Explicitly, it consists of a symmetric sequence $\PP$ together with morphisms of symmetric sequences $\mu:\PP \circ \PP \rightarrow \PP$, called the \textit{multiplication}, and $\eta: \mathcal{J} \rightarrow \PP$, called the \textit{unit}, such that the following diagrams commute. 
\[\begin{tikzcd}

	{\PP \circ \PP} && {\PP \circ \PP} \\
	& \PP
	\arrow["{{{a_{\PP,\PP,\PP}}}}", from=1-1, to=1-3]

	\arrow["\mu"', from=2-1, to=3-2]
	\arrow["\mu", from=2-3, to=3-2]
\end{tikzcd}\]
\[\begin{tikzcd}

	& \PP &&&& \PP
	\arrow["{{\eta \circ \id_{\PP}}}", from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow["{{l_{\PP}}}"', from=1-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow["\mu", from=1-3, to=2-2]
	\arrow["{{\id_{\PP} \circ \eta}}", from=1-5, to=1-7]
	\arrow["{{r_{\PP}}}"', from=1-5, to=2-6]
	\arrow["\mu", from=1-7, to=2-6]

{"assumptions":["Independent coordinates, arbitrary measurable state spaces; measurable real f and E Z^2 finite","Each resampling copy independent of original coordinates","Coordinate-infimum application requires a real X_{-i}-measurable infimum; additive equality means equality almost surely"],"created_at":"2026-10-13T09:56:14+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_00a8a829ba7b0cabcfb6107b8a3fcda1a7239d151268d11bb0e4036b513850d6","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1,...,X_n be independent random variables on arbitrary measurable coordinate spaces, let f be measurable and real valued, and let Z=f(X_1,...,X_n) belong to L^2. For each i let X_i_prime be an independent copy of X_i, independent of all original coordinates, and let Z^{(i)} replace X_i by X_i_prime in f. Write X_{-i} for the other coordinates and m_i=E[Z|X_{-i}]. Then Var(Z)<=v:=sum_i E[(Z-m_i)^2]=(1/2)sum_i E[(Z-Z^{(i)})^2]=sum_i E[((Z-Z^{(i)})_+)^2]. For arbitrary real X_{-i}-measurable Z_i, Var(Z)<=sum_i E[(Z-Z_i)^2], interpreted in the extended nonnegative sense; if the right side is finite, each Z_i is square integrable. In particular v is the minimum over such square-integrable Z_i, attained at Z_i=m_i. A coordinate infimum inf_x f(X_1,...,X_{i-1},x,X_{i+1},...,X_n) may be used as Z_i only when it defines a real X_{-i}-measurable random variable; those properties are additional conditions, not automatic consequences of measurability of f on arbitrary spaces. Equality Var(Z)=v holds exactly when Z=c+sum_i g_i(X_i) almost surely for some square-integrable one-coordinate functions g_i and constant c. Equality in the arbitrary-Z_i bound holds exactly when this almost-sure additive condition holds and Z_i=m_i almost surely for every i. The Efron-Stein bound is Boucheron-Lugosi-Massart, Concentration Inequalities (2013), Theorem3.1, printedpages54-55; the iff equality characterization here is independently derived using the finite orthogonal Hoeffding decomposition, rather than attributed to the theorem text.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Perfectly correlated singleton Gaussian paths","K_n=2^(n^2)","L_n=n and beta_n=n"],"created_at":"2026-10-10T09:02:46.153228+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_012f82fc17167316ffc88c22134bf384fb77068dc27a4e5d38dd41edc08f13a3","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"For integer n>=1, let L_n=n, K_n=2^(n^2) singleton paths of unit weight, all X_i equal one shared N(0,1) variable Z, and beta_n=n. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:11:02.388533+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_012fc76db4c1344067509086d763ee972e513647c2c95d7417ad26418ba78088","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:goodset of arXiv:2507.10531, 'Quantitative central limit theorems for exponential random graphs'] For all small enough $\varepsilon > 0$, there are some $\eta, \gamma > 0$ such that for all large enough $n$ there is a set
$\Lambda^* \subseteq \mathcal{B}_p^\eta$ satisfying the following properties, where $X \sim \mu_\mathsf{H}^\eta(n,p)$ and $(X_t^x)$ is the
Glauber dynamics conditioned on $\mathcal{B}_p^\eta$ and started at $x$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\Roman*)]
    \item
    
    The set $\Lambda^*$ is large, i.e.\ we have
    \begin{equation}
        \mathbb{P}[X \in \Lambda^*] \geq 1 - e^{-\gamma n}.
    \end{equation}
    \item
    
    The chain started near $\Lambda^*$ stays in the good region.
    Namely, whenever $\mathbf{d}_\mathrm{Ham}(x,\Lambda^*) \leq 1$,
    \begin{equation}
        \mathbb{P}\mleft[X_t^x \in \Gamma_p^\varepsilon \cap \mathcal{B}_p^{\eta/2} \text{ for all } t < e^{\gamma n}\mright] \geq 1 - e^{-\gamma n}.
    \end{equation}
    \item
    
    The set $\Lambda^*$ is connected under the nearest-neighbor relation.
    Moreover, for any $x,x' \in \Lambda^*$, we have
    \begin{equation}
        \mathbf{d}_{\Lambda^*}(x,x') \leq 2 n^2,
    \end{equation}
    where $\mathbf{d}_{\Lambda^*}(x,x')$ denotes the distance within $\Lambda^*$, i.e.\ the length of the shortest nearest-neighbor
    path between $x,x'$ which stays inside $\Lambda^*$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:56:21.583397+00:00","domain":"mathematical logic","id":"claim_0143593c9533c892a728d6d489a657fa87d876ed1b66d476c0807d570b7c0586","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"For first-order logic, Godel's completeness theorem states that a formula is provable from a set of axioms by a standard formal proof system if and only if it is semantically entailed by those axioms, that is, true in every model satisfying them. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:56:21.583151+00:00","domain":"linear algebra","id":"claim_014678b4f3cb617ba9549a52110422cfba00bf13a4e692be47c4d2dce870cf79","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A be an n by n complex matrix with entries a_ij. For each row i, the Gershgorin disc D_i is the closed disc in the complex plane centered at the diagonal entry a_ii with radius R_i equal to the sum of the absolute values of the other, off-diagonal entries in row i. Every eigenvalue of A lies in at least one disc D_i. Moreover, if a union of k of these discs is disjoint from the remaining n-k discs, that union contains exactly k eigenvalues of A counted with multiplicity, and the complementary union contains the rest. Proved by Semyon Gershgorin in 1931.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["product measure","all the events increasing (the proof uses FKG on the decreasing complements)"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.542929+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_01ce16ef6218f32c1f9919a8d7c88e3c9ce4ae7ffd8d9803708ef6d53c50695b","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let P be a product measure on {0,1}^E and let A_1, ..., A_k be INCREASING events with the same probability. Then max_i P(A_i) = P(A_1) >= 1 - ( 1 - P( union_i A_i ) )^{1/k}. More generally, without assuming equal probabilities, max_i P(A_i) >= 1 - (1 - P(union_i A_i))^{1/k}. The name comes from the case k = 2, where the bound reads P(A_1) >= 1 - sqrt(1 - P(A_1 or A_2)): if the union is very likely then at least one of two increasing events is likely, quantitatively. This is the standard device for turning a statement like 'some crossing of a box occurs' into 'a crossing in a specific direction occurs with probability bounded below', and it is the engine of Zhang's argument that theta(1/2) = 0 for bond percolation on Z^2. The events must be INCREASING, since the proof is Harris-FKG applied to their complements; for arbitrary events the inequality is false. [standard; e.g. Grimmett, Percolation, 2nd ed., proof of Theorem 11.11, and Bollobas-Riordan, Percolation]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:54:12.250027+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_024d4e58d5540875d80cc3e02217a5b2b0aca72c63809dc5e0b5493afba2ff04","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma OU flow property of arXiv:2603.14163, '\LARGE \bf Tail Bounds for Queues with Abandonment: Constant, Moderate, Large Deviations, '] Let $p>1$ and let $X\in \mathbb{R}^d$ a random vector with law $\mathcal{L}(X)\in\mathcal{P}_p(\mathbb{R}^d)$. Let $T:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ be a Borel measurable map such that $Y:=T(X)$ is a real random variable with $\mathbb{E}|Y|^p<\infty$. Let $Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ be independent of $X$. For $t>0$ define
\[
F_t := e^{-t}Y + \sqrt{1-e^{-2t}}\,Z,
\]
and let $f_t$ denote the density of $F_t$ (w.r.t.\ Lebesgue measure). Then the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item (OU representation) \textnormal{[fang2022wasserstein]} The family $(F_t)_{t>0}$ is the Ornstein--Uhlenbeck semigroup acting on $Y$; equivalently, $(F_t)$ is a version of the solution to the SDE
        \[
            dF_t = -F_t\,dt + \sqrt{2}\,dB_t,\qquad F_0=Y,
        \]
        where $(B_t)$ is a standard Brownian motion independent of $Y$.

    \item (Smooth positive density) \textnormal{[johnson2001entropy]} For every $t>0$ the law of $F_t$ admits a strictly positive, smooth density $f_t$.
    \item (Commutation of OU semigroup and differentiation) \textnormal{[bakry2013analysis] [bonis2020steins]} For every $t>0 , k\in\mathbb{N}$, and $g \in C^{\infty}_c(\mathbb{R})$,
        \[
            \frac{d^k}{dx^k} P_t g(x) = e^{-kt} P_t\!\Bigl(\frac{d^k}{dx^k} g\Bigr)(x),\qquad x\in\mathbb{R},
        \]
        where $P_t g(x):=\mathbb{E}[g(F_t)\mid F_0=x]$ is the OU semigroup acting on $g$. Moreover,
        \[
         P_t \frac{d^k}{dx^k}g(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1- e^{-2t}}^k} \mathbb{E}[h_k(Z) g(e^{-t}x + \sqrt{1-e^{-2t}}Z)], \qquad x\in\mathbb{R},
        \]
        where $h_k(x) = (-1)^k e^{x^2/2} \frac{d^k}{dx^k}e^{-x^2/2}$ is the $k$-th Hermite Polynomial.

    \item (Continuity equation) For every $t>0$ the density $f_t$ satisfies the continuity equation
        \[
            \partial_t f_t(x) + \frac{d}{dx}\bigl(f_t(x)\,\rho_t(x)\bigr)=0,\qquad x\in\mathbb{R},
        \]
        where $\rho_t(x):=-\partial_x\log f_t(x)-x$ is the score function of $f_t$.

    \item (Score representation) \textnormal{[bonis2020steins]} For each $t>0$ the score admits the conditional expectation representation
        \[
            \rho_t(F_t)\;\overset{d.}{=}\; \mathbb{E}\!\Bigl[e^{-t}Y-\frac{e^{-2t}}{\sqrt{1-e^{-2t}}}\,Z\;\Big|\;F_t\Bigr],
        \]
        and, consequently,
        \[
            t\mapsto \|\rho_t(F_t)\|_{L^p(\mathcal{L}(F_t))}\in L^1((0,\infty)).
        \]

    \item (Moment bound and weak continuity) The curve $t\mapsto\mathcal{L}(F_t)$ is weakly continuous on $(0,\infty)$, and
        \[
            \sup_{t>0}\|F_t\|_{L^p}<\infty,
        \]
        (equivalently $\sup_{t>0}\|x\|_{L^p(\mathcal{L}(F_t))}<\infty$).
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:09:43.713008+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_02a3e89663d2a838b378f1c87f4faaa128fcd7cb762609d2de15867a092ed0c8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary cor:shot-nois-field of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] Consider a simple marked point process 
\(\tilde{\Xi} = \{ \tilde{x} = (x, U(x)) \}_{x \in \Xi}\) on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) 
with i.i.d.\ marks \(U(x)\) taking values in a Polish space \(\mathbb{K}\).  
Let the shot-noise field \(M\) on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) with values in \( \mathbb{R}\) be defined by
\[
M(x) := \sum_{y \in \Xi} \zeta(x, \tilde{y}), \quad x \in \mathbb{R}^d,
\]
for some measurable function \(\zeta : \mathbb{R}^d \times (\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{K}) \longrightarrow  \mathbb{R}\) 
such that \(\zeta(\tilde{x}, \tilde{y}) \le \phi(|x-y|)\)

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.191093+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_02f8ef901ce9a0e22850103c9eb2a8251cfa175ba32d3aa3ab18e07a105da31b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 110 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $f:\R\to[0,\infty)$ be a smooth function which integrates to one and has compact support. Then the derivative of $f^{1/2}$ is uniformly bounded, that is,
	\[ \|(f^{1/2})'\|_\infty
	= \frac12 \bigg\|\frac{f'}{f^{1/2}}\bigg\|_\infty
	\le O(1)\,,\]
where $O(1)$ indicates a constant depending on $f$.

\begin{proof}
Since $f$ is smooth, we have $\|f''\|_\infty \le C$ where $C$ is a constant depending only on $f$. Assume without loss that $C$ is large. Now suppose $f(y)>0$ is small while $|f'|$ is large, say
$f'(y) \ge 2 C f(y)^{1/2}$. The bound on $f''$ implies $f'(x) \ge C f(y)^{1/2}$ for all $|x-y| \le f(y)^{1/2}$. It follows that
	\[
	f\Big(y-f(y)^{1/2}\Big)
	\le f(y) - Cf(y)^{1/2} \cdot f(y)^{1/2}
	< 0\,,
	\]
contradicting the assumption that $f\ge0$. The case $f'(y) \le - 2 C f(y)^{1/2}$ leads to a similar contradiction, so we conclude 
	\[\bigg\|\frac{f'}{f^{1/2}}\bigg\|_\infty
	\le 2C\,,
	\]
which proves the claim.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X has independent coordinates and P is a product measure","for the corollary: f convex and 1-Lipschitz for the Euclidean norm, coordinates valued in [0,1]","the corollary centres at a MEDIAN, not the mean"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.628352+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_0376bec83a9d7056e168a9ba341af418dbb0c42d6ec3f78d13a9c52d6fe37ac1","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X = (X_1, ..., X_n) have INDEPENDENT coordinates taking values in arbitrary measurable spaces, and let P be the product law on the product space. For a subset A and a point x define the convex distance d_T(x, A) = sup { inf_{y in A} sum_{i=1}^n alpha_i 1{x_i != y_i} : alpha in R^n, alpha_i >= 0, |alpha|_2 <= 1 }. Then for every measurable A, E[ exp( d_T(X, A)^2 / 4 ) ] <= 1 / P(A), and consequently P(A) P( d_T(X, A) >= t ) <= exp( - t^2 / 4 ) for every t > 0. COROLLARY for convex Lipschitz functions: if f : [0,1]^n -> R is CONVEX and 1-Lipschitz with respect to the Euclidean norm and the coordinates of X are independent with values in [0,1], then for every t > 0, P( |f(X) - M| >= t ) <= 4 exp( - t^2 / 4 ) where M is a median of f(X). The hypotheses are exactly: independence, a product structure, and for the corollary convexity together with a bounded range. Convexity cannot be dropped - the conclusion is false for general Lipschitz functions of bounded independent variables at this strength, which is why the bounded-differences (McDiarmid) inequality with its sum-of-squared-ranges denominator is the general-purpose tool and Talagrand's is the sharp one for convex functionals. The centring is at a MEDIAN; converting to the mean costs an absolute constant. [Talagrand (1995), Publ. IHES 81; see Boucheron, Lugosi and Massart, Concentration Inequalities, Theorem 7.11 and Section 7.4]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-10T02:20:17.000000+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_038aeec00adcff1f433d16d10823ab9aa59fecfe5d9edd7e388f1e17d09b9549","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematics, the axiom of choice, abbreviated AC or AoC, is an axiom of set theory. Informally put, the axiom of choice says that given any collection of non-empty sets, one can identify another set containing one element chosen from each set, even if the collection is infinite. Formally, the axiom establishes existence rather than a construction; it states that for every set I and every I-indexed family (S_i)_{i in I} of nonempty sets, there exists an I-indexed set (x_i)_{i in I} of elements of the union of the S_i such that x_i in S_i for every i in I. {"assumptions":["A closed (so that the resolvent is bounded by the closed graph theorem) and the resolvent set nonempty.","The lower bound on the distance to the spectrum is an equality only for normal operators on Hilbert space;","for a non-normal operator the resolvent norm can be enormous far from the spectrum, which is the pseudospectrum phenomenon and the reason spectral information alone does not control transient behaviour."],"created_at":"2026-09-12T14:06:45.871209+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, operator theory","id":"claim_03d939c2a79f6b612a799b18298a7e6a00ccdd46f92d2f060d60503cc6b9e0b0","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A be a closed operator on a Banach space with resolvent set rho(A) and resolvent R(z) = (z I - A)^{-1}. Then: (i) the FIRST RESOLVENT IDENTITY R(z) - R(w) = (w - z) R(z) R(w) holds for z, w in rho(A), so resolvents at different points commute; (ii) rho(A) is OPEN and R is analytic on it, with the Neumann expansion R(z) = sum over k >= 0 of (w - z)^k R(w)^{k+1} valid whenever |z - w| is strictly less than 1 / ||R(w)||; (iii) consequently the distance from w to the spectrum is at least 1 / ||R(w)||, so the resolvent norm blows up at least like the reciprocal of the distance to the spectrum as z approaches it. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:31:02.815653+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_03f06e52dc29705b242d5d7c656625cc46770c1a358d4a41147671d7b0d59601","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:collision-exact-sequence of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] The map
\[

Then there is delta > 0 such that on the tubular neighbourhood { x : dist(x, S) < delta } the nearest point of S to x is UNIQUE, the projection map is C^{k-1}, and the signed distance function d is C^k with gradient of unit length equal to the outward normal at the projected point. on the time interval $q_0 \le t \le 1$, with $Z(q_0)\sim\acute{\zeta}$ and $Z^\Ising(q_0)\sim\acute{\zeta}^\Ising$. Assume the following:
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
\item 
The coefficients
$\ab,\asig,\aw$ are 
progressively measurable processes on the time interval $[q_0,1]$;

\item 
$\bE[(\aw_t)^2]=1$ for all $t\in[q_0, 1]$;

\item  $p\in\incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ with
$p(q_0)\ge 1/L$
and $\|p\|_{C^2([q_0,1])}\le L$;

\item 
The coefficients $\ab,\asig,\aw$ obey the budget constraints \eqref{eq:is-budget-constraint}, that is,
	\[
	\bE \bigg[(\ab_t)^2 + \frac{(tp)'(t)}{p(t)}(\asig_t-1)^2\bigg]
        \le \frac{(\bE \aw_t)^2 }{ \alpha}\,,\]
for all $t\in [q_0,1]$;

\item 
$|Z^{\Ising}(1)|=1$ almost surely;

\item 
$Z(q_0)=0$ almost surely, and $\bE[Z^{\Ising}(q_0)^2]=q_0$;

\item 
$\zeta^\Ising\in\cP([-1,1])$,
the space of Borel probability measures on $[-1,1]$.\footnote{We note that since $Z^\Ising$ is a martingale with $|Z^{\Ising}(1)|=1$ almost surely, the initial distribution cannot have support outside of $[-1,1]$.}
\end{enumerate}
Given any
$q_*,b,\sigma,w,p,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising$
(same $p$ as above),
let $X,X^\Ising$ be given by \eqref{e:sde.x} and \eqref{e:sde.x.ising} on the time interval $[q_*,1]$, with $X(q_*)\sim\zeta$ and $X^\Ising(q_*)\sim\zeta^\Ising$.
Then for any $\epsilon>0$ there exist parameters $q_*,b,\sigma,w,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising$ such that the following hold: 
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item 
$b_t= b(t,X_t)$, $\sigma_t=\sigma(t,X_t)$, and $w_t= w(t,X_t)$,
for $C$-Lipschitz functions
$b:[q_*,1]\times\R\to[-C,C]$
and $\sigma,w:[q_*,1]\times\R\to[0,C]$, for a constant $C=C(L,\epsilon)$.
 
\item 
 $|\bE[(w_t)^2] -1| \le\epsilon$
 for all $t\in[q_*,1]$. 
 
\item 
 $X$ and $X^{\Ising}$ approximately obey the budget constraints at each time $t$, that is,
	\[\bE \bigg[(b_t)^2 + \frac{(tp)'(t)}{p(t)}(\sigma_t-1)^2\bigg]
        \le \frac{(\bE w_t)^2 }{ \alpha}
        +\epsilon\]
for all $t\in[q_*,1]$.

\item  The initial distributions of $(X,X^\Ising)$ and $(Z,Z^\Ising)$ are close:
\[\begin{aligned}
\bbW_2(\zeta,\acute{\zeta}) &= 
\bbW_2(\Law(X(q_*)),\Law(Z(q_0)))
\leq \epsilon\,,\\
\bbW_2(\zeta^\Ising,\acute{\zeta}^\Ising)
&= \bbW_2(\Law(X^{\Ising}(q_*)),
        	\Law(Z^{\Ising}(q_0)))
\leq \epsilon\,.
\end{aligned}\]

\item  
The initial time $q_*$ lies in $[q_0,q_0+\epsilon]$.
\end{enumerate}
Lastly, we have
	\beq
    \begin{aligned}
	\bbW_2(\Law(X(1)),\Law(Z(1)))
	&\leq \epsilon\,,\\
	\bbW_2(\Law(X^{\Ising}(1)),
        	\Law(Z^{\Ising}(1)))
	&\leq \epsilon
    \end{aligned}
	\eeq
Thus the more general diffusions $(Z,Z^\Ising)$ are well approximated by the Markovian SDE solutions
$(X,X^\Ising)$. Finally, if $\Law(Z^{\Ising}(t))$ is even for each $t$, then we can take $w_t$ to be even for each $t$, that is, $w(t,x)=w(t,-x)$ for all $(t,x)\in [0,1]\times \bbR$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:52:08.666279+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_04dc9bb9f19fe88b29d641576bdef3842dd1498561b284e4d50c063f7c26580b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 7 (Fixed-threshold almost-flat/torus-bundle alternative) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Let \(M\) be \(\TT^3\), a compact \(\Nil\) torus bundle with nontrivial
unipotent monodromy, or a compact \(\Sol\) torus bundle with hyperbolic
monodromy, and let \(g(t)\) be an immortal Ricci flow on \(M\).  Let \(K\) be
a Type-III constant supplied by Proposition~\ref{input:bamler-typeIII}.
Fix any \(c_0\in(0,1)\) such that
\begin{equation}
        Kc_0^2<\eps_{\mathrm{af}}.
\end{equation}
The parameter \(c_0\) is used only as the diameter threshold separating the two
geometric alternatives below; it is not an analytic smallness parameter and will not
be decreased later to meet compactness or stability tolerances.

There exist a finite time \(T_B(c_0)<\infty\) and a nonincreasing function
\[
        \eps_B^{c_0}:[T_B(c_0),\infty)\longrightarrow(0,\tfrac12],
        \qquad \eps_B^{c_0}(t)\longrightarrow0,
\]
with
\begin{equation}
        \eps_B^{c_0}(t)<c_0,
        \qquad t\geq T_B(c_0),
\end{equation}
such that every \(t\geq T_B(c_0)\) belongs to exactly one of the following
diameter-defined alternatives.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
If
\begin{equation}
        \diam(M,g(t))<c_0\sqrt t,
\end{equation}
then
\begin{equation}
 \bigl(\sup_M|\sec_{g(t)}|\bigr)\diam(M,g(t))^2
 <Kc_0^2<\eps_{\mathrm{af}}.
\end{equation}
Thus the slice is quantitatively almost flat.

\item
If
\begin{equation}
        \diam(M,g(t))\geq c_0\sqrt t,
\end{equation}
then there exist a torus fibration \(\pi_t^B:M\to S_t^1\) and an invariant metric \(g_t^B\), in the sense described in
Subsection~\ref{subsec:torus-bundle-conventions}, such that
\begin{equation}
        (1+\eps_B^{c_0}(t))^{-1}g_t^B\leq g(t)
        \leq(1+\eps_B^{c_0}(t))g_t^B.
\end{equation}
Moreover, for every integer \(m\) with
\(0\leq m<\bigl(\eps_B^{c_0}(t)\bigr)^{-1}\), the metric
\(t^{-1}g_t^B\) is \(\eps_B^{c_0}(t)\)-close to \(t^{-1}g(t)\) in
\(C^m\), relative to \(t^{-1}g(t)\), and every fiber has
\(g(t)\)-diameter at most \(\eps_B^{c_0}(t)\sqrt t\).
\end{enumerate}
Labels~(\ref{item:bamler-small-slice}) and~(\ref{item:bamler-large-slice})
refer only to the diameter inequalities.  A torus comparison
may also exist in the first alternative, but it is not used there.  In the
second alternative the fibration, quotient circle, and comparison metric may
depend on \(t\), with no asserted compatibility or uniqueness. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:49:15.410225+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_04f9ecc29ba05404cd78b521f991ae28a1d4cfa0fe0fbd722d15bdb9818a7029","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem Inverse transport theorem of arXiv:2608.27248, 'Optimal Transport and the ABP Method in Higher Codimension'] Let $m\geq1$, let $X:\Sigma^n\to\mathbb{R}^{n+m}$ be a smooth immersion of a
compact manifold, possibly with smooth boundary, and let
$\mathcal K\subset\mathbb{R}^{n+m}$ be a bounded open convex set.  Let
$u\in C^{2,\alpha}(\Sigma)$, understood up to the boundary, for some
$\alpha\in(0,1)$.  If $\partial\Sigma\ne\varnothing$, assume
$\langle\nabla^\Sigma u,\eta\rangle=h_{\mathcal K}(\eta)$ on
$\partial\Sigma$.  With $v$, $Q$, $\Phi$, $\mathcal{C}$, and $\vartheta$ defined
above, the following conclusions hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item One has $Q_x(y)\geq0$ on $\mathcal{C}$ and, for every Borel function
$\varphi:\mathcal K\to[0,\infty]$,
\begin{equation}
 \int_{\mathcal{C}}\varphi(\Phi(x,y))\frac{\det Q_x(y)}{\vartheta(x)}
 \,\mathrm d\mu(x)\,\mathrm dy
 =\int_{\mathcal K}\varphi(\xi)\,\mathrm d\xi.
\end{equation}
Both sides are understood as extended nonnegative integrals.

\item Let $\rho$ be a nonnegative Borel function satisfying
$\int_{\mathcal K}\rho\,\mathrm d\xi=1$, and set
\[
 I_\rho(x)=\int_{\mathcal{C}_x}\rho(\Phi(x,y))\det Q_x(y)\,\mathrm dy,
 \qquad
 \mathrm d\lambda_{u,\rho}(x)=\frac{I_\rho(x)}{\vartheta(x)}\,\mathrm d\mu(x).
\]
By part \textup{(i)}, $I_\rho(x)<\infty$ for $\mu$-almost every $x$.
For $0<I_\rho(x)<\infty$, define
\begin{equation}
 \mathrm d\nu_{x,\rho}(y)
 =\frac{\rho(\Phi(x,y))\det Q_x(y)}{I_\rho(x)}
 \mathbf1_{\mathcal{C}_x}(y)\,\mathrm dy.
\end{equation}
On $\{I_\rho=0\}\cup\{I_\rho=\infty\}$ set
$\nu_{x,\rho}=\delta_0$.  Then $x\mapsto\nu_{x,\rho}$ is a Borel
probability kernel, $\lambda_{u,\rho}$ is a probability measure, and the plan
$\pi_{u,\rho}$ defined by
\begin{equation}
 \int \zeta\,\mathrm d\pi_{u,\rho}
 =\int_\Sigma\int_{N_x\Sigma}
 \zeta(x,v(x)+y)\,\mathrm d\nu_{x,\rho}(y)\,\mathrm d\lambda_{u,\rho}(x)
\end{equation}
for bounded Borel $\zeta$ has marginals $\lambda_{u,\rho}$ and
$\rho\,\mathrm d\xi$, and is optimal for
$c(x,\xi)=\frac12|X(x)-\xi|^2$.

\item Let
\begin{equation}
 \Psi(\xi)=\max_{z\in\Sigma}
 \{\langle X(z),\xi\rangle-u(z)\}.
\end{equation}
As a supremum of affine functions, $\Psi$ is convex and hence differentiable
almost everywhere.  Then $T=\nabla\Psi$ is the Brenier map from
$\rho\,\mathrm d\xi$ to $X_\#\lambda_{u,\rho}$ and
\begin{equation}
 T_\#(\rho\,\mathrm d\xi)=X_\#\lambda_{u,\rho}.
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:39:12.389301+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_0502692680db273a0e329c6eb9cb5c35f10de22c34a8d72d27ad5d72786013ee","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition of arXiv:2412.07936, 'Simple Norm Bounds for Polynomial Random Matrices via Decoupling'] [Graph matrix, see e.g. [RT23] Definition 4.4]
Given a shape $\tau$, the associated graph matrix ${\bf M}$ : $\Omega \rightarrow {\mathbb R}^{d_1 \times d_2}$ is a matrix-valued function such that
$$
{\bf M} [I,J] = \sum_{\substack{\varphi \in {\mathcal T}^k_n: \\ \varphi(U_\tau) = I, \varphi(V_\tau) = J }} \prod _{(u,v) \in E(\tau)} G_{\varphi(u),\varphi(v)}.
$$
In other words, ${\bf M}$ maps an input graph $G \in \Omega$ to a $\frac{n!}{(n-|I|)!} \times \frac{n!}{(n-|J|)!}$ matrix whose rows and columns are indexed by $I$ and $J$ respectively.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-23T08:42:36.709135+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_05325b965e8d415a9ca55cf42540127a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In statistics, the Neyman–Pearson lemma describes the existence and uniqueness of the likelihood ratio as a uniformly most powerful test in certain contexts. It was introduced by Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson in a paper in 1933. The Neyman–Pearson lemma is part of the Neyman–Pearson theory of statistical testing, which introduced concepts such as errors of the second kind, power function, and inductive behavior. The previous Fisherian theory of significance testing postulated only one hypothesis. By introducing a competing hypothesis, the Neyman–Pearsonian flavor of statistical testing allows investigating the two types of errors. The trivial cases where one always rejects or fails to reject the null hypothesis are of little interest but it does prove that one must not relinquish control over one type of error while calibrating the other. Neyman and Pearson accordingly proceeded to restrict their attention to the class of all $\\alpha$ level tests while subsequently minimizing type II error, traditionally denoted by $\\beta$. Their seminal 1933 paper, which includes the Neyman–Pearson lemma showed not only the existence of tests with the most power that retain a prespecified level of type I error ( $\\alpha$), but also provided a way to construct such tests. The Karlin-Rubin theorem extended the Neyman–Pearson lemma to settings involving composite hypotheses with monotone likelihood ratios.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:36:31.233054+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_056b1d82d89798fd61215d786f24f7e068d4bc4e15478fab9d7f57f5f028616d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorema 3 of arXiv:2609.00567, 'Hodge--Tate splitting and Akizuki--Nakano vanishing in positive characteristic'] Let \(k\) be a perfect field of characteristic \(p>0\).
\begin{enumerate}
\item
Let \(X\) be a smooth quasi-\(F\)-split \(k\)-variety, and let \(D\)
be a simple normal crossings divisor on \(X\).  Then \((X,D)\) is
log HT-split (\Cref{qFs-to-HT}).

\item
Let \(X\) be a smooth \(k\)-variety, and let \(D\)
be a simple normal crossings divisor on \(X\).
Let \((X,D)\) be a log HT-split pair, and let
\[
\pi\colon Y \defeq \operatorname{Bl}_Z(X) \to  X
\]
be the blow-up along a stratum \(Z\) of \(D\) and $D_Y \defeq (\pi^{-1}D)_{\red}$. 
Then \((Y,D_Y)\) is log HT-split.  In particular, \(Y\) is HT-split (\Cref{HT-ascent-stratum-blowup}).

\item
Let \(T\) be a toric variety with Cox ring \(S_T\).  
Suppose that a smooth
closed subvariety \(Z\subseteq T\) is defined by a homogeneous regular sequence.
Then \(Z\) is HT-split (\Cref{complete-intersection}).

\item Let $\pi \colon X \to Y$ be a morphism of smooth $k$-varieties.
If $\cO_Y \to R\pi_*\cO_X$ splits and $X$ is HT-split, then $Y$ is HT-split (\Cref{finite-cover}).
In particular, if $\pi$ is a linearly reductive good quotient and $X$ is HT-split, then $Y$ is HT-split.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a real or complex Banach space","A is linear on a subspace D(A)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.769837+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, operator semigroups","id":"claim_05b342a8dbfbe497827c01268d9e092d3b7a5c5940a131f4d29aa0e10be41ee7","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a Banach space with dual X*. The duality set of x ∈ X is J(x) = {x* ∈ X* : ⟨x, x*⟩ = ‖x‖² = ‖x*‖²}, which is nonempty by the Hahn-Banach theorem. A linear operator A: D(A) ⊂ X → X is dissipative if for every x ∈ D(A) there exists some j ∈ J(x) with Re⟨Ax, j⟩ ≤ 0. Equivalently (Lumer-Phillips lemma), ‖(λ − A)x‖ ≥ λ‖x‖ for all λ > 0 and all x ∈ D(A). In a Hilbert space (J(x) = {x}) this reads Re⟨Ax, x⟩ ≤ 0 for all x ∈ D(A). A is m-dissipative (maximal dissipative) if it is dissipative and Ran(λ − A) = X for some λ > 0 (then for every λ > 0). A is accretive (m-accretive) if −A is dissipative (m-dissipative). For a dissipative A, λ − A is injective for λ > 0 and its inverse on Ran(λ − A) has norm at most 1/λ.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-07T12:18:34.091638+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_05c2a6e5817a074dc3ef501ceb044cc3bcc71ebde6c2b5236144feeee975d9f0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 27 ({\cite[Lemma 3.4 and Remark 3.5) of arXiv:2507.06186, '2507.06186'] {Matsuda}}]

\begin{enumerate}[(1)]

\[\mbf E\big[\be^\eps_{[a,b]^2_\leq}(B^{0,0}_t)\big]
=\frac{b-a}{2\pi}\big(\log(1/\eps)+\log t\big)+\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{b-a}\log r-\log(t-r)\d r+o(1)\]
and
\[\mbf E\big[\be^\eps_{[a,b]^2_{\leq}}(B^0)\big]
=\tfrac{b-a}{2\pi}\big(\log(1/\eps)+\log(b-a)-1\big)+o(1).\]
\item If $0\leq a<b\leq c<d\leq t$, then as $\eps\to0$, one has

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:10:07.423380+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_06159cda4e4bf4ff6ad0642d28cae37c7e51d38a732a089d7e659a08cb286f43","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary Point-incoherent frames of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[corollary]{cor:point-incoherent}
Let \(\overline\sigma_{N-1}\) denote normalized surface measure on
\(\mathbb S^{N-1}(1)\), and define
\[
 D_{N,L}=\left\{x\in\mathbb S^{N-1}(1):
 \left\lVertx\right\rVert_\infty\le L\sqrt{\frac{\log N}{N}}\right\},
 \qquad
 \widehat\mathcal O_{N,L}
 =\{(v_1,\ldots,v_n,x)\in\mathbb O(N):x\in D_{N,L}\}.
\]
Let \(\widehat\mathcal Z_{N,L}^J\) be defined by replacing \(\mathcal O_{N,L}\) with
\(\widehat\mathcal O_{N,L}\) in (equation eq:Z-def of the paper).  Every conclusion of
(thm:bulk-universality of the paper) remains valid for
\(\widehat\mathcal Z_{N,L}^J\), with the same quantitative bound.  For Gaussian
disorder, (equation eq:Gaussian-Z-exact of the paper) remains valid with
\(\nu_N(\mathcal O_{N,L})\) replaced by
\(\overline\sigma_{N-1}(D_{N,L})\).  In particular, for \(L>L_0\) the
set \(D_{N,L}\) has spherical measure tending to one, while for every
fixed \(L>0\) the Gaussian variational pressure limit is unchanged.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Even fixed K>=2, N=Kn, n>=1, P>=1; independent Gaussian blocks and patterns","Hidden weights have norm sqrt(n), both readout signs occur K/2 times, threshold zero, ReLU hidden activation","Labels fixed or random independently of inputs; no balance or inter-label independence required for asymptotic exclusion","Every unit is inactive whenever its readout sign differs from the pattern label; arbitrary input-dependent assignments and same-sign overlaps are allowed"],"created_at":"2026-10-22T02:50:47.905518+00:00","domain":"statistical learning theory; Gaussian random constraint satisfaction","id":"claim_0624ebd58741ec6f217055c471d6888848d7dc2f311e49d732afec5f13380dfb","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Proof (unaudited), elementary route obstruction; no novelty claimed. Let K>=2 be even, N=Kn, and let a ReLU tree committee have independent standard Gaussian input blocks, spherical hidden weights of norm sqrt(n), fixed balanced readout signs and zero threshold. Labels are fixed independently of inputs. Restrict to classifiers in which every unit is inactive on every opposite-label pattern, but allow assignments to depend arbitrarily on all inputs and allow same-sign overlaps. Conditional on positive and negative label counts M_+,M_-, strict storage probability is at most q(M_-,n)^(K/2) q(M_+,n)^(K/2), where q(0,n)=1 and q(m,n)=2^(1-m) sum_{r=0}^{min(n-1,m-1)} binom(m-1,r) for m>=1. Uniformly in labels this is at most q(ceil(P/2),n)^(K/2), so for fixed K storage probability tends to zero when n tends to infinity and P/N tends to a>4/K. With balanced labels and P=4n the conditional bound is 2^-K. Thus positive sequential wide-limit load requires allowing wrong-sign active votes in this model; this is not an upper bound on unrestricted ReLU capacity.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:10:07.501490+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_062b22585439db726a0b6f470b0037a36b8af3520acc59696c5e337e8b8a8398","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma Strict finite-support profile of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[lemma]{lem:strict-profile}
Let \(K\) be a compact neighborhood in \(\mathbb S^{N-1}(1)\), let \(x_0\) lie in its relative interior, and suppose a continuous function \(P\) satisfies
\[
 P(x_0)=\max_KP,
 \qquad
 \Delta:=P(x_0)-\max_{\partial K}P>0.
\]
If \(\left\lVertr\right\rVert_\infty\le M\) and \(b\Delta>2M\), then \(bP+r\) has a local maximum in the interior of \(K\), with value in
\[
 [bP(x_0)-M,bP(x_0)+M].
\]
If \(P,r\) are \(C^1\), this point is a spherical critical point.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:12:46.874389+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_065ff3d17e006b24f4d31dfe2e0076ac6a6f5b33b738e19e4cc9d2d6dfcf0bd0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:kac-moment of arXiv:2608.08375, 'Algebraic formulas for first-passage times of Markov processes in the linear framework: ge'] Let $G$ be a strongly connected graph and choose $u \in \mathcal{V}(G)$. The $r$-th moment of the recurrence time to $u$ is given by,
\[
    \tau^{(r)}_u(G) = \frac{r!}{\left( \lambda_u(G) \, x_u^*(G) \right)^r} \sum_{(i_1, \dotsc, i_r) \in \mathcal{V}(G)^r}{\left( \prod_{j=0}^{r-1}{\psi_{i_{j+1}|i_j,u} \, x_{i_{j+1}}^*(G)} \right)} \,,
\]
where the exchange factor takes the form,
\begin{align*}
    & \psi_{i_{j+1}|i_j,u} = 1 \,\, + \\
    & \sum_{\substack{m \in \mathcal{V}(G) \setminus \{i_{j+1}\} \\ m \to_G u}}\left( \frac{w(\Phi_{\{u,i_{j+1}\} \to \{m,i_{j+1}\}}(G)) - w(\Phi_{\{i_j,i_{j+1}\} \to \{m,i_{j+1}\}}(G))}{w(\Phi_{\{i_{j+1}\}}(G))} \right) \ell(m \to_G u) \,.
\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Independent rate-one Poisson offspring displacement processes.","The layer-tail recursion is the one stated in the source paper."],"created_at":"2026-10-10T06:51:51.363857+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_066f8d6d147ffdc831735ab62b26710560d8571ba00afcc1c575fa46962eb6bf","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked; tested by direct Monte Carlo simulation of the Poisson-weighted infinite tree (4000 replicates, k=2,5,10,12), agreeing with the recursion within about 1.5 standard errors] This is the campaign's branching-walk identification behind Conjecture 1 of H. Stepanyants, P. L. Krapivsky, H. Hartle and D. Krioukov, The rank and layer distributions in random recursive trees, arXiv:2608.04303. Let the Poisson-weighted infinite tree have root position zero, with children of each vertex at the points of an independent rate-one Poisson process on (0,infinity), translated by their parent's position. Let M_k be the minimum position of generation k, and set M_0=0. Define s_0(y)=1 for y>=0 and s_k(y)=1-exp(-integral_0^y s_{k-1}(z)dz) for k>=1. Put bar_ell_k=integral_0^infinity s_k(y)exp(-y)dy and ell_k=bar_ell_k-bar_ell_{k+1}. In the source, ell_k is the limiting fraction of vertices in layer k of a random recursive tree, formed by joining each new vertex j uniformly to one of vertices 1,...,j-1. Layer zero consists of the initial leaves, and subsequent layers are obtained by successive leaf removals. For every k>=0 and y>=0, s_k(y)=P(M_k<=y). Consequently bar_ell_k=E[exp(-M_k)] and ell_k=E[exp(-M_k)-exp(-M_{k+1})]. This is an unrefereed campaign result.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.177505+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_06bcc8c744c35f9e53258930c2a42e4230c2963bfb9ddbaddd3c27b6b7d32b10","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 77 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\gamma:[q_0,1]\to[q_0,1]$ be a monotone and absolutely continuous function, and define its generalized inverse
	\[
	\lambda:[q_0,\gamma(1)]\to[q_0,1]\,,\quad
	\lambda(s)
	\equiv\inf\Big\{
	t : \gamma(t)>s
	\Big\}\,.
	\]
Then the set $\{s : \gamma'(\lambda(s))=0 \}$ has zero Lebesgue measure.

\begin{proof}
It is straightforward to verify that $\lambda$ is a right-continuous function with $\gamma(\lambda(s))=s$ for all $s$. For any measurable set $A\subseteq\R$, consider the preimage $\lambda^{-1}(A)$: we have $s\in \lambda^{-1}(A)$ if and only if $\lambda(s)\in A$, which implies $s=\gamma(\lambda(s)) \in \gamma(A)$. This proves that 
	\[\lambda^{-1}(A)
	\subseteq \gamma(A)\]
(the converse need not hold). Let $A=\{t\in[q_0,1] : \gamma'(t)=0\}$: by absolute continuity of $\gamma$, we have
	\[|\gamma(A)|
	= \int_{q_0}^1 \gamma'(t)
	\ind\{t\in A\}
	\,dt = 0\,.\]
Since $\lambda^{-1}(A)\subseteq \gamma(A)$, it follows that
	\[
	|\lambda^{-1}(A)|
	=\bigg| \Big\{s : \gamma'(\lambda(s))=0
	\Big\}\bigg|=0\,,
	\]
as claimed.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:38:58.683023+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_06d33a069c6151dab2253c61a92e30547b9d5481c5bbc8307bf1a1d01726dc1a","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma of arXiv:2510.18792, 'The frog model with death revisited'] \thlabel{lem:biased-walk-bounds}
Let $(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ be a nearest-neighbor random walk on $\mathbb Z$ with $X_0=n> 0$ that moves left with probability $0<p<1/2$ and right with probability $1-p$ at each step. Let $\rho = p/(1-p)$. We let $\Geo(r)$ denote the geometric distribution supported on the nonnnegative integers. 
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
\item
For $\tau_{n-1}=\inf\{t\ge1: X_t=n-1\}$, it holds that
$$\frac{\tau_n-1}{2} \preceq \Geo\left(r\right) \quad 
\text{ with } \quad r = \exp\left(-\frac{3(1 - 2p)^2}{2(1 + 4p)} \right).$$

\item Let $T_n = \max \{t \colon X_t =n\}$ be the time of the last visit to $n$. It holds that 
    $$\frac{T_n}{2}\ \preceq \Geo(s) \quad \text{ with } \quad s=(1-2p)r.$$
\item
Suppose the walk is conditioned to never go left of $n$ i.e.\ conditioned on the event $A=\{X_t \geq n \text{ for all $t \geq 0$}\}$. 
Let $T_n'$ denote the time of its last return to $n$. Then $T_n' \preceq T_n$. 

\end{enumerate}
It follows that the length of each excursion between steps taken by the recursive frog model on $\mathbb T_d$ is stochastically dominated by the $2\Geo((1-p)(1-\rho)r) +1$ distribution. Moreover, these excursion lengths are independent between non-backtracking steps by the strong Markov property of random walk.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the counterexample is a 2-dimensional real l^p computation (the ratio at (1, 1/2) is 1.7268 and the maximum over x = (1,t) is attained near t = 0.62 at about 1.7320)","complexification bound: ||T_C f||_q <= ||T u||_q + ||T v||_q for f = u + i v"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:36.553381+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis, interpolation of operators","id":"claim_0730394901107dee5537f5da05c6f3480958fb025978d553df02c49ce8dba25d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Two hypotheses of the Riesz-Thorin theorem are load-bearing and are routinely dropped in write-ups. (1) COMPLEX SCALARS. The proof interpolates through an analytic family f_z, so the conclusion ||T||_{p_theta -> q_theta} <= M_0^{1-theta} M_1^{theta} is a theorem about complex L^p spaces. Counterexample for real scalars: on R^2 with the l^p norms let T(x_1, x_2) = (x_1 - x_2, x_1 + x_2). Over the REALS, ||T||_{l^infinity -> l^1} = 2 (the maximum of |x_1-x_2| + |x_1+x_2| = 2 max(|x_1|,|x_2|) over the unit cube) and ||T||_{l^2 -> l^2} = sqrt(2) (T is sqrt(2) times a rotation). Interpolating the endpoints (p_0,q_0) = (infinity,1) and (p_1,q_1) = (2,2) at theta = 1/2 gives (p,q) = (4, 4/3) and the putative bound 2^{1/2} (sqrt 2)^{1/2} = 2^{3/4} = 1.6818...; but the real operator norm from l^4 to l^{4/3} is about 1.7320 (already the vector (1, 1/2) gives the ratio 1.7268 > 1.6818). No contradiction with the complex theorem: over C the norm ||T||_{l^infinity -> l^1} is 2 sqrt 2 (take (1, i)), and the complex bound becomes (2 sqrt 2)^{1/2} (sqrt 2)^{1/2} = 2, which is consistent. Remedy: for a real-linear T, complexification costs at most a factor 2, so the real conclusion holds with constant 2 M_0^{1-theta} M_1^{theta}. (2) LINEARITY. Riesz-Thorin is false as stated for merely sublinear operators, and it also requires STRONG endpoint bounds; an operator with only weak endpoint bounds, or one that is sublinear (such as a maximal operator), must be interpolated with the Marcinkiewicz theorem instead, whose constant is not M_0^{1-theta} M_1^{theta} and blows up at the endpoints.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f in the Schwartz space S(R^d)","convention e^{-2 pi i x.xi}"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:39.262703+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis on Euclidean space","id":"claim_074ce430a1974d3bf9b3b7f35a12df34a963afadada2d75fdc561987015f87ec","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"The Fourier transform $f\\mapsto\\hat f$, $\\hat f(\\xi)=\\int f(x)e^{-2\\pi i x\\cdot\\xi}dx$, maps $\\mathcal S(\\mathbb R^d)$ continuously and bijectively onto itself, with continuous inverse given for every $x$ (pointwise, not just a.e.) by $f(x)=\\int_{\\mathbb R^d}\\hat f(\\xi)e^{2\\pi i x\\cdot\\xi}d\\xi$. Moreover $\\hat{\\hat f}(x)=f(-x)$, so the transform has order 4, and $\\widehat{\\partial^\\beta f}=(2\\pi i\\xi)^\\beta\\hat f$, $\\widehat{x^\\alpha f}=(-2\\pi i)^{-|\\alpha|}\\partial^\\alpha\\hat f$. Also $\\int f\\bar g=\\int\\hat f\\,\\overline{\\hat g}$ on $\\mathcal S$, which together with density gives the Plancherel theorem, and $\\widehat{fg}=\\hat f*\\hat g$, $\\widehat{f*g}=\\hat f\\hat g$ within $\\mathcal S$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.357926+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_074da0e685fb432dc28bacba60057e21af057b6ad4f19b226aa9d9ae921892d7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 245 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Assume that $L\ge1$ and that condition \eqref{e:deriv.p.bound} holds. Let $\vX\equiv \vX^N$ be the process defined by \eqref{e:X.decomp} and \eqref{e:Delta.X.Ising}. Then the process $X^\RomI$ satisfies the estimate
	\[ \max_{a\in[M]}
	\E\bigg[ \max_{0\le d\le\dmax}
	 \Big(X^\RomI(q_d,a)
	 -\E X^\RomI(q_d,a)\Big)
	 ^8\bigg] \le L^{O(1)}\,,\]
with the estimate holding uniformly in $N$.
\begin{proof} Similarly as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:martingale.sup.bound.X.II.III.Ising}, let us abbreviate
	\[
	\frac{\Delta X^{\RomI}(q_d,a)}{\delta_d p'(q_d)^{1/2}}
	\equiv \mathfrak{y}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)
	\equiv \frac{(\bmeta^a(q_{d+1}),\by(q_{d+1}))}{N^{1/2}}\,.
	\]
Define truncated $\tilde{\bmeta}$ and $\tilde{\by}$ similarly as
in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:martingale.sup.bound.X.II.III.Ising}, and define
	\[
	\frac{\Delta \tilde{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)}{\delta_d p'(q_d)^{1/2}}
	\equiv \tilde{\mathfrak{y}}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)
	\equiv \frac{(\tilde{\bmeta}^a(q_{d+1}),
		\tilde{\by}(q_{d+1}))}{N^{1/2}}\,.
	\]
By the same argument as for \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l4.step2} or for \eqref{e:RomII.tilde.discrepancy.second.mmt.bound}, we have
	\beq
	\bigg|\E\bigg[
	\Big(
	\mathfrak{y}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)
	- \tilde{\mathfrak{y}}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)
	\Big)^8
	\bigg]\bigg|
	\le e^{-cN}\,.
	\eeq
Let $\tilde{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)$ be the process started from zero with increments
$\Delta \tilde{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)$. (As before, we regard this as a process indexed by time $q_d$, for fixed $a\in[M]$.) Applying \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l4.step2.RomI} gives
	\beq
	\E\bigg[ \max_{0\le d \le \dmax}\Big(
	X^{\RomI}(q_d,a)- \tilde{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)\Big)^8\bigg]
	\le o_N(1)\,.
	\eeq
Then consider the centered increments
	\begin{align*}
	\frac{\Delta \bar{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)}{\delta_d p'(q_d)^{1/2}}
	&\equiv
	\frac{\Delta \tilde{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)}{\delta_d p'(q_d)^{1/2}}
	-\E\bigg[
	\frac{\Delta \tilde{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)}{\delta_d p'(q_d)^{1/2}}
		\,\bigg|\, \cG(q_d)
		\bigg]\\
	&= \tilde{\mathfrak{y}}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)
	- \E\Big[\tilde{\mathfrak{y}}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)
		\,\Big|\,\cG(q_d)\Big]\,.
	\end{align*}
Each increment above is a Lipschitz function of the gaussian noise, with Lipschitz constant $L^{O(1)}\delta_d$, and has mean zero conditional on $\cG(q_d)$.
Let $\bar{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)$ be the process started from zero with increments
$\Delta \bar{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)$. (Again, we regard this as a process indexed by time $q_d$, for fixed $a\in[M]$.)
Then $\bar{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)$ is a \emph{martingale}, whose increments are subgaussian with variance proxy $L^{O(1)} (\delta_d)^2$. Similar arguments as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:martingale.sup.bound.X.II.III.Ising} give (cf.\ \eqref{e:bar.X.II.martingale.exponential.concentration})
	\[
	\E \Big[\exp\{ \theta \bar{X}^{\RomI}(1,a)\}\Big]
	\le \exp( \theta^2 L^{O(1)} \delta)\,,\]
and combining with Doob's $L^p$ martingale inequality gives (cf.\ \eqref{e:martingale.bar.X.II.application.of.Doob})
	\beq
	\E\Big[ \max_{0\le d\le \dmax}
	\bar{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)^8\Big] 
	\le L^{O(1)} \delta^4\,.
	\eeq
It remains to address the discrepancy between $X^{\RomI}$ and $\bar{X}^{\RomI}$. Since $\tilde{X}^{\RomI}$ has subgaussian increments, we have
	\[
	\E\bigg[
	\Big( \Delta \tilde{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a) - \E \Delta \tilde{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)
	\Big)^8\bigg] \le  L^{O(1)}\delta^8\,,
	\]
and summing over increments gives
	\beq
	\E\bigg[ \max_{0\le d\le \dmax}
	\Big(
	 \tilde{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a) - \E \tilde{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)\Big)^8\bigg]
	 \le L^{O(1)}\,.
	\eeq
It also follows from  
\eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l4.step2.RomI}
or \eqref{e:martingale.X.I.to.tilde.X.I.error}
that
 \beq
 \max_{0\le d\le \dmax}
 \bigg|\E \Big[ \tilde{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)
 - X^{\RomI}(q_d,a) \Big] \bigg| \le o_N(1)
 \eeq
 where we recall $\E X^{\RomI}(q_d,a)
 = \E X(q_d,a)$.  Combining \eqref{e:martingale.X.I.to.tilde.X.I.error}, \eqref{e:martingale.tilde.X.I.close.to.mean}, and \eqref{e:martingale.tilde.X.I.close.to.X.I} gives the conclusion.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

This is extremely useful because computations involving a diagonalizable matrix can often be reduced to much simpler computations involving the corresponding diagonal matrix of eigenvalues. The concept of diagonalization is relatively straightforward for operators on finite-dimensional vector spaces but requires some modification for operators on infinite-dimensional spaces. In general, the spectral theorem identifies a class of linear operators that can be modeled by multiplication operators, which are as simple as one can hope to find. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:38:37.404722+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_07d972dc39418d6c8b9cda8b07b6f6b0a63b4c93df3fe299b6305346c5da177f","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 18 of arXiv:2605.15501, 'Well-posedness of the obstacle problem for generalized Dean--Kawasaki equation\thanks{ The'] (Existence of
solutions to the penalized equation)
Let Assumption \ref{assu:assu for existence} and Assumption \ref{assu:assum for F} hold for some $p\in [2,\infty)$.

For fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, as $\alpha\to0$ and $n\to\infty$,
there exists a subsequence of $\{u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}\}_{(\alpha,n)\in(0,1)\times\mathbb{N}}$ that converges almost surely on the original probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$ in $L^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{d}\times[0,T])$ to some limit $u_{\varepsilon}$.
This limit $u_{\varepsilon}$ is a stochastic kinetic equation
of \eqref{eq:penalized eq} in the sense of Definition \ref{def:def of stochastic kinetic solution without obstacle}, meaning that the kinetic function $\chi_{\varepsilon}(x,\xi,t):=\mathbf{1}_{\{0<\xi<u_{\varepsilon}(x,t)\}}$ satisfies almost surely, for every $\phi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{d}\times(0,\infty)\times[0,T))$,
\begin{align}
& -\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\chi_{\varepsilon}(x,\xi,s)\partial_s\phi(x,\xi,s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}\xi\mathrm{d}s\\
 & =\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\bar{\chi}(u_{\mathrm{init}},\xi)\phi(x,\xi,0)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}\xi-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\Phi^{\prime}(u_{\varepsilon})\nabla_x u_{\varepsilon}\cdot(\nabla_x\phi)(x,u_{\varepsilon},s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber \\
 & \quad-\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\big(F_{1}(x)[\sigma^{\prime}(u_{\varepsilon})]^{2}\nabla_x u_\varepsilon+\sigma(u_{\varepsilon})\sigma^{\prime}(u_{\varepsilon})F_{2}(x)\big)\cdot(\nabla_x\phi)(x,u_{\varepsilon},s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber\\
 & \quad-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\partial_{\xi}\phi(x,\xi,s)\mathrm{d}m_\varepsilon(x,\xi,s)-\int_0^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\phi(x,u_\varepsilon,s)\nabla_x \cdot g(u_\varepsilon)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber \\
 & \quad+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\Big(\sigma(u_{\varepsilon})\sigma^{\prime}(u_{\varepsilon})\nabla_x u_\varepsilon\cdot F_{2}(x)+\sigma^{2}(u_{\varepsilon})F_{3}(x)\Big)(\partial_{\xi}\phi)(x,u_{\varepsilon},s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber \\
 & \quad-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\phi(x,u_{\varepsilon},s)\frac{1}{\varepsilon}(u_{\varepsilon}-\psi)^+\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\phi(x,u_{\varepsilon},s)\nabla_x\cdot(\sigma(u_{\varepsilon})f_{k})\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}B_{s}^{k},\nonumber
\end{align}
where the kinetic measure $m_{\varepsilon}\geq \delta_{0}(\xi-u_{\varepsilon})\Phi^{\prime}(\xi)|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}|^{2}$ is finite. Moreover, the following a priori estimates hold.
  \begin{align}
 & \sup_{t\in[0,T]}\mathbb{E}\Vert u_{\varepsilon}(t)\Vert_{L^{p}(\mathbb{T}^{d})}^{p}+\mathbb{E}\Vert|u_{\varepsilon}+1|^{\frac{p-2}{2}}\nabla_{x}\llbracket\sqrt{\Phi^{\prime}}\rrbracket(u_{\varepsilon})\Vert_{L^{2}(Q_{T})}^{2} \\
 & +\mathbb{E}\Vert|u_{\varepsilon}+1|^{\frac{p-2}{2}}\varepsilon^{-1}(u_{\varepsilon}-\psi)^{+}\Vert_{L^{2}(Q_{T})}^{2}+\mathbb{E}\Vert|u_{\varepsilon}+1|^{p-2}\varepsilon^{-1}(u_{\varepsilon}-\psi)^{+}\Vert_{L^{1}(Q_{T})} \nonumber\\
 & \leq C\Big(1+\mathbb{E}\Vert u_{\mathrm{init}}\Vert_{L^{p}(\mathbb{T}^{d})}^{p}+\mathbb{E}\Vert u_{\mathrm{init}}\Vert_{L^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{d})}^{m+p-1}\Big),\nonumber
\end{align}
  \begin{align}
 & \sup_{t\in[0,T]}\mathbb{E}\Vert u_{\varepsilon}(t)\Vert_{L^{2}(\mathbb{T}^{d})}^{2}+\mathbb{E}\Vert\nabla_{x}\llbracket\sqrt{\Phi^{\prime}}\rrbracket(u_{\varepsilon})\Vert_{L^{2}(Q_{T})}^{2}+\mathbb{E}m_\varepsilon(\mathbb{T}^d\times\mathbb{R}\times[0,T]) \\
 & \quad+\varepsilon^{-1}\mathbb{E}\Vert(u_{\varepsilon}-\psi)^{+}\Vert_{L^{2}(Q_{T})}^{2}+\mathbb{E}\Vert\varepsilon^{-1}(u_{\varepsilon}-\psi)^{+}\Vert_{L^{1}(Q_{T})}\nonumber\\

{"assumptions":["G is finite, connected, simple, distance-regular, and n>=2."],"created_at":"2026-10-10T06:51:51.364496+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_07e8c48717f2e4462cbff10644f98ed2bdee48e66a11c8ccf4e48c023be5f089","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked against a direct linear-algebra solve on twelve graphs, with the complete graph and the cycle as independent controls at the two extremes.] This is the proved identity behind the campaign reduction of Open Problem 7.31 in David Aldous and James Allen Fill's Reversible Markov Chains and Random Walks on Graphs, unfinished monograph (2002, recompiled 2014; official source https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/RWG/book.html). Let G be a finite connected simple distance-regular graph with n>=2 vertices, valency k, and diameter d: for vertices at distance i, the numbers of neighbors one step closer to or farther from the target are constants c_i and b_i depending only on i. Use c_1=1, b_0=k, b_d=0. Let k_i be the number of vertices at distance i from a fixed vertex, so k_0=1, k_1=k, k_{i+1} c_{i+1}=k_i b_i, and n=sum_{i=0}^d k_i. For the simple random walk, let T_y be the first hitting time of y, measured in steps, and define tau_0=max_{x,y} E_x[T_y]; here tau_0 is the maximum mean hitting time, not the spectral Kemeny sum. Then tau_0=k sum_{i=1}^d (k_i+k_{i+1}+...+k_d)/(k_i c_i). In particular tau_0>=n-1, with equality exactly for complete graphs. The distance to a fixed target is a birth-and-death chain with downward probability c_i/k, upward probability b_i/k, and stationary mass k_i/n, so the formula requires only the intersection array. This is an unrefereed campaign result.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:33:21.485041+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_0876afd796b8bfc599511bd3570d193cd72d6d77550ca9a72b7c7e3cb84d32e2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem Sharp small-hole eigenvalue asymptotic, \(d = 2\) of arXiv:2606.23025, 'Spectral-Capacitary Bounds for Homological Recovery from Reflected Brownian Trajectories'] Let \(d = 2\) and \(\partial M\)
uniformly of class \(C^{1,1}\), and write
\(\delta_{\varepsilon} = \operatorname{dist}\left( x_{\varepsilon},\partial M \right)\).
The planar boundary layer has three regimes:

(i) boundary-scale centers,
\(\delta_{\varepsilon}/\varepsilon = O(1)\) (including
\(\delta_{\varepsilon} = 0\)):

\[\lambda\left( B_{M}\left( x_{\varepsilon},\varepsilon \right) \right) = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{\pi}{|M|\,\log(1/\varepsilon)}\,\left( 1 + o(1) \right);\]

(ii) intermediate centers,
\(\varepsilon \ll \delta_{\varepsilon} \ll 1\) with
\(\theta: = limlog\left( 1/\delta_{\varepsilon} \right)/\log(1/\varepsilon) \in (0,1)\)
(equivalently
\(\delta_{\varepsilon} = \varepsilon^{\theta + o(1)}\)):

\[\lambda\left( B_{M}\left( x_{\varepsilon},\varepsilon \right) \right) = B(\theta) \cdot \frac{\pi}{|M|\,\log(1/\varepsilon)}\,\left( 1 + o(1) \right),\quad\quad B(\theta) = \frac{1}{1 + \theta};\]

(iii) macroscopically interior centers, \(\delta_{\varepsilon}\)
bounded below:

\[\lambda\left( B_{M}\left( x_{\varepsilon},\varepsilon \right) \right) = \frac{\pi}{|M|\,\log(1/\varepsilon)}\,\left( 1 + o(1) \right).\]

Here \(\theta \in \lbrack 0,1\rbrack\) is the logarithmic
boundary-layer parameter, with \(\theta = 0\) for macroscopically
interior centers (iii) and \(\theta = 1\) for boundary-scale
centers (i); the three regimes are the single asymptotic
\(\lambda\left( B_{M}\left( x_{\varepsilon},\varepsilon \right) \right) = B(\theta)\,\pi/\left( |M|\log(1/\varepsilon) \right)\,\left( 1 + o(1) \right)\)
with \(B(\theta) = 1/(1 + \theta)\). The profile \(B\)
acts on the eigenvalue --- and, by Proposition D.5, on the Neumann
capacity --- decreasing from the interior value \(B(0) = 1\) to
the boundary value \(B(1) = \frac{1}{2}\); the associated
hitting-time constant of Corollary D.9 is the reciprocal
\(1/B(\theta) = 1 + \theta\), increasing from \(1\) to
\(2\). Thus a boundary-scale target has half the eigenvalue, and
twice the hitting time, of a macroscopically interior one. In contrast
to \(d \geq 3\), every fixed rescaled distance
\(\delta_{\varepsilon}/\varepsilon\) corresponds to
\(\theta = 1\) and hence to the same boundary value; the
nontrivial planar transition occurs only on the logarithmic scale
\(\theta\).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["g Borel measurable","P(X in D_g) = 0, where D_g is the discontinuity set of g and X is the LIMIT","for the distributional case: a separable metric space, so that Skorokhod representation applies"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.752745+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_08bbed66bee85e7a43e037177ad373d4b632f7fc0a234cb4b033a85493a10a9f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_n and X be random elements of a metric space S and let g : S -> S' be a Borel measurable map whose set of discontinuity points D_g is a Borel set with P(X in D_g) = 0. Then: X_n => X in distribution implies g(X_n) => g(X); X_n -> X in probability implies g(X_n) -> g(X) in probability; X_n -> X almost surely implies g(X_n) -> g(X) almost surely. The hypothesis is that the LIMIT avoids the discontinuity set almost surely, not that g is continuous everywhere - which is what makes the theorem usable for maps such as x -> 1/x when the limit is almost surely nonzero, or x -> 1_{(a, infinity)}(x) when P(X = a) = 0. Without that hypothesis the conclusion fails: with X_n = 1/n deterministically, X = 0, and g = 1_{(0, infinity)}, we have g(X_n) = 1 for all n while g(X) = 0. D_g is always Borel for any g between metric spaces, so that part of the hypothesis is automatic. [standard; e.g. Billingsley, Convergence of Probability Measures, 2nd ed., Theorem 2.7]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Omega is a bounded open subset of R^N with N >= 2 and 1 < p < N","a(x,s,xi) is a Caratheodory Leray-Lions field: p-growth with k in L^{p'}, coercivity a.xi >= alpha |xi|^p, strict monotonicity in xi","f in L^1(Omega); the estimates are on weak solutions of approximating problems with L^1-bounded data","existence of a distributional W_0^{1,q} solution additionally needs p > 2 - 1/N","homogeneous Dirichlet boundary condition"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:23.251071+00:00","domain":"nonlinear elliptic PDE, L^1 data, truncation method, Marcinkiewicz estimates","id":"claim_091da16d48d2aaf84660ce50e0a871758dac4023b0cb663a0df7ad63ba360344","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Setting: $\\Omega \\subset \\mathbb{R}^N$ bounded open, $N \\geq 2$, $1 < p < N$. Let $a: \\Omega\\times\\mathbb{R}\\times\\mathbb{R}^N \\to \\mathbb{R}^N$ be a Caratheodory function (measurable in $x$, continuous in $(s,\\xi)$) satisfying, for a.e. $x$ and all $s, \\xi, \\eta$: growth $|a(x,s,\\xi)| \\leq \\beta\\,(k(x) + |s|^{p-1} + |\\xi|^{p-1})$ with $k \\in L^{p'}(\\Omega)$; coercivity $a(x,s,\\xi)\\cdot\\xi \\geq \\alpha|\\xi|^p$ with $\\alpha > 0$; strict monotonicity $(a(x,s,\\xi) - a(x,s,\\eta))\\cdot(\\xi-\\eta) > 0$ for $\\xi \\neq \\eta$ (a Leray-Lions operator, e.g. the $p$-Laplacian $a = |\\xi|^{p-2}\\xi$). Consider $-\\operatorname{div}\\,a(x,u,\\nabla u) = f$ in $\\Omega$, $u = 0$ on $\\partial\\Omega$, with $f \\in L^1(\\Omega)$. (Boccardo-Gallouet, J. Funct. Anal. 87 (1989); the estimates are the nonlinear form of Stampacchia's truncation estimates.) A PRIORI ESTIMATES. Let $u \\in W_0^{1,p}(\\Omega)$ be a weak solution for a datum $f \\in L^1 \\cap W^{-1,p'}$ (in practice the solutions $u_n$ of approximating problems with $f_n \\in L^\\infty$, $\\|f_n\\|_{L^1} \\leq \\|f\\|_{L^1}$; all constants below depend only on $N, p, \\alpha, \\|f\\|_{L^1}$, never on $n$). Then: (E1) for every $k > 0$, $\\alpha\\int_\\Omega|\\nabla T_k(u)|^p\\,dx \\leq k\\,\\|f\\|_{L^1}$; (E2) for every $k > 0$, $|\\{|u| \\geq k\\}| \\leq (S^p\\|f\\|_{L^1}/\\alpha)^{N/(N-p)}\\,k^{-N(p-1)/(N-p)}$, where $S$ is the Sobolev constant of $W_0^{1,p} \\hookrightarrow L^{p^*}$, $p^* = Np/(N-p)$; i.e. $u$ is bounded in the Marcinkiewicz space $M^{N(p-1)/(N-p)}(\\Omega)$; (E3) for every $h > 0$, $|\\{|\\nabla u| \\geq h\\}| \\leq C\\,h^{-N(p-1)/(N-1)}$, i.e. $|\\nabla u|$ is bounded in $M^{N(p-1)/(N-1)}(\\Omega)$; hence, $\\Omega$ being bounded, $u$ is bounded in $W_0^{1,q}(\\Omega)$ for every $q < N(p-1)/(N-1)$. EXISTENCE. If moreover $p > 2 - 1/N$ (equivalently $N(p-1)/(N-1) > 1$), there exists $u \\in W_0^{1,q}(\\Omega)$ for every $q < N(p-1)/(N-1)$, with $T_k(u) \\in W_0^{1,p}(\\Omega)$ for every $k$, $a(x,u,\\nabla u) \\in L^{r}(\\Omega)$ for some $r > 1$, and $\\int_\\Omega a(x,u,\\nabla u)\\cdot\\nabla\\varphi\\,dx = \\int_\\Omega f\\varphi\\,dx$ for all $\\varphi \\in C_c^\\infty(\\Omega)$ (a distributional solution). For $p = 2$ this is exactly Stampacchia's $q < N/(N-1)$. Sharp edges: (a) $q = N(p-1)/(N-1)$ is not attained - the fundamental solution of the $p$-Laplacian with $f = \\delta_0$ has $|\\nabla u| \\sim |x|^{-(N-1)/(p-1)}$, in $L^q$ iff $q < N(p-1)/(N-1)$; (b) for $1 < p \\leq 2 - 1/N$ the gradient of the solution is in general NOT in $L^1$, $u \\notin W^{1,1}$, and the distributional formulation is meaningless - one must use entropy or renormalized solutions defined through the truncations $T_k(u) \\in W_0^{1,p}$ and a generalized gradient; (c) existence is asserted, uniqueness is NOT: distributional $W^{1,q}$ solutions need not be unique (Serrin's pathological solutions of $\\operatorname{div}(A\\nabla u) = 0$ with $u \\in W^{1,q}$, $q < 2$, $u \\notin H^1_{loc}$, already for $p = 2$ and measurable coefficients); uniqueness holds in the entropy-solution class (Benilan, Boccardo, Gallouet, Gariepy, Pierre, Vazquez 1995) for $L^1$ data; (d) the estimates (E1)-(E3) require $T_k(u)$ to be an admissible test function, which is why they are proved on the approximations; (e) for measure data one gets the same $W_0^{1,q}$ bounds, but for a measure concentrated on a set of zero $p$-capacity the entropy uniqueness theory does not apply.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:38:11.735717+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_092f647668962c58af82e5e5f77ed3d543aea8d38795a25920ac1a86802cdd53","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:complex_cumu of arXiv:2504.00512, 'Localization-delocalization transition for a random block matrix model at the edge'] (Complex cumulant expansion) 
		Let $h$ be a complex random variable all of whose moments exist. The $(p,q)$-cumulant of $h$ is defined as
		$$
		\mathcal{C}^{(p,q)}(h)\mathrel{\vcenter{\baselineskip0.65ex \lineskiplimit0pt \hbox{.}\hbox{.}}}= (-\mathrm{i})^{p+q} \cdot \left(\frac{\partial^{p+q}}{\partial {s^p} \partial {t^q}} \log \mathbb{E} e^{\mathrm{i}sh+\mathrm{i}t\overline{h}}\right) \bigg{|}_{s=t=0}\,.
		$$
		Let $f:\mathbb C^2 \to \mathbb{C}$ be a smooth function, and we denote its holomorphic  derivatives by
		$$
		f^{(p,q)}(z_1,z_2)\mathrel{\vcenter{\baselineskip0.65ex \lineskiplimit0pt \hbox{.}\hbox{.}}}= \frac{\partial^{p+q}}{\partial z_1^p \partial z_2^q} f(z_1,z_2)\,.
		$$ Then, for any fixed $l \in \mathbb{N}$, we have
		\begin{equation} 
		\mathbb{E} f(h,\overline{h})\overline{h}=\sum\limits_{p+q=0}^l \frac{1}{p!\,q!}\mathcal{C}^{(p,q+1)}(h)\mathbb{E} f^{(p,q)}(h,\overline{h}) + R_{l+1}\,,
		\end{equation}
		given all integrals in ((5.16 of the paper)) exist. Here, $R_{l+1}$ is the remainder term depending on $f$ and $h$, and for any $\tau>0$, we have the estimate
		$$
			\begin{aligned}
			R_{l+1}=&\, \mathrm{O}(1)\cdot \mathbb{E} \big|h^{l+2}\mathbf{1}_{\{|h|>N^{\tau-1/2}\}}\big|\cdot \max\limits_{p+q=l+1}\big\| f^{(p,q)}(z,\overline{z})\big\|_{\infty} \\
			+&\,\mathrm{O}(1) \cdot \mathbb{E} |h|^{l+2} \cdot \max\limits_{p+q=l+1}\big\| f^{(p,q)}(z,\overline{z})\cdot \mathbf{1}_{\{|z|\le N^{\tau-1/2}\}}\big\|_{\infty}\,.
			\end{aligned}
		$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

	\[ S_\star\bigg(\lambda,\mu;
		\frac\epsilon5,
		\frac\epsilon2\bigg) 
	\subseteq \bigg[0,
		\frac8{\iota_0}
		\bigg]^{3r+s}\,.\]
where $\iota_0\equiv\iota \min\{1,\alpha\}$.
\begin{proof} Consider any $\YY$ belonging to the set on the left-hand side of the above display. By the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality,
    \[
        \Budget(\YY;\mu) \le \frac{1}{\alpha} (\mu,\vwww) = \frac{1}{\alpha}\,,
    \]
 Recall from the discussion after Proposition~\ref{p:fp}
 that  $\epsilon \le 1$. Then, for any $j\in [r]$, 
assumption~\eqref{e:def-Lambda} gives
    \[\max\bigg\{
            \vBBb_j,\vUUu_j,

        \bigg\}
        \le \frac{\Cost(\YY;\lambda)}{\iota}
        \le \frac{\Budget(\YY;\mu) + \epsilon/2}{\iota}
        \le \frac{2}{\iota\min\{1,\alpha\}}\,.
    \]
    This further implies (recalling $\iota,\epsilon \le 1$)
    \[
        \vvvv_j \le \vUUu_j + \bigg(1 +

	\bigg)^2

        \le \frac{8}{\iota \min\{1,\alpha\}}\,.
    \]
Finally, we can use the constraint $(\mu,\vwww) = 1$ to crudely bound
    \[

{"assumptions":["X is a compact metric space and T is continuous","the metric is fixed, but the notions defined are independent of the choice of a compatible metric on a compact space","Gamma_eps(x) is taken with forward iterates for a general continuous map and with two-sided iterates for a homeomorphism","Bowen's entropy h(T,Y) is used for arbitrary, possibly non-invariant, subsets Y"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.090635+00:00","domain":"topological dynamics, entropy","id":"claim_09ce2d5bcd2dcfca590ed7dbdf3202b050716fcf7e9c95e3a6d615cdc80401f0","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, d) be a compact metric space and T : X -> X continuous. For a subset Y of X (not assumed invariant or closed) Bowen's entropy of T on Y is h(T, Y) = lim as delta -> 0 of limsup_n (1/n) log r_n(delta, Y), where r_n(delta, Y) is the least cardinality of a set S that (n, delta)-spans Y, that is such that every y in Y admits s in S with d(T^i y, T^i s) <= delta for all 0 <= i < n. For eps > 0 and x in X put Gamma_eps(x) = { y in X : d(T^i x, T^i y) <= eps for all i >= 0 }, the set of points whose forward orbit shadows that of x at scale eps (for a homeomorphism one lets i range over all integers). DEFINITIONS: T is h-EXPANSIVE (Bowen) if there exists eps > 0 with h(T, Gamma_eps(x)) = 0 for every x in X. The TAIL ENTROPY of T is h*(T) = lim as eps -> 0 of sup over x in X of h(T, Gamma_eps(x)); the limit exists because the supremum is nondecreasing in eps. T is ASYMPTOTICALLY h-EXPANSIVE (Misiurewicz) if h*(T) = 0. Relations and cautions: expansive implies h-expansive (for small eps the sets Gamma_eps(x) are singletons, with the one- or two-sided convention matching the map), and h-expansive implies asymptotically h-expansive; neither implication reverses. Subshifts and expanding maps are expansive, hence h-expansive; every C^infinity diffeomorphism of a compact manifold is asymptotically h-expansive (Newhouse), while for finite smoothness this can fail. The quantity h*(T) measures the entropy invisible at any finite scale - the entropy 'in the tail' - and it is zero exactly when the system admits a principal symbolic extension (Boyle-Downarowicz theory); it is not the same as the topological entropy and carries no information about it.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f_n -> f in measure or mu-almost everywhere","uniform integrability of {f_n}","uniform tightness of {f_n}: on an infinite measure space this is an independent hypothesis"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.751693+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_0a5d28e3a2f0563534ddca90e6e5c1998a87b5c53300e2cd9dcf829e15f851d8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"On a FINITE measure space, uniform integrability plus convergence in measure gives L^1 convergence. On a general (for instance sigma-finite but infinite) measure space this is FALSE and a third hypothesis is needed. The correct statement: let (Omega, F, mu) be a measure space and f_n in L^1(mu) with f_n -> f in measure (or mu-a.e.). Then f_n -> f in L^1(mu) if and only if (i) {f_n} is uniformly integrable, meaning sup_n integral_{|f_n| > K} |f_n| dmu -> 0 as K -> infinity, AND (ii) {f_n} is uniformly tight, meaning for every eps > 0 there is a set A with mu(A) < infinity and sup_n integral_{Omega \\ A} |f_n| dmu < eps. Counterexample showing (ii) is not implied by (i): on R with Lebesgue measure take f_n = 1_{[n, n+1]}. Then |f_n| <= 1 so the family is uniformly integrable and dominated, f_n -> 0 pointwise everywhere, yet ||f_n||_1 = 1 for every n. Mass escapes to infinity; on a finite measure space it has nowhere to go, which is exactly why the finite-measure statement can omit (ii). [standard; e.g. Bogachev, Measure Theory, Vol. I, Section 4.5]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["i.i.d. rows C^{1/2} z with z having i.i.d. mean-zero unit-variance entries and finite twelfth moment","p/n -> q_0 in (0, infinity)","the population spectral distribution converges to a limit with bounded support","the formula is used inside the bulk; isolated spikes are handled by the BBP correction"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T05:50:37.943602+00:00","domain":"random matrix theory","id":"claim_0a70bf7dec2d4a8e97f8b3a3a903aaf467d73a6d689fe2fb896f6788c775985a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $E = \\frac{1}{n} X^T X$ be the sample covariance of $n$ i.i.d. rows in $\\mathbb{R}^p$ with population covariance $C$ (rows $C^{1/2} z_i$ with $z_i$ having i.i.d. entries of mean zero, variance one and finite twelfth moment), in the regime $p, n \\to \\infty$ with $q = p/n \\to q_0 \\in (0, \\infty)$, and assume the spectral distribution of $C$ converges to a limit with bounded support. Let $\\lambda_k, u_k$ be the sample eigenvalues and eigenvectors and let $g_E(z) = \\frac{1}{p}\\operatorname{tr}(z I - E)^{-1}$ be the Stieltjes transform of the sample spectrum, with $g(\\lambda - i0) := \\lim_{\\eta \\downarrow 0} g_E(\\lambda - i\\eta)$ inside the bulk. THEOREM (Ledoit and Peche, 2011, Theorem 4; in the form of Bun, Bouchaud and Potters 2017). The oracle eigenvalues $\\xi_k^{\\mathrm{or}} = u_k^T C u_k$ converge, uniformly in $k$ inside the bulk, to $$\\xi(\\lambda_k) = \\frac{\\lambda_k}{\\big|\\, 1 - q + q\\, \\lambda_k\\, g_E(\\lambda_k - i0) \\,\\big|^2}.$$ This limit depends on the population covariance $C$ only through the observable sample spectrum, so it is a consistent, computable estimator (the rotationally invariant estimator, RIE, or nonlinear shrinkage): replace each sample eigenvalue by $\\xi(\\lambda_k)$, keep the sample eigenvectors. In practice $g_E$ is evaluated at $\\lambda_k - i\\eta$ with a small $\\eta$ of order $n^{-1/2}$ times the eigenvalue scale, and the result is floored at a small positive fraction of the bulk level. When $C = \\sigma^2 I$ the formula returns $\\sigma^2$ for every eigenvalue (the Marchenko-Pastur spread is entirely removed); for a spike above the bulk it returns approximately the debiased population spike. Applying the formula to a matrix whose largest eigenvalue is a signal one is trying to keep, and flooring relative to that top eigenvalue, destroys the small eigenvalues that the inverse depends on.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["K compact and convex in a locally convex Hausdorff space","K metrizable for the measure to live on ext K itself"],"created_at":"2026-08-29T02:26:24.139081+00:00","domain":"functional analysis / convexity","id":"claim_0a8ceaa5f37b374709515e490798b2dbcdf330a9987e8089bd7542bf2dd180cd","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let K be a compact convex subset of a locally convex Hausdorff topological vector space, and suppose K is metrizable. Then the set ext K of extreme points of K is a G_delta set, and for every x in K there is a Borel probability measure mu on K, concentrated on ext K, whose barycenter is x: phi(x) = integral phi dmu for every continuous linear functional phi. Without metrizability, the Bishop-de Leeuw theorem gives a probability measure that vanishes on every Baire set disjoint from ext K. The Krein-Milman theorem, that K is the closed convex hull of ext K, is the qualitative counterpart. Uniqueness of the representing measure for every x characterises the Choquet simplices.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Zero-mean fixed finite-rank GP, supplied feature norms <=R, independent Gaussian noise variance s>0","At most n context labels; all input locations and context length jointly independent of latent GP and noises; iid tasks","Full original posterior is the target; only the predictor clips context labels at the explicit deterministic B"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T16:46:14.074691+00:00","domain":"Gaussian process predictive approximation; context truncation","id":"claim_0aac28c997e413b6e870c7d366e02430c9ded09828abe71420cb34a1f75fae4a","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"OWNER RESULT DRAFT, proof (unaudited), C007 v1; no novelty claim.
Let a fixed zero-mean finite-rank Gaussian process have a supplied feature map phi with ||phi(x)||<=R, independent Gaussian observation noise of variance s>0, and at most n context observations. All context/query input locations and context length are jointly independent of the GP and all noises. Context labels may be correlated and are not bounded or conditioned. Put V=s+R^2. Given the full original context W, let P_W=N(m,v) be the exact noisy posterior predictive. Clip each context label to [-B,B], B>0, and recompute the mean m_B with the same design; v is unchanged. Suppose a Gaussian predictor h_B=N(mhat,vhat), depending only on clipped context and supplied features, has vhat>=s and KL(N(m_B,v)||h_B)<=eps_c for every possible context and design. Then on the ORIGINAL unconditioned task law,
E_W KL(P_W||h_B) <= 2 eps_c + (2 sqrt(2) n^2 R^4 V/s^3) exp(-B^2/(4V)).
In particular, for eps>0, eps_c=eps/4 and B=sqrt(4V log(max(e,4 sqrt(2) n^2 R^4 V/(s^3 eps)))) make the expected KL at most eps. If nR=0 the bias is zero. This does not assert that N(m_B,v) is the conditional law given clipped labels. The supplied-feature comparator exists by the separately audited C002 construction; this clipping lemma itself awaits independent review.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Finite-dimensional Euclidean space; n>=2 components and K>=2 epochs","Convex C1 f_i with globally L_i-Lipschitz gradients, L_i>0","Proper closed convex psi and an attained finite minimum of F=f+psi","x_1 is in dom psi; eta is constant, positive, and satisfies the displayed K-dependent cap","For the expected random-reshuffling bound, use fresh independent uniform permutations","For the optimized-rate corollaries assume D>0; the fixed-step inequalities do not require D>0"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T15:34:11.132651+00:00","domain":"Liu Zhou; proximal shuffling; random reshuffling; last iterate; convex optimization","id":"claim_0ab04f1d8562a58b42caeb8c92cdff50dfe5a30627a7b67abd496813c58be7c6","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let n>=2, K>=2 and d>=1. Let each f_i:R^d->R be convex C1 with globally L_i-Lipschitz gradient, L_i>0. Let psi:R^d->R union {+infinity} be proper closed convex. Set f=(1/n)sum_i f_i, F=f+psi, and suppose x* minimizes F with F(x*) finite. Start at x_1 in dom psi. Write D=||x_1-x*||, Lbar=(1/n)sum_i L_i, Lmax=max_i L_i, s=1+log K, sigma_any^2=(1/n)sum_i ||grad f_i(x*)||^2 and sigma_rand^2=sigma_any^2+n||grad f(x*)||^2. Use a fixed positive step eta<=1/[4n sqrt(2 Lbar Lmax s)]. In epoch k, set z_0=x_k, take z_i=z_(i-1)-eta grad f_(sigma_i)(z_(i-1)) for i=1,...,n along a permutation sigma, and set x_(k+1)=prox_(n eta psi)(z_n), where prox_(n eta psi)(z) minimizes psi(x)+||x-z||^2/(2n eta). There is an absolute constant C such that, for every sequence of permutations, F(x_(K+1))-F(x*)<=C[D^2/(n eta K)+(n eta)^2 Lbar sigma_any^2 s]. If fresh independent uniform permutations are used in each epoch, E[F(x_(K+1))-F(x*)]<=C[D^2/(n eta K)+n eta^2 Lbar sigma_rand^2 s]. These are bounds for the last epoch iterate, with no strong-convexity assumption. For D>0, balancing eta under the stated cap gives respectively O(D^2 sqrt(Lbar Lmax s)/K+D^(4/3)(Lbar sigma_any^2 s)^(1/3)/K^(2/3)) and O(D^2 sqrt(Lbar Lmax s)/K+D^(4/3)(Lbar sigma_rand^2 s)^(1/3)/(n^(1/3) K^(2/3))). The fixed-step bounds also cover D=0. All norms are Euclidean. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-23T11:58:53.978374+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_0ab65f335e4846d89753e7dca87d1223","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Exact rank three for the bounded-density conjecture: what is proved and what is open. (1) The step 'a rank-three coarea bound ||p_S||_inf <= K ||rho||_inf^{2/3} for S = sum_{j<=3} lambda_j Y_j^2' is false for general bounded densities rho on R^3: a density rho <= B that puts mass 2hB A(s) on the shell {|S - s| < h} gives p_S about B A(s) near s, where A(s) = d/ds vol{S <= s} = 2 pi s^{1/2}/sqrt(lambda_1 lambda_2 lambda_3) for a definite form, unbounded as s grows; a bound needs regularity of rho beyond its supremum. (2) Orthonormal 3D projections of product densities have that regularity on spheres: their spherical means satisfy M_{y0}(r) <= 6/(pi r) uniformly in the centre, and definite rank-three forms have density <= 82 for every linear term.
