{"assumptions":["f is continuous on a closed cylinder around (t_0,y_0)","f is Lipschitz in y, uniformly in t, on that cylinder"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T14:20:41.451641+00:00","domain":"ordinary differential equations","id":"claim_0ad98344cc4c4b7f94070b09639fced6","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f: [t_0-a,t_0+a] x B(y_0,b) -> R^n be continuous, where B(y_0,b) subset R^n is the closed ball of radius b around y_0, and suppose f is Lipschitz in its second argument uniformly in the first: there is L >= 0 with |f(t,y_1)-f(t,y_2)| <= L|y_1-y_2| for all t in the interval and y_1,y_2 in B(y_0,b). Let M = max|f(t,y)| over this compact domain and h = min(a, b/M). Then the initial value problem y'(t) = f(t,y(t)), y(t_0)=y_0, has a unique solution y on [t_0-h, t_0+h]. (When M = 0, read b/M as infinity, so h = a.) Continuity alone does not give uniqueness: y' = 2 sqrt(|y|), y(0) = 0 has infinitely many solutions. If f is continuous and locally Lipschitz in y on an open domain D, the local solutions through (t_0, y_0) patch together into a unique maximal solution, which leaves every compact subset of D as t approaches either end of its interval.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:13:18.501965+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_0afdafd4b352c5fcad844d588f8048f7a3634622f9b8b5964f08fe8ff6f0d068","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theo 22 (Explicit threshold, compact-support branch and onset amplitude) of arXiv:2608.30578, 'Compactly Supported Solutions near a Nehari Critical Value'] Let $0<\alpha<1$ and $n\ge2$. Consider the problem
\[
\begin{cases}
	-u''=\lambda u+m_n(x)u^\alpha,& -1<x<1,\\
	u(-1)=u(1)=0.
\end{cases}
\]
Define
\[
\lambda_{c,n}:=
\frac{\pi^2}
{\left((1-\alpha)+\dfrac{1+\alpha}{n}\right)^2}.
\]
Then
\[
\frac{\pi^2}{4}
<
\lambda_{c,n}
<
\lambda_n^*.
\]
At $\lambda=\lambda_{c,n}$ there exists an even positive flat solution
$u_{c,n}$ satisfying $u_{c,n}(\pm1)=u_{c,n}'(\pm1)=0$. For every
$\lambda\in(\lambda_{c,n},\lambda_n^*)$ there exists a unique even
non-negative solution in the above class whose connected support is
\[
\operatorname{supp}u_{\lambda,n}
=
[-b_{\lambda,n},b_{\lambda,n}]
\Subset(-1,1),
\]
where
\[
b_{\lambda,n}
=
\frac{1}{1-\alpha}
\left(
\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{\lambda}}
-\frac{1+\alpha}{n}
\right).
\]
For $x\ge0$ the solution is
\[
u_{\lambda,n}(x)
=
\begin{cases}
	A_{\lambda,n}\cos(\sqrt{\lambda}\,x),
	& 0\le x\le\dfrac1n,\\[2mm]
	\displaystyle
	\left(
	\frac{2}{(1+\alpha)\lambda}
	\right)^{\frac1{1-\alpha}}
	\sin^{\frac{2}{1-\alpha}}
	\left[
	\frac{1-\alpha}{2}\sqrt{\lambda}\,
	(b_{\lambda,n}-x)
	\right],
	& \dfrac1n\le x\le b_{\lambda,n},\\[3mm]

	& b_{\lambda,n}\le x\le1,
\end{cases}
\]
and it is extended evenly to $(-1,0)$. Moreover,
\[
A_{\lambda,n}
=
\|u_{\lambda,n}\|_{L^\infty(-1,1)}
=
\left(
\frac{2}{(1+\alpha)\lambda}
\right)^{\frac1{1-\alpha}}
\cos^{\frac{1+\alpha}{1-\alpha}}
\left(\frac{\sqrt{\lambda}}{n}\right).
\]
For each fixed $n$, the mapping $\lambda\longmapsto A_{\lambda,n}$
is strictly decreasing on $(\lambda_{c,n},\lambda_n^*)$, and

\[

then
\[

\left[
\frac{2}{(1+\alpha)\pi^2}
\left(

\right)^2
\right]^{\frac1{1-\alpha}}
\cos^{\frac{1+\alpha}{1-\alpha}}
\left(

\]
and
\[
\lambda_{c,n}\uparrow
\lambda_{c,\infty}:=
\frac{\pi^2}{(1-\alpha)^2},
\]
while
\[
A_n\longrightarrow
A_\infty:=
\left[
\frac{2(1-\alpha)^2}
{(1+\alpha)\pi^2}
\right]^{\frac1{1-\alpha}}
>0.

Furthermore,
\[
\frac{\lambda_{c,n}}{\lambda_n^*}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Moreover, $H_\lambda(u_{\lambda,n})=M_n(u_{\lambda,n})<0$, and therefore

\ \sum_{f\in H_{\mathrm{new}}(N)}1

{"assumptions":["X compact, T continuous.","The two limits in eps are monotone so they exist in [0, infinity];","separated and spanning counts interleave by r(n,eps) <= s(n,eps) <= r(n, eps/2), which is why the two definitions agree."],"created_at":"2026-09-12T14:04:29.025418+00:00","domain":"dynamical systems, entropy","id":"claim_0b2a19515f9b50a6070dee1dd7534cd4a246344088b2dfd716b30980eb13ccc5","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X,d) be a compact metric space and T : X -> X continuous. Method: Examine the small parameter of the lace expansion and whether a different expansion parameter exists for d in {7,...,10}. Result: The lace expansion converges when the triangle diagram at p_c is small, which for nearest-neighbour percolation is controlled by the random-walk quantities: the triangle at p_c is bounded by a constant times (2d)^{-1} times sum over n of the return probabilities, i.e. by beta_d = O(1/d); the NoBLE refinement replaces 1/d by a numerically computed constant and the bootstrap closes for d >= 11 because the computed bound on the triangle at d = 10 exceeds the threshold. Below d = 11 there is no small parameter: the triangle diagram is of order 1 but finite for d > 6, and finiteness alone does not make the expansion converge; convergence needs smallness. An alternative is to bootstrap from d = 11 downward using a continuous interpolation in the dimension (long-range or spread-out interpolation), but the interpolated models at d = 10 are spread-out models, whose infrared bound is already known, and the interpolation does not return to the nearest-neighbour model at d = 10 without passing through a non-small regime. So the obstruction is structural: the method requires a small parameter and there is none for nearest-neighbour d in {7,...,10}. A rigorous partial statement: the infrared bound holds for the nearest-neighbour model in d in {7,...,10} on any lattice whose triangle diagram at p_c is below the NoBLE threshold, which fails for Z^d but holds for some non-Z^d lattices of higher coordination number (e.g. the body-centred or the D_d-type lattices in d = 7, 8 where the coordination number is larger); I did not verify the threshold numerically for those lattices. Obstruction: No small parameter for nearest-neighbour Z^d with 7 <= d <= 10.","status":"unverified"}

\log\frac{d\Prob_{\mathrm{true}}}{d\Prob_{\mathrm{dir}}}=\int_0^\tau\langle b^{-1}\Delta_t,dW_t\rangle-\frac12\int_0^\tau\|b^{-1}\Delta_t\|^2\,dt,
\]
where $\Delta_t=\gamma\,\sigma\big(s^{(v)}_t-\theta_{vu}\big)$ is the back-reaction drift. On the cascade timescale $\|\Delta_t\|=\Theta(1)$ whenever the child is active, so the quadratic-variation term is $\Theta(\tau)$ and the density is not tight toward $1$ as $G_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{BS}}T$. Hence Hypothesis~\ref{hyp:red} cannot be obtained by a change of measure showing $d\Prob_{\mathrm{true}}/d\Prob_{\mathrm{dir}}\to1$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.160341+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_0bce53c2a54a877341b0ab6914a27bb4ca63a6faae2fb61944aae563360a55f7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 4 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any constant $\delta > 0$, there exists $c = c(\alpha, L, \delta) > 0$ such that with probability $1-e^{-cN}$,
    \begin{align}
        
        \bigg|\frac{\|\bar{\bx}\|^2}{N} - 1\bigg| &\le \delta\,,\\
    
        \bigg|\frac{\E[ \|\hat{\by}\|^2 | \bG]}{N} - 1\bigg| &\le
        \frac{\delta}{2}\,.
    \end{align} 
Moreover, conditional on any realization of $\bG$ satisfying \eqref{e:fp-y-cond-conc} the following holds. Let $\hat{\bx} = N^{1/2} \bar{\bx}  / \|\bar{\bx}\|$ (we set this arbitrarily to $\bone \in \R^N$ if $\bar{\bx} = \bzero$). Let $\bXi'$ be an independent copy of $\bXi$ and $\hat{\by}' = \hat{\by}(\bG,\bXi')$. Then
    \beq
        
        \lt|\frac{\|\hat{\by}\|^2}{N} - 1\rt|\,,
        \frac{|(\hat{\bx},\hat{\by})|}{N},
        \frac{|(\hat{\by},\hat{\by}')|}{N} \le \delta
    \eeq
   with probability at least $1-e^{-cN}$.

\begin{proof}
    Since $\bG \mapsto \|\bar{\bx}\|$ is $L$-Lipschitz, $\|\bar{\bx}\|$ is $O(1)$-subgaussian by gaussian concentration of measure.
    Combined with $\E \|\bar{\bx}\|^2 = N$ this implies \eqref{e:fp-x-conc}.
    We next argue that the function
    \[
        f(\bG) = \E[ \|\hat{\by}(\bG,\bXi)\|^2 | \bG]^{1/2}
    \]
    is also $L$-Lipschitz. Indeed,
    \[
        \nabla f(\bG)
        = \frac{\E[ (\nabla_\bG \hat{\by}(\bG,\bXi))(\bG,\bXi) \hat{\by}(\bG,\bXi) | \bG]}{\E[ \|\hat{\by}(\bG,\bXi)\|^2 | \bG]^{1/2}}\,,
    \]
    and thus
    \[
        \|\nabla f(\bG)\|^2
        = \frac{\|\E[ (\nabla_\bG \hat{\by}(\bG,\bXi)) \hat{\by}(\bG,\bXi) | \bG]\|^2}{\E[ \|\hat{\by}(\bG,\bXi)\|^2 | \bG]}
        \le \frac{\E[ \|\nabla_\bG \hat{\by}(\bG,\bXi)\|_\op^2 \|\hat{\by}(\bG,\bXi)\|^2 | \bG]}{\E[ \|\hat{\by}(\bG,\bXi)\|^2 | \bG]}
        \le L^2\,.
    \]
    Thus $\E[ \|\hat{\by}\|^2 | \bG]^{1/2}$ is also $O(1)$-subgaussian.
    Combined with $\E \|\hat{\by}\|^2 = N$ this proves \eqref{e:fp-y-cond-conc}. 
    The first inequality of \eqref{e:fp-y-conc} follows similarly to \eqref{e:fp-x-conc}, applying gaussian concentration on $\bXi$ conditional on $\bG$.
    The second inequality of \eqref{e:fp-y-conc} holds by gaussian concentration because $\bXi \mapsto (\hat{\bx},\hat{\by}) / N$ is $L/N^{1/2}$-Lipschitz and $\E[\hat{\by} | \bG] = \bzero$. 
    The third inequality of \eqref{e:fp-y-conc} follows similarly, conditioning further on a realization of $\hat{\by}$ such that $\|\hat{\by}\| \le 2N^{1/2}$ (which holds with probability $1-e^{-cN}$).
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:33:11.960658+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_0be23745fcb7932124769ed07416e7cd81572a3e3125e91e92e0879df1c8b822","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:convex-corners of arXiv:2607.24018, 'Jeu de taquin forests \\ and the inverse infinite RSK correspondence'] \

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:29:21.917044+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_0c01392a1bd9c746e686d9a5483d0fcac5dfd5992ca13f504729f5d405f12239","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 1 (Extended mapping) of arXiv:2608.01516, 'Nondegeneracy and regularity of polynomial pushforwards'] Let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^n$, let $d\in\mathbb N$,
and let
$f=(f_1,\ldots,f_k)\colon \mathbb R^n\to \mathbb R^k$ be a measurable mapping
such that
\[
0<\sigma_{f_j}^2:=\operatorname{Var}_\mu(f_j)<\infty
\quad \forall j\in\{1,\ldots,k\}.
\]
Let
\[
\hat f_j
=
\sigma_{f_j}^{-1}
\biggl(f_j-\int_{\mathbb R^n} f_j\,d\mu\biggr)
\quad \forall j\in\{1,\ldots,k\},
\]
and set
$\hat f:=(\hat f_1,\ldots,\hat f_k)$.
Assume also that
\[
\hat f^{\mathbf m}:=\hat f_1^{m_1}\ldots \hat f_k^{m_k}\in L^2(\mu)
\quad \forall \mathbf m=(m_1,\ldots,m_k)\in\mathbb Z_+^k
\quad\text{with}\quad
1\le |\mathbf m|\le d^{k-1}.
\]
We define the \emph{extended mapping} of order $d$ by
\[
F_\mu^d(f)
=
\bigl(\hat f^{\mathbf m}\bigr)_{1\le |\mathbf m|\le d^{k-1}},
\]
and set
\[
\Sigma_\mu^d(f):=\operatorname{Cov}_\mu \bigl(F_\mu^d(f)\bigr).
\]
In other words, $\Sigma_\mu^d(f)$ is the matrix, in the monomial basis, of the quadratic form
\[
Q\mapsto \operatorname{Var}_\mu\bigl(Q(\hat f)\bigr),\quad Q\in\mathcal P_{d^{k-1}}(\mathbb R^k),\quad
Q(0)=0.
\]","status":"unverified"}

A probability measure is unimodal if, for some mode m, it is an atom at m plus an absolutely continuous measure whose density is nondecreasing to the left of m and nonincreasing to the right. Write boxplus for additive free convolution. For t>0 let S(0,t) be the centered semicircle law of variance t, with density sqrt(4t-x^2)/(2pi t) on |x|<=2sqrt(t). Let mu be compactly supported with positive diameter D=sup{|x-y|: x,y in supp(mu)}. Then mu boxplus S(0,t) is unimodal for every t>=D^2. Proof route: by the source's Lemma 3.1 (Biane's description), non-unimodality at time t gives some R>0 and a separating local minimum u_0 of xi_R with xi_R(u_0)<=1/t. The stationary-kernel lower bound, rescaled to diameter D, gives xi_R(u_0)>=1/D^2, so t<=D^2. At t=D^2, equality would hold in that lower bound. This forces mu to be the symmetric two-point law with atoms at u_0±D/2 and R^2=3D^2/4, which is unimodal at t=D^2 by the source's Example 2.1. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:52:47.241221+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_0cf57756fb303fe51c5a78510ee0ea2f61720aa84ba675a3743fecea3bf9f10c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 1 (local existence and uniqueness below the classical threshold) of arXiv:2609.01093, 'Ideal MHD below the classical well-posedness threshold'] Fix $\breg\in(\frac12,1)$. Let $n\ge2$, let $\frac{n+1}2<s\le\frac n2+1$, let
$\Bzero\equiv\Binf\in\Rn\setminus\{0\}$, and let $v_0\in H^{s}(\Rn)$ be divergence-free. There are
constants $C\ge1$ and $\delta\in(0,1)$, depending only on
$n,s,\breg$ and $v_{\rm A}$, and there exist a time $T_*>0$, a distributional
solution $(v,B, p)$ of \eqref{eq:mhd} on $[0,T_*]\times\Rn$ with data
$(v_0,\Binf)$, with the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}
\item writing $b:=B-\Binf$, the fields $v$, $b$ and $p$ lie in
$C([0,T_*],H^{s}(\Rn))$. The pressure is normalised by
\[
 p=\Riesz_i\Riesz_j
 \big(v^iv^j-\Binf^ib^j-b^i\Binf^j-b^ib^j\big),
\]
where $\Riesz_i$ are the Euclidean Riesz transforms;
\item writing $X=\mathrm{id}+w$, the solution is carried by a Lagrangian flow
$X:[0,T_*]\times\Rn\to\Rn$ with $X(0,\cdot)=\mathrm{id}$, uniformly bi-Lipschitz
and volume-preserving, $\det dX\equiv1$, such that $v=(\partial_tX)\circ X^{-1}$ and
$B=(\mathcal BX)\circ X^{-1}$;
moreover there is a spatially exact spacetime field
$\Ufield\in H^{s-1,1}_{\breg}(\Rst)$ such that
$\Ufield=dw$ on $[0,T_*]\times\Rn$ and, for constants fixed by
the standing parameters (one may take $C=2C_{\rm lin}$, with $C_{\rm lin}$
the constant of the linear estimate \eqref{eq:linear}),
\begin{equation}
 \|\Ufield\|_{H^{s-1,1}_{\breg}}
 \le C\|v_0\|_{H^s},
 \qquad
 \sup_{t\in[0,T_*]}\|dw(t)\|_{Y^{s-1,1}}\le\delta;
\end{equation}
here $\delta$ is chosen so that the second bound implies
$\|dw\|_{L^\infty_{t,y}}\le\frac12$;
\item the renormalised energy $E$ and cross helicity $H_{\rm c}$ of \eqref{eq:energy} are
conserved on $[0,T_*]$;
\item the solution is unique among all distributional solutions with the same
initial data for which $v$ and $B-\Binf$ belong to
$C([0,T_*],H^s)$. 
\end{enumerate}
The existence time is governed by the longitudinal regularity of the datum. We
distinguish the following two regimes.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\textbf{\emph{(R1)}}]  $T_*$ depends on $n,s,\breg,
v_{\rm A}$, on $\|v_0\|_{H^{s}}$ and on the function
$T\mapsto\omega_{v_0}(T)$ defined in \eqref{eq:datum-modulus}.
\item[\textbf{\emph{(R2)}}] If $\|\nabla v_0\|_{Y^{s-1,\rpar}}<\infty$
for some $\rpar\in(0,1]$, then $T_*$ depends on $n,s,\breg,\rpar,v_{\rm A}$
and on $\|v_0\|_{H^{s}}+\|\nabla v_0\|_{Y^{s-1,\rpar}}$ alone. Moreover,
the spacetime field in~(2) satisfies
\[
 \|\Ufield\|_{H^{s-1,1+\rpar}_{\breg}}
 \le C\|\nabla v_0\|_{Y^{s-1,\rpar}}.
\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["m a positive integer","The exact real symmetric 3-by-3 matrix family displayed above","Frobenius metric for the full Gram matrix; scalar Schur complement in its last coordinate","No identification of m with a realizable network depth"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T17:46:43.579570+00:00","domain":"probability and Gaussian conditioning","id":"claim_0d0af2cc485fae31c86ec03a77b28a1438b145446a35de781b46983c6a934c15","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"PROOF (UNAUDITED); elementary matrix example, no novelty claimed. For every integer m>=1, let rho=1-m^(-2), Y=[[1,rho],[rho,1]], b(t)=(1/(2m)+t)(1,-1)^T, and G(t)=[[Y,b(t)],[b(t)^T,1]], for 0<=t<=1/(8m). Every G(t) is positive definite of rank 3 with unit diagonal. Its Schur complement s(G(t))=1/2-2mt-2m^2t^2 lies in [7/32,1/2]. The endpoint Frobenius distance is 1/(4m), while the Schur-complement difference is 9/32 and its square-root difference is (4-sqrt(7))/(4sqrt(2)). Hence square-root sensitivity is >m/2. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:46:09.850320+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_0d13ae038fd9406c6117e2c0470b7b3883dd66014b46ac803d003bab28e95a0c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 1 (Log-concavity, PF$_2$, and TP$_2$) of arXiv:2605.18751, '\mytitle'] A positive function \(a:J\to(0,\infty)\) on an interval \(J\subseteq E\) is \emph{log-concave} if \(\log a\) is concave on \(J\). In the discrete case this is equivalent to \(\Delta^2\log a(k)\le0\) for every admissible \(k\in J\) and in the continuous case it is equivalent to \((\log a)''(x)\le0\) wherever the second derivative exists.

For a sequence \(b=(b_k)_{k\in\Z}\), we say that \(b\) is a \emph{P\'olya frequency sequence of order 2} (PF$_2$) if \(b_k\ge0\) for all \(k\), the support \(\{k:b_k>0\}\) is an interval in \(\Z\), and \(b\) is log-concave on its support.  A probability distribution \(F\) on \(\N_0\) is PF$_2$ if its mass sequence, extended by zero outside its support, is PF$_2$.

A nonnegative kernel \(M:I\times J\to[0,\infty)\) on two totally ordered sets is \emph{totally positive of order 2} (TP$_2$) if
\[
M(i,j)M(i',j')\ge M(i,j')M(i',j)
\]
whenever \(i\le i'\) and \(j\le j'\). See~\cite{Karlin1968} for the general total positivity theory.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:33:01.744633+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_0d9a176282a96c93b294a74a824ca937dc5efa7fe2e71bf4175a378aace79fca","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 10 of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] The ordinary generating function of $H$ is
  \[
    \phi_H(z) = (1-p)^m \binom{m/z - 1}{m}^{-1}.
  \]
  \begin{proof}
    We use the Laplace--Borel transform with $m$ applications of integration
    by parts:
    \begin{align*}
      \frac{\phi_H(x)}{(1-p)^m} &= \int_0^\infty
        \left( e^{xt/m} - 1 \right)^m
        e^{-t} \, dt\\
      &= \underbrace{\left. \left( e^{xt/m} - 1 \right)^m \left(-e^{-t}\right)
          \right|^{t=\infty}_{t=0}}_0\\
      &\quad + \int_0^\infty m\left( e^{xt/m} - 1 \right)^{m-1} \left(\frac{x}{m} \, e^{xt/m}\right)
      e^{-t} \, dt\\
      &= \frac{m\left(x/m\right)}{1} \int_0^\infty \left(e^{xt/m}-1\right)^{m-1}
            e^{-(1-x/m)t} \, dt\\
      &= \frac{m \left(m-1\right) (x/m)^2}{1-x/m} \int_0^\infty \left( e^{xt/m}-1\right)^{m-2}
            e^{-(1-2x/m)t} \, dt\\
      &\ \,\vdots\\
      &= \frac{m!\left(x/m\right)}{\left(m/x - 1\right)^{\underline{m-1}}} 
            \int_0^\infty e^{-(1-x)t} \, dt\\
      &= \frac{m!}{\left(m/x-1\right)^{\underline{m}}} = \binom{m/x - 1}{m}^{-1},
      \quad 0 < x < 1.
    \end{align*}
    The right-hand side is a rational function of $x$, say
    $f(x) / g(x)$ where $f(z)$ and $g(z)$ are real polynomials in $z$.
    Then $f(z) \, g(z)^{-1}$ is a well-defined object in the ring 
    of formal power series $\mathbb{R}[[z]]$ and we can
    restate our result for $\phi_H(z)$;
    see Section~\ref{language}.
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:37:25.925179+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_0dd4eeed3cc16d0d119ec6898bcb507f6d0169af673e54eb694a3ed0b621b1e9","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 26 of arXiv:2608.29585, '2608.29585'] For $m\ge0$, let
\[
 \mathscr P_m
 =\{\lambda:\ell(\lambda)\le n,\ |\lambda|\le m\},
 \qquad
 E_m=\bigl(G_\lambda(p_\mu)\bigr)_
       {\mu,\lambda\in\mathscr P_m},
\]
where
\[
 p_\mu=(Q^{\mu_1+n-1},Q^{\mu_2+n-2},\ldots,Q^{\mu_n}),
\]
and the rows and columns are ordered by any linear extension of
inclusion.  Then $E_m$ is lower triangular and
\[
 G_\lambda(p_\lambda)
 =u_\lambda\prod_{\square\in\lambda}
       (1-Q^{h(\square)}),
 \qquad u_\lambda\in R_{\mathrm{ev}}^\times.
\]
In particular,
\[
 D_m:=\det E_m\in R_{\mathrm{ev}}\setminus\{0\}
\]
is a Laurent unit times a product of cyclotomic polynomials, and
\[
 D_mE_m^{-1}=\operatorname{adj}(E_m)
 \in\operatorname{Mat}_{\mathscr P_m}(R_{\mathrm{ev}}).
\]

If $F=\sum_\lambda b_\lambda G_\lambda\in

\[
 \mathbf v_m(F)=\bigl(F(p_\mu)\bigr)_{\mu\in\mathscr P_m},
 \qquad
 \mathbf b_m(F)=\bigl(b_\lambda\bigr)_{\lambda\in\mathscr P_m},
\]
then
\begin{equation}
 \mathbf v_m(F)=E_m\mathbf b_m(F).
\end{equation}
Consequently, for every ideal $J\subseteq R_{\mathrm{ev}}$,
\[
 F(p_\mu)\in J\quad(\mu\in\mathscr P_m)
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 b_\lambda\in D_m^{-1}J
 \quad(\lambda\in\mathscr P_m).

{"assumptions":["H and K are complex Banach spaces","A and B are BOUNDED linear operators on H and K respectively","sigma(A) and sigma(B) are disjoint compact subsets of C","C is a bounded operator from K to H","Gamma is a cycle in the resolvent set of B winding once around sigma(A) and not at all around sigma(B)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.091249+00:00","domain":"operator theory, Sylvester equations, Riesz functional calculus","id":"claim_0ddcfb960219b5d37190ff5731d811c9cbc7554da88e7737e484070a46e2973a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"CAUTION ON THE NAME: this is the other result commonly called 'Rosenblum's argument' - the contour-integral solution of the Sylvester equation; the scattering-theory Hilbert-Schmidt estimate is a different theorem of the same author, so a citation naming Rosenblum must be matched to its context. STATEMENT: let H and K be complex Banach spaces, A a bounded operator on H, B a bounded operator on K, and suppose their spectra are disjoint: sigma(A) intersect sigma(B) is empty. Then for every bounded operator C from K to H the equation A X - X B = C has a UNIQUE bounded solution X from K to H, and it is given by X = (1 / (2 pi i)) times the contour integral over Gamma of (A - z)^(-1) C (B - z)^(-1) dz, where Gamma is a finite union of positively oriented rectifiable Jordan curves lying in the resolvent set of B, encircling sigma(A) once and sigma(B) not at all. WHERE IT FAILS: (i) disjointness of the spectra is what gives both existence and uniqueness. With A = B and C = 0 the equation A X - X A = 0 is solved by every operator commuting with A, so uniqueness fails badly; and with A = B = 0 on a one-dimensional space the equation is unsolvable for nonzero C. (ii) It is the SPECTRA, not the norms, that matter: no smallness of C is assumed, the solution depends linearly on C, and the bound on X is controlled by the length of Gamma and by the size of the two resolvents on Gamma - a bound that blows up as the spectra approach each other, which is the quantitative content usually needed in perturbation arguments. (iii) The theorem as stated is for BOUNDED A and B; for unbounded operators the analogous statement requires separate hypotheses (sectoriality, semigroup generation), and the contour formula must be justified anew. (iv) Finite-dimensional corollary: for matrices, A X - X B = C is uniquely solvable precisely when A and B have no common eigenvalue.","status":"unverified"}

# Target 1: two-cycle exclusion and necessary overshoot for periodic GD

Version 1, proof unaudited. This excludes possible third fates; it does not
classify all factored-GD trajectories or prove convergence.

Consider the factored model of claim 010 with any eta>0. More generally the
argument applies to any real update
 v_+=v+eta F(v,kq),
 k_+=k+delta q, q_+=q+delta k,
 delta=eta v G(v,kq),
where G is strictly positive at every finite point and F(0,s) has a unique
zero p_bar. The softmax logistic model satisfies these conditions.

1. Every orbit of period dividing two with k^2-q^2!=0 is a fixed point.
   It lies on v=0,kq=p_bar. This holds at every fixed step size.
2. Every nonstationary finite periodic orbit with k^2-q^2!=0 at one (hence
   every) iterate must contain an iterate with delta^2>=2. Equivalently,
   any periodic orbit on which |eta vG|<sqrt(2) throughout is stationary.

Neither statement excludes balanced-plane cycles, long cycles with large
overshoot, unbounded nonconvergent orbits, or nonperiodic bounded invariant
sets. This is a special obstruction result, not a scored global classification.

## Proof of two-cycle exclusion

Let U=k+q and D=k-q. Their exact simultaneous updates are
 U_+=(1+delta)U, D_+=(1-delta)D.
The nonzero imbalance is C=UD, so U,D are both nonzero initially.
For a returning two-step orbit, with a=delta_0,b=delta_1,
 (1+a)(1+b)=1, (1-a)(1-b)=1.
Expansion and addition yield 2ab=0; subtraction yields 2(a+b)=0.
Over the reals this forces a=b=0. Since eta>0 and G>0, v_0=v_1=0.
The factors therefore do not move. The head update then forces
F(0,kq)=0, hence kq=p_bar. This is a fixed point, as claimed.

## Proof of the overshoot requirement

The exact imbalance update is C_+=(1-delta^2)C. If an r-step orbit returns
with C_0!=0, no intermediate C can vanish, and
 product_{t=0}^{r-1}(1-delta_t^2)=1.
If every delta_t^2<2, every absolute factor is <=1, strictly less than 1
whenever delta_t!=0. The product can have absolute value 1 only if every
delta_t=0. Then every v_t=0, the factors stay fixed, and F(0,kq)=0.
Thus any nonstationary periodic orbit requires at least one delta_t^2>=2.

## Relation to the remaining gap

The flow's invariant imbalance is unavailable in GD, but its multiplicative
replacement still excludes every nonbalanced two-cycle, including at steps
beyond the normal-stability threshold of claim 013. A loss of an attracting
normal multiplier therefore does not by itself provide a two-cycle witness.
The unresolved step is controlling general, possibly large factor updates
well enough to show eventual entry into one of claim 010's escaping regions,
or finding a third fate that persists off the balanced planes.


# Target 1: exact balanced two-cycle and its transverse multiplier

Version 1, proof unaudited. Boundary check for claim 014, not a positive-volume
counterexample to an almost-everywhere theorem.

Fix any n>=2 and any distinct positive kappa_i. Put
 b_i=2 cosh(kappa_i)^2/kappa_i,
 a_i=b_i tanh(kappa_i).
These satisfy 0<a_i<b_i. In the usual coupled factored model
h_i(s)=a_i+b_i tanh(kappa_i s), all links have
 h_i(-1)=0, h_i'(-1)=2.

For EVERY fixed eta>0, simultaneous Euclidean GD on the average logistic
loss has an exact two-cycle
 (v,k,q)=(2/eta,1,-1) <-> (2/eta,-1,1).
At both points the loss is log 2, the product is -1, and k^2-q^2=0.
The two-step Jacobian has a transverse multiplier 9 normal to k=-q.
Thus the nonzero-imbalance assumption in 014 is necessary. This cycle
does not establish a positive-measure basin or rule out almost-everywhere
endpoint convergence.

## Proof

At either displayed state every h_i(kq)=0, so g_i=1/2, F=0 and
G=mean_i g_i h_i'=1. The head therefore stays fixed and
delta=eta vG=2. The factor update sends
 (k,q)->(k+2q,q+2k).
It exchanges (1,-1) and (-1,1). The cycle is nonstationary and has exact
period two; the loss remains log(1+exp(0))=log 2. The construction uses
different nonlinear scales, rather than requiring repeated identical examples.

The full factor-sum identity is U_+=(1+delta)U, U=k+q. At U=0 its
linearization gives dU_+=(1+delta)dU=3dU; the term U d(delta) vanishes.
After two steps dU_{++}=9dU, an exact normal multiplier even when v and
the product vary in the perturbation. No stability assertion at a unit
multiplier is involved.

The same constructed family has finite stationary points at v=0,kq=-1,
whereas the displayed periodic points have v=2/eta>0. Hence a classification
of every finite initialization by stationary points and escaping selections
alone would be false at any positive constant step. The exceptional balanced
plane must be allowed, as it is in claim 012's flow statement (which is a
different dynamical system).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["rows independent and identically distributed (the pairs bootstrap resamples rows, not residuals, so heteroscedasticity is allowed)","finite fourth moments and a converging empirical second-moment matrix (Freedman 1981); the predictor is a fixed measurable map of the sample, applied identically to every resample"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T12:03:52.456149+00:00","domain":"regression / resampling","id":"claim_0e4e01deefe6a25c51c622bfa99085bafd98403f8cc1a516a140a42803b61b73","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"For a least-squares predictor yhat(x) = x' beta_hat fitted on n rows, the textbook variance at a new point x is sigma^2 x'(X'SX)^(-1) x (sigma^2 times the leverage), and the hat matrix H = X(X'SX)^(-1)X'S has trace equal to the number of parameters. Both statements require X'SX to be invertible. On a design that is rank-deficient - here, an ensemble whose members include exact duplicates, so the member-prediction Gram of every output is singular by the number of duplicates - the leverage is undefined: the trace of the hat matrix drops to the rank (21 instead of 24 on the s104 Y1 cell of the EMIT pool), and inverting through a tiny ridge assigns any new point that leaves the duplicates' span an arbitrarily large leverage (a load 11.8 times the whole prediction error on that cell), which is a property of the ridge, not of the predictor actually used. The pairs bootstrap sidesteps this: resample the n rows with replacement B times, refit the predictor exactly as it is fitted in production (with its own ridge or pseudo-inverse and its own constraints), and take the empirical variance of the B predictions at x. Under Freedman's (1981) conditions for the pairs (correlation-model) bootstrap - independent rows, finite fourth moments of the regressors and errors, and a design whose empirical second-moment matrix converges - the bootstrap variance of a linear predictor is consistent for its sampling variance, and it remains well defined on a singular design because every resample is fitted by the same regularised map as the original. It is the right variance estimator when the estimator's regularisation, rather than an invertible Gram, determines its behaviour; it also applies unchanged to a constrained estimator (a long-only stack) for which no closed form exists. Cost: B refits per cell; B = 8 was enough to rank rows and cells in the RMT ensemble program (the ranking, not the level, was used).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:55:27.265312+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_0f8096492788892d5587c57e7fb8200627e06850fb3fd50cf9e2750d9523e4bc","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition AvoidBB of arXiv:2410.23899, 'Tightness for interlacing geometric random walk bridges'] Fix $k \in \mathbb{N}$. Let $\vec{x}, \vec{y} \in W_k^{\circ}$, $a,b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and $f: [a,b] \rightarrow (-\infty, \infty]$ and $g: [-\infty, \infty)$ be two continuous functions. The latter means that either $f: [a,b] \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is continuous or $f = \infty$ everywhere and similarly for $g$. We also assume that $f(t) > g(t)$ for all $t \in [a,b]$, $f(a) > x_1$, $f(b) > y_1$, $g(a) < x_k$ and $g(b) < y_k$. 

With the above data we define the $(f,g)$-avoiding Brownian line ensemble on the interval $[a,b]$ with entrance data $\vec{x}$ and exit data $\vec{y}$ to be the $\llbracket 1 , k \rrbracket$-indexed line ensemble $\mathcal{Q}$ on $\Lambda = [a,b]$ whose law is the same as that of $\{B_i\}_{i = 1}^k$ (with law $\mathbb{P}_{\operatorname{free}}^{a,b, \vec{x}, \vec{y}}$), conditioned on the event
$$E = \{f(r) > B_1(r) > B_2(r) > \cdots > B_k(r) > g(r) \mbox{ for all $r \in [a,b]$} \}.$$
We denote the law of $\mathcal{Q}$ by $\mathbb{P}_{\operatorname{avoid}}^{a,b,\vec{x},\vec{y},f,g}$, and expectations with respect to this measure by $\mathbb{E}_{\operatorname{avoid}}^{a,b,\vec{x},\vec{y},f,g}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["each F_n nondecreasing, right-continuous, with values in [0,1]","no tightness is assumed, and without it the limit can be defective"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.752559+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_0fba1416669badf1de8ab735445eeb6c5d50526da69885c6f0c2f43871a867fd","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (F_n) be a sequence of distribution functions on R, that is nondecreasing right-continuous functions with values in [0,1]. Then there exist a subsequence (F_{n_k}) and a nondecreasing right-continuous F : R -> [0,1] such that F_{n_k}(x) -> F(x) at every continuity point x of F. The limit F need NOT be a distribution function: mass can escape to plus or minus infinity, and with F_n the distribution function of the point mass at n one gets F identically 0. This is exactly the gap that tightness closes: the family is tight, meaning sup_n (1 - F_n(M) + F_n(-M)) -> 0 as M -> infinity, if and only if every such subsequential limit is a proper distribution function, which is Prokhorov's theorem on R. Nothing is assumed about the F_n beyond monotonicity, right-continuity and the range [0,1] - no continuity, no tightness, no common support. [standard; e.g. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 3.2.6]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:15:45.375658+00:00","domain":"general topology","id":"claim_0fc6ca3efccfbfb81740d50ff4b42e6d92b545e1d6116f465b8a720d7d0ba797","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A topological space X is compact if every open cover of X has a finite subcover: whenever X is the union of a family of open sets {U_i : i in I}, there are finitely many indices i_1, ..., i_n such that X is the union of U_(i_1), ..., U_(i_n). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:41:28.175431+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_0fe92c2c3a66065cf6b5bdef344e3592858a429adda497c795705a803f8618aa","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition $(r-2)_*$-BP of arXiv:2510.26724, 'Sharp Fuss-Catalan thresholds in graph bootstrap percolation'] Let $T$ be a $K_r$-tree
and $S\subset V(T)$ a set of {\it seeds}, 
which we consider to be initially {\it infected}. 
Then, in each step of the process, either 
\begin{itemize}
\item {\it (usual step)} some vertex $v$ with at least $r-2$ 
infected neighbors becomes infected; or else
\item {\it (special step)} if no such $v$ exists, but 
for some internal edge $e$, there are two cliques $H_i\neq H_j$ 
containing $e$ such that $H_i$ has $r-4$ infected vertices 
and $H_j$ has $1$ infected vertex,  
and all $r-3$ of these vertices are not in $e$, 
then  we infect an arbitrarily chosen vertex $u\in e$; and 
otherwise, 
\item {\it (terminal step)} if neither type of step is possible, 
then the process terminates. 
\end{itemize}
We call this process {\it $(r-2)_*$-BP} 
on $T$, 
and let $\langle S;T\rangle_*$ denote the set of 
eventually infected vertices in $T$ started with 
the seed set $S$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["U and V are open subsets of R^n of the same dimension n","phi : U -> V is a bijection, continuously differentiable, with continuously differentiable inverse (equivalently injective C^1 with nonvanishing Jacobian determinant and image V)","Lebesgue measure and Lebesgue measurable functions are used on both sides","f is measurable and either nonnegative or integrable"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.090563+00:00","domain":"real analysis, measure theory, integration in R^n","id":"claim_1047e7e34c38c2168c64f635d6e025f096e2d64b3ad9dc9fbd5d8a3856bb2cb5","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let U and V be open subsets of R^n and let phi : U -> V be a C^1 DIFFEOMORPHISM: phi is a bijection of U onto V, phi is continuously differentiable, and its inverse is continuously differentiable. (By the inverse function theorem it is equivalent to assume phi is injective, C^1, onto V, with det Dphi(x) nonzero for every x in U.) Let Dphi(x) denote the Jacobian matrix. Then for every Lebesgue measurable f : V -> [0, +infinity], the integral of f(y) dy over V equals the integral of f(phi(x)) |det Dphi(x)| dx over U, both sides being simultaneously finite or infinite; the same identity holds for complex-valued f, with f integrable over V if and only if (f composed with phi) times |det Dphi| is integrable over U. Taking f an indicator gives the measure statement: the Lebesgue measure of phi(E) equals the integral of |det Dphi| over E, for every measurable E contained in U. WHERE IT FAILS: (i) the ABSOLUTE VALUE of the determinant is required. The density is |det Dphi|; the sign records orientation and belongs to the theory of differential forms, not to Lebesgue integration. (ii) Injectivity cannot be dropped without paying for multiplicity: for a general C^1 map the correct statement is the area formula, the integral of f(phi(x)) |det Dphi(x)| dx over U equals the integral over V of f(y) N(y) dy, where N(y) is the number of preimages of y in U; N identically 1 is exactly injectivity. (iii) Smoothness cannot be relaxed to 'differentiable almost everywhere'. One needs the Luzin (N) property, that null sets map to null sets, which C^1 and Lipschitz maps have: in dimension one the Cantor function is continuous and nondecreasing with derivative 0 almost everywhere, yet it maps a null set onto a set of measure 1, and the naive substitution formula is false for it. (iv) The hypothesis is a diffeomorphism between OPEN sets; for maps defined on closed or lower-dimensional sets the statement must be routed through the area or coarea formula.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:41:28.165285+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_10481ef2ca34f8c3e5d918c755a8fb020f38f279aafadc53589ce33814706e5b","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition Order of TWGs of arXiv:2510.26724, 'Sharp Fuss-Catalan thresholds in graph bootstrap percolation'] The {\it order} $\vartheta(T)$ of a TWG

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:02:34.840473+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1058192005b327e28fcdebe84783f3b749482fd64fc92d01bddef62c5a66ea64","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 6 (Gaussian tail and conditional excess limit) of arXiv:2607.20714, 'High Minima of Gaussian Processes: Overshoots and Minimizer Locations'] Let $\boldsymbol X$ be a centred Gaussian vector in $\mathbb R^n$ with
positive definite covariance matrix $\Sigma$, and let $\boldsymbol p$ be
the minimizer of the following problem:
\[
 \sigma_*^2=\min_{\boldsymbol v\geq0,
             \,\boldsymbol1^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol v=1}
             \boldsymbol v^{\mathsf T}\Sigma\boldsymbol v.
\]
Put
\[
 I=\{i:p_i>0\},\qquad J=\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus I,
 \qquad  
 \qquad \boldsymbol\theta=\Sigma_{II}^{-1}\boldsymbol1_I.
\]
Then
\[
 \boldsymbol\theta=\frac{\boldsymbol p_I}{\sigma_*^2}>0,
 \qquad
 \boldsymbol r_J=\Sigma_{JI}\Sigma_{II}^{-1}\boldsymbol1_I\geq\boldsymbol1_J,
 \qquad
 \boldsymbol1_I^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\theta=\frac1{\sigma_*^2}.
\]
Write $r_j$ for the $j$th component of $\boldsymbol r_J$.
Let
\[
 P=\{j\in J:r_j=1\},\qquad N=\{j\in J:r_j>1\},
\]
and let $G_P$ be centred Gaussian with covariance matrix
\[
 \Gamma_P=\Sigma_{PP}-\Sigma_{PI}\Sigma_{II}^{-1}\Sigma_{IP}.
\]
Set $c_P=\Pp\{G_P>0\}$, with $c_P=1$ when $P$ is empty.  If
$M=\min_{1\leq i\leq n}X_i$, then, as $u\to\infty$,
\begin{equation}
 \Pp\{M>u\}\sim
 \frac{c_P}{(2\pi)^{|I|/2}\det(\Sigma_{II})^{1/2}
                  \prod_{i\in I}\theta_i}
 u^{-|I|}\exp\left\{-\frac{u^2}{2\sigma_*^2}\right\}.
 
\end{equation}
Let $(\xi_i)_{i\geq1}$ be independent unit exponential random variables.
If $P$ is nonempty, let $G_P^+$ have law
$\mathcal L(G_P\mid G_P>0)$ and be independent of $(\xi_i)_{i\geq1}$.
Furthermore, as $u\to\infty$,
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal L\left(
 \left(
   (u(X_i-u))_{i\in I},
   (X_j-u)_{j\in P},
   \frac{\boldsymbol X_N}{u}
 \right)
   \ \middle|\ M>u\right)
 \Longrightarrow
 \mathcal L\left(
   (\xi_i/\theta_i)_{i\in I},
   G_P^+,
   \boldsymbol r_N
 \right).
 
\end{equation}
The $G_P^+$ and $\boldsymbol r_N$ blocks are omitted
when $P$ and $N$, respectively, are empty. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.199654+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1071a2338358110494cec48ce2da366826450939e1b46a3f99b8559e9fb42441","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 133 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $t\notin \oJ$ (recall Lemma~\ref{l:bad.J}) and parameters as in \eqref{eq:order-of-limits}: 
    \[\bE\Big[|tp'(t) - \trrr_t|\Big]
    \leq  
    o_{\trK}(1)
    \]
for $ \trrr_t\equiv \trrr(t,X^\plus(t))$. 

\begin{proof}
Let $\bar{P}(t)$ be the temporal smoothing of $tp'(t)$. Then for $t\notin\bar{J}$ we have
	\[
    \bE\Big[|tp'(t) - \trrr_t|\Big]
    =
    \bE\Big[|tp'(t) - \bar P(t)|\Big]
    +\bE\Big[|\bar P(t) - \trrr_t|\Big]
    = O(\lambda)
    +\bE\Big[|\bar P(t) - \trrr_t|
    \Big]\,.
    \]
Let $\bar{P}^N$ be the temporal smoothing of $t(p^N)'(t)$. It follows from Lemma~\ref{l:limit.coefs} that $\bar{P}^N$ converges pointwise to $\bar{P}$, and $\trrr^N$ converges pointwise to $\trrr$. It follows by the bounded convergence theorem that we also have convergence in expectation, so
	\[
	\bE\Big[|\bar P(t) - \trrr_t|\Big]
	=\bE\Big[|\bar P^N(t) - (\trrr^N)_t|\Big] + o_N(1)\,.
	\] 
We then note that $\bar{P}^N-\trrr^N$ is the smoothing (via Definitions~\ref{d:sp.smooth} and \ref{d:t.smooth}) of 
	\begin{align} \nonumber
	A^N(t,\vy)
	&\equiv t(p^N)'(t)-\rrr^{\plus,N}(t,\vy)
	= t(p^N)'(t)-\sum_{B^\frozen \subseteq B^{\frozen,\coarse}}
    \frac{|B|}{|B^{\frozen,\coarse}|}
    \rrr^{\trunc,N}(t,B) 
    \\
	&\qquad= \bigg(
	1-\frac{|B^{\frozen,\coarse} \cap [M]|}{|B^{\frozen,\coarse}|} 
	\bigg)
	t(p^N)'(t)
	+ \sum_{B^\frozen \subseteq B^{\frozen,\coarse}} \frac{|B|}{|B^{\frozen,\coarse}|}
	\bigg(
	t(p^N)'(t) -
	\rrr^{\trunc,N}(t,B)\bigg)\,,
	
	 \end{align}
where the correspondence between $\vy$ and $B^{\frozen,\coarse}$ is as described around \eqref{e:review.P}. For the first term in
\eqref{e:P.N.r.frozen.twoterms}, at any fixed time $t$, we have
\[\bE\bigg[ 1-\frac{|B^{\frozen,\coarse} \cap [M]|}{|B^{\frozen,\coarse}|} \bigg]
    = 1 - \sum_{B^{\frozen,\coarse}}
    \frac{|B^{\frozen,\coarse}|}{M^\frozen}
    \frac{|B^{\frozen,\coarse} \cap [M]|}{|B^{\frozen,\coarse}|}

Interior H^2 regularity (u in H^2_loc with the corresponding estimate on compactly contained subsets) needs only a^{ij} in C^1(Omega) and no boundary hypothesis. The C^2 boundary hypothesis can be relaxed to C^{1,1}, and for L = -Laplacian to convexity of Omega, but it cannot be dropped: on a domain with a reentrant corner the conclusion is false.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(X_n) a submartingale for a filtration (F_n)","sup_n E[X_n^+] < infinity (for a martingale: sup_n E|X_n| < infinity)","no uniform integrability is assumed, and without it convergence is only almost sure"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.627158+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_111070f1050f003220fb4766d3ba4d411602ec9050d0c6e450a5eeb448ccb643","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X_n) be a submartingale with sup_n E[X_n^+] < infinity. Then X_n converges almost surely to a limit X_infinity with E|X_infinity| < infinity. For a MARTINGALE the hypothesis is equivalent to sup_n E|X_n| < infinity, since E[X_n] is constant and E|X_n| = 2E[X_n^+] - E[X_n]. Convergence is ONLY almost sure: it need not hold in L^1, and E[X_infinity] need not equal E[X_0]. Standard failure: let (X_n) be the product of independent nonnegative mean-one factors, for instance X_n = prod_{k <= n} (1 + eps_k) with eps_k = +1 or -1 with probability 1/2 each - equivalently X_n = 2^n on the event that all signs were +1 and 0 otherwise. Then X_n is a nonnegative martingale with E X_n = 1 for every n, so it is L^1-bounded and converges a.s., but the limit is 0 almost surely and E X_infinity = 0 != 1 = E X_0. Nonnegative supermartingales always converge a.s. because X_n^+ = X_n has bounded expectation; upgrading to L^1 convergence is exactly what uniform integrability supplies. [standard; e.g. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 4.2.11]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Bernoulli percolation on Z^d, 3 <= d <= 10","Barsky-Grimmett-Newman half-space theorem; Burton-Keane uniqueness"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T07:36:18.308377+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1153b816e6a41f1354e232183d6087dc0fec2193137621d7a5254bde6e25481c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"PRIVATE REDUCTION, author-recorded. Barsky-Grimmett-Newman: at p_c(Z^d) the half-space N x Z^{d-1} has no infinite cluster. To conclude theta(p_c) = 0 in Z^d (open for 3 <= d <= 10) one would show that a unique infinite cluster (Burton-Keane) cannot be made of infinitely many finite half-space clusters connected through the boundary hyperplane. In d = 2 this works because the half-plane susceptibility at p_c is infinite. The reduction: theta(p_c) = 0 in Z^d follows from (i) infinite half-space susceptibility at p_c(Z^d), and (ii) a gluing lemma showing that finite half-space clusters linked across the hyperplane force an infinite half-space cluster on one side at a slightly larger parameter. Both (i) and (ii) are open for 3 <= d <= 10; (i) is a natural intermediate target because it is a statement about a single half-space cluster rather than about the full-space cluster.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-06T03:36:16.690087+00:00","domain":"harvested statement (arXiv 2512.18592, 2025): mathematics","id":"claim_115c89f8a67d4fce88f37c87ae749bc1","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 2.4 (Erdős–Rényi, SBMs and logistic RDPGs) in the first version of arXiv:2512.18592, 'Wavelet Latent Position Exponential Random Graphs'] Fix $c\\in\\mathbb{R}$ and a real symmetric Hilbert–Schmidt matrix $S=(s_{rs})_{r,s\\geq 0}$, and let $G_{n}\\sim\\mathrm{WL\\mbox{-}ERG}(c,S)$ be generated as in Definitions 2.1 – 2.3. 1. (Erdős–Rényi.) If $s_{rs}=0$ for all $(r,s)\\neq(0,0)$, then $G_{n}$ is Erdős–Rényi $G(n,p)$ with $p=\\sigma(c+s_{00})$. 2. (Haar/SBM special case.) Assume the underlying wavelet system is the Haar system and fix an integer $J\\geq 0$. Let $\\{I_{\\ell,J}\\}_{\\ell=0}^{2^{J}-1}$ be the dyadic partition of $(0,1)$, define $\\phi_{\\ell,J}(x):=2^{J/2}\\mathbf{1}_{I_{\\ell,J}}(x)$, and let $V_{J}:=\\mathrm{span}\\{\\phi_{\\ell,J}:0\\leq\\ell\\leq 2^{J}-1\\}\\subset L^{2}(0,1)$. If the logit satisfies $f_{S}\\in V_{J}\\otimes V_{J}$, equivalently if there exist real coefficients $\\alpha_{\\ell k}$ such that $f_{S}(x,y)=\\sum_{\\ell,k=0}^{2^{J}-1}\\alpha_{\\ell k}\\,\\phi_{\\ell,J}(x)\\phi_{k,J}(y)\\quad\\text{in }L^{2}\\big((0,1)^{2}\\big),$ then $G_{n}$ is a stochastic block model with $2^{J}$ blocks. In particular, there are constants $\\beta_{\\ell k}:=2^{J}\\alpha_{\\ell k}$ such that $f_{S}(x,y)=\\beta_{\\ell k}$ for a.e. $(x,y)\\in I_{\\ell,J}\\times I_{k,J}$, and hence the block connectivity probabilities are $p_{\\ell k}=\\sigma(c+\\beta_{\\ell k})=\\sigma(c+2^{J}\\alpha_{\\ell k}).$ Under $U_{i}\\sim\\mathrm{Unif}(0,1)$, the block proportions are $\\pi_{\\ell}=2^{-J}$. 3. (Finite-rank PSD $\\Rightarrow$ logistic RDPG.) Assume $S$ is positive semidefinite as an operator on $\\ell^{2}$ and has finite rank $d$. Then there exist functions $g_{1},\\dots,g_{d}\\in L^{2}(0,1)$ such that $f_{S}(x,y)=\\sum_{k=1}^{d}g_{k}(x)g_{k}(y)\\quad\\text{in }L^{2}\\big((0,1)^{2}\\big).$ Consequently, for a measurable representative $\\Phi(x):=(g_{1}(x),\\dots,g_{d}(x))\\in\\mathbb{R}^{d}$ (defined a.e.), $W_{c,S}(x,y)=\\sigma\\!\\bigl(c+\\Phi(x)^{\\top}\\Phi(y)\\bigr)\\quad\\text{for a.e. }(x,y).$ Therefore $G_{n}$ is a logistic random dot product graph: with latent positions $X_{i}=\\Phi(U_{i})\\in\\mathbb{R}^{d}$, the edges are independent conditional on $X$ and satisfy $\\mathbb{P}(A_{ij}=1\\mid X)=\\sigma(c+X_{i}^{\\top}X_{j})$ for all $i<j$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["characteristic 0 (over Q or a field containing Q); the criterion needs the field to contain, or to be extended by, roots of unity","'general' means indeterminate coefficients; a particular polynomial of degree >= 5 may well be solvable (x^5 - 2 is)"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:05:27.626563+00:00","domain":"algebra","id":"claim_115d87a98ec962f9b30fe189acf038bc99ce62e12c2461843b01819a67bf4895","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"For n >= 5 the general polynomial equation of degree n, x^n + a_1 x^{n-1} + ... + a_n = 0 with independent indeterminate coefficients over Q (the field Q(a_1, ..., a_n)), is not solvable by radicals: there is no formula for its roots built from the coefficients by field operations and extraction of k-th roots. Moreover specific polynomials over Q are not solvable by radicals, for instance x^5 - x - 1 and x^5 - 4x + 2, whose Galois groups over Q are S_5. For n <= 4 the general equation IS solvable by radicals (the quadratic formula; Cardano's formula for cubics, 1545; Ferrari's method for quartics). GALOIS'S CRITERION, which subsumes the theorem: a polynomial over a field of characteristic 0 is solvable by radicals if and only if its Galois group is a solvable group.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["A a square complex matrix; eigenvalues counted with algebraic multiplicity in the refinement","the discs are closed; a point of the union may fail to be an eigenvalue (the theorem localises, it does not characterise)"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:31:12.479038+00:00","domain":"linear algebra","id":"claim_118eb1edbdd586661b78b6b8a406c50d9aa31e793c06b918802f39726a6468d2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A = (a_ij) be a complex n x n matrix and for each i let R_i = sum_{j != i} |a_ij| be the i-th deleted absolute row sum and D_i = { z in C : |z - a_ii| <= R_i } the i-th Gershgorin disc. Then every eigenvalue of A lies in the union of the discs D_1, ..., D_n. Applying the theorem to the transpose, every eigenvalue also lies in the union of the column discs (radii the deleted column sums), so the spectrum lies in the intersection of the two unions. Refinement: if a union of k of the discs is disjoint from the union of the other n - k, then exactly k eigenvalues (counted with algebraic multiplicity) lie in the union of those k discs. Consequences: a strictly diagonally dominant matrix (|a_ii| > R_i for all i) is invertible, since 0 lies in no disc; a Hermitian strictly diagonally dominant matrix with positive diagonal is positive definite; and the discs can be shrunk by a diagonal similarity D^{-1} A D, which changes the radii to sum_{j != i} |a_ij| d_j / d_i.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Discrete Gaussian free field on a two-dimensional lattice domain with Dirichlet boundary conditions","Gibbs-Markov (domain Markov) property and lattice Green function asymptotics","Random-walk-below-a-barrier (ballot) estimates for the scale walk"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.987849+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_11fcc5b0b92d4300329a446dd3a28c80e7535335cb27eaecb364b7fce9c12206","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). The concentric decomposition (Biskup-Louidor) describes the two-dimensional discrete Gaussian free field h in a box of side N as seen from a point x where the field is near its maximum. Around x one takes nested dyadic annuli; conditioning on the values of h on the boundaries of the concentric boxes, the Gibbs-Markov property splits h into (i) a random walk S_k along the scales, whose increments are the Gaussian binding fields' values at x, with variance of order g log 2 per scale, with the maximum constraint acting as a barrier the walk must stay below (entropic repulsion), (ii) independent zero-boundary fields in the annuli, and (iii) explicit bounded error terms from the non-exact scale invariance of the lattice Green function. The maximum-at-x event becomes a ballot-type event for the walk S_k, handled by random-walk-below-a-barrier estimates, which yield tightness of the centred maximum, the local limit law of the maximum, and the description of the cluster of near-maximal points around x (the cluster law nu). It is the tool behind the full extremal process of the DGFF (Biskup-Louidor 2016, 2018) and the intermediate level sets. It does not by itself give universality for other log-correlated fields: the binding-field structure uses the DGFF's exact Gibbs-Markov property. Typical failure: Treating the annulus fields phi_k as exactly independent rather than approximately so, and carrying a multiscale second-moment computation through without tracking the coupling error terms; because the GFF is only log-correlated rather than an exact branching random walk, the independence used in the concentric decomposition is an approximation that must be explicitly controlled, and skipping this step is a common source of unjustified exponent claims for GFF level-set percolation. Canonical reference: Biskup and Louidor, 2016, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Biskup and Louidor, 2018, Advances in Mathematics; Biskup, Extrema of the two-dimensional discrete Gaussian free field, PIMS-CRM lecture notes, 2020, Springer.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["G finite, connected, undirected, without isolated vertices (weighted graphs work verbatim with weighted degrees and volumes)","the spectral gap is that of the NORMALISED Laplacian; for regular graphs it is (d - mu_2)/d, and the unnormalised version scales by d","conductance is measured against volume; the vertex-count edge expansion h(G) is the same quantity only for regular graphs"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:49:11.846189+00:00","domain":"spectral graph theory","id":"claim_123dda5b10ef9e8af280ba37a63254fd3b1973ad6a342a5785086a24af3d21fc","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let G = (V, E) be a finite connected graph with vertex degrees d(v), volume vol(S) = sum_{v in S} d(v), and for a vertex set S with 0 < vol(S) <= vol(V)/2 let phi(S) = e(S, V - S) / vol(S) be its conductance, where e(S, V - S) counts the edges leaving S. The conductance (Cheeger constant) of G is phi(G) = min over such S of phi(S). Let 0 = lambda_1 < lambda_2 <= ... <= lambda_n <= 2 be the eigenvalues of the normalised Laplacian L = I - D^{-1/2} A D^{-1/2}. CHEEGER'S INEQUALITY (Alon-Milman, Sinclair-Jerrum, Dodziuk; the graph form of Cheeger's 1970 Riemannian inequality): lambda_2 / 2 <= phi(G) <= sqrt(2 lambda_2). For a d-regular graph with adjacency eigenvalues d = mu_1 >= mu_2 >= ..., lambda_2 = (d - mu_2)/d and the edge expansion h(G) = min e(S, V-S)/|S| (over |S| <= n/2) satisfies (d - mu_2)/2 <= h(G) <= sqrt(2 d (d - mu_2)). Both sides are sharp up to constants: the cycle C_n has phi of order 1/n and lambda_2 of order 1/n^2 (so the square root is needed), while the hypercube and expanders have phi and lambda_2 of the same order. Consequences: a graph is an expander (phi bounded below) if and only if it has a spectral gap bounded below; the mixing time of the random walk is O(log(n) / lambda_2) and at least of order 1/phi; the sweep cut of the second eigenvector (the proof of the upper bound) is the spectral partitioning algorithm, with the guarantee phi(S) <= sqrt(2 lambda_2) for the set it returns; higher-order Cheeger inequalities (Lee-Oveis Gharan-Trevisan) relate lambda_k to k-way partitions, and the improved Cheeger inequality bounds phi by lambda_2 / sqrt(lambda_3).","status":"unverified"}

p

{"assumptions":["mu is a product measure on {0,1}^n, or satisfies the FKG lattice condition (log-supermodular)","A and B are both increasing (or both decreasing) events; f and g both monotone in the same direction","the reversed inequality needs one increasing and one decreasing event","no conclusion for events that are not monotone, and none for a non-FKG measure"],"created_at":"2026-09-02T07:51:33.048644+00:00","domain":"percolation and correlation inequalities (hand-authored statement with hypotheses, 2026-09-02)","id":"claim_12642faa7ec3d8f83d07d4fc84666d17c25bf65b9cb7021607d2e1967b320070","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let mu be a product probability measure on {0,1}^n (Harris 1960), or more generally a measure on a finite distributive lattice satisfying the FKG lattice condition mu(x v y) mu(x ^ y) >= mu(x) mu(y) (Fortuin, Kasteleyn, Ginibre 1971). If A and B are both increasing events, then mu(A and B) >= mu(A) mu(B); equivalently, for increasing functions f and g, E[f g] >= E[f] E[g]. The same holds when both are decreasing. If one event is increasing and the other decreasing, the inequality reverses: mu(A and B) <= mu(A) mu(B). The inequality says nothing about a pair of events that are neither increasing nor decreasing, and it fails for a general (non-FKG) measure.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["i.i.d. observations with finite variance (Andrews states the result under moment conditions for the CLT)","the constraint is active at the true parameter (theta = 0); for theta > 0 the bootstrap is consistent"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T09:23:59.828365+00:00","domain":"resampling / constrained estimation","id":"claim_128317036fe4b38de221748567b9dd5e4b220bf4b14f749dabab4f8dd0bb0ff4","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $X_1, \\dots, X_n$ be i.i.d. with mean $\\theta \\ge 0$ and variance $\\sigma^2$, and let the estimator respect the constraint: $\\hat\\theta_n = \\max(0, \\bar X_n)$. When the true parameter is interior ($\\theta > 0$) the nonparametric bootstrap is consistent: the conditional law of $\\sqrt n(\\hat\\theta_n^* - \\hat\\theta_n)$ converges to $N(0, \\sigma^2)$, the law of $\\sqrt n(\\hat\\theta_n - \\theta)$. When the true parameter is on the boundary ($\\theta = 0$) it is not: $\\sqrt n(\\hat\\theta_n - \\theta) \\Rightarrow \\max(0, Z)$ with $Z \\sim N(0, \\sigma^2)$, a law with an atom of mass $1/2$ at zero, whereas the bootstrap law of $\\sqrt n(\\hat\\theta_n^* - \\hat\\theta_n)$ converges, conditionally on the data, to the law of $\\max(0, Z + \\zeta) - \\max(0, \\zeta)$ with $\\zeta \\sim N(0, \\sigma^2)$ a random shift that does not vanish - so the bootstrap distribution is random in the limit and does not equal the sampling distribution (Andrews 2000, Theorem 1). The same failure holds for maximum-likelihood and least-squares estimators under inequality constraints whenever the true parameter has an active constraint, in particular for nonnegatively constrained regression and portfolio weights with coordinates at zero: the bootstrap replicates flip the constrained coordinates between zero and positive values, and the spread of the replicates is not the spread of the estimator. Consistent alternatives: the $m$-out-of-$n$ bootstrap with $m \\to \\infty$, $m/n \\to 0$, and subsampling, both of which recover the limit law at the boundary.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:47:41.429782+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory","id":"claim_128a347949b062310df605967ebb97c6f0c93838dbb92f9d1f69184994c7496e","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X,Sigma,mu) be a probability space and T: X -> X a measure-preserving transformation. T is ergodic if every T-invariant measurable set has measure 0 or 1: whenever A in Sigma satisfies T^{-1}A = A up to a mu-null set, mu(A) is 0 or 1. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:33:01.740854+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_12b24723aa93f050871e7949f914605cbec33b4efdc7c35f81ec8af464b9628e","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 1 of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] Let $\{ C_n \}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be uniformly random elements of $[m]\coloneqq\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$, and let
$\{ U_n \}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be uniformly random elements of $(0, 1)$.
Assume the family $\{ U_n, C_n \}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is independent.
The random variable $C_n$ denotes the coupon type
obtained on day $n$.
Define the random variables
\[
  L(i, n) \coloneqq \sup\{ k \leqslant n \mid C_k = i \}, \quad i \in [m], \quad n > 0.
\]
Then $L(i, n)$ is the most recent day no later than $n$ that coupon
type $i$ was issued.
For clumsiness probability $p \in [0, 1)$, the 
clumsy coupon collection time can be defined by
\[
  T_{m, p} \coloneqq \inf \{ n > 0 \mid L(i, n) > 0 \ \text{and} \ U_{L(i, n)} \leq 1 - p \ 
    \text{for all $i \in [m]$} \},
\]
the first day that every coupon type has been updated, their most
recent updates all having been non-clumsy.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:10:07.530380+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_12cada61a0fe3477c1bfafbdeb2ef3132076cda06b26983b5dd3acb4db76c1c9","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition eq:residual-mixed-set of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[proposition]{prop:bulk-sparse-reduction}
Let \(V:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be Borel measurable and bounded below, and let
\(0<r_N\le1\) and \(1\le k_N\le N\) be arbitrary deterministic
sequences.  Write
\[
 D_{N,r_N}
 =\{x\in\mathbb S^{N-1}(1):\left\lVertx\right\rVert_\infty\le r_N\}
\]
and
\[
 \mathcal A_N(k_N,\rho)
 =\left\{x\in\mathbb S^{N-1}(1):
 \text{some \(S\subset[N]\), \(\left\lvertS\right\rvert\le k_N\), satisfies }
 \norm{x_{S^c}}_2\le\rho\right\}.
\]
For \(\rho>0\), define the residual mixed-profile set
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal R_N(r_N,k_N,\rho)
 :=
 \left\{x\in\mathbb S^{N-1}(1):
 \left\lVertx\right\rVert_\infty>r_N,\ 
 \inf_{\substack{S\subset[N]\\|S|\le k_N}}
 \norm{x_{S^c}}_2>\rho\right\}.
\end{equation}
Then the disjoint decomposition
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb S^{N-1}(1)
 =D_{N,r_N}\,\dot\cup\,
  \bigl(\mathcal A_N(k_N,\rho)\setminus D_{N,r_N}\bigr)
  \,\dot\cup\,\mathcal R_N(r_N,k_N,\rho)
\end{equation}
holds.  Suppose only that the exact bulk slice satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N
 \log\mathscr C_N^J(V;D_{N,r_N})
 =:\Phi\in\mathbb R.
\end{equation}
No independence, moment matching, tail, density, or nondegeneracy
condition is needed for the decomposition itself.
For \(\rho>0\), set
\begin{align*}
 \mathscr S_N(\rho)
 &:=
 \mathscr C_N^J\bigl(
 V;\mathcal A_N(k_N,\rho)\setminus D_{N,r_N}\bigr),\\
 \mathscr R_N(\rho)
 &:=
 \mathscr C_N^J\bigl(
 V;\mathcal R_N(r_N,k_N,\rho)\bigr),
\end{align*}
and define
\begin{align}
 \overline\Phi_{\rm sp}^J(V;r_\bullet,k_\bullet)
 &:=
 \lim_{\rho\downarrow0}\limsup_{N\to\infty}
 \frac1N\log\mathscr S_N(\rho),
 \\
 \overline\Phi_{\rm mix}^J(V;r_\bullet,k_\bullet)
 &:=
 \lim_{\rho\downarrow0}\limsup_{N\to\infty}
 \frac1N\log\mathscr R_N(\rho).
 
\end{align}
Then
\begin{equation}
 \limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathscr C_N^J(V)
 =
 \max\left\{
 \Phi,\,
 \overline\Phi_{\rm sp}^J(V;r_\bullet,k_\bullet),\,
 \overline\Phi_{\rm mix}^J(V;r_\bullet,k_\bullet)
 \right\}.
\end{equation}
Consequently, exact universality holds if and only if both nonbulk
upper exponents are at most \(\Phi\).

If \(k_N=o(N)\), \(({\rm PT})_p\), and
(equation eq:critical-count-ceiling of the paper) also hold, then
\begin{equation}
 \overline\Phi_{\rm sp}^J(V;r_\bullet,k_\bullet)
 \le\Xi_p^{\rm sp}(V).
\end{equation}
In particular, whenever the explicit sparse-rate compatibility condition
\begin{equation}
 \Xi_p^{\rm sp}(V)\le\Phi
\end{equation}
holds, exact universality is equivalent to the single residual condition
\begin{equation}
 \overline\Phi_{\rm mix}^J(V;r_\bullet,k_\bullet)
 \le\Phi.
\end{equation}
When the disorder and \(V\) satisfy the hypotheses of
(thm:growing-point-cutoff of the paper), and
(equation eq:growing-Haar-zero-cost-condition of the paper) and
\(q_N^{\rm gr}\to0\) hold, that theorem supplies the corresponding
universal regularized bulk pressure.  Controlling its one-sided
de-regularization defects is one sufficient route to
(equation eq:exact-growing-bulk-slice of the paper), with
\(\Phi=\Phi_p^{\rm bulk}(V)\).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:39:12.432703+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_13279b84b29dd341ec4ea79e17486be448a9a1e1f755f1def7f857a636231449","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 3. dfn: effective resistance between sets of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] [{Effective resistance between sets}]  
  Fix a resistance form $(\mathcal{E}, \mathcal{F})$ on $F$
  and write $R$ for the corresponding resistance metric.
  For sets $A, B \subseteq F$,
  we define
  \begin{equation}
    R(A,B)
    \coloneqq
    \left(
    \inf\{
    \mathcal{E}(f,f):
    f \in \mathcal{F},\
    f|_{A} \equiv 1,\
    f|_{B} \equiv 0
    \}
    \right)^{-1},
  \end{equation}
  which is defined to be zero if the infimum is taken over the empty set.
  Note that by (4. dfn cond: resistance forms condition 4 of the paper) 
  we clearly have $R( \{x\}, \{y\}) = R(x,y)$.","status":"unverified"}

Luce and Mallows'] Consider the secretary problem for a Mallows distribution with $q=q_n>1$ in the case that the largest number is  of highest rank.

\noindent i. Let $q_n=1+\frac cn$, where $c>0$. Then the asymptotically optimal strategy is $\mathcal{S}^\uparrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
\begin{equation}
M_n^*\sim n\Big(\frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{1-e^{-c}}{e-1+e^{-c}}\big)\Big),
\end{equation}
 and the corresponding  limiting probability of success
is $\frac1e$:
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}P_n^{\mathcal{M};q_n}(\mathcal{S}^\uparrow(n,M_n^*))=\frac1e.
$$
Also, $\lim_{c\to\infty} \frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{1-e^{-c}}{e-1+e^{-c}}\big)=0$ and $\lim_{c\to0} \frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{1-e^{-c}}{e-1+e^{-c}}\big)=\frac1e$.

\noindent ii.
Let $q_n=1+\frac c{n^\alpha}$, where $c>0$ and $\alpha\in(0,1)$. Then the asymptotically optimal strategy  is $\mathcal{S}^\uparrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
$$
M_n^*\sim\frac1c\left(1-\log(e-1)\right)n^\alpha\approx0.459\frac{n^\alpha}c,
$$
 and the corresponding limiting probability of success
is $\frac1e$:
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}P_n^{\mathcal{M};q_n}(\mathcal{S}^\uparrow(n,M_n^*))=\frac1e.
$$
\noindent iii. Let $q>1$.  Then the asymptotically optimal strategy  is $\mathcal{S}^\uparrow(n,M^*)$, where
$$
M^*=\begin{cases}&\max\left\{M\ge1: \sum_{j=M}^\infty\frac1{q^j-1}\ge\frac q{q-1}\right\}, \ \text{if}\ \sum_{j=1}^\infty\frac1{q^j-1}\ge \frac q{q-1};\\
&0,\ \text{if}\ \sum_{j=1}^\infty\frac1{q^j-1}<\frac q{q-1}.\end{cases}
$$
(If  $\sum_{j=M^*}^\infty\frac1{q^j-1}=\frac q{q-1}$, then $M^*-1$ is also optimal.)

\noindent The corresponding limiting probability of success is given by
\begin{equation}
\lim_{n\to\infty}P_n^{\mathcal{M};q}(\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M^*))=\begin{cases}&\frac{q-1}q(1-q^{-M^*})\sum_{j=M^*}^\infty\frac1{q^j-1}\ge\\
&(1-q^{-M^*}),\ \text{if}\ M^*\ge1;\\
&\frac{q-1}q>,\ \text{if}\ M^*=0.\end{cases}
\end{equation}
The limiting probability in (equation SuccessProbup of the paper) is always greater or equal to $\frac1e$ and is strictly greater than $\frac1e$ for all but at most a countable number of $q$ with no accumulation points in $(0,\infty)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["d-regular graphs on n vertices; tau_2 = the relaxation time (inverse spectral gap) of the natural random walk, maximised over all d-regular graphs on n vertices for fixed n","the d=3 (cubic) enumerations used are COMPLETE for n<=12 (counts 1,2,5,19,85 match the known sequence); the d>=4 enumerations are RANDOM SAMPLES (isomorphism-deduplicated, stopped after 4000 consecutive repeats) and are NOT certified complete, especially at n=12"],"created_at":"2026-09-24T23:46:59.998009+00:00","domain":"probability/Markov chains","id":"claim_13c3a894a23e44b0acdc4d79135f18d9","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"The paper proving the Aldous-Fill spectral gap conjecture leaves conditional the claim that for every sufficiently large even order n, the slowest d-regular graph (maximising relaxation time tau_2) is cubic (d=3); the finite crossover point is n=8. The 2-regular cycle has tau_2 = 1/(1-cos(2 pi/n)) ~ n^2/(2 pi^2), one third of the cubic asymptotic 3n^2/(2 pi^2), so cubic graphs must eventually overtake the cycle but do not lead at first: the slowest-known regular graph by order is 2-regular (the cycle) at n=4 (tau_2=1.0000) and n=6 (2.0000), then becomes 3-regular at n=8 (3.9271, versus the cycle's 3.4142), n=10 (13.5414, cycle 5.2361), and n=12 (17.8846, cycle 7.4641). Separately, the extremal cubic maxima (0.75, 1.50, 3.93, 13.54, 17.88 for n=4,6,8,10,12) jump by a factor of 3.5 from n=8 to n=10, out of line with the surrounding steps; this is because the extremal cubic graph acquires a BRIDGE at n=10 and CANNOT do so at any earlier order. Proof that a bridged cubic graph needs n>=10: if a cubic graph has a bridge uv, deleting it leaves a component A containing u where every vertex has degree 3 except u (degree 2), so the degree sum 3|A|-1 must be even, forcing |A| odd; |A|=1 would need a loop and |A|=3 would need four edges among three vertices (both impossible for a simple cubic graph), so both sides of any bridge are odd and at least 5, giving n>=10. This matches exact enumeration: no bridged cubic graph exists at n=4, 6, or 8; at n=10 there is exactly one bridged cubic graph and it IS the extremal one (tau_2=13.5414, versus 6.8423 for the best bridgeless cubic graph on 10 vertices); at n=12 there are four bridged cubic graphs and the extremal one among them is a 5|7 split (17.8846, versus 10.3190 for the best bridgeless cubic graph), a 6|6 split being impossible by the same parity argument. So the crossover at n=8 (cubic first overtakes the cycle, still bridgeless there, via a narrow 2-edge 4|4 cut) and the jump at n=10 (the bridge becomes possible) are two DIFFERENT events. NOT CERTIFIED: whether any regular graph of degree d>=4 ever competes with the cubic extremal graphs at these orders - only suggested: a 4-regular graph would need a second eigenvalue of 0.944 to compete, and the best 4-regular graph seen has 0.890; and a parity fact (a d-regular graph has a cut of size c across a vertex subset A only if c = d|A| mod 2, checked on 8400 random cuts with zero violations) shows a bridge is impossible outright for any EVEN degree d, which is suggestive but not a proof that odd degrees d>=5 cannot compete either.","status":"unverified"}

$$
g_n(\omega,t,y,z):=\inf_{\bar{z}\in{\mathbb R}^d}\{g(\omega,t,y,\bar{z})

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:52:47.241923+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_13f403f846aece457950973733524a242e3d522e0e374b1f613ac41dc742f4aa","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 4 (Wave--Hodge reduction) of arXiv:2609.01093, 'Ideal MHD below the classical well-posedness threshold'] Let $X=X(t,y)$ be smooth in spacetime, let $w:=X-\mathrm{id}$ and let
$\Kmat=(dX)^{-1}$.  Then the following statements hold.
 
\emph{(i) Algebraic pressure identity.}
Without using an evolution equation or the constraint $J=1$,
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal Q[dw]
 =-\tr \left(
   \Kmat\mathcal A^+(dw)\Kmat\mathcal A^-(dw)\right)
 =-\Kmat^a_i\Kmat^b_j
   Q_0(\partial_aw^j,\partial_bw^i).
\end{equation}
 
\emph{(ii) Smooth MHD reduction.}
Assume in addition that $X$ is the Lagrangian flow of a smooth solution of
\eqref{eq:mhd}, with $X(0)=\mathrm{id}$ and initial magnetic field $\Binf$.

$\mathcal Q[dw]\in L^{r_{\mathrm{HLS}}}(\mu)$ and the pressure is normalised so
that $(\nabla p)\circ X\in L^4(\mu)$ then
\[
 (\nabla p)\circ X=F[dw]=\mathcal{P}_{\gmetric[dw]}\mathcal Q[dw],
\]
and $(w,F[dw])$ satisfies \eqref{eq:auxiliary-system}. In particular, this holds when
$v,b\in C([0,T];H^\infty)$ decay together with all their derivatives and $p$ is
the Riesz pressure \eqref{eq:return-pressure}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["S is a finite subset of R^d","for the final claim: N <= d and x_1,...,x_N are linearly independent"],"created_at":"2026-08-20T03:43:30.215738+00:00","domain":"convex geometry","id":"claim_13f960d12d7361f53f8b9649a3a09792dc53550f7d06e91b0c0b658011ff3912","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $S=\\{x_1,\\dots,x_N\\}$ be a finite subset of $\\mathbb{R}^d$. The following are equivalent: (i) there is $y$ with $\\langle y,x_i\\rangle>0$ for every $i$; (ii) $0 \\notin \\operatorname{conv}(S)$. The frequently attempted substitute is FALSE: the condition that $\\operatorname{conv}(S)$ have empty interior does NOT imply (i). Counterexample in $\\mathbb{R}^2$ with $N=2$: take $x_1=e_1$ and $x_2=-e_1$. Their convex hull is a segment, which has empty interior, yet $0$ lies in it and no $y$ satisfies both inequalities. In particular, the observation that $N$ points in $\\mathbb{R}^N$ span an affine hull of dimension at most $N-1$, and so have a hull with empty interior, proves nothing about separation. What does suffice is linear independence: if $N \\le d$ and $x_1,\\dots,x_N$ are linearly independent then (i) holds, and an explicit witness solves $\\langle y,x_i\\rangle = 1$ for every $i$.","status":"unverified"}

Burdzy-Scheutzow (2014), Problem 7.5 asks whether a process with law equivalent to Wiener measure can receive a random finite prefix to become Brownian motion. Apply the forward filling lemma on two-sided Wiener paths with theta w(t)=w(t+1)-w(1) and density f equal to the desired future-law density. The selected future W(N+t)-W(N) has the desired law; prefixing W[0,N] recovers the original Wiener path. A standard Borel disintegration supplies the coupling for an already-given suffix process. Check earlier filling, shift-coupling, and Brownian embedding literature before any claim of novelty.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T01:10:08.701828+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_14409a5966b83008ac0af157fab8daf436e1e95c611ed920546016a5e84a2806","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm thm_gGE of arXiv:2411.17216, 'Large deviations of the empirical measures of a strong-Feller Markov process inside a subs'] Let $(\mathbb P_T)_{T>0}$ be a sequence of probability distribution on $\mathcal P(\mathscr S)$, such that:

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:27:56.773082+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1447ac7edeb187e1982ff160bc578d85fb9b1cf07f7630c9907d6544d4217793","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 1 (The \JKL{} formulation of Einstein areal flows) of arXiv:2608.31171, '\bf Finite-energy spacetimes with torus symmetry. \\ \Large Cauchy stability of Einstein--'] Consider four-dimensional spacetimes $(\Mcal,\guntrois)$ with spatial topology $\Tbb^3$ and two commuting spacelike Killing fields with closed orbits, admitting a foliation by the area~$|t|$ of the symmetry orbits. Consider a constitutive law $p=p(\mu)$ (pressure vs.\ mass-energy density) satisfying hyperbolicity and asymptotic conditions (stated in~\eqref{hyperbolic-eos-zero}, below). Then the following properties hold.
\bei

\item \textbf{Perfect-fluid matter model.} In the class of regular flows, the Einstein--Euler system 
\bel{equa-49F}
G^{\alpha\beta} = T^{\alpha\beta},
\qquad
\nabla_\alpha T^{\alpha\beta}=0
\ee
is equivalent to an \emph{evolution--constraint, first-order differential system} in terms of the variables \eqref{equa-phipsi}, as  given in \eqref{eq:T2-1234-def}--\eqref{equa-9385}, below, and referred to as the \JKL{} system. Its evolution subsystem has essentially \emph{quadratic nonlinearities} with a partial \emph{null structure} and, away from vacuum, is strongly hyperbolic.   All differential operators in the formulation 
remain defined on the full (closed) state space, including cavitation and near-light speed fluid propagation, although the hyperbolicity degenerates at non-zero null states.  

\item \textbf{Particle-production dissipative model.} Analogous properties hold for the following class of Einstein--Navier--Stokes systems
\bel{eq:pot-production-system0}
G^{\alpha\beta}=T_\chi^{\alpha\beta},
\qquad
\nabla_\alpha T_\chi^{\alpha\beta}=0,
\qquad
\nabla_\alpha A_\chi^{\alpha\beta\gamma}
=-\mathscr B^{\beta\gamma}, 
\ee
namely an extension of the Einstein--Euler system by adjoining to the fluid variables a symmetric two-tensor relaxation field~$\zeta$. The tensors $T_\chi$ and $A_\chi$ are defined from second-order derivatives
of a \emph{Navier--Stokes potential} denoted by~$\chi$, which is assumed to satisfy suitable equilibrium, dominant-energy, and causal-hyperbolicity conditions in \autoref{def-pot-hyperbolic}. The relaxation rate tensor~$\mathscr B$ is prescribed and satisfies suitable stable-equilibrium and positivity conditions in \autoref{def-pot-source}. In particular, the coupled evolution equations are symmetric hyperbolic in the interior of the state space, and both Einstein equations and Bianchi equations are satisfied.  The associated particle-number current~$\vNumb_\chi$ satisfies $\nabla_\alpha \vNumb_\chi^\alpha = \zeta_{\alpha\beta}\mathscr B^{\alpha\beta}\geq 0$.

\item \textbf{Dissipated-energy dissipative model.} 
Analogous properties also hold for the following class of Einstein--Navier--Stokes systems
\bel{eq:pot-dissipated-system0}
\begin{aligned}
G^{\alpha\beta}
&=T_\chi^{\alpha\beta}+T_{\rm aux}^{\alpha\beta}, \quad
&
\nabla_\alpha T_\chi^{\alpha\beta}
&=-\sigma n^\beta, \quad
&
\nabla_\alpha A_\chi^{\alpha\beta\gamma}
&=-\mathscr B^{\beta\gamma},
\end{aligned}
\ee 
with 
\be
\begin{aligned}
T_{\rm aux}^{\alpha\beta}
&=\sigma \underline\pi^{\alpha\beta},
&
\sigma & \coloneqq \frac{\zeta_{\alpha\beta} \mathscr B^{\alpha\beta}}{-n_\alpha\beta^\alpha} \geq 0. 
\end{aligned}
\ee 
Here $\underline\pi^{\alpha\beta}$ is the (rescaled) projection onto the symmetry orbits, $n_\alpha$ is the future-directed normal to the areal foliation, and $\beta$ is the rescaled fluid momentum.
The model includes an auxiliary stress tensor~$T_{\rm aux}$ (\autoref{def-diss-en}), which compensates the mass-energy dissipated by~$T_\chi$. In particular, the coupled evolution equations are symmetric hyperbolic in the interior of the state space, and both Einstein equations and Bianchi equations are satisfied.
The associated particle-number current~$\vNumb_\chi$ is divergence-free.
\eei
\noindent For all three systems, the Einstein constraints propagate from one areal hypersurface, and the metric variables are reconstructed from the transport, constraint, and periodicity equations. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

Let \(\sigma\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})\), and let \(W_L(\sigma)\) be the truncated Wiener--Hopf operator on \(L^2(0,L)\). Suppose that there exists a bounded determination \(\psi\) of \(\log\sigma\) whose inverse Fourier transform \(\check{\psi}\) satisfies
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}}|x|\,|\check{\psi}(x)|^2\,\mathrm{d}x<\infty.

Then \(W_L(\sigma)\exp(-W_L(\psi))\) is of determinant class, and
\[
\det\bigl(W_L(\sigma)\exp(-W_L(\psi))\bigr)

as \(L\to\infty\). If, in addition, \(\psi\in L^1(\mathbb{R})\), then

\right)
\to
\exp\left(
\int_0^{\infty}x\check{\psi}(x)\check{\psi}(-x)\,\mathrm{d}x
\right),
\]
where \(\det W_L(\sigma)\) denotes the Fredholm determinant of \(W_L(\sigma)=\operatorname{Id}+W_L(\sigma-1)\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}
