{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.165090+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_14c12419e48d441dc5aa5a7d5a0e080939ec89667ae7347c2f8743f09e0c5653","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 38 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] There exists a constant $C_8=C_8(\alpha,\iota)$ such that the following holds with probability at least $1-e^{-cN}$ over $\dot{\bg}_+, \hat{\bg}_+$, where $c$ is an absolute constant. 
    For any $\|\by\|^2=N$, the function
    \[
        \btheta_+ \mapsto
        \frac{2(\hbg_+,\btheta_+)}{M}
        + \frac{2\|\btheta_+\|(\dbg_+,\by)}{M\sqrt{N}}
        - \frac{((\hbD_+)^{-1} \btheta_+, \btheta_+)}{M}
    \]
    attains its supremum over $\R^{B_+}$ at some $\btheta_+$ satisfying
    $\|\btheta_+\| \le C_8N^{1/2}$.
    (We take the assertion to be vacuously true if $B_+ = \emptyset$.)

\begin{proof}
    Since the function tends to $-\infty$ as $\|\btheta_+\| \to +\infty$, the supremum is attained at a local maximizer $\btheta_+$.
    The function is differentiable everywhere except possibly at $\btheta_+=\bzero$, so the only possible local maximizer are $\btheta_+=\bzero$ and stationary points $\btheta_+$. 
    The stationarity condition gives
    \[
      \btheta_+
     =\hbD_+\bigg(   \hbg_+
        + \frac{(\dbg_+,\by) \btheta_+}{N^{1/2} \|\btheta_+\|}
        \bigg) \,.
    \]
With probability $1-e^{-cN}$, we have $\|\hbg_+\| \le 2 M^{1/2}$, $\|\dbg_+\| \le 2 N^{1/2}$, and consequently $|(\dbg_+,\by)| \le 2N$. Since the operator norm of $\hbD_+$ is at most $\hv_1$, it follows that any stationary point $\btheta_+$ must satisfy
    \[
        \|\btheta_+\|
        \le\hv_1 \bigg(
            \|\hbg_+\|
            + \bigg|
            \frac{(\dbg_+,\by) }{N^{1/2} }
            \bigg|
        \bigg)
        \le
        2\hv_1\Big( M^{1/2} + N^{1/2}
         \Big)
        \stackrel{\eqref{e:reduced-normalization}}{\le}
        \frac{4(\alpha^{1/2}+1)}{\iota} N^{1/2}\,.
    \]
This proves the claim.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:17:42.300829+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_150695aae1416938622114b2c4a679692c1815cb8ead848472a4025947266e99","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 6 (Main result in spatial dimension $d=1$) of arXiv:2510.22155, 'Random walks in space-time random media in all spatial dimensions: the full subcritical fl'] Let $\{K_n\}_{n\ge 1}$ denote an environment satisfying Assumption \ref{a1}, and let $\mathfrak H^N$ be as in \eqref{hn}. Assume as in Definition \ref{goodseq} that one has a good sequence of deterministic initial data $\mathfrak H^N(0,\bullet)$ converging weakly as measures to some limit $\mathfrak H_0$. There is an explicit Banach space $X$ of distributions on $\mathbb R$, which is continuously embedded in $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R)$, such that the rescaled and recentered collection $\{ \mathfrak F^N\}_{N \ge 1}$ is tight with respect to the topology of $C([0,T], X)$. Furthermore any limit point as $N\to \infty$ is as follows. 
\begin{itemize} 
\item (Bulk fluctuations in $d=1$) If $N^{1/2}\varsigma_N \to \boldsymbol{\varsigma} \text{ as } N\to\infty$, then the limit point is unique and coincides with the law of $(t,x)\mapsto e^{\varsigma\bullet x +\frac12 |\varsigma|^2 t} \mathcal U(t,x+\varsigma t)$ where $\mathcal U$ is the solution of the additive-noise SPDE \begin{equation}\partial_t \mathcal U(t, x) = \frac12\partial_x^2 \mathcal U(t, x) + \gamma_{\mathrm{ext}}\cdot \partial_x^p \big((\mathfrak H_0 *G_t)(x)\;\xi(t, x)\big),

\end{equation}started with initial data $\mathcal U(0, x)=0$. 
\end{itemize} Here $G_t(x) = G(t,x)= (2\pi t)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2t}$ is the standard heat kernel, $*$ denotes spatial convolution, and $ \xi$ is a standard space-time white noise defined on $\mathbb R_+\times \mathbb R.$ Furthermore in either case we have the noise coefficient $$\gamma_{\mathrm{ext}}^2:=  \frac1{(2p)!}\int_{I} \bigg[ \int_{I^2}( x- y)^{2p}\mu(\mathrm d x)\mu(\mathrm d y)-\int_I ( a- z)^{2p} \pdif( z,\mathrm d a)\bigg]
\pi^{\mathrm{inv}}(\mathrm d z).

{"assumptions":["sub-Gaussian increments with respect to the metric d","separability of the process, so that the supremum is measurable and the chaining series converges","convergence of the entropy integral"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.628694+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_15319d42d2a2e77a7eb628a9a06e56b61b321dba9d4e5dfffbd869a984b61dbb","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X_t)_{t in T} be a stochastic process on a metric space (T, d) with SUB-GAUSSIAN INCREMENTS, meaning P( |X_s - X_t| > u ) <= 2 exp( - u^2 / (2 d(s,t)^2) ) for all s, t and u > 0. Then there is an absolute constant C with E sup_{t in T} X_t <= C integral_0^{diam(T)} sqrt( log N(T, d, u) ) du, where N(T, d, u) is the covering number, the smallest number of d-balls of radius u needed to cover T. If the process is not centred one should read the statement for X_t - X_{t_0} with a fixed base point. Two standard cautions: the bound can be LOOSE - for a centred Gaussian process the sharp answer is Talagrand's generic chaining and the majorizing measure theorem, and Dudley's integral can overshoot by an unbounded factor; and the integral must converge, so a class with covering numbers growing faster than exp(u^{-2}) is not handled. Sudakov's minoration provides the matching lower bound E sup_t X_t >= c sup_{u > 0} u sqrt( log N(T, d, u) ) for centred GAUSSIAN processes, so the two differ exactly by the integral versus the supremum. [Dudley (1967); see Vershynin, High-Dimensional Probability, Theorem 8.1.6]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(a) f absolutely continuous with E|f'(Z)| finite","(c) the characterisation quantifies over a rich enough class of test functions","(d) the Gaussian vector must be CENTRED"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.543764+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1564c803ed1f4f740d9c5f603549c04916aaed26f09262fdb378ee739b59ba18","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"(a) Let Z be standard Gaussian on R and f absolutely continuous with E|f'(Z)| < infinity. Then E[ Z f(Z) ] = E[ f'(Z) ]. (b) Multivariate: if X is centred Gaussian on R^n with covariance Sigma and f is differentiable with the appropriate integrability, then E[ X_i f(X) ] = sum_j Sigma_{ij} E[ d f / d x_j (X) ]. (c) STEIN'S CHARACTERISATION: a real random variable Z is standard Gaussian IF AND ONLY IF E[ Z f(Z) ] = E[ f'(Z) ] for every bounded, continuously differentiable f with bounded derivative. This is the identity that makes Stein's method work: to show a law is close to Gaussian, one bounds E[ Z f(Z) - f'(Z) ] over a class of test functions f solving Stein's equation. (d) ISSERLIS-WICK FORMULA: for a centred Gaussian vector, E[ X_1 X_2 ... X_{2m} ] = sum over all PERFECT MATCHINGS of {1, ..., 2m} of the product of the covariances of the matched pairs, and any odd moment vanishes. For 2m = 4 this reads E[X_1X_2X_3X_4] = Sigma_{12}Sigma_{34} + Sigma_{13}Sigma_{24} + Sigma_{14}Sigma_{23}, and in particular E[Z^4] = 3 for a standard Gaussian, which is the '3' that the fourth moment theorem tests against. Centring is essential in (d); for a non-centred Gaussian one must first subtract the means. [standard; Isserlis (1918), Stein (1972); see Nourdin and Peccati, Normal Approximations with Malliavin Calculus, Chapter 3]","status":"unverified"}

			\Big) \le \delta

	\]

			\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)) \in \cP_2(\R,C)
		\bigg) \ge 1 - e^{-cN}\,.
	\eeq
We now define
	\[
		S_\delta \equiv
		\Big\{ \mu \in \cP_2(\R,C) : \bbW_\fq(\mu, \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)) \ge \delta \Big\}
	\]
(note this differs slightly from the set $S_\delta$ defined in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.lip.trunc.to.ideal}). 
	By Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.cPp.compact.Wq}, the space $\cP_2(\R,C)$ endowed with the $\bbW_\fq$ metric is compact.
	The set $S_\delta$ is closed with respect to the $\bbW_\fq$ metric, and therefore also compact. We may thus cover $S_\delta$ with finitely many $\bbW_\fq$-balls,
	\[S_\delta = \bigcup_{\mu \in T_\delta} \cB_{\fq,\delta/5}(\mu)
		\,,\]
	where $T_\delta \subseteq S_\delta$ is a finite set depending on only $\fq, \delta$, and
		\[\cB_{q,\delta/5}(\mu) 
		\equiv\bigg\{
			\mu' \in S_\delta : \bbW_\fq(\mu,\mu') \le 
			\frac{\delta}{5}
		\bigg\}\,.\]
	Note that for each $\mu \in S_\delta$, we have
	\begin{align*}
		\bbW_\fq(\mu(\cA_N),\mu) 
		&\ge \bbW_\fq(\mu,\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon))
		- \bbW_\fq(\mu(\cA_N),\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)) \\
		&\ge \delta - \bbW_\fq(\mu(\cA_N),\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon))\,,
	\end{align*}

\mu$, and is $o_N(1)$ by
	Proposition~\ref{p:confinement}. It follows that for $N$ large enough, we have
	\[
		\inf_{\mu \in S_\delta} \bbW_\fq(\mu(\cA_N),\mu) \ge 
		\frac{4\delta}{5}\,.
	\]
	For each $\mu \in T_\delta$,  Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.consequence.of.variance.bound} implies
	\[
		\E \bbW_\fq\Big(\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)),\mu\Big)
		\stackrel{\eqref{e:confinement.consequence.of.variance.bound}}{\ge} \bigg(\Big[\bbW_\fq(\mu(\cA_N),\mu)^2 - o_N(1)\Big]_+\bigg)^{1/2}
		\ge \frac{3\delta}{5}
	\]
	for sufficiently large $N$.
	Note that the $o_N(1)$ term above may depend on $\mu$; however, as $T_\delta$ is a finite set independent of $N$, the above estimate can be taken to hold simultaneously for all $\mu \in T_\delta$. By Lemma~\ref{l:Wq.lip.to.fixed.msr.conc} combined with a union bound over
$\mu \in T_\delta$, we obtain
	\[
		\P\bigg(
			\min_{\mu \in T_\delta} \bbW_\fq\Big(\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux),\mu\Big)
			\ge \frac{2\delta}{5}
		\bigg)
		\stackrel{\eqref{e:Wq.lip.to.fixed.msr.conc.tail}}{=} 1 - e^{-cN}\,.
	\]
	(This $c$ depends on $\alpha,L,\delta$ only, as $\epsilon,\fq$ affect only the $N$-independent number of terms $|T_\delta|$ in the union bound.)
	On this event, we further have
	\[\bbW_\fq\Big(\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)), S_\delta\Big)
		\ge \min_{\mu \in T_\delta} \bbW_\fq\Big(\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)),\mu\Big) - \frac{\delta}{5}
		\ge 
		\frac{\delta}{5}\,,\]
	and therefore $\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)) \not\in S_\delta$.
	Combining with \eqref{e:confinement.mu.bG.to.P2} shows that 
	\[
		\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)) \in \cP_2(\R,C) \setminus S_\delta
	\]
with probability $1-e^{-cN}$ (again adjusting $c$ appropriately). 
	On this event, we obtain the desired estimate
	\[
		\bbW_\fq\Big(\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)), \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)
		\Big) \le \delta\,.
	\]

{"assumptions":["All hypotheses, dimensions, step restrictions and observable norms in the statement; no independent audit."],"created_at":"2026-10-21T19:50:21.974827+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_15ae575f5cdf6ffb959dcd4d6db118bd84cd72568d605a4fd10d69cb34b06ab0","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"OWNER OWN WORK DRAFT; proof (unaudited), claim w730-T355-C009 v1; novelty unestablished.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.352475+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_15e330d2baaa644ec10bc714fcdd93a5b89163ac895e536f314465a8b83d5176","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Cor 195 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$, let $p^\sigma\equiv p^\sigma(\bXi)$ denote the empirical averages
	\[
	\frac1M\sum_{a\le M}
	\max_{0\le d\le \dmax}
	\ind \Big\{
	X^{\trunc,\sigma}(q_d,a)
	\notin  [-\trK,\trK)\Big\}\,.
	\]
Similarly, let $p^\Ising\equiv p^\Ising(\bXi)$ denote the empirical average
	\[
	\frac1N\sum_{i\le N}
	\max_{0\le d\le \dmax}
	\ind \Big\{
	X^{\trunc,\Ising}(q_d,i)
	\notin  [-\trK,\trK)\Big\}\,.
	\]
Then $p^\sigma(\bXi) \le o_{\trK}(1)$
for all $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}$, with probability
at least $1- \exp(-N^{1/2})$.

\begin{proof}
Let $\bar{p}^\sigma$ be defined as $p^\sigma$, but with $[-\trK+1,\trK-1)$ in place of $[-\trK,\trK)$.
Let $f:\R\to\R$ be the Lipschitz function defined by
	\[f(x)=\begin{cases}
	0 & \textup{if $|x|\le \trK-1$,}\\
	1 & \textup{if $|x|\ge \trK$,}\\
		|x|-(\trK-1)
		&\textup{if $\trK-1
			\le |x| \le \trK$}\,.
	\end{cases}\]
Since $\ind\{x\notin[-\trK,\trK)\} \le f(x)
\le \ind\{x\notin[-\trK+1,\trK-1)\} 
$, for $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$ we have
	\[p^\sigma(\bXi)
	\le
	F^\sigma(\bXi)
	\equiv
	\frac1M
	\sum_{a\le M}
	\max_{0\le d\le \dmax}
	f(X^{\trunc,\sigma}(q_d,a))
	\le \bar{p}^\sigma(\bXi)
	\,.
	\]
We first argue that the \emph{annealed} expectation of $\bar{p}^\sigma$ is small for each $\sigma$. Note that since $\vX^{\trunc,\RomI:\RomIII}$ is frozen upon leaving $[-\trK,\trK)^3$ (Definition~\ref{d:trunc}), the probability that $\vX^{\trunc,\RomI:\RomIII}(q_d,a)$ lies outside $[-\trK,\trK)^3$ is maximized at time $d=\dmax$. From the spatial rerandomization (Definition~\ref{d:rerand}), this is the same as the probability that $\vY^{\RomI:\RomIII}(q_d)$ lies outside $[-\trK,\trK)^3$ at time $d=\dmax$. This (annealed) probability can be bounded using the proof of  Proposition~\ref{p:tightness}: recall from \eqref{e:A.H} that the event $A(H)$ has probability tending to zero as $H\to\infty$. On the complement of $A(H)$, the paths
$\bar{D}^\RomI$,
$Y^\RomII$, $Y^\RomIII$, $Y^\Ising$
are all $\gamma$-H\"older with H\"older norm $O(H)$, and in particular the maximum deviation of each path must be $O(H)$.
Moreover, since $\mathcal{E}^N$ converges uniformly to zero, the discrepancy between $\bar{D}^\RomI$ and $Y^\RomI$ converges uniformly to zero, so we can conclude that the maximum deviation of $Y^\RomI$ is also $O(H)$.
If we take $H$ to be a small constant multiple of $\trK$, then we conclude that $\E[\bar{p}^\sigma(\bXi)] \le o_{\trK}(1)$ for $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$. A similar argument gives 
$\E[\bar{p}^\Ising(\bXi)] \le o_{\trK}(1)$. 

The above implies that the annealed expectation of each $F^\sigma$ is also small. It remains to show that $F^\sigma$ is highly concentrated about this expectation. For $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$,
it follows by Corollary~\ref{c:conc.empir.avg} 
that $F^\sigma$ is $(L^{O(1)}/(\delta N^{1/2}))$-Lipschitz on the set $U_\MAX$. It follows by 
Assumption~\ref{a:params} that this Lipschitz constant is very small, for instance,
	\[
	\frac{L^{O(1)}}{\delta N^{1/2}}
	\ll \frac{1}{N^{1/3}}\,.
	\]
By the Kirszbraun extension theorem, there exists a function $\tilde{F}^\sigma(\bXi)$ which agrees with $F^\sigma$ for $\bXi\in U_\MAX$, but such that $\tilde{F}^\sigma$ is $(1/N^{1/3})$-Lipschitz on the entire space. 
It follows by standard concentration bounds (see e.g.\ Lemma~\ref{l:lip.subgaus}) that $\tilde{F}^\sigma$ is highly concentrated about its mean $\E[\tilde{F}^\sigma(\bXi)]$. We finally bound
	\[
	\E\Big[\tilde{F}^\sigma(\bXi)\Big]
	\le \E\Big[F^\sigma(\bXi)\Big]
	+ \E\Big[\tilde{F}^\sigma(\bXi);(U_\MAX)^c\Big]
	\le 
	\E\Big[F^\sigma(\bXi)\Big]
	+\bigg\{ \E\Big[\tilde{F}^\sigma(\bXi)^2\Big]
	\P\Big((U_\MAX)^c \Big)
	\bigg\}^{1/2}
	\le o_{\trK}(1)\,.
	\]
In the last step, we used that $\tilde{F}^\sigma$ is Lipschitz so its second moment must be bounded, while  \eqref{e.MAX.bound} implies that $\P((U_\MAX)^c)$ is very small. This proves the claim for $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$, and a similar argum (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

On any event Z_n->z, the update forces X_n to converge to a binary vector x and hence eventually equal it. The bounded martingale-difference strong law gives x=Qz. The update limit gives z=(r x+f p)/(r+f). A binary coordinate of Qz can equal0 or1 only when all its positive-weight predecessors have the same x-value and matching p-value. The maximum principle can also be checked by propagating the set of zero coordinates backwards through irreducibility. Obstruction: This resolves the fixed-step convergence subquestion under the stated assumptions, but not the whole diffusion question. {"assumptions":["(a) f_n >= 0 measurable","(b) sum_n integral |f_n| dmu < infinity"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.752150+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_161f0473e05bf76a88262094c5be25c7d5ddcdbbee8494f99bd8cb784a8fb953","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (Omega, F, mu) be a measure space and f_n measurable. (b) If sum_n integral |f_n| dmu < infinity then sum_n f_n converges absolutely mu-almost everywhere, the sum is in L^1(mu), and integral sum_n f_n dmu = sum_n integral f_n dmu. Failure: on R with Lebesgue measure let f_n = 1_{[n, n+1]} - 1_{[n+1, n+2]} for n >= 0. Each integral f_n = 0 so sum_n integral f_n = 0, but the partial sums telescope to 1_{[0,1]} - 1_{[N+1, N+2]}, so sum_n f_n = 1_{[0,1]} pointwise off the integer endpoints, with integral 1. [standard; e.g. Folland, Real Analysis, 2nd ed., Theorem 2.15 and its corollary]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:48:47.287467+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1637051eb8cf9971561070e4866638ef1c48ccf7f1cba15a2067c2bee9fa4a90","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma Delta-bound of arXiv:2604.20660, 'The Legendre structure of the TAP complexity\\ for the Ising spin glass'] Fix $q\in[0,1)$ and let $\mu$ be a probability measure on $[-1,1]$ with
		$\int m^2\,\mu(\mathrm{d} m)=q$.
		For $\zeta\in\mathcal P([q,1])$, let $(X_t^{\mu,\zeta})_{t\in[q,1]}$ be the
		Auffinger--Chen process (equation eq:AC mu of the paper), set
		\[
		u_\zeta(t,x):=\partial_x\Phi_\zeta(t,x),
		\]
		and define
		\begin{equation}
			\Delta_\zeta^\mu
			:=
			\int_{[q,1]}
			\Bigl(\mathbb{E}\bigl[u_\zeta(t,X_t^{\mu,\zeta})^2\bigr]-t\Bigr)\,\zeta(\mathrm{d} t).
		\end{equation}
		Then:
		\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
			\item
			For every $\zeta\in\mathcal P([q,1])$,
			\[
			|\Delta_\zeta^\mu|\le 1.
			\]
			
			\item
			Let $\zeta_\mu$ be the unique minimizer of $\mathrm{TAP}(\mu,\cdot)$ on $\mathcal P([q,1])$.
			Assume that $\mu$ is supported in $[-1+\delta,1-\delta]$ for some
			$\delta\in(0,1)$, and let $\zeta\in\mathcal P([q,1])$ satisfy
			\[
			\zeta(\{q\})\ge u_0>0.
			\]
			Then there exists $C=C(\xi,u_0)$ such that
			\[
			|\Delta_\zeta^\mu|
			\le \frac{C}{\delta}\,\mathrm{dist}(\zeta,\zeta_\mu).
			\]
		\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

Moreover, the intermediate projections $\delta(t)$, $t\in(0,1)$ are the  graphs of bounded operators: $\delta(t)=P_{Gr(B(t))}$, where $B(t)\in\b(\h)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["T is measure-preserving on a probability space; for the one-sided version T need not be invertible","A is measurable with log^+ ||A|| integrable","the splitting version additionally needs T invertible, A(x) invertible a.e., and log^+ ||A^{-1}|| integrable","all statements hold for mu-a.e. x; exponents depend on mu"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T02:00:35.438459+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, Lyapunov exponents, smooth dynamics","id":"claim_1676fc5d4bd4204464d67994de31ed5e2340561ded554ac315e0ddd82660b53e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(X, \mathcal{B}, \mu, T)$ be a probability-preserving system and $A: X \to M_d(\mathbb{R})$ a measurable cocycle with $\log^+ \|A\| \in L^1(\mu)$; write $A^n(x) = A(T^{n-1}x)\cdots A(x)$.

ONE-SIDED (FILTRATION) VERSION - no invertibility of $T$ or of $A$ needed. For $\mu$-a.e. $x$: (a) the limit $\Lambda(x) = \lim_{n\to\infty} \big(A^n(x)^{\mathsf T} A^n(x)\big)^{1/2n}$ exists (a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix); (b) there are an integer $1 \le k(x) \le d$, exponents $\infty > \lambda_1(x) > \lambda_2(x) > \dots > \lambda_{k(x)}(x) \ge -\infty$ (only the smallest may be $-\infty$; this happens whenever $A$ is singular with positive probability, and can also happen for a.e.-invertible $A$ when $\log^+\|A^{-1}\|$ is not integrable), and a filtration of linear subspaces $\mathbb{R}^d = V_1(x) \supsetneq V_2(x) \supsetneq \dots \supsetneq V_{k(x)}(x) \supsetneq V_{k(x)+1}(x) = \{0\}$, measurable in $x$, such that $A(x) V_i(x) \subset V_i(Tx)$ and
$$\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac1n \log \|A^n(x) v\| = \lambda_i(x) \quad\text{for every } v \in V_i(x) \setminus V_{i+1}(x);$$
(c) $k$, the $\lambda_i$ and the multiplicities $m_i = \dim V_i - \dim V_{i+1}$ are $T$-invariant functions of $x$ (constants when $T$ is ergodic); (d) $\lim \frac1n \log |\det A^n(x)| = \sum_i m_i \lambda_i(x)$, and more generally $\lim \frac1n \log \|\Lambda^p A^n(x)\|$ (norm on the $p$-th exterior power) equals the sum of the $p$ largest exponents counted with multiplicity; (e) the $\lambda_i$ with multiplicities are exactly the limits $\lim \frac1n \log \sigma_j(A^n(x))$ of the singular values, i.e. the logarithms of the eigenvalues of $\Lambda(x)$.

TWO-SIDED (SPLITTING) VERSION. If moreover $T$ is invertible, $A(x) \in GL_d(\mathbb{R})$ a.e. and $\log^+ \|A^{-1}\| \in L^1(\mu)$, then for a.e. $x$ all exponents are finite and there is a measurable $A$-equivariant splitting $\mathbb{R}^d = E_1(x) \oplus \dots \oplus E_{k(x)}(x)$, $A(x)E_i(x) = E_i(Tx)$, $\dim E_i = m_i$, with $\lim_{n \to \pm\infty} \frac1n \log \|A^n(x) v\| = \lambda_i(x)$ for all $v \in E_i(x) \setminus \{0\}$ (the SAME exponent forwards and backwards), $V_i(x) = \bigoplus_{j \ge i} E_j(x)$, and the angles between the Oseledets subspaces decay subexponentially along orbits: $\lim_{n\to\pm\infty} \frac1n \log \sin\angle\big(E_i(T^n x), \bigoplus_{j\ne i} E_j(T^n x)\big) = 0$.

WHERE IT FAILS. (1) Without $\log^+\|A\| \in L^1$ the limits need not exist: for $d = 1$ the theorem IS Birkhoff's theorem for $\log|a|$, which fails when $\log^+|a| \notin L^1$. (2) Without $\log^+\|A^{-1}\| \in L^1$ (or with $T$ non-invertible) there is in general NO equivariant splitting, only the forward filtration: the subspaces of vectors with exponent exactly $\lambda_i$, $i \ge 2$, are not canonically defined and the 'slow' directions are not invariant under $A$. (3) The exponents depend on the measure $\mu$: different ergodic measures for the same $T$ and $A$ generally have different exponents, and a point outside the full-measure set need not have exponents at all. (4) Convergence is not uniform in $x$, and the Oseledets subspaces are only measurable, in general not continuous, in $x$. (5) The theorem is about $\|A^n(x)v\|$ along ONE orbit; it says nothing about eigenvalues of $A^n(x)$ or about $\|A^n\|$ averaged over $x$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:31:02.815410+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_16c4740aba5042f3ad9a84b6ae1bd62bd1bf991539a3fb69e1d53e6dcfa0170f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:cyclic-suspension of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Put $C=\Sigma_{\ell,c}A$ and $D=\max A$.  For
$q\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}$, let $L_q(A)$ be the real span of the homogeneous
relation vectors of relation degree at most $q$, and put
$r_q(A)=\dim L_q(A)$.  Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item For every $q\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}$,
\begin{equation}
 |qC|=\sum_{j=0}^{\min(q,\ell-1)}|(q-j)A|.
\end{equation}
Equivalently, for $X\in\{A,C\}$ put
\[
 \mathcal H_X(z)=\sum_{q\geq0}|qX|z^q.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal H_C(z)=\mathcal H_A(z)[\ell]_z,\qquad
 [\ell]_z=1+z+\cdots+z^{\ell-1}.
\end{equation}

\item Let
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 S_A&=K[x_0,\ldots,x_{m-1}],&
 \psi_A&:S_A\longrightarrow K[u,v],\\
 \psi_A(x_i)&=u^{D-a_i}v^{a_i},&
 I_A&=\ker\psi_A,\qquad R_A=S_A/I_A.
 \end{aligned}
\]
be the standard-graded projective semigroup ring of $A$.  Put
$S_C=S_A[y]$, and let $I_C$ be the kernel of the homogeneous toric map
\[
 x_i\longmapsto u^{\ell(D-a_i)}v^{\ell a_i},\qquad
 y\longmapsto u^{\ell D-c}v^c,
\]
so that $R_C=S_C/I_C$.  Then
\begin{equation}
 R_C\cong
 R_A[y]\big/\bigl(y^\ell-x_0^{\lambda_0}\cdots
 x_{m-1}^{\lambda_{m-1}}\bigr).
\end{equation}
The displayed polynomial is homogeneous and regular.  In particular, if
$R_A$ is Cohen--Macaulay, then so is $R_C$.

\item Define the ambient $K$-polynomials by
\[
 \mathcal K_A(z)=(1-z)^m\mathcal H_A(z),\qquad
 \mathcal K_C(z)=(1-z)^{m+1}\mathcal H_C(z).
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal K_C(z)=\mathcal K_A(z)(1-z^\ell).
\end{equation}
If $\beta^A_{i,j}$ and $\beta^C_{i,j}$ are the standard-graded Betti
numbers over $S_A$ and $S_C$, respectively, extended by zero outside their
natural homological and internal degree ranges, then
\begin{equation}
 \beta^C_{i,j}
 =\beta^A_{i,j}+\beta^A_{i-1,j-\ell}.
\end{equation}
Equivalently, with $\xi$ an indeterminate recording homological degree, put
\[
 \mathcal B_A(\xi,z)=\sum_{i,j}\beta^A_{i,j}\xi^iz^j,
 \qquad
 \mathcal B_C(\xi,z)=\sum_{i,j}\beta^C_{i,j}\xi^iz^j.
\]
Then
\[
 \mathcal B_C(\xi,z)=\mathcal B_A(\xi,z)(1+\xi z^\ell).
\]

\item Label the coordinates of $C$ by the tuple
$(\ell a_0,\ldots,\ell a_{m-1},c)$.  They need not be in increasing order;
this changes $L_q(C)$ only by a coordinate permutation.  Put
\[
 w_{\ell,c}=(\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_{m-1},-\ell).
\]
Under the old-coordinate embedding,
\begin{equation}
 L_q(C)=
 \begin{cases}
  L_q(A),&q<\ell,\\[2mm]
  L_q(A)\oplus\mathbb Rw_{\ell,c},&q\geq\ell.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
Hence
\begin{equation}
 r_q(C)=r_q(A)+
 \begin{cases}
  0,&q<\ell,\\
  1,&q\geq\ell,
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
and the multiset of active-relation birth degrees is the old multiset with
$\ell$ adjoined.

\item Define the order-$q$ Freiman dimension by
\[

Then for every t > 0, P(|X - mu| >= t) <= sigma^2 / t^2; equivalently P(|X - mu| >= k sigma) <= 1/k^2 for every k > 0. The inequality is sharp: for t >= sigma the variable taking the values mu - t and mu + t with probability sigma^2 / (2 t^2) each and the value mu otherwise has mean mu, variance sigma^2 and P(|X - mu| >= t) = sigma^2 / t^2 exactly. It gives no information for t <= sigma, and it is the classical route to the weak law of large numbers: for i.i.d. X_i with finite variance, P(|(X_1 + ... + X_n)/n - mu| >= eps) <= sigma^2 / (n eps^2) -> 0.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:18:27.580419+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1735778aaca10a65189fbd741cefd1c48f000341d27b9831055fcfa73b29880f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 18 (Bethe verification) of arXiv:2608.15987, 'Threshold cascades of interacting diffusions on unimodular random trees: a conditional bra'] On $T_d$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item (Hypothesis~\ref{hyp:red} is exact.) By vertex-transitivity all transmission probabilities equal a single $p=p^{\ex}$, the harmonic measure is uniform on the end space $\Sigma^{\mathbb N}$, $\Sigma=\{1,\dots,d-1\}$, there is no failure-strength heterogeneity across siblings (all forcings identical), and the failed cluster is exactly a Galton--Watson process with offspring law $\mathrm{Bin}(d-1,p)$. The mean matrix is the scalar $M=(d-1)p$, so $\rho(M)=(d-1)p$.
\item (Theorem~\ref{thm:gap} is an equality.) The boundary is homogeneous, $p_ew_e\equiv p$, so $\ell=\log(d-1)+\log p$ and $e^{\ell}=(d-1)p=\rho(M)=p_{\min}^{-\dimH}$ with $p_{\min}=1/d$; the Jensen gap is zero. At criticality $(d-1)p=1$ the weighted dimension is $0$.
\item (Theorem~\ref{thm:32}.) At criticality the offspring law is $\mathrm{Bin}(d-1,1/(d-1))$, mean $1$, variance $1-1/(d-1)<\infty$ for $d\ge3$, giving $C_d=(2\pi(1-1/(d-1)))^{-1/2}>0$ and the $n^{-3/2}$ tail. The binary tree $d=2$ is the degenerate variance-zero case and is excluded.
\item (Theorem~\ref{thm:stab}.) $\rho=(d-1)p(\theta,\gamma)$ with $p$ decreasing in $\theta$ and increasing in $\gamma$; $\mathcal M_+=\{p>1/(d-1)\}$ is convex, $\mathcal M_-$ its complement is contractible by the $\gamma$-retraction, the critical curve is smooth, and $(1-(d-1)p)^{-1}$ is the explicit expected cluster size.
\item (Theorems \ref{thm:pressure}, \ref{thm:dimS} and \ref{thm:crt}.) The pressure is affine, $\varphi(\beta)=\log(d-1)+\beta\log p$, so the convexity gap vanishes, consistent with item 2. In the supercritical regime $(d-1)p>1$ the failed boundary has $\dimH(\partial S)=\log((d-1)p)<\log(d-1)=\dimH(\partial T)$: the cascade survives along an exponentially thin bundle of rays, of relative codimension $\log(1/p)$. At criticality, the cluster is single-type with bounded offspring, so the exponential-moment hypothesis of Theorem~\ref{thm:crt} is automatic and the conditioned cluster rescaled by $\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{off}}}{2\sqrt n}$, $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{off}}=1-\frac{1}{d-1}$, converges to the CRT by Aldous' theorem \cite{Ald93}.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Recurrent symmetric Markov process; base point o; inverse local time at o","GFF with covariance the Green function of the process killed at o, independent of the process","Identity in law, not a pathwise coupling"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.988309+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_178ab0e20429fbcabddf72bded46fbdf579084e30b0d6607f8a57c199cde4f8b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). Generalised second Ray-Knight theorem (Eisenbaum, Kaspi, Marcus, Rosen and Shi, 2000): let X be a recurrent symmetric Markov process on a countable state space (for instance continuous-time random walk on a finite connected graph, or on Z^2), started at a base point o, and let tau(u) be the inverse local time at o, the first time the local time at o reaches u. Let (phi_x) be the Gaussian free field on the state space with covariance the Green function of X killed at o, independent of X. Then the field (L^{tau(u)}_x + (1/2) phi_x^2)_x has the same law as ((1/2)(phi_x + sqrt(2u))^2)_x. Dynkin-type isomorphisms exist for transient processes killed at an independent exponential time (there the shift is absent). Uses: transfer of DGFF extremal results to local-time level sets and cover times (Ding-Lee-Peres via the Gaussian free field maximum), thick points of random walk, and the Sabot-Tarres and Lupu loop-soup couplings. Limits: the isomorphism identifies laws, not couplings, of the two sides unless the stronger Lupu coupling is used; the sign of phi is lost in the square, so events about level sets of the local time correspond to two-sided level sets of phi + sqrt(2u). Typical failure: Using the generalized second Ray-Knight isomorphism but omitting or misplacing the additive shift sqrt(2T) term that appears when T is a fixed constant rather than an inverse-local-time stopping time, as in the classical Brownian motion Ray-Knight theorems; dropping or mislocating this shift silently changes which boundary or starting condition the isomorphism is actually describing. Canonical reference: Ray, 1963, Illinois Journal of Mathematics; Knight, 1963, Transactions of the American Mathematical Society; Eisenbaum, Kaspi, Marcus, Rosen and Shi, 2000, Annals of Probability; Lupu, 2016, Annals of Probability.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X's law absolutely continuous with respect to Brownian motion (weaker than the problem's equivalence)","theta the unit shift with recentering on two-sided Wiener space, ergodic and invertible"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:11:19.449623+00:00","domain":"probability, Brownian motion, ergodic theory","id":"claim_178be04644b922b0b199a99ca4c2e4d055a2ff13a8ecf4efb01dca25babd8550","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Burdzy and Scheutzow, Forward Brownian motion (arXiv:1302.6958), Problem 7.5 (p. 26) asks: for any process {X_t, t >= 0} whose law is equivalent to Brownian motion, can one find a random piece to put in front of X so that the new process is a Brownian motion? Our result (id P0032, 2026-09-08): YES - and under absolute continuity rather than equivalence, which is weaker than the problem assumes. The mechanism is a filling-scheme lemma: for theta an invertible ergodic measure-preserving transformation of a standard Borel space (E, P) and Q = f P, there is an almost surely finite integer N >= 0 with law(theta^N Z) = Q for Z distributed as P. Apply it with E = C_0(R) under two-sided Wiener measure and (theta w)(t) = w(t+1) - w(1), lifting the one-sided density of X's law to two-sided paths; the lemma returns a finite N for which {Z(N+t) - Z(N)} has X's law while {Z(t) - Z(0)} is a Brownian motion whose first N units are exactly the prefix. Verification as the source words it: the filling construction was implemented on a finite ergodic system (Z/n with the +1 shift) for n = 5, 7, 12, 60 with random densities - total accepted mass 1.000000000000 every time, the law of theta^N Z matching f P to about 1e-16, E[N] finite - and the negative control is the informative one, since with a non-ergodic theta exactly half the mass is ever accepted and half survives forever. The L^1 ergodic-theorem step in the infinite-dimensional setting was not verified, only read; it is standard but checked by eye only. NOVELTY IS THE WEAK POINT and the campaign's own proof file volunteers it: the lemma is a filling construction related to classical work of Chacon-Ornstein, Rost and Thorisson - sound mathematics, very likely a known consequence.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the signs are independent and symmetric; the identity E S^4 = 3 (sum a_i^2)^2 - 2 sum a_i^4 uses E epsilon_i^4 = 1 and E epsilon_i^2 epsilon_j^2 = 1 for i different from j","coefficients are real (the complex and vector-valued versions hold with modified constants; Kahane's inequality is the Banach-space extension)","dependent or asymmetric signs are not covered"],"created_at":"2026-09-02T07:51:33.049237+00:00","domain":"anti-concentration and moment inequalities (hand-authored statement with hypotheses, 2026-09-02)","id":"claim_1796c911ceeffee80cd7700c686eb05fc27456d52abdbb661721b8f2800206a5","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let epsilon_1, ..., epsilon_n be independent Rademacher signs (each +1 or -1 with probability 1/2) and a_1, ..., a_n real numbers, and write S = sum a_i epsilon_i and ||a||_2 = (sum a_i^2)^{1/2}. Khintchine's inequality (1923): for every 0 < p < infinity there are constants A_p, B_p depending only on p with A_p ||a||_2 <= (E|S|^p)^{1/p} <= B_p ||a||_2. The second moment is exact, E S^2 = ||a||_2^2. The fourth moment is an identity, not just a bound: E S^4 = 3 (sum a_i^2)^2 - 2 sum a_i^4, so E S^4 <= 3 ||a||_2^4 and B_4 <= 3^{1/4}, with the constant 3 approached as the coefficients spread out (many equal a_i) and never attained; this is the Gaussian fourth moment. Sharp constants: A_p = 1 for p >= 2 and B_p = 1 for p <= 2; A_1 = 1/sqrt 2 (Szarek 1976); for p >= 3, B_p equals the p-th moment of a standard Gaussian to the power 1/p (Haagerup 1981). The lower bound for p < 2 is the nontrivial direction and is what the fourth-moment identity gives via the Paley-Zygmund argument: E|S| >= (E S^2)^{3/2} / (E S^4)^{1/2} >= ||a||_2 / sqrt 3.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:33:01.752514+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_17d70e18ae0d318b2d606d663e30e9e5a5b56f4563f75fc3467328d3c16dfeae","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 27 (Critical shapes) of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] Let $p \sim c/m$ for some $c > 0$
  and let $\tau_c$ be the first hitting time of
  $0$ in the birth-death process defined by
  Lemma~\ref{thm:birth-death}.
  If $G$ is a standard Gumbel random variable,
  independent of $\tau_c$, then
  $(T_{m,p} - m\log{m})/m$ converges in law to $G + \tau_c$.
  \begin{proof}
    Lemma \ref{thm:coupling} reveals
    $(T_{m, p} - m\log{m})/m$ is the independent sum
    of $(T_{m,0} - m\log{m})/m$ and $(T_{m,p} - T_{m,0})/m$.
    The first term converges to $G$ weakly
    by Lemma~\ref{thm:subcritical}.

    The second term has \textsc{mgf} $I_{m,p}(t/m)$ for $t < 0$,
    \[
      M_{(T_{m,p} - T_{m,0})/m}(t)
      = (1-p)^m
      \left[
        1
        -
        \int_0^1 p \, m
        \left(1-x\right)^{m\exp(-t/m)-m}
        \left(1-p\,x\right)^{m-1} dx
      \right]^{-1}.
    \]
    Then since $p\,m \to c$ and $(1-p)^m \to e^{-c}$,
    the integrand is bounded and we have
    access to the dominated convergence theorem;
    for each $0 < x < 1$ it holds
    \[
      p\,m\left(1-x\right)^{m\exp(-t/m)-m} \left(1-p\,x\right)^{m-1}
      \longrightarrow e^{c} \left(1-x\right)^{-t}
      e^{-c x},
    \]
    which implies
    \[
      M_{(T_{m,p} - T_{m,0})/m}(t)
      \longrightarrow e^{-c} \left[
        1 - \int_0^1 c \left(1-x\right)^{-t} e^{-c x} \, dx \right]^{-1}.
    \]
    This is the \textsc{mgf} of $\tau_c$ (Lemma~\ref{thm:birth-death}).
    So, we have shown $M_{(T_{m, p} - m \log{m})/m}(t)
    \to M_G(t) \, M_{\tau_c}(t) = M_{G+\tau_c}(t)$
    for all negative $t$. The convergence theorem confirms
    $(T_{m,p} - m \log{m})/m \Rightarrow G + \tau_c$.
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

The slicing method controls a penalized or weighted supremum of a random process: cut the index set into slices on which the penalty lies between two levels, remove the penalty on each slice, and add the slice bounds with a union bound. Each remaining term is the supremum of a process without penalty, which chaining can control. van Handel, Section 5.4: writing X_t = E[X_t] + Z_t with subgaussian fluctuations Z_t, sup_t X_t = sup_t {Z_t + E[X_t]} is a penalized supremum of a subgaussian process with E[X_t] as the penalty, and chaining is suited to the fluctuations but not to the penalty. In the multiplicative setting (the additive one works the same way), for the weighted supremum of (X_t − X_s)/ρ(t, s), fix α_k ↓ 0 with ρ(s, t) ≤ α_0 for all s, t; on the slice {α_k ≤ ρ(s, t) ≤ α_{k−1}} the weight is bounded above and below, and a union bound gives P[sup_{s,t} (X_t − X_s)/ρ(t, s) ≥ x] ≤ Σ_{k≥1} P[sup_{ρ(s,t) ≤ α_{k−1}} {X_t − X_s} ≥ α_k x]. The sets {ρ ≤ α_{k−1}} shrink as k grows while the levels α_k x fall, so the penalty and the levels must be chosen to make the probabilities summable; that tuning is specific to each application. Worked example, Theorem 5.32 (modulus of continuity): if {X_t} is a separable subgaussian process on (T, d) and N(T, d, ε) ≥ (c/ε)^q for some c, q > 0 and all ε > 0, then ω(δ) = ∫_0^δ sqrt(log N(T, d, ε)) dε is a modulus of continuity for {X_t}, and E[sup_{t,s} (X_t − X_s)/ω(d(t, s))] < ∞. The proof slices with α_k = ω(Δ2^{−k}), Δ = diam(T), bounds each slice by the local chaining inequality (Proposition 5.35: P[sup_{d(t,s) ≤ δ} {X_t − X_s} ≥ C ∫_0^δ sqrt(log N(T, d, ε)) dε + x] ≤ C e^{−x²/(Cδ²)}), and uses ω(2δ) ≤ 2ω(δ). By Remark 5.34 the covering-number condition is technical: ω is still a modulus of continuity without it, by a more delicate tuning of slicing and chaining. Problem 5.12 (Empirical risk minimization I: slicing) applies the slicing argument to the excess risk R(t̂_n) − R(t*) of the empirical risk minimizer.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["each f_n differentiable on [a,b], with [a,b] a bounded interval","(f_n(x_0)) converges for at least one point x_0","f_n' -> g uniformly on [a,b]"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.751029+00:00","domain":"real analysis","id":"claim_18620c87505e98d6c532146546254519319c9d12188204bf60601298432ca6cc","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f_n : [a,b] -> R be differentiable on [a,b], suppose the numerical sequence (f_n(x_0)) converges for SOME x_0 in [a,b], and suppose f_n' -> g uniformly on [a,b]. Then f_n converges uniformly on [a,b] to a function f, f is differentiable, and f' = g. The hypothesis that must be uniform is on the DERIVATIVES: uniform convergence of f_n itself is neither necessary nor sufficient. Sufficiency fails: f_n(x) = sin(nx)/sqrt(n) converges to 0 uniformly on R while f_n'(x) = sqrt(n) cos(nx) diverges at every x with cos(nx) bounded away from 0. Convergence of f_n at one point cannot be dropped either: f_n = n has f_n' = 0 -> 0 uniformly and f_n converges nowhere. [standard; e.g. Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed., Theorem 7.17]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a topological space; no metrisability, compactness or separation axiom is required","each f_i is upper semicontinuous as a map into the extended reals (continuity is the special case used most often)","the family is nonempty; the index set may be uncountable","the infimum is taken pointwise, and values -infinity and +infinity are allowed"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.089930+00:00","domain":"general topology, semicontinuity","id":"claim_18da4caf8dac6a3433a1aa1a053da36b492c033651287018a2b335ad110cf583","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a topological space (no separation or countability axiom is needed) and let (f_i), i in I, be a nonempty family of functions f_i : X -> [-infinity, +infinity], each upper semicontinuous; in particular each f_i may be continuous. The index set I is arbitrary: finite, countable, or uncountable. Put f(x) = inf over i in I of f_i(x). Then f is upper semicontinuous: the set {x : f(x) < c} is open for every real c, equivalently limsup_{y -> x} f(y) <= f(x) at every point x. The standard consequence: an upper semicontinuous function on a nonempty compact space attains its supremum, so a variational problem whose objective is an infimum of continuous quantities always has a maximiser. WHERE IT FAILS: (i) the direction is not symmetric. A SUPREMUM of continuous functions is lower semicontinuous, not upper: on R, sup over n >= 1 of min(1, n|x|) is the indicator of {x nonzero}, which is lower but not upper semicontinuous at 0. Quoting this result for a supremum is the common misuse. (ii) The infimum of an INFINITE family of continuous functions is in general not continuous: on [0,1], inf over n of x^n equals 0 for x < 1 and 1 at x = 1. Only finite infima of continuous functions are continuous, so upper semicontinuity is the most one can claim. (iii) Upper semicontinuity of each member is exactly what is used; an infimum of merely lower semicontinuous functions has no semicontinuity property at all. (iv) The pointwise version localises: if each f_i is merely continuous AT a point x, the same proof gives limsup_{y -> x} f(y) <= f(x), i.e. upper semicontinuity at that one point, which is the form most often needed in practice.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:52:45.021618+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_18dc1002295738a96cf427e8ea34ea8b6e20b2184d1d1aee51f53342d98504b7","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 3 of arXiv:2606.06193, 'Peng's Maximum Principle for McKean-Vlasov Stochastic Differential Equations with Common N'] For $\varphi:\R^d\times\cP_2(\R^d)\to \R^m $ we say $\varphi\in C_b^{2,1}(\R^d\times\cP_2(\R^d),\R^m)$ if
    \begin{enumerate}[(i)]

{"assumptions":["independent coordinates with finite ranges","f real valued"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T08:50:16.134177+00:00","domain":"Hoeffding (ANOVA) decomposition on finite product spaces","id":"claim_18de152cd6b3f3dde27fe3acec21197ea05d1c17bca342890c19af231c9bf2ed","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X = (X_1, ..., X_n) have independent coordinates with finite ranges, f a real function of X, and f = sum over S of f_S its Hoeffding (ANOVA) decomposition over subsets S of {1, ..., n}: f_S depends only on X_S, f_empty = E f, and E[f_S | X_T] = 0 unless S is inside T. Put w_S = E[f_S^2] and W_k = sum over |S| = k of w_S, the variance at interaction order k. For 0 <= t <= n let A_t f be the average over t-element sets T of E[f | X_T], and for 0 <= k <= n put P_k = binom(n, k) sum_{t=0}^k (-1)^(k - t) binom(k, t) A_t. Then P_k f = sum over |S| = k of f_S: P_k is the orthogonal projector onto the order-k part, so P_j P_k = 0 for j != k, P_k^2 = P_k, sum_k P_k = I and ||P_k f||_2^2 = W_k. If K_r f(x) is the average over |A| = r of E[f(X^(A)) | X = x], with X^(A) redrawing X_A independently, then K_r = A_{n - r}, so the same alternating combination of the K_{n - t} recovers each order.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(X, M) is a measurable space","mu is sigma-finite (needed for the Radon-Nikodym density)","nu is sigma-finite (needed for existence of the decomposition); for signed or complex nu, finite total variation","absolute continuity and mutual singularity are with respect to the same sigma-algebra M"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:13:10.402094+00:00","domain":"measure theory, Radon-Nikodym and decomposition","id":"claim_18fa6795088dd8fb6799c6e0c0ce7eb13ec14601000f98529cdd5659c067baeb","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, M) be a measurable space and let mu and nu be SIGMA-FINITE positive measures on M. Then nu can be written as nu = nu_a + nu_s with nu_a absolutely continuous with respect to mu (nu_a << mu) and nu_s mutually singular with mu (nu_s perp mu), and this decomposition is unique. Combined with the Radon-Nikodym theorem, nu_a has a density: there is an M-measurable f >= 0, unique up to mu-null sets, with nu_a(E) = integral_E f dmu for all E in M; f is in L^1(mu) exactly when nu_a is a finite measure. The statement extends to nu a signed or complex measure of finite total variation with mu sigma-finite. WHERE IT FAILS: (a) sigma-finiteness of nu is essential for existence of the decomposition. Take X = [0,1] with the Borel sets, mu = Lebesgue measure and nu = counting measure. If nu = nu_a + nu_s with nu_a << mu and nu_s perp mu, pick E with mu(E) = 0 and nu_s(X minus E) = 0. For any x outside E we get nu({x}) = nu_a({x}), and mu({x}) = 0 forces nu_a({x}) = 0, contradicting nu({x}) = 1. So X minus E is empty, i.e. E = X, contradicting mu(X) = 1 > 0. (b) sigma-finiteness of mu is essential for the DENSITY. With mu = counting measure on [0,1] and nu = Lebesgue measure one has nu << mu, yet no f satisfies nu(E) = integral_E f dmu (evaluating on singletons forces f = 0). The decomposition itself survives here (nu_s = 0), but the Radon-Nikodym half does not. (c) Uniqueness is uniqueness of the pair of measures; the density f is only mu-almost everywhere unique.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:44:27.893196+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_19101d3b19fa7dede03e1f1d289b2f3b9303322e4f5bb44a12b4820ccaff511b","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 2 (Large deviations principle) of arXiv:2607.12666, 'Sample-path Large deviations for \\Scheduled Arrival Processes with Unpunctuality'] Let $(E,\mathcal{T})$ be a topological space. A sequence of random elements $\{X^{(n)}\}$ taking values in $E$ satisfies a large deviations principle with speed $n$ and rate function $I:E\to[0,\infty]$ if:
\begin{itemize}
\item for every closed set $F\subset E$,
\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\log \Pbb(X^{(n)}\in F)
\le -\inf_{x\in F} I(x),
\]
\item for every open set $G\subset E$,
\[
\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\log \Pbb(X^{(n)}\in G)
\ge -\inf_{x\in G} I(x).
\]
\end{itemize}
The rate function $I$ is called {\it good} if its level sets $\{x: I(x)\le M\}$ are compact for all $M<\infty$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["translation invariance","ergodicity under the translations","finite energy","an amenable transitive graph such as Z^d; the theorem FAILS on nonamenable graphs"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.543290+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_19571635c9811ef2c4fa9bf7413abff7ada34807a8dc3b1fc48636004a01b663","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let mu be a probability measure on {0,1}^{E(Z^d)} that is (i) invariant under the lattice translations, (ii) ERGODIC with respect to them, and (iii) has the FINITE ENERGY property: for every edge e, the conditional probability that e is open given the states of all other edges lies almost surely strictly between 0 and 1. Then the number of infinite open clusters is almost surely a constant taking the value 0 or 1. Each of the three hypotheses does work. Ergodicity is what makes the number a constant rather than a random variable; without it a mixture of two percolation measures is a counterexample. Finite energy is what rules out infinitely many infinite clusters, by allowing local modifications; a measure that deterministically forbids certain local patterns can have infinitely many. And the argument uses AMENABILITY of Z^d - on a regular tree or another nonamenable transitive graph there is genuinely a regime with infinitely many infinite clusters, so the theorem is false there. Bernoulli percolation satisfies all three hypotheses for every p, so its infinite cluster is unique whenever it exists. [Burton and Keane (1989), Comm. Math. Phys. 121; see Grimmett, Percolation, 2nd ed., Theorem 8.1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["a Markov chain, here a Galton-Watson branching process, with an identified P-harmonic function h appropriate to the conditioning event","for Kesten's tree specifically: finite-mean offspring distribution with criticality or subcriticality correctly identified, and a precisely specified conditioning event","existence of the relevant weak-convergence limit of the conditioned law to the h-transformed law, which must be checked rather than assumed","correct identification of the size-biased offspring law along the spine, which differs from the original offspring law"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.994756+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_195cce09417950c349c4fdda5edd9f33edbe4cce03fe18f997181d11d952556c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). Given a Markov chain with kernel P and a nonnegative P-harmonic function h, the Doob h-transform defines a new Markov chain with kernel P^h(x,y) = P(x,y) h(y)/h(x), representing the law of the original chain conditioned, in an appropriate limiting sense such as conditioning to survive forever or on an asymptotic event, to respect the weighting given by h. Applied to a critical or subcritical Galton-Watson branching process conditioned to survive forever, or, for critical trees, conditioned to have total size n with n -> infinity, the Kesten tree construction realizes the limiting law as an explicit infinite random tree: a single infinite spine, with each spine vertex additionally carrying an independent number of extra children distributed according to the size-biased-minus-one offspring law, each extra child then supporting an ordinary, unconditioned Galton-Watson subtree. This gives the exact local weak limit of large conditioned critical or subcritical branching trees and underlies scaling-limit results, such as convergence to the continuum random tree, that first pass through this explicit infinite-tree description. It does not directly give scaling limits of the whole tree's metric structure, which requires an additional contour or height-function argument, and the exact form of the spine's offspring law is specific to the conditioning event used, since conditioning on survival forever and conditioning on total size n give related but generally distinct limiting infinite trees. Typical failure: Confusing the different conditioning regimes for the conditioned Galton-Watson tree, such as conditioning on survival to infinity versus conditioning on total progeny exactly n as n -> infinity versus conditioning on height n, as if they all give the identical Kesten tree limit; they give related but generally distinct limiting infinite trees, differing in the spine's offspring bias and finer distributional details, and using one variant's known properties for a computation set up under a different conditioning is a frequent, easy-to-miss error. Canonical reference: Doob, 1957, Annales de l'Institut Fourier; Kesten, 1986, Annales de l'Institut Henri Poincare, Probabilites et Statistiques; Lyons, Pemantle and Peres, 1995, Annals of Probability.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:12:46.873192+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_196dc52f07f00d6043b3137b21fc6c200d1241e94baf64b25a1082e146b614ec","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:hill of arXiv:2608.08375, 'Algebraic formulas for first-passage times of Markov processes in the linear framework: ge'] The vertices of $\mathcal{H}_u[G]$ are the non-terminal vertices of $G$, $\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{H}_u[G]) = \overline{Z}$. The edges and labels of $\mathcal{H}_u[G]$ are acquired from those of $G$ through the following rules.
\begin{enumerate}[topsep=1em]
    \item If $j, k \in \overline{Z}$ are non-terminal vertices with $k \neq u$ ($j = u$ is allowed) and there is an edge $j \to_G k$, then there is an edge $j \to_{\mathcal{H}_u[G]} k$ with, 
    \[
        \ell(j \to_{\mathcal{H}_u[G]} k) = \ell(j \to_G k) \,.
    \]
    \item If $j \in \overline{Z}$ is a non-terminal vertex and there is an edge $j \rightarrow_G u$, then there is an edge $j \to_{\mathcal{H}_u[G]} u$ with, 
    \[
        \ell(j \to_{\mathcal{H}_u[G]} u) = \ell(j \to_G u) + \sum_{j \rightarrow_G z ,\, z \in Z} \ell(j \rightarrow_G z) \,.
    \]
    \item If $j \in \overline{Z}$ is a non-terminal vertex other than $u$ ($j \neq u$) without an edge to $u$ ($j \not\to_G u$) but with at least one edge, $j \to_G z$, to some $z \in Z$, then there is an edge $j \rightarrow_{\mathcal{H}_u[G]} u$ with, 
    \[
        \ell(j \rightarrow_{\mathcal{H}_u[G]} u) = \sum_{j \rightarrow_G z ,\, z \in Z} \ell(j \rightarrow_G z) \,.
    \]
\end{enumerate}
There are no other edges in $\mathcal{H}_u[G]$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the cleaners compared are consistent for the population covariance (sample, eta-RIE without floor, LW2020, NERCOME)","the ensemble error covariance is rank-deficient in practice (members near-collinear), so the unconstrained plug-in has near-null sample directions"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T07:18:07.916034+00:00","domain":"ensemble learning / covariance estimation","id":"claim_1979e55efac080980a9b8016771f4431a63d793eddbb97023ada620cc4079e30","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Read the ladder result (every consistent cleaner ties inside the long-only stack; floors and linear shrinkage lose) through the entrywise bound. Unconstrained minimum variance depends on $\\hat\\Sigma^{-1}$, so its error is governed by the SPECTRUM of $\\hat\\Sigma$: the ratio $q = M/n$, the bulk edge, the near-null directions - the territory of random-matrix cleaning, where the Ledoit-Peche oracle, its analytical estimate and NERCOME differ from the sample covariance by design. The long-only plug-in's excess risk is bounded by twice the ENTRYWISE error $\\varepsilon = \\max_{ij}|\\hat\\Sigma_{ij} - \\Sigma_{ij}|$, which is $O(\\sqrt{\\log M/n})$ for the sample covariance and of the same order for every consistent estimator (a consistent nonlinear shrinkage moves the eigenvalues by $O(n^{-1/2})$ relative, hence the entries by the same order) - so all of them obey the same bound and, on the well-conditioned active submatrix, produce the same weights. A fixed floor $f\\sigma^2$ on the small eigenvalues, or a linear shrinkage $\\rho(\\mu I - \\hat\\Sigma)$, is a BIAS of size $f\\sigma^2$ (or $\\rho|\\mu - \\Sigma_{ii}|$) in the entries spanned by those directions that does not vanish with $n$; it cannot tighten the bound and it displaces the plug-in wherever an active member has weight in a floored direction. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:22:08.302412+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_19a5425d5320073dffe4e7e97162d0002e041499308edf2a775c6e7dbda71421","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:band-limited-orbit-coding of arXiv:2607.25616, 'Stealthy point processes and lattice induction'] Fix
\[
    \frac12<\sigma<1.
\]
There exist $\tau\in(\frac12,\sigma)$ and a real entire function
$\psi$ such that
\[
    \psi(n)
    =
    \begin{cases}
        1,&n=0,\\
        0,&n\in\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\},
    \end{cases}
\]
and, for every $j,N\geq0$,
\[
    \left|\psi^{(j)}(x+iy)\right|
    \leq
    C_{j,N}
    e^{2\pi\sigma|y|}
    (1+|x|)^{-N}.
\]
Moreover,
\[
    \operatorname{supp}\widehat\psi
    \subset[-\tau,\tau].
\]

Let $b:Z\to[-1,1]$ be a Borel injection and define
\[
    H_z(w)
    :=

\]
The series and all its derivatives converge locally uniformly on
$\mathbb C$. The map
\[
    z\longmapsto H_z
\]
is Borel for the topology of locally uniform convergence, and
\[
    H_z(n)=b(T^nz),
    \qquad
    H_{Tz}(w)=H_z(w+1).
\]
For every $j\geq0$,
\[
    \left|H_z^{(j)}(x+iy)\right|
    \leq
    C_j e^{2\pi\sigma|y|}
\]
uniformly in $z\in Z$ and $x,y\in\mathbb R$. Finally,
\[
    \operatorname{supp}\widehat H_z
    \subset[-\tau,\tau]
    \qquad
    (z\in Z).
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.349210+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_19a76e2dc934a60d9e20f80a59b8a2a7bf1420c51133d0aa6b6a875b4fe6a527","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 168 (errors from spatial rerandomization) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\vY$ be the spatial rerandomization of $\vX^\trunc$, defined by \eqref{e:def.Y}
with indices $(a(q_0), \ldots, a(\dmax))$ sampled according to Definition~\ref{d:rerand}. Then we have
	\begin{align*} 
	\max\bigg\{
	\Big|\Delta Y^{\sigma}(q_d)
		-\Delta X^{\trunc,\sigma}(q_d, a(q_{d+1}))\Big|
		: \sigma\in\{
		\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII
		\}
		\bigg\}
		&\le 2\eta\,,\\
	\bigg|
	\Delta Y^{\Ising}(q_d)
	-\Delta X^{\trunc,\Ising}(q_d,i(q_{d+1}))
	\bigg|
	&\le2\eta\,.
	\end{align*}
for all $0\le d\le \dmax-1$. The same holds with $(\vY^\frozen,\vX^\frozen)$ in place of $(\vY,\vX^\trunc)$.

\begin{proof}
We prove the estimate for
$Y^{\RomI}$ versus $X^{\trunc,\RomI}$; the other bounds follow by the same argument. It follows from the definition~\eqref{e:def.Y} that
	\[
	\Delta Y^{\RomI}(q_d)
	= \sum_{a\in B(q_{d+1},a(q_{d+1}))}
	\frac{X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_{d+1},a)}{|B(q_{d+1},a(q_{d+1}))|}
	-\sum_{a\in B(q_d,a(q_d))}
	\frac{X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a)}{|B(q_d,a(q_d))|}\,.
	\]
Marginally, $a(q_d)$ is a uniformly random index from $[M]$. Conditional on $\cG(q_d)$, the index $a(q_{d+1})$ is sampled uniformly at random from  $B=B(q_d,a(q_d))$, the bucket at time $q_d$ that contains $a(q_d)$. 
It follows from the definitions of the buckets (see~\eqref{e:bucket}) that
	\begin{align*}
	\max\bigg\{ \Big|X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_{d+1},a)
	-X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_{d+1},a(q_{d+1}))\Big|
	: a\in B(q_{d+1},a(q_{d+1}))
	\bigg\} &\le \eta\,,\\
	\max\bigg\{ \Big|X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a)
	-X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))\Big|
	: a\in B(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))
	\bigg\} &\le \eta\,,
	\end{align*}
where the second bound uses that
$a(q_{d+1})$ and $a(q_d)$ are in the same bucket $B$ at time $q_d$.
Since $\vY(q_d)$ is obtained by averaging $\vX^\trunc(q_d,a)$ over $a\in B$, we immediately obtain
	\[
	\max\bigg\{
	\Big|Y^{\RomI}(q_d)
	- X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a(q_d))\Big|,
	\Big|Y^{\RomI}(q_d)
	- X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))\Big|
	\bigg\} \le\eta\,.
	\]
Likewise, since $\vY(q_{d+1})$ is obtained by averaging 
$\vX^\trunc(q_{d+1},a')$ over $a'\in B'=B(q_{d+1},a(q_{d+1}))$, we have
	\beq
	\Big|Y^{\RomI}(q_{d+1})
	- X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_{d+1},a(q_{d+1}))\Big| \le\eta\,.
	\eeq
Combining these gives the claimed bound.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["uniform product measure on the discrete cube {-1,1}^n","f real-valued and square integrable on the cube","C is a universal constant, in particular independent of n and of f"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.628427+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_19af561bcf040b56cc9b3aa80d52d5dd62e1e00c1b7ecb97b574cbacb19b5603","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f : {-1,1}^n -> R with the uniform product measure and let Delta_i f (x) = ( f(x) - f(x^{(i)}) ) / 2, where x^{(i)} flips coordinate i. Then there is a UNIVERSAL constant C with Var(f) <= C sum_{i=1}^n || Delta_i f ||_2^2 / ( 1 + log( || Delta_i f ||_2 / || Delta_i f ||_1 ) ), with the convention that a term is 0 when Delta_i f = 0. The unimproved bound Var(f) <= sum_i ||Delta_i f||_2^2 is the Efron-Stein inequality on the cube; Talagrand's refinement gains a LOGARITHMIC factor for every coordinate whose influence is spread out, that is whose L2 and L1 norms are far apart, and gains nothing for a coordinate whose discrete derivative is essentially an indicator. This is precisely the inequality Benjamini, Kalai and Schramm apply to first-passage percolation with two-valued weights to obtain Var <= C n / log n, and the reason their theorem carries a two-point weight hypothesis is that the L1-L2 comparison must be run on that specific cube structure. The p-biased and Gaussian analogues exist with modified constants; the Gaussian version replaces the log ratio by an entropy term (Falik-Samorodnitsky). [Talagrand (1994), 'On Russo's approximate zero-one law', Ann. Probab. 22; used in Benjamini-Kalai-Schramm (2003)]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the uniform product measure on {-1,1}^n","1 <= p <= q < infinity and 0 <= rho <= sqrt((p-1)/(q-1))","the constant is independent of n"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.628214+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_19e3e9af2b5ddcfa431ba08524a9369ff10ac214b8a1b8391f61eaf614565d0c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f : {-1,1}^n -> R with the uniform measure, with Fourier-Walsh expansion f = sum_{S subset [n]} fhat(S) chi_S where chi_S(x) = prod_{i in S} x_i. For 0 <= rho <= 1 define the noise operator T_rho f = sum_S rho^{|S|} fhat(S) chi_S. Then for all 1 <= p <= q < infinity, || T_rho f ||_q <= || f ||_p whenever rho <= sqrt( (p-1)/(q-1) ). Two standard specialisations: taking p = 2 gives || T_rho f ||_q <= || f ||_2 for rho = 1/sqrt(q-1); and for f of DEGREE at most d, meaning fhat(S) = 0 whenever |S| > d, one gets || f ||_q <= (q-1)^{d/2} || f ||_2 for every q >= 2, and by duality || f ||_2 <= (q-1)^{d/2} ||f||_{q'} for the conjugate exponent. The degree-d moment comparison is the workhorse: it says low-degree functions on the cube have all L^q norms comparable to their L^2 norm with a constant depending only on the degree and q, not on n, which is exactly the dimension-free input that KKL and Talagrand's variance inequality consume. The measure must be the UNIFORM (or a fixed p-biased, with a different constant) product measure - the theorem is about product measures on the cube. {"assumptions":["Omega is a bounded open subset of R^n, n >= 2","A is measurable, bounded and uniformly elliptic (no continuity assumed)","f is in L^1(Omega); the data may also be a bounded Radon measure with the same conclusions","the approximating data f_m are bounded, converge to f in L^1, and have L^1 norms bounded by ||f||_{L^1}","q is strictly less than n/(n-1)","conclusions are for the approximating sequence and its limit, not for an arbitrary distributional solution"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:13:10.396034+00:00","domain":"elliptic PDE, equations with measure or L^1 data","id":"claim_1a2ed3a0477ecc6b19ac15853dd25ba30feec9956659f5a93173e31f2bcfe10f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Omega be a bounded open subset of R^n with n >= 2, and let A be measurable, bounded and uniformly elliptic on Omega (alpha|xi|^2 <= A(x)xi.xi, |A(x)| <= Lambda, alpha > 0). Let f be in L^1(Omega) and let f_m be any sequence in L^infinity(Omega) with ||f_m||_{L^1} <= ||f||_{L^1} and f_m -> f in L^1 (for instance f_m = T_m(f), the truncation of f at level m). Let u_m in H^1_0(Omega) solve -div(A grad u_m) = f_m weakly. Then: (i) for every q with 1 <= q < n/(n-1) the sequence (u_m) is bounded in W^{1,q}_0(Omega) by a constant depending only on n, q, alpha, |Omega| and ||f||_{L^1}; (ii) up to a subsequence u_m converges strongly in W^{1,q}_0(Omega) and almost everywhere, together with its gradients, to a function u in W^{1,q}_0(Omega) which is a distributional solution: integral_Omega A grad u . grad phi = integral_Omega f phi for every phi in C_c^infinity(Omega); (iii) the limit satisfies the Marcinkiewicz (weak-Lebesgue) bounds u in M^(n/(n-2)) for n >= 3 and |grad u| in M^(n/(n-1)), with norms controlled by ||f||_{L^1}. {"assumptions":["A in C4(R,R^{q x q})","0<mI<=H<=MI globally","sup norm A prime<=D; sup norm H^(j)<=B_j, j=1..4","iid z independent of past, z equal in law to -z, EzzT=I, E|z|6 finite","sigma>=0; eta in (0,min(1,1/M)]","u0 deterministic; v0=0","F bounded C3 with bounded derivatives"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T19:48:21.750439+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_1acc06ed77c5a3544de7b5d174203e8bbf687cbf55975a914b5375320d1a09ac","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT. Status: proof (unaudited), claim w730-T355-C002 version 2; not independently checked. The scalar tangential coordinate is u in R; v is in R^q. Let A:R -> R^{q x q}
be C^4, q>=1 an integer, H=A^T A, and assume, globally,

    0 < m I <= H(u) <= M I,
    ||A'(u)|| <= D,  ||H^(j)(u)|| <= B_j, j=1,2,3,4.

Matrix norms are operator norms. Constants m,M,D,B_j are finite and independent
of eta. Let sigma>=0. The iid label noises z_k have a centrally symmetric law,
E z_k z_k^T=I, and mu_6=E|z_k|^6<infinity; put mu_4=E|z_k|^4. No almost-sure noise bound is assumed. In particular E z_k=0. Set
eta_0=min(1,1/M), 0<eta<=eta_0. Start from deterministic (u_0,0).
Consider full-vector label-noise SGD for residual A(u)v and loss
L(u,v)=|A(u)v|^2/2:

    d_k=u_{k+1}-u_k
       =-eta v_k^T H'(u_k)v_k/2 -eta sigma z_k^T A'(u_k)v_k,
    v_{k+1}=(I-eta H(u_k))v_k-eta sigma A(u_k)^T z_k.

On v=0 its noise covariance is sigma^2 Hess L. The limiting ODE is

    U'=b(U),  b(u)=-sigma^2 tr H'(u)/4,  U(0)=u_0.

This is the known limiting flow of Li-Wang-Arora, Corollary 5.2, arXiv
2110.06914v4, printed pp.8-9 and 33. Their Theorem 4.6 supplies convergence,
not the explicit error estimate below. The hardest quantitative step here
is averaging with a coefficient that depends on u and shares the same noise
as the normal update. Section 4 computes that correlation rather than
discarding it as a martingale.

## 1. Constants and conclusion

Let F:R^{1+q}->R be bounded C^3, with bounded derivatives. Write
f(u)=F(u,0), F_j=sup |f^(j)|, j=1,2,3, and
F_vv=sup ||D_v^2 F||. The displayed bound uses only these seminorms.
Define

    c2=sigma^2 q M/m,
    c4=[sigma^2 M(2q+4)c2 + sigma^4 M^2 mu_4]/m,
    c6=[sigma^2 M(3q+12)c4 + 15 sigma^4 M^2 mu_4 c2
        + sigma^6 M^3 mu_6]/m,
    J2=B_1^2 c4/4+sigma^2 D^2 c2,
    Jcv=B_1^2 c6/4+B_1^2 sigma^2 M q c4/4
         +sigma^2 D^2 q c4+sigma^4 D^2 M mu_4 c2.

For j=0,1,2,3 put beta_j=sigma^2 q B_{j+1}/4. For T>=0 set

    G1=F_1 exp(beta_1 T),
    G2=exp(2 beta_1 T)(F_2+beta_2 T F_1),
    G3=exp(3 beta_1 T)[F_3+3 beta_2 T F_2
                     +(beta_3 T+3 beta_2^2 T^2/2)F_1],
    Gtu=beta_1 G1+beta_0 G2,
    Gtt=beta_0 beta_1 G1+beta_0^2 G2.

Define

    S0=B_1/(2m),
    S1=(B_2+2B_1 S0)/(2m),
    S2=(B_3+2B_2 S0+4B_1 S1)/(2m),
    C0=G1 S0/2,
    C1=(G2 S0+G1 S1)/2,
    C2=(G3 S0+2G2 S1+G1 S2)/2,
    Ct=Gtu S0/2.

Finally let

    Qg=G2 J2/2 + Gtu sqrt(J2) + Gtt/2,
    Qc=C0 M^2 c2
       +C1 B_1(c4+sigma^2 q M c2)/2
       +2 sigma^2 C1 sqrt(M) D c2
       +2 C2 Jcv + Ct c2,
    C(T)=(C0+F_vv/2)c2 + T(Qg+Qc).

Then, simultaneously for all integers 0<=k<=T/eta^2,

    |E F(u_k,v_k)-F(U(k eta^2),0)| <= C(T) eta.       (1)

The exponent is a=1. The finite constant is explicit in the hypotheses and
the stated observable seminorms. H and H' need not commute. This includes
every finite normal dimension q, and arbitrary smooth rotating output
frames A satisfying the bounds. The tangential dimension remains one.
It permits unbounded symmetric noise, including Gaussian labels. Fixed
off-manifold initialization is not addressed.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:39:41.441547+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1ad3e11fcf1a534b4a0bea93886abc8c9d9a7f3110ce39a1c7d21980402469d5","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 4 of arXiv:2604.07478, 'Mixing Times and Cutoff for the Rook's Walk'] The Rook's Walk with dimension $d\in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 2}$ and board length $n\in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 3}$ is transitive.
  \begin{proof}
  Fix $x,y\in \Omega$ and let $d = (y-x \bmod n+1)$. Define, $\xi_{(x,y)}: \Omega \to \Omega$ as,
  \[v \overset{\xi_{(x,y)}}{\longmapsto} v + d,\quad  \quad \forall v\in \Omega\]
  Now, notice that,
  \begin{align*}
   \xi_{(x,y)}(x) &= x + d\\
   &= (x\bmod n+1) + (y-x \bmod n+1)\\
   &= (y\bmod n+1)\\
   &= y
  \end{align*}
  Therefore, $\xi_{(x,y)}$ satisfies our first condition. Now, fix $z,w \in \Omega$. Notice that the transition probability $P(z,w)$ is dependent only on the Hamming distance between $z$ and $w$ (Recall that $||z-w||_0$ is the Hamming distance). Further we have,
  \[||\xi_{(x,y)}(z) - \xi_{(x,y)}(w)||_0 = ||(z+d)-(w+d)||_0= ||z-w||_0\]
  That is, Hamming distance is invariant under $\xi_{(x,y)}$ and, by extension, \[P(z,w) = P(\xi_{(x,y)}(z), \xi_{(x,y)}(w))\]
  Therefore, the Rook's Walk is transitive.
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:48:47.287978+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1af3bd520266f791e66f402c3180bffd80ccb737cd4d487899c876d22d3d6be6","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma det app of arXiv:2604.20660, 'The Legendre structure of the TAP complexity\\ for the Ising spin glass'] Fix $q\in(0,1)$, $\delta\in(0,1)$, and let $\zeta\in\mathcal P([0,1])$.
		For every $s\in[0,1]$, set
		\[
		\pi_s\zeta:=\zeta|_{(s,1]}+\zeta([0,s])\delta_s,

		\qquad m\in[-1,1].
		\]
		Assume that there exist $\varepsilon_0>0$ and $u_0>0$ such that
		\[
		[q-\varepsilon_0,q+\varepsilon_0]\subset (0,1)
		\qquad\text{and}\qquad
		\zeta([0,s])\ge u_0
		\quad\text{for every } s\in[q-\varepsilon_0,q+\varepsilon_0].
		\]
		Let $0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0$, let $\mathbf{m}\in[-1+\delta,1-\delta]^N$ satisfy
		\[
		q_\mathbf{m}\in(q-\varepsilon,q+\varepsilon),
		\qquad
		\mathrm{dist}\!\bigl(\zeta_\mathbf{m},\pi_q\zeta\bigr)\le \varepsilon,
		\]
		and let $f\in\mathbb{R}$. Writing $T_\zeta:=T_{\zeta,q}$, one has
		\begin{multline}
			\log \mathbb{E}\Bigl[
			\bigl|\det(\nabla^2F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m}))\bigr|
			\;\Bigm|\;
			\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})=0,\,
			F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})=Nf

\begin{equation}
 J(x)=\det DT(x)>0,

\end{equation}
Let $U\subset B_{10}$ be any open set such that
$T|_U:U\to V:=T(U)$ is a $C^2$ diffeomorphism.
Then the restriction $Y|_U$ parametrizes the graph of a function
$\widetilde u\in C^2(V)$; that is,
\[
 Y(U)=\{(y,\widetilde u(y)):y\in V\}.
\]
Moreover,
\begin{equation}
  D_y\widetilde u(y)=Du(x),
 \qquad y=T(x), \qquad x\in U.
\end{equation}

{"assumptions":["1 ≤ p < ∞","(A): u ∈ W^{1,p}_0(Ω), Ω contained in a slab of finite width d (no boundary regularity needed)","(B): Ω bounded, connected, Lipschitz boundary (or convex), u ∈ W^{1,p}(Ω)"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:57.492434+00:00","domain":"Sobolev inequalities, elliptic PDE, coercivity","id":"claim_1b864127f2bba872e9317da0f8bb92499ed6de1b5bd8779daf961da7ad1cb410","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Ω ⊂ R^n be open and 1 ≤ p < ∞.

(A) Poincaré–Friedrichs inequality (zero boundary values). Suppose Ω is bounded in one direction: Ω ⊂ {x : a < x_1 < a + d} for some a and some finite d (in particular any bounded Ω, with d = diam Ω). Then for every u ∈ W^{1,p}_0(Ω)
   ||u||_{L^p(Ω)} ≤ d ||∂_1 u||_{L^p(Ω)} ≤ d ||∇u||_{L^p(Ω)}.
For p = 2 the sharp constant for a slab of width d is d/π: ||u||_{L^2} ≤ (d/π)||∇u||_{L^2} for u ∈ H^1_0(Ω). NO regularity of ∂Ω is required and Ω need not be connected. Consequently ||∇u||_{L^p} is a norm on W^{1,p}_0(Ω) equivalent to the full W^{1,p} norm, the Dirichlet form ∫|∇u|^2 is coercive on H^1_0(Ω), and for bounded Ω the best constant C_P in ||u||_2 ≤ C_P||∇u||_2 satisfies 1/C_P^2 = λ_1(Ω), the first Dirichlet eigenvalue of −Δ.

(B) Poincaré–Wirtinger inequality (mean-zero functions). Suppose Ω is bounded, connected, and has Lipschitz boundary (or is bounded, connected and convex; more generally a bounded connected W^{1,p}-extension domain). Then there is C = C(Ω, p) with
   ||u − u_Ω||_{L^p(Ω)} ≤ C ||∇u||_{L^p(Ω)}  for all u ∈ W^{1,p}(Ω),  u_Ω = (1/|Ω|) ∫_Ω u dx.
For convex Ω and p = 2 the sharp constant is diam(Ω)/π (Payne–Weinberger). Consequently u ↦ ||∇u||_{L^p} + |∫_Ω u| is a norm on W^{1,p}(Ω) equivalent to the W^{1,p} norm, and the Neumann problem is coercive on the mean-zero subspace.

Where it fails. (A) fails without zero boundary values: constants lie in W^{1,p}(Ω) with zero gradient. (A) fails on any domain containing balls of arbitrarily large radius (R^n, half-spaces, exterior domains): dilating one test function shows no constant works. (B) fails for disconnected Ω (a function equal to different constants on two components). (B) fails on some bounded connected domains with bad boundary (rooms-and-passages domains, sufficiently sharp outward cusps), where functions that are ≈0 in one part and ≈1 in another can have arbitrarily small gradient energy; Lipschitz boundary rules this out. In (B) the constant depends on Ω and blows up as the domain degenerates (e.g. a thin neck).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["H is a complex Hilbert space","T is densely defined (needed for T* to be an operator)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.769532+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, unbounded operators, spectral theory","id":"claim_1b902b4a41e8c34e8b840d74a6ef14815baf6efeb2a8a6cb619f154eae6d0982","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let H be a complex Hilbert space (inner product linear in the first slot) and T: D(T) ⊂ H → H linear and densely defined. The adjoint T* has domain D(T*) = {y ∈ H : x ↦ ⟨Tx, y⟩ is bounded on D(T)}, and for y ∈ D(T*), T*y is the unique z ∈ H with ⟨Tx, y⟩ = ⟨x, z⟩ for all x ∈ D(T) (uniqueness uses density of D(T); without density T* is not a well-defined operator). T is symmetric (Hermitian) if it is densely defined and ⟨Tx, y⟩ = ⟨x, Ty⟩ for all x, y ∈ D(T), i.e. T ⊂ T*. T is self-adjoint if T = T*, which includes the equality of domains D(T) = D(T*). T is essentially self-adjoint if it is symmetric and its closure T̄ is self-adjoint (equivalently, T is symmetric and has exactly one self-adjoint extension). For a closed symmetric T the deficiency subspaces are K_+ = ker(T* − i) = Ran(T + i)^⊥ and K_- = ker(T* + i) = Ran(T − i)^⊥, and the deficiency indices are n_± = dim K_± ∈ {0, 1, 2, ..., ∞}. A symmetric T is bounded below (semibounded) with bound c ∈ ℝ if ⟨Tx, x⟩ ≥ c‖x‖² for all x ∈ D(T); positive if c = 0 works. For symmetric T one always has T ⊂ T̄ ⊂ T* and T̄ = T**.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:32:23.588420+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1bbdc0671006af81fc37c9885d0816b787449a4a45694ffba824f88710fd9496","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm RT of arXiv:2603.15323, '\Large \bf Small-time heat decay for stable processes on fractal drums'] Suppose that a map $f:{\mathbb R}\to {\mathbb R}$ satisfies the renewal equation (equation eqn:RE of the paper) with
\[
\lim_{z\to-\infty}f(z)=0,
\]
and 
\[
|\phi(z)|\leq c_{1}e^{-c_{2}|z|}, \quad z\in {\mathbb R},
\]
for some constants $c_1,c_2>0$. Then, the solution of the renewal equation (equation eqn:RE of the paper) is given by
\[
f(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}L^{n}\phi(z)=\phi(z)+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\sum_{i_1,\cdots, i_n} 
c_{i_1}\cdots c_{i_n}L_{\gamma_{i_1}}\cdots L_{\gamma_{i_{n}}}\phi(z),
\]
where $i_1,\cdots, i_n$ take values from 1 to $N$ and are not necessarily different.

$$
f(z)=\frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}c_{j}\gamma_{j}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\phi(x)dx +o(1) \text{ as } z\to\infty.
$$ 
If $\{\gamma_{j}\}$ is arithmetic with span $\gamma$, then
$$
f(z)=\frac{\gamma}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}c_{j}\gamma_{j}}\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}\phi(z-k\gamma) +o(1) \text{ as } z\to\infty.
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}
