{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:51:26.590254+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1c10fe6b4003997db129ff47f14d2f95ef1ffc18f1857fb25ac7eadd1b3625ad","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:existence of arXiv:2606.02003, 'Higher-Order Multifractional Stable Motion:\\ Definition and Fundamental Properties'] Under Assumption~(ass:params of the paper), the following hold.

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item \textbf{Well-definedness.}
  For each $t \in \mathbb{R}$,
  $f_n(t,\cdot;H,\alpha) \in L^\alpha(\mathbb{R})$,
  so $X^{(n)}_H(t)$ is a well-defined S$\alpha$S random variable.

\item \textbf{Finite-dimensional distributions.}
  For any $m \in \mathbb{N}^*$, $t_1,\ldots,t_m \in \mathbb{R}$,
  and $\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_m \in \mathbb{R}$:
  \begin{equation}
  
  \mathbb{E}\!\left[
  \exp\!\Bigl(i\sum_{j=1}^m\theta_j X^{(n)}_H(t_j)\Bigr)
  \right]
  = \exp\!\left(
  -\int_\mathbb{R}\Bigl|\sum_{j=1}^m\theta_j f_n(t_j,u)\Bigr|^\alpha\,du
  \right).
  \end{equation}

\item \textbf{S$\alpha$S property.}
  For any $\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_m \in \mathbb{R}$,
  the linear combination $\sum_{j=1}^m\theta_j X^{(n)}_H(t_j)$
  is S$\alpha$S. In particular, $(X^{(n)}_H(t_1),\ldots,X^{(n)}_H(t_m))$
  is a jointly S$\alpha$S random vector.

\item \textbf{Scale.}
  $\bigl\|X^{(n)}_H(t)\bigr\|_\alpha^\alpha
  = \int_\mathbb{R}|f_n(t,u)|^\alpha\,du < \infty$.

\item \textbf{Higher-order increment stationarity.}
  For $H$ constant ($H(t) \equiv H \in (n-1,n)$), the
  $n$-th order increment process
  \begin{equation}
  
  \Delta^n_h X^{(n)}_H(t)
  := \sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^{n-k}\binom{n}{k}X^{(n)}_H(t+kh),
  \quad h \in \mathbb{R},
  \end{equation}
  is stationary in $t$. For functional $H(\cdot)$, the distribution
  of $\Delta^n_h X^{(n)}_H(t)$ depends on $t$ only through the
  values $H(t), H(t+h), \ldots, H(t+nh)$.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Bernoulli percolation with the ghost-field magnetisation M(p,h)","Russo's formula and the pivotal decomposition (Simon-Lieb type inequality)","Conclusions are one-sided mean-field bounds and sharpness, never continuity at p_c"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.988803+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1c135835662116d8bd927dc5acd650b6de0faa870e088f5dd7fd1ab1414511d1","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). Aizenman-Barsky (1987), for Bernoulli percolation on Z^d (and general transitive graphs), work with the magnetisation M(p,h) = P(0 is connected to a ghost vertex attached to every site with probability 1 - e^{-h}) and prove two differential inequalities: M <= h dM/dh + M^2 + p M dM/dp and dM/dp <= |J| M dM/dh (|J| the coordination constant), the first of Simon-Lieb type via the pivotal decomposition, the second from Russo's formula. Integrating them gives: (i) sharpness of the phase transition, i.e. the susceptibility chi(p) is finite for every p < p_c, hence exponential decay of connectivities below p_c; (ii) the mean-field bounds M(p_c,h) >= c h^{1/2} (delta >= 2) and theta(p) >= c (p - p_c) for p > p_c (beta <= 1). What they do NOT prove: continuity of theta at p_c (theta(p_c) = 0 is open for 3 <= d <= 10), or the matching upper bounds beta >= 1, delta <= 2 (those need the triangle condition, i.e. the lace expansion in high dimensions). The same inequalities transfer to the Ising model via the random-current representation (Aizenman-Barsky-Fernandez). Typical failure: Conflating the auxiliary percolation ghost field h with an actual physical parameter of the underlying model, or applying the conclusion theta(p_c)=0 to a percolation variant where FKG fails for the ghost-augmented measure, such as certain dependent percolation models; the entire argument rests on FKG holding for the specific augmented construction, and this needs to be re-verified for each new model rather than assumed to transfer automatically from ordinary Bernoulli percolation. Canonical reference: Aizenman and Barsky, 1987, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Aizenman, Kesten and Newman, 1987, Communications in Mathematical Physics.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["complex (or real) terms; the ratio test needs a_n != 0 eventually","limsup and liminf are taken in [0, infinity]; when the limits exist the tests read with the plain limit"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:31:12.479169+00:00","domain":"real analysis","id":"claim_1c217f746d95c3909891090744a766ac7bb7f0c720afa221f92c52b6b464afc1","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let sum a_n be a series of complex numbers. ROOT TEST (Cauchy): put L = limsup |a_n|^{1/n}. If L < 1 the series converges absolutely; if L > 1 it diverges (the terms do not tend to 0); if L = 1 the test is inconclusive. RATIO TEST (d'Alembert): suppose a_n != 0 for large n. If limsup |a_{n+1}/a_n| < 1 the series converges absolutely; if liminf |a_{n+1}/a_n| > 1 (in particular if |a_{n+1}/a_n| >= 1 for all large n) it diverges; otherwise the test is inconclusive. Comparison: for every sequence, liminf |a_{n+1}/a_n| <= liminf |a_n|^{1/n} <= limsup |a_n|^{1/n} <= limsup |a_{n+1}/a_n|, so whenever the ratio test decides, the root test decides the same way, and the root test is strictly stronger: for a_n = (1/2)^n for n even and (1/3)^n for n odd, the ratios oscillate between (2/3)^n -> 0 and (3/2)^{n} -> infinity so the ratio test says nothing, while |a_n|^{1/n} takes the values 1/2 and 1/3, limsup 1/2 < 1, and the series converges. Both tests are inconclusive for sum 1/n (divergent) and sum 1/n^2 (convergent), which have L = 1; the radius of convergence of a power series sum c_n z^n is 1 / limsup |c_n|^{1/n} (Cauchy-Hadamard), the root test in its most used form.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:55:18.060710+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1d14d0b7e9076743e4b8eb70c925c6f8a70259997b39f59d9cc901a99a3944d0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 3 of arXiv:2606.17381, 'Large deviation principle for friendship-biases\\ in Galton--Watson trees'] {\bf [LDP for type fractions along a random path]}

Under the joint law of the Galton--Watson tree $\mathcal{T}_\infty$ and the random exploration path, the family of random variables $\{\Upsilon_j\}_{j\in\N_4}$ satisfies the LDP in the Polish space $(0,\infty) \times \mathcal{S}_2$ with rate $j$ and with good rate function $J$ given by
\[
J(x,s) = \inf_{\nu \in \Phi(x,s)} I(\nu), \qquad x \in (0,\infty),\, s \in \mathcal{S}_2.
\]
Here,
\begin{itemize}
\item 
$I\colon\,\mathcal{P}(E) \to [0,\infty]$ is the good rate function given by
\[
I(\nu) =
\begin{cases}
H\left(\nu\,\middle\|\, \pi_{1,2}\nu \otimes \zeta^{\otimes 2}\right), & \text{if } \pi_{1,2}\nu=\pi_{2,3}\nu,\\[1ex]
\infty, & \text{otherwise,}
\end{cases}
\]
where $H(\cdot\, \|\, \cdot)$ denotes relative entropy and $\pi_{1,2}$, $\pi_{2,3}$ denote the projection onto the first two, respectively, the last two of the three coordinates.
\item
The constraint on $\nu$ is to the subset of $\mathcal{P}(E)$ given by
\[
\Phi(x,s) = \big\{\nu \in \mathcal{P}(E)\colon\,\|G(\nu)\|_1 = x,\,G(\nu)/\|G(\nu)\|_1 = s\big\},
\qquad x \in (0,\infty),\,s \in \mathcal{S}_2,
\]
where $G = (G^\chi)_{\chi \in S}$ with $G^\chi\colon\,\mathcal{P}(E) \to [0,\infty]$ is given by
\[
G^\chi(\nu) = \int_{E} h^\chi\,\mathrm{d}\nu
\]
with $h^\chi\colon\,E \to \N_0$ given by
\[
\begin{aligned}
h^{-}\big((a,a^\prime),(b,b^\prime),(c,c^\prime)\big)
&= \mathbbm{1}_{\{c>0\}}
+ \mathbbm{1}_{\{b=0,\, c>0\}}
+ \mathbbm{1}_{\{b=0,\,c=0,\, c^\prime>0\}}, \\[6pt]
h^{0}\big((a,a^\prime),(b,b^\prime),(c,c^\prime)\big)
&= c-\mathbbm{1}_{\{c>0\}}-\mathbbm{1}_{\{c>1\}}
+ \mathbbm{1}_{\{b=0,\,c=0,\,c^\prime=0\}}, \\[6pt]
h^{+}\big((a,a^\prime),(b,b^\prime),(c,c^\prime)\big)
&= \mathbbm{1}_{\{c>0\}} + \mathbbm{1}_{\{c>1\}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:57:30.978046+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1d74d4ba9a11466bf703dc94769a7cfc89489e8fd69fc29e5ce730c1a2df9a97","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 22 (\textsf{Zero-set bound}) of arXiv:2608.12451, '2608.12451'] Let

$
be nonzero with $s\in\N_0$, and let $r:=\deg(P)\leq s$.

$
 D_{i_r}\cdots D_{i_1}P\not\equiv 0,
$

 \geq\eps^r
 \geq\eps^s.
 
\end{align}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:09:49.837035+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1d89905cc9835ea4fa57ea2b1c995a93c5373524fcdcfe9b9ec4687392771569","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 33 of arXiv:2609.03070, 'Variants of order semicontinuity in Banach lattices'] Assume that $F$ is $r$-demicontinuous. Then:
\item[(i)] $F^{L}$ is an $r$-monotonically complete Banach lattice.
\item[(ii)] The norm of $F$ has an $r^{2}$-demicontinuous extension to $F^{L}$, equivalent to $\|\cdot\|_{L}$.
\item[(iii)] The norm completion of $F$ is $r^{2}$-demicontinuous.
\item[(iv)] If $T:F\to E$ is a contractive order continuous homomorphism into a demicontinuous normed lattice, then there is a unique order continuous extension $T^{L}:F^{L}\to E^{L}$ of $T$. Moreover, $T^{L}$ is a contractive homomorphism.
\item[(v)] If $G$ is a normed lattice which isomorphically contains $F$ as an order dense sublattice, then there is a unique injective order continuous homomorphism $J:G\to F^{L}$ which leaves $F$ in place.
\item[(vi)] If $F$ is $r$-semicontinuous, then so is $F^{L}$. In particular, the Lorentz completion preserves topological semicontinuity.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-11-02T23:06:16.395782+00:00","domain":"dynamical systems","id":"claim_1d935f08a980ccb3970b38e8e040329a1218f9d5da5957ad912737706c91e750","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Publication record. Y. Shmalo, Partition quadratic stochastic operators converge to the empty body (2026). An F-quadratic stochastic operator acts on the simplex over types {0, 1, ..., m}, where 0 is the empty body: parents of the same sex, or a pair containing 0, produce 0; Rozikov and Zhamilov proved that every such operator has the unique fixed point e_0 and that every trajectory converges to it exponentially fast. Problem 10 of Ganikhodzhaev, Mukhamedov and Rozikov, Quadratic stochastic operators and processes: results and open problems (arXiv:0902.4207), asks whether the same holds when the two sexes are replaced by the blocks E_1, ..., E_q of an arbitrary partition of {1, ..., m}, with same-block pairs producing the empty body. The answer is yes: with y = 1 - x_0, every such operator V satisfies y(V(x)) <= (1 - 1/q) y(x)^2, so e_0 is the unique fixed point and y(V^n(x)) <= c^{-1} (c y(x))^{2^n} with c = 1 - 1/q, and the inequality is an equality at every step along some trajectories for each q. Without the rule that pairs containing 0 produce 0 the statement fails: (x_0, x_1) -> (x_0^2 + x_1^2, 2 x_0 x_1) has a second, attracting fixed point (1/2, 1/2). Exact rational checks and a Lean 4 file accompany the paper. Paper and code: https://github.com/yspennstate/partition-qso-empty-body (commit f3a2991ab8c5). Not refereed.","status":"unverified"}

$(\widetilde C_k^m,  \tilde\nu_k^m,\tilde s_k^m)
_{k \geq 1}$ 
the excursion decomposition of $\tilde \phi_m$, where 
$\widetilde C_k^m$ are the connected components of 
$\{\tilde \phi_m \neq 0\}$, 
$\tilde \nu_k^m$ are given by $|\tilde \phi_m|$ restricted to $\widetilde C_k^m$, and $\tilde s_k^m$ are the sign of 
$\phi_m$ on $\widetilde C_k^m$. 
Moreover, the clusters are ordered by decreasing size of diameter.

$\tilde\nu_k^{(m)}\to \nu_k$ and $\tilde s_k^{(m)}\to s_k$ as $m\to \infty$, in the Hausdorff topology\footnote{This is the topology on closed sets given by the Hausdorff distance.} for the first component, and in the weak topology of measures for the second component. Let ${\bf x} = \{x_i\}_{i = 1}^n$ be a sequence of i.i.d random variables with ${\mathbb E} x_i= 0$,  ${\mathbb E} x_i^2= 1$ and $|x_i| \leq L$ for all $1\leq i \leq n$. \item Suppose that $(D;\ul{x}) \in \markeddomain{2N}$, and we have a non-crossing collection of paths $\ul{\eta} = (\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_N)$ in $D$ where each $\eta_i$ connects a distinct pair of marked points. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.167563+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1dc5a679e2211368b630985d58800be61bf289fc83995d52c07c31a39ab91041","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 57 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $\star$ as in \eqref{e:star.options} and $\mu \in \sM^\star(\alpha,q_0)$, we have
        \[\|\mu\|_{L^2}^2 \le
    \frac{10}{\alpha}
    +6 + O(\epsilon)\,.\]
\begin{proof}
Let $X$ be given by \eqref{e:formal.sde.main}. Let us write
$X(1)= X(q_*)+\textup{(a)}+\textup{(b)}$ where (a) denotes the drift term and (b) denotes the martingale term.
We have $\bbE[X(q_*)^2] \le \epsilon$ under either of the initialization conditions \ref{it:6.1} or \ref{it:6.2}. Next, using the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality, we have
    \begin{align*}
    \E[\textup{(a)}^2]
    &= \E\bigg[
    \bigg(\int_{q_*}^1
    p'(t)^{1/2} b_t\,dt\bigg)^2
    \bigg]
    \le \E\bigg[
    \bigg(\int_{q_*}^1 p'(t)\,dt\bigg)
    \bigg(\int_{q_*}^1 (b_t)^2 \,dt
        \bigg)\bigg]
    \le
    \int_{q_*}^1 \E[(b_t)^2] \,dt\\
    &\le \int_{q_*}^1 \Cost(t)\,dt
    \le \int_{q_*}^1 \budget(t;\alpha)\,dt + \epsilon
    \le \frac{1+\epsilon}{\alpha} + \epsilon\,,
    \end{align*}
where the last two inequalities hold under any of the budget conditions
\ref{it:4.1}, \ref{it:4.2}, or \ref{it:4.3}
combined with either condition
\ref{it:2.1} or \ref{it:2.2}. Lastly, we have from \eqref{e:loc.mg.L2.bounded} that 
    \[
    \E[\textup{(b)}^2]
    \le \int_{q_*}^1 s(t)^2
    \E[(\sigma_t)^2] \,dt
    \le 2\bigg\{ \frac{1+\epsilon}{\alpha}
        + \epsilon + 1\bigg\}\,.\]
Combining the above bounds gives altogether
    \[
    \E[X(1)^2]
    \le 3\bigg\{
    \E[X(q_*)^2]
    +\E[\textup{(a)}^2]
    +\E[\textup{(b)}^2]\bigg\}
    \le 3\bigg\{
    \frac{3(1+\epsilon)}{\alpha}
    +2 + 4\epsilon\bigg\}\,,
    \]
proving the claim.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Ω ⊂ R^n open","F continuous on Ω × R × R^n","u continuous on Ω"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.415708+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: Hamilton-Jacobi equations","id":"claim_1e25d63418d6f4a5169a94db2c01063496e715960b47674a81764905279ec8b8","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Ω ⊂ R^n be open and F: Ω × R × R^n → R continuous. A function u ∈ C(Ω) is a viscosity subsolution of F(x,u,Du) = 0 in Ω if for every φ ∈ C^1(Ω) and every x0 ∈ Ω at which u - φ has a local maximum, F(x0, u(x0), Dφ(x0)) ≤ 0. It is a viscosity supersolution if for every φ ∈ C^1(Ω) and every x0 ∈ Ω at which u - φ has a local minimum, F(x0, u(x0), Dφ(x0)) ≥ 0. It is a viscosity solution if it is both. For the evolution equation u_t + H(x,Du) = 0 in R^n × (0,T) apply the definition in the variables (x,t), with test functions φ(x,t) of class C^1 and F((x,t), r, (p,s)) = s + H(x,p); so at a local maximum of u - φ one requires φ_t + H(x0, Dφ) ≤ 0, and at a local minimum φ_t + H(x0, Dφ) ≥ 0. Equivalent variants giving the same class: C^1 test functions may be replaced by C^2 or C^∞ ones, local extrema by strict local extrema, and one may normalize φ(x0) = u(x0). The definition is NOT invariant under F ↦ -F: in general the viscosity solutions of F = 0 and of -F = 0 differ. The correct symmetry is: u is a viscosity subsolution of F(x,u,Du) = 0 iff -u is a viscosity supersolution of G(x,r,p) = 0, where G(x,r,p) := -F(x,-r,-p).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Discrete Gaussian free field on a two-dimensional lattice domain with Dirichlet boundary conditions","Gibbs-Markov (domain Markov) property and lattice Green function asymptotics","Random-walk-below-a-barrier (ballot) estimates for the scale walk"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T16:00:40+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1e595d1ddd4d31f5d20f20448b8cd74340f097f418011ebff2ea7ceb8a77b1af","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). The concentric decomposition (Biskup-Louidor) describes the two-dimensional discrete Gaussian free field h in a box of side N as seen from a point x where the field is near its maximum. Around x one takes nested dyadic annuli; conditioning on the values of h on the boundaries of the concentric boxes, the Gibbs-Markov property splits h into (i) a random walk S_k along the scales, whose increments are the Gaussian binding fields' values at x, with variance of order g log 2 per scale, with the maximum constraint acting as a barrier the walk must stay below (entropic repulsion), (ii) independent zero-boundary fields in the annuli, and (iii) explicit bounded error terms from the non-exact scale invariance of the lattice Green function. The maximum-at-x event becomes a ballot-type event for the walk S_k, handled by random-walk-below-a-barrier estimates, which yield tightness of the centred maximum, the local limit law of the maximum, and the description of the cluster of near-maximal points around x (the cluster law nu). It is the tool behind the full extremal process of the DGFF (Biskup-Louidor 2016, 2018) and the intermediate level sets. It does not by itself give universality for other log-correlated fields: the binding-field structure uses the DGFF's exact Gibbs-Markov property. Typical failure: Treating the scale walk S_k as an exact random walk with identically distributed increments, as if the field were an exact branching random walk, and carrying a multiscale second-moment computation through without tracking the error terms; because the GFF is only log-correlated rather than an exact branching random walk, the comparison of S_k with a random walk (scale-dependent variances, the bounded error terms (iii)) must be explicitly controlled, while the Gibbs-Markov pieces themselves are exactly independent; skipping this control is a common source of unjustified exponent claims for GFF level-set percolation. Canonical reference: Biskup and Louidor, 2016, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Biskup and Louidor, 2018, Advances in Mathematics; Biskup, Extrema of the two-dimensional discrete Gaussian free field, PIMS-CRM lecture notes, 2020, Springer.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["each K_eps is Lebesgue integrable"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:39.262329+00:00","domain":"real and harmonic analysis","id":"claim_1e5d0188dd28e245626b909ca5c58042ec03419fa53232852fb9172b6eb55d7d","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A family $(K_\\varepsilon)_{\\varepsilon>0}$ in $L^1(\\mathbb R^d)$ (or a sequence $K_N$ with $N\\to\\infty$; the same definition works on $\\mathbb T$) is an approximate identity if (i) $\\int K_\\varepsilon=1$ for every $\\varepsilon$; (ii) $\\sup_\\varepsilon\\|K_\\varepsilon\\|_1<\\infty$; (iii) for every $\\delta>0$, $\\int_{|x|\\ge\\delta}|K_\\varepsilon(x)|\\,dx\\to0$ as $\\varepsilon\\to0$. If $K\\in L^1(\\mathbb R^d)$ with $\\int K=1$, the dilates $K_\\varepsilon(x)=\\varepsilon^{-d}K(x/\\varepsilon)$ form an approximate identity. Standard examples: the Gauss-Weierstrass (heat) kernel $\\varepsilon^{-d}e^{-\\pi|x|^2/\\varepsilon^2}$, the Poisson kernel of the half-space, the Fejer kernel $F_N$ and the Poisson kernel $P_r(x)=\\sum_n r^{|n|}e^{2\\pi i n x}$ ($r\\uparrow1$) on $\\mathbb T$. Non-example: the Dirichlet kernel $D_N$ satisfies (i) but not (ii), since $\\|D_N\\|_1\\to\\infty$; this is the root of the divergence phenomena for Fourier series. Some texts add the stronger condition $\\sup_{|x|\\ge\\delta}|K_\\varepsilon(x)|\\to0$, which is the convenient hypothesis for convergence at a point of continuity of a merely integrable $f$ (the tail is then controlled by $\\|f\\|_1$). Almost-everywhere convergence at Lebesgue points needs more than either condition: the usual hypothesis is the dilation structure $K_\\varepsilon(x)=\\varepsilon^{-d}K(x/\\varepsilon)$ together with an integrable radially nonincreasing majorant of $|K|$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the entries a_i are real and nonnegative","in the weighted form the weights are nonnegative and sum to exactly 1","the geometric mean is the nonnegative real root of the product","the convention 0^0 = 1 is used for zero weights"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.090495+00:00","domain":"real analysis, classical inequalities","id":"claim_1f1e654f8c410c52b8d725a17d45f62a04496de0ecc32675cb38e67a595827dd","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"For NONNEGATIVE real numbers a_1, ..., a_n, (a_1 + ... + a_n)/n >= (a_1 a_2 ... a_n)^(1/n), with equality if and only if a_1 = ... = a_n. WEIGHTED FORM: if w_1, ..., w_n >= 0 with w_1 + ... + w_n = 1 and a_1, ..., a_n >= 0, then w_1 a_1 + ... + w_n a_n >= a_1^(w_1) ... a_n^(w_n), with the convention 0^0 = 1, and with equality if and only if all a_i with w_i > 0 are equal. WHERE IT FAILS: (i) nonnegativity is essential. With n = 2 and a_1 = a_2 = -1 the arithmetic mean is -1 while the product is 1 and its positive square root is +1, so the inequality as usually read reverses; the theorem is about nonnegative entries, never about arbitrary reals. (ii) With at least one zero entry and n >= 2 the geometric mean is 0 and the inequality is strict unless every entry is 0. (iii) The weights must be nonnegative AND sum to 1; dropping the normalisation makes the statement false, and the correct inhomogeneous relative is Young's inequality ab <= a^p/p + b^q/q with 1/p + 1/q = 1. (iv) The inequality is homogeneous of degree one, so it can be rescaled but never used to compare means of different orders; that is the power mean inequality, of which AM-GM is the limiting case as the exponent tends to 0.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["H is a complex Hilbert space","A is self-adjoint","B is symmetric with D(B) ⊃ D(A)","relative bound a < 1 in ‖Bx‖ ≤ a‖Ax‖ + b‖x‖ on D(A)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.770689+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, perturbation theory, Schrodinger operators","id":"claim_1f4ab59f173a44abadbf58bf5376c8c9b2832575e6d08115bf54538bf8f08703","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A be a self-adjoint operator on a complex Hilbert space H and let B be symmetric with D(A) ⊂ D(B) and ‖Bx‖ ≤ a‖Ax‖ + b‖x‖ for all x ∈ D(A), where 0 ≤ a < 1 and b ≥ 0. Then A + B, defined on D(A + B) = D(A), is self-adjoint, and it is essentially self-adjoint on every core of A. If in addition A is bounded below by M, then A + B is bounded below by M − max{b/(1 − a), a|M| + b}. (Wüst's theorem covers the borderline a = 1: if B is symmetric with D(A) ⊂ D(B) and ‖Bx‖ ≤ ‖Ax‖ + b‖x‖, then A + B is essentially self-adjoint on D(A), though possibly not self-adjoint there.) {"assumptions":["E contains the empty set and admits countable covers of X, so every subset has at least one admissible cover","rho : E -> [0, +infinity] with rho(empty set) = 0; nonnegativity is essential for the rearrangement of the double sum","the family (A_n) is countable; the sets need not be measurable, disjoint or nested","the conclusion is an inequality only; additivity requires the Caratheodory criterion"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:13:10.402499+00:00","domain":"measure theory, outer measures","id":"claim_1f8c36eb2db254c54ff701dd08d6243e0a9c40ab1d83ef4c3b9be279b1744140","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let E be a family of subsets of a set X with the empty set in E and with X covered by countably many members of E, let rho : E -> [0, +infinity] satisfy rho(empty set) = 0, and define mu*(A) = inf { sum over k of rho(E_k) : E_k in E, A contained in the union of the E_k } for every subset A of X. Then mu* is an outer measure: mu*(empty set) = 0; A contained in B implies mu*(A) <= mu*(B); and for EVERY countable family (A_n) of subsets of X, measurable or not, mu*(union of the A_n) <= sum of mu*(A_n). In particular Lebesgue outer measure on R^n is countably subadditive on all subsets of R^n, and finite subadditivity follows by padding the family with empty sets. WHERE THE INEQUALITY CANNOT BE IMPROVED: (a) equality fails in general even for pairwise DISJOINT sets. Let V be a Vitali set in [0,1] (one representative of each coset of the rationals) and let V_q = V + q for q in a countable enumeration of the rationals in [-1,1]. The V_q are pairwise disjoint, their union contains [0,1] and is contained in [-1,2], and by translation invariance all of them have the same Lebesgue outer measure; countable additivity would force that common value to be simultaneously 0 (giving outer measure 0 for [0,1]) and positive (to fill [0,1]), so the outer measure of the disjoint union is strictly less than the sum. Additivity is recovered exactly on the Caratheodory measurable sets. (b) Countable is sharp: the inequality does not extend to uncountable families - [0,1] is the union of its singletons, each of Lebesgue outer measure 0, while the union has outer measure 1. (c) No structure on rho is needed - rho need not be monotone, additive or a premeasure; that is why the construction is so robust, and also why mu* generally does not extend rho (mu*(E) <= rho(E) always, and equality for E in E requires rho to be a premeasure and E to be well behaved).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:27:36.725532+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1f96d6cd70eada662d44338b599396678b2f0ab12197c3cde9e08652b29c65ca","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 40 of arXiv:2511.13559, 'Asymptotic analysis of rare events in high dimensions'] Suppose $\g\in C^{2L}(\us(R\e)), \z \in C^{2L+2}(\us(R\e))$, $R^4d^2/\la\leq\CR$, $R\geq1$, and

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:33:01.751928+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1fc20a5681643b475f0f39f7026b6a8536ea7fa315fd2f91358dbeb6b84e3c43","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 26 of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] Fix $c > 0$ and let $Q_t$ be the birth-death process
  with
  \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
    \item $Q_0 \sim \operatorname{Poisson}(c)$;
    \item $n \mapsto n +1$ transitions of rate $c$; and
    \item $n \mapsto n - 1$ transitions of rate $n$.
  \end{enumerate}
  Then the first hitting time of $0$,
  \[
    \tau_c \coloneqq \inf\{ t \geqslant 0 \mid Q_t = 0 \},
  \]
  has Laplace transform
  \[
    \E e^{-s\tau_c} = e^{-c}
    \left[1 - c\int_0^1 \left(1-x\right)^{s} e^{-cx} \, dx
    \right]^{-1},
    \quad s \geqslant 0.
  \]
  \begin{proof}
    Fix $s > 0$. By total expectation,
    \[
      \E e^{-s \tau_c}
      = \sum_{n = 0}^\infty
      \E\left(e^{-s\tau_c} \middle| Q_0 = n\right)
      \PP(Q_0 = n)\\
      = e^{-c} \sum_{n = 0}^\infty \frac{c^n}{n!}\, \phi_n(s)
    \]
    where $\phi_n(s) \coloneqq \mathbb{E}(e^{-s\tau_c} \mid 
    Q_0 = n)$. So if $\Phi_s$ is defined on $[0, c]$ by
    \begin{equation}
      
      \Phi_s(y) \coloneqq \sum_{n=0}^\infty
      \phi_n(s) \, \frac{y^n}{n!}
      \quad \text{then} \quad
      \E(e^{-s\tau_c}) = e^{-c} \, \Phi_s(c).
    \end{equation}
    Clearly $\phi_0(s) = 1$ and first-step analysis gives
    \[
      (c+n+s) \, \phi_n(s) = 
      n \, \phi_{n-1}(s) + c \, \phi_{n+1}(s),
      \quad n > 0.
    \]
    By taking a weighted sum of this recurrence,
    \[
      \sum_{n = 1}^\infty
      \frac{y^n}{n!} \left(c + n + s \right)
      \phi_n(s) = \sum_{n = 1}^\infty
      \frac{y^n}{n!}
      \left[ n \, \phi_{n-1}(s)
      + c \, \phi_{n+1}(s)\right].
    \]
    The left-hand side is
    \[
      (c+s) \sum_{n=1}^\infty
      \frac{y^n}{n!} \, \phi_n(s)
      + y \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{y^{n-1}}{(n-1)!} \, \phi_n(s)
      =
      (c+s)\left[\Phi_s(y) - 1\right]
      + y \, \Phi_s'(y)
    \]
    while the right-hand side is
    \[
      y \sum_{n=1}^\infty
      \frac{y^{n-1}}{(n-1)!} \, \phi_{n-1}(s)
      + c \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{y^n}{n!} \, \phi_{n+1}(s)
      = y \, \Phi_s(y) + c
      \left[ \Phi_s'(y) - \phi_1(s)\right].
    \]
    We are left with the differential equation
    \[
      (c+s) \left[\Phi_s(y) - 1\right]
      + y \, \Phi_s'(y)
      = y \, \Phi_s(y) + c
      \left[\Phi_s'(y) - \phi_1(s) \right]
    \]
    or equivalently,
    the initial value problem
    \begin{align}
      
      \left(c-y\right) \Phi_s'(y)
      + \left(- c + y - s\right) \Phi_s(y)
      &= \overbrace{c \, \phi_1(s) - c - s}^{-K}\\ \notag
      \Phi_s'(y) + \left(-1-\frac{s}{c-y}\right) \Phi_s(y)
      &= -\frac{K}{c-y}
    \end{align}
    with condition $\Phi_s(0) = 1$.
    Use the integrating factor $I_s(y) = e^{-y} \, (c-y)^s$ to write
    \begin{align*}
      \left[e^{-y} \left(c-y\right)^s \Phi_s(y)\right]'
      &= \frac{-K}{c-y} \, e^{-y} \left(c-y\right)^s\\
      e^{-y} \left(c-y\right)^s \Phi_s(y)
      - e^{-0} \left(c - 0\right)^s \Phi_s(0) 
      &= \int_0^y \frac{-K}{c-x} \, e^{-x} \left(c - x\right)^s \, dx
      \intertext{for any $y < c$. It's clear from \eqref{eq:Phi} that
      $\Phi_s$ is continuous, so take the $y \uparrow c$ limit:}
      \frac{c^s}{\int_0^c e^{-x} \left(c-x\right)^{s-1} dx}
      &= K.
    \end{align*}
    Finally, the $y \uparrow c$ limit of \eqref{eq:IVP}
    informs us $-s \, \Phi_s(c) = -K$, thus
    \begin{align*}
      \E e^{-s\tau_c}
      &= e^{-c} \, \Phi_s(c)
      = \frac{e^{-c}\, c^s}{\int_0^c e^{-x} \, s \left(c-x\right)^{s-1} dx}\\
      &= \frac{e^{-c} \, c^s}{c^s - \int_0^c e^{-x} \left(c-x\right)^s dx}
      = \frac{e^{-c} \, c^s}{c^s - \int_0^1 c \, e^{-cx} \left(c-c\,x\right)^s dx}\\
      &= e^{-c} \left[1 - c \int_0^1 \left(1-x\right)^s e^{-cx}\, dx \right]^{-1}.
      \qedhere
    \end{align*}
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["psi(lambda) = log E e^{lambda X} finite for some lambda > 0 (otherwise the bound is vacuous)","for the i.i.d. rate statement: independent and identically distributed summands"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.627588+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1fe4f3b747b727689cb17f579418ee4b2fd98070d9ff3fa9527f2e43df172cf8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a random variable with cumulant generating function psi(lambda) = log E[exp(lambda X)], finite on an interval containing 0 in its interior on the right. Then for every t, P(X >= t) <= exp(-psi^*(t)) where psi^*(t) = sup_{lambda >= 0} (lambda t - psi(lambda)) is the (one-sided) Legendre transform of psi. If X = sum_{i=1}^n X_i with the X_i independent and identically distributed with cumulant generating function psi_1, then psi = n psi_1 and P(X >= n t) <= exp(-n psi_1^*(t)): the exponent is LINEAR in n with rate psi_1^*(t), the Cramer rate function. Cramer's theorem says this exponential rate is exactly right, that is (1/n) log P(X >= n t) -> -psi_1^*(t) for t > E[X_1] under a finiteness condition on psi_1 near 0, so the Chernoff bound loses nothing at the level of the exponential rate although it can lose polynomial factors. The method requires SOME finite exponential moment: without it psi^* is identically 0 for t above the mean and the bound is vacuous, which is the correct behaviour for heavy-tailed laws. [standard; e.g. Dembo and Zeitouni, Large Deviations Techniques and Applications, 2nd ed., Chapter 2]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["a probability space (or a finite measure space)","G convex, nondecreasing, superlinear at infinity; the constant sup_i E[G(|X_i|)] must be uniform over the family"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.751629+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_2009470175a95a3c30c51a0b9029476dfd66707c810383993ea647e49b0c988a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (Omega, F, P) be a probability space and {X_i : i in I} a family of random variables. The family is uniformly integrable if and only if there exists a nondecreasing convex function G : [0, infinity) -> [0, infinity) with G(t)/t -> infinity as t -> infinity such that sup_{i in I} E[G(|X_i|)] < infinity. The sufficiency direction is the one used in practice: a uniform bound on any superlinear moment, for example sup_i E[|X_i|^p] < infinity for a single p > 1, or sup_i E[|X_i| log^+ |X_i|] < infinity, forces uniform integrability. A uniform bound on the FIRST moment does not: on ([0,1], Lebesgue) the family X_n = n 1_{(0,1/n)} has E|X_n| = 1 for all n and is not uniformly integrable. [standard; e.g. Dellacherie and Meyer, Probabilities and Potential, or Williams, Probability with Martingales, Section 13.3]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:16:18.686380+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_20379a5dab6d932dbb7f2d5de4b388201a8eeacc73402556dcd59bdc4ce9d0cc","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 15 (Resonant skew-Hermitian endpoint identity) of arXiv:2607.26377, '\textbf{Entire Logarithmic Signatures\\ of Bounded-Variation Paths in Finite Dimensions}'] Let $\Lambda\subset 2\pi\Q$ be finite and symmetric, and choose $m\geq1$ such that
\[
m\omega\in2\pi\Z
\qquad(\omega\in\Lambda).
\]
Let $\Gamma=\gamma^{*m}$ be the $m$-fold concatenation of $\gamma$, naturally parametrised on $[0,mT]$.
Fix $r\geq1$, frequencies $\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_r\in\Lambda$, and real covectors $\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_r\in W^*$. No distinctness is assumed: the frequencies and covectors may repeat.
Choose real numbers $\sigma_0,\ldots,\sigma_r$ satisfying
\begin{equation}
\sigma_{j-1}-\sigma_j=\omega_j
\quad(1\leq j\leq r),
\qquad
m\sigma_j\in2\pi\Z
\quad(0\leq j\leq r).
\end{equation}
Set $D=i\diag(\sigma_0,\ldots,\sigma_r)$, write $I=I_{r+1}$, and, for $u=(u_1,\ldots,u_r)\in\R^r$, define
\begin{equation}
\rho_u(a)
 =\ell(a)D
  +\sum_{j=1}^r
   u_j\eta_j(a)(E_{j-1,j}-E_{j,j-1}),
\end{equation}
first as a real-linear map $V\to\uLie(r+1)$. Denote its complex-linear extension by
\[
\rho_{u,\C}:V_{\C}\longrightarrow M_{r+1}(\C).
\]
If $U^u$ is the right development
\[
\dd U_s^u=U_s^u\rho_u(\dd\Gamma_s),
\qquad U_0^u=I,
\]
then
\begin{equation}
U_{mT}^u=I
\qquad(u\in\R^r).
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:32:35.610180+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_2047058969970faf847b7f2324be353be0b235fdd8f019ee565f68c8925fae8c","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma Monotonicity of arXiv:2606.13264, 'Interference Queueing Networks: A Replica Mean-Field Approach in the Symmetric Setting'] The Markov chain $Q$ is monotone with respect to the arrival rate, the initial condition, and the departure rate. More precisely:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Monotonicity in the arrival rate.} If $\lambda_1 < \lambda_2$, then the chains $Q^{(1)}$ and $Q^{(2)}$ defined by \emph{(2)} with arrival rates $\lambda_1$, $\lambda_2$ and $Q^{(1)}(0)=Q^{(2)}(0)$ satisfy
    \[
    Q^{(1)} \leq_{\mathrm{st}} Q^{(2)}.
    \]

    \item \textbf{Monotonicity in the initial condition.} If $x \leq y$, then the chains $Q^x$ and $Q^y$ defined by \emph{(2)} with initial conditions $Q^x(0)=x$ and $Q^y(0)=y$ satisfy
    \[
    Q^x \leq_{\mathrm{st}} Q^y.
    \]

    \item \textbf{Monotonicity in the departure rate.} If for all $i \in [1;N]$, $f \leq \mu_i$ (resp. $f \geq \mu_i$), and $Q^f(0)=Q(0)$, then the chain $Q^f$ defined by \emph{(2)} with departure rate $\mu_i = f$ for every $i$ satisfies
    \[
    Q \leq_{\mathrm{st}} Q^f
    \qquad (\text{resp. } Q^f \leq_{\mathrm{st}} Q).
    \]
\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.348858+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_208f7c4d1a65f4167efac3277e11eddaa90b1e153739b4d3e12334ae49c18c70","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 165 ($\by$ is Lipschitz) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Take $\by\equiv \by(q_{d+1})$ as in \eqref{e:normalized.vectors.y}, so it is measurable with respect to $\cG(q_{d+1})$, as defined by \eqref{e:gaus.filt}. 
Conditional on $\cG(q_d)$,
the random vector $\by$ has mean zero, and is subgaussian with variance proxy $L^{O(1)}$.

\begin{proof} Let us abbreviate
	\[
	\bXi
	\equiv \bXi^{d+1}
	\equiv \frac{\bG(q_{d+1})
		-\bG(q_d)}{\sqrt{p_{d+1}-p_d}}\,,
	\]
so this is a gaussian independent of $\cG(q_d)$. Then we can express
	\begin{align*}
	\sqrt{\delta_d}\by
	&\stackrel{\eqref{e:normalized.vectors.y}}{=}
	\E\bigg[ \cA\Big(
		\bG(q_d)
		+(p_{d+1}-p_d)^{1/2}\bXi
		+ (1-p_{d+1})^{1/2} \bG'\Big)\,\bigg|\,\bG(q_d),\bXi
		\bigg]\\
	&\qquad-\E\bigg[ \cA\Big(
		\bG(q_d)
		+(p_{d+1}-p_d)^{1/2}\bXi
		+ (1-p_{d+1})^{1/2} \bG'\Big)\,\bigg|\,\bG(q_d)\bigg] \,.
	\end{align*}
Thus, conditional on $\cG(q_d)$,
the vector $\by$ has mean zero.
It follows by the assumption on $\cA$ together with assumption~\eqref{e:deriv.p.bound} that
 $\by$ is $L^{O(1)}$-Lipschitz in $\bXi$, so the subgaussian claim follows using Lemma~\ref{l:lip.subgaus}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a topological space and T: X → X a map","for the orbit-closure characterization, T is continuous"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:57:26.111010+00:00","domain":"topological dynamics","id":"claim_20ab9dec4c9cbfd28df1fff4fca5251efcaf20965cb1e82ec6c01020cfd918be","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a topological space and T: X → X a map. A set A ⊂ X is (forward) invariant if T(A) ⊆ A. A minimal set is a nonempty closed invariant set M that contains no proper nonempty closed invariant subset. Some authors require T(M) = M (strict invariance); for a continuous T on a compact Hausdorff space a minimal set in the above sense automatically satisfies T(M) = M, since T(M) is then itself nonempty, closed (compact image) and invariant, hence equal to M. Characterization (T continuous): a nonempty closed invariant M is minimal if and only if for every x ∈ M the forward orbit {Tⁿx : n ≥ 0} is dense in M. Proof of the equivalence: for x ∈ M the orbit closure cl{Tⁿx : n ≥ 0} is nonempty, closed, contained in M, and invariant because continuity gives T(cl O) ⊆ cl T(O) ⊆ cl O; so minimality forces it to equal M; conversely, if every orbit in M is dense and N ⊂ M is nonempty closed invariant, any x ∈ N has its orbit inside N, so M = cl(orbit) ⊆ N. The system (X,T) itself is called minimal if X is a minimal set, i.e. every forward orbit is dense. Examples: a periodic orbit is a minimal set; an irrational rotation of the circle is minimal; the closure of a non-periodic orbit is in general NOT minimal (e.g. the orbit closure of a point of the doubling map whose orbit is dense contains the fixed point 0 as a smaller minimal set). Continuity is used in the orbit-closure characterization; the definition of a minimal set itself does not need it. For flows and group/semigroup actions the same definitions apply with 'orbit' read as the (semi)group orbit.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0129-recurrence-transience-criterion-for-excited-random-walks-under-station","No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:26:45.048084+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_20d91e1f2f967bd5c7191a2142a497f6f5c041cbfb86f3a0ac001391879cb602","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Examine the branching-process-with-migration proof and where i.i.d. is used. Result: The proof of Theorem 3.10 under (3.10) translates the walk into a branching process with migration whose offspring law at site k is determined by the cookie stack at k; under (IID) the branching process is homogeneous in space and the criterion delta > 1 is the criterion for the branching process to die out... under (SE) the process is a branching process in a stationary ergodic environment (BPRE with migration), whose survival criterion is governed by the Lyapunov exponent of the environment, i.e. by an ergodic average of log-means, not by the mean delta of the drift. For genuinely random ergodic environments a similar averaging holds if the migration is additive, which it is (the number of cookies eaten per visit adds). So the expected answer is YES for (SE) with the same delta, and the obstruction to a proof is that the branching-process comparison uses independence between the offspring at different sites when computing the extinction probability of the process with migration; with dependence one needs an ergodic theorem for the total progeny, available via the Kesten-Kozlov-Spitzer approach only for i.i.d.. {"assumptions":["INFINITE exchangeability; the theorem is false for finite exchangeable sequences","values in a Polish space, so that regular conditional distributions and a countable determining class exist"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:40.781914+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_20e7e94fd93a2e51ba5becdbc47068b21245cc7d9d4def4e9e32ec611d9265ad","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, X_2, ... be an INFINITE exchangeable sequence of random variables taking values in a Polish space S, meaning that for every n the law of (X_1, ..., X_n) is invariant under permutations of the n coordinates. Then there is a random probability measure Theta on S, measurable with respect to the exchangeable sigma-algebra, such that CONDITIONALLY on Theta the X_i are i.i.d. with common law Theta. Equivalently the law of the sequence is a MIXTURE of i.i.d. laws, and Theta is the almost sure limit of the empirical measures (1/n) sum_{i <= n} delta_{X_i}. The theorem is FALSE for finite exchangeable sequences. Counterexample with n = 2: let (X_1, X_2) be uniform on {(0,1), (1,0)}. This is exchangeable, but any mixture of i.i.d. Bernoulli sequences has Cov(X_1, X_2) = E[p^2] - (E p)^2 = Var(p) >= 0, whereas here E[X_1] = E[X_2] = 1/2 and E[X_1 X_2] = 0 give Cov = -1/4 < 0. Sampling without replacement is exactly the mechanism, and it produces the negative correlation that no mixture of i.i.d. can. What DOES survive in finite length is a quantitative approximation, due to Diaconis and Freedman: an exchangeable sequence of length n, restricted to k of its coordinates, is close in total variation to a mixture of i.i.d. sequences, with an error of order k/n. So infinite exchangeability is the hypothesis and it is not decorative; 'exchangeable' alone, applied to a finite sample, does not license treating the data as conditionally i.i.d. [de Finetti (1931); Hewitt and Savage (1955) for the general Polish case; Diaconis and Freedman (1980) for the finite version]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the chain is reversible with respect to pi (real eigenvalues); the bounds are stated for the absolute spectral gap","aperiodicity (e.g. laziness) so that gamma* > 0","the upper bound carries the factor log(1/pi_min); the lower bound holds for epsilon < 1/2"],"created_at":"2026-09-02T07:51:33.049135+00:00","domain":"Markov chains and mixing (hand-authored statement with hypotheses, 2026-09-02)","id":"claim_2114caacee9ef704ca7243abee0f8be7a280413638cb34b387097351ec0f2be3","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let P be the transition matrix of an irreducible, reversible Markov chain on a finite state space with stationary distribution pi, and let gamma* = 1 - max{|lambda| : lambda an eigenvalue of P other than 1} be the absolute spectral gap, with relaxation time t_rel = 1/gamma*. Then for every epsilon in (0, 1/2) the total-variation mixing time satisfies (t_rel - 1) log(1/(2 epsilon)) <= t_mix(epsilon) <= t_rel log(1/(epsilon pi_min)), where pi_min is the smallest stationary probability (Levin, Peres, Wilmer, Theorems 12.4 and 12.5). Mixing time is therefore the relaxation time up to a factor between log(1/(2 epsilon)) and log(1/(epsilon pi_min)); on a state space of size N the gap between the two sides can be as large as log N, and neither side can be dropped in general. For a lazy chain (holding probability at least 1/2) all eigenvalues are nonnegative, so the absolute gap equals the ordinary gap 1 - lambda_2; a periodic chain (a simple random walk on a bipartite graph) has an eigenvalue -1, gamma* = 0, and never mixes.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Arbitrary Borel probability measure mu on R; t>0 is the semicircular variance, not its standard deviation."],"created_at":"2026-10-21T15:23:58.847983+00:00","domain":"Free additive convolution and free heat regularity","id":"claim_2150603dbb29e550419a3132c576044838a7255dc53cbc4b5f04d0e912b173d2","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Biane semicircular density parametrization. Let mu be any Borel probability measure on R, let t>0, and let mu_t=mu free-additive-convolved with the centered semicircle of variance t. Set U_t={u: integral (u-y)^(-2) mu(dy)>1/t}, with the integral allowed to be infinite, and v_t(u)=inf{v>=0: integral ((u-y)^2+v^2)^(-1) mu(dy)<=1/t}. Then v_t is continuous, is positive exactly on U_t, and is real analytic there. Define psi_t(u)=u+t integral (u-y)/((u-y)^2+v_t(u)^2) mu(dy). At boundary points where numerator and denominator both vanish, use the continuous Cauchy-transform extension, equivalently the integrable boundary limit. The map psi_t is an increasing homeomorphism R to R, and mu_t has a continuous density p_t satisfying p_t(psi_t(u))=v_t(u)/(pi*t). In particular p_t is real analytic wherever positive, and 0<=p_t<=1/(pi*sqrt(t)). No moment, initial density, or compact-support assumption on mu is required. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:10:07.530224+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_21d2a5018cf74284bf204467cf2d5730a77c94fcd7b28d93caf66cb23f5f62f9","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition eq:cutoff-event of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[proposition]{prop:quenched-cutoff}
Fix \(0\le\varepsilon<1/2\) and a Borel set \(B\subset\mathbb R\), with no
independence, identical-distribution, density, or genericity condition.
Set
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal T_{N,\varepsilon}
 =\left\{\max_{I\in[N]^p}|J_I|
 \le N^{1/2-\varepsilon}\right\},\qquad
 \delta_{N,\varepsilon}
 =\mathbb P(\mathcal T_{N,\varepsilon}^c),
\end{equation}
and, whenever the conditioning event has positive probability, write
\(\mathbb P_{N,\varepsilon}^{\mathrm{cut}}
:=\mathbb P(\,\cdot\mid\mathcal T_{N,\varepsilon})\).  If merely
\(\delta_{N,\varepsilon}=o(1)\), then the event has positive probability
for all sufficiently large \(N\), and
\[
 \left\lVert\nu-\nu'\right\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}
 :=\sup_A\left\lvert\nu(A)-\nu'(A)\right\rvert
\]
satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \left\|
 \mathcal L_{\mathbb P}\bigl(Q_N^J(B)\bigr)
 -\mathcal L_{\mathbb P_{N,\varepsilon}^{\mathrm{cut}}}
 \bigl(Q_N^J(B)\bigr)
 \right\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
 \le\delta_{N,\varepsilon}.
\end{equation}
Consequently, for every deterministic sequence \(a_N\), every
\(\eta>0\), and every bounded measurable
\(\varphi:[0,\infty]\to\mathbb R\),
\begin{align}
 &\left|
 \mathbb P\bigl(\left\lvertQ_N^J(B)-a_N\right\rvert>\eta\bigr)
 -\mathbb P_{N,\varepsilon}^{\mathrm{cut}}
  \bigl(\left\lvertQ_N^J(B)-a_N\right\rvert>\eta\bigr)
 \right|
 \le\delta_{N,\varepsilon},\\
 &\left|\mathbb E\varphi(Q_N^J(B))
 -\mathbb E_{N,\varepsilon}^{\mathrm{cut}}\varphi(Q_N^J(B))\right|
 \le2\left\lVert\varphi\right\rVert_\infty\delta_{N,\varepsilon}=o(1).
 
\end{align}
In particular, convergence of \(Q_N^J(B)\) in probability to a
deterministic limit is equivalent under the original and conditioned
laws.

The hypothesis \(\delta_{N,\varepsilon}=o(1)\) follows, for example,
from the marginal bound
\[
 \sup_{I\in[N]^p}\mathbb E\exp(J_I^2/K^2)\le2,
\]
which requires no independence and gives
\begin{equation}
 \delta_{N,\varepsilon}
 \le2N^p\exp\{-K^{-2}N^{1-2\varepsilon}\}=o(1).
\end{equation}
Mean comparison needs only a separate integrability input.  In
particular, if \(0\le Q_N^J(B)\le M_N\) almost surely and
\(M_N\delta_{N,\varepsilon}\to0\), then
\begin{equation}
 \left|\mathbb E Q_N^J(B)
 -\mathbb E_{N,\varepsilon}^{\mathrm{cut}}Q_N^J(B)\right|
 \le M_N\delta_{N,\varepsilon}=o(1).
\end{equation}
The critical-count ceiling \({\rm(CC)}_p\) is sufficient, with
\[
 M_N=\frac1N\log(1+D_{N,p})=O(1).
\]
Algebraic genericity gives the explicit \(N\)-independent choice
\begin{equation}
 M_N=M_p:=
 \log(p-1)+\log\left(1+\frac2{p-2}\right).
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:19:47.300957+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_21d4f49bfcd68c408ad18811bd2404c7533fb5adcca2d0064c2d79ca3e22ca91","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition The distributions $\wishart$ and $\gaussmat$ of arXiv:2602.11129, 'Information-Theoretic Thresholds for Bipartite Latent-Space Graphs Under Noisy Observation'] We let $\mathbb{W}(n, m, p, d)$ be the distribution over $n \times m$ matrices with entries in $\{0,1\}$ obtained as follows.     Define further the threshold $\tau = \tau(d, p)$ such that for any $u \in L, v \in R$, we have $
        \Prnop{d^{-1/2}\langle \mathbf{x}_u, \mathbf{x}_v \rangle \le \tau} = p.

    Then, after drawing $(\mathbf{x}_{u})_{u \in R}$ and $(\mathbf{x}_{u})_{u \in L}$,  determine each entry of $W\sim \mathbb{W}(n, m, p, d)$ by thresholding\footnote{Instead of thresholding using the indicator $d^{-1/2}\langle \mathbf{x}_u, \mathbf{x}_v \rangle \le \tau$, we could also use $d^{-1/2}\langle \mathbf{x}_u, \mathbf{x}_v \rangle \ge \tau$ instead and our results would remain valid, up to some flipped signs. } $$

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:32:20.761755+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_2247540e3bd73e1f9ac070e833ce77db0f12f0ee46a5765eaef048b9e6d5d91f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 21 of arXiv:2609.00448, 'Equivariant formality and representation theory'] Let $G$ be a compact connected Lie group of rank $n$, $S$ a torus subgroup of dimension being $n-1$, $T$ a maximal torus of $G$ containing $S$, $\mu\in \chi(T)$ a primitive character of $T$ such that $S=\text{ker }\mu$, $L$ a primitive weight in the weight lattice $\mathfrak{t}^*_\mathbb{Z}$ corresponding to $\mu$ after exponentiation, and $W$ the Weyl group of $G$. Define
	\[\Phi_L:=\left(\prod_{w\in W/W_{[L]}} wL\right)^{n(L)}\in \text{Sym}^*(\mathfrak{t}^*)^W,\]
	where $W_{[L]}$ is the stabilizer of $[L]:=\{\pm L\}\in \mathfrak{t}^*/\{\pm 1\}$, $n(L)=1$ or 2 depending on whether $\displaystyle\prod_{w\in W/W_{[L]}}wL$ is $W$-invariant or $W$-anti-invariant, i.e. 
	\[\displaystyle w'(\prod_{w\in W/W_{[L]}}wL)=\text{sgn}(w')\prod_{w\in W/W_{[L]}}wL\text{ for all }w'\in W.\] 
	Then $(G, S)$ is isotropy formal if and only if $\Phi_L\notin (f_1, \cdots, f_n)^2$, where $f_1, \cdots, f_n$ are the fundamental $W$-invariant homogeneous polynomials on $\mathfrak{t}$, i.e. $\text{Sym}^*(\mathfrak{t}^*)^W=\mathbb{R}[f_1, \cdots, f_n]$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["characteristic zero (or the general polynomial over any field of characteristic zero)","n >= 5","coefficients are independent indeterminates: particular degree-5 polynomials over Q may still be solvable by radicals"],"created_at":"2026-08-29T02:26:24.137447+00:00","domain":"algebra / Galois theory","id":"claim_2256ca4481d9e0acf08c9c091382001ee523cf5d05e7ef315770d80b729f7390","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let n >= 5 and let K = Q(a_0, ..., a_{n-1}) be the field of rational functions in independent indeterminates. The general polynomial x^n + a_{n-1} x^{n-1} + ... + a_1 x + a_0 over K is not solvable by radicals: no root of it lies in any radical extension of K (a tower K = K_0 < K_1 < ... < K_m in which each K_{i+1} = K_i(r) with r^{k} in K_i for some k >= 1). The reason is Galois' criterion: a polynomial is solvable by radicals exactly when its Galois group is a solvable group, and the general polynomial has Galois group the full symmetric group S_n over K, which is not solvable for n >= 5. For n <= 4 such formulas exist.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:07:35.020004+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_22579e0013e3790d51f813ba1becd014cb593a5097ee0a2b9087ed0d03bfb032","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 35 of arXiv:2609.02878, '2609.02878'] Let \(Z\) be a connected normal complex space whose dense analytic
regular locus \(\cR\) carries a K\"ahler structure \((g,J)\).  Assume
that the analytic and metric topologies agree, that \(d|_{\cR}\) is the
intrinsic length distance, and that \((Z,d)\) is a complete locally
compact length space equal to the metric completion of \((\cR,g)\).
Assume also that \(Z\) is klt, that \(\omega_g\) extends locally as a
positive current with bounded potential, and that every point has a
local closed holomorphic embedding
\(V\hookrightarrow\Omega_V\subset\C^L\) for which
\begin{equation}
                     \omega_g\ge c_V\omega_{\C^L}
                     \quad\text{on }V\cap\cR.
\end{equation}
Let $G:Z\to\C^r$ be continuous and holomorphic, and
assume on $\cR$ that
\begin{equation}
 \nabla dG^a=0,\qquad
 \left[\langle dG^a,d\overline{G^b}\rangle_{g^{-1}}\right]_{a,b=1}^r
 \text{ is positive definite}.
\end{equation}
Then, after composing \(G\) with an element of
\(\mathrm{GL}(r,\C)\), without translating the target, there is a global
biholomorphic isometry
\begin{equation}
                         Z\cong\C^r\times Z'
\end{equation}
under which $G$ is the projection.  The factor $Z'$ is connected, complete,
normal, and klt; write \(g'\) for its induced regular K\"ahler metric.
It inherits the bounded-local-potential K\"ahler current
and the local ambient metric lower bound of $Z$, and
\begin{equation}
                         \Sing Z=\C^r\times\Sing Z'.
\end{equation}

If, in addition, $f$ is locally Lipschitz on $Z$, smooth on $\cR$, and
satisfies \(\Rc+\nabla^2f=g/2\) on $\cR$, then
\[
                 f(z,y)=\frac{|z|^2}{4}+\ell(z)+f'(y),
\]
where $\ell$ is real affine-linear and $f'$ is locally Lipschitz; if $f$
is proper, then $f'$ is proper.  If also
\begin{equation}
                         \int_{\cR}e^{-f}\,dV_g<\infty,
\end{equation}
then \(\int_{\Reg Z'}e^{-f'}\,dV_{g'}<\infty\).  Finally, assume that
the flow of \(\nabla f\) is complete and preserves \(\cR\), and that its
canonical self-similar maps extend to the metric completions.  Then the
same Euclidean factor is static on every negative-time slice in that
canonical gauge. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Bernoulli percolation on the discrete torus, d > 6","Mean-field cluster geometry (intrinsic diameter m^{1/2}, Euclidean diameter m^{1/4})"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T07:48:45.952251+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_2279334a78f40f9f470203698541f2090e13571639d4fc686f5a52efb3646d33","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"PRIVATE MECHANISM NOTE, author-recorded. On the torus T_{n,d} with volume V, a critical cluster of size V^{2/3} has intrinsic geometry of a critical tree embedded four-dimensionally, so its Euclidean diameter is of order (V^{2/3})^{1/4} = V^{1/6}, while the torus side is V^{1/d}. Since V^{1/6} > V^{1/d} iff d > 6, above six dimensions the window clusters wrap around the torus many times and see the torus uniformly; this is why the exploration process should have the same global (mass-proportional) depletion as in G(n,p), which is what the multiplicative-coalescent scaling limit (Heydenreich-van der Hofstad Open Problems 13.3 and 13.5) needs. The torus plateau theorem (Hutchcroft-Michta-Slade) is the two-point version of this uniformity; the open step is the exploration-level (higher-point) version. Same reason makes eps >> V^{-1/3} lie above the correlation-length crossover eps >> V^{-2/d} for d > 6 (Open Problem 13.2).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Galton-Watson with P(D=2) = 3/5, P(D=3) = 2/5","consistent equivariant flow rule choosing uniformly among same-coloured children"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:11:19.450036+00:00","domain":"probability, trees, ergodic theory","id":"claim_22df461caf6d08479ba0f1da9d8fdedbb4603bca52d4395ae62573d0bad9bec1","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Lyons and Peres, Probability on Trees and Networks (version 19 August 2026), Question 17.18 (p. 575) asks whether a consistent equivariant flow rule admitting a stationary measure EQUIVALENT to Galton-Watson measure must induce an ergodic Markov chain; their Proposition 17.17 proves it when all child weights are strictly positive, and Exercise 17.22 gives a non-ergodic example whose stationary measure is only absolutely continuous, so equivalence is the point of the question. Our result (id P0033, 2026-09-08): NO. Take Galton-Watson with P(D=2) = 3/5, P(D=3) = 2/5 (mean 12/5) and an isomorphism-invariant colour in {0,1} defined by AND at two-child vertices and OR at three-child vertices; both preserve unanimity, so every vertex has at least one child of its own colour, and the flow chooses uniformly among those. Galton-Watson measure is stationary, the root colour is invariant along the chain and takes each value with probability 1/2 - a non-constant invariant function, hence no ergodicity - and the stationary measure equals Galton-Watson measure, trivially equivalent to it. The colour exists because F(p) = (3/5) p^2 + (2/5)[1 - (1-p)^3] fixes 1/2, and r_n = E[q_n^2] satisfies r_{n+1} = 3/10 + (3/5) r^2 + (2/5) r^3 whose increment factors as (r - 1/2)[(2/5) r^2 + (4/5) r - 3/5], driving r_n from r_0 = 1/4 up to 1/2 and giving E[q(1-q)] = 0. Verification as the source words it: the step the proof leaves implicit, and which was checked, is that Galton-Watson really is stationary - it holds because, conditioned on the children's colours, the child subtrees are independent, each distributed as Galton-Watson conditioned on its own colour, so the chosen subtree is exactly GW given colour = c, the uniform choice adds no bias, and mixing over c returns GW. Prior art unchecked; the tree-automaton and factor-of-iid literature is where to look.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X compact metric, T continuous and topologically exact","T is a local homeomorphism with finite fibres, so that L maps C(X) into C(X)","the weight w is continuous and strictly positive everywhere","there exist lambda > 0 and h in C(X) with h > 0 everywhere and L h = lambda h","there exists a Borel probability measure nu with L* nu = lambda nu (used only for algebraic simplicity)","the conclusion is about the eigenvalues of L acting on C(X); no Banach space of Holder or bounded-variation functions and no quasi-compactness is assumed"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.090835+00:00","domain":"thermodynamic formalism, transfer operators, Perron-Frobenius theory","id":"claim_237e639d0e9ed9df151e70d43e37add45d9d02ba588674ca6999612a5fb36cf3","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"SETTING: X a compact metric space; T : X -> X a continuous, topologically exact map which is a local homeomorphism with finite fibres (so that the operator below sends continuous functions to continuous functions); w : X -> (0, infinity) a continuous weight. Define the transfer (Ruelle) operator on complex continuous functions by (L f)(x) = the sum of w(y) f(y) over the finitely many y with T(y) = x; L is a bounded positive operator on C(X). Assume the Perron data exist: a number lambda > 0 and a strictly positive h in C(X) with L h = lambda h, together with a Borel probability measure nu with L* nu = lambda nu, i.e. the integral of L f with respect to nu equals lambda times the integral of f with respect to nu for all f in C(X). CONCLUSION: (1) if f in C(X) is complex-valued and L f = z f with |z| = lambda, then z = lambda and f is a constant multiple of h - so lambda is the only eigenvalue of modulus lambda in C(X) and its eigenspace is one dimensional; (2) lambda is ALGEBRAICALLY simple: there is no f in C(X) with L f - lambda f = h, hence no Jordan block at lambda. WHERE THE HYPOTHESES BITE: (i) exactness cannot be weakened to minimality, unique ergodicity or transitivity. Take X the circle, T an irrational rotation and w identically 1, so that L f = f composed with T^{-1}: every character exp(2 pi i n x) is an eigenfunction with an eigenvalue of modulus 1, so the peripheral spectrum is infinite - and the system is minimal and uniquely ergodic but not exact (it is invertible, hence never exact). (ii) Strict positivity of the weight is essential. If w may vanish, the irreducibility can become periodic: in the finite-state model, where L is a nonnegative matrix, the statement above is the PRIMITIVE case of the Perron-Frobenius theorem, and an irreducible matrix of period p > 1 has exactly p eigenvalues of modulus equal to its spectral radius, so simplicity of the peripheral eigenvalue genuinely fails. (iii) The conclusion concerns the peripheral eigenvalue only and gives NO spectral gap: to place the rest of the spectrum in a strictly smaller disc one needs quasi-compactness (a Lasota-Yorke or Ionescu-Tulcea-Marinescu inequality on a Holder or bounded-variation space), a separate hypothesis on the regularity of w and the expansion of T. (iv) The existence of h and nu is assumed here, not proved; producing them is the other half of the Ruelle-Perron-Frobenius theorem and needs its own hypotheses.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["A finite with at least two elements (for N = 1 the maximum has mean 0)","the signs are independent and symmetric; the bound is on the expectation over the signs only, the vectors are fixed"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:40:13.706093+00:00","domain":"probability and learning theory","id":"claim_238153b7dd2c94196c2f503107fe4086af1bd720d344b15f76689b1605667c76","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A be a finite subset of R^n with N = |A| >= 2 elements, and let r = max_{a in A} ||a||_2. Let sigma_1, ..., sigma_n be independent Rademacher signs (uniform on {-1, +1}). Then E_sigma [ max_{a in A} sum_{i=1}^{n} sigma_i a_i ] <= r sqrt(2 log N), and consequently E_sigma [ max_{a in A} (1/n) sum_i sigma_i a_i ] <= r sqrt(2 log N) / n. Two consequences used constantly in learning theory: (1) for a finite class F of functions bounded by B on a sample x_1, ..., x_n, the empirical Rademacher complexity satisfies R_hat_S(F) = E_sigma sup_{f in F} (1/n) sum_i sigma_i f(x_i) <= B sqrt(2 log |F| / n), since each vector (f(x_1), ..., f(x_n)) has Euclidean norm at most B sqrt(n); (2) for a class C of sets of VC dimension d, restricting to the sample leaves at most s(C, n) <= (e n / d)^d distinct indicator vectors (Sauer-Shelah), each of norm at most sqrt(n), so R_hat_S(C) <= sqrt(2 d log(e n / d) / n) for n >= d. The logarithm cannot be removed at this generality: for A = {-1, +1}^n (N = 2^n, r = sqrt(n)) the maximum is exactly n while the bound reads n sqrt(2 log 2), so the lemma is sharp up to the constant sqrt(2 log 2) = 1.18; for VC classes Dudley's chaining removes the logarithm, R_hat_S(C) <= C sqrt(d / n).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:56:21.583278+00:00","domain":"graph theory","id":"claim_2391dac5df9a90395b1af7a294eca603716608168823cf2e7908d46e42b93d6a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In any bipartite graph, the maximum size of a matching (a set of edges no two of which share an endpoint) equals the minimum size of a vertex cover (a set of vertices meeting every edge). Let $B\subset E$ be a nearly Borel set with compact closure $\overline{B}$.

 \[

# C017 v1: rescaled noise restores two roots in the iid-head frozen precursor
Status: proof (unaudited). Kind: bound. Target:1. Novelty unestablished.
A supporting frozen-model result, not full Target1 and not yet a nonlinear-network result.

## 1. Model and precise limit
For 0<e<1/4 set D=1+e^2+e^4 and x_(s,t)=(1,es,e^2t)/sqrt(D), s,t=+/-1.
Use the uniform four-point population and teacher direction
u_e=(0,e,1)/sqrt(1+e^2). The letter u_e denotes this direction, not
nu, the fixed readout magnitude in (0,1]. Set c_e=e^2/sqrt(D(1+e^2)),
alpha=c_e/2, g(x)=ReLU(u_e.x)-c_e/2. Its Walsh coefficients in modes
0,s,t,st are (0,alpha,alpha,alpha).
Initialize independent neurons with W_j~N(0,I_3) and heads independently +/-nu.
First take width to infinity at every fixed e, obtaining initial Gaussian
Walsh coefficients Z_(e,h). This is the ordinary fixed-width CLT of C016.
Then train the FROZEN deterministic full kernel
 H(x,z)=E[ReLU(W.x)ReLU(W.z)+nu^2 1{W.x>0,W.z>0}x.z]
with discrete step1/2. Write b_h=-log(1-lambda_h/2) for the normalized
four-point eigenvalues lambda_h. Use the settled clock premises
 b_s~nu^2 e/(4pi), b_t~b_st~nu^2 e^2/(8pi), b_0 bounded away from0.
Thus eta=(b_t+b_st)/b_s~e and b_t/(b_t+b_st)->1/2.

For fixed kappa>0 choose effective Walsh noise variance alpha^2 rho_e,
 rho_e=kappa/sqrt(e).
Four independent errors +/-sigma_e with sigma_e=2alpha sqrt(rho_e)
realize exactly this variance. In particular sigma_e~sqrt(kappa)e^(7/4),
so label noise remains <=1 for small e, but is not fixed as e decreases.
The noise-averaged clean risk conditional on initialization, in real-time
spectral interpolation of discrete GD, is
 Q_e(t)=sum_h [exp(-2b_h t)(Z_(e,h)-theta_h)^2
             +alpha^2 rho_e(1-exp(-b_h t))^2].             (1)
At integer t this is exactly discrete kernel GD. Real t is used only to
locate extrema of its spectral interpolation; no GD-to-flow limit is taken.

## 2. Joint initial-output covariance, on the relevant scales
Let phi_h(W)=(1/4)sum_(s,t) h(s,t) ReLU(W.x_(s,t)), and
lambda_h^RF=E phi_h(W)^2. The initial covariance is diagonal in Walsh modes,
Var(Z_(e,h))=nu^2 lambda_h^RF, by Gaussian coordinate sign symmetry.
In the Gaussian limit these modes are therefore independent.
C016 establishes lambda_s^RF/e^2->1/2 and the bounds
|phi_t|,|phi_st|<=e^2|W_2|/sqrt(D).
For W_0!=0, all four preactivations eventually have its sign. Consequently
phi_t/e^2 -> W_2 1{W_0>0}, and phi_st/e^2 ->0 almost surely.
Dominated convergence with the preceding bounds gives
 lambda_t^RF/e^4->1/2, lambda_st^RF/e^4->0.                (2)
On one probability space take independent standard normals G_0,G_s,G_t,G_st
and set Z_(e,h)=nu sqrt(lambda_h^RF)G_h for every e. This coupling has exactly
the required Gaussian law at each e. Since alpha~e^2/2, writing
A_(e,h)=(Z_(e,h)/alpha-theta_h/alpha)^2, we get almost surely
 e^2 A_(e,s)->a=2nu^2 G_s^2,
 A_(e,t)->(sqrt(2)nu G_t-1)^2, A_(e,st)->1.                (3)
Define B=((sqrt(2)nu G_t-1)^2+1)/2 >=1/2.
Here a>0 almost surely and a is independent of B. Independence is used only
after the joint Gaussian limit, not for finite-width output coefficients.

## 3. The new central derivative limit
For real s in a fixed compact interval set
 t_e(s)=((3/2)log(1/e)+s)/b_s, z=exp(-s).
Then q_s=exp(-b_s t_e(s))=e^(3/2)z exactly.
Normalize the risk derivative by 2alpha^2(b_t+b_st). Its fast contribution is
 [rho_e q_s-(A_(e,s)+rho_e)q_s^2]/eta
 =kappa(e/eta)z-[(e^2 A_(e,s))(e/eta)+kappa e^(5/2)/eta]z^2
 -> kappa z-a z^2.                                      (4)
For each slow mode q_h=1-O(e log(1/e)) uniformly on the compact interval.
Thus rho_e q_h(1-q_h)=O(sqrt(e)log(1/e))->0, while A_(e,h)q_h^2
has the limits in (3). The rate weights tend to1/2, giving their combined
contribution -B. The constant-mode contribution vanishes: its exponent
decays faster than every power of e and Z_(e,0)=O(1) in this coupling.
The same calculation after differentiating in s is valid: slow terms gain
a factor b_h/b_s=O(e), and even rho_e times that factor tends to0;
constant-mode exponentials dominate the additional polynomial factors.
Hence, almost surely in this coupling, uniformly on each compact s interval,

 Q'_e(t_e(s))/(2alpha^2(b_t+b_st)) -> H_kappa(s)
                                      =kappa exp(-s)-a exp(-2s)-B,
 and the derivatives in s converge too.                  (5)

## 4. Two-root criterion and peak time
On the event Delta=kappa^2-4aB>0 define
 z_+=(kappa+sqrt(Delta))/(2a), z_-=(kappa-sqrt(Delta))/(2a).
Both are positive and z_+>z_-. The classification is the elementary quadratic
criterion already used in C012, now with random coefficients a and B.
As s increases, H is negative, positive, then negative across
 s_min=-log z_+ and s_max=-log z_-.
The roots are simple. Uniform C1 convergence in (5) gives, for every such
fixed Gaussian realization, one nearby minimum and one nearby maximum of
the frozen interpolation for all sufficiently small e, converging to these
locations. Derivative convergence also gives strict decrease immediately
after the maximum. Thus there are two descents separated by a rise.
More precisely the peak satisfies
 b_s t_peak-(3/2)log(1/e) -> -log z_-,
 t_peak~(6pi/nu^2)e^(-1)log(1/e).                         (6)
The statements are pathwise in the coupling, on Delta>0. Random compact
neighborhoods are allowed: convergence on every integer-sized compact set
holds on one probability-one event. No deterministic width rate is asserted.
On Delta<0, H is negative on every compact s interval; this only addresses
this particular time window, not global absence of DD. Delta=0 is not treated.

For value-based nonlinear transfer, a useful additional consequence is this:
 d/ds [Q_e(t_e(s))/(2alpha^2 eta)] converges to H_kappa(s).
Therefore differences of the normalized risks converge to differences of
 V(s)=-kappa exp(-s)+(a/2)exp(-2s)-Bs.
Values across the two simple extrema have strict gaps of order alpha^2 eta.
An o(alpha^2 eta) uniform risk error over a containing compact interval would
preserve appropriately chosen decrease/rise/decrease witnesses and interval
peak localization. Such a nonlinear error is NOT supplied in this claim.

## 5. A tunable probability lower bound
The Gaussian independence in Section2 gives E a=2nu^2 and E B=1+nu^2,
so E[4aB]=8nu^2(1+nu^2). Markov's inequality yields
 P(Delta>0) >= 1-8nu^2(1+nu^2)/kappa^2.                   (7)
Choose kappa^2>8nu^2(1+nu^2)/delta for any prescribed delta in (0,1).
Then the frozen limiting construction has two simple central extrema with
probability greater than1-delta. The noise amplitude still tends to zero.
This is an initialization probability bound, with risk already averaged over
labels; it is not concentration for one realized label vector.
For fixed kappa the exact event probability need not equal this lower bound.

## 6. Scope and next unpaid step
C016's failed rho~1 route is avoided by changing BOTH noise scale and time
center; fixed nu and the unit-norm single-index teacher are retained.
This lemma concerns the balanced four-point frozen precursor only. It does
not yet prove the result for actual nonlinear GD, continuous iid input laws,
fixed label-noise amplitude, macroscopic feature learning, or full Target1.
The next step is a uniform-in-time risk transfer at order o(alpha^2 eta),
with nonzero iid initial output retained. C009's finite-horizon strategy is
a candidate; C015's zero-output paired argument cannot simply be substituted.
Independent mathematical and novelty review is pending. No paper-level
priority claim is made. Sources: own C009 clocks, C012 quadratic-root tool,
C016 Gaussian covariance and exact risk formula; the added slow-mode limits
and derivative scaling are proved above.","status":"unverified"}

For A_N={a_0 connects to a_N}, for every fixed t>=0 the conditional exponential moment E_{1/2}[exp(t N_{A_N})|A_N] is bounded uniformly in N; the conditional mean is less than 3. Yet for every 0<a<1/2 its integrated conditional pivotal cost from a to 1/2 tends to infinity. There is almost surely one infinite critical cluster. Gamma is simple and locally finite but has unbounded degrees and is not transitive, so it is not a counterexample to the Z^d target.","status":"unverified"}

    Then for

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:19:06.750407+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_25bd8c4419c5cfebdbe654d2feb419773e19601d2dc4f7acbb5dc20133c485ec","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary cor:scalar-dyadic-interval-formula-paper of arXiv:2606.08683, 'Exact Fourier dimensions of dyadic Mandelbrot cascades under minimal integrability'] Let \(W\ge0\) satisfy
\[
    \mathbb{E} W=1,\qquad
    \mathbb{E}[W\log_2^+W]<\infty,\qquad
    \mathbb{E}[W\log_2 W]<1.
\]
Let \(W_0,W_1\) be independent copies of \(W\), define
\[
    X_i=\frac{W_i}{2},
    \qquad i=0,1,
\]
and let \(\mu\) be the corresponding scalar dyadic Mandelbrot cascade measure
on \([0,1]\).  Set \(M=\mu([0,1])\).  Then, almost surely on \(\{M>0\}\),
\begin{equation}
    \dim_{\mathrm F}(\mu)
    =
    \dim_{\mathrm E}(\mu)
    =
    \dim_2(\mu)
    =
    D^+(W),
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}
D^+(W)
=
\sup_{1<q<2}
\max\left\{
0,\,
2-\frac2q\bigl(1+\log_2\mathbb{E}[W^q]\bigr)
\right\},
\end{equation}
with the convention that the corresponding term is interpreted as \(0\)
whenever \(\mathbb{E}[W^q]=\infty\).  In particular, on the same event, if
\(D^+(W)>0\), then for every \(0<\sigma<D^+(W)\) there are finite random
constants \(C_\sigma(\omega),R_\sigma(\omega)<\infty\) such that
\begin{equation}
    |\widehat{\mu}(\xi)|
    \le
    C_\sigma(\omega)|\xi|^{-\sigma/2}
    \qquad (|\xi|\ge R_\sigma(\omega)).
\end{equation}
If \(D^+(W)=0\), the decay assertion is vacuous.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:00:46.822597+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_25d0ebf9f483b8c580212f3e0ad5e9867056252c8bd3c689d12ac82eac4e7189","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 24 of arXiv:2608.13208, 'Universality in dimension $1$ of kinetically constrained lattice gases'] Fix $\omega\in\Omega_{0}$. We construct a legal
path $\omega_{0}=\omega,\omega_{1}=\omega_{0}^{x_{0}-1,x_{0}},\dots,\omega_{2n+1}=\omega_{2n}^{x_{2n}-1,x_{2n}}=\omega^{-1,0}$
(with $n$ depending on $\omega$). We do it in three phases:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Begin with a path $\omega_{0}=\omega,\omega_{1}=\omega_{0}^{x_{0}-1,x_{0}},\dots,\omega_{n}=\omega_{n-1}^{x_{n-1}-1,x_{n-1}}$,
whose last configuration satisfies $c(-1,0,\omega_{n})\neq0$ (here
$c=c^{\land}$ by Observation \ref{obs:D_and}). Recall Lemma \ref{lem:and_move_0},
and that $(k+1)F_{l(\omega)}(\omega)<l(\omega)$. If $c(-1,0,\omega)\neq0$
we are done (taking $n=0$). Otherwise, there exists $x\in[2,l(\omega)]$
with $\omega(x)=0,\ \omega(x-1)=1,\ c(x-1,x,\omega)=1$. Set $x_{0}$
to be the minimal such $x$, and $\omega_{1}=\omega^{x_{0}-1,x_{0}}$.

Continue by induction: assume that we constructed $\omega_{m}$. If
$c(-1,0,\omega)\neq0$ we move to phase 2. Otherwise, set $x_{m}$
to be the minimal $x\in[2,l(\omega)]$ such that $\omega_{m}(x)=0,\ \omega_{m}(x-1)=1,\ c(x-1,x,\omega_{m})=1$,
and $\omega_{m+1}=\omega_{m}^{x_{m}-1,x_{m}}$.

This procedure is valid, since we only exchange sites in $[1,l(\omega)]$,
so the condition $(k+1)F_{l(\omega)}(\omega_{m})<l(\omega)$ holds
for all $m$. Moreover, it must end: at each step the center of mass
$\sum_{x=1}^{l(\omega)}x\eta(x)$ increases by $1$, and it cannot
exceed $\sum_{x=1}^{l(\omega)}x\cdot1\le l(\omega)^{2}.$
\item Next, exchange $-1$ and $0$, choosing $x_{n}=0$ and $\omega_{n+1}=\omega_{n}^{-1,0}$.
\item Finally, wind back the path of phase 1: for $m\in\{n+1,\dots2n\}$
we set $x_{m}=x_{2n-m}$, and $\omega_{m+1}=\omega_{m}^{x_{m}-1,x_{m}}$.
Since all these transitions are in $[1,L]$ they do not depend on
the configuration at $-1$ and $0$, hence they are all legal and
end at $\omega_{2n+1}=\omega^{-1,0}$.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

Result: Upper bound: the infrared bound gives <sigma_0 sigma_x> <= C |x|^{-(d-2)} = C|x|^{-1} in d = 3, and improving to |x|^{-(1+eps)} is the statement eta > 0 (anomalous dimension), known numerically eta = 0.036; an argument would need to show the two-point function is strictly smaller than the Gaussian one in a scale-invariant way, e.g. via the random-current intersection probabilities (the same quantity that gives non-triviality, C0052): if two independent currents from 0 to x and from y to z intersect with probability bounded below uniformly, one gets a strict improvement of Simon-Lieb at every scale which iterates to a power gain.
