{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.188469+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_2ec5da81fe4cd2bf3338598e43e8f927a872bec8bec1db320915c7db24db5994","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 100 (comparison of Fokker--Planck equations) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let
$\hvY(t) = \vY(t-\sss)+\xxx$
where $(\sss,\xxx)\sim\varphi$.
Let $\hvX$ be the SDE solution from Definition~\ref{d:intro.SDE.coefs}.
Assume the coefficients $B^i$ and $\Sigma^{ij}$ of \eqref{e:intro.occ.ratio.drift} and \eqref{e:intro.occ.ratio.qv} are bounded and Lipschitz. Then the processes $\hvX$ and $\hvY$ satisfy the same Fokker--Planck equations. Consequently, for each fixed $t$, the marginal law of $\hvX(t)$ agrees with the marginal law of\/ $\hvY(t)$.

\begin{proof}
Abbreviate $\rho\equiv\rho_{\vY}$ for the occupation density of $\vY$, and recall from Lemma~\ref{l:ideal.smoothed.occ.msr} that $\hvY$ has occupation density $\nu\equiv\rho_{\vY}*\varphi$.
Let $\mu$ denote the occupation density of $\hvX$.
 Let $f:\R^d\to\R$ be a smooth compactly supported test function. 
\smallskip

\noindent
\textbf{Fokker--Planck equations for $\hvY(t) = \vY(t-\sss)+\xxx$.} We will calculate
	\[
	\bE\Big[ f(\vY(T))-f(\vY(0))\Big]
	= \int_{s,x} \varphi(s,x)
	\bE\Big[ f(Y(T-s)+x)
	-f(Y(-s)+x)\Big]
	\,ds\,dx
	=\textup{(dr)}+\textup{(qv)}
	\]
where $\textup{(dr)}$
and $\textup{(qv)}$
denote the contributions from the drift and covariation respectively:
	\begin{align*}
	\textup{(dr)}
	&= \sum_{i=1}^d \textup{(dr)}^i
	= \sum_{i=1}^d
	\int_{s,x}\varphi(s,x)
	\int_{-s}^{T-s}
	\partial_i f(Y(t)+x)\,dD^i(t)
	\,ds\,dx \,,\\
	\textup{(qv)}
	&= \sum_{i,j=1}^d \textup{(qv)}^{ij}
	= \frac12
	\sum_{i,j=1}^d
	\int_{s,x}\varphi(s,x)
	\int_{-s}^{T-s}
	\partial_i\partial_j
	f(Y(t)+x)\,dQ^{ij}(t)
	\,ds\,dx\,.
	\end{align*}
Abbreviate $I_T(s)\equiv \ind\{s\in[0,T]\}$. The above can be further simplified as follows:
	\begin{align*}
	\textup{(dr)}^i
	&= \int_{s,x}\varphi(s,x)
	\int_{t,y} I_T(t+s)
	\partial_i f(y+x)
	\,\rho_{D^i}(dt\,dy)\,ds\,dx \\
	&=
	\int_{s',x'}
	I_T(s')\partial_i f(x')
	\bigg\{\int_{t,y} 
	\varphi(s'-t,x'-y)
	\,\rho_{D^i}(dt\,dy)
	\bigg\}\,ds'\,dx'\\
	&=
	\int_{t,y}
	I_T(t)\partial_i f(y)
	\frac{\rho_{D^i}*\varphi(t,y)}
	{\rho*\varphi(t,y)}
	\nu(dt\,dy)\,,
	\end{align*}
recalling at the last step that $\nu=\rho*\varphi$ is the occupation density of $\hvY$.\smallskip

\noindent
\textbf{Fokker--Planck equations for SDE solution $\hvX$.}
 If $f:\R^d\to\R$ is a smooth compactly supported test function, define
	\[
	L_t f(x)
	= \sum_{i=1}^d
	B^i(t,x)
	\partial_i f(x)
	+\frac12\sum_{i,j=1}^d
	A^{ij}(t,x)
	\partial_i\partial_j f(x)
	\]
Then, by It\=o's formula, the process
	\[
	N(t)
	= f(\hvX(t))-f(\hvX(0)) - \int_0^t L_s f(\hvX(s))\,ds
	\]
is a local martingale. Since we assumed the coefficients are bounded, we can conclude that $N$ is a true martingale, and the optional stopping theorem gives
	\[
	\bE\Big[ f(\hvX(T))-f(\hvX(0))\Big]
	= \bE \int_0^T L_t f(\hvX(s))\,ds
	= \textup{(Dr)}+\textup{(QV)}\,,
	\]
where $\textup{(Dr)}$ and $\textup{(QV)}$ denote the contributions from the drift and covariation respectively:
	\begin{align*}
	\textup{(Dr)}
	&= \sum_{i=1}^d \textup{(Dr)}^i
	=\sum_{i=1}^d
	\bE \int_0^T \partial_i f(\hvX(t))
	B^i(t,\hvX(t))\,dt\,,\\
	\textup{(QV)}
	&= \sum_{i,j=1}^d \textup{(QV)}^{ij}
	=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^d
	\bE \int_0^T 
	\partial_i\partial_j f(\hvX(t))
	A^{ij}(t,\hvX(t))\,dt\,.
	\end{align*}
Again abbreviate $I_T(s)\equiv \ind\{s\in[0,T]\}$. The above can be further simplified as
	\begin{align*}
	\textup{(Dr)}^i
	&= \int I_T(t)
	\partial_i f(y) 
	\frac{\rho_{D^i}*\varphi(t,x)}
		{\rho*\varphi(t,x)}
	\mu(dt\,dy)\,,\\
	\textup{(QV)}^{ij}
	&= \int I_T(t)
	\partial_i\partial_j f(y) 
	\frac{\rho_{Q^{ij}}*\varphi(t,x)}
		{\rho*\varphi(t,x)}
	\mu(dt\,dy)
	\end{align*}
recalling that $\mu$ is the occupation density of $\hvX$, and using the definitions \eqref{e:intro.occ.ratio.drift} and \eqref{e:intro.occ.ratio.qv} of $B^i$ and $A^{ij}$.

Comparing the expressions for $\hvX$ and $\hvY$ shows that $\mu$ and $\nu$ satisfy the same Fokker--Planck equations. We now apply \cite[Lem.~2.3]{MR2375067}: this is a general result applying to $\R^d$-valued stochastic differential equations
such as \eqref{e:abstract.sde}, with a given law fo (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X_i independent (not necessarily identically distributed)","F countable, or measurable in the sense that the suprema are measurable","eps_i Rademacher, independent of the sample"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.628563+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_2f07d4d2760bb3a92f148947533c45743c582d35923c10aa7b5e5c8d1a13a9d0","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, ..., X_n be independent random elements and let F be a countable class of measurable real functions (countability, or a suitable separability/measurability condition, is needed so the suprema are measurable). Let eps_1, ..., eps_n be independent Rademacher signs, independent of the X_i. Then E sup_{f in F} | sum_{i=1}^n ( f(X_i) - E f(X_i) ) | <= 2 E sup_{f in F} | sum_{i=1}^n eps_i f(X_i) |, and in the other direction E sup_{f in F} | sum_{i=1}^n eps_i ( f(X_i) - E f(X_i) ) | <= 2 E sup_{f in F} | sum_{i=1}^n ( f(X_i) - E f(X_i) ) |. The constant 2 in the first inequality is the standard one and is not claimed sharp. Symmetrization is what allows one to work CONDITIONALLY on the data, replacing an empirical process by a Rademacher process whose conditional law is sub-Gaussian with an explicit variance proxy, which is the entry point for chaining bounds and Rademacher complexity. The X_i need not be identically distributed. Note the direction of the useful inequality: it bounds the centred empirical process by the Rademacher process, which is the one that can be chained. [standard; e.g. van der Vaart and Wellner, Weak Convergence and Empirical Processes, Lemma 2.3.1]","status":"unverified"}

Positive-probability restricted four-atom single-label result, not full Target1.

# C020 v2: a shifted peak for ONE realized label vector
Status: proof (unaudited). Kind: narrowed. Target: 1. Novelty unestablished.
General T267 remains open. This is a restricted four-atom width-first theorem.

## 1. Model and precise probability statement
For 0<e<1/4 put D=1+e^2+e^4, x_(s,t)=(1,es,e^2t)/sqrt(D),
s,t in {-1,1}. The population is uniform on these four atoms and the
training set contains one observation at each atom (stratified, not iid).
Set u_e=(0,e,1)/sqrt(1+e^2), c_e=e^2/sqrt(D(1+e^2)), alpha_e=c_e/2,
and g_e(x)=ReLU(u_e.x)-c_e/2. Thus ||u_e||=1 and its four Walsh
coefficients (0,s,t,st) are (0,alpha_e,alpha_e,alpha_e).
Fix 0<nu<=1 and kappa>0. Independently draw four noise signs xi_(s,t),
each uniform {-1,1}, and label y_i=g_e(x_i)+sigma_e xi_i, where
 sigma_e=2alpha_e sqrt(kappa/sqrt(e))~sqrt(kappa)e^(7/4).
Initialize f_m(x)=m^(-1/2)sum_j a_j ReLU(w_j.x), with iid w_j~N(0,I_3)
and independent iid a_j uniform {-nu,nu}. Both layers undergo simultaneous
GD with step gamma=1/2 on loss (1/8)sum_i(f_m(x_i)-y_i)^2, using gate
derivative zero at zero. The individual clean risk is
 R_(e,m,xi)(k)=(1/4)sum_i(f_(m,xi)(x_i;k)-g_e(x_i))^2.
There is NO noise average anywhere in the claim.

Let H(x,z)=E[ReLU(W.x)ReLU(W.z)+nu^2 1{W.x>0,W.z>0}x.z], and let
lambda_h be the Walsh eigenvalues of H(X,X)/4, b_h=-log(1-lambda_h/2),
eta_e=(b_t+b_st)/b_s. C009's clock premises are
 b_s~nu^2 e/(4pi), b_t~b_st~nu^2 e^2/(8pi), eta_e~e,
with b_0 bounded away from zero.
For epsilon>0 let E_(e,m,xi)(epsilon) mean that there exist integer
k0<k1<k2<k3 with k0>=0, satisfying
 R(k0)>R(k1), R(k2)>R(k1), R(k2)>R(k3),                   (1)
 |k1/((3pi/nu^2)e^(-1)log(1/e))-1|<epsilon,
 |k2/((9pi/nu^2)e^(-1)log(1/e))-1|<epsilon,
and k2 is an interior maximum on a nontrivial integer interval [l,k3]
with k1<l<k2<k3 and both endpoint risks strictly below R(k2).
Ties between interior maximizing indices are allowed. The claim is
 liminf_(e downarrow0) liminf_(m to infinity)
 P_(xi,initialization)(E_(e,m,xi)(epsilon)) >= 1/16.       (2)
For each fixed chi in {-1,1}, conditional on xi_(s,t)=chi*s, the lower
bound over initialization alone is 1/2. The time k1 is a low-risk
cancellation WITNESS, not a claimed uniquely located stationary minimum.
The time k2 is an interval peak, not a unique stationary point theorem.
Equation (1) is the finite-witness meaning of two descents separated by a rise;
no monotonicity of every intervening nonlinear GD step is asserted.

## 2. Gaussian-width precursor and its exact unaveraged risk
C016/C017 supply, after the fixed-e width limit, independent Gaussian
Walsh initial outputs Z_(e,h) with covariance nu^2 lambda_h^RF. Couple them
for all e using independent standard G_0,G_s,G_t,G_st. Set
 U_(e,h)=Z_(e,h)/alpha_e-theta_h/alpha_e.
Then almost surely
 e U_(e,s)->L=sqrt(2)nu G_s,
 U_(e,t)->L_t=sqrt(2)nu G_t-1, U_(e,st)->-1.
These convergences are uniform when the four Gaussian coordinates range
over a fixed bounded set; the scalar variance coefficients are deterministic.
The constant initial output Z_(e,0)=O(1) in this coupling.

Fix the single label branch xi_(s,t)=chi*s. Its only nonzero normalized
noise Walsh coefficient is N_s=d e^(-1/4), d=2sqrt(kappa)chi;
N_0=N_t=N_st=0. Write N=N_s. The exact frozen clean risk is
 Q_(e,chi)(t)=alpha_e^2 sum_h [q_h U_(e,h)+(1-q_h)N_h]^2,
 q_h=exp(-b_h t).                                       (3)
At integer times this is discrete kernel GD, not gradient flow. In real
time it is only the spectral interpolation used to select integer witnesses.
Use the favorable initialization event chi*L<0, of probability1/2.
Every assertion below first refers to a fixed Gaussian realization in
this event, then is made probabilistic through compact exhaustion.

## 3. Early cancellation and two large value gaps
For small e, N and U_(e,s) have opposite signs. Thus
 q_*=-N/(U_(e,s)-N) belongs to (0,1),
 q_*~(-d/L)e^(3/4).
The fast residual N+q_*(U_(e,s)-N) is EXACTLY zero. Define
 t_1=-log(q_*)/b_s, t_0=-log(2q_*)/b_s.
Both are nonnegative for small e, t_0<t_1, and
 b_s t_1=(3/4)log(1/e)-log(-d/L)+o(1).                 (4)
Round these to nearest integers k0,k1. Their separation is (log2)/b_s,
which tends to infinity, so rounding preserves their order. A time change
of at most1/2 multiplies q_s by exp(O(b_s))=1+O(e). The residual error at
k1 is therefore O(|N|e)=O(e^(3/4)); at k0 it is -N+O(|N|e).
Slow-mode q_h tend to1 at both times and their U_h stay bounded. The
constant-mode residual is negligible faster than every power of e because
its initial normalized coefficient is O(e^(-2)) and b_0 is positive.
It follows that
 Q(k1)/alpha_e^2 -> L_t^2+1=2B,
 Q(k0)/(alpha_e^2 e^(-1/2)) -> d^2=4kappa,
where B=(L_t^2+1)/2>=1/2. In particular Q(k0)>Q(k1).
This proves the first descent witness and its leading clock; no derivative
argument or minimum uniqueness is needed.

## 4. The later single-label peak
Set t_e(v)=((9/4)log(1/e)+v)/b_s and z=exp(-v). Then q_s=e^(9/4)z.
Differentiate (3), using the exact derivative identity of C019:
 Q'(t_e(v))/(2alpha_e^2(b_t+b_st))
 =sum_h [b_h/(b_t+b_st)]
   [q_h N_h(N_h-U_h)-q_h^2(U_h-N_h)^2].                 (5)
The fast term -q_s N U_s/eta_e converges to -dL z=A z,
with A=-dL>0. Its other four expansion terms vanish uniformly on bounded
v intervals. Their orders are respectively e^(3/4), e^(3/2), e^(9/4), e^3,
for q_s N^2/eta_e, q_s^2 U_s^2/eta_e, q_s^2 U_s N/eta_e,
and q_s^2 N^2/eta_e. The slow terms, with N_t=N_st=0, tend to -B,
since their weights tend to1/2 and q_t,q_st=1-O(e log(1/e)).
The constant term is again exponentially negligible. Hence locally uniformly
 Q'(t_e(v))/(2alpha_e^2(b_t+b_st)) -> A exp(-v)-B.         (6)
Integration on bounded intervals gives convergence of centered risk differences:
 [Q(t_e(v))-Q(t_e(0))]/(2alpha_e^2 eta_e)
 -> V(v)-V(0), V(v)=-A exp(-v)-Bv.                     (7)
The function V is strictly concave, with its unique maximum at
 v_*=log(A/B), and has strict value gaps to either endpoint of any compact
interval containing v_* in its interior. Also, uniformly on compact v sets,
 Q(t_e(v))/(alpha_e^2 e^(-1/2)) -> d^2=4kappa.            (8)
Indeed q_s U_s=O(e^(5/4)) is negligible relative to N=O(e^(-1/4));
slow risk is O(alpha_e^2) and the constant-mode risk is negligible.
Equations (8) and Section3 give the second strict gap Q(peak)>Q(k1).
Equation (7) gives the third strict gap to a later time, now of order
alpha_e^2 eta_e. It is much smaller than the two early value gaps.

Round all central t_e(v) to the integer grid. The mesh in v is b_s->0,
so (7) remains uniform on the grid. On a fixed compact interval containing
v_* inside, an integer maximizing index is interior and its v coordinate
tends to v_*. This uses the positive gap between V(v_*) and the compact
complement of any neighborhood of v_*, not derivatives of nonlinear GD.
The central maximizing time consequently has leading term
 (9pi/nu^2)e^(-1)log(1/e).                              (9)
The early cancellation witness (4) precedes the entire central interval,
since their b_s-scaled time separation is (3/2)log(1/e)+O(1).
This completes the Gaussian frozen-array witness construction.

## 5. Probability and transfer to the actual BOTH-layer nonlinear updates
For an integer M>=1 restrict to the compact Gaussian event
 K_M={chi L<=-1/M, |G_0|,|G_s|,|G_t|,|G_st|<=M}.
These increasing events exhaust {chi L<0}. On K_M, A is bounded above
and away from zero and B is bounded above and below. Thus v_*, the offset
in (4), and all coefficients used above lie in deterministic bounded sets.
All estimates in Sections3-4 are uniform on K_M: the U limits have deterministic
coefficients linear in bounded G, the denominator L is bounded away from0,
and the exponentially small constant-mode bounds are uniform as well.
Choose a deterministic central v interval [-J,J] whose interior contains
all possible v_* on K_M, with a margin of at least1. Strict concavity and
compactness give uniform positive endpoint gaps for V. The two large early
gaps are also uniform. For small e, the entire central grid interval lies
inside the relative time tolerance epsilon in (2), and the cancellation
indices lie inside the stated earlier relative tolerance.

For each fixed e choose a finite integer horizon T_e(M) containing the
central grid interval and the possible earlier witnesses. C009 Section3,
as applied in C018 Section3, gives joint weak convergence of all actual
individual risks through that finite horizon to (3) when m tends to infinity.
The proof retains the actual nonzero initial output and controls both-layer
motion and gate-crossing remainders. The finite sixteen-label family is
covered, although here only the fixed single branch is used. Risk squaring
is continuous on the finite array, and the prediction arrays are tight.
No finite-width Gaussian-mode independence or e-uniform width bound is used.

For clarity about maxima and weak convergence, take the deterministic
central interval just specified. The event that there exist k0<k1 before
it and a grid index j in its interior, with the two early witness gaps
strictly positive and R(j) strictly above BOTH central endpoint values,
is open in the finite risk array: it is a finite union of finite intersections
of strict inequalities. Restrict k1 to its required relative time band.
The frozen arrays on K_M satisfy this open event for sufficiently small e.
Any maximum k2 over that central interval then lies in its interior;
replacing j by k2 only increases the witness gaps. The right endpoint is
k3, and k1 precedes the central interval. The entire central interval is
already in the required peak-time band, so all maximizers qualify.
The open-set Portmanteau inequality transfers the LOWER probability bound
to actual nonlinear risk arrays for each fixed e. Thus the two ordered
liminf limits have conditional probability at least P(K_M). Let M increase
to infinity to obtain the conditional lower bound1/2. This argument sends
width to infinity separately at every e and finite horizon, before e tends
to zero. No infinite-horizon NTK statement or interchange of limits occurs.

Finally the two noise events xi=+s and xi=-s are disjoint and each has
probability1/16 under the original four independent sign errors. Noise is
independent of initialization. Summing their conditional lower bounds gives
(1/16)(1/2)+(1/16)(1/2)=1/16, proving (2). Other sign patterns might add
probability, but they are not analyzed or counted in this claim.

## 6. Limits and unresolved piece
This is a single REALIZED label vector result, unlike C017/C018. It is
consistent with C019: its peak is at the later (9/4)log(1/e) clock, while
C019 addresses bounded offsets around (3/2)log(1/e).
The four input atoms cluster as e decreases; training inputs are stratified,
noise amplitude shrinks, width is taken first, and only a positive-probability
noise/initialization event is proved. No full typical-data theorem, macroscopic
feature learning, fixed-noise theorem, unique stationary points or complete
noise window is claimed. The hardest unpaid step is a general single-dataset
result beyond this shrinking four-atom, positive-probability construction.
Dependencies C009,C016,C017,C018,C019 and this claim all remain unaudited.
Independent correctness and novelty review are pending; no priority claim
is made. Sources: the named own proof files; the full ReLU kernel and clock
premises come from C009, with Heckel-Yilmaz 2007.10099v2 Section3 as its
primary kernel source. No new external literature result is claimed here.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the sequence is independent AND identically distributed","A invariant under permutations of finitely many coordinates"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:40.781848+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_2f498bfa2a2e45261395e21060f28261d050042661f5980c3c3857ba42765667","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, X_2, ... be INDEPENDENT AND IDENTICALLY DISTRIBUTED. Call an event A EXCHANGEABLE if it is invariant under every permutation of finitely many indices, that is A is unchanged when the values of any finite set of coordinates are permuted. Then P(A) is 0 or 1 for every exchangeable A. This is strictly stronger than Kolmogorov's 0-1 law, which applies to TAIL events: every tail event is exchangeable, but not conversely. The standard separating example is A = { S_n = 0 for infinitely many n } for a simple random walk, which is exchangeable but NOT a tail event, since changing X_1 changes every partial sum. Identical distribution is essential and cannot be relaxed to mere independence. Minimal counterexample: let X_1 be Bernoulli(1/2) and let X_n = 0 deterministically for every n >= 2. These are independent but not identically distributed, and the event A = { x : x_n = 1 for some n } is invariant under every finite permutation of the coordinates, hence exchangeable, yet P(A) = P(X_1 = 1) = 1/2. The proof below breaks exactly where one needs it to: the permutation swapping the first n coordinates with the next n is not measure preserving unless the coordinates share a law. A standard use: for an i.i.d. sequence the events {limsup S_n = + infinity} and {liminf S_n = - infinity} are exchangeable, because permuting finitely many summands changes S_n for only finitely many n, so each has probability 0 or 1; for a non-degenerate mean-zero law a short further argument then shows both probabilities are 1, but that conclusion is NOT delivered by the 0-1 law alone. [Hewitt and Savage (1955); see Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 4.1.1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.176790+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_2fdcbd29342bc81581ff221e1335d681186fe635fa373907a7fd8c6b9238e08b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 72 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For all $q_0 \in [0,1)$, we have 
\begin{align*}
\sM^{\sx}(\alpha,q_0) 
&\subseteq \sM^{\sxii}(\alpha,q_0)\,,\\
\sM^{\six}(\alpha,q_0) 
&\subseteq \sM^{\sidealast}(\alpha,q_0)\,.
\end{align*}

\begin{proof}
We repeat the most relevant part of Definition~\ref{d:SDE.classification} for this proof:
	\begin{center}
	\begin{tabular}[h]{r|cccccccc}
	\MSRheader\\
	\hline
	\PRFTWOdefn\\
	\PRFFOURdefn\\
	\PRFONEHALFdefn\\
	\SUPERPERFECTASTdefn
	\end{tabular}
	\end{center}
The classes only differ in the conditions on the function $p$.

    Consider any $\mu \in \cM^{\sx}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)$ where $\epsilon < 1/2$. 
    Then $\mu$ is of the form $\mu = \mu(q_*=q_0,b,\sigma,p,\zeta = \delta_0)$ for some $(q_*=q_0,b,\sigma,w,p,\zeta = \delta_0,\zeta^\Ising) \in \Adm^{\sx}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)$.
    Since $p$ satisfies condition~\ref{it:3.1}, $p$ is twice differentiable and therefore continuous, and further satisfies $p(q_0) \le \epsilon$.
    So we can find $q' \in (q_0,1)$ such that $p(q') = 2\epsilon$, and define $\tilde p \in \incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ by
    \[
        \tilde p(t) = \begin{cases}
            2\epsilon (t - q_0) / (q' - q_0) & t \in [q_0,q')\,, \\
            p(t) & t \in [q',1]\,.
        \end{cases}
    \]
    In particular $\tilde p(q_0) = 0$, so $\tilde p$ satisfies condition~\ref{it:3.5withzero}, as required for the $\sxii$ class.
    Since $p$ and $\tilde p$ agree on $[q',1]$, we have
    \[
        \|p'-\tilde p'\|_1
        = \int_{q_0}^{q'} |p'(t) - \tilde p'(t)|\,dt
        \le \int_{q_0}^{q'} (p'(t) + \tilde p'(t))\,dt
        \le p(q') + \tilde p(q')
        = 4\epsilon\,.
    \]
Recalling Definition~\ref{d:X.adm}, we have $\mu \in \cM(q_0;p,f)$ for budget function
$f(t) = (\E w_t)^2 / \alpha$. Applying
    Proposition~\ref{p:continuity.in.p} gives the existence of a measure
    \[
        \tilde\mu \in \cM(q_0;\tilde p,f)
        \subseteq \cM^{\sxii}(\alpha,q_0)
    \]
    with $\bbW_2(\mu,\tilde \mu)^2 \le 6(1+1/\alpha) \cdot 4\epsilon$.
    Since this holds for all $\mu \in \cM^{\sx}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)$ with $\epsilon < 1/2$, we conclude
    \[
        \cM^{\sx}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon) \subseteq \cB_{\tilde\epsilon}\Big(\cM^{\sxii}(\alpha,q_0)\Big)
    \]
    for some $\tilde\epsilon$ tending to $0$ with $\epsilon$.
    By adjusting $\tilde\epsilon$ we can also ensure
    \[
        \cB_{\epsilon}\Big(\cM^{\sx}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)\Big) \subseteq \cB_{\tilde\epsilon}\Big(\cM^{\sxii}(\alpha,q_0)\Big)\,.
    \]
 Recall \eqref{e:measure.classes.simplification.without.L0}: taking a union over $L$ and an intersection over $\epsilon$ proves the first assertion, $\sM^{\sx}(\alpha,q_0) \subseteq \sM^{\sxii}(\alpha,q_0)$.

    The proof of the second assertion $\sM^{\six}(\alpha,q_0) \subseteq \sM^{\sidealast}(\alpha,q_0)$ is very similar, so we only describe the differences.
    Consider any $\mu \in \cM^{\six}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)$ where $\epsilon < 1/2$, realized by controls $(q_*=q_0,b,\sigma,w,p,\zeta = \delta_0,\zeta^\Ising) \in \Adm^{\six}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)$.
    In this case $p$ satisfies condition~\ref{it:3.1concave}, so $p$ is concave in addition to the properties of condition~\ref{it:3.1} used above.
    Let $q'$ and $\tilde p$ be defined as above.
    Since $p(q_0) \ge 0$ and $p(q') = 2\epsilon$, the concavity of $p$ implies $p(t) \ge \tilde p(t)$ for all $t\in [0,q']$.
    Thus $\tilde p$ is also concave, and in particular satisfies condition~\ref{it:3.3}, as required for the $\sidealast$ class.
Then, arguing identically as above completes the proof.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.751901+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_302068305216ae5c066735895bb24468a7e83b19c56defd1453da6e28734f134","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TYPEWRITER (L^p convergence does not imply almost-everywhere convergence). On [0,1] write n = 2^k + j with 0 <= j < 2^k and let f_n be the indicator of [j 2^{-k}, (j+1) 2^{-k}). Then ||f_n||_p^p = 2^{-k} -> 0, so f_n -> 0 in L^p for every p < infinity and in measure. But for every x in [0,1) and every k there is exactly one j with f_{2^k + j}(x) = 1, so f_n(x) equals 1 for infinitely many n and 0 for infinitely many n: the sequence converges at NO point. This is why one extracts an a.e. convergent subsequence rather than hoping for the full sequence. SLIDING BUMP (pointwise convergence does not imply L^1 convergence). On [0,1] let g_n = n 1_{(0, 1/n)}. Then g_n(x) -> 0 for every x in (0,1], indeed the convergence is pointwise everywhere on (0,1], yet integral g_n = 1 for every n. The mass does not disappear, it concentrates. The dominated convergence theorem excludes exactly this: no integrable g dominates all g_n, since any such g would satisfy g >= n on (0,1/n) for every n, forcing integral_{(0,1/n)} g >= 1 for all n and contradicting absolute continuity of the integral. ESCAPING MASS is the third, distinct failure and lives on infinite measure spaces: h_n = 1_{[n, n+1]} on R is uniformly bounded, converges to 0 everywhere, and has ||h_n||_1 = 1. Three different mechanisms, three different repairs: a subsequence, a dominating function, and a tightness condition. [standard; the typewriter sequence is sometimes attributed to Kolmogorov]","status":"unverified"}

Then the closed unit ball B of X* is metrizable in the relative weak-star topology if and only if X is separable; in that case every bounded subset of X* is weak-star metrizable, and a compatible metric is d(f,g) = sum over n of 2^(-n) min(1, |f(x_n) - g(x_n)|) for any dense sequence (x_n) of the unit sphere of X. Combined with Banach-Alaoglu (B is weak-star compact), separability of X gives that B is weak-star compact and metrizable, hence weak-star SEQUENTIALLY compact: every bounded sequence in X* has a weak-star convergent subsequence. The dual statement also holds: for a Banach space X, the closed unit ball of X is metrizable in the weak topology sigma(X, X*) if and only if X* is separable. WHERE IT FAILS: (a) 'bounded' is essential - the weak-star topology on ALL of X* is metrizable only when X is finite dimensional; indeed if it were metrizable with countable base (U_m) at 0 and X is infinite dimensional, each U_m contains a nonzero subspace (it is cut out by finitely many functionals), so one can pick f_m in U_m with ||f_m|| >= m, and then f_m converges weak-star to 0 while being unbounded, contradicting the uniform boundedness principle; (b) the two directions are not interchangeable - separability of X does not imply separability of X*: X = l^1 is separable, so B of (l^1)* = l^infinity is weak-star metrizable, but (l^1)* = l^infinity is not separable, so the unit ball of l^1 is NOT weakly metrizable; (c) the metric above is not translation-invariantly compatible on the whole of X* and the equivalence is genuinely a statement about the relative topology on bounded sets; (d) for X = l^infinity, which is not separable, the unit ball of (l^infinity)* is weak-star compact but not weak-star metrizable, and weak-star compactness there is not sequential compactness.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:49:49.204148+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_306e084e1cb887edf036fb5c0c3c7f11d4d1df89e4517f85f314907966879a51","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 2 (Sampling active subspaces~\protect{\cite[Thm.~3.7) of arXiv:2604.27119, '\Large Applied Random Matrix Theory\relatedversion'] {Con15:Active-Subspaces}}]
Let $f : \R^d \to \R$ be $L$-Lipschitz and differentiable.
As in~\cref{eqn:sensitivity-matrix,eqn:empirical-sensitivity},
consider the sensitivity matrix $\mtx{\Sigma} \in \Sym_d(\R)$
and the empirical approximation $\widehat{\mtx{\Sigma}}_n \in \Sym_d(\R)$
determined by $n$ gradient samples.  The expectation of the relative approximation error satisfies
\[
\Expect\left[ \frac{ \norm{ \widehat{\mtx{\Sigma}}_n - \mtx{\Sigma} }}{\norm{\mtx{\Sigma}}} \right]

	\beta_n \coloneqq \frac{L^2 \log(2d)}{\norm{\mtx{\Sigma}}} \cdot \frac{1}{n}.

\]

results in expected relative error at most $\eps$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.346979+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3083b9a91b3bfb645dd1208a02f4f9ee20f6b1c4e5780669c6f1d7c2726f9b6f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 149 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Fix $(b,\sigma,w,p,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising)$ satisfying the conditions of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-centered}. 
Fix any vectors $\bx^{\dagger,0},\prxbx^{\dagger,0}\in\bbR^M$, and let $\tilde{\cA}^\dagger$ be the centered IAMP specified by Definition~\ref{d:centered.iamp}. 
Then, for $C\equiv C(L,\epsilon,\delta)$, 
there exists a $C$-Lipschitz map $\cA^\dagger$ which agrees
with $\tilde{\cA}^\dagger$ with probability $1-\exp(-cN)$, and satisfies
	    \[
    \cA(-\bG,-\bg^\aux)
    =
    -\cA(\bG,\bg^\aux)\,.
    \]
In particular, it follows that $\bbE[\cA(\bG,\bg^{\aux})~|~\bx^{\dagger,0},\prxbx^{\dagger,0}]=\bzero\in\bbR^N$.
\begin{proof}
    Let $(\hat\by^{\dagger,k},\hat\prxby^{\dagger,k},\hat\bx^{\dagger,k},\hat\prxbx^{\dagger,k})$ be the IAMP iterates corresponding to $(-\bG,- \bg^{\aux})$.
    We claim that for all $0\leq k\leq \ubl$ we have
    \begin{align*}
    (\hat\prxby,\hat\by,\hat\bu,\hat\bw)^{\dagger,k}
    &=
    (-\prxby,-\by,-\bu,\bw)^{\dagger,k}
      \,\\
    (\hat\prxbx,\hat\bx,\hat\bv,
    \hat\bm,\hat\bsig,\hat\bb)^{\dagger,k}
    &=
    (\prxbx,\bx,\bv,
    \bm,\bsig,\bb)^{\dagger,k}\,.
    \end{align*}
Indeed, the base case for the first statement above holds easily since
$w$ is even by the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main} \eqref{i:IAMP-main-centered}, the functions
 $\psi$ and $\prxpsi$ are odd (Lemma~\ref{lem:even-manual-init}), 
the vectors $(\by,\prxby,\hat{\by},\hat{\prxby})^{\dagger,0}$ are defined by \eqref{eq:mean-0-initialization},  and  we defined $\bu^{\dagger,0}=\hat{\bu}^{\dagger,0}=\bzero\in\R^M$.
The remaining statements follow by 
induction, using the formulas \eqref{eq:proxy-y-amp-def}--\eqref{eq:x-amp-def}. 

The above shows the desired symmetry for the mapping $\tilde{\cA}^\dagger$, and we must now transfer it to $\cA^\dagger$. This proceeds similarly as in the \hyperlink{proof:t.IAMP.main.main}{proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-main}}, using the Kirzsbraun extension theorem, except that we now need to ensure that the symmetry requirement is satisfied. 
First, we have by easy induction that $\tilde{\cA}^\dagger$ is $C$-Lipschitz on a subset $\mathcal{U}^{\dagger}\subseteq \bbR^{MN+N_{\aux}}$, similarly to the \hyperlink{proof:t.IAMP.main.main}{proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-main}}. To be precise, 
    \[\mathcal{U}^{\dagger}
    =\bigg\{
    \begin{array}{c}
    (\bG,\bg^\aux) : 
    \textup{$\bG_\circ$
    satisfies \eqref{eq:Brownian-bridge-condition},
    $\|\bG\|_\textup{op}\le C_0
    (M^{1/2}+N^{1/2})$,}\\
    \textup{$\|\bar\bg^{\ell}\|\leq 2\sqrt{N}$
    for all $0\le\ell\le\ubl$, and
    $\|\bar\bg^{\init}\|\leq 2\sqrt{N}$}
    \end{array}
    \bigg\}\,.
    \]
In particular, this choice of $\mathcal{U}^{\dagger}$ is origin-symmetric. 
(Again, see e.g.\ the discussion on ``standard optimization algorithms'' in \cite{HuangSellke2021} for the Lipschitz bound on such a domain.)

Thus, let $S=\{\bg_1,\bg_2,\dots\}$ be a countable dense set in $\bbR^{MN+N_{\aux}}$.
    For each $\bg_i$, we assume $\tilde\cA^{\dagger}$ has been extended to a $C$-Lipschitz function on $\mathcal{U}^{\dagger,i}\equiv \mathcal{U}^{\dagger}\cup \{\bg_1,-\bg_1,\dots,\bg_i,-\bg_i\}$.
    Then by the Kirzsbraun extension theorem, there exists a $C$-Lipschitz extension to $\mathcal{U}^{\dagger,i}\cup \{\bg_{i+1}\}$.
    Since 
  $\mathcal{U}^{\dagger,i}$ is symmetric,  
the unique odd extension to $\mathcal{U}^{\dagger,i+1}$ is still $C$-Lipschitz. Continuing in this way yields a $C$-Lipschitz extension to $ \mathcal{U}^\dagger\cup S\cup -S$. This set is dense by definition of $S$, so the result follows by continuously extending to all of $\R^{MN+N_{\aux}}$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:27:56.778420+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3094139d6c32ee053ca7cdcf1a48243f534a519ed5d8e61476f08327de9b8c55","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 16 of arXiv:2608.31171, '\bf Finite-energy spacetimes with torus symmetry. \\ \Large Cauchy stability of Einstein--'] A \textbf{Navier--Stokes triple} \((\mathscr F,\chi,\mathscr B)\) is called \textbf{admissible} provided the following \textbf{invariant-domain property} holds for each of the two associated Einstein--Navier--Stokes models 
\eqref{eq:pot-production-system} and \eqref{eq:pot-dissipated-system}, as follows. 

Let \(\{\Sigma_t\}_{t_0\leq t<t_1}\) be a spacelike foliation of a compact spacetime slab, and let \((g,\beta,\zeta)\) be a regular solution of the corresponding hyperbolic evolution-constraint system\footnote{A gauge must be chosen to deal with the spacetime metric and formulate a well-posed initial value problem; this is a standard topic, not reviewed here \cite{Choquet-book}.} on \([t_0,t_1)\). Assume that
\be
\zeta(t_0,\Sigma_{t_0})\subset\mathcal K_0
\qquad\text{for some closed fiber subset }\mathcal K_0\Subset\mathscr F.
\ee
Then one has
\be
\zeta(t,\Sigma_t)\subset\mathscr F
\qquad\text{for every }t_0\leq t<t_1.
\ee
Moreover, if the fields admit a continuous limit in the ambient bundles as \(t\uparrow t_1\), while the nonsingular coefficients in the equation for~\(\zeta\) remain bounded, then the terminal relaxing field satisfies
\be

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:09:41.186720+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_31199ef303ea3dc048a12dfd4ffe05c9131d850a43b8c0ee851330f431bc4f9f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematics, Schur's lemma is an elementary but useful statement in representation theory of groups and algebras. In the group case it says that if M and N are two finite-dimensional irreducible representations of a group G and φ is a linear map from M to N that commutes with the action of the group, then either φ is invertible, or φ = 0. An important special case occurs when M = N, i.e. φ is a self-map; in particular, for representations over an algebraically closed field, any element of the center of a group must act as a scalar operator on M. The lemma is named after Issai Schur who used it to prove the Schur orthogonality relations and develop the basics of the representation theory of finite groups. Schur's lemma admits generalisations to Lie groups and Lie algebras, the most common of which are due to Jacques Dixmier and Daniel Quillen.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-05T06:00:09.358403+00:00","domain":"ensemble learning","id":"claim_3164e6f087edcf03d0ed5dc5b5362a181abb5563823cfe1cedcf020aa6b01bc9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Fitting a per-output affine stack directly in the per-sample relative metric - weighted least squares with case weights $1/\\|y_i\\|^2$, or a per-output simplex fit with the same weights - overfits badly: the weights concentrate the effective sample on the handful of smallest-norm cases and $M + 1$ coefficients fitted to them are unusable out of sample (measured on the EMIT pool, seed 101: 0.1236 against 0.0465 for ordinary least squares on Y1, 0.1591 against 0.1292 on Y2; cross-validation on the weighted fit chooses to discard it entirely). The same objective becomes the best available estimator when it is reached through the error covariance rather than through the regression: form the error covariance in the relative metric, replace its sample eigenvalues by the Ledoit-Peche nonlinear-shrinkage values (floored at a small fraction of the bulk level), and take the sum-to-one minimum-variance weights with the intercept closing the weighted mean error, with no cross-validation anywhere. Measured on the same three cells (Y1, Y2, Y4): 0.0451 / 0.1190 / 1.799 against ordinary least squares 0.0465 / 0.1292 / 1.898 (+3.0 / +7.9 / +5.2 percent), matching the cross-validated best heuristic of the pool twice and beating it once; with the residual shrink toward the pooled simplex weights on top (cross-validated amount 0.2-0.4) it is the best estimator on all three cells, +4.1 / +11.7 / +6.7 percent over least squares and +3.4 to +3.9 percent over the pool's best. Two ingredients do the work: the nonlinear shrinkage tames the heavy-tailed spectrum that the small-norm cases create, and the sum-to-one constraint removes the scale and intercept freedom those cases exploit. In this metric the random-matrix cleaning is not a small correction on top of least squares; it is the difference between an unusable fit and the best one. Three cells of one seed at the time of writing; the seventy-cell population test on both corpora was running.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:47:41.428399+00:00","domain":"Riemannian geometry","id":"claim_31b886d6ae5e89d7ba86732be244fd5ceb8c845f680edca8ffdf80a466f188ad","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (M,g) be a Riemannian manifold with Levi-Civita connection nabla. A smooth curve gamma: I -> M on an interval I subset R is a geodesic if its velocity field is parallel along itself: nabla_{gamma'(t)} gamma'(t) = 0 for every t in I. Equivalently, in local coordinates x^1,...,x^n a curve gamma(t) = (x^1(t),...,x^n(t)) is a geodesic iff it satisfies the second-order ODE system d^2x^k/dt^2 + sum_{i,j} Gamma^k_{ij}(gamma(t)) (dx^i/dt)(dx^j/dt) = 0 for k=1,...,n, where Gamma^k_{ij} are the Christoffel symbols of g. Geodesics are the critical points of the energy functional among curves with fixed endpoints, and, when locally minimizing, are the locally shortest paths between nearby points.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-23T07:57:26.142189+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_31bf23c8569447ad87fe2691c4a7ab91","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematics, Schur's lemma is an elementary but useful statement in representation theory of groups and algebras. In the group case it says that if M and N are two finite-dimensional irreducible representations of a group G and φ is a linear map from M to N that commutes with the action of the group, then either φ is invertible, or φ = 0. An important special case occurs when M = N, i.e. φ is a self-map; in particular, for representations over an algebraically closed field (e.g. $\\mathbb {C}$), any element of the center of a group must act as a scalar operator (a scalar multiple of the identity) on M. The lemma is named after Issai Schur who used it to prove the Schur orthogonality relations and develop the basics of the representation theory of finite groups. Schur's lemma admits generalisations to Lie groups and Lie algebras, the most common of which are due to Jacques Dixmier and Daniel Quillen.","status":"unverified"}

Leskela (Queueing Systems 100 (2022), 213-215, Problem 3) asked whether some stationary ergodic chain that is not stochastically monotone becomes smaller in the supermodular order of processes as it is speeded up. {"assumptions":["l^p norm on R^2","axis direction","d/r -> 0 asymptotics"],"created_at":"2026-08-10T04:06:41.000000+00:00","domain":"convex geometry / first-passage percolation limit shapes","id":"claim_32cba36e9ea9ba0c5d9ba247f3e15cf592fb208e4bcf772a85f058485b81ff96","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"For the l^p norm on R^2 and the axis direction e_2, the dogleg excess of a midpoint-displaced point v = (d, r/2) is exactly asymptotic to (2^p/p) d^p / r^{p-1} as d/r -> 0 (second-order Taylor of (1 + x^p)^{1/p}). Consequently the enclosing-ball (quadratic lower) curvature condition excess >= c d^2/r holds at the axis if and only if p <= 2: for p < 2 the excess is of larger order than quadratic (the condition holds with room), at p = 2 it is exactly quadratic with constant 2, and for every p > 2 the contact is quartic or flatter and the enclosing-ball constant is ZERO. The curvature hypothesis consumed by localization arguments is therefore genuinely restrictive - entire familiar norm families fail it at their axis directions - and cannot be discharged by convexity or symmetry alone. Numerically verified: measured excess/predicted ratios 0.9995-1.0000 across p in {1.5, 2, 3, 4} at two offsets, and the quadratic test excess/(d^2/r) converges to a constant for p <= 2 and to zero for p > 2.","status":"derived_in_campaign_refereed"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-23T07:57:26.300439+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_32db5e05c2234ca8a4c051e226a841c9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematics, the free group $F_{S}$ over a given set $S$ consists of all words that can be built from members of $S$, considering two words to be different unless their equality follows from the group axioms (e.g. $st=suu^{-1}t$ but $s\\neq t^{-1}$ for $s,t,u\\in S$). The members of $S$ are called generators of $F_{S}$, and the number of generators is the rank of the free group. For fixed j the function k/(K+K*j/G-2k) increases with k on the
feasible positive-denominator range: cross multiplication cancels the
quadratic terms and leaves K*(1+j/G)*(k_2-k_1)>=0. Thus its maximum
is at k=k_j. Formula (4) proves max_world H(g)>=the value (2).
It does not assume arbitrary bins are homogeneous in truth status.

## Attainer for each j

Fix any j and k=k_j. Choose k known L truths for a safe group T;
put all other L atoms in B*. In R put r*j/G-k known truths and
F*j/G outside-C_R atoms into B*. Put k of the remaining known R
truths in T alongside its k known L truths. Put all remaining R atoms
in Z. These choices are possible: k<=s and k<=r*j/G; also j<=G
ensures enough R known truths remain for T.

The groups have these source-invariant counts and scores:

* B*: K+K*j/G-2k atoms, score (3) with w=0;
* T: 2k known true atoms, score (1/r+1/K)/(2N), omitted if k=0;
* Z: r*(G-j)/G known R truths and F*(G-j)/G outside atoms,
  total K*(G-j)/G atoms, score lambda, omitted if j=G;
* fixed S atoms: score lambda.

T has source mass k/(Nr)+k/(NK). Z has source mass (G-j)/(GN)
in either orientation. B* has the remaining pair mass, or its
invariance follows directly from F*(u+k)=r*v. Thus every group has
an invariant p mass and g is its uniform coarsening; equal lambda
scores merge harmlessly. The total is one and g is robustly calibrated
with zero budget in every compatible world.

If L=A its F false atoms all lie in B*, giving H_L=F*q*. If R=A,
H_R=(F*j/G)*q*+F*(1-j/G)*lambda. Since q*<=lambda, H_R>=H_L.
The worst risk is exactly F*lambda*(1-a_j). Maximizing a_j attains
the lower bound, proving (2).

The attaining rule uses only the observed known-truth unions and the
given model parameters: choose j by the explicit optimization, and
choose the displayed subsets of those known unions. It never reads
the hidden orientation or unobserved truth labels. Those labels enter
only the subsequent all-world verification and lower-bound argument.

## Consequences and relation to the earlier obstruction

If G=1, the only improving choice is j=1,k=s. Formula (2) becomes
the earlier smaller-count expression (K-r)*b_s. Thus the saturated
unequal case still has that expression when r and K-r are coprime.
When G>1, additional neutral truth/false bundles may improve it.

For C016's family K=3m,r=3(m-1),s=2(m-1),m>=5, G=3. The reductions
a_j for j=1,2,3 are respectively

 1/[6(m+1)], 4/[3(m+4)], 1/(m+2).

The middle value is largest: it beats the last iff m>4 and beats
the first since 24(m+1)>3(m+4). Thus C016's feasible generator is
in fact OPTIMAL in the conditional zero-budget game, with exact value

 V_sat(0)=lambda*(3m+8)/(m+4).                           (5)

This upgrades a route obstruction to an exact infinite-family frontier,
within the stated single-pair regime. It does not solve the full
arbitrary-d/global expected targets. Together with the unsaturated
C017 result and the fully-known-both-sides C013 case it gives an exact
single-pair zero-budget case map, but no larger claim is inferred.

{"assumptions":["all examples are for Lebesgue measure on [0,1] or R, and counting measure on N"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:36.553628+00:00","domain":"real analysis, Lp spaces","id":"claim_33568bddd455c11696bbce09e0ff678cc9dd457d94aed6dcd3a4a493975ad160","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"There is NO inclusion between L^p and L^q on a general measure space, and the two familiar inclusions run in OPPOSITE directions. (a) Finite measure (mu(X) < infinity), p < q: L^q is contained in L^p, with ||f||_p <= mu(X)^{1/p - 1/q} ||f||_q; the inclusion is strict, e.g. on [0,1], f(x) = x^{-1/2} is in L^1 but not L^2. (b) Counting measure, p < q: l^p is contained in l^q, with ||a||_q <= ||a||_p - the reverse containment; strictness: a_n = 1/n is in l^2 but not l^1. (c) Lebesgue measure on R^n: NEITHER containment holds. On R, |x|^{-1/2} 1_{{|x|<1}} is in L^1 but not L^2, while (1 + |x|)^{-1} is in L^2 but not L^1 - the first fails by a local singularity, the second by slow decay at infinity. What IS always true is the interpolation statement: for p_0 < p < p_1, L^{p_0} intersect L^{p_1} is contained in L^p, with ||f||_p <= ||f||_{p_0}^{1-theta} ||f||_{p_1}^{theta}. So a step 'f in L^2 hence f in L^1' is only legitimate after the measure has been declared finite (with the factor mu(X)^{1/2} exhibited), and 'f in L^1 hence f in L^2' only on an atomic space with atoms bounded below.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the factors are independent","entries i.i.d. centered Gaussian, variance 1/n","square factors of equal dimension","the largest-singular-value claim needs strong convergence, which is stronger than convergence of the spectral distribution"],"created_at":"2026-08-20T03:43:30.216158+00:00","domain":"random matrix theory","id":"claim_33a8efc37836202fed9468a5983040948a4b1e47488753c7edb06802b1e30ddb","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $G_1,\\dots,G_p$ be independent $n \\times n$ matrices with i.i.d. $\\mathcal{N}(0,1/n)$ entries. The limiting singular value distribution of the product $G_p \\cdots G_1$ is the Fuss-Catalan law of order $p$, whose upper edge is $(p+1)^{(p+1)/2}p^{-p/2}$. For $p=1$ this is $2$, recovering the square Gaussian case; for $p=2$ it is $3^{3/2}/2=\\sqrt{27/4}=2.5980\\ldots$; for $p=3$ it is $3.0792\\ldots$. Moreover the largest singular value itself converges to that edge, not merely the bulk. This last point matters and is strictly stronger: convergence of the spectral distribution locates the edge but by itself does not exclude an outlier above it, so a bound that needs no outlier cannot be justified by the Fuss-Catalan law alone.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Z has i.i.d. mean-zero unit-variance entries with finite fourth moment (orthogonally invariant, e.g. Gaussian, for the sharpest vector statements)","rank(X) = r fixed, its nonzero singular values fixed on the noise scale","m/n -> beta in (0, 1]; the loss is Frobenius"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T05:37:33.911379+00:00","domain":"random matrix theory","id":"claim_33ac0767a68834a907f3d5ea4c4652965bbd6ad4e44964080117e92a26c8252f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $Y_n = X_n + \\sigma Z_n$ where $Y_n$ is $m \\times n$ with $m/n \\to \\beta \\in (0, 1]$, $Z_n$ has i.i.d. entries of mean zero, variance one and finite fourth moment, and $X_n$ has fixed rank $r$ with singular values $\\sigma\\sqrt{n}\\, x_1, \\dots, \\sigma\\sqrt{n}\\, x_r$ (so the $x_k$ are the signal singular values on the scale of the noise, $x_k > 0$ fixed). Write the singular values of $Y_n$ on the same scale, $y_k := s_k(Y_n) / (\\sigma \\sqrt{n})$. THEOREM (Gavish and Donoho, 2017). (i) For each $k \\le r$: if $x_k > \\beta^{1/4}$ then $y_k \\to \\sqrt{(x_k^2 + 1)(x_k^2 + \\beta)} / x_k$, and if $x_k \\le \\beta^{1/4}$ then $y_k \\to 1 + \\sqrt\\beta$ (the bulk edge); every other singular value of $Y_n$ converges to the bulk. (ii) Among all estimators of the form $\\hat X = \\sum_k \\eta(y_k)\\, \\sigma\\sqrt{n}\\; \\hat u_k \\hat v_k^T$ that keep the sample singular vectors and replace each singular value by a function $\\eta$ of it, the one minimizing the asymptotic Frobenius loss $\\lim \\|\\hat X - X_n\\|_F^2 / (\\sigma^2 n)$ is $$\\eta^*(y) = \\frac{1}{y}\\sqrt{(y^2 - \\beta - 1)^2 - 4\\beta} \\quad \\text{for } y \\ge 1 + \\sqrt\\beta, \\qquad \\eta^*(y) = 0 \\quad \\text{for } y < 1 + \\sqrt\\beta.$$ (iii) The asymptotic loss of $\\eta^*$ is strictly smaller than that of hard thresholding at any threshold and of soft thresholding at any threshold whenever some $x_k > \\beta^{1/4}$; on a pure-noise matrix ($r = 0$) $\\eta^*$ returns the zero matrix. The rule selects the rank (the number of $y_k$ above the edge $1 + \\sqrt\\beta$) and the amount of shrinkage of each retained component from the data, without cross-validation; with $\\sigma$ unknown it is combined with the median estimate $\\hat\\sigma = y_{\\mathrm{med}}/\\sqrt{n \\mu_\\beta}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:50:30.561190+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_33e69b85bbda2e6b5c4901506497b4e7355a6989661fdf4996b65e442b91ac5e","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 3 of arXiv:2605.30560, 'Projected McKean--Vlasov Dynamics for Entropic Weak Optimal Transport'] A map $F:\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R}^d)\to\mathbb{R}$ admits a

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:20:07.935355+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_33f9b35e85453ac9d7e9c8f68c998c618e25afd4de9adf09b1aabeac2b561e50","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:twodir of arXiv:2608.30254, 'Exact Recovery Thresholds for Weighted Data Selection\\ in Vector-Valued Linear Regression'] Suppose the atoms take exactly two directions. Then the directions are
antipodal, each class has total weight $\frac12$ and zero conditional mean,
and $C(q)=\frac12(|m_+|^2+|m_-|^2)$ where $m_\pm$ are the conditional means
of the selected weights. Consequently
\[
  \inf_{|\operatorname{supp} q|\le4}C\le\frac E4,\qquad
  \inf_{|\operatorname{supp} q|\le3}C\le\frac{5E}8 ,
\]
and both constants are attained: for six equally weighted atoms with
$z$-values the cube roots of unity over each direction, the three-point
optimum is exactly $\frac{5E}8$ and the four-point optimum exactly
$\frac E4$. Equality at $\frac{5E}8$ forces both classes to have equal
energy, conditional weights $\frac13$ each, and equilateral $z$-triangles of
equal radius. Furthermore, for five-atom two-direction systems the sharp
constant at three points is $\frac47<\frac58$ (attained by an equilateral
triple against an antipodal pair with energy ratio $4{:}3$).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:13:49.971829+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_340e082d40e3c67119e2b8e18d01a4edc01332ad451a5e2e17fa94a8e3d2aba1","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:sections of arXiv:2411.07157, 'Rough differential equations in the flow approach'] Given $\tau \in \mathfrak{T}$, we define $\text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\tau] \subset \prod_{\underline{\tau} \in \tau} \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\underline{\tau}]$ 
by setting 
\begin{equs}
\text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\tau]
\eqdef
\big\{ 
\big(F_{\underline{\tau}}\in \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\underline{\tau}] : \underline{\tau} \in \tau\big): \enskip 
\forall \underline{\tau}, \underline{\tau}' \in \tau\;\text{and}\; f \in \mathrm{Iso}(\underline{\tau},\underline{\tau}')\,,\; \mathbf{f} F_{\underline{\tau}} =  F_{\underline{\tau}'}
\big\}\,.
\end{equs}
We define $\text{${\mcb{C}}$}[\tau]\subset \prod_{\underline{\tau} \in \tau} \text{${\mcb{C}}$}[\underline{\tau}]$ analogously. 

Moreover, for $\underline{\tau} \in \tau \in \mathfrak{T}$, let $\iota_{\tau,\underline{\tau}}: \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\tau] \rightarrow \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\underline{\tau}]$ be the ``fiber'' map $\big(F_{\underline{\tau}'}\in\mathcal{H}^{\underline{\tau}'} : \underline{\tau}' \in \tau\big) \mapsto F_{\underline{\tau}}$. 
Observe that $\iota_{\tau,\underline{\tau}}$ has a left inverse given by the ``section'' map $\pi_{\tau,\underline{\tau}}: \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\underline{\tau}] \rightarrow \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\tau]$ defined by setting
\[
\text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\underline{\tau}]\ni F_{\underline{\tau}}\mapsto\pi_{\tau,\underline{\tau}}F_{\underline{\tau}}\eqdef\Big(\frac{1}{|\mathrm{Iso}(\underline{\tau},\underline{\tau}')|}
\sum_{f \in \mathrm{Iso}(\underline{\tau},\underline{\tau}')} \text{$\mathbf{f}$} F_{\underline{\tau}} : \underline{\tau}'\in\tau\Big)\in \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\tau]
\,.
\] 
We use the same notation for the analogous maps between $\text{${\mcb{C}}$}[\underline{\tau}]$ and $\text{${\mcb{C}}$}[\tau]$. 

Note that $|\mathrm{Iso}(\underline{\tau},\underline{\tau}')|$ actually does not depend on the choice of $\underline{\tau},\underline{\tau}'\in\tau$. In the sequel, we therefore just write $|\mathrm{Aut}(\tau)|\eqdef |\mathrm{Aut}(\underline{\tau})|$ for any $\underline{\tau}\in\tau$.

Finally, for $\underline{\tau} \in \tau$ we sometimes write $\iota_{\underline{\tau}} \eqdef \iota_{\tau,\underline{\tau}}$ and $\pi_{\underline{\tau}} \eqdef \pi_{\tau,\underline{\tau}}$ to lighten subscripts.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["i.i.d. nonnegative weights on Z^d","existence holds in case (a) d=2 with no hypothesis, case (b) F(0) < p_c, case (c) F(0) > p_c with E tau_e < infinity; case (d) F(0) = p_c with d > 2 is OPEN","F continuous is a SUFFICIENT condition for uniqueness","the statement is about FINITE geodesics only"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.542657+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3439799dcf869b96ef8603273809d352afd98579ca6a151dff8f1d66fd0af028","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Consider i.i.d. first-passage percolation on Z^d with weight law F. EXISTENCE of a finite geodesic between every pair of vertices, almost surely and simultaneously over all pairs, is known in each of the following cases, and the case division matters. (a) d = 2 and F ARBITRARY: Wierman and Reh proved that for any passage time distribution, with probability one there is a geodesic between any two points of Z^2. (b) Any d, with F(0) < p_c(d): existence follows from standard subcritical estimates. (c) Any d, with F(0) > p_c(d) and E[tau_e] < infinity: existence was proved by Zhang. (d) The remaining case F(0) = p_c(d) with d > 2 is STILL UNRESOLVED in general, though existence is known for distributions with F(0) = F(delta) = p_c for some delta > 0 in sufficiently high dimensions. So it is WRONG to say that geodesics need F(0) < p_c; that condition is sufficient and convenient, not necessary, and supercritical zero-weight percolation does not by itself destroy existence. UNIQUENESS is a separate matter: a continuous F is a SUFFICIENT condition for the model to be uniquely geodesic, since two distinct finite paths then have equal passage time with probability zero and there are countably many pairs of paths. With atoms - a two-valued weight law, say - ties are genuine and multiple geodesics occur with positive probability. All of the above is about FINITE geodesics; the existence, direction, uniqueness and coalescence of semi-infinite geodesics is a separate and largely open subject whose known results require differentiability or curvature assumptions on the limit shape. [Wierman and Reh (1978); Kesten, Aspects of First Passage Percolation, (9.23); Zhang; verified against Auffinger, Damron and Hanson, 50 Years of First-Passage Percolation, Section 4.1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:31:49.844542+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_343f93727fc15914326f1ba88eeac6b98ee395a33c7c9486b4201a9d20a1a38e","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:expectation-taylor of arXiv:2608.23742, 'Second-order fusion asymptotics for $\Sine_\beta$ correlation functions'] Let $d\ge1$, $\gamma>0$, and put $D=d\gamma$. Let $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be compact. Suppose that real random variables $X,Y,M$ satisfy, for some $p,q$,
\begin{equation}
p>\max\{2,D\},\qquad q>\max\{1,D\},\qquad
2q\left(1-\frac1p\right)>1,
\end{equation}
and $X\in L^p$, $Y,M\in L^q$. Suppose, uniformly for $b\in K$ and $1\le j\le d$,
\begin{equation}
U_j(t,b)=tb_jX+\frac{t^2b_j^2}{2}Y+R_j(t,b),
\qquad |R_j(t,b)|\le C_K|t|^3M.
\end{equation}
Then, with
\[
F(u):=\prod_{j=1}^d|1+u_j|^\gamma,
\qquad A(b):=\sum_jb_j,
\qquad B(b):=\sum_jb_j^2,
\]
one has, uniformly for $b\in K$,
\begin{align}
\mathbb E F(U(t,b))
&=1+\gamma tA(b)\mathbb E X\\
&\quad+\frac{t^2}{2}\left\{\gamma B(b)\mathbb E Y+
\left[\gamma(\gamma-1)B(b)+\gamma^2(A(b)^2-B(b))\right]\mathbb E X^2\right\}
+o(t^2).\notag
\end{align}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.354793+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3476ca2b2d66e332b342e3b77d62e015071a36e4b7a149dab3b5a797c97a4393","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Ppn 216 (constraints on $(\bbb,\vvv,\uuu,\rrr,\www)^{\frozen,\coarse,N}$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For the coefficients defined by \eqref{e:b.plus.coarse}--\eqref{e:w.plus.coarse},
with high probability,
the following hold simultaneously for all $0\leq d\leq d_{\max}-1$:
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
\item 
     
    The ``domain constraint'': for all 
    $B^{\frozen,\coarse} \in \mathcal{C}^\frozen(q_d)$,
    \beq
    \vvv^{\frozen,\coarse,N}(q_d,B^{\frozen,\coarse}) 
    \ge 
    q_d p'(q_d)
    \frac{\uuu^{\frozen,\coarse,N}(q_d,B^{\frozen,\coarse})^2 }
    {\rrr^{\frozen,\coarse,N}(q_d,B^{\frozen,\coarse})}
    - \frac{\eta^2}{2}\,.
    \eeq
(If $\uuu^{\frozen,\coarse,N}$ and $\rrr^{\frozen,\coarse,N}$ are both zero, we interpret the ratio on the right-hand side as zero.)
 \item
 
The ``budget constraint'' for the spherical perceptron:
    \beq
    
    \bE_{\bG^N}
    \bigg[ \Cost\Big(
        \bbb^{\frozen,\coarse,N}(q_d),
        \vvv^{\frozen,\coarse,N}(q_d),
            \uuu^{\frozen,\coarse,N}(q_d)
        \Big) \bigg]
    \le \frac{1}{\alpha} 
    + \epsilon^\circ
 .
    \eeq
\item 
The ``budget constraint'' for the Ising perceptron:
    \beq
    
    \bE_{\bG^N}\bigg[ \Cost\Big(
        \bbb^{\frozen,\coarse,N}(q_d),
        \vvv^{\frozen,\coarse,N}(q_d),
        \uuu^{\frozen,\coarse,N}(q_d)
        \Big) \bigg]
    \le \frac{\bE_{\bG^N}[
    \www^{\frozen,\coarse,N}(q_d)^{1/2}]^2}{\alpha} 
    + \epsilon^\circ\,.
    \eeq
\item  The ``diffusivity'' for the Ising perceptron:
    \[\Big|\bE(\www^{\frozen,\coarse,N}(q_d)) -1\Big|
    \le\epsilon^\circ\,.\]
\end{enumerate}

\begin{proof}
Assertions
\eqref{it:spherical-budget-constraint-plus-coarse}--\eqref{it:Ising-w-constraint-plus-coarse} follow straightforwardly from Jensen's inequality. For assertion \eqref{it:domain-constraint-plus-coarse}, note 
from \eqref{e:indicator.qd.less.than.qT},
 \eqref{e:def.r}, and \eqref{e:P.plus.hist}
that Proposition~\ref{p:budget-constraints-HIST}\ref{it:domain-constraint-plus-HIST} can be rewritten as
	\[
	\vvv^{\frozen,N}(q_d,B^\frozen) 
    \ge  q_d p'(q_d) 
    I(B^\frozen)
	\frac{\uuu^{\frozen,N}(q_d,B^\frozen)^2}
		{\rrr^{\frozen,N}(q_d,B^\frozen)}
    - \frac{\eta^2}{2}\,,
	\]
where we again interpret a $0/0$ ratio as zero, and
	\[I(B^\frozen)\equiv \ind\bigg\{|B^\frozen \cap[M]| \ge 
		\frac{M}{\BUCKETS^2}
		\bigg\}\,.\]
If $I(B^\frozen)=0$ for all $B^\frozen\in B^{\frozen,\coarse}$,
then the bound \eqref{e:domain.plus.coarse} follows.
Otherwise, consider a discrete probability measure $\pi$, and random variables $v_j,u_j,r_j$ which are zero on a set of indices $Z$, and otherwise satisfy
	\[
	v_j \ge A' \frac{(u_j)^2}{r_j} - a'\]
Assume $\pi_+ \equiv 1-\pi(Z)\in(0,1]$. Then Jensen's inequality gives
	\[
	\frac{\sum_j \pi_j v_j}{\pi_+}
	\ge \frac{1}{\pi_+}
	\sum_{j\notin Z} \pi_j \bigg\{
	A' \frac{(u_j)^2}{r_j} - a'\bigg\}
	\ge A'
	\bigg(\frac{1}{\pi_+}\sum_j \pi_j u_j\bigg)^2\bigg/
	\bigg(
	\frac{1}{\pi_+}\sum_j \pi_j r_j
	\bigg) - a'
	\]
and rearranging gives
	\[
	\sum_j \pi_j v_j
	\ge
	A' \bigg(\sum_j \pi_j u_j\bigg)^2\bigg/
	\bigg(\sum_j \pi_j r_j
	\bigg)
	-a'\pi_+\,.
	\]
If we apply the above inequality with the probability measure $\pi$
over buckets $B^\frozen\in B^{\frozen,\coarse}$ with probabilities 
$\pi(B^\frozen)=|B^\frozen|/|B^{\frozen,\coarse}|$, then we obtain the desired conclusion.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["one-dimensional, nearest-neighbor random walk in an i.i.d. random environment","existence of kappa in (0,2) solving E[rho^kappa]=1 for the environment's local odds ratio rho","transience of the walk, or the appropriate directional condition for the regime under study","technical non-lattice or non-degeneracy conditions on the environment law needed for the stable-law convergence"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.989782+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_34a6da748207f4cd112326dff5e5e3f10da84d0a5a8d231a18afecb144c6023f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For one-dimensional nearest-neighbor random walk in an i.i.d. random environment in the subballistic or intermediate regime, parametrized by an index kappa solving E[rho^kappa]=1 for rho the local odds ratio of the environment, hitting times of successive integers admit a classical Kesten construction as a branching process with migration: individuals reproduce according to an environment-dependent offspring law with an added immigration/emigration term reflecting the local environment. The Kesten-Kozlov-Spitzer theorem shows that for kappa in the relevant range below 2, the hitting time of level n, normalized by n^{1/kappa}, converges to a kappa-stable distribution, via a result on the total population size of the associated branching-with-migration process, which itself has heavy-tailed, stable-scaling behavior. This gives the precise non-Gaussian scaling limits characterizing anomalous, subdiffusive or index-dependent, behavior in one-dimensional random walk in random environment, a phenomenon absent for simple random walk. It does not extend to higher dimensions, since the explicit branching correspondence is a genuinely one-dimensional, nearest-neighbor phenomenon, and it requires the environment to be i.i.d. with a moment condition admitting a solution kappa in the relevant range. Typical failure: Extending the branching-process-with-migration correspondence and its kappa-stable scaling conclusion to multi-dimensional random walk in random environment, or to environments with dependence rather than i.i.d. structure, where no analogous exact combinatorial bijection to a branching process is known; the Kesten construction is a special, essentially exact identity in one dimension that does not generalize by analogy, so claiming kappa-stable scaling outside the one-dimensional i.i.d. setting requires an entirely separate justification. Canonical reference: Kesten, Kozlov and Spitzer, 1975, Compositio Mathematica.","status":"unverified"}

\eta_t
:=
C_{t_0}e^{-\rho_\chi(t-t_0)},
\qquad t\geq t_0,
\end{equation}
for some \(t_0\geq0\), \(C_{t_0}<\infty\), and \(\rho_\chi>0\), where \(P_t\) and \(\Pi_0\) denote the laws with densities \(p_t\) and \(\pi_0\), respectively. For the OU potential~\eqref{eq:ou-potential}, the inequality~\eqref{eq:chi2-transfer-assumption} holds under the assumptions of~\cite{belomestny-morozova-ou}, with
\(
C_{t_0}=\chi^2(P_{t_0}\Vert\Pi_0).
\)
Let \(X_1^{T_n},\ldots,X_n^{T_n}\) be independent observations from \(P_{T_n}\) for some \(T_n>0\), and let \(G_{M_n}\) be the event on which~\eqref{eq:full-mle-oracle-transfer} holds. Under the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:oracle}, it holds that
\[
P_{T_n}^{\otimes n}(G_{M_n}^c)
\leq
\delta+n\tau_0(M_n)
+
\frac12\sqrt{(1+\eta_{T_n})^n-1}.
\]
Indeed,
\[
1+\chi^2(P_t^{\otimes n}\Vert\Pi_0^{\otimes n})
=
\left(1+\chi^2(P_t\Vert\Pi_0)\right)^{n}
\leq
(1+\eta_t)^n,
\]
and therefore
\(
\TV(P_t^{\otimes n},\Pi_0^{\otimes n})
\leq
0.5\sqrt{(1+\eta_t)^n-1}.
\)
The claimed bound follows from
\(
P_{T_n}^{\otimes n}(G_{M_n}^c)
\leq
\Pi_0^{\otimes n}(G_{M_n}^c)
+
\TV(P_{T_n}^{\otimes n},\Pi_0^{\otimes n})
\)
and
\(
\Pi_0^{\otimes n}(G_{M_n}^c)
\leq\delta+n\tau_0(M_n).
\)
Consequently, if
\(
n\eta_{T_n}\longrightarrow0
\)
and
\(
n\tau_0(M_n)\longrightarrow0,
\)
then the stationary oracle inequality and the rates in~\eqref{eq:kl-rate} remain valid for observations from \(P_{T_n}\). Under~\eqref{eq:chi2-transfer-assumption}, it is sufficient to choose, for any \(\varepsilon>0\),
\(
T_n
\geq
t_0+(1+\varepsilon)\rho_\chi^{-1}\log n,
\)
which guarantees
\(
n\eta_{T_n}
\leq
C_{t_0}n^{-\varepsilon}
\longrightarrow0
\)
as \(n\to\infty\).
Since by Lemma~\ref{lem:explicit-tails}
it holds that
\(
\tau_0(M)\lesssim e^{-c_a(M-v_\star)},
\)
taking
\(
M_n=v_\star+C_{\mathrm{tr}}\log n
\)

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:33:01.745954+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_34eded4e47fda8bfa953967f1708fed3055331411980a025ddafe2c472a1c787","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 19 of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] Within our coupling of the collection times (Definition~\ref{def:coupling}),
  $T_{m,0}$ is independent of $T_{m,p} - T_{m,0}$ and this difference
  has \textsc{mgf}
  \[
    M_{T_{m, p} - T_{m, 0}}(t) = I_{m, p}(t), \quad t \leqslant 0.
  \]
  \begin{proof}
    If $T_{m, 0} = k$, then the value of $T_{m, p} - T_{m, 0}$
    is a deterministic function of the initial clumsiness $\{ U_{L(i,k)} \}_{i \in [m]}$,
    the future updates $\{ C_n \}_{n > k}$,
    and the future clumsiness $\{ U_n \}_{n > k}$. Call this function $f$.
    We will make $f$ explicit. Consider an initial clumsiness vector
    $\mathbf{x} = (x_1, \dots, x_m)^\top \in [0, 1]^m$,
    coupon updates $\mathbf{y} = (y_n)_{n > 0} \in [m]^\mathbb{N}$,
    and future clumsiness $\mathbf{z} = (z_n)_{n > 0} \in [0, 1]^\mathbb{N}$.
    Then define
    $L'(i, n; \mathbf{y})$ as the most recent update of coupon $i$
    no later than $n$,
    \[
      L'(i, n; \mathbf{y}) \coloneqq
      \sup\{ k \leqslant n \mid y_k = i \}, \quad
      i \in [m], \quad n \geqslant 0,
    \]
    where naturally $\sup\emptyset = -\infty$ and $L'(i, 0; \mathbf{y}) = -\infty$.
    Define
    \begin{align*}
      f(\mathbf{x}; \mathbf{y}; \mathbf{z})
      \coloneqq \inf \{ n \geqslant 0 \mid {} &\text{for all $i \in [m]$,}\\
          &\text{if $x_i > 1-p$ or $L'(i, n; \mathbf{y}) > 0$,}\\
          &\text{then $L'(i, n; \mathbf{y}) > 0$
          and $z_{L'(i, n; \mathbf{y})} \leq 1-p$}
          \}.
    \end{align*}
    Thus, for any integers $\ell \geqslant m$ and $x \geqslant 0$,
    \begin{align*}
      \PP\left( T_{m,p} - T_{m,0} = x \right)
      &= \sum_{k \geqslant m}
        \PP\left( T_{m,p} - T_{m,0} = x \mid T_{m,0} = k\right)
        \PP(T_{m,0} = k)\\
      &= \sum_{k \geqslant m} \PP\left(f(U_{L(1, k)}, \dots, U_{L(m, k)};
      C_{k+1}, C_{k+2}, \dots;
      U_{k+1}, U_{k+2}, \dots) = x\right)\\
      &\qquad \qquad \qquad \times \PP\left(T_{m,0} = k\right)\\
      &= \sum_{k \geqslant m} \PP\left(f(U_{L(1, \ell)}, \dots, U_{L(m, \ell)};
      C_{\ell+1}, C_{\ell+2}, \dots;
      U_{\ell+1}, U_{\ell+2}, \dots) = x\right)\\
      &\qquad \qquad \qquad \times \PP\left(T_{m,0} = k\right)\\
      &= \PP\left(f(U_{L(1, \ell)}, \dots, U_{L(m, \ell)};
      C_{\ell+1}, C_{\ell+2}, \dots;
      U_{\ell+1}, U_{\ell+2}, \dots) = x\right)\\
      &\qquad \qquad \qquad \times \underbrace{
        \sum_{k \geqslant m} \PP\left(T_{m,0} = k\right)
      }_1\\
      &= \PP\left(T_{m,p} - T_{m,0} = x \mid T_{m,0} = \ell\right).
    \end{align*}
    The third line uses our i.i.d.~assumptions from
    Definition~\ref{def:coupling}.
    This proves the independence of $T_{m,0}$ and $T_{m,p} - T_{m, 0}$.
    Hence the factorisation
    $M_{T_{m,0}}(t)\,M_{T_{m,p} - T_{m,0}}(t) = M_{T_{m,0}}\,I_{m,p}(t)$.
    These quantities are non-zero; divide both sides to conclude the proof.
    
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:36:44.551748+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_34fd9fae7b41cda5283a1108094a574e2c1ee96b6cfe04afedd622806387eefe","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 20 of arXiv:2604.01978, 'Homogenized Transformers'] Fix $i,j\in[n]^2$ and define
\(
R_{ij}(t)\coloneqq \langle x_i(t),x_j(t)\rangle.
\)
We have
\begin{equation}
\de R_{ij}(t)
=
\de M_{ij}(t)
+
\cD_{ij}(t)\,\de t,
\end{equation}
where the local martingale part is
\begin{equation}
\de M_{ij}(t)
=
\int_\Uptheta
\left(\langle G_i(t,\bm{\theta}),x_j(t)\rangle+\langle x_i(t),G_j(t,\bm{\theta})\rangle\right)
\,\mathsf{W}(\de\bm{\theta},\de t),
\end{equation}
and the drift is
\begin{align}
\cD_{ij}(t)
&=
\frac1d\left(d-2+R_{ij}(t)^2\right)\,s_{\mu(t)}(x_i(t),x_j(t))\nonumber\\
&-
\frac{(d-1)}{2d}\,R_{ij}(t)\left(s_{\mu(t)}(x_i(t))+s_{\mu(t)}(x_j(t))\right),
\end{align} 
where $\mu(t) = \mu_{X(t)}$ and 
\begin{align*}
s_\mu(x)&\coloneqq \E\left\|\mathsf{m}_{\upbeta,\bA}[\mu](x)\right\|^2,\nonumber\\
s_\mu(x,x')&\coloneqq \E\left\langle \mathsf{m}_{\upbeta,\bA}[\mu](x),\mathsf{m}_{\upbeta,\bA}[\mu](x')\right\rangle.
\end{align*}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:05:28.080749+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_357284b985ff888d2c1c29af9510420130262d1665162bbe9a236df7a5cd3cbf","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem maintheorem2 of arXiv:2601.20502, 'Optimal matching under size priority'] Let $G_n=(V_n,E_n)$ be a sequence of random graphs and choose a root $\overset{\rightarrow}{o}_n$ uniformly among the vertices.
    Suppose that the sequence of rooted weighted random graphs $(G_n,o_n)$ converges locally to an (vertex-rooted) Unimodular Bienaymé-Galton-Watson (UBGW) tree $(\mathbb{T},o)$ with reproduction law $\pi$. Assume further that the ratio $\frac{2|E_n|}{|V_n|}$ converges in probability to the expectation of $\pi$ and that the hypothesis of Theorem~(maintheorem of the paper) holds on the UBGW tree. Now assign i.i.d weights $(w_n(e))_{e \in E(G_n)}$ of distribution $\omega$ on the edges of $G_n$. We have
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item There exists a sequence $(M_n)_n$ of matchings of $G_n$ such that $(G_n,o_n,M_n)$ converges locally to $(\mathbb{T},{o},\mathbb{M}_{\mathrm{opt}})$ given by Theorem~(maintheorem of the paper).
        In particular, we have that:

         \[
        \lim_{n \to \infty} 
        \left(  \mathbb{P}\left( \exists v \sim o_n, \{o_n,v\} \in M_n\right),\mathbb{E}\left[ \sum_{v\sim o_n}w_n(o_n,v)\mathbbm{1}_{\{o_n,v\} \in M_n}\right]\right) = \perfE(\mathbb{T},o,\mathbb{M}_{\mathrm{opt}}),
        \]
        
        \item Reciprocally, for any sequence $(M_n)_n$ of matchings of $G_n$, take $(a,b)$ to be any subsequential limit of
        \[ \left(  \mathbb{P}\left( \exists v \sim o_n, \{o_n,v\} \in M_n\right),\mathbb{E}\left[ \sum_{v\sim o_n}w_n(o_n,v)\mathbbm{1}_{\{o_n,v\} \in M_n}\right]\right) ,\]
        then we must have that 
        \[ (a,b)\overset{\mathrm{lex}}{\leq} \perfE(\mathbb{T},o,\mathbb{M}_{\mathrm{opt}}).
        \]
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["F_q finite with q = p^m","sum_i deg f_i < n (total degrees); the bound is sharp, as the norm form shows","Chevalley's form needs the f_i to vanish at the origin"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:05:27.626667+00:00","domain":"number theory and algebra","id":"claim_35ee79c9fa9041171e62a639c4595448b33224c480be67a60335a1ce17158a8a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let F_q be the finite field with q = p^m elements (p prime) and let f_1, ..., f_r be polynomials in F_q[x_1, ..., x_n] with sum_i deg f_i < n. WARNING (1935): the number N of common zeros of f_1, ..., f_r in F_q^n is divisible by p. CHEVALLEY (1935): if in addition every f_i has zero constant term (so 0 is a common zero), then there is another common zero; in particular a homogeneous form of degree d in more than d variables has a nontrivial zero over F_q, so finite fields are quasi-algebraically closed (C_1 fields). Strengthenings: Ax (1964) showed q^b divides N with b = ceil((n - sum deg f_i) / max deg f_i) (Ax-Katz); the theorem gives the Erdos-Ginzburg-Ziv theorem (among 2n - 1 integers some n have sum divisible by n) by applying it to two forms of degree p - 1 in 2p - 1 variables.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Primary-source scope record, not a new polynomial-gap theorem","Matrix sensing application assumes 1/20-RIP on all rank-at-most-2k matrices","The actual row has iid Gaussian rank-one measurements and m at least C d log^3 d"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T20:04:21.099115+00:00","domain":"sampling and nonconvex learning","id":"claim_35f9c193fc020fba4b06d0f0b693bea38742862f79e20a892b24d653fe16ba68","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"# Moitra-Risteski: relevant decomposition, uncovered phase-retrieval hypotheses

T321 Target 2. Literature applicability finding, not a new proof of Target 2.
Source: Fast Convergence for Langevin Diffusion with Manifold Structure,
arXiv:2002.05576, primary PDF saved under papers/.

Section 2, PDF page 3, requires the matrix-sensing operator to satisfy
(19/20)||M||_F^2 <= ||A(M)||_2^2 <= (21/20)||M||_F^2
for every matrix M of rank at most 2k. This is an operator-wide assumption,
not concentration for a fixed deterministic M.

For phase retrieval take k=1 and A_ph(M)_j=(a_j^T M a_j)/sqrt(m), so the
squared residual is precisely the normalized empirical quartic loss.
For every nonzero measurement a_i, set u=a_i/||a_i|| and M=uu^T. Then
rank(M)=1, ||M||_F=1 and

 ||A_ph(M)||_2^2=(1/m)sum_j(a_j.u)^4 >= ||a_i||^4/m.

Thus the upper RIP inequality would force
m >= (20/21)max_i||a_i||^4. The witness is allowed to depend on the sample,
because RIP quantifies over EVERY rank-one matrix. This is the exact
deterministic fourth-moment obstruction already relevant to this row,
applied to the paper's stated hypothesis; it is not presented as new.
For Gaussian measurements, ||a_1||^2/d tends to 1 in probability. Therefore
for m=C d log^3 d with fixed C, this necessary inequality fails with
probability tending to 1 as d grows. Multiplication by any fixed scalar
normalization of A_ph does not remove the growing d/log^3 d obstruction.
No claim is made here about operators obtained by data-dependent weighting,
truncation or a changed loss; those require their own arguments.

Section 4.1, Theorem 4, PDF page 7, is nevertheless a relevant generic
decomposition framework: along-level and across-level Poincare control,
control of changing conditional density/Jacobian, and finite-time retention
near the minimizer manifold combine into convergence to a restricted law.
These are hypotheses to establish, not consequences of benign landscape
alone. Our C007 is a different polar decomposition with the same unresolved
need for one conditional spectral-gap estimate.

Section 4.2, Theorem 5, PDF pages 7-8, assumes the matrix measurement
conditions above, a sufficiently large beta, and an absolutely continuous
initial law supported near one minimizer component. The target p_i is
defined just before the theorem as the Gibbs law restricted to points
closer to component E_i than the other component. The theorem's displayed
TV error includes an additive epsilon, as well as a decaying chi-square
term. It is not a statement of the full unrestricted even Poincare constant
for the empirical rank-one measurement model at beta~d/epsilon_loss.
The TV accuracy epsilon in the paper must not be identified silently with
the row's optimization/loss tolerance epsilon_loss.

The discussion on PDF page 9 explicitly leaves reaching the prescribed
initialization by unmodified Langevin for future work, while explaining
that optimization can supply such an initialization in the stated models.
Even if a warm-start sampling guarantee were imported, an additive-error
TV guarantee alone is not a variational Poincare inequality for the full law.

NEXT: adapt the near-well decomposition and retention estimates using the
actual rank-one measurement geometry, without imposing false global RIP;
then control the rest of the quotient to obtain the full polynomial gap.
No claim of a solved parameter range or a scored frontier move is made.
The rank-one diagnostic is analytic and unaudited, not a numerical bound
or a Lean-certified assertion.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:07:56.656926+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3602a942d36037448d060dcd4dbbb50334b9b3583ef08c8588a2ae0bde45bc33","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:BESQflow of arXiv:2411.04773, 'Meeting of squared Bessel flow lines and application to the skew Brownian motion'] Let $\delta \in {\mathbb R}$.  We call ${\rm BESQ}^\delta$ flow  driven by $\mathcal W$ a collection ${\mathcal S}$ of continuous processes $({\mathcal S}_{r,x}(a),\, x\ge r)_{r\in {\mathbb R},a\ge 0}$ such that: 
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item
for each $(a,r)\in {\mathbb R}_+\times {\mathbb R}$, the process $({\mathcal S}_{r,x}(a),\, x\ge r)$ is almost surely the strong solution of the following SDE  
\begin{equation}
{\mathcal S}_{r,x}(a) = 
a + 2 \int_r^x  {\mathcal W}([0,{\mathcal S}_{r,s}(a)], \, \mathrm{d} s) + 
\delta (x-r) 
,\, x\ge r
\end{equation}
 and which, in the case $\delta<0$, is absorbed when hitting $0$.
 \item Almost surely,
 \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
 \item for all $r\in {\mathbb R}$ and $a\ge 0$, $ {\mathcal S}_{r,r}(a)=a$,
 \item for all $r\le x$, $a\mapsto  {\mathcal S}_{r,x}(a)$ is c\`adl\`ag,
 \item (Perfect flow property) for any $r\le x \le y$ and $a\ge 0$, $\mathcal S_{r,y}(a)=\mathcal S_{x,y}\circ \mathcal S_{r,x}(a)$. 
\end{enumerate} 
\end{enumerate}

We call killed ${\rm BESQ}^\delta$ flow driven by $\mathcal W$ the flow obtained from the ${\rm BESQ}^\delta$ flow by absorbing at $0$ the flow line $\mathcal S_{r,\cdot}(a)$ at time $\inf\{x>r\,:\,\mathcal S_{r,x}(a)=0\}$. 

We call general ${\rm BESQ}^\delta$ flow  a  ${\rm BESQ}^\delta$ flow or a  killed ${\rm BESQ}^\delta$ flow.","status":"unverified"}
