{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:09:43.679895+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_361f42eb61d6fe1bdebc4e7242f48e8e7bbfcbe17746fb8281f8c3d49b30fa88","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma p:mppmixcl_double of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] Fix $p,q \in \mathbb{N}$ and $r \in (0, \infty)$.
Assume that we are given
\begin{enumerate}[wide,label=(\roman*),labelindent=0pt,partopsep=0pt,topsep=0pt,parsep=0pt]
\item  a marking function $\xi: \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{K} \times \mathcal{N}_{\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{K}} \to \mathbb{K}'$, and
\item  
a marked point process $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$ on $\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{K}$ having  $\mathbb{B} $-mixing  correlations
as in  Definition (B-omega-mixing of the paper)(Bmixing of the paper)
with correlation decay functions $\omega_{k}(s) = C_k  \phi(s)$, $k \in \mathbb{N}$, 
where $(C_k)_{k \geq 1}$ is a non-decreasing sequence such that for some fixed $\epsilon \in (0,1)$, we have

\begin{equation}  
\sum_{l = 1}^{\infty}  \frac{ ({w}_0(1 + \epsilon)\kappa_0^{1 + \epsilon})^l }{l!} C_{l + p + q}  < \infty,
\end{equation}

with  ${w}_0= 4(p+q)\theta_d r^d$ and where $\kappa_0 = \max\{1, \sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^d}\rho^{(1)}(x)\}$ is related to the ground process $\mathcal{P}$.
\end{enumerate}

\vskip.2cm
Then for  all $f \in \mathbb{B} ((\mathbb{K}')^p),$   $g \in \mathbb{B} ((\mathbb{K}')^q)$ and for almost all $\bk x1{p+q}\in\mathbb{R}^{d(p+q)}$ such that $s:=d(\bk x1p,\bk x{p+1}{p+q}) >4r$ we have

\begin{align} \nonumber
& \Big| \mathbb {E} _{\bk x1{p+q}}[f(\bk{{\xi}^{\cup(r)}}{1}{p}(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}}))g(\bk{{\xi}^{\cup(r)}}{p+1}{p+q}(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}}))]\rho^{(p+q)}(\bk x1{p+q})  \\
&  \qquad - \,
\mathbb {E} _{\bk x1p}[f(\bk{{\xi}^{\cup(r)}}{1}{p}(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}}))] \rho^{(p)}(\bk x1{p}) \; \mathbb {E} _{\bk x{p+1}{p+q}}[g(\bk{{\xi}^{\cup(r)}}{p+1}{p+q}(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}}))]\rho^{(q)}(\bk x{p+1}{p+q}) \Big|  \nonumber \\
& \le 
\phi( \frac{s}{2})\sum_{l=1}^\infty \frac{w_0^l}{l!}  C_{l+p+q}
=:\phi( \frac{s}{2})\hat{C}_{p+q}<\infty.
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["entries of Z i.i.d., mean zero, variance one (finite second moment suffices for the almost-sure convergence in the Bai-Silverstein form)","the spectral distribution of Sigma converges weakly to H; p/n -> c in (0, infinity)","Sigma and Z independent (Sigma may be random)"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T16:00:40+00:00","domain":"random matrix theory","id":"claim_3625ab2a19639ec1e18b098bfb508774dc8680a3563d30345ceda3df84ad0c18","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $X = Z\\Sigma^{1/2}$ be $n \\times p$ with $Z$ having i.i.d. entries of mean $0$ and variance $1$, $\\Sigma$ positive semidefinite, and let $S = \\frac{1}{n}X^T X$. Assume $p/n \\to c \\in (0, \\infty)$ and that the empirical spectral distribution of $\\Sigma$ converges weakly to a probability measure $H$ on $[0, \\infty)$. Then almost surely the empirical spectral distribution of $S$ converges weakly to a nonrandom probability measure $F = F^{c, H}$, characterised as follows: with $\\underline F = (1 - c)\\delta_0 + cF$ (the limiting spectral distribution of the $n \\times n$ companion $\\frac{1}{n}XX^T$) and $\\underline m(z) = \\int \\frac{d\\underline F(t)}{t - z} = -\\frac{1 - c}{z} + c\\,m_F(z)$, for every $z \\in \\mathbb{C}^+$ the value $\\underline m(z)$ is the unique solution in $\\mathbb{C}^+$ of $$z = -\\frac{1}{\\underline m} + c\\int \\frac{\\tau\\, dH(\\tau)}{1 + \\tau\\,\\underline m}.$$ Equivalently, $m_F$ solves $m_F(z) = \\int \\frac{dH(\\tau)}{\\tau\\,(1 - c - c z\\, m_F(z)) - z}$. For $H = \\delta_1$ (identity population covariance) the equation reduces to the quadratic $z\\,\\underline m^2 + (z + 1 - c)\\,\\underline m + 1 = 0$ for the companion transform (equivalently $c z\\, m_F^2 + (z - 1 + c)\\, m_F + 1 = 0$ for $m_F$ itself), whose solution is the Stieltjes transform of the Marchenko-Pastur law with ratio $c$; the support of $F$ and its density are read off by Stieltjes inversion, and the density is analytic inside the support and vanishes like a square root at each edge of the support other than $0$: for $c = 1$ the left edge is the hard edge $0$, where the density blows up like $x^{-1/2}$, and for $c > 1$ the measure $F$ also carries an atom of mass $1 - 1/c$ at $0$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Ω ⊂ R^n open","u continuous on Ω","F continuous on Ω × R × R^n (for part (b))"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.416110+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: viscosity solution theory","id":"claim_367dca126752a97158c2d321bbcf3990dfd46c533d360292e0deac44d1f630d1","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Ω ⊂ R^n be open and u ∈ C(Ω). For x0 ∈ Ω define the superdifferential D^+u(x0) = { p ∈ R^n : limsup_{x→x0} ( u(x) - u(x0) - p·(x-x0) ) / |x - x0| ≤ 0 } and the subdifferential D^-u(x0) = { p : liminf_{x→x0} ( u(x) - u(x0) - p·(x-x0) ) / |x-x0| ≥ 0 }. Then: (a) p ∈ D^+u(x0) if and only if there exists φ ∈ C^1(Ω) with Dφ(x0) = p such that u - φ has a local maximum at x0; symmetrically for D^-u(x0) and local minima. (b) Hence, for continuous F, u is a viscosity subsolution of F(x,u,Du) = 0 iff F(x, u(x), p) ≤ 0 for every x ∈ Ω and every p ∈ D^+u(x), and a viscosity supersolution iff F(x,u(x),p) ≥ 0 for every x ∈ Ω and every p ∈ D^-u(x). (c) u is differentiable at x0 if and only if D^+u(x0) and D^-u(x0) are both nonempty, and in that case D^+u(x0) = D^-u(x0) = {Du(x0)}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0044-zero-one-law-for-directional-transience-in-dimensions-d-3","No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:26:45.040705+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_372d2aafaafb697b2a7c3c66368c6ae5c2e757ce647bd528fceebd3b13c28630","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Analyse where the Zerner-Merkl planar argument uses d = 2. Result: Zerner-Merkl show P_0[A_l intersection A_{-l}] = 0 using that in d = 2 two independent walks in the same environment started at distant points on a line perpendicular to l must, with positive probability, have paths that intersect (planarity), which lets one derive a contradiction from the walk going to +infinity and -infinity in direction l with positive probability each. In d >= 3 paths of two walks need not intersect, and the known partial result (Kalikow's 0-1 law: P_0[A_l union A_{-l}] in {0,1}) does not exclude the mixed event. A candidate counterexample structure in d >= 3 would be an i.i.d. environment where the walk is guided to +l or -l depending on a local feature it meets first; the i.i.d. assumption and the fact that the walk visits infinitely many independent regions make such a persistent memory implausible but not provably impossible: the walk in direction +l sees fresh environment forever, and the event that it turns around is a tail event of the walk but not of the environment. I checked that the natural martingale argument (P_omega(A_l) as a function of the environment at the current position) fails because P_omega(A_l) is not measurable with respect to a finite region. No result. Obstruction: Planarity is essential to the d = 2 proof; no substitute in d >= 3.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:22:59.738751+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_372e91d43434e1c705419dae497552bb85dd4bdd022859b7c2c089e67ee1bb2e","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn def:mostlytrans of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] Let $\mathcal{G}$, $\mathcal{G}'$ be two $C^0$-foliations on $\mathbb{T}^2$. We say that $\mathcal{G}$ and $\mathcal{G}'$ are \textbf{mostly-transverse} if there exist open sets $W \Subset V \subset \mathbb{T}^2$ such that
    \begin{itemize}
        \item On a neighborhood of $\mathbb{T}^2 \setminus V$, the leaves of $\mathcal{G}$ and $\mathcal{G}'$ coincide,
        \item On a neighborhood of $\overline{V} \setminus W$, $\mathcal{G}$ and $\mathcal{G}'$ are smooth,
        \item On $V \setminus W$, $T\mathcal{G}$ and $T\mathcal{G}'$ coincide, and on $W$, $T\mathcal{G}$ is positively transverse to $T\mathcal{G}'$,
        \item For every $p \in \mathbb{T}^2$, the leaf of $\mathcal{G}$ passing through $p$ intersects $W$ on both sides of $p$.
    \end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:47:40.724355+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_375b2b51a05ee14834c28f13b0b6c3d12063d8b90da949dff2c7b81304ae6af6","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:good_parameters of arXiv:2604.18558, 'Uniform analyticity of local observables in FK-percolation and analyticity of the Ising sp'] Define $\mathcal G_{\mathsf{FK}}$ to be the set of triplets $(d,p,q)$ such that the FK measures in finite volumes $\phi_{\Lambda_n, p, q}$ satisfy the following hypotheses. 
\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{Exponential weak mixing property}: for any $\alpha > 1$, there exists $c > 0$ such that for any $n \geq 0$ sufficiently large\footnote{$\mathrm{d}_{\mathsf{TV}}$ denotes the classical total variation distance between probability measures, and for any measure $\mu$, $\mu( \cdot_{|\Lambda_n})$ denotes the restriction of the measure $\mu$ to the box $\Lambda_n$.}, 
\[
\mathrm{d}_{\mathsf{TV}}( \phi^1_{\Lambda_{\alpha n}, p,q}( \cdot_{|\Lambda_n} ), \phi^0_{\Lambda_{\alpha n}, p,q}( \cdot_{|\Lambda_n} ) ) < \exp(-cn). 
\]
\item One of the two following conditions holds:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textit{Exponential decay}: for any $\alpha > 1$, there exists $c>0$ such that for any $n \geq 0$ large enough, 
\[
\phi^1_{\Lambda_{\alpha n, p ,q}}[A_n] < \exp(-cn),
\]
where $A_n$ is the event that $\Lambda_n$ contains a cluster of diameter greater than $n/100$.
\item \textit{Local uniqueness}: for any $\alpha > 1$, there exists $c>0$ such that for any $n \geq 0$ large enough, 
\[
\sup_\eta \phi^\eta_{\Lambda_{\alpha n, p ,q}}[U_n^c] < \exp(-cn),
\]
where the local uniqueness event $U_n$ is the event that $\Lambda_n $ contains a \emph{crossing} cluster and all the other clusters have diameter less than $n/100$, where a crossing cluster is a cluster that connects all the sides of the box $\Lambda_n$. The event $U_n^c$ is the complement of $U_n$.
In the last property, the supremum is taken over all the boundary conditions on the box $\Lambda_{\alpha n}$. 
\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:50:30.562372+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_376f73ec0e4a8fa79094fd56bcc2e399117f8992563f9193bea8b6347e7d3bba","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 17 of arXiv:2605.30560, 'Projected McKean--Vlasov Dynamics for Entropic Weak Optimal Transport'] Let $p>d+2$, let $\P_0\in\Pc(\Xc\times\R^d)$, and let
\[
b:\R_+\times\Xc\times\R^d\longrightarrow\R^d
\]
be a Borel-measurable vector field. Assume that there exists a weak solution to
\[
dY_t
=
b(t,X,Y_t)\,dt+\sqrt{2} \,dB_t,
\qquad
(X,Y_0)\sim\P_0,
\qquad
(X, Y_0) \independent B,
\]
where $\independent$ denotes the indepenance. 
For $T>0$ and $R>0$, define
\begin{equation} 
C_1(R,T,b)
:=
\int_0^T
\left\{
\E\Big[
|b(t,X,Y_t)|^p\mathbf{1}_{\{|Y_t|\le R\}}
\Big]
+
\int_{\Xc} \int_{B(0,R)} |b(t,x,y)|^p\,dy\,\mu(dx)
\right\}
dt.
\end{equation}
Assume that $C_1(R,T,b)<\infty$ for every $R>0$. Then the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), ref=(\roman*)]
    \item 
    For every $t\in(0,T]$, the law
    \[
    \P_t:=\Lc(X,Y_t)
    \]
admits a density with respect to $\mu \otimes \mathrm{L}$,
    still denoted by $\tilde{\P}_{t,x}(y)$. 
    Moreover, for every $R>0$ and every
    $t\in(0,T]$, there exists a constant $K_{T,R}>0$ such that
    \begin{equation} 
    \big\|
    \tilde{\P}_t\,\mathbf{1}_{\{|y|\le R\}}
    \big\|_{\L^p(\mu\otimes \mathrm{L} ) }
    \le
    K_{T,R} \bigl(1+C_1(R,T,b)\bigr).
    \end{equation}

    \item 
    Assume furthermore that the second marginal of $\P_t$ is given by
    \[
    \Lc(Y_t)=\nu(dy)=e^{-V(y)} \,dy, \quad \forall \, t \in \R_+.
    \]
    For every bounded Borel function $\phi:\Xc\to\R$, define
    \[
    w_\phi(t,y):=\E[\phi(X)\mid Y_t=y].
    \]
    Equivalently, for $\nu$-a.e.\ $y$,
    \begin{equation} 
    w_\phi(t,y)
    =
    \int_{\Xc} \phi(x)\,\tilde{\P}_{t,x}(y)\,\mu(dx)\,e^{V(y)}.
    \end{equation}
    Then, for every $R>0$ and every $\delta>0$, there exist constants
    $\alpha,\beta,K>0$, depending only on $C_1(R,T,b)$, $R$, and $\delta$, such
    that for all $y,y'\in B(0,R)$ and all $t,t'\in[\delta,T]$ satisfying
    $|t-t'|\le1$,
    \begin{equation} 
    |w_\phi(t',y')-w_\phi(t,y)|
    \le
    K\|\phi\|_\infty
    \Big(
    |y-y'|^\alpha + |t-t'|^\beta
    \Big).
    \end{equation}
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

If E[Y] < infinity then the limit mu(e_1) = lim_{n -> infinity} T(0, n e_1)/n exists almost surely and in L^1 and is a deterministic constant in [0, infinity), and the same holds along every lattice direction, defining mu on Z^d and by homogeneity and convexity on all of R^d, invariant under the symmetries of the lattice; mu is either identically 0 or a genuine norm. Three companion facts, each with its own status. (ii) 0 <= mu(e_1) <= E[tau_e], the upper bound by taking the direct path and applying the law of large numbers - so the finiteness of E[tau_e] gives the bound but is NOT needed for existence. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:11:09.317791+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_379223428004d7efd78d22695193deeb16dd036ad798e8757d892ce06ac2b383","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:restriction-to-a-subset of arXiv:2411.06195, 'Restrictions of some reinforced processes to subgraphs'] \mbox{}\\
  Let $(X_n,T_n)_{n\in{\mathbb N}_0}$ be a continuous-time jump process on $G$.
  Recursively, we take $\sigma_0:=0$ and for $n\in{\mathbb N}$, on the event
  $\{\sigma_{n-1}<\infty\}$, we define 
  $\sigma_n:=\inf\{l>\sigma_{n-1}:X_l\neq X_{\sigma_{n-1}}\}$ to be the index
  of the next jump to a different location. 
  The process with self-loops removed is defined by 
  $(X^{\neq},T^{\neq})=(X^{\neq}_n,T^{\neq}_n)_{n\in{\mathbb N}_0}:=(X_{\sigma_n},\sum_{l=\sigma_n}^{\sigma_{n+1}-1}T_l)_{n\in{\mathbb N}_0}$
  on the event $\{\sigma_n<\infty\text{ for all }n\in{\mathbb N}\}$. 

  Let $\emptyset\neq J\subseteq\Lambda$. We set recursively $\tau_0=0$, 
  $\tau_n=\inf\{ l>\tau_{n-1}: X_l\in J\}$
  for $n\in{\mathbb N}$. In other words, on the event $\{X_0\in J\}$, 
  $\tau_n$ denotes the number of jumps up to the $n$-th return to $J$. 
  The restriction of the process to $J$ is defined
  on the event $\{\tau_n<\infty\text{ for all }n\in{\mathbb N}\}$ by
  $(X^J,T^J)=(X_n^J,T_n^J)_{n\in{\mathbb N}_0}:=(X_{\tau_n},T_{\tau_n})_{n\in{\mathbb N}_0}$.

  The notation $(X^{J\neq},T^{J\neq})$ means that both operations have
  been applied to the process $(X,T)$, first the restriction to $J$ and
  then self-loop removal.","status":"unverified"}

		$t$, the map $\zeta\mapsto u_t(x)$ is convex and satisfies
		\[

			\left(\sum_{z\in\mathbb{Z}^d}g_t(x,z)^2\right)^{1/2}
			\|\zeta-\eta\|_{\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^d)}\, .
		\]
		For every $p\geq2$ with $\mathbb{E}|\zeta(0)|^p<\infty$ there is

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:12:19.464074+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_37f9e23eb13e2294349f0aaf2da4b0ccc2ed76095064b4331de2e8d3720977fc","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 12 (Consistency of the Lipschitz-case powers) of arXiv:2608.17540, 'Pathwise stability for one-dimensional SDEs driven by Brownian motion and a symmetric stab'] Let $p=\alpha-1\in(0,1)$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item \textup{Initial value perturbation.} Let
\[
  X_t=x_0+W_t+Z_t,
  \qquad
  \wt X_t=\wt x_0+W_t+Z_t.
\]
Then
\[
  \sup_{0\le t\le T}\E|X_t-\wt X_t|^p=|x_0-\wt x_0|^p.
\]
Thus the initial error exponent $p=\alpha-1$ is exact.

\item \textup{Drift perturbation.} Let
\[
  X_t=bt,
  \qquad
  \wt X_t=\wt b t.
\]
Then
\[
  \sup_{0\le t\le T}\E|X_t-\wt X_t|^p=T^p|b-\wt b|^p.
\]
Since $B=T|b-\wt b|$, this is exactly $B^p$.

\item \textup{Brownian diffusion perturbation.} Let
\[
  X_t=aW_t,
  \qquad
  \wt X_t=\wt a W_t.
\]
Then
\[
  \sup_{0\le t\le T}\E|X_t-\wt X_t|^p
  =m_p T^{p/2}|a-\wt a|^p,
\]
where $m_p=\E|N(0,1)|^p$. Since $A=T^{1/2}|a-\wt a|$, this is $m_p A^p$.

\item \textup{Stable jump coefficient perturbation.} Let
\[
  X_t=\sigma Z_t,
  \qquad
  \wt X_t=\wt\sigma Z_t.
\]
Then
\[
  \sup_{0\le t\le T}\E|X_t-\wt X_t|^p
  =\E|Z_1|^p T^{p/\alpha}|\sigma-\wt\sigma|^p.
\]
Since $S=T^{1/\alpha}|\sigma-\wt\sigma|$, this is $\E|Z_1|^pS^p$.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently, when $\wt\eta=1$, the powers $|x_0-\wt x_0|^{\alpha-1}$, $B^{\alpha-1}$, $A^{\alpha-1}$ and $S^{\alpha-1}$ agree with the exact scaling of the four elementary perturbation mechanisms.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:25:06.200908+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3868ed49fdf830327ebcf31c5da52e30f470519cbe34592632474628329eb581","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 21 of arXiv:2608.22636, 'Q-Learning with Stable Infinite-Dimensional \\Linear Function Approximation'] Fix real numbers $\alpha\ge 1$ and $T>0$, and integers $n\ge0$ and $n_0>0$. \begin{equation}
        m+n_0+1
        \le
        e^{T/\alpha}(n+n_0+1).
        
\end{equation}

If $m_\vee=\max\cW(n,T)$ and $\alpha_{n+1}\le T/2$, then the end time satisfies
\begin{equation}
        \frac{T}{2}
        \le
        \tau(n,m_\vee)
        \le
        T.
        
\end{equation}

If either $T=1/4$ and $n+n_0\ge8$, or
$T=1/5$ and $n+n_0\ge10$, then
\begin{equation}
        m+n_0
        \le
        \frac32(n+n_0),
        \quad \forall m\in\cW(n,T).
        
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.360578+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3886ad8530baeb3a3681c5a268cbb86bf82b63c3a3aa5a6382e8733a6fb1dffa","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Ppn 256 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] In both the spherical and Ising settings, there exists $c>0$ and $C = C(\alpha) > 0$ such that the following holds.
    Let $\cA^\circ$ be a $L$-Lipschitz algorithm with $L\ge 1$.
    Let $\chi^\circ \equiv \chi_{\cA^\circ}$ and $q_0 \equiv \chi^\circ(0)$, and suppose $q_0 < 1$.
    Then, there exists an $L$-Lipschitz algorithm $\cA$ such that the following hold:
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
\item $\chi \equiv \chi_{\cA}$ satisfies $\chi(0) = q_0$ and
    \[
        \chi'(0) \ge  \frac1{L^2}\,.
    \]
In fact, we can take
    \[
        \chi(p) = \bigg(1-\frac{1}{(1-q_0)L^2}\bigg) \chi^\circ(p)+ \frac{q_0 + (1-q_0)p}{(1-q_0)L^2}\,.
    \]

\item 
The perturbed algorithm $\cA$ approximates the original algorithm $\cA^\circ$ in the sense that
    \[
        \frac{1}{N} \E\Big[\|\cA^\circ(\bG,\bg^{\aux}) - \cA(\bG,\bg^{\aux})\|^2\Big]
        \le \frac{2}{(1-q_0)L^2}\,.
    \]

\end{enumerate}
We remark that the above error should be considered small, since we will prove later in Lemma~\ref{l:sM.Lip.1.trivial} that a sequence of algorithms with $q_0$ tending to one can only achieve the gaussian distribution.

\begin{proof} 
Let $\dot{\bg}$ be a standard gaussian in $\bbR^N$ independent of $\bg^{\aux}$, and
let $\bv$ be a deterministic element of $S_N$ with 
 $(\bv,\bbE \cA^\circ(\bG,\bg^{\aux})) = 0$. The perturbed algorithm $\cA$ is defined by
    \[\cA(\bG, (\bg^{\aux}, \dot{\bg} )) 
        = \bigg\{1-\frac{1}{(1-q_0)L^2}
            \bigg\}^{1/2}
        \cA^\circ(\bG,\bg^{\aux}) 
        + \bigg(\frac{q_0}{1-q_0}\bigg)^{1/2} \frac{\bv}{L}
        + \frac{\dot{\bg}}{L} \,.
    \]
Then the gradient of $\cA$ can be bounded as
    \begin{align*}
        \|\nabla\cA
            (\bG,(\bg^{\aux}, \dot{\bg})) \|^2
        &= \|\nabla_{\bG,\bg^{\aux}}
            \cA(\bG,(\bg^{\aux}, \dot{\bg} )) \|^2
        + \|\nabla_{\dot{\bg}} 
            \cA(\bG,(\bg^{\aux},\dot{\bg})) \|^2 \\
        &\le \bigg\{1-\frac{1}{(1-q_0) L^2}   \bigg\} L^2 
            + \frac1{L^2}
        \le L^2\,.
    \end{align*}
Since $\bv$ is deterministic and orthogonal to $\bbE \cA^\circ(\bG,\bg^{\aux})$,
 $\dot{\bg}$ is independent of $(\bG,\bg^{\aux})$, and $\bbE[\|\dot{\bg}\|^2] = N$, we have
    \[\frac{\bbE[
             \|\cA(\bG,(\bg^{\aux},\dot{\bg}))\|^2]}{N}
    =\bigg\{ 1-\frac1{(1-q_0)L^2}\bigg\}
    	+\frac{q_0}{(1-q_0)L^2}
	+\frac{1}{L^2}
    = 1\,,
    \]
where the last step follows from the trivial inequality $1-q_0\le1\le L^2$.  The above two displays show that $\cA$ is an $L$-Lipschitz algorithm in the sense of Definition~\ref{d:Lip}. Moreover, recalling the abbreviations $\chi\equiv\chi_\cA$ and $\chi^\circ\equiv\chi_{\cA^\circ}$, for any $0\le p\le1$ we have
    \[\chi(p) 
    = \bigg(1-\frac1{(1-q_0)L^2}\bigg) \chi^\circ(p) + \frac{q_0+(1-q_0)p}{(1-q_0)L^2}\,,
    \]
which implies $\chi(0)=q_0$.
   As noted above, $\chi^\circ$ is nondecreasing, which implies $\chi'(0)\ge 1/L^2$. This proves part~\eqref{it:wlogable.PERTURBED.CHI}. 

Next, since $|a^{1/2}-b^{1/2}| \le |a-b|^{1/2}$ for all $a,b\ge0$, we can bound
    \begin{align*}
        \frac{1}{N} \E\bigg[\Big\|\cA^\circ(\bG,\bg^{\aux}) - \cA(\bG,\bg^{\aux})\Big\|^2\bigg]
        &= \bigg(1 - \bigg(1-\frac{1}{(1-q_0)L^2}\bigg)^{1/2}\bigg)^2
        + \frac{q_0}{(1-q_0)L^2} + \frac{1}{L^2} \\
        &\le \frac{1}{(1-q_0)L^2} + \frac{q_0}{(1-q_0)L^2} + \frac{1}{L^2}
        = \frac{2}{(1-q_0)L^2}\,.
    \end{align*}
This proves part~\eqref{it:wlogable.PERTURBED.APPX}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["mu satisfies the FKG lattice condition, automatic for independent product measures but requiring verification for dependent Gibbs measures","f, g, or the events A, B, are both increasing, or both decreasing, with respect to the same partial order","the state space is finite or otherwise compactified so that all expectations involved are well defined"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.973188+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_38b7645fc7da6a9d085dab2a80793f9ef28cf412f7ea823995207adfbe1333e1","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). Let mu be a probability measure on a finite distributive lattice satisfying the FKG lattice condition mu(x v y) mu(x ^ y) >= mu(x) mu(y) for all x, y, a condition automatically satisfied by any product measure on {0,1}^E, in which case the conclusion is called the Harris inequality. Then for any two increasing (or two decreasing) functions f, g in L^2(mu), E[fg] >= E[f]E[g]; equivalently, for increasing events A, B, mu(A ^ B) >= mu(A) mu(B), so increasing events are positively correlated. This is the basic monotone-coupling tool throughout percolation and interacting particle systems, lower-bounding joint probabilities of increasing events, such as several disjoint crossings occurring together, by the product of their individual probabilities, and it justifies a wide range of comparison and sprinkling arguments. It does not give any upper bound on the correlation, which requires separate and generally harder tools such as the van den Berg-Kesten inequality for disjoint occurrence; it does not apply to a mix of an increasing and a decreasing event without flipping a sign; and the strength of the positive correlation is not quantified beyond nonnegativity. Typical failure: Applying FKG to a pair of events where one is increasing and the other decreasing without flipping the sign, which reverses the direction of the inequality; or invoking FKG for a non-product Gibbs measure, such as a random-cluster model outside the ferromagnetic regime with cluster weight q<1, without checking the lattice condition, which is known to fail there. Canonical reference: Fortuin, Kasteleyn and Ginibre, 1971, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Harris, 1960, Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Ω ⊂ R^n open; derivatives taken in the distributional sense"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:57.492362+00:00","domain":"Sobolev spaces, functional analysis for PDE","id":"claim_38c3cd05223b169021fe1f60a1ce84a3a15d39f588dd388ecea15bbf6fdb3634","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Ω ⊂ R^n be open, 1 ≤ p ≤ ∞ and k ≥ 1 an integer. W^{k,p}(Ω) is the set of u ∈ L^p(Ω) all of whose distributional derivatives D^α u with |α| ≤ k lie in L^p(Ω): for each α there is g_α ∈ L^p(Ω) with ∫_Ω u D^α φ dx = (−1)^{|α|} ∫_Ω g_α φ dx for every φ ∈ C_c^∞(Ω); one writes D^α u = g_α (the weak derivative, unique a.e.). The norm is ||u||_{W^{k,p}} = ( Σ_{|α| ≤ k} ||D^α u||_{L^p}^p )^{1/p} (maximum over α for p = ∞). W^{k,p}(Ω) is a Banach space, separable for p < ∞ and reflexive for 1 < p < ∞. H^k(Ω) := W^{k,2}(Ω) is a Hilbert space with ⟨u, v⟩ = Σ_{|α| ≤ k} ∫_Ω D^α u D^α v dx. W^{k,p}_0(Ω) is the closure of C_c^∞(Ω) in W^{k,p}(Ω) (functions 'vanishing on the boundary' together with derivatives of order < k); H^1_0(Ω) := W^{1,2}_0(Ω). The Sobolev conjugate of p < n is p* = np/(n − p), i.e. 1/p* = 1/p − 1/n.\n\nFacts: C^∞(Ω) ∩ W^{k,p}(Ω) is dense in W^{k,p}(Ω) for p < ∞ and any open Ω (Meyers–Serrin); restrictions of C^∞(R^n) functions are dense when Ω is bounded with Lipschitz boundary; W^{k,p}_0(R^n) = W^{k,p}(R^n); for bounded Ω, W^{1,p}_0(Ω) is a proper closed subspace of W^{1,p}(Ω) (nonzero constants are excluded by the Poincaré inequality). On an interval, W^{1,p} functions have absolutely continuous representatives; in dimension n ≥ 2 a W^{1,p} function with p ≤ n can be unbounded and discontinuous. For a bounded Lipschitz domain, W^{1,∞}(Ω) is the space of Lipschitz functions on Ω̄.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:09:41.192539+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_38c908d6d617590f98221d7a1608eff9bf05db02ce35b5c55d59b799004eb09e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In computational complexity theory, NP-complete problems are the hardest of the problems to which solutions can be verified quickly. Somewhat more precisely, a problem is NP-complete when:It is a decision problem, meaning that for any input to the problem, the output is either \"yes\" or \"no\". Each input to the problem is associated with a collection of short solutions, which might or might not validly solve the input. The output is \"yes\" when at least one of these solutions is valid, and \"no\" when none of them are. The validity of each solution can be verified quickly, and a brute-force search algorithm can find a valid solution by trying all possible solutions. The problem can be used to simulate every other problem for which we can verify quickly that a solution is valid. Hence, if we could find valid solutions of some NP-complete problem quickly, we could quickly find valid solutions for every other problem in which a given solution can be easily verified.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:23:03.033543+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_39189ad78c197f73292494ba14447706a1b7c8cc2e534c93d9a79bda2361d8c4","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 10 (Decay of the first derivatives of the decoupled flow) of arXiv:2605.03057, 'Uniform-in-time quantitative fluctuations of large scale interacting particle systems'] Assume Assumption~\ref{ass:coeff-level-new}. Fix $ x \in \R^d $, $ \mu \in \Ptwo $, let
$ X_t^{x,\mu} $ be the decoupled flow, and $\omega$ be the constant
defined in \eqref{eq:def-omega-uniform-time}. Then, the following hold.

\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] For every $ h \in \R^d $, the first spatial derivative
$ \partial_x X_t^{x,\mu}\left[ h \right] $ exists and solves
\begin{equation}

d\left( \partial_x X_t^{x,\mu}\left[ h \right] \right)
=
\partial_x b\left( X_t^{x,\mu}, \mu_t^\mu \right)
\partial_x X_t^{x,\mu}\left[ h \right] dt
+
\partial_x \sigma\left( X_t^{x,\mu}, \mu_t^\mu \right)
\partial_x X_t^{x,\mu}\left[ h \right] dB_t,
\end{equation}
with initial condition $\partial_x X_0^{x,\mu}\left[ h \right] =
h$. Moreover, for every $ p \in \mathcal P $ and all $t \ge 0$,
\begin{equation}

\E\left(
\abs{\partial_x X_t^{x,\mu}\left[ h \right]}^p
\right)
\le
e^{-\frac{p\kappa_p}{2} t} \abs{h}^p
\le
e^{-p\omega t} \abs{h}^p.
\end{equation}

\item[(ii)] For every $ v \in \R^d $, the Lions derivative
$ \partial_\mu X_t^{x,\mu}\left( v \right) $ exists and solves
\begin{align}

d\left( \partial_\mu X_t^{x,\mu}\left( v \right) \right)
&=
\Bigg(
\partial_x b\left( X_t^{x,\mu}, \mu_t^\mu \right)
\partial_\mu X_t^{x,\mu}\left( v \right)
+
\widetilde{\E}\left(
\partial_\mu b\left( X_t^{x,\mu}, \mu_t^\mu \right)
\left( \widetilde{X}_t^{v,\mu} \right)
\partial_x \widetilde{X}_t^{v,\mu}
\right)
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\widetilde{\E}\left(
\partial_\mu b\left( X_t^{x,\mu}, \mu_t^\mu \right)
\left( \widetilde{X}_t^{\widetilde{\xi},\mu} \right)
\partial_\mu \widetilde{X}_t^{\widetilde{\xi},\mu}\left( v \right)
\right)
\Bigg) dt
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\Bigg(
\partial_x \sigma\left( X_t^{x,\mu}, \mu_t^\mu \right)
\partial_\mu X_t^{x,\mu}\left( v \right)
+
\widetilde{\E}\left(
\partial_\mu \sigma\left( X_t^{x,\mu}, \mu_t^\mu \right)
\left( \widetilde{X}_t^{v,\mu} \right)
\partial_x \widetilde{X}_t^{v,\mu}
\right)
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\widetilde{\E}\left(
\partial_\mu \sigma\left( X_t^{x,\mu}, \mu_t^\mu \right)
\left( \widetilde{X}_t^{\widetilde{\xi},\mu} \right)
\partial_\mu \widetilde{X}_t^{\widetilde{\xi},\mu}\left( v \right)
\right)
\Bigg) dB_t,
\end{align}
with initial condition $\partial_\mu X_0^{x,\mu}\left( v \right) =
0$. Moreover, for every $ p \in \mathcal P $, there exists a constant
$ C_p > 0 $ such that, for all $t \ge 0$,
\begin{equation*}
\sup_{x,\mu,v}
\E\left(
\abs{\partial_\mu X_t^{x,\mu}\left( v \right)}^p
\right)
\le
C_p e^{-p\omega t}.
\end{equation*}
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["pointwise form: u ∈ C^2(Ω) (or H^2_loc, a.e.)","integrated form: Ω bounded with Lipschitz boundary, u ∈ C^2 up to the boundary or u ∈ H^2(Ω)","eigenvalue formula: additionally u = 0 on ∂Ω and −Δu = λu in Ω"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:57.492269+00:00","domain":"elliptic PDE, Rellich and Pohozaev identities, Dirichlet eigenvalues","id":"claim_39490348519396f0628002960648e225d47916ef40d2fa4016bd80557364979d","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Pointwise identity. Let Ω ⊂ R^n be open, x the position vector, and u ∈ C^2(Ω). Then, everywhere in Ω,
   div( (x·∇u) ∇u − (1/2)|∇u|^2 x ) = (x·∇u) Δu − ((n−2)/2) |∇u|^2.
The same holds almost everywhere for u ∈ H^2_loc(Ω) (all terms are then in L^1_loc). Replacing x by x − x_0 for any fixed x_0 gives the same identity (translation invariance).

Integrated form (Rellich). Let Ω be a bounded open set with Lipschitz boundary, ν the outward unit normal, dS surface measure, and u ∈ C^2(Ω̄), or u ∈ H^2(Ω) with the boundary integrals read through the L^2(∂Ω) traces of ∇u. Then
   ∫_Ω (x·∇u) Δu dx = ((n−2)/2) ∫_Ω |∇u|^2 dx + ∫_∂Ω [ (x·∇u)(∂_ν u) − (1/2)|∇u|^2 (x·ν) ] dS.

Dirichlet case. If in addition u = 0 on ∂Ω (trace sense), then the tangential gradient vanishes on ∂Ω, ∇u = (∂_ν u) ν there, and the boundary term collapses to (1/2) ∫_∂Ω (x·ν) (∂_ν u)^2 dS. If moreover −Δu = λu in Ω, then
   λ ∫_Ω u^2 dx = (1/2) ∫_∂Ω (x·ν) (∂_ν u)^2 dS,
the Rellich formula expressing a Dirichlet eigenvalue by a boundary integral; equivalently 2λ||u||^2_{L^2(Ω)} = ∫_∂Ω (x·ν)(∂_ν u)^2 dS. For a domain star-shaped with respect to the origin (x·ν ≥ 0 on ∂Ω) the right side is nonnegative term by term. The same computation with −Δu = f(u), u = 0 on ∂Ω, is the Pohozaev identity.

Where it fails / hypotheses that matter. The integrated form needs enough regularity to give ∇u a boundary trace: u ∈ H^2(Ω) (or C^2 up to the boundary). A Dirichlet eigenfunction on a Lipschitz domain that is not convex (a re-entrant corner) need not belong to H^2(Ω), and the identity is then not available in this form without a separate justification. Without u = 0 on ∂Ω the tangential gradient contributes and the simplified boundary term (1/2)∫(x·ν)(∂_ν u)^2 is wrong: the full bracket must be kept. The sign of x·ν is not fixed for a general domain, so conclusions that use x·ν ≥ 0 (star-shapedness, Pohozaev-type nonexistence) fail otherwise. In dimension n = 2 the interior term ((n−2)/2)∫|∇u|^2 vanishes. The identity is for the Laplacian; for a variable-coefficient operator div(A∇u) extra terms involving x·∇A appear.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.197503+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3974ceafccda88625c19a4b09749f8b173b7dd31b03e4232755106f3683a1951","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 119 (continuous-time smoothed coefficients) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Analogously to Definition~\ref{d:sp.smooth}, we define the spatially smoothed continuous-time coefficients

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:52:08.670984+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_39c92a21ce09e808fb46f2dd1cc54ccba0953444b48886fc35c59e2aadc175f0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 27 (Block contraction theorem) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Under the standing fixed-threshold application, fix \(\delta_0\geq c_0\).
There are constants
\[
        T_{\mathrm{blk}}<\infty,\qquad
        \eta_{\mathrm{blk}}>0,\qquad
        \theta_{\mathrm{blk}}>0,\qquad
        \Lambda_*<\infty
\]
with the following property.  The constants
\(\eta_{\mathrm{blk}},\theta_{\mathrm{blk}},\Lambda_*\) depend only on
\(K,\delta_0,N,\sigma\).  The start-time threshold \(T_{\mathrm{blk}}\) may
additionally depend on the fixed Bamler tail data \(T_B(c_0)\) and
\(\eps_B^{c_0}\) for the given flow.

Let \(p(\tau)\) be a parabolically rescaled \(\delta_0\)-large block starting
at \(S\geq T_{\mathrm{blk}}\), fix a torus fibration \(\pi:M\to S^1\), and put
\[
        q(1)=p(1),\qquad r(1)=\overline{q(1)}.
\]
Suppose that \(r(1)\) is Riemannian and, with
\[
 b=\|q(1)-r(1)\|_{C^{N,\sigma}(M,r(1))},
 \qquad d=d_{\TT^2}(r(1)),
\]
one has
\[
        b<\eta_{\mathrm{blk}},\qquad
        d<\theta_{\mathrm{blk}},\qquad
        \BG_N(r(1);\Lambda_*).
\]
Equivalently, \((q(1),r(1))\) is an admissible stage start in the sense of
Definition~\ref{def:admissible-stage-start}, with constants
\(\Lambda_*,\eta_{\mathrm{blk}},\theta_{\mathrm{blk}}\).
Then the invariant Ricci flow \(r\) and the Ricci--DeTurck flow \(q\) relative
to it exist on \([1,100]\).  At the rescaled endpoint, put
\[
        q^+(1)=100^{-1}q(100),\qquad
        \rho^+=100^{-1}r(100),\qquad
        r^+(1)=\overline{q^+(1)},
\]
and set
\[
        b^+=\|q^+(1)-r^+(1)\|_{C^{N,\sigma}(M,r^+(1))}.

Then \(r^+(1)\) is Riemannian and

        b^+\leq\tfrac12 b,\qquad
        d_{\TT^2}(r^+(1))<\theta_{\mathrm{blk}},\qquad
        \BG_N(r^+(1);\Lambda_*).

Thus the same admissible-start conditions hold at the restart.  The ordinary
Ricci flow corresponding to \(q\) is \(p\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.162189+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_39ef52ee75249f5f440b1e1246bef6c63616758f5dffa470be1204a3dd78e398","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Cor 17 (\cite{MR51275}; see also \cite{MR317760}) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Take $A,b,C,d$ as in Theorem~\ref{t:hoffman} with $(b,d)\in F(A,C)$.
Let $B(M_0)$ denote the ball of radius $M_0$ in $\R^n$, centered at the origin.
\begin{enumerate}[a.]
\item  Suppose $(b',d')\in F(A,C)$, and
suppose further that the (nonempty) sets
$S_{A,C}(b,d)$ and $S_{A,C}(b',d')$ are both contained in $B(M_0)$.
Then
	\[d_H\Big(S_{A,C}(b,d),S_{A,C}(b',d')\Big)
	\le c\left\| \begin{pmatrix}
	b-b'\\d-d'\end{pmatrix}\right\|_2
	\]
where $c$ is a finite constant depending only on $A,C,M_0$.
\item 
Now suppose we have $(A,b,C,d)'$ of the same dimensions,
with $(b',d')\in F(A',C')$. 
Suppose further that the (nonempty) sets
$S\equiv S_{A,C}(b,d)$ and $S'\equiv S_{A',C'}(b',d')$ are both contained in $B(M_0)$.
Then, for any $x'\in S'$ there exists $x\in S$ with
	\[\|x-x'\|_2
	\le c \left\| \begin{pmatrix} A-A'\\ C-C'\\
	b-b'\\d-d'\end{pmatrix}\right\|_2\,,
	\]
where $c$ is a finite constant depending only on $A,C,M_0$, and on the right-hand side we treat $A$ and $C$ as vectors of length $mn$ and $qn$ respectively.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{proof}
Suppose $x'\in S'$. Then
	\[
	Ax'-b
	=[A'+(A-A')] x'- [b' + (b-b')]
	\le (A-A')x'-(b-b')\,,
	\]
from which it follows that
	\[
	\|(Ax'-b)_+\|
	\le \| [(A-A')x'-(b-b')]_+\|
	\le \|A-A'\|_\textup{op} M_0 + \|b-b'\|\,.
	\]
Similarly, we can bound
	\[

{"assumptions":["The standard thirteen-graph cubic distance-regular classification.","The values are reported computations from the campaign record."],"created_at":"2026-10-10T06:51:51.364653+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_39f9c09b53339b708c3cfa454baf0d76df290fd6db9f1e7d7a2a93b62a11785e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14; values computed exactly from the intersection-array identity tau_0 = k sum_{i=1}^d (k_i+...+k_d)/(k_i c_i). That identity was checked against a direct linear-algebra solve on twelve graphs, among them the cubic graphs K_{3,3}, Q_3, Petersen, Heawood, Pappus, Desargues and the dodecahedron, with the complete graph and the cycle as independent controls.] This is the cubic case of Open Problem 7.31 in David Aldous and James Allen Fill's Reversible Markov Chains and Random Walks on Graphs, unfinished monograph (2002, recompiled 2014; official source https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/RWG/book.html). For a finite connected simple distance-regular graph G with n vertices, let tau_0 = max_{x,y} E_x[T_y] for simple random walk. By the known classification, there are exactly thirteen cubic (valency-three) distance-regular graphs. Their (n, tau_0) values are: K_4 (4, 3); K_{3,3} (6, 6); cube Q_3 (8, 10); Petersen (10, 12); Heawood (14, 19); Pappus (18, 27); Desargues (20, 65/2); dodecahedron (20, 35); Coxeter (28, 45); Tutte-Coxeter (30, 48); Foster (90, 675/4); Biggs-Smith (102, 195); Tutte 12-cage (126, 234). Hence, given the classification, the maximum of tau_0/(n-1) over all cubic distance-regular graphs is 195/101 (about 1.9307), attained uniquely by the Biggs-Smith graph. This reproduces exactly the value Aldous and Fill attribute to Biggs and settles, for valency three, Biggs's outlined claim that it is the largest. The general O(n) conjecture over non-cycle distance-regular graphs is not settled by this computation. This is an unrefereed campaign result.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Sign convention: L u = -a^{ij} u_{x_i x_j} + b^i u_{x_i} + c u, subsolution means u_t + Lu <= 0","c identically zero for the full maximum principle","c >= 0 for the version with the positive part","bounded c of any sign for the comparison (sign) principle only"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:49.107002+00:00","domain":"parabolic partial differential equations","id":"claim_3a4cafe9e19336aa105a2005fb7c65fd586ea28dc22562c2af3b9b1faed19d02","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"For $u_t+Lu\\le0$ with $Lu=-a^{ij}u_{x_ix_j}+b^iu_{x_i}+cu$, the identity $\\max_{\\overline{U_T}}u=\\max_{\\Gamma_T}u$ requires $c\\equiv0$; with $c\\ge0$ only the weaker $\\max_{\\overline{U_T}}u\\le\\max_{\\Gamma_T}u^+$ survives; with $c$ of arbitrary sign even that fails. Heydenreich-van der Hofstad Open Problem 13.4 asks that the second largest cluster at p_c(1 + eps) on {0,1}^d match, to leading order, the largest cluster at p_c(1 - eps), eps >> 2^{-d/3}. G(n,p) has this through the discrete duality principle: after the giant is removed, the rest is close in law to a subcritical G(n', p) with the dual mean (an asymptotic statement, not an exact symmetry); the hypercube has no such principle, so it must come from tails: the subcritical largest cluster is Theta(eps^{-2} log(eps^3 2^d)) once the tail P(|C| >= k) >= c k^{-1/2} exp(-c' eps^2 k) holds with the SHARP rate in eps^2 k (the upper bound is known, the sharp lower bound is the missing half), and the supercritical second-largest needs the same tail for the clusters after removal of the giant, which is the geometric-depletion question of the exploration process. So the duality principle is reduced, heuristically, to two tail statements, one subcritical with a sharp rate and one post-giant; turning tails into the size of the largest cluster also needs control of the number of clusters and of their dependence, so this is not an equivalence.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.543633+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3a7f53cc4f4c10093c8e4e07c223f18d52212a9c7d6f98c1196f104f16111a3d","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let gamma be the standard Gaussian measure on R^n. The ORNSTEIN-UHLENBECK SEMIGROUP is defined by MEHLER'S FORMULA P_t f(x) = integral f( e^{-t} x + sqrt(1 - e^{-2t}) y ) gamma(dy) for t >= 0. It is a Markov semigroup: P_0 = identity, P_{s+t} = P_s P_t, P_t 1 = 1, P_t preserves nonnegativity, gamma is INVARIANT (integral P_t f dgamma = integral f dgamma), and P_t is SELF-ADJOINT on L^2(gamma). Its generator is L f = Laplacian f - x . grad f, which satisfies the integration-by-parts identity integral (L u) v dgamma = - integral grad u . grad v dgamma. The Hermite polynomials diagonalise it: L He_alpha = - |alpha| He_alpha and P_t He_alpha = e^{-|alpha| t} He_alpha, so the n-th Wiener chaos is the eigenspace of eigenvalue -n. The COMMUTATION RELATION grad P_t f = e^{-t} P_t grad f follows by differentiating Mehler's formula under the integral. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:31:02.820761+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3ab938b4d4cb0291e52c58efecec41c9b61657b15af69c0bf3f08bdc1bef47be","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:root-sweep-dictionary of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Let $h\geq1$ and $k\geq2$.  One has the exact difference identity
\begin{equation}
 E_{h,k}-E_{h,k}=h\mathsf R_{k-1}\cap\mathsf A_{k-1}.
\end{equation}
For an ordered real tuple $a=(a_1<\cdots<a_k)$, write
\({\bf1}=(1,\ldots,1)\in\mathbb R^k\) and let
$a^\circ=a-k^{-1}(\sum_i a_i){\bf1}$ be its centered representative.  Let
$F_h(a)$ be the face of $\mathfrak Z_{h,k}$ exposed by $a^\circ$.  The
following data determine one another:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item the total preorder on $E_{h,k}$ induced by $u\mapsto u\cdot a$
      (equivalently, its ordered weak partition into level sets);
\item the complete ordered $h$-addition table of $a$, including ties;
\item the face $F_h(a)$.
\end{enumerate}
The dimension of $F_h(a)$ is the active relation rank $r_h(a)$.  In the
ambient space ${\bf1}^{\perp}$, its normal cone has dimension
$k-1-r_h(a)$, and the relative interior of that cone consists precisely of
the centered weights inducing the same complete table.  Moreover, the same
face determines every ordered addition table in degrees $1\leq j\leq h$.

Fix any field $K$.  If $a\in\mathbb Z^k$, put
$A=\{a_1,\ldots,a_k\}$ and define
\[
 \varphi_a:K[x_1,\ldots,x_k]\longrightarrow K[u,t,t^{-1}],
 \qquad x_i\longmapsto u t^{a_i},
 \qquad I_a=\ker\varphi_a,
\]
where $\deg u=1$ and $\deg t=0$.  Then the number of blocks in the face
label is the Hilbert value
\begin{equation}
 |hA|=\dim_K\bigl(K[x_1,\ldots,x_k]/I_a\bigr)_h.
\end{equation}
Thus the face records the equality rank and Hilbert/block label, while its
normal cone encodes the normalized shape, realization frequency, and integer
compression developed below.","status":"unverified"}

A bounded operator T: H -> K is Hilbert-Schmidt if sum_{i in I} ||T e_i||^2 < infinity for some orthonormal basis (e_i)_{i in I} of H. The sum is then the same for every orthonormal basis of H, and ||T||_2 = (sum_i ||T e_i||^2)^{1/2} is the Hilbert-Schmidt norm. Equivalently, T is compact and sum_n s_n(T)^2 < infinity, with ||T||_2^2 = sum_n s_n(T)^2. Properties: ||T|| <= ||T||_2; ||T*||_2 = ||T||_2; every Hilbert-Schmidt operator is compact (it is the ||.||_2-limit, hence operator-norm limit, of finite-rank operators); the Hilbert-Schmidt operators S_2(H,K) form a Hilbert space under <A,B>_2 = sum_i <A e_i, B e_i> = tr(B*A), independent of the basis; and they form an ideal: ||A T B||_2 <= ||A|| ||T||_2 ||B|| for bounded A, B. Basis independence follows from sum_i ||T e_i||^2 = sum_i sum_j |<T e_i, f_j>|^2 = sum_j ||T* f_j||^2 for any orthonormal basis (f_j) of K.","status":"unverified"}

For Bernoulli percolation, and more generally for FKG-satisfying, translation-invariant models with finite energy (including the random-cluster model for cluster weight q>=1), the sharpness-of-phase-transition theorem shows that below the critical point p_c, the probability of connection to distance n decays exponentially in n, proved without duality via a finite-size criterion: a box functional phi_p(S), built from crossing probabilities and a weighted sum over pivotal edges, is shown to satisfy a differential inequality in p that forces it to either stay bounded (subcritical, exponential decay) or blow up past a threshold (supercritical), with the threshold identified as p_c. This unifies and reproves the classical results of Menshikov and of Aizenman-Barsky with a single argument that is robust enough to extend to Z^d for every d, to general transitive graphs, and to the random-cluster model. The theorem does not give the exact value of p_c, does not determine critical behavior exactly at p_c (critical exponents are a separate, generally much harder, question), and the exponential-decay rate produced is not claimed to be sharp or explicit. Typical failure: Assuming the Duminil-Copin-Tassion argument extends automatically to a non-FKG regime, such as random-cluster parameters q<1 or certain long-range or antiferromagnetic models, where positive association fails; the driving differential inequality depends essentially on FKG-type monotonicity and on finite energy, and dropping either hypothesis breaks the exponential-decay conclusion outright rather than merely weakening it. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.544171+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3b43ec8f5d0fa6d27d0e5752777028d785fae794a67b64a293ba500ca12736e7","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"The GAUSSIAN ORTHOGONAL ENSEMBLE GOE_n is the law of a real symmetric n by n matrix H whose entries are independent up to symmetry with H_{ii} distributed as N(0, 2/n) and H_{ij} distributed as N(0, 1/n) for i < j. Its density with respect to Lebesgue measure on the space of real symmetric matrices is proportional to exp( - (n/4) trace(H^2) ), and the law is invariant under H -> O H O^T for every orthogonal O. The GAUSSIAN UNITARY ENSEMBLE GUE_n is the law of a Hermitian H with H_{ii} distributed as N(0, 1/n) real and, for i < j, H_{ij} = x + i y with x and y independent N(0, 1/(2n)), so that E|H_{ij}|^2 = 1/n; its density is proportional to exp( - (n/2) trace(H^2) ) and it is invariant under H -> U H U^* for every unitary U. With THESE normalisations the empirical spectral distribution of either ensemble converges to the semicircle law on [-2, 2], the largest eigenvalue converges to 2, and the edge fluctuations are of order n^{-2/3} with Tracy-Widom limits (beta = 1 for GOE, beta = 2 for GUE). The DIAGONAL VARIANCE DIFFERS BETWEEN THE TWO ENSEMBLES - 2/n for GOE, 1/n for GUE - and that is what makes both densities come out as the invariant exponential of the trace; getting it wrong changes the density but not the limiting spectral law. Normalisation conventions vary widely across the literature: some authors use unnormalised entries of variance 1 and divide by sqrt(n) afterwards, some put the semicircle on [-1,1] or [-2 sqrt(2), 2 sqrt(2)], and some use exp(-trace(H^2)/2) with n absorbed elsewhere. Any imported constant must be checked against the convention it was derived under. [standard; e.g. Anderson, Guionnet and Zeitouni, An Introduction to Random Matrices, Sections 2.5 and 2.6]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:00:46.819743+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3b587371cf631eb291613b05dab51097d529d27dc0b183b1d5fa8c0a7277305f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 1 of arXiv:2608.13208, 'Universality in dimension $1$ of kinetically constrained lattice gases'] A kinetically constrained lattice gas is a Markov
process on $\Omega=\{0,1\}^{\Z}$ with generator 
\begin{equation}
\cL f(\eta)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{x,y\in\Z}c(x,y,\eta)(f(\eta^{xy})-f(\eta)),
\end{equation}
where $\eta^{xy}$ is the configuration after exchanging $x$ and
$y$. The rates are given by the \emph{constraint function} $c:\Z\times\Z\times\Omega\to[0,\infty]$
satisfying:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Nearest-neighbor jumps: $c(x,y,\eta)=0$ if $\left|x-y\right|\neq1$.
By convention $c(x,y,\eta)=c(y,x,\eta)$.
\item Translation invariance: $c(x,y,\eta)=c(x+z,y+z,\tau_{z}\eta)$ for
all $x,y,z$, where $\tau_{z}$ is the translation by $z$.
\item $c(x,y,\eta)$ does not depend on the occupation at $x$ and $y$,
i.e., $c(x,y,\eta)=c(x,y,\eta^{xy})$.
\item Finite range: there exists $r>0$ such that $c(x,y,\eta)$ depends
only on the configuration in $x+[-r,r]$.
\item Monotonicity: if $\eta(x)\le\omega(x)$ for all $x$, then $c(x,y,\eta)\ge c(x,y,\omega)$.
That is, adding vacancies speeds up transitions.
\end{enumerate}
We can also define the process on a finite segment $[a,b]$ of $\Z$
by fixing boundary conditions; in this article we always consider
filled boundary, i.e., for $x,y\in[a,b]$ the constraint in the segment
is given by $c_{[a,b]}(x,y,\eta)=c(x,y,\tilde{\eta})$ where $\tilde{\eta}$
agrees with $\eta$ on $[a,b]$ and equals $1$ outside.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:15:54.903423+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3b6077a432a793f0a80f87dc5e6644dd149f2797ff4b881d43f56274b79cacdb","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:block of arXiv:2608.28007, 'Exact Risk Ratios for Weighted Data Selection in Linear Regression'] A whitened system $\{(\xi_i,\eta_i)\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$ has \emph{orthogonal

gradients means a set of indices whose gradients $g_i=\eta_i\xi_i$ carry a
strictly positive zero-sum relation, minimal with respect to support. Write

{"assumptions":["rows iid","S and T are distinct (m-1)-subsets of row indices","the span of the shared rows has full rank almost surely"],"created_at":"2026-09-23T13:16:40.830294+00:00","domain":"random matrix theory","id":"claim_3b6ac9ae92b563a93f51075f27414a262a50f1204b39ef9ae9ea1f99cf7277e6","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $X_1,\\dots,X_m$ be iid random rows in $\\mathbb{R}^m$ and let $S, T$ be two distinct $(m-1)$-subsets of row indices. Put $A = S \\cap T$, $B = S \\setminus T$, $C = T \\setminus S$ and $D = m - |A|$, so that $|B| = |C| = D - 1$. Condition on the rows indexed by $A$, let $E_A = \\operatorname{span}(A)^{\\perp}$, which has dimension $D$ almost surely, and let $Q_A : \\mathbb{R}^D \\to E_A \\subset \\mathbb{R}^m$ be any isometry (an $m \\times D$ matrix with orthonormal columns). Then the unit null normals $u_S, u_T$ of the two $(m-1) \\times m$ row submatrices satisfy $u_S = Q_A v$ and $u_T = Q_A w$, where $v, w \\in S^{D-1}$ are the null directions of the residual matrices $U = B Q_A$ and $V = C Q_A$. Conditionally on $A$ the matrices $U$ and $V$ are independent, each with iid rows of law $Q_A^{\\top} X$, and the pair correlation is preserved exactly: $\\rho_{ST}^2 = \\langle u_S, u_T \\rangle^2 = \\langle v, w \\rangle^2$. Writing $M_A = \\mathbb{E}[v v^{\\top} \\mid A]$ for the conditional second-moment matrix of the residual null line, $\\mathbb{E}[\\langle v,w\\rangle^2 \\mid A] = \\operatorname{tr}(M_A^2)$. {"assumptions":["f integrable on R","the pointwise identity is claimed at a specific point (typically x = 0)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:39.264346+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis, common errors","id":"claim_3b718e0037a91db9c64b0a4706cc1000aa0a6e3fe12673010be7f29fee1bf2dc","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypotheses: the periodization $Pf(x)=\\sum_nf(x+n)$ must be continuous at the point where the identity is evaluated, and its Fourier series must converge there (absolute summability of $(\\hat f(k))_k$ is the usual sufficient condition). For a general $f\\in L^1(\\mathbb R)$ all that is true is $\\widehat{Pf}(k)=\\hat f(k)$, i.e. Poisson summation as an identity of Fourier series of an $L^1(\\mathbb T)$ function - which says nothing pointwise. Concrete failure: $f=\\mathbf 1_{[0,1]}$ (with $f(0)=f(1)=1$). Then $\\sum_nf(n)=f(0)+f(1)=2$, while $\\hat f(0)=1$ and $\\hat f(k)=\\int_0^1e^{-2\\pi ikx}dx=0$ for $k\\ne0$, so $\\sum_k\\hat f(k)=1\\ne2$. The periodization equals $1$ off $\\mathbb Z$ and $2$ on $\\mathbb Z$: it is discontinuous exactly where the identity is being evaluated, and the Fourier series converges to the midpoint $1$. Redefining $f(0)=f(1)=1/2$ restores the identity. Second trap: pure decay of $f$ is not enough - one needs decay (or summability) on the transform side as well, since the right-hand series must converge; $f$ continuous and integrable with $\\hat f$ merely tending to zero gives no pointwise statement. When quoting a rate, the clean hypothesis is $|f(x)|\\le C(1+|x|)^{-1-\\delta}$ and $|\\hat f(\\xi)|\\le C(1+|\\xi|)^{-1-\\delta}$ with $f$ continuous, or simply $f\\in\\mathcal S$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0054-localisation-of-all-bulk-states-for-two-dimensional-random-band-matric","No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:26:45.042114+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3bf6be9ae3842b9ca1fdd761e2056571214bc8ce381c2922ab547980201cf160","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Try a fractional-moment (Aizenman-Molchanov) argument adapted to band matrices at fixed W in d = 2. Result: The fractional-moment method proves localisation when the expected s-th moment of the Green function E|G_{xy}(E + i eta)|^s decays exponentially in |x - y|; for band matrices at fixed W in d = 2 the required a priori bound is a decoupling of the moment across a band-width-sized block, which for the Anderson model comes from the rank-one structure of the diagonal disorder. Band matrices have no rank-one structure: the randomness at a site is a W^2-dimensional block, and the decoupling lemma degrades by a factor that grows with W^2, so the method proves localisation only for W <= W_0 small (large disorder regime), not for every fixed W. The conjectured localisation length exp(W^2) matches the expected scaling of the failure of the fractional-moment bound: the moment decays only after distances of order exp(cW^2), consistent with the conjecture but not proving it. A rigorous partial statement I can defend: for every fixed W there is a positive density of localised states at the spectral edges (Lifshitz-tail regime), by the standard edge-localisation argument, which does not touch the bulk. $$

$$
and
$$

$$
In particular, we have$:$
$$

$$

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:47.651862+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3c2a73cc53296bd38cbc69e9d18f9715c6a949b5dec9214a445ecf905510450a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop 11 of arXiv:2605.07050, 'Universality of the fluctuations of the free energy in generalized Sherrington--Kirkpatric'] Suppose that the random variables $\{ P^{(n)}_{ij} \}_{i<j}$ ($n=1, 2, 3, 4$) satisfy the following:
\begin{itemize}

\item For any $n$, $\E[P^{(n)}_{ij}] = 0$ and $\E[(P^{(n)}_{ij})^2] = \cn_n$ for some ($N$-independent) constants $\cn_n$.
\item $\E[P^{(1)}_{ij} P^{(2)}_{ij}] = \E[P^{(2)}_{ij} P^{(3)}_{ij}] = \E[P^{(3)}_{ij} P^{(4)}_{ij}] = \E[P^{(1)}_{ij} P^{(4)}_{ij}] = 0$ and $\E[P^{(1)}_{ij} (P^{(2)}_{ij})^2] = 0$.

\begin{itemize}

\item For any $n$, $\E[P^{(n)}_{d,kk}] = 0$ and $\E[(P^{(n)}_{d,kk})^2] = \cn'_n$ for some ($N$-independent) constants $\cn'_n$.

In addition, we also assume that for any $n=1, 2, 3, 4$, $m=1, 2$, $i<j$ and $k$, $P^{(n)}_{ij}$ and $P^{(m)}_{d,kk}$ are independent.
Fix $\epsilon \in (0, 1/60)$ and let
\[
	\Omega_\caX^\epsilon := \{ \max_{1 \leq k \leq N} |x_k| \leq N^{-1/2 +\epsilon} \} \cap \{ | \| \bsx \| - 1 | \leq N^{-1/5} \}.
\]
Suppose that Assumption \ref{assump:second_moment} holds with $\SNR_c$. If $\F < \SNR_c$,
\beq \begin{split} 
	&\log \E_\caX \left[ \indi(\Omega_\caX^\epsilon) \prod_{i<j} \left( 1 + P^{(1)}_{ij} \sqrt{N} x_i x_j + P^{(2)}_{ij} N x_i^2 x_j^2 + P^{(3)}_{ij} N^{3/2} x_i^3 x_j^3 + P^{(4)}_{ij} N^2 x_i^4 x_j^4 \right) \right. \\

as $N \to \infty$, where

	\rho:= -\frac{1}{4} \left( \log (1-\F) + (\F - 2 \F') + \frac{\F^2}{2} \right) + \frac{\G}{4}.
\]
Similarly, under the same assumption
\beq \begin{split}

	&\qquad \qquad \left. \times \prod_{k=1}^N \left( 1 + P^{(1)}_{d,kk} \frac{\sqrt{N} x_k^2}{\| \bsx \|^2} + P^{(2)}_{d,kk} \frac{N x_k^4}{\| \bsx \|^4} \right) \right] \Rightarrow \caN(-\rho, 2\rho)
\end{split} \eeq
as $N \to \infty$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(X,B,mu) is a probability space and T preserves mu","the partitions P_k are countable, measurable, and increasing: P_{k+1} refines P_k","H_mu(P_k) < infinity for each k","the union of the P_k generates B modulo mu-null sets","h_mu(T) is defined as the supremum of h_mu(T,Q) over countable partitions Q of finite entropy"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.090319+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, entropy, generators","id":"claim_3c3e128038c699e9bd64175dd57d1489d79b6bc2f84bbdbc616d67a216487a92","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, B, mu) be a probability space and T : X -> X measure-preserving (invertibility is not assumed). Let P_1 <= P_2 <= ... be an increasing sequence of countable measurable partitions (each P_{k+1} refines P_k) with H_mu(P_k) < infinity for every k, and assume the sequence GENERATES: the sigma-algebra generated by the union of the P_k equals B up to mu-null sets. Then h_mu(T) = lim_k h_mu(T, P_k) = sup_k h_mu(T, P_k), where h_mu(T) is the supremum of h_mu(T,Q) over all finite-entropy partitions Q. The classical generator form is the special case: for an invertible T and a partition P with H_mu(P) < infinity whose two-sided join over all integer translates generates B, take P_k = the join of T^{-n}P over |n| <= k and conclude h_mu(T) = h_mu(T,P); for non-invertible T take the one-sided join over 0 <= n <= k. WHERE IT FAILS: (i) generation is the entire content. If the union of the P_k generates only a proper sub-sigma-algebra, the limit computes the entropy of the corresponding sub-process and can be strictly smaller than h_mu(T); with every P_k trivial the limit is 0 for a system of arbitrarily large entropy. In particular a partition that separates points topologically but only generates a smaller sigma-algebra modulo mu is not enough. (ii) Monotonicity of the sequence (or at least H_mu(Q | P_k) -> 0 for every finite-entropy Q) is used; an arbitrary sequence of partitions that 'converges' in some other sense need not have monotone entropies and the comparison step breaks. (iii) H_mu(P_k) < infinity is needed for the comparison inequality. (iv) Generation is modulo mu-null sets only, and the conclusion says nothing pointwise. (v) For non-invertible T the one-sided generator computes h_mu(T); using the two-sided join for a non-invertible map is meaningless.","status":"unverified"}

(a) Free homotopy: γ₀ and γ₁ are homotopic through closed curves in ℂ \\ {z₀} (a continuous H: [0,1]×[0,1] → ℂ \\ {z₀} with H(0,·) = γ₀, H(1,·) = γ₁ and H(s,0) = H(s,1) for every s) if and only if n(γ₀, z₀) = n(γ₁, z₀). (b) Based version: if γ₀(0) = γ₁(0) = p, they are homotopic through loops based at p in ℂ \\ {z₀} if and only if their winding numbers about z₀ agree. (c) Consequently the map π₁(ℂ \\ {z₀}, p) → ℤ, [γ] ↦ n(γ, z₀), is a well-defined group isomorphism; every integer k is realized by the circle t ↦ z₀ + r e^{2πikt} (moved to the base point along a path), and a loop in ℂ \\ {z₀} is null-homotopic exactly when its winding number about z₀ is zero. {"assumptions":["n ≥ 2"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:51.723666+00:00","domain":"dispersive partial differential equations","id":"claim_3c61dddc2341b2fe03846c34c5f8fd2adaac49c5e5184bddc378dc2b3677df6a","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let n ≥ 2. A pair (q,r) is wave-admissible (in the sense of Keel–Tao) if 2 ≤ q ≤ ∞, 2 ≤ r ≤ ∞, 1/q + (n−1)/(2r) ≤ (n−1)/4, and (q,r,n) ≠ (2,∞,3). It is sharp wave-admissible when equality holds, 1/q + (n−1)/(2r) = (n−1)/4. The exponent (n−1)/2 is the dispersive decay rate of frequency-localized waves; the associated regularity s is fixed separately by the scaling relation 1/q + n/r = n/2 − s. Examples in n = 3: (4,4) with s = 1/2, (5,10) and (4,12) with s = 1, and (∞,2) with s = 0, which is the bound ‖u‖_{L^∞_t L²_x} ≲ ‖u0‖_{L²} + ‖u1‖_{Ḣ^{−1}}. Note that the energy bound ‖u‖_{L^∞_t Ḣ¹} + ‖∂_t u‖_{L^∞_t L²} ≲ ‖u0‖_{Ḣ¹} + ‖u1‖_{L²} is not a different admissible pair: it is the pair (∞,2) applied at regularity s = 1, i.e. to |∇|u. The scaling relation always ties s to (q,r), so s = 0 is the only value that goes with (q,r) = (∞,2) in the Lebesgue-norm form of the estimate. Also note that r = ∞ is allowed in this definition but not in the Lebesgue-space wave Strichartz theorem, which requires r < ∞.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:36:31.221997+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3c9dbb84370f01449a45a358af3c4e2180aca4413319da51186af6baec056e3a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 1 (Unique finite-time limit) of arXiv:2609.00501, 'Uniqueness of Finite-Time Varifold Limits for the M\"obius-Invariant Willmore Flow'] Let $F\colon[0,T)\times\Sigma\to\Sph^3$ be a smooth MIWF of a compact
torus, where $T<\infty$, and write $F_t:=F(t,\cdot)$.  Let $A_t^0$
denote the trace-free second fundamental form of $F_t$.  Put
\[
 W(t):=\Will(F_t),\qquad W_0:=W(0),\qquad
 \mu_t:=\mu_{F_t^*g_{\Sph^3}}.
\]
Assume that
for some $c_0>0$,
\[
 \inf_{0<t<T}\min_{x\in\Sigma}|A_t^0(x)|^2\geq c_0.
\]
Let $\Var_t$ denote the multiplicity-counting integral two-varifold in
$\R^4$ induced by $F_t$, and set
$\lambda_t:=\lVert\Var_t\rVert=(F_t)_\#\mu_t$.
Then there exists a unique integral two-varifold
$\Var_T$ in $\R^4$, possibly the zero varifold, such that, with
$\rightharpoonup$ denoting weak varifold convergence,
\begin{equation}
 
 \Var_t\rightharpoonup\Var_T
 \qquad\text{as }t\nearrow T.
\end{equation}
No reparametrizations of $\Sigma$ and no M\"obius transformations of
$\Sph^3$ are required.

More precisely, there are finite nonnegative Radon measures $\mu_T$ on
$\Sigma$ and $\lambda_T=\lVert\Var_T\rVert$ on $\Sph^3$ such that
$\mu_t\to\mu_T$ in total variation and
$\lambda_t\to\lambda_T$ in the bounded-Lipschitz distance
$d_{\BL}$ defined in \eqref{eq:bl-distance}.  Setting
\[
 W_T:=\lim_{t\nearrow T}W(t),
\]
there holds, for every $0<s<T$,
\begin{align}
 
 \lVert\mu_T-\mu_s\rVert_{\TV}
 &\leq \frac{2\sqrt{W_0}}{c_0}
 \sqrt{(T-s)\bigl(W(s)-W_T\bigr)},\\
 
 d_{\BL}(\lambda_T,\lambda_s)
 &\leq \frac{2\sqrt{W_0}}{c_0}
 \sqrt{(T-s)\bigl(W(s)-W_T\bigr)}.
\end{align}
Moreover, $\Var_T$ has generalized Euclidean mean-curvature vector
$H_{\Var_T}^{\R^4}\in L^2(\lVert\Var_T\rVert;\R^4)$ and
\begin{equation}
 
 \frac14\int_{\R^4}|H_{\Var_T}^{\R^4}|^2
 \dd\lVert\Var_T\rVert\leq W_T.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["reflection positivity of the Gibbs measure with respect to lattice reflections","translation invariance, typically verified on a torus with periodic boundary conditions","finite-range or sufficiently decaying interaction with a well-defined quadratic energy function E(k)","dimension d>=3 so the infrared integral of 1/E(k) is finite"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.972375+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3d1b7483c816df0af33429f02689b300652fb53dd58b9e9c714fd05827ae29f6","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For statistical mechanics models on a torus whose Hamiltonian and lattice satisfy reflection positivity across midplanes between sites, the Gaussian domination (infrared) bound gives an upper bound on the Fourier transform of the two-point function: hat{G}(k) <= C / (beta E(k)), where E(k) is the quadratic energy form of the interaction (e.g. E(k)=sum_i (1-cos k_i) for nearest-neighbor coupling) and C is an explicit constant (often 1/2; exact value depends on normalization and is not always recalled precisely across variants). Combined with a spin-wave/Gaussian domination inequality this yields, for models such as the classical Heisenberg or XY model in dimension d>=3, or the Ising model in sufficiently high dimension, existence of long-range order at low temperature via a second-moment argument applied to the infrared-bounded Fourier integral. It does not give critical exponent values, does not apply in dimension d<=2 where the infrared integral diverges (consistent with the Mermin-Wagner theorem ruling out continuous-symmetry breaking there), and requires the specific reflection-positive algebraic structure; it gives no control for models lacking this symmetry, such as many disordered, frustrated, or non-bipartite systems. Typical failure: Assuming reflection positivity survives a seemingly minor modification of the Hamiltonian, such as adding next-nearest-neighbor terms, a random field, or working on a non-bipartite lattice, without re-checking the checkerboard decomposition; reflection positivity is a delicate algebraic property that most natural perturbations destroy, so the infrared bound and everything built on it, including the Frohlich-Simon-Spencer long-range order conclusion, silently stops applying. Canonical reference: Frohlich, Simon and Spencer, 1976, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Frohlich, Israel, Lieb and Simon, 1978, Communications in Mathematical Physics.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.626929+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3d2eccef094bb69e406fac092e701dccd48b74c6119162e597a97768bad97898","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (Omega, F, P) be a probability space with a filtration (F_n)_{n >= 0}, an increasing family of sub-sigma-algebras of F. A sequence (X_n)_{n >= 0} of random variables is a MARTINGALE with respect to (F_n) if (i) X_n is F_n-measurable for every n (adapted), (ii) E|X_n| < infinity for every n (integrable), and (iii) E[X_{n+1} | F_n] = X_n almost surely for every n. It is a SUBMARTINGALE if (iii) is weakened to E[X_{n+1} | F_n] >= X_n almost surely, and a SUPERMARTINGALE if E[X_{n+1} | F_n] <= X_n almost surely. Mnemonic: a supermartingale decreases in expectation, so it is what a gambler faces in an unfair game. All three notions are relative to a specified filtration; a process can be a martingale for its own natural filtration and fail to be one for a larger filtration. Integrability in (ii) is part of the definition, not a consequence: without it the conditional expectation in (iii) need not exist. If (X_n) is a martingale and phi is convex with phi(X_n) integrable for every n, then (phi(X_n)) is a submartingale by conditional Jensen; in particular |X_n| and X_n^2 are submartingales when integrable. [standard; e.g. Williams, Probability with Martingales, Chapter 10]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:16:18.685575+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3d503c6327a83a68e621770de7b4c70c36649a0faac6888735187552b9fc9369","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 11 (Exact matrix isospectrality) of arXiv:2607.26377, '\textbf{Entire Logarithmic Signatures\\ of Bounded-Variation Paths in Finite Dimensions}'] Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space, let $\gamma:[0,T]\to V$ be continuous and of bounded variation, put $g=S(\gamma)$, let $l=\log g=\sum_{n\geq 1}l_n$, and put $v=l_1$.
Assume $R(l)=\infty$.
For every $q\geq1$ and every complex-linear map $\Phi:V_{\C}\to M_q(\C)$, write $I=I_q$ and define
\[
A_{\Phi}(z)=\sum_{n\geq 1}z^n\Phi^{(n)}(l_n).
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
\det(\zeta I-A_{\Phi}(z))
 =\det(\zeta I-z\Phi(v))
\end{equation}
for all $z,\zeta\in\C$.
Thus $A_{\Phi}(z)$ and $z\Phi(v)$ have the same eigenvalue multiset, counted with algebraic multiplicity, and
\[
\tr\bigl(A_{\Phi}(z)^p\bigr)
 =z^p\tr\bigl(\Phi(v)^p\bigr)
\qquad (p\geq1).
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:37:25.962857+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3d5328bdd4ebe6b72b68f980656a4c0448e98ebdec29d3620703043d747138a8","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 9 of arXiv:2608.29713, '\textbf{A Cartan geometry from a correspondence space in Riemannian geometry}'] Let $(p:\mathcal P\to N,\omega)$ be a Cartan geometry of type $(G,H)$, and let $K^\omega=d\omega+\frac12[\omega,\omega]$ be its curvature form.  The torsion of $\omega$ is the $\mathfrak m$-part of its curvature function
$\kappa^\omega$, that is, the map
\[
T^\omega:=\operatorname{pr}_{\mathfrak m}\circ\,\kappa^\omega\colon
\mathcal P\longrightarrow\Lambda^2\mathfrak m^*\otimes\mathfrak m,
\qquad
T^\omega(u)(X,Y)=\operatorname{pr}_{\mathfrak m}\left[K^\omega(u)\big(\omega^{-1}(X)(u),\omega^{-1}(Y)(u)\big)\right].
\]
We say that $\omega$ is normal if $\partial^*T^\omega=0$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:39:12.411917+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3d56675b7ac3f548f6c515c6bf0a4f66919263cf75af1747133e295ecf14107d","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 2. thm: precompactness in sP of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] [{Precompactness in $\mathscr{P}(S)$}]

{"assumptions":["A and B are linear operators in the same Banach space","D(A) ⊂ D(B)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.769951+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, perturbation theory of operators","id":"claim_3e4fa40fff097dc9c86af5298ab723946a61639931a25125440e3ee34a2b916e","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A and B be linear operators in a Banach space X. B is relatively bounded with respect to A (A-bounded) if D(A) ⊂ D(B) and there are constants a, b ≥ 0 with ‖Bx‖ ≤ a‖Ax‖ + b‖x‖ for all x ∈ D(A). The infimum of all admissible a is the A-bound (relative bound) of B; the corresponding b usually grows as a approaches the infimum, and the infimum itself need not be attained. In a Hilbert space the condition ‖Bx‖² ≤ a'²‖Ax‖² + b'²‖x‖² defines the same relative bound. Relative bound 0 means: for every ε > 0 there is b_ε with ‖Bx‖ ≤ ε‖Ax‖ + b_ε‖x‖. If A is closed, B is closable, and D(A) ⊂ D(B), then B is automatically A-bounded (closed graph theorem applied to B on the Banach space (D(A), graph norm of A)). The form analogue: for A ≥ 0 self-adjoint with form q_A(x) = ‖A^{1/2}x‖² on Q(A) = D(A^{1/2}), a symmetric form β is A-form-bounded with bound a if Q(A) ⊂ D(β) and |β(x, x)| ≤ a q_A(x) + b‖x‖² for x ∈ Q(A). Operator-boundedness with bound a implies form-boundedness with bound at most a, not conversely.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.179244+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3e7c028e15ea54077751c874676a322fafb4f9ef09b31515f5992a62c85933b6","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 91 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] We have $\sM^{\IAMP,\sym}(\alpha,0) \subseteq \sM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha,0)$.
\begin{proof} Consider any $\mu \in \cM^{\IAMP,\sym}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)$.
    Then, there exists
    \[
        (q_*,b,\sigma,w,p,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising) \in \Adm^{\IAMP,\sym}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)
    \]
    such that $\mu^{\sym}(q_*,b,\sigma,p,\zeta) = \mu$.
    Let $\tilde p$ denote the restriction of $p$ to $[q_*,1] \subseteq [q_0,1]$.
    Note that $(b,\sigma,w,\tilde p,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising)$ satisfies the assumptions of
    Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-chaotic} with $q_*$ in place of $q_0$.
    Indeed, conditions~\ref{it:1.1}, \ref{it:2.1}, \ref{it:3.1}, \ref{it:4.2}, \ref{it:5.1}, and \ref{it:6.1} provide assumptions~(\ref{i:IAMP-main-coefs}), (\ref{i:IAMP-main-diffusivity}), (\ref{i:IAMP-main-p}), (\ref{i:IAMP-main-budget}), (\ref{i:IAMP-main-endpt}), and (\ref{i:IAMP-main-init}) of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}.

    By Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-chaotic}, there exists $\iota = \iota(\epsilon)$ with $\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0} \iota(\epsilon) = 0$ such that for all (sufficiently large) $N$, there exists a $C(L,\epsilon)$-Lipschitz algorithm $\cA_N$ with
    \[
        \WERR^\sym(\cA_N,\mu)=
        \max\bigg\{
            \bbW_2\Big(\sym(\mu(\cA_N)), \mu\Big),
            \bbW_2\Big(\mu^{\Ising}(\cA_N), \cP(\{\pm 1\})\Big)
        \bigg\}
        \le \iota\,,

    which furthermore satisfies $\chi_{\cA_N}(0) = 0$ and $\chi_{\cA_N}(1-\iota) \le \iota$.
    This implies
    \[
        \cM^{\IAMP,\sym}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon) \subseteq \cM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha,0;C(L,\epsilon),\iota(\epsilon))\,.
    \]
    The rest of the proof is identical to that of Lemma~\ref{l:IAMP.in.Lip}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:18:19.416907+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3eac84abad9b502298a028b9a6f478f1cf091c793852e6752a1d843bffcc747e","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:prelimit_barcode_kernel of arXiv:2507.22011, 'Random Lozenge Waterfall:\\Dimensional Collapse of Gibbs Measures'] Let $L$ be a positive integer.

	\draw[thick] (0,0)--++(1,0)--++(0,1)--++(-1,0)--cycle;

{"assumptions":["Finite d,q; constant SPD H with spectrum in [m,M]","Adapted states, deterministic u0, v0=0; jointly sampled oracle noise centered conditional on the past","Normal conditional covariance <=sigma^2 H; tangential conditional second moment <=sigma^2 D^2 |v|^2","0<rho<2; 0<eta<=rho/M; sigma,D>=0; F in C_b^2","Unbiased gradient oracle; individual random sample-loss gradient representation not asserted","For the proportional-covariance target subclass require normal covariance equality on v=0; proportionality is on the manifold only"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T19:49:38.596602+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_3eb7dc9fd7523a133f226b8bdae7ac45699057680f6ac8b7e79453b8cfe1178d","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Status: proof (unaudited). C006 v1. Novelty unestablished.

Let d,q>=1 be finite, H a constant symmetric positive definite q by q
matrix, and 0<m<=lambda(H)<=M. Fix sigma,D>=0, 0<rho<2 and
0<eta<=rho/M. Let (F_k) be a filtration and (u_k,v_k) adapted, with
deterministic u_0 and v_0=0. At each step let the jointly sampled oracle
noise (xi_k^u,xi_k^v) in R^d x R^q be F_{k+1}-measurable, with

    E[xi_k^u|F_k]=0, E[xi_k^v|F_k]=0,
    E[xi_k^v (xi_k^v)^T|F_k] <= sigma^2 H,
    E[|xi_k^u|^2|F_k] <= sigma^2 D^2 |v_k|^2.           (1)

The matrix inequality is in Loewner order and holds almost surely.
The two noise components may be dependent; their law may depend on the
entire past and on k. No iid, Markov, symmetry or higher-moment hypothesis
is imposed. Consider the unbiased stochastic-gradient oracle recursion
for the population loss L(u,v)=v^T H v/2:

    u_{k+1}=u_k-eta xi_k^u,
    v_{k+1}=B v_k-eta xi_k^v, B=I-eta H.               (2)

Here "oracle" means an unbiased estimator of grad L; this theorem does
not assert that every allowed noise field is the gradient of an individual
random sample loss. The label-gradient models of C005 are included.

For F in C_b^2(R^{d+q}), let f(u)=F(u,0), a(u)=D_v F(u,0), and define

    F_2=sup ||D^2 f||_op,
    F_vv=sup ||D_v^2 F||_op,
    F_uv=sup ||D_u a||_op,
    c=sigma^2 q/(2-rho), gamma=min{m,M(2-rho)/rho}.

Then, for every T>=0,

    sup_{integer 0<=K<=T/eta^2}
      |E F(u_K,v_K)-F(u_0,0)| <= eta C(T),
    C(T)=c[F_vv/2+T sigma^2 D^2 F_2/2+F_uv sigma D/gamma]. (3)

Thus a=1. If, in addition, the normal conditional covariance equals
sigma^2 H on the event v_k=0, then (1) forces xi_k^u=0 there almost
surely. Consequently the full noise covariance on the minimizing
manifold is sigma^2 diag(0,H), proportional to the population Hessian.
That equality is the target-compatible subclass; the estimate itself
uses only domination. No global covariance proportionality is asserted.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X, Y Banach spaces"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:57.492197+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, operator theory","id":"claim_3ecf47d2e1941e3ed3b704c1615dceb455e30d7da6c0085069f13dc22e065c98","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X, Y be Banach spaces. A linear operator K : X → Y is compact if it maps the closed unit ball of X onto a relatively compact subset of Y; equivalently, for every bounded sequence (x_n) in X the sequence (Kx_n) has a norm-convergent subsequence. Compact operators are bounded. They form a norm-closed two-sided ideal in the bounded operators: norm limits of compact operators are compact, and BK and KB are compact whenever K is compact and B is bounded. Every bounded finite-rank operator is compact; in a Hilbert space (and in every Banach space with the approximation property) every compact operator is a norm limit of finite-rank operators. K is compact iff its adjoint K* is compact (Schauder). The identity of an infinite-dimensional space is not compact (Riesz), so on an infinite-dimensional space a compact operator never has a bounded inverse. A compact operator maps weakly convergent sequences to norm-convergent sequences; the converse (complete continuity implies compactness) holds when X is reflexive, e.g. a Hilbert space, but fails in ℓ^1 (Schur property).\n\nExamples: diag(λ_n) on ℓ^2 is compact iff λ_n → 0; integral operators with L^2 kernels (Hilbert–Schmidt operators) are compact; the embedding H^1_0(Ω) → L^2(Ω) for bounded open Ω is compact (Rellich), so the inverse of the Dirichlet Laplacian is a compact self-adjoint operator on L^2(Ω). Non-examples: the shift operators on ℓ^2; multiplication by a function f on L^2[0,1] is compact only when f = 0 a.e.","status":"unverified"}
