{"assumptions":["a_n >= 0 and a_{n+1} <= a_n for all n (eventually monotone suffices, discarding finitely many terms)","a_n -> 0"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:05:27.626008+00:00","domain":"real analysis","id":"claim_3ede50b815234b74f1e55e9ad1f6d4885c71980e05d39b628eeab4be161774f2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (a_n)_{n >= 0} be a nonincreasing sequence of nonnegative reals with a_n -> 0. Then the alternating series S = sum_{n >= 0} (-1)^n a_n converges, and for every N the remainder satisfies |S - S_N| <= a_{N+1}, where S_N = sum_{n=0}^{N} (-1)^n a_n; moreover S lies between any two consecutive partial sums, and S - S_N has the sign of the first omitted term (-1)^{N+1} a_{N+1}. {"assumptions":["Finite state/action MDP; bounded rewards with the stated conditional mean","Fixed target and behavior policies; ergodic behavior state-action chain with positive stationary law","0<gamma<1; eta>0; xi in (0,1)","Feature matrix full column rank with ||X||<C0","Both projections with C1<R1 and R1-xi<R2<R1","Positive deterministic nonincreasing nonsummable square-summable main and target step sequences","Some p>0 with sum(beta_t/alpha_t)^p finite","theta_0 in B1; finite main-network initial vector"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T15:45:20.889958+00:00","domain":"reinforcement learning; two-timescale stochastic approximation","id":"claim_3f07ee78748cf1e9fa6f5abfedb2e5b220908088b1235f80d6a1e385cfd05dcb","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Consider a finite-state finite-action discounted MDP, bounded rewards with conditional mean r(s,a), discount 0<gamma<1, fixed target policy pi, and a fixed behavior policy mu whose state-action chain is ergodic with stationary vector d_mu>0. \[
u_j\colon K\to\mathbb R,

\]
be continuous functions. Let $P_{u_1,\ldots,u_p}(K)\ne\emptyset$ be the set of all

\quad j=1,\ldots,p.

Let
\[

\[
\dim S(\nu)\le p.

Consequently,
\[
\sup_{\mu\in P_{u_1,\ldots,u_p}(K)} \Phi(\nu)
=
\sup_{\substack{\nu\in P_{u_1,\ldots,u_p}(K)\\ \dim S(\nu)\le p}}

\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a compact metric space and T is continuous","the metric enters only through the compact topology"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T02:00:35.438163+00:00","domain":"topological dynamics, entropy","id":"claim_3fe95da80d1756dae2bb8c43b479ad29fb9efff8bf12406c39a668547d7335d9","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $T: X \\to X$ be a continuous map of a compact metric space $(X, d)$. For $n \\ge 1$ define the dynamical metric $d_n(x, y) = \\max_{0 \\le k < n} d(T^k x, T^k y)$. A set $E \\subset X$ is $(n, \\varepsilon)$-separated if $d_n(x, y) > \\varepsilon$ for all distinct $x, y \\in E$; let $s(n, \\varepsilon)$ be the maximal cardinality of such a set (finite by compactness). A set $F$ is $(n, \\varepsilon)$-spanning if every $x \\in X$ has $d_n(x, y) \\le \\varepsilon$ for some $y \\in F$; let $r(n, \\varepsilon)$ be the minimal cardinality. The topological entropy is\n$$h_{top}(T) = \\lim_{\\varepsilon \\to 0} \\limsup_{n \\to \\infty} \\frac{1}{n} \\log s(n, \\varepsilon) = \\lim_{\\varepsilon \\to 0} \\limsup_{n \\to \\infty} \\frac{1}{n} \\log r(n, \\varepsilon) \\in [0, \\infty],$$\nusing $r(n,\\varepsilon) \\le s(n,\\varepsilon) \\le r(n, \\varepsilon/2)$; the limit in $\\varepsilon$ exists by monotonicity, and replacing the $\\limsup$ in $n$ by a $\\liminf$ gives the same value. The value is independent of the compatible metric (this uses compactness) and coincides with the open-cover definition $h_{top}(T) = \\sup_{\\mathcal{U}} \\lim_n \\frac1n \\log N(\\mathcal{U}^n_0)$ where $N$ counts the minimal subcover of the join $\\mathcal{U}^n_0 = \\bigvee_{k<n} T^{-k}\\mathcal{U}$. Basic properties: $h_{top}(T^m) = m\\, h_{top}(T)$ for $m \\ge 1$; $h_{top}(T^{-1}) = h_{top}(T)$ for homeomorphisms; $h_{top}$ is an invariant of topological conjugacy; a Lipschitz map of a compact metric space of finite box dimension has finite entropy, but a continuous map of a compact metric space can have $h_{top} = \\infty$. On a NON-compact space the separated-set quantity depends on the metric, not merely on the topology, and the equalities above can fail.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:52:08.674398+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3ff619da11f26838eeebd63e4e7ab7d17c07daa25e94177b4f2168ecd887ce56","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 42 (Difference equation for two Ricci--DeTurck solutions) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Let \(s(t)\) be a Ricci-flow background and let \(v_0(t)\) and \(v_1(t)\)
be two positive definite solutions of the Ricci--DeTurck equation relative to
\(s(t)\) on the same time interval.  Put
\[
        U=v_1-v_0,
        \qquad v_\vartheta=v_0+\vartheta(v_1-v_0),
        \quad 0\leq\vartheta\leq1,
\]
and assume that every \(v_\vartheta\) is positive definite.  With \(\nabla\)
the connection of \(s(t)\), the difference satisfies a homogeneous linear
system
\begin{equation}
        \partial_tU-P^{pq}\nabla_p\nabla_qU
        =B^p\nabla_pU+CU,
\end{equation}
where the second-order part is diagonal in the tensor components: in a fixed
frame, every component \(U^A\) is acted on by the same operator
\(P^{pq}\nabla_p\nabla_q\), and no second derivative of a different component
occurs.  More precisely, for
\[
        \mathcal Q_s(v)=-2\Ric(v)+\Lie_{W(v,s)}v,
\]
one has the structural formula
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
        \mathcal Q_s(v)
        ={}&v^{pq}\nabla_p\nabla_qv
        +v^{-1}*v^{-1}*\nabla v*\nabla v \\
        &\quad+\mathcal R(\Rm(s),v,v^{-1}),
\end{split}
\end{equation}
and the mean-value identity
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
        \partial_tU
        &=\mathcal Q_s(v_1)-\mathcal Q_s(v_0)\\
        &=\int_0^1D\mathcal Q_s|_{v_\vartheta}[U] \,d\vartheta.
\end{split}
\end{equation}
Differentiating \eqref{eq:rdt-structural-form} gives
\begin{equation}
        D\mathcal Q_s|_{v_\vartheta}[Z]
        =v_\vartheta^{pq}\nabla_p\nabla_qZ
          +\mathcal B_\vartheta^p\nabla_pZ+\mathcal C_\vartheta Z,
\end{equation}
with
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
        \mathcal B_\vartheta
        &=v_\vartheta^{-1}*v_\vartheta^{-1}*\nabla v_\vartheta,\\
        \mathcal C_\vartheta
        &=v_\vartheta^{-1}*v_\vartheta^{-1}*\nabla^2v_\vartheta
          +v_\vartheta^{-1}*v_\vartheta^{-1}*v_\vartheta^{-1}
             *\nabla v_\vartheta*\nabla v_\vartheta\\
        &\qquad+\mathcal R_1(\Rm(s),v_\vartheta,v_\vartheta^{-1}).
\end{split}
\end{equation}
Here \(*\) denotes universal tensor contractions, and \(\mathcal R\) and
\(\mathcal R_1\) are algebraic in the displayed arguments; in particular,
\(\mathcal R_1\) contains no derivatives of \(v_\vartheta\).  The
coefficients in \eqref{eq:rdt-difference-system} are
\[
 P^{pq}=\int_0^1v_\vartheta^{pq}\,d\vartheta,
 \qquad B^p=\int_0^1\mathcal B_\vartheta^p\,d\vartheta,
 \qquad C=\int_0^1\mathcal C_\vartheta\,d\vartheta.
\]
Consequently, uniform metric equivalence and finite-order bounds for
\(v_0,v_1\), and \(s\) give the corresponding ellipticity and H\"older bounds
for \(P,B,C\).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:51.726542+00:00","domain":"dispersive partial differential equations","id":"claim_4035e0f47d8f89385856e3a0fa89ee495b32f2ab6d982252999b8813bc8feedd","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: finite speed of propagation and the domain-of-dependence cone are properties of the wave equation (and of symmetric hyperbolic systems), proved by a local energy identity on the cone. The Schrödinger equation has no such identity and propagates instantaneously. Concrete counterexample: let f ∈ L¹(R^n) be nonzero and compactly supported and let t ≠ 0. By the kernel formula, e^{itΔ}f(x) = (4πit)^{−n/2} e^{i|x|²/(4t)} · G(x/(2t)) where G is the Fourier transform of the compactly supported integrable function y ↦ e^{i|y|²/(4t)}f(y). By the Paley–Wiener theorem G extends to an entire function on C^n, and it is not identically zero, so its zero set contains no nonempty open set. Hence e^{itΔ}f is nonzero almost everywhere on every open subset of R^n at every t ≠ 0: compactly supported data instantly become globally supported. The same phenomenon rules out any cone-shaped domain of dependence, and the heat equation behaves the same way. What survives for Schrödinger are local smoothing, dispersive decay and (pseudo)locality statements about wave packets moving at velocity ≈ 2ξ, not a finite propagation speed; the wave equation's finite-speed argument must never be transplanted to a dispersive or parabolic equation.","status":"unverified"}

\(

\)

sequences of i.i.d. Rademacher random variables. Let
$\{\lambda_r(K)\}_{r\geq1}$ and
$\{\lambda_r(K')\}_{r\geq1}$ denote the nonzero eigenvalues of
$T_K$ and $T_{K'}$, respectively, repeated according to

\[
\begin{pmatrix}
\displaystyle
\frac{1}{2N}

\\[4mm]

\frac{1}{2N}

\end{pmatrix}

\begin{pmatrix}
\displaystyle
\frac12\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}
\lambda_r(K)(X_r^2-1)

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:17:42.312267+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_40871787fc45aea8c87bcfc71952dd37f18724345a7ff0c0c4b0ecef144b6d99","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 20 of arXiv:2608.05931, 'Effective Lagrangian regularity and the uniqueness threshold for random H\"older velocity '] For a function $g : X \to Y$, where $X = \T^d$ or $\R^d$ and $Y$ is a Banach space, we define for $s \geq 0$ the (semi)norm space $\mathcal{C}^s$ as follows. For $s=0$, we let
    \[\|g\|_{\mathcal{C}^0(X) Y} := \sup_{x \in X} \|g(x)\|_Y.\]
    For $s \in (0,\infty)$---letting $s = n + r$ where $r \in (0,1]$ and $n \in \N$---we define $\mathcal{C}^s(X)$ as a seminorm on a subspace of $C^n(X)$ by
    \[\|g\|_{\mathcal{C}^s(X) Y} := \sup_{x,x' \in X, x \ne x'} \frac{\|\nabla^n g(x) - \nabla^ng(x')\|_Y}{|x-x'|^r}.\]
    We note in particular that $\mathcal{C}^1$ is the Lipschitz seminorm and that $\mathcal{C}^0$ is the natural norm on the space of bounded functions---rather than $C^1$ and $C^0$ which have additional qualitative regularity hypotheses that we do not want to require, as we will frequently be working with Lipschitz functions that are not $C^1$.

    We also consider for $p \in [1,\infty), s\geq 0$ the fractional Sobolev (semi)norm spaces $W^{s,p}$. For $s \in \N$, we just let $\|g\|_{W^{s,p}(X)Y} := \|\nabla^s g\|_{L^p(X)Y}$, and for $s>0$ and $s \not \in \N$, we again write $s = n+r$ where $r \in (0,1)$ and $n \in \N$ and define
    \[\|g\|_{W^{s,p}(X) Y} := \Big(\int_X \int_X \frac{\|\nabla^n g(x) - \nabla^n g(x')\|^p_Y}{|x-x'|^{d + rp}}\,dx\,dx'\Big)^{1/p}.\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:57:28.721388+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_40ca71dd6ef3c68ffc4d0f55c284dac5dd8311461393016f2d79d105c2651331","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 3 of arXiv:2609.01190, 'Rough differential equations on manifolds via natural bundles'] Let $m,n,\ell\in\Nsf$, let $U\subseteq\Rsf^m$ be an open convex set, and let $\phi:U\to\Rsf^\ell$ be a smooth function. Let $p\in [1,3)$, let $\omega$ be a control function on interval $[S,T]$, and let $X=(X^\tau)$ be an $n$-dimensional branched rough path on interval $[S,T]$ with regularity $p$ and control $\omega$. Let $Y: [S,T]\to U$ be a continuous curve in $U$ and let $f_\tau^i:U\to\Rsf$ (for $\tau\in\Fcal_n^2$ and $i\in\llbracket 1,m \rrbracket$) be smooth functions. Assume that there exists $C\in (0,\infty)$ such that the inequality 
	\begin{equation}
	
		\bigg| 
			Y^i(t) - Y^i(s) 
			- f_{\ta}^i(Y(s)) X^{\ta}(s,t) 
			- \frac{1}{2} f_{\tab}^i(Y(s)) X^{\tab}(s,t) 
			- f_{\tc}^i(Y(s)) X^{\tc}(s,t) 
		\bigg| 
		\leq C \omega(s,t)^\frac{3}{p}
	\end{equation}
holds for every $i\in\llbracket 1,m \rrbracket$ and $(s,t)\in\Delta[S,T]$. Then there is a constant $\widetilde{C}\in (0,\infty)$ such that 
	\[
		\bigg|
			\phi^i(Y(t)) - \phi^i(Y(s)) 
			- g^i_{\ta}(Y(s))X^{\ta}(s,t) 
			- \frac{1}{2} g^i_{\tab}(Y(s)) X^{\tab}(s,t) 
			- g^i_{\tc}(Y(s))X^{\tc}(s,t) 
		\bigg| 
		\leq \widetilde{C}\omega(s,t)^\frac{3}{p},
	\]
where 
	\[
		g^i_{\ta} := \frac{\partial\phi^i}{\partial y^j}f_{\ta}^j, 
			\quad 
		g_{\tab}^i := \frac{\partial\phi^i}{\partial y^j}f_{\tab}^j + \frac{\partial^2 \phi^i}{\partial y^j\partial y^k} f_{\ta}^jf_{\tb}^k, 
			\quad\mbox{and}\quad  
		g_{\tc}^i := \frac{\partial\phi^i}{\partial y^j}f_{\tc}^j,
	\]
holds for every $i\in \llbracket 1,\ell \rrbracket$ and $(s,t)\in\Delta[S,T]$.","status":"unverified"}

Fix L>0 and eta>0. For each n let X be a deterministic real n by n matrix with operator norm at most L, and w_1,...,w_n independent N(0,I_n) vectors. Put h_j=ReLU(Xw_j), mu=E h_j, z_j=h_j-mu, Phi=E[h_j h_j^T], and Sigma=E[z_j z_j^T]. Let R_j be real symmetric, measurable in X and the columns w_k with k!=j (and optionally auxiliary randomness independent of all feature weights), with operator norm at most 1/eta almost surely. The recorded unaudited derivation gives, for each fixed epsilon>0, P(max_j |z_j^T R_j z_j/n-Tr(Sigma R_j)/n|>epsilon)<=C n exp[-c n min(epsilon^2,epsilon)], with C,c depending only on L,eta. The centering step uses the exact identity z^T R z-Tr(Sigma R)=h^T R h-Tr(Phi R)-2 mu^T R(h-mu) for deterministic symmetric R. Louart-Liao-Couillet quadratic-form concentration controls the raw term. Gaussian Lipschitz concentration controls the mean correction. Indeed mu_i=||x_i||/sqrt(2 pi), ||mu||^2<=n L^2/(2 pi), and w->mu^T R ReLU(Xw) is Lipschitz with constant at most sqrt(n/(2 pi))*L^2/eta. Condition on all columns except j before applying those bounds; integrate and take a union bound, without asserting independence between deviation events. Thus the method allows correlations among coordinates within each feature column, but R_j must exclude the tested column. For X=I and eta=1, taking the same-column R=zz^T/||z||^2 makes z^T R z/n tend to kappa=1/2-1/(2 pi)>0 while Tr(Sigma R)/n=kappa/n, illustrating failure if this independence hypothesis is removed. For random X independent of all w_j with tight operator norm, conditioning first on ||X||<=L and then letting L grow gives convergence in probability, rather than a uniform unconditional exponential rate. This is a fixed-positive-ridge concentration ingredient; it supplies neither an edge law nor a justification for a ridge tending to zero. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:47:22.245900+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_414774552018474bc5ee76321ba5e7b66cb73ff5fb105f49125c1862c38a7ec9","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 19 of arXiv:2605.26664, 'Mixing times for Glauber dynamics of lozenge tilings of the hexagon'] [Liquid and frozen region, arctic boundary]
  Given any open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$, we call a function $F : \overline{\Omega} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ \emph{admissible} if $F$ is $1$-Lipschitz and satisfies $\nabla F (z) \in \overline{\mathcal{T}}$ for Lebesgue almost every $z \in \Omega$. Let $\Adm (\Omega)$ denote the set of admissible functions $F : \overline{\Omega} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ and, for any function $f : \partial \Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, let $\Adm (\Omega; f)$ denote the set of $F \in \Adm (\Omega)$ satisfying $F |_{\partial \Omega} = f$.  Define the \emph{liquid region} $\mathfrak{L}_F \subseteq \Omega$ associated with an admissible height function $F \in \Adm (\Omega)$ by 
         \begin{flalign*}
         	\mathfrak{L}_F = \big\{ z \in \Omega : \nabla F(z) \in \mathcal{T} \big\},
         \end{flalign*}
         where the condition $\nabla F(z) \in \mathcal{T}$ in particular implies that $\nabla F(z)$ exists.

         In particular, we define the liquid region of $\cH_{q;a,b,c}$ as
         \[\mL_{q;a,b,c}:=\mL_{\cH_{q;a,b,c}}.\] The  boundary
        $\mathfrak A_{q;a,b,c}:=\partial\mL_{q;a,b,c}$ is called the
        \emph{arctic boundary} and the interior of
        $\mX_{a,b,c}\setminus\mL_{q;a,b,c}$ is called the \emph{frozen
        region}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-12T07:22:43.761193+00:00","domain":"graph theory","id":"claim_41f1607fe0ca61747b32e0ca370c278bba715b149e9ab306a7f07d7712059878","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A graph G = (V, E) is a finite set V of vertices together with a set E of edges, each an unordered pair of vertices; G is simple if it has no loops or repeated edges. {"assumptions":["X and Y are Banach spaces","T is linear on a linear subspace D(T) of X"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.769166+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, unbounded operators","id":"claim_41fdcf41b301c72abeac970dc8d13d7e8412473ffc482e2582494edf964e1f49","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X, Y be Banach spaces and T: D(T) ⊂ X → Y a linear operator defined on a linear subspace D(T). Its graph is G(T) = {(x, Tx) : x ∈ D(T)} ⊂ X × Y. T is closed if G(T) is closed in X × Y; equivalently, whenever x_n ∈ D(T), x_n → x in X and Tx_n → y in Y, then x ∈ D(T) and Tx = y. Equivalently, D(T) is complete under the graph norm ‖x‖_T = ‖x‖ + ‖Tx‖. S is an extension of T (written T ⊂ S) if D(T) ⊂ D(S) and Sx = Tx for x ∈ D(T). T is closable if it has a closed extension; equivalently, x_n ∈ D(T), x_n → 0 and Tx_n → y imply y = 0; equivalently, the closure of G(T) is the graph of an operator, called the closure T̄ (the smallest closed extension). If T is closed, a subspace D_0 ⊂ D(T) is a core for T if D_0 is dense in D(T) for the graph norm, i.e. the closure of T restricted to D_0 equals T. A closed operator need not be bounded, and being closed says nothing about D(T) being dense; by the closed graph theorem a closed operator with D(T) = X is bounded.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.349563+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4227cc72423df9e86220706666cf0c5942ecb93c47543ebc0343a142107821ab","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 171 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let indices $a(q_d),a^\frozen(q_d)$

For $N$ large enough, we have
	\[\max_{\sigma\in\{\RomII,\RomIII\}}
	\E\bigg[

{"assumptions":["X a normed space; no completeness of X is needed","for metrizability and sequential compactness of the ball: X separable","Tychonoff (hence a form of the axiom of choice) in the general case"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T15:38:23.784925+00:00","domain":"functional analysis","id":"claim_424daabf6bab4c23b100ce5671977a4d","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a normed vector space over R or C. The closed unit ball B of the dual space X^* is COMPACT in the weak-* topology, that is the topology of pointwise convergence on X. Two refinements matter. (a) If X is SEPARABLE then the weak-* topology restricted to B is metrizable and B is weak-* SEQUENTIALLY compact, so bounded sequences of functionals have weak-* convergent subsequences; without separability compactness need not give sequential compactness. (b) The general theorem uses Tychonoff's theorem for a product of compact scalar discs and therefore, in ZF, is not provable without some choice; the separable case needs only a diagonal argument. The theorem does NOT say the ball is norm-compact: by Riesz's lemma the closed unit ball of a normed space is norm-compact if and only if the space is finite-dimensional. Nor does it say the ball of X itself is weakly compact - that characterises reflexivity (Kakutani). [standard; e.g. Rudin, Functional Analysis, 2nd ed., Theorem 3.15]\n\nFor every neighborhood U of 0 in X, its polar U^circ = {phi in X^*: |phi(u)| <= 1 for every u in U} is weak-* compact. Here X^* is the continuous dual and the weak-* topology is pointwise convergence on X; neither completeness nor separability of X is needed.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X_n => X in distribution","Y_n -> c in probability with c a CONSTANT (not a random variable)","for the quotient: c != 0"],"created_at":"2026-10-07T01:09:09+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_42d5d8144efc7c7815ae88f7a13799ed","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_n converge in distribution to a real random variable X and let Y_n converge in probability to a real constant c. Then (X_n,Y_n) converges jointly in distribution to (X,c). Consequently X_n+Y_n converges in distribution to X+c, X_n Y_n converges in distribution to cX, and, if c!=0, X_n/Y_n converges in distribution to X/c. For the quotient, define its value arbitrarily on {Y_n=0} when necessary; that event has probability tending to zero. Convergence Y_n=>c in distribution is equivalent to convergence Y_n->c in probability, so either hypothesis gives the same conclusion for a constant target. With a nonconstant target, separate marginal convergence alone does not identify the joint limit: if X is a nondegenerate symmetric random variable, X_n=X and Y_n=-X, then both marginal laws converge to the law of X, but X_n+Y_n=0 does not converge to the law of 2X. A random second limit is allowed when joint convergence (X_n,Y_n)=>(X,Y) is supplied; the continuous mapping theorem then gives the corresponding sum and product limits, and the quotient limit if P(Y=0)=0. [Re-derived local source, M9; textbook cross-reference: van der Vaart, Asymptotic Statistics, Theorem 2.8.]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["i.i.d. rows C^{1/2} z with z having i.i.d. mean-zero unit-variance entries and finite twelfth moment","p/n -> q_0 in (0, infinity)","the population spectral distribution converges to a limit with bounded support","the formula is used inside the bulk; isolated spikes are handled by the BBP correction"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T15:09:50+00:00","domain":"random matrix theory","id":"claim_4371e12019521ab578f7c0a985513fd3b35fa6f43b024c62adc7360470e48a4a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $E = \\frac{1}{n} X^T X$ be the sample covariance of $n$ i.i.d. rows in $\\mathbb{R}^p$ with population covariance $C$ (rows $C^{1/2} z_i$ with $z_i$ having i.i.d. entries of mean zero, variance one and finite twelfth moment), in the regime $p, n \\to \\infty$ with $q = p/n \\to q_0 \\in (0, \\infty)$, and assume the spectral distribution of $C$ converges to a limit with bounded support. Let $\\lambda_k, u_k$ be the sample eigenvalues and eigenvectors and let $g_E(z) = \\frac{1}{p}\\operatorname{tr}(z I - E)^{-1}$ be the Stieltjes transform of the sample spectrum, and $g(z) = \\int (z - x)^{-1} F(dx)$ that of its almost-sure limit $F$, the limiting sample spectral distribution, with $g(\\lambda - i0) := \\lim_{\\eta \\downarrow 0} g(\\lambda - i\\eta)$ inside the bulk (the finite-sample $g_E(\\lambda - i\\eta)$ has no useful limit as $\\eta \\downarrow 0$: it diverges at each sample eigenvalue and is real between them). THEOREM (Ledoit and Peche, 2011, Theorem 4; in the form of Bun, Bouchaud and Potters 2017). The oracle eigenvalues $\\xi_k^{\\mathrm{or}} = u_k^T C u_k$, as the weighted measure $\\frac{1}{p}\\sum_k \\xi_k^{\\mathrm{or}} \\delta_{\\lambda_k}$, converge almost surely to $\\xi(\\lambda) F(d\\lambda)$ on $(0, \\infty)$, where $$\\xi(\\lambda) = \\frac{\\lambda}{\\big|\\, 1 - q_0 + q_0\\, \\lambda\\, g(\\lambda - i0) \\,\\big|^2};$$ informally $\\xi_k^{\\mathrm{or}} \\approx \\xi(\\lambda_k)$ for sample eigenvalues inside the bulk (the theorem is about the weighted measure, not a limit for each $k$). This limit depends on the population covariance $C$ only through the observable sample spectrum, so it is a consistent, computable estimator (the rotationally invariant estimator, RIE, or nonlinear shrinkage): replace each sample eigenvalue by $\\xi(\\lambda_k)$, keep the sample eigenvectors. In practice $g_E$ is evaluated at $\\lambda_k - i\\eta$ with a small $\\eta$ of order $n^{-1/2}$ times the eigenvalue scale, and the result is floored at a small positive fraction of the bulk level. When $C = \\sigma^2 I$ the formula returns $\\sigma^2$ for every eigenvalue (the Marchenko-Pastur spread is entirely removed); for a spike above the bulk it returns approximately the debiased population spike. Applying the formula to a matrix whose largest eigenvalue is a signal one is trying to keep, and flooring relative to that top eigenvalue, destroys the small eigenvalues that the inverse depends on.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["alpha,rho,lambda are fixed strictly positive real numbers","M_N=floor(exp(alpha N)); the energies within each N are independent N(0,rho^2/N)","All arrays are on a common probability space; arbitrary dependence across different N is permitted","For the pattern interpretation, x_N has norm rho sqrt(N) and is independent of every competing Gaussian pattern"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T15:33:41.510256+00:00","domain":"random energy model; REM; Derrida; Gaussian noise; quenched free energy; condensation threshold; dense associative memory","id":"claim_4498555a06d1cc33d3838c2b27ffe673f5b4cd6f3617e875afcf85b094a712bb","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Fix alpha>0, rho>0 and lambda>0, all independent of the positive integer N. For each N let M_N=floor(exp(alpha N)), and let epsilon_(1,N),...,epsilon_(M_N,N) be independent centered Gaussian variables, each of variance rho^2/N. Define phi_N=(1/(lambda N)) log(sum_(mu=1)^(M_N) exp(lambda N epsilon_(mu,N))). On any common probability space for these arrays, phi_N converges almost surely to alpha/lambda+lambda rho^2/2 when lambda<=lambda_c=sqrt(2alpha)/rho, and to rho sqrt(2alpha) when lambda>=lambda_c. The two expressions agree at lambda_c. Independence is required within each N; no independence across different N is needed. Equivalently, for independent Gaussian patterns xi_mu~N(0,I_N) and a state x_N of norm rho sqrt(N), chosen independently of these patterns, one may take epsilon_(mu,N)=<x_N,xi_mu>/N. The result applies to that fixed state or independently chosen state sequence. It does not assert a uniform limit over pattern-dependent states or along an adaptive retrieval trajectory. This is the classical Gaussian random energy model condensation formula, used as a noise free-energy computation, not a retrieval or basin theorem. {"assumptions":["the perturbation K is compact","lambda is a nonzero scalar","the ambient space is a Banach space (Hilbert space for the adjoint form with conjugated lambda)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.573224+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, Fredholm theory","id":"claim_44c2b247a9f29b24f5479cb03b211daeeab0cd1b96adb5f6a3837b72135ca330","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The alternative 'injective implies surjective' for operators of the form lambda I - K is carried entirely by two hypotheses: K is compact, and lambda is nonzero. (1) Compactness is load-bearing. On l^2 the unilateral shift S(x_1, x_2, ...) = (0, x_1, x_2, ...) is bounded and injective but not surjective, and S = I - K with K = I - S bounded but not compact; its index is -1, not 0. So for a general bounded perturbation of the identity the two alternatives can both fail to be the right dichotomy: the equation x - K x = y can be uniquely solvable for some y and unsolvable for others, with no finite-dimensional solvability condition of equal dimensions on the two sides. What actually powers the alternative is that the index is 0, which compactness guarantees; a Fredholm operator of nonzero index (like S) is a counterexample to the dichotomy but not to Fredholm theory. (2) lambda nonzero is load-bearing. Take K = diag(1, 1/2, 1/3, ...) on l^2, which is compact and injective, with dense but proper range (the sequence (1/n) is not in ran K, since it would need preimage (1, 1, 1, ...)). So for lambda = 0, 'injective' does not give 'surjective', the range is not closed, and 0 is in the spectrum of every compact operator on an infinite-dimensional space. (3) In the Hilbert-space version the solvability condition uses the conjugate: lambda x - K x = y is solvable exactly when y is orthogonal to ker(conjugate of lambda times I - K*), not to ker(lambda I - K*); forgetting the conjugation is a common slip for complex lambda. (4) The dimension identity dim ker(lambda - K) = dim ker(lambda - K') is an identity of the two kernels, not a claim that the kernels correspond naturally, and it fails for non-compact perturbations (for S, ker S = 0 while ker S' is one-dimensional).","status":"unverified"}

For a class C of subsets of X and points x_1, ..., x_n, the number of distinct traces |{ A intersect {x_1, ..., x_n} : A in C }| is at most 2^n; the growth (shatter) function is s(C, n) = max over all n-point sets of this number; the VC dimension d = VC(C) is the largest n with s(C, n) = 2^n (infinite if s(C, n) = 2^n for all n). Sauer-Shelah: if d < infinity then s(C, n) <= sum_{i <= d} binom(n, i) <= (e n / d)^d for n >= d. THEOREM (Vapnik and Chervonenkis, 1971). Let X_1, ..., X_n be i.i.d. from P and P_n the empirical measure. For every eps > 0 and n >= 2 / eps^2, P( sup_{A in C} |P_n(A) - P(A)| > eps ) <= 4 s(C, 2n) exp( -n eps^2 / 8 ); a form valid for all n is P( sup_{A in C} |P_n(A) - P(A)| > eps ) <= 8 s(C, n) exp( -n eps^2 / 32 ). COROLLARIES. If VC(C) = d < infinity, then sup_A |P_n(A) - P(A)| -> 0 almost surely for EVERY P (C is a uniform Glivenko-Cantelli class), with E sup_A |P_n(A) - P(A)| <= C_0 sqrt(d / n) for an absolute constant C_0 (Talagrand's sharpening of the log-free bound); the sample size n = O( (d log(1/eps) + log(1/delta)) / eps^2 ) makes the sup at most eps with probability 1 - delta; and the condition is also necessary: if VC(C) = infinity there is a distribution P for which the sup does not converge to 0 in probability (Vapnik-Chervonenkis; Assouad; Dudley). In learning: for a class of classifiers of VC dimension d, every classifier's true error is within eps of its training error simultaneously once n is of order d / eps^2 (up to logarithms), so empirical risk minimisation is consistent exactly for finite VC dimension (the fundamental theorem of statistical learning, PAC learnability iff finite VC dimension).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["A measurable, uniformly parabolic with constants lambda, Lambda; divergence form","u >= 0 and a local weak solution on the whole cylinder B_{2r} x (t_0 - 4r^2, t_0)","the two cylinders are separated in time, with Q^- earlier than Q^+"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:49.106483+00:00","domain":"parabolic partial differential equations / Harnack inequalities","id":"claim_44dbfa0199ed26c36b75aa732eeca6cc025e4e1a57803299d2f6b3708baf81ca","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $A$ be measurable and uniformly parabolic with constants $\\lambda,\\Lambda$ and let $u\\ge0$ be a local weak solution of $\\partial_tu=\\mathrm{div}(A\\nabla u)$ in $B_{2r}(x_0)\\times(t_0-4r^2,t_0)$. Set $Q^-=B_r(x_0)\\times(t_0-3r^2,t_0-2r^2)$ and $Q^+=B_r(x_0)\\times(t_0-r^2,t_0)$. Then $\\sup_{Q^-}u\\ \\le\\ C\\,\\inf_{Q^+}u$ with $C=C(n,\\lambda,\\Lambda)$. The time lag is essential and so is the direction: the past cylinder's supremum is controlled by the future cylinder's infimum, never the reverse, and no inequality of this form holds on a single time slice. Nonnegativity on the whole cylinder $B_{2r}\\times(t_0-4r^2,t_0)$ is required. Consequences: interior Holder continuity of solutions, the near-diagonal lower bound for the fundamental solution, and (through chaining) Aronson's Gaussian lower bound; the inequality is equivalent to the conjunction of the volume doubling property and a Poincare inequality in the Grigor'yan-Saloff-Coste characterization on manifolds and graphs.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:58:49.164270+00:00","domain":"functional analysis","id":"claim_44eebfa67f00c602e0e7fbbc83a9b119a28016877ee79d496a128f66be871a6f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let 1 <= p < infinity and let Omega be a bounded connected open subset of R^n with Lipschitz boundary. Poincare-Wirtinger form: there is a constant C depending only on p and Omega such that ||u - u_Omega||_{L^p(Omega)} <= C ||grad u||_{L^p(Omega)} for every u in W^{1,p}(Omega), where u_Omega denotes the average of u over Omega. Zero-boundary form: for u in W_0^{1,p}(Omega), with Omega merely bounded in one direction, ||u||_{L^p(Omega)} <= C ||grad u||_{L^p(Omega)}, so the gradient term alone is an equivalent norm on W_0^{1,p}(Omega). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:51:30.076170+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4527e58724eb5ad3a0b5956fdb92b0df82b829e9a4270dbdd40f6f94392f0fab","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 21 of arXiv:2606.02036, 'Self-intersection local times for Volterra Gaussian processes in stochastic flows with int'] A family of random maps $\{\phi_{s,t}:\mbR^d\times\Omega\to\mbR^d,\ 0\leqslant s\leqslant t<\infty\}$ is called a stochastic flow of homeomorphisms if for $\prob$-almost all $\omega\in\Omega:$

 \item $\phi_{s,t}(\omega)=\phi_{r,t}(\omega)\circ\phi_{s,r,}(\omega)\ \text{holds for all}\ s\leqslant r\leqslant t.$

 \end{enumerate}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-23T07:57:26.273086+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_453cdc3caad94d439041d887f802b242","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In information theory, the entropy of a random variable quantifies the average level of uncertainty or information associated with the variable's potential states or possible outcomes. This measures the expected amount of information needed to describe the state of the variable, considering the distribution of probabilities across all potential states. Given a discrete random variable $X$, which may be any member $x$ within the set ${\\mathcal {X}}$ and is distributed according to $p\\colon {\\mathcal {X}}\\to [0,1]$, the entropy is $\\mathrm {H} (X):=-\\sum _{x\\in {\\mathcal {X}}}p(x)\\log p(x),$ where $\\Sigma$ denotes the sum over the variable's possible values. The choice of base for $\\log$, the logarithm, varies for different applications. Base 2 gives the unit of bits (or \"shannons\"), while base e gives \"natural units\" nat, and base 10 gives units of \"dits\", \"bans\", or \"hartleys\". An equivalent definition of entropy is the expected value of the self-information of a variable.","status":"unverified"}

\[\|B\|^2_{L_2(U,H)}\le\frac{1}{4}\lambda\nu^3 c_0^2,\]

Then the Markovian Feller semigroup $(P_t)_{t\ge 0}$ of the stochastic incompressible 2D Navier-Stokes equations~(equation eq:2DNSE of the paper) with degenerate additive Wiener noise possesses a unique invariant measure $\mu_\ast$ with second moments in $V$.

Then q is the SMALLEST root in [0,1] of the equation f(s) = s, and: if m < 1 (subcritical) then q = 1; if m = 1 (critical) then q = 1 UNLESS p_1 = 1, in which case the process is deterministic and never dies; if m > 1 (supercritical) then q < 1. The critical case is the one that gets misquoted: a critical branching process dies out almost surely even though E[Z_n] = 1 for every n, so the population is not uniformly integrable and the mean survives while the process does not. Excluding the degenerate p_1 = 1 is necessary. A second standard trap: q < 1 does not mean the process survives with probability 1 - it survives with probability exactly 1 - q, and conditioned on survival Z_n grows geometrically at rate m. [standard; e.g. Athreya and Ney, Branching Processes, Chapter I, or Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Section 4.3.3]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["H a real or complex Hilbert space; X a normed space for the general remarks"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:57.492120+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, weak topologies","id":"claim_46001c947b4cab76c499d85088d68c6f5587b6afdebff362beafde43fb023003","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"In a Hilbert space H a sequence (x_n) converges weakly to x, written x_n ⇀ x, if ⟨x_n, y⟩ → ⟨x, y⟩ for every y ∈ H; by the Riesz representation theorem this is convergence against every bounded linear functional. The weak topology on H is the coarsest topology making every functional x ↦ ⟨x, y⟩ continuous. Norm convergence implies weak convergence; the converse fails in infinite dimensions (an orthonormal sequence e_n converges weakly to 0 while ||e_n|| = 1). Weak limits are unique; weakly convergent sequences are norm-bounded (Banach–Steinhaus); the norm is weakly lower semicontinuous (||x|| ≤ liminf ||x_n|| when x_n ⇀ x); norm-closed convex sets are weakly closed (Mazur), and in infinite dimensions the weak closure of the unit sphere is the closed unit ball. If x_n ⇀ x and ||x_n|| → ||x|| then x_n → x in norm (Radon–Riesz property of Hilbert spaces). Bounded operators preserve weak convergence; compact operators turn weak convergence into norm convergence.\n\nIn a general normed space X the weak topology is the coarsest topology making every f ∈ X* continuous, and the weak-* topology on X* is the coarsest making every evaluation f ↦ f(x), x ∈ X, continuous. The weak-* topology on X* is in general coarser than the weak topology of X* (which is induced by X**); the two coincide when X is reflexive. In a Hilbert space, after identifying H* with H, weak and weak-* convergence are the same notion.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:52:08.674798+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_46721de49b735f82f6a6bb879f2e793467e77ac0d3aee9e7e16d9f0b3761dd8a","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 45 (Local one-derivative gain for Ricci--DeTurck systems) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Fix an integer \(k\geq2\) and \(\sigma\in(0,1)\).  Let \(Q\) and \(Q'\) be
concentric coordinate cylinders in a fixed spatial chart, with \(Q'\) having
smaller spatial radius and a positive time gap from the lower time face of
\(Q\); the two cylinders may share their upper time face.  Let \(r(t)\) be a
smooth reference metric on \(Q\), and let \(q(t)\) be a smooth positive
definite solution of the Ricci--DeTurck equation relative to \(r(t)\).  In a
fixed tensor frame this equation has the scalar-principal form
\begin{equation}
 \partial_tq^A-q^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jq^A
 =\mathcal F^A\bigl(x,t,q,q^{-1},\partial q;
                 r,\partial r,\partial^2r\bigr),
\end{equation}
where \(\mathcal F\) is a universal smooth expression and contains no second
spatial derivatives of \(q\).  Suppose, in the fixed coordinates, that
\[
 \lambda I\leq(q_{ij})\leq\Lambda I,
 \qquad
 \|q\|_{C^{k+\sigma,(k+\sigma)/2}(Q)}
 +\|r\|_{C^{k+1+\sigma,(k+1+\sigma)/2}(Q)}\leq A.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \|q\|_{C^{k+1+\sigma,(k+1+\sigma)/2}(Q')}
 \leq C,
\end{equation}
where \(C\) depends only on the displayed bounds, the rank and dimension, and
the fixed spatial and lower-time separations between \(Q'\) and \(Q\).
Consequently, the estimate is uniform in any bounded-geometry atlas with fixed
nested-cylinder ratios.","status":"unverified"}

Fix \(A,\sigma_0>0\) and \(R\in(0,\infty]\).

  \begin{enumerate}
    \item A function \(B:\overline{\mathbb B}_A\times \mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{S}}\times (0,\sigma_0]\to\mathbb
    R\) belongs to \(\mathfrak B_\ell\) if its pullback \( B(a,\varphi (\theta),\sigma)\) is
    \(C^\ell\) in \((a,\theta, \sigma)\) and, for every \(\gamma\) with \(|\gamma| \leqslant \ell\),
    \begin{equation*}
      \sup_{{\mathcal D}_{A,\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{S}},\sigma_0}} \bigl| \partial_{a,\theta,\sigma}^{\gamma}
      B(a,\varphi(\theta),\sigma) \bigr|<\infty.
    \end{equation*}

    \item A function \(E:\overline{\mathbb B}_A \times\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{S}}\times (0,\sigma_0]\to\mathbb
    R\) belongs to \(\mathfrak E_\ell^\omega\) if its pullback \( E(a, \varphi (\theta),\sigma)\) is
    \(C^\ell\) in \((a, \theta, \sigma)\), and there exists \(c>0\) such that, for every \(\gamma\)
    with \(|\gamma|\leqslant\ell\), there is a constant \(C_\gamma>0\) satisfying
    \begin{equation*}
      \bigl|\partial_{a,\theta,\sigma}^{ \gamma} E(a,\varphi(\theta),\sigma) \bigr|
      \leqslant C_\gamma e^{-c/\sigma^{\omega}},\quad
      \forall (a,\varphi(\theta),\sigma)\in {\mathcal D}_{A,\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{S}}, \sigma_0}.
    \end{equation*}

    \item A function \(P: \mathcal D_{R, A, \mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{S}}, \sigma_0} \to\mathbb R\) belongs to
    \(\mathfrak P_\ell \) if it is measurable in \(\zeta\) and its pullback
    \(P(\zeta;a,\varphi(\theta),\sigma)\) is \(C^\ell\) in the
    parameter variables \((a,\theta, \sigma)\), for every fixed \(\zeta\), and there exists
    \(n\geqslant 0\) such that
    \begin{equation*}
      \bigl| \partial_{a,\theta,\sigma}^{\gamma} P(\zeta; a,\varphi(\theta),\sigma) \bigr|
      \leqslant C_\gamma \bigl(1 + \|\zeta\|^n\bigr)
    \end{equation*}
    for every \(\gamma\) with \(|\gamma|\leqslant\ell\), uniformly on \(\mathcal D_{R, A,
    \mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{S}}, \sigma_0} \).

    \item A function \(G: \mathcal D_{R, A,\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{S}}, \sigma_0} \to\mathbb R\) belongs to
    \(\mathfrak G_\ell\) if it is measurable in \(\zeta\) and its pullback
    \(G(\zeta;a,\varphi(\theta),\sigma)\) is \(C^\ell\) in the
    parameter variables \((a,\theta,\sigma) \), for every fixed \(\zeta\), and there exist \(c_0>0,
    n\geqslant 0\) such that
    \begin{equation*}
      \bigl| \partial_{a,\theta,\sigma}^{\gamma} G(\zeta;a,\varphi(\theta),\sigma) \bigr|
      \leqslant C_\gamma\bigl(1+\|\zeta\|^n\bigr)\Gamma_{c_0}(\zeta;a)
    \end{equation*}
    for every \(\gamma\) with \(|\gamma|\leqslant\ell\), uniformly on \({\mathcal
    D}_{R,A,\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{S}},\sigma_0}\).
  \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:07:35.023126+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_470563666c43e815c543f1b6933b2a06a328112f8ece79973a7b6369423d7206","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 3 of arXiv:2609.02879, 'On the cut locus of Hamilton--Jacobi equations I: structure and propagation via the touchi'] Let \( \Omega \subset \R^n \) be an open convex subset and $\phi\in\text{\rm SCL}\,(\Omega)$.

		\]

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:54:53.448922+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_47287f87e721bff4b685bf2abd0ba02ebf431dad6a65e37235c7ff6e1a2bf8db","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 12 (Block stratification) of arXiv:2606.16005, '\bfseries An Algebraic Matrix Spencer Theorem'] Let
\[
H=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\mathcal B}H_\alpha
\]
be a fixed common block decomposition, and write $b_\alpha:=\dim H_\alpha .$ A \emph{block stratification} is a partition
\[
\mathcal B=\mathcal P_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup \mathcal P_J
\]
of the block index set into nonempty groups, called strata. For a stratum $\mathcal P_j$, define
\[
\cH_{\mathcal P_j}:=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\mathcal P_j}\cH_\alpha,
\qquad
h_j:=\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal P_j} b_\alpha,
\qquad
m_j:=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal P_j} b_\alpha,
\]
and $q_j:=h_jm_j$. The total stratified block complexity is $Q(\mathcal P):=\sum_{j=1}^J q_j= \sum_{j=1}^J h_jm_j$.

We also write
\[
\cH_{\max}:=\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal B}b_\alpha,
\qquad
M:=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal B}b_\alpha,
\]
for the largest block size and total ambient dimension of the compressed block system.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.166483+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_478a1bb27d1aaedfc6391e6abf27228a54f343f81889aff4908cd268ecc37ea2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 48 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Suppose $J_+ \neq \emptyset$, and define
    \begin{align}
        
        \Delta_+(\vartheta) 
        &\equiv \vartheta + \gamma_+(z_\star) - \gamma_+(\beta_\star(\gamma_\star + \vartheta))
        \,,\\
        
        \Delta_-(\vartheta) 
        &\equiv \vartheta + \gamma_+(\beta_\star(\gamma_\star - \vartheta)) - \gamma_+(z_\star)\,.
    \end{align}
These functions are continuous and strictly increasing on the intervals $[0,+\infty)$ and $[0,\vartheta_{-,\max})$ respectively, where in the latter case we define
    \[
        \vartheta_{-,\max} \equiv \sup\lt\{
            \vartheta \ge 0 : \beta_\star(\gamma_\star - \vartheta) > z_0
        \rt\}\,.
    \]
    Furthermore, $\Delta_+(0) = \Delta_-(0) = 0$ and 
    \beq
        
        \lim_{\vartheta \uparrow +\infty} \Delta_+(\vartheta)
        = \lim_{\vartheta \uparrow \vartheta_{-,\max}} \Delta_-(\vartheta)
        = +\infty\,.
    \eeq
    In particular, for any $\delta > 0$, there exist (unique) solutions $\vartheta_+ \in (0,+\infty)$, $\vartheta_- \in (0,\vartheta_{-,\max})$ to the equations
    \beq
        
        \Delta_+(\vartheta_+) = \Delta_-(\vartheta_-) = \delta\,.
    \eeq
\begin{proof}
    Since $J_+ \neq \emptyset$, we have $\hv_1 > 0$ and $z_0 = m^{-1}(\alpha / \hv_1)$, and thus case \eqref{i:fp-case2} or \eqref{i:fp-case3} of Remark~\ref{r:fp.cases} holds. In either case, we have $z_\star > z_0$. Note that $\gamma_+$ is strictly decreasing for $z > z_0$. Since $\beta_\star(\gamma_\star) = z_\star$, we have $\Delta_+(0) = \Delta_-(0) = 0$.
Recall that $\beta_\star$ is nondecreasing by Lemma~\ref{l:fp-g2}\eqref{i:fp-beta-incr}; it follows that $\beta_\star(\gamma_\star - \vartheta) > z_0$ for all $\vartheta \in [0,\vartheta_{-,\max})$. Moreover, $\beta_\star$ is continuous, so $\Delta_+$ and $\Delta_-$ are continuous and strictly increasing on their respective domains. It remains to verify \eqref{e:fp-vartheta-limit}.
Since $\Delta_+(\vartheta)\ge\vartheta$, it is clear the limit involving $\Delta_+$ is $+\infty$.
Similarly, since $\Delta_-(\vartheta)\ge\vartheta$, 
 the limit involving $\Delta_-$ is also clearly $+\infty$ in the case $\vartheta_{-,\max} = +\infty$.
    Otherwise, we must have $\beta_\star(\gamma_\star - \vartheta) \downarrow z_0$ as $\vartheta \uparrow \vartheta_{-,\max}$, so $\gamma_+(\beta_\star(\gamma_\star - \vartheta)) \uparrow +\infty$.
    This proves \eqref{e:fp-vartheta-limit}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

Method: Identify what makes q = 1 and q = 2 expandable and whether a q-analogue of the random-current switching lemma exists. Result: q = 1 is Bernoulli percolation (independence gives the pivotal decomposition); q = 2 is expandable through the random-current representation and the switching lemma (Sakai's lace expansion for the Ising model). For integer q >= 3 the Potts model has a random-current-like representation (the 'random-current representation for Potts' via the Edwards-Sokal coupling with q colours) but the switching lemma fails because currents are Z_q-valued and the pairing structure that gives the switching identity is specific to Z_2. A lace expansion needs a 'pivotal' notion for which the model factorises across the pivotal: in FK with general q the cluster weight q^{k(omega)} couples the two sides of a pivotal edge only through the count of clusters, which changes by one when the pivotal is closed; this suggests an expansion in which each pivotal carries a factor q or 1 depending on whether closing it splits a cluster, i.e. a lace expansion for the two-point function with the cluster count as an extra variable, which is exactly the generating function in the number of clusters, i.e. the Tutte polynomial. So the expansion would be an expansion of the Tutte polynomial's two-point version, which is #P-hard to evaluate in general, suggesting no simple diagrammatic expansion exists for generic q; for the infrared bound one might instead use reflection positivity (available for integer q and for the FK model on Z^d with q >= 1 via the Potts representation), which gives the infrared bound for the Potts spin-spin covariance directly for integer q >= 1 (Frohlich-Simon-Spencer), without a lace expansion. Recorded: for integer q the infrared bound is available by reflection positivity (this is classical), so the source's 'and use it to derive an infrared bound' is partly moot for integer q; the genuinely open content is the expansion itself and the non-integer q infrared bound. Key identity: Reflection positivity gives the infrared bound for integer-q Potts covariances without any expansion; the open part is non-integer q and the expansion. Obstruction: No switching lemma for Z_q currents; the natural expansion variable is a Tutte-polynomial quantity.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(M,g) complete, without boundary, Ric >= 0 (M = R^n is the model case)","u > 0 everywhere on M x (0,infinity) and smooth","u solves the heat equation u_t = Delta u","in the integrated form: 0 < t_1 < t_2 and d the Riemannian distance"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:49.106567+00:00","domain":"parabolic partial differential equations / geometric analysis","id":"claim_47db85f6916ac54d9a66f428afda4251cde272229adb51598e29f6604b83e38b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(M,g)$ be a complete Riemannian manifold of dimension $n$ with nonnegative Ricci curvature and without boundary (for instance $M=\\mathbb R^n$), and let $u>0$ be a smooth solution of $u_t=\\Delta u$ on $M\\times(0,\\infty)$. Then the differential Harnack (Li-Yau) inequality holds pointwise: $\\frac{|\\nabla u|^2}{u^2}-\\frac{u_t}{u}\\le\\frac{n}{2t}$, equivalently $-\\Delta\\log u\\le\\frac n{2t}$. Integrating along geodesics gives the classical Harnack form: for $x_1,x_2\\in M$ and $0<t_1<t_2$, $u(x_1,t_1)\\le u(x_2,t_2)\\Big(\\frac{t_2}{t_1}\\Big)^{n/2}\\exp\\Big(\\frac{d(x_1,x_2)^2}{4(t_2-t_1)}\\Big).$ Both are sharp: equality in the differential form holds for the Gaussian $u=\\Phi(x,t)$ on $\\mathbb R^n$. Positivity of $u$ on the whole of $M\\times(0,\\infty)$ and $\\mathrm{Ric}\\ge0$ are both needed; if $\\mathrm{Ric}\\ge-K$ with $K>0$ the estimate degrades to $\\alpha\\frac{|\\nabla u|^2}{u^2}-\\frac{u_t}{u}\\le\\frac{n\\alpha^2}{2t}+\\frac{n\\alpha^2K}{2(\\alpha-1)}$ for any $\\alpha>1$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:51:26.626563+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_48340aeb574eab5abf6373f7f0b60fd2e1a2e55246c7d5648c8bca05e6e6445f","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma L:massOutofCompact of arXiv:2606.03079, 'Mean Field Limits for Stochastic, Underdamped Reactive Langevin Dynamics Models'] There exists a sequence of $C_{b}^{2}(\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^d)$ functions $\{f_{m}(x,v)\}_{m \geq 0}$ with $f_{0} \equiv 1$ such that

f_{m}(x,v) &=1 \text { when }\|x\|+ \|v\|>m \\
0 \leq f_{m}(x,v) & \leq 1 \text { when } m-1<\|x\| + \|v\|\leq m .
\end{aligned}
$$
Additionally, $\displaystyle\sup _{m \geq 0}\|f_{m}(x,v)\|_{C_{b}^{2}(\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^d)}:=\sup _{m \geq 0} \mkern22mu \smashoperator{\sup_{\substack{ x \in \mathbb{R}^{d},v \in \mathbb{R}^{d},\\ |\alpha| \leq 2\strut}}}|D_{\alpha} f_{m}(x,v)|<\infty$. $$
for all $j=1,2, \cdots, J$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:35:59.919814+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_483cd18548c66865eb587d5699726e9efe451a77592960583f3002e1f7e0377d","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 11 of arXiv:2608.26084, 'Localic Esakia Duality\\via Conic Frames'] A \emph{monotone map} $f\colon (X,R)\to (Y,Q)$ between locales equipped with localic relations consists of a locale map~${f\colon X\to Y}$ satisfying:
	\[
	
	\begin{tikzcd}[cramped]
		R & Q \\
		{X\times X} & {Y\times Y.}
		\arrow["{\exists \bar f}"', dashed, from=1-1, to=1-2]
		\arrow[tail, from=1-1, to=2-1]
		\arrow[tail, from=1-2, to=2-2]
		\arrow["{f\times f}"', from=2-1, to=2-2]
	\end{tikzcd}
	\]
	The map $\bar f$ is unique if it exists. The commutativity of the square above is equivalent to saying that the \emph{source} and \emph{target squares} commute:
	\[\begin{tikzcd}[cramped]
		R & Q \\
		X & Y
		\arrow["{\bar f}", from=1-1, to=1-2]
		\arrow["{s_R}"', from=1-1, to=2-1]
		\arrow["{s_Q}", from=1-2, to=2-2]
		\arrow["f", from=2-1, to=2-2]
	\end{tikzcd}
	\qquad\text{and}\qquad
	\begin{tikzcd}[cramped]
		R & Q \\
		X & {Y.}
		\arrow["{\bar f}", from=1-1, to=1-2]
		\arrow["{t_R}"', from=1-1, to=2-1]
		\arrow["{t_Q}", from=1-2, to=2-2]
		\arrow["f", from=2-1, to=2-2]
	\end{tikzcd}\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:16:33.595230+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4896c8b55d37f829d79b5f233564c7c457174235883befac4f901fc73efbc473","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Abstract of arXiv:2609.02320, 'Analysis of Triggered Packet Streams: A Matrix-Analytic Method for Exponential Triggering...'] In many communication networks, the transmission of a packet may automatically trigger the transmission of a subsequent packet from the same source after a (possibly random) delay, without requiring acknowledgment or feedback. Such behavior arises in multi-stage status updating, proactive protocols, and other applications where users generate causally dependent packet streams. In this paper, in order to analyze these systems, we introduce the $\\mathrm{M^T/G/1}$ queue. In this model, primary customers arrive according to a Poisson process, and each primary customer triggers a secondary customer to join the queue after an independent delay. This arrival mechanism falls outside the scope of classical queueing models with renewal arrival processes. When the triggering delays follow an exponential distribution, we exploit the memoryless property to set up a tractable Markov description. By truncating the number of pending secondary customers, we derive a finite system of linear algebraic equations in the Laplace--Stieltjes transform domain and solve them using matrix-analytic methods. Based on the resulting workload distribution, we compute class-specific performance metrics using PASTA for primary customers and Palm conditioning for secondary customers. Finally, we validate the accuracy of this truncation through numerical experiments.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:59:45.016441+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_48e4d2ea8c30d4fe0f66ec87e43cbd4ff0f35b4a3b079b4da623b51ee1862ec3","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:Idot_well_def_and_rep of arXiv:2605.15401, 'Noise Tradeoffs, Stationary Information Flow, and Structural Balance in Unit-Birth Network'] Fix $i \in \{1,\dots, N\}$.

\[
(\dot I)_{X_i}
=
\sum_{n\ge0}\sum_v
\left(

{"assumptions":["mu satisfies a logarithmic Sobolev inequality with constant C","F is 1-Lipschitz with respect to the Euclidean metric","E_mu[F] finite"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.628148+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_48fde4b77a642071372ff1e759485d91cb6b61684b8d1f88e8b46b8a726cbc0f","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let mu be a probability measure on R^n satisfying a logarithmic Sobolev inequality with constant C, that is Ent_mu(f^2) <= 2 C E_mu[|grad f|^2] for all locally Lipschitz f. Then for every 1-Lipschitz F with E_mu[F] finite and every real lambda, E_mu[ exp( lambda (F - E F) ) ] <= exp( C lambda^2 / 2 ), and consequently mu( F - E F >= t ) <= exp( - t^2 / (2C) ) for every t > 0, with the same bound for the lower tail. For the standard Gaussian, C = 1 by the Gaussian logarithmic Sobolev inequality, giving the sharp Gaussian concentration bound exp(-t^2/2) for 1-Lipschitz functions. The argument converts a functional inequality into an exponential moment bound and is the reason log-Sobolev, rather than Poincare, is the inequality one wants: Poincare alone yields only exponential, not Gaussian, tails. The hypothesis is a Lipschitz bound on F with respect to the EUCLIDEAN metric; changing the metric changes the effective constant. [Herbst, unpublished; see Ledoux, The Concentration of Measure Phenomenon, Chapter 5]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0074-scaling-limit-of-random-walk-on-the-high-dimensional-incipient-infinit","No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:26:45.044664+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_49130968f69d04518594feadc86c7254295245afe5504bce42258268d1cce6aa","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Reduce to the scaling limit of the IIC itself (C0077) plus a homogenisation of the walk on the limit tree. Result: If the IIC converges (as a measure-valued process indexed by intrinsic distance) to incipient infinite super-Brownian motion, then the walk on the IIC should converge to the Brownian motion on the associated continuum random tree embedded in R^d, time-changed by the IIC volume measure, i.e. to the 'Brownian motion on the ISE-type tree' with spatial displacement given by the embedding (the Ben Arous-Cabezas-Fribergh limit). The walk on the discrete tree structure of the IIC is a random walk on a graph that is tree-like at all scales in d > 6 (the number of cycles at scale r is bounded), so the spatial position is a Brownian motion time-changed by the intrinsic clock; the intrinsic clock converges by the tree scaling limit; the embedding of the tree in R^d is a branching random walk-type embedding whose limit is the ISE embedding. Each step is known for the branching random walk trace (BCF 2016) and the difficulty for the IIC is the dependence between the tree structure and the embedding (loops, self-intersections). The rigorous reduction: the walk's scaling limit follows from (i) the IIC tree scaling limit with its embedding, (ii) a resistance estimate showing the effective resistance across the IIC at intrinsic distance r is of order r (tree-like), which is known up to constants from Kozma-Nachmias-type estimates. So the problem is subsumed by C0077 plus a resistance-form convergence theorem (Croydon's framework), which needs the convergence of the IIC as a resistance metric space, a stronger statement than the measure-valued convergence in the source. Obstruction: Resistance-metric convergence of the IIC in d > 6 is not established.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.165760+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4997649fea6ac3b1d570818aa0d47cc348dd0bd69b6f01bace7d030ace220912","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 43 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Recall the function $V_\gamma(\by)$ from \eqref{e:def-V-gamma-y}.
For any $\gamma \ge 0$, any local maximizer of $V_\gamma(\by)$ on the sphere $\{\|\by\|^2=N\}$ is of the form
    \beq
        
        \by =\dbA_\beta\Big(\gamma^{1/2}\dbg+\dbX\by\Big)\,,
    \eeq
    where we recall $\dbA_\beta \equiv (\beta \bI_N - \dbD)^{-1}$. Furthermore, for any such $\by$ we must have $\beta \ge \hw_1$.
\begin{proof}
We apply the method of Lagrange multipliers with the Lagrangian $\Lagr(\by;\beta)$ as defined in \eqref{e:fp-y-lagrangian}. Note that the Lagrangian Hessian (with respect to $\by$) is given by
    \[
        \nabla^2 \Lagr(\by;\beta)
        = -\frac{2}{N} \Big(
            \beta \bI_N - \dbD - \dbX
        \Big)\,.
    \]
At any local maximum, this Hessian must be negative semi-definite. Recall the definitions of $\dbD$ and $\dbX$ from \eqref{e:fp.dbD} and \eqref{e:fp.dbX} respectively. Since $|B_1|\ge\iota N$ by the assumption $(\lambda,\mu) \in \Lambda$, we can find a non-zero vector $\bv$ that is zero outside the coordinates of $B_1$, and is additionally orthogonal to each of the vectors $\tbmeta^j$ ($1\le j\le r'$) in the definition \eqref{e:fp.dbX} of $\dbX$. It follows that
    \[
    0 \le \bv^\st \Big(\beta -\dbD-\dbX \Big)\bv
    =\bv^\st \Big(\beta -\dbD \Big)\bv
    =(\beta-\hw_1)\|\bv\|^2\,,
    \]
so we conclude $\beta\ge\hw_1$. 
For any local maximizer $\by$ satisfying $\|\by\|^2=N$, stationarity of $\Lagr$ at $\by$ yields the expression~\eqref{e:fp-g-prep2-stationarity}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Fresh mutually independent Gaussian inputs","Noiseless labels","t deterministic, including any finite first expected-risk hit; not a sample-path stopping time","alpha>1 and gamma>alpha+1; fixed eta>0; B positive integer; n positive integer","Independent audit pending; no whole-theorem formal certificate."],"created_at":"2026-10-21T19:58:24.779201+00:00","domain":"stochastic optimization","id":"claim_49faa9192c7b291553081217a714e6fa79ce2dfe68b1cb7571c24cfe0aeea4ee","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"PROOF (UNAUDITED), w741-T422-C05 v1. Not independently checked.
# T422 Target 2: an explicit lower tail bound for instantaneous noise scales

Status: proof (unaudited), C05 v1. This strengthens the positive-probability
scope obstruction C04. It is not an upper tail estimate or a typical-scale
calibration, and it makes no literature-priority claim.

## Statement and all constants

Use the noiseless fresh Gaussian online model of C04. Let alpha>1,
gamma>alpha+1, h_j=j^(-alpha), and deterministic e_0,j satisfy
e_0,j^2=j^(-(gamma-alpha)). Each update averages B independent samples,
B>=1 integer, with a fixed step eta>0. Fix finite integer t>=1, ell in {1,2},
and integer n>=1. Let u_n denote the nth coordinate unit vector, and put

    m=gamma-alpha>1, M=||e_0||=sqrt(zeta(m)), c=M/2,
    y=c u_n, A=<e_0-y,e_0>=M^2-c e_0,n,
    u=(e_0-y)/sqrt(eta A), R=||u||+1,
    r=c h_n^((ell+1)/2)/4,
    T=(1+eta R^2)^t-1,
    rho=min(1, r R/(4 M T)).

Here A>=M^2/2>0, T>0, M,R,r,rho>0. Every division is well defined.
The norm in R is explicit:

    ||u||^2=(M^2-2c e_0,n+c^2)/(eta A).

Choose the following explicit finite truncation:

    N=ceil(max(n,1,
         [16/(eta A (m-1)rho^2)]^(1/(m-1)),
         [32/((alpha-1)rho^2)]^(1/(alpha-1)))).

For a prescribed center w equal to either 0 or u, define

    a=rho/(2 sqrt(N)),
    P_N(w)= (1/2) [rho/sqrt(2 pi N)]^N
             (product_(j=1)^N h_j^(-1/2))
             exp[-(1/2) sum_(j=1)^N (|w_j|+a)^2/h_j].

These are finite explicit strictly positive real numbers, not floating-point
certificates. Put

    pi_event=P_N(0)^(B(t-1)) P_N(u)^B >0,
    L_n=1+(9/25)zeta(ell alpha)n^(ell alpha).

For the conditional single-example instantaneous scale R_ell of C04,

    P(e_t!=0 and R_ell(e_t)>=L_n) >= pi_event.             (Q1)

In particular, for any finite L choose n with L_n>L; the same explicit
pi_event lower-bounds P(e_t!=0 and R_ell(e_t)>L).
The theorem also applies when t is any finite first EXPECTED-risk hitting
index, since that index is deterministic. It does not apply to a realized-risk
stopping time chosen from the samples without an additional stopping argument.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["translation invariance, or more generally a transitive amenable group action, of the percolation measure","ergodicity of the measure under the translation group, needed to conclude N is almost surely constant","amenability of the underlying graph, i.e. subexponential boundary-to-volume ratio along a Folner sequence","finite energy or insertion and deletion tolerance for each edge's conditional state"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.981600+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4a75ca0603a5987c8ea2229b5f254b315be024ca14b43e8bb06290ff87223753","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For a translation-invariant, ergodic percolation measure on Z^d, or more generally on an amenable transitive graph, satisfying finite energy (insertion and deletion tolerance for each edge conditionally on the rest of the configuration), the number N of infinite open clusters is almost surely a constant in {0, 1, infinity}, and Burton and Keane's argument rules out 2 <= N < infinity as well as N = infinity: if there were at least two infinite clusters with positive density, a positive density of trifurcation points (local configurations forcing at least three disjoint infinite paths) would be forced, but a discrete isoperimetric counting argument on a large box shows the number of trifurcation points cannot exceed a quantity of the order of the box's boundary, contradicting positive density in the bulk unless N <= 1. It follows that N is almost surely 0 or 1. The argument does not apply to non-amenable graphs, where coexistence of infinitely many infinite clusters is a genuine, well-studied phenomenon rather than a proof artifact, and constancy of N itself (ruling out a mixture over the value of N) is a separate ergodic-theory step, not part of the trifurcation-counting argument. Typical failure: Applying Burton-Keane uniqueness to a non-amenable graph, such as a regular tree or a graph with exponential volume growth, and expecting a unique infinite cluster; the trifurcation-point isoperimetric argument fundamentally requires amenability, and on non-amenable graphs the coexistence of infinitely many infinite clusters, studied by Haggstrom, Peres and others, is a real phenomenon that this theorem simply does not rule out. Canonical reference: Burton and Keane, 1989, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Gandolfi, Keane and Newman, 1992, Probability Theory and Related Fields.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:57:28.228397+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4ad62140468ebb8bbab6129a8630c718c54d71548ce60b7e2aaabeb2fee419de","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 1 ({\cite[Definition 10.1) of arXiv:2607.18104, '2607.18104'] {DOV:DirectedLandscape}}]
We denote by $\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}(x,s;y,t)$ the \textbf{(full-space) directed landscape}, a four parameter random function in $\mathcal{C}(\R^{4}_{\uparrow},\R)$. It satisfies:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] The marginals laws are given by the Airy sheet, i.e., for any $t,s>0$, the increment over the time interval $[t,t+s^3)$
\begin{equation}
(x,y) \mapsto \mathcal{L}(x,t;y,t+s^3)
\end{equation} is an Airy sheet $\mathcal{S}^{(s)}$ of scale $s$.
\item[(ii)] The metric composition law
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{L}(x,s;y,t) = \sup_{z \in \R} \big(\mathcal{L}(x,s;z,r) + \mathcal{L}(z,r;y,t) \big)
\end{equation} holds almost surely for any $s< r < t$ and $x,y \in \R$. The supremum in \eqref{eq:InvTriangleSup} is attained. 

\item[(iii)] For all $(t_i)_{i\in \lbr \ell \rbr}$ and $(s_i)_{i \in \lbr \ell \rbr}$ with $\ell \in \N$ such that $(t_i,s_i)_{i \in \lbr \ell \rbr}$ are disjoint intervals, the random functions $
\mathcal{L}(\cdot,t_i;\cdot,s_i)
$ are independent. 
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the underlying space is a Lebesgue probability space (the unit interval with Lebesgue measure, after normalisation)","the construction uses three cuts and exactly one spacer above the middle subcolumn at every stage, with h_0 = 1 and h_{n+1} = 3h_n + 1","T is the induced a.e.-defined invertible measure-preserving map"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:07:38.814795+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, mixing and rank-one constructions","id":"claim_4b4d539c3f629ff9022575793ca66b8a2b15d3199dbed5c40bec97bddfa73324","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Chacon's transformation is the invertible, rank-one, measure-preserving transformation T of a Lebesgue probability space produced by the following cutting-and-stacking construction. Start with the column C_0 consisting of the single interval [0,1), of height h_0 = 1. Given the column C_n, a stack of h_n disjoint intervals ('levels') of equal width w_n, cut it vertically into three subcolumns of equal width w_n/3, place one new 'spacer' interval of width w_n/3, taken from the not-yet-used part of the line, on top of the MIDDLE subcolumn, and stack the three pieces in order: subcolumn 1 at the bottom, then subcolumn 2 with its spacer on top of it, then subcolumn 3. The result is the column C_{n+1} of height h_{n+1} = 3 h_n + 1. The map T sends each point of a level to the point directly above it in the current column; the columns exhaust the space in the limit, T is defined almost everywhere, is invertible, and preserves Lebesgue measure normalised to a probability measure. The same system appears symbolically as the subshift generated by the blocks B_0 = 0, B_{n+1} = B_n B_n 1 B_n, whose lengths satisfy the same recursion. STANDARD FACTS about this system: it is ergodic; it has rank one, hence simple spectrum and ZERO entropy; it is WEAKLY MIXING but NOT strongly mixing; del Junco, Rahe and Swanson proved that it has minimal self-joinings, from which it follows that it is prime (its only factors are the trivial ones) and that its centraliser consists of the powers of T alone. WHY MIXING FAILS, in one line one can check: let I be a level of C_n and let I_1, I_2, I_3 be the three pieces into which the cut splits I inside C_{n+1}, each of measure mu(I)/3. By construction T^{h_n} carries I_1 onto I_2, and I_2 is a subset of I; hence I_1 is contained in I ∩ T^{-h_n} I, so mu(I ∩ T^{-h_n} I) >= (1/3) mu(I). The same argument applied at every later stage m >= n gives mu(A ∩ T^{-h_m} A) >= (1/3) mu(A) for every A which is a union of levels of C_n and every m >= n. Mixing would force these correlations to converge to mu(A)^2, which is smaller than (1/3) mu(A) as soon as mu(A) < 1/3. SHARP EDGES. (a) This is THE standard witness that weak mixing does not imply strong mixing; do not use it as an example of a mixing system, and do not expect quantitative decay of correlations from it - along the tower heights h_n the correlations do not decay at all. (b) Its zero entropy and simple spectrum show that weak mixing carries no entropy or spectral-multiplicity information whatsoever. (c) Rank one and minimal self-joinings are properties of this specific construction, not of cutting-and-stacking systems in general; changing the number of cuts or the spacer pattern changes the mixing behaviour (some cutting-and-stacking constructions are mixing).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:05:37.779544+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4b75e7a086585552bf28502d2c0e068613ba7db7687de5740338c7d078c90f00","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:ehr-kraw of arXiv:2608.01253, 'The pseudo-quantum representation of \\finite reversible Markov chains'] Let $u_m$, $m=-\tfrac n2,\dots,\tfrac n2$, be the orthonormal eigenvectors of
$A_{\mathrm{sym}}$ with eigenvalue $2m/n$. Then the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.7em,itemsep=2pt,topsep=2pt]
\item $u_m$ is the $J_x$ eigenvector of eigenvalue $m$. In the $J_z$ basis its
entries are, up to a column phase, the entries of the spin-$\tfrac n2$ rotation by
$\tfrac\pi2$ about the $y$ axis,

\[
u_m(k)=\langle k-\tfrac n2\rvert\,e^{-i\tfrac\pi2 J_y}\,\lvert m\rangle,
\]

the Wigner rotation matrix at $\tfrac\pi2$, which is real.
\item The rescaled entries $\mathrm K_m(k):=u_m(k)/\sqrt{\nu_k}$ are polynomials of
degree $\tfrac n2-m$ in $k$, the (normalised, symmetric) Krawtchouk polynomials,
orthogonal with respect to the binomial weight $\nu$,
$\sum_k\nu_k\,\mathrm K_m(k)\mathrm K_{m'}(k)=\delta_{mm'}$.
\item The semigroup has the exact spectral (Karlin--McGregor) form

\begin{equation}
\bigl(e^{tQ}\bigr)_{kl}
=\frac{\sqrt{\nu_l}}{\sqrt{\nu_k}}\sum_{m=-n/2}^{n/2}
e^{(2m-n)t}\,u_m(k)\,u_m(l)
=\nu_l\sum_{m}e^{(2m-n)t}\,\mathrm K_m(k)\,\mathrm K_m(l).

\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["P and Q are probability measures on one measurable space"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T07:39:17.917728+00:00","domain":"total variation, Kullback-Leibler divergence and two-point lower bounds","id":"claim_4b7b88b0a274034c33250c07a3aedbb06cfa837fecc4c43b4b9429a74ecd76ec","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"For probability measures P and Q on one space, TV(P, Q) = sup_A |P(A) - Q(A)| and D = D(P || Q) is the Kullback-Leibler divergence in nats (+infinity unless P << Q). For every event A, P(A^c) + Q(A) >= 1 - TV(P, Q), with equality for A = {p >= q}. So the smallest average error of a test between P and Q under equal priors is R* = (1 - TV)/2, and by the Bretagnolle-Huber inequality R* >= (1 - sqrt(1 - exp(-D)))/2 >= (1/4) exp(-D).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:13:18.505546+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4b9123247713378b8558488734fb1bf861f944969c4f7845ce04589a7418ded1","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 6 (Compatibility with separable tensor products) of arXiv:2608.30589, 'Vector-Valued Wavelet Bases as Hilbert $\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})$-Module Bases: A Construc'] Let $d_1,d_2\ge 1$ and $m\ge 1$.
Let $f,r\in L^2(\mathbb{R}^{d_1},\mathbb{R}^m)$ and $g,u\in L^2(\mathbb{R}^{d_2},\mathbb{R}^m)$.
Define $h,k\in L^2(\mathbb{R}^{d_1+d_2},\mathbb{R}^m)$ by
\[
h(x,y):= f(x)\odot g(y),\qquad
k(x,y):= r(x)\odot u(y),
\]
where $\odot$ denotes the componentwise product: $(a\odot b)_i:=a_i b_i$.
This compatibility will be used later in our separable construction of multivariate vector-valued wavelets.
Then

\[
\langle h,k\rangle_{\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})}
=
\langle f,r\rangle_{\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})}\ \odot\ \langle g,u\rangle_{\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})},
\]
where on the right-hand side $\odot$ denotes the Hadamard (entrywise) product of matrices:
$(A\odot B)_{ij}:=A_{ij}B_{ij}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:29:00.764167+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4b95f56b3aa2c2a48195d7504d1791b22a87845ca2e88f9e10ef07cc41467bf6","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 1 of arXiv:2512.04807, 'Existence and uniqueness of the canonical Brownian motion in non-simple conformal loop ens'] Suppose that we have the setup described just above. We say that a resistance form $(\rform{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma}, \rfdomain{\Gamma})$ on $\Upsilon_\Gamma$ is a \clekp{} resistance form if the following holds. For each $V \in \metregions$, there exists a resistance form $(\rformres{V}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma}, \rfdomainres{V}{\Gamma})$ on $\ol{V} \cap \Upsilon_\Gamma$  such that the following properties are satisfied.
\begin{enumerate}[I.]
\item $(\rform{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma}, \rfdomain{\Gamma})$ is a local, regular resistance form, and its associated resistance metric $\rmet{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma}$ is topologically equivalent to $\dpathY$.
\item Let $V_1,\ldots,V_n \in \metregions$, $n \in \N$, such that $V_i \cap V_j = \emptyset$ for $i \neq j$ and $\bigcup_i \ol{V_i} \cap \Upsilon_\Gamma = \Upsilon_\Gamma$. Then
 \begin{align*}
  \rfdomain{\Gamma} &= \{ f : f|_{\ol{V_i} \cap \Upsilon_\Gamma} \in \rfdomainres{V_i}{\Gamma} \text{ for each } i \} ,\\
  \text{and}\quad
  \rform{f}{f}{\Gamma} &= \sum_i \rformres{V_i}{f|_{\ol{V_i} \cap \Upsilon_\Gamma}}{f|_{\ol{V_i} \cap \Upsilon_\Gamma}}{\Gamma} .
 \end{align*}
 See Figure~\ref{fi:cle_rf_locality}.
\item If $V,V' \in \metregions$, $V \subseteq V'$, and $f\colon \ol{V'} \cap \Upsilon_\Gamma \to \R$ is a continuous function that is constant on each $\dpathY$-connected component of $\ol{V'} \cap \Upsilon_\Gamma \setminus \ol{V}$, then
\begin{align*}
 & f \in \rfdomainres{V'}{\Gamma} \text{ if and only if } f|_{\ol{V} \cap \Upsilon_\Gamma} \in \rfdomainres{V}{\Gamma} \\
 \text{and}\quad & \rformres{V'}{f}{f}{\Gamma} = \rformres{V}{f}{f}{\Gamma} .

\item For each open, simply connected $U \subseteq \C$, the collection $(\rformres{V}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma})_{V \in \metregions[U]}$ is a.s.\ determined by $(\Gamma_{U^*}, \dpathY[U])$.
\item Let $U \subseteq \C$ be open, simply connected, and $z \in \C$. Then
\[ (\rformres{V}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma_{U^*}})_{V \in \metregions[U]} = (\rformres{V+z}{T_{z}\cdot}{T_{z}\cdot}{\Gamma_{U^*}+z})_{V \in \metregions[U]} \quad\text{a.s.,} \]

{"assumptions":["Both layers trained, centered C1 activation with positive derivative at zero and Lipschitz derivative.","Explicit separable signed-data family and small-radius cone conditions in statement.","Proof (unaudited), T368-w734-C004 version 1; no novelty claim and no nonlinear-trajectory conclusion."],"created_at":"2026-10-21T19:11:08.040824+00:00","domain":"neural network optimization","id":"claim_4bb554719dde5321414420959e9349ee40e3a9c952810414469e359add77b2c7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Own-work proof (unaudited), C004 v1, route-failure for T368 Target 2; no novelty or GD nonconvergence claim. Let p>q>=1, tau=(p-q)/(p+q), and a,b>0 satisfy a^2+b^2<=1 and a^2<tau*b^2. Take p signed samples z_i=y_i*x_i=(a,b) and q signed samples (a,-b), with arbitrary labels +/-1 and x_i=y_i*z_i. These data are separated by (1,0) with margin a. Their signed mean mu=(a,tau*b) has negative inner product with the minority samples. Put e=mu/||mu|| and kappa=(tau*b^2-a^2)/||mu||>0. For f(theta,x)=m^-1 sum_j a_j phi(w_j dot x), width m>=1, centered C1 activation phi(0)=0, c=phi'(0)>0 and beta-Lipschitz derivative beta>=0, let P be the orthogonal projection onto the per-neuron spans of (1,e), and Q=I-P. This is the positive expanding eigenspace of simultaneous both-layer logistic-GD linearization at zero for any positive step. Write U=||Ptheta||>0, V=||Qtheta||, R=||theta||. If V<=epsilon*U, epsilon>0, epsilon+epsilon^2/2<=kappa/4, and beta*R*(1+epsilon^2)<=c*kappa/4, then every minority sample has y_i*f(theta,x_i)<=-c*kappa*U^2/(8m)<0. For beta=0 the radius condition is automatic. The cone is nonempty at arbitrarily small radii. The strict data inequalities persist under perturbations when a^2+b^2<1, giving an open family. For general data with nonzero signed mean, that mean separates all samples exactly when all signed Gram row sums sum_l z_i dot z_l are positive; existence of some separator does not imply this. Thus local saddle escape or arbitrarily close expanding alignment alone cannot establish positive margins. This does not control nonlinear trajectories after escape or refute eventual Gaussian burn-in. The exact rational example p=3,q=1,a=3/10,b=4/5 has e=(3/5,4/5), kappa=23/50.
