{"assumptions":["gamma the standard Gaussian measure on R^n","f locally Lipschitz with f and grad f in L^2(gamma)","the generator normalisation L = Laplacian minus x . gradient, which fixes the constant 2"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.628082+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4bdeb13cc86ab526b0013e02b6024d3dede00f91d34eca4a10273fa64375e52c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let gamma be the standard Gaussian measure on R^n. For every locally Lipschitz f with f and grad f in L^2(gamma), Ent_gamma(f^2) <= 2 E_gamma[ |grad f|^2 ], where Ent(g) = E[g log g] - E[g] log E[g] for g >= 0. The constant 2 is sharp, with near-equality for exponentials f = e^{a . x / 2}. As with the Poincare inequality the constant is DIMENSION-FREE, obtained from the one-dimensional case by tensorization of entropy. Gross's theorem states that this inequality is EQUIVALENT to Nelson's hypercontractivity for the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup, and it implies the Gaussian Poincare inequality by linearisation. Combined with the Herbst argument it yields Gaussian concentration for Lipschitz functions with the sharp sub-Gaussian variance proxy equal to the square of the Lipschitz constant. Care with normalisation: the inequality is often written as Ent(f) <= 2 E[ |grad sqrt(f)|^2 ] for f >= 0, which is the same statement after substituting f -> f^2, and some sources carry a factor 1/2 from using a different generator normalisation; the version stated here is the one matching the standard Gaussian and the generator L = Laplacian minus x . gradient. [Gross (1975); see Bakry, Gentil and Ledoux, Analysis and Geometry of Markov Diffusion Operators, Chapter 5]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-02T01:20:52.931336+00:00","domain":"harvested statement (arXiv 2605.24611, 2026): owner_math","id":"claim_4bfb4312751e7b4b65a99c25a8bda6a321b048b42ff129e2faf2efae009dfffa","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 2 (Limit cycle and basin of attraction) of arXiv:2605.24611, 'Beyond Fixed Points: Superpolynomial Capacity of Asymmetric Hopfield Networks'] A limit cycle of period P ≥1 is a set of distinct states C = {x(0), x(1), . . . , x(P −1)} such that, for the synchronous update map F : {−1, 1}n → {−1, 1}n, we have F(x(i)) = x(i+1) for i = 0, . . . , P −2 and F(x(P −1)) = x(0). {"assumptions":["f is holomorphic on a neighborhood of the closed disk |z| ≤ R","f(0) ≠ 0 (otherwise divide by z^m)","zeros in the open disk are listed with multiplicity","no zeros on |z| = R in the stated form (the formula extends to that case)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:42.483367+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_4c20bd0201a9aff751ded5583603d49c0ce62d6d31f19a6b630a6fd68f837cd3","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let R > 0, let f be holomorphic on an open set containing the closed disk |z| ≤ R, with f(0) ≠ 0 and f having no zeros on the circle |z| = R. Equivalently, (1/2π)∫_0^{2π} log|f(Re^{iθ})| dθ - log|f(0)| = Σ_k log(R/|a_k|) = ∫_0^R n(t) dt/t, where n(t) is the number of zeros of f in |z| ≤ t counted with multiplicity. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:48:25.142700+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4c46c6a1dbe7ddf1cd9704d0a1a1e438449cf0a0452e6aa8850046fbeeae9192","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:three-causes of arXiv:2607.04620, 'The Exact Ville Identity\\ \large From the Absorbing Case to the General Law\\ with an App'] For a nonnegative supermartingale $(M_n)$ with $M_0=1$ crossing the level $b>1$:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item The martingale-versus-supermartingale gap governs $D_b$. If $(M_n)$ is a martingale then $\delta_n\equiv0$ and $D_b=0$; the loss term is nonzero precisely to the extent that the process is a strict supermartingale, that is, sheds predictable mass before crossing.
\item Bounded overshoot governs $O_b$. If the conditional landing value satisfies $\mathbb{E}[M_{T_b}\mid \mathcal{F}_{T_b-1},T_b=n]\le b+\omega$ a.s. for a constant $\omega$, then $O_b\le\omega$ ((sec:overshoot of the paper)); on a lattice that includes $b$, $O_b=0$. \item Wobbling governs $R_b$. If, in the martingale case, conditions (i)--(ii) of (thm:wobbling of the paper) hold (sufficient wobbling and bounded overshoot), then $\mathbb{P}(T_b<\infty)=1$, so the survival event is null and $R_b=0$. \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:31:20.615284+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4c6c543f211775f81e17258e84be6b56ba7c5c724d2ea53c655e440161959d78","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 20 of arXiv:2608.25785, 'Proper Actions on Homogeneous Spaces of the Upper Triangular Matrix Group via Coarse Geome'] Let $(S,\mathcal{E})$ and $(T,\mathcal{F})$ be coarse spaces.
A map $f : S \rightarrow T$ is called: 
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \emph{controlled} (cf.~\cite{BunkeEngel2020}) if, for each $E\in \mathcal{E}$, 
    \[
    \Ad_f(E) = \{ (f(x_1),f(x_2)) \mid (x_1,x_2) \in E \} \subset T \times T
    \]
    is an entourage on $T$, 
    \item  \emph{coarsely proper} (cf.~\cite{LeitnerVigolo2023}) if the set $f^\dagger[D]=f^{-1}(D)$ is bounded in $S$ for any bounded subset $D$ of $T$,  
    \item \emph{coarse} (cf.~\cite{Roe2003LectureCoarse}) if it is controlled and coarsely proper,
    \item  \emph{effectively proper} (cf.~\cite{DikranjanZavaCatCoarseGp2020}) if, for any $F\in \mathcal{F}$, the relation 
    \[
    \Ad_{f^\dagger}F = \{ (p,q) \mid (f(p),f(q)) \in F \} \subset S \times S
    \]
    is also an entourage on $S$,
    \item   \emph{a coarse embedding} (cf.~\cite{DikranjanZavaCatCoarseGp2020}) if $f$ is controlled and effectively proper,
    \item  \emph{coarsely surjective} (cf.~\cite{LeitnerVigolo2023}) if there exists $F\in \mathcal{F}$ such that $F[f(S)] = T$,
    \item  \emph{a coarse equivalence} (cf.~\cite{DikranjanZava2017}) if $f$ is controlled and there exists a controlled map $h: T\to S$ such that $h\circ f\sim \id_S$ and $f\circ h\sim \id_T$.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

Y. Shmalo, A Brownian piece in front of a process absolutely continuous with respect to Brownian motion (2026). Burdzy and Scheutzow (Forward Brownian motion, Probab. Theory Related Fields 160 (2014), Problem 7.5) asked whether, for every process X whose law is equivalent to Wiener measure, a random piece of path can be put in front of X so that the new process is a Brownian motion. The paper proves that absolute continuity with respect to Wiener measure is enough: on an extension of the probability space there are a standard Brownian motion B and an almost surely finite random integer N >= 0 with X_t = B_{N+t} - B_N for all t >= 0; N cannot in general be a stopping time for B. More generally, for an invertible measure-preserving map theta of (E, P) and a target law fP, a forward shift theta^N with N built from a P-distributed point and independent uniforms carries P to fP if and only if E[f | I] = 1, I the invariant sigma-field; without the auxiliary uniforms only integer-valued densities can be reached. The construction is Rost's filling scheme (Chacon-Ornstein, Rost 1971) for the unit shift of two-sided Brownian motion. \cref{sp:prop:limiting-package}: it is the intrinsic completion
of its K\"ahler regular locus, is normal and klt, carries the normalized
shrinker measure and complete soliton flow, and has smooth
metric--complex--density convergence and the local ambient metric lower
bound.  Let \(A\) be the nonnegative
self-adjoint operator associated with the closure of
\[
 \cE_0(\phi,\psi)=
 \int_{\cR}\langle\nabla\phi,\nabla\overline\psi\rangle\,d\mathfrak m,
 \qquad \phi,\psi\in C_c^\infty(\cR).
\]

\begin{equation}
                     \sigma(A)\subset\{0\}\cup[1/2,\infty),
                     \qquad\ker A=\C1.
\end{equation}

\(u\in L^2(Z,\mathfrak m)\), and
\begin{equation}
 A\left(u-\int_Zu\,d\mathfrak m\right)
 =\frac12\left(u-\int_Zu\,d\mathfrak m\right),
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
          \nabla^2\Re u=\nabla^2\Im u=0\qquad\text{on }\cR.
\end{equation}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:37:08.955794+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4d0850de5b28c4a7bc8e53651048f9d8d7a85ebea2650c557730166733bc5f7a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:variance_explicit of arXiv:2609.01581, 'Concentration of additive functionals of Stratonovich-type'] Consider the empirical density $\overline{\rho}_t(V)$ (Definition~(def:empirical_density of the paper))
and empirical current $\overline J_t(U)$ (Definition~(def:empirical_current of the paper))

\begin{align}
  \mathrm{Var}_\mu(\overline\rho_t)
    &\leq \frac{2\mathrm{Var}_\mu(V)}{\lambda_\mathrm{gap}t},
  \\

    &\leq \frac{1}{t}\left(2\E^\mu[Q]
      +\frac{2\mathrm{Var}_\mu(W)}{\lambda_\mathrm{gap}}\right)
      \leq \frac{1}{t}\left(2\|Q\|_{L^\infty(\mu)}
      +\frac{2\mathrm{Var}_\mu(W)}{\lambda_\mathrm{gap}}\right),
  
\end{align}
where $\lambda_\mathrm{gap}$ denotes the spectral gap~(equation eq:gap_variational of the paper) of $\mathcal{L}_S$

\begin{align}

	\quad\quad
  \sigma_{J,\infty}^2\leq 2\E^\mu[Q]+\frac{2\mathrm{Var}_\mu(W)}{\lambda_\mathrm{gap}}

{"assumptions":["G finite, p prime with p dividing |G|"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:31:12.478772+00:00","domain":"group theory","id":"claim_4d35593daa64c444cac9ce0985344a1fd51aea56f0ba9d34f01bd81800978194","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let G be a finite group and p a prime dividing the order |G|. Then G contains an element of order exactly p, hence a subgroup of order p. More precisely (McKay), the number of solutions to x^p = e in G is a multiple of p, and since x = e is one of them, there are at least p - 1 elements of order p; in fact the number of elements of order p is congruent to -1 modulo p. Cauchy's theorem is the p^1 case of Sylow's first theorem (a subgroup of order p^a exists whenever p^a divides |G|) and is the converse of Lagrange's theorem for prime orders; the converse of Lagrange fails in general (A_4 has order 12 and no subgroup of order 6).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:35:04.097652+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4d4bc2c914255102e0b0fa0df3fd56d972fe9eab9b698b26f4419da6aace4953","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:singleton-renewal of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] For a Kac plane $i$, let
\[
 W_i^\circ=\Pi_{\mathcal W}(\mathsf P_i-N^{-1}I_W)
\]
be its pure-Weyl coefficient.  On the common star space, with an arbitrary
passive ancillary Hilbert space $E$, put
\[
 (\mathsf M h)(i,\theta)=(W_i^\circ\otimes I_E)h(i,\theta),
 \qquad \mathsf J=\mathscr E^*\mathscr E,
 \qquad \mathsf Q=I-\mathsf J.
\]
Relative to $\operatorname{ran}\mathsf J\oplus
\operatorname{ran}\mathsf Q$, write
\[
 \mathsf M=
 \begin{pmatrix}0&\mathsf S^-\\ \mathsf S^+&\mathsf V\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{3.2.10n}
\]
We call $0,\mathsf S^-,\mathsf S^+,\mathsf V$ the four
\emph{star statuses} of a passive singleton; a status record chooses one
of these four blocks for every singleton after equal-time fusion.  These
statuses are distinct from the derivative-placement coefficients
$(\alpha,\beta)$ used in the Ricci root calculus.
Then
\[
 \|\mathsf S^-\|=\|\mathsf S^+\|
 \le\sqrt{\frac{n-3}{N(n-1)}}\le N^{-1/2},
 \qquad \|\mathsf V\|\le2,
\tag{3.2.10o}
\]
and the one-sided utilized-step maps factor through the innovation:
\[
 \mathscr E\mathsf M\mathscr T=\mathscr E\mathsf M\mathscr G,
 \qquad
 \mathscr T^*\mathsf M\mathscr E^*
 =\mathscr G^*\mathsf M\mathscr E^*.
\tag{3.2.10p}
\]
Consequently a passive singleton isolated between invariant separators is
zero.  A run of $s\ge2$ passive singletons with $s-1$ prescribed finite
Green gates has norm at most
\[
 \frac{2^{2s-3}}N.
\tag{3.2.10q}
\]
Thus its two endpoints create one $N^{-1}$ resource and every interior
singleton transports that same resource; no additional token is created.
The same conclusion holds when an endpoint is a $\mathscr D$- or
$\mathscr L$-incidence, with the corresponding mixed bound of
(lem:riesz of the paper) and with the already existing root or packet token
transported.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["F entire on C (or C^d)","claims of band limitation require the growth bound off the real axis","L^2 version needs square integrability on R; distributions need the polynomial-growth version"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:39.264631+00:00","domain":"complex and harmonic analysis, common errors","id":"claim_4d88e0d15b6e8881d2eb18cd54107f75b8c1834afa521c13029e34cc2e348e2d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypotheses: (1) the growth bound $|F(z)|\\le Ce^{A|z|}$ must hold for all complex $z$, not merely on $\\mathbb R$; (2) $F$ must be square integrable on $\\mathbb R$ (for the $L^2$ version) or have controlled polynomial growth (for the distributional version). Failure of (1): $F(z)=e^{-z^2}$ is entire and its restriction to $\\mathbb R$ is in $L^2$, yet $|F(iy)|=e^{y^2}$, so $F$ is of order 2, not of exponential type; its Fourier transform is a Gaussian, supported everywhere - no band limitation. Failure of (2): $F(z)=\\cos(Az)$ is entire of exponential type exactly $A$ and bounded on $\\mathbb R$, but not in $L^2(\\mathbb R)$; it is not $\\int_{-A}^A\\varphi(t)e^{itz}dt$ for any $\\varphi\\in L^2$, only for the measure $\\frac12(\\delta_A+\\delta_{-A})$ - the correct statement in that regime is the Paley-Wiener-Schwartz theorem for compactly supported distributions, with a polynomial factor $(1+|\\zeta|)^N$ allowed. Similarly $F(z)=e^{Az}$ has type $A$ but grows on the real axis. Two further traps: the exponential factor in Paley-Wiener-Schwartz measures the support of the transform only through the supporting function of its convex hull, so the theorem detects $\\operatorname{ch}(\\operatorname{supp}u)$, not the support itself; and no such function can have both itself and its transform compactly supported, since a nonzero entire function cannot vanish on an open set (see Benedicks' theorem for the measure-theoretic strengthening).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X_1, ..., X_n independent","Z = f(X) nonnegative with E[Z log Z] finite"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.627951+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4dc336ffe1859932768872cd898d8a70b2b6935d4bd7b90c575ded181869d08f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, ..., X_n be independent random variables and let Z = f(X_1, ..., X_n) be a nonnegative random variable with E[Z log Z] finite. Write Ent(Z) = E[Z log Z] - E[Z] log E[Z] and let Ent^{(i)}(Z) denote the same functional computed with respect to X_i alone, with the other coordinates held fixed. Then Ent(Z) <= sum_{i=1}^n E[ Ent^{(i)}(Z) ]. The same statement with variance in place of entropy is the Efron-Stein inequality, and the two are the p = 2 and p = 1 members of a family of phi-entropies that all tensorize. Tensorization is what converts a ONE-DIMENSIONAL functional inequality into an n-dimensional one with no loss of constant: if each coordinate's law satisfies a logarithmic Sobolev inequality with constant C, then the product law satisfies it with the SAME constant C, independent of n. That dimension-free feature is the whole reason the entropy method produces concentration bounds that do not degrade as n grows. Independence of the coordinates is essential. [standard; e.g. Boucheron, Lugosi and Massart, Concentration Inequalities, Theorem 4.10 and Section 4.1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:11:11.695099+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4e2841da640a398408c72f98a4c00ba304f3a51379b2beecfbd04e38294d3c1f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:whole-plane-persistence of arXiv:2609.00645, 'Global persistence of nearly radial concentrated vortices in a bounded domain'] Fix $\kappa,M,R>0$.  Then there exists $C=C(\kappa,M,R)>0$ such that the following
holds.  For $\varepsilon>0$, let
$\omega_{\varepsilon,0}\in L^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$ satisfy
\begin{equation}
  \omega_{\varepsilon,0}\geq0,\qquad
  \int_{\mathbb R^2}\omega_{\varepsilon,0}\,\mathrm d\mathbf x=\kappa,
  \qquad
  \|\omega_{\varepsilon,0}\|_\infty\leq M\varepsilon^{-2},
  \qquad
  \operatorname{supp}\omega_{\varepsilon,0}
  \subset B_{R\varepsilon}(\mathbf0).
\end{equation}
Let $\omega_{\varepsilon,t}$, $t\in\mathbb R$, be the corresponding Yudovich
solution of the two-dimensional Euler equation in $\mathbb R^2$.  Then
\begin{equation}
  \sup_{t\in\mathbb R}\mathcal A(\omega_{\varepsilon,t})^2
  \leq C\mathcal A(\omega_{\varepsilon,0}).
\end{equation}
If, in addition,
\begin{equation}
  \mathcal A(\omega_{\varepsilon,0})\leq\frac{\kappa^2}{C},
\end{equation}
then, with
\[
  \mathbf X_\varepsilon
  :=\frac1\kappa\int_{\mathbb R^2}\mathbf x
  \omega_{\varepsilon,0}(\mathbf x)\,\mathrm d\mathbf x,
\]
one has
\begin{equation}
  \sup_{t\in\mathbb R}\ \sup_{\mathbf b\in\mathsf C(\omega_{\varepsilon,t})}
  |\mathbf b-\mathbf X_\varepsilon|
  \leq (1+\sqrt2)R\varepsilon.
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}
  \sup_{t\in\mathbb R}\ \sup_{\mathbf b\in\mathsf C(\omega_{\varepsilon,t})}
  |\mathbf b|
  \leq(2+\sqrt2)R\varepsilon.
\end{equation}
In particular, for any family of initial data satisfying
(equation eq:whole-plane-initial-data of the paper) with the same $\kappa,M,R$, if
$\mathcal A(\omega_{\varepsilon,0})\to0$ as $\varepsilon\to0$, then
\[
  \sup_{t\in\mathbb R}\mathcal A(\omega_{\varepsilon,t})\longrightarrow0,
  \qquad
  \sup_{t\in\mathbb R}\ \sup_{\mathbf b\in
  \mathsf C(\omega_{\varepsilon,t})}|\mathbf b|\longrightarrow0.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["both sequences (or functions) monotone in the same direction; opposite directions reverse the inequality","no independence or product structure needed beyond the single variable; the n-variable generalization is Harris-FKG"],"created_at":"2026-09-02T07:51:33.049386+00:00","domain":"correlation inequalities (hand-authored statement with hypotheses, 2026-09-02)","id":"claim_4e33e7a855f3b1ed38c5b184f81787d0bc6049fa0a51bfd8ff8f2972faba1f89","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"If a_1 >= a_2 >= ... >= a_n and b_1 >= b_2 >= ... >= b_n (both sequences sorted the same way), then (1/n) sum a_i b_i >= ((1/n) sum a_i) ((1/n) sum b_i); if one sequence is increasing and the other decreasing, the inequality reverses. The integral form: for f and g both monotone in the same direction on [0,1], the integral of f g is at least the product of the integrals. This is the one-dimensional case of the Harris-FKG inequality (a product of two increasing functions of one uniform variable has nonnegative covariance), and its proof is the identity 2(n sum a_i b_i - sum a_i sum b_j) = sum_{i,j} (a_i - a_j)(b_i - b_j) >= 0.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Y = sum_{k>=0} B_k (2/3)^k with i.i.d. digits B_k, P(B_k=1)=p (the biased-coin Bernoulli convolution at contraction ratio lambda=2/3, equivalently the same non-Pisot ratio 3/2 used elsewhere in this campaign)","elementary dimension bound only: Hochman's theorem is NOT used; only the entropy-over-Lyapunov upper bound on dimension and the fact that a measure on R of dimension below 1 cannot be absolutely continuous"],"created_at":"2026-09-24T23:46:59.956588+00:00","domain":"probability/Bernoulli convolutions","id":"claim_4e3f794ecd634c87b21e676f1227583d","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"For the biased Bernoulli convolution at ratio 2/3 - the law of sum_k B_k (2/3)^k with B_k i.i.d., P(B_k = 1) = p - the measure is singular for every p < p* = 0.140277, where p* solves H(p) = log(3/2) in natural logarithms (H(p)/log(3/2) = 0.4896, 0.8018, 1.2341, 1.7095 at p = 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 1/2). Proof: the dimension of the measure is at most the entropy-over-Lyapunov ratio H(p)/log(3/2), and a measure on the line of dimension below one is not absolutely continuous; Hochman's theorem is needed only for the matching lower bound dim = min(1, H(p)/log(3/2)), which this does not use. Two further thresholds govern the Fourier criterion at this ratio. The biased factor |(1-p) + p e^{i phi}|^2 = 1 - 2p(1-p)(1 - cos phi) has arithmetic mean 1 - 2p(1-p) over the phase, which gives the annealed (main-term) exponent alpha(p) = 1 + log(1 - 2p(1-p))/log(3/2), zero at p(1-p) = 1/6, i.e. p = (1 - 3^{-1/2})/2 = 0.211325; and log-mean 2 log(1-p), which gives the quenched (typical) threshold (3/2)(1-p)^2 = 1 at p = 0.183503. As a calibration control for statistics on the unbiased Bernoulli convolution at 2/3 (the same ratio, frequencies and arithmetic, only the weights changed): below p* the measure is singular and a detection is expected; above 0.2113 the main term decays and a pass is expected; between 0.1403 and 0.2113 the measure has dimension one while the main term already diverges, so a reading there means nothing - controls belong at p <= 0.12 and p >= 0.35. Unlike the Pisot control lambda = 1/phi, where one localised cell forces the reading a priori, the absence of such a cell at ratio 3/2 is Mahler's open problem on ||(3/2)^m xi||, so the control's genuineness rests on an empirical extensiveness test: a flat per-step rate means one cell forces the reading, a wobbling rate means a real measurement (flat to 0.0005 at 1/phi from K = 8; wobbling by 0.028 at the unbiased 2/3).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:57:28.723939+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4e92ce6e9b8fc59cb1d4748bc8c36496d4a69b015f697587300eb89a24e12c0a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 22 of arXiv:2609.01190, 'Rough differential equations on manifolds via natural bundles'] Let $f:\Rsf^m\to\Rsf$ be a smooth, compactly supported function and let $\varepsilon, \tilde{\varepsilon}, \delta, \zeta\in [0,\infty)$ and $a,b, \tilde{a},\tilde{b}\in\Rsf^m$ be such that 
	\[
		|b-a|\leq \varepsilon, 
			\quad 
		|\tilde{b}-\tilde{a}|\leq \tilde{\varepsilon}, 
			\quad 
		|\tilde{a}-a|\leq \delta, 
			\quad\mbox{and}\quad 
		|\tilde{b}-\tilde{a} - (b-a)| \leq \zeta.
	\]
Let also $T_0,T_1: \Rsf^m\times\Rsf^m\to\Rsf$ be defined by 
	\begin{align*}
		& T_0(x,y):= f(y)-f(x),\\
		& T_1(x,y):= f(y)-f(x)- \frac{\partial f}{\partial x^j}(x)(y^j-x^j)
	\end{align*}
for $x,y\in\Rsf^m$. Then
	\[
		\left|T_0(a,b)\right|  \lesssim \varepsilon 
		\quad\mbox{and}\quad
		|T_0(\tilde{a},\tilde{b})-T_0(a,b)| \lesssim \varepsilon(\delta + \zeta) + \zeta,
	\]
and
	\[
		 |T_1(a,b)| \lesssim \varepsilon^2
		 \quad \mbox{and}\quad 
		 |T_1(\tilde{a},\tilde{b})-T_1(a,b)| \lesssim \varepsilon^2(\delta + \zeta) + (\varepsilon + \tilde{\varepsilon})\zeta
	\]
where the constants are non-decreasing functions of $C^1$, $C^2$, $C^2$, and $C^3$ norm of $f$, respectively. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["entries independent up to symmetry with mean 0 and variance 1 before scaling by 1/sqrt n","moments bounded uniformly in n (finite fourth moment suffices for the semicircle limit of the empirical spectral distribution; the diagonal entries may have a different variance)","the moment method identifies the limit because the semicircle law is determined by its moments (compact support)"],"created_at":"2026-09-02T07:51:33.049288+00:00","domain":"random matrix theory (hand-authored statement with hypotheses, 2026-09-02)","id":"claim_4f1567c38734286426940b4f4f52f264db38c2264b6a25725643dc91aea4918c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"For the semicircle density (1/(2 pi)) sqrt(4 - x^2) on [-2, 2] (mean 0, variance 1), all odd moments vanish and the 2k-th moment equals the Catalan number C_k = (1/(k+1)) binom(2k, k): 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, 132, ... . A semicircle of radius R has 2k-th moment C_k (R/2)^{2k}. In the moment method for a Wigner matrix W = X / sqrt n, where X is real symmetric with independent entries above the diagonal, mean 0 and variance 1, the normalized traces satisfy E tr(W^{2k}) / n -> C_k: expanding the trace as a sum over closed walks of length 2k on the index set, only walks whose edges are each traversed exactly twice and whose underlying graph is a tree survive as n grows, and such walks are counted by C_k; the Catalan numbers determine the semicircle law uniquely because it has compact support. Wigner's theorem then follows from convergence of moments plus a variance bound (or a concentration bound on the trace) giving weak convergence of the empirical spectral distribution in probability.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:42.499458+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_4f46b2de22e7549670bcc1dce7b0f972c96bfd2b3336d5d4426cf06f59a598fa","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The Weierstrass convergence theorem (a locally uniform limit of holomorphic functions is holomorphic and derivatives converge locally uniformly) has no real-variable analogue and does not upgrade to uniform convergence on the whole domain. (1) Real failure: f_n(x) = sin(n^2 x)/n converges to 0 uniformly on R, but the derivatives f_n'(x) = n cos(n^2 x) do not converge to the derivative of the limit — at x = 0, f_n'(0) = n → ∞ — so uniform convergence of real functions carries no information about derivatives. More dramatically, by the Weierstrass approximation theorem every continuous nowhere differentiable function on [0,1] is a uniform limit of polynomials, so uniform limits of real-analytic functions need not be differentiable anywhere. The complex proof uses the Cauchy estimates, which need holomorphy on a two-dimensional neighborhood: a bound on |g| on a disk controls all derivatives at the center. (2) Only locally uniform: f_n(z) = z^n/n converges to 0 uniformly on all of D, yet f_n'(z) = z^{n-1} has supremum 1 on D for every n and does not converge uniformly on D. So the derivative statement must be quoted with 'uniformly on compact subsets'; deducing a uniform derivative bound up to the boundary from a uniform bound on the functions is a genuine error, and controlling it requires extra input (a larger domain of holomorphy, or boundary regularity). (3) The hypothesis is convergence on compact subsets of the open set, not convergence on the closed set: a sequence converging uniformly on the closed unit disk still gives derivative convergence only on |z| ≤ r < 1 unless the functions are holomorphic on a larger disk.","status":"unverified"}

The order of f is ρ = limsup_{r→∞} (log log M(r))/(log r) in [0, ∞]; equivalently ρ = inf{λ ≥ 0 : M(r) ≤ exp(r^λ) for all sufficiently large r}, with the infimum of the empty set taken to be ∞. Constant functions are assigned order 0. If 0 < ρ < ∞ one further distinguishes the type σ = limsup_{r→∞} log M(r)/r^ρ. Examples: every nonconstant polynomial has order 0; exp(z), sin z, cos z and 1/Γ have order 1; exp(z^n) has order n; cos(sqrt z) has order 1/2; exp(exp(z)) has infinite order. If f has finite order ρ and nonzero zeros (a_n) listed with multiplicity, then Σ_n |a_n|^{-s} < ∞ for every s > ρ; the exponent of convergence of the zeros, λ = inf{s > 0 : Σ_n |a_n|^{-s} < ∞}, satisfies λ ≤ ρ, and the inequality can be strict (exp(z) has order 1 and no zeros at all).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f ∈ C^1","u is a weak solution which is piecewise C^1 with C^1 shock curves and one-sided traces (the equivalence as stated is for this piecewise-smooth class; Kruzhkov's definition is what governs general L^∞ solutions)","the chord condition must hold at EVERY point of EVERY discontinuity curve","Rankine-Hugoniot alone is not sufficient: it fixes σ but permits inadmissible jumps"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.417666+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: hyperbolic conservation laws","id":"claim_502c4a8cf7e11bf1fd64197cea9e23277293f004895262e4972b802ea4718867","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f ∈ C^1(R) and let u ∈ L^∞(R × (0,∞)) be a weak solution of u_t + f(u)_x = 0 that is piecewise C^1: away from finitely many disjoint C^1 curves x = s_i(t) it is C^1, and it has C^1 one-sided traces u_-(t) (from x < s_i(t)) and u_+(t) (from x > s_i(t)) on each curve. Each curve then satisfies Rankine-Hugoniot, σ := s_i'(t) = ( f(u_-) - f(u_+) ) / ( u_- - u_+ ) when u_- ≠ u_+. Such a u is a Kruzhkov entropy solution if and only if at every point of every discontinuity curve the chord condition holds: for every k strictly between u_- and u_+, ( f(k) - f(u_-) ) / ( k - u_- ) ≥ σ ≥ ( f(k) - f(u_+) ) / ( k - u_+ ). Equivalently: if u_+ < u_-, the graph of f on [u_+,u_-] lies on or below the chord joining (u_+,f(u_+)) to (u_-,f(u_-)); if u_- < u_+, the graph of f on [u_-,u_+] lies on or above that chord. If f is strictly convex, this is equivalent to the Lax shock inequalities f'(u_-) ≥ σ ≥ f'(u_+), i.e. to u_- > u_+: a strictly convex flux admits only downward jumps.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:34:33.543870+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_503a791b1755d53c7385e64d56512fef661f8ac68a58a89821ec3caef72ecfb3","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 30 (Coordinate representation) of arXiv:2603.28734, 'Free energy analyticity of the disordered XY model and Debye screening in the 2D Coulomb g'] Let $G$ be a finite graph and $\beta\in[0,\infty)$.
    Define $\mu_{G,\beta}'$ as the probability measure on
    \[
        \tau:=(\alpha,\omega,\eta)\in [0,\tfrac\pi2]^V\times\{0,1\}^E\times\{0,1\}^E:=\Pi_G
    \]
    with density
    \begin{align}
        &
        \diff\mu_{G,\beta}'(\tau)
        \propto
        \textstyle
        \left(\prod_{u\in V}\diff\alpha_u\right)
        \\
        &
        \qquad\qquad
        \textstyle
        \cdot
        2^{k(\omega)}
        \left(
            \prod_{uv\in \omega}
                (1-\e^{-2\beta(\cos\alpha_u)(\cos\alpha_v)})
            \middle)\middle(
            \prod_{uv\not\in\omega}
                e^{-2\beta(\cos\alpha_u)(\cos\alpha_v)}
            \right)
            \\&
            \qquad\qquad
            \textstyle
            \cdot
            2^{k(\eta)}
            \left(
                \prod_{uv\in \eta}
                     (1-\e^{-2\beta(\sin\alpha_u)(\sin\alpha_v)})
                \middle)\middle(
                \prod_{uv\not\in\eta}
                    e^{-2\beta(\sin\alpha_u)(\sin\alpha_v)}
                \right).
    \end{align}
    Here $k(\rho)$ denotes the number of connected components of $(V,\rho)$.

    Now obtain a sample $\sigma\in(\S^1)^V$ as follows:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item Sample $\tau\sim\mu_{G,\beta}'$,
        \item Sample $\xi\in\{-1,+1\}^V$ by flipping a fair coin for each connected component of $\omega$,
        \item Sample $\zeta\in\{-1,+1\}^V$ by flipping a fair coin for each connected component of $\eta$,
        \item Set $\sigma_u:=\xi_u\cos\alpha_u + i\cdot \zeta_u\sin\alpha_u$ for each $u\in V$.
    \end{itemize}
    Then $\sigma\sim\mu_{G,\beta}$.","status":"unverified"}

The self-duality of Z^2 bond percolation at p = 1/2 - the dual of the open configuration at parameter p is a configuration at parameter 1 - p on an isomorphic lattice - makes 1/2 the ONLY candidate but does not by itself decide the critical behaviour, which is why the theorem is hard. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:59:45.016200+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_50c533f92eee13c94cf75100e67172a0b364f9929664e26acbecb80a0b4c4b82","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:stationarity_L1 of arXiv:2605.15401, 'Noise Tradeoffs, Stationary Information Flow, and Structural Balance in Unit-Birth Network'] Consider a CTMC on a countable state space $S$ with transition rates $q(x,y)$
and total exit rate $\Lambda(x)=\sum_{y\neq x}q(x,y)$. Suppose $\pi$ is a
stationary distribution with full support and
\[
\mathbb{E}_\pi[\Lambda(X)]<\infty.
\]
Let $\varphi:S\to\mathbb{R}$ satisfy
\begin{equation}
\sum_{x\in S}\pi(x)\sum_{y\neq x}q(x,y)|\varphi(y)-\varphi(x)|<\infty.
\end{equation}
Then, for every $x\in S$, the series
\[
\sum_{y\neq x} q(x,y)\,|\varphi(y)-\varphi(x)|
\]
is finite, and hence
\[
(L\varphi)(x):=\sum_{y\neq x} q(x,y)\big(\varphi(y)-\varphi(x)\big)
\]
is absolutely convergent and well defined. Moreover, $L\varphi\in L^1(\pi)$
and
\[
\mathbb{E}_\pi\!\big[(L\varphi)(X)\big]=0.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:35:04.096313+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_521d8b2552ac54fe398b53b3651e9496b3fe562d609da8d501e77cfd5cdd303b","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:ricci-removal of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] Let $P_z$ be the rank-one projector onto a unit decomposable bivector and
$C_z=P_z-N^{-1}I_W$.  If $L_z=-2z_{\rm mat}^2$ is the orthogonal
projector onto the plane of $z$, put
\[
 B_z=\frac{L_z-(2/n)I_H}{n-2}.
\tag{2.6.2}
\]
Then the orthogonal curvature decomposition is
\[
 C_z=W_z+X_{B_z},\qquad W_z\in\mathcal W,
 \qquad X_B(u\wedge v)=Bu\wedge v+u\wedge Bv,
\tag{2.6.3}
\]
with no scalar or $\Lambda^4H$ summand, and
\[
 \|B_z\|_\mathrm{op}=\frac1n,\qquad
 \|B_z\|_F^2=\frac{2}{n(n-2)},\qquad
 \|X_B\|_2^2=(n-2)\|B\|_F^2,\qquad
 \|X_B\|_\mathrm{op}\le2\|B\|_\mathrm{op}.
\tag{2.6.4}
\]

In the cumulative moving frame the transported $B_z$ are reverse
martingale differences.  If $\mathfrak B_r$ is their sum, then
\[
 \mathbb E\|\mathfrak B_r\|_F^2=\frac{2r}{n(n-2)},\qquad
 \mathbb E\|\mathfrak B_r\|_F^4
 \le C\frac{r^2}{n^2(n-2)^2},
\tag{2.6.5}
\]
and, for fixed $c$, uniformly over $r\le cN$,
\[
 \max_{r\le cN}\|\mathfrak B_r\|_\mathrm{op}=o_{\mathbb P}(1).
\tag{2.6.6}
\]
More quantitatively, for every fixed $L$ and $1\le p\le L\log n$,
\[
 \left(\mathbb E\max_{r\le cN}\|\mathfrak B_r\|_\mathrm{op}^p\right)^{1/p}
 \le C_{c,L}\left(
 \sqrt{\frac{p+\log n}{n}}+\frac{p+\log n}{n}
 \right)=o(1).
\tag{2.6.6a}
\]
The same martingale satisfies the dimension-free Frobenius estimate
\[
 \left(\mathbb E\max_{r\le cN}\|\mathfrak B_r\|_F^p\right)^{1/p}
 \le C_c\sqrt p,
 \qquad 2\le p\le L\log n.
\tag{2.6.6b}
\]

Finally let $A_i=\operatorname{ad}_{a_i}$.  For traceless symmetric $B$
on $H$ and arbitrary $Z\in\operatorname{End}(W)$, define
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathcal R_i(B,Z)&=\{X_B,[A_i,Z]\}a_i,&
 U_i(B,Z)&=\{X_B,Z\}a_i,\\
 E_i(B,Z)&=\{X_{[a_i,B]},Z\}a_i,&
 \bar E(B,Z)&=N^{-1}\sum_iE_i(B,Z).
\end{aligned}

\]
Put $\Psi(T)=\sum_jA_jTa_j$ and

\[

 -\frac1N\sum_jA_jV_j-H_B(Z)},

and its star-normalized square functions obey

 \frac1N\sum_i\|E_i-\bar E\|^2
 &\le\frac{64}{n-1}\|B\|_F^2\|Z\|_\mathrm{op}^2.

The residue obeys

 \|H_B(Z)\|

        \qquad \Sigma_0>0,
\]

$\widetilde\mu_t$ denote the mean-field solution and let
\[
        \widetilde\mu_t^N:=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\delta_{Y_i(t)}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:42:16.238847+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_52c6d6dde6b7ad7904d5ef61529b9276d55a0cc8fb989cb44357dd27568b6c31","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:jw-degree-law of arXiv:2607.00731, 'Sharp Asymptotics for the Largest Component in the Subcritical Regime of Preferential Atta'] Let $Y_1,\dots,Y_n$ be i.i.d.\ random variables with
\[
\mathbb P(Y_i=k)=\binom{\alpha+k-1}{k}(1-p_n)^{\alpha}p_n^k,
\]
where $$p_n=\frac{2m}{\alpha n+2m}=\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\alpha+2-\varepsilon}.$$
Then
\[
d\bigl(G_{n,m}^{\alpha,\ast}\bigr)\overset{d}= (Y_1,\dots,Y_n)\,\big|\,\{Y_1+\cdots+Y_n=2m\}.
\]
In particular, if $Y^{(n)}\sim\operatorname{NBin}(\alpha,p_n)$, then for every fixed integer $k\ge 0$ and every fixed integer $r\ge 1$,
\[
\pi_k(d)=\mathbb P\bigl(Y^{(n)}=k\bigr)+O_p(n^{-1/2}),
\]
and
$$\mu_r(d)=\mathbb E\bigl[(Y^{(n)})^r\bigr]+O_p(n^{-1/2}).$$
For each fixed $r\ge 1$ one also has $\mathbb E\bigl[(Y^{(n)})^r\bigr]=O(1)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.160651+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_53144a8d46bb675c6426a29502ef6aad25df8a850910735bdde4294bf23b9834","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 6 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Recall the definition of $\Surplus(\YY;\lambda,\mu)$ from the statement of Proposition~\ref{p:convex.body.polytope.bound.new}. 
Recall $\cD_+$ from \eqref{e:cD-plus}.
Given any $\mu$, define 
    \[
        \cD_{+,\mu}(2) \equiv \Big\{
            \YY = (\BBb,\vvv,\UUu,\www) \in \cD_+ : (\mu, \www) \le 2
        \Big\}\,,
    \]
For $(\lambda,\mu) \in \Lambda$ and $\dot{\YY}, \ddot{\YY} \in \cD_{+,\mu}(2)$, we have
    \[\Big|\Surplus(\dot{\YY};\lambda,\mu) - \Surplus(\ddot{\YY};\lambda,\mu)\Big|
        \le
        \frac{4\|\Delta\YY\|_2
            +  6\|\Delta\YY\|_2^{1/2}}{\iota \min\{1,\alpha\}}\,,
    \]
where we abbreviate $\Delta\YY \equiv \dot{\YY} - \ddot{\YY}$. 
That is, $\YY \mapsto \Surplus(\YY;\lambda,\mu)$ is uniformly continuous in $\cD_{+,\mu}(2)$, uniformly in $(\lambda,\mu) \in \Lambda$.

\begin{proof}
We will bound separately the differences 
	\baln
	\Delta\Cost
	& \equiv\Cost(\dot{\YY};\lambda) - \Cost(\ddot{\YY};\lambda)\,,\\
	\Delta\Budget
	& \equiv\Budget(\dot{\YY};\mu) - \Budget(\ddot{\YY};\mu)\,.
	\ealn
Note that for any $\xxxx \in \bbR^r$, the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality gives
    \[
        \sum_{j=1}^r \lambda_j |\xxxx_j|
        \le \bigg(\sum_{j=1}^r \lambda_j |\xxxx_j|^2\bigg)^{1/2}
        \le \|\xxxx\|_2\,.
    \]
    Thus, abbreviating $\Delta\YY
    \equiv(\Delta\vBBb,\Delta\vvvv,\Delta\vUUu,\Delta\vwww)
    \equiv\dot{\YY}-\ddot{\YY}$, we have
    \baln
        |\Delta\Cost|
        &\le \sum_{j=1}^r \lambda_j \bigg\{
            |\Delta\vBBb_j|
            + |\Delta\vUUu_j|
            + \Big|
            (\dot{\vvvv}_j-\dot{\vUUu}_j)_+ - (\ddot{\vvvv}_j-\ddot{\vUUu}_j)_+
            \Big| 
            + 2 \Big|(\dot{\vvvv}_j-\dot{\vUUu}_j)_+^{1/2} - (\ddot{\vvvv}_j-\ddot{\vUUu}_j)_+^{1/2} 
            \Big|
        \bigg\} \\
        &\le \|\Delta\vBBb\|_2
        + \|\Delta\vUUu\|_2
        + \Big\|(\dot{\vvvv}-\dot{\vUUu})_+ - (\ddot{\vvvv}-\ddot{\vUUu})_+
        	\Big\|_2 
        + 2\Big\|(\dot{\vvvv}-\dot{\vUUu})_+^{1/2} - (\ddot{\vvvv}-\ddot{\vUUu})_+^{1/2}
        \Big\|_2\,,
    \ealn
    where the operations $x\mapsto x_+$ and $x\mapsto (x_+)^{1/2}$ are applied entrywise.
    Since $x\mapsto x_+$ is a contraction,
    \[
        \|(\dot{\vvvv}-\dot{\vUUu})_+ - (\ddot{\vvvv}-\ddot{\vUUu})_+\|_2
        \le \|(\dot{\vvvv}-\dot{\vUUu}) - (\ddot{\vvvv}-\ddot{\vUUu})\|_2
        \le \|\Delta\vvvv\|_2 + \|\Delta\vUUu\|_2\,.
    \]
Furthermore, since $|a^{1/2}-b^{1/2}| \le |a-b|^{1/2}$ for all $a,b\ge0$, for any vectors $\vec{a},\vec{b}\in[0,\infty)^r$ we can bound
	\[
	\Big(\|\vec{a}^{1/2}-\vec{b}^{1/2}\|_2\Big)^2
	=\sum_{j=1}^r \Big((a_j)^{1/2}-(b_j)^{1/2}\Big)^2
	\le \sum_{j=1}^r |a_j-b_j| = \|\vec{a}-\vec{b}\|_1\,.
	\]
Applying this estimate gives 
    \baln
        &\bigg(\Big\|(\dot{\vvvv}-\dot{\vUUu})_+^{1/2} - (\ddot{\vvvv}-\ddot{\vUUu})_+^{1/2}\Big\|_2\bigg)^2
        \le 
        \Big\|(\dot{\vvvv}-\dot{\vUUu})_+ - (\ddot{\vvvv}-\ddot{\vUUu})_+
        \Big\|_1 \\
        &\qquad \le 
            \|\Delta\vvvv\|_1
            + \|\Delta\vUUu\|_1 
            \le r^{1/2} \Big(
            \|\Delta\vvvv\|_2
            + \|\Delta\vUUu\|_2
        \Big)\,.
    \ealn
    Finally, crudely upper bounding 
$\|\Delta\vBBb\|_2,
        \|\Delta\vvvv\|_2,
        \|\Delta\vUUu\|_2$ by $\|\Delta\YY\|_2$,
    we obtain
    \[
        |\Delta\Cost|
        \le 4 \|\Delta\YY\|_2
        + 2
        \Big(2 r^{1/2} \|\Delta\YY\|_2 \Big)^{1/2} \,.
    \]
This gives a continuity estimate for the $\Cost$ function.

We next turn to the $\Budget$ function.
    For all $\YY  \in \cD_{+,\mu}(2)$, we have
    \[
        0\le \alpha \cdot \Budget(\YY;\mu) \le (\mu,\vwww) \le 2\,,
    \]
    where the intermediate step is by the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality.
    Therefore,
    \baln
        \alpha |\Delta\Budget| 
        &= \alpha^{1/2} \Big|
        \Budget(\dot{\YY};\mu)^{1/2} + 
        \Budget(\ddot{\YY};\mu)^{1/2}\Big| 
        \cdot 
        \alpha^{1/2} \Big|
        \Budget(\dot{\YY};\mu)^{1/2}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:57:31.001970+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_536b82a2c9a400575b888014cb1a91c6c6308f0a6c2ce3f0df34ef821b5ab280","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 56 (No mass at chaos degree infinity) of arXiv:2608.12492, 'Weak Limits of Wiener Chaos: Primitive--Fock Classification and Hilbert--Stein Extraction'] Let $\mathcal U$ be a free ultrafilter and put
\[
 \cH_q=(H_n^{\odot q},\ip{\cdot}{\cdot})_{\mathcal U}.
\]
Here the factorial normalization has already been absorbed into
$x_{n,a,q}=\sqrt{q!}\,f_{n,a,q}$.
All tensor norms below are the ordinary tensor norms of these scaled coordinates.  The
product transported by the primitive--Fock unitary is the normalized product
\begin{equation}
 u\wtensor_{\mathrm{nor}}v
 =
 \sqrt{\frac{q!}{p!(q-p)!}}\,
 \Sym(u\otimes v),
 \qquad
 u\in H^{\odot p},\quad v\in H^{\odot(q-p)}.
 
\end{equation}
The raw contractions of Section~\ref{all:sec:infinite-feedback} are ordinary
Hilbert tensor contractions of the scaled coordinates.  The dictionary
between the two normalisations used in this paper is therefore
\[
 \underbrace{(H_n^{\odot q},q!\ip{\cdot}{\cdot})_{\mathcal U}}
 _{\text{Parts II--IV, kernels }f_{n,a,q}}
 \;\xrightarrow{\ f\,\mapsto\,x=\sqrt{q!}f\ }\;
 \underbrace{(H_n^{\odot q},\ip{\cdot}{\cdot})_{\mathcal U}}
 _{\text{Parts V--VI, coordinates }x_{n,a,q}},
\]
an isometry which carries $\wtensor$ to $\wtensor_{\mathrm{nor}}$ and
multiplies an $s$-fold contraction of a weight-$p$ by a weight-$q$ coordinate
by $\sqrt{p!\,q!/(p+q-2s)!}$.  No statement below depends on the choice, but
all displayed constants refer to the scaled coordinates.

$x_{a,q}=[x_{n,a,q}]_{\mathcal U}$ satisfy
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{a,q}\norm{x_{a,q}}_{\cH_q}^2
 =
 \lim_{\mathcal U}\sum_{a,q}\norm{x_{n,a,q}}^2.
 
\end{equation}

$\bigoplus_{q\ge1}\cH_q$ and has no additional component at an infinite chaos grade.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:48:47.287549+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_53a63231a14d32986d7b01d953bf29a23589cb9731216344d145a1b7856dcfd9","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma gradient TAP of arXiv:2604.20660, 'The Legendre structure of the TAP complexity\\ for the Ising spin glass'] Recall $\mathrm{TAP}$ from (equation def:TAPmu of the paper) and $k_\zeta$ from~(equation def:kqm of the paper).

		Let $\zeta$ be a probability measure on $[q,1]$. Then for every $i\in[N]$:
		\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
			\item (\emph{Exact gradient at the minimizer}) If $\zeta_\mathbf{m}$ is the minimizer in Definition~(def:zetam of the paper), then
			\begin{equation}
				\partial_i \mathrm{TAP}(\mu_N^{(\mathbf{m})})=-\frac{1}{N}k_{\zeta_\mathbf{m}}(q,m_i).
			\end{equation}
			
			\item (\emph{Exact defect formula and explicit boundary stability}) One has
			\begin{equation}
				-N\partial_i \mathrm{TAP}(\mu_N^{(\mathbf{m})},\zeta)
				=
				k_\zeta(q,m_i)-m_i\,\xi''(q)\,\Delta_\zeta^{\mu_N^{(\mathbf{m})}},
			\end{equation}
			where $\Delta_\zeta^{\mu_N^{(\mathbf{m})}}$ is defined in (equation eq:def-Delta of the paper).
			Consequently, if
			\[
			\max_{j\in[N]}|m_j|\le 1-\delta
			\qquad\text{for some }\delta\in(0,1),
			\]
			and
			\[
			\zeta(\{q\})\ge u_0>0,
			\]

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:15:45.376271+00:00","domain":"general topology","id":"claim_53b62a4d4b0ea879e3c5457fa6f8ecdb78aba2e92827a95ead2ce3351cd5f4ff","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A sequence (x_n) in a metric space (X, d) is Cauchy if for every epsilon > 0 there is an index N such that d(x_m, x_n) < epsilon for all m, n >= N. The metric space (X, d) is complete if every Cauchy sequence in X converges to a point of X. Every convergent sequence is Cauchy, but not conversely in general: the rationals with the usual distance are not complete, while the real line R and Euclidean space R^n are complete. A closed subset of a complete metric space is complete, and a complete subspace of any metric space is closed in it.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["F is continuous","u is continuous on Ω","the equation is written in the form F = 0 with a fixed sign convention"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:57:26.110816+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations, Hamilton–Jacobi equations","id":"claim_53dfc94ed0a9e05577bb2bf64ec2af288dc9f26b2353c233536514d102e5795c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Ω ⊂ ℝⁿ be open and F: Ω × ℝ × ℝⁿ → ℝ continuous; consider the equation F(x, u(x), Du(x)) = 0 in Ω. A function u ∈ C(Ω) is a viscosity SUBsolution if for every φ ∈ C¹(Ω) and every point x₀ ∈ Ω at which u − φ has a local maximum, F(x₀, u(x₀), Dφ(x₀)) ≤ 0. It is a viscosity SUPERsolution if for every φ ∈ C¹(Ω) and every local minimum point x₀ of u − φ, F(x₀, u(x₀), Dφ(x₀)) ≥ 0. It is a viscosity solution if it is both. (Equivalent reformulations: replace 'local' by 'strict local' or 'global' max/min, or use C^∞ test functions, or use super-/subdifferentials D⁺u(x₀) and D⁻u(x₀): the conditions read F(x₀, u, p) ≤ 0 for all p ∈ D⁺u(x₀) and ≥ 0 for all p ∈ D⁻u(x₀).) Every classical C¹ solution is a viscosity solution, and a viscosity solution that is differentiable at x₀ satisfies the equation pointwise there. For time-dependent equations u_t + H(x, Du) = 0 on Ω × (0,T) apply the same definition with the gradient variable (u_t, Du) and test functions of (x,t). SHARP EDGE — the sign of F matters: writing the same equation as −F = 0 interchanges the roles of sub- and supersolutions, so the two forms have DIFFERENT viscosity solutions. Example: on (−1,1) with boundary values u(±1) = 0, the function 1 − |x| is a viscosity solution of |u'| − 1 = 0 but NOT of 1 − |u'| = 0, while |x| − 1 is a viscosity solution of 1 − |u'| = 0 but not of |u'| − 1 = 0 (at the kink x = 0, a concave kink admits only test functions touching from above, and a convex kink only test functions touching from below). Viscosity solutions are in general only continuous, are stable under uniform limits, and for convex H coincide with Lipschitz solutions that are semiconcave; the notion is designed so that comparison/uniqueness theorems hold where classical and a.e. solutions are non-unique.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.348469+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5416a777be1cc30c7c8f9a9bebbe4d2ca70960a8272285b96d45fe6a1e694b32","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 162 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $I$ be a finite, nonempty index set. Let 
  \[
    \lt(\Theta, 
    \vec{\hat{Z}}\equiv
    (\hat Z_i)_{i\in I},
    \vec{\tilde{Z}}
    \equiv(\tilde Z_i)_{i\in I}\rt)
  \]
  be a random variable where
  $(\vec{\hat{Z}},\vec{\tilde{Z}})$
  are centered, jointly gaussian, and independent of $\Theta$. 
  Assume that $\vec{\hat{Z}}$ and $\vec{\tilde{Z}}$ are equidistributed,
 and that, for distinct $i,k\in I$,
  \[
    \bbE[\hat Z_i\hat Z_k]
    =\bbE[\tilde Z_i\tilde Z_k]
    =\bbE[\hat Z_i\tilde Z_k]=0.
  \]
Let $F$ and $G$ be measurable functions
such that $F(\Theta,\hat Z)$ and 
$G(\Theta,\hat Z)$ have finite variance, and such that
	\beq
    \bbE\Big[F(\Theta,\hat Z) 
    	\,\Big|\, \Theta\Big] = 0 = 
    \bbE\Big[G(\Theta,\tilde Z) 
    	\,\Big|\, \Theta\Big]\,,
    \eeq
  $\Theta$-almost surely.
Then the covariance between $F(\Theta,\hat{Z})$ and $G(\Theta,\tilde{Z})$ is bounded by
  \beq
    \lt| \bbE[F(\Theta,\hat Z) G(\Theta,\tilde Z)] \rt|
    \le
    \rho_{\max} \cdot
    \bbE[F(\Theta,\hat Z)^2]^{1/2}
    \bbE[G(\Theta,\tilde Z)^2]^{1/2}\,, 
    
  \eeq
where $\rho_i\in[-1,+1]$ denotes the correlation between $\hat{Z}_i$ and $\tilde{Z}_i$, and 
$\rho_{\max} 
   \equiv\max\{|\rho_i|: i\in i\}$.
 
\begin{proof}
Let $\sigma_i$ denote the standard deviation of $\hat{Z}_i$, and denote
  \[
    \hat W_i \equiv 
    \frac{\hat Z_i}{\sigma_i}\,, \quad
    \tilde W_i 
    \equiv \frac{\tilde Z_i}{\sigma_i}\,,
  \]
which are marginally standard gaussians. It follows from the assumptions that
$(\hat W_i,\tilde W_i)$ are independent over $i\in I$, and $\bbE[\hat W_i\tilde W_i]=\rho_i$.
Let $(h_m)_{m\geq 0}$ denote the orthonormal Hermite polynomials for the
one-dimensional standard gaussian measure. We note that if $W$ and $\tilde{W}$ are marginally standard gaussians, and $(W,\tilde{W})$ is jointly gaussian and $\rho$-correlated, then it is straightforward to verify that
	\beq
	\E[ h_n(W) h_m(\tilde{W})]
	= \ind\{n=m\} \rho^n\,.\eeq
 For a multi-index $\vec n=(n_i)_{i\in I}\in\bbZ_{\ge 0}^I$, define the multivariate Hermite polynomial
  \[
    H_{\vec n}(w)
    \equiv\prod_{i\in I}h_{n_i}(w_i).
  \]
  We expand $F,G$ in the Hermite bases of $\hat W$ and $\tilde W$ respectively, conditional on $\Theta$, to obtain Hermite coefficients $a_{\vec n}(\Theta)$ and $b_{\vec n}(\Theta)$ such that
  \begin{align*}
    F(\Theta,\hat Z)
    &= \sum_{\vec n}a_{\vec n}(\Theta)
        H_{\vec n}(\hat W)\,, \\
    G(\Theta,\tilde Z)
    &= \sum_{\vec n}b_{\vec n}(\Theta)
        H_{\vec n}(\tilde W)\,.
  \end{align*}
  The assumption \eqref{e:conditional-centering} ensures $a_{\vec 0}(\Theta)=b_{\vec 0}(\Theta)=0$, $\Theta$-almost surely.
  Consequently, expanding in the Hermite bases and applying \eqref{e:hermite.corr.ip} gives
  \begin{align*}
    &\bigg|
      \bbE\Big[
        F(\Theta,\hat Z)G(\Theta,\tilde Z) \,\Big|\, \Theta
      \Big]
    \bigg|
    \le
      \sum_{\vec n\neq\vec 0}
         |a_{\vec n}(\Theta)b_{\vec n}(\Theta)|
         \prod_{i\in I}|\rho_i|^{n_i}\\
    &\qquad\le
      \rho_{\max}
      \bigg(\sum_{\vec n\neq\vec 0}
        a_{\vec n}(\Theta)^2
        \bigg)^{1/2}
      \bigg(\sum_{\vec n\neq\vec 0}
        b_{\vec n}(\Theta)^2
        \bigg)^{1/2}
    =\rho_{\max}
      \bbE\Big[F(\Theta,\hat Z)^2 
      	\,\Big|\, \Theta\Big]^{1/2}
      \bbE\Big[G(\Theta,\tilde Z)^2 
      	\,\Big|\, \Theta\Big]^{1/2}\,.
  \end{align*}
  Taking expectation over $\Theta$ and again applying the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality proves the conclusion.
\end{proof}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:32:23.712545+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_541bc79eaed85f810b8436319a9cd709cd15a1e8f1e30341ff0cfb0f3701102a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem th:Foster-Liapunov of arXiv:2603.20078, '\bf \Large Gated Infinite Server Queues in Light Traffic'] Suppose

{"assumptions":["the operator is densely defined but not assumed symmetric or closed","a closure or a core argument is being invoked"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.772684+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, unbounded operators","id":"claim_54940f80014d70dd9eb95c49c095eba47a53c4de71e730a15c0f74ec018b6e59","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: 'take the closure of T' presupposes that T is closable, i.e. that x_n ∈ D(T), x_n → 0 and Tx_n → y force y = 0; equivalently (in a Hilbert space) that D(T*) is dense. What fails: without closability the closure of the graph is not a graph, and 'the smallest closed extension' does not exist. Counterexample: H = ℓ², D(T) = finitely supported sequences, T x = (Σ_n x_n) e_1. T is densely defined and linear. Take x^{(k)} = (1/k, ..., 1/k, 0, 0, ...) with k entries: ‖x^{(k)}‖ = 1/√k → 0 while T x^{(k)} = e_1 for every k, so the graph closure contains both (0,0) and (0, e_1) and T is not closable. Consistently, ⟨Tx, y⟩ = (Σ x_n) conj(y_1) is ℓ²-bounded in x only if y_1 = 0, so D(T*) = {y : y_1 = 0} is not dense - exactly the criterion. The same phenomenon occurs for pointwise evaluation f ↦ f(0)g on L²(ℝ) restricted to continuous L² functions. Related traps: (i) an operator can be closable while its closure has strictly larger domain on which a defining formula no longer holds pointwise, so identities proved on D(T) must be re-derived by continuity in the graph norm; (ii) symmetry rescues closability (a symmetric operator is always closable, since T ⊂ T* and T* is closed), which is why this pitfall bites mainly for non-symmetric operators such as first order operators with unbalanced boundary conditions or multiplication-composition operators; (iii) a core argument ('it suffices to verify on a dense subspace') is valid only if the subspace is dense in the graph norm of the closed operator, not merely dense in the ambient space.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:17:10.025497+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_54ae114798ca9a256a2c70700fa791a86f298aba79d645fb75c2a110914ca5b2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 16 (Kac's walk applied to the Johnson--Lindenstrauss transform) of arXiv:2608.17374, '\textbf{On the Pseudo-Mixing of Kac's Walk}'] There is a universal constant $C_{\mathrm{JL}}<\infty$ such that the following holds. Let $n\geq 2$, let $x\in\So{n}$, and let $M\sim\kacdist_{n,T,x}$ be the endpoint of $T$ steps of Kac's walk started from $x$. Let $\mathcal X\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ have $N\geq2$ points, and let $0<\varepsilon,\delta<1/2$. Set
\be 
r=\left\lceil \log\frac{N}{\delta}\right\rceil,
\ee
and assume $4r<n$. Let $\ell$ be an integer satisfying
\be 
C_{\mathrm{JL}}\varepsilon^{-2}r\leq \ell<n.
\ee

If
\be 
T\geq
C_{\mathrm{JL}}\,n(4r+\log n)\left(r\log\frac{n}{\varepsilon}+\log\frac{N}{\delta}\right),
\ee
then, with probability at least $1-\delta$ over $M\sim\kacdist_{n,T,x}$,
\be 
(1-\varepsilon)\|x_i-x_j\|_2^2
\leq
\|A_M(x_i-x_j)\|_2^2
\leq
(1+\varepsilon)\|x_i-x_j\|_2^2
\ee
for every pair $1\leq i<j\leq N$.

In particular, for fixed $\varepsilon$ and $N/\delta\leq n^A$, with $A<\infty$ fixed, the usual Johnson--Lindenstrauss target dimension $\ell=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(N/\delta))=O_A(\varepsilon^{-2}\log n)$ \vnote{Isn't the JL target dimension $\epsilon^{-2}\log N$? EDIT: Ah, I see what's going on, $N$ is set to polynomial in $n$. But see below.} is achieved by taking $T\geq C_A n\log^3 n$. \vnote{I am worried that this is not the best illustration of our bound. In particular, when $N$ is polynomial in $n$, the JL embedding dimension $\ell$ is already $O(\log n)$ and so applying the matrix already only costs $O(n\log n)$. Shouldn't we be thinking about very large point sets of size, say $2^{n^{\epsilon'}}$ for some constant $0 < \epsilon' < 1$.} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.751292+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_54d64fad1e4608f5ad2108eaf3e69d53ceffd8a53470cf0276a225deb916e63a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Tonelli's theorem needs BOTH measures sigma-finite and the integrand nonnegative and product-measurable; it then asserts that the double integral and both iterated integrals agree in [0, infinity], with no integrability assumption. Fubini's theorem needs both measures sigma-finite and f in L^1(mu tensor nu); it then asserts the same equality with all three quantities finite. Two failure modes are standard and are NOT the same failure. (1) Integrability dropped, sigma-finiteness kept: on (0,1)^2 with Lebesgue measure take f(x,y) = (x^2 - y^2)/(x^2 + y^2)^2. Since d/dy [ y/(x^2+y^2) ] = (x^2 - y^2)/(x^2+y^2)^2, the inner integral over y in (0,1) is 1/(1+x^2), so integrating in x afterwards gives pi/4; f is antisymmetric under swapping x and y, so the other order gives -pi/4. Both iterated integrals exist and are finite and they differ, so f cannot be in L^1 of the product. (2) sigma-finiteness dropped, nonnegativity kept: let mu be Lebesgue measure on [0,1], nu counting measure on [0,1], and f the indicator of the diagonal. Then integral over x of (integral over y of f dnu) dmu = integral 1 dmu = 1, while integral over y of (integral over x of f dmu) dnu = integral 0 dnu = 0. Tonelli's conclusion fails although f >= 0, because nu is not sigma-finite. A third, quieter caveat: for COMPLETE measure spaces the correct statement is that ALMOST every section is measurable, not every section, since a null set in the product can have non-measurable sections; the theorem for the completed product measure is stated that way. In practice the usable recipe is: apply Tonelli to |f| first to decide integrability, then apply Fubini to f. [standard; e.g. Folland, Real Analysis, 2nd ed., Theorems 2.37 and 2.39]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:35:19.876191+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_550f9f8a3b419eb6f07e3074b654c0e830eb5b9c8987ff82123178743b7fdb0e","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn of arXiv:2608.27939, 'Entropy and domination for quasi-Hitchin representations'] Let $X$ be a marked hyperbolic structure on $S$, let
$\rho_0:\pi_1(S)\to\mathrm{PSL}(2,\mathbb R)$ be its holonomy, and identify
$\widetilde X$ with $\mathbb{H}^2$. Given a representation
$\rho:\pi_1(S)\to\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{C})$, a \emph{$\rho$-equivariant pleated plane}
is a continuous map  $\Psi:\widetilde X\longrightarrow \mathbb{H}^3$
such that
\[
        \Psi\bigl(\gamma \cdot x\bigr)
        =\rho(\gamma)\Psi(x)
        \qquad
        \text{for every $\gamma\in\pi_1(S)$ and $x\in\widetilde X$,}
\]
and with the following properties:

(i) There is a geodesic lamination $\lambda$ on $X$ such that $\Psi$ is a totally-geodesic embedding on the closure of every complementary component of its lift $\tilde{\lambda} \subset \tilde{X}$. Such a component $P$ is called a \textit{plaque} and its $\Psi$-image lies on a totally-geodesic copy of the hyperbolic plane $H_P \subset \mathbb{H}^3$, called the \emph{support plane} of $P$.

(ii) $\Psi$ is path-isometric: for every rectifiable arc
$a\subset\widetilde X$, $\ell_{\mathbb{H}^3}(\Psi(a))
        =\ell_{X}(a)$, 
where the length on the left is the length of the parametrized
image. The smallest geodesic lamination for which these properties
hold is the \emph{pleating locus}.

(iii) The pleating locus is equipped with a transverse measure recording
the bending angles. More precisely, if a leaf $\ell\subset \widetilde\lambda$, of weight
$\theta\in(0,\pi]$ separates two plaques $P_-$ and $P_+$, the support plane $H_{P_+}$ is obtained from
$H_{P_-}$ by an elliptic rotation about the geodesic
$\Psi(\ell)$ through angle $\theta$; the direction of rotation is
determined by the chosen orientations.

More generally, let $a$ be an oriented arc transverse to
$\widetilde\lambda$, with endpoints in plaques $P$ and $Q$.
Approximating the measured lamination in a neighborhood of $a$ by
finitely many weighted leaves, one may compose, in their order along
$a$, the rotations through the corresponding bending angles about
the successive images of their leaves. The convergence theorem for
quakebend cocycles (see
[EpsteinMarden], and also
[BonShear]) implies that these ordered products converge in
$\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{C})$ to an isometry  $B_{\widetilde\lambda}(P,Q)\in\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{C})$. 
The limit is independent of the finite approximation and satisfies
\begin{equation*} 
    B_{\widetilde\lambda}(P,R)
        =
                B_{\widetilde\lambda}(P,Q) 
        B_{\widetilde\lambda}(Q,R)
\end{equation*} 
where the composition is from left to right. This $B_{\widetilde\lambda}$ is the
\emph{bending cocycle} (see also [Dumas]). 
The rotation-angle component of the bending defines a transverse measure  on $\widetilde\lambda$; from the equivariance it descends to a measured
geodesic lamination $\lambda$ on $X$ that we call the \textit{bending lamination}. Moreover, 

the \emph{straightening} of $\Psi$ is obtained by replacing the bending cocycle by the trivial cocycle; its intrinsic hyperbolic structure is $X$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(L1) subadditivity","(L2) stationarity of the sequence of blocks of each fixed length","(L3) the row law does not depend on the starting index","(L4) E[X_{0,1}^+] finite and a linear lower bound on E[X_{0,n}]","ergodicity of the block sequences is needed only for a constant limit"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.542341+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory","id":"claim_5512c8e378a10d1dd7b71a2d5741379e9a70c5f5d022ab969d1836e21965a057","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let {X_{m,n} : 0 <= m < n} satisfy: (L1) X_{0,n} <= X_{0,m} + X_{m,n} for every 0 < m < n; (L2) for each m >= 1 the sequence {X_{nm, (n+1)m} : n >= 1} is STATIONARY; (L3) the distribution of the row {X_{m, m+k} : k >= 1} does not depend on m; (L4) E[X_{0,1}^+] < infinity and E[X_{0,n}] >= -c_0 n for every n, for some finite c_0. Then: (a) gamma = lim_n E[X_{0,n}]/n = inf_n E[X_{0,n}]/n exists in [-c_0, infinity); (b) X = lim_n X_{0,n}/n exists almost surely and in L^1, with E[X] = gamma; (c) if in addition all the stationary sequences in (L2) are ERGODIC then X = gamma almost surely. The difference from Kingman is that (L2) and (L3) together are strictly WEAKER than joint stationarity of the whole array: they demand stationarity only along each fixed block length and equality of the row laws, not invariance of the full joint distribution. That weakening is what lets the theorem apply to models where the array is not generated by a single measure-preserving transformation. Note also that (L4) asks only for the POSITIVE part of X_{0,1} to be integrable, weaker than Kingman's E|X_{0,1}| < infinity. Quoting Kingman's hypotheses when using Liggett's conclusion, or the reverse, is the standard misquotation here. [Liggett (1985), 'An improved subadditive ergodic theorem', Ann. Probab. 13, 1279-1285; textbook form in Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 6.6.1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["targets at every design point are mean plus noise with the noise independent of the calibration sample (so Cov(e, f(x)) = 0)","the weights on each point set sum to one; the family f_t is any family of fitted predictors (linearity in t is not needed for the identity, only for the cheap computation of the blend's cross-validated and bootstrap predictions)"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T12:56:40.878952+00:00","domain":"regression / model assessment / transductive selection","id":"claim_553662417244b971618b1a8e4cc64e9cead1479c7050963b070adb0204ea329f","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f be a predictor fitted on a calibration sample, evaluated at design points x with targets y = mu(x) + e, where e has mean zero and variance sigma^2(x) and is independent of the sample. For a weighted average over a set of evaluation points E and the same average over the calibration points C (weights w_x summing to one on each set), write R_E = sum_E w_x E(y - f(x))^2 for the expected weighted risk on E, R_C the same on C, V_S = sum_S w_x Var f(x) for the average estimation variance on a set S, B_S = sum_S w_x (mu(x) - E f(x))^2 for the average squared bias, and N_S = sum_S w_x sigma^2(x) for the average noise. Then R_E = R_C + (V_E - V_C) + (B_E - B_C) + (N_E - N_C). Consequently, for a family of predictors f_t indexed by t (for instance a blend that is linear in t between two fitted bases), the minimiser over t of R_E(t) is the minimiser of R_C(t) + [V_E(t) - V_C(t)] + [B_E(t) - B_C(t)], the noise difference being free of t. A label-free criterion that replaces R_C(t) by the cross-validated risk on the calibration rows and V_E(t), V_C(t) by pairs-bootstrap estimates - the transductive covariance penalty used to choose the amount of simplex constraint at the scored rows - is this identity with the bias-shift term dropped; its single assumption is that the squared bias of the family shifts between the two point sets by an amount that does not depend on t, or does so less than the variance shift. What it cannot see is exactly the bias shift, which needs the targets at the new points; that is why such a criterion recovers only part of the hindsight-best t and errs toward the endpoint the calibration rows favour.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X_i independent with E[X_i] = 0","one-sided bound X_i <= b almost surely (no lower bound needed for the upper tail)","v = sum_i E[X_i^2] finite"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.627726+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5539ab1dd12776494ca55d16665e0670d5e85f01452dc2694daade30bd0d0cca","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, ..., X_n be independent random variables with E[X_i] = 0 and X_i <= b almost surely for every i - a ONE-SIDED bound suffices for the upper tail - and let v = sum_{i=1}^n E[X_i^2]. Then for every t > 0, P( sum_i X_i >= t ) <= exp( - (v/b^2) h(bt/v) ) where h(u) = (1+u) log(1+u) - u. Bennett's inequality implies Bernstein's inequality through h(u) >= u^2/(2(1 + u/3)), which gives the familiar P(sum X_i >= t) <= exp(-t^2/(2(v + bt/3))), and it is strictly sharper in the large-deviation regime bt/v large, where Bennett decays like exp(-(t/b) log(bt/v)) - a Poisson tail - while Bernstein decays only like exp(-3t/(2b)). This is the right inequality when the summands are bounded but their variance is much smaller than the square of the bound, the regime where Hoeffding's inequality is badly lossy. [Bennett (1962); see Boucheron, Lugosi and Massart, Concentration Inequalities, Theorem 2.9]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-06T03:36:16.697768+00:00","domain":"harvested statement (arXiv 2512.18592, 2025): mathematics","id":"claim_553e933b88264eee9732d2a61a730e1b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 3.3 (Adaptive wavelet estimation) in the first version of arXiv:2512.18592, 'Wavelet Latent Position Exponential Random Graphs'] Assume that conditional on observed latent positions $U_{1},\\dots,U_{n}\\in[0,1]$, the edges $\\{A_{ij}:1\\leq i<j\\leq n\\}$ are independent with $A_{ij}\\mid(U_{k})_{k=1}^{n}\\sim\\mathrm{Bernoulli}\\bigl(W(U_{i},U_{j})\\bigr),$ for a symmetric graphon $W:[0,1]^{2}\\to[0,1]$. Let $N_{n}:=\\binom{n}{2}$ and assume $W\\in\\mathcal{F}^{s}_{p,q}(M)\\cap[0,1],\\qquad s>0,\\quad 1\\leq p\\leq 2,\\quad 0<q\\leq\\infty,$ where $\\mathcal{F}^{s}_{p,q}(M)$ is the Besov ball from Definition 3.1. Let $\\{\\Psi_{\\lambda}\\}_{\\lambda}$ be an orthonormal tensor-product wavelet basis of $L^{2}([0,1]^{2})$ of regularity $r>s$, and assume there exists $C_{\\Psi}<\\infty$ such that $\\|\\Psi_{\\lambda}\\|_{\\infty}\\leq C_{\\Psi}\\,2^{j(\\lambda)}$ for all indices $\\lambda$. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:35:19.873914+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5547254edcb16a77cf208749f2a9dea83f0c9955664164ca7d90e3604a1b049e","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn lengths of arXiv:2608.27939, 'Entropy and domination for quasi-Hitchin representations'] Given a representation $\rho:\pi_1(S)\to \mathrm{PSL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ and $\gamma\in\pi_1(S)$, let $A\in \mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ be a determinant-one  lift of $\rho(\gamma)$ and let $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$ be the eigenvalues of $A$ ordered so that $|\lambda_1|\le\cdots\le |\lambda_n|$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The \emph{Hilbert length} of $\gamma$ with respect to $\rho$ is
\[
\ell^H_{\rho}(\gamma):=\log\Bigg|\frac{\lambda_n}{\lambda_1}\Bigg|.
\]
\item The \emph{translation length} of $\gamma$ with respect to $\rho$ is the translation length of $\rho(\gamma)$ in the symmetric space $\mathbb{X}_n=\mathrm{PSL}_n(\mathbb{C})/\mathrm{PSU}(n)$, namely
\[
\ell_{\rho}(\gamma):=\ell_{\mathbb{X}_n}(\rho(\gamma))
=\sqrt{2\big((\log|\lambda_1|)^2+\cdots+(\log|\lambda_n|)^2\big)}.
\]
\end{enumerate}
(These expressions are well-defined, i.e.\ independent of the choice of the determinant-one lift $A$; two such lifts differ by multiplication by an $n$-th root of unity.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.190459+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_556f2b6181c59184ef7ab9c6102e0e7432deb1fea508d31399e6848f0fcaf303","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 106 (SDE coefficients with spatial smoothing
	and coordinate sum projection) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\sphicirc:\R\to[0,\infty)$ be a smooth nonnegative function that integrates to one and has support $[-1,1]$. We also assume that we have

	\beq

 Recall from Definition~\ref{d:projected.coeffs} the notation $\rho\mapsto\bar{\rho}$ for the coordinate sum projection.

	\begin{align*}

{"assumptions":["(X, B, mu, T) is an invertible measure-preserving system on a standard (Lebesgue) probability space","T is ergodic with respect to mu","G is a compact metrizable group with normalized Haar measure m","phi : X -> G is measurable and the extension is T_phi(x,g) = (Tx, phi(x) g) on mu x m","solutions F of the transfer equation are required only to be measurable (matrix-valued), not continuous"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:09:43.732127+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, skew products, cocycles and group extensions","id":"claim_55b03d25b04f083e6d2634636c495b808dc293ac41f7f84754595cf15210a9be","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, B, mu, T) be an invertible measure-preserving system on a standard probability space with T ERGODIC. Let G be a compact metrizable group with normalized Haar measure m, let phi : X -> G be measurable, and let T_phi(x, g) = (T x, phi(x) g) be the associated group extension of (X x G, mu x m). Then:

  T_phi is ergodic  <=>  for EVERY nontrivial irreducible unitary representation pi : G -> U(d_pi), the functional (transfer) equation
        F(T x) = pi(phi(x)) F(x)      for mu-a.e. x
  has no nonzero MEASURABLE solution F : X -> M_{d_pi}(C).

Equivalently, ergodicity fails exactly when some nontrivial pi admits such a nonzero F. A nonzero solution can always be normalized so that its Hilbert-Schmidt norm is constant, because ||F(x)||_HS is then a T-invariant function and T is ergodic.

Abelian case (the form most often used). If G is abelian, the irreducible representations are the characters chi in the dual group, and the criterion reads: T_phi is ergodic if and only if for every nontrivial character chi there is NO measurable h : X -> S^1 with h(T x) = chi(phi(x)) h(x); i.e. no nontrivial character of phi is a measurable multiplicative coboundary. For G = S^1 and phi written additively this is: for every nonzero integer n, the equation u(T x) - u(x) = n * phi(x) (mod 1) has no measurable solution u.

SHARP EDGES. (1) Ergodicity of the BASE T is a hypothesis, not a conclusion: if T is not ergodic then T_phi is not ergodic either (invariant sets of the base lift), and the displayed equivalence is false as stated without it. (2) Compactness of G is essential -- the proof uses the Haar PROBABILITY measure and the Peter-Weyl decomposition of L^2(G); for noncompact G (e.g. G = R, cylinder flows) the natural invariant measure is infinite and ergodicity is a genuinely different problem. (3) 'Measurable' cannot be weakened to 'continuous': a cocycle can be a measurable coboundary without being a continuous one, so verifying that the equation has no CONTINUOUS solution does not certify ergodicity. (4) Every nontrivial irreducible pi must be tested, not one convenient one. Example: G = S^1 and phi taking values in {+1, -1} with the induced two-point extension ergodic. Then for the character chi_1(z) = z the equation has no solution (that is exactly ergodicity of the two-point extension), yet chi_2(z) = z^2 satisfies chi_2(phi(x)) = 1, so h identically 1 solves the equation for chi_2 -- and indeed T_phi is not ergodic, since phi lives in the proper closed subgroup {+1,-1}.","status":"unverified"}

There is a subcollection S of pairwise DISJOINT balls such that every B_i is contained in 3B for some B in S, where 3B denotes the ball with the same centre as B and three times the radius. Consequently the union of all the B_i is contained in the union of the dilates 3B over B in S, and in R^d with Lebesgue measure |union_i B_i| <= 3^d sum_{B in S} |B|. The constant 3 is what makes the greedy argument work; 2 + eps also works for any eps > 0 with a slightly more careful selection, but 2 does not. In a general metric space the same greedy proof works for a finite family; for infinite families one needs either uniformly bounded radii (the 5r covering lemma) or a Vitali-type fine-cover hypothesis. [standard; e.g. Stein and Shakarchi, Real Analysis, Lemma 1.2 of Chapter 3]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["1 <= p < infinity","all three conditions (boundedness, uniform translation-continuity, uniform tightness); on a bounded domain tightness is automatic"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.752488+00:00","domain":"functional analysis","id":"claim_55f7009e84a2c8aa0d6a0ebd9fd1b1397cfed669b44ad4e89536ea54eab897b5","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let 1 <= p < infinity. A subset F of L^p(R^d) is relatively compact in the norm topology if and only if all three of the following hold: (i) F is BOUNDED, sup_{f in F} ||f||_p < infinity; (ii) F is uniformly continuous under translation, sup_{f in F} ||f(. + h) - f||_p -> 0 as h -> 0; (iii) F is uniformly TIGHT, sup_{f in F} integral_{|x| > R} |f|^p dx -> 0 as R -> infinity. Conditions (ii) and (iii) are each independent of the rest and cannot be dropped: the family {n^{d/p} 1_{B(0,1/n)}} is bounded in L^p and tight but not uniformly translation-continuous, since for |h| >= 2/n the translate is disjoint from the original; and the family {1_{[n, n+1]}} is bounded and uniformly translation-continuous but not tight, and has no L^p-convergent subsequence. Boundedness is listed as a separate condition here for safety - some treatments observe that it can be derived from the other two - and stating it explicitly costs nothing. On a bounded domain condition (iii) is automatic and the criterion reduces to (i) and (ii). The criterion is FALSE for p = infinity, where the analogue is Arzela-Ascoli on compacts plus a suitable equicontinuity. This is the L^p analogue of Arzela-Ascoli, with translation-continuity playing the role of equicontinuity. [Kolmogorov (1931), M. Riesz (1933), Frechet (1937); see Hanche-Olsen and Holden, 'The Kolmogorov-Riesz compactness theorem', Expo. Math. 28 (2010)]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T00:41:11.649647+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5616c88e86c184a5906752e46579ef1877c0cc14aab314dc20269c1a16f40246","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop generator_continuous_process of arXiv:2411.13964, 'Long-time analysis of a pair of on-lattice and continuous run-and-tumble particles with ja'] Let $\mathcal L$ be
  the generator of the continuous process. Its domain $D(\mathcal L)$
  is the set of bounded measurable functions
  $f : E_D \rightarrow \mathbb R$ such that
\begin{itemize}
\item for $\sigma \in \Sigma_+ \setminus \Sigma_-$ the function
  $f( \cdot, \sigma)$ is absolutely continuous on $[0, \ell)$ and
  $\lim_{x \rightarrow \ell} f(x, \sigma) =
  f\left(\ell,*_\sigma^\ell\right)$,
\item for $\sigma \in \Sigma_+ \setminus \Sigma_-$ the function
  $f(\cdot, \sigma)$ is absolutely continuous on $(0, \ell]$ and
  $\lim_{x \rightarrow 0} f(x, \sigma) = f\left(0, *_\sigma^0\right)$.
\end{itemize}

For $f \in D(\mathcal L)$ one has that
\begin{itemize}
\item in the bulk $\cup_{\sigma \in \Sigma} E_\sigma$ the generator
  comprises a transport term and a jump term
\begin{align*}
\mathcal L f(x, (\sigma^1, \sigma^2)) = &\underbrace{(\sigma^2 - \sigma^1) \partial_x f(x, (\sigma^1, \sigma^2))}_{\text{\normalfont transport term}} \\
&\quad + \underbrace{\lambda(x,\nu) \int_{E_D} \left(f(\tilde x, \tilde \nu) - f(x, (\sigma^1, \sigma^2))\right) dQ\left((x, (\sigma^1, \sigma^2)); (\tilde x, \tilde \nu)\right)}_{\text{\normalfont jump term}},
\end{align*}
\item whereas for boundary states
  $(x, \nu) \in \cup_{\nu \in \partial K} E_\nu$ the generator is
  given only by the jump term
$$
\mathcal L f(x, \nu) = \lambda(x, \nu) \int_{E_D} \left(f(\tilde x, \tilde
  \nu) - f(x, \nu)\right) dQ((x, \nu); (\tilde x, \tilde \nu))
$$
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the joint law of the points is invariant under reflection of any subset through the origin","the points are almost surely in general position (every d or fewer are linearly independent)","independence of the points is not required"],"created_at":"2026-08-20T03:43:30.215579+00:00","domain":"geometric probability","id":"claim_5624e3058d31a9a0d57cd8be58c608b9944691397689c7cd52a7d35a6247e504","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $x_1,\\dots,x_N$ be random points in $\\mathbb{R}^d$ whose joint law is invariant under reflection of any subset of them through the origin, and which are almost surely in general position. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:52:08.674656+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_563635ce248309438812ffeb056905e9e435f832b097a31d3275e454fae19268","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 44 (Uniform lifted linear Schauder estimate) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Fix \(m\geq2\) and \(\sigma\in(0,1)\).  Let \(s(t)\), \(a\leq t\leq b\),
be a Ricci flow satisfying \(\PBG_m(s;\Lambda;[a,b])\) for some \(\Lambda\geq1\).
Let \(E\) be a fixed finite-rank tensor bundle and consider,
on the universal cover and in the charts of
Lemma~\ref{lem:uniform-parabolic-atlas}, a system
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal P U
 =\partial_tU-a^{ij}\nabla_i\nabla_jU-B^i\nabla_iU-CU=F.
\end{equation}
Assume that the second-order part is diagonal in the bundle components and
uses the same coefficient matrix \(a^{ij}\) on every component.  For fixed
constants \(0<\lambda_-\leq\lambda_+<\infty\), suppose that
\[
 \lambda_- s^{ij}\xi_i\xi_j\leq a^{ij}\xi_i\xi_j
 \leq\lambda_+ s^{ij}\xi_i\xi_j,
\]
and that the local
\(C^{m-2+\sigma,(m-2+\sigma)/2}\)-norms of \(a,B,C\) are bounded by
\(A_0\).

Every smooth bounded solution on the universal cover satisfies, for
\(\theta>0\) with \(a+\theta\leq b\),
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
 \|U\|_{C^{m+\sigma,(m+\sigma)/2}_{\mathrm{uloc}}
          (\widetilde M\times[a+\theta,b],s)}
 \leq C_\theta\bigl(&
       \|U\|_{C^0(\widetilde M\times[a,b],s)}\\
       &+\|F\|_{C^{m-2+\sigma,(m-2+\sigma)/2}_{\mathrm{uloc}}}\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
For the global estimate, assume in addition that \(\mathcal P\) is
deck-invariant, equivalently that the coefficient fields \(a,B,C\) descend to
\(M\).  If \(U\) and \(F\) are deck-invariant and descend to tensors \(u\)
and \(f\) on \(M\), with \(u(a)\in C^{m,\sigma}\) and
\(f\in Y_s^m[a,b]\), then
\begin{equation}
 \|u\|_{X_s^m[a,b]}
 \leq C\left(
      \|u(a)\|_{C^{m,\sigma}(M,s(a))}
      +\|f\|_{Y_s^m[a,b]}\right).
\end{equation}
The constants depend only on
\(m,\sigma,\Lambda,\lambda_-,\lambda_+,A_0\), on \(\theta\) in the interior
estimate, and on an upper bound for \(b-a\).  The interior and initial-face
estimates are based, respectively, on Lieberman's interior Schauder theorem
\cite[Theorem~4.9, p.~59]{Lieberman} and his Cauchy--Dirichlet Schauder theorem
\cite[Theorem~4.28, p.~77]{Lieberman}.  All atlas-radius, overlap, and cutoff
constants, fixed-coordinate ellipticity constants, localized initial-face
boundary-chart constants, and coefficient H\"older constants are uniform over
the admissible family specified by \(\PBG_m\) and the displayed bounds.  In
particular, the constants are independent of collapse of the compact quotient.","status":"unverified"}
