{"assumptions":["(X, Sigma, mu) is a measure space","f is Sigma-measurable","0 < p < infinity for the quasi-norm formula"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:36.551797+00:00","domain":"real analysis, Lp spaces","id":"claim_56428cce7b939634b8046806c62ca819a8a8f81caa9b6e1f7436a073f0e11f58","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"For a measurable f on a measure space (X, Sigma, mu), the distribution function is d_f(t) = mu({x : |f(x)| > t}) for t > 0; it is nonincreasing and right-continuous. For 0 < p < infinity the weak L^p quasi-norm is ||f||_{L^{p,infinity}} = sup_{t>0} t * d_f(t)^{1/p}, and weak L^p = L^{p,infinity}(mu) is the set of (a.e.-classes of) measurable f with this quantity finite; by convention L^{infinity,infinity} = L^infinity. It is a quasi-norm: ||f+g||_{L^{p,infinity}} <= max(2, 2^{1/p}) (||f||_{L^{p,infinity}} + ||g||_{L^{p,infinity}}), from d_{f+g}(t) <= d_f(t/2) + d_g(t/2). Chebyshev's inequality gives L^p contained in L^{p,infinity} with ||f||_{L^{p,infinity}} <= ||f||_p, and the inclusion is strict in general: on R^n, |x|^{-n/p} lies in L^{p,infinity} but not in L^p. For 1 < p < infinity, L^{p,infinity} admits an equivalent norm; L^{1,infinity}(R^n) admits none.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a compact metric space","for the homeomorphism notion f is invertible; for positive expansiveness f is only assumed continuous"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T02:00:35.437766+00:00","domain":"topological dynamics","id":"claim_5676c1f151b4a57362148ab72f2407ae791df1e012af3b7099cc8435b4d96949","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(X, d)$ be a compact metric space. A homeomorphism $f: X \\to X$ is expansive with expansivity constant $\\varepsilon > 0$ if whenever $x \\ne y$ there is some $n \\in \\mathbb{Z}$ (positive OR negative) with $d(f^n x, f^n y) > \\varepsilon$; equivalently, $d(f^n x, f^n y) \\le \\varepsilon$ for all $n \\in \\mathbb{Z}$ forces $x = y$. A continuous map $f: X \\to X$ (not necessarily invertible) is positively expansive (forward expansive) with constant $\\varepsilon$ if $d(f^n x, f^n y) \\le \\varepsilon$ for all $n \\ge 0$ forces $x = y$. Positive expansiveness is much stronger than expansiveness: a positively expansive HOMEOMORPHISM of a compact metric space exists only when $X$ is finite (Schwartzman; Keynes-Robertson), so for an infinite compact space the notion is meaningful only for genuinely non-invertible maps such as expanding maps and one-sided shifts. On a compact space the property (with some constant) does not depend on the choice of compatible metric, though the constant does. Expansiveness is preserved by passing to $f^{-1}$ and to $f^k$, $k \\ne 0$; positive expansiveness is preserved by passing to $f^k$, $k \\ge 1$.","status":"unverified"}

The coordinate e is PIVOTAL for A at omega if exactly one of omega^e, omega_e lies in A; Piv_A(omega) is the set of pivotal coordinates and its size |Piv_A| is the number of pivotal coordinates. THEOREM (Margulis 1974, Russo 1981). For every event A, p |-> P_p(A) is a polynomial in the p_e and, for every coordinate e, d/dp_e P_p(A) = P_p(A^e) - P_p(A_e). {"assumptions":["m is Lebesgue measure on R^n and L is its completion of the Borel sigma-algebra B","f is Lebesgue measurable with values in the extended reals","for part (i): Lebesgue measure is sigma-finite and outer regular, which is what supplies the Borel hull and kernel","for part (iii): (X, M-bar, mu-bar) is the completion of a measure space (X, M, mu)","the conclusion is equality off a null set, not everywhere"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:13:10.402310+00:00","domain":"measure theory, Borel versus Lebesgue measurability","id":"claim_56d067a642318476c9ea2c21c69cf1a4651cbf39b9d439c61824ee18654d3860","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let m denote Lebesgue measure on R^n, let B be the Borel sigma-algebra and let L be the Lebesgue sigma-algebra; recall that (R^n, L, m) is the completion of (R^n, B, m). (i) SETS: if E is in L then there are Borel sets B_1 contained in E contained in B_2 with m(B_2 minus B_1) = 0; consequently E = B_1 union N with N contained in a Borel set of measure zero, and every Lebesgue measurable set differs from a Borel set by a null set. (ii) FUNCTIONS: if f : R^n -> [-infinity, +infinity] is Lebesgue measurable, then there is a BOREL measurable g : R^n -> [-infinity, +infinity] and a Borel set N with m(N) = 0 such that g(x) = f(x) for every x outside N. One may take g with the same pointwise bounds as f (if a <= f <= b a.e. then a <= g <= b everywhere, and if f >= 0 then g >= 0). (iii) The same holds verbatim for the completion of any measure space: an M-bar-measurable function on the completion (X, M-bar, mu-bar) of (X, M, mu) agrees mu-almost everywhere with an M-measurable function. WHERE IT FAILS: (a) 'almost everywhere' cannot be strengthened to 'everywhere': let N be a non-Borel subset of the Cantor set (such subsets exist since the Cantor set has cardinality the continuum and carries continuum-many subsets, while there are only continuum-many Borel sets and all subsets of the Cantor set are Lebesgue null hence Lebesgue measurable); then the indicator of N is Lebesgue measurable but not Borel. (b) 'Borel' cannot be upgraded to 'continuous': Lusin's theorem only gives continuity of the restriction after deleting a set of arbitrarily small measure, not a continuous function agreeing almost everywhere (the indicator of [0,1] is a counterexample). (c) The distinction is not cosmetic in compositions: if h is continuous and f is Lebesgue measurable, f composed with h need not be Lebesgue measurable, whereas g composed with h is Borel measurable whenever g is Borel; this is the standard reason to replace f by its Borel representative before composing or before invoking a change of variables. (d) Statement (i) uses that Lebesgue measure is sigma-finite and Borel-regular; for a general non-regular measure there is no such inner and outer Borel approximation.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Countable underlying graph","Tail-trivial forest law","For the FUSF corollary use Lyons-Peres Theorem 10.18"],"created_at":"2026-10-10T08:08:30.940046+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_56d0ba3d36dbdba6d3c440c370af60307ea514a7e76d292c612048a660c35d55","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"For any random spanning forest on a countable graph with trivial edge-tail sigma-field, the event that it has infinitely many components has probability zero or one. {"assumptions":["independence within each row (nothing assumed across rows)","mean zero and finite variances, with sum_i E[X_{n,i}^2] -> sigma^2 > 0","Lindeberg's condition for sufficiency; additionally uniform asymptotic negligibility for the converse"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:40.781577+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_56f2f3ba378c4a6f96900d8c87012af674a778ae0963a2aedce836ff95c4516e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"For each n let X_{n,1}, ..., X_{n,k_n} be INDEPENDENT random variables within each row, with E[X_{n,i}] = 0 and sum_{i=1}^{k_n} E[X_{n,i}^2] -> sigma^2 in (0, infinity). Suppose the LINDEBERG CONDITION holds: for every eps > 0, sum_{i=1}^{k_n} E[ X_{n,i}^2 1{ |X_{n,i}| > eps } ] -> 0 as n -> infinity. Then S_n = sum_i X_{n,i} converges in distribution to N(0, sigma^2). FELLER'S CONVERSE: if in addition the row is UNIFORMLY ASYMPTOTICALLY NEGLIGIBLE, max_{i <= k_n} E[X_{n,i}^2] -> 0, and S_n converges in distribution to N(0, sigma^2), then the Lindeberg condition holds - so under negligibility the condition is necessary as well as sufficient. LYAPUNOV'S CONDITION, sum_i E|X_{n,i}|^{2 + delta} -> 0 for some delta > 0, IMPLIES Lindeberg and is usually easier to check. Two things the theorem does not require: identical distribution within a row, and any relation between rows. Two things it does require: independence WITHIN each row, and the variance sum converging to a strictly positive limit. Without negligibility the converse fails - a single summand can already be Gaussian and carry the whole limit while the others are wild. [Lindeberg (1922), Feller (1935); see Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorems 3.4.10 and 3.4.11]","status":"unverified"}

Then Σ_n |a_n|^{-(k+1)} < ∞ and f(z) = z^m exp(Q(z)) Π_n E_k(z/a_n), where E_k is the Weierstrass elementary factor and Q is a polynomial of degree at most k (equivalently, of degree at most ρ). {"assumptions":["A small parameter: bubble (SAW), triangle (percolation) or square (lattice trees) diagram small at criticality","Above the upper critical dimension: d > 4 (SAW), d > 6 (percolation), d > 8 (lattice trees)","Nearest-neighbour models need d >= 5 (SAW) or d >= 11 (percolation) with current methods"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T12:13:53+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_57375976b63bf663a8210d0e4c836fb9befaf15f16d6294ef02907a3056e8fcc","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). The lace expansion writes the two-point function of self-avoiding walk, Bernoulli percolation, oriented percolation or lattice trees as a renormalised random-walk Green function plus a correction series: for SAW, c_n(x) = sum_y D(y) c_{n-1}(x - y) + sum_{m=2}^{n} sum_y pi_m(y) c_{n-m}(x - y), with pi_m the alternating-sign lace coefficients obtained by inclusion-exclusion over self-intersections (for percolation the analogous expansion is in terms of pivotal bonds and sausages). The expansion is an exact identity; its use requires a bootstrap showing the coefficients are small in a norm controlled by a random-walk diagram: the bubble diagram for SAW (finite for d > 4), the triangle diagram for percolation (finite for d > 6) and the square diagram for lattice trees (d > 8). Proved regimes: nearest-neighbour SAW for d >= 5 (Hara-Slade), spread-out SAW for d > 4, nearest-neighbour percolation for d >= 11 (Fitzner-van der Hofstad) and spread-out percolation for d > 6 (Hara-Slade). Conclusions there: mean-field exponents (gamma = 1, eta = 0, beta = 1 and delta = 2 in bounded-ratio senses), Gaussian or super-Brownian scaling limits, and asymptotic expansions of critical points. It gives nothing at or below the upper critical dimension, and for nearest-neighbour percolation in 7 <= d <= 10 there is no small parameter, so the expansion holds only as an identity, not as a bound. Typical failure: Applying the expansion's mean-field conclusions (eta=0, Gaussian or super-Brownian scaling limit) to a model at or below its upper critical dimension without re-verifying the triangle or bubble condition; the coefficients pi_m are not shown small there, the bootstrap can fail to close, and the diagrammatic control silently assumed at the outset is exactly the open problem, which is why mean-field behaviour of nearest-neighbour percolation in dimensions 7 <= d <= 10 remains unproved although the spread-out (d > 6) and nearest-neighbour d >= 11 cases are resolved (below d = 6 mean-field behaviour is not expected, and at d = 6 logarithmic corrections are expected). Canonical reference: Hara and Slade, 1990, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Madras and Slade, The Self-Avoiding Walk, 1993, Birkhauser.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Eikonal equation |u'| = 1 on (-1,1) with zero boundary data","The correct symmetry is: u solves F = 0 in the viscosity sense iff -u solves -F(x,-r,-p) = 0; simply flipping the sign of F does not preserve the solution set","The sign convention pairs with vanishing viscosity: the viscosity solution of F = 0 is the limit of solutions of F(x,u_ε,Du_ε) - εΔu_ε = 0"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.418207+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: viscosity solution theory","id":"claim_573bfbe8e5c9cedb4b4e443a344bb159372ae5341600e867e80decd2533c1068","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing convention: the definition of viscosity solution is tied to the SIGN with which the equation is written (with the convention that F is nonincreasing in the second-order term, i.e. that the vanishing-viscosity approximation is F(x,u,Du) - εΔu = 0). Multiplying the equation by -1 changes the solution. Concrete counterexample: on Ω = (-1,1) with boundary data u(-1) = u(1) = 0, consider |u'| = 1. Written as F(x,r,p) = |p| - 1 = 0, the viscosity solution is u(x) = 1 - |x| (the distance to ∂Ω): at x = 0 the function has a concave kink, no C^1 function touches it from below there, and the subsolution test at the kink only requires |p| - 1 ≤ 0 for p ∈ [-1,1]. Written as G(x,r,p) = 1 - |p| = 0 (the same equation pointwise!), the viscosity solution is u(x) = |x| - 1: at its convex kink at x = 0 the supersolution test requires 1 - |p| ≥ 0 for the touching slopes p ∈ [-1,1], which holds. Moreover 1 - |x| is NOT a viscosity solution of G = 0 (the subsolution test at the concave kink would demand 1 - |p| ≤ 0 for p = 0) and |x| - 1 is not a viscosity solution of F = 0. Both functions are Lipschitz with |u'| = 1 a.e. and the same boundary data. Auditor's check: before citing a comparison or uniqueness theorem, verify that the equation is written in the same sign convention as the theorem (this bites when a Hamiltonian is moved across the equality, when time is reversed in u_t + H = 0, or when a maximization problem is rewritten as a minimization).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.164539+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_57969f10100f2bd46f36781f2fd50d579fc3fad2b1b29097213972227544a36f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 34 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Recall the definition of $z_\star$ from \eqref{e:fp.z.star}.
Recalling the expression for $V'(z)$ from \eqref{e:fp-V-pr}, define
    \beq
    \gamma(z)
    \equiv
    \alpha \sum_{j=1}^r \lambda_j
    \bigg(
    \frac{ \hv_j}{\alpha - \hv_j m(z)}
    \bigg)^2\,.\eeq
Then, writing $\gamma_\star\equiv\gamma(z_\star)$, we have $\beta_\star(\gamma_\star) = z_\star$.

\begin{proof}
We divide the proof according to the cases from the definition
\eqref{e:fp.z.star} of $z_\star$:
\begin{itemize}
\item   First suppose $z_\star = z_{\min}$.
    Then, recalling \eqref{e:fp-V-pr}, we see that $z_\star$ solves the equation
    \[
    0 = V'(z_\star)
    = 1- m_2(z_\star) \gamma(z_\star)\,,
    \]
which rearranges to
$m_2(z_\star) = 1/\gamma_\star$.
This is precisely the characterization of $\beta_{\min}(\gamma_\star)$, so we conclude $ \beta_{\min}(\gamma_\star)=z_\star=z_{\min}$.
    Finally, since $z_\star = z_{\min}$, we have \[\hx \le
    \frac{\alpha}{m(z_{\min})}
    = \frac{\alpha}{m(\beta_{\min}(\gamma_\star))}
    \,,\] and therefore $\beta_\star(\gamma_\star) = \beta_{\min}(\gamma_\star) = z_\star$.
\item In the other case, we must have $\hx>0$, and
    \[
    z_\star = m^{-1}\bigg(\frac{\alpha}{\hx}\bigg) > z_{\min}\,.
    \]
Abbreviate $\beta_\star\equiv\beta_\star(\gamma_\star)$ and $\beta_{\min}\equiv\beta_{\min}(\gamma_\star)$.
We want to again conclude that $\beta_\star=z_\star$, so suppose for contradiction that this does not hold, in which case it follows from \eqref{e:fp-betast} combined with the above that
    \[
    \beta_\star
    =\beta_{\min}
    > m^{-1}\bigg(\frac{\alpha}{\hx}\bigg)
     = z_\star > z_{\min}\,.
    \]
Now we recall that $z_{\min}$ satisfies $V'(z_{\min})=0$, which by \eqref{e:fp-V-pr} rearranges to
    \beq
    1 = m_2(z_{\min})
    \gamma(z_{\min})
    =
    \frac{m_2(z_{\min})}{m(z_{\min})^2}
    \Big[
    m(z_{\min})^2\gamma(z_{\min})
    \Big]
    \,.\eeq
Meanwhile, $\beta_{\min}$ is characterized by the equation
    \beq
    1
    = m_2(\beta_{\min})
    \gamma(z_\star)
    = \frac{m_2(\beta_{\min})}
        {m(z_\star)^2}
    \Big[
    m(z_\star)^2\gamma(z_\star)
    \Big]
    \,.\eeq
We saw in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:freeprob.V.convex} that
the function $m_2(z)/m(z)^2$ is nonincreasing in $z$. Since $m_2$ is strictly decreasing in $z$, it follows that
\[
    \frac{m_2(\beta_{\min})}
    {m(z_\star)^2}
    <\frac{m_2(z_\star)}
    {m(z_\star)^2}
    \le \frac{m_2(z_{\min})}
    {m(z_{\min})^2}
    \]
We also saw in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:freeprob.V.convex} that
the function $m(z)^2\gamma(z)$ is strictly decreasing in $z$, which implies
$m(z_\star)^2\gamma(z_\star)<
    m(z_{\min})^2\gamma(z_{\min})$. This shows that the above equations \eqref{e:fp.char.of.zmin} and \eqref{e:fp.char.of.betamin} cannot hold simultaneously, a contradiction.
\end{itemize}
Thus we have shown in all cases that $\beta_\star(\gamma_\star)=z_\star$, as claimed.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["i.i.d. observations with finite variance (Andrews states the result under moment conditions for the CLT)","the constraint is active at the true parameter (theta = 0); for theta > 0 the bootstrap is consistent"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T09:15:04.118127+00:00","domain":"resampling / constrained estimation","id":"claim_5803afc2cb107c5851acbdda8fe0e490d3b03266f3d6e659e596fdbcafb115fe","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $X_1, \\dots, X_n$ be i.i.d. with mean $\\theta \\ge 0$ and variance $\\sigma^2$, and let the estimator respect the constraint: $\\hat\\theta_n = \\max(0, \\bar X_n)$. When the true parameter is interior ($\\theta > 0$) the nonparametric bootstrap is consistent: the conditional law of $\\sqrt n(\\hat\\theta_n^* - \\hat\\theta_n)$ converges to $N(0, \\sigma^2)$, the law of $\\sqrt n(\\hat\\theta_n - \\theta)$. When the true parameter is on the boundary ($\\theta = 0$) it is not: $\\sqrt n(\\hat\\theta_n - \\theta) \\Rightarrow \\max(0, Z)$ with $Z \\sim N(0, \\sigma^2)$, a law with an atom of mass $1/2$ at zero, whereas the bootstrap law of $\\sqrt n(\\hat\\theta_n^* - \\hat\\theta_n)$ converges, conditionally on the data, to the law of $\\max(0, Z + \\zeta) - \\max(0, \\zeta)$ with $\\zeta \\sim N(0, \\sigma^2)$ a random shift that does not vanish - so the bootstrap distribution is random in the limit and does not equal the sampling distribution (Andrews 2000, Theorem 1). The same failure holds for maximum-likelihood and least-squares estimators under inequality constraints whenever the true parameter has an active constraint, in particular for nonnegatively constrained regression and portfolio weights with coordinates at zero: the bootstrap replicates flip the constrained coordinates between zero and positive values, and the spread of the replicates is not the spread of the estimator. Consistent alternatives: the $m$-out-of-$n$ bootstrap with $m \\to \\infty$, $m/n \\to 0$, and subsampling, both of which recover the limit law at the boundary.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-23T13:15:27.869621+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_581c9552f43e1f4cf92726d32a39b9a4720c921de8094cf33857ac37ef5fce39","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"FIRES WHEN a detection or coverage problem in a moving Boolean model has been reduced, correctly, to the volume of a union of swept regions, and you are about to call the problem solved. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:18:27.580325+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_583a6a2d58ab2641021ba72d33552a23bcc7fcdd59ee5d70ec39e158a910086e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 17 (Stability of the subcritical domain; conditional on Hypothesis~\ref{hyp:red}) of arXiv:2608.15987, 'Threshold cascades of interacting diffusions on unimodular random trees: a conditional bra'] Let $\mathcal M_-=\{\theta:\rho(M(\theta))<1\}$ and $\mathcal M_+=\{\theta:\rho(M(\theta))>1\}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item ($\mathcal M_-$ is open.) $\rho(M(\cdot))$ is continuous (indeed real-analytic where $M$ is irreducible), so $\mathcal M_-$ is open and $\partial\mathcal M_-=\{\rho(M)=1\}$ is, where the gradient is nonzero, a smooth codimension-one submanifold (Proposition~\ref{prop:PF}(3) and the implicit function theorem).
\item (Convexity goes to $\mathcal M_+$, not $\mathcal M_-$.) In the scalar (Bethe) case $\rho=(d-1)p$, with $p$ log-concave, $\mathcal M_+=\{p>1/(d-1)\}$ is a superlevel set of a log-concave function, hence convex; $\mathcal M_-$ is its complement and is in general non-convex. Explicitly, if $p$ is jointly log-concave in $(\theta,\gamma)$ then $\mathcal M_-$ is the non-convex exterior of a convex region. Convexity of $\mathcal M_-$ cannot be deduced from log-concavity of $p$: the implication ``sublevel sets of a concave function are convex'' is false (it is superlevel sets that are convex).
\item ($\mathcal M_-$ is contractible.) $\mathcal M_-$ is star-shaped toward the zero-coupling locus $\{\gamma=0\}$: holding $(\theta,\alpha,\mu)$ fixed and sending $\gamma\downarrow0$ decreases every $p_{d,d'}$ (transmission increases in coupling), hence decreases $\rho(M)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:PF}(2)), keeping the path in $\mathcal M_-$. The straight-line homotopy $\gamma\mapsto(1-t)\gamma$ therefore retracts $\mathcal M_-$ to a point; $\mathcal M_-$ is contractible.
\item (Resolvent and gap.) On $\mathcal M_-$ the resolvent $R=(I-M)^{-1}=\sum_{k\ge0}M^k$ converges (finite matrix, $\rho(M)<1$) to a bounded nonnegative matrix; the halting probability is $\Prob(|S|<\infty)=1$; the expected cluster size is $\E|S|=\one^\top R\,\pi$, real-analytic in $\theta$; and the spectral gap $g(\theta)=1-\rho(M(\theta))>0$ gives quantitative stability: any $\Delta\theta$ with $\|\Delta\theta\|<g(\theta)/\|\nabla_\theta\rho\|$ keeps $\theta+\Delta\theta\in\mathcal M_-$.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:31:02.820998+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_589202f03b99b9f1482c8a4024de03ebf8483baf5b41dc2e63ebbc1c538e4c68","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:compression-master of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Let $h\geq1$, $k\geq2$, and let
$A=(a_0<a_1<\cdots<a_{k-1})$ be an ordered real $k$-set.  If
$r=r_h(A)$, define its successive active-relation degrees by
\[
 p_i(A)=\min\{p\in\mathbb Z_{\geq1}:\dim L_p(A)\geq i\},
 \qquad 1\leq i\leq r.
\]
Put $d_A=k-1-r$.  Since $r\leq k-2$, one has $d_A\geq1$.
Then there is an integer set
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 A^*&=(0=a_0^*<a_1^*<\cdots<a_{k-1}^*),\\
 a_{k-1}^*
 &\leq d_Ah^{d_A-1}\prod_{i=1}^{r}p_i(A)
 \leq(k-1-r)h^{k-2},
 \end{aligned}
\]
where the empty product is one,
such that, simultaneously for every $1\leq j\leq h$ and every
$u,v\in\mathcal U_{j,k}$,
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{sgn}\bigl((u-v)\cdot A^*\bigr)
 =\operatorname{sgn}\bigl((u-v)\cdot A\bigr).
\end{equation}
Thus the ordered addition tables are identical in every degree $1\leq j\leq h$;
in particular, $|jA^*|=|jA|$ for $1\leq j\leq h$.

There is a complementary intrinsic statement.  Suppose $k\geq3$ and
\[
 B=(0=b_0<b_1<\cdots<b_{k-1}=d),
 \qquad \gcd(b_1,\ldots,b_{k-1})=1.
\]
For $1\leq i\leq k-2$, define the successive relation degrees
\[
 p_i(B)=\min\{p\in\mathbb Z_{\geq1}:\dim L_p(B)\geq i\}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{ndiam}(B)=d\leq\prod_{i=1}^{k-2}p_i(B).
\end{equation}
Consequently, for $h\geq2$,
\begin{equation}
 \max_{\substack{B\subset\mathbb Z,\ |B|=k\\r_h(B)=k-2}}
       \operatorname{ndiam}(B)=h^{k-2}.
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.179777+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_58c2f90a212f274a241ad1ba9cc4d9d7695182d21fe0fbe058f607ce2eb09584","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 95 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Fix $L,\alpha>0$ and let $(\cA_N)^\circ$ be a sequence of $L$-Lipschitz algorithms in the sense of Definition~\ref{d:Lip}. Let $\cA_N$ be the perturbation of $(\cA_N)^\circ$ from Proposition~\ref{p:wlogable}. By passing to a subsequence $N_j\to\infty$, we assume that $\chi_{\cA_N}$ converges to a limiting function $\chi$, pointwise and in $L^1$. Denote $q_0\equiv \chi(0)\in[0,1]$. The function $p\equiv\chi^{-1}$ belongs to $\incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ and is concave, with
\[\frac1{L^2}
\le p'(q) \le L^2\] for all $q\in [q_0,1]$. Suppose $(\mu,\mu^\Ising)$ satisfies 
	\beq
	\bbW_2\big(\mu,\mu(\cA_N)\big)
	+\bbW_2\big(\mu^\Ising,
		\mu^\Ising(\cA_N)\big)
		\le \epsilon_\textup{apx}
		\,.
	\eeq
Then there exist $C(L) > 0$ and $q_*,b,\sigma,w,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising$ such that the following hold. Let $B(t)$ and $W(t)$ be standard Brownian motions and
\begin{align} 
        dX(t)
        &= p'(t)^{1/2} b_t\,dt
        + s(t) \sigma_t\,dB(t)\,,
        \\
        dX^{\Ising}(t)
        &= w_t\,dW(t) 
        \end{align}
on the time interval $q_* \le t \le 1$, with $X(q_*)\sim\zeta$ and $X^\Ising(q_*)\sim\zeta^\Ising$.  Then: 
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item 
$b_t=b(t,X(t))$,
$\sigma_t=\sigma(t,X(t))$,
and $w_t=w(t,Y(t))$ 
for functions $b:[q_*,1]\times \bbR\to[-C(L),C(L)]$ and $\sigma,w:[q_*,1]\times \bbR\to[0,C(L)]$, such that the functions $p'(t)^{1/2} b(t,x), s(t) \sigma(t,x), w(t,x)$, are $C(L)$-Lipschitz in $(t,x)$.
\item 
We have the diffusivity constraint
        \beq
            \max\bigg\{
            \Big|\bbE[w(t,X^\Ising(t))^2]-1
            	\Big|
	:q_* \le t\le 1
\bigg\} \leq  o(1)\,.
\eeq

\item 
    We have the approximate budget constraints
       \beq 
            \int_{q_*}^1
            \bigg\{
            \bbE\bigg[ b(t,X(t))^2+ \frac{(tp)'(t)}{p(t)}
            	(\sigma(t,X(t))-1)^2\bigg]
            -
            \frac{(\bbE w(t,X^\Ising(t)) )^2}{\alpha}
            \bigg\}_+
            \de t
            \leq o(1)\,.\eeq

 \item  The initial measures $\zeta,\zeta^\Ising$ satisfy $|\bE[X(q_*)^2]|\leq o(1)$ and  $|\bE[X^\Ising(q_*)^2] - q_*|\leq o(1)$.
\item  The initial time $q_*$ lies in $[q_0,q_0+ o(1)]$ and satisfies $p(q_*) \le o(1)$. 
\end{enumerate}
Lastly, we have
\beq
\begin{aligned}
	\bbW_2(\Law(X(1)),\mu)
	&\leq 
	O(\epsilon_\textup{apx}) 
	+ o(1)\,,\\ 
	\bbW_2(\Law(X^{\Ising}(1)),\mu^{\Ising})
	&\leq  O(\epsilon_\textup{apx})
	+ o(1)\,.
\end{aligned}
\eeq
In all the above assertions, the $o(1)$ denotes an error which can tend to zero as $L^{-\Theta(1)}$. Thus, the distributions $\mu,\mu^\Ising$ are well approximated by the distributions of the endpoints of the solution to the constrained SDE described above. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:29:21.917510+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_58ffc21014799f6ba9dde03765b16731732113257ed5337a11b7a7e9422e4c49","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 5 of arXiv:2608.01516, 'Nondegeneracy and regularity of polynomial pushforwards'] Let $a,b\in(0,+\infty)$, $\eta>0$, $k,d\in\mathbb N$, and $d\ge2$. There exists
a constant $C:=C(a,b,\eta,k,d)>0$ such that, for every
$X=(X_1,\ldots,X_k),Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_k)\in\mathcal P_{d,k}^{\rm lc}$
satisfying
\[
a\le \operatorname{Var}(X_j)\le b,
\quad
a\le \operatorname{Var}(Y_j)\le b
\quad
\forall j\in\{1,\ldots,k\},
\]
and
\[
\det \Sigma^d(X)\ge \eta,
\quad
\det \Sigma^d(Y)\ge \eta,
\]
one has
\[
d_{\rm TV}(X,Y)
\le
C d_{\rm KR}(X,Y)^{\frac{1}{k(d-1)+2}}.
\]

In particular, if a sequence
$X_n\in\mathcal P_{d,k}^{\rm lc}$ converges in distribution to an
$\mathbb R^k$-valued random vector $X_\infty$ whose distribution is absolutely
continuous, then the convergence holds in total variation and
\[
d_{\rm TV}(X_n,X_\infty)
\le
C d_{\rm KR}(X_n,X_\infty)^{\frac{1}{k(d-1)+2}}
\]
for some constant $C>0$ depending on the sequence and on the limiting
distribution. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

bi-Lipschitz map with $d\mu=J dy$.  Fix $1<p<n$ and put

For every $q\in L^p(\mu)$ there is a unique vector field $F=F^i\eframe_i$ along $X$, whose Cartesian components belong to

distributional sense: equivalently, $u:=F\circ X^{-1}$ satisfies
\[
 \partial_{x^i}u^j-\partial_{x^j}u^i=0,

 \quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\Real_x^n).

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:58:09.068015+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5aa29bffd3f775401eb1d40c41db493c2a9c756795dd6c968fe81383a4f82057","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 1 (Standard asymptotic characterization) of arXiv:2606.27774, 'Variational Formulas for the Spectrum of\\ Block Wishart Matrices'] Assume the rows $\bx_i\in\C^{p}$ are i.i.d., centered (i.e., $\E[\bx_i] =\bzero$), and isotropic
(i.e., $\E[\bx_i\bx_i^*] = \bI_p$). Assume further that there exists 
$\sfK \in (0,\infty)$
such that, for each $i\in[n]$, all deterministic $\bA\in \C^{p\times p}$, and all $t>0$,

\begin{equation}

   \P\Big( \big|\bx_i^*\bA \bx_i - \Tr(\bA)\big| \ge t \Big)
   \le
   2 \exp\bigg\{-c \min\bigg(\frac{t^2}{\sfK^4 \|\bA\|_\Fnorm^2},\, 
   \frac{t}{\sfK^2 \|\bA\|_\op}\bigg)\bigg\}\, ,
\end{equation}
for some universal constant $c>0$, where $\|\bA\|_\Fnorm$ and $\|\bA\|_\op$ denote 
the Frobenius and operator norms of $\bA$, respectively.
Fix integer $k\ge 1$, $\alpha \in (0,\infty)$ and
let $\nu\in\cuP_0(\sa{k}{\C})$.
Define
\begin{equation}

    \bK_\up{\alpha,\nu}(\bS) := \int  \bT(\bI + \bS\bT)^{-1} \nu(\de \bT) - \frac1\alpha\bS^{-1},\quad\quad \bK_\up{\alpha,\nu}:\C^{k\times k} \to\C^{k\times k}.
\end{equation}

For any $z \in\bbH_+$, there exists a unique 
solution 
$\bS_\up{\nu,\alpha}(z)$
to
\begin{equation}

    \bK_\up{\alpha,\nu}(\bS) = z\bI,\quad\quad \bS\in\bbH_+^k := \{\bB\in \C^{k\times k}: \Im(\bB) \succ\bzero\}.
\end{equation}
Furthermore,
    \begin{equation}
        s_\up{\nu,\alpha}(z) := 
         \frac{\alpha}{k} \Tr(\bS_\up{\alpha,\nu}(z))\quad\quad\textrm{for}\quad z\in\bbH_+
    \end{equation}
is the Stieltjes transform of a probability measure 
$\mu_\up{\alpha,\nu}\in\cuP(\R)$ such that, almost surely
\begin{equation}
    \hmu_{\bW_k} \Rightarrow \mu_\up{\alpha,\nu} \quad\quad \textrm{almost surely, as} \quad\quad n\to\infty,\;\frac{n}{p} \to\alpha,
\end{equation}
where $\hmu_{\bW_k}$ is the empirical spectral distribution of $\bW_k$ and $\Rightarrow$ denotes weak convergence of probability measures.

Finally, if $\dist(\{\bT_i:i\le n\},\supp(\nu))\to 0$ (with $\dist$ denoting
Hausdorff distance between sets in $(\reals^k,\|\,\cdot\,\|$), then,
almost surely,

\begin{align}
\dist\big(\supp(\hmu_{\bW_k}),\supp (\mu_\up{\alpha,\nu})\big) \to 0\, .
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:21:10.889137+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5aa7b9e481e70b09648267e9bf18116ec1f80bfa8b76f43f5556e3f678d682a8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 38 (MTP for the marked Poisson point process) of arXiv:2504.02435, 'Poisson-Voronoi percolation in higher rank'] Let $G$ be a non-compact connected semisimple real Lie group and $(X,d_X)$ be its symmetric space.
Let ${\bf Y}^{(\lambda)}$ be the marked Poisson point process on $X$ with intensity $\lambda \, {\rm vol}$ for some $\lambda>0$.
Let ${\bf Y}^{(\lambda)}_o={\bf Y}^{(\lambda)} \cup \{\mathbf o\}$, where~$\mathbf o$ is equipped with an independent ${\rm Unif}[0,1]$-mark.
Then
\begin{equation*} 
\mathbb E \bigg[ \sum_{i\in \mathbb{N}} F(o,Y^{(\lambda)}_i,{\bf Y}_o^{(\lambda)}) \bigg] = \mathbb E \bigg[ \sum_{i\in \mathbb{N}} F(Y^{(\lambda)}_i,o,{\bf Y}_o^{(\lambda)}) \bigg]
\end{equation*}
for every measurable $F : X\times X\times \mathbf M(X\times[0,1]) \to [0,\infty]$ such that 
$$
F(\tau(x),\tau(y),\tau \circ \overline \eta) = F(x,y, \overline \eta)
$$
for every $\overline\eta \in\mathbf M(X\times[0,1])$ and every $x,y\in X$ and $\tau\in{\rm Isom}(X)$ which interchanges $x$ and $y$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["conjugate exponents with 1 <= p <= 2","convention e^{-2 pi i x . xi}, for which the constant 1 is available on R^d","on T the transform is the coefficient sequence, with the counting measure on Z"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:39.264720+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis, common errors","id":"claim_5aeb07b2cba38ad9cc3665ecb9550bf24a5d74fc445f8cf0332b5120f3c59861","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The inequality $\\|\\hat f\\|_{p'}\\le\\|f\\|_p$, $\\frac1p+\\frac1{p'}=1$, holds for $1\\le p\\le2$ (Riesz-Thorin interpolation between $\\|\\hat f\\|_\\infty\\le\\|f\\|_1$ and Plancherel) - and only there. The restriction $p\\le2$ is load-bearing: (i) On $\\mathbb T$, $L^p\\subset L^2$ for $p>2$, so the coefficients are automatically in $\\ell^2$, but no better exponent is available: Carleman's example provides a continuous (hence in every $L^p$) function $f$ on $\\mathbb T$ with $\\sum_n|\\hat f(n)|^q=\\infty$ for every $q<2$. So no bound $\\|\\hat f\\|_{\\ell^{p'}}\\le C\\|f\\|_{L^p}$ with $p'<2$ can hold for any $p>2$. (ii) On $\\mathbb R^d$ and $p>2$, the Fourier transform of an $L^p$ function exists only as a tempered distribution and need not be representable by a locally integrable function, so the left-hand side of the inequality is not even defined in general. (iii) The direction matters too: the dual statement '$\\hat f\\in L^{p'}$ implies $f\\in L^p$' is false in general; what is true is the companion inequality $\\|f\\|_{p'}\\le\\|\\hat f\\|_p$ for $1\\le p\\le2$. (iv) On $\\mathbb R^d$ the constant $1$ is not sharp: Babenko-Beckner give $\\|\\hat f\\|_{p'}\\le\\big(p^{1/p}/(p')^{1/p'}\\big)^{d/2}\\|f\\|_p$ for $1<p<2$, attained by Gaussians, whereas on $\\mathbb T$ and $\\mathbb Z$ the constant $1$ is sharp.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f in L^2(R)","the Fourier transform vanishes a.e. outside [-W,W] (bandlimited)","the identity is for the continuous representative of f, at the sample rate 2W"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:39.264078+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis, signal analysis","id":"claim_5b13f31813707effd67637d18a57d7f164f03bdd14f035e44aa83cc3dc91a5ef","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Convention $\\hat f(\\xi)=\\int f(x)e^{-2\\pi i x\\xi}dx$. Let $W>0$ and let $f\\in L^2(\\mathbb R)$ satisfy $\\hat f=0$ a.e. outside $[-W,W]$. Then $\\hat f\\in L^1$, so $f$ has a (unique) continuous representative $f(x)=\\int_{-W}^{W}\\hat f(\\xi)e^{2\\pi i x\\xi}d\\xi$, and for that representative $$f(x)=\\sum_{n\\in\\mathbb Z}f\\!\\left(\\frac{n}{2W}\\right)\\operatorname{sinc}(2Wx-n),\\qquad \\operatorname{sinc}(t)=\\frac{\\sin(\\pi t)}{\\pi t},$$ the series converging in $L^2(\\mathbb R)$ and uniformly on $\\mathbb R$. Moreover $\\sum_n|f(n/2W)|^2=2W\\|f\\|_2^2$, so the samples determine $f$ isometrically. The sampling rate $2W$ (the Nyquist rate) is critical: functions bandlimited to $[-W,W]$ are in general not determined by samples at a slower rate, and the theorem's conclusion uses $f\\in L^2$ - the distributionally bandlimited function $\\sin(2\\pi Wx)$ has all samples $f(n/2W)=0$ without being zero, and it is excluded only because it is not in $L^2$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.357189+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5b6f7b66106ac510bc178ea79662cbf40119d6a1b20f404e79fcc46b2807147f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 239 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Fix any $\alpha,L > 0$, $\fq \in [1,2]$, and $\mu \in \cP_2(\R)$. 
	Then, for any $L$-Lipschitz algorithm $\cA_N$,
	\begin{align}
		(\E \bbW_\fq(\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)),\mu))^2
		&\ge \bbW_\fq(\mu(\cA_N),\mu)^2 - o_N(1)\,,\\
	
		(\E \bbW_2(\EmpDist(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)),\cP(\{\pm 1\})))^2
		&\ge \bbW_2(\mu^\Ising(\cA_N),\cP(\{\pm 1\}))^2 - o_N(1)\,.
	\end{align}
where $o_N(1)$ denotes a term tending to $0$ as $N\to\infty$, which may depend on $\alpha,L,\mu$.

\begin{proof}
	Abbreviate $X = \bbW_\fq(\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)),\mu)$.
	By Jensen's inequality, we have
	\[
		\E[X^\fq]^{2/\fq} 
		\le \E[X^2] 
		= (\E X)^2 + \E[(X-\E X)^2] \stackrel{\eqref{e:Wq.lip.to.fixed.msr.conc.var}}{=} (\E X)^2 + o_N(1)\,.
	\]
By convexity of $\bbW_\fq(\cdot,\cdot)^\fq$, we have
	\[
		\E[X^\fq] = \E [\bbW_\fq(\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)),\mu)^\fq] \ge \bbW_\fq(\mu(\cA_N),\mu)^\fq\,.
	\]
	Rearranging yields the first assertion \eqref{e:confinement.consequence.of.variance.bound}.
	The second assertion
	\eqref{e:confinement.consequence.of.variance.bound.ising} is proved in the same way, replacing $X$ with $J \equiv \bbW_2(\EmpDist(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)),\cP(\{\pm 1\}))$ in the above argument and using \eqref{e:Wq.lip.to.fixed.msr.conc.var.ising} from Lemma~\ref{l:Wq.lip.to.fixed.msr.conc} in place of \eqref{e:Wq.lip.to.fixed.msr.conc.var}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Lebesgue measure on R^n (for a general Radon measure on a locally compact Hausdorff space, density of C_c in L^p, p < infinity, still holds)","1 <= p <= infinity as indicated"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:36.553780+00:00","domain":"real analysis, Lp spaces","id":"claim_5bc45a179230b3bc44038a44275348cd59550ba798a4169de50c05821e9e46a5","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Standard approximation arguments in L^p silently use p < infinity. On R^n with Lebesgue measure: (1) DENSITY. Continuous compactly supported functions are dense in L^p for 1 <= p < infinity, but their closure in L^infinity is C_0(R^n) (continuous functions vanishing at infinity), a proper closed subspace; L^infinity(R^n) is not separable, while L^p(R^n) is for p < infinity. (Simple functions are dense in L^p for every p including infinity; simple functions with support of FINITE measure are dense only for p < infinity.) (2) MOLLIFICATION. If phi is an approximate identity then phi_eps * f -> f in L^p for 1 <= p < infinity, but not in L^infinity: for f = 1_{[0,infinity)} each phi_eps * f is continuous, and any continuous g satisfies ||g - f||_infinity >= 1/2, so the convergence fails; in L^infinity one only gets convergence at points of continuity (and weak-* convergence). (3) TRANSLATION. h -> f(. - h) is continuous from R^n to L^p for p < infinity; in L^infinity it is not: for f = 1_{[0,infinity)}, ||f(. - h) - f||_infinity = 1 for every h not equal to 0. Consequences for proofs: any argument that proves an estimate for nice functions and 'passes to the limit by density', or that uses continuity of translation (Riemann-Lebesgue, convolution identities, Lebesgue differentiation via density), must be carried out in L^p with p < infinity, or re-done by a separate weak-* / pointwise argument at p = infinity.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the ambient space is R^d with Lebesgue outer measure defined by countable covers by boxes","L is the sigma-algebra of Caratheodory-measurable sets and lambda = lambda* restricted to L","R^d is sigma-compact, locally compact and second countable, and lambda is finite on bounded sets - this is what drives regularity","the axiom of choice is used only for the remark that non-measurable sets exist"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:07:38.815011+00:00","domain":"measure theory, real analysis","id":"claim_5be137db7963f504ae7ade7e44a43ba8c850915205425ffc83a5dcc77d7cfe50","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let lambda* denote Lebesgue outer measure on R^d, defined by lambda*(E) = inf of sum of volumes of countably many open boxes covering E, let L be the sigma-algebra of Caratheodory-measurable (Lebesgue measurable) sets, and let lambda = lambda* restricted to L. Then: (1) OUTER REGULARITY, valid for EVERY set E contained in R^d, measurable or not: lambda*(E) = inf { lambda(U) : U open, U contains E }. (2) MEASURABILITY CRITERION: E is in L if and only if for every eps > 0 there is an open U containing E with lambda*(U \\ E) < eps, if and only if there is a G_delta set G containing E with lambda(G \\ E) = 0, if and only if there is an F_sigma set F contained in E with lambda(E \\ F) = 0. (3) INNER REGULARITY by compact sets, valid for every E in L: lambda(E) = sup { lambda(K) : K compact, K contained in E } (both sides may be +infinity). Equivalently, for E in L with lambda(E) < infinity and eps > 0 there is a compact K contained in E with lambda(E \\ K) < eps. Thus lambda is a Radon measure: it is finite on compacta, outer regular and inner regular. (4) COMPLETENESS: if lambda*(N) = 0 then N is in L and lambda(N) = 0, and hence every subset of a null set is measurable with measure zero. Equivalently, (R^d, L, lambda) is the completion of (R^d, Borel, lambda|Borel): L = { B union Z : B Borel, Z a subset of a Borel null set }. SHARP EDGES. (a) The Borel sigma-algebra itself is NOT complete: the Cantor set is Borel and null, it has 2^continuum subsets, all of them Lebesgue null and hence Lebesgue measurable, while there are only continuum many Borel sets; so L is strictly larger than the Borel sigma-algebra, and 'measurable' must never be silently upgraded to 'Borel'. (b) Regularity statements about the MEASURE are for measurable sets. Outer regularity in the form (1) does hold for arbitrary sets because it is the definition of the outer measure, but inner regularity fails badly for non-measurable sets: a Vitali set has inner measure 0 and positive outer measure, so the two approximations do not meet. It is exactly the meeting of the two that measurability expresses. (c) Completeness is what makes 'a.e. defined' harmless: if f = g almost everywhere and f is measurable then g is measurable. That inference is FALSE in the Borel sigma-algebra, and is a frequent silent error. (d) Regularity is not automatic for general Borel measures: on a non-sigma-compact or non-locally-compact space a finite Borel measure need not be inner regular by compact sets. Lebesgue measure is regular because R^d is sigma-compact, locally compact and second countable, and because lambda is finite on boxes. (e) Not every set is measurable: the existence of a non-measurable set uses the axiom of choice, and translation invariance plus countable additivity forbid extending lambda to all subsets of R^d.","status":"unverified"}

For the Ising model, or more generally ferromagnetic spin systems with finite-range or summable interactions, let G(x,y) = <sigma_x sigma_y> be the two-point function. The Simon-Lieb inequality bounds G(x,y) across any finite set Lambda separating x from y (x in Lambda, y outside Lambda) by G(x,y) <= sum_{u in Lambda, v not in Lambda, u~v} G(x,u) J_{uv} G(v,y), a one-step recursive bound relating the two-point function across a separating surface to the two-point function up to the boundary of Lambda times the coupling crossing it. Iterating the inequality over a sequence of nested separating sets, such as concentric boxes, yields exponential decay of G(x,y) once the associated generating function drops below its self-consistency threshold, giving a classical route, predating and complementary to the Duminil-Copin-Tassion approach, to sharpness of the phase transition and analyticity of the free energy in the high-temperature regime. It does not determine the exact critical temperature directly, only characterizing it implicitly through the inequality's self-consistency condition, and it applies specifically to ferromagnetic spin systems with a workable notion of finite separating surfaces; it does not transfer automatically to percolation, which uses combinatorially different, though philosophically related, inequalities. Typical failure: Iterating the Simon-Lieb inequality across many nested separating surfaces while implicitly assuming a geometric decay rate that has not actually been verified to be summable; turning the one-step recursive bound into exponential decay requires checking that the relevant generating function, summing G times J over the boundary, lies strictly below its self-consistency threshold, and this check is exactly where the difficulty of locating beta_c resides, so skipping it silently assumes the conclusion. Canonical reference: Simon, 1980, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Lieb, 1980, Communications in Mathematical Physics.","status":"unverified"}

\begin{enumerate}

The nerve $N(\\mathcal{A})$ of $\\mathcal{A}$ is the simplicial complex with vertex set $I$ where a non-empty finite subset $\\sigma \\subseteq I$ forms a simplex in $N(\\mathcal{A})$ if and only if $\\bigcap_{i \\in \\sigma} A_i \\neq \\emptyset$. {"assumptions":["(X, B, mu) is a probability space and T is measure-preserving","the partition is finite or countable and consists of measurable sets","for the two-sided join T must be invertible"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:23.250796+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, entropy","id":"claim_5c8ad06c4539071020c4a52ccb50fab1a5b23a0b5f4b9e11e00d40a599f8d3a6","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(X, \\mathcal{B}, \\mu, T)$ be a measure-preserving system on a probability space with $T$ invertible (a measure-preserving automorphism). A finite or countable measurable partition $\\xi = \\{A_1, A_2, \\dots\\}$ of $X$ is a (two-sided) generator if the smallest $\\sigma$-algebra containing all the sets $T^{-n} A_i$, $n \\in \\mathbb{Z}$, coincides with $\\mathcal{B}$ up to $\\mu$-null sets; in join notation, $\\bigvee_{n=-\\infty}^{\\infty} T^{-n}\\xi = \\mathcal{B}$ (mod $\\mu$). For a non-invertible $T$ one uses the one-sided join $\\bigvee_{n=0}^{\\infty} T^{-n}\\xi$ and speaks of a one-sided (strong) generator. Why it matters: by the Kolmogorov-Sinai theorem, if $\\xi$ is a generator with finite entropy $H_\\mu(\\xi) < \\infty$ then the measure-theoretic entropy of the system equals the entropy relative to $\\xi$, $h_\\mu(T) = h_\\mu(T, \\xi)$; no supremum over partitions is needed. Existence (Krieger): an ergodic automorphism of a Lebesgue probability space with $h_\\mu(T) < \\log k$ has a generator with $k$ atoms; a system with infinite entropy has no finite generator. Sharp edges: a partition may generate for one invariant measure and not another; the join over $n \\geq 0$ alone need not generate for an automorphism (e.g. the time-zero partition of a two-sided shift does not generate one-sidedly); and 'generates' is a statement mod null sets, not about separating every pair of points, although separating points does imply generating (see the Walters entry).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0117-concentration-of-the-cover-time-at-the-scale-of-the-maximal-hitting-ti","No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:26:45.047330+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5cda397e692b4a69754f60cde69a564791ae71e4aad95958ba9d8c25ac49f973","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Test the claim on the extreme families and derive the one-sided bound from Matthews-type arguments. Result: Upper tail: for any graph, P(tau_cov > t_cov + s t_hit) <= e^{-cs}? The standard argument: after time 2 t_hit... using the Markov property at multiples of the 'maximal hitting time' scale, the probability that a fixed uncovered vertex remains uncovered for another 2 t_hit is at most 1/2 by Markov's inequality on hitting times, but the union over uncovered vertices costs the number of uncovered vertices, so the naive bound gives only P(tau_cov > t_cov + s t_hit) <= n 2^{-s}, i.e. exponential decay after a log n shift, not at scale t_hit from the mean unless t_cov - t_cov... For the complete graph, tau_cov is a coupon-collector time with standard deviation of order n ~ t_hit, and the centred cover time divided by t_hit converges to a Gumbel, which has exponential tails: consistent. For the cycle Z_n, t_hit ≍ n^2 ≍ t_cov and tau_cov/n^2 converges to a non-degenerate law with exponential tail (the cover time of the cycle is the time for the range to reach n, a functional of Brownian motion with Gaussian-type tails): consistent, and the standard deviation is of order n^2 = t_hit: consistent. For the two-dimensional torus, t_hit ≍ n^2 log n... t_cov ≍ n^2 (log n)^2, and the cover time fluctuations are known to be of order n^2 log n (Belius-Kistler / Abe: the cover time of the 2D torus has fluctuations of order t_hit... the second-order term is of order n^2 log n times a random variable), consistent with the question. So the conjecture passes all the standard test cases; the general lower-tail statement (tau_cov not much smaller than t_cov) is the hard side because early coverage requires all vertices to be hit quickly, which involves correlations of hitting times; via the GFF isomorphism (Ding-Lee-Peres) the cover time corresponds to the level at which the GFF maximum exceeds a threshold, and concentration of the cover time at scale t_hit corresponds to tightness of the GFF maximum at scale sqrt(t_hit/|E|), which is tightness of the maximum of the Gaussian free field on the graph in the correct units; tightness of the GFF maximum is known for the 2D torus and trees but not for general graphs. Reduction: the question is essentially equivalent to tightness of the graph GFF maximum in units of the maximal hitting time. Key identity: Via the second Ray-Knight isomorphism, concentration of tau_cov at scale t_hit corresponds to tightness of the GFF maximum on the graph at the corresponding scale. Obstruction: Tightness of the GFF maximum on general graphs is not known.","status":"unverified"}

\(\mathcal{W} = \{ W_{1},\ldots,W_{m}\}\) of measurable subsets of \(M\)

\(G\) if every continuous path

\(\iota_{*}\), the detection guarantee of the Remark above. A
degree-\(q\) class --- and the \emph{feature} it represents --- is
\emph{detectable} at scale \(\varepsilon\) by \(m\) witnesses if the
line it spans admits such a witness family of cardinality \(m\)
consisting of intrinsic balls \(B_{M}\left( x_{i},\varepsilon \right)\);
the feature is \emph{robust} if \(m\) may be taken bounded independently

# C018 v1: finite-width nonlinear transfer of the iid-head construction
Status: proof (unaudited). Kind: narrowed. Target: 1. Novelty unestablished.
This is a four-point, label-noise-averaged witness theorem. It does not
claim double descent for one realized label vector or settle general T267.

## 1. Exact model and statement
Use C017's definitions: 0<e<1/4, D=1+e^2+e^4, uniform population on
x_(s,t)=(1,es,e^2 t)/sqrt(D), one training observation at each of these
four inputs, and u_e=(0,e,1)/sqrt(1+e^2). The teacher is
 g_e(x)=ReLU(u_e.x)-c_e/2, c_e=e^2/sqrt(D(1+e^2)), alpha_e=c_e/2.
Fix 0<nu<=1 and kappa>0. For each of the sixteen sign vectors
xi in {-1,1}^4, train a separate network with labels
 y_i=g_e(x_i)+sigma_e xi_i, sigma_e=2 alpha_e sqrt(kappa/sqrt(e)).
All sixteen networks share their initial parameters. At width m these are
 f_m(x)=m^(-1/2) sum_(j=1)^m a_j ReLU(w_j.x),
 w_j(0) iid N(0,I_3), a_j(0) iid uniform {-nu,nu}, independent of w_j(0).
Train BOTH layers by simultaneous discrete GD with step gamma=1/2 on
(1/8) sum_i (f_m(x_i)-y_i)^2. Set the derivative at a zero gate to zero.
No pairing, tying or resetting of the readout is imposed.
Define the clean population risk averaged over the sixteen trained networks:
 R_(e,m)(k)= (1/16) sum_xi (1/4) sum_i (f_(m,xi)(x_i;k)-g_e(x_i))^2.
Probability below is over initialization only. In particular R is NOT the
risk trajectory of any one of the sixteen networks.

Let lambda_h be the Walsh eigenvalues of C=H/4, where
 H(x,z)=E[ReLU(W.x)ReLU(W.z)+nu^2 1{W.x>0,W.z>0}x.z],
and let b_h=-log(1-lambda_h/2), eta_e=(b_t+b_st)/b_s.
The clock premises proved in C009 are b_s~nu^2 e/(4pi), eta_e~e.
Let independent standard normals G_s,G_t define
 a=2nu^2 G_s^2, B=((sqrt(2)nu G_t-1)^2+1)/2,
 p=P(kappa^2>4aB).

For every epsilon>0 define E_(e,m)(epsilon) as existence of integers
0<=k0<k1<k2<k3 such that
 R(k0)>R(k1), R(k2)>R(k1), R(k2)>R(k3),
and k2 maximizes R on the integer interval [k1,k3], with
 | k2 / ((6pi/nu^2)e^(-1)log(1/e)) - 1 | < epsilon.
Then
 liminf_(e downarrow 0) liminf_(m to infinity) P(E_(e,m)(epsilon)) >= p
 >= max(0,1-8nu^2(1+nu^2)/kappa^2).                       (1)
More precisely, for every zeta>0 there are constants c>0,L<infinity
such that the inner/outer liminf probability of witnesses with each of
the three displayed strict risk gaps >=c alpha_e^2 eta_e and
 |b_s k2-(3/2)log(1/e)|<=L
is at least p-zeta. Negative lower bounds are understood as vacuous.
This proves two descents separated by a rise in the finite-witness sense,
with an interior interval peak. It does not prove unique stationary points
or monotonicity of the intervening integer-time segments.

## 2. What the preceding proofs provide
C017 proves, in its joint Gaussian initialization coupling, locally uniform
convergence of centered risk differences
 [Q_e(t_e(s))-Q_e(t_e(0))]/(2alpha_e^2 eta_e)
       -> V(s)-V(0),
where t_e(s)=((3/2)log(1/e)+s)/b_s and
 V(s)=-kappa exp(-s)+(a/2)exp(-2s)-Bs.
The derivative converges too, although this proof only transfers values.
On Delta=kappa^2-4aB>0, V has a simple minimum r and a simple maximum v,
with r<v, decreasing before r, increasing on (r,v), decreasing after v.
Their formulas are r=-log((kappa+sqrt(Delta))/(2a)) and
v=-log((kappa-sqrt(Delta))/(2a)). The probability a=0 is zero.
C009 Section 3 proves the following finite-horizon fact for the SAME
nonzero iid initialization: for fixed e, bounded labels, and finite integer T,
actual nonlinear predictions at all four inputs, uniformly over k<=T and
all sixteen label patterns, approach frozen deterministic-C predictions
started from the actual initial vector, in probability as m tends to infinity.
That proof controls gates through initial weighted Gaussian bands and keeps
the exact simultaneous-update remainder. Its deterministic residual bounds
can use any finite initial residual bound; replacing its old teacher/labels
by the present bounded labels changes only this bound. Thus its argument
applies verbatim for each fixed e here. The small-e limit is taken AFTER the
width limit; no uniform width estimate in e or T is inferred.
These preceding claims are unaudited dependencies, not independent audits.

## 3. From nonlinear prediction transfer to the correct joint risk limit
For fixed e and T, the initial four-vector converges by the multivariate iid
CLT to C017's Gaussian Z_e (expressed in Walsh coordinates). The empirical
initial tangent kernel converges in probability to the deterministic C.
These facts hold jointly: no independence between the finite-width initial
output and its empirical kernel is needed, since the latter limit is constant.
C009's comparison is already to deterministic C with the same initial output.

Frozen predictions at times 0,...,T are affine continuous functions of the
initial four-vector, with labels fixed. For the finite sixteen-label family,
the corresponding frozen risk array is therefore a continuous function of
this vector. Actual and frozen risk arrays differ by o_P(1). Indeed for
vectors u,v measured in population L2, the exact bound
 | ||u-g||^2-||v-g||^2 | <= ||u-v||(2||v-g||+||u-v||)
applies; the finite frozen array is tight at fixed e,T by its continuous
Gaussian limit, and C009 supplies uniform o_P(1) prediction error. Averaging
a finite sixteen terms preserves this estimate. Slutsky then gives joint
weak convergence of the whole actual risk array to (Q_e(k))_(k=0)^T.
At fixed e, alpha_e^2 eta_e is strictly positive, so the same assertion holds
for risks centered at any fixed time and divided by this scale. There is
no claim that an unscaled o_P(1) error is uniform in e.

## 4. Finite witnesses, rounding, and the open-event argument
Fix a Gaussian realization in {Delta>0,a>0}. Choose small radii h0,h1>0
with r-h0<r<v<v+h1. Because V is strictly decreasing immediately before
r, increasing on (r,v), and decreasing after v, the values at
 r-h0, r, v, v+h1
have the required decrease/rise/decrease gaps. All are strict. On the
closed interval [r,v+h1], V has its unique global maximum at v. For any
sufficiently small d>0, the maximum over the complement of (v-d,v+d)
in that interval is strictly smaller than V(v), by continuity and compactness.

Convergence of centered risk differences locally uniformly in s therefore
preserves the three gaps, as well as the separated interval maximum, for
all sufficiently small e depending on this realization. Round all four
t_e anchor times to nearest integers. Their s coordinates change by at
most b_s/2, which tends to zero. They remain ordered because their fixed
s spacings are positive. The interpolation values at the rounded anchors
converge to the same V values. The same local uniform convergence controls
ALL integer times between the rounded second and fourth anchors. It gives
an interior maximizing grid index, with s coordinate in (v-d,v+d).
It follows pathwise that its s coordinate tends to v: apply this argument
for every rational d>0. Its peak-time leading coefficient is consequently
6pi/nu^2. This rounding step makes no claim about continuous interpolation
of actual nonlinear GD, which is only evaluated at integer times.

For precision in passing probabilities, fix zeta>0. The preceding pathwise
argument and a countable exhaustion allow deterministic c>0,L<infinity
such that, on an event of probability at least p-zeta, the three gaps of
the Gaussian-limit integer curves exceed 2c alpha_e^2 eta_e, all their
anchors lie in |s|<L-1, and an interior interval maximizer lies in |s|<L-1,
for all sufficiently small e in the following probabilistic sense: the
liminf of these event probabilities is at least p-zeta. One explicit
exhaustion bounds all four Gaussian coordinates, bounds a away from zero,
bounds Delta away from zero, bounds r and v, and then restricts each
positive limiting value gap and peak-separation margin away from zero.
These compact events exhaust {Delta>0,a>0}; local uniform convergence and
Fatou give the asserted liminf. Uniform convergence over compact Gaussian
parameters can also be used, but is not required.

For each fixed sufficiently small e, there are only finitely many indices
with |b_s k-(3/2)log(1/e)|<=L. Consider the following event in this FINITE
risk array: there exist k0<k1<j<k3 in this window such that all three
witness gaps at j exceed c alpha_e^2 eta_e, and every index in [k1,k3]
with a peak time outside the desired localization band has risk strictly
less than R(j). This is a finite union of finite intersections of strict
inequalities, hence open. If the excluded set is empty its inequalities
are vacuous. An interval maximizer then lies inside the desired band,
and substituting that maximizer for j preserves the three strict gaps.
The Gaussian arrays just constructed belong to such an open event (with
extra positive margins), taking either the band |s|<L or the relative
peak-time band of (1); for small e the whole fixed s window is inside the
relative band. Enlarge the finite horizon to include the whole window.
The joint weak convergence in Section 3 and the open-set Portmanteau
inequality transfer its probability LOWER bound to the nonlinear arrays.
Take liminf in e, then let zeta decrease to zero, proving (1).
For the refined gap statement retain zeta and c,L from the exhaustion.
Only fixed-e finite arrays are used in each width limit. There is no
exchange of the two limits, no infinite-horizon NTK claim, and no assertion
that finite-width Gaussian mode coefficients are independent.

## 5. Probability bound and scope
C017 gives E(4aB)=8nu^2(1+nu^2) using independence of G_s and G_t.
Markov's inequality bounds P(4aB>=kappa^2) and yields (1). Arbitrarily
large fixed kappa makes the bound approach one; sigma_e still tends to
zero and is <=1 for sufficiently small e. The teacher direction has norm
one. The input distribution is uniform on four shrinking, clustered atoms,
with a stratified training set of size four, not an iid Gaussian sample.
Width tends to infinity first, so this is an iterated-limit lazy-regime
result about actual nonlinear parameter updates, not macroscopic feature
learning. The risk average spans sixteen different GD trajectories.
The unresolved hardest piece for a one-dataset theorem is control of the
realized-noise cross terms on the alpha_e^2 eta_e central gap scale.
General Target 1, fixed-noise regimes, continuous iid-input extensions of
this particular iid-head construction, independent correctness review and
novelty review all remain open. Source dependencies: C009 Section 3,

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:42.499003+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_5dc3c47c9309dce7fd49bcf52a42480f0accb33ab54ce677db12baa123bb1e4e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Hurwitz's theorem is often quoted as 'a locally uniform limit of zero-free holomorphic functions is zero-free'. Three hypotheses carry that conclusion. (1) Connectedness of the domain. On U = D(0,1) union D(3,1) put f_n = 1/n on the first disk and f_n = 1 on the second; each f_n is holomorphic and zero-free on U and f_n converges locally uniformly, but the limit is 0 on one component and 1 on the other: neither zero-free nor identically zero. The correct statement is the dichotomy component by component. (2) The degenerate alternative cannot be dropped even on a connected domain: f_n(z) = exp(z)/n is zero-free on C and converges locally uniformly to the identically zero function. Likewise the injectivity version must allow constants: f_n(z) = z/n is injective on D and converges to the constant 0. (3) Holomorphy, not just real analyticity: on the real line f_n(x) = x^2 + 1/n has no real zeros and converges uniformly on compacts to x^2, which has a zero; the complex statement survives because the complex zeros ±i/sqrt(n) move to 0. (4) The counting form requires that the boundary circle avoid the zeros of the limit: f_n(z) = z - 1 + 1/n has one zero in the unit disk for every n, while f_n(z) = z - 1 - 1/n has none, and both converge to z - 1, whose only zero sits on the circle |z| = 1. Never conclude equal zero counts from a circle through a zero of the limit.","status":"unverified"}

The relation-type set R partitions into six pairwise-disjoint classes, R = R_causal U R_contain U R_temp U R_assoc U R_epist U R_spatial, each defined by an independent structural test below. A particular graph may employ only a subset; belief-graph and working-memory instantiations specify which classes appear in R_B and R_{W_t}. The six classes are: 1. Causal (R_causal). An edge (u, v) with tau(u, v) in R_causal asserts that node u produces, enables, probabilistically raises, or inhibits the occurrence of node v, independent of the payload types of u and v: R_causal = {r_causes, r_enables, r_inhibits, r_counterfactual}. Causal edges are antisymmetric: (u, v) in E_{R_causal} implies (v, u) not in E_{R_causal}. Acyclicity over R_causal is a structural forbidden pattern in S. When u is a distinguished agent node, an optional attribution tag a(u, v) in V records whose causal model the edge belongs to, e.g. 'agent a believes u causes v'. 2. Containment (R_contain). An edge (u, v) with tau(u, v) in R_contain asserts that v's existence or identity is nested inside u's scope, characterized by an existential-dependency test: (u, v) in E_{R_contain} iff removing u from G requires removing v as well. R_contain = {r_is-a, r_part-of, r_instance-of, r_role-of}. When v carries a graph payload G_v (Definition 2, item 5) or a structured perceptual payload (item 4), its internal subgraph is linked to v via r_part-of edges. Containment is transitive and irreflexive; a directed cycle over R_contain is a forbidden pattern in S. 3. Temporal (R_temp). An edge (u, v) with tau(u, v) in R_temp encodes ordering of nodes across time via a node timestamp function theta_V : V -> R (distinct from the working-memory time index t) such that (u, v) in E_{R_temp} implies theta_V(u) <= theta_V(v): R_temp = {r_before, r_after, r_during, r_next}. Here r_before and r_after are mutually exclusive on the same ordered pair (a predicate incompatibility in F); r_next is the sequential successor used in action-sequence and planning subgraphs. 4. Associative (R_assoc). An edge (u, v) with tau(u, v) in R_assoc encodes statistical co-occurrence or spreading-activation linkage with no stronger typed commitment: R_assoc = {r_related-to, r_co-occurs-with, r_similar-to}. Associative edges are undirected, represented as symmetric pairs (u, v), (v, u) in E with equal weights w(u, v) = w(v, u). This is the default class: any relation not warranting a stronger typed commitment from classes 1-3 or 5-6 defaults here. 5. Evidential (R_epist). An edge (u, v) with tau(u, v) in R_epist encodes inferential, evidential, or evaluative support between propositional or evaluative nodes: R_epist = {r_supports, r_contradicts, r_derived-from, r_supersedes}. Valence and deontic force are carried as signed edge weights on r_supports and r_contradicts edges (extending w to R on R_epist when needed); an obligation is an r_supports edge with |w(u, v)| = 1 directed at a norm node, and a prohibition is the corresponding r_contradicts edge. Here r_contradicts induces a conflict pair in (F, S); r_supersedes is generated by belief-update operators when a node is revised rather than deleted. 6. Spatial (R_spatial). An edge (u, v) with tau(u, v) in R_spatial encodes geometric relations, restricted to node pairs where at least one endpoint carries a perceptual or structured perceptual payload (Definition 2, items 3-4): R_spatial = {r_above, r_below, r_left-of, r_right-of, r_near, r_affords}. The sub-type r_affords links a body-schema node u to a perceptual node v, encoding a sensorimotor affordance relation. For any edge class R_k, write E_{R_k} = {(u, v) in E | tau(u, v) in R_k} for the induced edge set. For a subgraph Q of B, the restriction E_{R_k}(Q) = E_{R_k} intersected with (V_Q x V_Q) denotes the edges of that class internal to Q.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:16:49.564583+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5ddfd9d0ab688bc06a92f61e8f3e02a3043a9179149de3abc786a92d5ab0f31e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 16 (The uniform-grid fixed-rate optimum is within-group flatness) of arXiv:2608.25188, 'Transforms for LLM Quantization:\\ The Great Inversion and Format Co-Design'] Writing $E=\sum_k v_k^2$ for the total energy over coordinate magnitudes $v_k$,

\Cref{prop:schur}(ii) rederived from the quantizer's own step rule, satisfies
\[
D_{\mathrm{fr}}=\sum_g M_g^2 \;\ge\; \frac1G\sum_k v_k^2 \;=\; \frac{E}{G},
\]
with equality iff every group is internally \emph{uniform}. Thus, at fixed $E$, $D_{\mathrm{fr}}$
is minimized precisely by driving every within-group crest factor to its floor;
the \emph{across}-group energy profile is irrelevant once each group is internally
balanced. No within-group concentration step lowers $D_{\mathrm{fr}}$, and any such step that

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:29:28.004498+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5dee73bee296f03e350a4cd2bbdf785b59b51399763d5a081db38bf3d551d9a5","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 4 (Certified finite-direction radial reconstruction for $1<\beta<2$) of arXiv:2608.24964, 'Common-Center Geometry and Certified Radial Reconstruction for Energy-Form Full Conformal '] Assume
\[
m\ge2,
\qquad
1<\beta<2.
\]
Fix
\[
0\le\varepsilon<1
\quad\text{such that}\quad
1\le k=\lfloor(m+1)\varepsilon\rfloor\le m.
\]
Let $c$ be the common center from Corollary~\ref{cor:power} and define the explicit constants
\[
\mu_{-j},r_j,H_j,D_{ij},M_j,\lambda_j,\ell_j,L
\]
as above.  Then
\[
\operatorname{Lip}(R_j)\le\ell_j,
\qquad

where Lipschitz constants on $\mathbb S^{d-1}$ are taken in chord distance.

Let
\[
\mathcal U=\{u_\ell\}_{\ell=1}^N\subset\mathbb S^{d-1}
\]
be a nonempty finite directional set.  Assume certified radial intervals
\[
a_\ell\le R_\varepsilon(u_\ell)\le b_\ell,
\qquad
b_\ell-a_\ell\le\delta.
\]
Define
\[
\underline R(u)
=
\max\left\{
0,
\max_\ell\left[a_\ell-L\|u-u_\ell\|\right]
\right\},
\]
and
\[
\overline R(u)
=
\min_\ell\left[b_\ell+L\|u-u_\ell\|\right].
\]
Then
\[
\underline R(u)\le R_\varepsilon(u)\le\overline R(u)
\qquad\forall u\in\mathbb S^{d-1}.
\]
Let
\[
h_{\mathcal U}
=
\sup_{u\in\mathbb S^{d-1}}
\min_\ell\|u-u_\ell\|.
\]
Then
\[
\|\overline R-\underline R\|_\infty
\le
\delta+2Lh_{\mathcal U}.
\]
Define
\[
\underline\Gamma
=
\{c+ru:u\in\mathbb S^{d-1},\ 0\le r\le\underline R(u)\},
\]
and
\[
\overline\Gamma
=
\{c+ru:u\in\mathbb S^{d-1},\ 0\le r\le\overline R(u)\}.
\]
Then
\[
\underline\Gamma\subseteq\Gamma^\varepsilon\subseteq\overline\Gamma.
\]

\[
d_H(\underline\Gamma,\Gamma^\varepsilon)
\le
\|R_\varepsilon-\underline R\|_\infty
\le
\delta+2Lh_{\mathcal U},

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:06:07.076229+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5def13abd9a185d8778d9459f41284dc55818751be72eb691308f4c4b1be3300","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 2 (Microscopic second-moment universality) of arXiv:2608.27641, 'Hard-Edge Determinant Fields and Second-Moment Universality for Random Matrix Ratios'] Under Assumption~\ref{ass:matrix-atoms}, the following statements hold.

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
\item The rescaled spectrum converges to the infinite complex Ginibre process:
\[
\mathcal{Z}_n
\overset{\mathrm{d}}{\rightarrow}
\operatorname{Gin}_{\infty}
\qquad
\text{in }\mathcal{N}\left(\mathbb{C}\right).
\]

\item For every fixed \(k\geq 1\),
\[
\left(
\sqrt{n}R_{n,1},
\ldots,
\sqrt{n}R_{n,k}
\right)
\overset{\mathrm{d}}{\rightarrow}
\left(
R_1,\ldots,R_k
\right).
\]

\item For every fixed \(k\geq 1\),
\[
\left(
\frac{R_{n,n}}{\sqrt{n}},
\ldots,
\frac{R_{n,n-k+1}}{\sqrt{n}}
\right)
\overset{\mathrm{d}}{\rightarrow}
\left(
R_1^{-1},\ldots,R_k^{-1}
\right).
\]

\item In particular,
\[
\sqrt{n}\rho_{\min}\left(M_n\right)
\overset{\mathrm{d}}{\rightarrow}
R_1,
\qquad
\frac{\rho_{\max}\left(M_n\right)}{\sqrt{n}}
\overset{\mathrm{d}}{\rightarrow}
R_1^{-1}.
\]

\item If \(D\subset\mathbb{C}\) is a bounded Borel set whose boundary has zero planar Lebesgue measure, then
\[
\mathcal{Z}_n\left(D\right)
\overset{\mathrm{d}}{\rightarrow}
\operatorname{Gin}_{\infty}\left(D\right).
\]
\end{enumerate}

More explicitly, let
\(\left(\Gamma_j\right)_{j\geq 1}\) be independent random variables satisfying
\[
\Gamma_j\sim\operatorname{Gamma}\left(j,1\right).
\]
The Kostlan representation gives the equality in distribution of unordered point configurations
\[
\left\{
\left|Z\right|^2:
Z\in\operatorname{Gin}_{\infty}
\right\}
\overset{\mathrm{d}}{=}
\left\{
\Gamma_j:
j\geq 1
\right\};
\]
see \citet[Theorem~4.7.3 and Section~7.2]{HoughKrishnapurPeresVirag2009}.
Consequently, \(\left(R_1,\ldots,R_k\right)\) are the first \(k\) order statistics of
\[
\left\{
\sqrt{\Gamma_j}:
j\geq 1
\right\}.
\]

For \(a>0\), let
\[
D_a:=\left\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\left|z\right|\leq a\right\}.
\]
Then
\[
\operatorname{Gin}_{\infty}\left(D_a\right)
\overset{\mathrm{d}}{=}
\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}I_j\left(a\right),
\]
where the variables \(\left(I_j\left(a\right)\right)_{j\geq 1}\) are independent and
\[
I_j\left(a\right)
\sim
\operatorname{Bernoulli}\left(p_j\left(a\right)\right),
\qquad
p_j\left(a\right)
=
\Pr\left(\Gamma_j\leq a^2\right)
=
1-e^{-a^2}
\sum_{\ell=0}^{j-1}
\frac{a^{2\ell}}{\ell!}.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:48:35.822708+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5e122050edb6557373649e03968459177332b19aae2750bcdd716dc6cb4b4705","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition upper and lower incomplete gamma functions of arXiv:2411.09614, 'Moment estimates for the stochastic heat equation on Cartan-Hadamard manifolds'] For $s>0$, $x>0$, $\Gamma(s,x):=\int_x^{+\infty} t^{s-1}e^{-t}dt$ is the upper incomplete gamma function, and $\gamma(s,x):=\int_0^x t^{s-1}e^{-t}dt$ is the lower incomplete gamma function. For $s>0$ they satisfy $\Gamma(s)=\gamma(s,x)+\Gamma(s,x)$, where $\Gamma(s)$ is the well-known gamma function with domain $s>0$. The above additive relation tells us that for $s>0$,$$\sup_{x>0}\gamma(s,x)=\sup_{x>0}\Gamma(s,x)=\Gamma(s).$$
        If $s=0,$ the additive relation fails due to $\gamma(0,x)$ being undefined. However, we have $\Gamma(0,x)=-\text{Ei}(-x)$, where $\text{Ei}(z):=-\int_{-z}^{+\infty} \frac{e^{-t}}{t}dt$ is the exponential integral function. 
        The following asymptotic results follow from elementary calculus arguments.
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item For $s>0$, $\gamma(s,x)\sim_{x\downarrow 0}x^{s}.$
            \item For $s\geq 0$, $\Gamma(s,x)\sim_{x\uparrow+\infty}e^{-x}$.
            \item $-\text{Ei}(-x)\sim_{x\downarrow0}-\ln(x)$.
        \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.178838+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5e2101359573bb2632a50cc2ddb67dc0dbc17a37fe0265b093904237c1be96b0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 88 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $\mu \in \cP_2(\bbR_{\ge 0})$, the preimage
    \[
        \sym^{-1}(\mu) \equiv \Big\{
            \tilde \mu \in \cP_2(\bbR) : \sym(\tilde\mu) = \mu
        \Big\}
    \]
    is compact with respect to the $\bbW_2$ metric.

\begin{proof}
The set $\sym^{-1}(\mu)$ is clearly closed. Therefore, it suffices to show that any sequence $(\tilde \mu_n)_{n\ge1}$ in $\sym^{-1}(\mu)$ has a $\bbW_2$-convergent subsequence. The collection of measures $\sym^{-1}(\mu)$ is clearly tight, since we have 
	\[
	\tilde{\mu}([-K,K])
	=\mu([0,K]) 
	\stackrel{K\to\infty}{\longrightarrow} 1\,,
	\]
uniformly over all $\tilde{\mu}\in \sym^{-1}(\mu)$. 
    By Prohorov's theorem, any sequence $(\tilde \mu_n)_{n\ge 1}$ in $\sym^{-1}(\mu)$ must have a subsequence $(\tilde \mu_{n_j})_{j\ge 1}$ that converges weakly to some measure $\tilde{\mu}$, which is also clearly in $\sym^{-1}(\mu)$. 
By Skorokhod's theorem, we have can find random variables $X_n,X$ such that $X_n$ is distributed according to $\tilde{\mu}_{n_j}$, $X$ is distributed according to $\tilde{\mu}$, and $X_n$ converges to $X$ almost surely as $n\to\infty$. Then, for any finite $M$, we have
	\[
	\E\Big[
	(X_n-X)^2; \max\{|X_n|,|X|\} \le M
	\Big]
	\le \E\Big[\max\Big\{(X_n-X)^2
	; (2M)^2
	\Big\}
	\Big] \stackrel{n\to\infty}{\longrightarrow} 0
	\]
by the bounded convergence theorem. On the other hand,	since $|X_n|$ and $|X|$ are distributed as samples from $\mu$, we have
	\begin{align*}
	&\E\Big[
	(X_n-X)^2; \max\{|X_n|,|X|\} 
		> M
	\Big]
	\le 2\Big\{
	\E[(X_n)^2;|X_n|>M]
	+\E[X^2;|X|>M]\Big\} \\
	&\qquad= 4 \E[X^2;|X|>M]
	\le o_M(1)\,.
	\end{align*}
By sending $M\to\infty$ we conclude $\tilde \mu_{n_j} \rightarrow \tilde \mu$ in $\bbW_2$, from which the compactness claim follows.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:33:01.744430+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5e60c33256ee4ba64660d7396b4dfe1a06cb3f2aa69619263e8e47ea6aa36c9f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 8 of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] The language $H$ admits a well-defined decomposition into primitive languages:
\begin{align*}
  H = \Big[\Big(\C_1^{\geqslant 0} \circ \D_1^{\geqslant 0}\Big).\C_1\Big]
  \circ \cdots \circ
  \Big[
    \Big(\C_m^{\geqslant 0} \circ \D_m^{\geqslant 0}\Big).\C_m
  \Big].
\end{align*}
Its exponential generating function is hence
\[
  \hat\phi_H(z) = \left(1-p\right)^m \left(e^{z/m} - 1\right)^m.
\]
\begin{proof}
It holds for all $i$ that
\[
  \hat\phi_{\C_i^{\geqslant 0}}(z) = 
  e^{z(1-p)/m} \quad \text{and} \quad
  \hat\phi_{\D_i^{\geqslant 0}}(z) = 
  e^{zp/m} \quad \text{and} \quad 
  \phi_{\C_i}(z) = \frac{\left(1-p\right)z}{m}.
\]
Apply Proposition \ref{thm:shuffling} to find
\[
  \hat\phi_{{\C_i^{\geqslant 0}} \circ {\D_i^{\geqslant 0}}}(z)
  = \hat\phi_{\C_i^{\geqslant 0}}(z) \,
    \hat\phi_{\D_i^{\geqslant 0}}(z)
  = e^{z/m},
\]
then take the Laplace--Borel transform:
\[
  \phi_{{\C_i^{\geqslant 0}} \circ {\D_i^{\geqslant 0}}}(x)
  = \int_0^\infty e^{xt/m}\, e^{-t} \, dt
  = \int_0^\infty e^{-\left(1-x/m\right)t} \, dt
  = \frac{1}{1-x/m}, \quad 0 < x < 1.
\]
Therefore
\[
  \phi_{\left({\C_i^{\geqslant0}} \circ {\D_i^{\geqslant0}}\right).\C_i}(z)
    = \frac{\left(1-p\right)z}{m} \cdot \frac{1}{1-z/m}
  = \frac{\left(1-p\right)z}{m} \sum_{n=0}^\infty \left(\frac{z}{m}\right)^n
  = (1-p) \sum_{n=1}^\infty \left(\frac{z}{m}\right)^n,
\]
so by introducing the $n!$ terms,
\[
  \hat\phi_{\left(\C_i^{\geqslant0} \circ \D_i^{\geqslant0}\right).\C_i}(z)
  = (1-p)\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(z/m)^n}{n!}
  = (1-p)\left(e^{z/m} - 1\right).
\]
We find $\hat\phi_H(z) = \prod_i 
\hat\phi_{\left(\C_i^{\geqslant0} \circ \D_i^{\geqslant0}\right).\C_i}(z)
= (1-p)^m\left(e^{z/m} - 1\right)^m$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

d\ell

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:51:00.241593+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5ec83e8838255549a30a7a891bd8b4e6575b0da6a976936f541e4fe7a1ce1727","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem Varadhan of arXiv:2604.23751, 'Large deviation principles for pattern-avoiding permutations, and limit shapes for constra'] For any $n\ge 1,$ let $\mu_n$ denote the distribution of $X_n$ and assume that $(X_n)$ satisfies an LDP at speed $a_n$ with good rate function $I.$ Let $F:E \rightarrow \mathbb R$ be a bounded continuous function.  \[ \mathrm{d}\nu_n(x) := \frac{1}{Z_n} \textup{e}^{a_nF(x)} \mathrm{d}\mu_n(x),\]
 where $Z_n$ is a normalizing constant such that $\nu_n$ is a probability measure.
 Then we have
	\[ \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{a_n} \log Z_n = -  \inf_{y\in E} (I(y)- F(y)). \]

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:29:21.935843+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5ee0b14ac38b0293255ee1c978583a5c49649d3eccaaed32e8c99e73b4ec3728","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 22 of arXiv:2608.01516, 'Nondegeneracy and regularity of polynomial pushforwards'] Let $n,d,k\in\mathbb N$ and assume that $n\ge k$. There exist two functions
\[
\alpha_{n,d,k}\colon(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)
\quad\text{and}\quad
\beta_{n,d,k}\colon(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty),
\]
with the following property.

Let $\mu$ be an isotropic log-concave measure on $\mathbb R^n$,
and let
$f=(f_1,\ldots,f_k)\in \mathcal P_d(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R^k)$
be such that
\[
\operatorname{Var}_\mu(f_j)>0,
\quad
\forall j\in\{1,\ldots,k\}.
\]
Then, for every $a>0$,
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \Delta_{\hat{f}}\,d\mu\ge a
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\det \Sigma_\mu^d(f)\ge \beta_{n,d,k}(a),
\]
and, for every $b>0$,
\[
\det \Sigma_\mu^d(f)\ge b
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \Delta_{\hat{f}}\,d\mu\ge \alpha_{n,d,k}(b).
\]","status":"unverified"}
