{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:09:41.190331+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_6f5cfee93cb76cd8d74924060da891f5b4881b2215fe5aa410d44ee0474d26de","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematics, the term homology, originally introduced in algebraic topology, has three primary, closely related usages. First, there is the homology of a chain complex, a sequence of abelian groups, called homology groups, which are regarded as fundamental invariants of the chain complex. Secondly, when one can associate a chain complex to a different mathematical object, one can also associate its homology to that object. Distinct procedures of associating chain complexes to a given object are grouped into homology theories. Finally, homology is important in the study of topological spaces. Under nice conditions in which distinct homology theories for a single topological space produce the same homology groups, one can define a single homology of a topological space. This last notion of homology is closely related to topological ideas frequently discussed in popular mathematics such as the holes of a surface or the cycles of a graph. There is also a related notion of the cohomology of a cochain complex, giving rise to various cohomology theories, in addition to the notion of the cohomology of a topological space.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:35:04.094911+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6f628d213e948889bebd7b6cc96612958248be05cf576e45b6f16f5b6758c038","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:circuit-primitives of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] For an ordered finite set $S$ of oriented carrier labels, write
$\mathscr H_S=\bigotimes_{u\in S}H_u$, with every factor equipped with
the Euclidean Hilbert norm.  A \emph{normalized Brauer primitive} is a
signed carrier permutation, a wedge reversal, full transpose, a share
turn, a through string, the orthogonal antisymmetrizer, or a cup/cap
normalized so that its operator norm is one.  A share turn is the fixed
signed boundary permutation, possibly followed by full transpose,
induced when a principal pivot reverses one of the two ordered boundary
intervals.  The two coefficient primitives are
\[
 \widehat C_{uv}=\iota_{uv}C\pi_{uv}:H_u\otimes H_v\to H_u\otimes H_v,
\]
where $\pi_{uv}$ is the normalized orthogonal projection and
identification onto $\Lambda^2H$, and $\iota_{uv}=\pi_{uv}^*$; hence
$\widehat C_{uv}$ is zero on $\operatorname{Sym}^2H$ and has norm $K$.
The other coefficient primitive is the restriction/re-expression of
(eq:2.1.3 of the paper) as the Bianchi transfer
\[
 (\Phi_CY)_{ik}=\sum_{m,n}C_{in,mk}Y_{mn},
 \qquad Y\in\Lambda^2H.
\]
The first Bianchi identity identifies the latter with the physical action
of $C$.  A \emph{safe gate} is a typed composite of these primitives,
including the $AA$ words and correctly oriented $AB$ words used below.
Its degree is the number of coefficient primitives.  Thus a degree-$d$
safe gate $G:\mathscr H_S\to\mathscr H_T$ satisfies
$\|G\|_{\rm op}\le K^d$; untouched factors are ancillary identities.

A coefficient box has four darts
$L_{i,0},L_{i,1},R_{i,0},R_{i,1}$.  For a column pairing $q$, a
\emph{packet} is a connected component of the box-incidence graph whose
edges are the $q$-pairs joining different boxes.  A $q$-pair joining the
two darts of one wedge is forbidden and gives zero.  An allowed
\emph{smoothing} chooses at each box either
\[
 h_i^{\parallel}=\{L_{i,0}R_{i,0},L_{i,1}R_{i,1}\},\qquad
 h_i^{\times}=\{L_{i,0}R_{i,1},L_{i,1}R_{i,0}\}.
\]
The alternating circuits of $q\vee h$ are the \emph{smoothing
carriers}; adjoining one carrier means adjoining one identity factor
$I_H$.  The smoothing support $\operatorname{supp}_h(i)$ of a box is the
one- or two-element set of $q\vee h$ carriers containing its two
$h$-passages.  A \emph{ported pair comb} on two chosen carriers consists of all
boxes whose smoothing support is that pair, together with every singleton-support box
assigned to it exactly once; removing all other support groups leaves
their boundary darts as linearly ordered typed ports.  These definitions
fix the domains and codomains of every safe word, fold, comb, and
attachment below.

An \emph{ambient rooted ribbon record} $\Gamma$ consists of a common
finite dart set, its coefficient boxes and local wedge signs, a row
pairing $p$, a column pairing $q$, a rooted trace pairing $r$, and the
declared boundary/root data.  Thus $p\vee r$ is the disjoint union of the
original trace circuits in that record; its components, not temporary
proof cuts, receive the normalization bases below.  The more detailed
Weingarten data carried by $\Gamma$ are specified in
(def:ribbon-record of the paper).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:07:15.760628+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6f94ffa8dcd385e87271234f98eae453b37f436b5823899a6aa86c6878e3a5bb","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:measurable-operator-field-calculus of arXiv:2608.02459, 'Response Calculus for Spectral Simplicity\\ and Joint Eigenvalue Densities'] From the preceding definitions we obtain the following three properties.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:28:49.111650+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6f952793904c3731ea77d2e91a965f0d41c6dc1e24edd91e37d78c894d14ebe9","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:terminal-lift of arXiv:2608.16119, 'Fully nonlinear parabolic equations under a fixed reference diffusion: weighted \texorpdfs'] Assume Assumptions~(ass:reference-diffusion of the paper) and
(ass:drift-multiplier of the paper).  For every
regular weight $w$, every interval $I=(r_0,r_1)$, and
$
 F\in H_{x,w}^1(I),\, \eta\in H^1(\mu_{r_1}),
$
one has
\begin{equation}
 D_x\mathcal U_I(F,\eta)
 =\mathcal P_{1,I}^{-1}(D_xF,D_x\eta)
 \in H_{x,w}^1(I;\mathbb R^d).
 
\end{equation}
In particular, for $\psi\in H^1(\mu_T)$, recall
$v^\psi=\mathcal U(0,\psi)$ and set
\begin{equation*}
p^\psi:=\mathcal P_1^{-1}(0,D_x\psi).
\end{equation*}
The terminal identities are
\begin{equation}
 p^\psi=D_xv^\psi,\qquad D_xp^\psi=D_x^2v^\psi,\qquad
 \operatorname{Tr}_T^Xp^\psi=D_x\psi(X_T).
 
\end{equation}
Consequently, for every $\alpha\geq0$, $v^\psi$ is the unique
order-$\alpha$ occupation Sobolev solution with data $(0,\psi)$, and
there exists a constant $C=C(T,\lambda,\Lambda,M_1(a),\Lambda_b)>0$ such that
\begin{equation}
 \left\lVert v^\psi\right\rVert_0^2+\left\lVert D_xv^\psi\right\rVert_0^2
 +\left\lVert D_x^2v^\psi\right\rVert_0^2
 \leq C\norm\psi_{H^1(\mu_T)}^2.
 
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.351977+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6f97ed2f4a5f62c3336de36c19870ab905777e638f947f2f9b8aabcaf18277b6","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 191 (annealed first moment bounds for 
$E^{\sigma,\tau}$ and $E^{\frozen,\sigma,\tau}$
with $\sigma,\tau\in\{\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let
$Q^{\sigma,\tau}=E^{\sigma,\tau}+\tilde{Q}^{\sigma,\tau}$ as in Definitions~\ref{d:Q} and \ref{d:tQ}. Then, for $N$ large enough, we have
	\[\bbE
	\Big|\Delta E^{\sigma,\tau}(q_d)\Big| 
	\le L^{O(1)}\bigg\{\eta\delta^{1/2} + \frac{\BUCKETS\delta}{N}
	\bigg\}
	\]
for all $\sigma,\tau\in\{\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}$. The same bound holds with $E^\frozen$ in place of $E$.
\begin{proof}
This is similar
to the proof of Corollary~\ref{c:Q.first.quenched}. Recall 
that Lemma~\ref{l:qv.simplification} implies
	\[
	\Big|\Delta E^{\sigma,\tau}(q_d)\Big| 
	\le O\bigg(
	\eta^2
	+\sum_{\rho\in\{\sigma,\tau\}}\bigg[
	\eta\Big(\Delta\tilde{Q}^\rho(q_d)\Big)^{1/2}
	+\Big( \Delta \bar{D}^\rho(q_d)\Big)^2
	\bigg]\bigg)\,.
	\]
By Lemmas~\ref{l:barD.II.second}--\ref{l:barD.Ising.second}, for all $\sigma\in\{\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}$ we have
	\[\E\Big[\Delta\bar{D}^\sigma(q_d)^2\Big]
	\le\frac{ L^{O(1)}\BUCKETS\delta}{N}
	\,.\]
By Lemma~\ref{l:tQ.first.quenched} and the bound $\E[(\MAX_N)^2]\le L^{O(1)}$ from Proposition~\ref{p:Y.kolmogorov}, for all $\sigma\in\{\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}$ we have
	\[
	\E\bigg[\Big(\Delta\tilde{Q}^\sigma(q_d)\Big)^{1/2}\bigg]
	\le L^{O(1)} \delta^{1/2}\,.
	\]
Combining the bounds gives the claim, recalling that $\eta\ll\delta$ from Assumption~\ref{a:params}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:36:49.819860+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6ff4d4292755c3eb3d1be3283f166d79c3ecad66f3002c0fae4eb7df642710f2","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:convex-linear-bound of arXiv:2609.02829, 'Quantitative explosion and percolation of the divisible sandpile'] Let $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_N$ be i.i.d.\ mean-zero variables with finite
		variance. Let $F$ be convex in each
		coordinate and suppose that, $\mathbb{P}$-almost surely, for every $1\leq i\leq N$,
		\[
			0\leq\partial_i^+F\leq b_i\, ,
		\]
		where the $b_i$ are deterministic. Then there is a universal
		$C<\infty$ such that, for every $L>0$,
		\[
			\mathbb{E}\left[\left(
			F-\mathbb{E} F-\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbb{E}[\partial_i^+F]\xi_i
			\right)^2\right]
			\leq CL^2\sum_{i=1}^N\Var(\partial_i^+F)
			+C\eta(L)\sum_{i=1}^Nb_i^2\, ,
		\]
		where, for an independent copy $\xi_1'$ of $\xi_1$,
		\[
			\eta(L)\coloneqq
			\mathbb{E}\left[(\xi_1-\xi_1')^2
			\mathbf{1}_{\{|\xi_1-\xi_1'|>L\}}\right]\, .
		\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["alpha is irrational and satisfies ||q alpha|| >= C q^{-tau} for all integers q >= 1, with C > 0 and tau >= 1","||t|| denotes the distance from t to the nearest integer","in part (ii), f is C^infinity on the circle R/Z with mean zero, and the rotation is x -> x + alpha","solutions are sought up to an additive constant; L^2 and distributional solutions are compared by Fourier coefficients"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:09:43.732260+00:00","domain":"Diophantine approximation, small divisors, circle rotations","id":"claim_701f743bb2241950d3a8f90b87a8fd689c27198731a6afd43cc9166321190ecf","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"For a real number t write ||t|| for its distance to the nearest integer. Fix an irrational alpha and suppose alpha is DIOPHANTINE of type (C, tau): there are constants C > 0 and tau >= 1 with

  ||q alpha||  >=  C * q^{-tau}    for every integer q >= 1.

Then:

(i) (the small divisors are only polynomially small) for every nonzero integer q,
      | e^{2 pi i q alpha} - 1 |  =  2 | sin(pi q alpha) |  >=  4 ||q alpha||  >=  4 C |q|^{-tau}.
    The upper bound | e^{2 pi i q alpha} - 1 | <= 2 pi ||q alpha|| always holds, so the two sides are comparable to ||q alpha||.

(ii) (solving the cohomological equation) Let R_alpha(x) = x + alpha on the circle T = R/Z and let f be a C^infinity function on T with mean zero. Then the equation u(x + alpha) - u(x) = f(x) has a C^infinity solution u, unique up to an additive constant, given on Fourier coefficients by u-hat(q) = f-hat(q) / (e^{2 pi i q alpha} - 1) for q nonzero. Quantitatively |u-hat(q)| <= |q|^{tau} |f-hat(q)| / (4C), so one loses tau derivatives: in Sobolev scale ||u||_{H^{s - tau}} <= (4C)^{-1} ||f||_{H^s}, and the analogous statement holds in Holder scale with an epsilon loss.

(iii) (how common the hypothesis is) For every tau > 1, Lebesgue-almost every alpha is Diophantine of type (C, tau) for some C = C(alpha) > 0; for tau = 1 the alpha satisfying the condition are exactly the badly approximable ones (bounded partial quotients), a set of Lebesgue measure zero and full Hausdorff dimension; for tau < 1 no alpha satisfies it at all, by Dirichlet's theorem.

WHERE IT FAILS. If alpha is LIOUVILLE (no such C, tau exist), the conclusion of (ii) fails badly: choose q_1 < q_2 < ... with ||q_k alpha|| < q_k^{-k} and define f by f-hat(q_k) = f-hat(-q_k)-bar = ||q_k alpha||^{1/2} and all other coefficients zero. These coefficients decay faster than any power of q_k, so f is C^infinity with mean zero, yet |u-hat(q_k)| >= ||q_k alpha||^{1/2} / (2 pi ||q_k alpha||) = 1 / (2 pi ||q_k alpha||^{1/2}), which blows up faster than any polynomial in q_k. Hence no solution u exists in L^2, and not even a distributional solution exists. So the Diophantine condition is not a technical convenience: it is what separates solvability from non-solvability. Note also that (ii) gives no information at all about the SPEED of ergodic averages by itself, and that the estimates degrade as C -> 0, so any application that needs uniformity must track C and tau explicitly.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:16:18.692823+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_705cce3bc3c2f162b4275875c9b9a71f24d78fbec2f616fc38040dcbd9b51005","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 31 (Compatible prefix time) of arXiv:2607.26377, '\textbf{Entire Logarithmic Signatures\\ of Bounded-Variation Paths in Finite Dimensions}'] Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real normed vector space with
$\dim V\geq2$, and let
$\gamma\colon[0,T]\to V$ be a continuous bounded-variation path. Set
\[
l=\log S(\gamma),
\qquad
v=\gamma_T-\gamma_0,
\]
and assume that
\[
R(l)=\infty,
\qquad
v\neq0.
\]
Fix $\ell\in V^*$ such that $\ell(v)=1$, put $W=\ker\ell$, and write
\[
\gamma_t-\gamma_0=x_t v+X_t,
\qquad
x_t=\ell(\gamma_t-\gamma_0),
\qquad
X_t\in W.
\]

Give $W$ an auxiliary Euclidean norm and let $W_{\C}$ be its
complexification. For every finite symmetric set
$\Lambda\subset2\pi\Q$, define the real Hilbert space
\[
E_\Lambda
=
\set{(z_\omega)_{\omega\in\Lambda}
\in\prod_{\omega\in\Lambda}W_{\C}:
 z_{-\omega}=\overline{z_\omega}}
\]
with the norm inherited from the Hilbert direct sum, the decorated
transverse path
\[
B_t^\Lambda(\gamma)
=
\left(
\int_0^t \e^{i\omega x_s}\dd X_s
\right)_{\omega\in\Lambda},
\qquad 0\leq t\leq T,
\]
and the orthogonal map
\[
T_\Lambda\colon E_\Lambda\to E_\Lambda,
\qquad
(T_\Lambda z)_\omega=\e^{i\omega}z_\omega.
\]
Denote by the same symbol the induced graded automorphism of tensor
series, and set
\[
r_t^\Lambda
=S\bigl(B^\Lambda(\gamma)|_{[0,t]}\bigr),
\qquad
h_\Lambda=r_T^\Lambda.
\]

Then there exists $t_*\in[0,T]$ such that, for every finite symmetric
$\Lambda\subset2\pi\Q$,
\begin{equation}
h_\Lambda
=a_\Lambda T_\Lambda(a_\Lambda)^{-1},
\qquad
a_\Lambda=r_{t_*}^\Lambda.
\end{equation}
Equivalently,
\[
r_{t_*}^\Lambda
=h_\Lambda T_\Lambda\bigl(r_{t_*}^\Lambda\bigr)
\]
for every such $\Lambda$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:17:10.022418+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_70aaacc132bf006490a2efbd61e694a78c197fa1fcea406ad4ce694db2ff6bdd","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 3 of arXiv:2608.17374, '\textbf{On the Pseudo-Mixing of Kac's Walk}'] [Distinguishability With Respect to Fixed Sequences] 
Fix two sequences of distributions $\mu_{n}, \nu_{n}$ that take on values in the set $\mathcal{S}_{n}$, and let $f_{n}$ be a sequence of functions from $\mathcal{S}_{n}$ to $\mathbb{R}$.

We say the sequence $f_{n}$ \textit{weakly} distinguishes $\mu_{n}$ and $\nu_{n}$ if
\be 
\sqrt{\max(\Var_{\mu_{n}}(f_{n}),\Var_{\nu_{n}}(f_{n}))} = O(|\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{n}}[f_{n}] - \mathbb{E}_{\nu_{n}}[f_{n}] |),
\ee 
and \textit{strongly} distinguishes if the LHS is 
$o(|\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{n}}[f_{n}] - \mathbb{E}_{\nu_{n}}[f_{n}] |)$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f measurable and a.e. finite","|E| < infinity (or E sigma-finite, applied piecewise)","the measure is Borel regular, so that inner regularity by closed sets is available"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.751562+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_70f1790178f49b91f5ee0ff4790936831774e34f8e840b54c67bc80f664a49ab","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f : R^d -> C be Lebesgue measurable and finite almost everywhere, let E be a measurable set of FINITE measure, and let eps > 0. Then there is a CLOSED set F contained in E with |E \\ F| < eps such that the RESTRICTION of f to F is continuous. Moreover one may take g in C_c(R^d) with g = f on F and sup |g| <= sup |f|. The theorem does not assert that f is continuous AT the points of F as a function on R^d: the indicator of the rationals is nowhere continuous on R, yet it agrees with the zero function off a set of measure zero, and Lusin's F can be taken to be any closed set of irrationals of nearly full measure. Finiteness of |E| may be relaxed to sigma-finiteness by exhausting E, at the price of stating the conclusion with |E \\ F| < eps for each piece. [standard; e.g. Rudin, Real and Complex Analysis, 3rd ed., Theorem 2.24]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:28:49.121797+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_70f93b993bb6bb37c7bfcb078034702d78b2e5b7cd400a6962d5b950db4fff82","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:johnson-spectrum of arXiv:2608.18293, 'Critical tensor covariance at the Marchenko--Pastur threshold'] Assume $1\le q<n/2$. Let $A_q$ be the adjacency matrix of the Johnson graph
$J(n,q)$: two $q$-subsets are adjacent when their symmetric difference has size
two. For a $j$-subset $T$, define
\[
  f_T(I)=\1_{\{T\subseteq I\}},
  \qquad |I|=q,
\]
and let $U_j$ be the span of the functions $f_T$ with $|T|=j$. Then
\[
  U_0\subseteq U_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq U_q.
\]
Set $U_{-1}=\{0\}$. If $H_j=U_j\cap U_{j-1}^{\perp}$, then $A_q$ acts on $H_j$ by the scalar
\begin{equation}
  \alpha_j=(q-j)(n-q-j)-j,
  \qquad 0\le j\le q.
  
\end{equation}
In particular, when $q<n/2$, the largest eigenvalue of $A_q$ on the orthogonal complement of the constant vector is
\begin{equation}
  \alpha_1=q(n-q)-n.
  
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:20:33.752427+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7124a5917977f2ae5f1f94d056ca5a53354973487bc04d551754f7e5081dc684","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop 11 of arXiv:2609.03836, 'Koszul Orlik--Solomon Algebras from Non-supersolvable Arrangements'] Let $M$ be a matroid and $F, G \in \mathcal{L}(M)$.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item Suppose $F \subseteq G$,
        $F$ is modular in $M|_G$, and $G$ is modular in $M$. Then $F$ is modular in $M$.
        \item If $F$ is modular in $M$, then $F \cap G$ is modular in $M|_G$.
        \item If $F, G$ are modular in $M$, then $F \cap G$ is modular in $M$.
        \item If $F$ is modular in $M$, then $(F \vee G)-G$ is modular in $M/G$.
        \item If $F$ is modular in $M$ and $S \subseteq E(M)$ contains $F$, then $F$ is modular in $M|_S$.
        \item If $F$ is modular in $M$ and $M$ is connected, then $M|_F$ is connected.
    \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:47.652013+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7186db882c863ea9073dea828e7af3f00cab1a8dfbe5aaa44a03333a136d9bd8","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 13 ($\ell$-multigraph) of arXiv:2605.07050, 'Universality of the fluctuations of the free energy in generalized Sherrington--Kirkpatric'] We say that a multigraph $\gamma$ with nodes $1, 2, \dots, N$ is an $\ell$-multigraph if any pair of nodes can be connected by at most $\ell$ edges. The multiplicity $m^\gamma_{ij}$ between the nodes $i$ and $j$ is the number of separate edges connecting them, and we let $m^\gamma_{ij} = 0$ if the nodes $i$ and $j$ are not connected. (It is possible that $m_{kk}^{\gamma} > 0$, i.e., self-loops are allowed.) If $m^\gamma_{ij} = 1, 2, 3, 4$, we say that the edge between the nodes $i$ and $j$ is single, double, triple, quadruple, respectively.

The degree of the node $i$ is defined by
\[
	d^\gamma_i = m^\gamma_{ii} + \sum_{j=1}^N m^\gamma_{ij}.
\]
In particular, a single self-loop at the node $i$ increases the degree of the node $i$ by $2$. The size $m^\gamma$ and the length $n^\gamma$ of a multigraph $\gamma$ are defined by
\[
	m^\gamma = \sum_{i\leq j} m^\gamma_{ij} = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^N d^\gamma_i, \quad n^\gamma = \sum_{i\leq j} \indi(m^\gamma_{ij} > 0),
\]
respectively. The number of the single (respectively, double, triple, quadruple) edges $n_1^\gamma$ (respectively, $n_2^\gamma, n_3^\gamma, n_4^\gamma$) is defined by
\[
	n_r^\gamma = \sum_{i\leq j} \indi(m^\gamma_{ij} = r), \quad r=1, 2, 3, 4.
\]
Similarly, the number of the single (respectively, double) self-loops $\tilde n_1^\gamma$ (respectively, $\tilde n_2^\gamma$) is defined by
\[ \tilde n_r^\gamma = \sum_{k=1}^{N}\indi(m^\gamma_{kk} = r), \quad r=1,2.\]

The set of all $\ell$-multigraphs with single and/or double self-loops is denoted by $\caG^\ell$. (The empty graph is a multigraph and included in $\caG^\ell$.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:48:24.296611+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_71e0d9ba818881c73222688b9d12a1a5628ea07bb86c0ba813ab26f2112a95b4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem optimaliq>1 of arXiv:2605.10452, 'A secretary for Messrs. Luce and Mallows'] Consider the secretary problem
with either  the  Mallows distribution
or the $P_n^{\mathcal{L}_\text{inv};\{q_n^i\}_{i=1}^n}$-type Luce distribution with  $q=q_n\in(0,\infty)-\{1\}$
in the case that the smallest number is  of highest rank.

\noindent i. Let $q_n=1-\frac cn$, where $c>0$. Then the asymptotically optimal strategy is $\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
\begin{equation}
M_n^*\sim n\Big(\frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{1-e^{-c}}{e-1+e^{-c}}\big)\Big),
\end{equation}
 and the corresponding  limiting probability of success
is $\frac1e$

\noindent Also, $\lim_{c\to\infty} \frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{1-e^{-c}}{e-1+e^{-c}}\big)=0$ and $\lim_{c\to0} \frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{1-e^{-c}}{e-1+e^{-c}}\big)=\frac1e$.

\noindent ii.
Let $q_n=1-\frac c{n^\alpha}$, where $c>0$ and $\alpha\in(0,1)$. Then the asymptotically optimal strategy  is $\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
$$
M_n^*\sim\frac1c\left(1-\log(e-1)\right)n^\alpha\approx0.459\frac{n^\alpha}c,
$$
 and the corresponding limiting probability of success
is $\frac1e$.

\noindent iii.
Let $q\in(0,1)$.  Then the asymptotically optimal strategy  is $\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M^*)$, where
$$
M^*=\begin{cases}&\max\left\{M\ge1: \sum_{j=M}^\infty\frac{q^j}{1-q^j}\ge\frac 1{1-q}\right\}, \ \text{if}\ \sum_{j=1}^\infty\frac{q^j}{1-q^j}\ge\frac1{1-q};\\
&0,\ \text{if}\ \sum_{j=1}^\infty\frac{q^j}{1-q^j}<\frac1{1-q}.\end{cases}
$$
(If  $\sum_{j=M^*}^\infty\frac{q^j}{1-q^j}=\frac 1{1-q}$, then $M^*-1$ is also optimal.)

\noindent The corresponding limiting probability of success is given by
$$
\begin{cases}&(1-q)(1-q^{M^*})\sum_{j=M^*}^\infty\frac{q^j}{1-q^j}\ge(1-q^{-M^*}),\ \text{if}\ M^*\ge1;\\
&1-q>\frac1e,\ \text{if}\ M^*=0.\end{cases}
$$
This limiting probability is always greater or equal to $\frac1e$ and is
strictly greater than $\frac1e$ for all but at most a countable number of $q$ with no accumulation points in $(0,\infty)$.

\noindent iv. Let $q_n=1+\frac cn$, where $c>0$. Then the asymptotically optimal strategy is $\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
\begin{equation}
M_n^*\sim n\Big(\frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{e^c-1}e\big)\Big),
\end{equation}
 and the corresponding  limiting probability of success
is $\frac1e$.

\noindent Also, $\lim_{c\to\infty} \frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{e^c-1}e\big)=1$ and $\lim_{c\to0} \frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{e^c-1}e\big)=\frac1e$.

\noindent v.
Let $q_n=1+\frac c{n^\alpha}$, where $c>0$ and $\alpha\in(0,1)$. Then the asymptotically optimal strategy  is $\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
$$
n-M_n^*\sim\frac{n^\alpha}c,
$$
 and the corresponding limiting probability of success
is $\frac1e$.

\noindent vi. Let $q>1$.  Then the asymptotically optimal strategy  is $\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
$$
M_n^*=n-L, \ \text{where}\ L \ \text{satisfies}\ \frac1{q-1}\le L<\frac q{q-1}.
$$
The corresponding limiting probability of success is given by
$$
\frac{q-1}{q^L}L>\frac1e.
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

\begin{equation}
 
 \mathcal A_t\longrightarrow\mathcal A_T
 \qquad\text{in }\R/4\pi\mathbb Z .
\end{equation}
For \(t\) sufficiently close to \(T\), choose compatible real
representatives such that \(\mathcal A_t\to\mathcal A_T\).  Pinkall's

It satisfies
\[
 \tau_t\longrightarrow

\]

\begin{equation}
 
 \frac14\leq\operatorname{Im}\tau_T\leq\frac2\pi.
\end{equation}

\[
 [\tau_t]\longrightarrow[\tau_T]
 \qquad\text{in }\mathcal M_1=\mathbb H/\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb Z)
\]
have a unique finite-time limit, independent of the approaching time
sequence.  With the orientation induced by the fixed oriented profile

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-05T06:00:09.358321+00:00","domain":"ensemble learning","id":"claim_725b1291163158659b5a95f154eb99cbd5bf0e3c3895a5a6a7c646f4cd804d39","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In a multi-output stacking problem scored by the mean per-sample relative error $\\frac{1}{n}\\sum_i \\|\\hat y_i - y_i\\|/\\|y_i\\|$, the per-output least-squares stack minimises the unweighted squared error, which is dominated by the cases with the largest $\\|y_i\\|$, while the score is dominated by the cases with the smallest. Interpolating the per-output weights toward one pooled simplex weight vector fitted on the relative error therefore improves the score even IN-SAMPLE on the very calibration rows on which least squares is optimal in squared error - the signature that distinguishes an objective mismatch from a generalisation (variance) effect, which can only appear out of sample. Measured on the EMIT lookup-table pool (seed 101, component Y2, 23 members, 932 calibration rows, 285 outputs): in-sample relative error 0.1105 for least squares against 0.1026 at interpolation weight 0.4 (-7.2 percent), the in-sample optimum at the same weight as the out-of-sample optimum (0.1292 to 0.1186), while the in-sample squared error is minimal at least squares (8.8e-5 against 1.2e-4); the out-of-sample gain is +15.9 percent in the smallest-norm quartile of targets and -9.6 percent in the largest, and 45 percent of the least-squares score comes from its worst decile of cases. Consequently no model of the sampling noise of the weight rows reproduces the cross-validated interpolation weight: the known-noise James-Stein amount is 0.00 and the heteroscedasticity-robust amount 0.03-0.05 where cross-validation chooses 0.10-0.40. Shrinking toward the pooled UNCONSTRAINED least-squares weights (entries up to 90 in magnitude) or toward the mean of the rows is much worse; the simplex constraint together with the relative objective carries the effect. The practical rule: when a stack is scored in a metric that weights cases differently from the fitting loss, the first question is the objective, not the estimator's variance.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["𝔄 is a unital Banach algebra (e.g. bounded operators on a Banach space, or square matrices)","A and B are elements of 𝔄 (bounded operators)","AB = BA"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:57:26.111181+00:00","domain":"operator theory, matrix analysis, one-parameter groups","id":"claim_72638ddfde3be7c71bd07c8d293de0f5da0036958c9131cd1b17e4853a1f9986","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let 𝔄 be a unital Banach algebra (for instance the algebra B(E) of bounded linear operators on a Banach space E, or the n×n complex matrices), and for A ∈ 𝔄 define exp(A) = e^A := Σ_{k=0}^∞ A^k / k!, a series that converges absolutely in norm for every A (‖A^k/k!‖ ≤ ‖A‖^k/k!), so that ‖e^A‖ ≤ e^{‖A‖}. If A, B ∈ 𝔄 COMMUTE, AB = BA, then e^{A+B} = e^A e^B = e^B e^A. Consequences: for every A and all scalars s, t, e^{(s+t)A} = e^{sA} e^{tA} (the one-parameter group law), e^A is invertible with (e^A)⁻¹ = e^{−A}, e^0 = 1, and t ↦ e^{tA} is norm-differentiable with derivative A e^{tA} = e^{tA} A. If P is invertible, e^{PAP⁻¹} = P e^A P⁻¹. Sharp edges. (1) Commutativity cannot be dropped: for the 2×2 matrices A = [[0,1],[0,0]] and B = [[0,0],[1,0]] one has e^A = I + A, e^B = I + B, so e^A e^B = [[2,1],[1,1]], whereas A + B = [[0,1],[1,0]] gives e^{A+B} = [[cosh 1, sinh 1],[sinh 1, cosh 1]] ≠ e^A e^B (and e^B e^A = [[1,1],[1,2]] ≠ e^A e^B, so the two products differ as well). For non-commuting A, B the product e^A e^B is instead described by the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff series e^{A+B+[A,B]/2+…} when it converges, and by the Lie–Trotter formula e^{A+B} = lim_{n→∞} (e^{A/n} e^{B/n})ⁿ. (2) The converse is false in general: e^A e^B = e^{A+B} does not imply AB = BA (there are non-commuting complex matrices with e^A = e^B = e^{A+B} = I); it does hold for Hermitian (self-adjoint) matrices A, B, because then e^{A+B} Hermitian forces e^A e^B = (e^A e^B)* = e^B e^A, so the positive definite matrices e^A and e^B commute, and hence so do their unique Hermitian logarithms A and B. (3) For UNBOUNDED operators (generators of semigroups) the series definition is unavailable and 'commuting' must be formulated with care (e.g. commuting resolvents / commuting semigroups); this statement is only about bounded operators and Banach algebras.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["α irrational (for the rational case the expansion terminates)","regular (simple) continued fraction with integer partial quotients a_k ≥ 1 for k ≥ 1","||t|| denotes the distance from t to the nearest integer"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:57.492004+00:00","domain":"Diophantine approximation, circle rotations, continued fractions","id":"claim_7271e0510379bbe55262f0b504298ebded2c36c4dd6bb321ac077750203941b8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let α be irrational with regular continued fraction [a_0; a_1, a_2, ...], convergents p_n/q_n (p_{-1} = 1, q_{-1} = 0, p_0 = a_0, q_0 = 1, p_{n+1} = a_{n+1}p_n + p_{n-1}, q_{n+1} = a_{n+1}q_n + q_{n-1}) and complete quotients α_{n+1} = [a_{n+1}; a_{n+2}, ...], so a_{n+1} < α_{n+1} < a_{n+1} + 1. Write ||t|| = dist(t, Z) and δ_n = |q_n α − p_n| (so δ_{-1} = 1).

(1) Exact size and alternating sign. For all n ≥ 0, q_n α − p_n = (−1)^n / (q_n α_{n+1} + q_{n-1}). Hence 1/(q_n + q_{n+1}) < δ_n < 1/q_{n+1}, the errors alternate in sign, δ_n is strictly decreasing, and δ_n = ||q_n α|| for every n ≥ 1 (because q_{n+1} ≥ 2 gives δ_n < 1/2); for n = 0 this holds when a_1 ≥ 2.

(2) The distances obey the same recursion as the denominators: δ_{n-1} = a_{n+1} δ_n + δ_{n+1} for all n ≥ 0. Equivalently δ_n = 1/(α_1 α_2 ··· α_{n+1}).

(3) Closest returns (Lagrange's theorem on best approximations of the second kind). For every n ≥ 0 and every integer q with 1 ≤ q < q_{n+1}: ||q α|| ≥ δ_n, with equality if and only if q = q_n. In dynamical words: for the rotation t ↦ t + α (mod 1), among all times 1 ≤ q < q_{n+1} the orbit of any point comes closest to its starting point exactly at time q_n; the record-breaking (closest-return) times of the orbit are precisely the denominators q_0 (when a_1 ≥ 2), q_1, q_2, ..., and successive closest returns land on alternate sides of the starting point, at distances δ_n.

(4) Growth. q_{n+1} ≥ q_n + q_{n-1}, hence q_n ≥ F_{n+1} (Fibonacci) and q_n ≥ 2^{(n−1)/2} for n ≥ 1; the golden ratio (all a_k = 1) is the slowest case.

Where it fails. For rational α the expansion terminates, the last δ is 0 and the recursion (2) stops. Statement (3) is about ||qα|| = min_p |qα − p| (best approximations of the SECOND kind). For the FIRST-kind problem of minimising |α − p/q| over q ≤ Q, intermediate fractions (p_{n-1} + k p_n)/(q_{n-1} + k q_n) with k > a_{n+1}/2 can also be best approximations, so the two notions must not be conflated. When a_1 = 1 one has q_0 = q_1 = 1, the n = 0 case of (3) is vacuous, and ||α|| equals δ_1, not δ_0.","status":"unverified"}

If moreover X is Hausdorff and T is continuous, then M = cl{Tⁿx : n ≥ 0} for every x ∈ M, T(M) = M, and (X metrizable) M carries a T-invariant Borel probability measure by the Krylov–Bogolyubov theorem, so every compact metrizable system has an invariant probability measure supported on a minimal set. {"assumptions":["nonempty compact X subset R^d; d,p>=1; n>=0 integer; eps,s>0; B,R>=0","continuous symmetric PSD kernel, rank <=p, k(x,x)<=R^2, zero-mean GP","independent N(0,s) observation noise; new noisy predictive observation","an admissible r>0 with Omega(r)<=eta/(2sqrt(p)), and a fixed h-net G subset X, are specified or bounded from a known modulus and covering bound","normalized bidirectional residual ReLU attention plus residual ReLU tokenwise MLPs; arbitrary real weights; raw coordinates and role flags"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T16:45:13.561071+00:00","domain":"Gaussian-process prediction; transformer approximation","id":"claim_7287d4292b2f0eb19800316b0df51e29ade681fed86b320517d42dc0df5e0416","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"CURRENT AUDIT STATUS: independently checked proof, T336-w727-C005 v2; claude-5693aca3 PASS in AUDITS_FROM_REVIEWER.tsv. Exact proof SHA256 22df67c6b2aaec99499aac6bf3440e8d5d6305204deedcc98fe9b4a621583b40. No novelty or Lean certification is claimed. The following original submission text retains historical pre-audit status notices.

Every continuous real symmetric PSD kernel of rank <=p and diagonal <=R^2 on a nonempty compact X subset R^d admits an explicit raw-input normalized-ReLU-attention transformer for uniform noisy predictive forward KL <=eps, with positive noise s, labels bounded by B, and contexts <=n. The complete width/depth/MLP/head bound is given in C005 Section 1 in terms of the canonical kernel modulus Omega(r), a finite h-net cardinality J, and the solver constants. A fixed finite Gram factorization supplies all encoder feature values; no feature computation is hidden outside the count. Status: proof (unaudited), T336-w727-C005 v2. Complete theorem, constants and scope:
# Target 1 for continuous finite-rank kernels on compact raw domains

Claim T336-w727-C005 v2. Status: proof (unaudited), dependent on C002 v1 and the deterministic perturbation/encoder constructions in C004 v1. The entire result is not Lean-checked. No independent review or novelty certification is claimed.

The hardest step is removing the supplied-feature oracle without adding a hidden feature-computation cost. A finite Gram factorization fixes the encoder weights; a kernel modulus controls its error. The size explicitly includes the resulting encoder.

## 1. Statement and all parameters

Let X be a nonempty compact subset of R^d, d>=1. Let k:X times X -> R be a continuous real symmetric positive-semidefinite kernel of rank at most p, p>=1, with k(x,x)<=R^2 for R>=0. The prior is the zero-mean GP with kernel k. Observation noise is independent N(0,s), s>0. Labels are bounded by B>=0, contexts have length <=n with n>=0 an integer, and eps>0. The prediction concerns a new noisy observation.

Define the canonical kernel modulus in the ambient L1 metric by

    Omega(r)=sup_{x,y in X, ||x-y||_1<=r}
                sqrt(k(x,x)+k(y,y)-2k(x,y)).

The expression is nonnegative by positive semidefiniteness. Omega(r) tends to zero as r decreases to zero, as proved below.

Retain the following explicit constants from C004's deterministic perturbation bound:

    S=R+1, C_A=n(2R+1),
    C_m=nB[(R+S)/s+S C_A R/s^2],
    C_v=R+S+S^2 C_A/s>0,
    eta=min(1,sqrt(s eps)/(2(1+C_m)),s sqrt(eps)/(2C_v),s/(4C_v)),
    eps0=min(eps/4,1/16), e=eta/sqrt(p)>0.

Choose any **fixed admissible** r>0 with Omega(r)<=e/2. An explicit upper modulus for k can be used to choose r; continuity guarantees existence, not an algorithm for computing a modulus of an arbitrary black-box kernel. Put

    A_cone=(2R+e)/r>0, h=e/(2A_cone)>0.

Choose a finite h-net G contained in X, of cardinality J>=1. The size bound is explicit in J (or in a known upper bound for the covering number). For X=[0,1]^d one may take the regular grid with

    m=max(1,ceil(d A_cone/e)), J=(m+1)^d.

For the attention solver define

    kappa=1+max(1,n)S^2/s, M=nS^2B/s,
    delta0=min(1/2,s/(2S^2),sqrt(s eps0)/(1+M),s sqrt(eps0)/S^2),
    T=ceil(sqrt(kappa) log(2/delta0)/2).

There is a transformer, using normalized residual ReLU attention and tokenwise residual ReLU MLPs, with

    D=7p+6+d+Jd+pJ,
    H=2Jd+pJ+4p+1,
    L_total=T+5+ceil(log_2 J),
    at most five attention heads per layer,
    at most L_total(15D^2+2DH)+2D dense scalar parameters,

whose positive-variance Gaussian output has forward KL<=eps from the exact noisy GP predictive, uniformly over all admissible raw-input contexts and queries. Its input contains only raw coordinates, labels, fixed context/query flags, and constants. The encoder is counted. These are arbitrary-real-weight size bounds; no finite-bit, kernel-evaluation, offline factorization-time, SGD, or ERM-generalization bound is asserted.

## 2. Canonical finite-dimensional features and the kernel modulus

Form the vector space of finite formal combinations of symbols delta_x with bilinear form

    <sum_i a_i delta_{x_i},sum_j b_j delta_{y_j}>
       =sum_{i,j}a_i b_j k(x_i,y_j).

Positive semidefiniteness makes this a nonnegative quadratic form. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality follows by applying nonnegativity to u+t v for all real t; in particular a zero-norm vector is orthogonal to every vector. Quotient by the zero-norm subspace. For any finite list of symbols, the dimension of their quotient span is the rank of their Gram matrix. Every finite list of quotient vectors is contained in the span of finitely many symbols. Thus the dimension of the resulting inner-product space is the supremum of these Gram ranks, which is the kernel rank and is at most p. It is finite dimensional, so no completion issue remains.

Choose an orthonormal basis and pad with zeros in R^p. The coordinates z(x) of delta_x then satisfy

    k(x,y)=z(x)^T z(y), ||z(x)||<=R,
    ||z(x)-z(y)||^2=k(x,x)+k(y,y)-2k(x,y).

Thus z is continuous and ||z(x)-z(y)||<=Omega(r) whenever ||x-y||_1<=r. To justify Omega(r)->0 directly, suppose the contrary. There are sequences r_j->0 and x_j,y_j in X at distance <=r_j with feature distance bounded away from zero. Compactness supplies a subsequence x_j->x; then y_j->x as well. Continuity of k makes the squared feature distance tend to k(x,x)+k(x,x)-2k(x,x)=0, a contradiction. The supremum is finite because the kernel is continuous on the compact product. In particular every fixed positive e admits the required r.

The factorization at the finite net does not require evaluating any feature map on runtime inputs. Form the fixed J-by-J Gram matrix K_G=(k(a,b))_{a,b in G}. It is PSD of rank <=p, so a finite spectral factorization gives vectors v_a in R^p with v_a^T v_b=k(a,b). There is an isometry between the spans of z(a) and v_a: the map sum c_a z(a) -> sum c_a v_a is well defined and norm preserving because both squared norms equal c^T K_G c. Extend orthonormal bases of the two spans to R^p. The isometry extends to an orthogonal map on R^p. Applying it to all z(x) gives a representation, still called z, with z(a)=v_a for every a in G and with the same norm and modulus bounds.

Consequently **all feature values used as weights below can be obtained from the finite prior Gram matrix on G**. Computing this fixed factorization is preprocessing of the fixed prior, not an input-dependent inverse hidden in the predictive head. Its real entries are included in the encoder's parameter count.

## 3. Cone envelope for a general continuous feature map

Define, using the finite Gram feature values,

    ztilde_j(x)=min_{a in G}[v_{a,j}+A_cone ||x-a||_1].

This formula is valid even though z_j need not be Lipschitz. We claim |ztilde_j(x)-z_j(x)|<=e for every j,x.

For a with ||x-a||_1<=r, the modulus gives v_{a,j}>=z_j(x)-Omega(r)>=z_j(x)-e/2. Adding a nonnegative cone term preserves this lower bound. For a with ||x-a||_1>r, the coordinate bound |z_j|<=R gives

    v_{a,j}+A_cone ||x-a||_1
      >z_j(x)-2R+A_cone r=z_j(x)+e.

So every candidate is >=z_j(x)-e/2, and the finite minimum is too.

For the upper bound choose a net point with ||x-a||_1<=h. Since h=e r/(2(2R+e))<=r/2, the modulus bound applies. Therefore

    ztilde_j(x)<=z_j(x)+Omega(r)+A_cone h
                  <=z_j(x)+e/2+e/2=z_j(x)+e.

It follows that sup_x ||ztilde(x)-z(x)||<=sqrt(p)e=eta and ||ztilde(x)||<=R+eta<=S. All denominators above are positive, including R=0. For a cube grid, coordinate rounding gives L1 distance <=d/(2m)<=e/(2A_cone)=h, which verifies the displayed grid size.

## 4. Exact network realization and original-posterior KL

Use C004 Section 4's explicit register construction, with the J centers now the net points a and with the slope K in the cone layer replaced by A_cone. Layer 1 computes all Jd absolute differences with 2Jd ReLUs. Layer 2 forms the pJ affine cone values using these nonnegative absolute registers and the constant register. A balanced residual-min tournament takes ceil(log_2 J) layers, including zero layers when J=1. The last gating layer, using the binary context/query flags and |ztilde_j|<=S, writes the context/query feature registers exactly. For padding choose a fixed anchor point in X as its raw coordinates, rather than assuming the ambient origin belongs to X. Its flags are zero, so the computed features are gated to zero.

This uses E=3+ceil(log_2 J) encoder layers and precisely the width and hidden-width bounds in Section 1. This invokes the exact algebraic encoder construction, **not the Lipschitz-error assertion** of C004 Section 3. Section 3 above supplies the replacement uniform approximation guarantee.

C004 Section 2's perturbation proof uses only ||ztilde-z||<=eta<=1, not feature Lipschitzness. It therefore gives original-versus-encoded predictive errors

    |mu-mutilde|<=sqrt(s eps)/2,
    |v-vtilde|<=min(s/4,s sqrt(eps)/2).

Apply C002 v1 to the encoded features with bound S and accuracy eps0. The one-head query broadcast, T five-head Chebyshev layers, and four-head readout produce muhat,vhat with vhat>=s and errors

    |mutilde-muhat|<=sqrt(s eps)/2,
    |vtilde-vhat|<=min(s/4,s sqrt(eps)/2).

The original predictive variance is also >=s. Adding scalar errors gives |mu-muhat|<=sqrt(s eps) and |v-vhat|<=min(s/2,s sqrt(eps)). The Gaussian calculation in C002 Section 5 then yields forward KL<=eps from the **original kernel** predictive distribution to the transformer output. No triangle inequality for KL is used.

Combining the E encoder layers with the T+2 solver layers gives the depth. Count three D-by-D matrices for each of at most five heads, two MLP matrices of dimensions H-by-D and D-by-H per layer (even counting zeros), and a two-coordinate linear readout. This proves the displayed parameter bound.

## 5. Exact scope

C005 covers every continuous bounded finite-rank kernel on a nonempty compact Euclidean domain, with an explicit bound in terms of a kernel modulus and a finite covering number. It includes continuous kernels whose features are not Lipschitz. C004 gives the simpler closed grid formula when a coordinatewise Lipschitz feature bound is available. C002 is smaller when features are supplied directly.

C003 proves that the bounded-kernel statement without continuity can fail for continuous raw-input Gaussian-output architectures. Thus these results distinguish the feature-input interpretation from the regularity needed for a raw-input theorem. They do not claim that a raw-input size bound can ignore the fixed kernel's modulus or its feature-computation complexity. All three constructive claims remain independently unaudited.","status":"unverified"}

        \item One of the following is true:

        \]
        \item There exists a quadratic extension $L/\mathbb{Q}$, irreducible polynomials $f_1,\ldots,f_n\in \mathbb{Q}[x]$, $g_1,\ldots,g_m\in\mathbb{Q}[y]$ that split over $L$ into conjugate factors $f_i=f_{i1}f_{i2}$ and $g_j=g_{j1}g_{j2}$, and $c_1,\ldots,c_n\in L\setminus \mathbb{Q}$, $d_1,\ldots,d_m\in L\setminus \mathbb{Q}$ satisfying $c_i+\overline{c_i}=0,d_j+\overline{d_j}=0$ such that
        \[

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:52:08.667563+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_73d0c639faad0d6c7c76fd8740caf43e4cd9f3f12e44e8145caac13ef1aab777","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 17 (Fiber-equivalent torus fibrations) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Let
\[
        \pi_i:M\to S^1_i,\qquad i=0,1,
\]
be torus fibrations.  The target circles are not part of the fixed data and may
be different.  Choose a basepoint \(x\in M\) and, for each \(i=0,1\), an identification
\(\pi_1(S_i^1,\pi_i(x))\cong\ZZ\), and let
\[
        \alpha_{\pi_i,x}:\pi_1(M,x)\longrightarrow\ZZ,
\]
be the surjective homomorphism induced by \(\pi_i\).  Changing the
identification changes \(\alpha_{\pi_i,x}\) by a sign.  Equivalently, \(\pi_i\)
determines a cohomology class \([\pi_i]\in H^1(M;\ZZ)\), well-defined up to
sign.  We say that \(\pi_0\) and \(\pi_1\) are \emph{fiber-equivalent}
if
\[
        [\pi_0]=\pm[\pi_1]\in H^1(M;\ZZ).
\]
Equivalently, after choosing a common basepoint,
\[
        \ker\alpha_{\pi_0,x}=\ker\alpha_{\pi_1,x}\subset\pi_1(M,x).
\]
For a different basepoint, the two kernels are changed by the same conjugacy
convention.  Thus, in fiber-subgroup language, the definition says that the
images of the two fiber fundamental groups agree, up to this usual conjugacy
ambiguity.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(X,B,mu) is a probability space and T preserves mu (invertibility is not needed)","P and Q are countable measurable partitions","H_mu(P) < infinity and H_mu(Q) < infinity","entropies are taken with a fixed logarithm base throughout"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.090248+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, entropy","id":"claim_73e397e27849e65c29b0ad85dd4fc2d78bd89a46e9ea1748bcc9855a192424af","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let T be a measure-preserving transformation of a probability space (X, B, mu) and let P and Q be countable measurable partitions with H_mu(P) < infinity and H_mu(Q) < infinity. Write P_n for the join of T^{-i}P over 0 <= i <= n-1 and h_mu(T,P) = lim_n (1/n) H_mu(P_n) (the limit exists by subadditivity and equals the infimum over n). Then h_mu(T, Q) <= h_mu(T, P) + H_mu(Q | P). Two standard consequences: if P refines Q then H_mu(Q | P) = 0 and hence h_mu(T, Q) <= h_mu(T, P), so the partition entropy is monotone under refinement; and |h_mu(T,P) - h_mu(T,Q)| <= H_mu(P | Q) + H_mu(Q | P), i.e. the map P -> h_mu(T,P) is 1-Lipschitz for the Rokhlin metric. WHERE IT FAILS: finiteness of H_mu(P) and H_mu(Q) is used - with infinite-entropy partitions both sides can be infinite and the inequality carries no information. The inequality is one-sided: nothing bounds h_mu(T,P) from below in terms of h_mu(T,Q) unless the conditional entropy in the other direction is also controlled. It is an inequality between the entropies of PROCESSES, not of the partitions: H_mu(Q) <= H_mu(P) + H_mu(Q|P) is the (easier) static statement and must not be quoted in its place.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f in L^1(R^n) cap H^1(R^n)","n >= 1"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:49.106228+00:00","domain":"functional inequalities / heat kernel estimates","id":"claim_7400d6ae9d3f15fbe50c3a54d6a28b75f27f445c575bbc77e500b8b4210619ce","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"There is a constant $C_n<\\infty$ such that for every $f\\in L^1(\\mathbb R^n)\\cap H^1(\\mathbb R^n)$, $\\|f\\|_{L^2(\\mathbb R^n)}^{1+\\frac2n}\\le C_n\\,\\|f\\|_{L^1(\\mathbb R^n)}^{\\frac2n}\\,\\|\\nabla f\\|_{L^2(\\mathbb R^n)}.$ Both hypotheses are needed: the inequality interpolates the $L^2$ norm between the $L^1$ mass and the Dirichlet energy. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:19:42.577408+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7405fcfc60ba2e2b510f49b725ba23ec3d1ae5ec2bd38cd0f3790d4437a8427b","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 1 of arXiv:2609.03512, ''] Let $G$ be a simple connected graph with vertex set $V(G)=\{v_1,\ldots,v_n\}$, and let $m=(m_1,\ldots,m_n)$ be a vector of positive integers. The \emph{blow-up} $G\bigodot m$ is obtained from $G$ by replacing each vertex $v_i$ with an independent set
\[
V_i = \{v_i^1,\ldots,v_i^{m_i}\}
\]
of $m_i$ vertices, and joining $v_i^s$ to $v_j^t$ if and only if $v_iv_j\in E(G)$. We call $V_i$ the \emph{part of $G\bigodot m$ corresponding to $v_i$}, and say that $G\bigodot m$ is obtained from $G$ by \emph{multiplication of vertices} (Golumbic \cite{Graph-multiplication-Golumbic}, p.~53).

If $m_j=1$ for all $j\ne i$, we say $G\bigodot m$ is obtained from $G$ by \emph{multiplying the single vertex $v_i$}; if moreover $m_i=2$, this is called \emph{duplicating} $v_i$ (Henning and Southey \cite{Henning-Michael}). If $G$ has a vertex of degree $2$, \emph{degree-$2$ vertex duplication} denotes the operation of duplicating any such vertex.

For graphs $G_1,\ldots,G_k$, we write $\mathcal{M}(G_1,\ldots,G_k)$ for the family of all graphs obtainable from some $G_\ell$ by multiplication of vertices. Since $G\bigodot(1,\ldots,1)=G$, each $G_\ell$ itself belongs to $\mathcal{M}(G_1,\ldots,G_k)$.","status":"unverified"}

Assume that $d_{\cal D}(\mu_n, \mu) \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$. Then the following assertions hold:
\begin{itemize}

$$
{\mathbb P}_x \left( \lim_{k \to \infty} \sup_{0 \le s \le t} \left| \int_0^s 1_K(X_u) \, dA^{n_k}_u - \int_0^s 1_K(X_u) \, dA_u \right| = 0 \text{ for all } t > 0 \right) = 1, \quad \text{q.e. } x \in E.

\item[\rm (2)] Suppose there exists a compact nest $\{F_\ell\}$ satisfying the following tail estimate:
\begin{equation} 
\lim_{\ell \to \infty} \sup_{\nu \in {\cal S}_{c,00}^1} \left\{ \left( \sup_n \int_{F_\ell^c} U_1 \nu \, d\mu_n \right) \vee \int_{F_\ell^c} U_1 \nu \, d\mu \right\} = 0.
\end{equation}
Then, there exists a further subsequence $\{n'_k\}$ such that $A^{n'_k}$ converges to $A$ locally uniformly in $t$ on $[0,\infty)$, ${\mathbb P}_x$-a.s. for quasi every $x \in E$:
$$

\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:43:37.236900+00:00","domain":"category theory","id":"claim_74afa4479d3dad60357c9de74c72bf7b39271c211d26362c05beb1fb4b52a5ba","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let J be a small category (the index or diagram shape) and D: J -> C a functor (a diagram of shape J) into a category C. A cone over D is an object X of C together with morphisms mu_j: X -> D(j), one for each object j of J, such that for every morphism alpha: j -> j' in J, D(alpha) o mu_j = mu_{j'} (composing with D(alpha) recovers the other leg of the cone). A limit of D is a cone (L, (pi_j)) that is universal among cones over D: for every other cone (X, (mu_j)) there is a unique morphism u: X -> L in C such that pi_j o u = mu_j for every j. Dually, a cocone under D is an object Y with morphisms nu_j: D(j) -> Y such that nu_{j'} o D(alpha) = nu_j for every alpha: j -> j' in J, and a colimit is a universal such cocone (Co, (iota_j)): for every cocone (Y,(nu_j)) there is a unique morphism v: Co -> Y with v o iota_j = nu_j for every j. Products, equalizers, and pullbacks are examples of limits; coproducts, coequalizers, and pushouts are examples of colimits.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Omega open in R^n; bounded for the Poincare inequality, Rellich compactness and the boundary-inequality notion","C^1 boundary for the trace theorem","1 <= p < infinity for W^{1,p}_0 and the trace"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:46.146990+00:00","domain":"function spaces for PDE","id":"claim_75688d20df658563c0d5cdec11a2defadcf6ffdf77614990c3442038bc5af7c7","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Omega in R^n be open. H^1_0(Omega) = W^{1,2}_0(Omega) is the closure of C_c^infinity(Omega) in the norm ||u||_{H^1} = (||u||_{L^2}^2 + ||grad u||_{L^2}^2)^{1/2}; W^{1,p}_0(Omega) is the W^{1,p}-closure, 1 <= p < infinity. If Omega is bounded, the Poincare inequality ||u||_{L^2(Omega)} <= diam(Omega) ||grad u||_{L^2(Omega)} holds for u in H^1_0(Omega), so ||grad u||_{L^2} is an equivalent norm on H^1_0(Omega); and the embedding H^1_0(Omega) into L^2(Omega) is compact (Rellich), with no boundary regularity needed. If Omega is bounded with C^1 boundary there is a bounded trace operator T from W^{1,p}(Omega) to L^p(boundary), 1 <= p < infinity, with Tu = restriction of u for u in W^{1,p} continuous up to the boundary, and W^{1,p}_0(Omega) = kernel of T. Lattice facts: for u in H^1(Omega) and real k, (u - k)^+ is in H^1_loc(Omega) (in H^1(Omega) when k >= 0 or Omega is bounded) with grad (u - k)^+ = 1_{u > k} grad u a.e.; in particular grad u = 0 a.e. on every level set {u = k}. For bounded Omega and u in H^1(Omega) one says u <= k on the boundary (in the H^1 sense) if (u - k)^+ is in H^1_0(Omega), and defines sup over the boundary of u as inf{k real : (u - k)^+ in H^1_0(Omega)}; u = g on the boundary means u - g in H^1_0(Omega). These notions need no regularity of the boundary.","status":"unverified"}

The pair therefore records jump direction and the mechanism that controls the variance-exact sub-gamma pole.","status":"unverified"}

A cross-cut is an antichain C, containing neither 0 nor 1, that meets every maximal chain from 0 to 1. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:56:49.285532+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7664c648bde9d0f4fa2006ba0b3ef2f6099ff7fe0ef540d61d4f68dcdbd042ca","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 11 (Majority rule) of arXiv:2606.22960, '2606.22960'] Let \((T_n,(B_v)_{v\in[n]})\) be the broadcast-coloured tree of size \(n\), where
	\(B_v\in\{-1,1\}\) denotes the colour of vertex \(v\).
	The {\it majority rule} estimator is the \(\{-1,1\}\)-valued random variable
	\[
	\widehat B_{\mathrm{maj},n}
	:=
	\begin{cases}
		1, & \sum_{v=1}^n B_v > 0,\\
		-1, & \sum_{v=1}^n B_v < 0,\\
		\xi_n, & \sum_{v=1}^n B_v = 0,
	\end{cases}
	\]
	where \(\xi_n\) is independent of the broadcasting process and satisfies
	\[
	\mathbb P(\xi_n=1)=\mathbb P(\xi_n=-1)=\frac12.
	\]
	Its error probability is defined by
	\[
	R_{\mathrm{maj}}(n,q):=\mathbb P\!\left(\widehat B_{\mathrm{maj},n}\neq B_1\right),
	\qquad
	R_{\mathrm{maj}}(q):=\limsup_{n\to\infty} R_{\mathrm{maj}}(n,q).
	\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["finite reversible chain","continuous time"],"created_at":"2026-10-05T21:18:10.823960+00:00","domain":"probability/markov-chains/mixing","id":"claim_76b0d870245046ffaed4fd91ce5230e9","kind":"counterexample","schema_version":1,"statement":"Aldous-Fill Open Problem 4.48(a) is answered in the negative: tau_1 <= tau_0 fails. {"assumptions":["U ⊂ C is open","all members of the family are holomorphic (respectively meromorphic) on the same open set U"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:42.483658+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_778fb0bb31baea70fbabe9efe4cbc496909f379fa127979c6c8cf41293005128","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let U ⊂ C be open and F a family of holomorphic functions on U. F is normal (in the finite sense) if every sequence in F has a subsequence converging uniformly on every compact subset of U; the limit is then automatically holomorphic, and it need not belong to F. F is normal in the extended sense if every sequence in F has a subsequence which, on each connected component of U, either converges uniformly on compact subsets to a holomorphic function or tends to ∞ uniformly on compact subsets (equivalently, the reciprocals tend to 0 uniformly on compact subsets). For families of meromorphic functions, normality means that every sequence has a subsequence converging uniformly on compact subsets with respect to the chordal metric of the Riemann sphere; restricted to holomorphic families this coincides with the extended sense, because a spherical limit of zero-free reciprocals is, by Hurwitz's theorem, either holomorphic or identically ∞ on each component. Normality is a local property: F is normal on U if and only if every point of U has a neighborhood on which F is normal. Normality asserts the existence of convergent subsequences only; it does not assert convergence of the family itself, and the limit function may leave the family (for instance the limit of injective functions may be constant).","status":"unverified"}

Method: Locate the rate bottleneck in the Hermitisation argument. Result: The Hermitisation proof controls the log-potential U_n(z) = (1/n) log|det(n^{-1/2}M_n - z)| through the singular-value distribution of the shifted matrix; the error has three parts: (a) the rate in the Marchenko-Pastur-type convergence of the singular-value distribution, of order n^{-1/2}-ish under four moments and degrading to n^{-c(eps)} under 2+eps moments through the truncation at level n^{1/(2+eps)}; (b) the smallest singular value lower bound, which contributes only a log-factor to the log-potential error; (c) the conversion from log-potential convergence to weak convergence of the ESD, which costs a power through the smoothing of the Laplacian. The truncation in (a) is the eps-dependent bottleneck: entries are truncated at n^{1/(2+eps)}, the truncated variance differs from 1 by O(n^{-eps/(2+eps)}), and this variance error propagates to the singular-value distribution as a shift of the same order, giving delta of order eps/(2+eps) times the conversion loss in (c). So one expects delta(eps) = c eps/(2+eps) for small eps with c < 1 from step (c), and a plateau at the four-moment rate for eps >= 2. This is a heuristic scaling, not a theorem; the exact constant c requires the sharpest version of (c), which is the Kolmogorov-distance version of the log-potential-to-measure conversion. Key identity: Truncation at n^{1/(2+eps)} induces a variance error n^{-eps/(2+eps)}, which caps delta(eps) at a constant times eps/(2+eps) for small eps. Obstruction: Sharp conversion constant from log-potential to Kolmogorov distance.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Independent arrays and standard Gaussian channel noise; N,P>=2,M>=1; X=UV^T/sqrt(N)","Fixed centered unit-variance factor laws with finite fourth moments; bounded tau_U,tau_V","E[u h]=E[tau_U h'], E[(u^2-1)h]=E[eta_U h']; corresponding V identities and E[(tau_V-1)h]=E[zeta_V h'] for bounded C1 h with bounded derivative","Square-integrable eta_U,eta_V,zeta_V; precise constants and all rate bounds are in proof Eqs2,13","Positive finite convergent aspects only for limiting coefficient; no information-limit existence assumed"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T16:16:13.028659+00:00","domain":"probability; Gaussian channels; extensive-rank matrix factorization","id":"claim_77f6ac5e73d28069a2817defb72ab668c6f3bbc97c7a3b33f41566584c157634","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"OWNER OWN WORK, proof (unaudited), novelty unestablished.

U in R^(N by M), V in R^(P by M), N,P>=2,M>=1, have independent
iid real entries within each array; the arrays are independent.
Their fixed scalar laws u,v are centered with variance one and
finite fourth moments u4,v4. Assume measurable scalar functions
tau_U,eta_U,tau_V,eta_V,zeta_V satisfy, for bounded C1 functions h
with bounded derivative, including their bounded smooth compositions
in the proof,

 E[u h(u)]=E[tau_U(u) h'(u)],
 E[(u^2-1)h(u)]=E[eta_U(u) h'(u)],
 E[v h(v)]=E[tau_V(v) h'(v)],
 E[(v^2-1)h(v)]=E[eta_V(v) h'(v)],
 E[(tau_V(v)-1)h(v)]=E[zeta_V(v) h'(v)].             (1)

Assume |tau_U|<=T_U, |tau_V|<=T_V almost surely and
E eta_U^2,E eta_V^2,E zeta_V^2 finite. No differentiability of
these five functions and no posterior independence is assumed.
Bounded truncation of h(x)=x gives E tau_U=E tau_V=1.
Define the finite scalar constants

 t_U=E tau_U^2, t_V=E tau_V^2,
 e_U=E eta_U^2, e_V=E eta_V^2, z_V=E zeta_V^2,
 a_U=E[tau_U u^2], a_V=E[tau_V v^2],
 b_U=E[tau_U u], b_V=E[tau_V v],
 h_U=E eta_U, h_V=E eta_V,
 L_N=N-2+2*a_U^2+2*b_U^4.

Let independent Z have iid standard Gaussian entries, X=UV^T/sqrt(N),
Y=sqrt(s)X+Z, d=NP, alpha=P/N, beta=M/N, v_s=1+beta*s.
Set g=beta/v_s, m_N=E||X-E[X|Y]||^2/d and
B_N=log(v_s)/2-I(X;Y)/d, with natural logs.

## Explicit constants and result

Put A=beta^2*(N-1)*(P-1)/N^2 and

 E3=6*(N-1)*(P-1)*M*(t_U^2*t_V-1)/N^4,
 Ec=6*(N-1)/N^4 *
       [M*T_U^4*T_V^2*(v4+2*(P-1))+M*(M-1)*a_V^2],
 Eeta=2/N^3 * [M*P*e_U*T_V^2+M*(M-1)*h_U^2*b_V^2],
 Ezeta=2*N*M*z_V/N^3,
 E4=24*(N-1)*(P-1)/N^5 *
       [M*T_U^4*T_V^2*e_V*N+2*M*(M-1)*b_U^2*h_V^2],
 W=120*(N-1)*(P-1)*(P-2)/N^6 *
       [M*T_U^4*T_V^6*N*(N-1+u4)+M*(M-1)*L_N],
 F2=2*(Eeta+Ezeta), F3=2*(E3+Ec), F4=E4.            (2)

All constants are nonnegative. For all s>0,delta>0,

 g-m_N <= (1+delta)*s^3/v_s^2*(sqrt(A)+s*sqrt(W))^2
       +3*(1+1/delta)/v_s^2*(s^2*F2+s^3*F3+s^4*F4). (3)

For the exact R_N in038(10), define

 a=(N+u4-3)/N, b=(P+v4-3)/N,
 Q(s)=v_s^3+beta*(a+b)*v_s*s^2+beta*a*b*s^3,
 D(s)=v_s^2*Q(s), delta_N=1/floor(sqrt(N)),
 eps_N=delta_N*A+3*(1+1/delta_N)*(F2+F3+F4),
 K_N=A*(Q(1)-1)+(1+delta_N)*(A+2*W).

For 0<=s<=1 the requested estimate and its integral are

 0<=R_N(s)<=eps_N*s^2+K_N*s^4,                      (4)
 half integral_0^s R_N(t)dt<=eps_N*s^3/6+K_N*s^5/10. (5)

In particular the full finite-N two-sided information bound is

 -A*(D(1)-1)*s^5/10
 <= B_N(s)-A*s^4/8
 <= eps_N*s^3/6+K_N*s^5/10.                         (6)

For fixed priors with positive aspect ratios bounded above,
F2,F3,F4=O(1/N), W,A,Q(1) are uniformly bounded,
eps_N=O(N^(-1/2)), and K_N is uniformly bounded.
If alpha_N->alpha>0,beta_N->beta>0, every limiting information
envelope therefore satisfies

 B(s)=alpha*beta^2*s^4/8+O(s^5), 0<=s<=1,            (7)

with the explicit remainder constants in (6). Existence or uniqueness
of the information limit is not required. The finite-N error in (6)
is additive O(N^(-1/2)*s^3), not a pure uniform Taylor remainder
after dividing by s^4 arbitrarily close to zero.

Equivalently the normalized mutual information has the explicit
finite-N polynomial

 P4_N(s)=beta*s/2-beta^2*s^2/4+beta^3*s^3/6
                              -(beta^4+A)*s^4/8,

and

 -eps_N*s^3/6-K_N*s^5/10
 <= I(X;Y)/d-P4_N(s)
 <= [beta^5+A*(D(1)-1)]*s^5/10.                     (6a)

The elementary identity log(1+x)=x-x^2/2+x^3/3-x^4/4
+integral_0^x t^4/(1+t)dt, valid for all x>=0, pays the log remainder.
Thus the limiting quartic term in I/(NP) is
-(beta^4+alpha*beta^2)*s^4/8, and no prior fourth cumulant enters
at that order within this class. The channel parameter is s=1/Delta;
I(UV^T;Y)=I(X;Y) because deterministic nonzero rescaling of the
input is invertible.

## Non-Gaussian example and whole-family scope

Both priors may independently be uniform on [-sqrt(3),sqrt(3)].
For either law take tau(x)=(3-x^2)/2, eta(x)=x-x^3/3;
for the V law take zeta(x)=-eta(x)/2. Their endpoint values vanish,
and their negative derivatives are x, x^2-1, and tau(x)-1,
respectively. Ordinary one-dimensional integration by parts proves
(1), without a Gaussian prior or a boundary contribution.
Exact constants are T=3/2, fourth moment9/5, t=6/5,
e=8/35, z=2/35, a=3/5, b=h=0.
Gaussian priors also satisfy (1) with tau=1,eta=x,zeta=0.
The result applies to every fixed law satisfying the stated kernel
conditions, not just these examples. Discrete Rademacher priors do
not satisfy (1) for arbitrary smooth tests and are not covered.
Specifically choose a compact smooth cutoff of (3*x-x^3)/2 which
equals that polynomial near {-1,1}. At a Rademacher input, h(u)=u
and h'(u)=0, so E[u*h(u)]=1 while E[tau(u)*h'(u)]=0 for every
finite function tau on its support. This is an obstruction to
applying the present derivative-transfer route to that law, not a
counterexample to quartic universality for discrete priors.

More concretely, each of U and V may have any standardized beta
law, with its own arbitrary fixed positive shape parameters p,q.
Let k=p+q, C=1/k, B=(q-p)*sqrt(k+1)/(k*sqrt(p*q)), and
x=(t-p/k)/sqrt(p*q/[k^2*(k+1)]) for t~Beta(p,q). Then

 tau(x)=1+C+B*x-C*x^2,
 eta(x)=tau(x)*(x+B)/(1+C),
 zeta(x)=B*tau(x)-C*eta(x).

The beta density times tau vanishes at both endpoints, including
when the density itself is unbounded there, because p,q>0.
Direct integration of its derivative proves E[x h]=E[tau h'].
Writing Q=x^2-1, the identity tau-1=B*x-C*Q and applying this
first identity to x*h(x) give
(1+C)E[Q*h]=E[tau*(x+B)*h']; this proves the eta identity.
The zeta identity follows by the same linear relation tau-1.
All kernels are bounded on the compact standardized support, so
every hypothesis of (1) is paid. This covers two asymmetric beta
priors as well as the symmetric subfamily. For an asymmetric exact
check, Beta(2,3) standardized as x=5*t-2 has
tau=(6+x-x^2)/5, eta=tau*(1+5*x)/6, zeta=tau*(1-x)/6.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:16:33.595011+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_780a34cf99432152b10899cdd580dbdd2b800f24e54f58db93caaf547e75a987","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Abstract of arXiv:2609.02362, '\\textbf{Farthest-cell triplet entropy: high-dimensional shell limits and hyperbolic...'] We introduce farthest-cell triplet entropy, the conditional Shannon entropy of the farthest-prototype label given three random prototypes. For independent queries and prototypes, its estimator records only the farthest label, not coordinates or numerical distances. The statistic is bounded by $\\log 3$, is invariant under common strictly increasing transformations of the dissimilarities, and has an exact mutual-information interpretation. In high-dimensional isotropic radial models $X_d=R_dU_d$, the Euclidean ordering reduces to scores $\\lambda_d\\xi_{i,d}-Z_i$, where $\\lambda_d=\\sqrt d\\,\\operatorname{sd}(R_d)/\\E R_d$ and the $Z_i$ are independent standard Gaussian variables. This gives angular-dominated, intermediate, and radial-dominated entropy limits $\\log 3$, $\\Hinf(\\lambda;F)$, and $0$. In hyperbolic space of curvature $-\\kappa_d^2$, the same master curve appears at $\\lambda_{d,\\mathbb H}=\\sqrt d\\,\\tau_d A(s_d)$, where $\\tau_d=\\operatorname{sd}(R_d)/\\E R_d$, $s_d=\\kappa_d\\E R_d$, and $A(s)=s\\coth s$. With a calibrated radial law and $\\tau_d$, and a monotone operating interval, entropy inversion identifies the scale-invariant target $s_d^2$; absolute curvature requires an external length unit. CPU simulations give Euclidean and hyperbolic master-curve RMSEs of $0.0164$ and $0.0209$. Inversion from observed synthetic latent coordinates has a median relative error in $\\kappa$ of $6.6\\%$, while angular anisotropy increases this error to $68.9\\%$. Thus the entropy statistic is comparison-based, whereas curvature recovery remains model-calibrated, is not graph-only, and is not robust to anisotropy.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f(t, .) is mu-integrable for every t in the open interval I","t -> f(t, omega) is differentiable on I for mu-a.e. omega","a single g in L^1(mu) dominates |d_t f(t, omega)| for ALL t in I (or on a neighbourhood of each point of I)"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.751130+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_7822c113585052dd029ffd5524924ae4013b85f7e3c8560bfcb2f576ac848d43","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (Omega, F, mu) be a measure space, I a nonempty open interval of R, and f : I x Omega -> R with: (i) for every t in I the function omega -> f(t, omega) is mu-integrable; (ii) for mu-almost every omega the map t -> f(t, omega) is differentiable on I, with derivative d_t f(t, omega); (iii) there exists g in L^1(mu) with |d_t f(t, omega)| <= g(omega) for all t in I and mu-almost every omega. Then F(t) = integral f(t, omega) dmu(omega) is differentiable on I and F'(t) = integral d_t f(t, omega) dmu(omega). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:15:45.377679+00:00","domain":"set theory","id":"claim_783ee34fc14e104fa620373620d7e9f6dc197a014b894eb8ac44b832183c96a2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Two sets A and B are equinumerous (have the same cardinality, written |A| = |B|) when there exists a bijection from A onto B. One writes |A| <= |B| when there is an injection from A into B. Equinumerosity is an equivalence relation, and <= is reflexive and transitive; by the Schroder-Bernstein theorem it is antisymmetric up to bijection (|A| <= |B| and |B| <= |A| imply |A| = |B|), all without the axiom of choice. With the axiom of choice any two sets are comparable (trichotomy), and every set is equinumerous with a unique initial ordinal, its cardinal number. A set is finite if it is equinumerous with {1, ..., n} for some natural number n; countably infinite if equinumerous with the set N of natural numbers; countable if finite or countably infinite; uncountable otherwise. Strict inequality |A| < |B| means |A| <= |B| and there is no bijection between A and B.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:07:48.561153+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_78a6b372d2caafb8dcaa94c4880f0bf813456055361755f18780b8e73bb6314e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 2 (The transference principle) of arXiv:2609.01460, 'On cost-induced Santal\'o-type inequalities \\ in Polish measure spaces'] For $m\in\N$, let $(X_1,\mu_{X_1}),\dots, (X_m,\mu_{X_m})$ be Polish measure spaces. Let $c \colon X_1 \times\cdots \times X_m \to (-\infty,\infty)$ be a continuous cost function. Fix $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_m \in (0,1)$ such that $\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1$.

Consider collections, for $i=1,\dots,m$, $\mathcal{C}_{X_i}$ of $\mu_{X_i}$-measurable subsets of $X_i$. Let $a,b\in \R\cup\{\pm\infty\}$ be such that for all non-empty $A_i\in \mathcal{C}_{X_i}$, $\sup_{\substack{x_i\in A_i \\ 1\leq i \leq m}} -c(x_1,\dots,x_m) \in [a,b]$ and consider a continuous, non-decreasing function $F \colon (a,b]\to [0,\infty)$ satisfying $F(a^+)=0$.

Then, the following are equivalent:\begin{enumerate}
    \item For every non-empty $A_1\in \mathcal{C}_{X_1},\dots,A_m\in\mathcal{C}_{X_m}$, one has
    \[
\prod_{i=1}^m\mu_{X_i}(A_i)^{\lambda_i} \leq F\left(\sup_{\substack{x_i\in A_i \\ 1\leq i \leq m}} -c(x_1,\dots,x_m) \right).
\]
\item For every $(m+1)$-tuple of measurable functions $f_1 \in \mathcal{F}(\mathcal{C}_{X_1}),\dots, f_m\in \mathcal{F}\left(\mathcal{C}_{X_m}\right)$ and $\Omega \colon (a,b]  \to [0,\infty)$, where $\Omega$ is non-increasing, that satisfy
\begin{align*}
\prod_{i=1}^mf_i(x_i)^{\lambda_i} &\leq \Omega(-c(x_1,\dots,x_m)) \text{ for all } 
\\
&(x_1,\dots,x_m)\in X_1\times\cdots\times  X_m, \text{ with } -c(x_1,\dots,x_m)\in (a,b],
\end{align*}
one has
\[
\prod_{i=1}^m\left(\int_{X_i} f_i(x) d\mu_{X_i}(x) \right)^{{\lambda_i}} \leq \int_{a}^b \Omega(r) dF(r).
\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.197231+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_78b5f2af63677a8e0ff36d9d7c03fa4cefc36487dd925193649690b73fcabe8d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 117 (temporal smoothing of budget constraint) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Analogously to \eqref{e:budget.constraint.Ising.plus.coarse} and the bound from Lemma~\ref{l:sp.smooth.budget}, with high probability we have 
	\begin{align*}
	\breve{C}^N(t)
	- \frac{\bar{W}^N(t)^2}{\alpha} 
	\le
	\bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2 \TMAX_N \tep^{1/2}
	+ 3\epsilon^\circ
	\end{align*}
for all $t\in[q_*,1]$. Additionally, with $J^N\equiv J(p^N,\tep,\lambda)$ as  defined by \eqref{e:bad.times.J}, we have
	\[
	\Big|\breve{C}^N(t)
	-\bar{C}^N(t)
	\Big|
	\le \bigg(\frac{ \trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2
	\lambda^{1/2}
	\]
for all $t\in[q_*,1] \setminus J^N$.

\begin{proof}
We continue to use the abbreviations introduced above. The function $\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}$ is convex on the expanded domain $\{(b,v,u) : v \ge u^2-2\bar{\lambda}\}$. Recall $\tGam^N\equiv(\tbbb,\tvvv,\tuuu)^N$
and $\TGam^N\equiv(\Tbbb,\Tvvv,\Tuuu)^N$: we have from Lemma~\ref{l:t.smooth.domain} that
(with high probability)
 $\TGam^N(t,y)$ lies in the expanded domain for all $(t,y)\in[q_*,1]\times \R$, while
$\tGam^N(t,y)$ lies in the expanded domain for all $(t,y)\in ([q_*,1]\setminus J^N)\times \R$. Lemma~\ref{l:t.smooth.domain} implies, for $(t,y)\in ([q_*,1]\setminus J^N)\times \R$,
	\[
	\bigg|
	\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}
	\Big( \tGam^N(t,y)\Big)
	-\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}
	\Big( \TGam^N(t,y)\Big)
	\bigg|
	\le
	\bigg(\frac{ \trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2
	\lambda^{1/2}\,.
	\]
Integrating with respect to $\overline{\varrho_{\vY,N,t}*\sphi(y)}\,dy$ proves the second conclusion. For all $(t,y)\in[q_*,1]\times\R$, we can bound
	\begin{align*}
	& \Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}
	\Big(\TGam^N(t,y)\Big)
	=
	\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}\bigg( \tE \Big[\sGam(t-\sss,y)\Big]\bigg) \\
	&\qquad\le \tE\bigg[
	\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}\Big( \sGam(t-\sss,y)\Big)\bigg]
	= \int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)
	\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}( \sGam(s,y) )\,ds\,.
	\end{align*}
Integrating with respect to $\overline{\varrho_t*\sphi}(y)\,dy$ gives
	\begin{align*}
	&\breve{C}^N(t)
	=
	\int_{\R} \Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}\Big(\TGam^N(t,y)\Big)
	\overline{\varrho_t*\sphi}(y)\,dy
	\le
	\int_{\R}
	\bigg[
	 \int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)
	\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}( \sGam(s,y) )\,ds\bigg]
	\overline{\varrho_t*\sphi}(y)\,dy \\
	&\qquad=
	\int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)
	\bigg[\int_{\R}
	\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}( \sGam(s,y) )
	\overline{\varrho_s*\sphi(y)} \,dy\bigg]\,ds
	+O\bigg[ \bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2 \TMAX_N
	\tep^{1/2}\bigg]\\
	&\qquad=
	\int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)
	\tilde{C}^N(s)\,ds
	+O\bigg[ \bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2 \TMAX_N
	\tep^{1/2}\bigg]
	\,,
	\end{align*}
where the error estimate uses the bounds on $\sGam=(\sbbb,\svvv,\suuu)$ proved in Lemma~\ref{l:sp.smooth.reg}, along with the regularity of the map $t\mapsto \overline{\varrho_s*\sphi}$ proved in Lemma~\ref{l:sp.smooth.cty}. 
 Similarly, note that
	\[
	S_t(w)
	\equiv
	\bigg( \int_{\R} w(y)^{1/2} \varsigma_t*\sphi(y)\,dy\bigg)^2
	\]
is a concave function. It follows that
	\begin{align*}
	&\bar{W}^N(t)^2 
	=\bigg(\int_{\R} \twww(t,y)^{1/2} \varsigma_t*\sphi(y)\,dy\bigg)^2
	= S_t\bigg(\tE\Big[ \swww(t-\sss,\cdot)\Big]\bigg)
	\ge \tE\bigg[ S_t\Big( \swww(t-\sss,\cdot)\Big)\bigg]\\
	&\qquad= \int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)
	\bigg( \int_{\R} \swww(s,y)^{1/2} 
		\varsigma_t*\sphi(y)\,dy\bigg)^2\,ds\\
	&\qquad=
	\int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)
	\bigg( \int_{\R} \swww(s,y)^{1/2} 
		\varsigma_s*\sphi(y)\,dy\bigg)^2
	\,ds
	+
	O\bigg[ \bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2 \TMAX_N \tep^{1/2}\bigg]
	\\
	&\qquad=
	\int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)
	\tilde{W}^N(s)^2\,ds
	+
	O\bigg[ \bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2 \TMAX_N \tep^{1/2}\bigg]
	\end{align*}
where the error estimate again follows from Lemmas \ref{l:sp.smooth.reg} and \ref{l:sp.smooth.cty}. The claim then follows by combining with
Lemma~\ref{l:sp.smooth.budget}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:10:07.451152+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_78e7f9001e04ec0a27742070218a07fa32e55e4e094660e1750dd00ce2833cd7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem eq:abstract-pressure-bridge of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[theorem]{thm:conditional-transfer}
For all sufficiently large \(N\), suppose
\(\widehat Q_{N,L}\) and
\(\widehat P_{N,L}(\varepsilon,\eta)\) are finite for every
\(\varepsilon,\eta>0\).  Suppose also that there exist \(\Phi\in\mathbb R\) and a
function \(F\) on \((0,\infty)^2\) such that
\begin{equation}
 \widehat P_{N,L}(\varepsilon,\eta)\longrightarrow F(\varepsilon,\eta)
 \quad\text{for every fixed }\varepsilon,\eta>0,
 \qquad
 F(\varepsilon,\eta)\longrightarrow\Phi
 \quad\text{as }(\varepsilon,\eta)\to(0,0).
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{align}
 \limsup_{N\to\infty}\widehat Q_{N,L}
 &\le\Phi+\delta_{L,\mathrm{dr}}^{J,\mathrm{up}}(V),
 \\
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\widehat Q_{N,L}
 &\ge\Phi-\delta_{L,\mathrm{dr}}^{J,\mathrm{low}}(V).
 
\end{align}
Consequently,
\begin{align}
 \limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathscr C_N^J(V)
 &\le
 \max\{\Phi+\delta_{L,\mathrm{dr}}^{J,\mathrm{up}}(V),
            \overline\Lambda_L^J(V)\},\\
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathscr C_N^J(V)
 &\ge
 \max\{\Phi-\delta_{L,\mathrm{dr}}^{J,\mathrm{low}}(V),
            \underline\Lambda_L^J(V)\}.
 
\end{align}
If both de-regularization defects vanish, then
\begin{equation}
 \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N
 \log\widehat{\mathscr C}_{N,L}^J(V)=\Phi
\end{equation}
and the exact identities
\begin{align}
 \limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathscr C_N^J(V)
 &=\max\{\Phi,\overline\Lambda_L^J(V)\},
 \\
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathscr C_N^J(V)
 &=\max\{\Phi,\underline\Lambda_L^J(V)\}
 
\end{align}
hold.  In particular,
\begin{equation}
 \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathscr C_N^J(V)=\Phi
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \overline\Lambda_L^J(V)\le\Phi.
\end{equation}

A concrete sufficient condition for (equation eq:abstract-pressure-bridge of the paper)
is that, for any fixed \(L>0\), the disorder array and \(V\) satisfy the
hypotheses of (thm:bulk-universality of the paper) with \(m=2\).
Indeed, (equation eq:point-Haar-zero-cost of the paper) is automatic.  In this concrete
case,
\[
 \Phi=\Phi_p^{\rm bulk}(V)
 =\sup_{u\in\mathbb R}\{\theta_p(u)-V(u)\}.
\]
When the two de-regularization defects vanish,
(equation eq:exact-universality-iff-localized-defect of the paper) therefore gives a
criterion for the localized branch that is both necessary and sufficient. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}
