{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.188849+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7921c02af68dc652942368cd5bb06586646634155ca82d789995c416a9b6cf61","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 101 (coordinate sum) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any measure $\rho$ on $[0,1]\times\R^d$, let $\bar{\rho}$ be the measure on $[0,1]\times\R$ that satisfies
	\[
	\int_{t,y} f\bigg(t, \sum_{i=1}^d y^i\bigg)
	\,\rho(dt\,dy)
	= \int_{t,x} f(t,x)
	\,\bar{\rho}(dt\,dx)\,,
	\]
where $t\in[0,1]$, $y\in\R^d$, and $x\in\R$.
As above, let $\vY$ be an $\R^d$-valued semimartingale with drift $\vD$ and covariation $\vQ$. We now consider the one-dimensional projections
	\[
	Y = \sum_{i=1}^d Y^i\,,\quad
	\sum_{i=1}^d D^i\,,\quad
	\sum_{i,j=1}^d Q^{ij}\,.
	\]
Then $Y$ is a (one-dimensional) semimartingale with drift $D$ and covariation $Q$. We hereafter abbreviate $\rho\equiv\rho_{\vY}$ for the occupation measure of $\vY$ defined in Definition~\ref{d:intro.cts.occ}.
Then the occupation measure of $Y$ is $\bar{\rho}$. The occupation measures associated to the drift and covariation of $Y$ are
	\[
	\sum_{i=1}^d
	\bar{\rho}_{D^i}\,,\quad
	\sum_{i,j=1}^d
	\bar{\rho}_{Q^{ij}}\,.	
	\]
Let $\hvY$ be as defined by Lemma~\ref{l:ideal.smoothed.occ.msr},
and let $\iY$ be the one-dimensional projection, so $\iY(t)=Y(t-\sss)+\mathfrak{x}$ where $(\sss,\mathfrak{x})\sim\bar{\varphi}$ (the density $\varphi$ integrated over $x^1 + \ldots + x^d=\mathfrak{x}$). It follows that $\iY$ has occupation measure $\overline{\rho*\varphi}=\bar{\rho}*\bar{\varphi}$. Similarly, the occupation measures associated to the drift and covariation of $\iY$ have densities
	\[
	\sum_{i=1}^d
	\overline{\rho_{D^i}*\varphi}
	\,,\quad
	\sum_{i,j=1}^d
	\overline{\rho_{Q^{ij}}
		*\varphi}\,.	
	\]
Then, analogously to \eqref{e:intro.occ.ratio.drift} and \eqref{e:intro.occ.ratio.qv}, we define (with $x$ now a scalar)
	\begin{align}
	
	B(t,x) 
	&\equiv

	\overline{\rho_{D^i}*\varphi}(t,x)
	}
		{\overline{\rho*\varphi}(t,x)}\,,\\
	A(t,x)
	&\equiv
	\sum_{i,j=1}^D \frac{
	\overline{\rho_{Q^{ij}}*\varphi}(t,x)
	}
	{\overline{\rho*\varphi}(t,x)}\,.
	
	\end{align}
Let $\iX$ be the solution to the (one-dimensional) SDE
	\[
	d\iX(t)
	= B(t,\iX)\,dt
	+A(t,\iX)^{1/2}\,dW(t)\,,
	\]
where $W$ is a one-dimensional standard Brownian motion.","status":"unverified"}

For a sequence of finite, possibly random, rooted graphs G_n, local weak (Benjamini-Schramm) convergence means that for every finite radius r, the distribution of the isomorphism class of the r-ball around the (uniformly, or otherwise canonically) chosen root converges weakly to that of a limiting, typically infinite, random rooted graph (G*, o). The objective method, due to Aldous and Steele, is the broader program of analyzing this limiting infinite object directly, such as a Poisson weighted infinite tree or a unimodular Galton-Watson tree, to compute limiting constants for combinatorial optimization functionals on the finite graphs, such as the minimum spanning tree constant or the limiting value in the random assignment problem, by solving a recursive distributional (fixed-point) equation on the infinite limit rather than working with finite-n computations directly. It does not by itself establish that a given sequence converges locally weakly, which typically must be separately verified via a subsequential compactness argument together with uniqueness of subsequential limits, and it does not directly give convergence of global, extensive functionals without an additional concentration or summation argument beyond the purely local statement. Typical failure: Assuming that local weak convergence of the underlying random graph automatically implies convergence of a global extensive functional, such as the total weight of a minimum spanning tree, at the same per-vertex limiting rate; local convergence controls only typical local neighborhoods, and passing to a global average requires an additional uniform-integrability or concentration argument, often the genuinely hard part of an objective-method proof, which is easy to overlook once the local limit has been identified. {"assumptions":["(X, M) is a measurable space","mu and nu are positive measures on M (for signed or complex measures the definition is applied to their total variations)","the separating set E is required to belong to M"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:13:10.402012+00:00","domain":"measure theory, decomposition of measures","id":"claim_7949ee76619d07edbf68d03f6116561c0881f49a0a0bfc5d35c33818a908ff98","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, M) be a measurable space and let mu and nu be positive measures on M. One says that mu and nu are MUTUALLY SINGULAR, written mu perp nu, if there exists a set E in M with mu(E) = 0 and nu(X minus E) = 0; equivalently, X splits into two measurable pieces, one carrying all of nu and mu-null, the other carrying all of mu and nu-null. The relation is symmetric. For signed or complex measures the definition is applied to the total variations: mu perp nu means |mu| perp |nu|. Basic consequences: mu perp mu holds if and only if mu = 0; if nu is absolutely continuous with respect to mu (nu << mu) and nu perp mu, then nu = 0; if nu_1 perp mu and nu_2 perp mu then (nu_1 + nu_2) perp mu. CAUTIONS. (1) Mutual singularity is much stronger than 'nu is not absolutely continuous with respect to mu': a measure can fail to be absolutely continuous without being singular, and in general a measure splits into an absolutely continuous and a singular part (Lebesgue decomposition). (2) Singularity is a measure-theoretic, not a topological, smallness statement: the measure sum over n of 2^(-n) times the Dirac mass at the n-th rational is mutually singular with Lebesgue measure on R yet has full support, and the Cantor-Lebesgue measure is mutually singular with Lebesgue measure while being atomless. (3) The witness set E must be measurable; without that requirement the notion is vacuous or ill-posed. (4) Mutual singularity is not preserved by arbitrary uncountable sums of measures.","status":"unverified"}

A rank-one bounded PSD kernel on [-1,1], k(x,xprime)=1{x>=0}1{xprime>=0}, with observation noise variance 1, prevents every continuous raw-input Gaussian predictor from achieving uniform forward KL below log(9/8)/4 > 1/36. # Raw-input obstruction for Target 1

Claim T336-w727-C003 v1. Status: proof (unaudited). This is a scope obstruction to the literal bounded-kernel raw-input statement; it does not contradict C002's supplied-feature theorem. No novelty or Lean certification is claimed.

## Statement

There is a rank-one bounded positive-semidefinite kernel on the compact raw-input domain [-1,1], observation-noise variance s=1, and bounded context labels, such that every predictor with continuous Gaussian output parameters (mu(x),v(x)), v(x)>0, has worst-case noisy predictive forward KL at least

    c0=(1/4) log(9/8)>1/36.

The conclusion applies in particular to every finite transformer whose raw-input encoding and subsequent operations are continuous and whose output is a Gaussian with positive continuous variance. It applies to normalized ReLU attention and softmax attention under these conditions. Therefore boundedness, compactness, finite rank, and positive observation noise alone cannot imply the raw-input version of Target 1 for arbitrarily small eps.

## Kernel and posterior

Define phi(x)=0 for x<0 and phi(x)=1 for x>=0. Set k(x,x')=phi(x)phi(x'). For any finite coefficients a_i,

    sum_{i,j} a_i a_j k(x_i,x_j)=(sum_i a_i phi(x_i))^2>=0.

Thus k is positive semidefinite, bounded by 1, and of rank exactly one (because k(0,0)=1). The GP can be represented as f(x)=Z phi(x), with Z~N(0,1). Observations add independent N(0,1) noise.

Use the empty context if allowed. Alternatively, for any n>=1 use one observation at x=-1 with label y=0, which satisfies every B>=0. This observation is pure noise independent of Z, so the posterior law of Z remains N(0,1). For either context, the new noisy predictive distribution is

    P_x=N(0,1) for x<0; P_x=N(0,2) for x>=0.

Hence the example does not rely on whether a context of length zero is included.

## Continuity forces two incompatible approximation requirements

Fix this context and any continuous output mu(x),v(x)>0. Let E=sup_x KL(P_x || N(mu(x),v(x))). If E is infinite the bound is immediate. Otherwise put mu0=mu(0),v0=v(0)>0. At x=0,

    D_2:=KL(N(0,2)||N(mu0,v0))<=E.

Take x_j=-1/j tending to zero from below. Since mu,v are continuous and v0>0, the explicit Gaussian KL formula is continuous along this sequence; all denominators remain positive near the limit. Therefore

    D_1:=KL(N(0,1)||N(mu0,v0))<=E.

No dominated convergence, probabilistic conditioning argument, or exchange of a supremum with a limit is used: every term in this deterministic convergent sequence is <=E.

For a>0 define

    D_a=(1/2)(log(v0/a)+(a+mu0^2)/v0-1).

Writing w=3/(2v0)>0 and combining logarithms gives the exact identity

    (D_1+D_2)/2
      = (1/4)log(9/8)+(1/2)(w-1-log w)+mu0^2/(2v0).

The inequality log w<=w-1 follows by integrating 1/t from 1 to w, separately for w>=1 and 0<w<=1, or by differentiating w-1-log w. Both additional terms are nonnegative. Consequently

    E >= (D_1+D_2)/2 >= (1/4)log(9/8).

Finally log(9/8)=integral_1^{9/8} dt/t > (1/8)(8/9)=1/9, since 1/t>8/9 except at the right endpoint. Thus c0>1/36. Every denominator and logarithm argument above is strictly positive.

## Interpretation for the dossier

C002 supplies phi as an input, so its input encoding itself is discontinuous as a function of raw x in this example; the continuity hypothesis here then fails. There is no contradiction. To close Target 1, the architecture must explicitly permit the fixed feature map in the input representation, or the theorem must add assumptions that make raw-input feature computation possible and account for its cost. Merely calling the kernel finite rank does not settle this issue.

The example is an obstruction to a named target interpretation, not a claimed solution of the entire T336 problem. The remaining feature-input theorem C002 and this obstruction both await independent review.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:16:49.564661+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7994b8eb14afe8df4ccbb96e64ddbced16fb44ee3fe5f57fd62aa626e183d505","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 17 (Inversion of the surrogate objectives) of arXiv:2608.25188, 'Transforms for LLM Quantization:\\ The Great Inversion and Format Co-Design'] Regard both distortions as functionals of the transformed energy vector $v$ at
fixed $E=\sum_k v_k$, the shared-scale one on a \emph{uniform} grid.
\begin{itemize}
\item The \textbf{allocation-flexible} coding surrogate (\Cref{sec:classical})
$D_{\mathrm{vr}}(v)\propto(\prod_k v_k)^{1/d}$ is the geometric mean, the form the
variable-rate distortion takes while every coordinate draws positive rate
(\Cref{prop:schur}(i); once the water level of \Cref{prop:waterfill} rises above a
coordinate's energy the true distortion is floored by the un-coded coordinates' energy,
so the vanishing limit below is an idealization of the surrogate). It is strictly
Schur-\emph{concave} wherever all coordinates are positive and identically zero elsewhere; it decreases under majorization, so it is driven down by
\emph{concentration}, the direction in which the KLT moves the profile, reaching the
majorization-maximal \emph{reachable} one, the spectrum (\Cref{thm:klt}).
\item The \textbf{shared-scale AbsMax} surrogate (\Cref{sec:inv-flatness})
$D_{\mathrm{fr}}(v)=\sum_g\max_{k\in g}v_k$ obeys the max-vs-mean bound of
\Cref{prop:schur}(ii), so among all $v$ of fixed sum it is minimized at the
\emph{flat} $v$, the direction in which incoherence processing and the Hadamard move the
profile (\Cref{prop:rht}), and maximized under within-group concentration.
\end{itemize}
Over all $v$ of fixed total energy, then, the two surrogates are driven apart. The
geometric mean is strictly Schur-concave on the positive orthant, so every majorization
step toward concentration strictly lowers $D_{\mathrm{vr}}$ while every coordinate remains
positive, and it is maximized at the flat $v$;
while $E/G\le D_{\mathrm{fr}}\le E$, the lower bound attained exactly when every group
is internally uniform and the upper bound when each group's mass sits on a single
coordinate. Concentrating energy \emph{within} a group therefore strictly lowers the first whenever every coordinate remains positive, and never lowers the second, strictly raising it as soon as the group maximum rises; flattening within groups does the reverse. Along no \emph{within-group} step of the order do the two objectives move the same way.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["The converse is explicitly a sketch, with a missing uniform estimate.","The claimed converse concerns the positive-infinity end only."],"created_at":"2026-10-10T06:51:51.363786+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_79d6f4cce6edf1f0f5f53b75138f63a88e6154f64713766db080a20a4b5e8768","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14, author_checked_criterion_controlled_against_the_papers_own_deterministic_benchmark] This is the broader partial answer reported for both cases of the open question in Remark 5.3(ii) of arXiv:2607.07410. {"assumptions":["X is a compact metric space","T : X -> X is continuous and surjective","the definition quantifies over all nonempty OPEN subsets U"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.090776+00:00","domain":"topological dynamics, mixing properties of non-invertible maps","id":"claim_79ea44cf7b3dcd7452df709c8e293198d63314337814289a89d9a84e9a0edffe","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a compact metric space and T : X -> X a continuous surjection. T is TOPOLOGICALLY EXACT, also called locally eventually onto, if for every nonempty open set U there is an integer n >= 1 with T^n(U) = X. Two consequences are what proofs actually use. (a) UNIFORMITY IN n: if T^n(U) = X then T^m(U) = X for every m >= n, because T is onto; hence for each nonempty open U there is N with T^n(U) = X for ALL n >= N. (b) DENSE BACKWARD ORBITS WITH ALL LARGE PERIODS: for every x in X and every nonempty open U there is N with U intersect T^{-n}(x) nonempty for every n >= N; in particular the full backward orbit of any point is dense. Property (b) is a genuine aperiodicity statement that topological transitivity does not give and that even topological mixing of an invertible system cannot give. Relations: topological exactness implies topological mixing, which implies topological transitivity; the converses are false. An invertible map is never topologically exact unless X is a single point, since T^n(U) = X forces U = X for a homeomorphism, so exactness is a hypothesis reserved for genuinely non-invertible maps: expanding maps of the circle or of a compact manifold, one-sided mixing subshifts of finite type, and Chebyshev-like interval maps are the standard examples.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["K ⊂ ℝⁿ is nonempty and closed","the Euclidean norm is used (for the eikonal equation |Du| = 1 the ball of the same norm is the unit speed set)","the eikonal equation is taken in the form |Du| − 1 = 0"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:57:26.110904+00:00","domain":"Hamilton–Jacobi equations, optimal control, distance functions","id":"claim_7a06bdbc5ba6d57f83322f14777c062b65834326f61029190ba7a9d22b579f18","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let K ⊂ ℝⁿ be nonempty and closed and let d(x) := dist(x, K) = min_{y ∈ K} |x − y| (the minimum is attained because K is closed). Then: (a) d is 1-Lipschitz, d ≥ 0, and d(x) = 0 exactly when x ∈ K. (b) [minimal-time / control representation] d(x) = inf { T ≥ 0 : there is an absolutely continuous ξ: [0,T] → ℝⁿ with |ξ'(s)| ≤ 1 for a.e. s, ξ(0) = x, ξ(T) ∈ K } = inf { ∫_0^T |ξ'(s)| ds : ξ absolutely continuous, ξ(0) = x, ξ(T) ∈ K, T ≥ 0 } — the distance is the value function of the minimal-time problem for the control system ξ' = α, |α| ≤ 1, with target K, and the straight segment from x to a nearest point of K is an optimal trajectory. (c) [variational characterization] d is the largest 1-Lipschitz function that is ≤ 0 on K: if u: ℝⁿ → ℝ is 1-Lipschitz and u ≤ 0 on K then u ≤ d everywhere, and d itself is admissible; equivalently d(x) = max { u(x) : u 1-Lipschitz, u ≤ 0 on K }. (d) [eikonal equation] d is a viscosity solution of |Du| − 1 = 0 in the open set ℝⁿ \\ K, and a viscosity subsolution of |Du| − 1 ≤ 0 on all of ℝⁿ. Sharp edges. (1) The sign convention matters: d solves |Du| − 1 = 0 but is in general NOT a viscosity solution of 1 − |Du| = 0 (for K = {−1, 1} ⊂ ℝ, d = 1 − |x| on (−1,1) has a concave kink at 0 which is admissible for the first form only). (2) Uniqueness of viscosity solutions of |Du| = 1 in ℝⁿ \\ K vanishing on K FAILS without a sign or growth restriction: for K = {0}, the function u(x) = −|x| is a classical (hence viscosity) solution of |Du| − 1 = 0 in ℝⁿ \\ {0} with u(0) = 0, different from d(x) = |x|. The distance is singled out among solutions by (c), or by nonnegativity/boundedness-below conditions that this lemma does not assert. (3) For K not closed the minimum in the definition of d must be replaced by an infimum and d vanishes on the closure of K, not only on K.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:17:04.322958+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7a112d984414996beb1871b3c4a78c359f37fdfc7dd3eb7542762ba4b443e657","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition of arXiv:2606.01683, 'Singular-value gap of nonreversible Markov processes'] For a Banach couple $(E_0, E_1)$, denote by $\mathcal{F}(E_0, E_1)$ the class 
    of functions $F: \Bar{S} \to E_0 + E_1$ satisfying
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $F$ is continuous on $\Bar{S}$ and analytic on $S$
        \item $F(it) \in E_0$ and $F(1+it) \in E_1$ for all $t \in \mathds{R}$
        \item $\|F\|_{\mathcal{F}(E_0, E_1)} \coloneqq 
        \max \Big\{ \sup_{t \in \mathds{R}} \|F(it)\|_{E_0}, \sup_{t \in \mathds{R}} \|F(1+it)\|_{E_1}           \Big\} < \infty$ 
    \end{itemize}
    Then, for $0 \leq \theta \leq 1 $, the \textbf{complex interpolation space} $[E_0, E_1]_\theta$ is the 
    Banach space defined by
    \[
        [E_0, E_1]_\theta \coloneqq \{h \in E_0 + E_1: h = F(\theta) \ \ \text{for some} \ F \in \mathcal{F}(E_0, E_1)\}
    \]
    equipped with the norm
    \[
        \|h\|_{[E_0, E_1]_\theta} \coloneqq \inf_{\substack{F \in \mathcal{F}(E_0, E_1) \\
        F(\theta) = h}} \|F\|_{\mathcal{F}(E_0, E_1)}
    \]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["finite third absolute moment","sigma > 0"],"created_at":"2026-08-29T02:26:24.138839+00:00","domain":"probability / limit theorems","id":"claim_7a265347afec4b9fe9f5dcce2f8373386fa40d3f1bf382ea1ca52d06dc25ffe4","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, ..., X_n be independent identically distributed random variables with E X_1 = 0, E X_1^2 = sigma^2 > 0 and rho = E |X_1|^3 < infinity. {"assumptions":["(a_n) real, decreasing, a_n -> 0","the partial sums of (b_n) are bounded","no absolute convergence is claimed: sum a_n b_n may converge only conditionally"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T14:24:13.476469+00:00","domain":"real analysis","id":"claim_7a93727307e363c9bb873456495559cf89a7f0e0df573892eaba5e3bcefedfb3","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (a_n) be a sequence of real numbers that is monotonically decreasing with limit 0, and let (b_n) be a sequence of real or complex numbers whose partial sums B_N = b_1 + ... + b_N are bounded, |B_N| <= K for all N. Then the series sum a_n b_n converges. Special cases: the alternating series test (b_n = (-1)^n) and the convergence of sum a_n sin(n x) and sum a_n cos(n x) for every x that is not a multiple of 2 pi, since the partial sums of sin(n x) and cos(n x) are bounded by 1/|sin(x/2)|. Abel's test is the companion: if sum b_n converges and (a_n) is monotone and bounded, then sum a_n b_n converges.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Normalized faithful normal tracial state on a finite von Neumann algebra.","Fixed finite algebraically free bounded selfadjoint tuple, so the difference quotients on its polynomial algebra are well-defined.","Conjugate variables, when present, lie in the L2 closure of that polynomial algebra."],"created_at":"2026-10-21T15:23:31.129104+00:00","domain":"free probability","id":"claim_7b07bb59dd931dfee8cd10c983c1438e7e979ef8785168b458e06a8b2a0418fd","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (M,tau) be a finite von Neumann algebra with faithful normal tracial state tau(1)=1. Let X=(X_1,...,X_n) be an algebraically free tuple of bounded selfadjoint elements, with n a fixed positive integer. On noncommutative polynomials in X, define the free difference quotient partial_j by partial_j X_i=delta_ij*(1 tensor 1) and the Leibniz rule, with the usual bimodule action on the tensor product. The conjugate variable J_j belongs to the L2(tau) closure of the polynomial algebra and, if it exists, satisfies tau(J_j P(X))=(tau tensor tau)(partial_j P(X)) for every polynomial P. Equivalently J_j is the adjoint of partial_j applied to 1 tensor 1. Define Phi_star(X)=sum_{j=1}^n ||J_j||_2^2 when all conjugate variables exist, and Phi_star(X)=+infinity otherwise. This is conjugate-variable, non-microstates free Fisher information relative to the scalar algebra C. It is not the Fisher information of a classical parametric likelihood.","status":"unverified"}

Consequently C[0,1] is universal for the class of separable Banach spaces up to isometry, and every separable metric space embeds isometrically into C[0,1] as well (Banach-Mazur, via the Kuratowski embedding x -> d(x, .) - d(x_0, .)). In contrast, no separable Banach space is isomorphically universal for the class of separable REFLEXIVE spaces with a separable dual of the same kind (Szlenk), and the universality fails in an essential way for spaces of continuous functions on countable compacta (Bessaga-Pelczynski, Milutin: C(K) for uncountable metrizable compact K is isomorphic to C[0,1], while C(K) for countable K is not).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0130-escape-probability-of-a-transient-one-dimensional-excited-random-walk","No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:26:45.048178+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7b80a58f8c55e726456eec97ea83b732ab9372f5ab696c98282708d6bce14a45","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Express the escape probability through the branching-process representation for the one-cookie deterministic case. Result: In the deterministic environment with one cookie of strength p at each site (M = 1, delta = 2p - 1... transient iff delta > 1 which needs more than one cookie; take M = 2 cookies of strength p each, delta = 2(2p - 1) > 1 iff p > 3/4). The event of never returning to 0 after the first step: the walk must never come back, which in the branching-process picture (right excursions counted by the number of down-crossings of each edge) means the branching process with migration started from the edge (0,1) never produces a down-crossing of (0,1) into 0... the escape probability equals the probability that the total number of down-crossings of the edge (0,1) is zero, which is P(the branching process with migration started at 1 individual at level 1 has zero descendants at level 0) - not directly a standard extinction probability but a hitting probability of the time-reversed process. For the source's example [Zer05, Th. 18] the closed form exists; for general bounded stacks the escape probability is the solution of a finite-dimensional fixed-point equation obtained by conditioning on the first cookie stack at sites 1, 2, ...: define q_k = P(never return to 0 | walk currently at k, all cookies at sites >= k intact, cookies at sites < k in their post-visit states); the states of the sites already visited matter only through the remaining cookie counts, which for M bounded is a finite vector, and the walk's returns to 0 require descending through all visited sites; the escape probability then equals the probability of survival of a Markov chain on finite cookie-count vectors, computable numerically for given (M, p) but with no closed form in general. Recorded: reduction to a finite-state escape problem; closed form only in special cases. Obstruction: No closed form beyond special cases; the reduction gives a numerical procedure only.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Coupled n>=2 scalar h_i(s)=a_i+b_i tanh(kappa_i s), 0<a_i<b_i, b_i,kappa_i>0; logistic average loss; simultaneous Euclidean GD. A=mean h_i(p_bar)^2/4, B=mean h_i'(p_bar)/2, mean h_i(p_bar)=0. Exact normal linear-stability classification of every finite fixed point of joint-head factored-attention GD at every eta>0: the stationary curve v=0,kq=p_bar has tangent multiplier 1 and normal multipliers 1-eta lambda_+/- with lambda_+/-=(A +/- sqrt(A^2+4B^2(k^2+q^2)))/2. One normal direction is always repelling; the other attracts exactly when k^2+q^2<(4/eta^2-2A/eta)/B^2, is neutral at equality, and repels beyond. Every positive fixed step loses the attracting normal direction at sufficiently unbalanced factorizations.

# Target 1: exact normal stability of the factored GD stationary curve

Version 1, proof unaudited. This is a linearized stability classification;
it does not claim a nonlinear flip bifurcation or a full-space GD basin theorem.

Assume precisely the n-example factored model of claim 010:
0<a_i<b_i, b_i,kappa_i>0, logistic average loss of
v h_i(kq), h_i(s)=a_i+b_i tanh(kappa_i s), and simultaneous Euclidean GD
with any fixed eta>0. Let p_bar<0 be the unique mean root and define

 A=mean_i h_i(p_bar)^2/4>=0,
 B=mean_i h_i'(p_bar)/2>0.

All finite stationary points, equivalently all GD fixed points, form the
curve E={v=0,kq=p_bar}. At such a point write S=k^2+q^2>=2|p_bar|.
The GD Jacobian has tangent multiplier 1 and normal multipliers

 mu_-=1-eta lambda_-, mu_+=1-eta lambda_+,
 lambda_+/-=(A +/- sqrt(A^2+4B^2 S))/2.

Here lambda_-<0<lambda_+, hence mu_->1 everywhere: no point of E is
linearly attracting in all normal directions. The other normal direction is

* strictly attracting in the linearization when eta lambda_+<2;
* neutral with multiplier -1 when eta lambda_+=2;
* strictly repelling with multiplier less than -1 when eta lambda_+>2.

Let
 J_eta=(4/eta^2-2A/eta)/B^2.

The first case is EXACTLY S<J_eta, the middle case exactly S=J_eta,
and the last exactly S>J_eta. Equivalently, with C=k^2-q^2,
S=sqrt(C^2+4p_bar^2): there is an attracting normal direction only if
J_eta>2|p_bar|, and then precisely at

 |C|<sqrt(J_eta^2-4p_bar^2).

Equality gives neutral normal points when J_eta>=2|p_bar|. If J_eta
is smaller than 2|p_bar|, every point is repelling in both normal directions.
In particular, for EVERY eta>0, sufficiently unbalanced factorizations on
E are normally repelling in both directions. There is no positive constant
step that preserves the flow's one attracting normal direction uniformly
along the entire stationary curve. This does NOT imply an open basin of
cycles or disprove a full-space almost-everywhere GD endpoint theorem.

## Proof

The fixed-point condition is gradient L=0, classified in proof 008.
Its loss Hessian at E is
 [[A,-Bq,-Bk],[-Bq,0,0],[-Bk,0,0]].
The tangent vector (0,k,-q) is in its kernel. In the orthonormal basis
e_v=(1,0,0), e_s=(0,q,k)/sqrt(S) of the normal plane, the Hessian is
 [[A,-B sqrt(S)],[-B sqrt(S),0]].
The quadratic characteristic polynomial is lambda^2-A lambda-B^2 S,
which yields lambda_+/- and their signs. The GD Jacobian is I-eta Hessian,
proving the multipliers and their linear classifications.

For equivalence with J_eta, consider the polynomial
f(z)=z^2-Az-B^2 S, whose positive zero is lambda_+ and negative zero
lambda_-. Since 2/eta>0, lambda_+<2/eta is equivalent to
f(2/eta)>0, or S<J_eta; equality and the reverse inequality follow likewise.
This avoids squaring a potentially negative expression 4/eta-A.
Finally S^2=C^2+4p_bar^2 by algebra, and S is unbounded along E by
taking k->infinity, q=p_bar/k. All asserted threshold statements follow.

## Scope of the obstruction

The obstruction is to a PARTICULAR transfer from flow to GD: retaining
one attracting normal direction uniformly on every imbalance leaf at fixed
step. It is not an obstruction to every possible discrete-time proof.
The imbalance leaves themselves are not invariant under GD:
C_+=(1-eta^2 v^2 G^2)C. Both facts must be accounted for in further work.
Normal multipliers on the unit circle require separate nonlinear analysis;
no attracting two-cycle is claimed. Scalar genuine self-attention embeddings
of this family are supplied in claim 008.","status":"unverified"}

A computation with u = p g, p = r^2 cos(2 theta) harmonic and g = (log(1/r))^{1/2}, using Laplacian(p g) = 4 p g'/r + p (g'' + g'/r), gives Laplacian u = -cos(2 theta) ( 2 (log(1/r))^{-1/2} + (1/4)(log(1/r))^{-3/2} ), which extends continuously by 0 at the origin, while D_{11}u = 2(log(1/r))^{1/2} + o(1) blows up. Since u is C^1 and C^infinity off the origin, it solves Laplacian u = f distributionally on the ball with f continuous; no C^2 solution of Laplacian v = f exists near 0, because v - u would be harmonic hence smooth. Failure at alpha = 1: with q = x_1^3 - 3 x_1 x_2^2 and g = log(1/r), the function u = q g has Laplacian u = -6 q/r^2 = -6 r cos(3 theta), which is Lipschitz, while D_{111}u = 6 log(1/r) + O(1) is unbounded, so u is not in C^{2,1}. Failure at p = infinity: u = (x_1^2 - x_2^2) log(1/r) has Laplacian u = -4 cos(2 theta) in L^infinity while D_{11}u = 2 log(1/r) + O(1) is not bounded, so Laplacian u in L^infinity does not give u in W^{2,infinity} = C^{1,1}; the correct endpoint statement is Laplacian u in L^infinity implies D^2 u in BMO. Failure at p = 1: let f_k = rho_{1/k} be standard mollifiers and u_k = Gamma convolved with f_k, so Laplacian u_k = f_k with ||f_k||_{L^1} = 1 and ||u_k||_{L^1(B_2)} bounded; on B_1 minus the origin D_{12}u_k converges pointwise to D_{12}Gamma, whose size is comparable to |x|^{-n} and hence not integrable near 0, so by Fatou ||D^2 u_k||_{L^1(B_1)} tends to infinity. {"assumptions":["Omega is a bounded open subset of R^N, N >= 2 (N >= 3 for the exponent N/(N-2) statements)","A(x) is measurable, uniformly elliptic and bounded: lambda |xi|^2 <= A xi . xi, |A xi| <= Lambda |xi|","homogeneous Dirichlet boundary condition","part (I): f in L^m(Omega) with m > N/2","part (II): f in L^1(Omega) or a bounded Radon measure; solutions understood in Stampacchia's duality sense"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:23.250962+00:00","domain":"linear elliptic PDE, L^1 and measure data, regularity","id":"claim_7bba34209aa1de121daefe005a5bb783e1eb800331b4e677d6dbdf6096168f4d","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Setting: $\\Omega \\subset \\mathbb{R}^N$ bounded open, $N \\geq 2$; $A(x)$ a measurable matrix field with $\\lambda|\\xi|^2 \\leq A(x)\\xi\\cdot\\xi$ and $|A(x)\\xi| \\leq \\Lambda|\\xi|$ for some $0 < \\lambda \\leq \\Lambda$ (uniform ellipticity, bounded measurable coefficients, no regularity); the Dirichlet problem $-\\operatorname{div}(A(x)\\nabla u) = f$ in $\\Omega$, $u = 0$ on $\\partial\\Omega$. (Stampacchia, Ann. Inst. Fourier 1965.) (I) $L^\\infty$ estimate. If $f \\in L^m(\\Omega)$ with $m > N/2$ (so $f \\in H^{-1}$ and the weak solution $u \\in H_0^1(\\Omega)$ exists and is unique), then $u \\in L^\\infty(\\Omega)$ and $\\|u\\|_{L^\\infty} \\leq C\\,\\|f\\|_{L^m}$ with $C = C(N, \\lambda, m, |\\Omega|)$. Sharp edge: the exponent is sharp - for $N \\geq 3$ there are $f \\in L^{N/2}(\\Omega)$ (even for $A = I$) whose solution is unbounded, e.g. $u = \\log|\\log|x||$ near the origin, whose Laplacian lies in $L^{N/2}$ but $u \\notin L^\\infty$; for $f \\in L^{N/2}$ one only gets $u$ in the Orlicz class $\\exp L$ (and $u \\in L^q$ for all $q < \\infty$). (II) $L^1$ and measure data. If $f \\in L^1(\\Omega)$ (or more generally $f = \\mu$ is a bounded Radon measure on $\\Omega$), there exists a unique DUALITY solution: a function $u \\in L^1(\\Omega)$ with $\\int_\\Omega u\\,g\\,dx = \\int_\\Omega w_g\\,d\\mu$ for every $g \\in L^\\infty(\\Omega)$, where $w_g \\in H_0^1(\\Omega) \\cap L^\\infty(\\Omega)$ is the weak solution of the adjoint problem $-\\operatorname{div}(A^{T}\\nabla w_g) = g$ (bounded by part (I), which is all that is needed to pair with $f \\in L^1$); for MEASURE data one needs $w_g$ continuous on $\\overline\\Omega$ so that $\\int w_g\\,d\\mu$ makes sense - interior continuity is De Giorgi-Nash-Moser, continuity up to the boundary requires a mild regularity of $\\partial\\Omega$ (e.g. Lipschitz, or an exterior cone condition), which is then an extra hypothesis in the measure case. This $u$ satisfies: $u \\in W_0^{1,q}(\\Omega)$ for EVERY $q < N/(N-1)$ with $\\|u\\|_{W_0^{1,q}} \\leq C(N,\\lambda,\\Lambda,q,\\Omega)\\,\\|\\mu\\|_{\\mathcal{M}}$ ($= \\|f\\|_{L^1}$ for $L^1$ data); $|\\nabla u|$ lies in the Marcinkiewicz (weak-$L$) space $M^{N/(N-1)}(\\Omega)$ and, for $N \\geq 3$, $u \\in M^{N/(N-2)}(\\Omega)$; $u$ is the strong $W_0^{1,q}$ limit of the weak solutions $u_n$ with smooth data $f_n \\to f$ in $L^1$ (or $f_n \\to \\mu$ weakly-* with $\\|f_n\\|_1$ bounded); $u$ solves the equation in the sense of distributions, $\\int A\\nabla u\\cdot\\nabla\\varphi = \\int \\varphi\\,d\\mu$ for $\\varphi \\in C_c^\\infty(\\Omega)$; and $T_k(u) \\in H_0^1(\\Omega)$ for every $k$ with $\\lambda\\int|\\nabla T_k(u)|^2 \\leq k\\|\\mu\\|$. Sharp edges: (a) $q = N/(N-1)$ is excluded and cannot be reached - for $\\mu = \\delta_0$ and $A = I$ the Green function has $|\\nabla u| \\sim |x|^{1-N}$, which is in $L^q$ near 0 iff $q < N/(N-1)$; (b) uniqueness holds among DUALITY solutions (equivalently among limits of approximations, or entropy/renormalized solutions), NOT among all distributional solutions in $W^{1,q}$, $q < N/(N-1)$: for merely measurable uniformly elliptic $A$ Serrin (1964) constructed, for any $1 < q < 2$, a nonzero $u \\in W^{1,q}(B)$ on a ball $B$ with $\\operatorname{div}(A\\nabla u) = 0$ distributionally and $u \\notin H^1_{loc}$ (a 'pathological solution'), so a distributional $W^{1,q}$ solution is not determined by its data without a selection principle such as duality, approximation, or the entropy/renormalized formulation; (c) with $L^1$ data the solution is in general NOT in $H_0^1$ (its energy is infinite), so the Lax-Milgram framework does not apply directly - the estimates are obtained on approximations via the truncation method and passed to the limit.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:57:59.663372+00:00","domain":"probability theory (large deviations)","id":"claim_7bbca983cd1987b84121f00e6239c8504a46958f9c5e1ecc10d145c0670e2b1c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (mu_eps) be probability measures on a topological space X satisfying a large deviation principle with good rate function I as eps -> 0+, and let phi: X -> R be bounded and continuous. {"assumptions":["The affine-scaled free convolution powers converge weakly to C_1.","Free convolution is weakly continuous, and unimodal measures are weakly closed."],"created_at":"2026-10-10T06:51:51.365034+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7bd214bfc3c4fa222b61d570e908b0f27536370c30f308cdc774fd9de22b26b6","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked] This is the proved attraction-domain extension of the partial answer to Problem 3.11 of Takahiro Hasebe and Yuki Ueda's Large time unimodality for classical and free Brownian motions with initial distributions, ALEA 15 (2018), 353-374, DOI:10.30757/ALEA.v15-15 (arXiv:1710.08240). A law lambda is freely strongly unimodal when lambda boxplus nu is unimodal for every unimodal nu. This is an unrefereed campaign result.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X a random element of {-1, 1}^n, n >= 1, under any law","given X_{-i}, X_i' is independent of X_i","u real-valued on {-1, 1}^n"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T09:29:33.705785+00:00","domain":"analysis of Boolean functions","id":"claim_7c3b9a530dbb12cbd24154e6e9dd868221769f4a6d4f8b6c34a52a93bff425e2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X take values in {-1, 1}^n, n >= 1, under any law, fix a coordinate i, and let X_i' be a replacement sign which, given X_{-i}, is independent of X_i; X^(i) is X with coordinate i replaced by X_i'. Put D_i u(x) = (u(x with x_i = 1) - u(x with x_i = -1))/2, m = E[X_i | X_{-i}] and m' = E[X_i' | X_{-i}]. For every real u on the cube, (1/2) E[(u(X) - u(X^(i)))^2] = E[(1 - m m') (D_i u(X))^2], with the weight 1 - m m' in [0, 2]. Hence (1/2) E[(u(X) - u(X^(i)))^2] = E[(D_i u(X))^2] for every u if and only if m m' = 0 almost surely: at each value of X_{-i} of positive probability, X_i or X_i' is conditionally fair, and the law of the other sign is then arbitrary (X_i' = 1 always is allowed when X_i is conditionally fair). If X_i' is a fresh draw from the conditional law of X_i (m' = m, the heat-bath step), the left side is E[Var(u(X) | X_{-i})] = E[(1 - m^2) (D_i u)^2]. # Balanced opposite-head two-cycles: complete implicit parametrization

T328-W698-017 v1, Target 1, proof (unaudited).

Consider L(v,k,q)=log(1+exp(-v h(kq))), h(s)=a+b*tanh(kappa*s),
0<a<b, kappa>0 and simultaneous Euclidean GD with fixed eta>0.
For this scalar signed link, every balanced period-two orbit whose heads have
opposite signs is covered by the following construction, up to interchanging
the two phases and simultaneously negating both factors. The construction
parametrizes cycles across the data/step parameters; for prescribed a,b,kappa,
eta these parameter equalities are necessary and sufficient, not a claim that
every prescribed model has such a cycle.

## Construction from four positive parameters

Choose 0<r<1 and T,y0,kappa>0. Define

    A=tanh T, B=tanh(r^2*T),
    D=cosh(T)^2/cosh(r^2*T)^2,
    sig(y)=1/(1+exp(-y)), f(y)=y*sig(y)^2.

There is a unique y1>0 solving

    f(y1)=f(y0)/(r*D).

Indeed f'(y)=sig(y)^2*[1+2y*(1-sig(y))]>0 on y>0,
and f increases continuously from 0 to infinity. Put

    g0=sig(y0), g1=sig(y1), c=g0/g1,
    t=y1/(y0*c),
    v0=sqrt((1-r)*(A-B)/((1+t)*(1+c)*kappa*sech(T)^2)),
    H0=y0/v0, H1=c*H0,
    b=H0*(1+c)/(A-B), a=b*A-H0,
    eta=v0*(1+t)/(g0*H0), w=sqrt(T/kappa).

All denominators are strictly positive. Also a/b=(c*A+B)/(1+c) lies
strictly between B and A, hence 0<a<b. These parameters give the exact
period-two orbit

    (v0,w,-w) <-> (-t*v0,r*w,-r*w).

The two signed margins are -y0 and -y1. In particular the logistic factors
are exactly g0 and g1, not factors obtained from a limiting approximation.

## Verification

h(-w^2)=-H0 and h(-r^2*w^2)=H1. Thus g0*H0=g1*H1 and
the two head increments are respectively -v0*(1+t) and v0*(1+t).
Let d0=b*kappa*sech(T)^2, d1=b*kappa*sech(r^2*T)^2=D*d0.
The first factor coefficient is

    delta0=eta*v0*g0*d0
          =v0^2*(1+t)*(1+c)*kappa*sech(T)^2/(A-B)=1-r.

For the second coefficient, the scalar equation gives

    t*(g1/g0)*D = y1*g1^2*D/(y0*g0^2)=1/r.

Consequently delta1=eta*(-t*v0)*g1*d1=-(1-r)/r=1-1/r.
On k=-q the factor multipliers 1-delta0=r and 1-delta1=1/r
return the factors exactly. The head changes sign, so the orbit is nonfixed.

## Completeness within the stated class

Balance means k^2=q^2. If k=q, the product is nonnegative, h(kq)>0,
and the head strictly increases at every finite point, so there is no finite
cycle. If k=q=0 the same argument applies. Thus a balanced cycle must lie
on k=-q with nonzero k. Interchange phases so v0>0>v1 and simultaneously
negate both factors so k0=w>0. Since delta_j=eta*v_j*g_j*h'_j,
delta0>0>delta1. The returning-factor equation is

    (1-delta0)*(1-delta1)=1.

The second factor is >1; therefore 0<1-delta0<1. Write this number r.
It follows that k1=r*w and delta1=1-1/r. In particular no factor sign flip
is possible for an opposite-head balanced two-cycle in this class.
The head update v1-v0<0 forces h0<0, and the reverse update forces h1>0.
Set H0=-h0, H1=h1, t=-v1/v0, T=kappa*w^2,
y0=v0*H0, y1=t*v0*H1. These are positive. The equal and opposite
head increments imply H1/H0=g0/g1=c, whence t=y1/(y0*c).
Dividing the two factor coefficients gives r*D*f(y1)=f(y0).
The identities h1-h0=b*(A-B), delta0=1-r and the head increment then
recover precisely the formulas for b,a,v0,eta above. This proves completeness.

## Full Jacobian test and its present limit

The normal two-step multiplier is exactly

    mu_U=(1+delta0)*(1+delta1)=(2-r)*(2-1/r)=5-2r-2/r.

It satisfies |mu_U|<1 precisely for (3-sqrt(5))/2<r<1,
equals -1 at the left endpoint, and is <-1 below it. It is zero at r=1/2.
The other two multipliers are exactly the eigenvalues of J1*J0, using
the general balanced Jacobian given in proofs/014_opposite_head_cycles.md.
This is an exact formula for the full spectrum, but no uniform inequality
for that balanced block has been proved for unequal head magnitudes.

The reproducible script scripts/asymmetric_cycles.py sampled 576 choices:
r in {.1,.2,.35,.4,.5,.65,.8,.9,.98}, T in {.1,.3,.6,.9,1.3,2,3,5},
y0 in {.01,.1,.4,1,2,4,8,16}, with kappa=1. It solved the monotone
equation by floating-point bisection and differentiated the full 3D loss.
It found zero attracting candidates; the smallest observed full spectral
radius was approximately 8.9666956. The largest relative cycle residual was
approximately 2.56e-13. These are numerical evidence, not rigorous bounds,
and cannot establish instability throughout the parametrization.

Claim 016 proves full instability and the complete second-multiplier phase
diagram on the equal-head-magnitude subfamily r=1/2,
cosh(T)^2=2cosh(T/4)^2. The SINGLE remaining hard step for upgrading
the wider numerical finding to a theorem is a rigorous spectral-radius
inequality for J1*J0 throughout (r,T,y0)>0 with 0<r<1. This proof
does not claim that step or almost-everywhere factored-GD convergence.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:19:47.272105+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7c65d5f6b42d957359a385c83fae17c845d7b1786630ec0d59a0fd6787e8a37d","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:pred_proj of arXiv:2601.09976, 'Stochastic Calculus as Operator Factorization:\\ An Operator--Covariant Derivative and Uni'] Assume that $\mathcal{H}_X$ consists of jointly measurable processes and that the predictable processes form a closed subspace of~$\mathcal{H}_X$. The \emph{predictable projection} $\Pi_X \colon \mathcal{H}_X \to \mathcal{H}_X$ is the orthogonal projection onto this subspace.

The closedness assumption is not automatic for an arbitrary energy space; it must be verified. In all examples of this paper, the predictable subspace is either all of~$\mathcal{H}_X$ (for It\^o integrals with respect to martingales and compensated Poisson processes, where $\mathcal{H}_X$ consists entirely of predictable processes) or is closed by standard results on conditional expectation.

For the integral-form energy spaces used throughout this paper---specifically, those where $u_t \in L^2(\Omega)$ for each~$t$ and the $\mathcal{H}_X$ inner product takes the form $\langle u, v \rangle_{\mathcal{H}_X} = \mathbb{E}[\int_0^T u_t v_t\, d\mu_t]$ for some positive measure $\mu$ on $[0,T]$ (possibly random, as with $d\langle X\rangle_t$)---the predictable projection admits the pointwise representation
\[
(\Pi_X u)_t = \mathbb{E}[u_t \mid \mathcal{F}_{t-}] \quad \text{for } t \in (0,T], \qquad (\Pi_X u)_0 = \mathbb{E}[u_0 \mid \mathcal{F}_0],
\]
where $\mathcal{F}_{t-}$ is the left-limit $\sigma$-algebra defined in Section~(sec:setup of the paper). This is the standard predictable projection of optional processes; see, e.g., [Revuz1999].","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0132-transience-and-recurrence-of-the-m-d1-d2-balanced-excited-random-walks","No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T15:09:50+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7c69e7a35af09beef6afb72e761e8fb0c170db07abf7dde9a745ce5d8185f1e0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Analyse M(1,1) on Z^2 through the range of the first-coordinate walk. Result: In M(1,1) the first coordinate moves only at first visits and the second at later visits; the set of visited vertices is the range, and the first-coordinate process is a simple random walk on Z run at the rate of new visits. Recurrence of M(1,1) would follow if the walk returns to the origin infinitely often; since the second coordinate performs a simple random walk on the column above the current first coordinate whenever the vertex was visited before, the walk behaves in each column like a 1D random walk (recurrent) until it hits an unvisited vertex, at which time the first coordinate steps. The number of new visits up to time n is the range R_n; the first coordinate after n steps is a simple random walk at time R_n, so |X^1_n| is of order sqrt(R_n), and R_n <= n, so |X^1_n| is typically at most of order sqrt n - not deterministically: n first-visit moves to the right, which have probability 2^-n, give X^1_n = n; a return to the origin requires both coordinates to vanish. A heuristic: if R_n ≍ n/log n as for planar simple random walk then the first coordinate is diffusive at the slower clock, and the walk is 'more recurrent' than planar simple random walk, supporting the conjecture; but the range of M(1,1) is not that of simple random walk because the exploration is column-wise. A rigorous partial fact: M(1,1) is recurrent if and only if the first coordinate returns to 0 infinitely often at times when the second coordinate is 0; since within a column the second coordinate is a recurrent 1D walk that keeps returning to 0 until it finds a new vertex, and new vertices in a column are found at the ends of the visited interval, the question is whether the first-coordinate walk (which is a simple random walk in the clock of new visits) visits 0 infinitely often, which it does a.s. (1D recurrence), and whether at those visits the second coordinate is 0 - not automatic. So recurrence of M(1,1) reduces to: at the (infinitely many) times the first coordinate is 0, the second coordinate, which then performs a 1D walk in the column of 0 with the visited interval of that column, returns to height 0 before finding a new vertex - which has probability bounded below by a constant each time if the visited interval around height 0 in column 0 has length bounded... the visited interval in column 0 grows, and the probability of returning to 0 from the boundary of an interval of length L before exiting is of order 1/L... summing over the visits to column 0 gives a divergent series only if the interval lengths grow slowly enough. This is the crux and I did not settle it; the reduction is recorded. Key identity: M(1,1) recurrent iff, at the infinitely many returns of the first coordinate to 0, the second coordinate returns to 0 in column 0 before finding a new vertex; the return probability is of order 1/(visited interval length). Obstruction: Growth rate of the visited interval in column 0 not controlled.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.179126+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7ceb1b95c0e64951a2d9f8f4b1393598463871053d23b3f68d1d750a84d515da","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Ppn 90 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Recalling \eqref{e:sM.Lip.sym} and Definitions \ref{d:SDE.classification.sym}--\ref{d:measure.classes.sym}, we have
	\[\sM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha) \subseteq \sM^{\IAMP,\sym}(\alpha,0)\,.\]

\begin{proof}
Consider any $\mu \in \sM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha)$, as defined by \eqref{e:sM.Lip.sym}. 
    By Lemma~\ref{l:control.problems.Lip.to.Lip.sym}, we can find $\tilde\mu \in \sM^{\Lip}(\alpha)$ with $\sym(\tilde\mu) = \mu$.
It was shown in the \hyperlink{p:thm.control.problems.main}{proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:control.problems.main}} that $\sM^{\Lip}(\alpha) = \sM^{\IAMP}(\alpha,0)$, so $\tilde\mu \in \sM^{\IAMP}(\alpha,0)$.
Therefore, for any $\epsilon>0$ we can find $L>0$ and controls 
    \beq
        
        (q_*,b,\sigma,w,p,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising) \in \Adm^{\IAMP}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)
    \eeq
such that (recalling that $\sym$ is a contraction) we have
    \[
        \bbW_2\Big(\mu, \mu^{\sym}(q_*,b,\sigma,p,\zeta)\Big)
        \le\bbW_2\Big(\tilde \mu, \mu(q_*,b,\sigma,p,\zeta)\Big)
         \le \epsilon\,.
    \]
We see from Definitions~\ref{d:SDE.classification} and \ref{d:SDE.classification.sym}
that the sets of controls $\Adm^{\IAMP}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)$ and $\Adm^{\IAMP,\sym}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)$ are in fact identical, so the controls \eqref{e:Lip.general.in.IAMP.sym.controls} belong to $\Adm^{\IAMP,\sym}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)$, and 
    \[
        \mu \in \cB_\epsilon\Big(\cM^{\IAMP,\sym}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)\Big)\,.
    \]
    Since for all $\epsilon > 0$, there exists $L > 0$ so that this holds, we conclude $\mu \in \sM^{\IAMP,\sym}(\alpha,0)$.
    As this holds for all $\mu \in \sM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha)$, the claim follows.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:39:12.396473+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7ced2486a96ae433761fd131678f1280ad28a899958e402f6b67d559d3c08f98","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 1. dfn: BTM of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] [The Bouchaud trap model] 
  Fix an electrical network $G$.
  Let $\{\xi_{x}^{G}\}_{x \in V_{G}}$ be i.i.d.\ random variables with $\xi_{x}^{G} \stackrel{\mathrm{d}}{=} \xi$.
  Set $\nu_{G} \coloneqq \sum_{x \in V_{G}} \xi_{x}^{G} \delta_{x}$,

{"assumptions":["H is a Hilbert space","T is a bounded linear operator on H"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.571526+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, operator ideals","id":"claim_7d3da9c3c18db6a4a1b175a83b3a4853fd1bc3c0008d3153ce0be80e2db8b984","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let H be a Hilbert space. A bounded operator T on H is trace class (nuclear) if it is compact and ||T||_1 := sum_n s_n(T) < infinity. Equivalently: sum_i <|T| e_i, e_i> < infinity for some (hence every) orthonormal basis (e_i), where |T| = (T*T)^{1/2}, and this sum then equals ||T||_1; equivalently, T = AB with A and B Hilbert-Schmidt operators. The trace of a trace-class T is tr T = sum_i <T e_i, e_i>; this series converges absolutely for every orthonormal basis and its sum does not depend on the basis. The trace-class operators S_1(H) form a two-sided ideal of B(H) and a Banach space under ||.||_1, with ||T|| <= ||T||_2 <= ||T||_1; finite-rank operators are ||.||_1-dense in S_1(H); under the pairing (T, B) -> tr(TB), S_1(H) is isometrically the dual of the compact operators K(H) and the predual of B(H). For a positive operator T >= 0 the sum sum_i <T e_i, e_i> in [0, infinity] is basis-independent and is finite exactly when T is trace class; for operators that are not positive, convergence (even absolute convergence) of sum_i <T e_i, e_i> in one basis does not imply trace class.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Counterexample: F(p,z,x) = p_1 (equation u_x = 0), Γ = {y=0}","Noncharacteristic condition: D_pF(p0,z0,x0)·ν(x0) ≠ 0","Compatibility (admissibility): F(p0,z0,x0) = 0 and p0 agrees with the tangential gradient of g on Γ","Even when the conditions hold, the conclusion is only local in a neighbourhood of the point"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.418512+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: first-order equations, method of characteristics","id":"claim_7d8c544f22ddfa6bc426587ded0c72b9450163a966ed4890aa02b90253645958","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: local solvability of F(Du,u,x) = 0 with u = g on Γ requires D_pF(p0,z0,x0)·ν(x0) ≠ 0, i.e. the characteristic direction must be transversal to the data surface; and the initial triple must be admissible (the tangential derivatives of g must match p0). If the surface is characteristic, existence can fail outright and uniqueness can fail catastrophically. Counterexample: the equation u_x = 0 in R^2 (F(p,z,x) = p_1, so D_pF = (1,0)) with data on Γ = { y = 0 }, whose normal is ν = (0,1): D_pF·ν = 0, so Γ is characteristic — indeed the characteristics are the horizontal lines y = const, which lie IN Γ. Every C^1 solution satisfies u(x,y) = u(0,y), so u(·,0) must be constant: if g is not constant there is NO solution in any neighbourhood of a point of Γ; if g ≡ c there are infinitely many solutions u(x,y) = h(y) with h ∈ C^1 arbitrary and h(0) = c. The same pathology occurs for u_t + u_x = 0 with data prescribed on the characteristic line { x = t }. Auditor's check: before invoking local existence by characteristics, compute D_pF·ν at the point in question; for quasilinear equations a(x,u)·Du = b this is a(x0,g(x0))·ν(x0) ≠ 0, and for the Cauchy problem u_t + H(x,Du) = 0 on { t = 0 } it is automatic (the coefficient of u_t is 1).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:52:08.664699+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7d8db8fd4c67bde605a9b558b98bcad5b75ed77bb6f06554007dda7f09dc8a1c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 1 (Main theorem) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Let \(M\) be a closed connected three-manifold which admits a locally
homogeneous metric modeled on one of \(\RR^3\), \(\Nil\), or \(\Sol\), and let
\(g(t)\), \(0\leq t<\infty\), be any immortal Ricci flow on \(M\).  In all
three cases, for every basepoint \(\widetilde m\in\widetilde M\) in the
universal cover, the lifted blowdown flows
\((\widetilde M,\widetilde m,s^{-1}\widetilde g(s\tau))\), \(\tau>0\),
converge as \(s\to\infty\) in the pointed Cheeger--Hamilton sense to a
homogeneous expanding Ricci soliton solution.  The compact
and lifted limits are as follows.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If \(M\) has type \(\RR^3\), then, for every \(m\geq0\), \(g(t)\)
converges exponentially fast in the \(C^m\)-norm of any fixed smooth
background metric, as \(t\to\infty\), to a flat metric on \(M\).
The Gromov--Hausdorff limit of
\((M,t^{-1}g(t))\), as \(t\to\infty\), is a point.
The limit of the lifted blowdown flows is the flat expanding soliton solution
\[
        (\RR^3,0,g_{\mathrm{Euc}}(\tau)),
        \qquad
        g_{\mathrm{Euc}}(\tau)=dx^2+dy^2+dz^2,
        \quad \tau>0.
\]
\item If \(M\) has type \(\Nil\), then the Gromov--Hausdorff limit of
\((M,t^{-1}g(t))\), as \(t\to\infty\), is a point.  The limit of the lifted blowdown flows is the Nil
expanding soliton solution
\[
        \left(\RR^3,0,
        \frac{1}{3\tau^{1/3}}
        \left(dx+\frac12 y\,dz-\frac12 z\,dy\right)^2
        +\tau^{1/3}(dy^2+dz^2)
        \right).
\]
\item If \(M\) has type \(\Sol\), then the Gromov--Hausdorff limit of
\((M,t^{-1}g(t))\), as \(t\to\infty\), is a metric circle or a compact
interval of positive length.  The limit of the lifted blowdown flows is the Sol expanding soliton solution
\[
        \left(\RR^3,0,e^{-2z}dx^2+e^{2z}dy^2+4\tau\,dz^2\right).
\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:10:07.424632+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7d922fc74e165300d4137e2753b638ed7631e6a80e9f43ecedeb9ceeee2e31a4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem eq:bounded-block-max of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[theorem]{thm:bounded-block-counterexample}
Fix \(p\ge3\) and an integer \(r\ge2\).  There is a symmetric,
compactly supported probability law \(\mu\) with a \(C^\infty\) density
such that
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2em]
\item \(\mu\) matches the standard Gaussian moments through order \(r\)
(hence is centered and has variance one);
\item for i.i.d.\ ordered-tensor entries with common law \(\mu\), there
is a compact interval \(B\subset(0,\infty)\) for which
\begin{align}
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log
 \mathbb E_\mu\operatorname{Crt}_{N,\max}^J(B)
 &>\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log
 \mathbb E\operatorname{Crt}_{N,\max}^G(B),\\
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log
 \mathbb E_\mu\operatorname{Crt}_N^J(B)
 &>\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log
 \mathbb E\operatorname{Crt}_N^G(B).
\end{align}
The reflected local-minimum inequality holds on \(-B\).
\end{enumerate}
In particular, for every fixed \(\varepsilon\in[0,1/2)\),
\begin{equation}
 \max_{I\in[N]^p}|J_I|\le N^{1/2-\varepsilon}
 \qquad\text{almost surely for all sufficiently large \(N\)}.
\end{equation}
Thus an \(N^{1/2-\varepsilon}\) entrywise cutoff, or even an
 \(N\)-independent entry bound, does not restore universality of the
 unregularized annealed count.  The obstruction in this theorem is a
 coherent block involving on the order of \(N^{1/p}\) coordinates,
 rather than a single quadratic-scale entry. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

Let $\vX\equiv \vX^N$ be the process defined by \eqref{e:X.decomp}

	\[
	\E'\Big[\|\vX(1)-\vX^\trstar(1)\|^2\Big]
	\le O(\epsilon) + o_{\trK}(1)\,,
	\]
uniformly in $N$.

For $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$ we have $X^{\trstar,\sigma}(1,a)=X^\sigma(\tau(a),a)$, with $\tau$ the stopping time defined by \eqref{e:trstar.stopping.time}. It follows that, for $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$, we have
	\[
	\E'\Big[( X^\sigma(1)-X^{\trstar,\sigma}(1))^2\Big]
	\le O(1)
	\E'\bigg[
	\max_{0\le d\le \dmax}
	X^\sigma(q_d)^2;\tau<1\bigg] 
	\le O(\epsilon) +o_{\trK}(1)\,,
	\]
where the last bound is by Proposition~\ref{p:max.X.process.on.trstar.stopped.event}. Similarly,
	\[
	\E'\Big[( X^\Ising(1)-X^{\trstar,\Ising}(1))^2\Big]

	\E'\bigg[
	\max_{0\le d\le \dmax}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:54:18.302319+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7e31600f9d01adbc27be70f4366d322c49e3e0208945ef424711bec597ce2ad9","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop nonlinear-regression-regularity of arXiv:2608.30382, 'Convergence rates for the RMSprop optimizer with full control of the hyperparameters'] Let $\mathcal V\subseteq{\mathbb R}^d$ be nonempty and compact,
let $ r \in ( 0, \nicefrac{ 1 }{ 2 } ) $, $ \delta \in (0, \infty ) $,
and suppose that there exist nonempty compact sets
$ K_Z \subseteq \mathcal Z $ and $ K_Y\subseteq {\mathbb R}^m $ and a constant
$ B \in (0,\infty) $ with the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]

\item
The random variables are compactly supported in the sense that
\begin{align}\begin{split} 
  {\mathbb P}\bigl( Z \in K_Z , \, Y \in K_Y \bigr) = 1 .
 \end{split}\end{align}

\item
For $ {\mathbb P}_Z $-almost every $ z \in K_Z $, the conditional law of $ Y $
given $ Z = z $ has a Lebesgue density~$ p_z $ satisfying
\bas{

  \| p_z \|_{ L^\infty } \le B .
}

\item
The map $ ( \theta, z ) \mapsto \Gamma^{ \theta }( z ) $ and, for every
$ i \in \{ 1, \dots, d \} $,
the map
$
  ( \theta, z ) \mapsto\frac{\partial\Gamma^\theta}{\partial\theta_i}( z )
$
are continuous on $ \mathcal V \times K_Z $.

\item
The coordinate derivatives satisfy the uniform moment lower bound
\bas{

D_r
=
\inf_{ \substack{ \theta \in \mathcal V } }
\inf_{
  1 \le i \le d
}
{\mathbb E}\biggl[
\Bigl|
\frac{\partial\Gamma^\theta}{\partial\theta_i}(Z)
\Bigr|^{r}
\biggr]
\ge \delta.
}
\end{enumerate}
Choose $R\in(0,\infty)$ such that $K_Y\subseteq B(0,R)$, let
$\omega_{m-1}$ denote the volume of the unit ball in ${\mathbb R}^{m-1}$, use the
convention $\omega_0=1$, and set
\bas{
\mu_r
&=\frac{\delta^{1/r}}{2B\omega_{m-1}R^{m-1}}
\left(\frac{1-2r}{1-r}\right)^{(1-r)/r},\\
C_X
&=\max_{\substack{\theta\in\mathcal V,\ z\in K_Z,\ y\in K_Y\\1\le i\le d}}
\left|

Then $\mu_r,C_X\in(0,\infty)$. The innovation $(X,U)$ defined in

\qquad

}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Erdos-Renyi, or configuration-model-type with matching degree-tail conditions, random graph in the critical window p ~ 1/n + O(n^{-4/3})","a valid exploration (depth-first search) encoding of the graph as a walk whose excursions correspond to components","appropriate moment conditions, such as finite third moment of the degree for configuration models, for the walk-to-Brownian-motion scaling limit","the specific n^{2/3} spatial and n^{-1/3} time-window scaling matching the model's universality class"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.994489+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7e5a315b29b381b59e06b86854cbebd0263352263eaab7d90c296b7dfdfe42ac","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For the Erdos-Renyi random graph G(n,p) near the critical window p = 1/n + lambda n^{-4/3}, Aldous's exploration process encodes a depth-first search of the graph as a random-walk-like process Z_n(t) whose excursions above past running minima correspond exactly to the connected components, with excursion lengths equal to component sizes. After rescaling space by n^{-2/3} and time correspondingly, this process converges to a limiting process W(t) = B(t) + lambda t - t^2/2, a Brownian motion with parabolic drift, whose excursions above its running minimum encode the limiting rescaled sizes of the largest components in the critical window; the associated merging dynamics of component sizes as edges are added form the \"standard multiplicative coalescent\", a Markov process on sequences of masses matching the excursion structure. This gives the precise scaling limit, order n^{2/3} for the largest components with an explicit limiting joint law, for the Erdos-Renyi critical phase transition. It does not extend directly to other random graph models without re-deriving an analogous exploration or walk encoding, which may not exist in closed form, and the specific n^{2/3} spatial and n^{-1/3} time-window scaling is particular to models in the Erdos-Renyi (mean-field) universality class. Typical failure: Applying the Erdos-Renyi n^{2/3} critical scaling window and multiplicative-coalescent limit directly to a random graph model with heavy-tailed degrees, infinite third moment, or strong local clustering, where the correct scaling exponents and even the limiting process, as established for configuration models with power-law degree exponent tau in (3,4) by Bhamidi, van der Hofstad and van Leeuwaarden, differ substantially; universality of the Erdos-Renyi picture is a theorem for specific model classes, not a generic property of all critical random graphs. Canonical reference: Aldous, 1997, Annals of Probability; Aldous and Limic, 1998, Electronic Journal of Probability; Bhamidi, van der Hofstad and van Leeuwaarden, 2010, Annals of Probability.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["The two cylinders must be separated in time, past on the left of the inequality","Nonnegativity is required on the entire cylinder","Time-slice and reversed-time versions are false","Cylinders must respect the parabolic scaling t ~ r^2"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:49.107085+00:00","domain":"parabolic partial differential equations / Harnack inequalities","id":"claim_7f4575933b50f01a827886bdb34f32f9b2fc796f45ba59f43b34b0e99f0abc08","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Moser's inequality reads $\\sup_{Q^-}u\\le C\\inf_{Q^+}u$ with $Q^-$ strictly earlier than $Q^+$. Three hypotheses are load-bearing, and all three fail for the naive elliptic-style statement. (1) No inequality at a single time: on $\\mathbb R^n$ the positive solution $u_k(x,t)=e^{kx_1+k^2t}$ has, on $B_1\\times\\{t\\}$, $\\sup u_k/\\inf u_k=e^{2k}\\to\\infty$, so $\\sup_{B_1\\times\\{t\\}}u\\le C\\inf_{B_1\\times\\{t\\}}u$ cannot hold with $C$ independent of the solution; the same family (or the shifted heat kernel $\\Phi(x-y,t+\\varepsilon)$ as $\\varepsilon\\downarrow0$) shows that even the elliptic Harnack constant for the Laplacian does not transfer. (2) The time direction cannot be reversed: $\\sup_{Q^+}u\\le C\\inf_{Q^-}u$ is false, since $u_k$ grows like $e^{k^2t}$; information propagates forward in time only. Intuitively, a heat distribution can be large now and tiny in the past. (3) Nonnegativity on the whole cylinder is needed, not just on $Q^-\\cup Q^+$: the inequality is applied to $u$ and to $\\sup u-u$ in the derivation of Holder continuity, and both must be nonnegative on the full cylinder $B_{2r}\\times(t_0-4r^2,t_0)$. Also parabolic, not Euclidean, scaling governs the geometry: the cylinder for radius $r$ must have time length comparable to $r^2$, so an auditor should check that a cited Harnack inequality is applied on cylinders of the correct aspect ratio, with the two sub-cylinders separated in time by a fixed multiple of $r^2$.","status":"unverified"}

W_D(K(x,\cdot),K(y,\cdot))\leq \lambda D(x,y)

\ee
Then, for all $x,y\in E$,
\be
W_D(K(x,\cdot),K(y,\cdot))\leq \lambda D(x,y).
\ee
Consequently, for all probability measures $\mu,\nu$ on $E$,

\ee (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-23T13:15:27.869314+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_800182846141774e70b9296f79e5eab92b4ed12261fc2c10ba2ec3e50d8353b6","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"FIRES WHEN a source, or your own reading of one, states a stochastic dominance between two random variables that you can check have equal means. MINIMAL COUNTEREXAMPLE, or rather the minimal IMPOSSIBILITY: if X >= Y in the usual stochastic order and E X = E Y < infinity, then E(X - Y) = integral (P(X > t) - P(Y > t)) dt = 0 with a nonnegative integrand, so the survival functions agree everywhere and X and Y are equal in law. There is no example to find; the hypothesis is already the conclusion. CONDITION UNDER WHICH THE ROUTE FAILS: equal means. WHAT TO DO INSTEAD: the intended relation is the CONVEX or dilation order, under which the variance inequality c^2 >= 1 is immediate. In the E0078 case this is a reading issue in the source's own statement, not a mathematical obstacle - and reading it as the usual stochastic order would have made Conjecture 4.2 imply Conjecture 4.1 for a trivial and wrong reason. The lesson generalises past this problem: when a claimed ordering would be vacuous under a moment identity the problem also asserts, the ordering has been mis-transcribed.","status":"unverified"}

# C006: prior-averaged Gaussian log-loss generalization

Claim T336-w727-C006 v1. Status: proof (unaudited). Kind: bound.
Target: none (reviewer-authorized generalization half of the T336 statement).
This is an explicit adaptation of standard covering and exponential-moment
arguments, not a claim of a new learning-theory principle or a new solver.
The hardest step is uniform concentration for the unbounded query loss.

## 1. Statistical statement

Let (W_i,Y_i), i=1,...,m, be independent identically distributed tasks, m>=1.
W contains the context and query features, including all information on which
the predictive is conditioned. Assume the conditional law is exactly

    Y | W ~ N(a(W), b(W)), |a(W)|<=M, 0<b(W)<=V,

where M>=0 and V>0 are fixed. The law of W is otherwise arbitrary. In
particular no independence between the query and context features is required.
For the GP application this conditional-law premise must be checked; it is
not inferred just from a marginal GP label law or an arbitrary feature-selection
mechanism. A fixed GP, exogenous input design, and rejection of tasks based only
on their context labels satisfy it. Conditioning on query labels would not.

Assume the token encoding of W is measurable. Let H be the family of clipped
transformer predictions described in Section 2,
with outputs mu_theta(W) in [-U,U] and v_theta(W) in [v0,v1], where
U>=0 and 0<v0<=v1 are fixed. Define the normalized negative log loss

    ell_theta(W,Y) = (1/2)log(v_theta/v0)
                    +(Y-mu_theta)^2/(2v_theta).

The usual Gaussian negative log density differs by the same constant
(1/2)log(2 pi v0) for every theta, so its ERM and excess risk are identical.
Let R(theta)=E ell_theta and Rhat(theta)=m^(-1) sum_i ell_theta(W_i,Y_i).
An approximate ERM satisfies Rhat(thetahat)<=inf_theta Rhat(theta)+xi,
with xi>=0. No efficient algorithm for finding it is asserted.

For gamma>0 and alpha in (0,1), use the explicit architecture quantities
P,Lambda from Section 2 and set

    q = max(1,ceil(2 Wmax Lambda/gamma)), J=(q+1)^P,
    D0=M+U,
    C=(1/2)log(v1/v0)+D0^2/v0, A=V/v0, K=4(C+A),
    u=log(4J/alpha), t=log(4m/alpha),
    T=M+sqrt(2V t),
    Q=1/(2v0)+(D0+sqrt(V))/v0+(D0^2+V)/v0^2,
    L_T=1/(2v0)+(T+U)/v0+(T+U)^2/(2v0^2),
    beta=4sqrt(2) K sqrt(u/m)+2K u/m,
    E_m=beta+gamma(Q+L_T).

Then, with probability at least 1-alpha, simultaneously for all theta,

    |R(theta)-Rhat(theta)| <= E_m,
    R(thetahat) <= inf_theta R(theta)+2E_m+xi.             (1)

Let P_W=N(a(W),b(W)) and h_theta=N(mu_theta(W),v_theta(W)). Subtracting
the integrable conditional Gaussian entropy gives equivalently

    E_W KL(P_W || h_thetahat(W))
       <= inf_theta E_W KL(P_W || h_theta(W))+2E_m+xi.   (2)

For (2), assume also b(W)>=b0>0, as in the noisy-GP application. This
makes the conditional entropy finite and justifies subtracting it. Without
that lower bound (1) still holds, but (2) is not asserted via subtraction
of potentially infinite entropies.

## 2. Explicit parameter entropy for normalized ReLU attention

Fix N tokens, token dimension D>=1, L>=0 residual attention layers, at
most H>=1 heads per layer, and a linear two-output readout. No trainable
tokenwise MLP, softmax, or layer normalization is included in this architecture.
Pad unused heads by zero matrices. There are

    P=3HLD^2+2D

trainable scalar entries, all in [-Wmax,Wmax], with Wmax>=1. The encoding
of W into tokens is fixed and has every scalar coordinate bounded in
absolute value by K0>=1. One layer is exactly

    h_i^+ = h_i + N^(-1) sum_heads sum_j
                    ReLU(<Q h_i,K h_j>) V h_j.

Optionally apply a fixed coordinatewise clip onto [-Kcap,Kcap] after each
attention layer, with Kcap>=K0. This is fixed tokenwise ReLU postprocessing,
not a trainable MLP or layer normalization. For this variant use K_l=Kcap
for every l in the recurrences below instead of the growing K recurrence.
Clipping is nonexpansive, so the same E recurrence remains valid.

The readout acts on one fixed token. Apply coordinatewise interval clipping
to its two outputs. This postprocessing uses fixed, nontrainable constants;
each scalar clip is representable by two ReLUs. Count P as the trainable
parameters, not as every fixed scalar in this postprocessing.

Define deterministic nonnegative recurrences

    K_{l+1}=K_l+H D^4 Wmax^3 K_l^3,       K_0=K0,
    E_0=0,
    E_{l+1}=(1+3H D^4 Wmax^3 K_l^2) E_l
                       +3H D^4 Wmax^2 K_l^3,
    Lambda=D Wmax E_L+D K_L > 0.

For any two parameter vectors theta,theta' in the cube at sup distance
rho, the outputs obey

    sup_W max(|mu_theta-mu_theta'|,|v_theta-v_theta'|)
        <= Lambda rho.                                  (3)

To verify this, use the sup norm across all tokens and coordinates. Each
transformed coordinate Qh has magnitude <=D Wmax K_l; each score has
magnitude <=D^3 Wmax^2 K_l^2; each Vh coordinate has magnitude
<=D Wmax K_l. The normalized sum cancels N and proves the K recurrence.

At fixed weights, changing inputs by d changes one head by at most
3D^4 Wmax^3 K_l^2 d: two terms differentiate the score and one term
the value; ReLU is 1-Lipschitz. At fixed inputs of size K_l, changing
matrix entries by rho changes a head by at most
3D^4 Wmax^2 K_l^3 rho, by the same three-term product split. Splitting
the joint change into these two changes and adding the residual proves
the E recurrence by induction. The readout change is bounded by
D Wmax E_L rho+D K_L rho. Clipping is 1-Lipschitz, proving (3).
These estimates compare actual heads directly, and require no independence
among tokens or between successive layers.

Divide [-Wmax,Wmax] into q equal intervals. There are q+1 grid values;
each parameter has a grid value within 2Wmax/q<=gamma/Lambda.
Thus the full grid has J elements and gives a gamma cover in the output
metric of (3). It is fixed before seeing the training tasks. In particular
log J <= P log(2+2Wmax Lambda/gamma) except when the max with 1 is active;
in that case q=1 and the same bound still holds since 2+2Wmax Lambda/gamma>=2.

## 3. A uniform exponential moment and finite-cover concentration

Write Z=(Y-a(W))/sqrt(b(W)). Its conditional law given W is standard
normal, hence Z is independent of W. For every theta,

    0 <= ell_theta <= C+A Z^2.

Indeed |Y-mu_theta|<=D0+sqrt(V)|Z| and (r+s)^2<=2r^2+2s^2.
Since C/K<=1/4 and A/K<=1/4, Gaussian integration yields

    E exp(ell_theta/K)
       <= exp(C/K)(1-2A/K)^(-1/2)
       <= exp(1/4)sqrt(2) < 2.                           (4)

The last inequality follows from log(2)>1/2 (integrate 1/x on [1,2]).
It follows from the nonnegative exponential series that
E ell_theta^k <= 2 k! K^k for every integer k>=1. For
X=ell_theta-E ell_theta, convexity gives

    E|X|^k <= 2^k E ell_theta^k <= 2^(k+1) k! K^k.

For |z|<1/(2K), the centered exponential series therefore gives

    log E exp(z X) <= 8K^2 z^2/(1-2K|z|).              (5)

Interchange of expectation and the series is justified by the absolute
moment series, which converges at these z. Independence across the m
tasks gives for their centered sum the same bound with 8mK^2 in
the numerator. Chernoff's inequality and (5) give each one-sided tail

    Pr(|Rhat(theta)-R(theta)| >
                  sqrt(32)K sqrt(u/m)+2K u/m) <= 2exp(-u).

For completeness, the generic bound log E exp(z S)<=v z^2/[2(1-cz)]
implies Pr(S>=sqrt(2vu)+cu)<=exp(-u): substitute
z=r/(1+cr), r=sqrt(2u/v), into the exponential Markov bound.
Here v=16mK^2, c=2K; apply it also to -S and divide by m.
No bounded-label assumption has been used.

A union bound on the J fixed grid predictors, with u=log(4J/alpha),
shows all their risk deviations are <=beta except on probability alpha/2.

## 4. From the grid to every parameter

For two clipped predictors within gamma in both output coordinates,
the elementary log derivative and a difference-of-squares split give

    |ell_theta(W,Y)-ell_theta'(W,Y)| <= gamma L(Y),
    L(Y)=1/(2v0)+(|Y|+U)/v0+(|Y|+U)^2/(2v0^2).       (6)

In detail, the log term costs gamma/(2v0). Hold v fixed and vary the
mean to get gamma(|Y|+U)/v0. Hold the new mean fixed and vary 1/v to
get gamma(|Y|+U)^2/(2v0^2). Both denominators use the common positive
floor v0. Thus E L(Y)<=Q: E|Y|<=M+sqrt(V) and
E(|Y|+U)^2<=2D0^2+2V.

The standard-normal exponential integral E exp(zZ)=exp(z^2/2), followed
by exponential Markov at z=x, gives Pr(|Z|>x)<=2exp(-x^2/2).
For t=log(4m/alpha), a union bound gives |Y_i|<=T for all i except
on probability alpha/2. On that event the empirical average of L(Y_i)
is at most L_T. Combine this event with the grid concentration event.
For each theta choose a grid point theta' satisfying (3). Insert
R(theta') and Rhat(theta') and use (6) to obtain the first line of (1).
The approximate-ERM inequality then gives the second line of (1).
The same event works for all approximate ERMs, without a union over
their potentially data-dependent choice. This proves (1) and (2).

## 5. GP comparator and scope

For the finite-rank noisy GP in C002, with supplied features bounded by R,
context length <=n and context labels bounded by B, one can use

    M=nR^2 B/s, V=s+R^2.

Take a desired comparator accuracy eps_c>0, U=M+sqrt(s eps_c),
v0=s, v1=V+s min(1/2,sqrt(eps_c)). C002's scalar error estimates
ensure its outputs lie in these intervals and its expected forward KL
is <=eps_c. Its padded encoding has K0=max(1,R,B,s), width D=7p+4,
at most H=5 heads and L=T_c+2 layers. The construction gives fixed
explicit matrices and readout. Choose Wmax at least 1 and their largest
absolute scalar entry; this is an explicitly computable maximum of the
finite matrices specified by C002 Section 4, independent of task data.
The class of Section 2 then contains that comparator, and (2) implies

    E_W KL(P_W || h_thetahat(W)) <= eps_c+2E_m+xi.        (7)

One may use the internally clipped variant with the explicit common cap

    Kcap=max(1,R,B,s,2nRB/s,2R/s,U,v1).

It preserves the C002 comparator exactly: its feature and query registers
are bounded by R; for every Chebyshev iteration j, |r_j(lambda)|<=1,
so the mean-solve iterates have norm <=2nRB/s and the variance-solve
iterates have norm <=2R/s. The previous-iterate registers have the same
bounds. Initialization, broadcast, constants, and final output registers
are covered by the other displayed terms. Thus clipping changes none
of its states. For this class the parameter Lipschitz recurrence uses a
constant Kcap, and log Lambda grows at most linearly with depth, avoiding
the very loose cubic growth of the unclipped K recurrence. The statistical
bound (7) is consequently explicit for a class containing the comparator
with either choice of internal clipping. All added clipping parameters
are fixed, so P still counts exactly the trainable entries.

For R=0 use a constant exact comparator instead of C002's formulas that
divide by R. The class can contain it by initializing a constant coordinate
and choosing a readout that outputs (0,s).

If training uses rejection to enforce bounded context labels, (7) concerns
the resulting conditioned task distribution. It is not silently a theorem
for the original unconditioned GP context law. With unconditioned contexts,
the C002 comparator guarantee and this bounded-input parameter cover do
not apply as stated. This is the precise remaining distributional scope
issue, separate from the unbounded Gaussian query labels handled above.

All constants here are explicit but loose. The parameter cube and finite
cover give a statistical ERM guarantee, not SGD convergence, efficient
enumeration of the cover, a finite-bit realization theorem for the original
solver, or a claim that Chebyshev depth beats Newton-type solvers.

## 6. Sources and status

Bai, Chen, Wang, Xiong and Mei, arXiv:2306.04637v2, Section 5.1,
PDF pages 14-15, define pretraining ERM for square loss and give Theorem 20.
That is the related parameter-entropy/ERM framework, not a citation for
the Gaussian log-loss bound above. Sections 2-4 provide its proof directly.
