{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:16:33.593058+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_80ed7ce8bcd053f18c5f0449417c6ae0439ff84ff77bd1666aa15a0c0e560405","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Abstract of arXiv:2609.02829, 'Quantitative explosion and percolation of the divisible sandpile'] The divisible sandpile on $\\Z^d$ starts from i.i.d.\\ masses at each site, and, in each discrete time step, a site with mass above one keeps one unit and sends the excess equally to its neighbors. \\citet*{LMPU} showed that at mean one this process explodes, with every site emitting infinite mass. We show that the mass emitted from a site by time $t$ is of order $t^{(4-d)/4}$ for $d\\leq3$, of order $\\log t$ for $d=4$, and a tail-dependent, divergent rate for $d\\geq5$. We further show that the mass emitted, after diffusive rescaling, converges to a Brownian optimal-stopping value for $d\\leq3$ and to tail-dependent, weighted membrane fields for $d\\geq5$, while at the critical dimension $d=4$, after superdiffusive rescaling, it converges to the membrane model. Using these estimates, we prove that, for every $d\\geq2$, the set of sites that topple contains an infinite component at some mean below one, hence it has a non-trivial percolation phase transition. This answers a variant of a question of \\citet*{FMR}. The proof adapts ideas from the theory of level-set percolation of strongly correlated Gaussian fields.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a compact metric space","T is a homeomorphism of X (bijective, continuous, continuous inverse)","the expansive constant delta is strictly positive and depends on the metric"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:23.250591+00:00","domain":"topological dynamics, expansive maps","id":"claim_81a7ef561e0af1f85a9f7f77df488257576c032550ed3b546d86f1abbe6a19db","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space and $T: X \\to X$ a homeomorphism. $T$ is called expansive if there is a constant $\\delta > 0$ (an expansive constant) such that for every pair of distinct points $x \\neq y$ in $X$ there exists an integer $n \\in \\mathbb{Z}$ (positive, zero or negative) with $d(T^n x, T^n y) > \\delta$. Equivalently: two orbits that stay within distance $\\delta$ of each other for all times $n \\in \\mathbb{Z}$ are the same orbit, i.e. the same point. Any $\\delta' < \\delta$ is again an expansive constant; on a compact metric space the property (though not the constant) does not depend on the choice of a compatible metric. A map $T$ (not necessarily invertible) is positively expansive if the same holds with $n$ restricted to $n \\geq 0$. Examples: the full shift on $k$ symbols and every subshift (with $\\delta$ below the distance between two sequences differing in the zeroth coordinate); hyperbolic toral automorphisms; Axiom A restricted to a basic set. Non-examples: the identity, any isometry (e.g. a circle rotation), any map with a nontrivial equicontinuous factor of the same type. Warning: the definition uses two-sided time for homeomorphisms; a homeomorphism of an infinite compact metric space is never positively expansive.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:39:41.442291+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_81ecedcf9027ab2eb28dc45a41cba276d2abf045d2d0f17986054dd6fe69d60f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 13 of arXiv:2604.07478, 'Mixing Times and Cutoff for the Rook's Walk'] Let $(X_t)_{t\in \mathbb{N}}$ be a birth-death chain over state space $\Omega=\{0,\dots,d\}$ with transition probabilities from some $x\in \Omega$,
  \begin{align*}
   P(x+1,x) &= p_x\\
   P(x-1,x) &= q_x\\
   P(x,x) &= r_x = 1 - p_x-q_x\\
   P(x,y) &= 0, \quad \forall y \not\in\{x,x+1,x-1\}
  \end{align*}
  Additionally, assume that $p_x$ and $q_x$ are affine in $x$. That is, there exists $\alpha,\beta,\xi,\eta\in \mathbb{R}$ such that,
  \[p_x = \alpha + \beta x \quad \text{and} \quad q_x = \xi + \eta x\]
  Finally, let $(K_m)_{m=0}^d$ be a sequence of degree $m$ polynomials that are orthogonal with respect to $\langle\cdot ,\cdot \rangle_\pi$ where $\pi$ is the stationary distribution. Then, $(K_m)_{m=0}^d$ are the eigenfunctions of $P$.
  \begin{proof}
   Let $x\in \Omega$ and $j\in \{0,\dots,d\}$ and consider,
   \begin{align*}
      (PK_j)(x) &= \sum_{y\in \Omega} P(x,y)K_j(y)\\
      &= P(x,x+1)K_j(x+1) + P(x,x-1)K_j(x-1) + P(x,x)K_j(x)\\
      &= q_{x+1} K_j(x+1) + p_{x-1} K_j(x-1) + r_x K_j(x)\\
      &= (\xi + \eta (x-1))K_j(x+1) + (\alpha + \beta (x+1))K_j(x-1) +(1 -(\alpha +\xi) - (\beta + \eta)x) K_j(x)
   \end{align*}
   Now, let $c$ be the coefficient of $x^{j}$ in $K_j(x)$. That is,
   \[K_j(x) = cx^j + o(x^{j-1})\]
   At this point, we examine the coefficient of $x^{j+1}$ in $(PK_j)(x)$. Using the above form and considering only relevant terms we have
   \begin{align*}
   (PK_j)(x)&= (\xi -\eta + \eta x)K_j(x+1) + (\alpha + \beta + \beta x)K_j(x-1) +(1 -(\alpha +\xi) - (\beta + \eta)x) K_j(x)\\
   &= \eta xc(x+1)^j + \beta x c(x-1)^j - (\beta + \eta)x cx^j + o(x^j)\\
   &=  \eta  cx^{j+1}+ \beta cx^{j+1} - (\beta + \eta)cx^{j+1} +  o(x^j)\\
   &= 0\cdot x^{j+1} + o(x^j)
   \end{align*}
   Thus, the coefficient of $x^{j+1}$ in $(PK_j)(x)$ is $0$. Also, notice that $(PK_j)(x)$ has no terms of order larger than $x^{j+1}$. This implies that $PK_j \in \mathbf{P}_j$ where $\mathbf{P}_j$ is the vector space of polynomials with degree at most $j$. This means that $\mathbf{P}_j$ is an invariant subspace with respect to $P$. Now, for any fixed $m\in \{0,\dots,d\}$, we know that $\{K_0,\dots K_{m-1}\}$ are orthogonal and therefore linearly independent. Thus, $\{K_0,\dots K_{m-1}\}$ span $\mathbf{P}_{m-1}$. Hence, any polynomial in $\mathbf{P}_j$ where $j < m$ is also orthogonal to $K_m$ by linearity of the inner product. Thus, $PK_j \in \mathbf{P}_j$, is orthogonal to $K_m$. That is,
   \[\langle K_m, PK_j \rangle_\pi = 0\]
   Hence, by Lemma \ref{self_ajoint},
   \[\langle PK_m, K_j\rangle_\pi=0 \quad \text{for}\quad j<m\]
   Finally, $PK_m \in \mathbf{P}_m$ so it admits the following presentation,
   \[PK_m = a_0 K_0 + a_1 K_1 + \cdots + a_m K_m\]
   where $a_0,\dots, a_m$ are constants. Hence,
   \begin{align*}
   0&= \langle PK_m, K_j\rangle_\pi\\
   &= \langle a_0 K_0 + a_1 K_1 + \cdots + a_m K_m, K_j\rangle_\pi\\
   &= a_0\langle K_0, K_j\rangle + \cdots + a_m\langle K_m, K_j\rangle_\pi \tag{by linearity}\\
   &= a_j\langle K_j, K_j\rangle_\pi \tag{by orthogonality}
   \end{align*}
   Therefore, $a_j = 0$ for all $j<m$. Thus,
   \[PK_m = a_m K_m\]
   and therefore, $K_m$ is an eigenfunction.
   \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-07T14:01:11.606209+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_82b243bfd1bdebcf927fafa46de1d7d9","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 2.5 of arXiv:2512.19517v1, 'Spiking and Resetting' (Cédric Bernardin and Vsevolod Vladimirovich Tarsamaev); numbered Proposition 6 in the earlier card; corrected to the increment form]

## Proposition 2.5 (increment form)

Assume the standing hypotheses of Section 1: (f,h\in C^2([0,1])), (f(1)<0<f(0)), (h(1)=0), (h'(1)\ne0), and (h(x)>0) on ([0,1)). Let

\[
e_1^\varepsilon=\inf\{t\ge0:X_t^\varepsilon>y_*^\varepsilon\},\qquad
e_2^\varepsilon=\inf\{t\ge e_1^\varepsilon:X_t^\varepsilon=0\},
\]

and define the post-(e_1^\varepsilon) holding time

\[
d_2^\varepsilon:=e_2^\varepsilon-e_1^\varepsilon.
\]

Then, for every (t\ge0),

\[
\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\mathbb P(d_2^\varepsilon>t)=e^{f(1)t},
\]

so (d_2^\varepsilon\Rightarrow \operatorname{Exp}(-f(1))).

The proof in the paper restarts the deterministic flow at (e_1^\varepsilon) with local time (s=0); its displayed survival integral is therefore for (d_2^\varepsilon), not the absolute epoch (e_2^\varepsilon). The source says that after the stopping time “the process evolves deterministically until the next reset” (v1 HTML lines 252-257), which is precisely an increment statement.

## Later alternating holding-time sentence

For the recursively defined epochs (e_k^\varepsilon), the strong Markov property applies to the increments

\[
e_{2k+1}^\varepsilon-e_{2k}^\varepsilon,
\qquad
e_{2k+2}^\varepsilon-e_{2k+1}^\varepsilon,
\]

not to the increasing absolute epochs themselves. The alternating increments are the quantities that can be independent and have the two respective holding-time laws. Any downstream card should preserve this distinction.

## Why the absolute-time statement cannot hold as written

For every (\varepsilon), (e_2^\varepsilon\ge e_1^\varepsilon), hence

\[
\mathbb P(e_2^\varepsilon>t)\ge\mathbb P(e_1^\varepsilon>t).
\]

This stochastic order must persist at continuity points of any weak limits. Yet the paper permits (f(x)=1-3x) and (h(x)=1-x), for which (f(0)=1) and (f(1)=-2). Its two displayed absolute-time limits would require (e^{-2t}\ge e^{-t}) for (t>0), an immediate contradiction. No additional relation between (f(0)) and (f(1)) is present in the standing hypotheses.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T14:24:13.477078+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_82bf60ef29eb019353b57d9cb9b4acf8aa885aaabf0b0cca759d50f62863a1a2","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A standard Brownian motion, or Wiener process, is a real-valued stochastic process (W_t)_{t >= 0} on a probability space such that (i) W_0 = 0 almost surely; (ii) for 0 <= s < t the increment W_t - W_s is normally distributed with mean 0 and variance t - s; (iii) increments over disjoint time intervals are independent; (iv) almost every sample path t |-> W_t is continuous. Existence is Wiener's theorem (constructed for instance by the Levy-Ciesielski series or as the Kolmogorov-extension limit with continuity from Kolmogorov's criterion, since E|W_t - W_s|^4 = 3 (t - s)^2). Consequences packaged with the definition: the covariance is E[W_s W_t] = min(s, t); paths are almost surely nowhere differentiable and have unbounded variation on every interval, with quadratic variation t; Brownian scaling c^{-1/2} W_{c t}, time inversion t W_{1/t}, and reflection are again Brownian motions; W is a continuous martingale and a Markov process with transition density the Gaussian kernel. Conditions (i)-(iii) characterise the finite-dimensional laws; (iv) selects the continuous version, which is the object meant in every theorem about paths.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:07:56.709839+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_832623f4fb151fca5d4960658b8dfc5c81436aea135e9b4afa95c31912cd2cb3","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:vary of arXiv:2411.04773, 'Meeting of squared Bessel flow lines and application to the skew Brownian motion'] Let $\mathcal W$ be a white noise with respect to some filtration $\mathcal F$. Let $\overline{\delta}$ be a drift function with respect to $\mathcal F$. We call a collection of continuous processes $\mathcal S=(\mathcal S_{r,x}(a),\, x\ge r)_{r\in {\mathbb R},a\ge 0}$ a ${\rm BESQ}(\overline{\delta})$ flow driven by $\mathcal W$ if 
   
    (1) The restriction of $\mathcal S$ to each $A_i$ is a ${\rm BESQ}^{\delta_i}$ flow driven by $\mathcal W$.

    (2) The regularity conditions of Definition (def:BESQflow of the paper) hold.
 

If $E$ is a (possibly random) Borel set, we call $\rm BESQ(\overline{\delta})$ flow killed on $E$ the flow obtained from the $\rm BESQ(\overline{\delta})$ flow by absorbing the flow line $\mathcal S_{r,\cdot}(a)$ at $0$ at time $\inf\{x \in E\cap (r,\infty) \,:\, \mathcal S_{r,x}(a)=0\}$.

 If $E={\mathbb R}$, we will simply say that $\mathcal S$ is a killed  $\rm BESQ(\overline{\delta})$ flow. We call general  $\rm BESQ(\overline{\delta})$ flow a $\rm BESQ(\overline{\delta})$ flow or a  killed $\rm BESQ(\overline{\delta})$ flow.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:11:44.460227+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8326bce44c888e2b0437f2230fd0425e811f63e685f49590fb6fb1fa97d42591","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 11 of arXiv:2609.03191, 'On lifting representations and actions on curves of the metacyclic groups $C_{p^s}\rtimes '] Let $V$ be a $k[H]$-module. Let $R$ be such that it contains $R_s$. Let $t\in\mathbb Z\setminus p\mathbb Z$. Let $o$ be the order of $[t]_{p^s}\in (\mathbb Z/p^s\mathbb Z)^{\times}$. Then the following properties hold.

\medskip
{\bf (1)} The following statements are equivalent.

\medskip\noindent
{\bf (1.a)} The $k[H]$-module $V$ is cyclic.

\smallskip\noindent
{\bf (1.b)} The $k[H]$-module $V$ is indecomposable.

\smallskip\noindent
{\bf (1.c)} The $k[H]$-module $V$ is strongly indecomposable.

\smallskip\noindent
{\bf (1.d)} We have $\imath_V\in\{0,1\}$.

\smallskip\noindent
{\bf (1.e)} Each lift $\mathcal V$ of $V$ to $R$ is cyclic.

\smallskip\noindent
{\bf (1.f)} Each lift $\mathcal V$ of $V$ to $R$ is cyclic and strongly indecomposable.

\medskip
{\bf (2)} The $k[H]$-module $V$ has a lift $\mathcal H$ to $R$ which is an end-hull of $V$ and a direct sum of cyclic $R[H]$-modules. Moreover, if $\jmath_V=0$, then we can also assume that $r_{\mathcal H}=0$.

\smallskip
{\bf (3)} Suppose that $V$ is cyclic. Let $\mathcal V_1$ and $\mathcal V_2$ be two lifts of $V$. Then the $R[H]$-modules $\mathcal V_1$ and $\mathcal V_2$ are isomorphic if and only if the $B[H]$-modules $\mathcal V_1\otimes_R B$ and $\mathcal V_2\otimes_R B$ are isomorphic.

\smallskip
{\bf (4)} The $k[H]$-modules $V$ and $V^{(t)}$ are isomorphic.

\smallskip
{\bf (5)} The following statements are equivalent.

\medskip\noindent
{\bf (5.a)} There exists a lift $\mathcal V$ of $V$ to $R$ which is $t$-invariant and a direct sum of cyclic $R[H]$-modules (resp.\ which is $t$-invariant and a direct sum of cyclic $R[H]$-modules with $r_{\mathcal V^H}=0$).

\smallskip\noindent
{\bf (5.b)} For each $b\in\llbracket1,p^s\rrbracket\setminus o\llbracket1,\lfloor\frac{p^s}{t}\rfloor\rrbracket$ such that $\mu_V(b)\neq 0$, $\mu_V(b)$ is a sum of cardinals of orbits of the action of $[t]_{p^s}$ on $\mathcal P_b(\Xi_s)$ (resp.\ $\mathcal P_b(\Xi_s^{\ast})$), equivalently of subsets $\Phi$ of $\mathcal P_b(\Xi_s)$ (resp.\ $\mathcal P_b(\Xi_s^{\ast})$) with $[t]_{p^s}\cdot\Phi=\Phi$.

\medskip
{\bf (6)} Suppose that $p$ is odd, $[t]_{p^s}=[p^s-1]_{p^s}$ (equivalently, $o=2$) and $\dim_k(V)$ is even. Then $V$ has a lift to $R$ which is a direct sum of cyclic $R[H]$-modules and is $t$-invariant.

\medskip
{\bf (7)} Suppose that $p$ is odd, $[t]_{p^s}=[p^s-1]_{p^s}$, $\mu_V(d)$ is even for each odd $d\in\llbracket1,p^s\rrbracket$, and $\jmath_V=0$. Then $V$ has a lift $\mathcal V$ to $R$ which is a direct sum of cyclic $R[H]$-modules and is $t$-invariant with $r_{\mathcal V}=0$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the prescribed zeros form a sequence with no finite accumulation point (|a_n| → ∞ if infinite)","the integers p_n satisfy Σ_n (r/|a_n|)^{p_n+1} < ∞ for every r > 0","multiplicities are encoded by repetition in the list"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:42.483061+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_8351e8110eb79c81b9035b42e43878b64a0b2a5e2f562abb232805d1c7984b15","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Define the elementary factors E_0(w) = 1 - w and, for p ≥ 1, E_p(w) = (1 - w) exp(w + w^2/2 + ... + w^p/p). {"assumptions":["H is a complex Hilbert space","in (a): A is self-adjoint, not merely symmetric","in (b): U(t) unitary for every real t, group law on all of ℝ, and strong (or weak) continuity"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.771144+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, spectral theory, quantum dynamics","id":"claim_83536995a52f9d6f74e19531f52ed168e8c98c144cb0af2e28337b9615d9255d","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let H be a complex Hilbert space. (a) If A is self-adjoint on H, then U(t) = e^{itA} (Borel functional calculus) defines a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group: U(t + s) = U(t)U(s), U(0) = I, U(t)* = U(−t), and t ↦ U(t)x is continuous on ℝ for each x. Moreover D(A) = {x ∈ H : lim_{t→0} (U(t)x − x)/t exists} and for x ∈ D(A) that limit equals iAx; D(A) is invariant under each U(t). (b) Conversely, let (U(t))_{t ∈ ℝ} be a family of unitary operators with U(t + s) = U(t)U(s), U(0) = I, and t ↦ U(t)x continuous for each x ∈ H. Then there is a unique self-adjoint operator A with U(t) = e^{itA} for all t, namely Ax = lim_{t→0} (U(t)x − x)/(it) on the set where the limit exists. (c) Weak continuity suffices in (b): if t ↦ ⟨U(t)x, y⟩ is continuous for all x, y, the group is strongly continuous, since ‖U(t)x − x‖² = 2‖x‖² − 2Re⟨U(t)x, x⟩. If H is separable, weak measurability of t ↦ ⟨U(t)x, y⟩ already implies strong continuity (von Neumann). (d) A subspace D ⊂ D(A) that is dense in H and invariant under every U(t) is a core for A (Nelson's criterion via invariant domains).","status":"unverified"}

Let $P=(p_{i,j})_{i,j \in [n]}$ be a symmetric matrix of non-negative entries such that\footnote{We can think of $P$ as the transition matrix of a Markov chain which is killed at $i$ with probability $1-\sum_{j} p(i,j)$.} $\sum_{j \in [n]} p(i,j) \leq 1$ for all $i \in [n]$. Let $\Gamma$ be the set of all sequences $\gamma=(\gamma_0,\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_k)$ in $[n]$ (for any $k \geq 1$) with $\gamma_0=1$ such that the unique element $i\in [k]$ satisfying both $\gamma_i=1$ and $\{\gamma_0,\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_i\} = [n]$ is $i=k$.           p(\gamma) := \prod_{i=1}^k p\left(\gamma_{i-1},\gamma_i\right).

{"assumptions":["f in L^1(R^d) for the weak (1,1) bound; f in L^p for the strong bound","Lebesgue measure on R^d (the doubling property of the measure is what the proof uses)"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.751428+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis","id":"claim_83dc1a42b76b6de69325a6175207b7e1669093bf0f53df5985f5dc3e5cdce959","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"For f in L^1_loc(R^d) define the centred maximal function Mf(x) = sup_{r > 0} (1/|B(x,r)|) integral_{B(x,r)} |f(y)| dy. Then M is of WEAK type (1,1): for every f in L^1(R^d) and every lambda > 0, |{x : Mf(x) > lambda}| <= 3^d ||f||_1 / lambda. For 1 < p <= infinity, M is bounded on L^p: ||Mf||_p <= C(d,p) ||f||_p, with C(d,p) blowing up like p/(p-1) as p decreases to 1. M is NOT bounded on L^1: if f is not almost everywhere zero then Mf(x) >= c_d ||f||_1 / |x|^d for |x| large, which is not integrable, so Mf is in L^1 only when f = 0 a.e. The uncentred maximal function (supremum over all balls containing x) is comparable to the centred one, with constants depending only on d. [standard; e.g. Stein and Shakarchi, Real Analysis, Theorem 1.1 and Chapter 3]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X takes values in a finite set of size m","X_hat is a function of Y alone, so X -> Y -> X_hat is a Markov chain","P_e = Pr(X_hat != X)"],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:43:37.236127+00:00","domain":"information theory","id":"claim_83dc491008b3e031d0e3a0ac5475fb48986b2f077baf5876dcd333a684d89f6b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a discrete random variable taking values in a finite set of size m, let Y be any random variable jointly distributed with X, and let X_hat = g(Y) be any estimator of X computed from Y alone, so that X -> Y -> X_hat forms a Markov chain. Let P_e = Pr(X_hat != X) be the error probability. Then H(X|Y) <= H_b(P_e) + P_e * log(m-1), where H_b(p) = -p*log p - (1-p)*log(1-p) is the binary entropy function. Consequently, if the conditional entropy H(X|Y) is bounded away from 0, the error probability P_e cannot be made arbitrarily small.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Real Lebesgue density p supported on a finite interval; p>=m>0 almost everywhere","Mean zero and variance one; no continuity, derivative or upper density bound assumed","For the matrix corollary: fixed independent iid real factor laws, Gaussian observation noise, N,P>=2,M>=1, positive finite aspect limits"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T16:16:22.797292+00:00","domain":"probability; Stein kernels; Gaussian matrix channels","id":"claim_83f6a1f11daf0b73d42501d7da22edf147524c35169a2125815646401fbaafd6","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"OWNER OWN WORK, proof (unaudited); standard-form construction, novelty unestablished.
Let p be a Lebesgue density supported on a finite interval [a,b],
p(x)>=m>0 for almost every x in that interval. Assume E u=0,
E u^2=1. No continuity, differentiability, or upper bound on p is
assumed. Define, almost everywhere on its support,

 tau(x)=[integral_x^b y*p(y)dy]/p(x),
 eta(x)=[integral_x^b (y^2-1)*p(y)dy]/p(x),
 zeta(x)=[integral_x^b (tau(y)-1)*p(y)dy]/p(x).       (1)

Then, for every bounded C1 h with bounded derivative,

 E[u*h(u)]=E[tau(u)*h'(u)],
 E[(u^2-1)*h(u)]=E[eta(u)*h'(u)],
 E[(tau(u)-1)*h(u)]=E[zeta(u)*h'(u)],               (2)

and the explicit bounds are

 0<=tau<=1/m, E tau=1,
 |eta|<=2/m, |zeta|<=2/m.                           (3)


Matrix corollary: let U in R^(N by M), V in R^(P by M) be independent iid factor arrays with fixed real laws having the preceding compact-density, centering and variance hypotheses, each with its own positive density floor. The remainder constant depends on the fixed priors and aspect bounds, not the matrix dimensions. No assertion of information-limit uniqueness or discrete-prior coverage is made.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:36:12.177577+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_84005a70176ace5fabd3383c9436c04a93fc7c065d2fbc235871053976c83d35","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 106 of arXiv:2609.03875, 'Measure theory without infinities'] Let $\mf A$ be an HTM, $\sm{\mf A}{k\in K}{f(k)}$, and $x = \sum_{k\in K}f(k)$.
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item[(i)] Let $\sm{\mf A}{k\in K}{g(k)}$. Then $\sum_{k\in K}(f(k) + g(k)) = x + \sum_{k\in K}g(k)$.
  \item[(ii)] Let $\mf B$ be an HTM and $\varphi\colon\mf A\to\mf B$ be a continuous homomorphism. Then $\sum_{k\in K} \varphi(f(k)) = \varphi(x)$.   
  \item [(iii)] Suppose $\mf A$ is an HTG. Then $\sum_{k\in K}(-f(k)) = -x$.
  \item [(iv)] Suppose $\mf A$ is an HTG and $\sm{\mf A}{k\in K}{g(k)}$. Then $\sum_{k\in K}(f(k) - g(k)) = x - \sum_{k\in K}g(k)$.
  \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:43:37.236543+00:00","domain":"numerical analysis","id":"claim_8448b322d9af94267599948f7ac8e35e7642de9c07050163cb44f14c3c789388","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"An explicit s-stage Runge-Kutta method for the initial value problem y' = f(t,y), y(t_0) = y_0, advances y_n to y_{n+1} = y_n + h * sum_{i=1}^{s} b_i * k_i, where k_i = f( t_n + c_i*h, y_n + h*sum_{j<i} a_{ij}*k_j ), and the coefficients a_{ij}, b_i, c_i (the Butcher tableau) typically satisfy c_i = sum_{j<i} a_{ij}. The method has order p if, for sufficiently smooth f, its Taylor expansion in h agrees with the Taylor expansion of the exact solution through the h^p term (equivalently, the local truncation error is O(h^{p+1})). Matching these Taylor expansions imposes polynomial equations on (a_{ij}, b_i, c_i) called order conditions: for example, order 1 requires sum_i b_i = 1, and order 2 additionally requires sum_i b_i*c_i = 1/2. In Butcher's rooted-tree theory there is one order condition per rooted tree up to order p, and the number of independent conditions grows faster than the number of stages s, which is why, for instance, no explicit Runge-Kutta method can reach an order equal to its stage count once the order exceeds 4.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["The allocations are defined along sizes with positive conditioning probability.","0 < nu < lambda and the boundary-tilted law pi has generating-function radius one."],"created_at":"2026-10-12T15:09:50+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_844ce3c8e953cf9771d011278dae7176f5cf70c2fb67a2cf71d54183386d59e7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14, author_checked; reduction plus asserted conditional, not a solution] Svante Janson's Problem 18.39 in Simply generated trees, conditioned Galton-Watson trees, random allocations and condensation, Probability Surveys 9 (2012), arXiv:1112.0510, asks whether Y_(1)/n -> 0 in probability is possible in the condensation regime 0 < nu < lambda. Janson conjectures that it is not possible for the full sequence and, more strongly, that there are always epsilon > 0 and a subsequence along which Y_(1) >= epsilon n w.h.p. (Example 18.36 gives Y_(1)/n -> 0 in probability along a subsequence.) Setting: let w_k >= 0 with w_0 > 0, let Phi(z) = sum_k w_k z^k have radius rho in (0,infinity) with Phi(rho) < infinity, and put pi_k = w_k rho^k/Phi(rho), a law with generating-function radius one and finite mean nu > 0. Let m_n/n -> lambda > nu. (Y_1,...,Y_n) is n i.i.d. pi variables conditioned on sum m_n, Y_(1) = max_i Y_i, and M = (lambda-nu)n. Heuristic rate: carrying M in r = M/a boxes of size a has class weight binomial(n,r) pi_a^r up to the bulk's fluctuation, giving log P = M Lambda(a) + o(M) with Lambda(a) = [log pi_a + log(a/(lambda-nu)) + 1]/a. For pi_k ~ c k^(-beta) and for pi_a = exp(-a^gamma), 0<gamma<1, Lambda increases on large a, so the optimum is a = M (one box), matching the known condensation picture. Since limsup_a Lambda(a) = 0 and Lambda < 0 for large a, Lambda has infinitely many upper records a_1 < a_2 < ... (Lambda(a_j) > Lambda(a) for all a < a_j) exactly when Lambda(a) < 0 for every a; if Lambda(a) >= 0 for some a the maximum is attained and there are finitely many records (Lambda(1) = log pi_1 + log(1/(lambda-nu)) + 1 is positive once lambda - nu < e pi_1). The record asserts, as author-checked and with no proof given beyond reference to an analogous step for Problem 18.40 in a companion memo, the following Proposition: if for some epsilon > 0 and every C, along infinitely many records, Lambda(a_j) - max_{a <= epsilon a_j} Lambda(a) > C a_j^(-1/2), then along n_j = a_j/(lambda-nu), P(Y_(1) >= ((lambda-nu)/2) n_j) -> 1, so the conjecture holds. Caveat: the only derivation offered is the heuristic rate with an o(M) error, which is coarser than the order sqrt(a_j) resolution this hypothesis requires, so the record does not establish the Proposition. The record poses the open Question whether, for every law pi on Z_{>=0} with radius one and finite mean, [log pi_a + log a]/a has infinitely many records with gap exceeding a_j^(-1/2) below max_{a <= epsilon a_j} for some fixed epsilon > 0. This is not a proved equivalence with the conjecture. A negative answer would only give a candidate counterexample, still requiring proof that the allocation spreads. The Question's normalisation and fixed threshold also differ from the Proposition's hypothesis. The problem remains open. This is an unrefereed campaign result.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the group is the two-element Cayley group; the claim is a counterexample, not a general theorem","relaxation time is 1/(1 - lambda_2), the standard spectral-gap convention","the target is the geometric-time law of the base walk at tilt p"],"created_at":"2026-09-23T13:15:27.869264+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_8494f2b7e60391b8ead2ab87b96e7454cadc38307316484de8264628972059fc","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign status: author_checked_limited_argument - a first-pass structural calculation; no independent review, prior art unverified, and the other questions in the source are untouched] For Metropolis chains targeting a geometric-time law on a Cayley group, the source asks whether the relaxation time decreases monotonically in the tilt p. CLAIM: NO, and the counterexample is the smallest possible one - the two-element group - with relaxation defined the standard way as 1/(1 - lambda_2). (i) NONLAZY BASE. The base walk flips the two states; the target is mu_p = (1/(2-p), (1-p)/(2-p)); the Metropolis matrix is [[p, 1-p],[1, 0]], whose second eigenvalue is p - 1, so tau(p) = 1/(2 - p), STRICTLY INCREASING in p. (ii) LAZY BASE, which removes the convention ambiguity because its spectrum is nonnegative. The base matrix has all entries 1/2, mu_p = ((1+p)/2, (1-p)/2), the Metropolis off-diagonal rates are (1-p)/(2(1+p)) and 1/2, and tau(p) = 1 + p, again increasing. (iii) If laziness is imposed AFTER forming the nonlazy Metropolis kernel, tau(p) = 2/(2 - p), still increasing. WHAT THIS DOES NOT DO: it refutes the literal monotonicity direction only. It does not answer the source's other universal-bound questions and does not resolve its undefined tau(infinity). CONVENTION CAVEAT recorded with the result: if 'relaxation' meant the inverse absolute spectral gap of a nonlazy chain, that convention differs - the lazy example exists precisely to remove the ambiguity.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.353526+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_852b0d4dc9f07b4a7615f1f6a29dbffaeb09c786792fcf84fedbb2a651fa5708","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 204 (spatial rerandomization for spherical perceptron) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] We use the buckets from Definition~\ref{d:buckets} to
 define a new process $\vY\equiv\vY^{\RomI:\RomIII}$, as follows. First let $a(q_0)$ be sampled uniformly at random from $[M]$. Then, conditional on $a(q_0), \ldots, a(q_d)$, we let $a(q_{d+1})$ be sampled from the measure $\bP$ conditional on the bucket at time $q_d$, that is,
    \[a(q_{d+1})
    \sim \bP
    \bigg( a = \cdot \,\bigg|\, 
    a\in B(q_d,a(q_d)) \bigg)\,.
    \]
We then let $\vY(q_d)$ be the average of $\vX^\trunc$ over all the particles in the bucket containing $a(q_d)$, 
    \beq
    \vY(q_d)
    =
    \sum_{a\in B(q_d,a(q_d))}
    \frac{\vX^\trunc(q_d,a)}{|B(q_d,a(q_d))|}
    \,.
    \eeq
Informally, $\vY$ is the process $\vX^\trunc$ with ``spatial rerandomization at scale $\eta$.'' It is easy to check (by induction) that each $a(q_d)$ is marginally uniform on $[M]$, which implies that $\vX^\trunc(q_d)$ and $\vY(q_d)$ are within $W_{\infty}$ distance $O(\eta/\delta)$ for each fixed $d$.  Likewise, we define $\vY^\frozen\equiv\vY^{\frozen,\RomI:\RomIII}$ to be the spatial rerandomization of $\vX^\frozen$ at scale $\eta$, with random indices $a^\frozen(q_d) \in[M^\frozen]$

Among all estimators of the form $\\rho_1 I + \\rho_2 S$ with nonrandom $\\rho_1, \\rho_2$, the expected loss $E\\|\\hat\\Sigma - \\Sigma\\|^2$ is minimized by $$\\Sigma^* = \\frac{\\beta^2}{\\delta^2}\\, \\mu I + \\frac{\\alpha^2}{\\delta^2}\\, S,$$ a convex combination of the sample covariance and the scaled identity, with expected loss $\\alpha^2 \\beta^2 / \\delta^2$. The constants have consistent plug-in estimates under general asymptotics $p/n \\to \\gamma \\in (0, \\infty)$: $\\hat\\mu = \\operatorname{tr}(S)/p$, $\\hat\\delta^2 = \\|S - \\hat\\mu I\\|^2$, $\\hat{\\bar b}^2 = \\frac{1}{n^2}\\sum_i \\|x_i x_i^T - S\\|^2$, $\\hat\\beta^2 = \\min(\\hat{\\bar b}^2, \\hat\\delta^2)$, $\\hat\\alpha^2 = \\hat\\delta^2 - \\hat\\beta^2$, and the resulting estimator $\\hat\\Sigma^* = \\frac{\\hat\\beta^2}{\\hat\\delta^2}\\hat\\mu I + \\frac{\\hat\\alpha^2}{\\hat\\delta^2} S$ has the same asymptotic loss as $\\Sigma^*$, is always well conditioned and invertible, and is uniformly no worse than $S$. The shrinkage target is the scaled identity, so the estimator pulls all eigenvalues of $S$ toward their mean $\\hat\\mu$; when one eigenvalue of $\\Sigma$ dominates the trace (a strong spike), $\\hat\\mu$ is dominated by that spike and the target is far from the small eigenvalues.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f measurable and a.e. finite","|E| < infinity (or E sigma-finite, applied piecewise)","the measure is Borel regular, so that inner regularity by closed sets is available"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T17:07:35.550181+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_85c2d201a83f46e0b6df467d153d01f4","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f : R^d -> C be Lebesgue measurable and finite almost everywhere, let E be a measurable set of FINITE measure, and let eps > 0. Then there is a compact (hence closed) set F contained in E with |E \\ F| < eps such that the RESTRICTION of f to F is continuous. Moreover one may take g in C_c(R^d) with g = f on F and sup |g| <= sup |f|. The theorem does not assert that f is continuous AT the points of F as a function on R^d: the indicator of the rationals is nowhere continuous on R, yet it agrees with the zero function off a set of measure zero, and Lusin's F can be taken to be any closed set of irrationals of nearly full measure. Finiteness of |E| may be relaxed to sigma-finiteness by exhausting E, at the price of stating the conclusion with |E \\ F| < eps for each piece. [standard; e.g. Rudin, Real and Complex Analysis, 3rd ed., Theorem 2.24]\n\nConverse (Lusin's criterion): let E be a Lebesgue measurable subset of R^d of finite measure and let f:E->C be a function. If for every eps>0 there is a closed F contained in E with |E\\F|<eps such that f restricted to F is continuous, then f is Lebesgue measurable on E. {"assumptions":["H: R^n → R finite, convex, superlinear (continuity is automatic from finiteness and convexity)","L = H* so that L is finite, convex and superlinear and L* = H","g: R^n → R Lipschitz continuous","for (iv): g in addition bounded, and uniqueness asserted only among bounded Lipschitz viscosity solutions","(ii) asserts the equation only at points of differentiability; a.e. solutions are not unique, so (ii) alone does not characterize u"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.416738+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: Hamilton-Jacobi equations","id":"claim_8605a80c7ba9fce3f915b195f020fd3a05f4b232377c21c08db9a93c7b73dcf5","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let H: R^n → R be convex and superlinear (H(p)/|p| → ∞), let L = H* be its Legendre transform, and let g: R^n → R be Lipschitz. Then: (i) the minimum is attained, u(·,t) is Lipschitz with constant at most Lip(g) for every t > 0, and |u(x,t) - g(x)| ≤ C t with C = max( |L(0)| , max_{|p| ≤ Lip(g)} |H(p)| ); hence u is Lipschitz on R^n × [0,∞) and attains the initial data continuously. For f: {-1,1}^n -> R with Fourier-Walsh expansion f = sum_S hat{f}(S) chi_S and the noise operator T_rho, which independently resamples each coordinate to a fresh uniform sign with probability 1-rho (equivalently, flips each coordinate with probability (1-rho)/2, so that each coordinate keeps correlation rho with the input), the Bonami-Beckner inequality states ||T_rho f||_q <= ||f||_p whenever 1 <= p <= q and 0 <= rho <= sqrt((p-1)/(q-1)). Equivalently, T_rho f = sum_S rho^{|S|} hat{f}(S) chi_S, and the inequality forces the Fourier weight of f on high-degree levels to decay geometrically once rho<1, giving sum_S rho^{2|S|} hat{f}(S)^2 <= (E[|f|^p])^{2/p} for suitable p. This is the central tool converting L^2 Fourier information into higher-moment (typically L^4) control, and it underlies the Kahn-Kalai-Linial theorem on the existence of an influential coordinate, the Benjamini-Kalai-Schramm noise-sensitivity theorems, and Friedgut's junta theorem for low-influence functions. Canonical reference: Bonami, 1970, Annales de l'Institut Fourier; Beckner, 1975, Annals of Mathematics; O'Donnell, Analysis of Boolean Functions, 2014, Cambridge University Press.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:10:07.448983+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_86a001531250df0f32c57191dcebd574ecb4174b22edb3dac30086bc48aa9860","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary No finite-moment determination of annealed complexity of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[corollary]{cor:no-finite-moment}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:45:02.063106+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_86b3fa63a0310eb4b2320ffced0a75087f6a0711096dc40d34bee6ba13f5db0d","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn def:size-biased-tree of arXiv:2601.00119, 'The largest common subtree of two random trees'] Let $\tau_\infty$ be a random infinite plane tree and $U_\infty=(J_i)_{i\geq 1}$ be a sequence of random positive integers. Set $U_0=\varnothing$ and $U_n=(J_1,\ldots,J_n)$ for all $n\geq 1$. We say that $(\tau_\infty,U_\infty)$ is a \emph{size-biased Bienaymé tree with offspring distribution $\mu$} if it satisfies the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(a)] For all $n\geq 0$, $U_n$ is almost surely an element of $\tau_\infty$.
    
    \item[(b)] The random pairs $(\mathrm{k}_{U_n}(\tau_\infty),J_{n+1})$ for $n\geq 0$ are i.i.d.~and distributed as follows:
    \[\forall k,j\in\mathbb{N}^*,\quad \mathbf{P}(\mathrm{k}_{U_n}(\tau_\infty)=k\, ;\, J_{n+1}=j)={\mathbf 1}_{\left\{j\leq k\right\}}\mu(k)/m_\mu.\]
    
    \item[(c)] Conditionally given $(\mathrm{k}_{U_n}(\tau_\infty),J_{n+1})_{n\geq 0}$, the random plane trees $\theta_{U_n*(j)}\tau_\infty$ for $n\geq 0$ and $j\in \{1,\ldots,\mathrm{k}_{U_n}(\tau_\infty)\}\setminus\{J_{n+1}\}$ are independent Bienaymé trees with offspring distribution $\mu$.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X_1, ..., X_n independent (not necessarily identically distributed)","f(X) square-integrable","no boundedness or Lipschitz assumption; those are needed only for the exponential tail (McDiarmid), not for the variance bound"],"created_at":"2026-09-02T07:51:33.049339+00:00","domain":"concentration of measure (hand-authored statement with hypotheses, 2026-09-02)","id":"claim_86cf1e9337e554632973d7e667c68acea223b8cc18e958d4dd1752b1136526fa","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, ..., X_n be independent random variables and f a square-integrable function of them, Z = f(X_1, ..., X_n). Let X_1', ..., X_n' be an independent copy of the X_i and Z_i' = f(X_1, ..., X_i', ..., X_n) the value with the i-th coordinate resampled. Then Var(Z) <= (1/2) sum_{i=1}^n E[(Z - Z_i')^2] = sum_{i=1}^n E[(Z - E_i Z)^2], where E_i denotes expectation over X_i alone (Efron and Stein 1981; Steele 1986 for the constant 1/2). Equivalently Var(Z) <= sum_i E[Var_i(Z)]. The inequality is tight for linear f. It needs independence of the coordinates (it is the sum over coordinates of one-coordinate variances, a tensorization statement) but no boundedness; the bounded-differences (McDiarmid) inequality is the exponential-tail counterpart under the extra assumption that changing one coordinate changes f by at most c_i, in which case Var(Z) <= (1/4) sum c_i^2.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the domain is reflexive for the converse direction","compactness always implies complete continuity, with no reflexivity needed","terminology must be checked in older sources, where 'completely continuous' can mean 'compact'"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.573661+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, compact operators, Banach space theory","id":"claim_8709e389c807abb0604721e0033898acf007e6902456fe85b7b0c2585491a096","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Compact operators are completely continuous: they send weakly convergent sequences to norm convergent ones. The converse needs the domain to be reflexive, because the proof runs 'bounded sequence -> weakly convergent subsequence -> norm convergent image', and the first arrow is exactly reflexivity (with the Eberlein-Smulian theorem). The counterexample is the identity of l^1: by Schur's property, every weakly convergent sequence in l^1 converges in norm, so the identity is completely continuous, yet it is not compact because l^1 is infinite-dimensional. A related trap in the other direction is the use of weak sequential compactness of the unit ball: in a nonreflexive space such as c_0 or L^1([0,1]) a bounded sequence need not have any weakly convergent subsequence, so arguments of the form 'the sequence is bounded, so pass to a weakly convergent subsequence, and then apply compactness of T' are invalid there. Also note that the older literature uses 'completely continuous' as a synonym for 'compact'; when reading a classical source, check which meaning is in force before transporting a statement.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:16:18.684375+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_872275d9465d671e04c6a26b80dfce8663fa08fc9e3ab19fa8af73023d3c07f6","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 1 (Classification of entire logarithmic signatures) of arXiv:2607.26377, '\textbf{Entire Logarithmic Signatures\\ of Bounded-Variation Paths in Finite Dimensions}'] Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space, let $\gamma:[0,T]\to V$ be continuous and of bounded variation, and put

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.163448+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_87759836e81f17895efdf77150cc0707d64729d7d8cfffca25cd91b8db896b68","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Ppn 26 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Recall $F^{\riv}$ from \eqref{e:F.iv}, and
$F^{\rv}$ from \eqref{e:F.rv}. 
    For sufficiently large $N$, we have for all $t\in \R$
    \[
    \P(F^{\riv} \ge t)
    \le \P\bigg(
    F^{\rv}+ \frac{\epsilon'}{5}
    \ge t
    \bigg) + e^{-cN} \,.
    \]
That is, $F^{\rv}$
approximately stochastically dominates

\begin{proof}
For each $j\in[r]$, let
    \[\bv_1(B_j)\equiv
    \frac{\bz(B_j)}{\|\bz(B_j)\|}\,,\]
and complete this to a (Haar random)

    \begin{align*}

    &= \sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{\hv_j}{MN}
        \sum_{a=1}^{|B_j|}
        (
         \bv_a(B_j),\bG^{B_j} \by)^2
         \,,\\
    \bar{F}_U(\bG,\bz,\by)
    &= \sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{\tau_j \hU_j}{MN}
        ( \bv_1(B_j),\bG^{B_j} \by)^2\,.
    \end{align*}
If we split off the $a=1$ term of $F_v$ and combine it with $\bar{F}_U$, then we see that $F_v+\bar{F}_U$ is the same as the sum of the two terms
    \begin{align*}
    F_{v\setminus1}(\bG,\by)
    &= \sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{\hv_j}{MN}
        \sum_{a=2}^{|B_j|}
        (
         \bv_a(B_j),\bG^{B_j} \by)^2
         \,,\\
    \bar{F}_{U+}(\bG,\bz,\by)
    &= \sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{\hv_j+
            \tau_j \hU_j}{MN}
        ( \bv_1(B_j),\bG^{B_j} \by)^2\,.
    \end{align*}
Fix arbitrary representatives $a_j \in B_j$, and denote
    \begin{align*}
    \acute{F}_{v\setminus}
    (\bG,\by)
    &= \sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{\hv_j}{MN}
        \sum_{a\in B_j\setminus a_j}
        (\bg^a,\by)^2
    \le F_v(\bG,\by)\,, \\
    \acute{F}_{U+}
        (\tbmeta,\by)
    &= \sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{\hv_j+
            \tau_j \hU_j}{MN}
    (\tbmeta^{r+j},\by)^2\,.
    \end{align*}
Recalling $F_w$ from \eqref{e:F.w} and
$\bar{F}_B$ from \eqref{e:bar.F.B}, define
    \begin{align*}
    \acute{F}_-(\bG,\tbmeta,\by)
    &\equiv F_w(\by)
    +\acute{F}_{v\setminus}
        (\bG,\by)
    +\bar{F}_B(\tbmeta,\by)
    +\acute{F}_{U+}
        (\tbmeta,\by)
    \\
    &\le F_w(\by)
    +\acute{F}_v(\bG,\by)
        +\bar{F}_B(\tbmeta,\by)
        +\acute{F}_{U+}
        (\tbmeta,\by)
    \equiv\ddot{F}(\bG,\tbmeta,\by)
    \end{align*}
By gaussian rotational invariance,
$\bar{F}$ has the same distribution (as processes indexed by $\by$) as $\acute{F}_-$, which in term is dominated by $\ddot{F}$. Finally, the difference between $\ddot{F}$ and $\acute{F}$
is bounded, for all $\|\by\|^2=N$, by
\[
        \bigg|\sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{(\tau_j-1) \hU_j}{MN}
        (\tbmeta^{r+j}, \by)^2\bigg|
        \le \sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{|\tau_j-1| |\hU_j|}{M}
        \|\tbmeta^{r+j}\|^2\,.
    \]
It holds with probability at least $1-e^{-cN}$ that
    \[|\tau_j-1| \le \frac{\alpha \iota \epsilon'}{20r},\quad
    \max_{j\in[r]}
    \frac{\|\tbmeta^{r+j}\|}{N^{1/2}}
     \le 2\,.
    \]
On this event, the above quantity is bounded by 
    \[
        r \cdot \frac{\alpha \iota \epsilon'}{20} \cdot \frac{\|\hU\|_\infty}{M} \cdot 4N 
        \stackrel{\eqref{e:fp-normalization-bd}}{\le} \frac{\epsilon'}{5}\,,

{"assumptions":["mu_1 and mu_2 strictly positive on a common finite distributive lattice closed under meet and join","the pointwise Holley ratio condition mu_1(x v y) mu_2(x ^ y) >= mu_1(x) mu_2(y) holding for all pairs x, y","events being compared are increasing with respect to the same partial order used to define the lattice"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.972949+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8778e7a65e49c4be1f23175bfeb78103a14f5cdd5ed03f4f8cc84200ea1e4687","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). Let mu_1, mu_2 be strictly positive probability measures on a common finite distributive lattice (e.g. {0,1}^E ordered coordinatewise). If the Holley condition holds, mu_1(x v y) mu_2(x ^ y) >= mu_1(x) mu_2(y) for all configurations x, y, then mu_1 stochastically dominates mu_2, meaning mu_1(A) >= mu_2(A) for every increasing (monotone) event A. This is a purely combinatorial, pointwise sufficient condition for stochastic domination between two measures that need not be product measures, and it strictly generalizes the FKG inequality, which is recovered as the special case mu_1 = mu_2. It is the standard tool for comparing Gibbs measures with different boundary conditions or parameters in the Ising model, the random-cluster model, and other lattice systems, and for monotone-coupling arguments more generally. The theorem does not establish the Holley condition itself, which can be as hard to verify as the comparison one is trying to prove; it gives only qualitative stochastic domination, with no quantitative bound on the total-variation distance between mu_1 and mu_2; and it requires strict positivity of both measures on the entire lattice. Typical failure: Assuming the Holley condition holds because mu_1 looks larger than mu_2 in some averaged or marginal sense; the condition is a pointwise, multiplicative statement that must hold for every pair of configurations including their join and meet, and it can fail even when mu_1 does stochastically dominate mu_2 for unrelated reasons, or when only checked on a generating set of configurations rather than genuinely all pairs. Canonical reference: Holley, 1974, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Georgii, Haggstrom and Maes, 2001, in Phase Transitions and Critical Phenomena, vol. 18, Academic Press.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:48:25.143238+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_88171b3bff4767675288df1575dfdfc282982120431430153abd723045933ee1","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary cor:constant-overshoot-families of arXiv:2607.04620, 'The Exact Ville Identity\\ \large From the Absorbing Case to the General Law\\ with an App'] Consider the first passage of an additive mean-zero walk above an integer level.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item \emph{Bounded integer up-steps (C1).} If the increments take integer values with maximal up-step $+1$, the walk lands exactly one unit above the level, so $\omega=1$. (For any such $X$, $\mathbb{E}[X\mid X>0]=1$.)
\item \emph{Geometric positive increments (C(2,$\cdot$)).} If the positive increment has the geometric law on $\{1,2,\ldots\}$ with success probability $q\in(0,1)$, namely $\mathbb{P}(X=k)=q(1-q)^{k-1}$, then by the memorylessness of the geometric the conditional overshoot is again geometric with the same law, and $\omega=1/q$. (Equivalently, the companion's parametrization gives $\mathbb{E}[X\mid X>k]=k+p/(1-p)$ in the decay-ratio convention; see (rem:geometric-param of the paper).)
\item \emph{Exponential right tail (C(3,$a$)).} If the positive increment has an exponential right tail, $\mathbb{P}(X>y)=c e^{-ay}$, then by the memorylessness of the exponential the overshoot is exponential with mean $\omega=1/a$, and $\mathbb{E}[X\mid X>y]=y+1/a$ (the constant $c$ is irrelevant).
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(X,d) is a compact metric space","T: X -> X is continuous","for the non-compact extension, T is uniformly continuous and the entropy is taken as a supremum over compact subsets, and then depends on the uniform equivalence class of d"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:07:38.814666+00:00","domain":"topological dynamics, entropy","id":"claim_885e1c5ce5a142a5b0817a051568e1c6290d72f8e2a8225eed7dad76bf607388","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X,d) be a compact metric space and T: X -> X continuous. For n >= 1 define the Bowen metric d_n(x,y) = max_{0 <= i <= n-1} d(T^i x, T^i y). A set E contained in X is (n, eps)-SEPARATED if d_n(x,y) > eps for all distinct x, y in E; let s_n(eps) be the largest cardinality of an (n, eps)-separated set. A set F is (n, eps)-SPANNING if for every x in X there is y in F with d_n(x,y) <= eps; let r_n(eps) be the smallest cardinality of an (n, eps)-spanning set. Both are finite by compactness. THEOREM (Bowen, Dinaburg): h_top(T) = lim_{eps -> 0+} limsup_{n -> infinity} (1/n) log s_n(eps) = lim_{eps -> 0+} limsup_{n -> infinity} (1/n) log r_n(eps), and this common value coincides with the Adler-Konheim-McAndrew topological entropy defined through open covers. The limits in eps exist in [0, +infinity] because s_n(eps) and r_n(eps) are nonincreasing in eps, so the inner quantities are nonincreasing in eps. The two counts are comparable at shifted scales: r_n(eps) <= s_n(eps) <= r_n(eps/2). SHARP EDGES. (a) The order of the limits is not negotiable: for a FIXED eps the quantity limsup_n (1/n) log s_n(eps) is in general strictly smaller than h_top(T) (it is the 'entropy at scale eps'), and it is only after eps -> 0 that one gets the entropy. The single exception worth remembering is an expansive homeomorphism, where any eps below the expansive constant already gives the answer. (b) Compactness is used to make the counts finite and to make the value a topological invariant. Bowen's extension to a uniformly continuous map of a possibly non-compact metric space, taking the supremum of the above over compact subsets, defines a quantity h_d(T) that depends on the METRIC and not only on the topology: uniformly equivalent metrics give the same value, but merely topologically equivalent ones need not, so on non-compact spaces 'the topological entropy' is not well defined without naming the metric. (c) Separated and spanning counts measure ORBIT distinguishability over a finite time window; they say nothing by themselves about invariant measures. The link to measures is the variational principle, h_top(T) = sup over T-invariant Borel probabilities mu of h_mu(T), which is a separate theorem and is not proved by the counting argument below. (d) The definition uses only forward iterates 0, ..., n-1, and for a homeomorphism this already gives the entropy of T; the two-sided window max over |i| <= n gives the same number, not twice it.","status":"unverified"}

Let $m=d+1$, let $x_1,\ldots,x_m$ be unit vectors in $\mathbb R^d$, and let the
message $I$ be uniform on $\{1,\ldots,m\}$.  Under the channel
\[
  Y=\lambda x_I+Z,

\]
the average probability of correct maximum-likelihood decoding is no larger
than for a regular simplex.  For every fixed $\lambda>0$, equality holds if

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:52:47.242501+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_895cfe1f7a99a92e12ef6e3745b0d8f821e23c4dd41df6ec46a73ebf705ad4e4","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 8 (the constant-field Fourier representation) of arXiv:2609.01093, 'Ideal MHD below the classical well-posedness threshold'] With $(\tau,\xi)$ the spacetime Fourier variables, $\lambda$ as in

Consequently $D_\pm=-\mathrm i\mathcal A^\pm$ are commuting self-adjoint
operators on $L^2(dt dy)$ and, for every Borel function $\Phi$,

so these groups are isometries on every $L^p$ and unitary on $L^2$.  In particular,

 [\Lambda^{\sreg},\mathcal B]=0

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:45:38.340351+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_89ac5cad7b954e6da1ebf203c7018e3caa1dbffa166a9f1a94566752511ba361","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 1 (Averaged macroscopic-loop bounds) of arXiv:2604.20514, 'Macroscopic loops in the random loop model on sparse random graphs'] Fix \(u\in[0,1]\) and \(\theta>0\).

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(\roman*)}]
    \item \textbf{Random regular graphs.}
    Let \(d\ge 3\), let \(G_n\) be the random \(d\)-regular graph on \(n\) vertices, and let \(p_{d,n}\) denote its law. Assume
    \[
    d>2c_{\theta,u}
    =
    2\bigl(1+\theta\max\{u,1-u\}\bigr).
    \]
    Then there exist \(\eta>0\), \(s>0\), and \(c>0\) such that for every \(a\ge 0\),
    \[
    p_{d,n}\!\left(
    \frac1s\int_a^{a+s}\Pbb^{G_n}_{\theta,t,u}(A_\eta)\,\dd t \ge c
    \right)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}1.
    \]

    \item \textbf{Sparse Erd\H{o}s--R\'enyi graphs.}
    Let \(\lambda>0\), and let \(G_n\sim G(n,\lambda/n)\). Assume
    \[
    \lambda>2c_{\theta,u}
    =
    2\bigl(1+\theta\max\{u,1-u\}\bigr).
    \]
    Then there exist \(\eta>0\), \(s>0\), and \(c>0\) such that for every \(a\ge 0\),
    \[
    \Pbb\!\left(
    \frac1s\int_a^{a+s}\Pbb^{G_n}_{\theta,t,u}(A_\eta)\,\dd t \ge c
    \right)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}1.
    \]

    \item \textbf{Simple bounded-degree configuration model.}
    Let \(G_n\) be the simple graph obtained from the configuration model with degree sequence \((d_i^{(n)})_{i=1}^n\), that is, the pairing model conditioned on simplicity. Assume that
    \[
    1\le d_i^{(n)}\le \Delta
    \qquad\text{for all }i,n,
    \]
    and
    \[
    \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n d_i^{(n)}\to \rho.
    \]
    If
    \[
    \rho>2c_{\theta,u}
    =
    2\bigl(1+\theta\max\{u,1-u\}\bigr),
    \]
    then there exist \(\eta>0\), \(s>0\), and \(c>0\) such that for every \(a\ge 0\),
    \[
    \Pbb\!\left(
    \frac1s\int_a^{a+s}\Pbb^{G_n}_{\theta,t,u}(A_\eta)\,\dd t \ge c
    \right)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}1.
    \]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Prey density N >= 0 and predator density P >= 0","Parameters r, K, s, tau, c, d are strictly positive constants"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T10:45:59.532356+00:00","domain":"dynamical systems","id":"claim_8a203d63401fe04430436767ea217341366ff22c6f1274a378d505cf3a215162","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"The deterministic Rosenzweig-MacArthur predator-prey model is the planar autonomous dynamical system for prey density N >= 0 and predator density P >= 0 given by dN/dt = r*N*(1 - N/K) - (s*N*P)/(1 + s*tau*N) and dP/dt = -c*P + d*(s*N*P)/(1 + s*tau*N), where r > 0 is the intrinsic prey growth rate, K > 0 is the prey carrying capacity, s > 0 is the predator search rate, tau > 0 is the prey handling time, c > 0 is the predator mortality rate, and d > 0 is the conversion efficiency. {"assumptions":["H is a complex Hilbert space","A and B are self-adjoint","A + B is essentially self-adjoint on D(A) ∩ D(B) (in particular this intersection is dense)","for the semigroup form: A, B bounded below and Q(A) ∩ Q(B) dense"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.771844+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, operator semigroups, quantum dynamics, Feynman path integrals","id":"claim_8a42ecd9291b18c555dbdf4b4b8eeec51666c9820d4d30934c9988c54e0e2269","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A and B be self-adjoint operators on a complex Hilbert space H and suppose that A + B, defined on D(A) ∩ D(B), is essentially self-adjoint (for example self-adjoint) there; write C for its closure. {"assumptions":["g a norm on R^2, even in the transversal coordinate","axis-aligned span"],"created_at":"2026-08-10T03:48:49.000000+00:00","domain":"convex geometry / first-passage percolation limit shapes","id":"claim_8a7b59a8053743091e4ad8ab9f95efc7b0a8f53dbde795774d159a9d7518d243","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let g be a norm on R^2 even in the first coordinate (every lattice-symmetric FPP limit-shape norm qualifies). Fix a transversal offset h and span length r, and for a dogleg from (0,0) through v = (h, j) to (0, r) consider F(j) := g((h, j)) + g((h, r-j)) (the second leg g((0,r) - v) = g((-h, r-j)) equals g((h, r-j)) by evenness). F is convex in j (a sum of compositions of g with affine maps) and satisfies F(r - j) = F(j), so it is symmetric about j = r/2 and therefore minimized there: F(j) >= F(r/2) for EVERY real j, including j < 0 and j > r. Consequence: any lower bound on the dogleg excess assumed only for the MIDPOINT-displaced point (the enclosing-ball statement as classically printed) extends free of charge to every longitudinal position at the same transversal offset - for axis-aligned spans, the 'displaced point arbitrary at its distance' reading is a theorem, not an added assumption. For tilted spans the reflection symmetry fails and the extension is genuinely false (measured deficits up to 4.5 percent at small tilts), so this reduction is exactly the boundary of what symmetry buys. Verified: zero violations over 80,000 fresh trials on four norms (weighted p-norms and a polygonal norm), worst ratio 1 + 2e-12; independently verified by its originating referee at zero violations over 5 norms x 3 scales x 5 offsets x 1401 positions.","status":"derived_in_campaign_refereed"}

process
\begin{equation*}
t\mapsto \langle \eta_t,f\rangle
\end{equation*}
is a continuous semimartingale admitting a decomposition
\begin{equation}

\langle \eta_t,f\rangle
=
\langle \eta_0,f\rangle + \int_0^t \langle \eta_s, \mathcal G_s f\rangle ds + M_t(f),
\end{equation}
where $(\mathcal G_s)_{s\in[0,T]}$ is a (possibly random, but progressively measurable) family of linear operators on $C_b^2(\R^d)$

\begin{equation}

d\langle \eta_t,\psi_t\rangle
=
\langle \eta_t,\partial_t\psi_t\rangle dt

+dM_t(\psi_t).

{"assumptions":["f ∈ C^2 with f'' > 0 everywhere (genuine nonlinearity); for nonconvex f the Riemann solution is a composite of shocks and rarefactions given by the convex/concave hull construction","initial datum exactly the two-state Riemann datum","entropy (Kruzhkov / Oleinik) admissibility is what excludes the nonphysical expansion shock when u_l < u_r"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.418000+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: hyperbolic conservation laws","id":"claim_8ac03e996b3b87a605fc6323901992a6fdd8ce364550e7a1265b2c2093413b70","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f ∈ C^2(R) with f''(s) > 0 for all s, and let u_l, u_r ∈ R with initial datum u0(x) = u_l for x < 0 and u0(x) = u_r for x > 0. The unique Kruzhkov entropy solution of u_t + f(u)_x = 0 is: (a) if u_l > u_r (shock): u(x,t) = u_l for x < σ t and u(x,t) = u_r for x > σ t, with σ = ( f(u_l) - f(u_r) ) / ( u_l - u_r ); this jump satisfies the Lax inequalities f'(u_l) > σ > f'(u_r); (b) if u_l < u_r (rarefaction wave): u(x,t) = u_l for x ≤ f'(u_l) t, u(x,t) = (f')^{-1}( x/t ) for f'(u_l) t ≤ x ≤ f'(u_r) t, u(x,t) = u_r for x ≥ f'(u_r) t; this function is continuous on t > 0 and Lipschitz away from t = 0. (c) if u_l = u_r the solution is constant. For Burgers' equation f(u) = u^2/2 these read: shock speed (u_l+u_r)/2 when u_l > u_r, and the rarefaction u = x/t between the lines x = u_l t and x = u_r t when u_l < u_r. {"assumptions":["f continuous (or merely integrable) on the circle","symmetric partial sums S_N of the Fourier series"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:39.264258+00:00","domain":"Fourier series, common errors","id":"claim_8ac39be5488e62ef2062744a8805090f4ff3f7a198a608caf56cfdc735eca673","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: a local regularity condition (Dini, Holder, bounded variation), not mere continuity. The evaluation functionals $f\\mapsto S_Nf(0)$ on $C(\\mathbb T)$ have norms equal to the Lebesgue constants $\\|D_N\\|_{L^1}=\\frac4{\\pi^2}\\log N+O(1)\\to\\infty$, so by Banach-Steinhaus the set of continuous $f$ with $\\sup_N|S_Nf(0)|=\\infty$ is a dense $G_\\delta$ in $C(\\mathbb T)$; du Bois-Reymond (1873) gave the first explicit example. Kahane-Katznelson: for every set $E\\subset\\mathbb T$ of measure zero there is a continuous $f$ whose Fourier series diverges at every point of $E$. Kolmogorov (1926): there is $f\\in L^1(\\mathbb T)$ whose Fourier series diverges at every point. What is true: Carleson (1966) - $f\\in L^2(\\mathbb T)$ implies $S_Nf\\to f$ a.e.; Hunt - the same for $L^p$, $p>1$; Riesz - $S_Nf\\to f$ in $L^p$ for $1<p<\\infty$, but this fails in $L^1$ and in the uniform norm; Fejer - $\\sigma_Nf\\to f$ uniformly for continuous $f$. Also note convergence in norm does not repair the pointwise picture near a jump: for a function with a jump $J$, the partial sums overshoot by $\\big(\\frac1\\pi\\int_0^\\pi\\frac{\\sin t}{t}dt-\\frac12\\big)J\\approx0.0895\\,J$ on each side (Gibbs phenomenon), so $\\|S_Nf-f\\|_\\infty$ does not tend to 0 even though $\\|S_Nf-f\\|_2\\to0$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:12:19.464282+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8ad4850031c2ab1371de9a748b4112ddc273de39142211075fea80bfc430bccc","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 14 (Explicit log-annular mollifier) of arXiv:2608.17540, 'Pathwise stability for one-dimensional SDEs driven by Brownian motion and a symmetric stab'] Let $\varphi\in C_c^\infty((0,1))$ satisfy
\[
  \varphi\ge0,\qquad \int_0^1\varphi(r)\dd r=1.
\]
For $\delta\ge2$, $\eps\in(0,1)$, put $L_\delta:=\log\delta$. For $y\ne0$, define
\[
  r_{\delta,\eps}(y):=\frac{\log(\eps/|y|)}{L_\delta}
\]
and
\begin{equation}
  \psi_{\delta,\eps}(y)
  :=\frac{1}{2L_\delta |y|}\,\varphi\!\left(r_{\delta,\eps}(y)\right),
  \qquad y\ne0,
\end{equation}
while setting $\psi_{\delta,\eps}(0)=0$. Then
\[
  \psi_{\delta,\eps}\in C_c^\infty(\R),\qquad
  \psi_{\delta,\eps}\ge0,
  \qquad
  \int_\R\psi_{\delta,\eps}(y)\dd y=1,
\]
and
\[
  \supp\psi_{\delta,\eps}\subset\{y:\eps/\delta<|y|<\eps\}.
\]
Moreover, there exists a constant $C_\varphi>0$, independent of $\delta$ and $\eps$, such that
\begin{align}
  \|\psi_{\delta,\eps}\|_\infty
  &\le C_\varphi\frac{\delta}{\eps\log\delta}, \\
  \|\psi_{\delta,\eps}'\|_\infty
  &\le C_\varphi\frac{\delta^2}{\eps^2\log\delta}, \\
  \|\psi_{\delta,\eps}''\|_\infty
  &\le C_\varphi\frac{\delta^3}{\eps^3\log\delta}. 
\end{align}
Finally,
\begin{equation}
  0\le \psi_{\delta,\eps}(y)
  \le \frac{C_\varphi}{|y|\log\delta},
  \qquad \eps/\delta<|y|<\eps.
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:48:47.288460+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8b48d1fb2f8277d09f6ad093ef1d58264cd1b64e6f2141ec05c6e7ade8fab195","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition pr:apriori of arXiv:2604.21142, 'Gaussian fluctuations for Internal DLA on cylinders'] Let $(A(t))_{t \geq 0}$ be an IDLA process on $V_N \times {\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}} $ starting from $A(0) = R_0$.

	\[ {\ensuremath{\mathbb P}}  \big( A(T) \nsubseteq R_{\b \log N} \big) \leq N^{-(\b - 1)}\,. \]

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:48:24.523060+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8b4ccfb1ea9be15a5382c6a8a12d74db0cab088d801f920c266b141becb20844","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop separation-intro-permutations of arXiv:2512.20338, 'Up-down chains and scaling limits: \\ application to permuton- and graphon-valued diffusio'] Let $  \mathbb S  _n$ be the set of permutations or graphs of size $n$
	and $  X _n $ the up-down chain defined above on $   \mathbb S  _n $.
	Let $ \Delta _n(m)$ denote the separation distance between $  X _n( m ) $ and the stationary distribution $  M _n $ (for the worst initial distribution).
	Then we have the identity
  \begin{equation}
  
   \Delta _n(m)
  	= 
		\sum_{j=1}^{n-1} 
			(-1)^{j-1} 
			(2j+1) 
			\frac{(n-1)!n!}{(n-1-j)!(n+j)!} 
			\bigg(1-\frac{j(j+1)}{n(n+1)}\bigg)^m
  	,
		\qquad
		n \ge 2,
		\,
		m \ge 0
	.
  \end{equation}

    \noindent
    Let now $  \Delta _ F  $ be the separation distance associated with the limiting diffusion of the $  X _n $.
    Then {$ \Delta _ F $ is given by the following monotonic limit and series}:
	
    
     \begin{equation}
      
        \Delta _n(\lfloor t n ( n + 1 ) \rfloor)
    		\underset{ n \to \infty}{{\nearrow}}
    	 \Delta _ F ( t )
    		=
    			\sum_{ j = 1 }^\infty 
					( -1 )^{ j - 1 } ( 2j + 1 ) 
    				e^{ -t j ( j + 1 ) }
    		,
				\qquad
				t > 0
			.
         \end{equation}
    
    \noindent
    Moreover, $  \Delta _ F  $ exhibits the following properties:
    \begin{enumerate}[ label = (\roman*)]
    
    \item
    
    $
    	 \Delta _ F (t)
    		=
    			1
    			-
    			\prod_{ j = 1 }^\infty
    				( 1 - e^{ - 2 j t } )^3
    		=
    			1
    			-
    			e^{ t/4} 
				\eta^3( i t/\pi )
    $
    for $ t > 0 $,
  \item 
	$
		1 -  \Delta _ F ( t )
			=	
				\exp\big( -\frac{ \pi^2 }{ 4 t } + \frac{ t }{ 4 } \big)
				\left(
					\frac{ \pi }{ t }
				\right)^{ 3/2 }
				\big( 1 -  \Delta _ F \big( \frac{ \pi^2 }{ t } \big) \big)
	$
	for $ t > 0 $,

  \item 
    $  \Delta _ F ( t ) \sim 3 e^{ - 2 t } $ as $ t \to \infty $,
    
    \item 
	$
		1 -  \Delta _ F ( t )
			\sim	
				e^{ -\frac{ \pi^2 }{ 4 t } }
				\left(
					\frac{ \pi }{ t }
				\right)^{ 3/2 }
	$
    as $ t \to 0 $,
    and

  \item 
      $ \Delta _ F $ is in $C^\infty[0, \infty )$ and its successive derivatives
    satisfy
    $ 
    	\orange{
		 \Delta _ F ^{(k)}( t ) = 0 
		}
	$ for $ k \ge 1 $.
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["a product probability measure on independent, not necessarily identically distributed coordinates","the function or event of interest admits a certifiable Lipschitz-type structure with bounded, possibly nonuniform, weights","measurability of the relevant sets","typically only median concentration is obtained directly; mean concentration needs a separate argument"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.985402+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8bc6218023d8f024ef67f80f2057021b0e367a5c321ceeb28f5937f91f9987b7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). On a product probability space (Omega_1 x ... x Omega_n, mu), define the convex distance d_T(x,A) = sup_{alpha>=0, |alpha|=1} inf_{y in A} sum_i alpha_i 1_{x_i != y_i}, a weighted Hamming-type distance from x to a set A, maximized over convex combinations of nonnegative unit-norm weight vectors. Talagrand's inequality states integral exp(d_T(x,A)^2/4) dmu(x) <= 1/mu(A), which implies mu(A) mu({x : d_T(x,A) >= t}) <= exp(-t^2/4), a strong concentration of any set A around itself in convex distance. Applied to a function f that is certifiable, meaning any difference f(x) - f(y) can be witnessed by a bounded number of coordinates with bounded weight, this yields subgaussian concentration of f around its median without requiring f to be linear or even close to it, making the method far more flexible than Azuma-Hoeffding for combinatorial optimization functionals such as the longest increasing subsequence, bin-packing cost, or chromatic number. It does not directly give concentration around the mean, only the median, so a separate median-to-mean gap argument is needed, and it requires exhibiting an explicit certificate structure for f, which can be technically demanding to construct. Typical failure: Applying Talagrand concentration by treating f as ordinary Hamming-Lipschitz (uniform weight 1 per coordinate change) when the natural certificate for f actually requires nonuniform or superlinear weighting, since changing one coordinate can move f by an amount depending on many other coordinates; using the wrong or absent certificate yields either the wrong concentration scale or, more commonly, no valid proof at all, since the convex-distance formulation is easy to state and easy to misapply. Canonical reference: Talagrand, 1995, Publications Mathematiques de l'IHES; Steele, Probability Theory and Combinatorial Optimization, 1997, SIAM.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Orientation-preserving, irrational rotation number, and log f' of bounded variation (C^2 suffices, C^1 does not).","The conjugacy produced is a homeomorphism;","its smoothness requires Diophantine conditions on alpha and much more regularity (Herman-Yoccoz theory)."],"created_at":"2026-09-12T14:04:29.025227+00:00","domain":"dynamical systems, circle diffeomorphisms","id":"claim_8c52739a81eba24dccec57aa97bd0aa341782637f37c8ae8fba3edff78cde085","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f be an orientation-preserving C^1 diffeomorphism of the circle with irrational rotation number alpha, and suppose log f' has BOUNDED VARIATION (in particular this holds if f is C^2). The engine is Denjoy's inequality: for every n the distortion is controlled, exp(-V) <= (f^n)'(x) / (f^n)'(y) <= exp(V) where V is the total variation of log f', valid whenever the intermediate iterates of the interval between x and y are disjoint - which the combinatorics of closest returns to an irrational rotation number supplies. {"assumptions":["each F_n nondecreasing, right-continuous, with values in [0,1]","no tightness is assumed, and without it the limit can be defective"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T12:13:53+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8c5cd17030a65ecdbe60f4f7255a5f34afa5ee5bff2e761be63adba0ecc0f134","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (F_n) be a sequence of distribution functions on R, that is nondecreasing right-continuous functions with values in [0,1]. Then there exist a subsequence (F_{n_k}) and a nondecreasing right-continuous F : R -> [0,1] such that F_{n_k}(x) -> F(x) at every continuity point x of F. The limit F need NOT be a distribution function: mass can escape to plus or minus infinity, and with F_n the distribution function of the point mass at n one gets F identically 0. This is exactly the gap that tightness closes: when every F_n is a proper distribution function (F_n(x) -> 0 as x -> -infinity and F_n(x) -> 1 as x -> +infinity), the family is tight, meaning sup_n (1 - F_n(M) + F_n(-M)) -> 0 as M -> infinity, if and only if every such subsequential limit is a proper distribution function, which is Prokhorov's theorem on R (without properness the 'if' fails: a single improper F_1 makes the family non-tight while every subsequential limit can be proper). For the selection itself nothing is assumed about the F_n beyond monotonicity, right-continuity and the range [0,1] - no continuity, no tightness, no common support. [standard; e.g. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 3.2.6]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the series is real-valued and conditionally convergent","for the affine-subspace conclusion: finite-dimensional target R^d and a convergent (not necessarily conditionally convergent) series"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.752356+00:00","domain":"real analysis","id":"claim_8cac9c7bdc207f01ab297921ae09bfe7234b1fd5d6dee6f7121badbca7085a69","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let sum_n a_n be a series of REAL numbers that converges but not absolutely (a conditionally convergent series). Then for every alpha in the extended reals [-infinity, +infinity] there is a permutation sigma of the indices with sum_n a_{sigma(n)} = alpha, and there are permutations for which the partial sums have any prescribed pair liminf <= limsup in the extended reals. Consequently a real series is unconditionally convergent (every rearrangement converges to the same sum) if and only if it is absolutely convergent. In R^d with d >= 2 the analogous statement is FALSE and is replaced by the Levy-Steinitz theorem: the set of sums achievable by rearranging a convergent series in R^d is an AFFINE SUBSPACE of R^d, that is a translate of a linear subspace, so it can be a single point, a line, a plane, or all of R^d, but never for instance a disc or two isolated points. In infinite-dimensional Banach spaces unconditional and absolute convergence differ (Dvoretzky-Rogers), so the equivalence in the first sentence is a strictly finite-dimensional phenomenon. [Riemann (1854); Levy (1905) and Steinitz (1913); Dvoretzky and Rogers (1950)]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-13T08:46:06.530785+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_8ce9d8dfa1be2b877f4ce98ce70b432c3025bc0db33c8705aa274cf7bb3cee4a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a square-integrable function of independent coordinates and X^L its value after an independent resampling of a block L, and suppose the pair (X, X^L) is exchangeable (automatic for independent block resampling). Proof in two lines from facts that hold separately: exchangeability gives E[(X - X^L)^2] = 2 Var(X) - 2 Cov(X, X^L), and the symmetry of X^L - X gives E[(X - X^L)^2] = 2 E[((X^L - X)^+)^2]; equate. Consequences: Cov(X, X^L) <= Var(X) always; summing over a partition of blocks turns Efron-Stein into the exact statement Sum_L E[((X^L - X)^+)^2] = Sum_L (Var(X) - Cov(X, X^L)), so bounding the positive-part functionals a resampling engine consumes is EXACTLY the problem of lower-bounding the block covariances. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:12:19.463392+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8cfbbbfae6ef8cb054756ae2bedca712ddcc3f6c041825aaa81da7892b85ed4b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 6 (A mixed example with all three coefficient distances) of arXiv:2608.17540, 'Pathwise stability for one-dimensional SDEs driven by Brownian motion and a symmetric stab'] Let $\wt\eta\in(1/\alpha,1)$, let $0<\lambda<1$, let $\varpi>0$, and let $b_0,a_0\in\R$. Let $\beta\in L^1(0,T)$ and $r\in L^2(0,T)$ be deterministic. Consider
\[
  b(t,x)\equiv b_0,
  \qquad
  \wt b(t,x)=b_0+\beta(t),
\]
\[
  a(t,x)\equiv a_0,
  \qquad
  \wt a(t,x)=a_0+r(t),
\]
and
\[
  \sigma(t,x)=1+\lambda\bigl(|x|^{\wt\eta}\wedge1\bigr),
  \qquad
  \wt\sigma(t,x)=1+\varpi+\lambda\bigl(|x|^{\wt\eta}\wedge1\bigr).
\]
Then both stable coefficients are bounded, bounded away from zero, and H\"older while failing to be Lipschitz at the origin. For any coupled solution pair satisfying Assumption~\ref{ass:solutions}, the coefficient distances satisfy
\[
  B=\|\beta\|_{L^1(0,T)},
  \qquad
  A=\|r\|_{L^2(0,T)},
  \qquad
  S=\varpi T^{1/\alpha}.
\]
Consequently, if $x_0=\wt x_0$ and these three quantities are smaller than one, then Theorem~\ref{thm:noncritical} gives
\[
\sup_{0\le t\le T}\E|X_t-\wt X_t|^{\alpha-1}
\le C\max\left\{
\|\beta\|_{L^1(0,T)}^{\frac{\alpha\wt\eta-1}{\alpha\wt\eta-\alpha+1}},
\|r\|_{L^2(0,T)}^{\frac{2(\alpha\wt\eta-1)}{\alpha\wt\eta-\alpha+2}},
(\varpi T^{1/\alpha})^{\alpha-1/\wt\eta}
\right\}.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["U ⊂ C is open","every member of F is holomorphic on U","F is uniformly bounded on each compact subset of U"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:42.482349+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_8d2196586281fbe29fe2e8e264eed8aa8081e271ecbfcd1b06c6fdf3c582a836","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let U ⊂ C be open and let F be a family of holomorphic functions on U that is locally uniformly bounded: for every compact K ⊂ U there is M_K < ∞ with |f(z)| ≤ M_K for all f in F and all z in K (equivalently, every point of U has a neighborhood on which F is uniformly bounded). Then F is a normal family: every sequence in F has a subsequence converging uniformly on every compact subset of U, and the limit is holomorphic on U (it need not belong to F). Conversely, a family of holomorphic functions in which every sequence has a locally uniformly convergent subsequence with finite limit is locally uniformly bounded. Pointwise boundedness alone is not sufficient.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:16:49.564045+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8d2e8f2054037a3aa67dfe4d17486e3a47ccd5a351b6caf3fa68bd2949d01ced","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 9 (Majorization) of arXiv:2608.25188, 'Transforms for LLM Quantization:\\\\ The Great Inversion and Format Co-Design'] For $a,b\\in\\R^d_{\\ge0}$ with equal sums, $a$ \\emph{majorizes} $b$ ($a\\succeq b$) if $\\sum_{i=1}^k a_{[i]}\\ge\\sum_{i=1}^k b_{[i]}$ for all $k$, where $x_{[1]}\\ge\\cdots\\ge x_{[d]}$ are the sorted entries. Intuitively $a$ is ``more concentrated'' than $b$.\\footnote{A terminology caution held throughout the survey: we use \\emph{concentration} in the transform-coding sense: energy packed onto few coordinates. Part of the quantization literature uses the word in the \\emph{opposite} sense, for low distributional spread, so that a Hadamard, which we call \\emph{flattening}, \\emph{increases} their ``concentration'' \\citep{federici2026dissecting}. The two senses are inverses; we always mean the former.} A function $f$ is \\emph{Schur-convex} if $a\\succeq b\\Rightarrow f(a)\\ge f(b)$, and \\emph{Schur-concave} if the inequality reverses. Fixing the partition of the coordinates into scale groups, we write $a\\succeq_G b$ ($a$ majorizes $b$ \\emph{within groups}) when the two agree on every group's sum and the restriction of $a$ to each group majorizes the restriction of $b$. A block-diagonal doubly stochastic map is doubly stochastic, so $a\\succeq_G b$ implies $a\\succeq b$, and every Schur-concave function is therefore monotone along $\\succeq_G$ as well. The converse fails, and that failure is what matters below: a sum of per-group maxima depends on the grouping, so it is not a functional of $\\succeq$ at all, and the opposition of \\Cref{prop:schur} is stated along $\\succeq_G$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:17:10.022631+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8d5f8f36991a87d02005e3dc57145bee06eb21048ffbbb137fd8e7c9e8069d70","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 6 of arXiv:2608.17374, '\textbf{On the Pseudo-Mixing of Kac's Walk}'] [Computational Mixing Time, or Pseudo-mixing Time]
Fix a sequence of Markov chains $\{X_{t}^{(n)}\}$ indexed by a size parameter $n$ and with unique stationary measures $\mu^{(n)}$. Fix a degree parameter $d > 0$ and a tolerance $\varepsilon > 0$. Define 
\be 
\tau_{\mathrm{comp}} = \min \{t > 0 \, : \, d_{\mathrm{comp}}(\mathcal{L}(X_{t}^{(n)}), \mu^{(n)}; n,d) \leq \varepsilon \}.
\ee 
where $\mathcal{L}(X_t^{(n)})$ is the probability law corresponding to the random variable $X_t^{(n)}$.","status":"unverified"}
