{"assumptions":["X is a compact metric space","T is continuous","the supremum is over T-invariant Borel probability measures; it need not be attained"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T02:00:35.438290+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, topological dynamics, entropy","id":"claim_95cd3f5a581ee5b3b33c5ba6ef9422e6da7205ab57a2fb35db6f9be50cdf92b0","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $T: X \to X$ be a continuous map of a COMPACT metric space and let $M(X, T)$ be the (nonempty, by Krylov-Bogolyubov) set of $T$-invariant Borel probability measures. Then
$$h_{top}(T) = \sup\{ h_\mu(T) : \mu \in M(X, T) \},$$
and the supremum may be restricted to ERGODIC invariant measures. The inequality $h_\mu(T) \le h_{top}(T)$ for every invariant $\mu$ is Goodwyn's half; the existence, for every $c < h_{top}(T)$, of an invariant $\mu$ with $h_\mu(T) > c$ is the Dinaburg-Goodman half (Misiurewicz's proof below). Both sides may be $+\infty$. A measure attaining the supremum is a measure of maximal entropy; it need NOT exist for a general continuous $T$ (there are continuous maps, and even homeomorphisms, with $h_{top} < \infty$ and no measure of maximal entropy), but it exists whenever $\mu \mapsto h_\mu(T)$ is upper semicontinuous, e.g. for expansive maps and for $C^\infty$ maps of compact manifolds. The variational principle is the case $\varphi = 0$ of the variational principle for topological pressure, $P(T, \varphi) = \sup_\mu \{ h_\mu(T) + \int \varphi\,d\mu \}$.

WHERE IT FAILS OR NEEDS CARE. (1) Non-compact $X$: the statement depends on which notion of topological entropy is used; for the Bowen metric entropy on a non-compact space the supremum over invariant measures can be strictly smaller, and $M(X,T)$ may be empty (translation on $\mathbb{R}$). (2) The supremum need not be a maximum (see above). (3) Restricting to a non-invariant measure is meaningless: $h_\mu(T)$ is defined only for invariant $\mu$. (4) The principle relates ENTROPY to entropy; it does not say that a generic point has orbit-growth rate $h_{top}$, nor that the measure of maximal entropy is unique (uniqueness = intrinsic ergodicity, a much stronger property that holds e.g. for topologically mixing shifts of finite type but fails for many systems).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:56:17.350956+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_96027ba99f974b0687326acd85db9973cfc6afa77a4001809717ec87c7567825","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop P:only-easy-consequences of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] Take any half-space pre-landscape $\mathcal{M}^\rho$ continuously extended to $\mathbb{H}^2_\uparrow$. Let $\mathcal{K}^\rho(x, s; y, t) = \mathcal{M}^\rho(x, s; y, t) + \frac{(x-y)^2}{(t-s)}$ for any $(x,s;y,t)\in \mathbb{H}^2_\uparrow$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textup{(Modulus of continuity, analogue of [DOV]).} For any $b \ge 2, \epsilon \le 1$, define
$$
K^\epsilon_b = \{(x, t; y, t + s) \in \mathbb H^2_\uparrow : s \in [\epsilon, b], \text{and } |t|, x, y \le b \}.
$$
For two points $u_i = (x_i, t_i; y_i, s_i)\in K^\epsilon_b$, $i = 1, 2$, let 
\begin{align*}
    \tau &= \tau(u_1, u_2) = \|(t_1, s_1) - (t_2, s_2)\|_2, \\
    \xi &= \xi(u_1, u_2) = \|(x_1, y_1) - (x_2, y_2)\|_2.
\end{align*}
Then if $\tau^{1/3} + \xi^{1/2} \le \min(\epsilon/b, 1/(\rho \vee 0))$, we have
$$
|\mathcal{K}^\rho(u_1) - \mathcal{K}^\rho(u_2)| \le M \left(\tau^{1/3}\log^{2/3}(\tau^{-1}) + \xi^{1/2}\log^{1/2}(4b\xi^{-1}) \right),
$$
with a random variable $M$  satisfying
$\mathbb{P}(M > a) \le b^{4}[(b/\epsilon)^{10} + (\rho \vee 0)^{10}] \exp(-ca^{3/2})$
for all $a > 0$. Here $c>0$ is a universal constant.
\item \textup{(Shape bound, analogue of [DOV]).} Fix $\rho_0 > 1$ and assume $\rho < \rho_0$. Then there exists $c > 0$ depending on $\rho_0$ such that the following holds. For all $u = (x, t; y, t + s) \in \mathbb H^2_\uparrow$ with $s \le \rho_0$, we have
$$
\left|\mathcal{K}^\rho(u) \right|\le M s^{1/3} \log^2\left(\frac{2\|u\|_2}{s}\right),
$$
where $M > 0$ is a random variable satisfying
$\mathbb{P}(M > a) \le 2\exp(-ca^{3/2})$
for all $a > 0$.
\item \textup{(Metric composition holds everywhere, analogue of [DOV])}
For each $u = (x, r;y, t) \in \mathbb H^2_\uparrow$ and $s \in (r, t)$, define
	$f_{u, s}(z) = \mathcal{M}^\rho(x,r;z,s)+\mathcal{M}^\rho(z,s;y,t)$. Then on an event of probability $1$, $\mathcal{M}^\rho$ satisfies the metric composition law
	\begin{equation}
	
	\mathcal{M}^\rho(u)=\max_{z \in \mathbb R} f_{u, s}(z)
	\end{equation}
	for every $u = (x, r;y, t) \in \mathbb H^2_\uparrow$ and $s \in (r, t)$. Moreover, for any compact set $K \subset \mathbb H^2_\uparrow$, there exists a random variable $B_K$ such that for all $u = (x, r;y, t) \in K$ and $s \in (r, t)$, the set where $f_{u, s}$ attains its maximum is contained in the interval $[-B_K, B_K]$.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["p, q probability mass functions on one finite set","p(A) > 0 and q(A) > 0","total variation is half the L1 distance"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T08:13:40.804747+00:00","domain":"total variation and couplings of finite probability laws","id":"claim_96788e32b7dc3e972356e5ee47f8562428e089141e06a6ce5f93c02ce9f3d9b2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let p and q be probability mass functions on a finite set S and A a subset of S with a = p(A) > 0 and b = q(A) > 0. {"assumptions":["K is a compact metric space","F is a uniformly bounded family in C(K)","F is equicontinuous on K"],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:15:45.377034+00:00","domain":"functional analysis","id":"claim_969621bacd8c4d8d1d18dc91064c5582eb98fa2cd21ef76831aadd2757e586da","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let K be a compact metric space and let F be a family of real- or complex-valued continuous functions on K. Suppose F is (i) uniformly bounded: there is M with |f(x)| <= M for all f in F and all x in K, and (ii) equicontinuous: for every epsilon > 0 there is delta > 0 such that d(x, y) < delta implies |f(x) - f(y)| < epsilon for every f in F simultaneously. Then every sequence in F has a subsequence converging uniformly on K (to a continuous limit); equivalently, F is relatively compact in C(K) with the supremum norm. Conversely, a relatively compact subset of C(K) is uniformly bounded and equicontinuous. (Pointwise boundedness plus equicontinuity already implies uniform boundedness on compact K; the classical statement on K = [a,b] is the special case.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:45:27.985537+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_96f2b3bdc8daa0bfa8767478b4f984f2bb860c9486cc22822685a699c603df5c","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:prop_adm_classes of arXiv:2607.04514, 'Boundary-layer asymptotics for Gaussian-smoothed singular measures'] Fix \(A,\sigma_0>0\), and \(R\in(0,\infty]\). Let \(\omega,\omega'>0\) and \(\ell\in\mathbb N\).
  All classes below are taken with respect to the same domain \( \mathcal D_{A, \mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{S}},
  \sigma_0}\) or \( \mathcal D_{R,A, \mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{S}}, \sigma_0}\). The following stability
  properties hold.

  \vspace*{-10pt}
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item 
    The classes \(\mathfrak B_\ell\), \(\mathfrak E_\ell^\omega\), \(\mathfrak P_\ell\) and
    \(\mathfrak G_\ell\) are vector spaces. Moreover, \(\omega\geqslant\omega'\) entails that
    \(\mathfrak E_\ell^{\omega}\subset\mathfrak E_\ell^{\omega'}\subset \mathfrak B_\ell\).

    \item 
    Let \(B\in\mathfrak B_\ell\), \(E\in\mathfrak E_\ell^\omega\), \(P\in\mathfrak P_\ell\) and
    \(G\in\mathfrak G_\ell\). Then the product functions \(BE,BP\) and \(BG\) satisfy
    \begin{equation*}
      BE\in\mathfrak E_\ell^\omega, \qquad BP\in\mathfrak P_\ell, \qquad BG\in\mathfrak G_\ell.
    \end{equation*}
    If, in addition, for \(i=1,2\), \(E_i\in\mathfrak E_\ell^{\omega_i}\), \(P_i\in\mathfrak P_\ell\),
    \(G_i\in\mathfrak G_\ell\), then, with \(\bar\omega=\min\{\omega_1,\omega_2\}\),
    \begin{equation*}
      E_1E_2 \in\mathfrak E_\ell^{\bar\omega}, \quad P_1P_2 \in\mathfrak P_\ell,
      \quad P_1G_2\in\mathfrak G_\ell, \quad G_1G_2\in\mathfrak G_\ell.
    \end{equation*}

    \item 
    If \(B\in\mathfrak B_\ell\) then \(B^{-1}\in\mathfrak B_\ell\) provided that
    \begin{equation*}
      \inf_{\|a\|\leqslant A,\ x\in\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{S}},\ 0<\sigma\leqslant\sigma_0} |B(a,x,\sigma)|>0.
    \end{equation*}
    \item 
    If \(P\in\mathfrak P_\ell\), then, for every \(c_0>0\), \(\Gamma_{c_0}P \in\mathfrak G_\ell\).

    \item 
    If \(R=\infty\), \(G\in\mathfrak G_\ell\) and \(B(a,x,\sigma) = \int_{\mathbb
    H_c^m}G(\zeta;a,x,\sigma)\,\mathrm{d}\zeta\), then \(B\in\mathfrak B_\ell\).

    \item 
    Let \(q\ge1\), let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^q\) be open, and let \(\psi\in C^\infty(\Omega)\).
    \begin{enumerate}
      \item[(a)] If \(B=(B_1,\dots,B_q)\),  with \(B_i\in

      \mathfrak P_\ell\), and the range of \(P\) on \(\mathcal D_{R,A,\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{S}},\sigma_0}\)
      is contained in a compact set \(K_\psi\Subset\Omega\), then \(\psi\circ P\in\mathfrak
      P_\ell\).
    \end{enumerate}
    The same conclusions hold without the compact-range assumption if \(\psi\) and all of its
    derivatives up to order \(\ell\) are globally bounded on \(\Omega\).

    \item
    
    Let \(B\in\mathfrak B_\ell\), \(E\in\mathfrak E_\ell^\omega\), \(P\in\mathfrak P_\ell\) and

    If \(M\in\mathbb N\) and \(E\in\mathfrak E_\ell^\omega\), then \(\sigma^{-M}E \in \mathfrak

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.161845+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_97106abd4033274e1b7b80450f58f510f15be0af5ab0bb57db151ea3e1c2915f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 14 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $(\lambda,\mu) \in \Lambda$, 
there exists a closed $\cD_\mu$-polytope $P$ such that
    \beq
       K_1 \equiv S_\star(\lambda,\mu)[\epsilon']
        \subseteq P
        \subseteq S_\star\bigg(\lambda,\mu;
        	\frac\epsilon5,\frac\epsilon2\bigg) 
	\equiv K_2\,,
    \eeq
where $K_1,K_2$ are both
 $\cD_\mu$-convex bodies.

\begin{proof}
Note that $\Cost(\YY;\lambda)$, $(\|\BBb\|_2)^2$, and $-\Budget(\YY;\mu)$ are all convex functions of $\YY\in\cD_\mu$. (This uses the fact that for $\YY \in \cD_\mu$, the input to the $(\cdot)_+$ in $\Cost(\YY;\lambda)$ is always nonnegative.) This immediately implies that $K_2$ is a $\cD_\mu$-convex body. It also implies that $S_\star(\lambda,\mu)$ is a $\cD_\mu$-convex body, and therefore so is its $\epsilon'$-neighborhood $K_1$.

We now turn to the construction of the polytope $P$. Lemma~\ref{l:S.star.nbd.in.S.star.eps} gives
    \beq 
        K_1 \subseteq S_\star\bigg(\lambda,\mu;
        		\frac\epsilon5,\frac{\epsilon}{3}
		\bigg)
        \subseteq (K_2)^\circ\,,
    \eeq
    where $(K_2)^\circ$ denotes the interior of $K_2$ relative to the topology of $\cD_\mu$. We let $C$ denote the boundary of $K_2$ relative to the topology of $\cD_\mu$, that is,
	\[
	C\equiv \partial K_2
	\equiv K_2 \setminus (K_2)^\circ\,.
	\]
Note that $C$ is a compact set in the topology of $\cD_\mu$. It follows from \eqref{e:S.star.nbd.in.S.star.eps.consequence} that $K_1$ and $C$ are disjoint.

Recall from \eqref{e:D.mu.affine.closure} that we use $\mathcal{F}_\mu$ to denote the affine closure of $\cD_\mu$.
For each $\YY\in C$, by the (strict) hyperplane separating theorem, there exists an open half-space $U_\YY$ of $\mathcal{F}_\mu$ such that $\YY\in U_\YY$ and $U_\YY\cap K_1=\emptyset$. Then $V_\YY\equiv \cD_\mu \cap U_\YY$ is open in the $\cD_\mu$-topology, and we have an open cover
	\[
	C\subseteq
	\bigcup_{\YY\in C} V_\YY\,.
	\]
Since $C$ is compact, this must admit a finite subcover, so there exists finite $S\subseteq C$ such that
	\[
	C\subseteq
	\bigcup_{\YY\in S} V_\YY\,.
	\]
Let $A_\YY \equiv \mathcal{F}_\mu\setminus U_\YY$, a closed half-space of $\mathcal{F}_\mu$. It follows that we can express $A_\YY = \mathcal{F}_\mu \cap H_\YY$ where $H_\YY$ is a closed half-space of the full space $\R^{3r+s}$. We then define the closed $\cD_\mu$-polytope 
	\[
	P\equiv
	\cD_\mu\cap
	\bigg( \bigcap_{\YY\in S} H_\YY
	\bigg)\,.
	\]
Since each $U_\YY$ is disjoint from $K_1$, each $H_\YY$ must contain $K_1$, so we have $K_1\subseteq P$.
On the other hand, since 
	\[
	\cD_\mu \setminus P
	= \cD_\mu \cap 
	\bigg( \bigcup_{\YY\in S} U_\YY
	\bigg)
	\supseteq C\,,
	\]
we see that $P$ does not intersect $C$. Since $P$ is convex, it must be fully contained in either $(K_2)^\circ$ or
$(\cD_\mu\setminus K_2)^\circ$.
Since we already saw that $K_1\subseteq P$, the former must hold, so $P\subseteq K_2$ as claimed.\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:17:33.988198+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_972c739154c7e2110889a4975117f4b3dd1b77d6106c90295eaf4331c4898e73","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 4 of arXiv:2609.03386, 'Twisted Gradient Flow Approach to Vegetation-Rainfall-Bushfire Interactions Model'] For every $\delta \in (1,\infty)$ and $\bar{z} \in L^2(\Omega)$ the bilinear form  
$(\cdot,\cdot)_{\text{{\tiny $\delta,\!\bar{z}$}}}:L^2(\Omega) \times L^2(\Omega) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ defined by (\ref{Equation-2-18}) is a quasi-variational inner
product on $L^2(\Omega)$.\\
\indent
Moreover, for each $\delta \in (1,\infty)$ the class of inner products 
$\{(\cdot,\cdot)_{\text{{\tiny $\delta,\!\bar{z}$}}}\,;\,\bar{z} \in L^2(\Omega)\}$ satisfies the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}\leftskip6pt
\item[(1)] There exist constants $C_1>0$ and $C_2>0$ such that

\begin{equation*}
\delta^{-\frac{1}{2}} C_1 \|v\|_{L^2(\Omega)} \le \|v\|_{\text{{\tiny $\delta,\!\bar{z}$}}} \le \delta^{\frac{1}{2}} C_2 \|v\|_{L^2(\Omega)}, 
\quad \forall v \in L^2(\Omega),~\forall \bar{z} \in L^2(\Omega).
\end{equation*}

\item[(2)] There exists a constant $C_3>0$ such that 

\begin{equation*}
\left| \|v\|_{\text{{\tiny $\delta,\!\bar{z}_1$}}}^2-\|v\|_{\text{{\tiny $\delta,\!\bar{z}_2$}}}^2 \right| 
\le \delta^3 C_3 \|\bar{z}_1-\bar{z}_2\|_{L^2(\Omega)} \|v\|_{\text{{\tiny $\delta,\!\bar{z}_1$}}}^2, 
\quad \forall \bar{z}_1,\bar{z}_2 \in L^2(\Omega),\,\forall v \in L^2(\Omega).
\end{equation*}

\end{enumerate}
where for every $\delta \in (1,\infty)$ and $\bar{z} \in L^2(\Omega)$ we set 
$\|\,\cdot\,\|_{\text{{\tiny $\delta,\!\bar{z}$}}}:=\displaystyle{\sqrt{(\,\cdot\,,\,\cdot\,)_{\text{{\tiny $\delta,\!\bar{z}$}}}}}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:39:12.397124+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9739eb0e75593e2c95007cdf00188d8ee52693da3ab680e344f398fd24707878","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 2. dfn eq: restriction of a measure to a closed ball of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] [{The vague metric $d_{V}^{S, \rho_{S}}$}]

  \begin{equation}  
    \mu^{(r)}(\cdot)

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:46:09.850529+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_974f993ea55dbb51cf199b61cd33a42054dbbddaf02c8c5467ece11aa1fdcab6","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 2 of arXiv:2605.18751, '\mytitle'] Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be probability measures on \(E\), with likelihood ratio \(\ell\) as in~\eqref{def.ell}.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]

\item \emph{Usual stochastic order} ($\st$): \(P\st Q\) if
\(\bar F_P(x)\le\bar F_Q(x)\) for every \(x\in E\).

\item \emph{Hazard-rate order} ($\hr$): \(P\hr Q\) if \(\bar F_P(x)/\bar F_Q(x)\) is nonincreasing wherever \(\bar F_Q(x)>0\) (equivalently, \(h_P(x)\ge h_Q(x)\) wherever both hazard rates are defined).

\item \emph{Likelihood-ratio order} ($\lr$): \(P\lr Q\) if \(\ell\) is nonincreasing on \(\supp(P)\cup\supp(Q)\).

\item \emph{Relative log-concavity} ($\lc$): when \(\supp(P)\) is an interval contained in \(\supp(Q)\), \(P\lc Q\) if \(\log\ell\) is concave on \(\supp(P)\).
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["F a class of measurable functions with values in a bounded interval [a, b] (for the two-sided form with the stated constant the class should be closed under negation or one accepts an extra factor; see the references)","the sample is i.i.d. from P; delta in (0, 1)","measurability of the suprema (a countable class, or the usual separability assumptions) is assumed throughout"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:40:13.706434+00:00","domain":"statistical learning theory","id":"claim_97839b3fb5a128a097b064c2e4b18409edd68bbc82e49a4901fe22e9f110c5d0","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"DEFINITIONS. Let F be a class of measurable functions f: X -> [a, b], let S = (X_1, ..., X_n) be an i.i.d. sample from a distribution P on X, and let sigma_1, ..., sigma_n be independent Rademacher signs, independent of S. The empirical Rademacher complexity of F on S is R_hat_S(F) = E_sigma [ sup_{f in F} (1/n) sum_{i=1}^{n} sigma_i f(X_i) ], and the Rademacher complexity is R_n(F) = E_S [ R_hat_S(F) ]. Write P f = E f(X) and P_n f = (1/n) sum_i f(X_i). THEOREM. For every delta in (0, 1), with probability at least 1 - delta over the sample, simultaneously for all f in F: P f - P_n f <= 2 R_n(F) + (b - a) sqrt( log(1/delta) / (2n) ), and also P f - P_n f <= 2 R_hat_S(F) + 3 (b - a) sqrt( log(2/delta) / (2n) ) (a bound computable from the data). If F is closed under negation (f in F implies -f in F), the two-sided version sup_{f in F} |P f - P_n f| <= 2 R_n(F) + (b - a) sqrt(log(2/delta) / (2n)) holds with probability at least 1 - delta (for a general F apply the one-sided bound to F and to -F, each with delta/2, which replaces R_n(F) by R_n(F union -F)). Since E sup_f (P f - P_n f) <= 2 R_n(F), a class is uniformly Glivenko-Cantelli whenever R_n(F) -> 0. Standard values of R_n: a finite class bounded by B has R_n <= B sqrt(2 log |F| / n) (Massart); a class of indicators of VC dimension d has R_n <= sqrt(2 d log(e n / d) / n) and in fact O(sqrt(d / n)) (Dudley); linear predictors x -> <w, x> with ||w||_2 <= Lambda on inputs with ||x||_2 <= r have R_n <= Lambda r / sqrt(n); and for L-Lipschitz phi, R_n(phi o F) <= L R_n(F) (Ledoux-Talagrand contraction), which is how the bound passes from a class of predictors to a class of losses. In learning, with f the loss of a hypothesis, the theorem says the true risk of EVERY hypothesis in the class exceeds its empirical risk by at most 2 R_n plus a term of order sqrt(log(1/delta)/n), the modern replacement for VC bounds when the class is not a class of sets.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:18:19.220183+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_97a72a1847f5a25f10ab1d841c3f1b73d0d91735389913491d547e16332d393e","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 17 of arXiv:2608.29075, 'The 2-Monoidal Structure of Symmetric Sequences'] Let $(\catname{C},\square, I, \circ, J)$ be a 2-monoidal category. A \textit{double monoid} in $\catname{C}$ is an object $A$ equipped with morphisms
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=scriptsize]
	{A \square A} & A && I & A && {A \circ A} & A && {J } & A,
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow[from=1-4, to=1-5]
	\arrow[from=1-7, to=1-8]
	\arrow[from=1-10, to=1-11]
\end{tikzcd}\]
    which turn $A$ into a monoid in both $(\catname{C},\square,I)$ and $(\catname{C},\circ,J)$, and make the following diagrams commute.
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	{(A \circ A) \square (A \circ A)} && {(A \square A) \circ (A \square A)} \\
	{A \square A} & A & {A \circ A}
	\arrow["{\zeta_{A,A,A,A}}", from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow[from=1-3, to=2-3]
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow[from=2-3, to=2-2]
\end{tikzcd}\]
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	{J \square J} & {A \square A} && {I \circ I} & {A \circ A} \\
	J & A && I & A
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow["{\mu_J}"', from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow[from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow[from=1-4, to=1-5]
	\arrow[from=1-5, to=2-5]
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow["{\Delta_I}", from=2-4, to=1-4]
	\arrow[from=2-4, to=2-5]
\end{tikzcd}\]
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	& A \\
	I && J
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow["{{\iota_J = \epsilon_I}}"', from=2-1, to=2-3]
	\arrow[from=2-3, to=1-2]
\end{tikzcd}\]
    Dually, one can define \textit{double comonoids}. 

    A morphism between two double (co)monoids is a morphism of the two underlying (co)monoids. 
    
    The categories of double (co)monoids in the 2-monoidal category $(\catname{C},\square, I, \circ, J)$ are denoted by $\text{dMon}(\catname{C},\square, I, \circ, J)$ and by $\text{dComon}(\catname{C},\square, I, \circ, J)$, respectively.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:39:12.431561+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_97e3804b3bd38df4c13bb36d47f9c369e4c2f55b1ab653dbdcb41f9e1e5abb51","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 4. dfn: resistance forms of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] [{Resistance form and resistance metric, [Kigami_12_Resistance]}] 
  
  Let $F$ be a non-empty set.
  A pair $(\mathcal{E}, \mathcal{F})$ is called a \textit{resistance form} on $F$ if it satisfies the following conditions.
  \begin{enumerate} [label=(RF\arabic*), leftmargin = *]
    \item 
          The symbol $\mathcal{F}$ is a linear subspace of the collection of functions $\{ f : F \to \mathbb{R} \}$ 
          containing constants,
          and $\mathcal{E}$ is a non-negative symmetric bilinear form on $\mathcal{F}$
          such that $\mathcal{E}(f,f)=0$ if and only if $f$ is constant on $F$.
    \item 
          Let $\sim$ be the equivalence relation on $\mathcal{F}$ defined by saying $f \sim g$ if and only if $f-g$ is constant on $F$.
          Then $(\mathcal{F}/\sim, \mathcal{E})$ is a Hilbert space.
    \item
          If $x \neq y$, then there exists a function $f \in \mathcal{F}$ such that $f(x) \neq f(y)$.
    \item 
          For any $x, y \in F$,
          \begin{equation} 
            R_{(\mathcal{E}, \mathcal{F})}(x,y)
            \coloneqq
            \sup
            \left\{
            \frac{|f(x) - f(y)|^{2}}{\mathcal{E}(f,f)}
            :
            f \in \mathcal{F},\
            \mathcal{E}(f,f) > 0
            \right\}
            < \infty.
          \end{equation}     
    \item
          If $\bar{f}\coloneqq  (f \wedge 1) \vee 0$,
          then $\bar{f} \in \mathcal{F}$ and $\mathcal{E}(\bar{f}, \bar{f}) \leq \mathcal{E}(f,f)$ for any $f \in \mathcal{F}$.
  \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:05:09.629919+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_97e92b713f5fb0ae485923c164806f6eca2dc22232484a3f8e3e4538afc5727a","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:tech_extent_lowerbound of arXiv:2411.03609, 'Asymptotically optimal Wasserstein couplings for the small-time stable domain of attractio'] Let $\bm{Y}$ be a nonzero pure-jump L\'evy process on $\mathbb{R}^d$, let $\psi_{\bm{Y}}(\bm{u})$ denote its L\'evy-Khintchine exponent and $\nu_{\bm{Y}}$ its L\'evy measure.\\
{\normalfont(a)} If $\bm{Y}$ has finite variation and nonzero drift with direction $\bm{u}_*\in \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$. Then $|\psi_{\bm{Y}}(x\bm{u}_*)|\geqslant cx$ for some $c>0$ and all sufficiently large $x>0$.\\
{\normalfont(b)} Suppose there exist a locally finite measure $\rho$ on $(0,\infty)$ and a probability measure $\sigma$ on $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ with
\[
\nu_{\bm{Y}}(A)
\geqslant \int_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}\int_{(0,\infty)}\1_A(x\bm{v})\rho(\mathrm{d} x)\sigma(\mathrm{d}\bm{v}),
\qquad A\in\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d_{\bm{0}}).
\]
Define $\Upsilon(x):=\int_{(0,x)}r^2\rho(\mathrm{d} r)$ for $x>0$, and, given any $c\in (0,1)$, suppose that $C_{c,\bm{u}_*}\coloneqq\{\bm{v}\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}:|\langle \bm{u}_*,\bm{v}\rangle|\geqslant c\}$ has positive $\sigma$-measure $m:=\sigma(C_{c,\bm{u}_*})>0$ for some $\bm{u}_*\in \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$. Then we have
\[
|\psi_{\bm{Y}}(x\bm{u}_*)|\geqslant \frac{c^2m}{3}r^2\Upsilon(x^{-1})
\qquad\text{for all }x>0.
\]
In particular, if $c_\delta:=\inf_{x\in(0,1)}x^{\delta-2}\Upsilon(x)>0$ for some $\delta\in(0,2)$, then $|\psi_{\bm{Y}}(x\bm{u}_*)|\geqslant (c_\delta c^2m/3)x^{\delta}$, $x>1$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:57:30.994414+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_97efde84c687734e23b1ce3ae8052542c0c176f8db17c62eaa957917a20a6546","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 42 (Physical fourth-moment theorem: exact zero stratum) of arXiv:2608.12492, 'Weak Limits of Wiener Chaos: Primitive--Fock Classification and Hilbert--Stein Extraction'] Let $q\ge2$ and
\[
 X_{n,a}=I_q^{W_n}(f_{n,a}),
 \qquad
 \sup_n\sum_{a=1}^dq!\norm{f_{n,a}}^2<\infty.
\]
Write $\Sigma_n=\Cov(X_n)$, fix a free ultrafilter $\mathcal U$, and put
\[
 \xi_a=[f_{n,a}]_{\mathcal U}\in\cH_q,
 \qquad
 \Sigma=\Ulim\Sigma_n,
 \qquad
 \kappa_{n,a}=\E[X_{n,a}^4]-3\E[X_{n,a}^2]^2.
\]
The represented terminal has the intrinsic splitting
\begin{equation}
 T_a=\mathbb U_q^{-1}\xi_a
 =A_a^{\phys}+G_a^{\phys},
 \quad
 A_a^{\phys}=\mathbb U_q^{-1}P_{\cD_q}\xi_a,
 \quad
 G_a^{\phys}=\mathbb U_q^{-1}P_{\cK_q}\xi_a.
 
\end{equation}
The following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
 \item $\displaystyle\sum_{a=1}^d\mathfrak Q_q(\xi_a)=0$,
 equivalently $\Ulim\sum_a\kappa_{n,a}=0$;
 \item for every $a$ and $1\le r<q$,
 $
  \Ulim\norm{f_{n,a}\otimes_rf_{n,a}}=0
 $;
 \item $\xi_a\in\cK_q$ for every $a$, equivalently
 $P_{\cD_q}\xi=0$;
 \item $A^{\phys}=0$ (equivalently, the limiting active part of
 the reduced Hilbert--Stein trajectory vanishes) and the represented
 laws converge along $\mathcal U$ to $N_d(0,\Sigma)$;
 \item for every $a$,
 $
  \Ulim\E[X_{n,a}^4]=3\Sigma_{aa}^2
 $.
\end{enumerate}
When these conditions hold, every mixed proper contraction also
vanishes:
\begin{equation}
 \Ulim\norm{f_{n,a}\otimes_rf_{n,b}}=0
 \qquad(1\le r<q,\ 1\le a,b\le d).
 
\end{equation}
Moreover, there is a finite constant $C_{q,d}$, depending only on
$(q,d)$, such that for every $n$ and $t\in\R^d$,
\begin{equation}
 \left|
  \E e^{it\cdot X_n}
  -e^{-\frac12t^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_nt}
 \right|
 \le C_{q,d}|t|^2
 \left(\sum_{a=1}^d\kappa_{n,a}\right)^{1/2}.
 
\end{equation}
Componentwise, the exact carré-du-champ comparison is
\begin{equation}
 \frac1{3q}\kappa_{n,a}
 \le
 \Var\bigl(\Gamma(X_{n,a},X_{n,a})\bigr)
 \le
 \frac{q-1}{3q}\kappa_{n,a}.
 
\end{equation}
Thus the fourth cumulants detect exactly, and not merely sufficiently,
the disappearance of the decomposable physical sector.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["entries of Z i.i.d., mean 0, variance 1, finite fourth moment (necessary for the edge statements)","||Sigma_n|| bounded; spectral distribution of Sigma_n converges to H; p/n -> c in (0, infinity)","the interval [a, b] is outside the supports of the finite-n laws for all large n (not only outside the limiting support)"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T09:21:49.109871+00:00","domain":"random matrix theory","id":"claim_98405d3e08a3062d8207dc22178a18452e909979f29e46ab7d8122c66d7b17e8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $S_n = \\frac{1}{n} X_n^T X_n$ with $X_n = Z_n \\Sigma_n^{1/2}$, where $Z_n$ is $n \\times p$ with i.i.d. entries of mean $0$, variance $1$ and finite fourth moment, $\\Sigma_n$ is positive semidefinite with $\\|\\Sigma_n\\|$ bounded, $p/n \\to c \\in (0, \\infty)$, and the spectral distribution of $\\Sigma_n$ converges weakly to $H$. Let $F^{c,H}$ be the limiting spectral distribution of $S_n$ (the Marchenko-Pastur-Silverstein law) and let $[a, b]$ be a closed interval, $a > 0$, lying outside the support of $F^{c,H}$ and outside the supports of $F^{c_n, H_n}$ for all large $n$ (the finite-$n$ laws built from $c_n = p/n$ and $H_n$). Then almost surely no eigenvalue of $S_n$ lies in $[a, b]$ for all $n$ large enough: $\\mathbb{P}(\\text{no eigenvalue of } S_n \\text{ in } [a, b] \\text{ for all large } n) = 1$. Corollary (Bai-Yin 1993, the case $\\Sigma = I$): $\\lambda_{\\max}(S_n) \\to (1 + \\sqrt c)^2$ and, for $c < 1$, $\\lambda_{\\min}(S_n) \\to (1 - \\sqrt c)^2$ almost surely - the Marchenko-Pastur edges - and the finite fourth moment is necessary for the largest eigenvalue to converge. Consequence used throughout: an eigenvalue of a sample covariance strictly above $\\sigma^2(1 + \\sqrt c)^2$ (by a fixed margin) cannot come from an identity-covariance bulk, which is what licenses the bulk edge as a detection threshold in the spiked model, in Gavish-Donoho denoising, and in the median-based noise estimate.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["fixed design X of full column rank","independent errors with mean zero and possibly different variances","finite fourth moments of errors and regressors; (1/n) X'X -> positive definite; p fixed as n -> infinity for the consistency statement"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T05:50:37.943831+00:00","domain":"regression","id":"claim_985b54f9338db3244323dab66f1613e14302710ac7bfd8d3569800bb347b6e0c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $y = X\\beta + \\varepsilon$ with $X$ an $n \\times p$ design of full column rank (treated as fixed), $E[\\varepsilon] = 0$, and $\\operatorname{Var}(\\varepsilon) = \\Omega = \\operatorname{diag}(\\omega_1^2, \\dots, \\omega_n^2)$ - independent errors whose variances may differ across observations. Then the ordinary least-squares estimator $\\hat\\beta = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y$ is unbiased and its exact covariance is the sandwich $$\\operatorname{Var}(\\hat\\beta) = (X^T X)^{-1}\\, X^T \\Omega X\\, (X^T X)^{-1},$$ which reduces to the textbook $\\sigma^2 (X^T X)^{-1}$ only when all $\\omega_i^2 = \\sigma^2$. THEOREM (White, 1980). With $r = y - X\\hat\\beta$ the residuals, the estimator $\\hat V_{\\mathrm{HC0}} = (X^T X)^{-1}\\big(\\sum_i r_i^2 x_i x_i^T\\big)(X^T X)^{-1}$ is consistent for $\\operatorname{Var}(\\hat\\beta)$ in the sense that $n\\,\\hat V_{\\mathrm{HC0}} - n\\operatorname{Var}(\\hat\\beta) \\to 0$ in probability as $n \\to \\infty$ with $p$ fixed, under finite fourth moments of the errors and of the regressors (the rows $x_i$ bounded or with $\\frac{1}{n}\\sum_i \\|x_i\\|^4 = O(1)$) and $\\frac{1}{n}X^T X \\to$ a positive definite limit. No model for the $\\omega_i^2$ is needed. In the ill-conditioned directions of $X^T X$ (nearly collinear regressors) the sandwich can exceed the homoscedastic formula by a large factor when the large residuals fall on the observations that determine those directions; the homoscedastic formula then badly understates the sampling noise of the coefficients.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a set and mu* is defined on the entire power set of X","for the construction: E contains the empty set and some countable subfamily of E covers X, so that every subset has at least one admissible cover","rho maps E into [0, +infinity] with rho(empty set) = 0; no additivity or monotonicity of rho is assumed","countable, not arbitrary, families are used in the subadditivity axiom"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:13:10.402410+00:00","domain":"measure theory, Caratheodory construction","id":"claim_9861570c368e84c1c207e946455b7453e592c4255152ddc4ad3423bc0df71072","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a set. A function mu* from the FULL power set of X to [0, +infinity] is an OUTER MEASURE if (1) mu*(empty set) = 0, (2) it is monotone: A contained in B implies mu*(A) <= mu*(B), and (3) it is countably subadditive: mu*(union over n >= 1 of A_n) <= sum over n >= 1 of mu*(A_n) for every countable family of subsets A_n of X, MEASURABLE OR NOT. Note that subadditivity is part of the definition in the abstract setting; the mathematical content lies in the fact that the standard constructions produce it. CONSTRUCTION FROM A COVERING FAMILY (a gauge): let E be a family of subsets of X containing the empty set and covering X by countably many of its members, and let rho : E -> [0, +infinity] with rho(empty set) = 0. Define mu*(A) = inf { sum over k >= 1 of rho(E_k) : E_k in E for all k and A contained in the union of the E_k }, with the convention that the infimum of the empty set is +infinity. Lebesgue outer measure on R^n is the case where E is the family of boxes (or open boxes, or cubes) and rho is the elementary volume. A set A is CARATHEODORY MEASURABLE for mu* if mu*(T) = mu*(T intersect A) + mu*(T minus A) for every test set T; these sets form a sigma-algebra on which mu* restricts to a complete countably additive measure (Caratheodory's theorem). CAUTIONS: an outer measure is defined on all subsets but is in general NOT additive on disjoint sets; it is not a measure on the power set; and the Caratheodory criterion, not the mere inequality in (3), is what recovers additivity.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:13:49.971936+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9877467e026f00b612e50d498a661006fbc979653968f984138cef41b06c4d6f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition eq:deftildeupsilon of arXiv:2411.07157, 'Rough differential equations in the flow approach'] We define the family of elementary differentials $(\Upsilon^{\tau}: \tau\in\mathfrak{T})$, with $\Upsilon^{\tau} \in \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\tau]$, by using an induction in $\tau$. 
For the base case, we define  $\Upsilon^{\circ} = \big( \Upsilon^{\circ_{r}}\big)_{r \in \N} \in \prod_{r \in \N} \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\circ_{r}]$ by setting, in analogy with (equation eq:elem_diff1_base of the paper), 
\[
\Upsilon^{\circ_{r}}(x_{r}) = V(x_{r})\;.
\]
It is clear that one indeed has $\Upsilon^{\circ_{r}} \in \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\circ]$. 
In other words, we could have just fixed a single $r \in \N$, applied the above formula, and then defined $\Upsilon^{\circ} = \pi_{\circ,\circ_{r}} \Upsilon^{\circ_{r}}$ and our construction would be well-defined in that it didn't depend on our initial choice of $r$. 

We now proceed to the inductive step. 
Suppose we have $\tau=[\tau_1,\dots,\tau_k]$, where $k > 0$, the $\tau_1,\dots,\tau_k$ are unlabelled, and $[\cdot]$ denotes joining the roots of unlabelled trees at a new unlabelled root. 
Our inductive assumption is that we have been given $\Upsilon^{\circ} \in \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\raisebox{+0.05ex}{\includegraphics[scale=1.5]{figures/Xi.pdf}}]$, and $\Upsilon^{\tau_{j}} \in \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\underline{\tau}_j]$ for $1 \leqslant j \leqslant k$.

Next, fix any labelled $\underline{\tau} \in \tau$, and choose any labelled $\underline{\tau}_1,\dots,\underline{\tau}_k$ with $\underline{\tau}_j \in \tau_j$, such that $\underline{\tau} = [\underline{\tau}_1,\dots,\underline{\tau}_k]_{r}$ (here we use the notation of (equation eq:product_of_trees of the paper), and $r = r(\underline{\tau})$).
For every $\underline{\sigma}\in \{\circ_{r}, \underline{\tau}_1,\cdots,\underline{\tau}_k\}$, we first set
\begin{equs}
   \Upsilon^{\underline{\sigma}} \eqdef \iota_{\sigma,\underline{\sigma}} \Upsilon^{\sigma}\in\text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\underline{\sigma}]\,.
\end{equs}
We then define $\Upsilon^{\underline{\tau}} \in \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\underline{\tau}]$ in analogy with (equation eq:elem_diff1 of the paper) by setting
\begin{equ}
\Upsilon^{\underline{\tau}}(x_{N(\underline{\tau})})
=
\big( \mathrm{d}^{k} \Upsilon^{\circ_r}(x_{r(\underline{\tau})}) \big) \big[ \Upsilon^{\underline{\tau}_{1}}(x_{N(\underline{\tau}_1)}),\cdots, \Upsilon^{\underline{\tau}_{k}}(x_{N(\underline{\tau}_k)}) \big]\,,
\end{equ}
and finally we can set
\begin{equ}
\Upsilon^{\tau} \eqdef
\pi_{\tau,\underline{\tau}} \Upsilon^{\underline{\tau}}\;.
\end{equ}
In the next lemma we verify that $\Upsilon^{\tau}$ as defined above is well-defined, in that it does not depend on how we realised $\tau$ as the labelled tree $[\underline{\tau}_1,\dots,\underline{\tau}_k]_{r}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:15:45.375169+00:00","domain":"general topology","id":"claim_987a713ab2d41c965d796f3285a70f19fefacd5934de0e8382701f1d12d8b510","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A collection B of subsets of a set X is a basis (base) for a topology on X if (i) every point of X lies in at least one member of B, and (ii) whenever a point x lies in the intersection of two members B1, B2 of B, there is a member B3 of B with x in B3 and B3 contained in the intersection of B1 and B2. {"assumptions":["all F_k lie in the SAME fixed chaos of order n >= 2","E[F_k^2] -> sigma^2 > 0","the equivalence is FALSE for sequences not confined to one chaos"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.543836+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_987c81863f8063bc739cd937cd38fc426cd1f16bcd26e3a30b1ba5274965a462","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Fix an integer n >= 2 and let F_k = I_n(f_k) be a sequence living in the SAME n-th Wiener chaos, with E[F_k^2] = n! ||f_k||^2 converging to sigma^2 > 0. Then the following are EQUIVALENT: (i) F_k converges in distribution to N(0, sigma^2); (ii) E[F_k^4] -> 3 sigma^4; (iii) the contractions satisfy || f_k contracted with f_k at r indices || -> 0 for every r = 1, ..., n-1. The theorem replaces the infinitely many moment conditions of the method of moments by a SINGLE fourth-moment condition. The hypothesis that the chaos order n is FIXED and the same for every k is essential and is the standard misquotation: for a general sequence of random variables, or for a sequence whose chaos order drifts, matching the fourth moment says nothing about normality - the fourth moment of a suitable two-point law is also 3 times the square of its variance. Also essential is sigma^2 > 0; degenerating variance is excluded. The quantitative form is due to Nourdin and Peccati via Malliavin-Stein: for F in the n-th chaos with E[F^2] = sigma^2, the total variation distance to N(0, sigma^2) is bounded by a constant depending only on n times the square root of ( E[F^4] - 3 sigma^4 ), so the fourth cumulant controls the rate as well as the limit. [Nualart and Peccati (2005), Ann. Probab. 33; Nourdin and Peccati (2009); see Nourdin and Peccati, Normal Approximations with Malliavin Calculus, Theorem 5.2.7]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:33:01.744319+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_98b69e2fa8508940af6a1fbb1117af0e4f28eb9d10d8d89c31b39210aabbe69a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 7 of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] The language $H$ equals the well-defined concatenation $J.G$.
  \begin{proof}
    To every word $w \in H$ there is a \emph{coupon-counting
    function} $f_w\colon \{ 0, 1, \ldots, \lvert w \rvert \} \to \N$
    that tracks the current number of distinct coupons held.
    This means $f_w(0) = 0$ and $f_w(\lvert w \rvert) = m$.
    Choose the smallest $k$ for which $f(k) = m$ and let
    $j$ be the word formed from the first $k$ letters in $w$.
    Then $w$ has the decomposition $j.g$ for some word $g$
    of length $\lvert w\rvert - k$.
    But since $f(k) = f(\lvert w \rvert) = m$,
    each occurrence of $\D_i$ in $g$ must be eventually followed
    by $\C_i$. Hence $g \in G$. There can be no decomposition $j = u.v$
    with $u \in H$ and $v \neq \varepsilon$ because $k > 0$ was selected minimally.
    This establishes $j \in J$ and $w \in J.G$. Thus $H \subseteq J.G$.

    To show $J.G \subseteq H$, take some $j.g \in J.G$ and
    consider the coupon-counting function $f_{j.g}$.
    Then $f_{j.g}(\lvert j \rvert) = m$ but $g$
    recovers all coupons it drops,
    so $f_{j.g}(\lvert j\rvert + \lvert g \rvert) = 
    f_{j.g}(\lvert j \rvert) = m$. We conclude
    $j.g \in H$ and $H = J.G$.

    We could not have selected a longer word $j' \in J$ in the first
    paragraph because $j' = j.u$ would hold with $u \neq \varepsilon$.
    This gives the contradiction $j' \notin J$.
    So, the factorisation of words $w \mapsto (j, g)$ is unique;
    $J$ and $G$ are well-defined for concatenation.
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:42.499252+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_98c8bf02b194191751d59e544407d2b5ddcfe2816446a87e8a3d6e57a9ae7c3e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"(1) U ≠ C is essential: there is no biholomorphism from C onto D, since any holomorphic map C → D is bounded, hence constant by Liouville's theorem. C and D are the two conformal types of simply connected Riemann surfaces with the sphere. (2) Simple connectivity is essential and is not repaired by 'the domain has no holes that matter'. The punctured disk D minus {0} is not conformally equivalent to D: a biholomorphism F : D minus {0} → D would be bounded, hence extend holomorphically to 0 with |F(0)| ≤ 1; the extension maps the disk into D by the open mapping theorem, so F(0) = F(z1) for some z1 ≠ 0, and openness near both points contradicts injectivity on D minus {0}. Likewise two annuli {1 < |z| < R} and {1 < |z| < R'} are conformally equivalent only when R = R': conformal type has a modulus, so 'both are doubly connected' is not enough. (3) The conclusion is interior. The Riemann map need not extend continuously to the boundary, and when it does it need not be injective there. For the slit disk U = D minus [0,1) (which is simply connected), the inverse of the Riemann map extends continuously to the closed disk, but each point of the open slit is the image of two boundary points, so no homeomorphism of the closures exists. The correct boundary statement is Carathéodory's theorem: if U is bounded by a Jordan curve, then the Riemann map extends to a homeomorphism of the closed domains. (4) Normalization: the map is unique only after fixing F(z0) = 0 and F'(z0) > 0; without it the family of Riemann maps is a three-real-parameter family (compose with any automorphism of D).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:35:19.875197+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_98de3550e564e494cc44cf9a8e2c05a05b8422d924aa0d891a71d9af9ed4384d","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn slith of arXiv:2608.27939, 'Entropy and domination for quasi-Hitchin representations'] For a closed surface $S$ and a maximal lamination $\lambda$, let $\rho:\pi_1(S) \to \mathrm{PSL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ be an $n$-pleated representation (as in Definition (defn:pleat of the paper)), pleated along $\lambda$, with an associated $\rho$-equivariant limit map $\xi$ that assigns flags in $\mathbb{C}^n$ with the endpoints of leaves of $\tilde{\lambda}$. The \textit{slithering map} compatible with $\xi$  $$\Sigma:\tilde{\Lambda}^2 \to \mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{C})$$ defined on the space of pairs of leaves of $\lambda$, such that $\Sigma(g_1,g_2)$ is a matrix in $\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ that takes the transverse pair of flags associated with the endpoints of a leaf $g_2$ to that of a leaf $g_1$ (oriented in parallel), satisfying
\[
\Sigma(g,g)=\mathrm{id}, \qquad
\Sigma(g_1,g_3)=\Sigma(g_1,g_2)\Sigma(g_2,g_3),
\]
whenever $g_2$ separates $g_1$ from $g_3$. When $g_1$ and $g_2$ share an endpoint, $\Sigma(g_1,g_2)$ is the unique unipotent transformation that fixes the flag at the common endpoint and takes the flag at the other endpoint of $g_2$ to the flag at the other endpoint of $g_1$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(F_n) increasing, F_infinity generated by their union","Y integrable"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.627314+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_990c757f8a69205734bf9eaa5f8523ff03979cc297993560b1152fd27fd6f9f2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (F_n) be an increasing filtration with F_infinity the sigma-algebra it generates, and let Y be in L^1. Then E[Y | F_n] converges almost surely and in L^1 to E[Y | F_infinity]. Taking Y = 1_A for A in F_infinity gives LEVY'S 0-1 LAW: P(A | F_n) -> 1_A almost surely, so the conditional probability of any event in the limit sigma-algebra converges to 0 or 1. Applied to a tail event of an independent sequence, where F_n is generated by the first n variables and P(A | F_n) = P(A) by independence, this yields Kolmogorov's 0-1 law as a corollary. The theorem is about an INCREASING family; the corresponding statement for a decreasing family is Levy's downward theorem and needs its own proof. The limit is conditional on F_infinity and not on F - the two differ, and writing E[Y | F] would be wrong unless F_infinity = F up to null sets. [standard; e.g. Williams, Probability with Martingales, Theorem 14.2]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["H a complex Hilbert space","U(t) unitary for every t, U(0)=I, U(t+s)=U(t)U(s)","strong continuity: t ↦ U(t)x continuous for every x ∈ H"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:51.724385+00:00","domain":"functional analysis for evolution equations","id":"claim_9912107a207ac70d93e85b9b1c20a3238db259eabf01dc54cd86d39bfc304d7b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let H be a complex Hilbert space and (U(t))_{t∈R} a family of unitary operators on H with U(0) = I, U(t+s) = U(t)U(s) for all s,t ∈ R, and t ↦ U(t)x continuous for each x ∈ H (strong continuity). Then there is a unique self-adjoint, generally unbounded operator A with domain D(A) = { x ∈ H : lim_{t→0} (U(t)x − x)/t exists in H }, defined by iAx = lim_{t→0}(U(t)x − x)/t, such that U(t) = e^{itA} in the sense of the Borel functional calculus. D(A) is dense and invariant under each U(t), and for x ∈ D(A) the map t ↦ U(t)x is differentiable with d/dt U(t)x = iA U(t)x = i U(t) A x. Conversely, every self-adjoint A generates such a group via e^{itA}. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:32:58.337207+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_991d5798b8de0767e729044e4a21b100a516cecfcfd6964aec3452256c990153","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm exponent of arXiv:2505.24821, 'Asymptotics for the harmonic descent chain and applications to critical beta-splitting tre'] We have that

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:46.149419+00:00","domain":"elliptic regularity theory","id":"claim_994ea180f3136425e554f422a5cd28077f4672f5e5871e28d1685f524f0bcfca","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Three hypotheses of the De Giorgi-Nash-Moser theorem are load-bearing, and each fails concretely. (1) Scalar. The theorem is false for systems: De Giorgi (1968) exhibited, for n >= 3, a linear elliptic system with bounded measurable coefficients satisfying the Legendre-Hadamard and even the strong ellipticity condition whose weak solution is u(x) = x |x|^{-gamma} for an explicit gamma with 1 < gamma < n/2 - a solution in H^1 that is unbounded, hence not even locally bounded, let alone Hoelder. So a referee must check that an application of De Giorgi-Nash-Moser or of Moser's Harnack inequality is to a single equation, not to a system, and that the maximum-principle-based truncations used in the proof are available. (2) The energy class u in H^1_loc. A distributional solution whose gradient is only in L^p for some p < 2 need not be bounded. In the plane take A(x) = I + (mu - 1) x x^T/|x|^2 with mu > 1 (uniformly elliptic, bounded, measurable, discontinuous only at the origin). In polar coordinates div(A grad u) = (1/r) d/dr ( r mu u_r ) + (1/r^2) u_{theta theta}, so u = r^s cos(theta) solves the equation away from 0 exactly when mu s^2 = 1. The choice s = -1/sqrt(mu) in (-1,0) gives u = r^{-1/sqrt(mu)} cos(theta), which is unbounded at 0, lies in W^{1,p}_loc precisely for p < 2/(1 + 1/sqrt(mu)) < 2, and is a distributional solution across the origin (the flux through small circles tends to 0 because s > -1). (3) The Hoelder exponent depends on the ellipticity ratio and cannot be improved to Lipschitz. The same coefficients with s = +alpha, i.e. mu = 1/alpha^2, give the H^1 solution u = r^alpha cos(theta) of a uniformly elliptic equation with ellipticity ratio alpha^{-2}: it is exactly C^{0,alpha} at the origin and no better. Hence the exponent alpha(n, Lambda/lambda) in the theorem must degenerate to 0 as Lambda/lambda tends to infinity, and 'bounded measurable coefficients give Lipschitz solutions' is false. Gradient bounds require continuity (or Dini/Hoelder continuity) of the coefficients.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the walk is on the incipient infinite cluster or a similarly statistically self-similar critical random graph","a known or boundable volume-growth exponent d_f for balls in the cluster","a known or boundable effective-resistance-growth exponent reflecting the bottleneck/dangling-end structure","typically also requires the cluster's law to have appropriate scale-invariance, or at least comparable behavior across scales"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T15:09:50+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_995bb1851ff2b7c32ba0e7dcdd60e02e63ccc5cf1891c73d2c0eefad0e85bbb6","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For simple random walk on the incipient infinite cluster of critical percolation, or more generally on critical random media with anomalous volume growth, Kesten's argument establishes subdiffusive behavior, that the walk's typical displacement after n steps is of order n^{1/d_w} with walk dimension d_w > 2 rather than the diffusive n^{1/2}, by combining a volume-growth estimate showing balls of radius r typically contain of order r^{d_f} points, with d_f the fractal (volume) dimension of the cluster, and an effective-resistance estimate R_eff(0, B(0,r)^c) of order r^{zeta}, reflecting the long dangling ends and low-conductance bottlenecks characteristic of the critical cluster. The expected exit time from a ball of radius r is then of order r^{d_f+zeta} (volume times resistance: the Einstein relation d_w = d_f + zeta), so the displacement is of order n^{1/(d_f+zeta)}, subdiffusive when d_f + zeta > 2; the Nash/heat-kernel machinery or a direct expected-exit-time computation turns the two estimates into bounds. In balls of the intrinsic (graph) metric with unit conductances R_eff(0, B(0,r)^c) <= r, so zeta <= 1 there: for the high-dimensional incipient infinite cluster the intrinsic volume grows as r^2 and the resistance as r, giving d_w = 3. The argument does not give the exact value of the subdiffusivity exponent in most dimensions, only bounds, with the precise exponent known rigorously only in specific settings such as sufficiently high dimension or tree-like/hierarchical models, and it is specific to critical (not subcritical or supercritical) percolation geometry, where the fractal, tree-like structure with many bottlenecks is essential to the argument. Typical failure: Assuming the subdiffusivity exponent established for one setting, such as high-dimensional or tree-based incipient infinite clusters where exact computation is possible, transfers to two-dimensional critical percolation, where the exact random-walk dimension remains a major open problem; volume-growth and resistance-growth exponents are model- and dimension-specific quantities that must be independently estimated rather than imported across models with superficially similar critical geometry. Canonical reference: Kesten, 1986, Annales de l'Institut Henri Poincare, Probabilites et Statistiques; Barlow, Jarai, Kumagai and Slade, 2008, Communications in Mathematical Physics.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.542424+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9983acdd24bab7573598cbe43c588211e9e1d72227253d0cb43782e29ec19a49","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Fix d >= 2 and let E(Z^d) be the set of nearest-neighbour edges of the integer lattice. Assign to each edge e an independent random weight tau_e >= 0 with common distribution F; the collection (tau_e) is the environment. The PASSAGE TIME of a finite lattice path gamma is T(gamma) = sum over the edges of gamma of tau_e, and the passage time between vertices x and y is T(x,y) = inf over finite paths from x to y of T(gamma). T is a random pseudometric on Z^d: it is symmetric, satisfies the triangle inequality, and vanishes on the diagonal, but T(x,y) = 0 is possible for x != y when F has an atom at 0. A GEODESIC from x to y is a path attaining the infimum. Geodesics need not exist for a general F, and when F(0) is at least the critical probability p_c(d) the infimum can be 0 and attained by infinitely many paths; when F(0) < p_c a geodesic exists almost surely for every pair, and it is almost surely unique for every pair when F is continuous, since ties then have probability 0. The standing notation in the literature is T(0, x) for the point-to-point time, mu or g for the time constant, chi for the fluctuation exponent and xi for the wandering exponent; the store already records that those exponents are DEFINED differently by different theorems and are not interchangeable. [standard; e.g. Auffinger, Damron and Hanson, 50 Years of First-Passage Percolation, Chapters 1 and 4]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Burgers' equation f(u) = u^2/2 in one dimension","Weak solutions are only required to satisfy the integral identity; jumps must satisfy Rankine-Hugoniot but may still be inadmissible","Uniqueness is restored by the Kruzhkov entropy inequalities (equivalently, for piecewise smooth solutions, by Oleinik's chord condition at each jump)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.418611+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: hyperbolic conservation laws","id":"claim_99a13816dfad50d260100b726c1812dec833cb5ab9500c5108e4748d4cdc77db","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: uniqueness in Kruzhkov's theorem is for ENTROPY solutions; the integral (weak) formulation alone, even with Rankine-Hugoniot satisfied at every jump, does not determine the solution. Counterexample 1 (Burgers, f(u) = u^2/2, datum u0 ≡ 0): besides u ≡ 0 the function u(x,t) = 0 for x < -t/2, u = -1 for -t/2 < x < 0, u = 1 for 0 < x < t/2, u = 0 for x > t/2 is a weak solution — every jump satisfies Rankine-Hugoniot (speeds -1/2, 0, 1/2 respectively) — yet it is not an entropy solution (the jump from -1 up to 1 is an expansion shock violating Oleinik/Lax). Counterexample 2 (Burgers with u0 = 0 for x < 0, u0 = 1 for x > 0): the stationary-in-shape expansion shock u = 0 for x < t/2, u = 1 for x > t/2 satisfies Rankine-Hugoniot, but the entropy solution is the rarefaction u = 0 for x ≤ 0, u = x/t for 0 ≤ x ≤ t, u = 1 for x ≥ t. {"assumptions":["rows i.i.d. with finite twelfth moments (the Ledoit-Wolf condition)","M/n -> c in (0,1) for the stated form; the population spectral distribution has compact support (Ledoit-Peche take it bounded away from zero)","the sample eigenvalues are distinct (they are, almost surely)"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T06:40:20.562774+00:00","domain":"covariance estimation / random matrix theory","id":"claim_99cacf9752b7e70bfc79fa5a079c62ca089650407d9a61a19b42983a5a0f9318","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $S = n^{-1} X^T X = \\sum_{i=1}^M \\lambda_i u_i u_i^T$ be the sample covariance of $n$ i.i.d. rows in $\\mathbb{R}^M$ with population covariance $\\Sigma$, and let $M/n \\to c \\in (0,1)$. Among rotation-equivariant estimators $\\sum_i d_i u_i u_i^T$ the Frobenius-optimal choice is the oracle $d_i^* = u_i^T \\Sigma u_i$, whose large-dimensional limit is $\\lambda_i / |1 - c - c\\lambda_i \\breve m_F(\\lambda_i)|^2$ with $\\breve m_F(\\lambda) = \\lim_{\\eta \\downarrow 0} m_F(\\lambda + i\\eta)$, $m_F(z) = \\int dF(t)/(t - z)$ the Stieltjes transform of the limiting sample spectral distribution $F$ (Ledoit-Peche 2011). Ledoit and Wolf (2020) estimate $f$ and $H_f$ from the sample eigenvalues themselves with the Epanechnikov kernel $\\kappa(x) = \\tfrac{3}{4\\sqrt5}(1 - x^2/5)^+$ and the eigenvalue-proportional bandwidth $h_j = \\lambda_j n^{-1/3}$: $\\tilde f(x) = M^{-1}\\sum_j \\kappa((x - \\lambda_j)/h_j)/h_j$ and $\\tilde H_f(x) = M^{-1}\\sum_j H_\\kappa((x - \\lambda_j)/h_j)/h_j$, where $H_\\kappa(x) = -\\tfrac{3x}{10\\pi} + \\tfrac{3}{4\\sqrt5\\pi}(1 - x^2/5)\\log\\big|\\tfrac{\\sqrt5 - x}{\\sqrt5 + x}\\big|$. The resulting estimator $\\hat\\Sigma = \\sum_i \\tilde d_i u_i u_i^T$ has no tuning constant, is positive definite when $c < 1$, and its Frobenius loss (and its minimum-variance-portfolio loss) converges to the oracle's; for $c > 1$ a separate formula handles the $M - n$ null eigenvalues.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["R>=72; d>=2","Independent standard Gaussian inputs","LSI convention Ent(f^2)<=2 C_LS E||grad f||^2","Fixed exceptional observation; not a typical-observation guarantee","Score-only input model for the information-obstruction consequence"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T20:12:05.583953+00:00","domain":"posterior sampling and functional inequalities","id":"claim_9a4cfee7532e1d359fb034449676f341a43f25f9d713fd07004d3bd13051134c","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"DRAFT, proof (unaudited), T411-w740-C002/C003 v1. Let d>=2 and R>=72, T_R(z)=z+(z-R)_+, and let Z,W,Z2,...,Zd be independent standard Gaussians. Set P0=Law(Z+W,Z2,...,Zd) and P1=Law(T_R(Z)+W,Z2,...,Zd). Both priors have positive smooth densities and log-Sobolev constant at most 5 in the convention Ent(f^2)<=2 C_LS E||grad f||^2. The exact OU forward score of P0 has squared L2 error at most exp(-R^2/2)/4 under the forward law of P1 at every time. Under additive Gaussian smoothing with standard deviation u, the squared error is at most Pr(Z>R)/[(1+u^2)(2+u^2)]. For the normalized observation A=e1^T, noise variance 2/5, and fixed y=2R, the posteriors of P0 and P1 differ in TV by more than 3/8. The posterior of P1 has C_P and C_LS at least exp(R^2/960)/8, although the prior ratio ||A||^2 C_LS/sigma^2 is at most 25/2. A common approximate-score oracle therefore cannot guarantee posterior TV error 1/8 for every fixed observation; adding n independent exact prior samples requires n Pr(Z>R)>1/8. These are rare-observation obstructions only: they do not establish exact-score computational hardness, do not refute high-probability-over-observations posterior sampling, and do not claim that these explicitly described posteriors are hard to sample. No novelty or independent-check claim is made.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["u >= 0 on R^n x [0,T)","u continuous on R^n x [0,T), C^2_1 on R^n x (0,T)","u solves the heat equation on R^n x (0,T)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:49.105607+00:00","domain":"parabolic partial differential equations","id":"claim_9a5bad18bd9d3e1275fd6476bf5a6345e55dbed91dc58935fdaa7c480ad81ddc","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $T\\in(0,\\infty]$ and let $u\\ge0$ be continuous on $\\mathbb R^n\\times[0,T)$, of class $C^2_1$ on $\\mathbb R^n\\times(0,T)$, and satisfy $u_t-\\Delta u=0$ in $\\mathbb R^n\\times(0,T)$. Then, with $\\Phi(x,t)=(4\\pi t)^{-n/2}e^{-|x|^2/(4t)}$, $u(x,t)=\\int_{\\mathbb R^n}\\Phi(x-y,t)u(y,0)\\,dy$ for all $x\\in\\mathbb R^n$ and $0<t<T$; in particular $\\int e^{-|y|^2/(4t)}u(y,0)dy<\\infty$ for every $t<T$. Consequently a nonnegative solution in this class with $u(\\cdot,0)\\equiv0$ vanishes identically, and two nonnegative solutions with the same initial values coincide -- no growth hypothesis is needed, one-sided boundedness replaces it. (Widder 1944 for $n=1$; the general statement, with arbitrary nonnegative initial traces given by Borel measures when continuity at $t=0$ is dropped, is due to Widder and Aronson; the divergence-form analogue is Aronson's.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-24T23:47:01.939466+00:00","domain":"boolean functions/fourier analysis","id":"claim_9a9adddb76424d3b96eb917c2d999d1a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[DERIVED + CHECKED 09-08 07:3x] Bernoulli 2/3: rescaling a block by v=(3/2)^n w turns Q^2 into a RIESZ PRODUCT with ratio 3/2, and the criterion's coefficient c(n) is its Fourier coefficient at frequency (3/2)^(n+1). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:35:04.096419+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9b1afa08cb1432c416d963cee443bdd6994471bd1a5eb173411bb5775883801e","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:ribbon-record of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] A rooted orthogonal-Weingarten ribbon record $\Gamma$ of degree $m$
consists of the dart set
$\{1,\ldots,m\}\times\{L_0,L_1,R_0,R_1\}$; its coefficient boxes and
color labels; perfect matchings $p,q,r$ giving the row,
coefficient-column, and rooted trace wiring; all local wedge and
direct/cross signs; the distinguished root boundary; and the following
orthogonal-Weingarten path data.

Partition the darts into the independent Haar-color classes
$\mathscr H_\Gamma$ (there is one class when all entries come from one
Haar matrix).  If $a\in\mathscr H_\Gamma$ contains $m_a$ coefficient
occurrences, put $k_a=2m_a$, so it has $2k_a=4m_a$ darts, and denote by
$p_a,q_a$ the restrictions of $p,q$.  The rooted dart order chooses a
deterministic relabelling $\sigma_a$ with
$\sigma_a\cdot e_{k_a}=p_a$, where
\[
 e_k=\{\{1,2\},\{3,4\},\ldots,\{2k-1,2k\}\},
\]
and put
$\mathfrak m_a=\sigma_a^{-1}\cdot q_a\in\mathcal P_2(2k_a)$.
The orthogonal Weingarten graph has vertex set
$\bigsqcup_{j\ge0}\mathcal P_2(2j)$.  At level $j$ it has a solid arrow
\[
 \mathfrak n\longrightarrow(i,2j-1)\cdot\mathfrak n,
 \qquad 1\le i<2j-1,
\]
and it has a dashed arrow
$\mathfrak n\dashrightarrow\mathfrak n^\downarrow$ when
$\{2j-1,2j\}\in\mathfrak n$, where $\mathfrak n^\downarrow$ is
obtained by deleting that pair.  The record chooses, for every $a$, one
\emph{individual} path $\gamma_a$ from $\mathfrak m_a$ to the empty
pairing.  It uses exactly $k_a$ dashed arrows; write $s_a$ for its number
of solid arrows.  If $\mu_a$ is the coset type of $\mathfrak m_a$, define
\[
 d_a:=|\mathfrak m_a|=k_a-\ell(\mu_a)
      =k_a-\#(p_a\vee q_a),
 \qquad
 g_a:=s_a-d_a\ge0,
 \qquad
 g_{\rm Wg}:=\sum_{a\in\mathscr H_\Gamma}g_a.
\]
Thus $g_{\rm Wg}$ is the total number of solid arrows beyond shortest
orthogonal-Weingarten paths; unlike the unitary excess, it need not be
even.

Let $w_\Gamma$ be the scalar coefficient of this chosen product path,
including the bounded local wedge and direct/cross coefficients.  Write
$\operatorname{Contr}^{\rm raw}_{\Gamma,\tau}$ for the typed raw
contraction determined by the record and its circuit state, and put
\[
 F_\Gamma=\#(p\vee r),\qquad
 \ell_\Gamma=\#(p\vee q)
      =\sum_{a\in\mathscr H_\Gamma}\#(p_a\vee q_a),\qquad
 \omega_\Gamma=n^{F_\Gamma}w_\Gamma,\qquad
 \mathcal A_\Gamma=w_\Gamma
       \operatorname{Contr}^{\rm raw}_{\Gamma,\tau}.
\]
Thus $w_\Gamma$ is a scalar coefficient, not the value or norm of an
open contraction; $\omega_\Gamma$ merely expresses the same coefficient
in once-normalized original-circuit units.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:43:45.381691+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9b43cffbd6501c79cc4837c141bffc96c552b691fc97e21ec7d7ccb9a96ac2c6","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 37 of arXiv:2609.04033, 'From configuration spaces to graph complexes via $\mathbf{FA}$-modules'] Given $n$ and $r$ we define the chain complex $(\mathsf{TT}(n,r), d_{\mathsf{TT}})$ as follows. $$ \mathsf{TT}(n,r) = \left(\ds\bigoplus_{i=0}^{\lfloor (n-r+1)/2\rfloor} \Sigma^{2i-r+2}\mathsf{T}(n,2i+1,r-2)\right)\oplus \Sigma^{1-r}\mathsf{T}(n,0,r-1).$$

{"assumptions":["A square over a field (R or C in the numerical statements)","unit lower triangular L fixes the normalisation; L D U variants move the diagonal into D"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:31:12.479562+00:00","domain":"numerical linear algebra","id":"claim_9b87fdf50aa592bb2dcee21b2e13402fec32970a0b5820f287442e30505c9e85","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A be an n x n matrix over a field. A has a factorisation A = L U with L unit lower triangular (ones on the diagonal) and U upper triangular if and only if every leading principal submatrix A_k = A[1..k, 1..k], k = 1, ..., n - 1, is invertible (for invertible A this is equivalent to all n leading principal minors being nonzero); when it exists the factorisation is unique for invertible A, and u_kk = det A_k / det A_{k-1}. In general, for every A there is a permutation matrix P with P A = L U (Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting: at each step the row with the largest remaining entry in the pivot column is swapped into the pivot position); for invertible A the factors are then unique given P. The elimination costs 2 n^3 / 3 flops; solving A x = b afterwards costs 2 n^2 by one forward and one back substitution; the determinant is the product of the u_kk times the sign of P. {"assumptions":["T is measurable","invariance is expressed through preimages T^{-1}A"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T02:00:35.437948+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, foundations","id":"claim_9ba1defc34ee3afb4584a993f111afbfc82e7640f9230052afb1810248d72dbf","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(X, \\mathcal{B}, \\mu)$ be a measure space. A measurable map $T: X \\to X$ is measure-preserving if $\\mu(T^{-1} A) = \\mu(A)$ for every $A \\in \\mathcal{B}$ (preimages, not images: $T$ need not be injective, and for non-invertible $T$ the condition $\\mu(TA) = \\mu(A)$ is neither implied nor required). The system is a probability-preserving system when $\\mu(X) = 1$. A set $A$ is (strictly) invariant if $T^{-1}A = A$, and invariant mod $\\mu$ if $\\mu(T^{-1}A \\,\\triangle\\, A) = 0$; every set invariant mod $\\mu$ differs from a strictly invariant set by a null set. $T$ is ergodic if every invariant set has measure $0$ or full measure; equivalently (for a probability measure) every measurable $f$ with $f \\circ T = f$ a.e. is a.e. constant; equivalently every set $A$ with $T^{-1}A \\subset A$ mod $\\mu$ (or $T^{-1}A \\supset A$ mod $\\mu$) has measure 0 or 1. The invariant $\\sigma$-algebra $\\mathcal{I} = \\{A : T^{-1}A = A\\}$ is what the ergodic averages converge to conditional expectations onto. Ergodicity is not the same as mixing (mixing implies ergodic, not conversely: an irrational rotation of the circle is ergodic but not mixing), and it is not preserved by passing to powers ($T^2$ may fail to be ergodic when $T$ is, e.g. the rotation by $1/2$ on two points).","status":"unverified"}

Each vertex carries one of two colours, which we identify with the values \(-1\) and \(1\). The root vertex \(1\) is assigned a random bit \(B_1\in\{-1,1\}\), chosen uniformly at random. For each \(n\geq 1\), once the new vertex \(n+1\) has chosen its parent \(p_{n+1}\), it inherits the bit of its parent with probability \(1-q\) and flips it with probability \(q\), independently of the tree growth and all previous broadcasting steps. Equivalently,
	\[
	B_{n+1}=B_{p_{n+1}}Z_{n+1},
	\]
	where \((Z_n)_{n\geq 2}\) are independent \(\{-1,1\}\)-valued random variables satisfying
	\[
	\mathbb P(Z_n=-1)=q,
	\qquad
	\mathbb P(Z_n=1)=1-q.
	\]
	The parameter \(q\in[0,1]\) is called the bit-flip probability.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["examples use Lebesgue measure on [0,1] and a one-point space of infinite measure","statements about (L^infinity)* use the axiom of choice via Hahn-Banach","the degenerate exception in (1) is a measure that is a finite sum of atoms of finite measure"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:36.553548+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, Lp spaces","id":"claim_9c99a22f279aba04c24062eeaa629c6222d83b8f4cd18106908536d318f9894e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The identification of the dual of L^p has two genuine exceptions. (1) p = infinity fails in general: apart from the degenerate case of finitely many atoms all of finite measure (where L^1 = L^infinity is finite-dimensional and the duality is trivially true), L^1 is a proper closed subspace of (L^infinity)*. On [0,1] with Lebesgue measure, C[0,1] embeds isometrically in L^infinity (for continuous functions the sup norm equals the essential sup norm); extend the evaluation functional h -> h(0) from C[0,1] to a norm-one functional Lambda on L^infinity by Hahn-Banach. If Lambda were integration against some g in L^1, then taking continuous h_n with h_n(0) = 1, 0 <= h_n <= 1, supported in [0, 1/n], dominated convergence would give int h_n g -> 0 while Lambda(h_n) = 1. (Concretely, (L^infinity)* is the space of finitely additive bounded measures absolutely continuous with respect to mu.) (2) p = 1 without sigma-finiteness (or localizability) fails: let X = {pt} with mu({pt}) = infinity. Then L^1(mu) = {0}, so (L^1)* = {0}, while L^infinity(mu) is one-dimensional; the canonical map L^infinity -> (L^1)* is not injective, let alone onto. (3) For 0 < p < 1 and mu nonatomic (e.g. Lebesgue on [0,1]) the dual is trivial: (L^p[0,1])* = {0}, so no duality/Hahn-Banach argument survives below p = 1. {"assumptions":["two-dimensional planar lattice model satisfying the FKG inequality","translation invariance and, in the classical gluing constructions, reflection symmetry of the lattice","an a priori lower bound on square-crossing probabilities, which is a hypothesis to be separately established, not a free consequence of RSW","independence, or at least positive association, of the underlying edge or site variables"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T16:00:40+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9ca68baa0660aa59223fcaebbdec10b169d0c2892b9d78d08095d1f75675fc1d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). In two-dimensional critical or near-critical percolation, RSW theory states that if crossing probabilities of n x n squares are uniformly bounded away from 0 as n grows, then crossing probabilities of rho n x n rectangles, for any fixed aspect ratio rho, are also uniformly bounded away from 0 by a constant depending on rho but not on n. The matching bound away from 1 needs the same input for the dual model (at criticality on a self-dual lattice it follows by duality); a lower bound for the primal model alone does not give it, since in the supercritical phase both crossing probabilities tend to 1. The classical proof glues together several square-crossing events using the FKG inequality and translation and reflection symmetry of the lattice. RSW estimates are the essential multi-scale input for proving arm-exponent bounds, conformal-invariance-adjacent results, and, via the Duminil-Copin-Tassion approach, for establishing sharpness of the phase transition without relying on exact self-duality. RSW does not by itself prove existence of a scaling limit as n -> infinity, does not give the exact value of any crossing probability, only two-sided bounds; and the classical form required exact self-duality (p=1/2 on the square lattice), so extending the theory to general planar lattices or to p != 1/2 required a genuinely new, duality-free argument (Tassion, 2016). Typical failure: Assuming that RSW-type bounded-away-from-0/1 crossing estimates transfer automatically to a new planar model merely because it is monotone and planar; RSW requires either exact self-duality or the more robust but still nontrivial Tassion-style construction, and models without FKG, or with strong enough long-range dependence, can fail to admit the needed gluing arguments even though they look superficially similar to Bernoulli percolation. Canonical reference: Russo, 1978, Zeitschrift fur Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie und verwandte Gebiete; Seymour and Welsh, 1978, Annals of Discrete Mathematics; Tassion, 2016, Probability Theory and Related Fields.","status":"unverified"}

	\[
	\lim_{n\to\infty}
	\mathbb P_{\mu^n}^n
	\left(
	\left|
	X_k^{n,t}(f_k)

{"assumptions":["X is a Banach space","A is densely defined (automatic in reflexive X under the range condition)","A is dissipative","a range condition: Ran(λ_0 − A) = X (or dense) for some λ_0 > 0"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.771500+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, operator semigroups, evolution equations","id":"claim_9cc7074f8de110e84e704f7481a4bebc14d6b3c2eb606e5b71dc671682f7125e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a Banach space and A: D(A) ⊂ X → X linear and densely defined. (1) If A is dissipative and Ran(λ_0 − A) = X for some λ_0 > 0, then A is closed, Ran(λ − A) = X for every λ > 0, and A generates a contraction C_0-semigroup. (2) If A is dissipative and Ran(λ_0 − A) is merely dense for some λ_0 > 0, then A is closable, its closure Ā is dissipative with Ran(λ − Ā) = X for all λ > 0, and Ā generates a contraction C_0-semigroup. (3) Conversely, if A generates a contraction C_0-semigroup, then A is densely defined, closed, Ran(λ − A) = X for all λ > 0, and A is dissipative in the strong sense that Re⟨Ax, x*⟩ ≤ 0 for every x ∈ D(A) and every x* ∈ J(x). (4) If X is reflexive, a dissipative A with Ran(λ_0 − A) = X for some λ_0 > 0 is automatically densely defined. (5) Hilbert space corollary: if A is densely defined and closed and both A and A* are dissipative, then A generates a contraction C_0-semigroup; and a densely defined symmetric operator S with S ≤ 0 that is self-adjoint generates the contraction semigroup e^{tS}. {"assumptions":["X a Banach space","K compact and linear","the statement is about I - K; for lambda I - K with lambda not zero divide by lambda"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T14:24:13.476530+00:00","domain":"functional analysis","id":"claim_9cd24333d102074cf31fdaac1e3b28d41b51bfe803503d2d5cfac25fbe524fc7","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a Banach space, K : X -> X a compact linear operator, and T = I - K. Then: (i) ker T is finite-dimensional and the range of T is closed; (ii) T is injective if and only if it is surjective, and in that case T has a bounded inverse; (iii) dim ker T = dim ker T* where T* = I - K* is the adjoint on the dual X*, and the equation T x = y is solvable exactly when y annihilates ker T* (the closed-range theorem). So either T x = y has a unique solution for every y, or the homogeneous equation T x = 0 has a nontrivial finite-dimensional solution space and T x = y is solvable exactly for y orthogonal (in the duality sense) to the finitely many solutions of the adjoint homogeneous equation. For a Hilbert space and a self-adjoint compact K this is the classical alternative for integral equations of the second kind; the same conclusions hold for lambda I - K with any nonzero lambda.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.199499+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9cdd95b748fea298de1a2af88b5ce1ac2dba3e772343b6d54cc9e46d419d944e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Ppn 132 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $u,v$ be real numbers such that $v\geq u^2 - \bar{\lambda}$, and let $P_1,P_2>0$.
Set
\beq
    \sigma 
    \equiv
    \bigg(
    \frac{P_1v + 2
    (P_1P_2)^{1/2}
    u+P_2}{P_1+P_2}
    \bigg)^{1/2}
\eeq
Then we have the bound
\beq
  u^2 + \Big((v-u^2 + 2\bar{\lambda})^{1/2}-1\Big)^2 
  \ge \bigg(1+\frac{P_2}{P_1}\bigg)(\sigma-1)^2\,.
\eeq
Given any $\sigma\ge0$, if we let $(u,v)$ be defined by the equations
	\[
	u^2 = \frac{P_2}{P_1}(\sigma-1)^2 
	= v-\sigma^2 + 2\bar{\lambda}\,,
	\]
then $(u,v)$ achieves equality in both \eqref{e:sigma.of.u.v} and \eqref{eq:u-v-to-sigma-bound}. 

\begin{proof}
Denote $\tilde{v}\equiv v-u^2 + 2\bar{\lambda} \ge0$. The above definition of $\sigma$ can then be rewritten as
	\beq    
	(P_1+P_2)\sigma^2
	= P_1 \tilde{v}  +
	\Big( (P_1)^{1/2} u + (P_2)^{1/2}
	\Big)^2\,.
	\eeq
Consider optimizing the left-hand side of \eqref{eq:u-v-to-sigma-bound} subject to the constraint 
\eqref{eq:LM-constraint}: the Lagrangian is
	\[
	\mathscr{L}
	= u^2 + \Big(\tilde{v}^{1/2}-1\Big)^2 
	+ \lambda
	\bigg\{
	(P_1+P_2)\sigma^2
	- P_1 \tilde{v}  -
	\Big( (P_1)^{1/2} u + (P_2)^{1/2}
	\Big)^2
	\bigg\}\,.
	\]
The Lagrangian stationarity conditions are
	\begin{align*}
	0&=\frac{\partial\mathscr{L}}
		{\partial u}
	= 2u - 2\lambda (P_1)^{1/2}
	\Big( (P_1)^{1/2} u + (P_2)^{1/2}
	\Big)\,\\
	0&=\frac{\partial\mathscr{L}}
		{\partial\tilde{v}}
	= 1-\frac{1}{\tilde{v}^{1/2}}
	- \lambda P_1\,.
	\end{align*}
Simplifying the above equations gives
	\[
	u
	= \bigg(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\bigg)^{1/2}
	 \frac{\lambda P_1}{1-\lambda P_1}
	=
	\bigg(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\bigg)^{1/2}
	(\tilde{v}^{1/2}-1)
	\,.
	\]
Combining this with \eqref{eq:LM-constraint} gives $\sigma^2=\tilde{v}$. Substituting this back into the left-hand side of \eqref{eq:u-v-to-sigma-bound} gives
	\[
	u^2 + (\tilde{v}^{1/2}-1)^2
	= \bigg(1+ \frac{P_2}{P_1}\bigg)
	(\tilde{v}^{1/2}-1)^2
	= \bigg(1+ \frac{P_2}{P_1}\bigg)
	(\sigma-1)^2\,,
	\]
so \eqref{eq:u-v-to-sigma-bound} holds with equality in the case of an interior stationary point. It remains to check the boundary case $\tilde{v}=0$. In this case we have
	\[
	\sigma
	=\bigg|\bigg( \frac{P_1}{P_1+P_2}\bigg)^{1/2} u
	+\bigg( \frac{P_2}{P_1+P_2}\bigg)^{1/2}\bigg|
	\equiv
	\Big| (A_1)^{1/2} u + (A_2)^{1/2}
	\Big|\,,
	\]
with $A_1+A_2=1$. The desired bound \eqref{eq:u-v-to-sigma-bound} then simplifies to
	\begin{align*}
	u^2 + 1
	&= \bigg(\frac{-(A_2)^{1/2}\pm\sigma}{(A_1)^{1/2}}\bigg)^2+1
	= \frac{A_2 + \sigma^2
		\pm 2 (A_2)^{1/2}\sigma}{A_1}
		+1
	= \frac{1+\sigma^2
		\pm 2 (A_2)^{1/2}\sigma}{A_1}
	\\
	&\ge
	\frac{1 + \sigma^2-2\sigma}{A_1}
	= \bigg(1+\frac{P_2}{P_1}\bigg)(\sigma-1)^2\,,
	\end{align*}
which gives the bound for the boundary case $\tilde{v}=0$. This concludes the proof.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:19:06.752924+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9cf065791a3e5980ec2ec36b3a14353e971f7b5d512c0b7776f4e0f7e4b20567","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:stationary-derivative-band-partition-paper of arXiv:2606.08683, 'Exact Fourier dimensions of dyadic Mandelbrot cascades under minimal integrability'] There exists an absolute constant \(C\ge1\) such that, for every \(\xi\neq0\), there exist nonnegative \(C^1\) functions
\[
\chi_{\xi,\mathrm{stat}},
\qquad
\chi_{\xi,d}\quad(d\in\mathfrak D_\xi),
\]
on \(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}\), where \(\mathfrak D_\xi\) is a finite set of dyadic numbers, satisfying the following properties.

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item Partition of unity:
\[
\chi_{\xi,\mathrm{stat}}(t)+\sum_{d\in\mathfrak D_\xi}\chi_{\xi,d}(t)=1
\qquad(t\in\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}).
\]

\item Number of bands:
\[
\#\mathfrak D_\xi\le C(1+\log_2(2+\Lambda)).
\]

\item Stationary tube:
\[
\operatorname{spt}\chi_{\xi,\mathrm{stat}}
\subset
\{t:\operatorname{dist}(t,Z_\xi)\le C\Lambda^{-1/2}\}.
\]

\item Localization of derivative bands:
for every \(d\in\mathfrak D_\xi\),
\[
C^{-1}\Lambda^{-1/2}\le d\le C,
\]
and
\[
\operatorname{spt}\chi_{\xi,d}
\subset
\{t:C^{-1}d\le\operatorname{dist}(t,Z_\xi)\le Cd\}.
\]

\item Derivative size:
on \(\operatorname{spt}\chi_{\xi,d}\),
\[
C^{-1}\Lambda d\le \lvert\phi_\xi'(t)\rvert\le C\Lambda d.
\]

\item Cutoff derivative:
\[
\lvert\chi_{\xi,d}'(t)\rvert\le Cd^{-1}.
\]

\item Bounded overlap:
\[
\sum_{d\in\mathfrak D_\xi}\mathbf 1_{\operatorname{spt}\chi_{\xi,d}}(t)\le C
\qquad(t\in\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}).
\]
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

\[

\qquad
\Var(\bar\eta;[u_1,u_2])=u_2-u_1.
\]
When $L=0$, $\bar\eta$ is understood to be constant. Set
\[
r_t=S(\eta|_{[0,t]}),
