The following are equivalent:

\item if $r_s=r_t$ for $0\leq s<t\leq T$, then $\eta|_{[s,t]}$ is constant; equivalently, the prefix-signature lift is injective after constant waiting intervals are collapsed.
\end{enumerate}

Complete theorem, constants and scope:
# Target 1 with raw inputs and an explicit Lipschitz feature encoder

Claim T336-w727-C004 v1. Rung: proof (unaudited), subject to recorded checks and dependent on unaudited C002 v1. No Lean certification or independent audit is claimed. This gives a quantitative raw-input subclass of Target 1, rather than assuming exact feature computation outside the size count.

The hardest steps are the explicit residual-MLP encoder and the perturbation budget linking its feature errors to the original GP predictive distribution. The proof does not use a triangle inequality for KL.

## 1. Assumptions and explicit size

Fix integers d,p>=1,n>=0, real s>0, B>=0,R>=0,K>=0,eps>0. The raw domain is X=[0,1]^d. The fixed zero-mean GP prior has kernel k(x,x')=z(x)^T z(x'), where z:X->R^p satisfies ||z(x)||_2<=R and, for each coordinate j,

    |z_j(x)-z_j(x')|<=K ||x-x'||_1.

The observation noise is independent N(0,s). Context labels satisfy |y_i|<=B, and contexts have length t<=n. The target is the predictive law of a new noisy observation. The input encoding supplies only raw coordinates, labels, two binary role flags (context and query), and fixed constants. Zero padding fixes N=n+1 tokens. A padding token has raw coordinates zero and both flags zero; the query has only its query flag set; actual context tokens have only their context flag set. No label is supplied for the query.

Define the following fixed constants:

    S=R+1,
    C_A=n(2R+1),
    C_m=nB[(R+S)/s + S C_A R/s^2],
    C_v=R+S+S^2 C_A/s > 0,
    eta=min(1, sqrt(s eps)/(2(1+C_m)), s sqrt(eps)/(2 C_v), s/(4 C_v)),
    eps0=min(eps/4,1/16),
    m=max(1,ceil(K d sqrt(p)/eta)), J=(m+1)^d, E=3+ceil(log_2 J).

For the solver set

    kappa=1+max(1,n)S^2/s, M=nS^2B/s,
    delta0=min(1/2,s/(2S^2),sqrt(s eps0)/(1+M),s sqrt(eps0)/S^2),
    T=ceil(sqrt(kappa) log(2/delta0)/2).

There is a residual normalized ReLU-attention transformer (Bai et al. Definition 1 and Definition 2) with

    token width D=7p+6+d+Jd+pJ,
    depth L_total=E+T+2=T+5+ceil(log_2 J),
    at most five attention heads per layer,
    tokenwise MLP hidden width at most H=2Jd+pJ+4p+1,

whose Gaussian output satisfies forward KL<=eps uniformly over all these raw-input contexts and queries. A dense parameter upper bound is

    L_total(15D^2+2DH)+2D.

Fixed affine input placement is not counted; all nonlinear feature computation is counted. Every weight is specified below or in C002 v1 and depends only on the fixed prior feature map (through finitely many grid samples) and the displayed bounds, never on observed contexts, query labels, or future data. This is a real-weight size theorem, not a finite-bit complexity theorem or training guarantee.

## 2. Posterior perturbation caused by an approximate feature map

First suppose a map ztilde satisfies sup_x ||ztilde(x)-z(x)||<=eta<=1. Then ||ztilde||<=R+eta<=S. For any fixed admissible context and query, put

    A=sI+sum_i z_i z_i^T, b=sum_i z_i y_i, q=z(x_*),
    Atilde=sI+sum_i ztilde_i ztilde_i^T, btilde=sum_i ztilde_i y_i, qtilde=ztilde(x_*).

Both matrices are symmetric positive definite with inverse operator norm <=1/s. For vectors u,v,

    ||uu^T-vv^T||_op
      =||(u-v)u^T+v(u-v)^T||_op
      <=||u-v|| (||u||+||v||).

Thus

    ||A-Atilde||<=n(2R+eta)eta<=C_A eta,
    ||b-btilde||<=nB eta, ||b||<=nRB,
    ||A^{-1}-Atilde^{-1}||
      =||A^{-1}(Atilde-A)Atilde^{-1}||<=C_A eta/s^2.

The true and perturbed noisy predictive parameters are

    mu=q^T A^{-1}b, v=s+s q^T A^{-1}q,
    mutilde=qtilde^T Atilde^{-1}btilde,
    vtilde=s+s qtilde^T Atilde^{-1}qtilde.

Both variances are >=s. Add and subtract qtilde^T A^{-1}b and qtilde^T Atilde^{-1}b. Cauchy-Schwarz and the preceding bounds give

    |mu-mutilde|
      <=eta nRB/s + S C_A eta nRB/s^2 + S nB eta/s
      =C_m eta.

For the variance, first replace both q factors while retaining A^{-1}, and then replace the inverse. This gives

    |v-vtilde|
      <=s[eta(R+S)/s+S^2 C_A eta/s^2]=C_v eta.

The definition of eta ensures

    |mu-mutilde|<=sqrt(s eps)/2,
    |v-vtilde|<=min(s/4,s sqrt(eps)/2).

No probabilistic context distribution or independence between observed features is needed here.

## 3. A finite-grid cone encoder

Let G={0,1/m,...,1}^d, so |G|=J. For each feature coordinate define

    ztilde_j(x)=min_{a in G}[z_j(a)+K sum_{r=1}^d |x_r-a_r|].

The Lipschitz assumption shows every term in this minimum is >=z_j(x). Choose a nearest grid point coordinate by coordinate; its L1 distance is <=d/(2m). The same Lipschitz bound then gives

    0<=ztilde_j(x)-z_j(x)<=Kd/m.

Consequently ||ztilde(x)-z(x)||<=sqrt(p)Kd/m<=eta. This also holds for K=0, when the error is zero and m=1. In particular |ztilde_j(x)|<=||ztilde(x)||<=S on the whole input cube.

The encoder is exact as an implementation of this finite minimum, including all absolute values. It is not a numerical approximation to the finite minimum.

## 4. Exact tokenwise residual-MLP construction

Use the 7p+4 core registers of C002. Add d registers for raw x, Jd zero-initialized absolute-value registers, pJ zero-initialized cone registers, and two role flags. This is D=7p+6+d+Jd+pJ. Initially the feature registers z_c,z_q are zero. The core constant is one=1; the variance-output register starts at s, and the query/padding label register is zero. Encoder MLP layers preserve raw x, the flags, and all core constants.

Each MLP has the residual form h^+=h+W2 ReLU(W1 h), with a constant register implementing affine biases. All unspecified matrix entries are zero. The attention block in each encoder layer is the identity (all value matrices zero).

Layer 1 uses 2Jd hidden units for ReLU(x_r-a_r) and ReLU(a_r-x_r), for all a in G,r. Their sums are written into the initially zero absolute-value registers, yielding |x_r-a_r| exactly.

Layer 2 uses Jd identity-ReLU units on the nonnegative absolute registers and one unit on the constant one. Its output matrix writes

    F_{j,a}=z_j(a)+K sum_r |x_r-a_r|

into each initially zero cone register. Negative fixed grid values cause no difficulty: they occur in the output matrix applied to the constant unit.

Next compute the minimum independently for each coordinate j by a balanced binary tournament on the J cone registers. A pair of current registers u,v is replaced in the first slot by

    u-ReLU(u-v)=min(u,v),

leaving the other slot unused thereafter. This is one residual MLP unit: W1 reads u-v and W2 subtracts its ReLU from the u register. Distinct pairs at the same level use disjoint output slots. An unpaired register passes unchanged. After ceil(log_2 J) levels one designated cone slot contains ztilde_j(x). Each level uses at most p floor(J/2) units, bounded by pJ. This works for signed cone values and for every J, not only powers of two.

One final gating layer writes the feature registers. For any |f|<=S and binary flag r define

    g(f,r)=ReLU(f+S(r-1))-ReLU(-f+S(r-1)).

If r=1, this equals f; if r=0, both arguments are <=0 and it equals zero. Apply g to every computed feature with the context flag to populate z_c, and with the query flag to populate z_q. The registers start at zero, so the residual connection adds precisely the desired values. This uses 4p units. Query, padding, and context feature routing now matches C002 exactly. Both flags and the raw x registers are preserved throughout.

There are E=3+ceil(log_2 J) MLP encoder layers. The stated H bounds every hidden width. Biases are realized through the constant register, rather than being omitted from the construction. All grid feature values are fixed weights of the known prior; no context-dependent parameter is selected.

## 5. Solver composition and KL budget

Apply C002 v1 to ztilde with feature bound S and accuracy eps0. Its core 7p+4 registers embed in the larger width D; all additional registers are preserved by zero extension of its matrices. The solver uses its one-head broadcast layer, T five-head Chebyshev layers, and four-head readout layer. All solver MLPs are identities. The resulting parameters muhat,vhat obey

    vhat>=s,
    |mutilde-muhat|<=sqrt(s eps0)<=sqrt(s eps)/2,
    |vtilde-vhat|<=s sqrt(eps0)<=min(s/4,s sqrt(eps)/2).

Combine these with Section 2 using ordinary triangle inequalities for scalar errors, not for KL:

    |mu-muhat|<=sqrt(s eps),
    |v-vhat|<=min(s/2,s sqrt(eps)).

Since v,vhat>=s, put h=(v-vhat)/vhat in [-1/2,1/2]. As proved directly in C002 Section 5,

    KL(N(mu,v)||N(muhat,vhat))
      <=(mu-muhat)^2/(2s)+(v-vhat)^2/(2s^2)<=eps.

The depth is E+T+2. There are at most five heads, each with three D-by-D matrices. Counting two D-by-H/H-by-D MLP matrices at every layer, even when they are zero, and a two-coordinate linear readout, gives the stated dense parameter bound.

## 6. What this does and does not settle

This is a quantitative raw-input theorem for every bounded finite-rank GP feature map satisfying the displayed Lipschitz assumption, in every fixed input dimension. It counts the encoder rather than treating it as a free feature oracle. The bound is deliberately explicit and can be very large because J=(m+1)^d.

C003 shows that dropping all raw-feature regularity makes the literal bounded-kernel statement false for continuous Gaussian-output transformers. C004 therefore supplies a precise constructive assumption, while C002 remains the smaller theorem when features are supplied directly.

The finite-grid envelope and ReLU min/max identities are classical elementary constructions, not claims of new approximation theory. The claimed target contribution is their fully costed composition with the accelerated posterior solver and a uniform original-posterior forward-KL budget. C004 remains a proof candidate dependent on C002 until independent review passes both exact versions.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.348330+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9d9940d5d71c04317ee6bf6c7af44330e25833e47c30d0a08c189418c3460668","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 161 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For all $1 \leq \ell\leq \ubl$ we have:
  \begin{align}
  
  \bbE[\hat U^{\ell}-\hat U^{\ell-1}
  \,|\,
  \cF^{\hat U,\tilde U}(\ell-1)]
  &=0\,,
  \\
  
  \bbE[\hat Y^{\ell}-\hat Y^{\ell-1}
  ~|~
  \cF^{\hat Y,\tilde Y,\hat{\prxY},\tilde{\prxY}}(\ell-1)]
  =
  \bbE[\hat Y^{\ell}-\hat Y^{\ell-1}
  ~|~
  \cF^{\hat U,\tilde U}(\ell-1)]
  &=
  0\,,
  \\
  
  \bbE[\hat V^{\ell}-\hat V^{\ell-1}
  ~|~
  \cF^{\hat V,\tilde V}(\ell-1)]
  &=0\,,
  \\
  
  \bbE[\hat M^{\ell}-\hat M^{\ell-1}
  ~|~
  \cF^{\hat M,\tilde M}(\ell-1)]
  =
  \bbE[\hat M^{\ell}-\hat M^{\ell-1}
  ~|~
  \cF^{\hat V,\tilde V}(\ell-1)]
  &=
  0
  \,.
  \end{align}

\begin{proof}
  We will show inductively that
  \eqref{eq:pair-u-increments-orthogonal} implies
  \eqref{eq:pair-y-increments-orthogonal}, which implies
  \eqref{eq:pair-v-increments-orthogonal}, which implies
  \eqref{eq:pair-m-increments-orthogonal}, which implies
  \eqref{eq:pair-u-increments-orthogonal} with $\ell+1$ in place of $\ell$.
We therefore proceed with the inductive argument: 

\begin{itemize}
\item \eqref{eq:pair-u-increments-orthogonal} $\Rightarrow$
  \eqref{eq:pair-y-increments-orthogonal}: 
for this we use
the recursion \eqref{e:state.evol.x.y.increments.CHAOTIC}. Note that $w^{\ell-1}(\hat{\prxY}^{\ell-1})$ is measurable with respect to the $\sigma$-field $\cF^{\hat Y,\tilde Y,\hat{\prxY},\tilde{\prxY}}(\ell-1)$, which in turn is contained in the $\sigma$-field 
$\cF^{\hat U,\tilde U}(\ell-1)$. Therefore
  \[
  \bbE[\hat Y^{\ell}-\hat Y^{\ell-1}
    ~|~
    \cF^{\hat U,\tilde U}(\ell-1)]
  = \frac{w^{\ell-1}(\hat{R}^\eta\hat{\prxY}^{\ell-1}) }
    {\hat{\gamma}(\ell,\delta,\eta)}
  \E[\hat{U}^\ell-\hat{U}^{\ell-1}
  ~|~ \cF^{\hat U,\tilde U}(\ell-1)
  ]=0\,,
  \]
where the last step is by the inductive hypothesis \eqref{eq:pair-u-increments-orthogonal}. This implies
\eqref{eq:pair-y-increments-orthogonal}.

\item \eqref{eq:pair-y-increments-orthogonal} $\Rightarrow$ \eqref{eq:pair-v-increments-orthogonal}:
it follows from the state evolution definition that the random variables $\hat{V}^{\ell,k}$ and $\tilde{V}^{\ell,k}$ are jointly gaussian. Using the covariance formula \eqref{eq:state-evolution-setup}, for $0\le k\le s \le \ell-1$ we have
  \begin{align*}
  \E[(\hat{V}^{\ell,k}-\hat{V}^{\ell-1,k})
  \tilde{V}^{s,k}]
  &\stackrel{\eqref{eq:state-evolution-setup}}{=} \E\bigg[
   \Big(h_{\chaos,\ell,k}(\hat{U}[[\ell]])-
  h_{\chaos,\ell-1,k}
  (\hat{U}[[\ell-1]])
  \Big)
    h_{\chaos,s,k}
    (\tilde{U}[[s]])
    \bigg]\\
  &\stackrel{
  \eqref{e:f.h.l.k.explicit.CHAOTIC}
  }{=} (a_k)^2
  \E[(\hat{Y}^\ell-\hat{Y}^{\ell-1})
    \tilde{Y}^s]
  = 0\,,
  \end{align*}
where the last step is by the inductive hypothesis \eqref{eq:pair-y-increments-orthogonal}. A similar calculation gives the same identity but with $\hat{V}^{s,k}$ in place of $\tilde{V}^{s,k}$. Since the $V$ are jointly gaussian, this implies \eqref{eq:pair-v-increments-orthogonal}.

\item \eqref{eq:pair-v-increments-orthogonal} $\Rightarrow$ \eqref{eq:pair-m-increments-orthogonal}: this follows from the recursion \eqref{e:state.evol.x.y.increments.CHAOTIC}, by the same reasoning as for \eqref{eq:pair-u-increments-orthogonal} $\Rightarrow$ \eqref{eq:pair-y-increments-orthogonal} above.

\item
\eqref{eq:pair-m-increments-orthogonal}
$\Rightarrow$
\eqref{eq:pair-u-increments-orthogonal}:
this follows by similar reasoning as for
\eqref{eq:pair-y-increments-orthogonal}
$\Rightarrow$
\eqref{eq:pair-v-increments-orthogonal} above.
\end{itemize}
The above steps give one complete round of the induction, and the claim follows.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(X, Sigma, mu) is a measure space","f is Sigma-measurable","0 < p < infinity","for the general form: phi nondecreasing, absolutely continuous on compact subsets of [0, infinity), phi(0) = 0"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:36.552764+00:00","domain":"measure theory, Lp spaces","id":"claim_9e38ac0e8c4106fcc1e8205467e88e50a1fbd8020a43f3f60c9695127f1eb8c8","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, Sigma, mu) be a measure space, f measurable, and d_f(t) = mu({|f| > t}). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:51:26.730004+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9e422d4608cc0dee24fad17871092c60bbee41500f0d3abcf32ac100adefa6fc","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:blocks of arXiv:2606.08325, 'Digit Mixing under Polynomial Maps'] Fix integers \(d\ge2 , r\), and a positive real number $\beta>0$. 
			We define the functions
			$s :=\lfloor \beta n\rfloor+r$.
			and  $L:=\lfloor(\log n)^2\rfloor$.
			Given an integer $R$, we define the scale function
			$$H:= H(R) =\left\lfloor \frac{s}{L^R}\right\rfloor.$$
			Provided \(R=R(d)\) is chosen large enough, for
			all sufficiently large \(n\), there exist pairwise disjoint integer intervals
			\[ I_{j,k}\subset\mathbb N, \qquad 1\le j\le d,\quad 1\le k\le L,
			\]
			and an absolute constant $c_d$ (only depending on $d$)  with the following properties. \\	
			First, every \(i\in I_{j,k}\) satisfies
			\begin{equation}
				i\asymp_{\beta,d} n.
			\end{equation}
			Second, for each \(k\),
			\begin{equation}
				|\left\{(i_1,\ldots,i_d)\in I_{1,k}\times\cdots\times I_{d,k}:
				i_1+\cdots+i_d=s\right\}|
				\asymp_d H^{d-1}.
			\end{equation}
			Third, suppose that for every \(1\le k\le L\) one chooses a tuple
			$(i_{1,k},\ldots,i_{d,k}) \in I_{1,k}\times\cdots\times I_{d,k}$
			such that

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-12T06:09:38.198131+00:00","domain":"general topology","id":"claim_9e45874fad796149c5ac8f2b58760157b9ee22954ae7f56d86aa7e03bdd65509","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"For a subset A of a topological space X: the interior int(A) is the union of all open sets contained in A (the largest open set inside A); the closure cl(A) is the intersection of all closed sets containing A - which is closed, being an arbitrary intersection of closed sets, contains A, and lies inside every closed superset of A, hence is the smallest closed set containing A; the boundary is cl(A) minus int(A), equivalently cl(A) intersect cl(X\\A). Then A is open iff A = int(A) and closed iff A = cl(A). Point characterization: x is in cl(A) iff every open neighborhood of x meets A (if not, X\\cl(A) is an open neighborhood of x missing A; conversely a neighborhood U of x missing A makes X\\U a closed superset of A avoiding x). The closure operator satisfies the Kuratowski axioms - cl(empty)=empty, A subset of cl(A), cl(cl(A))=cl(A), cl(A union B)=cl(A) union cl(B) - and these four axioms on a set determine a unique topology whose closed sets are exactly the closure-fixed subsets.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.164817+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9e9fc1f22fbbd6aed0546c786bb0cc9eb865e002d311d3614d9fe68ef5df37cd","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 36 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] The following functions are $C_6$-Lipschitz, with $C_6 = 2/\iota$:
    \begin{enumerate}[(a)]
        \item  $z \mapsto m^{-1}(1/z)$, on $(0,+\infty)$.
        \item  $\gamma \mapsto g(\gamma^2)$, on $[0,+\infty)$.
        \item  $\gamma \mapsto \beta_\star(\gamma^2)$, on $[0,+\infty)$.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{proof}
    A routine calculation and application of Lemma~\ref{l:fp-m-fns-conversion} implies
    \[
        \frac{d}{dz} m^{-1}(1/z) = \frac{1/z^2}{m_2(m^{-1}(1/z))}
        \le \frac{1/z^2}{\iota / z^2} = \frac{1}{\iota}\,.
    \]
    This proves part~\eqref{i:fp-m-inv-lipschitz}.
    Since $m$ is strictly decreasing, and $\beta_\star \ge \beta_{
    \min}$, we also have, for $\gamma > 0$,
    \[
        \frac{d}{d\gamma} g(\gamma^2) 
        = 2\gamma m(\beta_\star(\gamma^2))
        \le 2\gamma m(\beta_{\min}(\gamma^2))
        = 2\gamma m(s_2(1/\gamma^2))
        \le \frac{2}{\iota^{1/2}}\,,
    \]
where the final inequality is by Lemma~\ref{l:fp-m-fns-conversion}.
This shows that $\gamma \mapsto g(\gamma^2)$ is $2/\iota^{1/2}$-Lipschitz on $(0,+\infty)$, and the estimate extends to $[0,+\infty)$ since $g$ was defined to be continuous on $[0,\infty)$ (see the comments below \eqref{e:freeprob.g.of.gamma}). 
    This proves part~\eqref{i:fp-g-sq-lipschitz}. For part~\eqref{i:fp-betast-sq-lipschitz}, it suffices to prove that the function
    \[
        \gamma \mapsto \beta_{\min}(\gamma^2)
        = s_2\bigg(\frac1{\gamma^2}\bigg)
    \]
    is $O(1)$-Lipschitz on $[0,+\infty)$. Similarly as above, a routine calculation and application of Lemma~\ref{l:fp-m-fns-conversion} shows that at any $\gamma > 0$, 
    \[
        \frac{d}{d\gamma} 
        s_2\bigg(\frac1{\gamma^2}\bigg)
        = \frac{1/\gamma^3}
            {m_3(s_2(1/\gamma^2))}
        \le \frac{1/\gamma^3}{\iota / \gamma^3}
        = \frac{1}{\iota}\,.
    \]
This shows that $\gamma \mapsto \beta_{\min}(\gamma^2)$ is $1/\iota$-Lipschitz on $(0,+\infty)$, and the estimate extends to $[0,+\infty)$ since the function $\beta_{\min}$ was defined to be continuous on $[0,\infty)$ (again we refer to the comments below \eqref{e:freeprob.g.of.gamma}). 
This proves part~\eqref{i:fp-betast-sq-lipschitz}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

By density the test class extends to phi in H^1(Omega) with compact support in Omega (phi >= 0 for the one-sided notions), and, when u in H^1(Omega) and f in L^2(Omega), to all phi in H^1_0(Omega) (nonnegative ones for the one-sided notions). If a^{ij} in C^1 and u in C^2, u is a weak solution iff it is a classical solution (integrate by parts). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:38:37.404623+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9f2d587caff488ee4b6cbc40da3bc5a5222c2231869c7d00bbf014685b39182a","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 17 of arXiv:2605.15501, 'Well-posedness of the obstacle problem for generalized Dean--Kawasaki equation\thanks{ The'] (Existence of solutions to the approximated penalized equation)
Let Assumption \ref{assu:assu for existence} and Assumption \ref{assu:assum for F} hold.
For $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\alpha,\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, there exists a solution $u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}$ of \eqref{eq:appro penalized eq}, defined on the original probability space $\Omega$, in the sense of Definition \ref{def:Weak solution approximating penalized}.
Furthermore, let $\chi_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}(x,\xi,t):=\mathbf{1}_{\{0<\xi<u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}(x,t)\}}$ be the kinetic function of $u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}$.
Then, $u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}$ satisfies that, almost surely for every $\phi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{d}\times(0,\infty)\times[0,T))$,
\begin{align}
& -\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\chi_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}(x,\xi,s)\partial_s\phi(x,\xi,s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}\xi\mathrm{d}s\\
 & =\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\bar{\chi}(u_{\mathrm{init}},\xi)\phi(x,\xi,0)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}\xi-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\Phi^{\prime}(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})\nabla_x u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}\cdot(\nabla_x\phi)(x,u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon},s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber \\
  & \quad-\alpha\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\nabla_{x}u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}\cdot(\nabla_{x}\phi)(x,u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon},s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber\\
 & \quad-\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\big(F_{1}(x)[\sigma_n^{\prime}(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})]^{2}\nabla_x u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}+\sigma_n(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})\sigma_n^{\prime}(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})F_{2}(x)\big)\cdot(\nabla_x\phi)(x,u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon},s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber\\
 & \quad-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\partial_{\xi}\phi(x,\xi,s)\mathrm{d}m_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}(x,\xi,s)-\int_0^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\phi(x,u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon},s)\nabla_x\cdot g(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber \\
 & \quad+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\Big(\sigma_n(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})\sigma_n^{\prime}(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})\nabla_x u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}\cdot F_{2}(x)+\sigma_n^{2}(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})F_{3}(x)\Big)(\partial_{\xi}\phi)(x,u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon},s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber \\
 & \quad-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\phi(x,u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon},s)\frac{1}{\varepsilon}(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}-\psi)^+\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\phi(x,u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon},s)\nabla_x\cdot(\sigma_n(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})f_{k})\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}B_{s}^{k},\nonumber
\end{align}
where the kinetic measure $m_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}$ is
\begin{align}\notag
m_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}&:=\delta_{0}(\xi-u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})\Big(\Phi^{\prime}(\xi)|\nabla u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}|^{2}+\alpha|\nabla u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}|^{2}\Big).
\end{align}
It follows from  (\ref{eq:priori}) that the $\{m_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}\}_{(\alpha,n)\in(0,1)\times\mathbb{N}}$ are finite kinetic measures.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:47.651277+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9f5a771b1ffe3a4acbf98295922ef93fd51f56c64993cc38d5117c6b2577103d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 2 of arXiv:2605.07050, 'Universality of the fluctuations of the free energy in generalized Sherrington--Kirkpatric'] Suppose that Assumption \ref{assump:decay} holds for $W$. Suppose that $\sqrt{N} x_k$  $(1 \leq k \leq N)$ are i.i.d., symmetric, and strictly sub-Gaussian random variables with variance $1$, independent of $W$. Define the likelihood ratios by
\beq
	 \caL(\SNR) := \E_\caX \left[ \prod_{i<j} \frac{p(\sqrt{N} W_{ij} - \sqrt{\SNR N} x_i x_j /\| \bsx \|^2)}{p(\sqrt{N} W_{ij})} \prod_k \frac{p_d(\sqrt{N} W_{kk} - \sqrt{\SNR N} x_k^2  /\| \bsx \|^2)}{p_d(\sqrt{N} W_{kk})} \right]
\eeq
and
\beq
	\ol \caL (\SNR) := \E_\caX \left[ \prod_{i<j} \frac{p(\sqrt{N} W_{ij} - \sqrt{\SNR N} x_i x_j)}{p(\sqrt{N} W_{ij})} \prod_k \frac{p_d(\sqrt{N} W_{kk} - \sqrt{\SNR N} x_k^2)}{p_d(\sqrt{N} W_{kk})} \right].
\eeq
Define
\[
	F_p:= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{(p'(x))^2}{p(x)} \dd x, \quad F_d:= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{(p_d'(x))^2}{p_d(x)} \dd x, \quad G_p:= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{(p''(x))^2}{p(x)} \dd x.
\]
Then, for any $\SNR \in (0, 1/F_p)$,
\[
	\log \caL(\SNR) \Rightarrow \caN(-\rho_L, 2\rho_L), \quad \log \ol \caL(\SNR) \Rightarrow \caN(-\rho_L, 2\rho_L),
\]
as $N \to \infty$, i.e., $\log \caL(\SNR)$ and $\log \ol\caL(\SNR)$ converge in distribution to the Gaussian with mean $-\rho_L$ and the variance $2\rho_L$ as $N \to \infty$, where
\[
	\rho_L:= -\frac{1}{4} \left( \log (1-\SNR F_p) + \SNR(F_p- 2F_d) + \frac{\SNR^2}{4} (2F_p^2 - G_p) \right).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.349925+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9f7133cf76bbe3c22618d5a11bf099dc0e39c448a3983850dae3d03d23b8a44c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 174 (eighth moment bounds for $X^{\Ising}$, $X^{\trunc,\Ising}$, and $X^{\frozen,\Ising}$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] The bound of Lemma~\ref{l:subgaus.X.II}
also holds with $X^{\Ising}$ in place of $X^{\RomII}$: for $N$ large enough, we have
	\[
	\E\bigg[\bigg(
	\sum_{\ell=a}^{b-1} 
	\Delta X^{\Ising}(q_d,
	{i(q_{d+1})})
	\bigg)^8\bigg]
	\le L^{O(1)} (q_b-q_a)^4
	\]
for all $0\le a\le b\le \dmax$. The same bound holds with 
$X^{\trunc,\Ising}$ or $X^{\Isplus}$ in place of $X^\Ising$. 

\begin{proof}
Recall from \eqref{e:Delta.X.Ising} that
	\[
	\Delta X^{\Ising}(q_d,i(q_{d+1}))
	= \sqrt{\delta_d}
	({\boldsymbol e}_i,\by(q_{d+1}))
	\]
where ${\boldsymbol e}_i$ is the $i$-th standard basis vector in $\R^N$.
The claim then follows essentially by the argument of Lemma~\ref{l:subgaus.X.II}, replacing $\bar{\bg}(q_d)/N^{1/2}$ with
${\boldsymbol e}_i$. (Moreover, since clearly $\|{\boldsymbol e}_i\|=1$, we can skip the step of restricting to the event that
$\|\bar{\bg}(q_d)\|$ is not atypically large.) It is straightforward to verify that the same argument applies with $X^{\trunc,\Ising}$ or $X^{\Isplus}$ in place of $X^\Ising$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:17:04.322866+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9f783b7c67d310c3d07d7f269bdbe98e95fe518fae819f01135ee0e55eb1d07d","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition symmetrized gap upper bound proposition of arXiv:2606.01683, 'Singular-value gap of nonreversible Markov processes'] Consider a jump process on a measurable space $S$ with generator (equation jump process generator of the paper)

{"assumptions":["All paired four-point model definitions and restrictions of C010","Noise-to-signal Walsh variance ratio rho>0 fixed as e decreases; actual noise standard deviation tends to zero","Width tends to infinity before feature scale decreases; nonlinear comparison is only through finite T_e for each fixed e","Clean risk averages over all sixteen training-label-noise sign patterns"],"created_at":"2026-10-22T00:34:45.041953+00:00","domain":"learning theory","id":"claim_9ffa636677134a5540e6a704a86f6f5fe37015b52ad2241f167a16f3bc581359","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"# Co-scaled noise phases: double descent versus preference for late stopping

T267 / Target 2 / C011 / proof draft (unaudited); novelty unestablished.
This is an asymptotic phase comparison in C010's restricted model, not
an exact finite-scale two-critical-noise-level theorem.

## 1. Model and statement

Keep the four-point design, unit-norm centered-ReLU teacher, paired
nonzero initialization and both-layer GD of BOUNDED_RELU_PAIRED.md.
Write alpha=alpha_e and replace label noise +/-2alpha by
+/-2alpha sqrt(rho), for any fixed rho>0. Thus the noise standard deviation
is c_e sqrt(rho), which tends to zero. Each Walsh noise variance is
rho alpha^2. Average clean risk over the sixteen noise patterns as before.
All width limits are over even widths m=2N, before e decreases to zero.

Let b_h be the full-kernel rates of C009, q_h=exp(-b_h), and define

K_e=ceil(e^(-3/2)), T_e=ceil(e^(-5/2)),
E(rho)=rho+2+rho/(1+rho),
L(rho)=2rho+2rho/(1+rho).

For small e, K_e<T_e. The following minima of the ACTUAL nonlinear risk
converge in probability in the iterated width-then-scale sense:

min_(0<=k<=K_e) Q_(m,e)(k)/alpha^2 -> min{3,E(rho)},
min_(K_e<=k<=T_e) Q_(m,e)(k)/alpha^2 -> L(rho),
min_(0<=k<=T_e) Q_(m,e)(k)/alpha^2 -> min{3,L(rho)}.

Here convergence means for every epsilon>0, lim_(e->0) limsup_(N->infinity)
P(absolute discrepancy>epsilon)=0. These statements do not control actual
nonlinear risk after T_e or exchange the two limits.

Moreover there are strict descent-rise-descent witnesses at every fixed
rho>0. With k0=ceil(e^(-1/2)),
k1=floor(log(1+1/rho)/b1), k2=K_e,
k3=floor(log(1+1/rho)/b2), their risks divided by alpha^2 converge to

rho+3, E(rho), 2rho+2, L(rho).

Their three limiting strict margins are
1/(1+rho), rho^2/(1+rho), 2/(1+rho).
For all fixed rho<1, the best risk in the late phase is strictly lower
than the best in the early phase with probability tending to one.
For all fixed rho>1, the early phase is strictly better. At rho=1 the
leading phase minima tie at 3; no finite-e ordering is asserted.

Thus rho=1 is the limiting late-versus-early preference boundary in this
model, whereas strict double descent survives on both sides. No lower
critical-noise rate or exact finite-e second threshold is established.

## 2. Exact frozen risk and nonlinear transfer

The frozen zero-output curve is

F_e(k)=Q_e^0(k)/alpha^2
      =rho(1-q0^k)^2
       +sum_(h=1,2,12)[q_h^(2k)+rho(1-q_h^k)^2].

This follows from Walsh Parseval, identical teacher coefficients alpha
and Walsh noise variances rho alpha^2. The paired initialization gives
zero output exactly. Let p_r(q)=q^2+rho(1-q)^2. Completing the square,

p_r(q)=(1+rho)(q-rho/(1+rho))^2+rho/(1+rho).

For each fixed e and rho the labels are bounded; indeed max|y_i| is at
most (3+2sqrt(rho))alpha, which tends to zero. For all sufficiently small
e the residual bound R_0=2 used in C010 is therefore valid. Its pairwise
finite-horizon transfer applies uniformly through T_e (a finite integer
for this fixed e), and over all noise patterns. It follows that

max_(k<=T_e)|Q_(m,e)(k)/alpha^2-F_e(k)| ->0 in probability as N->infinity.

For this step alpha^2 is a FIXED positive number; no uniform-in-e width
bound is inferred. Consequently it suffices to prove the deterministic
frozen limits for the two ranges and the four witnesses.

## 3. Early-phase minimum

At k=0, F_e=3 exactly. At
k1=floor(log(1+1/rho)/b1), the constant mode has learned, q1^k1 tends to
rho/(1+rho), and q2^k1,q12^k1 tend to one. Hence F_e(k1)->E(rho).
These give the upper bound min{3,E(rho)} for the limiting early minimum.

For the lower bound, take any sequence e->0 and early-phase integers
k_e<=K_e. Choose a subsequence such that k_e is bounded or tends to
infinity, and such that b1 k_e converges in [0,infinity].
If k_e is bounded, all nonconstant q_h^k_e tend to one, so liminf F_e>=3.
If k_e tends to infinity, q0^k_e tends to zero. Uniformly for k<=K_e,
b2 k and b12 k tend to zero, since b2 K_e=O(e^(1/2)). Thus the slow-mode
contribution tends to two, while the fast-mode contribution is at least
rho/(1+rho) by the exact completed square. The limit inferior is at least
E(rho), whether the fast scaled time is finite or infinite. This proves
the matching early lower bound. The subsequence argument applies to
minimizers, which exist because the integer range is finite.

## 4. Late-phase minimum

Uniformly for k>=K_e, q0^k and q1^k tend to zero, since b1 K_e tends to
infinity. Their combined risk tends to 2rho, uniformly in this range.
Each of the two slow contributions is bounded below by rho/(1+rho),
so the late minimum has limit inferior at least L(rho).
For k3=floor(log(1+1/rho)/b2), both slow q's tend to rho/(1+rho), because
b12/b2->1. Also K_e<k3<T_e for all small e, since b2 K_e->0 and
b2 T_e->infinity. Thus F_e(k3)->L(rho), proving the matching upper bound.
Combining Sections 3-4 gives the full finite-horizon minimum as
min{3,E(rho),L(rho)}. The simplification in Section 6 proves the stated
min{3,L(rho)} form.

## 5. Strict double-descent witnesses

At k0 all nonconstant modes remain at one and the constant noise mode
has saturated, so F_e(k0)->rho+3. At k1 the limit is E(rho).
At K_e fast q1 tends to zero and the slow q's to one, giving 2rho+2.
At k3 the limit is L(rho). Subtraction gives exactly the three positive
margins in Section 1. This applies to every fixed rho>0, including rho>1.
The strict finite-e margins transfer to nonlinear GD by Section 2.

For rho=0 the frozen curve is sum_(h=1,2,12)q_h^(2k), strictly decreasing.
This zero-noise frozen statement does not imply monotonic actual nonlinear
risk for all times, nor locate a finite-e onset as rho_e tends to zero.
Pointwise positive-rho results must not be promoted to such a uniform
noise-window theorem.

## 6. Which phase wins?

Exact subtraction yields

E(rho)-L(rho)=(2-rho^2)/(1+rho),
L(rho)-3=(rho-1)(2rho+3)/(1+rho).

If 0<rho<1, then L<3 and L<E, so late training beats the entire early
phase, not just its fast-mode stationary point. If rho>1, then L>3,
so the early phase containing k=0 beats the late phase. Also E>3 for
rho>1, since E-3=(rho^2+rho-1)/(1+rho)>0. Consequently the overall
minimum is min{3,L}. At rho=1 the leading early and late values both
are 3, so a finer expansion is needed to decide finite-scale ordering.

Comparing ONLY E and L would instead produce sqrt(2). That would be the
wrong early-stopping boundary because it omits the allowed initialization
time k=0. This is why the early-phase minimization includes every time
from zero rather than only the first fast-signal minimum. The tiny initial
transient may shift the finite-e preference threshold; it does not change
these strict comparisons for rho bounded away from one.

## Scope and source distinction

Stephenson--Lee, arXiv:2108.12006, Section4, EDD-NES/EDD-ES phases and
P3/P4, distinguish onset of double descent from the higher noise level
where early stopping is preferable. This source does not supply this
model's threshold. Our computation is self-contained and restricted to
the paired four-point model. The lower onset at finite scale, its rate,
a full two-threshold window, iid Gaussian inputs, fixed-positive-noise
unit-teacher dynamics, high probability over label noise, and actual
nonlinear convergence after T_e remain open. Mathematical and novelty
review are pending; no independent audit or full Target2 solution.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:38:37.403908+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a05a99961fccd76be10f8880990fae2a96c0e5a9c99ef183629288be063edf33","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 11 of arXiv:2605.15501, 'Well-posedness of the obstacle problem for generalized Dean--Kawasaki equation\thanks{ The'] For fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, a stochastic kinetic

\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] Preservation of mass: almost surely for every $\phi\in C_c^{\infty}([0,T))$,
\begin{align}
    -\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d} u_\varepsilon\partial_s\phi(s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s+\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\phi(s)\varepsilon^{-1}(u_\varepsilon-\psi)^{+}\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s=\int_{\mathbb{T}^d} u_{\mathrm{init}}\phi(0)\mathrm{d}x
\end{align}
\item[(ii)] $\sigma(u_\varepsilon)\in L^{2}(\Omega;L^{2}(Q_T))$,\quad $g(u_\varepsilon)\in L^{1}(\Omega;L^{1}(Q_T;\mathbb{R}^d))$.
\item[(iii)] For every $K\in\mathbb{N}$,
\[
[(u_\varepsilon\land K)\lor(1/K)]\in L^{2}(\Omega\times[0,T];H^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{d}))).
\]
Furthermore, there exists a kinetic measure $m_\varepsilon$ satisfying the following properties.
\item[(iv)] Almost surely as a nonnegative measure, $m_\varepsilon$ satisfies
\[
\delta_{0}(\xi-u_\varepsilon)\Phi^{\prime}(\xi)|\nabla u_\varepsilon|^{2}\leq m_\varepsilon\quad\text{on}\quad\mathbb{T}^{d}\times(0,\infty)\times[0,T].
\]
\item[(v)] (Vanishing)
\[
\lim_{N\to\infty}\mathbb{E}\big[m_\varepsilon(\mathbb{T}^{d}\times[N,N+1]\times[0,T))\big]=0.
\]
\item[(vi)] Preservation of energy: for every $\phi\in C_c^{\infty}([0,T))$,
\begin{align}
&-\mathbb{E}\int_0^T\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}u_\varepsilon^2(x,s)\partial_s\phi(s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s+\frac{2}{\varepsilon}\mathbb{E}\int_0^T\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\phi(s)\psi(x,s)(u_\varepsilon-\psi)^+\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\\
&+\frac{2}{\varepsilon}\mathbb{E}\int_0^T\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\phi(s)|(u_\varepsilon-\psi)^+|^2\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s+2\mathbb{E}\int_0^T\phi(s)\mathrm{d}m_\varepsilon(\mathbb{T}^d,[0,\infty),s)\nonumber\\
&=\mathbb{E}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}u^2_{\mathrm{init}}(x)\phi(0)\mathrm{d}x-\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\phi(s)\sigma^2(u_{\varepsilon})(\nabla_{x}\cdot F_{2}-2F_3)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s.\nonumber
\end{align}
\item[(vii)] For every $\phi\in C_{c}^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{d}\times(0,\infty)\times[0,T))$, the kinetic function $\chi_\varepsilon$ of $u_\varepsilon$ almost surely satisfies
\begin{align}
& -\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\chi_\varepsilon(x,\xi,s)\partial_s\phi(x,\xi,s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}\xi\mathrm{d}s\\
 & =\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\bar{\chi}(u_{\mathrm{init}},\xi)\phi(x,\xi,0)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}\xi-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\Phi^{\prime}(u_\varepsilon)\nabla_x u_\varepsilon\cdot(\nabla_x\phi)(x,u_\varepsilon,s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber \\
 & \quad-\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\big(F_{1}(x)[\sigma^{\prime}(u_\varepsilon)]^{2}\nabla_x u_\varepsilon+\sigma(u_\varepsilon)\sigma^{\prime}(u_\varepsilon)F_{2}(x)\big)\cdot(\nabla_x\phi)(x,u_\varepsilon,s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber\\
 & \quad-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\partial_{\xi}\phi(x,\xi,s)\mathrm{d}m_\varepsilon(x,\xi,s)-\int_0^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\phi(x,u_\varepsilon,s)\nabla_x\cdot g(u_\varepsilon)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber \\
 & \quad+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\Big(\sigma(u_\varepsilon)\sigma^{\prime}(u_\varepsilon)\nabla_x u_\varepsilon\cdot F_{2}(x)+\sigma^{2}(u_\varepsilon)F_{3}(x)\Big)(\partial_{\xi}\phi)(x,u_\varepsilon,s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber \\
 
 & \quad-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\phi(x,u_\varepsilon,s)\frac{1}{\varepsilon}(u_\varepsilon-\psi)^+\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\phi(x,u_\varepsilon,s)\nabla_x\cdot(\sigma(u_\varepsilon)f_{k})\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}B_{s}^{k}.\nonumber
\end{align}
\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:34:33.542748+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a066ca5a723bc272ac6d47762feb4e1ceb7b51afdba3eef74716a5638a577e0e","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 16 (Factor of i.i.d.) of arXiv:2603.28734, 'Free energy analyticity of the disordered XY model and Debye screening in the 2D Coulomb g'] Consider a locally finite transitive graph $G=(V,E)$
    (with respect to some group $\Theta\subset\operatorname{Aut}(G)$).
    Let $S$ denote a measurable space,
    and let $\mu$ denote the distribution of a $\Theta$-stationary random field on $S^V$.
    Let $(T,\lambda)$ denote a probability space, and consider $\P:=\lambda^V$.
    A \emph{factor of i.i.d.}\ (FIID) is a map $\phi:T^V\to S^V$
    with the following properties:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\phi$ is measurable with respect to the product $\sigma$-algebras on $T^V$ and $S^V$,
        \item $\phi$ is equivariant with respect to $\Theta$,
        \item If $X\sim\P$, then $\phi(X)\sim\mu$.
    \end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:57:07.195470+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a07189e4565bb2e03cc6c8ca76610f610b0d06d46c1290d122574b7a11b44785","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:gamma of arXiv:2509.04333, 'The limiting law of the Discrete Gaussian level lines'] Let $\\phi$ be a\n\t\t$\\mathbb Z$-valued height function on the vertices of a connected domain $V\\subset \\mathbb Z^2$. Associate to each bond $e\\in (\\mathbb Z^2)^*$, dual to some edge $(x,y)\\in\\mathbb Z^2$, the gradient $(\\nabla \\phi)_e := \\phi_x - \\phi_y$, where $x$ is taken to be the \\textsc{north} vertex if $(x,y)$ is vertical and the \\textsc{west} vertex if $(x,y)$ is horizontal. We say the bond $e$ is a \\emph{disagreement bond} of $\\phi$ if $(\\nabla\\phi)_e\\neq 0$ (including when $\\phi_x$ or $\\phi_y$ are specified by the boundary conditions). A \\emph{disagreement polymer}~$\\gamma$ is a (maximal) connected component of the disagreement bonds of $\\phi$, and we let $\\ensuremath{\\mathcal P}_\\phi$ denote the disagreement polymers in $\\phi$. Call the triple $(\\gamma, \\{D_i\\}, \\{h_i\\})$ a \\emph{labeled disagreement polymer}. For brevity,  we denote labeled disagreement polymers by $\\gamma$ (omitting the $\\{h_i\\}$ from the notation).","status":"unverified"}

orthonormal basis of $W=\mathfrak{so}(n)$, and put $A_i=\operatorname{ad}_{a_i}$.
Define
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathcal R_i(X,Z)&=\{X,[A_i,Z]\}a_i,&
 U_i(X,Z)&=\{X,Z\}a_i,\\
 E_i(X,Z)&=\{[A_i,X],Z\}a_i,&
 \bar E(X,Z)&=\frac1N\sum_iE_i(X,Z).
\end{aligned}
\tag{3.2.10a}
\]
Put $\Psi(T)=\sum_jA_jTa_j$.  Then, with no projection onto curvature
summands,
\[
 \mathcal R_i=A_iU_i-(E_i-\bar E)-\bar E,
 \qquad
 \bar E=\frac1N\sum_jA_jV_j+H(X,Z),\qquad V_j=XZa_j,
\tag{3.2.10b}
\]
where
\[
 H(X,Z)=\frac1N\{-X\Psi(Z)+Z\Psi(X)\}.
\tag{3.2.10b$'$}
\]
Moreover, writing $\|\cdot\|_2$ for Hilbert--Schmidt norm,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \frac1N\sum_i\|U_i\|^2
 &\le\frac4N\|X\|_2^2\|Z\|_\mathrm{op}^2,\\
 \frac1N\sum_j\|V_j\|^2
 &\le\frac1N\|X\|_2^2\|Z\|_\mathrm{op}^2,\\
 \frac1N\sum_i\|E_i-\bar E\|^2
 &\le\frac{16(n-2)}N\|X\|_2^2\|Z\|_\mathrm{op}^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{3.2.10c}
\]
The residue satisfies
\[
 \|H(X,Z)\|
 \le\frac{\sqrt{n-2}}N
 \bigl(\|X\|_\mathrm{op}\|Z\|_2+\|Z\|_\mathrm{op}\|X\|_2\bigr).
\tag{3.2.10e}
\]
If $X$ and $Z$ are symmetric, then $\Psi(X)=\Psi(Z)=0$, so $H=0$.
The identities and estimates remain valid when all maps are tensored by
an ancillary identity and the Hilbert--Schmidt norm is taken on the
amplified space.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["g a norm on R^2, even in the transversal coordinate"],"created_at":"2026-08-10T03:39:47.000000+00:00","domain":"convex geometry / first-passage percolation limit shapes","id":"claim_a12c2b183a67ea70d9e183fc859334195570a83942c6e5d103a55a95913d7a60","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let g be a norm on R^2 that is even in the first coordinate (g(-h, m) = g(h, m)), as every lattice-symmetric FPP limit-shape norm is. For fixed m, the map h -> g((h, m)) is even and convex, hence minimized at h = 0, so g((h, m)) >= g((0, m)) = |m| g(e_2). Consequently, for a dogleg from (0,0) through v = (h, j) to (0, r) with j = r + m, m > 0 (longitudinal overshoot past the far endpoint): g(v) + g((0,r) - v) - g((0,r)) >= (r + m) g(e_2) + m g(e_2) - r g(e_2) = 2 m g(e_2), and symmetrically for j = -m < 0. The dogleg excess grows at least LINEARLY in the overshoot, with the explicit constant 2 g(e_2), using convexity and symmetry alone - no curvature hypothesis of any kind. The bound is tight as h -> 0. Use: in localization arguments it kills union sites with longitudinal overshoot at a rate no curvature assumption needs to fund, letting curvature windows be quoted only where they are literally assumed. Numerical attack: 0 violations in 300,000 trials on an anisotropic convex norm, worst ratio 1.000019.","status":"derived_in_campaign_refereed"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:12:19.465306+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a17b601a05c2305dc15605532bfd096306cc24f9e9ae6a44baf32f4ec9a06b4b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 24 (Uniform convergence in probability) of arXiv:2608.17540, 'Pathwise stability for one-dimensional SDEs driven by Brownian motion and a symmetric stab'] Assume Assumptions~\ref{ass:baseline}--\ref{ass:solutions} and suppose $B,A,S<1$. Then there exists a constant $C>0$, independent of $h$, such that, for every $h>0$, if $\wt\eta\in(1/\alpha,1]$, then
\[
\Pbb\left(\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t-\wt X_t|^{\alpha-1}>h\right)
\le \frac{C}{h}\left[|x_0-\wt x_0|^{\alpha-1}
+\max\left\{
B^{\frac{\alpha\wt\eta-1}{\alpha\wt\eta-\alpha+1}},
A^{\frac{2(\alpha\wt\eta-1)}{\alpha\wt\eta-\alpha+2}},
S^{\alpha-1/\wt\eta}
\right\}\right].
\]
If $\wt\eta=1/\alpha$ and $\Theta=\max\{B,A,S\}\in(0,1)$, then
\[
\Pbb\left(\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t-\wt X_t|^{\alpha-1}>h\right)
\le \frac{C}{h}\left[|x_0-\wt x_0|^{\alpha-1}
+\left(\log\frac1\Theta\right)^{-1}\right].
\]
When $\Theta=0$, the right-hand side is interpreted as $C|x_0-\wt x_0|^{\alpha-1}/h$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:40:27.002426+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a1c23893a74f716fa52a5e6cb22597c721bec0b82d07cbeeabf6c4524271b20f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition of arXiv:2604.17253, 'Large Deviations for the Nonlinear Schrödinger Equation with Randomized Quasi-Periodic Ini'] The domain ${\mathrm D}^{(k,\gamma^{(k)})}$ admits a canonical identification with
\begin{align*}
{\mathscr D}^{(k,\gamma^{(k)})}=
\begin{cases}
\prod_{j=1}^d \mathbb{Z}^{\nu_j}, & \gamma^{(k)}=0,\ k\ge1;\\
\prod_{j=1}^d (\mathbb{Z}^{\nu_j})^3, & \gamma^{(1)}=1;\\
\prod_{j=1}^3 {\mathscr D}^{(k-1,\gamma_j^{(k-1)})}, & \gamma^{(k)}\in(\Gamma^{(k-1)})^3,\ k\ge2.
\end{cases}
\end{align*}
This identification is induced by coordinate-wise projection.

More precisely, for each $j=1,\dots,d$, we define the projection
\[
\iota_{x_j}:\left(\prod_{j=1}^d \mathbb{Z}^{\nu_j}\right)^s \to (\mathbb{Z}^{\nu_j})^s,
\quad
\iota_{x_j}\big((q_1^1,\dots,q_d^1),\dots,(q_1^s,\dots,q_d^s)\big)

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:25:06.154978+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a1e9b69ec562f848d9dbf92e1162e06410972cdaa65fb2afd9610ce9656eda79","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 12 (Kneser) of arXiv:2608.22534, 'Entropy power inequalities in compact groups'] Let $A,B$ be subsets of a locally compact, abelian group $G$ and let $\mu$ 
denote (a version of) the Haar measure on $G$. If there exists an open 
subgroup $H$ such that 
$$
A+B+H=A+B \quad\text{and}\quad \mu(A+B+H) = \mu(A+H) + \mu(B+H)-\mu(H),
$$
then 
$$
\mu(A+B) \geq \mu(A)+\mu(B)-\mu(H).
$$
Otherwise, 
$$
\mu^*(A+B) \geq \mu(A)+\mu(B),
$$
where $\mu^*$ denotes the inner measure induced by $\mu$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["n,L,M,D positive integers; D'>=0; B,R>0; B_y>=1; 0<xi<1","The n pretraining instances are iid from the same meta-distribution and the query label is bounded by B_y","Normalized ReLU attention, residual ReLU MLP, input and hidden-token Euclidean projection at radius R, and prediction clipping at B_y","The specified transformer parameter norm is at most B and hat theta is an exact constrained empirical risk minimizer"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T15:33:17.892015+00:00","domain":"transformer generalization; pretraining; in-context learning","id":"claim_a2089af688f2246e22d6df8c528ce0527f4e59ab5605bc65d29b77cbe833c673","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Choose positive integers n,L,M,D and D'>=0, parameter bound B>0, token clipping radius R>0, a label bound B_y>=1, and confidence 0<xi<1. A transformer has L residual blocks, each consisting of normalized ReLU attention followed by a residual two-layer ReLU MLP; it has token dimension D, at most M attention heads per block, and MLP hidden width at most D'. For S tokens, attention sends h_i to h_i+(1/S) sum_m sum_j ReLU(<Q_m h_i,K_m h_j>) V_m h_j. The MLP sends h to h+W_2 ReLU(W_1 h). Project every input token and every block's output token onto the Euclidean radius-R ball. Read out the designated label coordinate of the final query token and clip it to [-B_y,B_y]. {"assumptions":["weights in [a,b], a > 0","nearest-neighbour lattice paths"],"created_at":"2026-08-10T02:29:08.000000+00:00","domain":"probability (first-passage percolation)","id":"claim_a20ea460b9385928f93a270c12abee9681fa07dacff1bba16272f9d26d17697d","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"In first-passage percolation on Z^2 with edge weights confined to [a, b] with a > 0, any geodesic from the origin to (0, r) satisfies a DETERMINISTIC bound on its transversal excursion: it never attains transversal level D > r(b - a)/(2a). {"assumptions":["Allen-Cahn on the 1-d torus with 1-d quadratic noise, critical gamma^2 = 2","deterministic constant initial data u_0 = a > 0"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:11:19.448302+00:00","domain":"stochastic partial differential equations, critical spaces","id":"claim_a215289259f9cccbe1cb7c19d537e22e0c0239f3b17a21caf7771d147f98140b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Agresti and Veraar, Nonlinear parabolic stochastic evolution equations in critical spaces (journal version 2025, p. 130), Problem 4 asks whether in the variational setting of their Theorem 6.4 there is a constant C_T with E sup_{t <= T} ||u(t)||_H^2 <= C_T (1 + E ||u_0||_H^2) for all u_0 in L^2(Omega; H). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:31:02.815831+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a2166a98ab376a45c0d5df2ab5b5538d1c7067d53f83ae87c0936aa4c267691f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary cor:iterated-suspension of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Let $t\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}$ and put $A^{(0)}=A$.  For each $1\leq i\leq t$, choose an

\begin{align}
 \mathcal H_{A^{(t)}}(z)
 &=\mathcal H_A(z)\prod_{i=1}^t[\ell_i]_z,

 \\
 \operatorname{ndiam}(A^{(t)})&=R\operatorname{ndiam}(A).

If every $\ell_i\leq q$, then
\[
 r_q(A^{(t)})=r_q(A)+t,\qquad

If the starting projective coordinate ring is ACM, then the ACM property

{"assumptions":["(H_n) predictable: H_n is F_{n-1}-measurable","boundedness of H_n, or integrability of each H_n (X_n - X_{n-1})","for the supermartingale/submartingale versions: H_n >= 0"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.627067+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a26f5d17686c1e295dc0e7eed296742f44e2d3fbf07ead7842c7484b505a8f62","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X_n) be a martingale for (F_n) and let (H_n)_{n >= 1} be PREDICTABLE, meaning H_n is F_{n-1}-measurable. Define the transform (H . X)_n = sum_{k=1}^{n} H_k (X_k - X_{k-1}), with (H . X)_0 = 0. If each H_n is bounded (or, more generally, if H_n (X_n - X_{n-1}) is integrable for every n), then (H . X) is a martingale. If (X_n) is a SUPERMARTINGALE and in addition H_n >= 0 for every n, then (H . X) is a supermartingale; the same with submartingale. Predictability is the load-bearing hypothesis: H_n may depend on everything known strictly before time n but not on the outcome at time n. Without it the conclusion is false - taking H_n = sgn(X_n - X_{n-1}) gives (H . X)_n = sum |X_k - X_{k-1}|, which is nondecreasing and not a martingale unless the increments vanish. The nonnegativity requirement in the supermartingale case is also necessary, since multiplying by -1 turns a supermartingale into a submartingale. [standard; e.g. Williams, Probability with Martingales, Section 10.6]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:11:09.318165+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a2a0a49c4b2f8417ae837c75976b2291342732fc1d238860a6fcc3f6e736ddb1","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:from-r-to-l of arXiv:2411.06195, 'Restrictions of some reinforced processes to subgraphs'] Let the graph $G$ be finite and take $0\le l\le r$. We endow the subdivided graph $G_r$
  with i.i.d.\ edge weights $W_e>0$, $e\in E_r$. Consider the family $W^{(l)}$ of
  corresponding random weights
from Theorem (thm:vrjp-on-G-r-pos-rec of the paper), all realized on the same probability space
with expectation operator ${\mathbb E}$. We abbreviate
$C_\alpha:=2^{-\alpha}\Gamma(\tfrac12-\alpha)/\sqrt{\pi}$
for $0\le\alpha<\frac12$ and ${c_2}:=\gamma+\log 2=1.27036\ldots$, where 
\begin{align}
  
  \gamma=-\int_0^\infty e^{-t}\log t\, dt=0.57721\ldots
\end{align}
denotes the Euler Mascheroni constant. 
For all $\bar e\in E_l$ and $e'\in E_r$, one has
  \begin{align}
    
    {\mathbb E}[(W^{(l)}_{\bar e})^\alpha]
    &\le (2^{-\alpha})^{r-l}{\mathbb E}[W_{e'}^\alpha]
    &\hspace{-1cm}\text{ for } \alpha\in[0,1],\\
    
    {\mathbb E}[(W^{(l)}_{\bar e})^\alpha]
     &\le \frac{1}{C_\alpha}\min_{m\in\{l,\ldots,r\}}\left(C_\alpha 
       (2^{-\alpha})^{r-m}{\mathbb E}[W_{e'}^\alpha]\right)^{2^{m-l}}
     &\hspace{-1cm}\text{ for } \alpha\in[0,\tfrac12),
    \\
      
    {\mathbb E}[\log W^{(l)}_{\bar e}]
    &\le \min_{m\in\{l,\ldots,r\}}
      2^{m-l}\left({\mathbb E}[\log W_{e'}]-(r-m)\log 2+{c_2}\right)-{c_2}.
  \end{align}
  Set $m_0:=r-2-\lfloor\alpha^{-1}\log_2(C_\alpha {\mathbb E}[W_{e'}^\alpha])\rfloor$
  and $m_1:=r-2-\lfloor(\log 2)^{-1}({\mathbb E}[\log W_{e'}]+{c_2})\rfloor$.
  If $m_0\in\{l,\ldots,r\}$, a minimizer in (equation eq:combined-alpha of the paper)
  is given by $m=m_0$. If $m_0<l$ or $m_0>r$, it is given by
  $m=l$ or $m=r$, respectively. The analogous statement holds for $m_1$
  with (equation eq:combined-alpha of the paper) replaced by (equation eq:combined-log of the paper). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["phi is continuous on the unit circle (for merely bounded measurable symbols the criterion is different)","T_phi acts on the Hardy space H^2 of the circle","the winding number is that of the curve phi about 0, defined because phi is nonvanishing"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.573131+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, Toeplitz operators, index theory","id":"claim_a336e41f1363f4a04acdf30204d079af81761e9aab33543cfff3898ac6f7532f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let H^2 be the Hardy space of the unit circle T, realised as the closed subspace of L^2(T) spanned by the exponentials z^n with n >= 0, and let P: L^2(T) -> H^2 be the orthogonal projection. For a continuous symbol phi in C(T) define the Toeplitz operator T_phi on H^2 by T_phi f = P(phi f); the bound ||T_phi|| <= ||phi||_infinity is immediate from ||P|| = 1, and in fact ||T_phi|| = ||phi||_infinity. Then T_phi is Fredholm if and only if phi has no zero on T, and in that case ind T_phi = - wind(phi), the negative of the winding number of the closed curve phi about the origin. In particular T_phi is invertible if and only if phi is nonvanishing with winding number 0, and a Fredholm Toeplitz operator with continuous symbol is never invertible when its winding number is nonzero, even though it may be injective or surjective.","status":"unverified"}

\begin{proof}

    Consider any $\mu \in \cM^{\Lip,\chaos}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)$ (recall \eqref{e:cM.Lip.0.chaos}), where $L$ is sufficiently large depending on $\alpha,\epsilon$.
    There exists a sequence of $L$-Lipschitz $((\cA_{N_j})^\circ)_{j\ge 1}$ such that
    \[
    \WERR((\cA_{N_j})^\circ,\mu)
    =
        \max\bigg\{
            \bbW_2\Big(\mu((\cA_{N_j})^\circ), \mu\Big),
            \bbW_2\Big(\mu^{\Ising}((\cA_{N_j})^\circ), \cP(\{\pm 1\})\Big)
        \bigg\} \le \epsilon\,,
    \]
    and the correlation functions $\chi_{(\cA_{N_j})^\circ}$ satisfy $\lim_{j\to\infty} \chi_{(\cA_{N_j})^\circ}(0) = 0$ and
    \beq
        
        \chi_{\cA_{N_j}^\circ}(1-\epsilon) \le \epsilon\,.
    \eeq
    That is, we have the same information about the algorithms $((\cA_{N_j})^\circ)_{j\ge 1}$ as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:Lip.in.BOGP} (instantiated with $q_0 = 0$), and in addition the estimate \eqref{e:Lip.in.BOGP.sym.chaos}.
    For $\cA_{N_j}$ the perturbation of $(\cA_{N_j})^\circ$ given by Proposition~\ref{p:wlogable},  the estimate \eqref{e:Lip.in.BOGP.sym.chaos} implies
    \[

        = \bigg(1-\frac{1}{L^2}\bigg) \chi_{\cA_{N_j}^\circ}(1-\epsilon)
        + \frac{1-\epsilon}{L^2} 
        \le \bigg(1-\frac{1}{L^2}\bigg) \epsilon + \frac{1-\epsilon}{L^2} 
        \le 2\epsilon\,,

        \subseteq \cB_{\hat\epsilon}\Big(
            \cM^{\BOGP,\chaos}(\alpha,0;\tilde C(L),\hat\epsilon)
        \Big)\,.
    \]
    Taking a union in $L$ and intersection in $\epsilon$, and applying $\sym$ to both sides, shows
    \begin{align*}

        \bigcap_{\epsilon > 0} \bigcup_{L>0}

        \Big)
        \stackrel{\eqref{e:measure.classes.sym.cM}}{=} \sM^{\BOGP,\sym}(\alpha,0)\,.

{"assumptions":["functions are smooth and complex-valued on R^d"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:39.262238+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis and distribution theory","id":"claim_a3e4ba3ae35124d3df8338899c6caae2cb3b9e9058c11269d43533b68c3fc893","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"The Schwartz space $\\mathcal S(\\mathbb R^d)$ is the set of $f\\in C^\\infty(\\mathbb R^d;\\mathbb C)$ such that $p_{\\alpha,\\beta}(f)=\\sup_{x\\in\\mathbb R^d}|x^\\alpha\\partial^\\beta f(x)|<\\infty$ for all multi-indices $\\alpha,\\beta$. With the countable family of seminorms $p_{\\alpha,\\beta}$ it is a Frechet space. It contains $C_c^\\infty(\\mathbb R^d)$ and the Gaussians $e^{-\\pi a|x|^2}$ ($a>0$); it is contained in $L^p(\\mathbb R^d)$ for every $1\\le p\\le\\infty$, is dense in $L^p$ for $1\\le p<\\infty$, and is closed under multiplication by polynomials, differentiation, products and convolution. Its continuous dual $\\mathcal S'(\\mathbb R^d)$ is the space of tempered distributions; the Fourier transform extends to $\\mathcal S'$ by $\\langle\\hat T,\\varphi\\rangle=\\langle T,\\hat\\varphi\\rangle$, which is consistent with the integral definition on $L^1$ and with Plancherel on $L^2$. Note $C_c^\\infty$ is not closed under the Fourier transform (a nonzero compactly supported function has a transform that is not compactly supported), while $\\mathcal S$ is.","status":"unverified"}

 such that

The minimum-variance weights subject to $\\mathbf{1}^T w = 1$ are $w^* = \\Sigma^{-1}\\mathbf{1} / (\\mathbf{1}^T \\Sigma^{-1}\\mathbf{1})$ with risk $R^* = w^{*T}\\Sigma w^* = 1/(\\mathbf{1}^T \\Sigma^{-1}\\mathbf{1})$. In the limit $M, n \\to \\infty$ with $q = M/n \\in (0, 1)$: (i) the true (out-of-sample) risk of the plug-in portfolio satisfies $\\hat w^T \\Sigma \\hat w / R^* \\to \\frac{1}{1 - q}$; (ii) the in-sample risk $\\hat w^T S \\hat w / R^* \\to 1 - q$; so the realized risk exceeds the optimum by the factor $1/(1-q)$ while the naive in-sample estimate understates the optimum by the factor $1 - q$, the two differing by $1/(1-q)^2$. {"assumptions":["A Hermitian (symmetric in the real case)","positive definite for existence with a strictly positive diagonal and for uniqueness"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:31:12.479375+00:00","domain":"numerical linear algebra","id":"claim_a456a3e325bc76743808041802880a3b7d0b3e39a7260821e678465f0bff4aaf","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"A Hermitian matrix A in C^{n x n} is positive definite if and only if it can be written as A = L L^* with L lower triangular having strictly positive real diagonal entries; when it exists this factorisation is unique. For real symmetric positive definite A the factor L is real, A = L L^T. Equivalently A = R^* R with R = L^* upper triangular. The factor is computed by the Cholesky algorithm in n^3 / 3 flops (half the cost of LU, no pivoting needed): for j = 1..n, l_jj = sqrt(a_jj - sum_{k<j} |l_jk|^2) and l_ij = (a_ij - sum_{k<j} l_ik conj(l_jk)) / l_jj for i > j; the algorithm is backward stable (Wilkinson), and it fails - a nonpositive quantity under the square root - exactly when A is not positive definite, which makes it the standard numerical test of positive definiteness. For positive semidefinite A a factorisation A = L L^* with nonnegative diagonal still exists but is no longer unique. Uses: solving A x = b by two triangular solves, sampling Gaussian vectors with covariance A (x = mu + L z), least squares via the normal equations, and the Kalman filter.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:12:19.465515+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a45a72bfc64e74cfef4e08b50d6102d0cbcdff0f7d9df796c17622d71b8bde30","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 26 (Coefficient approximation) of arXiv:2608.17540, 'Pathwise stability for one-dimensional SDEs driven by Brownian motion and a symmetric stab'] Let $X$ solve the baseline equation \eqref{eq:X}. Suppose that $X^{(n)}$ solves
\[
X_t^{(n)}=x_0^{(n)}+\int_0^t b_n(X_s^{(n)})\dd s
+\int_0^t a_n(X_s^{(n)})\dd W_s
+\int_0^t \sigma_n(X_{s-}^{(n)})\dd Z_s.

Assume that there exist common constants $L_b,L_a,L_\sigma$ and exponents $\eta_n\in[\wt\eta,1]$, with $\wt\eta\in[1/\alpha,1]$, such that for all $n$ and all $x,y\in\R$,
\[
|b_n(x)-b_n(y)|\le L_b|x-y|,
\qquad
|a_n(x)-a_n(y)|\le L_a|x-y|,
\]
and
\[

Then the family satisfies Assumption~\ref{ass:perturbed} uniformly with exponent $\wt\eta$. Define
\begin{align*}

Suppose that $B_n,A_n,S_n\to0$ and $x_0^{(n)}\to x_0$. Then

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:07:35.022614+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a4a66c5ef2226c51ee2d48c031c804bf32596f1676b64aa001aab18fe4e7a945","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 56 of arXiv:2609.02878, '2609.02878'] Let \(U\subset Y^{\rm rv}\) be a Zariski-open product region.  Suppose
\[
 q_i\longrightarrow q_\infty\in U,
 \qquad x_i\in F_{q_i},
 \qquad t_i\nearrow T.
\]
Set \(\tau_i=T-t_i\) and assume that
\begin{equation}
             \tau_i|\Rm(g(t_i))|_{g(t_i)}(x_i)\longrightarrow\infty.
\end{equation}
Choose nested coordinate sets
\[
 q_\infty\in V_0\Subset V_a\Subset V_b\Subset V\Subset U
\]
and holomorphic coordinates \(w=(w^1,\ldots,w^m)\) on \(V\).  After
discarding finitely many terms, assume that \(q_i\in V_0\).

Then there are \(\sigma_j\searrow0\) and a subsequence
\(i(j)\nearrow\infty\) such that the pointed flows
\begin{equation}
 \widehat g_j(t)
 =\frac{1}{\sigma_j\tau_{i(j)}}
   g\bigl(t_{i(j)}+\sigma_j\tau_{i(j)}t\bigr),
 \qquad
 -\frac{t_{i(j)}}{\sigma_j\tau_{i(j)}}\le t\le0,
\end{equation}
have the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.4em]
\item Equipped with the point conjugate heat kernels based at
$(x_{i(j)},0)$, the flows converge in $\mathbb F$, and smoothly on the
full regular spacetime, to a connected noncollapsed K\"ahler shrinking
soliton \(\mathcal Z\).  Write \((Z,g_Z)=\mathcal Z_{-1}\) and
\[
 d\nu_{Z,-1}=(4\pi)^{-(m+1)}e^{-f_Z}\,dV_{g_Z}
\]
for its distinguished shrinker probability measure.  Its normalized
Nash entropy satisfies
\[
 \mathcal N(Z):=
 \int_{\Reg Z}f_Z\,d\nu_{Z,-1}-(m+1)<0.
\]

\item On the localized convergence charts, the maps
\begin{equation}
 \widehat H_j
 =\frac{(w-w(q_{i(j)}))\circ\pi}
        {\sqrt{\sigma_j\tau_{i(j)}}}
\end{equation}
converge smoothly on compact subsets of the regular spacetime to a map
$H_Z$.  Its time-$-1$ restriction extends uniquely to a globally
Lipschitz holomorphic map $H_Z:Z\to\C^m$ satisfying on $\Reg Z$
\begin{equation}
 \nabla^{g_Z}dH_Z=0,
 \qquad
 c|a|^2\le |d(a\cdot H_Z)|_{g_Z}^2\le C|a|^2
 \quad(a\in\C^m).
\end{equation}

\item The time-$-1$ space is smooth.  More precisely, there exists
\(L\in\mathrm{GL}(m,\C)\), with no target translation, such that
\begin{equation}
 Z\cong\C^m\times\PP^1,
 \qquad LH_Z=\operatorname{pr}_{\C^m},
\end{equation}
where $\PP^1$ carries the round metric normalized by
$\Rc(g_{S^2})=\frac12g_{S^2}$.

\item The convergence is realized on a regular exhaustion by embeddings
$\Psi_j$ for which
\begin{equation}
 \Psi_j^*\widehat g_j(-1)\longrightarrow g_Z,
 \qquad
 \widehat H_j\circ\Psi_j\longrightarrow H_Z
\end{equation}
smoothly on compact subsets of \(Z=\Reg Z\).  For every \(U'\Subset Z\)
and all sufficiently large \(j\),
\begin{equation}
 \Psi_j(U')\cap\widehat H_j^{-1}(0)
 =\Psi_j(U')\cap F_{q_{i(j)}}.
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:33:01.746840+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a5abe4b7b2f1bbaf1c1f7056fab6f5392aea2c743002878883712dc250b6d979","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 24 of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] If $p = \omega(1/m)$ then
  $p\,(1-p)^m\,(T_{m,p} - T_{m,0})$ converges
  in law to an exponential distribution
  with rate $1$.
  \begin{proof}
    Fix $t < 0$ and recall definition \eqref{eq:extra term}.
    The reciprocal of the
    moment-generating function of
    $p\,(1-p)^m\,(T_{m,p} - T_{m,0})$ is
    \begin{align*}
      \frac{1}{I_{m,p}(p\,(1-p)^m\,t)}
      &=
      (1-p)^{-m} - (1-p)^{-m} \int_0^1 p\,m
      \left(1-x\right)^{m\exp(p\,(1-p)^m\,(-t))-m}
      \left(1-p\,x\right)^{m-1} dx \\
      &=
        (1-p)^{-m} - (1-p)^{-m} \int_0^1 p\,m
      \left(1 + x\,t\,p\,m\,(1-p)^m\right)
      \left(1-p\,x\right)^{m-1} dx + o(1)
    \intertext{where we have used the binomial approximation
      $(1-x)^\alpha = 1 - \alpha \, x + O(\alpha^2)$, uniform in $x$,
      and a first-order expansion
      $m\exp(p\,(1-p)^m \, (-t)) - m = p\,m\,(1-p)^m\,(-t)
      + O(p^2\,m\,(1-p)^{2m})$.
      Together these give
      $(1-x)^{m\exp(p\,(1-p)^m\,(-t)) - m}
      = 1 + x\,t\,p\,m\,(1-p)^m + O(p^2\,m^2\,(1-p)^{2m})$.
      This error suffices because, upon distribution to form another integral,
      we are left with a trivial term
      $O(p^3\,m^3\,(1-p)^m) \int_0^1 \left(1-p\,x\right)^{m-1} dx =
      O((p\,m)^3 \, e^{-2pm}) = o(1)$, which we have written above.
      The remaining steps involve the dominated convergence theorem:
      }
      &=
        (1-p)^{-m} - (1-p)^{-m} \int_0^{pm}
      \left(1 + x\,t\,(1-p)^m\right)
      (1-x/m)^{m-1}\, dx + o(1)\\
      &= (1-p)^{-m} - (1-p)^{-m} \underbrace{\int_0^{pm} 
          \left(1-x/m\right)^{m-1} dx}_{1-(1-p)^m}\\
      &\quad\, -
        {\underbrace{\int_0^{pm}
          x\,t
          \left(1-x/m\right)^{m-1} dx}_{t+o(1)}} + o(1) \\
      &= 1 - t + o(1).
    \end{align*}
    The \textsc{mgf} of a rate $1$ exponential is

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:50:30.561430+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a5ccff55c3ae9cd79f5eecd8fb93ddf1c696d6f6e33af9f6efdfe65708ab4622","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 6 of arXiv:2605.30560, 'Projected McKean--Vlasov Dynamics for Entropic Weak Optimal Transport'] Under Assumptions~\ref{ass:cost}, problem~\eqref{eq:WOT}
admits a unique minimizer $\pi^*\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)$, and there exists a pair of
potentials $(\phi,\psi)\in L^1(\mu)\times L^1(\nu)$ such that
\begin{align*}
c(x,\rho)+\varepsilon H(\rho\,\|\,\nu)
&\;\geq\;\phi(x)+\rho(\psi),
&&\forall\,(x,\rho)\in\Xc\times\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^d),
\\
c(x,\pi^*_x)+\varepsilon H(\pi^*_x\,\|\,\nu)
&\;=\;\phi(x)+\pi^*_x(\psi),
&&\mu\text{-a.e.\ }x.
\end{align*}
In particular, $\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)} J(\pi) = \mu(\phi)+\nu(\psi)$.

Moreover, the optimal coupling is given explicitly in
terms of the dual potential $\psi$ and the cost gradient $\hat{c}$
of~\eqref{eq:def-chat} by
\begin{equation}
\frac{d\pi^*}{d(\mu\otimes \nu)}(x,y)
\;=\;
\exp\!\left(\tfrac{1}{\varepsilon}\big(\phi(x)+\psi(y)
-\delta_m c(x,\pi^*_x)(y)\big)\right).
\end{equation}
Equivalently, the disintegration of the optimal coupling is 
\begin{equation}
\pi^*_x(dy)
\;=\;
\frac{1}{Z(x)}\,
\exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\,\delta_m c(x,\pi^*_x)(y)
\;+\;\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\,\psi(y)\right)\nu(dy),
\qquad \mu\text{-a.e.\ }x,
\end{equation}
where $Z(x)$ is the normalizing constant
\[
Z(x)\;=\;\int\exp\!\left(-\tfrac{1}{\varepsilon}\delta_m c(x,\pi^*_x)(y)
+\tfrac{1}{\varepsilon}\psi(y)\right)\nu(dy)
\;=\;\exp\!\big(-\tfrac{1}{\varepsilon}\phi(x)\big).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

Then for every t > 0, P(|X - mu| >= t) <= sigma^2 / t^2; when sigma > 0 this is equivalent to P(|X - mu| >= k sigma) <= 1/k^2 for every k > 0 (for sigma = 0 the standardized form fails: X = mu almost surely and the left side is 1). The inequality is sharp: for t >= sigma the variable taking the values mu - t and mu + t with probability sigma^2 / (2 t^2) each and the value mu otherwise has mean mu, variance sigma^2 and P(|X - mu| >= t) = sigma^2 / t^2 exactly. It gives no information for t <= sigma, and it is the classical route to the weak law of large numbers: for i.i.d. X_i with finite variance, P(|(X_1 + ... + X_n)/n - mu| >= eps) <= sigma^2 / (n eps^2) -> 0.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:31:02.822396+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a5fc660422e9240690fbda2573a1fda3e134f9c7a7f3d2a56d7cdd9c943cb562","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:primitive-lattice-shell of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Fix integers $D\geq3$ and $1\leq s<D$.  A sublattice
$\Lambda\subset\mathbb Z^D$ is called primitive when
$\Lambda=(\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\Lambda)\cap\mathbb Z^D$, and we
write
\[
 \Lambda^\perp=
 (\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\Lambda)^\perp\cap\mathbb Z^D.
\]
An orientation of $\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\Lambda$, together with
the standard orientation of $\mathbb R^D$, induces the orientation on
$\Lambda^\perp$ used below.
Write
\[
 \mathcal X_j=\operatorname{SO}_j(\mathbb R)\backslash
 \operatorname{SL}_j(\mathbb R)/\operatorname{SL}_j(\mathbb Z)
\]
for Horesh--Karasik's shape space of oriented rank-$j$ lattices, equipped
with the invariant quotient Radon measure induced from Haar measure, with any
fixed normalization.  Write $\operatorname{Gr}^+(s,D)$ for the oriented
Grassmannian of $s$-planes in $\mathbb R^D$, equipped with its invariant
measure.  Let $\Phi\subset\operatorname{Gr}^+(s,D)$ and
$E\times F\subset\mathcal X_s\times\mathcal X_{D-s}$ be positive-measure
boundary-controllable sets (BCSs) in the sense of
[HoreshKarasik2023], with $E$ and $F$ relatively
compact.  Relatively compact domains with piecewise $C^1$ boundary suffice.
Let $N(T)$ be the number of oriented primitive rank-$s$ lattices
$\Lambda\subset\mathbb Z^D$ such that
\[
 \begin{gathered}
  \dfrac{T}{2}<\operatorname{covol}(\Lambda)\leq T,\qquad
  \operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\Lambda\in\Phi,\\
  \operatorname{shape}(\Lambda)\in E,\qquad
  \operatorname{shape}(\Lambda^\perp)\in F.
 \end{gathered}
\]
Then, as $T\to\infty$,
\begin{equation}
 N(T)=\Theta_{D,s,\Phi,E,F}(T^D).
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:31:20.614997+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a60c8d34088faa4a63346f8001f0a7499f02270e227006a669b2f5464feb89f8","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 17 of arXiv:2608.25785, 'Proper Actions on Homogeneous Spaces of the Upper Triangular Matrix Group via Coarse Geome'] Let $S$ be a set.
    A family $\mathcal{E}\subset \mathcal{P}(S\times S)$ is called a \emph{coarse structure} on $S$ if it satisfies the following five conditions (see Section \ref{subsection:notation} for notation):
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\diag(S) \in \mathcal{E}$.
        \item $E \in \mathcal{E}$ implies $E^\dagger \in \mathcal{E}$.
        \item $E_1, E_2 \in \mathcal{E}$ implies $E_1 \cup E_2 \in \mathcal{E}$.
        \item $E_1, E_2 \in \mathcal{E}$ implies $E_1\circ E_2\in \mathcal{E}$.
        \item $E \in \mathcal{E}$ implies $E' \in \mathcal{E}$ for each $E' \subset E$.
    \end{enumerate}
    The pair $(S, \mathcal{E})$ is called a \emph{coarse space} and 
    each element of $\mathcal{E}$ is referred to as an \emph{coarse entourage} or simply an \emph{entourage}.
    An entourage $E\in \mathcal{E}$ is called \emph{symmetric} if the equality $E=E^\dagger$ holds.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:09:44.799493+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_a69b4271c80fa20aa2fea9d95ad80807bc72e1765e618476cb1e679b00be37b2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In the mathematical field of graph theory, the Erdős–Rényi models are two closely related models for generating random graphs and the evolution of a random network. These models are named after Hungarian mathematicians Paul Erdős and Alfréd Rényi, who introduced one of the models in 1959. Edgar Gilbert introduced the other model contemporaneously with and independently of Erdős and Rényi. In the model of Erdős and Rényi, all graphs on a fixed vertex set with a fixed number of edges are equally likely. In the model introduced by Gilbert, also called the Erdős–Rényi–Gilbert model, each edge has a fixed probability of being present or absent, independently of the other edges. These models can be used in the probabilistic method to prove the existence of graphs satisfying various properties, or to provide a rigorous definition of what it means for a property to hold for almost all graphs.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["U ⊂ C is open and connected","f is holomorphic on U","f is not constant on U"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:42.482048+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_a6b99002ecb79eae7c982d9fde341aac0683db46b4f620776ddcbf4a03879dbe","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let U be a connected open subset of C and f : U → C holomorphic and not constant. Then f(V) is open for every open V ⊂ U. More precisely, if z0 is in U and f - f(z0) has a zero of order m ≥ 1 at z0, then for every sufficiently small r > 0 there is δ > 0 such that every w with 0 < |w - f(z0)| < δ has exactly m preimages (counted with multiplicity, in fact m distinct simple preimages when r is small enough) in the disk |z - z0| < r. Consequences: a nonconstant holomorphic function on a connected open set cannot have locally constant modulus, real part, or argument, and an injective holomorphic map has nonvanishing derivative and holomorphic inverse. Connectedness can be replaced by: f is nonconstant on every connected component of U.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["independent (product) Bernoulli measure, possibly with coordinate-dependent parameters","A is a monotone (increasing) event depending on finitely many coordinates","differentiability in p, automatic for finite-dimensional product measures"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.974074+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a6e95b98b55e5073a7f62110341ac5fe86d89ae81b909d71bb1c753c13feb7de","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For the product measure mu_p on {0,1}^E with each coordinate independently open with probability p and an increasing event A depending on finitely many edges, Russo's formula states d/dp mu_p(A) = sum_{e in E} mu_p(e is pivotal for A), where e is pivotal for A at a configuration omega if flipping the state of e changes the indicator of A. When different edges carry different parameters p_e, the analogous statement is d/dp_e mu(A) = mu(e is pivotal for A). This identity converts questions about how quickly an event's probability crosses a threshold into questions about counting or bounding pivotal edges, which is the basic engine behind sharp-threshold theorems when combined with the Margulis-Russo framework and tools such as hypercontractivity, the Benjamini-Kalai-Schramm influence bound, or the OSSS inequality. Russo's formula does not by itself give sharp thresholds; it requires monotonicity of A, since non-monotone events need a more complex signed-pivotal generalization; and it is stated for independent-coordinate measures, so applying it to dependent measures such as the random-cluster model requires a separate Glauber-dynamics-based generalization rather than the naive product-measure formula. Typical failure: Using Russo's formula on a non-monotone event without its signed-pivotal generalization, or applying the plain product-measure version of the formula to a dependent measure such as a random-cluster or Ising Gibbs measure, where the correct analogue requires the generator of an associated Glauber dynamics rather than a simple coordinatewise derivative; both errors produce a derivative formula that looks structurally similar but is simply wrong. Canonical reference: Russo, 1981, Zeitschrift fur Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie und verwandte Gebiete; Margulis, 1974, Problemy Peredachi Informatsii; Grimmett, Percolation, second edition, 1999, Springer, Chapter 2.","status":"unverified"}
