{"assumptions":["X is a compact metric space and T : X -> X is continuous","M(X,T) carries the weak-star topology and is nonempty (guaranteed by Krylov-Bogolyubov)","h*(T) = 0 (asymptotic h-expansiveness); h-expansiveness and expansiveness are sufficient special cases","h_mu(T) is the Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy of the measure-preserving system (X, mu, T)","the existence corollary uses the variational principle, which itself needs only compactness and continuity"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.090700+00:00","domain":"topological dynamics, entropy, measures of maximal entropy","id":"claim_a77bafb383fb156acf97fdf0ec6338f3cdb7ec81469c4cf42ee27a80550d59df","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a compact metric space, T : X -> X continuous, and let M(X,T) be the set of T-invariant Borel probability measures with the weak-star topology, a nonempty compact convex metrisable set. Suppose T is ASYMPTOTICALLY h-EXPANSIVE, i.e. its tail entropy h*(T) = lim as eps -> 0 of sup over x of h(T, Gamma_eps(x)) vanishes; this holds in particular when T is h-expansive, and a fortiori when T is expansive. THEN the entropy map mu -> h_mu(T) is upper semicontinuous on M(X,T): whenever mu_k -> mu weak-star inside M(X,T), limsup_k h_{mu_k}(T) <= h_mu(T). CONSEQUENCES: an upper semicontinuous function on a nonempty compact set attains its supremum, so by the variational principle a measure of maximal entropy exists and h_top(T) = max over mu in M(X,T) of h_mu(T); the entropy function is then a bounded, affine, upper semicontinuous function on a Choquet simplex, which is what makes the theory of maximal measures and of symbolic extensions run. WHERE IT FAILS: (i) some hypothesis of this kind is necessary. For a general continuous map the entropy map need not be upper semicontinuous and a measure of maximal entropy need not exist; this is why smoothness matters - Newhouse proved that C^infinity diffeomorphisms of compact manifolds are asymptotically h-expansive and therefore always carry maximal measures, while for finite smoothness there are counterexamples. (ii) The conclusion is strictly one-sided and cannot be improved to continuity even for expansive systems: in a mixing shift of finite type the periodic-orbit measures, all of entropy 0, are weak-star dense, so they converge to the measure of maximal entropy and the entropy map is not lower semicontinuous. (iii) Compactness of X (hence of M(X,T)) is what converts upper semicontinuity into existence of a maximiser; on a noncompact space the existence conclusion fails even when the map is upper semicontinuous. (iv) The implication is stated in one direction only: upper semicontinuity of the entropy map is a strictly weaker property than asymptotic h-expansiveness, so do not run the criterion backwards.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["two independent centered Gaussian fields on a common finite or suitably truncated index set","existence and enough regularity of the covariance functions to differentiate the interpolated expectation under the integral","a consistent-sign comparison, or specific structural relation, between the two covariance kernels","the test functional F smooth with the correct sign of mixed partial derivatives for the interpolation identity to yield a useful inequality rather than an uncontrolled remainder"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.986351+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a7b6b7b2b6ff3d35232e25a83c85018f52e970e60f45507e62d94c80f06513bc","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For two independent centered Gaussian fields X, Y indexed by a common finite (or suitably truncated) set T with covariance functions C_X, C_Y, Kahane's interpolation forms Z(t,u) = sqrt(u) X(t) + sqrt(1-u) Y(t) for u in [0,1] and computes d/du E[F(Z(.,u))] for a smooth test function F, obtaining an integral expression involving (C_Y(s,t) - C_X(s,t)) times a mixed second derivative of F, evaluated against the law of Z(.,u). When C_X <= C_Y pointwise (or the relevant difference has a consistent sign) and F is chosen with matching sign of mixed partials, this yields a comparison inequality between functionals of X and Y, an approach that both generalizes Slepian-type comparisons and, in the Gaussian multiplicative chaos literature, is used to show that different regularizations of a log-correlated field, such as the two-dimensional Gaussian free field, converge to the same limiting chaos measure regardless of the approximation scheme, a key technical step in constructing Liouville quantum gravity measures. It does not apply to non-Gaussian fields, it requires the two fields being compared to be independent for the interpolation construction itself, and the sign or convexity conditions on F needed to obtain a clean inequality must be verified case by case rather than assumed. Typical failure: Applying the interpolation to fields that are not independent, or to a family of regularizations whose covariance difference does not have a consistent sign across the whole index set, which is common when comparing regularizations of a log-correlated field near its singular set; either error breaks the monotonicity the interpolation is meant to exploit, and the resulting comparison can go in the wrong direction with no explicit error term to control it. Canonical reference: Kahane, 1986, Annales des Sciences Mathematiques du Quebec; Robert and Vargas, 2010, Comptes Rendus Mathematique; Berestycki, 2017, Electronic Communications in Probability.","status":"unverified"}

For f: {-1,1}^n -> R with Fourier-Walsh expansion f = sum_S hat{f}(S) chi_S and the noise operator T_rho, which independently resamples each coordinate to a fresh uniform sign with probability (1-rho)/2, the Bonami-Beckner inequality states ||T_rho f||_q <= ||f||_p whenever 1 <= p <= q and 0 <= rho <= sqrt((p-1)/(q-1)). Equivalently, T_rho f = sum_S rho^{|S|} hat{f}(S) chi_S, and the inequality forces the Fourier weight of f on high-degree levels to decay geometrically once rho<1, giving sum_S rho^{2|S|} hat{f}(S)^2 <= (E[|f|^p])^{2/p} for suitable p. This is the central tool converting L^2 Fourier information into higher-moment (typically L^4) control, and it underlies the Kahn-Kalai-Linial theorem on the existence of an influential coordinate, the Benjamini-Kalai-Schramm noise-sensitivity theorems, and Friedgut's junta theorem for low-influence functions. It does not directly give influence bounds without further combination with such machinery, and the sharp constant and range of rho given here hold for the uniform measure on {-1,1}^n; biased-p product measures or non-product (dependent) measures require different, generally weaker, p-biased or dependency-adjusted hypercontractive inequalities. Typical failure: Applying the sharp uniform-measure {-1,1}^n hypercontractive constant to a biased-p product measure or to a dependent measure such as the random-cluster or Ising Gibbs measure without switching to the correct p-biased or dependency-adjusted hypercontractivity inequality, whose constants generally degrade as p approaches 0 or 1; this silently invalidates quantitative noise-sensitivity conclusions claimed for critical percolation at p != 1/2 or for genuinely non-product models. Canonical reference: Bonami, 1970, Annales de l'Institut Fourier; Beckner, 1975, Annals of Mathematics; O'Donnell, Analysis of Boolean Functions, 2014, Cambridge University Press.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f : {-1,1}^n -> {0,1} Boolean, uniform product measure","c is a universal constant","the conclusion bounds only the MAXIMUM influence, not any specific coordinate"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.628283+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a7d3fa81d9e828619a0897ad9b5e1de549e37211c93fe093b3a6f7e2f0ac728c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f : {-1,1}^n -> {0,1} be a Boolean function on the uniform product measure, and define the influence of coordinate i as Inf_i(f) = P( f(X) != f(X^{(i)}) ) where X^{(i)} flips the i-th coordinate. Then there is a universal constant c > 0 with max_{i <= n} Inf_i(f) >= c Var(f) log n / n, where Var(f) = p(1-p) with p = E[f]. Equivalently the TOTAL influence satisfies sum_i Inf_i(f) >= c Var(f) log n. The bound is SHARP up to the constant: the tribes function, a read-once DNF on blocks of size about log_2 n - log_2 log_2 n, is balanced and has all influences of order log n / n. The theorem is about the uniform measure on the cube; the analogous statement for p-biased measures carries an extra factor and is the Friedgut-Kalai sharp-threshold machinery. Note what it does NOT say: it does not bound the influence of any PARTICULAR coordinate, only the maximum, and it says nothing when Var(f) is 0, that is when f is constant. [Kahn, Kalai and Linial (1988); see O'Donnell, Analysis of Boolean Functions, Chapter 9]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["No finiteness, countability or uniformity assumption on the family;","values in the extended reals are allowed."],"created_at":"2026-09-12T14:01:51.298864+00:00","domain":"real analysis, topology","id":"claim_a7d6b373429f32266ad5157b4e9a016da414a695cb09150843502c65cad89b8f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a topological space and let (f_i) be an arbitrary family of functions on X with values in the extended reals. If every f_i is upper semicontinuous - in particular if every f_i is continuous - then the pointwise infimum inf_i f_i is upper semicontinuous. Dually, a pointwise supremum of lower semicontinuous functions is lower semicontinuous. The family may be uncountable, and no uniformity is needed. The DIRECTION matters and is the standard place to slip: a supremum of upper semicontinuous functions need not be upper semicontinuous, and an infimum of lower semicontinuous functions need not be lower semicontinuous.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["H is a complex Hilbert space","T is symmetric (densely defined and T ⊂ T*)","for the semibounded variant, T ≥ c and μ < c is real"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.770179+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, spectral theory, mathematical physics","id":"claim_a7fcd1c8ead2f74dd2cfb25a1c05adbe2e24b4b7b1fc4d1b01ea88381a77748c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let T be a symmetric operator on a complex Hilbert space H. The following are equivalent: (a) T is self-adjoint; (b) T is closed and ker(T* − i) = ker(T* + i) = {0}; (c) Ran(T + i) = Ran(T − i) = H. Likewise the following are equivalent: (a') T is essentially self-adjoint; (b') ker(T* − i) = ker(T* + i) = {0}; (c') Ran(T + i) and Ran(T − i) are both dense in H. The pair ±i may be replaced by any pair λ, λ̄ with Im λ ≠ 0. If moreover T is bounded below, ⟨Tx, x⟩ ≥ c‖x‖² on D(T), then T is self-adjoint iff Ran(T − μ) = H for some real μ < c, and T is essentially self-adjoint iff ker(T* − μ) = {0} for some real μ < c (equivalently Ran(T − μ) dense). Consequences for self-adjoint A: σ(A) ⊂ ℝ, and for Im z ≠ 0, ‖(A − z)^{-1}‖ ≤ 1/|Im z|.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:46.149018+00:00","domain":"elliptic partial differential equations, maximum principles","id":"claim_a7ff9de16f2bbefc6c4fe4f5adbe349d50f8611965c390800f138c4833c83567","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: c <= 0 in the nondivergence convention Lu = sum a^{ij}D_{ij}u + b.Du + cu (equivalently c >= 0 in the divergence convention -div(A grad u) + b.grad u + cu). Without it every conclusion of the weak maximum principle, of comparison and of uniqueness can fail, and no smallness of the coefficients repairs it on a large domain. Counterexample: on Omega = (0, pi) in R^1 take u(x) = sin x. Then u'' + u = 0, so Lu = 0 with c = +1 > 0; u = 0 at both endpoints while u > 0 inside, so sup over Omega of u = 1 > 0 = sup over the boundary of u^+. The same function shows uniqueness fails: u and 0 both solve the Dirichlet problem. In n dimensions the first Dirichlet eigenfunction of the Laplacian does the same on any bounded domain. Sharp form: for L = Laplacian + c with constant c on a bounded Omega, the weak maximum principle in the H^1 sense (if u in H^1(Omega), Lu >= 0 weakly and u^+ in H^1_0(Omega), then u <= 0) holds if and only if c < lambda_1(Omega), the first Dirichlet eigenvalue. Proof of the positive half: test with u^+ to get integral |grad u^+|^2 <= c integral (u^+)^2, which contradicts the Rayleigh quotient bound lambda_1 integral (u^+)^2 <= integral |grad u^+|^2 unless u^+ = 0. Failure for c >= lambda_1: the positive eigenfunction phi_1 satisfies Laplacian phi_1 + c phi_1 = (c - lambda_1) phi_1 >= 0 with phi_1 = 0 on the boundary and phi_1 > 0 inside. Second, finer point: even with c <= 0 the conclusion is only sup u <= sup over the boundary of u^+ and not sup u <= sup over the boundary of u. Example: on (-1,1), u(x) = -cosh x satisfies u'' - u = 0 (so c = -1 <= 0), u(0) = -1 while u(-1) = u(1) = -cosh 1 which is about -1.543; the interior supremum strictly exceeds the boundary supremum, and only the truncation at 0 saves the statement. No sign condition on the drift b is needed; only its boundedness relative to the ellipticity constant.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X integrable with X in an open interval I almost surely","phi convex on I","E[phi(X)^-] < infinity, so that E[phi(X) | G] is defined"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.752623+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a82c08a702478464e662ccbbaeeea30b77120ba9b85679d10ca8d340f884bc36","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be an integrable random variable taking values almost surely in an open interval I of R, let phi : I -> R be convex, and let G be a sub-sigma-algebra. If phi(X) is integrable, or more generally if E[phi(X)^-] < infinity so that E[phi(X) | G] is well defined in (-infinity, +infinity], then phi(E[X | G]) <= E[phi(X) | G] almost surely. Taking G trivial recovers the unconditional Jensen inequality. Two hypotheses do real work: X must lie in the interval where phi is convex, and some one-sided integrability of phi(X) is needed for the right-hand side to be defined. Convexity cannot be weakened to midpoint convexity without measurability, and the inequality REVERSES for concave phi. A standard consequence is that for a convex phi and a martingale (M_n), the process phi(M_n) is a submartingale whenever it is integrable. [standard; e.g. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 4.1.10]","status":"unverified"}

\]

{"assumptions":["X and Y are Banach spaces over the same field","T is a bounded linear operator from X to Y"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.571248+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, Fredholm theory","id":"claim_a8d654dd18a265403bd8a3b84aa51c1024872fabf26f962e91167e35b5920dca","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X and Y be Banach spaces and T in B(X,Y) a bounded linear operator. T is a Fredholm operator if (a) its kernel ker T is finite-dimensional and (b) its range ran T has finite codimension, i.e. the quotient vector space Y / ran T is finite-dimensional. The index of a Fredholm operator is the integer ind T = dim ker T - dim(Y / ran T). The range of a Fredholm operator is automatically closed (a bounded operator between Banach spaces whose range has finite algebraic codimension has closed range), so texts that add 'ran T is closed' to the definition define the same class. For Fredholm T one has dim(Y / ran T) = dim ker T', where T': Y' -> X' is the Banach-space adjoint, so ind T = dim ker T - dim ker T'. Examples on l^2: an invertible operator has index 0; the unilateral shift S(x_1, x_2, ...) = (0, x_1, x_2, ...) is injective with range of codimension 1, so ind S = -1, and its adjoint (the backward shift) has index +1; I + K with K compact has index 0. The set of Fredholm operators X -> Y is written Phi(X,Y).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["R associative with identity; 'semisimple' means semisimple as a left module over itself (equivalent to the right-module version)","the division rings need not be commutative (the real quaternions H occur, e.g. in R[Q_8])"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:31:12.479831+00:00","domain":"ring theory and representation theory","id":"claim_a8dff8cc7fd1ebc995d2f1c2cd5a96f7c66d395874540b73e9f3e7c21eab6fcc","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"A ring R (associative, with 1) is semisimple - every left R-module is a direct sum of simple modules, equivalently R is a finite direct sum of simple left modules, equivalently R is left Artinian with zero Jacobson radical - if and only if R is isomorphic to a finite product of matrix rings over division rings: R = M_{n_1}(D_1) x ... x M_{n_r}(D_r). The integers r and n_i and the division rings D_i (up to isomorphism) are determined by R: r is the number of isomorphism classes of simple left R-modules, and the simple module S_i = D_i^{n_i} has End_R(S_i) = D_i (opposite conventions aside). A simple left Artinian ring is a single matrix ring M_n(D). Consequences: for a finite group G and a field k of characteristic not dividing |G| (Maschke), the group algebra k[G] is semisimple, so k[G] = prod M_{n_i}(D_i); over an algebraically closed field the D_i are k itself, the n_i are the degrees of the irreducible representations, r is the number of conjugacy classes, and |G| = sum n_i^2. A commutative semisimple ring is a finite product of fields. Wedderburn's little theorem (finite division rings are fields) then gives: a finite semisimple ring is a product of matrix rings over finite fields.","status":"unverified"}

with $\MAX_N$ as in Proposition~\ref{p:Y.kolmogorov}. The same bound holds with $\vY^\frozen$ in place of $\vY$. 

\begin{proof} It follows using

	\[\bE\Big(

	+ O(\eta)\bigg\{ \bE\Big| \Delta X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))\Big|
	+ \eta\bigg\}\,.\]
From the spatial rerandomization (Definition~\ref{d:rerand}), the index $a(q_{d+1})$ is a uniformly random sample from $[M]$, even if we condition on the gaussian disorder. 	\]
using that $\MAX_N\ge1$ and $\eta\ll\delta$ from Assumption~\ref{a:params}. This proves \eqref{e:Y.I.second.quenched}, and the analogous bound for $Y^{\frozen,\RomI}$ follows by the same argument.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.356775+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a995d06274ddf557e5d3170e4d4483f83f08209bad25e038d38c0297bc13eb05","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 236 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For all $1\le \fq < \fp$ and $C > 0$, the spaces $\cP_\fp(\R,C)$ and $\cP_\fp(\R_{\ge0},C)$, endowed with the $\bbW_\fq$ metric,
are compact.

\begin{proof}
	We will show compactness of $\cP_\fp(\R,C)$, as compactness of $\cP_\fp(\R_{\ge0},C)$ is proved analogously.
	It suffices to show that every sequence $(\mu_n)_{n\ge 1}$ in $\cP_\fp(\R,C)$ has a subsequence converging in $\bbW_\fq$ to a measure in $\cP_\fp(\R,C)$.
	Consider any such sequence $(\mu_n)_{n\ge 1}$.
	The set of measures $\cP_\fp(\R,C)$ is clearly tight, so by Prohorov's theorem there exists a weakly convergent subsequence $(\mu_{n_j})_{j\ge 1}$. 
Let $\mu$ be its weak limit. By Skorokhod's theorem, we can find a coupling of random variables $X_j\sim\mu_{n_j}$ and $X\sim\mu$ such that
$X_j\to X$ almost surely. Then, by Fatou's lemma, we have
	\[
		\|\mu\|_{L^\fp}^\fp 
	=\E[|X|^p]^{1/p}
		\le
		\liminf_j \E[|X_j|^p]^{1/p}
		= \liminf_{j\to\infty} \|\mu_{n_j}\|_{L^\fp}^\fp
		 \le C\,,
	\]
	so $\mu \in \cP_\fp(\R,C)$. 
	It remains to show $(\mu_{n_j})_{j\ge 1}$ converges to $\mu$ in the $\bbW_\fq$ metric.
	 Note that for any $\nu \in \cP_\fp(\R_{\ge0},C)$, Markov's inequality implies
	\[
	\nu(|x|>K) 
	\le \frac{1}{K^\fp}\int
		|x|^\fp \,d\nu
		 \le \frac{C}{K^\fp}\,.
	\]
Combining this with H\"older's inequality gives
	\beq
		\int_{|x|>K} |x|^\fq \,d\nu
		\le \nu(|x|>K)^{1 - \fq/\fp} \bigg(
			\int |x|^\fp \,d\nu
		\bigg)^{\fq/\fp}
		\le \frac{C}{K^{\fp - \fq}}\,.
	\eeq
	By \eqref{e:confinement.cPp.compact.Wq.tail} and the weak convergence $\mu_{n_j} \rightarrow \mu$,
	\begin{align*}
		\limsup_{j\to\infty} \bigg|
			\int |x|^\fq \,d\mu_{n_j}
			- \int |x|^\fq \,d\mu
		\bigg|
		&\le \limsup_{j\to\infty} \bigg|
			\int
			\max\{|x|,K\}^\fq
			\,d\mu_{n_j}
			- \int
			\max\{|x|,K\}^\fq
			 \,d\mu
		\bigg|\\
		&\qquad + \limsup_{j\to\infty} \int_{|x| > K} |x|^\fq \,d\mu_{n_j}
		+ \int_{|x| > K} |x|^\fq \,d\mu
		\le \frac{2C}{K^{\fp-\fq}}\,.
	\end{align*}
	Since $K$ was arbitrary, we infer the convergence of $\fq$-th moments
	\[
		\lim_{j\to\infty} 
		\E[|X_j|^p]
		=\lim_{j\to\infty} 
		\int |x|^\fq \,d\mu_{n_j}
		= \int |x|^\fq \,d\mu
		= \E[|X|^p]\,.\]
This implies that the random variables $\{X_j\}$ are uniformly integrable, so
	\begin{align*}
	&\bbW_\fq(\mu_{n_j}, \mu)^\fq
	\le \E[|X_j-X|^\fq]\\
	&\le\E\Big[
	\max\{|X_j-X|,2K\}^\fq\Big]
	+\E\Big[|X_j| ; |X_j|\ge K\Big]
	+ \E\Big[|X| ; |X|\ge K\Big]
	\\
	&\le o_j(1) + o_K(1)+ o_K(1)\,.
	\end{align*}
Since the left-hand side does not depend on $K$, we conclude that
$\mu_{n_j} \rightarrow \mu$ in the $\bbW_\fq$ metric.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["independent coordinates with finite ranges","f real valued"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T08:50:16.133603+00:00","domain":"Hoeffding (ANOVA) decomposition on finite product spaces","id":"claim_a9c9615f822d7eeb848e1824aaacf3ac69fc9a75c4061f0fa09662553259da87","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X = (X_1, ..., X_n) have independent coordinates with finite ranges, f a real function of X, and f = sum over S of f_S its Hoeffding (ANOVA) decomposition over subsets S of {1, ..., n}: f_S depends only on X_S, f_empty = E f, and E[f_S | X_T] = 0 unless S is inside T. {"assumptions":["the semicircle law normalised to [-2,2], corresponding to Wigner matrices with entry variance 1/n","the convention m(z) = integral (x - z)^{-1} d mu(x); the opposite sign convention changes the equation"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.544103+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a9f9a8f598dab28e0957ae56e87073ce26d8a3b6d7df827c75290aa5f4b04b18","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let mu_sc be the semicircle law with density (1/(2 pi)) sqrt(4 - x^2) on [-2, 2]. Its Stieltjes transform m(z) = integral (x - z)^{-1} mu_sc(dx) satisfies the self-consistent equation m(z)^2 + z m(z) + 1 = 0 for every z in C^+, equivalently m(z) = -1/( z + m(z) ), and is the UNIQUE solution of that equation with Im m(z) > 0 for z in C^+; explicitly m(z) = ( -z + sqrt(z^2 - 4) )/2 with the branch of the square root chosen so that m(z) is asymptotic to -1/z as |z| tends to infinity. This equation is the fixed point that resolvent proofs of Wigner's theorem converge to: the Schur complement identity applied to the resolvent of a Wigner matrix gives (1/n) tr (H - z)^{-1} approximately equal to -1/(z + (1/n) tr (H - z)^{-1}) up to errors that vanish as n grows, and stability of the fixed point then forces the empirical Stieltjes transform to converge to m. # Target 1: scalar three-token self-attention under joint training

Version 1, unaudited. Owner own work; novelty not established globally.
This extends the scalar family, not arbitrary vector-valued token geometry.

## Data, model and conclusions

For each i=1,...,n, n>=2, take a label y_i in {-1,+1} and three distinct
signed token values c_ij. Their minimum m_i is negative, maximum M_i positive,
and the FIRST token c_i1 is positive. Let raw tokens x_ij=y_i c_ij and use
the actual first token x_i1 as the self-attention query. With jointly trained
scalar head v and scalar attention weight p, signed prediction is v h_i(p),

 h_i(p)=sum_j c_ij exp(zeta_i c_ij p)/sum_j exp(zeta_i c_ij p),
 zeta_i=c_i1>0.

The loss is average logistic loss. Let
 H=max_i max(|m_i|,|M_i|), D=max_i zeta_i(M_i-m_i)^2,
 eta_*=min(2/H^2,1/(2D)).

For every fixed eta in (0,eta_*], simultaneous GD in (v,p) has precisely
three possible limits: the unique finite saddle (0,p_bar), where
mean_i h_i(p_bar)=0; matching-positive escape v,p->+infinity; or
matching-negative escape v,p->-infinity. The saddle's global stable set is
planar null. Both escaping basins are open and nonempty. Their hard selections
are respectively the maximum signed token in EVERY example and the minimum
signed token in EVERY example. No interior token, or mixed pattern of extrema,
is a hard-selection limit in this scalar model. On escaping trajectories
p=O(log |v|), loss->0 and the normalized joint directions are (+1,0),(-1,0).
The corresponding minimum signed margins, normalized by sqrt(v^2+p^2),
are Gamma_+=min_i M_i and Gamma_-=min_i(-m_i).

In addition, for EVERY eta>0 the regions
 Q_+={v>0,p>max_i rho_i}, Q_-={v<0,p<min_i rho_i},
where h_i(rho_i)=0, are forward invariant and satisfy the same respective
escape/margin conclusions. Thus if Gamma_+>Gamma_-, the inferior basin is
open and positive measure even without a step-size restriction. A sufficient
strict inequality is M_i+m_i>0 for every example.

## Scalar softmax link estimates

Write alpha_ij(p) for the three softmax weights. Direct differentiation gives
h_i'=zeta_i[sum alpha_ij c_ij^2-h_i^2]
     =zeta_i sum_{j<l} alpha_ij alpha_il(c_ij-c_il)^2>0.
Also |h_i|<=H, h_i'<=zeta_i(M_i-m_i)^2<=D, and h_i tends to m_i,M_i
at the two infinities. Thus each root rho_i exists uniquely.

Let delta be the minimum over i of zeta_i times either adjacent gap of its
sorted three token values. It is strictly positive. For p>=0, the total
softmax mass on nonmaximum tokens is <=2 exp(-delta p).
Variance is no larger than the second moment about the maximum token,
so h_i'(p)<=2D exp(-delta p). Reflecting yields the same upper bound
2D exp(-delta |p|) for p<=0. Every h_i is real analytic, strictly increasing,
bounded, and has exponentially decaying derivative.

## Full-plane trapping and escape

For g_i=(1+exp(v h_i(p)))^-1 put F=mean g_i h_i and G=mean g_i h_i'>0.
GD is v_+=v+eta F, p_+=p+eta vG. The following estimates are identical
to those needed in proof 005, now established for genuine three-token links:

 -H^2/4<=F_v<=0,
 F(0,p)=mean h_i(p)/2=:F_0(p), 0<F_0'<=D/2, G<=D.

There is a unique mean root p_bar. Set u=p-p_bar, A=H^2/4.
In v,u>0, v_+>=(1-eta A)v+eta F_0(p)>0 and p increases; reflecting gives
invariance in v,u<0. In a bad quadrant v>0,u<0, v decreases and u increases
until it exits or converges to the saddle. Double crossing would require

 (1-eta A)v<=eta(D/2)|u|<=eta^2 D^2 v/2,

impossible since eta A<=1/2 and eta D<=1/2. The other bad quadrant is the
reflection. An axis point other than the saddle enters a good quadrant after
one step. A bad-quadrant orbit staying there is bounded and monotone; continuity
of increments gives vG=F=0 at its limit, hence the saddle.

Consider a positive good-quadrant orbit. If p had a finite limit P and v were
bounded, compactness would give G bounded below; Delta p->0 would force v->0,
but F_0(P)>0 contradicts convergence of v to zero. If v were unbounded and
P<=R:=max rho_i, an example with root R has h_j(p)<=0 and therefore g_j>=1/2.
On the compact p interval its derivative is bounded below, so
Delta p>=eta d v/(2n), contradicting finite P. If P>R, eventually all links
are >=c>0; v then increases without bound and
Delta p/Delta v>=d v/H again contradicts finite P. Thus p->infinity.
Eventually all h_i>=c, forcing v->infinity (bounded v would keep the g_i
uniformly positive). Negative escape follows by reflection using -h_i(-p).

This proof also applies directly within Q_+ or Q_- at any eta>0: both
coordinates are monotone from the start and all signed links are positive
after reflection. Only the full-plane trapping argument uses eta_*.

## Rates, margin, and the null exceptional set

On a positive escaping trajectory, h_i>=c>0 eventually, so
Delta p<=eta D v exp(-cv)->0. Moreover
Delta p/Delta v<=2D v exp(-delta p)/c.
Once Delta p<=1, the mean value theorem gives
Delta exp(delta p)<=C v Delta v. Telescoping against v^2 gives
exp(delta p)<=C'(1+v^2), so p=O(log v). Reflection proves the other branch.
Loss and normalized margin limits now follow. For any parameter pair,
the endpoint bounds and sqrt(v^2+p^2)>=|v| show the normalized minimum
margin cannot exceed max(Gamma_+,Gamma_-); the larger branch attains it.

At the saddle, the update Jacobian is
[[1-eta A_s,eta B_s],[eta B_s,1]],
where A_s=mean h_i(p_bar)^2/4<=A and B_s=mean h_i'(p_bar)/2 in (0,D/2].
Its determinant >=7/16 and det(DT-I)<0: one eigenvalue lies in (0,1),
the other exceeds 1. The analytic update map has a Jacobian determinant
not identically zero; the zero set is null. Away from that set its local
inverse maps preserve null sets. By a countable cover, preimages of null
sets are null. The local stable-manifold theorem and countably many iterated
preimages therefore give a null global stable set. Each escaping basin is
the union of preimages of its open good quadrant, hence open. This is the
same null-preimage argument detailed in proofs/003 and 005, not an assumption
that the GD map is globally invertible.

## Which locally optimal selections, and comparison with prior art

For p->+infinity only the largest signed c_ij can dominate; for p->-infinity
only the smallest can dominate. Because all zeta_i>0 these choices must be
consistent across examples. At finite p all weights are strictly positive,
so an interior token cannot become a hard selection. For a fixed v>0, the
maximum-token pattern is the only locally optimal feasible hard selection;
for fixed v<0 the minimum-token pattern is the only one. Both are stable
under joint training, by the open basins above. The minimum pattern can
nevertheless be inferior when comparing the two JOINT normalized margins.

Tarzanagh et al., 2306.13596, Definition 2 (PDF p.5) compares the chosen token
score only to its active SVM neighbors, with a FIXED head. Their Theorem 3
(PDF p.6) gives convergence from cones C_{mu,R} around such locally optimal
directions. It already includes a three-token illustration immediately after
the theorem. The present scalar result is not the discovery of that phenomenon:
it classifies the scalar joint-head basins and excludes mixed/interior hard
patterns in this stated geometry. General vector-valued three-token locally
optimal selections and their joint-head basins remain open here.

## Explicit distinct mixed-label witness

Take signed triples (3/2,1/4,-1/2) and (3/2,1/8,-1), with labels +1,-1.
Raw triples are (3/2,1/4,-1/2),(-3/2,-1/8,1); actual first-token queries
are 3/2,-3/2. Both zeta_i=3/2. H=3/2, D=75/8, eta_*=4/75.
Gamma_+=3/2 and Gamma_-=1/2. The conditions are strict and persist in an
open neighborhood of these data. This witness is illustrative; the theorem
covers the whole family above rather than just this isolated case.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:35:04.164461+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_aa7ee49186ba658d9c910cdec1f29ecb659b7af0bd7ea0dc6a4fb81c9c4eb808","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 27 of arXiv:2608.30059, 'Multihomogeneous Measures and Stochastic Polar Representations'] For the fixed admissible gauge \(\tau\), with
\(C_\star=(1,2]^q\) and \(d_\alpha=m_\alpha(C_\star)\), set  
\begin{equation}

s_\tau
:=
\varsigma_\tau(\Sigma_\tau)
=
\frac{1}{d_\alpha}
\int_{\{\tau\in C_\star\}}
\chi_\alpha(\tau(x))\,\nu(dx)
=
\frac{\nu\{\tau\in C_\star\}}
{\vartheta_\alpha(C_\star)}
\in(0,\infty].
\end{equation}
Every stochastic representer \(Z\) of \(\nu\) satisfies
\[
\E{\chi_\alpha(R_Z)}=s_\tau.
\]
The following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[\rm(i)]
\item
Some stochastic representer \(Z\) has \(R_Z\perp Y_Z\).

\item
\(s_\tau<\infty\).

\item
\(\nu\{\tau\in C_\star\}<\infty\).
\end{enumerate}

If \(s_\tau<\infty\), put
\[
\bar\alpha:=\sum_{i=1}^q\alpha_i,
\qquad
a_\tau:=s_\tau^{1/\bar\alpha}\boldsymbol1 
\]
and  for any stochastic representer \(Z\)  define
\begin{equation}

\frac{d\mathbb P_Z^\tau}{d\mathbb P}
:=
\frac{\chi_\alpha(R_Z)}{s_\tau},
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}

Z_\tau^\circ
:=
S_{a_\tau}Y_Z
=
S_{a_\tau R_Z^{-1}}Z.
\end{equation}
Under \(\mathbb P_Z^\tau\),
\[
Y_Z\sim\frac{\varsigma_\tau}{s_\tau},
\qquad
\tau(Z_\tau^\circ)=a_\tau,
\qquad
\nu_{Z_\tau^\circ}=\nu,
\]
and
\[
\mathcal L(Z_\tau^\circ)
=
(S_{a_\tau})_\#
\left(\frac{\varsigma_\tau}{s_\tau}\right).
\]
Consequently, every stochastic representer \(W\) satisfying
\(\tau(W)=a_\tau\) almost surely has this law.

Finally, for \(Z\) concentrated on \(E_\tau\) with \(R_Z\perp Y_Z\),
\[
\nu_Z=\nu
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
Y_Z\sim\frac{\varsigma_\tau}{s_\tau}
\ \text{ and }\
\E{\chi_\alpha(R_Z)}=s_\tau.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-23T13:15:27.869212+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_ab403eae02babe283bdaed7631d179880589c9cff81d8649db11e29a3ce1de2c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign status: candidate_full_solution - author-checked with a scope caveat; NO independent review - the parent that reviewed it had itself supplied two of the argument's steps, so its review does not certify the amended proof; no Lean] van Handel, The strong convergence phenomenon, arXiv:2507.00346v2 (11 February 2026), Section 6.9, pp. 69-70, asks whether strong convergence of a family of random matrices forces the empirical complex-eigenvalue measures of every noncommutative polynomial to converge to the corresponding limiting Brown measure. Problem 6.9 states it for ARBITRARY strongly convergent families - no independence, no independent entries, no freeness of the limit - and that literal generality is what is addressed. CLAIM: no. Fix an irrational theta and reduced approximants p_j/q_j -> theta; with omega_j = exp(2 pi i p_j / q_j) put U_j e_k = omega_j^k e_k, S e_k = e_{k-1} and V_j = e^{pi i / q_j} S. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:33:01.753254+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ab44bddca90c995f912e92cf910d2083e736574934b0f5e966f17663146713e6","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 29 (Mean) of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] The first moment of $T_{m, p}$ is
  \[
    \E T_{m, p} = m \, H_m + 
      \frac{(1-p)^{-m}}{p}
      \left[
      (p\,m)^2\left(1-p\right)^{m-1}
      +
      \int_0^1 p^3 \, m^2 \left(m-1\right)
      \left(1-p\,x\right)^{m-2} L(x) \, dx
      \right]
  \]
  where $H_m$ is the $m^\text{th}$ harmonic number
  and $L(x) \coloneqq x + (1-x) \log(1-x)$.
  If $p = p_m$ is an $o(1/m)$ sequence then this becomes
  \[
    \E T_{m, p} = m\,H_m
    + p\,m^2 + \frac{1}{4} \, p^2 \, m^3
    + O\left(p^2 \, m^2\right) + O\left(p^3 \, m^4\right).
  \]
  as $m \to \infty$. If $p \sim c/m$ then
  \[
    \E T_{m, p} = m\,H_m + \left(1 + o(1)\right)
      m \left[ c + c^2 \int_0^1 e^{-cx} \, L(x) \, dx\right].
  \]
  If $p = \omega(1/m)$ then
  \[
    \E T_{m,p} = m\,H_m + \frac{(1-p)^{-m}}{p} \left(1
    + O\left(\frac{1}{p\,m}\right)\right).
  \]
  In particular, for $p$ constant,
  \begin{align*}
    \E T_{m,p}
    = m \, H_m
    + \frac{(1-p)^{-m}}{p}&\Bigg\{
      1 + \left(-6p + 5 + \frac{1}{p}\right) m^{-1}\\
    &\phantom{\Bigg\{} {} + \left(45\,p^2 - 62\,p + 8 + \frac{7}{p} + \frac{2}{p^2} \right) m^{-2}
      + O\left(m^{-3}\right)
    \Bigg\}.
  \end{align*}
  \begin{proof}
    The difference $T_{m, p} - T_{m, 0}$ has \textsc{mgf}
    $I_{m, p}(t)$. Corollary~\ref{thm:mgf} implies
    the \textsc{mgf} of $T_{m, p} - T_{m, 0}$
    exists on a neighbourhood of the origin, hence
    $\E [T_{m, p} - T_{m, 0}] = \lim_{t \uparrow 0} I_{m,p}'(t)$.
    With the knowledge 
    \begin{equation}
      
      \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \left( 1 - x \right)^{m \exp(-t) - m}
      = \log\left(\frac{1}{1-x}\right) \, m \, e^{-t}
      \left( 1 - x \right)^{m \exp(-t) - m},
    \end{equation}
    we differentiate the integral expression of
    \eqref{eq:extra term} to find
    \begin{align}
      \notag
      \E \left[T_{m,p} - T_{m,0}\right]
      &= (1-p)^m
      \left[
        1 - \overbrace{\int_0^1 p\, m\left(1-p\,x\right)^{m-1}
        \, dx}^{1 - (1-p)^m} 
      \right]^{-2}\\
      \notag
      &\quad \times \int_0^1 p\,m^2 \left(1-p\,x\right)^{m-1}
      \log\left( \frac{1}{1-x} \right) dx\\
      
      &= \frac{(1-p)^{-m}}{p}
      \int_0^1 (p\,m)^2 \left(1-p\,x\right)^{m-1}
      \log\left( \frac{1}{1-x} \right) dx.
      \intertext{Notice that $L(x) = x + (1-x) \log(1-x)$
      is an antiderivative of $-\log(1-x)$ that
      increases from $L(0) = 0$ to $L(1) = 1$. Hence, by an
      integration by parts,}
      
      &= \frac{(1-p)^{-m}}{p}
      \left[
      (p\,m)^2\left(1-p\right)^{m-1}
      +
      \int_0^1 p^3 \, m^2 \left(m-1\right)
      \left(1-p\,x\right)^{m-2} L(x) \, dx
      \right].
  \end{align}
    Add on $\E T_{m,0} = m \, H_m$ to find our expression for
    the first moment.

{"assumptions":["the operator is compact on a Hilbert space","self-adjointness or normality is what the eigenbasis conclusion needs","for a general compact operator only the Riesz-Schauder conclusions and the singular value decomposition are available"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.573312+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, spectral theory of compact operators","id":"claim_ab876a6af8757c91d5eb78a56fd013d6691bfc416c7fa2ac4c3ae96614531a82","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators (an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, real eigenvalues tending to 0, ||T|| = max |eigenvalue|, min-max characterisation of eigenvalues) requires self-adjointness or at least normality. Compactness alone gives only the Riesz-Schauder picture: the nonzero spectrum consists of eigenvalues of finite algebraic multiplicity accumulating only at 0, and the set of such eigenvalues may be empty. The standard counterexample is the Volterra operator on L^2([0,1]), (V f)(x) = integral from 0 to x of f(t) dt, which is Hilbert-Schmidt (kernel k(x,t) = 1 for t < x, 0 otherwise) hence compact, but has no eigenvalues at all: V f = lambda f with lambda nonzero forces f to be absolutely continuous with f' = f/lambda and f(0) = 0, so f = 0; and V f = 0 forces f = 0 a.e. Thus sigma(V) = {0}, spectral radius 0, while ||V|| = 2/pi; the singular values of V are 1/((n + 1/2) pi), n >= 0, so V is Hilbert-Schmidt but not trace class, and the moduli of its eigenvalues (all zero) are nowhere near its singular values. Consequences for an auditor: (a) 'compact, so expand in eigenfunctions' is invalid without normality; the right substitute is the Schmidt decomposition in singular values, which always exists; (b) 'compact, so the spectral radius equals the norm' is false; (c) Rayleigh-quotient and min-max formulas for eigenvalues are statements about self-adjoint operators and become statements about singular values otherwise; (d) Mercer-type positivity conclusions require a self-adjoint positive kernel, not just an L^2 kernel.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["finite, non-zero variance; with infinite variance the limit, when it exists, is a stable law","independence (identically distributed in the Lindeberg-Levy form, the Lindeberg condition otherwise)"],"created_at":"2026-08-29T02:26:24.138989+00:00","domain":"probability / limit theorems","id":"claim_ac161ddb19210d474662f30b6da4aeb7e8bb6e0e063392305d5b99c6a5de00cf","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Lindeberg-Levy form: let X_1, X_2, ... be independent identically distributed random variables with mean mu and finite variance sigma^2 > 0, and let bar X_n = (X_1 + ... + X_n) / n. Lindeberg-Feller form: for a triangular array of independent, mean-zero rows with s_n^2 = sum_k Var(X_{n,k}), the normalised sums S_n / s_n converge to N(0, 1) provided the Lindeberg condition holds: for every epsilon > 0, (1 / s_n^2) sum_k E[X_{n,k}^2 ; |X_{n,k}| > epsilon s_n] -> 0.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.199182+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ac3b35e8d69c8916a75f31a260dd4f7e833a3c597539ff4b35fbe5e35e24ce2c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 130 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $X^1$ and $X^2$ be solutions to SDEs
    \[
    dX^i(t)
    =
    b^i(t,X^i(t))\,dt
    +
    \sigma^i(t,X^i(t))\,dB_t\,,
    \]
such that $X^1(q_*)$ and $X^2(q_*)$ are equidistributed.
Suppose for some finite constant $\oL$ that the SDE coefficients $b^i$ and $\sigma^i$ are uniformly bounded by $\oL$, and moreover are $\oL$-Lipschitz in the space coordinate. Lastly suppose
	\[
    \sup_{(t,x)\in [q_*
    ,1]\times \mathbb R}
    \bigg\{
    \Big|b^1(t,x) - b^2(t,x)\Big|
    +
 	\Big|\sigma^1(t,x)-\sigma^2(t,x)\Big|
    \bigg\}
    \le \epsilon\,.
    \]
Then the marginal laws of $X^1$ and $X^2$ are close in $L^2$-Wasserstein distance for all time: more precisely, there is a coupling of $X^1$ with $X^2$ under which
	\[
	\sup\bigg\{
	\E\bigg[\Big(X^1(t)-X^2(t)\Big)^2\bigg] 
	: t\in[q_*
        ,1]
	\bigg\} \le 
	C(\oL) \epsilon^2\,,
	\]
where $C(\oL)$ denotes a constant depending only on $\oL$.

\begin{proof}
Couple $X^1$ and $X^2$ with the same Brownian motion $B$, and same initial value (almost surely). For this coupling let $Z(t) = X^1(t)-X^2(t)$, and $E(t) = \E[Z(t)^2]$. By It\=o's formula, for any
$0\le t\le t'\le1$, we have
	\[
	E(t')-E(t)
	=\E \int_t^{t'} \bigg\{
		2 Z(s)
		\Big(b^1(s,X^1(s))-b^2(s,X^2(s))
		\Big)
	+\Big( \sigma^1(s,X^1(s))
		-\sigma^2(s,X^2(s))
		\Big)^2
		\bigg\}\,ds\,.
	\]
For $s\in[q_*,1]$, using that $b^1$ and $b^2$ are $\epsilon$-close to one another, and $\oL$-Lipschitz in the space coordinate, gives
	\[
	\Big|b^1(s,X^1(s))-b^2(s,X^2(s))
	\Big|
	\le \oL\Big| X^1(s)-X^2(s)\Big|
		+ \epsilon
	=\oL |Z(s)|
		+ \epsilon\,.
	\]
A similar bound holds with $\sigma^i$ in place of $b^i$. It follows that 
for $[t,t']\subseteq[q_*,1]$, we have
	\[
	E(t')-E(t)
	\le 3
	\E \int_t^{t'}
	\Big(\oL |Z(s)| + \epsilon\Big)^2\,ds
	\le 6 \bigg\{
	\oL^2 \int_t^{t'} E(s)\,ds
	+ \epsilon^2 (t'-t)
	\bigg\}\,.
	\]
The claimed bound follows from Gr\"onwall's inequality. More precisely, we can use the form stated in \cite[Lem.~6.1]{MR1071170} which says that if for all $t\in[q_*
    ,1]$ we have
	\[
	E(t) \le a(t) +\int_{q_0}^t b(s) E(s)\,ds
	\]
with $a,b$ continuous nonnegative functions, then it holds that
	\[
	E(1)
	\leq 
	E(q_*)
	+
	\int_{q_*
        }^1
	a(s)b(s)
	\exp
	\lt(
	\int_s^1 b(r)\,dr
	\rt)\,ds.
	\]
In our setting $E(q_*)=0$, $b(t)=6\oL^2$, and $a(t)=6\epsilon^2(t-q_*)$. Therefore
$a(1) \le 6\epsilon^2$, and the claimed bound follows.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["N>=3,K>=2,1<=r<K,0<=s,t<=r integers","One arbitrary and one systematic context, remaining contexts known S; source uniform contexts then uniform truths","Known truth identities from actual untagged factual samples and optional verifier; all compatible supports/orientations allowed","Robust source exact-level zero miscalibration; arbitrary generators"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T21:03:49.822810+00:00","domain":"statistical learning; robust calibration; truth support identification","id":"claim_ac4030be2b43ae3f012bf4d5561467d93512ee60948bd24529927d6d06add842","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT; proof (unaudited); independent mathematical, priority and target-scope audit pending. # Neutral truth/false bundles defeat the smaller-count hypothesis

T379-C016 v2, proof (unaudited), exact checks PASS; independent audit pending.
Targets 1/2: auxiliary-route failure, no target score claimed.

For every integer m>=5 and N>=3 set K=3m,r=3(m-1),d=1. In the two
variable contexts L,R suppose the known truth unions have sizes
s=2(m-1),t=r, respectively. There are N-2 fixed known S contexts.
No partition tags are supplied. Both orientations remain compatible:
if L is A its r-support contains C_L of size s; if R is A its support
is exactly C_R of size r. Such unions have positive probability from
actual untagged factual samples with ell=0, e.g. one occurrence of
every known truth, n=s+r. The identities can be permuted within each
context without affecting the construction or source probabilities.

Put lambda=1/(NK). Partition the variable-context atoms as follows:

* B: all K-s=m+2 atoms outside C_L and two atoms outside C_R;
* T: all s known L truths and any s of the known R truths;
* Z: the remaining m-1 known R truths and its one remaining outside atom.

B has m+4 atoms; T has 4(m-1); Z has m. In either orientation and
for EVERY compatible residual L support, their source masses are

 p(B)=lambda*(m+2),
 p(T)=lambda*(4m-2),
 p(Z)=lambda*m.

For B, if L is A its residual true count is r-s=m-1, so
p(B)=(m-1)/(Nr)+2/(NK)=lambda*(m+2). If R is A the same mass comes
from K-s systematic L atoms and no R truths. T's mass is always
s/(Nr)+s/(NK). Z's mass is (m-1)/(Nr)=m/(NK) when R is A and is
also m/(NK) when R is S. This checks invariance directly from p.

Define g as the uniform coarsening of these groups:

 g(B atom)=lambda*(m+2)/(m+4)=q,
 g(T atom)=lambda*(2m-1)/(2(m-1)),
 g(Z atom)=lambda,
 g(fixed S atom)=lambda.

The total is one and all probabilities are nonnegative. Equal lambda
scores merge Z and fixed S; their source masses remain invariant.
Thus g is source Mis_infinity=0 for every compatible world, not just
on average or conditional on a correct orientation prediction.

If L is A all three false atoms lie in B, giving H_L=3q.
If R is A two false atoms lie in B and one in Z, giving H_R=2q+lambda.
Since q<lambda, the worst-world false mass is

 max H=lambda*(3m+8)/(m+4).                              (1)

C016 v1 conjectured that the smaller known count alone gives the exact
value. Here h=s yields that conjectured value

 V_small=3lambda*(m+1)/(m+2).

The actual feasible worst risk (1) is strictly smaller, by

 V_small-max H=lambda*(m-4)/((m+2)(m+4))>0.               (2)

For m=5,N=3 these are 2/35 versus 23/405, gap 1/2835.
This refutes the entire proposed smaller-count formula; it does not
establish the optimal risk in this family. In particular the nine
complete small-alphabet score-partition checks were consistent with
the conjecture but insufficient to prove it. No general lower bound
was promoted from those computations.

The neutral Z group contains truths and possible falsehoods in exactly
the systematic true-density ratio. Its p mass is orientation-invariant
even though the known truth counts are unequal. This mechanism is
invisible to a rule that discards all surplus known truths. A general
unequal-count frontier must account for invariant weighted count
identities, not merely the minimum count or posterior risk ordering.
This is a route obstruction, not a solution of the unrestricted target.
Primary calibration basis: Kalai--Vempala 2311.14648v3 Definitions 1--2.

Verification: logs/neutral_bin_counterexample_check.json records 33
exact rational parameter cases and 582 compatible-world source-bin
calibration checks. It exhausts residual L supports for m=5,6,7;
larger m use the displayed general cardinality proof plus one
representative support, without claiming exhaustive enumeration there.","status":"unverified"}

Facts (Jordan, Lebesgue): (1) f is of bounded variation if and only if f = g - h with g and h nondecreasing on [a, b] (Jordan decomposition; one may take g(x) = V(f; [a, x]), the variation function, and h = g - f, both nondecreasing); (2) a BV function is bounded, has one-sided limits at every point, has at most countably many discontinuities, all of them jumps, and is differentiable Lebesgue-almost everywhere with f' integrable and integral_a^b |f'(x)| dx <= V(f; [a, b]), with equality if and only if f is absolutely continuous; (3) monotone functions and Lipschitz functions are BV (a Lipschitz function with constant L has V <= L (b - a)), while a continuous function need not be: x sin(1/x) on (0, 1] (extended by 0) has infinite variation, and the Cantor function is continuous, nondecreasing, BV, yet has f' = 0 almost everywhere with total variation 1 (so it is not absolutely continuous); (4) BV[a, b] is a Banach space under ||f|| = |f(a)| + V(f; [a, b]); (5) f is BV exactly when the Riemann-Stieltjes integral integral_a^b g df exists for every continuous g, and then g -> integral g df is a bounded linear functional on C[a, b] of norm V(f; [a, b]) - the Riesz representation of the dual of C[a, b] (normalised BV functions correspond to finite signed Borel measures). In higher dimensions BV functions are those whose distributional gradient is a finite vector measure.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:46.149510+00:00","domain":"elliptic regularity, L^p theory","id":"claim_ac7bfef65ba08df89da6d269b48b216132d2600e11e7ada5844f2602810376eb","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: in the Calderon-Zygmund theory for Lu = sum a^{ij}D_{ij}u + b.Du + cu the leading coefficients must be continuous (uniform continuity on the relevant compact set), or at least of vanishing mean oscillation; only then does the freezing-and-absorption step work for every 1 < p < infinity. Mere measurable uniform ellipticity is not enough, and the failure is not a technicality: both the estimate and uniqueness fail. Counterexample (Gilbarg-Serrin type): on the unit ball B_1 in R^n, n >= 2, fix lambda in (0,1) and set a^{ij}(x) = delta^{ij} + beta x_i x_j/|x|^2 with 1 + beta = (n-1)/(1 - lambda) > 0. These coefficients are bounded, symmetric, uniformly elliptic (eigenvalues 1 with multiplicity n-1 and (n-1)/(1-lambda)) and continuous except at the origin. For radial u, D_{ij}u = u''(r) x_i x_j/r^2 + (u'(r)/r)(delta_{ij} - x_i x_j/r^2), hence Lu = (1 + beta) u'' + (n-1) u'/r, and u(x) = |x|^lambda gives Lu = r^{lambda - 2} [ (1 + beta) lambda(lambda - 1) + (n-1) lambda ] = 0. Now w = |x|^lambda - 1 lies in W^{2,p}(B_1) for every p < n/(2 - lambda), lies in W^{1,p}_0(B_1) for those p, satisfies Lw = 0 almost everywhere, and is not identically zero (w(0) = -1). Consequences: the Dirichlet problem is not uniquely solvable in W^{2,p} intersect W^{1,p}_0 for p < n/(2 - lambda), so no global estimate ||w||_{W^{2,p}} <= C ||Lw||_{L^p} can hold there; the maximum principle also fails for such strong solutions (w attains its minimum -1 at an interior point while Lw = 0 and w = 0 on the boundary). Note n/(2 - lambda) < n and lambda may be taken as close to 1 as desired, so the failure reaches every exponent below n. What survives with only measurable coefficients: the Aleksandrov-Bakelman-Pucci estimate and Krylov-Safonov theory, both of which require the solution to be in W^{2,n}_loc - which is exactly the class this example escapes.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.357576+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ac81b303f3d1341ca273c97542be91edbaf419690548b6ea7476e7328eb55d4a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 242 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Fix any $\phi \in C_b(\R,\R)$ and define the domain
	\[
		\ocM^{\Ising+}(\alpha) = \Big\{

		\Big\}\,.
	\]
	Then the function
	\[
		f_\phi(\mu) \equiv \int \phi\,d\mu
	\]
	is uniformly continuous on $\ocM^{\Ising+}(\alpha)$ equipped with the $\bbW_1$ metric.

Since $\phi$ was assumed to be a bounded continuous function, we obtain 
	 \[\lim_{n\to\infty} f_\phi(\mu_n) = f(\mu)\,.\]

\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X a normed space; no completeness of X is needed","for metrizability and sequential compactness of the ball: X separable","Tychonoff (hence a form of the axiom of choice) in the general case"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.752423+00:00","domain":"functional analysis","id":"claim_ad0f3a207b3c5379410429f086bcbbeb1babd7dfb64560bd3c03ab098d3b5d3e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a normed vector space over R or C. The closed unit ball B of the dual space X^* is COMPACT in the weak-* topology, that is the topology of pointwise convergence on X. Two refinements matter. (a) If X is SEPARABLE then the weak-* topology restricted to B is metrizable and B is weak-* SEQUENTIALLY compact, so bounded sequences of functionals have weak-* convergent subsequences; without separability compactness need not give sequential compactness. (b) The general theorem uses Tychonoff's theorem for a product of compact scalar discs and therefore, in ZF, is not provable without some choice; the separable case needs only a diagonal argument. The theorem does NOT say the ball is norm-compact: by Riesz's lemma the closed unit ball of a normed space is norm-compact if and only if the space is finite-dimensional. Nor does it say the ball of X itself is weakly compact - that characterises reflexivity (Kakutani). [standard; e.g. Rudin, Functional Analysis, 2nd ed., Theorem 3.15]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:26:26.807268+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ad2577d53d461574b2aa13e7c5473ca3510eb25e4462f7d955d961221f62d0ed","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:read-k of arXiv:2608.06159, 'Majority Dynamics on Resampled Sparse Erd\H{o}s--R\'enyi Graphs:\\[0.5ex] Gaussian Winner '] {gavinsky2015tail}}]
    
     Let \(\{\rY_j\}_{j\in[r]}\) be a read-\(k\) family of indicator random variables with \(p_j \coloneqq\P(\rY_j=1)\), and denote their average by \(\bar p \coloneqq r^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^r p_j\).
    If \(0<\bar p<1\), then
    \begin{subequations}
    \begin{align}
    \P\bigg(
    \sum_{j=1}^r \rY_j\ge (\bar p+\varepsilon)r
    \bigg)
    &\le
    \exp\bigg(
    -\frac{r}{k}\D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\bar p+\varepsilon\|\bar p)
    \bigg),
    &&0<\varepsilon\le1-\bar p,
    \\
    \P\bigg(
    \sum_{j=1}^r \rY_j\le (\bar p-\varepsilon)r
    \bigg)
    &\le
    \exp\bigg(
    -\frac{r}{k}\D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\bar p-\varepsilon\|\bar p)
    \bigg),
    &&0<\varepsilon\le\bar p.
    \end{align}
    \end{subequations}
    where the Kullback-Leibler divergence is defined as
    \[
    \D_{\mathrm{KL}}(u\|v)\coloneqq
    u\log(u/v)+(1-u)\log((1-u)/(1-v)).
    \]
    We use the standard convention \(0\log0=0\) at \(u\in\{0,1\}\).
    If \(\bar p\in\{0,1\}\), all the indicators are almost surely constant and
    the corresponding tail statements are trivial. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-13T08:46:06.530543+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_adaa019d5495d3e53729b4d371baf52eb8ec09e6bd00a9d24fb8b0ddda8d06b1","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"For the l^p norm on R^2 and the axis direction e_2, the dogleg excess of a midpoint-displaced point v = (d, r/2) is exactly asymptotic to (2^p/p) d^p / r^{p-1} as d/r -> 0 (second-order Taylor of (1 + x^p)^{1/p}). {"assumptions":["(X, Sigma, mu) is a measure space","1 <= p < infinity (the statement is false for p = infinity)","for p = 1: mu sigma-finite (or localizable) for surjectivity; mu semifinite for isometry","scalars real or complex"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:36.552519+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, Lp spaces","id":"claim_adee9ce43c73105fd97da47f2239ef349918c1fc447cc025fb6cb07edd000262","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, Sigma, mu) be a measure space and 1 <= p < infinity with conjugate exponent p'. For g in L^{p'}(mu) define Lambda_g(f) = int_X f g dmu. (a) If 1 < p < infinity, then g -> Lambda_g is an isometric isomorphism of L^{p'}(mu) onto the dual space (L^p(mu))*, for an arbitrary measure space. (b) If p = 1 and mu is sigma-finite (more generally, localizable), then g -> Lambda_g is an isometric isomorphism of L^infinity(mu) onto (L^1(mu))*. In particular L^p is reflexive for 1 < p < infinity. For 1 < p < infinity the map is isometric over every measure space; for p = 1 it is isometric as soon as mu is semifinite, and without sigma-finiteness (or localizability) it need not be surjective. The case p = infinity is genuinely different and is NOT covered: the analogous map L^1(mu) -> (L^infinity(mu))* is isometric when mu is semifinite but in general not surjective, so (L^infinity)* is in general strictly larger than L^1 (see the pitfall).","status":"unverified"}

For an energy E in R define the Schrodinger cocycle (T, A^E) over (Omega,T), where A^E(omega) is the SL(2,R) matrix with rows (E - V(omega), -1) and (1, 0); its iterates are A^E_n(omega) = A^E(T^{n-1}omega) ... A^E(omega), and they transfer solutions of the difference equation u(n+1) + u(n-1) + V(T^n omega)u(n) = E u(n). The cocycle is UNIFORMLY HYPERBOLIC if there is a continuous T-invariant splitting R^2 = E^s(omega) + E^u(omega) and constants C > 0, lambda > 1 with ||A^E_n(omega)v|| <= C lambda^{-n}||v|| for v in E^s(omega) and ||A^E_{-n}(omega)v|| <= C lambda^{-n}||v|| for v in E^u(omega), for all n >= 0 and all omega; equivalently (for SL(2,R) cocycles over a compact base) ||A^E_n(omega)|| >= C lambda^n for all omega and all n >= 0. THEOREM (R. Johnson): E belongs to R \\ Sigma if and only if the cocycle (T, A^E) is uniformly hyperbolic. Equivalently, Sigma is exactly the set of real energies at which the Schrodinger cocycle fails to be uniformly hyperbolic. The same statement holds in the continuum setting for Schrodinger operators -u'' + V(T_t omega)u on the line with a minimal flow, which is Johnson's original formulation, and it is the standard dictionary between spectral theory and the dynamics of the transfer-matrix cocycle. SHARP EDGES. (a) UNIFORM hyperbolicity is far stronger than a positive Lyapunov exponent, and this is the single most often misused point. In the supercritical almost Mathieu operator, and more generally in the localisation regime, the Lyapunov exponent L(E) is positive at EVERY energy of the spectrum; those energies are in Sigma, so the cocycle there is non-uniformly hyperbolic. 'Positive exponent' therefore does NOT imply 'in the resolvent set'; only uniformity does. (b) Minimality of the base is used twice: to make sigma(H_omega) independent of omega, and to propagate the exponential dichotomy from one orbit to all of Omega. For a non-minimal base the spectrum can genuinely depend on omega and the statement must be reformulated (typically with the union of the spectra over the support of an ergodic measure, or over the whole base), so do not apply the equivalence verbatim outside minimality. (c) The theorem characterises the RESOLVENT set, which is open; correspondingly uniform hyperbolicity is an open condition in E and in the cocycle, whereas positivity of the Lyapunov exponent is not open. (d) The statement is for real E; for non-real E the operator is invertible anyway and the associated cocycle is not an SL(2,R) cocycle.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a topological space","f takes values in the extended reals (-infinity, +infinity]","for the liminf characterisation, X is first countable (e.g. metric)","for the attainment-of-the-infimum statement, X is compact","for the approximation by Lipschitz functions, X is metric and f is bounded below"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:07:38.814277+00:00","domain":"general topology, real analysis, calculus of variations","id":"claim_ae0d76cf084a3679aa5c60bc21a5f1aa5a7d55e81a31da780dbc20178aa9cae5","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a topological space and f: X -> (-infinity, +infinity] an extended-real function. f is lower semicontinuous (lsc) at a point x0 if for every real a < f(x0) there is a neighbourhood U of x0 with f(x) > a for all x in U. f is lsc on X iff any one of the following equivalent conditions holds: (i) the superlevel set {x : f(x) > a} is open for every real a; (ii) the sublevel set {x : f(x) <= a} is closed for every real a; (iii) the epigraph {(x,t) in X x R : t >= f(x)} is closed in X x R. If X is first countable (in particular metric), lower semicontinuity at x0 is equivalent to liminf_{x -> x0} f(x) >= f(x0). f is upper semicontinuous iff -f is lsc, and f is continuous iff it is both. Standard facts, each of which is the reason lsc is worth naming: (1) the pointwise SUPREMUM of an arbitrary family of lsc functions is lsc; (2) a sum of finitely many lsc functions is lsc provided no (+infinity) + (-infinity) occurs, and a nonnegative multiple of an lsc function is lsc; (3) a nondecreasing pointwise limit of continuous functions is lsc, and conversely on a METRIC space every lsc function bounded below is the pointwise nondecreasing limit of a sequence of Lipschitz functions (Baire); (4) the indicator 1_A is lsc iff A is open; (5) WEIERSTRASS FORM: if X is compact and f is lsc then f attains its infimum on X, because the sublevel sets {f <= a} are closed and have the finite intersection property. This is the form in which lsc is used in the direct method of the calculus of variations: coercivity plus lsc on a compact (or weakly compact) set yields a minimiser. SHARP EDGES, i.e. what is NOT true. (a) lsc buys you MINIMA only, never maxima: on the compact space [0,1] the function f(x) = x for x < 1, f(1) = 0 is lsc (every superlevel set {f > a} is (a,1) or [0,1] or empty), its supremum is 1 and it is not attained. (b) The supremum of lsc functions is lsc but the INFIMUM of infinitely many lsc functions need not be: on R the continuous functions f_n(x) = max(0, 1 - n|x|) have pointwise infimum the indicator of {0}, whose superlevel set {f > 1/2} = {0} is not open. (c) 'lsc at every point' is genuinely weaker than continuity; an lsc function may be discontinuous on a dense set. (d) Statement (3) uses metrizability of X; on a general topological space an lsc function need not be a pointwise limit of continuous functions (it is a supremum of continuous functions on compact Hausdorff or, more generally, normal spaces, by Urysohn/Katetov-Tong, but for arbitrary X no such representation is available). (e) In integration theory the useful instance is Fatou's lemma, which says exactly that f -> integral f is lsc along pointwise convergence of nonnegative measurable functions; no upper semicontinuity holds there without a domination hypothesis.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["A is a square real matrix with nonnegative entries"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T02:00:35.438555+00:00","domain":"linear algebra, nonnegative matrices","id":"claim_ae5c6a4cb8084ef24a18e45632bcc8943945094a5e71de887f9245aa6e393816","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A real $n \\times n$ matrix $A = (a_{ij})$ is nonnegative ($A \\ge 0$) if all entries are $\\ge 0$, and positive ($A > 0$) if all entries are $> 0$. Associate to $A \\ge 0$ the directed graph $G(A)$ on vertices $1, \\dots, n$ with an edge $i \\to j$ iff $a_{ij} > 0$; then $(A^m)_{ij} > 0$ iff there is a walk of length $m$ from $i$ to $j$. $A$ is irreducible if $G(A)$ is strongly connected (every vertex reaches every other), equivalently if there is no permutation matrix $P$ with $P A P^{\\mathsf T} = \\begin{pmatrix} B & C \\\\ 0 & D\\end{pmatrix}$ with $B, D$ square nonempty blocks, equivalently (for $n \\ge 2$) if $(I + A)^{n-1} > 0$; a $1 \\times 1$ matrix is irreducible by convention (some authors exclude the zero $1\\times1$ matrix). The period (index of imprimitivity) $h$ of an irreducible $A$ is the greatest common divisor of the lengths of all closed walks in $G(A)$; it does not depend on the vertex, and $h = 1$ iff $A$ is aperiodic. $A$ is primitive if $A \\ge 0$ and $A^m > 0$ for some $m \\ge 1$; for nonnegative matrices, primitive $\\iff$ irreducible and aperiodic, and then $A^m > 0$ for all $m \\ge (n-1)^2 + 1$ (Wielandt's bound). Every positive matrix is primitive. Warnings: irreducible does not imply primitive (the cyclic permutation matrix of an $n$-cycle is irreducible with period $n$); a matrix with a positive diagonal entry that is irreducible is automatically primitive; irreducibility is a property of the zero pattern only, not of the magnitudes; a matrix with some negative entries is outside this theory entirely.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:33:46.767216+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ae806e2d14ac53d071e815421fa3fd8d8dd630356962ffc4f1102a910336673a","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 8 of arXiv:2603.24616, 'Pinning in non-critical half-space geometric last passage percolation'] Let $\\Sigma \\subseteq \\mathbb{Z}$ and $\\Lambda \\subseteq \\mathbb{R}$ be an interval. A {\\em $\\Sigma$-indexed line ensemble $\\mathcal{L}$} is a random variable defined on a probability space $(\\Omega, \\mathcal{F}, \\mathbb{P})$ that takes values in $\\left(C (\\Sigma \\times \\Lambda), \\mathcal{C}_{\\Sigma}\\right)$. Intuitively, $\\mathcal{L}$ is a collection of random continuous curves (sometimes referred to as {\\em lines}), indexed by $\\Sigma$, each of which maps $\\Lambda$ into $\\mathbb{R}$. We will often slightly abuse notation and write $\\mathcal{L}: \\Sigma \\times \\Lambda \\rightarrow \\mathbb{R}$, even though it is not $\\mathcal{L}$ which is such a function, but $\\mathcal{L}(\\omega)$ for every $\\omega \\in \\Omega$. For $i \\in \\Sigma$, we write $\\mathcal{L}_i(\\omega) = (\\mathcal{L}(\\omega))(i, \\cdot)$ for the curve of index $i$ and note that the latter is a map $\\mathcal{L}_i: \\Omega \\rightarrow C(\\Lambda)$, which is $\\mathcal{F}/\\mathcal{C}$ measurable. \n\nWe say that a line ensemble $\\mathcal{L}$ is {\\em non-intersecting} if $\\mathbb{P}$-almost surely $\\mathcal{L}_i(t) > \\mathcal{L}_j(t)$ for all $i < j$ and $t \\in \\Lambda$. We say that a line ensemble $\\mathcal{L}$ is {\\em ordered} if $\\mathbb{P}$-almost surely $\\mathcal{L}_i(t) \\geq \\mathcal{L}_j(t)$ for all $i < j$ and $t \\in \\Lambda$. If $[a,b] \\subseteq \\Lambda$, we let $\\mathcal{L}_i[a,b]$ denote the restriction of $\\mathcal{L}_i$ to $[a,b]$, and note that the latter is a measurable map $\\mathcal{L}_i[a,b]: \\Omega \\rightarrow C([a,b])$. If $\\Sigma_1 \\subseteq \\Sigma$ and $[a,b] \\subseteq \\Lambda$, we let $\\mathcal{L}\\vert_{\\Sigma_1 \\times [a,b]}$ denote the restriction of $\\mathcal{L}$ to $\\Sigma_1 \\times [a,b]$, which is a measurable map $\\mathcal{L}\\vert_{\\Sigma_1 \\times [a,b]}: \\Omega \\rightarrow C(\\Sigma_1 \\times [a,b])$.","status":"unverified"}

\[

Because each operator is self-adjoint, the resolvent (A_n - z)^(-1) is bounded with norm at most 1 / |Im z|, so the family is uniformly bounded and it is enough to verify the convergence for a SINGLE non-real z: one z in the upper half plane suffices, the conjugate point following by taking adjoints and the remaining z by the resolvent identity together with the uniform bound. The NORM RESOLVENT SENSE is the same statement with convergence in operator norm; it implies the strong resolvent sense and is strictly stronger. Practical criterion: if all the A_n and A are essentially self-adjoint on a common core D and A_n psi -> A psi for every psi in D, then A_n -> A in the strong resolvent sense. Without such a hypothesis convergence on a dense subspace says nothing, which is precisely why the resolvent formulation, and not naive pointwise convergence of unbounded operators, is the notion that interacts with the spectral theorem.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["real variable on [-1, 1] for the extremal statements; the polynomials themselves are defined on all of R and C"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:31:12.479741+00:00","domain":"approximation theory","id":"claim_af2c306d13e82f8e10b1a499cd863744a70e37247652744c79e094c450f9b166","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"The Chebyshev polynomials of the first kind are defined on [-1, 1] by T_n(cos theta) = cos(n theta), n = 0, 1, 2, ...; equivalently T_0 = 1, T_1 = x and T_{n+1}(x) = 2 x T_n(x) - T_{n-1}(x). Facts: (1) T_n is a polynomial of degree n with leading coefficient 2^{n-1} for n >= 1, and T_n(x) = ((x + sqrt(x^2 - 1))^n + (x - sqrt(x^2 - 1))^n) / 2 for all real x (cosh(n arccosh x) for x >= 1); (2) |T_n(x)| <= 1 on [-1, 1], with T_n(cos(k pi / n)) = (-1)^k at the n + 1 extremal points and zeros at cos((2k - 1) pi / (2n)), k = 1..n, all in (-1, 1); (3) orthogonality: integral_{-1}^{1} T_m(x) T_n(x) dx / sqrt(1 - x^2) = 0 for m != n, pi for m = n = 0, pi/2 for m = n >= 1; (4) MINIMAX (Chebyshev): among all monic polynomials of degree n, 2^{1-n} T_n has the smallest maximum absolute value on [-1, 1], namely 2^{1-n}, and it is the unique minimiser; equivalently x^n is best approximated in the sup norm on [-1, 1] by polynomials of degree < n with error 2^{1-n}; (5) Chebyshev interpolation at the zeros of T_{n+1} has Lebesgue constant O(log n) and the Chebyshev series of a Lipschitz function converges uniformly, which is why Chebyshev nodes replace equispaced nodes (Runge's phenomenon) in numerical analysis. The polynomials of the second kind U_n are defined by U_n(cos theta) sin theta = sin((n+1) theta) and satisfy the same recurrence with U_1 = 2x.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:42:16.236249+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_af301d480ff0d63b1823f79073205a288d43b79de86ce0d2782100e31d4bfd4e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem kpartW1 of arXiv:2607.00149, '\bf Uniform-in-time Propagation-of-Chaos for\\ Stein Variational Gradient Descent'] Let Assumption~(ass:w1-normalized-matern of the paper) hold and suppose the joint initial law of the particles is exchangeable. For fixed \(k\ge1\), define
the random \(k\)-fold empirical occupation measure
\[
        \widehat\mu_T^{N,k}
        :=
        \frac1T\int_0^T (\mu_t^N)^{\odot k}\,dt,
        \qquad
        \overline{\mu^{\otimes k}}_T
        :=
        \frac1T\int_0^T \mu_t^{\otimes k}\,dt,
\]
where
\[
(\mu_t^N)^{\odot k}
:=
\frac{1}{(N)_k}
\sum_{\substack{1\le i_1,\ldots,i_k\le N\\
i_1,\ldots,i_k\ {\rm distinct}}}
\delta_{\bigl(x_{i_1}^N(t),\ldots,x_{i_k}^N(t)\bigr)},
\qquad
(N)_k:=N(N-1)\cdots(N-k+1).
\]
Let \(W_1^{(k)}\) be the Wasserstein distance on \((\mathbb R^d)^k\)
associated with the product cost
\(
        d_k(x,y):=\sum_{\ell=1}^k \|x_\ell-y_\ell\| .
\)
Then, with $\gamma$ as in Theorem~(prop:uniform-time-averaged-w1 of the paper),
\begin{equation}
\lim_{M \to \infty} \, \limsup_{N \to \infty}\,\sup_{T>0}
\mathbb P\left(
W_1^{(k)}
\left(
\widehat\mu_T^{N,k},
\overline{\mu^{\otimes k}}_T
\right)
>
M(\log \log N)^{-\gamma/2}
\right)=0.
\end{equation}
Moreover, suppose the initial distributions satisfy (equation Gaussexp of the paper). 
Define, for $k \ge 1$,
\[
        \bar\mu_T^{N,k}
        :=
        \frac1T\int_0^T
        \mathcal L(x_1^N(t),\ldots,x_k^N(t))\,dt,
        \qquad
        \overline{\mu^{\otimes k}}_T
        :=
        \frac1T\int_0^T \mu_t^{\otimes k}\,dt ,
\]
where $L(x_1^N(t),\ldots,x_k^N(t))$ denotes the joint law of $(x_1^N(t),\ldots,x_k^N(t))$.
Then there is \(C_k<\infty\) such that, for all sufficiently large \(N\),
\begin{equation}
        \sup_{T>0}
        W_1^{(k)}
        \left(
        \bar\mu_T^{N,k},
        \overline{\mu^{\otimes k}}_T
        \right)
        \le
        C_k(\log\log N)^{-\gamma/2}.
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:09:43.682340+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_af46b4cf56dd51b7cb69e8bc90c8cf2f734de6ab113c1193e9b207638b55d439","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma NEW-l:pre-Gron of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] Consider Lipschitz diffusion  coefficients $(b,\sigma)$ as defined in Definition~(NEW-d:lip_assum of the paper). Let $\{X[x]\}_{x\in{\cal X }}$ and $\{X'[x]\}_{x\in{\cal X }}$ be two families of  continuous  processes in $\mathbb{R}^{d'}$ adapted to the filtration generated by the family of i.i.d. standard Brownian motions $\{Z_x(\cdot)\}_{x \in {\cal X }}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d'}$ on $[0,t_0]$ 
and $\mathbb{E} [\|X[x]\|^2]<\infty$, $\mathbb{E} [\|X'[x]\|^2]<\infty$ for all  $x\in{\cal X }$.
Consider  the family of stochastic processes $\{Y[x]\}_{x\in{\cal X }}$ on $\mathbb {M} $, defined on $[0,t_0]$ by
\begin{equation}
   
Y(x,t):= Y(x,0)+\int_0^t b(t, X[x], X[N_x])\, \mathrm{d} t + \sigma(t, X[x], X[N_x])\, \mathrm{d} Z_x(t),
\end{equation}
along with the family of stochastic processes $Y'(x,t)$ on $\mathbb {M} $ defined as above but with $X'$ instead of $X$.
These processes are indexed by the vertices $x\in{\cal X }$, they utilize the graph neighborhood $N_x=\{y\in{\cal X }:y\sim x\}$ on a given graph $\Psi({\cal X })$
and they share the same initial conditions $Y(x,0)=Y'(x,0)$.
Then for any $x\in{\cal X }$ and $t\in[0,t_0]$, we have
\begin{equation}

\mathbb{E}  [\| Y[x,t] - Y'[x,t] \|^2]

{"assumptions":["i.i.d. nonnegative weights on Z^d, d >= 2","F(0) < p_c(d), so the time constant is a norm and the shape is bounded","E min{t_1^d, ..., t_{2d}^d} < infinity, equivalently E[Y^d] < infinity for Y the minimum of 2d independent copies of tau_e - and this condition is necessary, not just sufficient","no curvature, strict convexity or differentiability of B_nu is asserted; those are open"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.542575+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_af7572591de074922b3c8bcd06ef7d3cfa5df7ed73222e70cd4667e68059f97c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Consider i.i.d. first-passage percolation on Z^d, d >= 2, with edge-weight law nu. Assume the two conditions (i) E min{ t_1^d, ..., t_{2d}^d } < infinity, where the t_i are 2d independent copies of tau_e - equivalently E[Y^d] < infinity where Y is the MINIMUM of 2d copies, the two being the same because x -> x^d is increasing on [0, infinity) - and (ii) F(0) < p_c(d). Let B(t) = {x : T(0, x) <= t}, the random ball. Then there is a DETERMINISTIC, convex, COMPACT set B_nu in R^d with NON-EMPTY INTERIOR, symmetric about the axes, such that for every eps > 0, P( (1-eps) B_nu is contained in B(t)/t which is contained in (1+eps) B_nu for all large t ) = 1. The set B_nu is the unit ball of the time constant. Condition (i) is NOT merely convenient: if it fails then for every C > 0 the sum over x of P(m(x) > C|x|) diverges, where m(x) is the minimum weight over the edges at x, and Borel-Cantelli forces T(0,x)/|x| > C for infinitely many x almost surely, so the shape statement itself fails. Condition (ii) is what keeps the shape bounded: if F(0) >= p_c then zero-weight edges percolate, the time constant vanishes and B_nu is all of R^d. What is NOT known, and is repeatedly imported elsewhere as an unproven hypothesis: whether the boundary of B_nu is STRICTLY CONVEX, whether it is DIFFERENTIABLE, and whether it has uniformly positive CURVATURE. Those are open for every non-degenerate weight distribution in every dimension, which is why the Newman-Piza exponent bounds and the directed-geodesic results carry non-constructive curvature or differentiability hypotheses. B_nu is not computed explicitly for any non-trivial F. [Cox and Durrett (1981), verified against Auffinger, Damron and Hanson, 50 Years of First-Passage Percolation, Section 2.2]","status":"unverified"}

This is the first-moment method (a union bound over the C(n,k) cliques); only linearity of expectation is used, and no clique needs to be independent of another. With Stirling's formula the same count gives R(k,k) >= (1 + o(1)) (k / (e sqrt 2)) 2^{k/2}; the Lovasz local lemma (Spencer 1975) improves the constant to (1 + o(1)) (sqrt 2 / e) k 2^{k/2} and nothing better than the exponent k/2 is known. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:00:45.293139+00:00","domain":"QA-corrected (round 3, audit-driven)","id":"claim_b001d8d08609b01c87ed8063363f8c26b11381d1d2005d334f2cefdcc2f036a8","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Schwarz lemma: Let D = {z in C : |z| < 1} be the open unit disk and let f : D -> D be a holomorphic map with f(0) = 0. Then |f(z)| <= |z| for every z in D, and |f'(0)| <= 1. Moreover, if |f(z_0)| = |z_0| for some z_0 in D with z_0 nonzero, or if |f'(0)| = 1, then f is a rotation, i.e. f(z) = a z for some constant a with |a| = 1.
