{"assumptions":["N>=5,d=2,K=3,r=2,ell=0,n=6; two A/S pairs and remaining known S contexts","Actual iid factual samples without tags; p uniform on contexts then true candidates; all A truth supports allowed","Each data-dependent generator robustly exact-level source-calibrated at zero in every compatible world","Conditional V(D) maximizes after data; global Gamma_N maximizes over a fixed world before data"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T21:04:18.141881+00:00","domain":"statistical learning; calibrated generation; global minimax and actual iid data","id":"claim_b06700a866ade064c72020029c1c0095e0197f769e2a689f4972776a20807bd5","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT; proof (unaudited), independent mathematical, priority and target-scope review pending. # A genuine zero-budget global averaging obstruction from repeated facts

T379-C020 v2, proof (unaudited), exact all-world checks PASS; audit pending.
Target 1, secondary target 2: auxiliary-route obstruction, not an exact
global frontier. This concerns actual iid training, not only an
artificial conditional posterior or a handpicked world.

## Experiment and objectives

Fix any N>=5. Set d=2,K=3,r=2,ell=0,n=6. There are two A/S pairs,
one A and one S each, and N-4 fixed S contexts. A has an arbitrary
uniform two-element truth support; S has all three truths. Source p
chooses contexts uniformly and then truths uniformly. Observe six
iid factual samples WITHOUT orientation labels or verifier information.
Require every data-dependent generator to have source Mis_infinity=0
in EVERY world compatible with its observed facts, at exact score bins.

For data D let V(D) be the conditional minimum over robustly calibrated
generators of their maximum compatible-world false mass. Let

 B_N=E_w[V(D)],
 Gamma_N=inf_policy max_fixed_world w E_w[H(policy(D))].

B_N is independent of the fixed actual world w: sibling permutations
and within-context candidate permutations map any world to any other,
preserve the model and compatibility, and carry source calibration,
false mass and V(D) with them. The data laws are carried along by the
same bijections. Thus V(D)'s distribution is identical in all worlds.

The candidate strict inequality is

 Gamma_N <= B_N-5/(1008*N^7) < B_N.                      (1)

No numerical value of B_N or Gamma_N is claimed. The point is that
expected conditional worst-world risk overstates global expected
minimax risk even at ZERO source calibration budget.

## Finite conditional selectors exist

There are finitely many actual worlds and finitely many score
partitions of the NK atoms. For a zero-calibrated g its score partition
Pi satisfies g=p_w,Pi for every compatible w, so a fixed Pi admits at
most one such g. Merging equal-score cells preserves this property.
The one-cell uniform generator is always feasible, so each V(D) is
attained among finitely many candidates. Choose any deterministic
conditional minimizer g*_D by a fixed tie rule. This selector is an
existence construction, not a claim of computational efficiency.
For every actual w it satisfies H_w(g*_D)<=V(D) pointwise.
Datasets incompatible with every source world may use the uniform
fallback; they have probability zero under every actual world.

## Observable rare event and its conditional value

Let E be the event that all six samples have this pattern:

* Four copies of ONE candidate in ONE context of one pair;
* one fact in each of the two contexts of the other pair;
* no other observations.

The pair roles, repeated context, candidate identities and sample
order are unrestricted. E is recognizable from the data alone.
Its known-truth counts are (1,0) in the repeated pair and (1,1) in
the other pair, all strictly below r=2. Thus C017's exact zero-budget
frontier, with pairwise minima 0 and 1, gives

 V(D)=1/(3N)+7/(24N)=5/(8N) on E.                        (2)

For clarity, the (1,0) pair's zero-calibrated bins must contain whole
contexts: support swaps make each uncertified set constant-score and
orientation invariance with the zero-known sibling leaves no known
truths available to peel from that context. Forgetting the repeated
fact therefore preserves all source-bin and false-count information.
The resulting balanced (0,0)/(1,1) game has artificial mean densities
1/(3N),7/(24N) on its residual groups, with false risks 1/6,1/4;
safe densities are higher. The per-bin low-density tail argument
gives the lower value (2), and the invariant-group mean attains it
worldwise. This is a conditional worst-world assertion, not an
actual-orientation posterior calculation.

## A causal calibrated generator on E

Let x be the observed four-repeat context. Let a,b be the two contexts
of the other pair and let their single observed candidates be c_a,c_b.
Form B from ALL THREE atoms of x plus the four atoms of a,b other
than c_a,c_b. Its source mass is 1/N+7/(6N)=13/(6N) in every
compatible world; its seven atoms get score q=13/(42N).
Give the two observed atoms in a,b score 5/(12N). Give every other
atom score lambda=1/(3N), including the untouched sibling of x and
all fixed S contexts. The group masses sum to one. All source group
masses are invariant across orientations and supports, so exact-score
mergers preserve source Mis_infinity=0. The rule uses observed context
counts and observed truths only; it never reads the hidden orientation.

If x is actually A, false mass is H_A=2q=13/(21N).
If x is actually S, false mass is H_S=q+lambda=9/(14N).
These identities hold for every compatible truth-support choice.

## Fixed-world event probabilities, not a posterior shortcut

In ANY fixed actual world, summing over the repeated candidate
identity gives repeated-four-fact weights proportional to

 r*(1/(Nr))^4=1/(N^4*r^3) for the A context,
 K*(1/(NK))^4=1/(N^4*K^3) for the S context.

Consequently, conditional on E, the repeated context is actually A
with probability K^3/(K^3+r^3)=27/35, uniformly in every fixed world.
The exponent is THREE, not four: the number of available true
candidate identities must be included. The other pair's one sample
per context contributes 1/N^2 after its identities are summed out.

There are two choices of repeated pair and 6!/(4!1!1!)=30 orders.
Thus in every fixed world

 P_w(E)=60/N^6*(1/8+1/27)=175/(18N^6),                  (3)
 E_w[H_pool|E]=(27/35)*13/(21N)+(8/35)*9/(14N)
             =153/(245N),
 V(E)-E_w[H_pool|E]=1/(1960N).                           (4)

These are ordinary disjoint-event sums under the fixed sampling law;
no independence of learned events or hidden labels is assumed.

## Global policy and strict separation

Use the explicit pooling generator on E and g*_D otherwise. Every
outcome is robustly zero-calibrated. For every fixed actual world,

 E_w H <= E_w[1_{not E}V(D)]+P_w(E)*153/(245N)
       =B_N-P_w(E)/(1960N)
       =B_N-5/(1008N^7).

Taking the maximum over w proves (1). At N=5 the exact strict gap
certified by this construction is 1/15750000. This is an upper bound
on Gamma_N relative to B_N, not an exact value for either objective.

The result complements C014's positive-budget example and C015's
single-outcome pointwise control. Here the improvement is realized
under actual iid data, uniformly for EVERY fixed world, at zero
budget. A global expected lower bound must therefore use a valid
fixed-prior/per-world argument rather than average conditional maxima.
Primary statistic: Kalai--Vempala 2311.14648v3 Definitions 1--2 pp.8--9.

N=5,6,9, totaling 6480 positive-probability source-calibration checks

event outcomes worsen risk, so the improvement is genuinely in
expectation. A three-repeat fault produces the wrong sign in all
108 world/parameter cases. The general finite-selector and symmetry
proof supplies the global conclusion; neither B_N nor Gamma_N is
estimated numerically.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:36:44.552249+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b0be67e39a0d300955fb603890c21971ebe679661fbaf4e11e148a94b91923d6","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 26 of arXiv:2604.01978, 'Homogenized Transformers'] Let $f:(\S^{d-1})^n\to \reals$ be $C^2$, and let $\tilde f$ be a $C^2$ extension of $f$ to a
neighborhood of $(\S^{d-1})^n$ in $\reals^{d\times n}$.
Then the Riemannian gradient of $f$ on $(\S^{d-1})^n$ is
\begin{equation*}
\grad f(X)=\proj_X \nabla \tilde f(X),
\end{equation*}
where $\nabla \tilde{f}$ denotes the Euclidean gradient in $\reals^{d\times n}$ of $\tilde f$.

For any tangent vector $V\in \mathsf{T}_X(\S^{d-1})^n$, the Riemannian Hessian satisfies
\begin{equation*}
\Hess f(X)[V]
=\proj_X\left(\nabla^2 \tilde f(X)[V] - V\,\Diag\left(\diag(X^{\sT}\nabla \tilde f(X))\right)\right).
\end{equation*}
Equivalently, component-wise,
\[
\left(\Hess f(X)[V]\right)_i
=\proj_{x_i}\left(\nabla^2_{x_i}\tilde f(X)[V]_i - \langle x_i,\nabla_{x_i}\tilde f(X)\rangle\,v_i\right).
\]
If $V$ is a $C^1$ vector field on $(\S^{d-1})^n$ and $f$ is smooth, then the second-order operator
$V^2$ is
\[
(V^2 f)(X)= V(V f)(X)
= \Hess f(X)[V(X),V(X)] + \langle \grad f(X),(\nabla_V V)(X)\rangle,
\]
where $\nabla_V$ is the Levi--Civita connection on $(\S^{d-1})^n$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f in C^2_1(R^n x [0,infinity)) with compact support (boundedness of f and its first two space derivatives and first time derivative suffices for the same conclusion)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:49.106060+00:00","domain":"parabolic partial differential equations","id":"claim_b0e94f995d33a364f8dd3e8bbfae914375ff61ea21fbef6596900a51304730ca","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $f\\in C^2_1(\\mathbb R^n\\times[0,\\infty))$ have compact support, and let $\\Phi(x,t)=(4\\pi t)^{-n/2}e^{-|x|^2/(4t)}$ for $t>0$. Define $u(x,t)=\\int_0^t\\!\\!\\int_{\\mathbb R^n}\\Phi(x-y,t-s)f(y,s)\\,dy\\,ds$. Then $u\\in C^2_1(\\mathbb R^n\\times(0,\\infty))$, $u_t-\\Delta u=f$ in $\\mathbb R^n\\times(0,\\infty)$, and $u(x,t)\\to0$ as $(x,t)\\to(x_0,0)$ for every $x_0$. In semigroup notation $u(t)=\\int_0^te^{(t-s)\\Delta}f(s)\\,ds$: the inhomogeneous solution is the superposition of homogeneous evolutions started at each time $s$ with initial datum $f(\\cdot,s)$. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:58:01.552948+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b0e9d0c9b19fa91febc0442ad4646b769c80e5e0b0a7c82036daa4f5d12b7244","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 9 of arXiv:2608.27143, 'An approximate zero bias transformation for random sums: Applications to sampling with out'] Let $n_1\in \mathbb{N}.$ Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be mean zero random variables with finite variances.
Suppose that
$X_1,\ldots,X_{n_1} \text{ and }
X_{n_1+1}, X_{n_1+1},\ldots$
form two independent groups of i.i.d.\ random variables, where the distributions may differ
between the two groups. Let $W=\sum_{i=1}^N X_i$, where $N$ is  a binomial random variable  with parameters $n$ and $p$, independent of $\{X_i\}_{i=1}^\infty$, and let $\sigma^2$ be defined as in \eqref{TH:IC1}.  
   Then
			\begin{align*}
				d_1\left(\mathcal{L}(W/\sigma), \mathcal{L}(Z) \right)
				&\le \frac{1}{\sigma^3}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{1}} \left(\E|X_1|^3 + 2\E X_1^2 \E|X_1|\right) P^2(N \ge i) \\
				&\quad + \frac{1}{\sigma^3} \sum_{i=n_{1}+1}^{n} \left(\E|X_{n_{1}+1}|^3 + 2\E X_{n_{1}+1}^2  \E|X_{n_{1}+1}|\right) P^2(N \ge i) \\
				&\quad + \frac{2\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{\pi}} \left(1 - \sum_{i=1}^{n_1}\frac{\Var(X_1)}{\sigma^2} \, {P}^2(N \ge i) -\sum_{i=n_1+1}^{n}\frac{\Var(X_{n_1+1})}{\sigma^2} \, {P}^2(N \ge i)\right),
			\end{align*}
			where $Z$ is a standard normal random variable. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:52:32.341091+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b0f815421f3b2f989c85c8b5cd8272474e5a34b17699414d207493caba6f0ab6","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Def of arXiv:2609.04023, 'Characterizing Contractions and Weighted Blowdowns'] {{[QR]}}
   A {\em weighted embedding} $Y_\bullet \hookrightarrow X$ is defined by a sequence of closed embeddings $\{Y_n = V(I_n) \hookrightarrow X\}_{n \ge 0}$ such that $\bigoplus_{i \ge 0} I_n t^n$ defines a \textit{Rees algebra} that is, a quasicoherent, finitely-generated, graded $\mathcal{O}_X$-subalgebra of $\mathcal{O}_X[t]$, satisfying
   \begin{enumerate}
      \item[(i)] $I_0 \supset I_1 \supset I_2 \supset \cdots$
      \item[(ii)] $I_nI_m \subset I_{n+m}$
      \item[(iii)] Locally in the smooth topology on $X$, there exists a sufficiently large positive integer $d$ such that for each $n \ge 1$,
      \[
       I_n = \left ( I_1^{l_1} I_2^{l_2} \cdots I_d^{l_d} \ : \ l_i \in \mathbb{N}, \ \sum_{i=1}^d il_i = n \right )
      \]
      in which case we say $I_\bullet$ is generated in degrees $\le d.$ 
   \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["H must be convex and superlinear for the Hopf-Lax (Lax-Oleinik) representation with L = H*","The Hopf formula requires convex initial datum g instead, with H merely continuous","Counterexample: H(p) = (p^2-1)^2, g(x) = x/2, where Hopf-Lax returns the solution for H** and misses the flux by H(1/2) - H**(1/2) = 9/16"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.418414+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: Hamilton-Jacobi equations","id":"claim_b153eb3a5fb04c6f5b11975f8d220003ec053be109078039e18bb58d9896bdc1","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: in u(x,t) = min_y ( t L((x-y)/t) + g(y) ) with L = H*, the Hamiltonian H must be CONVEX (and superlinear). For a nonconvex H the formula does not solve u_t + H(Du) = 0: since H* = (H**)*, the formula reproduces the equation with H replaced by its convex envelope H**. Counterexample (n = 1): H(p) = (p^2 - 1)^2 is continuous and superlinear but not convex, and H**(p) = 0 for |p| ≤ 1, H**(p) = H(p) for |p| ≥ 1. Take the Lipschitz datum g(x) = x/2. The true solution is the classical (hence viscosity) solution u(x,t) = x/2 - t H(1/2) = x/2 - (9/16) t. The Hopf-Lax expression gives min_y ( tL((x-y)/t) + y/2 ) = x/2 - t L*(1/2) = x/2 - t H**(1/2) = x/2, which satisfies u_t + H(u_x) = 0 + (1/4 - 1)^2 = 9/16 ≠ 0 at EVERY point — it is not even an almost-everywhere solution. The correct nonconvex counterpart is the Hopf formula u(x,t) = sup_p ( x·p - t H(p) - g*(p) ), valid for continuous H when the DATUM g is convex; for nonconvex H and general Lipschitz g there is no closed formula and one works with viscosity solutions directly. Auditor's check: whenever a proof writes a value function / Hopf-Lax representation, confirm convexity (of H for Hopf-Lax, of g for Hopf) before trusting it; the corresponding control interpretation (L as a running cost) also fails without convexity.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:17:42.303248+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b162c9199bd7f4aff140db2ccfaf697b85dbc8d4301da1e2c5cd8d3f236c2d8d","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 37 (SRI chain) of arXiv:2510.22155, 'Random walks in space-time random media in all spatial dimensions: the full subcritical fl'] Fix some integers $k,d\ge 1$, and let $I$ as always be an additive locally compact subgroup of $\mathbb R^d$. Consider a Markov kernel $\br(\x,\mathrm d \mathbf y)$ on $I^k$. We say that the $q^{th}$ moments of $\br$ are bounded by $M$ if\begin{align}\sup_{\mathbf x \in I^k} \int_{I^k}|   y_i-   x_i|^q \br(\x,\mathrm d \mathbf y)&\leq M,\text{ for all } 1\le i \le k,

\end{align} Let $F: [0,\infty) \to [0,\infty)$ be a decreasing function. Let $\nu$ be some probability measure on $I$, and let $M>0$.  
A $k\times d$ \textbf{SRI chain with base measure $\nu$ and decay function $F$} is defined as a Markov kernel $\br$ on $I^k$, satisfying 
\begin{align}\| \br(\x,\bullet) - \nu^{\otimes k} (\mathbf x-\bullet)\|_{TV} &\leq F\big(\min_{1\le i<j\le k} |    x_i-   x_j|\big)\;\;\text{ for all } \x\in I^k .
\end{align} Here $\mathbf x = (   x_1,...,   x_k) \in I^k \subset \mathbb R^{kd}$. 
We denote by $\mathcal E^{\mathrm{SRI}}_{k\times d}(q,M,F)$ the set of all SRI chains on $I^k$ whose $q^{th}$ moments are bounded by $M$, and such that \eqref{tvb2} holds with $F$ on the right side, though we allow the base measure $\nu$ to vary between different elements of $\mathcal E^{\mathrm{SRI}}_{k\times d}(q,M,F)$. 

We furthermore say that the SRI chain is \textbf{centered} if $$\int_{I^k} (y_j-x_j) \br (\x,\dr\y) = \int_I    u \;\nu(\dr    u),\;\; \x\in I^k, 1\le j \le k.$$

We will say that an SRI chain is $\delta$-\textbf{repulsive} 
$$\int_{I^k} |   y_i-   y_j-(   x_i-   x_j)| \br(\x ,\dr \y) 
> \delta
\text{ for all $\x\in I^k$ and all $1\le i <j \le k$.}$$","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.161181+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b16dada1d2b6d35b3428c8fda0e031d4e220ce870a3028c903adf0c090078896","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 10 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For $\mu,\mu'$ satisfying condition~\eqref{e:def-Lambda},
if we have $\vwww'\ge0$ with $(\mu',\vwww')=1$,
then we can find $\vwww\ge0$ with $(\mu,\vwww)=1$ 
such that
	\[
	\|\vwww-\vwww'\|_1
	\le \frac{\|\mu-\mu'\|_\infty}{\iota^2}
	\,.\]
Note if $\YY' \equiv (\vBBb,\vvvv,\vUUu,\vwww)'\in\cD_{\mu'}$, and we find $\vwww$ as above, then
    $\YY=(\vBBb',\vvvv',
    \vUUu',\vwww)\in\cD_\mu$.

\begin{proof}
We start with $\vwww'\ge0$ satisfying $(\mu',\vwww')=1$, which by condition~\eqref{e:def-Lambda} implies that
	\[\|\vwww'\|_1
	\le \frac{(\mu',\vwww')}{\iota}
	=\frac{1}{\iota}\,.
	\]
Abbreviating $\delta\equiv \|\mu-\mu'\|_\infty$, it follows that
	\[
	\Big|(\mu,\vwww')-1\Big|
	=  \Big|(\mu-\mu',\vwww')\Big|
	\le \|\mu-\mu'\|_\infty \|\vwww'\|_1
	\le \frac{\delta}{\iota}\,.
	\]
We then choose $\vwww$ to satisfy $(\mu,\vwww)=1$, which we can do with a similar construction as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:random-YY-in-cD}: if $(\mu,\vwww')\ge1$
(resp.\ $(\mu,\vwww')<1$), let $\vwww$ be any vector with $\vwww\le\vwww'$ (resp.\ $\vwww\ge\vwww'$) such that $(\mu,\vwww)=1$. Then, similarly as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:random-YY-in-cD}, we can use the above to bound
	\[\frac{\delta}{\iota}
	\ge
	\Big|(\mu,\vwww')-1\Big|

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:44:27.969581+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b185048fd62fc19c53bbeb26857b05a7b1655ae296ab13fa91660bdc7f1a7a56","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 6 of arXiv:2607.13273, 'Asymptotics of transition densities for L\'evy processes with stochastic resetting'] Let $\alpha\in(0,2)$ and $Y_t$ be a cylindrical $\alpha$-- stable process in $\Rd,$ i.e.,
    \[
       \mE e^{i\langle \xi, Y_t \rangle } = \prod_{k=1}^d e^{-t|\xi_k|^\alpha} = e^{-t\sum_{k=1}^d|\xi_k|^\alpha},\quad \xi\in\Rd, t>0.

    Let $\theta\in \mathbb{S}^{d-1} = \{y\in\Rd:\: |y|=1\} $ and let $m$ denote a number of non--zero coordinates of $\theta.$

    \[
       C_{\alpha,d} = \mathcal{A}_{1,\alpha}^m \Gamma\left(\frac{m-d}{\alpha}+m+1\right)\left(\frac{\Gamma(\frac{1}{\alpha})}{\alpha\pi}\right)^{d-m}.

For every a > 0, P(X - mu >= a) <= sigma^2 / (sigma^2 + a^2), and by symmetry P(X - mu <= -a) <= sigma^2 / (sigma^2 + a^2). For sigma^2 > 0 this is strictly smaller than the bound min(1, sigma^2 / a^2) that Chebyshev's inequality gives for the one-sided tail; at sigma^2 = 0 both are 0. The bound is attained for every sigma^2 > 0 and a > 0: the law that puts mass sigma^2 / (sigma^2 + a^2) at mu + a and mass a^2 / (sigma^2 + a^2) at mu - sigma^2 / a has mean mu, variance sigma^2 and P(X - mu >= a) = sigma^2 / (sigma^2 + a^2).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-09T13:38:08+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b1aa480f1b67138f42975b167f14a82eb6515e69096e662d374bfe60b1b23eb8","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (Omega, F, (F_t)_{0 <= t <= T}, P) be a filtered probability space and let N^1, N^2 be Poisson processes on [0, T] with rates lambda_1, lambda_2 >= 0 with respect to this one filtration: each N^i is cadlag and adapted with N^i(0) = 0, and for 0 <= s <= u <= T the increment N^i(u) - N^i(s) is independent of F_s and Poisson distributed with mean lambda_i (u - s). Then N^1 and N^2 are independent if and only if almost surely they have no common jump time in [0, T]. {"assumptions":["Omega is bounded and open in R^n","L is locally uniformly elliptic: a^{ij} symmetric with a^{ij} xi_i xi_j >= lambda(x)|xi|^2, lambda(x) > 0 in Omega","|b^i|/lambda is bounded on Omega","c <= 0 in Omega (identically 0 for the sharper form (i))","u is in C^2(Omega) and continuous up to the closure of Omega","the differential inequality L u >= 0 holds pointwise in Omega"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:13:10.396277+00:00","domain":"elliptic PDE, maximum principles","id":"claim_b1af22df20531351edcba66ebf511db40a02c503c0d643a4140f3798e72e41d2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Omega be a BOUNDED open subset of R^n and let L u = a^{ij}(x) D_{ij} u + b^i(x) D_i u + c(x) u with a^{ij} = a^{ji}, L locally uniformly elliptic in the sense that a^{ij}(x) xi_i xi_j >= lambda(x)|xi|^2 with lambda(x) > 0 for every x in Omega, and with |b^i(x)|/lambda(x) bounded on Omega. Let u be in C^2(Omega) intersect C^0(closure of Omega). (i) If c is identically 0 and L u >= 0 in Omega, then max over the closure of u = max over the boundary of u (and if L u <= 0, min over the closure = min over the boundary). (ii) If c <= 0 in Omega and L u >= 0 in Omega, then max over the closure of u <= max over the boundary of u^+, where u^+ = max(u, 0); if L u <= 0 then min over the closure of u >= -max over the boundary of u^-. (iii) If c <= 0 and L u = 0, then max over the closure of |u| = max over the boundary of |u|. Nothing is assumed about continuity of the coefficients, and no sign condition is placed on a^{ij} beyond positive definiteness. WHERE IT FAILS: (a) the sign condition c <= 0 cannot be dropped - on Omega = (0,pi) x (0,pi) the function u(x_1,x_2) = sin(x_1) sin(x_2) satisfies Laplacian(u) + 2u = 0 (so c = 2 > 0), vanishes on the whole boundary and is strictly positive inside; (b) with c <= 0 but not identically 0 the positive part in (ii) is necessary: on Omega = (0,1) with L = d^2/dx^2 - k^2 the function u(x) = -cosh(k(x - 1/2))/cosh(k/2) solves L u = 0, equals -1 at both endpoints and equals -1/cosh(k/2) > -1 at the midpoint, so max over Omega of u strictly exceeds max over the boundary of u, while remaining below max of u^+ = 0; (c) boundedness of Omega cannot be dropped - u(x) = x_n is harmonic on the half-space {x_n > 0}, vanishes on its boundary and is unbounded above; on unbounded domains one needs a Phragmen-Lindelof growth restriction; (d) |b|/lambda must be bounded and lambda > 0 - degenerate ellipticity or unbounded drift relative to lambda destroys the auxiliary-function step. The conclusion is a bound by boundary values only, with no gradient information; the strong maximum principle (Hopf) is a separate statement requiring connectedness and local uniform ellipticity.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["members fitted on training rows only; calibration and evaluation rows are disjoint subsets of the test rows","paired comparisons cell by cell; small-calibration arms use the same subsample draws for every estimator"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T09:17:06.630206+00:00","domain":"ensemble learning","id":"claim_b1af80c830980c68889b9acac6f530d6836b4a70edf57875df3cb64a911900ce","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Measured 2026-09-05 on two stacking pools with the same protocol (test rows split 40/60 by a fixed permutation into calibration and evaluation, per-sample relative $L_2$ metric, paired gains): EMIT (10 seeds x 4 components = 40 cells; 23 members, 285 outputs, 932 calibration rows) and OCO-2 (10 seeds x 3 bands = 30 cells; 18 members, 40 outputs, 800 rows). The cross-validation-free estimator - error covariance in the relative metric, centred with an intercept, long-only minimum-variance weights, no cleaning constant - against the pool's best heuristic (per-output least squares shrunk toward the pooled simplex weights by a cross-validated amount): EMIT $+4.6$ percent at full calibration (33 of 40 cells; $+8.8$ over least squares; $+9.3$ on the physical radiance metric, 10 of 10 seeds), $+4.6/+5.1/+4.9$ at $n = 60/120/240$ calibration rows on the same draws, sign preserved under a second split ($+2.5$ mean); OCO-2 $-1.3$ percent at full calibration (0 of 30 cells; $-0.3$ against least squares) and $-4.4/-2.2/-1.3$ at $n = 60/120/240$, sign preserved under a second split ($-1.5$, correlation 0.89). Tempering the metric weighting ($\\|y\\|^{-2\\gamma}$, $\\gamma < 1$) does not help either corpus: at full calibration $\\gamma = 1$ is best or within $0.5$ percent on the median cell, on the ten EMIT cells with effective sample size below 20 at $n = 60$ the oracle $\\gamma$ is worth $+0.5$ percent on average, and a rule choosing $\\gamma$ by the effective sample size loses $4.4$ percent - the reported metric's weighting is right at every calibration size and its small effective sample size is a diagnostic, not a lever.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:07:15.774583+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b1fcdbf5e423a491c5c66fbee6023c3bd7d71bb383190f85b60655b82350babb","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:wn of arXiv:2608.05089, 'Correlation decay in area-tilted line ensembles'] The set $\mathcal{W}_N$ consists of all collections $\mathbf{W}$ of $n$ random walk trajectories $\mathbf{W} = (W^i : i \in \{1,\dotsc,n\})$,
where each $W^i$ is a function $[\ell,r]_N \to \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}} \mathbb{Z}$, such that $\mathbf{W}$ satisfies the following conditions.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item For each $i \in \{1,\dotsc,n\}$ and all $t_1, t_2 \in [\ell,r]_N$ with $|t_1 - t_2| = \frac{1}{N}$, we have
    $\mleft| W^i(t_1) - W^i(t_2) \mright| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}$, so that $W^i$ is a diffusively rescaled random walk trajectory.
    \item For each $t \in [\ell,r]_N$, we have the nonintersection constraint $W^1(t) > \dotsb > W^n(t)$.
    \item For each $i \in \{1,\dotsc,n\}$, the trajectory $W^i$ has appropriate boundary conditions, which we now explain.
    We would like to have $W^i(\ell_N) = x^i + O(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}})$ and $W^i(r_N) = y^i + O(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}})$,
    but some care is needed here.
    First, if $x^i$ and $x^{i+1}$ are very close (or equal), then choosing arbitrary discrete approximations of the boundary conditions
    may violate the strict ordering of the random walk trajectories.
    Furthermore, since the parity of the two boundary conditions must be compatible in order for $W^i$ satisfying the above conditions to exist,
    we will need to correct this issue if it arises.
    So we will impose the boundary conditions
    \begin{equation}
        W^i(\ell_N) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}} \mleft( \mleft\lfloor \sqrt{N} x^i \mright\rfloor + 2 (n-i) \mright)
        \qquad \text{ and } \qquad
        W^i(r_N) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}} \mleft( \mleft\lfloor \sqrt{N} y^i \mright\rfloor + 2(n-i) + \epsilon^i \mright),
    \end{equation}
    where $\epsilon^i \in \{0,1\}$ is chosen (depending on $x^i, y^i$, and $N$) to mitigate the parity issue,
    and the term $2(n-i)$ is added to ensure strict ordering of the boundary conditions.
    \item For each $t \in [\ell,r]_N$ and each $i \in \{1,\dotsc,n\}$ we have the floor and ceiling constraints.
    To state these constraints, we introduce the linear interpolation $\widetilde{\mathbf{W}} = (\widetilde{W}^i)_{i=1}^n$ of $\mathbf{W}$, which is a continuous function
    $[\ell,r] \to \mathbb{A}_+^n$ obtained by interpolating $\mathbf{W}$ linearly between points of $[\ell,r]_N$, and extending by a constant
    in $[\ell,r] \setminus [\ell,r]_N$ (i.e.\ at the edges).
    The floor and ceiling constraint is then that $\widetilde{W}^i(t) \in (f^i(t), g^i(t))$ for all $t \in [\ell,r]$. 
\end{enumerate}
This completes the definition of our set of possible states $\mathcal{W}_N$ in the
discrete model of a line ensemble. Note that due to our choices of boundary
conditions,
$\mathcal{W}_N$ is nonempty as long as $N$ is large enough and the
boundary conditions are compatible with the floors and ceilings.

For example,
to construct one element $\mathbf{W} \in \mathcal{W}_N$, we may first let $W^n_\ell$ take
downwards steps away from the left boundary, only taking upwards steps when a
downwards step would intersect $f^n$.  Similarly, we may let $W^n_r$ take
downwards steps away from the right boundary, and set $W^n =
\max\{W^n_\ell,W^n_r\}$.  Then we may inductively construct $W^i$ in the same
way, ensuring that it also does not intersect $f^i$ or $W^{i+1}$.  As long as
$N$ is large enough, the ceiling constraint will also be satisfied since there
is some constant minimum amount of room between $f^i$ and $g^i$ as $\mathbf{f} \prec
\mathbf{g}$ and these functions are continuous on a compact interval.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.357023+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b246d11cd7903d8c6088cf77c46e0bfd50f8b07422a32d6f33af4b4d07225324","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 238 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $\alpha,L,\delta>0$ there exists $c = c(\alpha,L,\delta) > 0$ such that the following holds for all $\fq\in [1,2]$ and all sufficiently large $N$.
Recall $\mu_\bG(\bx)$ defined in \eqref{eq:proj-pursuit-def}. For any fixed $\mu \in \cP_2(\R)$ and $L$-Lipschitz algorithm $\cA_N$, abbreviate $\bx\equiv\bx_N\equiv \cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)$ as before, and define the random variables
	\begin{align*}
	X&\equiv X_N
	\equiv X(\bG,\bg^\aux)
	\equiv \bbW_\fq\Big(\mu_\bG(\bx_N),\mu\Big)\,,\\
	J&\equiv J_N
	\equiv J(\bG,\bg^\aux)
	\equiv 
	\bbW_\fq\Big(
	\EmpDist(\bx_N),\cP(\{\pm1\})
	\Big)\,.
	\end{align*}
 We then have the bounds
\begin{align}
		\bbP\Big(
			|X_N - \E X_N|
			\le \delta
		\Big)
		& \ge 1-e^{-cN}\,,\\	
		\bbE\Big[
			(X_N - \E X_N)^2
		\Big] 
		&= o_N(1)\,,\\
		
		\bbP\Big(
			|J_N - \E J_N|
			\le \delta
		\Big)
		& \ge 1-e^{-cN}\\

		\bbE\Big[
			( J_N - \E J_N)^2
		\Big] 
		&= o_N(1)\,.
	\end{align}
where $o_N(1)$ denotes a term tending to $0$ as $N\to\infty$, which may depend on $\alpha,L,\mu$.
	Analogous inequalities to \eqref{e:Wq.lip.to.fixed.msr.conc.tail} and  \eqref{e:Wq.lip.to.fixed.msr.conc.var} hold with $\mu_{\bG,\sym}(\bx_N)$ in place of $\mu_\bG(\bx_N)$, and $\mu \in \cP_2(\R_{\ge 0})$.
\begin{proof}
	Throughout this proof, $c$ denotes a constant that depends on $\alpha,L,\delta$, which can change line by line.
	Let $C = C(\alpha)$ be given by Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.subgaussian.basic}. As in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound}, let
	\[\bar{\bx}
	\equiv\bar\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux) 
		\equiv \bx \min \bigg\{
			1, \frac{2N^{1/2}}{\|\bx\|}\bigg\}\,.\] 
However, in contrast with the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound}, we now let $\bar{\bg}^a$ denote the $a$-th row of 
	\[\bar\bG = \bG \min\bigg(1,\frac{CN^{1/2}}{\|\bG\|_{\op}}\bigg)\,.\]
 We then define the measure
	\[
		\bar\mu(\bG,\bg^\aux) = \EmpDist\bigg(\frac{\bar\bG \bar{\bx}}{N^{1/2}}\bigg)
		\equiv \frac{1}{M} \sum_{a=1}^M \delta\bigg\{
		\frac{(\bar\bg^a, \bar{\bx})}{N^{1/2}}\bigg\}\,,
	\]
	By  the bound \eqref{e:confinement.subgaussian.basic.tail} from Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.subgaussian.basic}, the event
	\[
		\cE = \bigg\{
			\frac{\|\bG\|_{\op}}{N^{1/2}} \le C \textup{ and }
			\frac{\|\bx\|}{N^{1/2}} \le 2
		\Big\}\,.
	\]
occurs with probability at least $1-e^{-cN}$. We abbreviate
	\[Y \equiv Y_N
	\equiv Y(\bG,\bg^\aux) 
	\equiv \bbW_\fq\Big(\bar\mu(\bG,\bg^\aux),\mu\Big)\]
We will first show that
	\beq
		\max_{\fp \in \{1,2\}}
		\Big|\E[X^\fp] - \E[Y^\fp]
		\Big| \le e^{-cN}\,.
	\eeq
		Note the trivial bound $\bbW_2(\nu,\mu) \le \|\nu\|_{L^2} + \|\mu\|_{L^2}$. Thus, for $\fp \in \{1,2\}$,
	\[
		\bbW_2(\nu,\mu)^\fp \le 2\Big\{
		(\|\nu\|_{L^2})^\fp + 
		(\|\mu\|_{L^2})^\fp
		\Big\}\,.
	\]
	Note also that on event $\cE$, $X=Y$. Thus, for each $\fp \in \{1,2\}$, we have
	\begin{align*}
		&|\E[X^\fp] - \E[Y^\fp]|
		\le \E\Big[
		(X^\fp + Y^\fp);\cE^c\Big] 
		\le \E\bigg[
			\Big\{
			\bbW_2\Big(\mu_\bG(\bx),\mu\Big)^\fp + \bbW_2\Big(\bar\mu(\bG,\bg^\aux),\mu\Big)^\fp
		\Big\}
		;\cE^c\bigg]\\
		&\qquad\le 2\E\bigg[
		\Big\{
		(\|\mu_\bG(\bx)\|_{L^2})^\fp 
		+ (\|\bar\mu(\bG,\bg^\aux)\|_{L^2})^\fp 
		+ 2(\|\mu\|_{L^2})^\fp
		\Big\}
		;\cE^c
		\bigg] \\
		&\qquad\stackrel{*}{\le} 4\E\bigg[ \Big\{
			(\|\mu_\bG(\bx)\|_{L^2})^\fp 
			+ (\|\mu\|_{L^2})^\fp\Big\}
		;\cE^c
		\bigg] 
		= 4\E\bigg[
		\bigg(
				\frac{\|\bG \bx\|^\fp}{(MN)^{\fp/2}}
				+ (\|\mu\|_{L^2})^\fp
			\bigg)
			;\cE^c
		\bigg] \\
		&\qquad\le 4\E\bigg[
			\ind\{\cE^c\}\bigg(
				\frac{(\|\bG\|_{\op})^\fp \|\bx\|^\fp}{(MN)^{\fp/2}}
				+ (\|\mu\|_{L^2})^\fp
			\bigg)
		\bigg]\,.
	\end{align*}
	The  inequality marked $*$ uses that $\|\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux))\|_{L^2}$ stochastically dominates $\|\bar\mu(\bG,\bg^\aux)\|_{L^2}$. Using H\"older's inequality, the above is
	\[\le
		\frac{4\P(\cE^c)^{1/2}
		\E[\|(\bG\|_{\op})^{4\fp}]^{1/4}
		\E[\|\bx\|^{4\fp}]^{1/4}}{(MN)^{\fp/2}}
		+ 4\P(\cE^c) 
		(\|\mu\|_{L^2})^\fp\,.
	\]
Recalling Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.subgauss","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:47:21.728611+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b2490336f73fbeeb6e8df50d887bdab4fbb3e307126a9e4934e613b04d678d08","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma SnikfeatFy of arXiv:2412.09290, 'Asymptotics of Harish-Chandra transform and infinitesimal freeness'] Let $n$ be a positive integer and $P \subseteq \{(a, b)
  \in \mathbb{N}^2 : 1 \leq a < b \leq n\}$. Moreover, let $f (z_1, \ldots,
  z_n)$ be a function and consider its symmetrization with respect to $P$,
  \[ f_P (z_1, \ldots, z_n) := \frac{1}{n!} \sum_{\pi \in S (n)} \frac{f
     (z_{\pi (1)}, \ldots, z_{\pi (n)})}{\prod_{(a, b) \in P} (z_{\pi (a)} -
     z_{\pi (b)})} . \]
  Then, the following holds:
  \begin{enumerate}
    {\item If $f$ is an analytic function in a neighborhood of $0^n$,
    then $f_P$ is also an analytic function in a neighborhood of $0^n$.}{\item
    If $(f^{(m)} (z_1, \ldots, z_n))_{m \in \mathbb{N}}$ is a sequence of
    analytic functions converging to zero uniformly in a neighborhood of
    $0^n$, then so is the sequence $f_P^{(m)}$.}
  \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["L is a vector lattice of real-valued (finite everywhere) functions on a set X","Stone's condition: f in L implies min(f,1) in L","I : L -> R is linear","I is positive: f >= 0 implies I(f) >= 0","Daniell continuity: f_n in L with f_n decreasing pointwise to 0 implies I(f_n) -> 0","for the uniqueness clause only: there are f_n in L increasing pointwise to the constant 1","no topology on X is assumed, and no regularity of the resulting measure is claimed"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.090141+00:00","domain":"measure theory, integration, representation of positive functionals","id":"claim_b330fea79f8371289214536b62fd4e02f8348d302f06b862ea12c798689edb94","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a nonempty set and let L be a vector lattice of real-valued functions on X: L is a real vector space of functions X -> R, and f, g in L implies max(f,g) and min(f,g) are in L. Assume STONE'S CONDITION: f in L implies min(f, 1) in L. Let I : L -> R satisfy (i) linearity; (ii) positivity: f >= 0 pointwise implies I(f) >= 0 (equivalently f <= g implies I(f) <= I(g)); (iii) the DANIELL CONTINUITY CONDITION: whenever f_n in L decrease pointwise to 0 at every point of X, I(f_n) -> 0. Granted (i) and (ii), condition (iii) is equivalent to: f_n in L increasing pointwise to f with f in L implies I(f_n) -> I(f). CONCLUSION (Daniell-Stone): there is a measure mu on sigma(L), the smallest sigma-algebra on X making every member of L measurable, such that every f in L is mu-integrable and I(f) equals the integral of f with respect to mu. If moreover there exist f_n in L increasing pointwise to the constant function 1 (an exhaustion, i.e. sigma-finiteness along L), then mu is unique on sigma(L). WHERE IT FAILS: (a) condition (iii) is the whole content and cannot be dropped. On X = (0,1] take L to be the set of restrictions to (0,1] of the continuous functions on the closed interval [0,1] - a vector lattice satisfying Stone's condition - and let I(f) be the limit of f(x) as x decreases to 0, which exists for every member of L. This I is linear and positive, but f_n(x) = max(0, 1 - n x) lies in L and decreases pointwise to 0 on (0,1] while I(f_n) = 1 for every n, and I is not integration against any Borel measure on (0,1]: the 'missing' representing measure is a unit mass at the point 0, which does not lie in the space. A positive linear functional on a lattice always yields a finitely additive set function; (iii) is exactly what upgrades finite additivity to countable additivity. (b) Stone's condition is what manufactures indicator functions: for f in L and c > 0 the functions min(n (f - c)^+, 1) lie in L and increase pointwise to the indicator of {f > c}, which is how the measure of a generating set is defined. Without it one still gets a representation, but on a lattice of sets rather than on a sigma-algebra. (c) Without the exhaustion hypothesis uniqueness can fail: sets that no member of L 'sees' are unconstrained. Example: X = {p} union (0,1] with L the continuous compactly supported functions on (0,1] extended by the value 0 at p; then {p} lies in sigma(L) but its measure may be chosen freely without changing any I(f). (d) The theorem produces a measure on sigma(L) only; regularity (inner or outer) of mu is NOT part of the conclusion and needs topological hypotheses, which is where Riesz-Markov-Kakutani differs from Daniell-Stone.","status":"unverified"}

	\frac{\sqrt{q_d (p_{d+1}-p_d)}
		(\bmeta^{a(q_{d+1})}(q_{d+1}),
		\bar{\bx}(q_d)
		)}{N^{1/2}}\,.
	\]
In this case, $\bar{\bx}(q_d)$ is measurable with respect to $\cFt(q_d)$, while $\bmeta(q_{d+1})$ is a standard gaussian vector in $\R^N$ that is measurable with respect to
$\cFt(q_{d+1})$. We can then repeat the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:subgaus.X.II} with $\bar{\bx}(q_d)$ taking the place of $\bar{\bg}(q_d)$, and $\bmeta(q_{d+1})$ taking the place of $\by(q_{d+1})$.
In place of \eqref{e:control.norm.event} we let
	\[E_d\equiv \bigg\{
	\frac{\|\bar{\bx}(q_d)\|^2}{N} \le  L^{O(1)}
	\bigg\} \in \cFt(q_d)\,,\quad
	E_\star=\bigcap_{d=a}^{b-1} E_d\,,\]
so the events have very high probability by Lemma~\ref{l:bar.x.subgaus} (which also holds with $\cFt(q_d)$ in place of $\cG(q_d)$) and Lemma~\ref{l:sg.norm.bound}. It is again straightforward to verify that the same argument applies with $X^{\trunc,\RomIII}$ or $X^{\frozen,\RomIII}$ in place of $X^{\RomII}$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["T is measurable with respect to Σ","invariance is defined through preimages T⁻¹(E), not images T(E)"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:57:26.110366+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, measure-preserving dynamics","id":"claim_b37bfdbafedccacf12edc1ee9bd940c9966158655c818a0c9f8f9b11bdc70a19","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, Σ) be a measurable space and T: X → X a measurable map (T⁻¹(E) ∈ Σ for every E ∈ Σ). A measure μ on Σ is T-invariant (equivalently: T preserves μ, or T is a measure-preserving transformation of (X, Σ, μ)) if μ(T⁻¹(E)) = μ(E) for every E ∈ Σ, i.e. the push-forward T_*μ := μ∘T⁻¹ equals μ. Equivalent formulation for a finite measure: ∫ f∘T dμ = ∫ f dμ for every bounded measurable f; when X is a compact metrizable space with its Borel σ-algebra and T is continuous, it suffices to test f ∈ C(X), because finite Borel measures on such a space are determined by their integrals against continuous functions. Note the direction: invariance is stated with the PREIMAGE T⁻¹(E), not the image T(E); for non-injective T the image condition μ(T(E)) = μ(E) is a different (and generally false) statement, e.g. the doubling map x ↦ 2x mod 1 preserves Lebesgue measure but doubles the length of short intervals. For a flow (φ_t)_{t∈ℝ} invariance means φ_t*μ = μ for every t.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:59:24.051330+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b3903b89a7eaa60ceeeff7cede0f154048d81e0924f3173b5e0a1e46026d2709","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm aronsson-package of arXiv:2608.30847, 'An Almgren-type formula for planar $p$-harmonic functions'] Let $u$ be a nonconstant $p$-harmonic function in a planar domain $\Omega$.
\begin{enumerate}[\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item The critical set
$$
  \operatorname{Crit}(u):=\{x\in\Omega:D u(x)=0\}
$$
is discrete.  In particular, if $x_0\in\operatorname{Crit}(u)$, then there exists $\rho>0$ such that $D u\ne0$ in $B_\rho(x_0)\setminus\{x_0\}$.

\item If $x_0\notin\operatorname{Crit}(u)$, then $u$ is real analytic in a neighborhood of $x_0$.

\item Let $x_0\in\operatorname{Crit}(u)$.  Then there are an integer $N\ge1$, a number $\delta>0$, and a nonzero homogeneous $p$-harmonic function $P$ in $\mathbb R^2$ such that, after subtracting the constant $u(x_0)$,
$$
  P(r\theta)=r^{\lambda_N(p)}\Phi(\theta),
  \qquad \theta\in\mathbb S^1,
$$
and, uniformly for $\theta\in\mathbb S^1$ as $r\to0$,
$$
  u(x_0+r\theta)-u(x_0)=P(r\theta)+O(r^{\lambda_N(p)+\delta}),
$$
$$
  D u(x_0+r\theta)=D P(r\theta)+O(r^{\lambda_N(p)-1+\delta}).
$$
Moreover $|D P(\theta)|>0$ on $\mathbb S^1$, and the hodograph representation gives the logarithmic-gradient expansion
$$
  \partial_r\log |D u(x_0+r\theta)|
  =
  \frac{\lambda_N(p)-1}{r}+O(r^{-1+\delta})
$$
uniformly in $\theta$.
\end{enumerate}
Here
$$
  \lambda_N(p)=\frac{\beta_{N+1}(p)}{\beta_{N+1}(p)-1},
$$
with
$$
  \beta_{N+1}(p)
  =
  \frac{\sqrt{(p-2)^2+4(p-1)((N+1)/N)^2}-(p-2)}{2}.
$$
For $p=2$, the same statement is understood in the classical harmonic sense and gives $\lambda_N(2)=N+1$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["γ is a continuous closed curve in ℂ","z₀ does not lie on the image of γ"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:57:26.110598+00:00","domain":"algebraic topology, complex analysis","id":"claim_b3a02e8f0726857a802fa42855fcd7acf8b442a81228e97aa6f877a727c5c99f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let γ: [a,b] → ℂ be a continuous closed curve (γ(a) = γ(b)) and let z₀ ∈ ℂ be a point NOT on the curve, z₀ ∉ γ([a,b]). Because γ(t) − z₀ never vanishes, there is a continuous function θ: [a,b] → ℝ (a continuous choice of argument) with γ(t) − z₀ = |γ(t) − z₀| e^{iθ(t)}; θ is unique up to adding a constant integer multiple of 2π. The winding number of γ about z₀ is n(γ, z₀) := (θ(b) − θ(a)) / (2π). It is an integer (since γ(b) = γ(a) forces θ(b) − θ(a) ∈ 2πℤ) and does not depend on the choice of θ. For piecewise C¹ curves it equals the contour integral (1/2πi) ∮_γ dz/(z − z₀). Basic properties: z₀ ↦ n(γ, z₀) is constant on each connected component of ℂ \\ γ([a,b]) and equals 0 on the unbounded component; it is additive under concatenation of closed curves at a common point and changes sign when the orientation of γ is reversed; it is invariant under homotopies of closed curves that avoid z₀ (see the classification theorem). The circle t ↦ z₀ + r e^{2πikt}, t ∈ [0,1], k ∈ ℤ, has winding number k about z₀ and winding number 0 about any point with |z − z₀| > r. The winding number is NOT defined when z₀ lies on the curve, and it is not a homotopy invariant for homotopies that are allowed to cross z₀ (the circle about z₀ is null-homotopic in ℂ but has winding number 1).","status":"unverified"}

that a recombination occurs at time
$r\in(0,y)$, the detached lineage recoalesces with either of the
two existing lineages at rate $1$ each (total rate $2$). If recoalescence
occurs with its own ancestral lineage before time $y$, then the recombination
is \emph{silent} and the state does not change. Otherwise---either
if recoalescence occurs with the other lineage, or if no recoalescence
occurs before time $y$---the recombination is \emph{visible}, and
the process jumps to a new TMRCA determined by the time of this coalescence
event.
The probability of a visible recombination at current TMRCA $s$ is
\begin{equation}
p_{\mathrm{vis}}(s)=\frac{2s+1-e^{-2s}}{4s},\qquad
p_{\mathrm{sil}}(s)=1-p_{\mathrm{vis}}(s).

\end{equation}

Equivalently, one may construct $(Y'_{\ell})$ from its embedded jump
chain and holding times as follows. Let $(X'_{n})_{n\ge0}$ be the
jump chain, and let $(E_{n})_{n\ge0}$ be i.i.d.\ $\mathrm{Exp}(1)$
random variables, independent of the chain. Given $X'_{n}$, define
the holding time 
\[
\Delta\ell_{n}:=\frac{E_{n}}{X'_{n} p_{\mathrm{vis}}(X_{n}')}
\]
and the jump locations $\ell_{0}:=0$, $\ell_{n+1}:=\ell_{n}+\Delta\ell_{n}$.
Then define 
\[
Y'_{\ell}:=X'_{n}\quad\text{for }\ell\in[\ell_{n},\ell_{n+1}),
\]
and $X'_{n+1}\sim q_{\mathrm{SMC}'}( \cdot \mid X_{n}'),$ where
\[
q_{\mathrm{SMC}'}(t\mid s)=\begin{cases}
\dfrac{2(1-e^{-2t})}{2s+1-e^{-2s}}, & 0<t<s,\\[10pt]
\dfrac{2(1-e^{-2s})}{2s+1-e^{-2s}} e^{-(t-s)}, & t\ge s.
\end{cases}
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.353731+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b40af3e81c72a4ce10a935f62c759802cbf86a6cda64dd369431078cb576df5b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 206 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\cA_N=\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)$ be a sequence of $L$-Lipschitz algorithms, as in Definition~\ref{d:Lip}.     \]

Consider a Brownian bridge terminating at $(\bG,\bg^\aux)$, and let $\vX^N\equiv (\vX^{\RomI:\RomIII},X^\Ising)^N$ be the resulting $\R^4$-valued process defined by \eqref{e:X.decomp}--\eqref{e:vX}. Let $\vX^{\trunc,N}$ be the truncation given by Definitions~\ref{d:trunc}--\ref{d:buckets.Ising}, and let $\vY^N$ be the spatial rerandomization of $\vX^{\trunc,N}$ from Definitions~\ref{d:rerand} and \ref{d:rerand.Ising}. We make
$(\vY,\vD,\vQ)^N$ into continuous-time $\R^{18}$-valued processes by taking the linear interpolation on each time interval $[q_d,q_{d+1}]$. We also denote the piecewise constant variants $(\vY,\vD,\vQ)^{\bullet,N}$, so for example $\vY^{\bullet,N}(t)=\vY^N(q_d)$ for all $[q_d,q_{d+1})$. Let $\mu_{\bG^N}$ be the law of $(\vY,\vD,\vQ)^N$ conditional on the disorder $\bG^N$, and let $\Q_N$ be the law of $\mu_{\bG^N}$. If $\Q_N\to\Q$ along an integer subsequence $N\to\infty$, then we have $\Q_{\bullet,N}\Rightarrow\Q_N$ along the same subsequence. {"assumptions":["both processes centred and Gaussian","Sudakov-Fernique: increment variances compared; conclusion only for expected suprema","Slepian: additionally equal pointwise variances; conclusion is distributional"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.628762+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b4b2e0be77f5756917d65ef45275366760a72b9a8c024ebef3f9c4928a398295","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X_t) and (Y_t) be CENTRED Gaussian processes indexed by a finite set T. SUDAKOV-FERNIQUE: if E[(X_s - X_t)^2] <= E[(Y_s - Y_t)^2] for all s, t in T, then E[ sup_t X_t ] <= E[ sup_t Y_t ]. Note that only the increment variances are compared and the individual variances may differ; the conclusion is about EXPECTED suprema only. SLEPIAN: if in addition E[X_t^2] = E[Y_t^2] for every t - so that the increment comparison is equivalent to E[X_s X_t] >= E[Y_s Y_t] for all s, t - then the stronger distributional conclusion P( sup_t X_t >= u ) <= P( sup_t Y_t >= u ) holds for every u, and indeed the whole joint law is stochastically ordered coordinatewise. Slepian's extra hypothesis of equal variances is not decorative: without it the distributional conclusion is false, while the Sudakov-Fernique conclusion about expectations survives. Both require CENTRED and GAUSSIAN; there is no comparable general statement for non-Gaussian processes. The finite index set is a convenience; both extend to separable processes by approximation. [Slepian (1962), Sudakov (1971), Fernique (1975); see Adler and Taylor, Random Fields and Geometry, Chapter 2, or Boucheron-Lugosi-Massart Section 13.3]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["d >= 3, G connected and d-regular (bipartite graphs have lambda_n = -d, which is excluded from the Ramanujan condition together with +d)","the Alon-Boppana bound is asymptotic in n for fixed d","existence results are cited, not proved"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T15:17:03.041240+00:00","domain":"spectral graph theory","id":"claim_b4cff0d243e113602094a9e01462d26887e25896b93bb86c6b28ac1795f048d4","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let G be a connected d-regular graph on n vertices with adjacency eigenvalues d = lambda_1 >= lambda_2 >= ... >= lambda_n >= -d. G is Ramanujan if every eigenvalue other than +-d satisfies |lambda| <= 2 sqrt(d - 1); the number 2 sqrt(d-1) is the spectral radius of the infinite d-regular tree. Alon-Boppana theorem: for every fixed d >= 3 and every epsilon > 0, every d-regular graph with sufficiently many vertices has lambda_2 >= 2 sqrt(d - 1) - epsilon; more precisely lambda_2 >= 2 sqrt(d-1) (1 - O(1/ log^2 n)) (Friedman; Nilli). So Ramanujan graphs are the best possible spectral expanders. Existence: Lubotzky, Phillips and Sarnak (1988) and independently Margulis constructed explicit infinite families of (p+1)-regular Ramanujan graphs for every prime p congruent to 1 mod 4 (Cayley graphs of PSL(2, Z/qZ) or PGL(2, Z/qZ) according to the Legendre symbol of p modulo q, the eigenvalue bound coming from the Ramanujan-Petersson conjecture for modular forms proved by Deligne), later extended to all prime powers (Morgenstern 1994); Marcus, Spielman and Srivastava proved by the method of interlacing families, non-constructively, that infinite families of bipartite Ramanujan graphs of every degree d >= 3 exist (Ann. Math. 2015, via 2-lifts) and then that bipartite Ramanujan graphs of every degree exist on every even number of vertices (interlacing families IV, 2018); Friedman (2008) proved Alon's conjecture that a random d-regular graph is nearly Ramanujan, lambda_2 <= 2 sqrt(d-1) + epsilon with high probability, and Bordenave (2020) gave a shorter proof. Ramanujan graphs give the optimal expander mixing lemma constant and near-optimal derandomisation gadgets.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:34:20.780114+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b4f235e2b06442818fd884bddd4367ab19bed442956ab0b85d8eb8bfc3e45ca0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theo 4 of arXiv:2609.02261, 'Quantization and process'] i) For all $F\in D_h( \R^{2n})$,  we have,

       F^{\rm ext} \Big(  T+\frac{Z}{2} , T-\frac{Z}{2}\Big )

      for any $T\in \R^{2n}$.
      
      
    ii) The operator $H_h$ maps $D_h (\R^{2n})$ into

    iii)  Let  $F\in D_h( \R^{2n})$. There exists a function $\widetilde F$ on $\C^{2n} \simeq \R^{4n} $ which is holomorphic in the following sense,     
    \be (\partial _1 + i \partial _2 ) \widetilde F = 0,\
    (\partial _3  + i \partial _4 ) \widetilde F = 0
  \ee 
    
   with a restriction to $\R^{2n}$ 
     equals to $F$, that is to say,  $\widetilde F (x , 0, \xi , 0) = F(x , \xi)$. Moreover, for $X,Y\in\R^{2n}$,
      
      \be   | \widetilde F (X+iY) |  \leq 
    ( 4 \pi h)^{-n}   \Vert \psi_F \Vert _{L^1 (\R^{2n})} 
  \  e^{  \frac {1}  {h}   |Y|^2 }, \ee 
  
that is to say, for any $(x_1 , x_2 , x_3 , x_4)\in\R^{4n}$,
  
  $$  | \widetilde F (x_1 , x_2 , x_3 , x_4) | \leq

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:54:12.567230+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b4f25deea9780b6bdb90adecee88856eb26387cc9e629b62d09a06f15e34c6df","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop P:half-space-horizon-marginals of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] As $n\to\infty$, the process $R^{(n)}$ has a distributional limit $R^{\mathsf{DL}}=\{R^{\mathsf{DL}}_i\}_{i=1}^k$, under the uniform-on-compact topology. 
    We can describe the process $R^{\mathsf{DL}}$ explicitly as follows.
	
Let $\mathcal{B} = (\mathcal{B}_1, \mathcal{B}_2, \ldots, \mathcal{B}_{2k})$ be $2k$ independent Brownian motions on $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ of diffusivity $2$, drift $\lambda_i$ for $\mathcal{B}_i, i\in\llbracket1, k \rrbracket$ and $-\lambda_i$ for $\mathcal{B}_{2k+1-i}$. Next, let $\{X(-i, j) : i\in\llbracket1, k \rrbracket, j \in \llbracketi +1, 2k +1 - i \rrbracket\}$ be an array of exponential random variables, independent of each other and $\mathcal B$, satisfying 
\[
X(-i, j) \sim \begin{cases}
\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda_i/2 - \lambda_j/2), \qquad &j \in \llbracketi + 1, k \rrbracket, \\
\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda_i/2 + \lambda_{2k + 1 -j}/2), \qquad &j\in\llbracketk + 1, 2k - i \rrbracket, \\
\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda_i/2 - \rho), \qquad &j=2k + 1- i.
\end{cases}
\]
We turn this array into a 
sequence of cadlag functions $X = (X_1, \dots, X_{2k})$ on $(-\infty, 0]$ by the rule that $X_j(0) = 0$ for all $j$, and the measure $dX$ has atoms of size $X(-i, j)$ at each coordinate $(-i, j)$ where $X(-i, j)$ is defined (and is supported on these points). Equivalently, the path $X_j$ has a jump of size $X(-i, j)$ at location $-i$.

Let $X \mathcal{B}$ be the concatenation of $X$ and $\mathcal{B}$. (See Figure (fig:hfsh of the paper) for an illustration.) Then:
$$
R^{\mathsf{DL}}_i(x) = \begin{cases}
X\mathcal{B}(-i, i; x, 2k) - X\mathcal{B}(-i, i; 0, 2k), \qquad &x \ge 0, \\
X\mathcal{B}^{\Delta_{2k+1}}(-i, i; |x|, 2k) - X\mathcal{B}(-i, i; 0, 2k), \qquad &x \le 0.
\end{cases}
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X_1, ..., X_n independent (arbitrary measurable state spaces, not necessarily identically distributed)","E[Z^2] < infinity","X_i' an independent copy of X_i"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.627864+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b4f8bc22f460f25f8d49dffc484368ee58c01fdabcf876f2f9b6345b6ceebd5f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, ..., X_n be INDEPENDENT random variables taking values in arbitrary measurable spaces - they need NOT be identically distributed and need not be real-valued - and let Z = f(X_1, ..., X_n) with E[Z^2] < infinity. Let X_i' be an independent copy of X_i, independent of everything else, and put Z^{(i)} = f(X_1, ..., X_{i-1}, X_i', X_{i+1}, ..., X_n). Then Var(Z) <= (1/2) sum_{i=1}^n E[ (Z - Z^{(i)})^2 ] = sum_{i=1}^n E[ ((Z - Z^{(i)})_+)^2 ]. Equivalently, and often more convenient, Var(Z) <= sum_{i=1}^n E[ (Z - Z_i)^2 ] for ANY random variables Z_i that are measurable functions of the n-1 variables other than X_i; taking Z_i = inf over the i-th coordinate of f gives the version used for suprema and for first-passage times. Equality holds if and only if f is a sum of functions of the individual coordinates. Independence is the only structural hypothesis and it is essential; the inequality is FALSE for dependent coordinates. Applied with a bounded-difference function it recovers the variance half of McDiarmid's inequality; applied to first-passage percolation with the geodesic length as the influence bound it produces the linear variance upper bound. [Efron and Stein (1981), Steele (1986); see Boucheron, Lugosi and Massart, Concentration Inequalities, Theorem 3.1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:31:02.828010+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b53b0a23500cb6be305f31581dcfc273c83e174f8830ff85d12eb075a9c4f4bc","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary cor:label-configuration-reversal of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] For fixed $h\geq2$ and $k\geq3$, as $q\to\infty$ a uniformly random
$A\in\binom{[q]}k$ satisfies
\[
 \mathbb P(A\text{ is not }B_h)
 =\frac{k!K_{h,k}}q+O_{h,k}(q^{-2}),
 \qquad K_{h,k}\asymp_k h^{k-2}.
\]
For each $2\leq r\leq h$,
\[
 \mathbb P(|hA|=M_{h,k}-M_{h-r,k})
 =\frac{k!\kappa_{k,r}}q+O_{h,k}(q^{-2}).
\]
Moreover,
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
  \mathbb P\bigl(r_{h,k}(|hA|)\leq1\bigr)
   &=1-O_{h,k}(q^{-2}),\\
  \mathbb P\bigl(r_h(A)=1\mid A\text{ is not }B_h\bigr)
   &=1-O_{h,k}(q^{-1}).
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
By contrast, if $k\geq4$ is fixed and $N_{h,k}$ is uniform in the finite set
$\mathcal R(h,k)$, then, as $h\to\infty$,
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb P\bigl(r_{h,k}(N_{h,k})\leq1\bigr)
 =\frac{h}{|\mathcal R(h,k)|}
 =h^{-(k-2)+o_k(1)}\longrightarrow0.
\end{equation}
Thus principal labels are asymptotically negligible among attainable
cardinalities, although their realizations account for asymptotically almost
every fixed-order configuration in a growing interval.
Here $h$ is fixed before $q\to\infty$;
no joint $(h,q)$ assertion is made.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["H: R^n → R is finite everywhere and convex (hence continuous)","H is superlinear: H(p)/|p| → ∞ as |p| → ∞","for part (iv): H ∈ C^2 and D^2H ≥ θI with θ > 0 (which already implies superlinearity)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.415976+00:00","domain":"convex analysis for Hamilton-Jacobi equations","id":"claim_b547a366acd0d9caa05bd0fd6c74e4b7c9b6d81ddd9e55157d9fc2c6927f0355","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let H: R^n → R be convex and superlinear, i.e. H(p)/|p| → +∞ as |p| → ∞. Its Legendre (Fenchel) transform is L(q) := sup_{p ∈ R^n} ( p·q - H(p) ), q ∈ R^n, and L is called the Lagrangian associated with H. Then: (i) the supremum is attained for every q, and L is finite, convex and superlinear; (ii) L* = H, i.e. H(p) = sup_q ( p·q - L(q) ) (duality of H and L); (iii) Fenchel-Young: p·q ≤ H(p) + L(q) for all p,q, with equality iff q ∈ ∂H(p) iff p ∈ ∂L(q); (iv) if in addition H ∈ C^2 with D^2H(p) ≥ θ I for all p and some θ > 0, then DH: R^n → R^n is a bijection, L ∈ C^1, DL = (DH)^{-1}, DL is Lipschitz with constant 1/θ, and consequently L(q+w) + L(q-w) - 2L(q) ≤ |w|^2/θ for all q,w.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:11:44.461095+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b5aca9b87a0a53a376c1614a4e342956b8df7107e354946f0c5c2d4ce94de36a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 19 of arXiv:2609.03191, 'On lifting representations and actions on curves of the metacyclic groups $C_{p^s}\rtimes '] We consider a cyclic $C_{p^s}$-extension of $k((t))$, its lower jumps $l_1<\cdots <l_s$, and its upper jumps $u_1<\cdots<u_s$. Then the following properties hold. 

\medskip
{\bf (1)} The lower and upper jumps determine uniquely each other by the recursive identities $l_1:=u_1$ and $l_i:=l_{i-1}+p^{i-1}(u_i-u_{i-1})$ for each $i\in\llbracket2,s\rrbracket$. 

\smallskip
{\bf (2)} For each $j\in\llbracket1,s\rrbracket $ we have $l_j=u_1+\sum_{i=1}^{j-1} p^i(u_{i+1}-u_i)$.

\smallskip
{\bf (3)} For each $j\in\llbracket1,s\rrbracket$ we have identities 
$$\sum_{i=1}^j \frac{l_i}{p^i}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^j p^{i-1}u_i}{p^j}$$
and
$$p^{j-1}u_j:=l_j+(p-1)\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}l_ip^{j-i-1}.$$

{\bf (4)} For $b\in\llbracket0,p^s-1\rrbracket$, write
\[
b=\delta_{1,b}+\delta_{2,b}p+\cdots+\delta_{s,b}p^{s-1}
\]
with $\delta_{i,b}\in\llbracket0,p-1\rrbracket$ for each $i\in\llbracket1,s\rrbracket$ and define
\[
N_{s,b}:=\sum_{i=1}^s p^{s-i}\bigl[p-1+(p-1-\delta_{i,b})l_i\bigr].
\] Then for each $b\in \llbracket1,p^s-1\rrbracket$, if $j\in\llbracket0,s-1\rrbracket$ is the largest such that $p^j\mid b$, then we have identities 
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
N_{s,b-1}-N_{s,b}&=p^{s-j-1}\Big[l_{j+1}-(p-1)\sum_{i=1}^j p^{j+1-i}l_i\Big]\\
&=p^{s-j-1}[l_1+\sum_{i=1}^j p^i(u_{i+1}-pu_i)].
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
In particular, $N_{s,b-1}-N_{s,b}\ge p^{s-j-1}l_1\ge l_1>0$ and therefore we have $\frac{l_{j+1}}{p^{j+1}}-(p-1)\sum_{i=1}^j\frac{l_i}{p^i}\ge\frac{l_1}{p^{j+1}}>0$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:30:50.736425+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b5d8543c9bd227108d68554601febd42d403b33ede6e56d56b42dcea4e6a21a2","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lemm_BH of arXiv:2503.24372, 'A criterion on the free energy for log-Sobolev inequalities in mean-field particle systems'] Let $N \geq 1$ and $\mu$ be a probability measure on $\R^N$ satisfying a log-Sobolev inequality with constant $\gamma_{\rm LS}>0$.

Then:

\begin{equation} 

\cov_{\mu}(F^2,H)^2
\leq 
\frac{4}{\gamma_{\rm LS}^2}  \sup_{x\in\R^N}|\nabla H (x)|^2 \, 
\E_{\mu}[F^2] \; \E_{\mu}\big[|\nabla F|^2\big],
\end{equation}

with the notation $|\nabla H (x)| = \big( \sum_{i =1}^N (\partial_{x_i}  H (x))^2 \big)^{1/2}$.
The same bound holds for a vector valued function $H(x)\in\R^d$.

Let $H_i:\R\to\R$ be Lipschitz ($1\leq i\leq N$) and let $F:\R^N\to\R$ be smooth and compactly supported. Then:

\begin{equation}

\sum_{i=1}^N\cov_{\mu}(F^2,H_i(x_i))^2
  \leq 
  \frac{4}{\gamma_{\rm LS}^2} \max_{1\leq i\leq N}\|H'_i\|^2_\infty \;  \E_{\mu}[F^2] \;  \E_{\mu}\big[|\nabla F
  |^2\big] 
  .
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

The argument does not give the exact value of the subdiffusivity exponent in most dimensions, only bounds, with the precise exponent known rigorously only in specific settings such as sufficiently high dimension or tree-like/hierarchical models, and it is specific to critical (not subcritical or supercritical) percolation geometry, where the fractal, tree-like structure with many bottlenecks is essential to the argument. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.360475+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b6037c8c8459122d7c3759452aab6b463cb95829c2fce94e8bb116ffceef2ba7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Ppn 255 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] We have $\chi'(1) \le L^2$.

\begin{proof}
Throughout this proof we abbreviate $\bg\equiv(\bG,\bg^\aux)$.  Consider small positive $\delta$, and define
    \[\begin{aligned}
    \bx&=\cA( (1-\delta)^{1/2}\bg+\delta^{1/2}\bg')\,,\\
    \by &= \E(\bx\,|\, \bg)\,,\\
    \bz &= \bx-\by\,.
    \end{aligned}\]
By iterated expectations, we have
    \[
    \frac{\E(\by,\by)}{N}
    =\frac{\E(\bx,\by)}{N}
    =\chi(1-\delta)\,, 
    \]
as well as $\E(\by,\bz)=0$. It follows that
    \beq
    \chi(1)
    =\frac{\E(\bx,\bx)}{N}
    =\frac{\E(\by,\by)}{N}+\frac{\E(\bz,\bz)}{N}
    =\chi(1-\delta) + \frac{\E(\bz,\bz)}{N}\,.\eeq
Let us treat $\bz$ as a function of $\bg'$ for fixed $\bg$. Note that $\E(\bz\,|\,\bg)=0$. Since $\cA$ is $L$-Lipschitz, we see that $\bz$ is $(L\delta^{1/2})$-Lipschitz as a function of $\bg'$. It follows (using e.g.\ Lemma~\ref{l:lip.subgaus}) that
    \[
    \frac{\E(\bz,\bz)}{N} \le O(L^2\delta)\,.
    \]
Recalling \eqref{eq:bz}, we see that $\chi(1-\delta) \ge \chi(1)-O(L^2\delta)$, which implies $\chi'(1) \le L^2$ as claimed. 
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the pool protocol: members fitted on training data, the test rows split 40/60 into calibration and evaluation with a fixed permutation, metric = mean per-sample relative L2","the small-calibration arms subsample the calibration rows only; evaluation rows are never touched"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T07:18:07.915757+00:00","domain":"ensemble learning / covariance estimation","id":"claim_b65e4f03214b2aa782f369b54d75f83a80e5af182457d205fd6bc537075ff3c0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Measured 2026-09-05 on the EMIT and OCO-2 stacking pools (23 and 18 members; 285 and 40 outputs; 932 and 800 calibration rows; the per-sample relative metric; 70 cells, paired). The error covariance of the members is rank-deficient in practice: $\\lambda_{\\max}/\\lambda_{\\min}$ of $10^{6}$ to $10^{17}$, three to five eigenvalues below $0.05\\,\\sigma^2$ (members that are near-linear combinations of one another). Inside the long-only minimum-variance stack, eight cleaners of that covariance were compared on the same cells, the same split and the same small-calibration draws: the raw sample covariance, the $\\eta$-regularised rotationally invariant estimator with floors $0, 0.05, 0.2, 1.0\\,\\sigma^2$, Ledoit-Wolf 2004 linear shrinkage, Ledoit-Wolf 2020 analytical nonlinear shrinkage and Lam's NERCOME. Result, paired gains against the $0.05$-floor RIE: the raw covariance, the eta-RIE without floor, LW2020 and NERCOME tie at full calibration (median paired gain 0.00 on both corpora; means +0.05, +0.04, +0.09, -0.86 on 40 EMIT cells, the last from one cell at -16; +0.16, +0.01, +0.15, +0.09 on 30 OCO-2 cells), while at $n = 60$ the eta-RIE itself is the worst of them: on OCO-2 raw +6.4, LW2020 +6.0, NERCOME +4.9 percent over it on 30 of 30 cells (on EMIT +0.6, +1.3, +1.0 with 20-28 of 40 wins), and at $n = 240$ on OCO-2 +1.1, +1.0, +0.8 on 30 of 30 at full calibration and in the $n = 60/120/240$ arms; the floors $0.2$ and $1.0$ lose 1.2 and 6.5 percent on EMIT at full calibration (0.2 and 1.1 on OCO-2), 4.5 percent for the heavy floor at $n = 60$ on EMIT; linear shrinkage loses 6.3 percent on EMIT at full calibration and 15 percent at $n = 60$ (a wash on OCO-2, where the members are fewer and the shrinkage target closer); and the sum-to-one (unconstrained-sign) forms of the same cleaners lose 2 to 7 percent at full calibration on EMIT and 13 to 105 percent at $n = 60$; on OCO-2 the raw sum-to-one form is off by factors of 30 to 3,000 (an 18-member rank-deficient covariance inverted). Mechanism (seed 101, medians over outputs): the constraint keeps 7-11 of 23 members; the condition number falls from $10^{6}$-$10^{17}$ on the full covariance to $4\\times10^{2}$-$3\\times10^{4}$ on the active principal submatrix; eigenvalues under the floor fall from 3-5 to 0-1; the active sets of raw, RIE and LW2020 overlap at Jaccard 0.86-0.90 (0.80-0.83 at $n = 60$); the floors and the linear shrinkage keep MORE members active (EMIT: raw 7.2, RIE 7.6, RIE with the 0.05 floor 8.3, floor 0.2 9.4, floor 1.0 12.2, linear shrinkage 13.9, LW2020 7.3, NERCOME 9.6 of 23; OCO-2: 6.9, 7.5, 8.0, 9.1, 11.3, 8.9, 7.1, 7.2 of 18), which is how they lose - a lifted small eigenvalue makes a duplicate look independent. By the active-set lemma the weights depend on the covariance only through $S_{AA}$, which is well conditioned, and there every consistent cleaner is close to the identity; by the entrywise risk bound all of them obey the same $O(\\sqrt{\\log M/n})$ excess-risk guarantee while a floor is a bias that does not vanish with $n$. The reading of the whole program: random-matrix theory identifies what to clean (the error covariance, in the reported metric, with an intercept) and why the plug-in fails (the near-null directions of a collinear ensemble); the fix that survives the population is the long-only constraint, itself a data-determined covariance shrinkage, and the spectral cleaners are interchangeable inside it. The pre-registered contrary hypothesis - that the floor was a kernel-bandwidth artefact which LW2020's theory-fixed bandwidth would remove - was refuted on its first cell: consistent estimators correctly keep the tiny eigenvalues, because in the population they are tiny.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:45:38.340592+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b6703bad009d889652cc64f04abead235202be056bb91938fe6e010ea70e1bed","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 2 (Pointwise macroscopic-loop bounds for integer loop weights) of arXiv:2604.20514, 'Macroscopic loops in the random loop model on sparse random graphs'] Fix \(u\in[0,1]\) and \(\theta\in\mathbb N\) with \(\theta>1\).

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(\roman*)}]
    \item \textbf{Random regular graphs.}
    Let \(d\ge 3\), let \(G_n\) be the random \(d\)-regular graph on \(n\) vertices, and let \(p_{d,n}\) denote its law. Assume
    \[
    d>2c_{\theta,u}
    =
    2\bigl(1+\theta\max\{u,1-u\}\bigr).
    \]
    Then for every \(\delta>0\) there exist \(\eta>0\) and \(c>0\) such that for every
    \[
    t\ge T_{\theta,u}(d)+\delta,
    \]
    one has
    \[
    p_{d,n}\!\left(
    \Pbb^{G_n}_{\theta,t,u}(A_\eta)\ge c
    \right)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}1.
    \]

    \item \textbf{Sparse Erd\H{o}s--R\'enyi graphs.}
    Let \(\lambda>0\), and let \(G_n\sim G(n,\lambda/n)\). Assume
    \[
    \lambda>2c_{\theta,u}
    =
    2\bigl(1+\theta\max\{u,1-u\}\bigr).
    \]
    Then for every \(\delta>0\) there exist \(\eta>0\) and \(c>0\) such that for every
    \[
    t\ge T_{\theta,u}(\lambda)+\delta,
    \]
    one has
    \[
    \Pbb\!\left(
    \Pbb^{G_n}_{\theta,t,u}(A_\eta)\ge c
    \right)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}1.
    \]

    \item \textbf{Simple bounded-degree configuration model.}
    Let \(G_n\) be the simple graph obtained from the configuration model with degree sequence \((d_i^{(n)})_{i=1}^n\), that is, the pairing model conditioned on simplicity. Assume that
    \[
    1\le d_i^{(n)}\le \Delta
    \qquad\text{for all }i,n,
    \]
    and
    \[
    \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n d_i^{(n)}\to \rho.
    \]
    If
    \[
    \rho>2c_{\theta,u}
    =
    2\bigl(1+\theta\max\{u,1-u\}\bigr),
    \]
    then for every \(\delta>0\) there exist \(\eta>0\) and \(c>0\) such that for every
    \[
    t\ge T_{\theta,u}(\rho)+\delta,
    \]
    one has
    \[
    \Pbb\!\left(
    \Pbb^{G_n}_{\theta,t,u}(A_\eta)\ge c
    \right)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}1.
    \]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["1 ≤ p < ∞","Ω = R^n, or Ω bounded open with Lipschitz boundary (an extension domain); for W^{1,p}_0 any open Ω","compactness statements require Ω bounded"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:57.492521+00:00","domain":"Sobolev spaces, embedding theorems, compactness","id":"claim_b6b2ca78bf6d58de47692329336d31951c68502f00143a7631b268179675e75b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let n ≥ 1, 1 ≤ p < ∞, and let Ω ⊂ R^n be either all of R^n or a bounded open set with Lipschitz boundary (more generally a bounded W^{1,p}-extension domain). For p < n write p* = np/(n − p) (Sobolev conjugate, 1/p* = 1/p − 1/n).

(i) Subcritical case p < n (Gagliardo–Nirenberg–Sobolev). W^{1,p}(Ω) ↪ L^{p*}(Ω) continuously. On R^n one has the scale-invariant form ||u||_{L^{p*}(R^n)} ≤ C(n,p) ||∇u||_{L^p(R^n)} for every u ∈ W^{1,p}(R^n). For bounded Ω, W^{1,p}(Ω) ↪ L^q(Ω) for every 1 ≤ q ≤ p*, and the embedding is COMPACT for every q < p* (Rellich–Kondrachov), but not for q = p*.

(ii) Critical case p = n ≥ 2. W^{1,n}(Ω) ↪ L^q(Ω) for every q ∈ [1, ∞), compactly when Ω is bounded, but W^{1,n}(Ω) is NOT contained in L^∞(Ω): in the unit disc of R^2, u(x) = log log(1 + 1/|x|) belongs to W^{1,2} and is unbounded. (For n = 1, W^{1,1} on an interval consists of absolutely continuous functions and does embed into the continuous functions.)

(iii) Supercritical case p > n (Morrey). W^{1,p}(Ω) ↪ C^{0,γ}(Ω̄) with γ = 1 − n/p: every u ∈ W^{1,p}(Ω) has a representative that is Hölder continuous with exponent γ, and ||u||_{C^{0,γ}(Ω̄)} ≤ C ||u||_{W^{1,p}(Ω)}. For bounded Ω the embedding into C^{0,β}(Ω̄) is compact for every β < γ, in particular into C(Ω̄).

(iv) Higher order, Ω bounded Lipschitz, k ≥ 1. If kp < n then W^{k,p}(Ω) ↪ L^q(Ω) with 1/q = 1/p − k/n, compactly into L^r for r < q. If kp > n then W^{k,p}(Ω) ↪ C^{k − ⌊n/p⌋ − 1, γ}(Ω̄), where γ = ⌊n/p⌋ + 1 − n/p when n/p is not an integer, and γ is any number in (0,1) when n/p is an integer.

(v) Zero boundary values. Every statement holds for W^{1,p}_0(Ω) (resp. W^{k,p}_0) on an ARBITRARY open set Ω, bounded for the compactness claims, with no regularity of ∂Ω, because such functions extend by zero to W^{1,p}(R^n).

Where it fails. Without an extension property (Lipschitz or comparable boundary) the embedding W^{1,p}(Ω) ↪ L^{p*}(Ω) can fail for bounded Ω: there are bounded domains with a sufficiently sharp outward cusp on which it is false. Compactness fails at the critical exponent q = p* (the rescaled bubbles u_λ(x) = λ^{(n−p)/p} u(λx) keep constant L^{p*} norm and W^{1,p} seminorm but converge weakly to 0) and fails on unbounded domains such as R^n (translates of one bump). The inequality ||u||_{L^q(R^n)} ≤ C||∇u||_{L^p(R^n)} is FALSE for every q ≠ p*: dilation invariance forces q = p*. W^{1,n} ↪ L^∞ fails for n ≥ 2 as shown. The Hölder exponent in (iii) cannot be improved beyond 1 − n/p in general.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["independent (product) probability measure on the input coordinates","f is a bounded, typically boolean, function of finitely many coordinates","existence of a randomized decision tree computing f exactly, with well-defined per-coordinate revealments","revealments computed under the same measure used for Var(f) and Inf_i(f)"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.972746+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b71abce6cf84475d6e6984b0c6a4d7ee2a29f331d669301354889ab502d006c7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). Let f: {0,1}^n -> {0,1} be evaluated exactly by a randomized decision-tree algorithm T that, over its internal randomness, queries coordinate i with probability delta_i(T) (its revealment), and let Var(f) denote the variance of f under a product probability measure on the input. The OSSS inequality states Var(f) <= sum_{i=1}^n delta_i(T) Inf_i(f), where Inf_i(f) is the influence of coordinate i under the same measure. Consequently, exhibiting an algorithm with small maximal revealment forces the sum of influences to be large, giving lower bounds on total influence and noise sensitivity via algorithmic constructions; for critical planar percolation, an exploration-path algorithm gives revealments comparable to arm-event probabilities, and combined with quasi-multiplicativity this yields sharp bounds on noise sensitivity and, via the Duminil-Copin-Raoufi-Tassion route, on sharpness of the phase transition in all dimensions without reflection positivity or duality. The inequality does not directly compute Inf_i itself, does not apply to non-product (dependent-coordinate) measures without a separate generalization, and it is an inequality rather than an identity, so it can be loose or even vacuous if the algorithm chosen is not well matched to f's structure. Typical failure: Plugging in a naive, non-adaptive algorithm (e.g. querying coordinates in a fixed deterministic order) and expecting a sharp bound; the inequality is only informative when the algorithm is cleverly matched to the function's geometric structure, such as an exploration process for a crossing event, and a poorly chosen algorithm produces a valid but essentially vacuous bound that is easy to mistake for a genuine obstruction to sharper influence or sensitivity estimates. Canonical reference: O'Donnell, Saks, Schramm and Servedio, 2005, Proceedings of the 46th Annual IEEE Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science; Duminil-Copin, Raoufi and Tassion, 2019, Annals of Mathematics.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:57:59.664058+00:00","domain":"geometric group theory","id":"claim_b73f8461b2ef4f5c7e5cfc231d8998c646a1b130245d4d4d51ae1850a21946ab","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let G be a finitely generated group and, for a finite generating set, let gamma(n) count the elements of G expressible as a word of length at most n. G has polynomial growth if gamma(n) <= C n^d for constants C, d and all n. Gromov's theorem states that G has polynomial growth if and only if G is virtually nilpotent, i.e. has a nilpotent subgroup of finite index. Virtually nilpotent groups have polynomial growth by an earlier theorem of Wolf and Milnor; Gromov proved the converse using a compactness argument for rescaled Cayley graphs. Due to Mikhail Gromov, 1981.","status":"unverified"}
