{"assumptions":["X_1, ..., X_n independent (arbitrary measurable state spaces, not necessarily identically distributed)","E[Z^2] < infinity","X_i' an independent copy of X_i"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T04:29:00.269210+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b7911cc88f0c4e9cbcd38f7c8f3a5c04","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, ..., X_n be INDEPENDENT random variables taking values in arbitrary measurable spaces - they need NOT be identically distributed and need not be real-valued - and let Z = f(X_1, ..., X_n) with E[Z^2] < infinity. Let X_i' be an independent copy of X_i, independent of everything else, and put Z^{(i)} = f(X_1, ..., X_{i-1}, X_i', X_{i+1}, ..., X_n). Then Var(Z) <= (1/2) sum_{i=1}^n E[ (Z - Z^{(i)})^2 ] = sum_{i=1}^n E[ ((Z - Z^{(i)})_+)^2 ]. Equivalently, and often more convenient, Var(Z) <= sum_{i=1}^n E[ (Z - Z_i)^2 ] for ANY random variables Z_i that are measurable functions of the n-1 variables other than X_i; taking Z_i = inf over the i-th coordinate of f gives the version used for suprema and for first-passage times. Equality in the replace-one bound (in either form) holds if and only if f is a sum of functions of the individual coordinates; equality in the bound with arbitrary Z_i holds if and only if, in addition, Z_i = E[Z | X_j, j != i] almost surely for every i. Independence is the only structural hypothesis and it is essential; the inequality is FALSE for dependent coordinates. Applied with a bounded-difference function it recovers the variance half of McDiarmid's inequality; applied to first-passage percolation with the geodesic length as the influence bound it produces the linear variance upper bound. [Efron and Stein (1981), Steele (1986); see Boucheron, Lugosi and Massart, Concentration Inequalities, Theorem 3.1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Nonzero feasible rank-at-most-r target; full-row-rank design and noiseless labels","B0=0; nondegenerate Gaussian A0","Step schedule fixed conditional on design independently of A0","Isotropic population prediction risk"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T20:54:30.733548+00:00","domain":"LoRA gradient dynamics and excess risk","id":"claim_b794a3607b41a0b1d035b802d142402b820e6cfccddde42c0fd0b798721070a7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT; T419-C006 v1, proof (unaudited), no novelty claim. Let Delta be any nonzero m-by-p matrix of rank at most r and X a fixed full-row-rank p-by-n design. For noiseless Y=Delta X, the global rank-r empirical least-squares estimate equals Delta, so its isotropic population parameter risk is zero. Simultaneous factor GD from B0=0 and nondegenerate Gaussian A0, with any step schedule fixed conditional on X independently of A0, almost surely has B_t A_t != Delta at every finite t. Each finite-iterate entry is a polynomial in A0; at A0=0 both factors remain zero, so a residual entry corresponding to nonzero Delta_ij has a nonzero constant term. Its zero set is Lebesgue-null, and a countable union over t remains null. This also excludes exact recovery at an almost-surely finite integer stopping time selecting these iterates. Consequently a finite-time constant-factor comparison to the noiseless zero-risk benchmark needs a limit, an additive optimization tolerance or other qualification. This does not cover arbitrary initialization-dependent adaptive step rules and does not refute the intended infinite-time or noise-dependent-stopping target.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T01:41:54.341806+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b7e9ae5d7f8dc9a0e31d70cdf304972c9704a43153c4e3ed8f7ba3e1bbbc9b99","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:KPS of arXiv:2412.01381, 'Ergodicity and mixing for locally monotone stochastic evolution equations'] We say that $\{P_{t}\}_{t\ge0}$ is \emph{weak$^\ast$-mean
ergodic} if there exists a Borel probability measure $\mu_\ast$ on ${\mathcal B}(H)$, such that
\begin{equation}\text{w-}\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\int_0^T P_t^\ast\mu\,\mathrm{d} t=\mu_\ast\quad\text{for every }\quad
\mu\in{\mathcal M}_1(H,{\mathcal B}(H)),
\end{equation}
where the limit is in the sense of weak convergence of probability measures.

We say that the \emph{weak law of large numbers} holds for $\{P_{t}\}_{t\ge0}$, for a function $F\in\operatorname{Lip}_{b}(H)$ and for a probability measure $\mu$ on ${\mathcal B}(H)$ if
\[\mathbb{P}_\mu\text{-}\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\int_0^T F(X_t^\mu)\,\mathrm{d} t=\int_H F\,\mathrm{d}\mu_\ast,\]
where $\mu_\ast$ denotes the invariant probability measure of $\{P_{t}\}_{t\ge 0}$ and $\{X_t^\mu\}_{t\ge 0}$ denotes the Markov process related to $\{P_{t}\}_{t\ge 0}$ whose initial distribution is $\mu$ and whose path measure is $\mathbb{P}_\mu$, and where the convergence takes place in $\mathbb{P}_\mu$-probability.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["i.i.d. nonnegative edge weights on Z^2 with F(0) = 0","mu is the axial time constant; the comparison is with the expectation of the minimum of four independent weights","the refutation is Ahlberg's (2019/2020); this is a rederivation with an explicit instance"],"created_at":"2026-09-23T13:15:27.869107+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_b80639d38026a14989da0a86aa6755d6ea3593aa2551d349ffb00e6d55126985","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign status: literature_counterexample_rederived - the primary two-page proof was read and the arithmetic author-checked; the result is Ahlberg's, not ours, and novelty is not claimed] For i.i.d. nonnegative edge weights on Z^2 with F(0) = 0, Auffinger, Damron and Hanson (50 years of first-passage percolation, Question 12) ask whether the axial time constant mu is at least the expected minimum of four independent edge weights. CLAIM: NO, and the question was already settled in the literature by Ahlberg (2019/2020), whose bound mu <= 2 t_{2/3} - twice the 2/3-quantile - refutes it. EXPLICIT INSTANCE: take tau = eta + epsilon U with P(eta = 0) = 3/4 and U uniform on [0,1]. For epsilon > 0 this law is atomless and bounded with F(0) = 0. Solving (3/4) t / epsilon = 2/3 gives t_{2/3} = 8 epsilon / 9, hence mu <= 16 epsilon / 9. The expected four-edge minimum is at least 1/256, the probability of the event that all four edges are expensive. At epsilon = 1/1024, mu <= 16/(9 x 1024) = 1/576 < 1/256, so the proposed inequality is reversed. All sufficiently small epsilon do the same. THIS IS NOT AN OPEN PROBLEM and the store's earlier node for P0096 records only a bounded-search exclusion; this node records what the counterexample actually is.","status":"unverified"}

Hence L_NUV>=sum_v d_v-max_v d_v. For unit-intensity planar Poisson points, Palm P(d_v>r)=exp(-pi*r^2), so E d_v=1/2. In the complete graph with independent mean-n exponential edge lengths, the analogous bound gives liminf E L_NUV/n>=1. Check: The mean-field minimum at each vertex has mean n/(n-1), and a union bound gives expected maximum O(log n); independence between vertices is unnecessary for these expectation bounds. The Euclidean boundary affects only a vanishing bulk fraction for the lower bound, and the maximum estimate follows from empty-ball bounds. Obstruction: These are lower constants only and may be weaker than established optimized-tour bounds. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:09:23.967682+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b8af826c0cd9366894fae1ba5a6454ce9f31cafe8f46b48911fc599e3dcb8bba","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop 11 of arXiv:2607.22416, 'A multi-player optimal stopping game based on a spider Brownian bridge'] Fix $d>0$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T16:46:51.523624+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_b903e3cee17593fc48f4bd33bca8ffaec7da904c9cb287cd97d6c703cf6ff573","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematical analysis, the Kakutani fixed-point theorem is a fixed-point theorem for set-valued functions. It provides sufficient conditions for a set-valued function defined on a convex, compact subset of a Euclidean space to have a fixed point, i.e. a point which is mapped to a set containing it. The Kakutani fixed point theorem is a generalization of the Brouwer fixed point theorem. The Brouwer fixed point theorem is a fundamental result in topology which proves the existence of fixed points for continuous functions defined on compact, convex subsets of Euclidean spaces. Kakutani's theorem extends this to set-valued functions.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["a well-defined electrical network with nonnegative conductances, on a finite graph or an infinite graph with appropriate limiting or boundary conditions","the comparison is between two networks differing only in conductance values on a common edge set, or related by a clean edge addition, deletion, or vertex identification","finite total energy for the relevant flows or potentials, so the variational characterization is well posed","for random-walk conclusions, the standard correspondence between the electrical network and a reversible Markov chain"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.993128+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b9387245512e1cdb33d492e04652cfd536ce550cebd97a2fc52f4dd9dc6c0a91","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For an electrical network on a graph with nonnegative edge conductances c_e, the effective resistance R_eff(a,b) between vertices a, b is defined variationally, via Thomson's principle, as the minimum of sum_e (1/c_e) i_e^2 over unit flows i from a to b obeying Kirchhoff's node law, or equivalently via Dirichlet's principle over voltage functions. Rayleigh's monotonicity law states that R_eff(a,b) is monotone nonincreasing as a function of each conductance: increasing any conductance, adding an edge, or short-circuiting (identifying) any pair of vertices can only decrease or preserve R_eff(a,b), while decreasing a conductance, or deleting an edge, can only increase or preserve it. This purely variational fact underlies comparisons between random walks on different graphs via the resistance-recurrence correspondence, that a network is recurrent for its associated random walk if and only if R_eff(a,infinity)=infinity, comparisons of hitting and commute times, and resistance-based bounds on percolation-type crossing quantities. It gives only monotone comparisons, no quantitative rates, and using it for random-walk conclusions requires the standard electrical network-reversible Markov chain correspondence, with conductances proportional to transition rates, to be correctly set up first. Typical failure: Applying Rayleigh monotonicity to compare effective resistances between two networks that differ in more than conductance values on a shared edge set, such as networks on genuinely different vertex sets or after a modification that is not literally a conductance increase/decrease, edge addition/deletion, or vertex identification; the monotonicity is a coupling statement about the same underlying network with modified weights, and applying it across structurally different networks without an explicit embedding produces an unjustified comparison. Canonical reference: Rayleigh, 1871, Philosophical Magazine; Doyle and Snell, Random Walks and Electric Networks, 1984, Mathematical Association of America; Lyons and Peres, Probability on Trees and Networks, 2016, Cambridge University Press.","status":"unverified"}

A strongly continuous semigroup (C_0-semigroup) on X is a family (T(t))_{t ≥ 0} of bounded linear operators on X with T(0) = I, T(t + s) = T(t)T(s) for all t, s ≥ 0, and t ↦ T(t)x continuous from [0, ∞) to X for every x ∈ X (for a semigroup this is equivalent to T(t)x → x as t ↓ 0 for every x, and also equivalent to weak continuity, i.e. continuity of t ↦ ⟨T(t)x, x*⟩ on [0, ∞) for every x ∈ X and every x* ∈ X*). Every C_0-semigroup is exponentially bounded: there are M ≥ 1 and ω ∈ ℝ with ‖T(t)‖ ≤ M e^{ωt} for all t ≥ 0; the growth bound is ω_0 = inf of such ω. It is a contraction semigroup if ‖T(t)‖ ≤ 1 for all t, and quasi-contractive if ‖T(t)‖ ≤ e^{ωt}. Its (infinitesimal) generator is the operator A with D(A) = {x ∈ X : lim_{t↓0} (T(t)x − x)/t exists} and Ax equal to that limit. One says A generates T and writes T(t) = e^{tA}. Norm continuity of t ↦ T(t) at 0 (a uniformly continuous semigroup) holds if and only if the generator is bounded, in which case T(t) = Σ t^n A^n / n!; the typical generators of PDE semigroups are unbounded and the semigroup is only strongly continuous.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["kappa nonnegative, integrable, compactly supported in [-a, a]","the moment series is used only for |x| > a (outside the support)"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T06:40:20.563000+00:00","domain":"integral transforms / numerical analysis","id":"claim_b9ee277fe9277799995aafa9bbf22addcb7c57f6a68beedf566b986ef748d965","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $\\kappa \\ge 0$ be a kernel supported in $[-a, a]$ with $\\int\\kappa = 1$ and moments $m_k = \\int t^k \\kappa(t)\\,dt$, and let $H_\\kappa(x) = \\pi^{-1}\\,\\mathrm{PV}\\!\\int \\kappa(t)/(t - x)\\,dt$. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:13:49.971281+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ba65bdb4fb4702396eb99a75d308c021109013d901d6f043c5a2f29df77b540d","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition of arXiv:2411.07157, 'Rough differential equations in the flow approach'] Given $\underline{\tau}, \underline{\sigma} \in \boldsymbol{\mathfrak{T}}$, we call a bijection $f: N(\underline{\tau}) \rightarrow N(\underline{\sigma})$ an \textit{isomorphism} from $\underline{\tau}$ to $\underline{\sigma}$ if $f\big(r(\underline{\tau})\big) = r(\underline{\sigma})$, and if the induced mapping $\vec{f}: E(\underline{\tau}) \rightarrow \big(N(\underline{\sigma})\big)^{(2)}$ given by $e = \{v,\bar{v}\} \mapsto \vec{f}(e) = \{f(v),f(\bar{v})\}$ is in fact a bijection between $E(\underline{\tau})$ and $E(\underline{\sigma})$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:32:23.644900+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ba82d5c3ae169f44f642125574eddc29a0eec3d9ef0b0eec62da8b3fa48128ad","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn def:TSAW of arXiv:2603.17858, 'Decay of correlations and zeros for the hard-core model'] Given a graph $G=(V,E)$ and a vertex $v$, the \emph{tree of self avoiding walks} is the tree $T_{\mathrm{SAW}(G,v)}$ obtained from $(G,v)$ as follows.
    Fix a total ordering of the vertices of $G$.
    We define the tree $T_{\mathrm{SAW}(G,v)}$ recursively. 
    If the component of $G$ containing $v$ consists of a single vertex $v$, then $T_{\mathrm{SAW}(G,v)}=\{v\}$.
    In case the component of $G$ containing $v$ consists of more than $1$ vertex, let $v_1,\ldots,v_d$ denote the neighbours of $v$ in $G$.
    Let for $i=1\ldots d$, $G_i$ be the graph obtained from $G$ by removing $v,v_1,\ldots,v_{i-1}$ from $G$.
    Denote for $i=1,\ldots, d$, $T_i=T_{\mathrm{SAW}(G_{i},v_{i})}$.
    Then $T_{\mathrm{SAW}(G,v)}$ is defined as the tree obtained from the disjoint union of the $T_i$ adding a vertex $v$ connecting it to each of the $v_1,\ldots,v_d$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:44:39.744180+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_baa0c5750edf13d2bf2a79502e882f1c7a537514c09efc8bb48bf15384df680f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 4 (Stochastic domination) of arXiv:2608.29872, 'Local Laws and Outlier Eigenvalues for Spiked Separable Covariance Matrices'] (i) Let
\[\xi=\left(\xi^{(n)}(u):n\in\bb N, u\in U^{(n)}\right),\quad \zeta=\left(\zeta^{(n)}(u):n\in\bb N, u\in U^{(n)}\right)\]
be two families of non-negative random variables, where $U^{(n)}$ is a parameter set depending on $n$. We say that $\xi$ is stochastically dominated by $\zeta$, uniformly in $u$, if for any fixed (small) $\epsilon>0$ and (large) $D>0$, 
\[\sup_{u\in U^{(n)}}\bb P\left[\xi^{(n)}(u)>n^\epsilon\zeta^{(n)}(u)\right]\le n^{-D}\]
holds for large enough $n\ge n_0(\epsilon, D)$, denoted by $\xi\prec\zeta$. Throughout this paper, the stochastic domination will always be uniform in all parameters that are not explicitly fixed (such as matrix indices, and $z$ that takes values in some compact set). Note that $n_0(\epsilon, D)$ may depend on quantities that are explicitly constant, such as $\tau$ in Assumption \ref{assm_big1} and \eqref{assm_gap}. If for some complex family $\xi$ we have $|\xi|\prec\zeta$, then we will also write $\xi \prec \zeta$ or $\xi=\OO_\prec(\zeta)$.
\medskip

\noindent (ii) We extend the definition of $\OO_\prec(\cdot)$ to matrices in the weak operator sense as follows. Let $A$ be a family of random matrices and $\zeta$ be a family of nonnegative random variables. Then $A=\OO_\prec(\zeta)$ means that $\left|\left\langle\mathbf v, A\mathbf w\right\rangle\right|\prec\zeta \| \mathbf v\|_2 \|\mathbf w\|_2 $ uniformly in any deterministic vectors $\mathbf v$ and $\mathbf w$. Here and throughout the following, whenever we say ``uniformly in any deterministic vectors", we mean that ``uniformly in any deterministic vectors belonging to certain fixed set of cardinality $n^{\OO(1)}$".

\medskip

\noindent (iii) We say that an event $\Xi$ holds with high probability if $\mathbbm{1}_{\Xi^c}\prec0$, or equivalently, for any constant $D>0$, $\mathbb P(\Xi)\ge 1- n^{-D}$ for large enough $n$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["mu is a probability measure","T is measure-preserving, not necessarily invertible","mu(A) > 0","the value 1/mu(A) for the mean return time requires ergodicity; the general identity does not"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T12:13:53+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, recurrence, induced maps","id":"claim_baade9096b6824c73152f5700a64977d653156c661b715154a8e597b0e136142","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(X, \mathcal{B}, \mu)$ be a probability space, $T: X \to X$ measure-preserving (not necessarily invertible), $A \in \mathcal{B}$ with $\mu(A) > 0$, and $n_A(x) = \min\{n \ge 1 : T^n x \in A\}$ the first return time (finite for a.e. $x \in A$ by Poincare recurrence; set $n_A = \infty$ where no return occurs). Then, in general,
$$\int_A n_A\,d\mu = \mu\Big(\bigcup_{j \ge 0} T^{-j} A\Big),$$
the measure of the set of points whose forward orbit ever meets $A$. In particular $\int_A n_A\,d\mu \le 1$ always, so $n_A$ is integrable over $A$ for EVERY positive-measure set in a probability-preserving system, ergodic or not. If $T$ is ERGODIC, the union has full measure and
$$\int_A n_A\,d\mu = 1, \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \frac{1}{\mu(A)} \int_A n_A\,d\mu = \frac{1}{\mu(A)}:$$
the mean return time to $A$, with respect to the normalised measure $\mu_A = \mu(\cdot \cap A)/\mu(A)$, is exactly $1/\mu(A)$. The induced (first-return) map $T_A = T^{n_A}$ on $A$ preserves $\mu_A$. When $T$ is invertible and ergodic, $(X, \mu, T)$ is isomorphic mod 0 to the tower (Kakutani skyscraper) over $(A, \mu_A, T_A)$ with height $n_A$, of total mass $\int_A n_A\,d\mu / \mu(A)$ in units of $\mu_A$; for non-invertible $T$ the tower map $(x, j) \mapsto T^j x$ is in general only a factor map (for the doubling map with $A = [0, 1/2)$ it is many-to-one).

WHERE IT FAILS. (1) Without ergodicity the mean return time can be strictly less than $1/\mu(A)$: if $A$ is itself invariant then $n_A = 1$ on $A$ and $\int_A n_A = \mu(A) < 1$. (2) In an infinite measure space $\int_A n_A\,d\mu$ can be infinite even for a conservative ergodic $T$ (in fact for an ergodic conservative infinite-measure system it is always infinite for sets of finite positive measure), so 'mean return time $= 1/\mu(A)$' is a finite-measure statement. (3) The lemma controls only the MEAN of $n_A$: no bound on its variance or tail follows; $n_A$ need not be in $L^2$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:31:02.822289+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_baf5e47187f91040484bfb7aaa40f81cd892329cac0240baf3e68d8d844bbe86","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary cor:addition-type-frequency of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Fix $h\geq2$ and $k\geq3$.  For a strictly increasing
$a=(a_1,\ldots,a_k)$, let $\mathsf T_h(a)$ be the equivalence relation on
$\mathcal U_{h,k}$ defined by
\[
 u\sim_{\mathsf T_h(a)}v
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 u\cdot a=v\cdot a.
\]
Equivalently, after quotienting the forced permutation symmetries, this is
O'Bryant's weak type of the $h$-fold addition table
[OBryant2025].
Let $\mathfrak T_{h,k}$ be the finite set of types realized by strictly
increasing integer $k$-tuples.  For $\mathsf T\in\mathfrak T_{h,k}$, put
\[
 r(\mathsf T)=\dim_{\mathbb R}
 \operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}
 \{u-v:u\sim_{\mathsf T}v\}
\]
and
\[
 F^{(k)}_{h,\mathsf T}(q)=
 \#\left\{A\in\binom{[q]}k:\mathsf T_h(A)=\mathsf T\right\}.
\]
Then $F^{(k)}_{h,\mathsf T}(q)$ is a quasipolynomial in $q-1$, valid for
every positive integer $q$, of degree exactly $k-r(\mathsf T)$.  In
particular, there is an effectively computable
$c_{h,k,\mathsf T}\in\mathbb Q_{>0}$ such that
\begin{equation}
 F^{(k)}_{h,\mathsf T}(q)
 =c_{h,k,\mathsf T}q^{k-r(\mathsf T)}
  +O_{h,k,\mathsf T}\!\left(q^{k-r(\mathsf T)-1}\right).
\end{equation}
Moreover,
\begin{equation}
 F^{(k)}_{h,n}(q)=
 \sum_{\substack{\mathsf T\in\mathfrak T_{h,k}\\
 |\mathcal U_{h,k}/\mathsf T|=n}}
 F^{(k)}_{h,\mathsf T}(q).
\end{equation}
Hence summing over weak types with $n$ equivalence classes recovers
Theorem~(thm:rank-frequency of the paper).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:34:33.540266+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_bb24e81ec438e42a0c90a144e24a2769f3d899f78c54b6945278ad382471f715","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 8 (XY model) of arXiv:2603.28734, 'Free energy analyticity of the disordered XY model and Debye screening in the 2D Coulomb g'] Fix $d\in\Z_{\geq 1}$ and $\beta\in\R_{\geq 0}$.
    For any domain $\Lambda$ and $\zeta:\Z^d\to\S^1$,
    the \emph{XY model} on $\Lambda$ with boundary condition $\zeta$
    at inverse temperature $\beta$ is the probability measure  on $\sigma\in(\S^1)^\Lambda$ given by
    \[
        \diff\mu_{\XYM,\Lambda,\beta}^\zeta(\sigma) = \frac1{Z_{\XYM,\Lambda,\beta}^\zeta} e^{-\beta H_{\XYM,\Lambda}^\zeta(\sigma)} \diff\sigma,
    \]
    where $Z_{\XYM,\Lambda,\beta}^\zeta$ is the normalising constant,
    $\diff\sigma$ the Haar measure, and
    \[
        H_{\XYM,\Lambda}^\zeta(\sigma) := \sum_{\substack{\{x,y\}\subset\Lambda\\x\sim y}} |\sigma_x-\sigma_y|^2/2 + \sum_{\substack{x\in\Lambda,\,y\in\Lambda^c\\x\sim y}} |\sigma_x-\zeta_y|^2/2.
    \]
    The \emph{critical inverse temperature} is defined as the largest $\beta_c=\beta_c(d)\in(0,\infty)$
    such that $\mu_{\XY,\Lambda_n,\beta}^{+1}[\sigma_0]$ decays exponentially fast in $n$
    for any fixed $\beta\in[0,\beta_c)$.
    Classical arguments based on correlations inequalities imply the existence of an infinite-volume Gibbs measure with $+1$ boundary conditions at inverse temperature $\beta\geq 0$, that we refer to as $\mu^{+1}_{\XY, \beta}$.
    The label $\XYM$ is omitted from notations when it is clear from the context.","status":"unverified"}

	\[

{"assumptions":["mu is a probability measure","T is measure-preserving, not necessarily invertible","mu(A) > 0","the value 1/mu(A) for the mean return time requires ergodicity; the general identity does not"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T02:00:35.438087+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, recurrence, induced maps","id":"claim_bb6dcbe5ce02085d2e2e48afcaee2028d3f09a38e89e185dcbbbb02136dd47f5","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(X, \mathcal{B}, \mu)$ be a probability space, $T: X \to X$ measure-preserving (not necessarily invertible), $A \in \mathcal{B}$ with $\mu(A) > 0$, and $n_A(x) = \min\{n \ge 1 : T^n x \in A\}$ the first return time (finite for a.e. $x \in A$ by Poincare recurrence; set $n_A = \infty$ where no return occurs). Then, in general,
$$\int_A n_A\,d\mu = \mu\Big(\bigcup_{j \ge 0} T^{-j} A\Big),$$
the measure of the set of points whose forward orbit ever meets $A$. In particular $\int_A n_A\,d\mu \le 1$ always, so $n_A$ is integrable over $A$ for EVERY positive-measure set in a probability-preserving system, ergodic or not. If $T$ is ERGODIC, the union has full measure and
$$\int_A n_A\,d\mu = 1, \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \frac{1}{\mu(A)} \int_A n_A\,d\mu = \frac{1}{\mu(A)}:$$
the mean return time to $A$, with respect to the normalised measure $\mu_A = \mu(\cdot \cap A)/\mu(A)$, is exactly $1/\mu(A)$. Equivalently, the induced (first-return) map $T_A = T^{n_A}$ on $A$ preserves $\mu_A$ and $(X, \mu, T)$ is recovered from $(A, \mu_A, T_A, n_A)$ as a tower of total mass $\int_A n_A\,d\mu / \mu(A)$.

WHERE IT FAILS. (1) Without ergodicity the mean return time can be strictly less than $1/\mu(A)$: if $A$ is itself invariant then $n_A = 1$ on $A$ and $\int_A n_A = \mu(A) < 1$. (2) In an infinite measure space $\int_A n_A\,d\mu$ can be infinite even for a conservative ergodic $T$ (in fact for an ergodic conservative infinite-measure system it is always infinite for sets of finite positive measure), so 'mean return time $= 1/\mu(A)$' is a finite-measure statement. (3) The lemma controls only the MEAN of $n_A$: no bound on its variance or tail follows; $n_A$ need not be in $L^2$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:44:27.903838+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_bbb809515616a783f0c0917647a9502220a6adee29ae22b1068da7aa5c3bc432","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 7 of arXiv:2607.12666, 'Sample-path Large deviations for \\Scheduled Arrival Processes with Unpunctuality'] The sequence $\{\bar A^{(n)}\}_{n\ge1}$ satisfies a large deviations principle on $D([0,T])$, equipped with the Skorokhod $J_1$ topology, with speed $n$ and good rate function
\[
I_T(\phi)
=
\sup_{m\ge1}\sup_{0<t_1<\cdots<t_m\le T}
I_{t_1,\dots,t_m}\bigl(\phi(t_1),\dots,\phi(t_m)\bigr),
\]
where, for each $0<t_1<\cdots<t_m\le T$,
\[
I_{t_1,\dots,t_m}(x)
=
\sup_{\alpha\in\mathbb R^m}
\left\{
\sum_{\ell=1}^m \alpha_\ell x_\ell-\Lambda_{t_1,\dots,t_m}(\alpha)
\right\}.
\]
Moreover, the rate function admits the variational representation
\begin{equation}
    I_T(\phi) = \sup_{\theta\in C([0,T]),\gamma\in\R} \left\{ \int_0^T \theta(t) \phi(t)\, dt + \gamma\phi(T) - \Lambda_T(\theta,\gamma)\right\},
\end{equation}
with $\Lambda_T(\theta,\gamma)$ given by
\begin{equation}
    \Lambda_T(\theta,\gamma):=\log \E \exp \left(\int_0^T \theta(t)A(t)\, dt + \gamma A(T)\right).
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.346762+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_bbc2bafb891aee173d5635f3b393a3305101bdc2922d2e3a43e5ecdb751f17b9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 147 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $Z$ be a standard gaussian random variable, and suppose $Y(q_0)\sim\zeta^\Ising$ satisfies assumption~\eqref{i:IAMP-main-init} of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}. Then for any $\eta>0$ there exists an odd function $\prxpsi:\bbR\to\bbR$ with bounded Lipschitz norm $\|\prxpsi\|_{\textup{Lip}}\leq \overline{L}(\eta,\zeta^{\Ising})$ such that $\bbW_2\big(\prxpsi(Z),\zeta^{\Ising}\big)\leq \eta$. Additionally, we have $|\bbE[\prxpsi(Z)^2] - q_0| \le 4\epsilon^{1/2}$.

\begin{proof}
    Using a standard quantile coupling, there exists an odd measurable function $\hat\psi\in L^2(\bbR)$ such that the law of $\hat\psi(Z)$ is precisely $\zeta^{\Ising}$. Since bounded Lipschitz functions are dense in $L^2$, there exists a bounded Lipschitz function $\tilde\psi:\bbR\to\bbR$ with $\bbW_2\big(\tilde\psi(Z),\zeta^{\Ising}\big)\leq \min\{\eta, \epsilon^{1/2}\}$.
The first assertion of the lemma immediately follows by taking $\prxpsi=\tilde\psi$.  For the second assertion, recall that under assumption~\eqref{i:IAMP-main-init} of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}, the random variable $Y(q_0)\sim\zeta^\Ising$ satisfies
	\[\Big|\E[Y(q_0)^2-q_0]
	\Big|\le\epsilon\,.\]
Under the $\bbW_2$-optimal coupling of $\prxpsi(Z)$ with $Y(q_0)$, we have
	\begin{align*}
	&\bigg|\E[\prxpsi(Z)^2]
	-\E[Y(q_0)^2] \bigg|
	=\bigg|\E\Big[
	(\prxpsi(Z)-Y(q_0))
	(\prxpsi(Z)-Y(q_0)
		+2Y(q_0))
	\Big]\bigg|\\
	&\qquad=\bigg| \E\Big[
	(\prxpsi(Z)-Y(q_0))^2
	\Big]
	+ 2\E\Big[
	(\prxpsi(Z)-Y(q_0)) Y(q_0)\Big]
	\bigg|
	\le \epsilon + 2 \epsilon^{1/2}
		\E[Y(q_0)^2]^{1/2} \le 3\epsilon^{1/2}\,.
	\end{align*}
Combining these gives
	\[
	\Big|\E[\prxpsi(Z)^2-q_0]
	\Big|
	\le 4\epsilon^{1/2}\,,
	\]
as claimed.\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-23T13:16:35.596991+00:00","domain":"statistical learning theory","id":"claim_bbd3a83729c8d9e501cff01bc27d1df869d97b124fee1913e254632b046cae12","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"For kernel ridge regression with power-law spectrum $\\eta_k = k^{-\\alpha}$ ($\\alpha>1$, the capacity) and teacher coefficients $\\theta_k = k^{-(1+\\alpha(2r-1))/2}$ ($r \\ge 0$, the source), with label noise of variance $\\sigma^2$ and ridge $\\lambda = n^{-\\ell}$, the excess risk of the ridgeless estimator ($\\ell \\ge \\alpha$, including interpolation) is of order $\\max(\\sigma^2, n^{-2\\alpha\\min(r,1)})$, while the optimally regularised excess risk is of order $n^{-2\\alpha\\min(r,1)}$ for $n$ below a crossover $n_* \\asymp \\sigma^{-1/(\\alpha\\min(r,1))}$ and of order $n^{1/(1+2\\alpha\\min(r,1)) - 1}$ above it (Cui, Loureiro, Krzakala, Zdeborova, NeurIPS 2021). Two consequences that a learning-curve experiment can test directly: (i) with no label noise the interpolant is the optimum of the whole path, so the ratio of the interpolant's risk to the best risk on the path is $1$; (ii) with noise, once $n$ is past the crossover, that ratio grows like $n^{2\\alpha\\min(r,1)/(1+2\\alpha\\min(r,1))}$, and a tenfold increase in the noise level moves the crossover by a factor $10^{1/(\\alpha\\min(r,1))}$ in $n$. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.360381+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_bbfda4e6f0c5e19e51593f8e671456cc0b18e76af6dcad38839849dfac646379","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 254 ($\bbW_2$-stability of $\mu_\bG(\bx)$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For all $\bx,\bx' \in \bbR^N$, we have
    \[
        \bbW_2(\mu_\bG(\bx),\mu_\bG(\bx'))
        \le \frac{\|\bG\|_\op \|\bx-\bx'\|}{(MN)^{1/2}}\,.
    \]
\begin{proof}
The $\bbW_2$ distance can be bounded by
    \[
        \bbW_2(\mu_\bG(\bx),\mu_\bG(\bx'))^2
        \le \frac{1}{M} \sum_{a=1}^M \frac{(\bg^a,\bx-\bx')^2}{N}
        = \frac{\|\bG (\bx-\bx')\|^2}{MN}
        \le \frac{(\|\bG\|_\op \|\bx-\bx'\|)^2}{MN}\,.
    \]
This proves the claim.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["v_1, ..., v_n linearly independent in a real or complex inner product space","for a dependent family the process produces a zero u_k, which is skipped and yields an orthonormal basis of the span"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T14:24:13.476812+00:00","domain":"linear algebra","id":"claim_bc01791ccad0fb7bcf635158f0db13bcca11c5b76eca0ae6dceb03aec1fed455","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let v_1, ..., v_n be linearly independent vectors in an inner product space. Define recursively u_1 = v_1 and u_k = v_k - sum_{j < k} <v_k, e_j> e_j with e_j = u_j / |u_j|. Then every u_k is nonzero, the vectors e_1, ..., e_n are orthonormal, and span(e_1, ..., e_k) = span(v_1, ..., v_k) for every k; the e_k are unique up to the sign (or unit scalar) of each vector given this nested-span condition. Applied to a countable linearly independent sequence the process yields an orthonormal sequence with the same nested spans, which is why every separable Hilbert space has an orthonormal basis. In matrix language, applying it to the columns of an m x n matrix A of full column rank gives the QR factorisation A = Q R with Q having orthonormal columns and R upper triangular with positive diagonal. (Numerically the modified Gram-Schmidt variant, which subtracts each projection as soon as it is formed, loses orthogonality far more slowly in floating point.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:12:19.463035+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_bc1bf5998e3b309547a77e1eac6e21c17c6647f058c7d8fe8674eba401ecf57a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 3 (A non-Lipschitz example in the non-critical regime) of arXiv:2608.17540, 'Pathwise stability for one-dimensional SDEs driven by Brownian motion and a symmetric stab'] Let $\wt\eta\in(1/\alpha,1)$ and fix $0<\lambda<1\wedge T^{-1/\alpha}$. Consider the time-homogeneous coefficients
\[
  b(t,x)=\wt b(t,x)\equiv0,
  \qquad
  a(t,x)=\wt a(t,x)\equiv0,
  \qquad
  \sigma(t,x)\equiv1,
  \qquad
  \wt\sigma(t,x)=1+\lambda\bigl(|x|^{\wt\eta}\wedge1\bigr).
\]
Then $\wt\sigma$ is bounded, bounded away from zero, and fails to be Lipschitz at the origin, while satisfying Assumption~\ref{ass:perturbed} with exponent $\wt\eta$. Moreover, there is a coupled pair of solutions driven by the same stable process $Z$ for which Assumption~\ref{ass:solutions} holds and
\[
  B=A=0,
  \qquad
  S^\alpha\le \lambda^\alpha T<\infty.
\]
Consequently, $S<1$, and the non-critical estimate of Theorem~\ref{thm:noncritical} applies to a non-Lipschitz stable coefficient. In particular, if $x_0=\wt x_0$, then
\[
  \sup_{0\le t\le T}\E|X_t-\wt X_t|^{\alpha-1}
  \le C\lambda^{\alpha-1/\wt\eta},
\]
where $C$ depends on $T,\alpha,\wt\eta$ and the fixed coefficient bounds, but not on $\lambda\in(0,1\wedge T^{-1/\alpha})$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:42:39.077210+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_bc304c101f3314e56fcb13bffecb2f3de6cbfcc859a9262a52dfb793aaddd513","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn A. dfn item: epsilon condition for metric on hatC_c of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] [{The metric $d_{\hat{C}_{c}(\cdot, \Xi)}^{M}$}]
  For $f, g \in \widehat{C}_{c}(M, \Xi)$ and $\varepsilon>0$, 
  consider the following condition.
  \begin{enumerate} [label = ($\widehat{C}_{c}(\varepsilon)$), leftmargin=*]
    \item 
      For any $x \in \dom(f)$, there exists an element $y \in \dom(g)$ such that 
      $d^{M}(x, y) \vee d^{\Xi}(f(x), g(y)) \leq \varepsilon$.
      Similarly,
      for any $y \in \dom(g)$, there exists an element $x \in \dom(g)$ such that 
      $d^{M}(x,y) \vee d^{\Xi}(f(x), g(y)) \leq \varepsilon$.
  \end{enumerate}
  We define
  \begin{equation}
    d_{\hat{C}_{c}(\cdot, \Xi)}^{M}(f, g) 
    \coloneqq
    \inf 
    \{
      \varepsilon > 0 \mid \varepsilon\ \text{satisfies (A. dfn item: epsilon condition for metric on hatC_c of the paper) with respect to}\ f, g
    \} 
    \wedge 1,
  \end{equation}
  where the infimum over the empty set is defined to be $\infty$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:06:21.712845+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_bc4c6d339716deba8578fb81c0c8d06aa9f50f49ae5da7f92c53fd366c551960","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 6 ({\cite[Theorem~4.3 and Lemma~4.4) of arXiv:2607.21374, 'Local structure at the maximum and sharp persistence asymptotics of rough fractional Brown'] {moench2026horizonProblem}}]

Let \(F\subset\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\) be finite and nonempty.  Then
\(B_F\) is nondegenerate and its precision matrix is Stieltjes: it is
symmetric positive definite with nonpositive off-diagonal entries.  Let
\(a\in\mathbb R^F\).  Here a coordinate conditioning means a normalised
density section obtained by fixing any subset of the current coordinates,
and a coordinate rectangle is a product of intervals in the current
coordinate space.  Any law obtained from \(a+B_F\) or \(a-B_F\) by finitely
many such conditionings, coordinate-rectangle restrictions, and coordinate
marginalisations is MTP\(_2\), provided every required section or restriction
normaliser is finite and strictly positive.  Every such law is therefore
associated, i.e., if \(X\) has one of these laws and \(f,g\) are bounded
coordinatewise nondecreasing functions, then
\begin{equation}
  \EE[f(X)g(X)]\geq \EE f(X)\,\EE g(X).
  
\end{equation}
Whenever the procedure uses only coordinate conditionings and
marginalisations and at least one coordinate remains, its result is a
nondegenerate Gaussian law with Stieltjes precision.  For a split into
retained and exposed blocks, write this precision as
\[
  P=\begin{pmatrix}P_{RR}&P_{RE}\\P_{ER}&P_{EE}\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Then the regression matrix of the retained block on the exposed block is
\(-P_{RR}^{-1}P_{RE}\), which is entrywise nonnegative because
\(P_{RR}^{-1}\geq0\) and \(P_{RE}\leq0\) entrywise. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:55:18.059726+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_bce04e98f027f497450ce13161a7d475c48ab45fc166d30c658b2e138400299a","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 7 (Local normalization and decoupled normal form) of arXiv:2606.16662, '2606.16662'] Fix a cutoff and a dyadic block \((N,Q,M)\).  Consider either one value of the
centered kernel, one increment between two Volterra pairs, or one member of
the finite cutoff family used in the tail argument.  In an increment
estimate, collect jointly all first-Wiener kernels at the two endpoints and
in the finite telescope connecting them.  There exists an integer \(d_0\),
depending only on the finite color family and on the number of telescope
terms, with the following properties.

For every \(\underline m\in\Z^d_+\), there is a standard real Gaussian vector
\[
        G_{\underline m}
        =(G_{\underline m,\mu})_{1\le\mu\le d_0},
\]
and these vectors are independent for distinct representatives.  With
\[
        a=(\underline\ell,\mu),\qquad
        b=(\underline r,\lambda),\qquad c=q,\qquad e=n,
\]
the centered kernel has a finite expansion
\begin{equation}

        =\sum_{\nu}\sum_{a,b}
        H_{\nu;a,b,c,e}(t,s)
        \wick{G_{\underline\ell,\mu}G_{\underline r,\lambda}} .
\end{equation}
The pattern index \(\nu\) contains the two Fourier signs, together with the
finite sine--cosine, color and cutoff choices.  For fixed \(\nu\), there are
signs \(\epsilon_{\nu,1},\epsilon_{\nu,2}\in\{+1,-1\}\) such that the
coefficient tensor is supported by
\begin{equation}
        n=q+\epsilon_{\nu,1}\underline\ell
              +\epsilon_{\nu,2}\underline r,
        \qquad |\underline\ell|\sim|\underline r|\sim N,
        \qquad |q|\sim Q,
        \qquad |n|\sim M,
        \qquad Q\le c_{\rm ap}N,
\end{equation}
up to the fixed Littlewood--Paley overlap, and
\begin{equation}
        |H_{\nu;a,b,c,e}(t,s)|
        \lesssim N^{-\Gamma_{i;j,k}}.
\end{equation}

increment factor from Assumption~\ref{ass:coeff}.  The number of patterns
and the auxiliary dimension \(d_0\) are uniform in the dyadic scales,
cutoff and time points.

family \((C_{a,b})\subset X\), and every \(p\ge2\), write
\(G_a=G_{\underline\ell,\mu}\) for \(a=(\underline\ell,\mu)\),

\begin{equation}
        \left\|\sum_{a,b}C_{a,b}\wick{G_aG_b}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.166318+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_bd0f46b82c7f0fbe5c37a69d3f09f939b26009d922195892b76d6bf129874120","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 47 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Suppose $J_+ \neq \emptyset$.
    Then, the supremum in \eqref{e:fp.F.rviii} is attained at a point of the form
    \[
        \btheta_+ = \hbA_+(\gamma) \hbg_+\,,
    \]
where we define
    \begin{align}
        
        \gamma
        &\equiv 
        \gamma(\btheta_+)
        \equiv \frac{\|\btheta_+\|^2}{M\alpha} + \gamma_-\,,\\
        
        \hbA_+(\gamma)
        &\equiv \bigg((\hbD_+)^{-1} -
        \frac{m(\beta_\star(\gamma))}{\alpha} \bI_{B_+} \bigg)^{-1}\,.
    \end{align}
    Furthermore, this value of $\gamma$ satisfies
    \beq
        
        m(\beta_\star(\gamma)) \le \frac{\alpha}{\hv_1}\,.
    \eeq

\begin{proof}
Recall that Lemma~\ref{l:fp-g2}\eqref{i:fp-g-growth} shows that $g(\gamma) = \Theta(\gamma^{1/2})$ as $\gamma \to \infty$. It follows that $F^{\rviii,+}(\btheta_+) \to -\infty$ as $\|\btheta_+\| \to +\infty$, so the supremum of $F^{\rviii,+}(\btheta_+)$ is attained at a local maximizer $\btheta_+$.
    We will show that this local maximizer must in fact be a stationary point.
    By Lemma~\ref{l:fp-g2}\eqref{i:fp-g-diff}, $g$ is differentiable on $(0,+\infty)$. Therefore, the only possible non-stationary local maximum $\btheta_+$ must satisfy $\gamma = 0$, which implies $\gamma_-=0$ and $\btheta_+=\bzero$. However, in this case let us consider a small $\bv \in \bbR^{B_+}$ with $(\bv,\hbg_+) = 0$. For such $\bv$, we have
    \[
        F^{\rviii,+}(\bv) - F^{\rviii,+}(\bzero) 
        = g\bigg(\frac{\|\bv\|^2}{M\alpha}\bigg) - g(0)
        - \frac{((\hbD_+)^{-1} \bv,\bv)}{M}\,.
    \]
Lemma~\ref{l:fp-g2}\eqref{i:fp-g-diff} characterizes the behavior of $g(\gamma)$ as $\gamma\downarrow0$, and implies that the above is positive for sufficiently small $\|\bv\|$.
    Thus $\btheta_+=\bzero$ is not a local maximizer, and the only possible local maximizers are stationary points $\btheta_+$.
Therefore, consider any stationary local maximizer $\btheta_+ \in \bbR^{B_+}$ of $F^{\rviii,+}(\btheta_+)$.
    Stationarity implies
    \[
        \btheta_+ = \bigg((\hbD_+)^{-1} -
        \frac{g'(\gamma)}{\alpha} \bI_{B_+} \bigg)^{-1} \hbg_+
    \stackrel{\eqref{e:fp-viii-hbA}}{=}
    \hbA_+(\gamma) \hbg_+\,.
    \]
    In the last equality, we used Lemma~\ref{l:fp-g2}\eqref{i:fp-g-diff} with the above observation that $\gamma>0$. This proves \eqref{e:fp-gamma-btheta-plus}.
    Similarly, for any $\bv$ orthogonal to $\btheta_+$
    (or, if $\btheta_+=\bzero$, for any $\bv$), we have 
    \[
        \frac{d^2}{dt^2}
        F^{\rviii,+}(\btheta_+ + t\bv)
        \bigg|_{t=0}
        = -\frac{2}{M} \bv^\st \bigg(
        (\hbD_+)^{-1} -
        \frac{m(\beta_\star(\gamma))}{\alpha} \bI_{B_+}
        \bigg) \bv\le0\,,
    \]
where the last inequality is because 
$\btheta_+$ is a maximizer. Since $(\hbD_+)^{-1}$ has smallest eigenvalue $1/\hv_1$ with multiplicity at least $\iota N$ (because $(\lambda,\mu) \in \Lambda$), this implies the bound \eqref{e:fp-m-betast-gamma-bd}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:20:15.584932+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_bda04e7f40323579d237bb825d0b41a752af6cdc3e28266bafa3f02e8bf1ab82","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:admissible-classes of arXiv:2609.00777, 'Universal murmuration and Hecke augmentation'] Suppose that $P\nmid rd$.  There is a set

\[
\mathcal A_{r,d}(Q)
=

\mu^2(N)=1,\ P\nmid N,\
N\bmod d^2\in\mathcal R_{r,d}(Q)
\right\}.
\]
Every class in $\mathcal R_{r,d}(Q)$ is coprime to $d$, and
\[
\#\mathcal R_{r,d}(Q)
=
\begin{cases}
1,&(r,d)=1,\quad 2\nmid rd,\\
1,&(r,d)=1,\quad 2\mid r,\\
1,&(r,d)=2,\quad 2\Vert d,\\
2,&(r,d)=2,\quad 4\mid d,\\

\]
If $d$ is even, every integer represented by an admissible class is odd.
Writing
\[
s=\frac{N(r^2N-4Q)}{d^2},
\]
the parity information is
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{case}&\text{parity of }s\\ \hline
2\Vert d,\ 2\Vert r&\text{even}\\
2\Vert d,\ 4\mid r&\text{odd}\\

\end{array}
\]
In particular, the number and parity type of these classes are independent of $k$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:20:33.755725+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_bdab94d6dc55189695d026f0ba5482683d76fc5a471b7f35270ed45a35685535","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 48 (\cite{Falk01}*{Theorem 3.7}) of arXiv:2609.03836, 'Koszul Orlik--Solomon Algebras from Non-supersolvable Arrangements'] \label[Thm]{prop:tensorreducedos}
    Let $M$ and $N$ be matroids and let us identify the symbol $f$ with an element in each.
    Then we have the graded $\QQ$-algebra isomorphism
    \[
        \rOS(P_{f}(M, N)) \cong \rOS(M)\otimes_{\QQ} \rOS(N).
    \]
    \begin{proof}
        Let $E_0 = E(M) - \{f\}$ and $E_1 = E(N) - \{f\}$.
        We will prove the isomorphism 
        $$\OS(\mathbf{d}_f P_{f}(M, N)) \cong \OS(\mathbf{d}_f M)\otimes_{\QQ} \OS(\mathbf{d}_f N).$$
        Both sides are canonically quotients of the free exterior algebra 
        $A = \bigwedge(E_0 \sqcup E_1)$.
        We will show that the kernel ideals are equal.
        As discussed in \Cref{subsec:OS_algebras},
        $\OS(\mathbf{d}_f P_{f}(M, N))$ is the quotient of $A$ by 
        (i) the monomials 
        $e_D$ for subets $D \subseteq E_0 \sqcup E_1$ containing $f$ in their span
        and (ii) the elements $\partial e_C$ for all circuits of $P_f(M, N)\del f$.
        Since a subset of $E_0$ (or $E_1$) spanning $f$ still spans it in $P_f(M, N)$ and since every circuit of $M \del f$ (or $N \del f$) is a circuit of $P_f(M, N) \del f$, every relation in the defining ideal of 
        $\rOS(M)\otimes_{\QQ} \rOS(N)$ lies in the defining ideal of
        $\OS(\mathbf{d}_f P_{f}(M, N))$. The converse follows from the following two observations:
        \begin{itemize}
            \item If $D \subseteq E_0 \sqcup E_1$ contains $f$ in its span in $P_f(M, N)$, then so does at least one of $D \cap E_0$ or $D \cap E_1$.
            \item If $C \subseteq E_0 \sqcup E_1$ is a circuit of $P_f(M, N)$ then either $C \subseteq E_0$, or 
            $C \subseteq E_1$, or else both 
            $C \cap E_0$ and $C \cap E_1$ contain $f$ in their span.
        \end{itemize}
        The first observation shows that every element of type (i) in the defining ideal of $\OS(\mathbf{d}_f P_{f}(M, N))$ is a multiple of an element of type (i) in the defining ideal of 
        $\rOS(M)\otimes_{\QQ} \rOS(N)$. 
        The second observation shows that every element of type (ii) in the defining ideal of $\OS(\mathbf{d}_f P_{f}(M, N))$ is either equal, up to sign, to a type (ii) element for $\rOS(M)\otimes_{\QQ} \rOS(N)$ or else every term in its expansion into monomials is a multiple of an element of type (i) in the defining ideal of $\rOS(M)\otimes_{\QQ} \rOS(N)$.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

Discrete form: for a_n >= 0 and 1 < p < infinity, sum_{n>=1} ((a_1 + ... + a_n)/n)^p <= (p/(p-1))^p sum_{n>=1} a_n^p, again with the sharp constant. At p = infinity the operator is bounded on L^infinity with norm exactly 1, consistent with p/(p-1) -> 1.","status":"unverified"}

WHAT HAPPENED: the first exact check of det(z I - U_q - V_q) reduced over Z[m] modulo m^q + 1, which m = e^{i pi / q} certainly satisfies, and reported nonzero coefficients for odd q - which reads exactly like a refutation of the nilpotency claim. {"assumptions":["the cleaners compared are consistent for the population covariance (sample, eta-RIE without floor, LW2020, NERCOME)","the ensemble error covariance is rank-deficient in practice (members near-collinear), so the unconstrained plug-in has near-null sample directions"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T07:07:18.954358+00:00","domain":"ensemble learning / covariance estimation","id":"claim_be3490f4cbcedf62ac943e2d6db3d9c77b884a50d5bcd0fb5f57c27a6283efd2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Read the ladder result (every consistent cleaner ties inside the long-only stack; floors and linear shrinkage lose) through the entrywise bound. Unconstrained minimum variance depends on $\\hat\\Sigma^{-1}$, so its error is governed by the SPECTRUM of $\\hat\\Sigma$: the ratio $q = M/n$, the bulk edge, the near-null directions - the territory of random-matrix cleaning, where the Ledoit-Peche oracle, its analytical estimate and NERCOME differ from the sample covariance by design. The long-only plug-in's excess risk is bounded by twice the ENTRYWISE error $\\varepsilon = \\max_{ij}|\\hat\\Sigma_{ij} - \\Sigma_{ij}|$, which is $O(\\sqrt{\\log M/n})$ for the sample covariance and of the same order for every consistent estimator (a consistent nonlinear shrinkage moves the eigenvalues by $O(n^{-1/2})$ relative, hence the entries by the same order) - so all of them obey the same bound and, on the well-conditioned active submatrix, produce the same weights. A fixed floor $f\\sigma^2$ on the small eigenvalues, or a linear shrinkage $\\rho(\\mu I - \\hat\\Sigma)$, is a BIAS of size $f\\sigma^2$ (or $\\rho|\\mu - \\Sigma_{ii}|$) in the entries spanned by those directions that does not vanish with $n$; it cannot tighten the bound and it displaces the plug-in wherever an active member has weight in a floored direction. With case weights $s_i$ (the per-sample relative metric $s_i = 1/\\|y_i\\|^2$) the bound holds with $n$ replaced by the effective sample size $n_{\\mathrm{eff}} = (\\sum s_i)^2/\\sum s_i^2$, which a few tiny-norm cases can make much smaller than $n$: that is why the relative-metric fit overfits without the constraint and why the long-only form still pays a little at very small $n$. Measured on the EMIT pool (2026-09-05, seed 101): the bound holds on every output of Y1/Y2/Y4 at n = 932 and of Y2/Y4 at n = 60, and is loose by one to three orders of magnitude (median $2\u000barepsilon$ over the oracle risk 10-1000 against a realised excess of 0.02-0.5 at full calibration) - it delivers finiteness and the right dependence, not a tight number; the unconstrained plug-in on the same matrices carries weights of median absolute size 68,000 on Y1 and 1,800 on Y2; the effective sample size of the $1/\\|y\\|^2$ weighting is 150 of 932 rows on Y2 (615 on Y1) and 8.7 of 60 in the $n = 60$ arm.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["i.i.d. summands with mean zero and finite variance","the constant sqrt(2) inside the normalisation is not adjustable; it is the correct almost sure envelope"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:40.781780+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_be6c233b3f80b2ad7b180f07b82c12b5a10e4b84732b718a58c52d3c3540a594","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, X_2, ... be i.i.d. with E[X_1] = 0 and E[X_1^2] = sigma^2 < infinity, and let S_n = X_1 + ... + X_n. Then almost surely limsup_{n -> infinity} S_n / sqrt( 2 n log log n ) = sigma and liminf_{n -> infinity} S_n / sqrt( 2 n log log n ) = - sigma. Consequently the set of limit points of S_n / sqrt(2 n log log n) is exactly the interval [-sigma, sigma], and the sequence oscillates: it comes arbitrarily close to both endpoints infinitely often and does not converge. STRASSEN'S CONVERSE: if limsup_n |S_n| / sqrt( 2 n log log n ) < infinity with positive probability, then E[X_1] = 0 and E[X_1^2] < infinity, so the two-moment hypothesis is exactly right and not merely convenient. The theorem sits strictly between the strong law, which says S_n/n -> 0, and the central limit theorem, which describes S_n/sqrt(n) in distribution but says nothing about the almost sure oscillation; in particular the CLT does NOT imply that S_n/sqrt(n) is almost surely bounded, and indeed it is not - the iterated logarithm is the correct almost sure envelope. [Hartman and Wintner (1941); Strassen (1966); see Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 8.5.2]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.349683+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_bef4771e153a1f5e86b37a54bbe4a60748ab9c190eab12bc6913e7cd9c207f24","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 172 (eighth moment bounds for $X^{\RomII}$, $X^{\trunc,\RomII}$, and $X^{\frozen,\RomII}$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $(a(q_d):0\le d\le \dmax)$
and $(a^\frozen(q_d):0\le d\le \dmax)$
be sampled as in Definition~\ref{d:rerand}.
For $N$ large enough, we have
	\[
	\E\bigg[\bigg(
	\sum_{\ell=a}^{b-1} 
	\Delta X^{\RomII}(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))
	\bigg)^8\bigg]
	\le L^{O(1)} (q_b-q_a)^4
	\]
for all $0\le a\le b\le \dmax$. The same bound holds 
with $\Delta X^{\trunc,\RomII}(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))$
or $\Delta X^{\frozen,\RomII}(q_d,a^\frozen(q_{d+1}))$
in place of $\Delta X^{\RomII}(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))$.

\begin{proof}
Let $\Delta_d$ be as in Remark~\ref{r:fourth.mmt}. We first define the (high probability) events
	\beq
	E_d\equiv \bigg\{
	\frac{\|\bar{\bg}(q_d)\|^2}{N} \le 2
	\bigg\} \in \cFt(q_d)\,,\quad
	E_\star=\bigcap_{d=a}^{b-1} E_d\,.
	\eeq
It follows using Lemma~\ref{l:y.subgaus} (with $\cFt(q_d)$ in place of $\cG(q_d)$, as discussed above) that, for any $\vartheta\in\R$,
	\[
	\ind\{E_d\}
	\E\Big[ \exp(\vartheta \Delta_d) \,\Big|\,\cFt(q_d)\Big]
	\le \ind\{E_d\}
	\exp \bigg\{ L^{O(1)} \delta
	\vartheta^2 \frac{\|\bar{\bg}(q_d)\|^2}{N} 
	\bigg\}
	\le \exp\Big(L^{O(1)} \delta\vartheta^2\Big)\,.
	\]
Recall that $\Delta_{a,b} \equiv \Delta_a + \ldots + \Delta_{b-1}$. Then
	\begin{align*}
	&\E\Big[ \exp( \vartheta \Delta_{a,b})
		\ind\{E_\star\} \,\Big|\,
		\cFt(q_{b-1})\Big]
	=\E\bigg[ \exp\bigg( \vartheta\sum_{d=a}^{b-1} \Delta_d\bigg)
		\ind\{E_\star\}
		\,\bigg|\,
		\cFt(q_{b-1})\bigg] \\
	&\qquad=
	\bigg\{ \exp\bigg( \vartheta\sum_{d=a}^{b-2} \Delta_d\bigg)
	\prod_{d=a}^{b-2} \ind\{E_d\}\bigg\}
	\cdot
	\ind\{E_{b-1}\}
	\E\Big[ \exp(\vartheta \Delta_{b-1})
		\,\Big|\,
		\cFt(q_{b-1})\Big]\\
	&\qquad\le
	\bigg\{ \exp\bigg( \vartheta\sum_{d=a}^{b-2} \Delta_d\bigg)
	\prod_{d=a}^{b-2} \ind\{E_d\}\bigg\}
	\cdot \exp\Big(L^{O(1)} \delta\vartheta^2\Big)\,.
	\end{align*}
Applying the same argument recursively gives
	\[
	\E\Big[ \exp( \vartheta \Delta_{a,b})
	\ind\{E_\star\}\Big]
	\le \exp\Big(L^{O(1)} (b-a) \delta \vartheta^2\Big)
	\le \exp\Big(L^{O(1)} (q_b-q_a) \vartheta^2\Big)
	\]
It follows by a Chernoff bound (using only $\P(E_\star)\ge1/2$)
	\[
	\P( |\Delta_{a,b}| \ge y \,|\,E_\star)
	\le 2 \exp\bigg( -\frac{y^2}{4 L^{O(1)} (q_b-q_a)}\bigg)\,,
	\]
and integrating this bound gives (cf.\ \eqref{e:subgaus.mmt})
	\[
	\E\Big[ (\Delta_{a,b})^8 \,\Big|\, E_\star\Big]
	\le \int_0^\infty 8y^{7}
	\P( |\Delta_{a,b}| \ge y \,|\,E_\star)\,dy
	\le L^{O(1)} (q_b-q_a)^4\,.
	\]
On the event $(E_\star)^c$ we can use the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality to bound
	\[
	\E\Big[ (\Delta_{a,b})^8 ; (E_\star)^c\Big]
	\le \Big( \E[(\Delta_{a,b})^{16}] \P(( E_\star)^c) \Big)^{1/2}
	\le \frac{L^{O(1)} (q_b-q_a)^4}{\delta^{O(1)}\exp(\Omega(N))}\,,
	\]
where the bound on $\E[(\Delta_{a,b})^{16}]$ follows very similarly to \eqref{e:weak.fourth.mmt.bound}. This is negligible since we assume  $\delta\gg 1/N$ (see Assumption~\ref{a:params}), and the claim follows.  It is straightforward to verify that the same argument applies with $X^{\trunc,\RomII}$ or $X^{\frozen,\RomII}$ in place of $X^{\RomII}$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.543499+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_bf1628660619b55d7ec07f62522563b7d539708a5746d597fc84c4bf7fb10937","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"The PROBABILISTS' Hermite polynomials He_n are defined by He_n(x) = (-1)^n e^{x^2/2} d^n/dx^n e^{-x^2/2}, equivalently by the generating function exp(t x - t^2/2) = sum_{n >= 0} t^n He_n(x)/n!. The first few are He_0 = 1, He_1 = x, He_2 = x^2 - 1, He_3 = x^3 - 3x. They satisfy He_n' = n He_{n-1}, the three-term recursion He_{n+1}(x) = x He_n(x) - n He_{n-1}(x), and the orthogonality relation E[ He_m(Z) He_n(Z) ] = n! times the Kronecker delta, for Z standard Gaussian. Hence { He_n / sqrt(n!) } is an ORTHONORMAL BASIS of L^2 of the standard Gaussian measure on R, and the normalised basis satisfies the derivative relation d/dx ( He_n/sqrt(n!) ) = sqrt(n) ( He_{n-1}/sqrt((n-1)!) ). The PHYSICISTS' Hermite polynomials H_n(x) = (-1)^n e^{x^2} d^n/dx^n e^{-x^2} are orthogonal with respect to the weight e^{-x^2} instead, and the two families are related by H_n(x) = 2^{n/2} He_n( sqrt(2) x ), equivalently He_n(x) = 2^{-n/2} H_n( x / sqrt(2) ). Constants such as the sharp constant in the Gaussian Poincare inequality or the coefficients in a chaos expansion depend on which family is meant, so the convention must be stated. In several variables one takes products He_alpha(x) = prod_i He_{alpha_i}(x_i) over a multi-index alpha, with orthogonality E[He_alpha He_beta] = alpha! delta_{alpha beta} where alpha! = prod_i alpha_i!. [standard; e.g. Nualart, The Malliavin Calculus and Related Topics, 2nd ed., Section 1.1]","status":"unverified"}

The essential idea is that if the best linear approximation to the function at a point is invertible, then with sufficient regularity assumptions, the function should also be invertible near that point. In its simplest form, the theorem states that if a real function f is differentiable in an open interval, with a continuous derivative, then in a neighborhood of any point where the derivative is not zero, f has an inverse function. The inverse function is also continuously differentiable, and the inverse function rule expresses its derivative as the multiplicative inverse of the derivative of f.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["M is a compact Riemannian manifold and f a C^1 diffeomorphism of M","mu is an f-invariant Borel probability measure (compactness makes the Oseledets integrability condition automatic)","the exponents and multiplicities are measurable and f-invariant, constant a.e. when mu is ergodic; the subspaces are measurable and Df-equivariant","the Oseledets splitting is measurable, generally not continuous, and the Pesin blocks are not invariant"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T16:00:40+00:00","domain":"smooth ergodic theory, Lyapunov exponents","id":"claim_bf769101c6fe8505c33df1958690eca784e10a921c4b8007d731b67c59e25eca","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f be a C^1 diffeomorphism of a compact Riemannian manifold M and mu an f-invariant Borel probability measure. Since M is compact, log of the norm of Df and of Df^{-1} are bounded, hence integrable, so Oseledets' multiplicative ergodic theorem applies: for mu-a.e. x there are finitely many numbers lambda_1(x) > lambda_2(x) > ... > lambda_{k(x)}(x) (the LYAPUNOV EXPONENTS at x) and a Df-invariant splitting of the tangent space

  T_x M = E_1(x) + ... + E_{k(x)}(x),   Df_x E_i(x) = E_i(f x),

such that for every nonzero v in E_i(x) the limit of (1/n) log |Df^n_x v| as n -> +-infinity exists and equals lambda_i(x). The functions x -> lambda_i(x) and the multiplicities dim E_i(x) are measurable and f-invariant, and if mu is ergodic they are constant almost everywhere; the subspaces E_i(x) are measurable and Df-equivariant, Df_x E_i(x) = E_i(fx). The splitting is in general only MEASURABLE, not continuous, and the convergence is not uniform in x.

Two structural facts that every application uses. (1) TEMPEREDNESS: any measurable positive function that is subexponential along orbits -- such as the angle between the Oseledets subspaces, or the norm of the change to Lyapunov (adapted) coordinates -- can be chosen tempered, meaning (1/n) log of its value at f^n x tends to 0; this is what lets one build Lyapunov charts in which Df is uniformly contracting on the negative-exponent bundle at the cost of a chart size that shrinks subexponentially along the orbit. (2) PESIN BLOCKS: for each l one collects the points where the Oseledets estimates hold with uniform constants depending on l; the resulting sets Lambda_l are COMPACT (after discarding a null set and restricting the subbundles continuously), increase in l, exhaust a full-measure set, and carry uniform hyperbolic-like estimates. They are NOT f-invariant -- an orbit wanders between blocks -- which is exactly why non-uniformly hyperbolic statements are local-and-measurable rather than uniform.

A point x is called (non-uniformly) hyperbolic when no exponent at x is zero; the stable bundle E^s(x) is the sum of the E_i(x) with lambda_i(x) < 0 and the unstable bundle the sum of those with lambda_i(x) > 0. Zero exponents are the obstruction: nothing in this framework says anything about directions with zero exponent.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f in L^1_loc(R^d), Lebesgue measure","averaging sets shrink nicely to x (bounded eccentricity); unbounded eccentricity breaks the theorem"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.751496+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_bf8b9a4334173b1b42ad155604b5dabb90ceb6c0b2b33e20cc69bf001127fc26","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f be in L^1_loc(R^d). Then for Lebesgue-almost every x, (1/|B(x,r)|) integral_{B(x,r)} |f(y) - f(x)| dy -> 0 as r -> 0; such an x is called a Lebesgue point of f. In particular the averages of f over shrinking balls converge to f(x) for a.e. x. The result persists if balls are replaced by any family of sets U_r shrinking NICELY to x, meaning U_r is contained in B(x,r) and |U_r| >= c |B(x,r)| for a fixed c > 0 (cubes centred at x, for instance). It FAILS for families of arbitrary eccentricity: in R^2 there is an integrable f whose averages over rectangles centred at x with sides parallel to the axes and both side lengths tending to 0 fail to converge at almost every x, because the strong maximal function is not of weak type (1,1). The a.e. exceptional set genuinely depends on f and cannot be taken empty. [standard; e.g. Stein and Shakarchi, Real Analysis, Chapter 3, Corollary 1.5 and Section 1.4]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:57:30.969953+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_bfaf6c758aebeb9ade6830f3d3db0a0f0ff9ce1c2b2b960272aa4c5c4020aac9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 1 (\textsf{Dominant chaos with lower-order perturbations}) of arXiv:2608.12451, '2608.12451'] Fix $\mathsf{S}\in\{{ \mathsf{P}},{\mathsf{R}}\}$, $r\in\N$, and
$\lambda\in(0,\infty)$.  For each $n\in\N$, let\footnote{The sum $\sum_{j=1}^0$ is understood to be empty.}

\noi
\begin{align*}
 F_n\in\cC_{r}^{\mathsf{S}}\cap L^4(\PP),
 \quad
 B_n=\sum_{j=1}^{r-1}B_{n,j},
\AND
 B_{n,j}\in\cC_{j}^{\mathsf{S}}\cap L^4(\PP).
\end{align*} 

\noi
Suppose that $F_n+B_n$ satisfies the lattice condition
\eqref{cond_La} with shift $\theta_n>0$, and define
$X_n:=\theta_n+F_n+B_n$.  Put
$\eps_n:=\sum_{j=1}^{r-1}\norm{B_{n,j}}_4$.
For every $n$ such that $\theta_n>0$, with
$c_{\theta_n}:=(1-e^{-\theta_n})/\theta_n$, define

\noi
\begin{align}
 \mathfrak{R}_{\theta_n}(F_n,\eps_n)
 :=
 c_{\theta_n}\bigg[ 2 \|F_n\|_4\eps_n+\eps_n^2+\frac{\eps_n}{2}
 + 14\bigl(1+ \|F_n\|_4+\eps_n\bigr)^3\eps_n  \bigg]
 +\left(1+\frac{c_{\theta_n}}2\right)\eps_n.
 
\end{align}
Then,

\noi
\begin{align} 
\begin{aligned}
 \dTV\bigl( X_n,  P_{\theta_n}\bigr)  
   & \leq
 c_{\theta_n}\bigg[  | m_2(F_n)-\theta_n|  + \frac{2r-1}{2r}\sqrt{\mathfrak{d}_{\mathsf{S}}(F_n)} \\
 &\qquad\qquad\qquad  + \frac23\sqrt{m_2(F_n)\mathfrak d_{\mathsf{S}}(F_n)}
 +b_{\mathsf{S}}\mathfrak d_{\mathsf{S}}(F_n)  \bigg]  
   +\mathfrak R_{\theta_n}(F_n,\eps_n).
\end{aligned}
\end{align}

\noi
In particular, $\mathfrak R_{\theta_n}(F_n,0)=0$.  Hence, when
$\eps_n=0$, one has $B_n=0$ and \eqref{pert_main_bdd} reduces exactly
to Corollary~\ref{cor_P_quant} if $\mathsf{S}={ \mathsf{P}}$ and to
Corollary~\ref{cor_R_quant} if $\mathsf{S}={\mathsf{R}}$.

If, in addition,
$
 \big(\theta_n,  m_2(F_n), \mathfrak{d}_{\mathsf{S}}(F_n)\big)
 \xrightarrow{n\to+\infty}(\lambda, \lambda, 0)$
and
 $\eps_n\to0$,
then
$\dTV(X_n, P_\lambda)\to0$,
the first four moments of $X_n$ converge to those of
$P_\lambda$, and $(X_n^4)_{n\geq1}$ is uniformly integrable.
In the Rademacher case, under $m_2(F_n)\to\lambda$, the condition
$\mathfrak{d}_{\mathsf{R}}(F_n)\to0$ is equivalent to
$\cR(F_n)\to0$ and $\cM(F_n)\to0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:31:02.817132+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_bfe34b4620b759b26ab1274ad07ca3b34dc6edf94c99aebfc801f306734a9364","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:shift-stable-chart of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Fix an integer $d\geq1$ and $0<\gamma<1$.  A \emph{shift-stable $d$-chart
of depth $\gamma h$} is a family
$(B_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta_h}$, indexed by all sufficiently large integers
$h$ with $\Theta_h\ne\varnothing$, of primitive
$(d+1)$-subsets of $\mathbb Z_{\geq0}$ containing zero for which there are
fixed integers $s\geq1$ and $c_1,\ldots,c_s$, and integer residuals
$x_\nu(\theta,h)$, such that, uniformly for $\theta\in\Theta_h$ and
$J\in\mathbb Z$ with $0\leq J\leq\gamma h$,
\begin{equation}
 |(h-J)B_\theta|
 =\sum_{\nu=1}^{s}c_\nu
  \binom{x_\nu(\theta,h)-J+d}{d},
 \qquad x_\nu(\theta,h)-J\geq0.
\end{equation}
Terms for which $x_\nu(\theta,h)-J<0$ throughout the shift window are
omitted.  This condition is satisfied, in particular, when the family
remains in one finite Hilbert-numerator chamber throughout the window.
Here $d=|B_\theta|-1$ is the dimension of the ambient simplex and the degree
of the binomial coefficient as a polynomial in its upper index; it is not
the dimension of the associated projective curve.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Fixed finite d,n,T and step gamma>0; bounded nonzero training inputs and bounded nonzero-input population independent of initialization","m=2N independent Gaussian hidden pairs with opposite fixed heads +/-nu,0<nu<=1; all parameters subsequently trained without tying","Squared empirical loss normalized by n; bounded labels; zero ReLU derivative at zero","Width tends to infinity before any time, sample-size or input-law limit; mathematical and literature review pending"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T18:15:10.683358+00:00","domain":"two-layer ReLU learning; population neural tangent kernel limits","id":"claim_c05778d0768f5d9377765bf96953205bc672897c685dd1f7ce32845f258f62b0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT; proof (unaudited); independent mathematical review pending; novelty unestablished. This is a finite-horizon supporting method, not full Target1 closure.

## 1. Finite-horizon transfer statement
Fix finite d,n,T, gamma>0, 0<nu<=1, Y<infinity, nonzero training inputs
x_1,...,x_n with norms <=M, and a probability law P supported on nonzero
inputs of norm <=M. Inputs and P are independent of initialization.
The loss is (1/(2n)) sum_i (f(x_i)-y_i)^2, with |y_i|<=Y.
Use m=2N neurons, f(x)=m^(-1/2) sum_j a_j ReLU(w_j.x).
For each independent W_l~N(0,I_d), initialize one pair at (nu,W_l),
(-nu,W_l); update every parameter by ordinary simultaneous GD of step gamma,
with derivative 1{w.x>0}. The pairing is only at initialization, not enforced.
Let H be the deterministic full initial kernel from C014 Section2:
H(x,z)=E[ReLU(W.x)ReLU(W.z)+nu^2 1{W.x>0,W.z>0}x.z].
Let f^H_k be zero-start kernel GD with this H, the same sample and labels.
Then, as N tends to infinity,

 max_{k<=T} ||f_k-f^H_k||_{L2(P)} -> 0 in probability.       (1)

The event bounds proving this hold uniformly for every y in [-Y,Y]^n.
No positive training eigenvalue or nonzero gate margin is assumed. T is
fixed before this width limit; constants below can grow rapidly with T.

## 2. Width-independent finite-horizon bounds
Write u_j=1+||w_j(0)||. The empirical mean S_m=m^(-1)sum u_j^2 is a pair
average and tends almost surely to E(1+||W||)^2. Fix S above that expectation
and work on S_m<=S, an event eventually true almost surely.
Define H_0=D_0=0, R_0=Y. Given H_k,D_k,R_k, set
 A_k=1+H_k, B_k=1+D_k, c_k=gamma M R_k,
 H_{k+1}=H_k+c_k B_k, D_{k+1}=D_k+c_k A_k,
 R_{k+1}=R_k+M c_k S[B_k(B_k+c_k A_k)+A_k^2].
Induction gives, uniformly over the label cube,
 |a_j(k)-a_j(0)|<=H_k u_j/sqrt(m),
 ||w_j(k)-w_j(0)||<=D_k u_j/sqrt(m),
 |a_j(k)|<=A_k u_j, ||w_j(k)||<=B_k u_j,
 ||r_k||/sqrt(n)<=R_k, where r_i=f_k(x_i)-y_i.
Indeed Cauchy-Schwarz in the exact parameter updates gives
 |Delta a_j|<=c_k B_k u_j/sqrt(m),
 ||Delta w_j||<=c_k A_k u_j/sqrt(m).
ReLU is 1-Lipschitz and homogeneous, so at every ||x||<=M,
 |Delta f_k(x)|<=||x|| c_k S[B_k(B_k+c_k A_k)+A_k^2].
This proves the induction and a finite uniform output bound through T.
Let H,D,A,B,c denote maxima of these constants through the required steps.

## 3. Population gate bands shrink in L2, not just on the sample
Put L_m(x)=m^(-1)sum_j u_j^2 1{|w_j(0).x|<=D u_j||x||/sqrt(m)}.
For each training x_i, L_m(x_i)->0 almost surely. Also

 ||L_m||_{L2(P)} -> 0 almost surely.                         (2)

Proof: for fixed q>0, the pair-averaged integrable function
 Z_q(W)=(1+||W||)^2 P_x{|W.x|<=q(1+||W||)||x||}
has its empirical average tending to E Z_q by the ordinary scalar SLLN.
For m large with D/sqrt(m)<=q, integral L_m dP is bounded by that average.
For every fixed nonzero x, Gaussian W.x has no atom at zero; Fubini and
dominated convergence imply E Z_q->0 as q decreases to zero. Apply SLLN
simultaneously on countably many q=1,1/2,1/3,..., then let q decrease.
Thus integral L_m->0 almost surely. Since 0<=L_m<=S_m, its squared L2 norm
is at most S_m integral L_m. The finite training-point assertion follows
by the same fixed-q argument without integration over P.
This is uniform over trajectories obeying Section2; no independence between
trained gates and initialization is asserted or needed.

## 4. Both train and cross kernels remain close
Let H^m_k be the empirical full tangent kernel at step k. Product expansion
and the movement bounds give, for every training point x_i,

 |H^m_k(x,x_i)-H^m_0(x,x_i)|
 <= ||x||||x_i|| [C S/sqrt(m)+nu^2(L_m(x)+L_m(x_i))],       (3)

where C=D(B+1)+H(A+1) is finite. The RF-product part is bounded by
D(B+1)u_j^2/sqrt(m). The readout-square change is bounded by
H(A+1)u_j^2/sqrt(m). A changed gate at x forces the initial weight into
the band defining L_m(x); likewise at x_i. These inequalities remain valid
when a trained preactivation equals zero, using the stated derivative.
Equations (2),(3) imply uniform-in-k convergence of the training normalized
Gram matrices and of the population cross rows, relative to their INITIAL
empirical kernels. In particular define K^m_k=(H^m_k(x_i,x_l)/n),
b^m_k(x)=(H^m_k(x,x_i)/sqrt(n))_i. Their respective operator and L2(row)
differences from step0 tend to zero; the latter is bounded by
M^2[C S/sqrt(m)+nu^2(||L_m||_2+max_i L_m(x_i))].

At initialization, each independent pair contributes the same feature
kernel F_W(x,z)=ReLU(W.x)ReLU(W.z)+nu^2 1{W.x>0,W.z>0}x.z.
It satisfies |F_W(x,z)|<=M^2(||W||^2+1). Its squared envelope is integrable.
Thus the empirical initial training kernel tends to K=(H(x_i,x_l)/n).
For the population cross row b(x)=(H(x,x_i)/sqrt(n))_i, independence of pairs
and Fubini give E||b^m_0-b||_2^2<=M^4 E(||W||^2+1)^2/N.
Hence this difference tends to zero in probability too. This explicitly
controls the missing test-to-training kernel; it is not inferred from K.

## 5. Discrete-step gate remainder off the sample
The exact prediction update is
 f_{k+1}(x)=f_k(x)-gamma b^m_k(x).v_k+Z_k(x), v_k=r_k/sqrt(n),
where, writing h=ReLU(w.x), h'=ReLU((w+Delta w).x),
 Z_k(x)=m^(-1/2)sum_j[Delta a_j(h'-h)
             +a_j(h'-h-1{w.x>0}Delta w_j.x)].
If the second summand is nonzero, the segment from w to w+Delta w crosses
its gate at x. Because both endpoints are within the Section2 cumulative
radius of w(0), the initial preactivation lies in the D-band above.
The Lipschitz inequality therefore gives

 |Z_k(x)|<=||x||[c^2 A B S/sqrt(m)+c A^2 L_m(x)].           (4)

It follows that max_{k<T}||Z_k||_{L2(P)}->0 and max_{k<T,i}|Z_k(x_i)|->0.
No approximation replaces discrete GD by flow.

## 6. Close the training and population prediction recurrences
Let v^H_{k+1}=(I-gamma K)v^H_k, v^H_0=-y/sqrt(n).
The true normalized residual update is
 v_{k+1}=(I-gamma K^m_k)v_k+z_k,
where ||z_k||<=max_i |Z_k(x_i)|. Sections2,4,5 imply by finite induction
max_{k<=T}||v_k-v^H_k||->0 in probability, uniformly over bounded labels.
For example each error is bounded by ||I-gamma K|| times the previous
error plus gamma ||K^m_k-K|| R_k+||z_k||. The multiplier is finite; neither
a contraction nor a spectral gap is required at this finite horizon.
Both output initializations are exactly zero. Sum the prediction updates:
 f_k-f^H_k=-gamma sum_{j<k}[(b^m_j-b).v_j+b.(v_j-v^H_j)]
                         +sum_{j<k}Z_j.
The population L2 norm is bounded by the sum of cross-kernel errors times
R_j, deterministic ||b||_2 times training residual errors, and remainder
norms. Every term tends to zero by the preceding sections, proving (1).
The same controlling random bounds work for all bounded label vectors.
For any bounded teacher, clean risks averaged over the bounded independent
label noises consequently converge uniformly through T in probability,
by Cauchy-Schwarz and the finite uniform output bound from Section2.


Here zero-start kernel GD means f^H_{k+1}(x)=f^H_k(x)-(gamma/n)sum_i H(x,x_i)(f^H_k(x_i)-y_i), with f^H_0=0.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:07:15.755110+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c05ff4c09ef60b1f7cf58fab071a24827d69eb7c5fde2e3587fd82d0cfe9bd78","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:abstract-kato-slice of arXiv:2608.02459, 'Response Calculus for Spectral Simplicity\\ and Joint Eigenvalue Densities'] For every $t_0\in\mathbb R^N$, there exists a complex neighborhood
$\mathcal U\subset\mathbb C^N$ of $t_0$ such that the following assertions hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(\roman*)}]
\item The family of sesquilinear forms $(a_z)_{z\in\mathcal U}$, defined by
\begin{equation}
 a_z(u,v):=\mathcal E(m_zu,m_{\bar z}v),
 \qquad \operatorname{Dom} a_z=V_{\mu_0}^{\mathbb C},
 
\end{equation}
is a holomorphic family of closed sectorial forms with common domain; in Kato's
terminology, it is a family of type~\textnormal{(a)}.  Let $\widehat A_z$
denote the associated $m$-sectorial operator.  For real $t\in\mathcal U\cap\mathbb R^N$,
this agrees with the previously defined $\widehat A_t$.
\item For every $z\in\mathcal U$, the operator $\widehat A_z$ has compact
resolvent, and the map

\begin{equation}
 R_{\Gamma}(t)
 =\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{\Gamma}
   (\zeta-\widehat A_t)^{-1}\,d\zeta
 
\end{equation}
is a real-analytic family of finite-rank projections satisfying
\begin{equation*}
 \rankR_{\Gamma}(t)=\rankR_{\Gamma}(t_0).
\end{equation*}
The coefficients of the characteristic polynomial of
$\widehat A_t|_{\operatorname{Ran}R_{\Gamma}(t)}$, and hence its
discriminant, depend real-analytically on $t$.
\end{enumerate}
If $t\mapsto(\lambda(t),\Phi(t))$ is a local real-analytic eigenpair branch of
$\widehat A_t$, normalized by
$\left\|\Phi(t)\right\|_{L^2(\mu_0)}=1$, then $\Phi$ is real analytic as a map with
values in $V_{\mu_0}^{\mathbb C}$ and
\begin{equation}
 \partial_{t_k}\lambda(t)
 =(\partial_{t_k}a_t)(\Phi(t),\Phi(t)),
 \qquad 1\le k\le N.

For each $h\geq2$, put
\[
 H_{h,k}=(k-1)h^{k-2},\qquad
 \mathcal M_{h,k}
 =\{A\subseteq\{0,\ldots,H_{h,k}\}:0\in A,\ |A|=k\}.
\]
The maps from $\mathcal M_{h,k}$ onto the realized weak types and onto the
realized ordered $h$-addition-table types are surjective.  Moreover, as

\[
 |\mathcal M_{h,k}|=\binom{H_{h,k}}{k-1}
 =\Theta_k\!\left(h^{(k-1)(k-2)}\right),
\]
and both target sets have the same order of magnitude.  Consequently, the
average fibre of either type map has order $\Theta_k(1)$, and choosing one
representative from each fibre gives a positive-proportion subfamily on which

be chosen entirely among representatives of maximal-rank weak types, and

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:51:11.953522+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c0f6569fe40b75e82233252e0aa32767f8b51829c2c878837afe78f36ffb1f4e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 6 (Gaussian-noise bulk and full-trace LSS) of arXiv:2608.07820, 'Linear Spectral Statistics for Entrywise-Transformed Spiked Wigner Matrices under Shifted '] Let $f$ satisfy \eqref{eq:Gaussian-f-assumptions-main}, let $\lambda\ge0$ be
fixed, and suppose that the deterministic spike obeys
\begin{equation}
 \norm{x}_2=1,
 \qquad
 \norm{x}_\infty=o(N^{-1/4}),
 \qquad
 \sum_{i=1}^N x_i=O(N^{o(1)}).
\end{equation}
Let $\Gamma$ satisfy (G1)--(G4) with $\theta_{f,\nu}$ replaced by $\theta_f$,
and let $\varphi_1,\ldots,\varphi_k$ be analytic on a neighborhood of
$\overline{D_\Gamma}$ and real-valued on its intersection with $\mathbb R$.
Then
\begin{equation}
 \left(
 \mathcal L_{M_{N,\gamma}^f}^{\Gamma}(\varphi_\ell)
 -N\int_{-2}^2\varphi_\ell(t)\rho_{\scal}(t)\,\dd t
 -m_{\varphi_\ell,\Gamma}^{\gamma,f}
 \right)_{\ell=1}^k
 \Longrightarrow
 (G_{\varphi_\ell})_{\ell=1}^k,
\end{equation}
where the limiting vector is centered Gaussian with
\begin{equation}
 \Cov(G_\varphi,G_\psi)
 =\mathcal V_{\kappa_f}^{\Gamma}(\varphi,\psi).
\end{equation}
If $|\theta_f|\le1$, then
$\mathcal L_{M_{N,\gamma}^f}^{\Gamma}(\varphi)
=\Tr\varphi(M_{N,\gamma}^f)$ with probability tending to one, so
\eqref{eq:Gaussian-bulk-CLT-main} is the full-trace CLT.  If
$|\theta_f|>1$ and each $\varphi_\ell$ is also analytic and real-valued on the
real axis near
\begin{equation}
 \rho_f:=\theta_f+\theta_f^{-1},
\end{equation}
then the full-trace CLT is obtained from
\eqref{eq:Gaussian-bulk-CLT-main} by replacing the statistic there with
\begin{equation}
 \left(
 \Tr\varphi_\ell(M_{N,\gamma}^f)
 -N\int_{-2}^2\varphi_\ell(t)\rho_{\scal}(t)\,\dd t
 -m_{\varphi_\ell,\Gamma}^{\gamma,f}
 -\varphi_\ell(\rho_f)
 \right)_{\ell=1}^k
 \Longrightarrow
 (G_{\varphi_\ell})_{\ell=1}^k,
\end{equation}
with the covariance \eqref{eq:Gaussian-covariance-main}.
In particular, all these conclusions hold for every centered and
variance-normalized polynomial-growth transform.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.351460+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c0fc8f01bf0470a4e19c40cfcbd48f63ad3e9919d3e37b9d46aff505e0204a9c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 187 (approximate quadratic variation processes) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For $\sigma,\tau\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$, define $\tilde{Q}^{\sigma,\tau}$ to be the piecewise linear process with increments
	\beq

	\Big(\Delta X^{\trunc,\tau}(q_d,a)\Big)\,.
	\eeq
For the Ising case, we also define
	\beq
	\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\sigma,\Ising}(q_d)

	\sum_{a\in B,i\in B^{\Ising}}
