{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:29:00.766306+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c8f269c00a0b2323cc27ad2722d492913ab2f66a9ea2c9b39e621b44966c2522","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 25 of arXiv:2512.04807, 'Existence and uniqueness of the canonical Brownian motion in non-simple conformal loop ens'] Suppose that we have a family $(\rmetres{V}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma})_{V \in \metregions}$ of resistance metrics coupled with $\Gamma$ where $\rmetres{V}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma}\colon (\ol{V} \cap \Upsilon_\Gamma) \times (\ol{V} \cap \Upsilon_\Gamma) \to [0,\infty)$. Then it is associated with a weak \clekp{} resistance form if and only if the following hold.
 \begin{enumerate}[(a)]
  \item The metric $\rmetres{C}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma}$ is continuous with respect to $\dpathY$.

  \item Let $U \subseteq \C$ be open, simply connected. The conditional law of the collection $(\rmetres{V}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma})_{V \in \metregions[U]}$ given $\Gamma\setminus\Gamma_{U^*}$ and $(\rmetres{V'}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma})_{V' \in \metregions[\C\setminus\ol{U}]}$ is almost surely measurable with respect to~$U^*$.

  \item Let $U \subseteq \C$ be open, simply connected. There exists a probability kernel $\mu^{U^*}$ such that for each $z \in \C$, the conditional law of $(\rmetres{V}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma})_{V \in \metregions[U+z]}$ given $(U+z)^*$ is $(T_z)_* \mu^{U^*}(\cdot -z)$ where $T_z \FR(x,y) = \FR(x-z,y-z)$ denotes translation by $z$.

  \item Let $V,V' \in \metregions$, $V \subseteq V'$, and $x,y \in \ol{V} \cap \Upsilon_\Gamma$ such that for every $u \in V' \setminus V$ there is a point $z \in \ol{V}$ that separates $u$ from $x,y$ in $\ol{V'} \cap \Upsilon_\Gamma$. Then
  \[ \rmetres{V}{x}{y}{\Gamma} = \rmetres{V'}{x}{y}{\Gamma} . \]

  \item Suppose that $V_1,V_2 \in \metregions$ with $\ol{V_1} \cap \ol{V_2} = \{z\}$ (where the closure is taken with respect to $d_{\ol{V}}$, see Section~\ref{subsec:main_results}). If $x \in \ol{V_1} \cap \Upsilon_\Gamma$, $y \in \ol{V_2} \cap \Upsilon_\Gamma$, then
  \[ \rmetres{V_1 \cup V_2}{x}{y}{\Gamma} = \rmetres{V_1}{x}{z}{\Gamma} + \rmetres{V_2}{z}{y}{\Gamma} . \]

  \item There exists a countable set $\{z_m\}_{m \in \N} \subseteq \Upsilon_\Gamma$ that is dense with respect to $\dpathY$ and such that the following holds. Suppose that $V \in \metregions$ consists of a single connected component and let $\CL \in \Gamma$ be a loop contained in $\ol{V}$ and intersecting $\partial V$. Then there exist two distinct points $a,b \in \CL \cap \partial V$ such that the following holds for sufficiently large $m \in \N$. Let $V_{a,b}$ (resp.\ $V_{b,a}$) be the collection of components of $V \setminus \CL$ that are connected to the counterclockwise arc of $\partial V$ from $a$ to $b$ (resp.\ from $b$ to $a$) by an admissible path within $V$. Let $A = \{z_1,\ldots,z_m\}$, $A_{a,b} = A \cap \ol{V_{a,b}}$, $A_{b,a} = A \cap \ol{V_{b,a}}$, and let $w, w_{a,b}, w_{b,a}$ be the weight functions associated with $\rmetres{V}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma}|_{A}$, $\rmetres{V_{a,b}}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma}|_{A_{a,b}}$, $\rmetres{V_{b,a}}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma}|_{A_{b,a}}$, respectively. Then
  \[
   w(x,y) =
   \begin{cases}
    w_{a,b}(a,b)+w_{b,a}(a,b) ,& \{x,y\} = \{a,b\} ,\\
    w_{a,b}(x,y) ,& x,y \in A_{a,b} ,\, \{x,y\} \neq \{a,b\} ,\\
    w_{b,a}(x,y) ,& x,y \in A_{b,a} ,\, \{x,y\} \neq \{a,b\} ,\\
    0 ,& \text{otherwise.}
   \end{cases}
  \]
 \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:53:31.969854+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c8f57e2680c04ac242ec7835ed2fb41fb03221ccff9cf4931faafcaa20e6a0b9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[1 6 (\cite{HX24a}) of arXiv:2606.10058, 'Mean First Passage Times and Fundamental Tensors of Higher Order Markov Chains'] If the chain $X$ is ergodic, then its mean first passage times are all finite and satisfy 
\be

\mu_{i_1i_2\ldots i_m}=1+\sum_{j \in S, j \ne i_1}\mu_{i_1ji_2\ldots i_{m-1}}p_{ji_2\ldots i_m}
\ee
for any $i_1, i_2, \ldots, i_m \in S$. In tensor form, (\ref{mfpteqn}) can be written as 
$$\mu={\cal E}+(\mu-\mu_d)\boxtimes {\cal P},$$

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-13T08:46:06.530321+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_c8fa8f9d294eb2cc481cd757521911b88d376297acef16fe77c553f47331f843","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let g be a norm on R^2 that is even in the first coordinate (g(-h, m) = g(h, m)), as every lattice-symmetric FPP limit-shape norm is. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:16:18.691651+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c91bb9984ea148e40ded2a45ac845506a68bfcb1c39e0f6c9edc1af271c4cc7f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 30 (Finite-frequency prefix factorisation) of arXiv:2607.26377, '\textbf{Entire Logarithmic Signatures\\ of Bounded-Variation Paths in Finite Dimensions}'] Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real normed vector space with
$\dim V\geq2$, and let
$\gamma\colon[0,T]\to V$ be a continuous bounded-variation path. Set
\[
l=\log S(\gamma),
\qquad
v=\gamma_T-\gamma_0,
\]
and assume that
\[
R(l)=\infty,
\qquad
v\neq0.
\]
Choose $\ell\in V^*$ such that $\ell(v)=1$, put $W=\ker\ell$, and write
\[
\gamma_t-\gamma_0=x_t v+X_t,
\qquad
x_t=\ell(\gamma_t-\gamma_0),
\qquad
X_t\in W.
\]

Let $\Lambda\subset2\pi\Q$ be finite and symmetric, so that
$\Lambda=-\Lambda$. Give $W$ an auxiliary Euclidean norm, let $W_{\C}$
be its complexification, and define the real Hilbert space
\[
E_\Lambda
=
\set{(z_\omega)_{\omega\in\Lambda}
\in\prod_{\omega\in\Lambda}W_{\C}:
 z_{-\omega}=\overline{z_\omega}}
\]
with the norm inherited from the Hilbert direct sum. Define the decorated
transverse path
\[
B_t^\Lambda(\gamma)
=
\left(
\int_0^t \e^{i\omega x_s}\dd X_s
\right)_{\omega\in\Lambda},
\qquad 0\leq t\leq T,
\]
and the orthogonal map
\[
T_\Lambda\colon E_\Lambda\to E_\Lambda,
\qquad
(T_\Lambda z)_\omega=\e^{i\omega}z_\omega.
\]
Denote by the same symbol the induced graded automorphism of tensor
series, and set
\[
r_t^\Lambda
=S\bigl(B^\Lambda(\gamma)|_{[0,t]}\bigr),
\qquad
h_\Lambda=r_T^\Lambda.
\]

Then there exists $t_\Lambda\in[0,T]$ such that
\begin{equation}
r_{t_\Lambda}^\Lambda
=h_\Lambda T_\Lambda\bigl(r_{t_\Lambda}^\Lambda\bigr).
\end{equation}
Equivalently, with
\[
a_\Lambda=r_{t_\Lambda}^\Lambda,
\]
one has
\begin{equation}
h_\Lambda
=a_\Lambda T_\Lambda(a_\Lambda)^{-1}.
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:43:37.236802+00:00","domain":"game theory","id":"claim_c9565091907e96d8504914374b1b2370362648e70aac2f39f97cdfa7046dceb0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Solving a finite two-player zero-sum game with m x n payoff matrix A (row player maximizing, column player minimizing the same quantity) is equivalent to solving a pair of dual linear programs. The row player's LP is: maximize v subject to sum_{i=1}^{m} x_i * A_{ij} >= v for all j=1,...,n, x_i >= 0, sum_i x_i = 1. The column player's LP, minimize w subject to sum_{j=1}^{n} A_{ij} * y_j <= w for all i=1,...,m, y_j >= 0, sum_j y_j = 1, is exactly the LP dual of the row player's program. {"assumptions":["K compact","each f_n continuous","for each x the sequence f_n(x) is monotone in n, in the same direction for every x","the pointwise limit f is continuous"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.751214+00:00","domain":"real analysis","id":"claim_c9b13faaa47bc5e4c48eaac0e195f673c255de2096f3e248b1dfd899c8f459b1","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let K be a compact topological space and f_n : K -> R continuous. Suppose the sequence is monotone in n at every point (f_n(x) <= f_{n+1}(x) for all n and all x, or the reverse for all n and all x), that f_n -> f pointwise, and that the limit f is continuous. Then f_n -> f UNIFORMLY on K. All four hypotheses carry weight: (a) compactness - on the non-compact [0,1) the sequence f_n(x) = x^n decreases continuously to the continuous limit 0 but not uniformly; (b) continuity of the limit - on the compact [0,1] the same f_n(x) = x^n is monotone and continuous with a discontinuous limit and the convergence is not uniform; (c) monotonicity - the moving bump f_n which is the piecewise-linear tent of height 1 on [1/(n+1), 1/n] and 0 elsewhere on [0,1] converges pointwise to 0 with all data continuous and compact, but sup |f_n| = 1; (d) continuity of each f_n - on [0,1] the indicators of the OPEN intervals, f_n = 1_{(0, 1/n)}, decrease pointwise to the identically zero function, which is continuous, on a compact space, so every hypothesis except the continuity of the f_n holds, yet sup |f_n| = 1 for every n. Monotonicity is required POINTWISE IN THE SAME DIRECTION for all x, not merely that each f_n is a monotone function of x. [standard; e.g. Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed., Theorem 7.13]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:00:45.292926+00:00","domain":"QA-corrected (round 3, audit-driven)","id":"claim_c9b6d95c44e30bbf0aba5f38e4fd929fea5c1f7eb1dd7adbd897cf92e839250a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Implicit function theorem (planar case): Let F be a real-valued function that is continuously differentiable on an open subset of R^2 containing a point (a, b), with F(a, b) = 0 and F_y(a, b) = (partial F / partial y)(a, b) nonzero. Then there are open intervals I containing a and J containing b and a unique continuously differentiable function g : I -> J such that g(a) = b and, within the rectangle I x J, the solution set of F(x, y) = 0 is exactly the graph {(x, g(x)) : x in I}; moreover g'(x) = -F_x(x, g(x)) / F_y(x, g(x)). Example: for F(x, y) = x^2 + y^2 - 1 (the unit circle) at (a, b) = (0, 1) one gets g(x) = sqrt(1 - x^2), the upper semicircle; no such g exists near (1, 0), where F_y = 0. General version: if F : R^{n+m} -> R^m is C^1 near (a, b), F(a, b) = 0, and the m x m Jacobian of F with respect to the y-variables at (a, b) is invertible, then near (a, b) the equation F(x, y) = 0 determines a unique C^1 map y = g(x) with g(a) = b and F(x, g(x)) = 0.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:18:27.580085+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c9d342de5d2740b126d2418ad05e8c8a337104c8b8bb0b44fac37cd61368b81c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 14 (Simplicity, positivity, monotonicity, analyticity) of arXiv:2608.15987, 'Threshold cascades of interacting diffusions on unimodular random trees: a conditional bra'] Let $M(\theta)$ have entries $M_{d,d'}(\theta)=m_*q(d')p_{d,d'}(\theta)$, with $\theta\mapsto p_{d,d'}(\theta)$ real-analytic (it is a ratio of analytic Wald integrals \eqref{eq:wald}).
\begin{enumerate}
\item (Krein--Rutman is unnecessary.) $\rho(M)$ is a simple, isolated eigenvalue with a strictly positive right eigenvector $\psi$ and left eigenvector $\phi$, by the Perron--Frobenius theorem for irreducible nonnegative matrices.
\item (Monotonicity.) $\rho(M)$ is nondecreasing in each entry of $M$, strictly so under irreducibility, since $\rho(M)=\lim_n\|M^n\|^{1/n}$ and $M^n$ is entrywise monotone.
\item (Analyticity and the gradient.) $\theta\mapsto\rho(M(\theta))$ is real-analytic on the region where $M$ is irreducible (a simple eigenvalue of an analytic matrix family is analytic, Kato \cite{Kato66}, finite-dimensional case, with no eigenvalue crossing at the top because the Perron root is simple and isolated), and
\[
\partial_{\theta_i}\rho(M)=\frac{\phi^\top(\partial_{\theta_i}M)\psi}{\phi^\top\psi}\qquad(\ne0\text{ generically, since }\partial_{\theta_i}M\ge0\text{ with a positive entry}).
\]
\item (Operator van den Driessche--Watmough lift is unnecessary.) Writing $M=FV^{-1}$ with $V=\diag(\alpha_d)$ and $F$ the $m\times m$ fertility block, the finite-dimensional next-generation theorem \cite{vdDW02} gives directly: $s(J)<0\Leftrightarrow\rho(M)<1$ and $s(J)>0\Leftrightarrow\rho(M)>1$, where $J=F-V$ is the linearised drift and $s(\cdot)$ its spectral abscissa.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:37:08.954998+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ca0d7ebacf2e9376009eb20f6df8f422c6b2ba7331c4a878f5ae0a04951f9ed2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:explicit_density of arXiv:2609.01581, 'Concentration of additive functionals of Stratonovich-type'] Let $(X_t)_{t\geq 0}$ be an ergodic diffusion with invariant measure $\mu$ whose
symmetric part $\mathcal{L}_S$ satisfies the Poincar\'e inequality~(equation eq:poincare of the paper)
with spectral gap $\lambda_\mathrm{gap}>0$ (by Assumptions~(ass:dynamics of the paper)). 
Let $\overline{\rho}_t(V)$ denote the empirical density according to Definition~(def:empirical_density of the paper)
with ergodic mean $\E^\mu[\overline{\rho}_t(V)]=\E^\mu[V]$,
and let $\nu\ll\mu$ with $\mathrm{d}\nu/\mathrm{d}\mu\in L^2(\mu)$.
Then for all $t > 0$ and $a > 0$,
\begin{align}
  \mathbb{P}^\nu\left(\overline{\rho}_t(V) - \E^\mu[\overline{\rho}_t] \geq a\right)
  \leq
  \left\|\frac{\mathrm{d}\nu}{\mathrm{d}\mu}\right\|_{L^2(\mu)}
  \exp\left[-t \frac{\tilde\sigma_\rho^2}{c_\rho^2} h\left(\frac{c_\rho a}{\tilde\sigma_\rho^2}\right)  \right],
  
\end{align}
where $h(u) \equiv 1 + u - \sqrt{1 + 2u}$ and we define 
\begin{align}
  \tilde\sigma_\rho^2 \equiv \frac{2\mathrm{Var}_\mu(V)}{\lambda_\mathrm{gap}},
  \qquad
  c_\rho \equiv \frac{\|V - \E^\mu[V]\|_{L^\infty(\mu)}}{\lambda_\mathrm{gap}}.
\end{align}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Integer n>=1; the threshold v has the same parity as n.","Codes may have at most 2n distinct codewords; repeated matrix rows are allowed."],"created_at":"2026-10-10T06:51:51.365448+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ca4ed2ec9c98afcf226b7ce43abe286b6ff980864f4e57a05f9d4b8c1b9fafc9","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked] This is the proved elementary covering-code reduction for Afonso S. Bandeira's Open Problem 11, How many deviations are needed afterall?, in Did just a couple of deviations suffice all along? (problems 10-14), Randomstrasse 101 (19 December 2024; https://randomstrasse101.math.ethz.ch/posts/HowManyDeviations/). For an n-by-n matrix A with entries in {+1,-1}, define disc(A)=min_{x in {+1,-1}^n} ||Ax||_infinity, where ||y||_infinity=max_i |y_i|, and let D_n=max_{A in {+1,-1}^{n-by-n}} disc(A). For r,x in {+1,-1}^n let d_H(r,x) be the number of differing coordinates and let the complement of r be -r. For an integer v in [0,n] with the same parity as n, |r dot x|>=v exactly when d_H(r,x)<=(n-v)/2 or d_H(-r,x)<=(n-v)/2. Thus disc(A)>=v exactly when the rows of A and their complements cover the sign cube within radius (n-v)/2. For a complement-closed nonempty code C contained in {+1,-1}^n, define its covering radius rad(C)=max_x min_{c in C} d_H(x,c), and define rho_n as the minimum of rad(C) over such C with at most 2n codewords. Then D_n=n-2rho_n. If K(n,R) is the least number of unrestricted binary codewords of length n covering the cube within an integer radius R, K(n,R)<=n certifies D_n>=n-2R, while K(n,R)>2n rules out D_n>=n-2R. This is an unrefereed campaign result.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Dirichlet case: U bounded in at least one direction gives lambda_1 > 0","Neumann case: U bounded, connected, Lipschitz, and the datum must be measured against its mean","Reaction terms shift the rate by sup c"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:49.107251+00:00","domain":"parabolic partial differential equations","id":"claim_ca75748799e3142c7793ceaf79dab6a7fc33eb9daceaf19a3c9b6049728cbd2e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The estimate $\\|u(t)\\|_{L^2}\\le e^{-\\lambda_1t}\\|u(0)\\|_{L^2}$ comes from the Poincare inequality $\\|\\nabla v\\|^2\\ge\\lambda_1\\|v\\|^2$ on $H^1_0(U)$, i.e. from a positive spectral gap; it is not a property of the heat equation as such. (1) Unbounded domains: on $U=\\mathbb R^n$ the Dirichlet spectrum is $[0,\\infty)$, $\\lambda_1=0$, and $\\|e^{t\\Delta}\\|_{L^2\\to L^2}=1$ for every $t$, so no rate is uniform over the unit ball of $L^2$; individual solutions do decay, but only algebraically in general -- for $g=\\Phi(\\cdot,1)$ one has $\\|u(t)\\|_{L^2}=(8\\pi(t+1))^{-n/4}$. Half-spaces and cones behave the same way. (2) Neumann boundary conditions: constants solve the Neumann heat equation, $u\\equiv1$ does not decay at all. The correct statement is decay to the mean: for $U$ bounded, connected and Lipschitz (so that $H^1(U)\\hookrightarrow L^2(U)$ is compact and the Neumann spectrum is discrete), $\\|u(t)-\\bar g\\|_{L^2}\\le e^{-\\mu_2t}\\|g-\\bar g\\|_{L^2}$, where $\\bar g$ is the mean of $g$ and $\\mu_2>0$ is the first nonzero Neumann eigenvalue. (3) Zeroth-order terms: for $u_t=\\Delta u+cu$ the decay rate becomes $\\lambda_1-\\sup c$, which is a growth rate as soon as $\\sup c>\\lambda_1$. Auditor's check: whenever an exponential-decay claim appears, identify the eigenvalue being used, verify it is positive on the stated function space, and verify that the domain's geometry (boundedness in at least one direction for Dirichlet, connectedness and mean-zero for Neumann) actually supplies the gap.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:48:47.287033+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_caaf82ba26dd526b12d4960d0679adfbfe0cf5e77618ccf990d13e89716944b2","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma xxphi of arXiv:2604.20660, 'The Legendre structure of the TAP complexity\\ for the Ising spin glass'] Let $\zeta\in\mathcal P([0,1])$ and fix $q\in[0,1]$.
		Let $(X_t)_{t\in[q,1]}$ solve the Auffinger--Chen SDE 
		\[
		\mathrm{d} X_t=\xi''(t)\,\zeta([0,t])\,\partial_x\Phi_\zeta(t,X_t)\mathrm{d} t+\sqrt{\xi''(t)}\,\mathrm{d} B_t.
		\]
		Write $u(t,y):=\partial_x\Phi_\zeta(t,y)$. Then for every $x\in\mathbb{R}$,
		\begin{equation}
			\partial_{xx}\Phi_\zeta(q,x)
			=1-\zeta\bigl([0,q)\bigr)\,u(q,x)^2
			-\int_{[q,1]}\mathbb{E}\!\left[u(t,X_t)^2\,\middle|\,X_q=x\right]\zeta(\mathrm{d} t).
		\end{equation}
		Consequently,
		\[
		\mathbb{E}\big[\partial_{xx}\Phi_\zeta(q,X_q)\big]
		=1-\zeta\bigl([0,q)\bigr)\,\mathbb{E}\big[u(q,X_q)^2\big]
		-\int_{[q,1]}\mathbb{E}\big[u(t,X_t)^2\big]\,\zeta(\mathrm{d} t).
		\]
		Moreover, if $\mathbb{E}[u(t,X_t)^2]=t$ for $\zeta$-a.e.\ $t\in[q,1]$
		and also $\mathbb{E}[u(q,X_q)^2]=q$,
		then
		\[
		\mathbb{E}\big[\partial_{xx}\Phi_\zeta(q,X_q)\big]
		=1-\zeta\bigl([0,q)\bigr)\,q-\int_{[q,1]}t\,\zeta(\mathrm{d} t)
		=\int_q^1 \zeta([0,t])\mathrm{d} t.
		\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:58:53.190810+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cb0d9ad222facc8d59b1559d22cc9305191285dcd3ed707c0b3ada8b0bc9e12c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 6 of arXiv:2606.31287, '\bf Heat kernel lower bound estimates for symmetric pure jump processes via averaged jump '] \rm 
 Let $(\sX,d,m,\sE, \sF)$ be an MMD space.
\begin{enumerate}  
\item[\rm (i)] We say that the Dirichlet form $(\sE, \sF)$ is conservative if its associated Hunt process is conservative. 

\item[\rm (ii)] We say that the transition density upper bound estimate ${\rm UHK}(\phi)$ holds for the Dirichlet form $(\sE, \sF)$ if the Hunt process $X$ associated with $(\sE, \sF)$  has a jointly continuous density function
 $p(t, x, y)$ on $(0, \infty )\times \sX \times \sX$ with respect to the measure $m$ and there is a positive constant $c_{\ref{e:2.6}} >0 $ so that 
\begin{equation}
 p(t, x, y) \leq c_{\ref{e:2.6}}\left( \frac{1}{V(x, \phi^{-1}(t))} \wedge
\frac{t}{V(x, d(x,y))\phi (d(x, y))} \right)
\end{equation}
for any $t > 0$ and $x, y \in \sX$.  
Here $\phi^{-1}$ denotes the inverse function of $\phi$.
 
\item[\rm (iii)] We say that the near diagonal lower bound estimate ${\rm NLHK}(\phi)$
 holds for the Dirichlet form $(\sE, \sF)$ if the Hunt process $X$ associated with $(\sE, \sF)$  has a jointly continuous density function $p(t, x, y)$ on $(0, \infty)\times \sX \times \sX$ with respect to the measure $m$ and there exist constants $\e_{\ref{e:1.9}} \in (0,1)$ and $c_{\ref{e:1.9}} > 0$ such that  
\be 
p(t, x ,y )\ge \frac{c_{\ref{e:1.9}}}{V(x , \phi^{-1}(t))} \quad \hbox{for any } x ,y \in \sX
\hbox{ with }  d(x, y) < \e_{\ref{e:1.9}}\phi^{-1}(t)  .
\ee

 \item[\rm (iv)]  We say that the transition density lower bound estimate for the Dirichlet transition density, ${\rm NDL}(\phi)$ for short, holds for the Dirichlet form $(\sE, \sF)$ if the Hunt process $X$ associated with $(\sE, \sF)$   has a jointly continuous density function $p(t, x, y)$ on $(0, \infty)\times \sX \times \sX$ with respect to the measure $m$ and there exist  $\e_{\ref{e:2.15}} \in (0, 1)$ and $c_{\ref{e:2.15}} > 0$ so that for every $x_0 \in \sX$, $r > 0$, $t\in (0, \phi (\e_{\ref{e:2.15}}r))$ and

 \begin{equation}
 p^B(t, x, y) \geq   \frac{c_{\ref{e:2.15}}}{V(x_0, \phi^{-1}(t))}  \quad \hbox{for } x, y \in B(x_0, \e_{\ref{e:2.15}} \phi^{-1}(t)).

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.350975+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cb10364dace7dba743898e874e7664b4dd7421f41ae9cdd370defd519baac0d2","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 184 (quenched second moment bounds for 
$\bar{D}^{\Ising}$ and 
$\bar{D}^{\frozen,\Ising}$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] In addition to Lemma~\ref{l:barD.Ising.second} we have the quenched second moment bound
	\[\max\bigg\{
	\bE\Big[\Delta\bar{D}^{\Ising}(q_d)^2\Big]
	: 0\le d\le\dmax-1
	\bigg\}
	\le \frac{\SMAX_N(\Ising)^2\BUCKETS\delta}{N}\]
where $\SMAX_N(\Ising)$ is a random variable satisfying the bound
	\[\P\Big(\SMAX^N(\Ising) \ge \log N\Big)
	\le \exp
	\bigg(
	-\frac{(\log N)^2}{L^{O(1)}}
	\bigg)
	\,.\]
The same bound holds with $\bar{D}^{\frozen,\Ising}$ in place of
$\bar{D}^{\Ising}$.

\begin{proof}
Recall that we can rewrite \eqref{e:drift.error.Ising} as
	\[
	\frac{\Delta \bar{D}^{\Ising}(q_d)}{(\delta_d)^{1/2}}
	=\frac{1}{|B|^{1/2}}
	\bigg(\sum_{i\in B}
	\frac{\be_i}{|B|^{1/2}},
	\by\bigg)
	\equiv \frac{(\be_B,\by(q_{d+1}))}{|B|^{1/2}}\,,
	\]
where we abbreviate $B\equiv B^\Ising$.
If we define the random variable
	\[
	\SMAX_N(\Ising)
	\equiv\max
	\bigg\{
	\Big|( \be_B,\by(q_{d+1}))\Big|
	: 
	0\le d\le \dmax-1, B\in \mathcal{B}^\Ising(q_d)
	\bigg\}\,,
	\]
then we have the quenched second moment bound
	\[
	\bE[\Delta \bar{D}^{\Ising}(q_d)^2]
	= \frac{\delta_d}{N}
	\sum_{B\in \mathcal{B}^\Ising(q_d)}
	(\be_B,\by(q_{d+1}))^2
	\le  \frac{\SMAX_N(\Ising)^2\BUCKETS\delta}{N}\,.
	\]
The bound on $\SMAX_N(\Ising)$ follows by a similar argument as the bound for $\SMAX_N(\RomII)$ from Lemma~\ref{l:barD.II.second.quenched}, with the simplification that $\|\be_B\|=1$ is trivially bounded. 
This proves the claim for $\bar{D}^{\Ising}$, and the claim for
$\bar{D}^{\frozen,\Ising}$ follows by using \eqref{e:barD.vs.plus}.
\end{proof}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:25:49.850549+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cb20fbc476e426f62cbb0a29e7dfcaa83cec9e888814ebaa77c1bc7165ffc280","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 3 of arXiv:2609.02017, 'Optimal girth-dependent bounds for the Bethe approximation of the permanent'] For $\bs{q}=(q_1,\ldots,q_d)\in\Delta_d$, let
\[
  H(\bs{q}):=-\sum_{i=1}^d q_i\log q_i
\]
denote the usual Shannon entropy, and define the complementary entropy functional
\[
  H_{\mr c}(\bs{q}):=-\sum_{i=1}^d(1-q_i)\log(1-q_i).
\]
We call the difference
\[
  S(\bs{q}):=H(\bs{q})-H_{\mr c}(\bs{q})
\]
the local Bethe entropy functional.
If $\mu$ is a
probability distribution on a finite set, we write $H(\mu)$ for the
entropy of its probability vector; for a finite random variable $U$, we write $\mc{L}(U)$ for its law and set $H(U):=H(\mc{L}(U))$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.198595+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cb2b906f97a626a6ba6ab61c535750b890261c0d31521b6dc09d068d7788a706","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Ppn 127 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Take independent random variables $\sss\sim\tphi$ and $\xxx\sim\sphi$.
Let $\vY^\frozen$ be a subsequential limit of the $\vY^{\frozen,N}$ processes, and let $\hvY^\frozen(t)\equiv \vY^\frozen(t-\sss)+\xxx$. Take the coordinate sum
	\beq
	\iY^\frozen\equiv
	\sum_{\sigma\in\{\RomI,
		\RomII,\RomIII\}}
	\iY^{\frozen,\sigma}\,.\eeq
Let $\iX^\frozen$ and $\iX^{\frozen,\Ising}$ be the unique solutions of the SDEs \eqref{e:iX.sde} such that  $\iX^\frozen(q_*)$ is equidistributed as $\iY^\frozen(q_*)$, and 
$\iX^{\frozen,\Ising}(q_*)$ is equidistributed as $\iY^{\frozen,\Ising}(q_*)$. Then the (one-dimensional) processes 
$\iX^\frozen$ and $\iY^\frozen$
satisfy the same Fokker--Planck equations on the time interval $[q_*,1]$.
As a consequence, for each fixed $t$ the marginal law of $\iX^\frozen(t)$ agrees with the marginal law of $\iY^\frozen(t)$.
The same statements hold for $\iX^{\frozen,\Ising}$ and $\iY^{\frozen,\Ising}$.

\begin{proof}
This follows from Lemma~\ref{l:projected.fokker.planck},  using the regularity estimates from Corollary~\ref{c:reg.in.limit}. 
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["both measure spaces sigma-finite (needed for Tonelli and for L^p-L^q duality)","f product-measurable and nonnegative, or with a finite right-hand side","1 <= p <= infinity"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.752220+00:00","domain":"real analysis","id":"claim_cb6ac42afbf5cb613a530cbb8393109c2b97fb3282b5e1c27ca1629a6a611759","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, mu) and (Y, nu) be sigma-finite measure spaces, 1 <= p <= infinity, and f : X x Y -> [0, infinity] product-measurable. Then the L^p(mu) norm of the y-average dominates in the direction: || integral_Y f(., y) dnu(y) ||_{L^p(dmu)} <= integral_Y || f(., y) ||_{L^p(dmu)} dnu(y). For signed or complex f the same holds provided the right-hand side is finite, and then the inner integral converges absolutely for mu-a.e. x. The inequality is the continuous form of the triangle inequality for the L^p norm and reduces to it when nu is counting measure on two points. The reverse inequality is false for p > 1 and TRUE for 0 < p <= 1 with the roles of the two sides exchanged. Special case worth naming: taking nu counting measure on the integers gives || sum_n f_n ||_p <= sum_n || f_n ||_p. [standard; e.g. Stein, Singular Integrals and Differentiability Properties of Functions, Appendix A.1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:10:07.473363+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cb79141dcb1fc490b9d4b16fe109e95273ae65cd23a5e2b93b438fb424cfff0d","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma eq:mixture-remainder-X of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[lemma]{lem:product-mixture-path}
Let \(\mu_i\) and \(\gamma_i\), \(1\le i\le M\), be probability laws whose
moments agree through order \(m\), and put
\[
 \mu_{i,t}=(1-t)\mu_i+t\gamma_i,
 \qquad \lambda_t=\bigotimes_{i=1}^M\mu_{i,t},
 \qquad A(t)=\int_{\mathbb R^M}F(z)\,\lambda_t(\,\mathrm d z),
\]
where \(F:\mathbb R^M\to(0,\infty)\) is \(C^{m+1}\).  Let
\(Z\sim\lambda_t\), \(X_i\sim\mu_i\), and \(Y_i\sim\gamma_i\) be
independent.  Assume \(0<A(t)<\infty\) on \([0,1]\), that the
expressions below are absolutely integrable, and that differentiation
under the finite product measure is justified.  Set
\(\Delta_i^X=X_i-Z_i\) and \(\Delta_i^Y=Y_i-Z_i\).  If, uniformly in
\(t\in[0,1]\),
\begin{align}
 &\sum_{i=1}^M\mathbb E\left[
  \left\lvert\Delta_i^X\right\rvert^{m+1}
  \int_0^1(1-s)^m
  \abs{\partial_i^{m+1}F(Z+s\Delta_i^Xe_i)}\,\mathrm d s\right]
 \le R A(t),\\
 &\sum_{i=1}^M\mathbb E\left[
  \left\lvert\Delta_i^Y\right\rvert^{m+1}
  \int_0^1(1-s)^m
  \abs{\partial_i^{m+1}F(Z+s\Delta_i^Ye_i)}\,\mathrm d s\right]
 \le R A(t),
\end{align}
then
\begin{equation}
 \left\lvert\log A(1)-\log A(0)\right\rvert\le \frac{2R}{m!}.
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:51:26.589301+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cb7cc8fd1114c41bfc16383467dd69f2f04c77f37babab12ced15ff799e959af","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:SaS-measure of arXiv:2606.02003, 'Higher-Order Multifractional Stable Motion:\\ Definition and Fundamental Properties'] Let $(E,\mathcal{E})$ be a measurable space with $\sigma$-finite measure $m$.
Set $\mathcal{E}_0 := \{A \in \mathcal{E} : m(A) < \infty\}$.
A mapping $M_\alpha : \mathcal{E}_0 \to L^0(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$
is a \emph{S$\alpha$S random measure with control measure $m$} if:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item For every $A \in \mathcal{E}_0$:
  $M_\alpha(A) \sim \mathrm{S}\alpha\mathrm{S}(m(A)^{1/\alpha})$, i.e.,
  \begin{equation}
  
  \mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{i\theta M_\alpha(A)}\bigr]
  = e^{-|\theta|^\alpha m(A)},
  \quad \theta \in \mathbb{R}.
  \end{equation}
\item For pairwise disjoint $A_1, A_2, \ldots \in \mathcal{E}_0$,
  the variables $M_\alpha(A_1), M_\alpha(A_2), \ldots$ are independent.
\item For pairwise disjoint $\{A_j\} \subset \mathcal{E}_0$ with
  $\bigcup_j A_j \in \mathcal{E}_0$:
  $M_\alpha\!\left(\bigcup_j A_j\right) = \sum_j M_\alpha(A_j)$
  almost surely.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:39:11.667269+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cb97ee9edeea22349ada59114228c7916782a63e40120b33671714dfc9e37161","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 11 of arXiv:2608.04644, 'Khinchin's and Chung's Laws of the Iterated Logarithm at Time Zero for the Linear Stochast'] \cite[Theorem 2.4]{T1994}
Let $\{X(t)\}_{t\in S}$ be a mean-zero continuous Gaussian process.
Denote $\sigma^2 := \sup_{t\in S} \|X(t)\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2$. Suppose that  there exist constants $M > \sigma$, $p > 0$, and $0 < \varepsilon_0 \leqslant \sigma$ such that
\[
N(S, d_X, \varepsilon) \leq (M/\varepsilon)^p \quad \text{for all } \varepsilon < \varepsilon_0.
\]
Then, for any $u > \sigma^2[(1 + \sqrt{p})/\varepsilon_0]$, the following holds:
\[
\mathbb{P}\left\{ \sup_{t\in S} X(t) \geq u \right\} \leq \left(\frac{KMu}{\sqrt{p}\,\sigma^2} \right)^p \Phi\left(\frac{u}{\sigma} \right),
\]
where $\Phi(x) = (2\pi)^{-1/2} \int_x^\infty e^{-y^2/2}\,dy$ and $K$ is a universal constant. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-05T05:37:33.911677+00:00","domain":"ensemble learning","id":"claim_cb9f0a5bfb69e6d801c7f9b4c969831d7a650fa1a7cd92d88cc350fba9aa3034","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $M$ predictors $f_1, \\dots, f_M$ of a target $y$ have errors $e_m = f_m - y$ with error covariance $\\Sigma_E$ (the $M \\times M$ covariance of the vector $(e_1, \\dots, e_M)$ over the population of inputs). An affine stack $\\sum_m w_m f_m + b$ with $\\sum_m w_m = 1$ has error $\\sum_m w_m e_m + b$, so after the intercept removes the mean error its risk is $w^T \\Sigma_E w$, and the optimal weights are the minimum-variance portfolio $w^* = \\Sigma_E^{-1}\\mathbf{1} / (\\mathbf{1}^T \\Sigma_E^{-1}\\mathbf{1})$; without the sum constraint the least-squares stack is the ordinary regression of $y$ on $(f_1, \\dots, f_M, 1)$. Consequently every random-matrix result about the noisy-covariance portfolio problem transfers to ensemble weighting with $q = M / n_{\\mathrm{cal}}$, $n_{\\mathrm{cal}}$ the number of calibration cases the weights are fitted on: the plug-in (least-squares) stack's out-of-sample risk is inflated by the factor $1/(1 - q)$ relative to the optimum, its in-sample risk understates the optimum by $1 - q$, and any cleaning of the covariance must be applied to $\\Sigma_E$. The covariance of the predictions themselves, $\\operatorname{Cov}(f_1, \\dots, f_M)$, is NOT the object to clean: writing $f_m = y + e_m$ it equals $\\operatorname{Var}(y)\\mathbf{1}\\mathbf{1}^T + (\\text{cross terms}) + \\Sigma_E$, a rank-one spike of the size of the signal variance over the error covariance. The stacking weight's departure from equal weights, $w - \\mathbf{1}/M$, is orthogonal to $\\mathbf{1}$, so it lives entirely in the small-eigenvalue subspace of the prediction covariance; a bulk-versus-spike cleaner applied to that matrix (Marchenko-Pastur truncation, shrinkage toward $\\operatorname{tr}/p \\cdot I$, a rotationally invariant estimator floored relative to the top eigenvalue) keeps the signal spike and destroys exactly the directions stacking needs. At $q = 0.025$ (23 members, 932 calibration rows) the whole prize from cleaning $\\Sigma_E$ is bounded by about $2.5$ percent; the prize grows like $q/(1-q)$ as the calibration set shrinks.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["convention with kernel e^{-i x . zeta} (with e^{-2 pi i x . zeta} the exponent becomes 2 pi R |Im zeta|)","support contained in the closed ball of radius R (for a general compact convex K replace R|Im zeta| by the supporting function of K evaluated at Im zeta)","(b): u is a distribution with compact support and finite order; the polynomial exponent equals the order only in the forward direction"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:39.263692+00:00","domain":"distribution theory and complex analysis","id":"claim_cba247c3ed3e796918e204e741c567b552748af03769e8d7a590344a31b7acf4","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Use the convention $\\hat\\varphi(\\zeta)=\\int_{\\mathbb R^d}\\varphi(x)e^{-ix\\cdot\\zeta}dx$ for $\\zeta\\in\\mathbb C^d$, and let $R\\ge0$, $B_R=\\{x\\in\\mathbb R^d:|x|\\le R\\}$. (a) Test functions: $\\varphi\\in C_c^\\infty(\\mathbb R^d)$ with $\\operatorname{supp}\\varphi\\subset B_R$ if and only if $\\hat\\varphi$ extends to an entire function on $\\mathbb C^d$ satisfying, for every $N\\in\\mathbb N$, a bound $|\\hat\\varphi(\\zeta)|\\le C_N(1+|\\zeta|)^{-N}e^{R|\\operatorname{Im}\\zeta|}$. (b) Distributions: if $u\\in\\mathcal E'(\\mathbb R^d)$ has $\\operatorname{supp}u\\subset B_R$ and order at most $N$, then $\\hat u(\\zeta)=\\langle u,e^{-ix\\cdot\\zeta}\\rangle$ is entire on $\\mathbb C^d$ and $|\\hat u(\\zeta)|\\le C(1+|\\zeta|)^{N}e^{R|\\operatorname{Im}\\zeta|}$. Conversely, if an entire $U$ on $\\mathbb C^d$ satisfies $|U(\\zeta)|\\le C(1+|\\zeta|)^{N}e^{R|\\operatorname{Im}\\zeta|}$ for some constants $C,N$, then $U=\\hat u$ for a unique $u\\in\\mathcal E'(\\mathbb R^d)$ with $\\operatorname{supp}u\\subset B_R$. The support-and-growth correspondence is an exact equivalence; the order is not preserved in both directions - the forward implication gives the exponent $N$ from the order $N$, while the converse only returns a distribution of order at most $N+d+1$. Consequence: the exponential factor records the size of the (convex hull of the) support, the polynomial factor records smoothness versus singularity order. Corollary: a nonzero compactly supported distribution never has compactly supported Fourier transform, since a nonzero entire function cannot vanish on a nonempty open subset of $\\mathbb C^d$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:39:41.443181+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cbe1d106d31bbfccb55cb83bd63076c04f8b9acb51cde99d137a30200c0b3de4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 23 of arXiv:2604.07478, 'Mixing Times and Cutoff for the Rook's Walk'] Let $n,d$ be any parameters for the Rook's Walk. Then for $\epsilon\in(0,1)$,
   \[t_\text{mix}(\epsilon) \leq \frac{d(n-1)}{2n} \log d + c_u(\epsilon) \frac{d(n-1)}{n}\]
   where $c_u(\epsilon)$ is a constant dependent only on $\epsilon$.
   \begin{proof}
      Let $u=4\epsilon^2+1$. Then,
      \[u^{1/d} =e^{\log(u^{1/d})}=e^{\frac{1}{d}\log(u)}\]
      Now, $e^x$ is concave up so the first order Taylor approximation is a lower bound; That is, $e^x \geq 1+x$. Therefore,
      \[e^{\frac{1}{d}\log (u)} \geq 1+ \frac{1}{d}\log( u)\]
      or equivalently,
      \[u^{1/d} -1 \geq \frac{\log u}{d}\]
      Now, recall our upper bound from Theorem \ref{main1} and substitute,
      \begin{align*}
          t_\text{mix}(\epsilon) &\leq -\frac{d(n-1)}{2n}\log\left((4\epsilon^2+1)^{1/d}-1 \right)\\
          &= \frac{d(n-1)}{2n}\log\left(\frac{1}{(4\epsilon^2+1)^{1/d}-1 }\right)\\
          &\leq \frac{d(n-1)}{2n}\log\left(\frac{d}{\log (4\epsilon^2 +1)}\right)\\
          &= \frac{d(n-1)}{2n}\left(\log(d) -\log\log(4\epsilon^2+1)\right)\\
          &= \frac{d(n-1)}{2n}\log(d) +c_u(\epsilon) \frac{d(n-1)}{n}
      \end{align*}
      as required.
      
   \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.163974+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cc1b2d0e0e60b2fab206e1bb831beb4f89e5103ec099debaccf925d39496b78b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 30 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Recall from Lemma~\ref{l:freeprob.V.convex} that $z_{\min}$ is the unique minimizer of $V$ on the interval $[z_0,\infty)$.
    We have $z_{\min} = z_0$ if and only if
    \beq
        
        \alpha \le \mu_1 \textup{ and } \hv_1 < 0\,.
    \eeq
    If \eqref{e:zmin-equal-z0} does not hold, $z_{\min}$ is the unique solution to the equation $V'(z) = 0$ for $z\in(z_0,\infty)$.

\begin{proof}
Recall that if $\hv_1 > 0$, then $V(z)\uparrow\infty$ as $z\downarrow z_0$, so in this case clearly $z_{\min} > z_0$.
If instead $\hv_1 < 0$, then $z_0 = \hw_1$, so we have $z_{\min}=z_0$ if and only if the derivative $V'$ stays nonnegative as $z\downarrow \hw_1$. To this end, recall that as $z\downarrow \hw_1$ we have $m(z)\uparrow\infty$, so
    \[\sum_{j=1}^r \lambda_j \bigg(
        \frac{\hv_j m(z)}{\alpha - \hv_j m(z)}\bigg)^2
        \longrightarrow \sum_{j=1}^r \lambda_j = 1\,.\]
We also have $m_2(z)/m(z)^2 \to 1/\mu_1$, and substituting into
\eqref{e:fp-V-pr} gives
    \[
        V'(z)
        \longrightarrow 1 - \frac{\alpha}{\mu_1}
    \]
   as $z\downarrow\hw_1$. This is nonnegative if and only if $\alpha \le \mu_1$, which yields the condition \eqref{e:zmin-equal-z0}. Otherwise, we must have $z_{\min} > z_0$; in this case, since $V$ is strictly convex and twice differentiable, the value $z_{\min}$ must be the unique solution to the equation $V'(z) = 0$ for $z\in(z_0,\infty)$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

Our result (id P0341, 2026-09-08): BOTH parts are FALSE, on the single observation that a(n,n) = 1 exactly - the chain starts at n, so it visits n surely. Verification as the source words it: each piece re-derived (the asymptotics of a(j) and a(j) j, the summability of a(2^r), the polynomial-growth hypothesis for both test functions, and a(n,n) = 1 from the definition); no rate of convergence and no numerical evaluation is needed anywhere. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.168228+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ccc0df09822bfa3a5d90fb1bef1737321977369413bb52b928df8763118ba57f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 62 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For all $q_0 \in [0,1)$, we have $\sM^{\Lip}(\alpha,q_0) \subseteq \sM^{\BOGP}(\alpha,q_0)$.
\begin{proof}
    This is a consequence of Theorem~\ref{thm:BOGP-hardness-main}.
    Consider any $\mu \in \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)$, where $L$ is sufficiently large depending on $\alpha,q_0,\epsilon$. Recalling \eqref{e:cM.Lip.q0}, this means there exists a sequence of $L$-Lipschitz algorithms $(\cA_j)^\circ$ (acting in $N_j$ dimensions) such that
    \begin{align} \nonumber 
    &\WERR( (\cA_j)^\circ,\mu)
 \le \epsilon\,,\\
        
   &     q_0(j)
        \equiv \chi_{ (\cA_j)^\circ}(0)
         \stackrel{j\to\infty}{\longrightarrow} q_0\,.
    \end{align}
    Let $(\cA_j)_{j\ge 1}$ be the perturbations of the $( (\cA_j)^\circ)_{j\ge 1}$ given by Proposition~\ref{p:wlogable}, which are also $L$-Lipschitz.
    Proposition~\ref{p:wlogable} further yields
    \[
        \frac{1}{N} \bbE \Big[\| (\cA_j)^\circ(\bG,\bg^{\aux}) 
        	- \cA_j(\bG,\bg^{\aux})\|^2\Big]
        \le \frac{2}{(1-q_0(j))L^2}\,.
    \]
Thus Lemma~\ref{l:control.problems.approx} implies that for $c_0$, $C_1(\alpha)$ and $C_2(\alpha,L)$ given therein,
	\[
	\WERR(\cA_j,(\cA_j)^\circ)
	\le 
	\bigg\{
        C_1(\alpha) \cdot \frac{2}{(1-q_0(j))L^2} + C_2(\alpha,L) e^{-c_0N_j}
        \bigg\}^{1/2} 
        \le \epsilon \]
    where the last inequality holds if $L$ is sufficiently large depending on $\alpha,q_0,\epsilon$ (consistent with our assumptions), and $j$ sufficiently large depending on $q_0,\epsilon,L$. Hence, by omitting finitely many $j$, we can assume it holds for all $j$ that
    \beq
        
        \WERR(\cA_j,\mu)=
        \max\bigg\{
            \bbW_2\Big(\mu(\cA_j), \mu\Big),
            \bbW_2\Big(\mu^{\Ising}(\cA_j), \cP(\{\pm 1\})\Big)
        \bigg\}
        \le 2\epsilon\,,
    \eeq
By passing to a further subsequence of the $j$'s, we can assume that for all $j$ we have 
    \[
         \max\bigg\{
            \bbW_2\Big(\mu(\cA_j), \mu\Big),
            \bbW_2\Big(\mu^{\Ising}(\cA_j), \mu^\Ising\Big)
        \bigg\}
         \le 3\epsilon
    \]
for some fixed $\mu^\Ising \in \cP(\{\pm 1\})$.
    By passing to a further subsequence, we can assume (as in Theorem~\ref{thm:BOGP-hardness-main}) that $\chi_{\cA_j}$ converges to a limiting function $\chi$, both pointwise and in $L^1$.
    Since Proposition~\ref{p:wlogable} ensures 
    \[
        \chi_{\cA_j}(0) = \chi_{\cA^\circ_j}(0) = q_0(j)\,,
    \]
    by \eqref{e:Lip.in.BOGP.q0.limit} we have $\chi(0) = q_0$.

We now apply Theorem~\ref{thm:BOGP-hardness-main} to the sequence $(\cA_j)_{j\ge 1}$ where, treating $\epsilon$ as a function of $L$ tending to $0$ sufficiently slowly, the hypothesis \eqref{e:BOGP-hardness-main-hypothesis} holds by \eqref{e:Lip.in.BOGP.hardness.hypothesis}.
    Then, for some $\tilde\epsilon = \tilde\epsilon(\epsilon)$ tending to $0$ sufficiently slowly as $\epsilon\rightarrow 0$, Theorem~\ref{thm:BOGP-hardness-main} provides controls $(q_*,b,\sigma,w,p\equiv \chi^{-1},\zeta,\zeta^\Ising)$ satisfying the conclusions of that theorem, where all $o_L(1)$ error terms are replaced by $\tilde\epsilon$. We assume without loss that $\tilde{\epsilon}\le1$. 
    We will now verify that for $C(L)$ given by Theorem~\ref{thm:BOGP-hardness-main},
    \beq
        
         (q_*,b,\sigma,w,p\equiv \chi^{-1},\zeta,\zeta^\Ising) 
         \in \Adm^{\BOGP}\Big(
         \alpha,q_0;
         \tilde C = \max\{C(L),L^2\}, \tilde\epsilon 
         \Big)\,.
    \eeq
    Indeed, we verify each of the conditions from Definition~\ref{d:SDE.classification} specifying the $\Adm^{\BOGP}$ class:
    \begin{itemize}
\item Theorem~\ref{thm:BOGP-hardness-main}\ref{it:BOGP-hardness-main-Lip}
    implies condition~\ref{it:1.1bogp};

\item Theorem~\ref{thm:BOGP-hardness-main}\ref{it:BOGP-hardness-main-diffusivity}
    implies condition~\ref{it:2.1}; 

\item We have $p(q_0) = 0$ because we defined $\chi(0) = q_0$. 
        Theorem~\ref{thm:BOGP-hardness-main} asserts $p(q_*) \le \tilde\epsilo (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.352896+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ccec066ffa0ec9499357e450b8a09d076a5e7a35b2314061cdccc3fc37f950af","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 198 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\cA$ be an $L$-Lipschitz algorithm, and let $\bx(q_d)$ be as defined by
\eqref{e:x.q.mean}. Then
    \[
    \P\bigg(\bigg|
    \frac{(\bx(q_d),\bx(q_\ell))}{N}-q_{\min\{d,\ell\}}
    \bigg|\ge
    \frac{1}{N^{1/3}}\bigg) 
    \le \exp(-N^{0.1})\,.
    \]

\begin{proof}
This follows easily from gaussian Lipschitz concentration (see e.g.\ Lemma~\ref{l:lip.subgaus}).
Indeed note that $\|\cA(\bG,  \bg^\aux)\|_2\leq N^{1/2}$ almost surely, while by definition $\bx(q_d)$
is an $L$-Lipschitz function of the gaussian vector $(\bG(q_d),\bg^\aux(q_d))$. It follows that for $\ell \le d$, the normalized inner product
    \[\frac{(\bx(q_d),\bx(q_\ell))}{N}\]
is an 
 $O(LN^{-1/2})$-Lipschitz function of 
    \[\Big(\bG(q_\ell),
    \bg^\aux(q_\ell),
    \bG(q_d) - \bG(q_\ell),\bg^\aux(q_d) - \bg^\aux(q_\ell)\Big)\,.\]
 Therefore it concentrates around its mean by Lemma~\ref{l:lip.subgaus}, which gives the conclusion.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Counterexample: u_t + (u^2/2)_x = 0 versus (u^2/2)_t + (u^3/3)_x = 0 with left state 1 and right state 0","Rankine-Hugoniot: σ = [flux]/[density], so both entries matter","Chain-rule manipulations of the flux are valid only where the solution is C^1"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.418709+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: hyperbolic conservation laws","id":"claim_cd2c0cd0a6c998918c8d20dec220a3380322e8bf670c19046ddde117aec30ea3","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: the Rankine-Hugoniot condition, and hence the whole notion of weak solution, is attached to a specific pair (conserved density, flux) — not to the PDE as an equation for smooth functions. Two equations with identical classical solutions can have different weak solutions. Counterexample: for smooth u, Burgers' equation u_t + (u^2/2)_x = 0 is equivalent to (u^2/2)_t + (u^3/3)_x = 0 (multiply the first by u; conversely divide where u ≠ 0). But a jump from u_l = 1 (left) to u_r = 0 (right) travels with speed [f]/[u] = (1/2 - 0)/(1 - 0) = 1/2 for the first form, and with speed (1/3 - 0)/(1/2 - 0) = 2/3 for the second: the two weak solutions are genuinely different. The same phenomenon makes the nonconservative form u_t + u u_x = 0 meaningless across a shock (the product u u_x is not a distribution for discontinuous u). Physically, the model must specify which quantity is conserved; numerically, only schemes written in the conservative form of the true conserved quantity (Lax-Wendroff theorem) converge to the correct shock speeds. Auditor's check: when a proof rewrites the flux (multiplying the equation by a function of u, changing variables u = φ(v), or using a chain rule), the manipulation is legitimate for smooth solutions only; across discontinuities it changes the answer.","status":"unverified"}

Method: Tightness of the path via the exponential metric (Liouville first passage percolation) comparison. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:09:41.190407+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_cd8b3fd8a8f4ae722c7b30ce5ede1b8d61ec46e770d6d666a20852c38aba2023","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematics, specifically in homology theory and algebraic topology, cohomology is a way of attaching algebraic invariants to a topological space or other mathematical object that encode its properties in a way that is often computable. Cohomology is often related to questions of whether some local property of the space is obstructed when passing to a global property. For example, the Möbius strip is not the product space of a line segment with a circle, but locally on any segment of the circle it resembles an ordinary rectangle without the global twist. The obstruction to making the product structure global is encoded in the first cohomology of the underlying circle, which classifies the two inequivalent ways a line can twist around a circle. The fact that there are only two inequivalent ways of twisting a line around a circle is encoded in the relevant cohomology group which can be computed as isomorphic to the group where corresponds to an even number of twists, and to an odd number.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:34:33.544042+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cdc32c6a7be0c770379c13c38cb0e7ab1ad4655c10de13426f6d3ee3de387d5d","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 32 (Monotonicity of angles) of arXiv:2603.28734, 'Free energy analyticity of the disordered XY model and Debye screening in the 2D Coulomb g'] Fix a finite graph $G$, some $\beta\in[0,\infty)$.
    Let $u$ denote some vertex, and let $E_u$ denote the set of edges incident to $u$.
    Pick
    \[
        \tau'=(\alpha',\omega',\eta')\in [0,\pi/2]^{V\setminus\{u\}}\times\{0,1\}^{E\setminus E_u}\times\{0,1\}^{E\setminus E_u},
    \]
    Let $\mu_{\tau'}$ denote the measure
    $\mu_{G,\beta}$ conditioned on \[\{\tau|_{(V\setminus\{u\})\times (E\setminus E_u) \times (E\setminus E_u)}=\tau'\}.\]
    Then the density of $\alpha_u$ on $[0,\pi/2]$ under $\mu_{\tau'}$
      is proportional to
    \begin{align}
        \textstyle
        \left(
        \prod_{\Gamma\in C(\omega')}
        \textstyle
        2\cosh(\beta\cos\alpha_u\sum_{v \in \Gamma}\cos\alpha_v')
        \right)
        \left(
        \prod_{\Gamma\in C(\eta')}
        \textstyle
        2\cosh(\beta\sin\alpha_u\sum_{v\in \Gamma}\sin\alpha_v')
        \right),
\end{align}
where $C(\rho)$ is the partition of $\{v\in V:v\sim u\}$ into $\rho$-connected components.

In particular, if $\mu^{\alpha_u}_{\tau'}$ denotes the law of $\alpha_u$ under $\mu_{\tau'}$, then
\[
    \tau'\preceq\tau''
    \qquad
    \implies
    \qquad
    \mu^{\alpha_u}_{\tau'}\leqstoch\mu^{\alpha_u}_{\tau''}.
\]","status":"unverified"}

In the two regimes not covered by the finite-variance mean-conditioning theorem, (c) lambda = nu with sigma^2 = infinity and (d) lambda > nu, the natural analogue of the Gaussian limit has variance sigma_d^2 = pi_d(1-pi_d). {"assumptions":["T is consistent","T is effectively axiomatized (computably enumerable axiom set)","T interprets Robinson arithmetic Q"],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:15:45.378582+00:00","domain":"mathematical logic","id":"claim_cde8bcbf7d8ce7708f2314743185825fb5c4235f909300f46e471371d1a885c8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let T be a first-order theory satisfying all three hypotheses: (i) T is consistent; (ii) T is effectively axiomatized: its set of axioms is computably enumerable (equivalently, by Craig's trick, computably decidable after re-axiomatization), so theoremhood is computably enumerable; (iii) T interprets enough arithmetic - it suffices that T contains or interprets Robinson arithmetic Q. Then T is incomplete: there is a sentence G in the language of T (arithmetical under the interpretation) such that T proves neither G nor the negation of G. Consequently no consistent, effectively axiomatized theory interpreting Q is complete; in particular Peano arithmetic and ZFC, if consistent, are incomplete. Godel's original 1931 argument additionally assumed omega-consistency to rule out T proving the negation; Rosser's 1936 refinement, stated here, needs only consistency. All three hypotheses are necessary: complete consistent extensions of Q exist but are not effectively axiomatized (e.g. true arithmetic), effectively axiomatized complete consistent theories exist that do not interpret Q (e.g. the theory of dense linear orders, or Presburger arithmetic), and an inconsistent theory proves everything.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["A increasing and depending on finitely many coordinates","product measure with a common density p","for general events use the Margulis-Russo form with signed summands"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.543078+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ce028eff08f7ef08cc636b492788f905d03b4c3fa8e4ee1b14f0bc0ea2dcd3a1","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A be an INCREASING event depending on the states of a FINITE set E of edges, and let P_p be the product measure with density p. Then p -> P_p(A) is a polynomial in p, hence smooth, and d/dp P_p(A) = sum_{e in E} P_p( e is pivotal for A ) = E_p[ N(A) ], where N(A) is the number of pivotal edges. Equivalently the derivative is the TOTAL INFLUENCE. The monotonicity hypothesis matters: for a general event the correct statement is the Margulis-Russo formula d/dp P_p(A) = sum_e [ P_p(A with e open) - P_p(A with e closed) ], whose summands can be negative and which reduces to Russo's formula exactly when A is increasing. Russo's formula is the bridge from influence estimates - Kahn-Kalai-Linial, Talagrand, Friedgut-Kalai - to SHARP THRESHOLDS: a lower bound on the total influence of order log(1/(p(1-p))) forces P_p(A) to rise from eps to 1 - eps over a parameter window of width O(1/log n). [Russo (1981), Margulis (1974); see Grimmett, Percolation, 2nd ed., Theorem 2.25]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["The stated published minimum-location, tail, and limit theorems apply to this Poisson branching walk."],"created_at":"2026-10-10T06:51:51.363927+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ce056cd6340bc4912f6868fe54fad0f2450076e2feff0e1ef5d3b6511feace21","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked; the recursion is integrated exactly against two published closed-form values as a control] This is the campaign answer to Conjecture 1 of H. Stepanyants, P. L. Krapivsky, H. Hartle and D. Krioukov, The rank and layer distributions in random recursive trees, arXiv:2608.04303. Let the Poisson-weighted infinite tree have root position zero, with children of each vertex at the points of an independent rate-one Poisson process on (0,infinity), translated by their parent's position. Let M_k be the minimum position of generation k, and set M_0=0. Define s_0(y)=1 for y>=0 and s_k(y)=1-exp(-integral_0^y s_{k-1}(z)dz) for k>=1. Put bar_ell_k=integral_0^infinity s_k(y)exp(-y)dy and ell_k=bar_ell_k-bar_ell_{k+1}. In the source, ell_k is the limiting fraction of vertices in layer k of a random recursive tree, formed by joining each new vertex j uniformly to one of vertices 1,...,j-1; layer zero consists of the initial leaves, and subsequent layers are obtained by successive leaf removals. Let e be the base of the natural logarithm. There is a constant C_star in (0,infinity) such that bar_ell_k exp(k/e) k^(3/(2e)) -> C_star and ell_k exp(k/e) k^(3/(2e)) -> (1-exp(-1/e)) C_star. More precisely, if M_star denotes the distributional limit of M_k-[k/e+(3/(2e))log k] furnished by the cited branching-random-walk minimum theorem, then C_star=E[exp(-M_star)]. In particular both tails have order exp(-k/e) k^(-3/(2e)). The proof uses Addario-Berry and Ford's Poisson-Dirichlet branching random walks, Annals of Applied Probability 23 (2013), Theorems 1.1-1.2, and Aidekon's Convergence in law of the minimum of a branching random walk, Annals of Probability 41 (2013), as stated in the record. This is an unrefereed campaign result.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:23:05.285568+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ce2854bc46715b64a84e17e7e82c740cce538870a762eb52c14617533264e705","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 10 of arXiv:2608.21551, '\bf Sparse Separable Factor Analysis in the Complex Domain with an Application to Local Fi'] For $j=1,\ldots,d$, let $\Lambdab_j\in\CC^{p_j\times k_j}$ denote the true loading matrix and $\widehat{\Lambdab}_j$ denote its estimate. Define the orthogonal projectors onto their column spaces by
\begin{align*}
  \Pb_j
  &=
  \Lambdab_j
  \left(
    \Lambdab_j^\star\Lambdab_j
  \right)^+
  \Lambdab_j^\star,
  \qquad
  \widehat{\Pb}_j
  =
  \widehat{\Lambdab}_j
  \left(
    \widehat{\Lambdab}_j^\star
    \widehat{\Lambdab}_j
  \right)^+
  \widehat{\Lambdab}_j^\star,
\end{align*}
where $+$ denotes the Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse. The null-space projection error is
\begin{align}
  \operatorname{err}_{\Pb_j}^2
  &=
  \left\|
    \left(
      \Ib_{p_j}-\widehat{\Pb}_j
    \right)
    \Pb_j
  \right\|_F^2.
  
\end{align}
Let
\begin{align*}
  r_j
  &=
  \operatorname{rank}(\Lambdab_j),
  \qquad
  \widehat{r}_j
  =
  \operatorname{rank}(\widehat{\Lambdab}_j),
  \qquad
  r_{\min,j}
  =
  \min(r_j,\widehat{r}_j).
\end{align*}
Denote the principal angles between the column spaces of $\Lambdab_j$ and $\widehat{\Lambdab}_j$ by
\begin{align*}
    0
  \leq
  \theta_{(j)1}
  \leq
  \cdots
  \leq
  \theta_{(j)r_{\min,j}}
  \leq
  \frac{\pi}{2}.
\end{align*}
Then,
\begin{align}
  \operatorname{err}_{\Pb_j}^2
  &=
  r_j-r_{\min,j}
  +
  \sum_{i=1}^{r_{\min,j}}
  \sin^2\left(\theta_{(j)i}\right),
  
\end{align}
where the sum \eqref{eq:appendix-null-err-proj-angle} is interpreted as zero when $r_{\min,j}=0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:09:41.191908+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_ce28db6406ddd1775473d2f98feeb5d35ef4dd3ce7888de7d1bef852dd5fbb5f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematics, philosophy, linguistics, and computer science, first-order logic (FOL), also called predicate logic, predicate calculus, or quantificational logic, is a type of formal system. First-order logic uses quantified variables over non-logical objects, and allows the use of sentences that contain variables. Rather than propositions such as \"all humans are mortal\", in first-order logic one can have expressions in the form \"for all x, if x is a human, then x is mortal\", where \"for all x\" is a quantifier, x is a variable, and \"... is a human\" and \"... is mortal\" are predicates. This distinguishes it from propositional logic, which does not use quantifiers or relations; in this sense, first-order logic is an extension of propositional logic.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:17:42.300287+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cee543072473629441b91ef51c460c6ff61a63e7f9c8c712992ffa41242103d2","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 1 (Markov Kernels) of arXiv:2510.22155, 'Random walks in space-time random media in all spatial dimensions: the full subcritical fl'] Fix $d\ge 1$. Let $I$ be any locally compact additive subgroup of $\mathbb R^d$, for example $I=\mathbb R^d$ or $I=A \mathbb Z^d$ where $A$ is some nonsingular $d\times d$ matrix. Let $\mathcal B(I)$ denote the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on $I$. 
A \textit{Markov kernel} on $I$ is a continuous function from $I\to \mathcal P(I)$, where $\mathcal P(I)$ is the space of probability measures on $(I,\mathcal B(I))$ equipped with the topology of weak convergence of probability measures. 

Any Markov kernel $K$ on $I$ shall be written as $K(   x,A)$, which is identified with the continuous function from $I\to \mathcal P(I)$ given by $x\mapsto K(   x,\cdot)$. We denote by $\mathcal M(I)$ the space of all Markov kernels on $I$.

We equip $\mathcal M(I)$ with the weakest topology under which the maps $T_{f,   x}:\mathcal M(I)\to \mathbb R$ given by $$K\stackrel{T_{f,   x}}{\mapsto}  \int_I f(   y)\;K(   x,\mathrm d   y)$$ 
are continuous, where one varies over all $x\in I$ and all bounded continuous functions $f:I\to \mathbb R$. This topology endows $\mathcal M(I)$ with a Borel $\sigma$-algebra which allows us to talk about random variables taking values in the space of Markov kernels. For $   a\in I$ define the translation operator $\tau_a:\mathcal M(I)\to \mathcal M(I)$ by $(  \tau_{   a} K)(   x,A):= K(x+   a,A+   a)$ which is a Borel-measurable map on this space.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:07:35.014637+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cef10872bc2f7d729fa12f1c6c789e180896bd4785f1feb1ccccd89e8218c046","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 12 of arXiv:2609.02878, '2609.02878'] A limiting point \(\xi=(\mu_t)_{t<T}\) is \emph{based at \(q\)} with
respect to the limiting morphism \(\pi\) if
\(\pi_*\mu_t\rightharpoonup\delta_q\).  Such a \(q\) is unique when it
exists, and we denote it by \(q_\pi(\xi)\).  It is
\emph{Type-I based at \(q\)} if there is \(C_\xi<\infty\) such that
\begin{equation}
 \int_Xd_\eta(\pi(x),q)^2\,d\mu_t(x)\le C_\xi(T-t)
 \qquad\text{for every }0\le t<T.
\end{equation}
If \(q\in Y^{\rm rv}\) and \(\rho_q\) is a localized
squared-distance barrier from \cref{def:squared-distance-barrier},
compactness and the defining comparisons for \(\rho_q\) show that this
is equivalent to
\[
 \int_X\rho_q\circ\pi\,d\mu_t\le C'_\xi(T-t).
\]
For an arbitrary holomorphic map, qualitative basing alone need not
imply this rate.  For the semiample K\"ahler--Ricci flow considered here,
\Cref{lem:automatic-label} proves that every limiting point is based at
a unique point \(q_\pi(\xi)\) and is Type-I based there.  Thus
\eqref{eq:label-moment} is never an additional hypothesis below.  When
\(q_\pi(\xi)\in Y^{\rm rv}\), we simply say that \(\xi\) is based at
the regular value \(q_\pi(\xi)\).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:57:07.195561+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cef74e96596ef283e611f566c0a608052515901afd67e8fb8a1c4e010f1e18a9","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:disagree-polymer-len-energy-decor of arXiv:2509.04333, 'The limiting law of the Discrete Gaussian level lines'] Let $(\gamma,\{D_i\},\{h_i\})$ be a labeled disagreement polymer. Its \emph{length} ${\ensuremath{\mathscr N}}(\gamma)$ and \emph{energy} 
		${\ensuremath{\mathscr E}}_\beta(\gamma)$ are defined as
		\[{\ensuremath{\mathscr N}}(\gamma)=\sum_{e\in\gamma}|(\nabla \phi)_e|\quad,\quad 
		{\ensuremath{\mathscr E}}_\beta(\gamma) := \beta\sum_{e \in \gamma} |(\nabla \phi)_e|^2\,.\]
		To describe the law of the disagreement polymer, we will use a family of decoration functions $\Phi$ on subsets ${\ensuremath{\mathsf W}}\subset \mathbb Z^2$---each referred to as a cluster if it is also connected---
        satisfying the following properties.
		\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
			\item  If ${\ensuremath{\mathsf W}}$ is not connected, then $\Phi({\ensuremath{\mathsf W}}) = 0$.
			
			\item 
			The function $\Phi$ is translation invariant, as well as invariant under a rotation by $\pi/2$ or reflection with respect to one of the axes.
			
			\item There exists a constant $C > 0$ such that for every ${\ensuremath{\mathsf W}}$, we have 
			$
			|\Phi({\ensuremath{\mathsf W}})| \leq \exp(-(\beta - C){\ensuremath{\mathbf d}}({\ensuremath{\mathsf W}}))
			$, 
			where ${\ensuremath{\mathbf d}}({\ensuremath{\mathsf W}})$ is the size of the smallest connected set of bonds in $(\mathbb Z^2)^*$ containing all the boundary bonds of ${\ensuremath{\mathsf W}}$.
		\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["M a local martingale with M_0 = 0","for 0 < p < 1: M continuous","for p >= 1: cadlag suffices","constants depend on p only"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.627451+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cf80a57cbccec160cd5893a5f18cbdc60f4fa6097c1a6f73d35f5f00697e2593","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let M be a local martingale with M_0 = 0, let M^*_T = sup_{t <= T} |M_t| for a stopping time T, and let [M] be the quadratic variation. There are constants 0 < c_p <= C_p < infinity depending ONLY on p such that c_p E[ [M]_T^{p/2} ] <= E[ (M^*_T)^p ] <= C_p E[ [M]_T^{p/2} ]. The admissible range of p differs by regularity: for CONTINUOUS local martingales the two-sided bound holds for every 0 < p < infinity; for general cadlag local martingales it holds for every p >= 1, and the case 0 < p < 1 genuinely requires continuity (Davis' theorem covers p = 1 in the general case). In discrete time the same holds with [M]_n = sum_{k <= n} (M_k - M_{k-1})^2 the square function, for 1 <= p < infinity. The constants are UNIVERSAL in the sense of depending on p alone - not on the martingale, the filtration, the time horizon or the dimension - and they blow up as p decreases to 0 and as p increases to infinity; explicit admissible choices grow like p for the upper constant. For p = 2 the inequality is an identity with c_2 = C_2 replaced by the Ito isometry together with Doob's L^2 maximal inequality, which is the cheap case one should reach for first. [Burkholder (1973), Davis (1970), Burkholder-Davis-Gundy (1972); see Revuz and Yor, Continuous Martingales and Brownian Motion, 3rd ed., Theorem IV.4.1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["finite nonempty dataset; n,d>=1,T>=2","fixed real tokens and queries, binary labels, fixed real linear prediction head","selected alpha has feasible unit-margin attention-SVM constraints"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T15:40:31.344626+00:00","domain":"learning theory","id":"claim_cf8d74fcc402639c49dd012b15ca4089db49d860df217f5a64f6e8fd2cd32852","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let n,d>=1 and T>=2 be integers. For each i in {1,...,n}, let tokens x_it in R^d, query z_i in R^d and label Y_i in {-1,+1} be fixed, and fix a linear prediction head v in R^d. Define token scores gamma_it=Y_i v^T x_it; globally optimal token indices satisfy opt_i in argmax_t gamma_it. Fix selected token indices alpha_i in {1,...,T}. Assume the attention-SVM constraints (x_i,alpha_i-x_it)^T W z_i>=1 for every i and every t!=alpha_i are feasible. Let W_alpha be the unique minimum-Frobenius-norm solution of these constraints, where ||W||_F=(sum_{a,b}W_ab^2)^(1/2). Equivalently it minimizes the squared Frobenius norm, a strictly convex objective. Define support indices T_i={t!=alpha_i:(x_i,alpha_i-x_it)^T W_alpha z_i=1}. The selection alpha is locally optimal exactly when gamma_i,alpha_i>gamma_it for every i and every t in T_i; W_alpha is then called a locally optimal direction. This condition compares the selected token only with support indices. It does not impose comparison with all non-support tokens. This card defines the fixed-head geometry; it makes no gradient-descent convergence assertion.","status":"unverified"}

\[
 \max_{1\le r\le m+1}\norm{V^{(r)}}_\infty<\infty.

Let \(\mathcal F_m\) be the Fourier--Wiener class of real-valued functions
\[
 f(x)=c+\int_\mathbb R e^{itx}\widehat f_0(t)\,\mathrm d t,
 \qquad c\in\mathbb R,
\]
where
\begin{equation}
 \int_\mathbb R(1+\left\lvertt\right\rvert^{m+1})\left\lvert\widehat f_0(t)\right\rvert\,\mathrm d t<\infty.
\end{equation}
Here \(\widehat f_0(-t)=\overline{\widehat f_0(t)}\), so \(f\) is real.

{"assumptions":["Little: f entire and nonconstant","Great: f holomorphic on a punctured disk about a with an isolated essential singularity at a"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T09:45:15.353295+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_cfb6b34b04c740458f4aa7f731e3fa6b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Little Picard theorem: if f is entire and nonconstant, then the complement of its image, C minus f(C), contains at most one point; i.e. a nonconstant entire function omits at most one complex value. Great Picard theorem: if f is holomorphic on a punctured disk 0 < |z - a| < r and has an essential singularity at a, then for every ε in (0,r) the image of the punctured disk 0 < |z - a| < ε is all of C with at most one point removed, and every value so attained (again with at most one exception) is attained infinitely often. Both exceptional values are genuinely possible and the count is sharp: exp(z) is entire and omits exactly the value 0, and exp(1/z) has an essential singularity at 0 and omits exactly 0 near 0. Meromorphic versions: a nonconstant meromorphic function on C omits at most two values of the Riemann sphere, and near an essential singularity a meromorphic function takes every spherical value with at most two exceptions. If f is entire and transcendental (not a polynomial), then f takes every complex value, with at most one exception, infinitely often.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:39:12.387907+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cfde59fe258dc90a0905f631a27d3f3cd24dfbc1d981f8c747ab9091a2e616cb","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem quadratic of arXiv:2412.07936, 'Simple Norm Bounds for Polynomial Random Matrices via Decoupling'] [Quadratic Recursion]

Let $\{x_i\}_{i = 1}^n$ be a sequence of i.i.d random variables with ${\mathbb E} x_i= 0$,  ${\mathbb E} x_i^2= 1$ and $|x_i| \leq L$ for all $1\leq i \leq n$. Let $\{{\bf A}_{i,j}\}_{(i,j) \in {\mathcal T}^2_n}$ be a double sequence of deterministic matrices of the same dimension. Define 
$$
{\bf F}({\bf x}) = \sum_{(i,j) \in {\mathcal T}^2_n} {\bf A}_{i,j} x_{i}x_{j}.
$$
Suppose that ${\bf F}({\bf x})$ is also permutation symmetric, i.e.,\xspace ${\bf A}_{i,j} = {\bf A}_{j,i}$, $\forall (i,j) \in {\mathcal T}^2_n$. Then for $a,b,c\in {\mathbb Z}_{\geq 0}$ and $2 \leq t < \infty$,
$$

$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["consistency of the finite-dimensional distributions under permutation and marginalisation","the state space Polish (or otherwise inner regular by compacts); the theorem fails for general measurable spaces","the conclusion is on the PRODUCT sigma-algebra only"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:40.781981+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cff4b22d3f4e9f129de820bfc924fd6ae8ae16e1c64314c11984e1f4a5a4588a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let T be an arbitrary index set and suppose that for every finite subset {t_1, ..., t_n} of T a probability measure mu_{t_1, ..., t_n} on R^n (or on S^n for a Polish space S with its Borel sigma-algebra) is given. Suppose the family is CONSISTENT: (i) permuting the indices permutes the measure correspondingly, and (ii) the marginal of mu_{t_1, ..., t_n, t_{n+1}} on the first n coordinates is mu_{t_1, ..., t_n}. Then there is a probability measure P on the product space S^T equipped with the PRODUCT sigma-algebra whose finite-dimensional marginals are exactly the given family, and P is unique. TWO LIMITATIONS, both routinely forgotten. FIRST, the topological hypothesis is essential: for general measurable spaces the theorem is FALSE, and there are consistent families with no extension (Andersen and Jessen); what is really needed is that the marginals be inner regular in a suitable sense, which Polish spaces provide. SECOND, the resulting measure lives on the PRODUCT sigma-algebra, every member of which is determined by countably many coordinates. When T is uncountable, sets such as {the path is continuous}, {sup_t X_t <= c}, or {the path is bounded} are therefore NOT measurable for that sigma-algebra, so the theorem does not by itself construct Brownian motion as a continuous process; it constructs a process with the right finite-dimensional laws, and a separate regularity theorem - Kolmogorov's continuity criterion - is needed to produce a modification with continuous paths. [Kolmogorov (1933); see Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 2.1.21, and Billingsley, Probability and Measure, Section 36]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T14:24:13.477019+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d007b509b76b2574e8db1cb4d99bb511beec50788f3846f5da7d43e190951280","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"For two probability measures mu and nu on a measurable space (S, A), the total variation distance is d_TV(mu, nu) = sup over A in A of |mu(A) - nu(A)|, a number in [0, 1]. If mu and nu have densities f and g with respect to a common reference measure lambda (which always exists, for instance lambda = mu + nu), then d_TV(mu, nu) = (1/2) integral |f - g| d lambda = 1 - integral min(f, g) d lambda, and the supremum is attained at A = { f > g }. Equivalent characterisations: d_TV is half the supremum of |integral h d mu - integral h d nu| over measurable h with |h| <= 1; and by the coupling characterisation, d_TV(mu, nu) = min P(X not equal to Y) over all couplings (X, Y) with X distributed as mu and Y as nu, the minimum being attained by the maximal coupling. Convergence in total variation is strictly stronger than weak convergence (point masses at 1/n converge weakly to the point mass at 0 but stay at total variation distance 1). The normalisation matters: some texts use the un-halved integral |f - g| d lambda, which lies in [0, 2].","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Boundedness of Omega is essential (the embedding is never compact on R^n, by translating a fixed bump), and for W^{1,p} rather than W_0^{1,p} some boundary regularity is needed so that an extension operator exists.","Compactness FAILS at the critical exponent q = p*, which is exactly the loss of compactness behind concentration phenomena in critical problems."],"created_at":"2026-09-12T14:06:45.870307+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations, Sobolev spaces","id":"claim_d00bdbb3a32698c4ecb614feccf503f1db25275537f989f81c44012bb8fa3418","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Omega be a bounded open subset of R^n with C^1 boundary (or any bounded extension domain, for instance a bounded Lipschitz domain), let 1 <= p < n and let p* = np/(n-p) be the Sobolev conjugate exponent. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:18:19.413234+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d01e9fd6f5dc66be51d583a10eeae66e3e2da0fe0e97e13aeb3758562c676ade","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:qRacah_tilings of arXiv:2507.22011, 'Random Lozenge Waterfall:\\Dimensional Collapse of Gibbs Measures'] We put a probability measure on the set of all
	nonintersecting path ensembles. The measure depends on the
	geometry of the hexagon (parametrized by $(T,S,N)$), and
	on two parameters $q>0$ and $\kappa\in
	\mathbf{i}\mathbb{R}$.
	The
	probability weight of a nonintersecting path ensemble is
	proportional to
	\begin{equation}
		
		\prod_{\textnormal{holes in the path ensemble}} \mathsf{w}_{q,\kappa}\bigl( x-\tfrac t2+1\bigr),
		\qquad
		\mathsf{w}_{q,\kappa}(j) \coloneqq \kappa q^{j-(S+1)/2}-\frac{1}{\kappa q^{j-(S+1)/2}}.
	\end{equation}
	Here the holes are points $(t,x)$ such that $x\notin X(t)$,
	but $x$ satisfies the inequalities
	(equation eq:hexagon_constraints of the paper). In other words,
	holes are lozenges of the type
	\begin{tikzpicture}[baseline = (current bounding box.south),scale=.25]
		\draw[thick] (0,0)--++(1,1)--++(1,0)--++(-1,-1)--cycle;
	\end{tikzpicture}.
	For example, in (fig:tiling_and_path_picture of the paper), right, the holes are $(1,2),(2,1),(2,4),(3,0),(3,2),(3,5),(4,2),(4,3),(5,3)$.
	The probability weights are normalized so that the total probability of all path ensembles is $1$.
	We call the resulting probability measure the \emph{$q$-Racah measure} on nonintersecting path ensembles
	(equivalently, on lozenge tilings of the hexagon).","status":"unverified"}

When lambda_n = m/n -> 0 the tilted laws degenerate - the mass at 0 tends to 1 and the variance to 0 - so the Gaussian local limit theorem has to be replaced by a Poisson-regime one and glued to the Gaussian regime when m is comparable to n. That uniform statement does not appear to exist in the literature, and without it the union bound has no input at all. CONDITION OF FAILURE: m/n -> 0, which is exactly the regime the conjecture is about. The heuristic the route does give is still useful as a target: P(Y_1 >= k) is about w_k tau_n^k / Phi(tau_n) with tau_n = tau(m/n) -> 0, so n P(Y_1 >= k) -> 0 once k >= (1 + eps) log n / log(1/tau_n), and that threshold is o(log n) precisely because tau_n -> 0.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["edges are present independently with the same probability p (the binomial model; the uniform model G(n,m) has the analogous statement with m = (n/2)(log n + c))","the statement is about the window p = (log n + c)/n with c fixed as n grows","the Poisson approximation is for the count of isolated vertices; other small components are negligible in this window"],"created_at":"2026-09-02T07:51:33.049186+00:00","domain":"random graphs (hand-authored statement with hypotheses, 2026-09-02)","id":"claim_d041dda48ec32c5f52986ec651884b81edb7100fb10f41b597a06330618dfc66","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In the binomial random graph G(n,p) with p = (log n + c)/n for a fixed real c, the number of isolated vertices converges in distribution to a Poisson random variable with mean e^{-c} (the method of moments: the factorial moments of the count converge to those of the Poisson law), and the probability that G(n,p) is connected tends to exp(-e^{-c}) (Erdos and Renyi 1959, 1960). The obstruction to connectivity in this window is isolated vertices alone: P(G connected) - P(G has no isolated vertex) tends to 0. Consequently p = log n / n is a sharp threshold: for p = (1 - epsilon) log n / n the graph is disconnected with probability tending to 1 (with a growing number of isolated vertices), and for p = (1 + epsilon) log n / n it is connected with probability tending to 1. Below the threshold at p = c'/n with c' > 1 the graph already has a unique giant component but is disconnected.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T00:41:11.649386+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d0b953cde21bb02b4b8e3d38e587b807a952d847c7a7db4d0208735c2b3b09c7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm summary of arXiv:2411.13964, 'Long-time analysis of a pair of on-lattice and continuous run-and-tumble particles with ja'] Let $\gamma_L=(L-1)/\ell$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:59:53.386594+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d0e74f929ce062ec42ed39aee3972e3d5cfb03147c9f5ca658e0a0b4d6c6e977","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:complexZero of arXiv:2608.18320, 'Asymptotics for Beta-Splitting Trees via Homogeneous Fragmentations and Meromorphic Potent'] Let $\beta>0$ be noninteger and let $      \beta=n_\beta+\theta_\beta$ with $       n_\beta=\lfloor\beta\rfloor$.

If $n_\beta$ is even, then $f_\beta$ has exactly $n_\beta$
nonreal zeros, counted with multiplicity. They occur in conjugate pairs.

Suppose that $n_\beta$ is odd. Let $q_\beta$ be the number of zeros
of $f_\beta$ in the upper half-plane, counted with multiplicity, and,
for $0\leq k\leq n_\beta+1$, let $M_k(\beta)$ be the total
multiplicity of the real zeros of $f_\beta$ in $\mathcal I_k$. Then
each $M_k(\beta)$ is odd and
\begin{equation}
        2q_\beta
        +
        \sum_{k=0}^{n_\beta+1}
        \left[M_k(\beta)-1\right]
        =
        n_\beta+1.
\end{equation}
In particular, $f_\beta$ has at most $n_\beta+1$ nonreal zeros,
counted with multiplicity.

Consequently, for every noninteger $\beta>0$, only finitely many zeros
of $f_\beta$ are nonreal or multiple. All the remaining zeros are real
and simple.","status":"unverified"}

For $\sigma\in\{\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}$,

\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}
