{"assumptions":["Full-support verification in every variable context including paired S, without orientations","Independent fair algorithmic orientation tie coins; robust source Mis_infinity<=c on every data/coin outcome","All other hypotheses and sample protocol exactly as C013, specialized as stated"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T21:03:25.815424+00:00","domain":"statistical learning; calibrated generation; verified truth supports","id":"claim_d17d974d73b26ffacf67c5e666254e1060bc965f7a41bc88aeee96c154a3cb86","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT; proof (unaudited); independent review pending. # Positive-budget global risk differs from expected conditional minimax risk

T379-C014 v2: proof (unaudited), exact rational checks PASS. Target 2;
route-failure of a tempting extension, not a new exact global frontier.

Use the full-verifier, untagged experiment of C013 with d=3,K=2,r=1,
n=1,N>=7. Write lambda=1/(2N), kappa=1/2 and choose robust calibration
budget c=2lambda=1/N. The three pairs are numbered 0,1,2. Conditional
on the verifier output, relabel each certified candidate as 0. Each A
therefore has only candidate 0 true; S has both candidates true. This
relabeling preserves all factual probabilities. Fixed S contexts are
6,...,N-1. The verifier supplies no orientation labels.

One factual sample outside the certified sets resolves exactly one
pair; otherwise all three are unresolved. Thus P(U=3)=1-3lambda and
P(U=2)=3lambda, uniformly in every fixed world and verifier output.
C013's conditional worst-world frontier is zero at U=2 and lambda/2
at U=3. Its expectation is

 E V(c,U)=lambda/2-3lambda^2/2.                         (1)

## Feasible asymmetric algorithm

On U=2, use C013's attainer, removing all posterior mass 2lambda from
the unresolved outside-certificate atoms and adding it to fixed S.
This has zero false mass in every compatible world and Mis<=2lambda.

On U=3, leave pair 0 balanced. For each of pairs 1 and 2, if the factual
sample is a certified candidate in that pair, predict that its context
is A. Otherwise predict either orientation by an independent fair coin.
This is a rule using observed data only. Form two sets of outside-
certificate atoms:

* B1: both atoms of pair 0 and the predicted-S atom of pairs 1 and 2;
* B2: the predicted-A atom of pairs 1 and 2.

Assign g=lambda/4 to each of B1's four atoms, g=0 to B2's two atoms,
g=3lambda/2 to each of the six certified atoms, and
g=lambda+lambda/(N-6) to each of the 2(N-6) fixed S atoms.
These masses sum to lambda+9lambda+2(N-6)lambda+2lambda=1.

For ANY compatible orientation let t be the number of true S atoms
in B1 from pairs 1 and 2. The source mass of B1 is lambda(1+t),
that of B2 is lambda(2-t), and that of the six certified atoms is
9lambda, all with the latter group assigned equal g. The fixed S
group receives exactly 2lambda extra g mass. Uniformly coarsening p
within these four groups gives TV to g equal to

 [t lambda+(2-t)lambda+2lambda]/2=2lambda.

Each group has constant g; the exact score partition can only merge
groups. Uniform averaging is TV-contractive and fixes g, so actual
source Mis_infinity<=2lambda even at N=8 where two scores coincide.
This verifies robust feasibility for every orientation and every coin
realization, without assuming that the orientation predictions are right.

Let E be the number of wrong orientation predictions in pairs 1 and 2.
Exactly one atom of pair 0 is false. Therefore on U=3 the ACTUAL false
mass is

 H=(lambda/4)(1+E).                                   (2)

For example, if both predictions happen to be right, H=lambda/4 is
strictly below the conditional minimax value lambda/2. For the opposite
orientations the same generator has H=3lambda/4. Thus a conditional
worst-world lower bound is not a lower bound in each actual world.

## Expectation in each fixed world

The one-sample categories below are disjoint. Each expected H averages
only the algorithm's independent fair tie coins; their probabilities
are factual sampling probabilities in a fixed actual world.

| Observation | Probability | Expected H |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Outside certificate in any S of the three pairs | 3lambda | 0 |
| Certified atom in pair 0 | 3lambda | lambda/2 |
| Certified atom in true A of pair 1 or 2 | 4lambda | 3lambda/8 |
| Certified atom in true S of pair 1 or 2 | 2lambda | 5lambda/8 |
| Fixed S context | 1-12lambda | lambda/2 |

Multiplying and summing gives, in EVERY fixed world and conditional
on EVERY verifier realization,

 E H=lambda/2-7lambda^2/4
     < lambda/2-3lambda^2/2=E V(c,U),                  (3)

with strict gap lambda^2/4=1/(16N^2). Thus the global minimax expected
value is at most the left expression and is strictly below the expected
conditional worst-world value. For N=7 these values are 3/112 versus
11/392, separated by 1/784. No optimality of this algorithm is asserted.

This does not contradict C013, whose exact GLOBAL value was asserted
only at c=0; its positive-budget conditional statement and global bracket
remain intact. This auxiliary-route counterexample is not claimed to
score as a target narrowing. Source calibration definition: Kalai--
Vempala 2311.14648v3, Definitions 1--2 pp.8--9. All other work here is
an owner-own-work unaudited draft. Priority and independent audit pending.

Exact verification: logs/positive_budget_separation_check.json records
13824 compatible-world feasibility checks, 1920 sample/coin outcomes,
32 fixed-world expectation checks and 384 pointwise negative controls.
The runs include N=7,8,9,12; N=8 checks the merged-score case directly.
The construction and expectation derivation above cover every N>=7.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:36:23.134099+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d194b3d064b052a65f243782076070b4a27cbb94744ff15e5bd7ecc64100ab1c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem MainSeriesKeyLem of arXiv:2506.18207, 'Cartan's Path Development, the Logarithmic Signature and a Conjecture of Lyons-Sidorova'] Let $L_{1},\cdots,L_{r}$ be given vectors
of positive integers and let $n_{0}\geqslant1$. Suppose that $|L_{1}|+\cdots+|L_{r}|+n_{0}=k\leqslant N.$
Then one has 
\begin{align}
 & \sum_{\xi_{0}+\xi_{1}+\cdots+\xi_{r}=l-r}{\rm ad}_{A}^{\xi_{r}}\circ{\rm ad}_{\hat{F}_{w}(H_{L_{r}})}\circ\cdots\circ{\rm ad}_{A}^{\xi_{1}}\circ{\rm ad}_{\hat{F}_{w}(H_{L_{1}})}\circ{\rm ad}_{A}^{\xi_{0}}\big(\hat{F}_{w}(D_{n_{0}}\tilde{L})\big)\nonumber \\
 & =\sum_{i}\sum_{\mu=1}^{r+1}\Theta_{L_{\mu-1},\cdots,L_{1},n_{0}}^{i}\cdot(b_{i}^{i+n_{0}^{\mu-1}-1})^{l+1-\mu}\nonumber \\
 & \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \sum_{I\in{\cal W}_{\mu,r}}\frac{(-1)^{\varepsilon(I)}\Psi_{I,n_{0}^{\mu-1}}^{{\bf L}_{{\bf p},{\bf q}}^{\mu,r}}\cdot}{b_{(i_{\mu}),n_{0}^{\mu-1}}^{{\bf n}_{{\bf p},{\bf q}}^{\mu,r}}b_{(i_{\mu},i_{\mu+1}),n_{0}^{\mu-1}}^{{\bf n}_{{\bf p},{\bf q}}^{\mu,r}}\cdots b_{I,n_{0}^{\mu-1}}^{{\bf n}_{{\bf p},{\bf q}}^{\mu,r}}}E_{i-|{\bf n}_{{\bf p}}^{\mu,r}|,i+n_{0}^{\mu-1}+|{\bf n}_{{\bf q}}^{\mu,r}|}.
\end{align}
Here \textcolor{black}{$\mathcal{W}_{\mu,r}$} denotes the set of words $I=(i_{\mu},i_{\mu+1},\cdots,i_{r})\in\{\pm1\}^{r-\mu+1}$. Given such a word $I$, the vector $\mathbf{p}$
denotes the subword of $(\mu,\cdots,r)$ which records the locations
of $-1$'s in $I$ and ${\bf q}\triangleq(\mu,\cdots,r)\backslash{\bf p}$.
The quantity $\varepsilon(I)$ denotes the length of ${\bf p}$ (i.e.
number of $-1$'s in $I$). The function $\Theta_{L_{\mu-1},\cdots,L_{1},n_{0}}^{i}$
is defined by 
\[
\Theta_{L_{\mu-1},\cdots,L_{1},n_{0}}^{i}\triangleq\Theta_{L_{\mu-1},\cdots,L_{1},n_{0},i}(b_{i},b_{i+1},\cdots,b_{i+k-1}),
\]
where $\Theta_{L_{\mu-1},\cdots,L_{1},n_{0},i}$ is a suitable meromorphic
function in $m$ complex variables ($m\triangleq n_{0}+|L_{1}|+\cdots+|L_{\mu-1}|$)
whose shape depends on $(L_{1},\cdots,L_{\mu-1}),n_{0}$ and $i$.
The family $\{\Theta_{L_{1},\cdots,L_{\mu-1},n_{0}}^{i}\}$ of functions
satisfy the following property: for any integer $i$, $1\leqslant\nu\leqslant r$
and any sequence of vectors ${\bf V}=(V_{1},\cdots,V_{r})$, under
the one-dimensional reduction $b_{j}\triangleq b_{j}^{*}+w$ the function
\begin{equation}
w\mapsto\sum_{\sigma\in{\cal S}_{\nu}}\Theta_{V_{\sigma(\nu)},\cdots,V_{\sigma(1)},n_{0}}^{i}
\end{equation}
is analytic near $w=0$ and vanishes at $w=0$. When $\mu=1,$ the
function $\Theta_{L_{\mu-1},\cdots,L_{1},n_{0}}^{i}$ depends only
on $n_{0}$ and $i$. As a convention, if $\mu=r+1$ the summation
$\sum_{I\in{\cal W}(\mu,r)}$ in ((lem:MainSeriesKeyLem of the paper)) is
set to be one and $|{\bf n}_{{\bf p}}^{\mu,r}|=|{\bf n}_{{\bf q}}^{\mu,r}|\triangleq0$
. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-10T02:20:17.000000+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_d1aff6012d9090d15df966b06f09c902bac2d9363713ed918c38f0539f817728","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Rouché's theorem, named after Eugène Rouché, states that for any two complex-valued functions f and g holomorphic inside some region K with closed contour partial K (the boundary of K), if |g(z)| < |f(z)| on partial K, then f and f + g have the same number of zeros inside K, where each zero is counted as many times as its multiplicity. {"assumptions":["1 < p <= q < infinity and e^{-t} <= sqrt((p-1)/(q-1))","the standard Gaussian measure and the generator normalisation L = Laplacian minus x . gradient","the constant in the contraction is exactly 1 and is dimension-free"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.543694+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d1cf7dae8a836624c27473f7845ae1273f14a2ce5a18a3ccc841f38670804eeb","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (P_t) be the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup on L^p of the standard Gaussian measure on R^n. For 1 < p <= q < infinity, || P_t f ||_q <= || f ||_p for every f, PROVIDED e^{-t} <= sqrt( (p-1)/(q-1) ). The constant is exactly 1 - the semigroup is a contraction from L^p to the strictly larger L^q, not merely bounded - and the condition on t is sharp. Two consequences used constantly: taking p = 2 gives || P_t f ||_q <= || f ||_2 for e^{-t} = 1/sqrt(q-1); and restricting to the n-th Wiener chaos, where P_t acts as multiplication by e^{-nt}, gives the MOMENT COMPARISON || F ||_q <= (q-1)^{n/2} || F ||_2 for every F in the n-th chaos and every q >= 2. That comparison is dimension-free and is the reason all L^q norms on a fixed chaos are equivalent, with a constant depending only on the chaos order and q. GROSS'S THEOREM: hypercontractivity of (P_t) with these exponents is EQUIVALENT to the logarithmic Sobolev inequality Ent(f^2) <= 2 E|grad f|^2 for the same measure; each implies the other by differentiating or integrating the relation at q = q(t). The discrete-cube analogue with the noise operator is the Bonami-Beckner inequality, and the Gaussian case follows from it by the central limit theorem. [Nelson (1966, 1973); Gross (1975); see Bakry, Gentil and Ledoux, Analysis and Geometry of Markov Diffusion Operators, Chapter 5]","status":"unverified"}

Let F be a class of functions parametrized by p real parameters (more precisely, with log covering number of order p). Then with high probability every f in F that fits the data to within a constant fraction of the noise level (a fraction of the sum of the y_i's conditional variances remains unexplained) has Lipschitz constant at least of order sqrt(n d / p), up to logarithmic factors. Proof in two lines from facts that hold separately: exchangeability gives E[(X - X^L)^2] = 2 Var(X) - 2 Cov(X, X^L), and the symmetry of X^L - X gives E[(X - X^L)^2] = 2 E[((X^L - X)^+)^2]; equate. Consequences: Cov(X, X^L) <= Var(X) always; summing over a partition of blocks turns Efron-Stein into the exact statement Sum_L E[((X^L - X)^+)^2] = Sum_L (Var(X) - Cov(X, X^L)), so bounding the positive-part functionals a resampling engine consumes is EXACTLY the problem of lower-bounding the block covariances. Numerically checked on a nonlinear functional (relative difference 0.008 at 200,000 samples).","status":"derived_in_campaign"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.172936+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d243b4959dfd7e7460c2fc178f0421f2cd926005a7671c561fb675cb6606f1ba","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Ppn 70 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $q_0 \in [0,1)$ and $p \in \incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$, 
the mapping $f\mapsto \cM(q_0;p,f)$,
as a function from
 $L^1([q_0,1];[0,+\infty))$ to $P(\cP_2(\bbR))$, is uniformly continuous:
    \[
        d_\cH\Big(\cM(q_0;p,f),\cM(q_0;p,\tilde f)\Big)^2
        \le 2 \|f-\tilde f\|_1\,,
    \]
where we recall that $P(\cP_2(\bbR))$ is metrized by the Hausdorff distance \eqref{e:hausdorff}. As a consequence, we have the inclusion  $\sM^{\sv}(\alpha,q_0)\subseteq\sM^{\svi}(\alpha,q_0)$.

\begin{proof}
Let $f,\tilde f \in L^1([q_0,1];[0,+\infty))$, and suppose $(b,\sigma)\in\Adm(q_0;p,f)$. Let
	\[
	a(t)
	\equiv \min\bigg\{
	\bigg(\frac{\tilde{f}(t)}
	{f(t)}\bigg)^{1/2}
	,1\bigg\} \in[0,1]\,,
	\]
so in particular if $f(t)=0$ then we take $a(t)=1$. Then define $\tilde{b}_t\equiv a(t) b_t$, and $(\tilde{\sigma}_t-1)\equiv a(t)(\sigma_t-1)$, and note that $\sigma\ge0$ implies
$\tilde{\sigma}_t \ge 1-a(t)\ge0$.  By definition, $(\tilde{b},\tilde{\sigma})$ satisfies condition~\eqref{e:budget-f}, hence it belongs to $\Adm(q_0;p,f)$ as specified by Definition~\ref{d:X.adm}. Let $X,\tilde{X}$ be the 
processes defined by 
\eqref{e:formal.sde.main} with controls $(b,\sigma)$ and $(\tilde{b}, \tilde{\sigma})$ respectively, coupled with the same initialization
$X(q_0) =\tilde{X}(q_0) = 0$ and the same Brownian motion $B$. Then, applying the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality similarly as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:L2-bound-on-stochastic-control}, we have
    \begin{align*}
       &\bbE\Big[(X(1) - \tilde{X}(1))^2\Big]
        \le 2 \bbE\bigg[ \bigg(
            \int_{q_0}^1
            p'(t)^{1/2} |b_t - \tilde b_t|\,dt
        \bigg)^2 \bigg]
        + 2 \int_{q_0}^1 
        s(t)^2
        \bbE\Big[ (\sigma_t
        -\tilde{\sigma}_t
        )^2\Big]\,dt \\
    &\qquad\le 2 \int_{q_0}^1
    \E\bigg[ (b_t - \tilde b_t)^2
    + s(t)^2 
    \Big( (\sigma_t-1)
    -(\tilde{\sigma}_t-1)\Big)^2\bigg]\,dt \\
    &\qquad= 2 \int_{q_0}^1
    (1-a(t) )^2
\E\Big[(b_t)^2 + s(t)^2 
(\sigma_t-1)^2\Big]\,dt \\
&\qquad\le
2 \int_{q_0}^1 (1-a(t) )^2
	 f(t)\,dt
	 \le 2\int_{q_0}^1 \Big(f(t)^{1/2}-\tilde{f}(t)^{1/2}\Big)^2\,dt
\le 2\|f-\tilde{f}\|_1\,.
\end{align*}
This proves the first assertion of the proposition.
For the second assertion, we repeat the most relevant part of Definition~\ref{d:SDE.classification}:

The $\sv$ and $\svi$ classes  differ only in the budget constraint: the $\sv$ class satisfies condition~\ref{it:4.1}, while the $\svi$ class satisfies condition~\ref{it:4.3}. Therefore, let us suppose we have 
	\begin{align*}
	&(q_*=q_0,b,\sigma,w,p,\zeta=\delta_0,\zeta^\Ising)
	\in
	\Adm^{\sv}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)\,,\\
	&\mu = \mu(q_*=q_0,b,\sigma,p,\zeta=\zeta_0)
 \in \cM^{\sv}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)\,.\end{align*}
Define the budget functions
        \[
        f(t) = \max\bigg\{
            \bbE\bigg[
            (b_t)^2 + \frac{s(t)^2}{p(t)}(\sigma_t-1)^2\bigg],
            \frac{(\bbE w_t)^2}{\alpha}
        \bigg\}, \quad
        \tilde f(t) =\frac{(\bbE w_t)^2}{\alpha}\,.

{"assumptions":["f lower semicontinuous AND bounded below (boundedness below can be relaxed to a linear minorant);","the approximation is from BELOW and increasing.","For an upper semicontinuous f bounded above the dual sup-convolution gives a decreasing sequence of Lipschitz functions."],"created_at":"2026-09-12T14:01:51.298930+00:00","domain":"real analysis, convex analysis","id":"claim_d260b03e2f3333274936e1cd451507f7f128ecfe5257b820323708fee2f6bbf4","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X,d) be a metric space and let f : X -> (-infinity, +infinity] be lower semicontinuous and bounded below. For each n define f_n(x) = inf over y in X of ( f(y) + n d(x,y) ). Then each f_n is real-valued and n-Lipschitz, the sequence is nondecreasing, f_n <= f for every n, and f_n(x) increases to f(x) at every x. So a lower semicontinuous function bounded below is the pointwise increasing limit of Lipschitz functions. On a Hilbert space with the quadratic kernel (1/(2t))||x-y||^2 in place of n d(x,y) the same construction gives the Moreau envelope of a convex f, which is convex, differentiable with Lipschitz gradient, and increases to f as t decreases to 0.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Injectivity of the solution map does not imply continuity of its inverse","The range of the forward solution operator is a proper dense subspace","Conditional (Holder) stability requires an a priori bound at the initial time and degenerates as t tends to 0"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:49.107167+00:00","domain":"parabolic partial differential equations / inverse problems","id":"claim_d293093269857df5a07b55e84088e12c20119ec34fc0008386b758c4e986eecc","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Backward uniqueness says the map from $u(\\cdot,T)$ to $u(\\cdot,0)$ is injective; it says nothing about continuity of that map or about its range, and both fail badly -- the backward heat problem is the standard ill-posed problem of Hadamard. (1) No stability: on $U=(0,\\pi)$ with Dirichlet data, $u_k(x,t)=e^{-k^2t}\\sin(kx)$ has $\\|u_k(\\cdot,T)\\|_{C^m}\\le k^me^{-k^2T}\\to0$ for every $m$ while $\\|u_k(\\cdot,0)\\|_{L^2}=\\sqrt{\\pi/2}$ is fixed. Hence there is no estimate $\\|u(\\cdot,0)\\|\\le C\\|u(\\cdot,T)\\|$ in any pair of norms, and numerical backward continuation must be regularized. (2) No solvability: $e^{T\\Delta_D}$ has range $\\{\\psi=\\sum_kc_k\\sin(kx):\\sum_k e^{2k^2T}c_k^2<\\infty\\}$, a dense but meagre subspace of $L^2$; for instance $\\psi(x)=\\sum_{k\\ge1}k^{-2}\\sin(kx)\\in L^2$ is not $u(\\cdot,T)$ for any solution with $u(\\cdot,0)\\in L^2$, since that would require coefficients $e^{k^2T}k^{-2}$ at time $0$. Backward-in-time data must be analytic-like (exponentially decaying spectral coefficients). (3) What does survive is conditional stability of logarithmic or Holder type: under the a priori bound $\\|u(\\cdot,0)\\|_{L^2}\\le M$, log-convexity gives $\\|u(\\cdot,t)\\|_{L^2}\\le M^{1-t/T}\\|u(\\cdot,T)\\|_{L^2}^{t/T}$ for $0<t<T$, with the estimate degenerating exactly as $t\\downarrow0$. An auditor should flag any argument that uses backward uniqueness to produce a bound at the earlier time without such an a priori bound.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:48:30.920892+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d2ee27e3fff78f733aab52028fa5098ce9d2e317533b205d04d28538bd7ce8b0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 12 (Partial Fraction Decomposition, {\cite[Theorem 2) of arXiv:2609.00974, 'On Algebraic Integrability\\ of Vector Fields \\ with Rational Function Coefficients\\ tha'] {PFD_euclidean_1989}}]
    Let $k$ be a field of any characteristic.
    Let $f\in k(x)$ be a rational function. Let $f=\frac{a}{b}$ be a presentation of $f$, where $a,b\in k[x]$ and $(a,b)=1$. Let $b=\prod_{i=1}^n p_i^{m_i}$ be a decomposition into pairwise distinct irreducible factors. Then, there exists the \textbf{partial fraction decomposition} (PFD) of $f$:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item A polynomial $Q\in k[x]$.
        \item For each $1\le i\le n$ and $1\le j\le m_i$ a polynomial $s_{ij}\in k[x]$ with $\op{deg}(s_{ij})<\op{deg}(p_i)$.
    \end{itemize}
    These polynomials are\textbf{ unique} such that the following equality holds:
    \[
    f=Q+\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^{m_i} \frac{s_{ij}}{p_i^j}.
    \]
    In particular, if $k$ is algebraically closed, then, without any loss of generality, we can assume that $p_i=x-a_i$, so $s_{ij}\in k$ and we define:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item Polynomial Part: $P(f)=Q$
        \item Logarithmic Part: $L(f)=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{s_{i1}}{x-a_i}$, and we call $s_{i1}$ the residue of $f$ at $a_i$.
        \item Higher Part: $H(f)=\sum_{i>1}^n\sum_{j=1}^{m_i} \frac{s_{ij}}{{(x-a_i)}^j}$
    \end{enumerate}
    In total, we have $f=PFD(f)=P(f)+L(f)+H(f)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["ferromagnetic pairwise interactions; the exponential-decay conclusion needs finite-range (or exponentially decaying) couplings, since G(x,y) >= tanh(beta J_xy) by Griffiths' inequality","finite volume, or an infinite-volume Gibbs state for which the relevant correlation inequalities (e.g. Griffiths inequalities) hold","existence of a family of finite sets separating the two points of interest","the model's symmetry, such as spin-flip Z_2 symmetry, used in the classical derivation of the inequality"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T12:13:53+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d393890b51a665689a58b52bbeacddfa45ba308a4e92ffc9e53fce0dc9def944","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For the Ising model, or more generally ferromagnetic spin systems with finite-range interactions (with merely summable long-range couplings G(x,y) >= tanh(beta J_xy) by Griffiths' inequality, so exponential decay can fail), let G(x,y) = <sigma_x sigma_y> be the two-point function. The Simon-Lieb inequality bounds G(x,y) across any finite set Lambda separating x from y (x in Lambda, y outside Lambda) by G(x,y) <= sum_{u in Lambda, v not in Lambda} G_Lambda(x,u) beta J_{uv} G(v,y), with G_Lambda the two-point function of the model restricted to Lambda (free boundary condition) and beta the inverse temperature (forms with tanh(beta J_{uv}) in place of beta J_{uv} are also used), a one-step recursive bound relating the two-point function across a separating surface to the two-point function up to the boundary of Lambda times the coupling crossing it. Iterating the inequality over a sequence of nested separating sets, such as concentric boxes, yields exponential decay of G(x,y) once the associated generating function drops below its self-consistency threshold, giving a classical route, predating and complementary to the Duminil-Copin-Tassion approach, to sharpness of the phase transition and analyticity of the free energy in the high-temperature regime. It does not determine the exact critical temperature directly, only characterizing it implicitly through the inequality's self-consistency condition, and it applies specifically to ferromagnetic spin systems with a workable notion of finite separating surfaces; it does not transfer automatically to percolation, which uses combinatorially different, though philosophically related, inequalities. Typical failure: Iterating the Simon-Lieb inequality across many nested separating surfaces while implicitly assuming a geometric decay rate that has not actually been verified to be summable; turning the one-step recursive bound into exponential decay requires checking that the relevant generating function, summing G times J over the boundary, lies strictly below its self-consistency threshold, and this check is exactly where the difficulty of locating beta_c resides, so skipping it silently assumes the conclusion. Canonical reference: Simon, 1980, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Lieb, 1980, Communications in Mathematical Physics.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["a specified target distribution with a known, workable Stein characterizing operator or equation","an auxiliary coupling structure connecting to W, such as an exchangeable pair, a size-biased coupling, or a dependency graph","sufficient smoothness or explicit derivative bounds on the solution f of the Stein equation for the specific target distribution","control of the resulting expectation bound in terms of the coupling's own closeness or error parameters"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.996944+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d39aa2bb9e25135cdd42c23538dfcea568834d63bc2b2b834c74380b75fd1b82","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). To bound the distance, in Kolmogorov, Wasserstein, or total variation metric, between the law of a random variable W and a target distribution, classically the standard normal but also Poisson, exponential, and other targets, Stein's method characterizes the target law via a characterizing (Stein) equation: for the normal, E[f'(Z) - Zf(Z)] = 0 for all sufficiently smooth f if and only if Z is standard normal. Given a test function h, one solves the associated Stein equation f'(x) - xf(x) = h(x) - E[h(Z)] for f, and then bounds E[f'(W) - Wf(W)] directly using structural information about W, typically supplied by an auxiliary coupling such as an exchangeable pair, a size-biased coupling, or a dependency-graph/local-dependence construction, without going through characteristic functions or moment matching. This yields explicit, often near-optimal-rate, quantitative bounds on distributional distance for sums of dependent or weakly dependent random variables and for counts in combinatorial structures, settings where classical central limit theorem machinery is difficult to apply directly because of dependence. It does not automatically give a good bound for an arbitrary random variable, since constructing the right coupling matched to the problem's dependence structure is the substantive and typically hardest step, and the quality of the final bound is entirely determined by the quality of that coupling. Typical failure: Treating Stein's method as an automatic black box that produces a good rate on its own, when in fact the rate is entirely determined by the quality of the coupling constructed for the specific problem, such as an exchangeable pair with a large error term or a dependency graph with high maximum degree; a poorly constructed coupling yields a valid but far-from-optimal, or even useless, bound, and this construction step, rather than the abstract Stein equation itself, is where nearly all the technical difficulty and risk of error lies. Canonical reference: Stein, 1972, Proceedings of the Sixth Berkeley Symposium on Mathematical Statistics and Probability; Chen, Goldstein and Shao, Normal Approximation by Stein's Method, 2011, Springer.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:41:29.024738+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d3e2c77622f8024859707cc8bf75fa031012b848d26a17bad25860cbfb4c5410","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2608.26490, 'Bayesian methods and Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms for curve reconstruction and poin'] For a fixed $n=1,\dots,N$, let $r_n$ be a random position generated according to the sampling scheme in \cref{eq:un,eq:sn,eq:pi,eq:L}. Then \cref{eq:rn} follows.
\begin{proof}
Given a geometry $G$, the position $r_n$ specifies and is specified by a global coordinate $v_n$ that equals the arc-length from $h^1$ along the curve $\mathcal{G}$ encoded by $G$. Consequently, it suffices to show that $v_n$ is uniformly distributed over $[0,L^G]$ where $L^G=\sum_{k=1}^K L_k^G$ is the total arc-length of $\mathcal{G}$.

Conditional on $s_n$ and $u_n$, such global coordinate $r_n$ is obtained deterministically by
\begin{align*}
v_n|s_n,u_n
&\sim\delta_{C^G_{s_n-1}+u_nL_{s_n}^G},
\end{align*}
where the cumulative segment lengths are defined by
\begin{align*}
C^G_0&=0,
\\
C^G_k&=\sum_{k'=1}^K L^G_{k'},
&
k&=1,\dots,K.
\end{align*}
According to the law of total probability, we obtain the marginal
\begin{align*}
p(v_n)
&=
\sum_{s_n=1}^K\int_0^1du_n\,
p(v_n|s_n,u_n)p(s_n,u_n),
\end{align*}
and, because of independence in \cref{eq:sn,eq:un}, we obtain
\begin{align*}
p(v_n)
&=
\sum_{s_n=1}^K\int_0^1du_n\,
p(v_n|s_n,u_n)p(s_n)p(u_n)
\\
&=
\sum_{s_n=1}^K\int_0^1du_n\,
\delta_{C^G_{s_n-1}+u_nL_{s_n}^G}(v_n)\pi_{s_n}^G
\\
&=
\sum_{s_n=1}^K\int_0^1du_n\,
\frac{1}{L_{s_n}^G}\delta_{u_n}\left(\frac{v_n-C^G_{s_n-1}}{L_{s_n}^G}\right)\frac{L_{s_n}^G}{L^G}
\\
&=\frac{1}{L^G}
\sum_{s_n=1}^K\int_0^1du_n\,
\delta_{u_n}\left(\frac{v_n-C^G_{s_n-1}}{L_{s_n}^G}\right)
\\
&=\frac{1}{L^G}
\end{align*}
indicating that, indeed, $v_n$ is uniformly distributed over $[0,L^G]$ which completes our proof. Here, the last equality holds because, from the $K$ different summands $\int_0^1du_n\,
\delta_{u_n}\left(\frac{v_n-C^G_{s_n-1}}{L_{s_n}^G}\right)$, only one integrates over the singularity.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T00:32:56.100267+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d418d5c7eb52ca818ca1e9c4347b8a9a10fdde559c2dab7d205f0e3ac6e5705f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition of arXiv:2411.13030, 'Classification of the limit shape for 1+1-dimensional FPP'] Let $G$ be non-deterministic and $B>t_{0}(G)$. For any edge $e$ of the lattice, we define the \emph{detour height} as the distance to an edge with small passage time:
\[
k_B(e):=\min\left (k\ge 1 | \,  \min( \tau(e+(0,k)),\tau(e-(0,k)))< B\right).
\]
The \emph{detour} of $e$ is the path that starts at one edge of $e$, goes $k_B(e)$ edges upwards or downwards, passes the horizontal edge with weight less than $B$ and goes $k_B(e)$ edges down back to the other endpoint of $e$. The \emph{detour time} $dt_B(e)$ is the passage time of the detour.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:32:28.952293+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d49600deb4bf0f37cf93bd3dbb35ca6a2e5e7a8b2f6730e47126fdeb1a6fc14f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:degeneracy of arXiv:2608.16915, 'Exact mean--covariance dynamics of the Weber field in the stochastic Lagrangian representa'] In centre and separation variables $c=\tfrac{x+y}{2}$, $r=x-y$,
\[
  (\nabla_x+\nabla_y)^2=\Delta_c,\qquad
  u(x)\cdot\nabla_x+u(y)\cdot\nabla_y
  =\frac{u_++u_-}{2}\cdot\nabla_c+(u_+-u_-)\cdot\nabla_r,
\]
with $u_\pm=u(t,c\pm r/2)$. The diffusion therefore acts on the centre variable only;
there is no $\Delta_r$. In particular the model equation
$\partial_tH-\nu(\nabla_x+\nabla_y)^2H=0$ admits every bounded profile
$H(t,x,y)=h(x-y)$ as a stationary solution, so no estimate can extract regularity in
$x-y$ from the common-noise diffusion alone.","status":"unverified"}

Let $(a_1, b_1)$ and $(a_2, b_2)$ be two buildings of $\landsc$. We say that $(a_2, b_2)$ is visible from $(a_1, b_1)$ if it is in range and there are no buildings above the segment from $(a_1, b_1)$ to $(a_2, b_2)$. In other words, if the following conjunction of events holds true:
\[\{(a_2, b_2)\text{ is in range from } (a_1, b_1)\} \cap \below{[a_1, a_2]}{(a_1, b_1)}{\frac{b_2-b_1}{a_2-a_1}}.\]

Thanks to this, we can define the relaying scheme $\tau$ as
\[\tau_{\mathrm{R}} (x, y, \landsc) = (x_b, y_b) := \underset{\substack{(a, b) \in \landsc\cap \mathrm{R}+(x, y) \\(a, b) \text{ visible from }(x, y)}}{\text{argmax}} \frac{b-y}{a-x}.\]
When this is well defined, and $\tau (x, y, \landsc) = (-\infty, -\infty)$ otherwise.

The blockage angle and its tangent are defined as usual in this context","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:57:28.725379+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d537d3ff9908c551b174be0816f534f466c2ed0a3a84ff44d09efc5670c6c38f","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 24 (Discrete local sewing) of arXiv:2609.01190, 'Rough differential equations on manifolds via natural bundles'] Let $\theta\in (0,1)$ and let $\Pcal=\{S = U_0<U_1<\ldots<U_N = T\}$ (with $N\in\Nsf$, $N\geq 2$) be a partition of the interval $[S,T]$ satisfying the following condition:

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.161511+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d595f6e2ed6ee8c526511a13862ba9d97f8c5f841ce447757b85a65986f3311f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Cor 12 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2,\epsilon\ge0$, 
and for $(\lambda,\mu) \in \Lambda$, 
the mapping
$(\lambda,\mu)\mapsto S_\star(\lambda,\mu;\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2)[\epsilon]$,
is continuous with respect to the Hausdorff metric $d_H$.

\begin{proof}
Fix $\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2,\epsilon\ge0$ and $\delta'>0$. By Lemma~\ref{l:S.star.cts.dH}, there exists $\delta>0$ such that if 
$(\lambda,\mu)\in\Lambda$ and 
$(\lambda',\mu')\in B_\delta(\lambda,\mu)$, then the sets
\begin{align*}
K&\equiv S_\star(\lambda,\mu;\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2)\,,\\
K'&\equiv S_\star(\lambda',\mu';\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2)
\end{align*}
lie within Hausdorff distance $\delta'$ of one another.
For any $\hat{\YY}\in K[\epsilon]$, there exists $\YY\in K$ with
$\|\hat{\YY}-\YY\|_2\le\epsilon$, and then there exists $\YY'\in K'$ with
$\|\YY-\YY'\|_2\le\delta'$. By Lemma~\ref{l:D.mu.continuity.w}, 
since $\hat{\YY}\in\cD_\mu$,
there exists $\tilde{\YY}\in\cD_{\mu'}$
with $\|\hat{\YY}-\tilde{\YY}\|_1\le\delta/\iota^2$. Then
	\[
	\|\tilde{\YY}-\YY'\|_2
	\le\|\tilde{\YY}-\hat{\YY}\|_2
	+ \|\hat{\YY} - \YY\|_2
	+ \|\YY - \YY'\|_2
	\le \epsilon + \delta' + \frac{\delta}{\iota^2}
	\le \epsilon + 2\delta'\,,
	\]
where the last inequality can be arranged by taking $\delta$ small enough (depending on $\delta'$).
Since $\YY'$ and $\tilde{\YY}$ both lie in $\cD_{\mu'}$, it follows by convexity of $\cD_{\mu'}$ that $\tilde{\YY}$ lies within distance
$2\delta'$ of a vector $\hat{\YY}' \in K'[\epsilon]$. We then finally have
	\[
	\|\hat{\YY}-\hat{\YY}'\|_2
	\le \|\hat{\YY}-\tilde{\YY}\|_2
		+ \|\tilde{\YY}-\hat{\YY}'\|_2
	\le\frac{\delta}{\iota^2} + 2\delta'
	\le 3\delta'\,.
	\]
This implies that $K[\epsilon]$ and $K'[\epsilon]$ lie within Hausdorff distance $3\delta'$ of one another, and the claim follows.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.160484+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d5c69f5a9def5c43ebde26912fc4597acbdf2cf9f029a385ff2b04326fee72b7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 5 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\YY = (\vBBb,\vvvv,\vUUu,\vwww)$ be the random vector defined in \eqref{e:freeprob.random.YY}, and $\mu(\bG,\omega)$ be defined in \eqref{e:lambda-mu-random}.
    For any $\epsilon'' > 0$ there exists $c = c(\alpha,\iota,\epsilon'') > 0$ such that
    \[
        \P\bigg(
            \inf\big\{
                \|\tilde \YY - \YY\|_2 : \tilde \YY \in \cD_{\mu(\bG,\omega)}
            \big\} \le \epsilon''
        \bigg)
        \ge 1 - e^{-cN}\,.
    \]
\begin{proof}
Throughout the proof, we abbreviate $(\lambda,\mu) = (\lambda(\bG,\omega),\mu(\bG,\omega))$, although we keep in mind that they are permitted to depend on $(\bG,\omega)$. We will construct $\tilde\YY = (\tilde\vBBb,\tilde\vvvv,\tilde\vUUu,\tilde\vwww) \in \cD_\mu$ such that $\|\tilde \YY - \YY\|_2 \le \epsilon''$ on an event with probability $1-e^{-cN}$.
    We set $(\tilde\vBBb,\tilde\vUUu) = (\vBBb,\vUUu)$, and $\tilde\vvvv = \max(\vvvv,\vUUu)$ where the maximum is taken entrywise.
    Note that for all $j\in [r]$, the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality gives
    \baln
        \vUUu_j - \vvvv_j
        &=
        \bigg(
            \frac{1}{|B_j|} \sum_{a\in B_j}
            \frac{(\bmeta^a,\bar{\bx})(\barbg^a,\hat{\by})}{N}
        \bigg)^2
        - \frac{1}{|B_j|} \sum_{a\in B_j}
        \frac{(\barbg^a,\hat{\by})^2}{N} \\
        &\le 
        \bigg(
            \frac{1}{|B_j|} \sum_{a\in B_j}
            \frac{(\barbg^a,\hat{\by})^2}{N}
        \bigg)
        \bigg(
            \frac{1}{|B_j|} \sum_{a\in B_j} \frac{(\bmeta^a,\bar{\bx})^2}{N} - 1
        \bigg)\,,
    \ealn
from which it follows that
    \[
        |\tilde\vvvv_j - \vvvv_j|
        = (\vUUu_j - \vvvv_j)_+
        \le \bigg(
            \frac{1}{|B_j|} \sum_{a\in B_j}
            \frac{(\barbg^a,\hat{\by})^2}{N}
        \bigg)
        \bigg|
            \frac{1}{|B_j|} \sum_{a\in B_j} \frac{(\bmeta^a,\bar{\bx})^2}{N} - 1
        \bigg|\,.
    \]
    By Lemma~\ref{l:fp-gc} and \eqref{e:wishart.bound.repeated}, with probability $1-e^{-cN}$,
    \[
        \frac{1}{|B_j|} \sum_{a\in B_j}
        \frac{(\barbg^a,\hat{\by})^2}{N}
        \le \frac{\|\hat{\by}\|^2 \|\bG\|_\op^2}{N|B_j|}
        \le \frac{(2N^{1/2})^2 (CN^{1/2})^2}{NM 
		\lambda_j}
        \le \frac{4C^2}{\alpha \iota}\,.
    \]
Set $\delta > 0$ small enough that
    \[
        [(1-\delta)^2,(1+\delta)^2] \subseteq \bigg[
            1 - \frac{\epsilon''\alpha\iota^2}{8C^2},
            1 + \frac{\epsilon''\alpha\iota^2}{8C^2}
        \bigg]\,.
    \]
    Since $(\bmeta^a : 1\le a\le M)$ are standard gaussians in $\bbR^N$ independent of $\bar{\bx}$ and $B_j$, we have
    \[
        \frac{1}{|B_j|} \sum_{a\in B_j} \frac{(\bmeta^a,\bar{\bx})^2}{N}
        \stackrel{d}{=}
        \frac{\|\bar{\bx}\|^2}{N} \cdot \frac{\|\bz\|^2}{|B_j|}
    \]
    where $\bz$ is a standard gaussian in $\bbR^{|B_j|}$.
    By Lemma~\ref{l:fp-gc} and a standard gaussian tail bound,
    \[
        \max\bigg\{
            \bigg|\frac{\|\bar{\bx}\|^2}{N} - 1\bigg|, 
            \bigg|\frac{\|\bz\|^2}{|B_j|} - 1\bigg|
        \bigg\} \le \delta
    \]
    with probability $1-e^{-cN}$.
It follows from the assumption on $\delta$ that
    \[
        \bigg| \frac{\|\bar{\bx}\|^2}{N} \cdot \frac{\|\bz\|^2}{|B_j|} - 1 \bigg|
        \le \frac{\epsilon''\alpha\iota^2}{8C^2}\,.
    \]
Combining the above bounds gives
    \beq
        |\tilde\vvvv_j - \vvvv_j|
        \le \frac{4C^2}{\alpha \iota}
        \cdot \frac{\epsilon''\alpha\iota^2}{8C^2}
        = \frac{\epsilon'' \iota}{2}\,.
    \eeq
    By a union bound, the above holds for all $j\in [r]$ with probability $1-e^{-cN}$.
    

    Next we set $\tilde\vwww$.
    If $(\mu,\vwww) \ge 1$ (resp. $(\mu,\vwww) < 1$), let $\tilde\vwww \in [0,+\infty)^s$ be any vector satisfying $\tilde\vwww \le \vwww$ (resp. $\tilde\vwww\ge \vwww$) with $(\mu,\tilde\vwww)=1$.
    Note that
    \[
        (\mu,\vwww)
        = \sum_{j=1}^s \mu_j \cdot 
        \frac{1}{|\BIsing_j|} \sum_{i\in \BIsing_j}
        (\be_i,\hat{\by})^2
        = (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-23T08:56:01.666630+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_d5dbdbda36dc4a8ea82d4464af1fb18e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematics, Minkowski's theorem is the statement that every convex set in $\\mathbb {R} ^{n}$ which is symmetric with respect to the origin and which has volume greater than $2^{n}$ contains a non-zero integer point (meaning a point in $\\mathbb {Z} ^{n}$ that is not the origin). {"assumptions":["C^1 regularity of both the integrand and the motion of the domain;","ONLY the NORMAL component of the boundary velocity appears, since tangential motion does not change the region.","Forgetting the boundary term - differentiating under the integral sign as if the domain were fixed - is the standard error when a domain depends on the parameter."],"created_at":"2026-09-12T14:06:45.871083+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations, continuum mechanics","id":"claim_d5ffd999e68cc75ac5f00be8da802c8611d11673b26d8fe31148291f77d131e2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Omega(t) be a family of bounded domains in R^n moving with a C^1 velocity field, whose boundary points move with normal speed V_n, and let f(x,t) be C^1. {"assumptions":["independence of the matrix entries or summands, each with finite moments up to the order being matched, typically four","matching of the first four (or the relevant number of) moments between the actual entry distribution and the Gaussian reference, up to a specified small error","sufficient smoothness, typically several bounded derivatives, of the test function F used in the swapping argument","a separate mechanism, such as local relaxation flow or a priori rigidity estimates, to transfer from smooth-test-function statements to the actual eigenvalue statistics of interest"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.997682+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d62d01195d629cfaace32a339dd8b3931fc1ee479898a520c29aeefdbd2472a7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). The Lindeberg exchange (swapping) principle proves distributional limit theorems by replacing the summands or matrix entries of a random object one at a time with Gaussian (or other reference) analogues, bounding the resulting change in E[F] for a sufficiently smooth test function F via a Taylor expansion at each swap, provided the relevant moments, typically up to third or fourth order depending on the smoothness assumed of F, agree between the original and replacement distributions. In random matrix theory, the Tao-Vu four-moment theorem states that for Wigner matrices, local eigenvalue statistics such as gap distributions at a fixed bulk location are universal, independent of the specific entry distribution, provided the first four moments of the off-diagonal entries match those of the Gaussian (GOE/GUE) case up to a small, quantified error, with a weaker three-moment matching sufficing for some global statistics; this is the primary technical engine behind Wigner-Dyson-Mehta universality results beyond the exactly solvable Gaussian ensembles. It does not apply directly to test functions or statistics that are insufficiently smooth, requiring a separate regularization step, typically via a local relaxation flow or Dyson Brownian motion argument, to pass from smooth test functions to eigenvalue counting functions or individual eigenvalue locations, and it requires the specific moment-matching order assumed, with fewer matched moments giving correspondingly weaker conclusions. Typical failure: Applying the four-moment theorem's universality conclusion directly to a non-smooth statistic, such as the exact location or gap of a specific eigenvalue or an indicator-type event, without the additional Green's function comparison or local relaxation machinery needed to pass from smooth test functions to such statistics; the raw Lindeberg swapping argument by itself only controls E[F(eigenvalues)] for smooth F, and asserting the full local universality conclusion from moment matching alone skips this substantial extra step. Canonical reference: Lindeberg, 1922, Mathematische Zeitschrift; Tao and Vu, 2011, Acta Mathematica; Erdos and Yau, A Dynamical Approach to Random Matrix Theory, 2017, American Mathematical Society (Courant Lecture Notes).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["mu is a T-invariant probability measure","partitions are finite or have finite static entropy"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T02:00:35.438227+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, entropy","id":"claim_d643cf301f6f85cdf8c9e8de5370d025f0501ae66a766e597b735e7610396bee","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(X, \\mathcal{B}, \\mu, T)$ be a probability-preserving system. For a finite (or countable, with finite entropy) measurable partition $\\xi = \\{A_1, \\dots, A_k\\}$ put $H_\\mu(\\xi) = -\\sum_i \\mu(A_i) \\log \\mu(A_i)$ (with $0 \\log 0 = 0$), and $\\xi^n_0 = \\bigvee_{j=0}^{n-1} T^{-j}\\xi$, the partition into sets $A_{i_0} \\cap T^{-1}A_{i_1} \\cap \\dots \\cap T^{-(n-1)}A_{i_{n-1}}$ (the $n$-step itineraries). The entropy of $T$ relative to $\\xi$ is $h_\\mu(T, \\xi) = \\lim_{n\\to\\infty} \\frac1n H_\\mu(\\xi^n_0)$ (the limit exists because $n \\mapsto H_\\mu(\\xi^n_0)$ is subadditive; it also equals $\\inf_n \\frac1n H_\\mu(\\xi^n_0)$ and $\\lim_n H_\\mu(\\xi \\mid \\xi^n_1)$). The Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy is $h_\\mu(T) = \\sup_\\xi h_\\mu(T, \\xi)$ over finite partitions, in $[0, \\infty]$. Facts used constantly: $h_\\mu(T, \\xi) \\le H_\\mu(\\xi) \\le \\log k$; $h_\\mu(T, \\xi) \\le h_\\mu(T, \\eta) + H_\\mu(\\xi \\mid \\eta)$ for partitions $\\xi, \\eta$; $h_\\mu(T^m) = m\\, h_\\mu(T)$ for $m \\ge 1$; the Kolmogorov-Sinai generator theorem: if $\\xi$ is a generator ($\\bigvee_{j \\ge 0} T^{-j}\\xi$ generates $\\mathcal{B}$ mod $\\mu$, or $\\bigvee_{j\\in\\mathbb{Z}}$ for invertible $T$) then $h_\\mu(T) = h_\\mu(T, \\xi)$; and if $\\xi_m$ is an increasing sequence of partitions generating $\\mathcal{B}$ then $h_\\mu(T, \\xi_m) \\uparrow h_\\mu(T)$. On a compact metric space, partitions of diameter $< \\varepsilon$ with $\\varepsilon \\to 0$ are such a sequence. The map $\\mu \\mapsto h_\\mu(T)$ on invariant measures is affine, but it is NOT in general continuous or even upper semicontinuous in the weak* topology; upper semicontinuity holds when $T$ is expansive (and for $C^\\infty$ maps of compact manifolds by Newhouse), which is what guarantees measures of maximal entropy exist in those cases.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0119-chaos-in-directed-polymers-in-dimensions-d-3","No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:26:45.047474+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d6482caf2a89870dd211b46bdfbffdf2f3b0e5124bf83645b39a0be761eb5611","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Check which steps of the d = 2 proof are dimension-dependent. Result: The source's d = 1+1 proof establishes superconcentration of the free energy (variance o(n)) via hypercontractivity and then chaos from superconcentration through the general equivalence theorem; the dimension-dependent step is the variance bound Var(log Z_n) = O(n/log n), obtained from the Benjamini-Kalai-Schramm influence inequality applied to the free energy with the influence of a single site bounded by the expected overlap of two polymers at that site, whose sum over sites is the expected overlap, of order n in the strong disorder regime. The BKS argument is dimension-free provided the polymer is in the strong disorder phase (positive overlap); in d >= 3 the strong disorder phase exists at low temperature (Comets-Yoshida), so the variance bound O(n/log n) transfers and superconcentration follows; the equivalence theorem then gives chaos at the level of the overlap between the polymers at slightly perturbed environments. So the obstruction the source mentions ('certain parts do not work in higher dimensions') must be in the identification that the overlap in the strong-disorder phase is of order n (needed for the influence sum to be order n and the BKS gain to be meaningful): in d >= 3 at low temperature the overlap is positive but the known lower bounds are only qualitative (positive limit of the overlap along the endpoint), not quantitative along the whole path. Rigorous partial: superconcentration (Var log Z_n = o(n)) in d >= 3 at low temperature follows from BKS if the expected path overlap is of order n, which is a consequence of the strong disorder characterisation via the endpoint overlap only if the overlap is positive at a positive fraction of times; this last step is plausible but I found no reference proving it in d >= 3. Reduction recorded. Obstruction: Quantitative (order n) path overlap in the strong disorder phase for d >= 3.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:34:20.799485+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d6544775dff5ffdceba5e0dcf81fee54f33d32943ffe0cb239fbd82a8b9bec16","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop 35 of arXiv:2609.02261, 'Quantization and process'] Let $A$ be a bounded   operator  in

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:51:11.961894+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d65917282c488bc9eb7ea0eef4f9980cf22c8524a931df98ba7ff5fc74cb9b66","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 5 of arXiv:2608.08242, 'Bang--bang representation of $3\times 3$ embeddable stochastic matrices'] The set $R_n\subseteq\mathcal M_+$ consists of the matrices $A$ for which

{"assumptions":["free entries independent standard Gaussian, H = W/sqrt(n)","f Lipschitz; no other regularity","the bound is around the mean, which is not identified here"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.544234+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d6862b4e3c8c63b6e20e398a7e0d94968e582011da1837ac900c1fbb41e8f5be","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let W be a real symmetric n by n matrix whose entries W_{ij} for i <= j are independent standard Gaussians, and let H = W / sqrt(n) with eigenvalues lambda_1, ..., lambda_n. Let f be Lipschitz with constant ||f||_L. Then for every t > 0, P( | (1/n) sum_{i=1}^n f(lambda_i) - E (1/n) sum_i f(lambda_i) | >= t ) <= 2 exp( - n^2 t^2 / (4 ||f||_L^2) ). The exponent scales like n^2 t^2, not n t^2: linear eigenvalue statistics are FAR more concentrated than an average of n independent samples would be, and their fluctuations are of order 1/n rather than 1/sqrt(n). This is a consequence of the eigenvalue repulsion built into the matrix model, and it is one of the few places where a naive independence heuristic gives the wrong exponent by a whole power of n. The result needs only Lipschitz f - no smoothness, no boundedness - and it is a statement about concentration around the MEAN, not about identifying the mean, which is the separate content of Wigner's theorem. The constant 4 in the denominator is tied to the stated normalisation (independent standard Gaussians for the free entries, then divided by sqrt(n)); a different convention rescales it. [standard; the argument is Hoffman-Wielandt plus Gaussian Lipschitz concentration, e.g. Anderson, Guionnet and Zeitouni, An Introduction to Random Matrices, Theorem 2.3.5]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a metric space","Y is a topological space (metric suffices, and is the usual case)","f: X x Y -> R is separately continuous: continuous in each variable with the other held fixed","for the residual-set-of-continuity-points consequence, X x Y is a Baire space (e.g. X, Y complete metric)","values are real (or in a metric space in which the partition-of-unity averaging makes sense, e.g. a locally convex space)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:07:38.815145+00:00","domain":"real analysis, Baire classes, separate continuity","id":"claim_d6a3e76764dc5394e33eca6c37c02af4c15a58c1386d4a14e4041123cff48df9","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Recall that a real function g on a topological space Z is of BAIRE CLASS ONE if it is the pointwise limit of a sequence of continuous real functions on Z. THEOREM (Baire for R x R; Rudin in this generality): let X be a METRIC space, let Y be a topological space (in particular a metric space), and let f: X x Y -> R be SEPARATELY CONTINUOUS, i.e. for each fixed y the map x -> f(x,y) is continuous on X and for each fixed x the map y -> f(x,y) is continuous on Y. Then f is of Baire class one on X x Y: there is a sequence of continuous functions f_n: X x Y -> R with f_n(x,y) -> f(x,y) for every (x,y). CONSEQUENCE (Baire's theorem on functions of the first class): if in addition X x Y is a Baire space - for instance if X and Y are both complete metric, or both locally compact Hausdorff - then the set of points at which f is JOINTLY continuous is a dense G_delta subset of X x Y, and its complement is meagre. So a separately continuous function is jointly continuous at 'most' points, in the sense of category. CLASSICAL EXTENSION: a function of n variables that is separately continuous in each variable is of Baire class n - 1 (Lebesgue); the case n = 2 is the theorem above. SHARP EDGES. (a) Separate continuity does NOT give joint continuity: f(x,y) = xy/(x^2 + y^2) with f(0,0) = 0 is separately continuous on R^2, indeed continuous on each line through the origin, and is discontinuous at the origin (it equals 1/2 on the diagonal). The theorem therefore cannot be strengthened to continuity anywhere in particular, only to a residual set of continuity points. (b) The metric structure of the first factor is essential to the proof, which builds a locally finite partition of unity on X; for arbitrary topological factors the statement requires extra hypotheses and should not be quoted in that generality. (c) The consequence about continuity points needs X x Y to be a Baire space; on a non-Baire domain 'dense G_delta' carries no information, and the conclusion is vacuous. (d) Baire class one is a statement about POINTWISE limits; it gives no uniform convergence, and the limit functions f_n constructed in the proof are not monotone in n. (e) The converse is false and is not being claimed: plenty of Baire class one functions on a product are not separately continuous.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:09:59.299744+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d6f29a6841e41be5378eec1bc15b94989400ec777035a848e170aed8277b1c90","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn contFV of arXiv:2608.06500, 'Free energy of Ising models under a spectral condition'] For $\alpha>0$, an \emph{$\alpha$-good potential} is a
    function $V:\mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$,  $(h,\varphi)\mapsto V_h(\varphi)$ 
    which is twice continuously differentiable 
    
    with 
    \[
        \sup_{\substack{|h|\le C \\ \varphi\in\mathbb{R}}}
        \left| \frac\partial{\partial h} V_h'(\varphi)\right| < \infty
    \]
    for all $C>0$ and $V_h''(\varphi)\in[\alpha,\alpha^{-1}]$
    for all $h,\varphi\in\mathbb{R}$ (where  $V_h'$ and $V_h''$ are the first and
     second  derivatives of $V_h$ with respect to $\varphi$). In other words, this family of potential
    functions is smooth and uniformly strongly convex with Lipschitz
    gradient, and furthermore $V_h'$ is Lipschitz in $h$. For
    $\text{\boldmath $h$}\in\mathbb{R}^N$, we define the potential

    \begin{align*}
V_\text{\boldmath $h$}(\text{\boldmath $\varphi$}):=\sum_{i=1}^NV_{h_i}(\varphi_i)\, .
\end{align*}

    Given an $\alpha$-good potential $V$ and
    a weighted graph $G=(\text{\boldmath $B$},\text{\boldmath $h$})$ on $[N]$ with $\text{\boldmath $B$}\succ-\alpha\text{\boldmath $I$}$,
    we consider the Gibbs measure on $\mathbb{R}^N$ with base measure
    $e^{-V_\text{\boldmath $h$}(\text{\boldmath $\varphi$})}{\rm d}\text{\boldmath $\varphi$}$ and quadratic Hamiltonian
    $-\frac12\<\text{\boldmath $\varphi$}, \text{\boldmath $B$}\text{\boldmath $\varphi$}\>$ and denote its free energy density
    by

    \begin{align*}
F_V(G)=F_V(\text{\boldmath $B$},\text{\boldmath $h$})=\frac1N \log \int_{\mathbb{R}^N} \exp\left( -\frac12
\<\text{\boldmath $\varphi$}, \text{\boldmath $B$}\text{\boldmath $\varphi$}\> \right) e^{-V_\text{\boldmath $h$}(\text{\boldmath $\varphi$})} {\rm d}\text{\boldmath $\varphi$}.
\end{align*}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Real compatible factors; differentiable loss depending only on the product","Constant-step summation is conditional on the stated sufficient decrease and lower bound"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T20:54:55.722211+00:00","domain":"LoRA factor gradient descent","id":"claim_d76476f244c48b4335361c25d6818f6fe34988dbd5c9e5aa0346ab1ea240500d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"For real factors B of size m-by-r and A of size r-by-p, and differentiable product loss F(BA), put G_B=grad F(BA) A^T, G_A=B^T grad F(BA), and D=AA^T-B^TB. Simultaneous factor gradient descent with step eta has the exact identity D_next-D=eta^2(G_A G_A^T-G_B^T G_B); the first-order terms cancel. Thus ||D_next-D||F<=eta^2(||G_A||F^2+||G_B||F^2). If a fixed eta>0 additionally satisfies the sufficient-decrease inequality f_next<=f-a eta ||grad f||F^2 for f(B,A)=F(BA), some a>0, and f is bounded below by f_star along the iterates, summation gives ||D_t-D_0||F<=(eta/a)(f_0-f_star). This implication assumes descent; it does not establish it or prove arbitrary-step convergence. The trace identity (||B||F^2+||A||F^2)^2<=r[||AA^T-B^TB||F^2+4||BA||F^2] then converts bounds on imbalance and product into a factor bound. Du-Hu-Lee, Algorithmic Regularization in Learning Deep Homogeneous Models: Layers are Automatically Balanced, arXiv:1806.00900, Theorem 2.2 gives continuous-time Gram invariance; Appendix B, Claim B.1 expands the discrete square-loss update. The conditional constant-step summation and trace inequality here are elementary method consequences, not their full GD convergence theorem. Their Theorem 3.1 instead uses small Gaussian initialization of both factors and decreasing steps.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:27:56.784061+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d770fd00e3be841d57d0052ff66900cc13317779c3f82c6c82309eeeb0bc3c20","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 29 (Geometric estimates from initial data) of arXiv:2608.31171, '\bf Finite-energy spacetimes with torus symmetry. \\ \Large Cauchy stability of Einstein--'] \bse
Fix an admissible Navier--Stokes triple $(\mathscr F,\chi,\mathscr B)$ as defined in \autoref{def-pot-admissible-triple}.
Let $(\Phi,\Psi,\zeta)$ with $\Phi=(\Jperp,\Jpar,\Pbb,\Qbb)$ and $\Psi=(\ell,\log\Omega,\Kpar)$ be a sufficiently regular dissipated-energy or particle-production Einstein--Navier--Stokes areal flow $(\Phi,\Psi,\zeta)$ on $[t_0,t_1]\times\Tbb^3$.  Denote the values at time $t=t_0$ by
\be
(\mathring\Phi,\mathring\Psi,\mathring\zeta) \coloneqq (\Phi,\Psi,\zeta)(t_0,\cdot) \quad \text{on } \Tbb^3 .
\ee
Then the following estimates hold, where implied constants depend on the Navier--Stokes potential $\chi$ and on $t_0,t_1$, but not on the relaxation structure~$\mathscr B$ nor on the solution $(\Phi,\Psi,\zeta)$.
\bei
\item \emph{Spatial energy.} The fluid variables, and the first-order geometric variables $\Pbb,\Qbb$ have
  \bel{estimate-SE}
    \int_{\{t\}\times \Tbb^3} \Bigl( T_\chi^{00} + \Ebf_0(\Pbb,\Qbb) \Bigr) \dVtrois
    \lesssim \|\mathring\Phi\|_{\mathrm{energy}} , \qquad t\in[t_0,t_1] .
  \ee

\item \emph{Conformal length and volume.}
  \bel{estimate-LV}
  \aligned
  & \mathcal L(t) \leq \mathcal L(t_0) , \quad \mathcal V(t) \leq |t/t_0|^{3/4} \mathcal V(t_0) , \qquad t_0 \leq t \leq t_1 < 0 \quad \text{(future-contracting regime)},
  \\
  & \mathcal L(t) \geq \mathcal L(t_0) , \quad \mathcal V(t) \geq |t/t_0|^{3/4} \mathcal V(t_0) , \qquad 0 < t_0 \leq t \leq t_1 \quad \text{(future-expanding regime)}.
  \endaligned
  \ee
  Furthermore, the minimum conformal length $\mathcal L_{\min}=\min_{t\in[t_0,t_1]} \mathcal L(t)\geq 0$ is reached at $t=t_1$ in the future-contracting regime and at $t=t_0$ in the future-expanding regime.
\eei
In the future-contracting regime, subsequent estimates require the assumption that $\mathcal L_{\min}>0$ and depend on $1/\mathcal L_{\min}$, which is \emph{not bounded} by the initial data.  In the future-expanding regime $\mathcal L_{\min}>0$ is part of the initial data.
The constants $C_1,C_2,\dots$ below depend on $\mathcal L_{\min}$ and on the finite-energy and bounded-variation norms of initial data.
\bei
\item \emph{Both-sided bounds on conformal length and volume.}
  \bel{both-sided-LV}
  (C_1)^{-1} \leq \mathcal L(t) \leq C_1 , \qquad (C_2)^{-1} \leq \mathcal V(t) \leq C_2 .
  \ee

\item \emph{Bounded variation in space.} The lapse, twist and conformal length measure satisfy
  \bel{spatial-bv}
    \|\ell\|_{\BVac(0,1)} + \|(\log\Omega,\Kpar)\|_{\BVac(\Tbb^3)}
    \leq C_3 , \qquad t \in [t_0,t_1] .
  \ee

\item \emph{Temporal integrals.} The (not necessarily positive) spatial stress~$T_\chi^{11}$ admits integrals on constant-$x$ slices
\bel{temporal-stress}
\biggl| \int_{[t_0,t_1]\times\Tbb^2} \Bigl( T_\chi^{11} + E_0(\Pbb,\Qbb) \Bigr) \dVundeux \biggr|
\leq C_4 , \quad x\in\Sbb^1 .
\ee
\eei
Assume further that the potential~$\chi$ is torus-adapted (\autoref{def-NS-torus-adapted}) and the stress-tensor satisfies the \emph{coercive stress condition} (\autoref{def-Tchi-coercive}, below), and assume that the parallel momentum per particle is bounded at initial time in the sense that $2|T_\chi^{02}|+2|T_\chi^{03}|\leq C^\parallel\Numb_\chi^0$ for some constant~$C^\parallel>0$.
Then \eqref{temporal-stress} are completed to an $L^2$~control of the whole fluid momentum~$\Jbb$ along timelike slices, and the following estimates are satisfied.
\bei
\item \emph{Bounded variation in time.} The lapse, twist and conformal length measure satisfy
  \bel{bv-time-bound}
    \|\ell\|_{\BVac(\Interval)} + \|(\log\Omega,\Kpar)\|_{\BVac(\Interval\times\Tbb^2)}
    \leq C_5 , \qquad x \in \Sbb^1 .
  \ee
\eei
Altogether, under the assumed coercive stress condition, the finite-energy and bounded-variation norms \eqref{equa-flow-energy-norm}--\eqref{equa-flow-variation-norm} of the areal flow are bounded by a function of its initial data and, in the future-contracting regime, of~$\mathcal L_{\min}$.
\ese (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["d is an integer >=2","Independent standard Gaussian input blocks a,b in R^d","Noiseless binary labels and disagreement loss","Independent training examples; randomized learners allowed","Orthogonal equivariance is required only for the single-target corollary","0<epsilon<c/2; fixed 0<delta<1 for the stated asymptotic; use epsilon<c/4 in the expected-risk formula"],"created_at":"2026-10-22T02:42:45.469501+00:00","domain":"statistical learning theory","id":"claim_d78c59562ff1370a5f041f4a2d1471299a379d138c7e30cc148d6d85948c6dce","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let d>=2 be an integer, let X=(a,b) have the standard Gaussian law on R^(2d), and let H_d={h_U(a,b)=sign(a^T U b): U in O(d)}. Define rho(h,g)=Pr[h(X)!=g(X)], and let D(H_d,rho,t) be its t-packing number. There is an absolute c>0 such that D(H_d,rho,t)>=(c/t)^(d(d-1)/2). Consequently any learner which, for each h in H_d, achieves disagreement error at most epsilon with probability at least 1-delta from n independent labeled examples must satisfy n >= (d(d-1)/2) log_2(c/(2epsilon)) + log_2(1-delta). This is useful for 0<epsilon<c/2 and fixed delta in (0,1). The class H_d is contained in the orthogonal orbit of f(x)=sign(sum_{i=1}^d x_i^2-sum_{i=d+1}^{2d} x_i^2). Thus an orthogonally equivariant learner of this single target under the standard Gaussian law has a fixed-confidence Omega(d^2 log(1/epsilon)) lower bound as epsilon decreases below an absolute constant. With expected disagreement risk epsilon, the corresponding explicit bound is (d(d-1)/2) log_2(c/(4epsilon))-1. This is an existing result of Li, Zhang and Arora, not new research; it concerns classification, not square-loss regression.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:25:41.597731+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d7dc728e4f45aa1bb5e1654709fbed1a4422baded7a647ef548d66d29c62a225","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition defn:axiomatic_shf of arXiv:2608.11603, 'Continuous-time directed polymers to the Critical SHF via moments'] {}
	A process $\mathcal{Z}^{\theta_{\star}}$ is called a Stochastic Heat Flow with strength $\theta_{\star}$, or $\mathsf{SHF}(\theta_{\star})$, if
    \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}, ref=\thedefinition\textup{(\roman*)}]
    	\item
    	 \textbf{(Continuity)} $\mathcal{Z}^{\theta_{\star}} = \{\mathcal{Z}^{\theta_{\star}}_{s,t}\} \in C(\mathbb{R}_{\leqslant}^{2}, \measspace{\mathbb{R}^2 \times \mathbb{R}^2})$. 
    	\item
    	\textbf{(Chapman--Kolmogorov)} For all $t_{0} < t_{1} < t_{2}$, there exists a sequence $\{u_{\ell}\}$ in $\mathcal{L}^{2}(\mathbb{R}^2)$ for which the operator $\psi \mapsto u_{\ell} \ast \psi$ converges strongly to the identity, such that the difference $\mathcal{Z}^{\theta_{\star}}_{t_{0},t_{1}} \bullet_{\ell} \mathcal{Z}^{\theta_{\star}}_{t_{1},t_{2}} - \mathcal{Z}^{\theta_{\star}}_{t_{0},t_{2}}$ is well-defined and converges to $0$ vaguely, in probability as $\ell \to \infty$.
    	\item 
    	\textbf{(Independent increments)} For all $ t_{0}  < \cdots < t_{k}$, the random variables $\mathcal{Z}^{\theta_{\star}}_{t_{0},t_{1}},  \ldots \mathcal{Z}^{\theta_{\star}}_{t_{k-1}, t_{k}}$ are independent.
    	\item
    	\textbf{(Delta-Bose Moments)} For $n = 1,2,3,4$, $s<t$ and $h, h' \in \mathcal{L}^{2}(\mathbb{R}^2)$, the following holds:
    	\begin{equation*}
    		\mathbf{E} \Big(\Big\langle h, \mathcal{Z}^{\theta_{\star}}_{s,t} h' \Big\rangle \Big)^{n} = \Big\langle h^{\otimes n}, \mathcal{Q}^{[\![n]\!], \theta_{\star}}(t-s) h'^{\otimes n} \Big\rangle \, .
    	\end{equation*} 
    \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.751964+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_d808bc15a0303b9690e36c075fb8407e6aa1c7ddf475cac89c2eb1a5636847d8","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The monotone convergence theorem for an INCREASING sequence 0 <= f_1 <= f_2 <= ... needs no integrability hypothesis at all: integral f_n dmu increases to integral (lim f_n) dmu in [0, infinity]. The downward statement is FALSE without an extra hypothesis. On R with Lebesgue measure, f_n = 1_{[n, infinity)} decreases pointwise to 0, yet integral f_n = infinity for every n. The correct downward version requires f_1 in L^1 (equivalently, on a finite measure space with a bounded f_1): if f_n decreases pointwise to f and f_1 is integrable then integral f_n -> integral f, which follows from applying upward monotone convergence to f_1 - f_n. FATOU'S LEMMA, integral liminf f_n <= liminf integral f_n for f_n >= 0, is strict in general and its strictness is exactly the escaping-mass and concentrating-mass phenomena: with f_n = 1_{[n, n+1]} on R, liminf f_n = 0 pointwise so the left side is 0 while the right side is 1; with f_n = n 1_{(0, 1/n)} on [0,1] the left side is 0 and the right side is again 1. Reverse Fatou, limsup integral f_n <= integral limsup f_n, requires an integrable UPPER bound f_n <= g in L^1, and fails without one: for f_n = n 1_{(0, 1/n)} on [0,1] the pointwise limsup is 0 with integral 0, while limsup integral f_n = 1, so the inequality is violated - and no integrable g dominates all the f_n. [standard; e.g. Folland, Real Analysis, 2nd ed., Theorems 2.14 and 2.15]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.345721+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d811d5a4f342b2ca990a543b016e9be538d352a4041c33ed5bb124df76084441","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 139 (IAMP mimicking BOGP SDE) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Recall from Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main} 
  the initial conditions $X(q_0)\sim\zeta$ and $Y(q_0)\sim\zeta^\Ising$. Now let
  \[
  \breve{X}(q_0)\equiv0\,,\quad
  \breve{Y}(q_0)\equiv
    \frac{Y(q_0) \sqrt{q_0}}{(\bbE[Y(q_0)^2])^{1/2}}\,.\]
If $Y(q_0)\equiv0$ then we (somewhat arbitrarily) set $\breve{Y}(q_0)\sim\cN(0,q_0)$.
Then $\E[\breve{Y}(q_0)^2]=q_0$ in either case,
and it follows from
assumption~(\ref{i:IAMP-main-init}) of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main} 
that
  \beq
    \bbE\bigg[
      \Big(
  Y(q_0)-\breve{Y}(q_0)
  \Big)^2\bigg]
  =\Big(
   \E[Y(q_0)^2]^{1/2}
   -  (q_0)^{1/2}\Big)^2
    \leq \Big|
    \bbE[Y(q_0)^2]-q_0\Big|
    \leq \epsilon\,.
    \eeq
We initialize vectors $\bx^0,\prxbx^0\in\R^M$ and 
$\by^0,\prxby^0\in\R^N$ as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item The coordinates of $\prxby^0$ are sampled i.i.d.\ from $\Law(Y(q_0))=\zeta^\Ising$. If $\bbE[Y(q_0)^2]>0$, then we set 
	\[\by^0 = \bigg(
	\frac{q_0}{\bbE[Y(q_0)^2]}
	\bigg)^{1/2} \prxby^0\,.\]
If $\bbE[Y(q_0)^2]=0$, then we let $\by^0\sim\mathcal{N}(0,q_0 I_N)$. 

\item the coordinates of $\prxbx^0$ are sampled i.i.d.\ from $\Law(X(q_0))=\zeta$, and we set $\bx^0 = \bzero \in \R^M$.
\end{itemize}
For fixed $\delta$ we abbreviate $ b^\ell(x)\equiv b_{q_0+\ell\delta}(x) \equiv b(q_0+\ell\delta,x)$, etc. We then introduce the vectors
\beq
\begin{aligned}
\bb^{\ell}
&\equiv
b^\ell(\prxbx^{\ell})
\equiv
b_{q_0+\ell\delta}(\prxbx^{\ell}) \in \bbR^M\,,\\
\bsig^{\ell}
&=
\sigma^\ell(\prxbx^{\ell})
\equiv
\sigma_{q_0+\ell\delta}(\prxbx^{\ell}) \in \bbR^M,
\\
\bw^{\ell}
&\equiv
w^\ell(\prxby^{\ell})
\equiv w_{q_0+\ell\delta}(\prxby^{\ell})
 \in \bbR^N, 
\end{aligned}\eeq
where the functions $b^\ell,\sigma^\ell,w^\ell$ are applied coordinate-wise. Let 
  \beqc_\ell(\epsilon)
  \equiv
  \bigg[\alpha\delta
  \Big( \budget(q_0+\ell\delta)+\epsilon-\Cost(q_0+\ell\delta) \Big)
    \bigg]^{1/2}\,.
  \eeq
As in \eqref{eq:IAMP-fully-general-fixed}, each $\bar{\bg}^\ell$ is an independent standard gaussian vector in $\R^N$. We let $\gamma(\ell,\delta)$ and $\prxgamma(\ell,\delta)$ be certain positive scalars, defined in \eqref{eq:proxy-C-ell-delta-def} below.  The IAMP iterates are as follows, with $\bu^0=\bzero \in \R^N$ and $\bm^{-1} = \bm^0=\bzero\in\R^M$: 
\begin{align}

  \prxby^{\ell+1}
  -
  \prxby^{\ell}
  &=
  \prxgamma(\ell,\delta)^{-1}
  \bw^{\ell}\odot(\bu^{\ell+1}-\bu^{\ell})
  \in\bbR^N,
  \\

  \by^{\ell+1}
  -
  \by^{\ell}
  &=
  \gamma(\ell,\delta)^{-1}
  \bw^{\ell}\odot(\bu^{\ell+1}-\bu^{\ell})\in\bbR^N\,,
  \\

  \bu^{\ell+1}
  -
  \bu^{\ell}
  &\equiv
  (\bA_\ell)^{\top}
  \big(
    \bm^{\ell}
    -
    \bm^{\ell-1}
  \big)
  + \delta^{1/2}
  (\bJ_{\ell+1})^\top\bb^\ell
  + c_\ell(\epsilon)
  \bar{\bg}^{\ell}
  -
  \ons_{\bu,\ell}
  \in\R^N\,,\\

  \bv^{\ell}&=\bA_{\ell}\by^{\ell}-\ons_{\bv,\ell-1}\in\bbR^M\,,
  \\

  \bm^{\ell+1}-\bm^{\ell}
  &=p(q_0+\ell\delta)^{-1}
  \big(\bsig^{\ell}
  -
  1
  \big)
  \odot
  \big(\bv^{\ell+1}-\bv^{\ell}\big)
  \in \bbR^M\,,
  \\

  \prxbx^{\ell+1}
  -
  \prxbx^{\ell}
  =
  \bx^{\ell+1}
  -
  \bx^{\ell}
  &=
  \bsig^{\ell}\odot
  \big(\bv^{\ell+1}-\bv^{\ell}\big)
  +
  \delta
  p'(q_0+\ell\delta)^{1/2}
  \,
  \bb^{\ell}
  \in 
  \bbR^M
  \,.
\end{align}
The Onsager terms $\ons_{\bu,\ell}$ and $\ons_{\bv,\ell-1}$ will be defined in \eqref{e:u.combined.ons} and \eqref{e:v.combined.ons} below. 
\textbf{We denote the above iteration by $\IAMP_N(\sigma,b,w,p,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising,\delta)$.} 
In the notation of Remark~\ref{rmk:omega-general-seed}, 
this algorithm will have random seed given by
	\beq
	\omega= \Big(
	\bG_\circ,
	(\bar\bg^\ell)_{1\le\ell\le\ubl},
	\bx[0], \by[0]\Big)\,.
	\eeq
For a fixed realization of $\omega$, this IAMP iteration will be a $C(L,\epsilon)$-Lipschitz function of the random matrix $\bG$ on an event with probability $1-e^{-cN}$, and the algorithm witnessing Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-main} is its globally Lipschitz extension.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:21:52.417902+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d81de109f8db617a4ce43541ecc65b56b261c3ecf52a6553603a73298e3547ad","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 110 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] In the setting of Lemma~\ref{Checkzw}, uniformly in any compact subset of $\mathcal{D}$, we have the asymptotic expansion as $\N \rightarrow \infty$
\[
\log \Z^{\textnormal{ref}}_{\N} = \N^2 \F^{[0],\textnormal{ref}} + \theta \hat{n}\,\N \log \N + \N\F^{[1],\textnormal{ref}} + \frac{1}{12}\bigg(\theta + \frac{1}{\theta} - 3\bigg)\log \N + \F^{[2],\textnormal{ref}} + O\bigg(\frac{1}{\N}\bigg).
\]
The coefficients $(\F^{[p],\textnormal{ref}})_{p = 0}^{2}$ are given using the notation \eqref{Ddefzw} by the following expressions
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\F^{[0],\textnormal{ref}} & = \frac{1}{\theta}\bigg[\mathrm{LLlog}(\theta\hat{n}) + \mathrm{LLlog}(\hat{D}' + \theta\hat{n}) - \mathrm{LLlog}(\hat{D}')  - \!\! \sum_{k,\ell = 1}^{2} \big(\mathrm{LLlog}(\hat{D}'_{k,\ell} + \theta\hat{n}) - \mathrm{LLlog}(\hat{D}_{k,\ell}')\big)\bigg] \\
\F^{[1],\textnormal{ref}} & = -  \hat{n}\log\big(2\pi \Gamma(\theta)\big) + \frac{\theta -1}{2\theta}\bigg[\mathrm{Llog}(\theta\hat{n}) - 5\big(\mathrm{Llog}(\hat{D}' + \theta\hat{n}) - \mathrm{Llog}(\hat{D}')\big) \\

Write B(Z) for the Borel sigma-algebra of a space Z and B(X) tensor B(Y) for the product sigma-algebra, i.e. the sigma-algebra on X x Y generated by the measurable rectangles A x B with A in B(X) and B in B(Y). (ii) If X and Y are both SECOND COUNTABLE (each has a countable base of open sets), then equality holds: B(X x Y) = B(X) tensor B(Y). In particular this applies to separable metric spaces, so B(R^(m+n)) = B(R^m) tensor B(R^n), and to Polish spaces and to countable products of second countable spaces. Practical consequence: for second countable targets, a map into X x Y is Borel measurable exactly when both components are, and Borel functions of two variables are jointly measurable in the product sense - which is what lets Fubini-Tonelli be applied to Borel functions. WHERE IT FAILS: second countability is not a technicality. Let X be a set of cardinality strictly greater than the continuum equipped with the discrete topology, so that B(X) is the full power set and X x X is discrete. The diagonal {(x,x)} is closed, hence Borel in X x X, but by a classical theorem (B. V. Rao) the diagonal of X belongs to P(X) tensor P(X) if and only if the cardinality of X is at most the continuum. So B(X x X) strictly contains B(X) tensor B(X). The underlying reason is structural: every set in a product sigma-algebra is already measurable with respect to a countably generated pair of sub-sigma-algebras, so a product sigma-algebra can only see countably many 'coordinates' at a time, while the product topology of a non-second-countable space produces open sets that need uncountably many. A second warning of the same kind: for Lebesgue sigma-algebras the analogous equality is FALSE - the Lebesgue sigma-algebra of R^(m+n) is strictly larger than the product of the Lebesgue sigma-algebras of R^m and R^n; it is its completion.","status":"unverified"}
