{"assumptions":["All restricted four-point, unit-norm centered-ReLU teacher and paired nonzero initialization assumptions of C010","Independent label noise amplitude sigma_e=c_e sqrt(kappa) eta_e^(1/4)~sqrt(kappa)e^(9/4)","Noise-averaged clean risk; simultaneous both-layer GD step 1/2; fixed nu in (0,1]","Even width limit precedes feature-scale limit; local windows only; eta_e is spectral ratio, not GD step size"],"created_at":"2026-10-22T00:34:50.829441+00:00","domain":"learning theory","id":"claim_d89b9de19b9c660b1053843fd221195d71bd568e8a0d66ceffe03289fef81a6d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"# Joint low-noise central-window bifurcation

T267 / Target 2 / C012 / proof draft (unaudited); novelty unestablished.
This is a local, rescaled noise-onset result in C010's restricted model.
It is not an exact global two-critical-noise-level theorem.

## 1. Precise scaling and result

Use C010's four-point stratified design, centered unit-norm ReLU teacher,
paired nonzero initialization with fixed nu in (0,1], both-layer GD with
step 1/2, and label-noise-averaged clean risk Q. Let alpha=alpha_e and
let b_h denote C009's full-kernel rates. Set

eta_e=(b2+b12)/b1 ~ e,
rho_e=kappa sqrt(eta_e), kappa>0 fixed,
sigma_e=2alpha sqrt(rho_e),
t0_e=log(1/sqrt(eta_e)).

Here sigma_e is the amplitude of independent symmetric label noise.
It is asymptotic to sqrt(kappa) e^(9/4). The network step size remains
1/2; eta_e in this proof is a spectral ratio, not that step size.

Let F_e(z) be the continuously interpolated frozen risk divided by
alpha^2. Define its central-time version
G_e(s)=F_e((t0_e+s)/b1). Then, uniformly on compact real s intervals,

G_e'(s)/(2 eta_e) -> H_kappa(s)
       =kappa exp(-s)-exp(-2s)-1,
G_e''(s)/(2 eta_e) -> H_kappa'(s)
       =-kappa exp(-s)+2exp(-2s).

Equivalently, the normalized value differences converge locally uniformly:

[G_e(s)-G_e(0)]/(2 eta_e) -> V_kappa(s)-V_kappa(0),
V_kappa(s)=-kappa exp(-s)+(1/2)exp(-2s)-s.

If kappa>2, define z_+=(kappa+sqrt(kappa^2-4))/2 and
z_-=(kappa-sqrt(kappa^2-4))/2. The frozen curve has a central strict local
minimum at scaled time tending to s_min=-log z_+, and a subsequent strict
local maximum at scaled time tending to s_max=-log z_-.
In small fixed neighborhoods of those two points there is exactly one
frozen stationary point of the indicated type for sufficiently small e.
The actual nonlinear discrete-GD risk has strict descent-rise-descent
witnesses near these points, with probability tending to one in the
iterated even-width-then-feature-scale limit. Its interval minimizers and
maximizers on these separate neighborhoods have the same scaled limits.
Its resulting central local peak obeys

b1 k_peak-t0_e -> s_max,
k_peak ~ (2pi/nu^2) e^(-1) log(1/e),

in that iterated probabilistic sense. The first assertion refers to every
maximizer in a chosen sufficiently small neighborhood of s_max; it does
not assert that all actual extrema are unique.

For 0<kappa<2, the FROZEN interpolated risk is strictly decreasing on any
fixed compact central s window for sufficiently small e. No monotonicity
of actual finite-width risk is asserted. At kappa=2 the leading derivative
has a degenerate zero; this proof does not resolve its finite-e unfolding.
Thus 2 is a threshold for this limiting central-window shape, not a proved
global critical noise level or a global absence theorem.

## 2. Uniform derivative limit

The exact frozen curve is
F_e(z)=rho_e(1-exp(-b0 z))^2
      +sum_(h=1,2,12)[exp(-2b_h z)+rho_e(1-exp(-b_h z))^2].
Its nonconstant h derivative with respect to z is
2 b_h q_h [rho_e-(1+rho_e)q_h], q_h=exp(-b_h z).
At z=(t0_e+s)/b1, q1=sqrt(eta_e)exp(-s). Therefore its contribution to
G_e'(s)/(2eta_e) is exactly
kappa exp(-s)-(1+kappa sqrt(eta_e))exp(-2s).

For h=2,12, b_h/b1=O(eta_e) and
q_h=1+O(eta_e log(1/eta_e)), uniformly on compact s sets. Their combined
contribution to G_e'(s)/(2eta_e) tends to -1, since their b_h/b1 weights
sum to eta_e. Differentiating with respect to s makes their contribution
tend to zero: the extra b_h/b1 factor is O(eta_e).
The constant-mode term and its s derivatives tend to zero after division
by eta_e. Indeed b0/b1 is of order 1/e, t0_e is of order log(1/e), and
exp[-(b0/b1)(t0_e+s)] decays faster than every power of e on compact s
sets. These exact formulas prove both uniform derivative limits.
Integration from zero proves the uniform value-difference limit.

## 3. Limiting stationary points and risk witnesses

Writing z=exp(-s)>0, H_kappa=kappa z-z^2-1.
For kappa>2 its roots are z_+>1 and z_-<1 with product one.
At s_min=-log z_+, H_kappa'=z_+ sqrt(kappa^2-4)>0;
at s_max=-log z_-, H_kappa'=-z_- sqrt(kappa^2-4)<0.
Thus V has a strict minimum then a strict maximum. Compact uniform
convergence of H and H' gives a unique frozen critical point near each,
of the same type; the derivative is bounded away from zero outside small
root neighborhoods inside a fixed central compact window.

Choose delta>0 sufficiently small. The four scaled times
s_min-delta, s_min, s_max, s_max+delta are increasing and have strict
limiting value inequalities descent-rise-descent. Rounded integer times
floor((t0_e+s)/b1) have scaled grid error at most b1, which tends to zero.
The associated frozen risk differences therefore have strictly positive
margins of order alpha^2 eta_e. The same value convergence provides a
strict gap away from the unique minimum or maximum in each separate
small neighborhood.

For 0<kappa<2, completion of the square gives
H_kappa=-(z-kappa/2)^2+kappa^2/4-1<0 for every z>0.
Its maximum is strictly negative, so compact uniform derivative
convergence implies the stated frozen decrease on each fixed compact
s window. This does not control scaled times escaping all compacts.

## 4. Actual nonlinear GD and order of limits

For each fixed e, rho_e, alpha_e and all interval endpoints are fixed
numbers, and all involved integer times lie below T_e=ceil(e^(-5/2))
for sufficiently small e. Labels remain bounded. C010's independent-pair
finite-horizon comparison therefore controls every involved actual risk
uniformly through T_e as width grows, including all sixteen noise
patterns. Multiplication of the error by the fixed positive factor
1/(alpha_e^2 eta_e) preserves convergence to zero for this FIXED e.
It follows, first taking width to infinity then e to zero, that the
actual risk value differences converge to the same V differences and
inherit the strict four witnesses. The positive local value gaps transfer
the interval minimizers and maximizers to s_min and s_max. No derivative
comparison for the actual nonlinear network is needed or claimed.

Finally eta_e~e, b1~nu^2 e/(4pi), so t0_e~(1/2)log(1/e) and the displayed
peak time follows. This theorem concerns a different joint-noise regime
from C011's fixed-rho phase comparison; neither proof exchanges limits.

## 5. Exact concrete witness certificate, kappa=5/2

Here z_+=2, z_-=1/2. Use z values 3,2,1/2,1/4 in decreasing order,
so the corresponding s=-log z and integer times increase. The primitive
values are respectively

-3+log 3, -3+log 2, -9/8-log 2, -19/32-2log 2.

Their required margins are
log(3/2), 15/8-2log 2, log 2-17/32, all strictly positive.
For fully checkable bounds, log(3/2)>1/3 and
7/12<log 2<3/4 follow from integrals of 1/t: the lower bound splits
[1,2] into [1,3/2] and [3/2,2] and uses right-endpoint rectangles.
For the upper bound write t=1+x and use
1/(1+x)<=1-x/2 on [0,1], strict in the interior, since the difference
has numerator x(1-x)/2. The margins exceed 1/3,3/8,5/96 respectively.
This certifies a specific joint-noise witness choice by exact rational
bounds, not a floating-point estimate of a bifurcation.

## Remaining scope

The exact finite-e global onset, the degenerate kappa=2 case, interaction
with the initial constant-mode transient, iid sampling, fixed-positive
noise and all-time nonlinear dynamics remain open. These restrictions
matter: a central-window derivative result cannot imply that no other
double-descent pattern occurs elsewhere in time. Pairing and finite

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:51.726283+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis / dispersive PDE","id":"claim_d948b0ea69eecd49bd6d6367620cfaf6003daf10d9fece613e380a2beca5623f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: the Christ–Kiselev lemma passes from an untruncated space-time bound L^p_t → L^q_t to its causal truncation ∫_{s<t} only when p < q strictly. At p = q the truncation can be unbounded even when the full operator is bounded. Concrete counterexample on L²(R): let K(t,s) = sin(t−s)/(t−s) (continuous, locally bounded). The full operator is convolution with the sinc kernel, whose Fourier multiplier is π·1_{[−1,1]}(ξ) (up to normalization), so it is bounded on L² with norm ≈ π. Its causal truncation is convolution with k(u) = 1_{u>0} sin(u)/u, whose multiplier is m(ξ) = ∫_0^∞ e^{−iuξ} sin(u)/u du; using ∫_0^∞ sin(u) sin(uξ)/u du = (1/2) log |(1+ξ)/(1−ξ)|, the imaginary part of m is −(1/2) log|(1+ξ)/(1−ξ)|, which is unbounded as ξ → ±1. A convolution operator on L²(R) is bounded if and only if its multiplier is in L^∞, so the truncated operator is unbounded on L²: p = q = 2 fails. Consequence for PDE: the retarded (Duhamel) Strichartz estimate at the double endpoint q = q̃ = 2 cannot be obtained from the untruncated estimate by Christ–Kiselev; it is exactly the case Keel–Tao had to prove directly. Any proof that claims the double-endpoint inhomogeneous estimate 'by Christ–Kiselev' is misapplying the lemma.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["for the smoothing transform: existence of alpha solving E[sum_i T_i^alpha]=1 in the admissible range, plus regularity conditions such as E[sum_i T_i^alpha log^+ T_i]<infinity from Durrett-Liggett/Biggins theory","for Poisson-Dirichlet: a well-defined subordinator, or fragmentation/coalescent structure, whose ranked, normalized jump sizes are being studied","independence of (T_i) from the i.i.d. copies (W_i) in the smoothing transform equation","non-degeneracy conditions ruling out the trivial Dirac-mass-at-0 solution"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.998030+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d95edc3570f77641129fb8247438ed5ea704bbccb6be4cad5233917af61c0692","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). The smoothing transform concerns fixed points of the distributional equation W =_d sum_i T_i W_i, where (T_i) is a given, typically random, sequence of nonnegative weights and (W_i) are i.i.d. copies of W independent of (T_i); such fixed points arise as limits of branching random walk martingales, including derivative martingale limits, or of Mandelbrot multiplicative cascades, and their tail behavior, characterized by a power-law index alpha solving E[sum_i T_i^alpha]=1 or a related equation, governs the limit's regular variation. Durrett and Liggett characterized the solution set of the smoothing transform equation, establishing existence, uniqueness up to a scaling constant, and the precise tail index under moment conditions on (T_i), a result foundational for analyzing branching random walk boundary and derivative martingale limits and related models such as the random energy model. Separately, Poisson-Dirichlet distributions PD(alpha,theta) arise as the limiting law of ranked, normalized jump sizes of a subordinator, of ranked cycle lengths in random permutations, or of ranked masses in fragmentation and coalescent processes, characterized via the stick-breaking (GEM) construction or via a Poisson process of jumps of a stable subordinator normalized by its total mass. Neither result gives an explicit closed-form density for the general fixed point or limit; the smoothing transform's fixed point is typically characterized only implicitly, through its tail index and functional equation, and both results require specific moment or regular-variation conditions on the input weights or subordinator to hold. Typical failure: Assuming the smoothing transform has a unique nontrivial fixed point up to scale without checking that the characteristic equation E[sum T_i^alpha]=1 actually has a solution in the admissible range, or without the Durrett-Liggett/Biggins regularity conditions, particularly in boundary cases such as the critical branching random walk where the derivative martingale, rather than the ordinary martingale, is the relevant object; applying the generic smoothing-transform tail behavior in a boundary or degenerate parameter regime without re-deriving it is a common source of incorrect tail-index claims. Canonical reference: Durrett and Liggett, 1983, Zeitschrift fur Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie und verwandte Gebiete; Biggins and Kyprianou, 2005, Electronic Journal of Probability; Pitman and Yor, 1997, Annals of Probability.","status":"unverified"}

It is studied in connection with the notion of universality in two-dimensional statistical physics models. While the connective constant depends on the choice of lattice so itself is not universal (similarly to other lattice-dependent quantities such as the critical probability threshold for percolation), it is nonetheless an important quantity that appears in conjectures for universal laws. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-02T00:34:53.675639+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_d97be235d01df4d78b67ce6366ce4d108aa22374e33abc12f3ab6cb220eb967c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In calculus and real analysis, absolute continuity is a regularity property of functions that is stronger than uniform continuity, and hence continuity. The notion of absolute continuity allows one to obtain generalizations of the relationship between the two central operations of calculus—differentiation and integration. This relationship is commonly characterized in the framework of Riemann integration, but with absolute continuity it may be formulated in terms of Lebesgue integration. For real-valued functions on the real line, two interrelated notions appear: absolute continuity of functions and absolute continuity of measures. These two notions are generalized in different directions. The usual derivative of a function is related to the Radon–Nikodym derivative, or density, of a measure. We have the following chains of inclusions for functions over an interval:Lipschitz continuous ⊆ absolutely continuous ⊆ uniformly continuous ⊆ continuous","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:23:03.034516+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d98feba1bb71e6e4d6980179a25205901c9d83096617fcde4b9b35c89fed88d3","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 20 (SDE for the second Malliavin derivative) of arXiv:2605.03057, 'Uniform-in-time quantitative fluctuations of large scale interacting particle systems'] Assume that Assumptions \ref{ass:smooth},
and \ref{ass:second-malliavin-uniform} hold. Fix
$ 0 \le r \le s \le t $, $ u \in [s,t] $,
$ i,j,k \in \left\{ 1,\dots,N \right\} $, and
$ \alpha,\beta \in \left\{ 1,\dots,m \right\} $.
Then, the process $\left(
D_r^{k,\beta} D_s^{j,\alpha} X_u^{i,N}
\right)_{u \in [s,t]}$ solves the SDE
\begin{align}

D_r^{k,\beta} D_s^{j,\alpha} X_u^{i,N}
&=
\mathcal I_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\int_s^u
\left(
\partial_x b\left( X_\rho^{i,N},\mu_\rho^N \right)
D_r^{k,\beta} D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{i,N}
+
G_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)
+
R_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)
\right)
d\rho
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\int_s^u
\left(
\partial_x \sigma\left( X_\rho^{i,N},\mu_\rho^N \right)
D_r^{k,\beta} D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{i,N}
+
H_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)
+
S_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)
\right)
dB_\rho^i ,
\end{align}
where $\mathcal I_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}$ denotes the initial
condition given by
\begin{align*}
\mathcal I_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}
&=
\mathbf{1}_{\left\{ i=j \right\}}
\partial_x \sigma\left( X_s^{i,N},\mu_s^N \right)
D_r^{k,\beta} X_s^{i,N}
e_\alpha
+
\mathbf{1}_{\left\{ r=s \right\}}
\mathbf{1}_{\left\{ i=k \right\}}
\partial_x \sigma\left( X_s^{i,N},\mu_s^N \right)
D_s^{j,\alpha} X_s^{i,N}e_\beta
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\mathbf{1}_{\left\{ i=j \right\}} \frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_\mu \sigma\left( X_s^{i,N},\mu_s^N \right)\left( X_s^{\ell,N} \right)
D_r^{k,\beta} X_s^{\ell,N} e_\alpha
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\mathbf{1}_{\left\{ r=s \right\}}
\mathbf{1}_{\left\{ i=k \right\}}
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_\mu \sigma\left( X_s^{i,N},\mu_s^N \right)\left( X_s^{\ell,N} \right)
D_s^{j,\alpha} X_s^{\ell,N} e_\beta ,
\end{align*}
with $ e_\alpha $ denoting the $ \alpha $-th vector of the canonical basis of $ \R^m $,
\begin{align}

G_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)
&=
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_\mu b\left( X_\rho^{i,N},\mu_\rho^N \right)\left( X_\rho^{\ell,N} \right)
D_r^{k,\beta} D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{\ell,N},
\end{align}
and $H_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho) $ is defined by the same formula, with
$ b $ replaced by $ \sigma $, while
\begin{align}

R_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)
&=
\partial_{xx}^2 b\left( X_\rho^{i,N},\mu_\rho^N \right)
\left[
D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{i,N}, D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{i,N}
\right]
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_\mu\left[ \partial_x b \right]
\left( X_\rho^{i,N},\mu_\rho^N \right)\left( X_\rho^{\ell,N} \right)
\left[
D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{\ell,N}, D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{i,N}
\right]
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_x\left[
\partial_\mu b\left( \cdot,\mu_\rho^N \right)\left( X_\rho^{\ell,N} \right)
\right]\left( X_\rho^{i,N} \right)
\left[
D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{i,N}, D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{\ell,N}
\right]
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_v\left[
\partial_\mu b\left( X_\rho^{i,N},\mu_\rho^N \right)
\right]\left( X_\rho^{\ell,N} \right)
\left[
D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{\ell,N}, D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{\ell,N}
\right]
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\frac1{N^2}\sum_{\ell=1}^N \sum_{q=1}^N
\partial_{\mu\mu}^2 b\left( X_\rho^{i,N},\mu_\rho^N \right)
\left( X_\rho^{\ell,N}, X_\rho^{q,N} \right)
\left[
D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{q,N}, D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{\ell,N}
\right],
\end{align}
and $ S_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho) $ is defined by the same formula, with
$ b $ replaced by $ \sigma $. Finally, there exists a constant $ C > 0 $, independent of
$ r,s,t,\rho,N,i,j,k,\alpha,\beta $, such that, for every $ \rho \in [s,t] $,
\begin{align}

\norm{R_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)}
+
\norm{S_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)}
&\le
C \Bigg(
\norm{D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{i,N}}
\norm{D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{i,N}}
+
\norm{D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{i,N}}
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\norm{D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{\ell,N}}
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\norm{D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{i,N}}
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\norm{D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{\ell,N}}
+
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\norm{D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{\ell,N}}","status":"unverified"}

Tile the bulk of the large square by unit cells. For fixed R and M, retain in each cell only the length, truncated at M, of routes between sampled endpoints within distance R of that cell. Its local binomial point configuration converges in total variation to the corresponding rate1 Poisson configuration. The retained length is bounded by M, so its expectation converges. {"assumptions":["n>=2 and K>0","All 2n coordinates of x and y are mutually independent and each has a Lebesgue density bounded a.e. by K","Z,u,v,w are deterministic real coefficients","rank(Z)>=2"],"created_at":"2026-10-07T01:09:09+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d9f3dbc365ca4e0870b0925e5f01e8fe","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let n>=2, K>0, and let x=(x_1,...,x_n) and y=(y_1,...,y_n) be real random vectors whose 2n coordinates are mutually independent, each with a Lebesgue density bounded almost everywhere by K. Let Z be a deterministic real n by n matrix, u,v deterministic real n-vectors, and w a deterministic real scalar. Write sigma_1(Z)>=...>=sigma_n(Z)>=0 for its singular values, and assume r=rank(Z)>=2. Then Q=x^T Z y+x^T u+v^T y+w has a Lebesgue density satisfying ||p_Q||_infinity <= 2(C_RV K)^2 sqrt(2e*pi) min_{2<=j<=r} [j^(-1/2) (product_{i=1}^j sigma_i(Z))^(-1/j)], where C_RV is the universal constant in the Rudelson-Vershynin bounded-density projection theorem. Equivalently one may minimize over 2<=j<=n, interpreting terms with zero singular-value product as infinity. This is the k=1 corollary of Banks, Garza-Vargas, Kulkarni and Srivastava, arXiv:2005.08930. No bounded-density bound is available in general at rank one: if U,V are independent uniform(0,1), UV has density -log(t) on 0<t<1, which is unbounded near zero. Independence only between the two vectors is insufficient even at rank two: x=(U,U), y=(V,V), Z=diag(1,-1) gives Q=0 almost surely. A quadratic-form application must independently verify the coordinate independence and rank hypotheses.","status":"unverified"}

with masses $s_0=s_3=s_6=s_7=\frac1{4(1+2\varepsilon)}$ and

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T16:46:51.518941+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_d9f8d662691360ba70c27634d29157ba859e2c7184c720c68306842f109cf517","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematics, the pigeonhole principle states that if n items are put into m containers, with n > m, then at least one container must contain more than one item. For example, of three gloves, at least two must be right-handed or at least two must be left-handed, because there are three objects but only two categories of handedness to put them into. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:36:31.235220+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dab15ba146eefad594bfb1127aa334a49aadee8418addb6be53fcfc3f5cb9226","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 19 of arXiv:2609.00567, 'Hodge--Tate splitting and Akizuki--Nakano vanishing in positive characteristic'] Let \(\iota \colon X \to S\) be a morphism of $\F_p$-stacks.
Let
\[
X^{(1)} \defeq X\times_{S,F_S}S
\]
be the relative Frobenius twist, and let
\[
F_{X/S}\colon X \to  X^{(1)}
\]
be the relative Frobenius.
  \begin{itemize}
      \item   The \emph{(absolute) de Rham stack} of \(X\) is defined as a functor
  \begin{equation*}
    X^{\dR} \colon \CAlg^{an}_{\setF_p} \to \Ani; \  R \mapsto X(W(R)/^L p),
  \end{equation*}
  where \(W(R)\) is the ring of Witt vectors of \(R\), \(-/^L p\) is the derived quotient by \(p\), and \(X(W(R)/^L p)\) is the mapping space \(\Map_{\dSch_{\setF_p}}(\Spec(W(R)/^L p), X)\) in the \(\infty\)-category of derived schemes over \(\setF_p\).
  Since this is isomorphic to the relative Hodge--Tate stack \((X/\setZ_p)^{\HT}\) of \(X\) relative to the crystalline prism \((\setZ_p, (p))\) introduced in \cite{bhatt2022Prismatization}*{Construction 7.1}, this is a stack on \(\CAlg^{an}_{\setF_p}\) (\cite{bhatt2022Prismatization}*{Lemma 7.3}).

  This is equipped with natural morphisms
  \begin{equation*}
    \pi_{X} \colon X \to X^{\dR} \quad \text{and} \quad \nu_X \colon X^{\dR} \to X
  \end{equation*}
  of \(\setF_p\)-stacks: For each \(R \in \CAlg^{an}_{\setF_p}\), each morphism is given by precomposition of morphisms
  \begin{equation*}
    R \xrightarrow{\Phi_R} W(R)/^L p \quad \text{and} \quad W(R)/^L p \xrightarrow{\res} R,
  \end{equation*}
  where \(\Phi_R\) is the animation of the morphism \(a \mapsto [a^p] \bmod p\) and \(\res\) is the restriction morphism.
  Note that the composition \(\nu_X \circ \pi_X\) is the absolute Frobenius morphism \(F_X \colon X \to X\) of \(X\).
\item The \emph{de Rham stack} of $X$ over $S$ is defined by
\[
(X/S)^{\dR} \defeq X^{\dR} \times_{S^{\dR},\pi_S} S.
\]
We define natural morphisms
  \begin{equation*}
    \pi_{X/S} \colon X \to (X/S)^{\dR} \quad \text{and} \quad \nu_{X/S} \colon (X/S)^{\dR} \to X^{(1)}
  \end{equation*}
  of \(\setF_p\)-stacks as follows:
The morphism $\pi_{X/S}$ is defined by
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
X \arrow[r,"\pi_{X/S}"'] \arrow[rd,bend right,"\iota"] \arrow[rr,bend left,"\pi_X"] & X^{\dR} \times_{S^{\dR}} S \arrow[r,"\pr_1"] \arrow[d,"\pr_2"] & X^{\dR} \arrow[d,"\iota^{\dR}"] \\
& S \arrow[r,"\pi_S"] & S^{\dR}.
\end{tikzcd}
\]
The morphism $\nu_{X/S} \colon (X/S)^{\dR} \to X^{(1)}$ is induced by the following commutative diagram
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
X^{\dR} \times_{S^{\dR}} S \arrow[r,"\pr_1"] \arrow[d,"\pr_2"] & X^{\dR} \arrow[d,"\iota^{\dR}"] \arrow[r,"\nu_X"] & X \arrow[d,"\iota"] \\
S \arrow[r,"\pi_S"] \arrow[rr,bend right,"F"] & S^{\dR} \arrow[r,"\nu_S"] & S.
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\item We assume that $\iota$ is smooth representable.
Then the cotangent complex \(L_{X/S}\) is a locally free \(\cO_X\)-module concentrated in degree \(0\).  
We set
\[
\Omega^1_{X/S} \defeq L_{X/S},
\qquad
\Omega^i_{X/S} \defeq 
\bigwedge_{\cO_X}^i\Omega^1_{X/S}.
\]
The universal \(S\)-derivation
\[
d_{X/S}\colon \cO_X \to  \Omega^1_{X/S}
\]
extends uniquely to the relative de Rham complex
\[
\Omega^\bullet_{X/S}
=
\left[
\cO_X
\xrightarrow{d_{X/S}}
\Omega^1_{X/S}
\xrightarrow{d_{X/S}}
\Omega^2_{X/S}
 \to \cdots
\right].
\]

We define a morphism of complexes of $\cO_{X^{(1)}}$-modules
\[
F^{\dR}_{X/S} \colon \cO_{X^{(1)}} \to F_{X/S,*}\Omega^{\bullet}_{X/S}
\]
as follows:
We have
\[
d_{X/S}\circ F_{X/S}^{\sharp}=0
\]
by checking smooth locally on \(X\).  
Therefore, the morphism
\[
F_{X/S}^{\sharp}\colon
\cO_{X^{(1)}} \to  F_{X/S,*}\cO_X
\]
defines a morphism of complexes
\[
F_{X/S}^{\dR}\colon
\cO_{X^{(1)}}
 \to 
F_{X/S,*}\Omega^\bullet_{X/S},
\]
whose degree \(0\) component is \(F_{X/S}^{\sharp}\) and whose
positive-degree components are zero.
\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:46.149110+00:00","domain":"elliptic partial differential equations, maximum principles","id":"claim_db0bd50e4b1d3185e597734ebdf3437ca5f83b01bff6e16e23fd7c464aeb3f41","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: Omega bounded. The proofs use boundedness twice - the auxiliary function exp(gamma x_1) must be bounded on Omega, and the maximum must be attained on a compact set. On unbounded domains the conclusion is false even for harmonic functions with zero boundary data. Unbounded counterexample: on the half-space {x_n > 0} the function u(x) = x_n is harmonic and vanishes on the whole boundary, yet u > 0 inside; sup u = infinity while sup over the boundary of u = 0. Bounded counterexample (so boundedness of u does not rescue the statement in general): for n >= 3 let Omega = {|x| > 1} and u(x) = 1 - |x|^{2-n}. Then u is harmonic in Omega, continuous up to the boundary, bounded with 0 <= u < 1, u = 0 on the boundary sphere, and sup over Omega of u = 1 > 0 = sup over the boundary of u^+. In the plane, u(x) = log|x| on {|x| > 1} is an unbounded version of the same phenomenon. What restores the principle: treat infinity as a boundary point, i.e. assume limsup of u(x) as |x| tends to infinity is <= 0 (then the principle holds on any unbounded Omega, by exhausting with large balls), or impose a Phragmen-Lindeloef growth restriction adapted to the geometry. The admissible growth is set by the opening of the domain, and a thinner domain permits faster growth, not slower: in a plane sector of opening pi/a the threshold is exp(|x|^a), so a narrow sector allows faster growth than a half-plane, and in a strip of width d the threshold is exp(pi|x|/d), the extremal being exp(pi x_1/d) cos(pi x_2/d). The same caution applies to the H^1 weak maximum principle: its proof uses the Sobolev inequality together with the fact that the level sets have finite measure.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:56:21.583768+00:00","domain":"algebraic geometry","id":"claim_db5eb654cfadf445fa059f8bceb44a8415837ad88ca812a4513a0ade0f74de10","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a smooth projective curve of genus g over an algebraically closed field, equivalently a compact Riemann surface, and let D be a divisor on X. Write l(D) for the dimension of the space of meromorphic functions on X whose poles are bounded by D and which have no other poles, and let K be a canonical divisor of X. The Riemann-Roch theorem states l(D) - l(K - D) = deg(D) + 1 - g, where deg(D) is the sum of the coefficients of D. Once deg(D) > 2g - 2 this gives l(D) = deg(D) + 1 - g exactly, since l(K-D) then vanishes. \[
Q_n(\alpha)

\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}
\left[

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.356901+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_db9918fbc671f11eee90cd6406606fa76cc6077e21fc89d28df52ffb173bfd87","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 237 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $\alpha,L,\epsilon,K>0$ and any sequence of $\epsilon$-approximate $L$-Lipschitz algorithms $(\cA_N)_{N\ge 1}$,
	\[
		\lim_{N\to\infty} \bbW_2\Big(\mu(\cA_{N[K]}), \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)\Big) 
		= \lim_{N\to\infty} \bbW_2\Big(\mu_{\sym}(\cA_{N[K]}), \cM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha;\epsilon)\Big)
		= 0\,.
	\]

\begin{proof}
	We only prove that the first limit is zero, as the second limit is proved analogously.
	Suppose for contradiction that there exists $\delta > 0$ such that $\bbW_2(\mu(\cA_{N[K]}), \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)) \ge \delta$ for infinitely many $N$.
	By \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l4} from Lemma~\ref{l:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound}, there exists $C = C(\alpha,L,K) > 0 $ such that for sufficiently large $N$, $\mu(\cA_{N[K]}) \in \cP_4(\R,C)$.
Then, for infinitely many $N$, we have
	\[\mu(\cA_{N[K]})\in
		S_\delta 
		\equiv \Big\{ \mu \in \cP_4(\R,C) : \bbW_2(\mu, \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)) \ge \delta 
		\Big\}\,.
	\]
	By Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.cPp.compact.Wq}, the space $\cP_4(\R,C)$ endowed with the $\bbW_2$ metric is compact.
	The set $S_\delta$ is closed with respect to the $\bbW_2$ metric, hence also compact. Therefore
 we may find $\mu \in S_\delta$ and a subsequence $(N_j)_{j\ge 1}$ such that
	\[
		\lim_{j\to\infty} \bbW_2\Big(\mu(\cA_{N_j[K]}),
		\mu\Big) = 0\,.
	\]
	As noted in Definition~\ref{d:truncated.lip.alg}, we have $\mu^{\Ising}(\cA_{N_j[K]}) = \mu^{\Ising}(\cA_{N_j})$: thus, since each $\cA_{N_j}$ is an $\epsilon$-approximate $L$-Lipschitz algorithm, so is each $\cA_{N_j[K]}$. It follows by omitting finitely many $j$'s that we have
	\[
	\WERR(\cA_{N_j[K]},\mu)
	=\max\bigg\{
	\bbW_2\Big(\mu(\cA_{N_j[K]}),
		\mu\Big),
	\bbW_2\Big(
		\mu^\Ising(\cA_{N_j[K]}),
		\cP(\{\pm1\})
		\Big)
	\bigg\}\le\epsilon
	\]
for all $j$. Recalling the definition \eqref{e:cM.Lip} of  $\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;L,\epsilon)$, this implies
	\[
		\mu \in \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;L,\epsilon) \subseteq \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)\,,
	\]
	which contradicts that $\mu \in S_\delta$.
\end{proof}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:51.726371+00:00","domain":"hyperbolic partial differential equations","id":"claim_dbf122d5a238489aa083fdb44f89336d4d034fb877e0be5e3ba3b1dc4f1ae3c4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: 'the solution at (t,x) depends only on the data on the sphere ∂B(x,t)', i.e. sharp propagation on the light cone with no tail, holds only in odd space dimensions n ≥ 3. Finite speed of propagation (support in {|x| ≤ t + R}) holds in every dimension; the sharp inner edge does not. Counterexample n = 1: with u0 = 0 and u1 = 1_{[−1,1]}, d'Alembert's formula gives u(t,x) = (1/2)∫_{x−t}^{x+t} u1, so u(t,0) = 1 for every t ≥ 1 — the disturbance never leaves the origin. Counterexample n = 2: with u0 = 0 and u1 = 1_{B(0,1)}, Poisson's formula gives u(t,0) = (1/2π)∫_{|y|<1} (t² − |y|²)^{−1/2} dy > 0 for every t > 1 — a decaying tail behind the wavefront (this is why a splash on a pond is felt long after the front passes, while a sound pulse in three dimensions is heard once). Practical consequence: statements like 'the data inside B(x,t) do not matter' or 'the solution vanishes after the front passes' are valid only for odd n ≥ 3, and any argument that tacitly extends them to n = 1, 2 or to even dimensions (or to variable-coefficient / curved-background wave equations, where strong Huygens generally fails even in odd dimensions) is unsound.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-22T11:15:24.943680+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_dc42d571cabd4fbbbe8af6d7e0fbaf69","kind":"heuristic","schema_version":1,"statement":"Method for the bounded-density-of-a-quadratic-form conjecture. Write the density by Fourier inversion p(y)=(1/2pi) integral e^{-ity} phi(t) dt with phi(t)=E[e^{itQ(X)}] the characteristic function; then ||p||_inf <= (1/2pi) integral |phi(t)| dt, so a bounded density follows from an L^1 bound on phi. phi(t) is an oscillatory integral integral e^{it Q(x)} prod f(x_i) dx with quadratic phase Q. Per large-eigenvalue direction, van der Corput / stationary phase gives decay |t lambda_j|^{-1/2} uniformly over amplitudes with density <=1 (since x^2 has nonvanishing second derivative); three eigenvalues with |lambda_j|>=1 give |phi(t)| <~ min(1,|t|^{-3/2}), which is integrable at infinity -> bounded density. The coupling between eigen-directions and the coordinate variables (Q not diagonal in the X_i) and degenerate phases are handled by resolution of singularities / Newton polyhedra (Varchenko oscillatory-integral asymptotics; the x^2-y^3 cusp is the model degenerate case), and Bai-Yin controls the eigenvalue configuration. The squaring/decoupling identity |phi(t)|^2=E_{X,X'}[e^{it(Q(X)-Q(X'))}] lowers the smoothness demanded of the densities. Related area: anti-concentration and local limit theorems for quadratic forms (Costello-Tao-Vu, Nguyen-Vu, Rudelson-Vershynin, Gotze-Sudakov-Tikhomirov).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["One FCFS server","Poisson arrival rate lambda>0","Independent exponential service rate mu>lambda","Deterministic nonnegative setup tau and grace g","Setup is never cancelled; setup arrivals queue"],"created_at":"2026-10-10T08:07:30.222044+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dc50cb5f4c5a6a66ee102e12be80846188e1dd3193d5b08d1f1fbd2280fd98f6","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"PROOF OF THE STATED SCOPED RESULT; independent audit pending. Consider one FCFS server with Poisson arrival rate lambda>0 and independent exponential service rate mu>lambda. After becoming empty it remains on for deterministic grace g in [0,infinity], then switches off. A cold arrival triggers deterministic setup tau>=0, which is never cancelled; arrivals during setup wait. Set p=exp(-lambda g), x=lambda tau and rho=lambda/mu. Busy, on-idle, off and setup occupy fractions rho, (1-rho)(1-p)/(1+xp), (1-rho)p/(1+xp), and (1-rho)xp/(1+xp). {"assumptions":["U open with lambda_1 > 0 on H^1_0(U) (e.g. U bounded, or bounded in one direction, or of finite measure)","g in L^2(U)","u the weak solution of the Dirichlet heat equation with u(0) = g","the equality case requires the infimum defining lambda_1 to be attained, e.g. U bounded"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:49.105957+00:00","domain":"parabolic partial differential equations","id":"claim_dccca23e6eedae7c488796bf4490a59edff019e1d479e546a6dbd3a3e781c655","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $U\\subset\\mathbb R^n$ be open with $\\lambda_1=\\inf\\{\\|\\nabla v\\|_{L^2}^2/\\|v\\|_{L^2}^2:v\\in H^1_0(U),v\\ne0\\}>0$; this positivity holds in particular when $U$ is bounded, when $U$ is merely bounded in one direction, and when $U$ has finite measure. Let $u$ be the weak solution of $u_t=\\Delta u$ in $U\\times(0,\\infty)$, $u=0$ on $\\partial U\\times(0,\\infty)$, $u(0)=g\\in L^2(U)$. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.176507+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dce2c5f1ca2ba7f115f24e4985d485e0ea81fbf2f9568b8bd5140a67410b7be1","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Ppn 71 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For fixed $q_0 \in [0,1)$ and $f \in L^\infty([q_0,1];[0,1/\alpha])$, the mapping $p \mapsto \cM(q_0;p,f)$, viewed as a function from $\incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ to  $P(\cP_2(\bbR))$, is uniformly continuous:
    \[
        d_\cH\Big(\cM(q_0;p,f),\cM(q_0;\tilde p,f)\Big)^2
        \le 6(1+\|f\|_\infty) \|p'-\tilde p'\|_1\,.
    \]
Here $\incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ is metrized by  $\mathsf{dist}(p,\tilde p) = \|p'-\tilde p'\|_1$, and we recall that  $P(\cP_2(\bbR))$ is metrized by the Hausdorff distance \eqref{e:hausdorff}. 

\begin{proof}
Let $p,\tilde p\in \incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ with $\|p'-\tilde p'\|_1 = \delta$.
Since $p(1) = \tilde p(1) = 1$, it follows by integrating that $|p(t) - \tilde p(t)| \le \delta$ for all $t\in [q_0,1]$, and so certainly we have $\|p-\tilde{p}\|_1\le\delta$. Recalling the notation of Definition~\ref{d:X.adm}, let $(b,\sigma)\in \Adm(q_0;p,f)$. We will construct modified controls $(\tilde b,\tilde \sigma) \in \Adm(q_0;\tilde p,f)$ such that the corresponding solutions to \eqref{e:formal.sde.main} approximate each other. Recall $s(t)\equiv (tp)'(t)^{1/2}$, and similarly denote
$\tilde{s}(t)\equiv (t\tilde{p})'(t)^{1/2}$.
We set $\tilde{b}=b$, and let $\hat \sigma$ be defined by the relation
	\[\hat{\sigma}_t-1
	= a(t) 
	(\sigma_t-1)\,,\quad
	a(t)
	\equiv 
	\frac{s(t)}{p(t)^{1/2}}
	\frac{\tilde{p}(t)^{1/2}}
		{\tilde{s}(t)}
	\]
for all $t\in[q_0,1]$. We note that 
	\[
	\frac{s(t)}{p(t)^{1/2}}
	= \frac{[p(t) + tp'(t)]^{1/2}}
		{p(t)^{1/2}} \ge 1\,,
	\]
so the ratio $a(t)$ can only be large if $p'(t)$ is very large, which occurs on a set of times of small measure. It is clear from the construction that $(\tilde b,\hat{\sigma})$ satisfies the budget constraint \eqref{e:budget-f} defining $\Adm(q_0;\tilde p,f)$, with the exception that $\hat{\sigma}$ is not necessarily non-negative. Let $X$ be given by \eqref{e:formal.sde.main} with controls $(b,\sigma)$, and $\hat X$ be given by \eqref{e:formal.sde.main} with controls $(\tilde b, \hat \sigma)$. We couple these processes with the same initialization $X(q_0) = \hat{X}(q_0) = 0$ and the same Brownian motion $B$. We will first show the endpoint laws of $X(1)$ and $\hat{X}(1)$ are close, then address the issue of $\hat{\sigma}$ being possibly negative. To this end, we recall from \eqref{e:formal.sde.main} that
  \[
        X(1) = \int_{q_0}^1 p'(t)^{1/2} b_t\,dt
        + \int_{q_0}^1 s(t)\,dB(t)
        + \int_{q_0}^1 s(t) (\sigma_t-1)\,dB(t)
        \,,
    \]
and similarly for $\hat{X}(1)$. This gives us a decomposition
$X(1)-\hat{X}(1) = \textup{(a)}+\textup{(b)}+\textup{(c)}$, and we proceed to bound each of the three terms:
    \begin{align*}\E[\textup{(a)}^2]
    &= \E \bigg[
    \bigg(\int_{q_0}^1 \Big(
        p'(t)^{1/2}
        - \tilde{p}'(t)^{1/2}\Big) b_t\,dt\bigg)^2\bigg]
    \le \bigg(
     \int_{q_0}^1\Big(
        p'(t)^{1/2}
        - \tilde{p}'(t)^{1/2}\Big)^2\,dt\bigg)
    \bigg( \int_{q_0}^1 \E[(b_t)^2]\,dt\bigg) \\
    &\le\bigg(\int_{q_0}^1 |p'(t)-\tilde{p}'(t)|\,dt\bigg)
    \bigg(\int_{q_0}^1 f(t)\,dt\bigg) 
    =  \delta \|f\|_1 \,,
    \end{align*}
having used the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality along with the budget constraint~\eqref{e:budget-f}. Next,
    \[\E[\textup{(b)}^2]
    = \int_{q_0}^1 \Big( s(t)-\tilde{s}(t) \Big)^2\,dt
    \le \int_{q_0}^1 \Big|s(t)^2 - \tilde{s}(t)^2\Big|\,dt
    \le \|p-p\|_1+\|p'-p'\|_1 \le 2\delta\,.\]
Lastly, using the above definition of $\hat\sigma$, we have
	\begin{align*}
	\E[\textup{(c)}^2]
    &= \int_{q_0}^1
    \Big( s(t) (\sigma_t-1)-\tilde{s}(t)(\hat{\sigma}_t
    -1)\Big)^2\,dt\\
    &= \int_{q_0}^1
    \frac{s(t)^2}{p(t)}
    \E[(\sigma_t-1)^2]
    \cdot p(t)
    \bigg( 1- 
    	\frac{\tilde{s}(t)}{s(t)} a(t)
    	 \bigg)^2
	\,dt\\
	&\le
	\|f\|_\infty
	\int_{q_0}^1
	p(t)
    \bigg( 1- \frac{\tilde{p}(t)^{1/2}}
		{p(t)^{1/2}}
    	 \bigg)^2
	\,dt 
	\le \|f\|_\infty \delta\,,
	\end{align*}
having used the budget constraint~\eqref{e:budget-f} along with the calculation from the bound on (a) above. Collec (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:54:53.443469+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dd038426f703dde2403154a36724715d1981820c0aa7f4d5dc7cdb10eb9bd4aa","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 1 (Multispecies mixed Ising model) of arXiv:2606.15432, 'A Concavity Theorem for the Parisi PDE'] Let $N\geq 1$, $D\geq 1$ and $\Sigma_N=\{\pm 1\}^N$.
For all $\bmx\in\mathbb R^D$, define the covariance function
\[
    \xi(\bmx)
    =
    \sum_{k\geq 1}
    \xi_k(\bmx)
    =
    \sum_{k\geq 1}
    \sum_{\substack{\bm p\in\mathsf P_k}}
    \Delta_{\bmp}^2\prod_{d=1}^D x_d^{p_d}.
\]
where $\bmDelta=(\Delta_{\bmp}^2:\bmp\in\mathsf P_k,\, k\geq 1)$ is a family of nonnegative coefficients and
where
\[
    \mathsf P_k
    =
    \{\bmp=(p_1,\ldots,p_D)\in\mathbb Z_+^D:
      |\bmp|:=p_1+\cdots+p_D=k\}.
\]
We also assume that $\xi((1+\varepsilon)\bm{1})<\infty$ for some $\varepsilon>0$.

For \(\sigma,\tau\in\SigN\), define the species overlap vector by
\[
    R_{N,d}(\sigma,\tau)
    =
    \frac1N\sum_{i\in I_{N,d}}\sigma_i\tau_i,
    \qquad
    \bmR_N(\sigma,\tau)=(R_{N,d}(\sigma,\tau))_{d=1}^D,
\]
where \(\bmI_N=\{I_{N,1},\ldots,I_{N,D}\}\) is a partition of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$.

The Hamiltonian of the \emph{multispecies mixed Ising model} is a centered Gaussian process
 \(H_N=(H_N(\sigma))_{\sigma\in\SigN}\)
with covariance
\[
    \mathbb E H_N(\sigma)H_N(\tau)
    =
    N\xi(\bmR_N(\sigma,\tau)),
    \qquad \sigma,\tau\in\SigN.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X and Y are Banach spaces","T is a bounded linear operator X -> Y","compactness of I - ST and I - TS (not merely boundedness) is what makes the criterion work"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.572195+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, Fredholm theory","id":"claim_dd902b48ae729c20df07599e1a8e793996632d7377d0e8bd78774bcd906c51d0","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X and Y be Banach spaces and T in B(X,Y). Then T is Fredholm if and only if T is invertible modulo compact operators, i.e. there is S in B(Y,X) with I_X - S T in K(X) and I_Y - T S in K(Y). Moreover, if T is Fredholm one may choose S (a Fredholm regularizer, or parametrix) so that I_X - S T and I_Y - T S have finite rank, namely the projection onto ker T along a closed complement and the projection onto a finite-dimensional complement of ran T along ran T; any such S is itself Fredholm with ind S = -ind T. For X = Y this says: T is Fredholm if and only if its class in the Calkin algebra B(X)/K(X) is invertible.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:29:00.764803+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dd9208166dd05484a23daf9673b9aef5c8e7dea3fc0576c4ede0e2f0feef7150","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 6 of arXiv:2512.04807, 'Existence and uniqueness of the canonical Brownian motion in non-simple conformal loop ens'] Consider the setup described just above where we let $\Gamma^\C$ be a nested whole-plane~\clekp{}. There exists a unique (up to a deterministic factor) collection of resistance forms $\rform{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C} = ((\rformres{k}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C}, \rfdomainres{\Upsilon_k}{\Gamma^\C}))_{k \in \N}$ that is measurable with respect to $\Gamma^\C$ and satisfies the following properties. There is a further collection of resistance forms $((\rformres{V}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C}, \rfdomainres{V}{\Gamma^\C}))_{V \in \metregions}$ such that the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}[I.]
 \item For each $k \in \N$ we have that $(\rformres{k}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C}, \rfdomainres{\Upsilon_k}{\Gamma^\C})$ is a local, regular resistance form on $\Upsilon_k$. Its associated resistance metric $\rmetres{k}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C}$ is topologically equivalent to $\dpathY[\Upsilon_k]$.
 \item Let $V_1,\ldots,V_n \in \metregions[k]$, $n \in \N$, such that $V_i \cap V_j = \emptyset$ for $i \neq j$ and $\bigcup_i \ol{V_i} \cap \Upsilon_k = \Upsilon_k$. Then
 \begin{align*}
  \rfdomainres{\Upsilon_k}{\Gamma^\C} &= \{ f : f|_{\ol{V_i} \cap \Upsilon_k} \in \rfdomainres{V_i}{\Gamma^\C} \text{ for each } i \} ,\\
  \text{and}\quad
  \rformres{k}{f}{f}{\Gamma^\C} &= \sum_i \rformres{V_i}{f|_{\ol{V_i} \cap \Upsilon_k}}{f|_{\ol{V_i} \cap \Upsilon_k}}{\Gamma^\C} .
 \end{align*}
\item If $V,V' \in \metregions[k]$, $V \subseteq V'$, and $f\colon \ol{V'} \cap \Upsilon_k \to \R$ is a continuous function that is constant on each $\dpathY$-connected component of $\ol{V'} \cap \Upsilon_k \setminus \ol{V}$, then
\begin{align*}
 & f \in \rfdomainres{V'}{\Gamma^\C} \text{ if and only if } f|_{\ol{V} \cap \Upsilon_k} \in \rfdomainres{V}{\Gamma^\C} \\
 \text{and}\quad & \rformres{V'}{f}{f}{\Gamma^\C} = \rformres{V}{f}{f}{\Gamma^\C} .
\end{align*}
 \item For each open set $U \subseteq \C$, the collection of forms $(\rformres{V}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C})_{V \in \metregions[U]}$ is a.s.\ a measurable function of $\Gamma^\C|_U$.
\item For each $z \in \C$, we have
\[ \rform{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C} = \rform{T_{z}\cdot}{T_{z}\cdot}{\Gamma^\C+z} \quad\text{a.s.,} \]
where $T_{z} f = f(\cdot -z)$ denotes translation by $z$.
\item There exists a constant $\resexp > 0$ so that for each $\lambda > 0$, we have
\[ \rform{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C} = \lambda^{\resexp}\rform{S_{\lambda}\cdot}{S_{\lambda}\cdot}{\lambda\Gamma^\C} \quad\text{a.s.,} \]
where $S_{\lambda} f = f(\lambda^{-1}\cdot)$.
\end{enumerate}
The analogous statement holds for the \clekp{} Brownian motion. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a Banach space over R or C","K: X -> X is compact","lambda is a nonzero scalar (for lambda = 0 every assertion can fail)","in the Hilbert-space form, H is a Hilbert space and K* is the Hilbert adjoint, so the relevant homogeneous adjoint equation uses the complex conjugate of lambda"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.572093+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, Fredholm theory, integral equations","id":"claim_ddaa1329528122fb80376912c0e3927070e563e1860806c39b21c8299d538814","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a Banach space over R or C, let K in K(X) be compact, let lambda be a nonzero scalar and set T = lambda I - K. Then: (i) ker T is finite-dimensional; (ii) ran T is closed; (iii) dim ker T = dim ker T' = dim(X / ran T) < infinity, where T' = lambda I - K' on the dual X'; in particular T is Fredholm with ind T = 0; (iv) ran T = {y in X : f(y) = 0 for every f in ker T'}. Consequently exactly one of the following holds: either lambda x - K x = y has a unique solution for every y in X (and the solution depends continuously on y), or the homogeneous equation lambda x - K x = 0 has a nonzero solution, in which case the solution space is finite-dimensional of dimension d, the adjoint homogeneous equation lambda f - K' f = 0 also has a d-dimensional solution space, and lambda x - K x = y is solvable exactly for those y annihilated by every solution f of the adjoint homogeneous equation (solutions then form an affine space of dimension d). In a Hilbert space H with K compact, the adjoint condition reads: lambda x - K x = y is solvable iff y is orthogonal to ker(conj(lambda) I - K*).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:50:48.848317+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ddbd361e7cd5ae1a97210c3759252a0a1a2c90c9e97f3b20d921b81cd1419b6c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:n2 of arXiv:2607.08551, 'Weighted-threshold Coupon Collection'] Consider the Zipf family with $N=2$:

w_2(s)=\frac{2^{-s}}{1+2^{-s}},

Then the expected quorum time has the explicit form
\[

\begin{cases}

Let X take values in a standard Borel space, let Z(X)>0 almost surely be measurable with E Z(X)<infinity, and fix 0<gamma<1. Among nonnegative randomized weights S satisfying E[S|X]=1 and E[P(S>0|X)]=gamma, the minimum of J(S)=E[S^2 Z(X)] is attained by S_star=I/pi_star(X), where I conditional on X is Bernoulli(pi_star(X)) and pi_star(X)=min(1,c*sqrt(Z(X))). {"assumptions":["(X, B, mu, T) is a measure-preserving system on a standard (Lebesgue) probability space","G is a compact metrizable group, m its normalized Haar measure","phi : X -> G is Borel measurable","the fibre action is by left translation, T_phi(x,g) = (Tx, phi(x) g)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:09:43.731878+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, skew products and cocycles","id":"claim_ddecdf9c38acba7f9d1a20280128c4273217092304e304e1c131cecbf3f30d61","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, B, mu, T) be a measure-preserving system on a standard probability space, let G be a compact metrizable group with normalized Haar measure m, and let phi : X -> G be measurable (the cocycle generator). The G-extension, or skew product, is the transformation

  T_phi(x, g) = (T x, phi(x) g)   on   (X x G, B x Borel(G), mu x m).

It preserves mu x m: for fixed x the fibre map g -> phi(x) g is a left translation, and Haar measure on a compact group is left invariant (compactness is what makes Haar a probability measure, so that mu x m is a probability measure). Iterating, T_phi^n(x, g) = (T^n x, phi_n(x) g) with the cocycle phi_n(x) = phi(T^{n-1} x) * ... * phi(T x) * phi(x), which satisfies the cocycle identity phi_{n+k}(x) = phi_k(T^n x) * phi_n(x).

Two standard obstructions to ergodicity are built into the definition. (i) If phi takes values in a proper closed subgroup H of G, then every set of the form X x (union of right cosets H g) is T_phi-invariant, so T_phi is not ergodic. (ii) More generally if there is a measurable u : X -> G with phi(x) = u(T x)^{-1} h(x) u(x) for h taking values in a proper closed subgroup, the same conclusion holds after the measurable change of coordinates (x, g) -> (x, u(x) g); cocycles differing in this way are called cohomologous, and ergodicity of T_phi depends only on the cohomology class. Note the sides: with the convention above the cocycle acts by LEFT translation and the invariant objects are RIGHT cosets; the opposite convention T_phi(x,g) = (Tx, g phi(x)) swaps them, and mixing the two conventions is the usual source of sign/side errors in the ergodicity criteria.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:30:52.746107+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_de12232140b00c54f654a321a766291084b9267f14677bea219692b0e6f96eed","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Define 5 of arXiv:2506.10522, 'On the Law of the Iterated Logarithm for $m$-dependent stationary random variables under s'] \begin{description}
  \item[ \rm (i)] ({\em Identical distribution}) Let $\bm X_1$ and $\bm X_2$ be two $n$-dimensional random vectors defined
respectively in sub-linear expectation spaces $(\Omega_1, \mathcal{H}_1, \mbE_1)$
  and $(\Omega_2, \mathcal{H}_2, \mbE_2)$. They are called identically distributed, denoted by $\bm X_1\overset{d}= \bm X_2$  if
$$ \mbE_1[\varphi(\bm X_1)]=\mbE_2[\varphi(\bm X_2)], \;\; \forall \varphi\in C_{b,Lip}(\mathbb R^n). $$
 A sequence $\{X_n;n\ge 1\}$ of random variables is said to be identically distributed if $X_i\overset{d}= X_1$ for each $i\ge 1$.
\item[\rm (ii)] ({\em Independence})   In a sub-linear expectation space  $(\Omega, \mathcal{H}, \mbE)$, a random vector $\bm Y =
(Y_1, \ldots, Y_n)$, $Y_i \in \mathcal{H}$ is said to be independent to another random vector $\bm X =
(X_1, \ldots, X_m)$ , $X_i \in \mathcal{H}$ under $\mbE$  if for each test function $\varphi\in C_{b,Lip}(\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n)$
we have
$ \mbE [\varphi(\bm X, \bm Y )] = \mbE \big[\mbE[\varphi(\bm x, \bm Y )]\big|_{\bm x=\bm X}\big].$
 \item[\rm (iii)] ({\em Independent random variables}) A sequence of random variables $\{X_n; n\ge 1\}$
 is said to be independent, if  $X_{i+1}$ is independent to $(X_{1},\ldots, X_i)$ for each $i\ge 1$.
 \item[\rm (iv)](m-dependence) A sequence of random variables(or random vectors) $\{X_n;n\geq 1\}$ is said to be $m$-dependent if there exists an integer $m$ such that for every $n$ and every $j\geq m+1$, $(X_{n+m+1},\cdots,X_{n+j})$ is independent of $(X_1,\cdots,X_n)$. In particular, if $m=0$, $\{X_n;n\geq 1\}$ is an independent sequence.
\item[\rm (v)](stationary) A sequence of random variables(or random vectors) $\{X_n;n\geq 1\}$ is said to be stationary if for every positive integers $n$ and $p$, $(X_1,\cdots,X_n)\overset{d}{=}(X_{1+p},\cdots,X_{n+p})$.
\item[\rm (vi)](linear stationary) A sequence of random variables(or random vectors) $\{X_n;n\geq 1\}$ is said to be linear stationary if for every positive integers $n$ and $p$, $X_1+\cdots+X_n\overset{d}{=}X_{1+p}+\cdots+X_{n+p}$.
 \end{description}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Finite exogenous time-homogeneous Markov chain with row-stochastic transition matrix P","Fixed finite real matrices A_i, vectors b_i and constant step alpha","Finite second moment of xi_0","Conditional independence of z_(k+1) and xi_k given z_k","Columnwise vectorization and stacking by chain state"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T16:05:57.431397+00:00","domain":"reinforcement learning; Markov jump linear systems","id":"claim_de1b5940314d04a7ddcbc45caa566cc8e834b108f83b393e8aa92596fbff4e17","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let z_k be an exogenous time-homogeneous Markov chain on {1,...,N}, with p_ij=P(z_(k+1)=j|z_k=i). Define p_k^i=P(z_k=i), q_k^i=E[xi_k 1_{z_k=i}], Q_k^i=E[xi_k xi_k^T 1_{z_k=i}]. Then p_(k+1)=P^T p_k, q_(k+1)^j=sum_i p_ij[H_i q_k^i+alpha p_k^i b_i], and Q_(k+1)^j=sum_i p_ij[H_i Q_k^i H_i^T+alpha(H_i q_k^i b_i^T+b_i(q_k^i)^T H_i^T)+alpha^2 p_k^i b_i b_i^T]. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:05:27.627278+00:00","domain":"functional analysis","id":"claim_de27015aaa0fed8be3e6e4717dc3b361b73aac1ab1054852f520fd6389b23345","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A linear operator T: X -> Y between Banach spaces is compact if the image T(B_X) of the closed unit ball is relatively compact in Y; equivalently, every bounded sequence (x_k) in X has a subsequence along which (T x_k) converges in Y. A compact operator is bounded. Facts: (1) the compact operators K(X, Y) form a closed linear subspace of the bounded operators B(X, Y), and compositions of a compact operator with bounded operators on either side are compact, so K(X) = K(X, X) is a closed two-sided ideal of B(X); (2) every finite-rank bounded operator is compact, and a norm limit of finite-rank operators is compact; when Y is a Hilbert space (more generally when Y has the approximation property) every compact operator is such a limit - for Banach spaces in general this fails (Enflo, 1973); (3) the identity of an infinite-dimensional Banach space is not compact (Riesz's lemma: the unit ball is not compact), so a compact operator on an infinite-dimensional space is never invertible; (4) Riesz-Schauder theory: for compact T on an infinite-dimensional Banach space the spectrum sigma(T) is a countable (possibly finite) set whose only possible accumulation point is 0, 0 belongs to sigma(T), every nonzero spectral value is an eigenvalue with finite-dimensional generalised eigenspace, and for lambda != 0 the operator lambda - T is injective if and only if it is surjective (the Fredholm alternative: either (lambda - T) x = y has a unique solution for every y, or the homogeneous equation has a nontrivial solution, and then the inhomogeneous one is solvable exactly for y annihilated by the kernel of the adjoint); (5) a compact self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors with real eigenvalues tending to 0 (the spectral theorem); (6) integral operators (Kf)(x) = integral k(x, y) f(y) dy with a continuous kernel on a compact domain, or with an L^2 kernel (Hilbert-Schmidt operators), are compact, and so is every diagonal operator on l^2 whose entries tend to 0. Compact perturbations preserve the essential spectrum and the Fredholm index (Atkinson).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.356404+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_de6ed04e0e0829407fc76e9f9053d5e379c62e487fac745c92001f9f22aa70f4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 233 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Suppose $\cA_N$ is a $L$-Lipschitz algorithm.
	Then there exists $C(\alpha) > 0$ depending on only $\alpha$ and $c = c(\alpha,L) > 0$ such that
	\beq
		\P\bigg(
			\frac{\|\bG\|_{\op}}{N^{1/2}}
			 \le C(\alpha)
			\,\,\text{and}\,\,
			\frac{\|\bx\|}{N^{1/2}} \le 2
		\bigg) \ge 1-e^{-cN}\,.
	\eeq
	Furthermore, for any $k\ge 1$, there exists $C(\alpha,k)$ such that for all sufficiently large $N$,
	\beq
		\max\bigg\{
			\frac{\E[(\|\bG\|_{\op})^k]}
				{N^{k/2}}, 
			\frac{\E[\|\bx\|^k]}{N^{k/2}}
		\bigg\} \le C(\alpha,k)\,.
	\eeq
\begin{proof}
	By Lemma~\ref{l:wishart}, there exists $C(\alpha)$ such that 
	\beq
		
		\P\bigg(
		\frac{\|\bG\|_{\op}}{N^{1/2}}
		 \le C(\alpha)
		\bigg) \ge 1-e^{-cN}\,.
	\eeq
Since the mapping $(\bG,\bg^\aux) \mapsto \|\bx\|$ is $L$-Lipschitz, the random variable $\|\bx\|$ is $L$-subgaussian.
	Combined with the equality $\E[\|\bx\|^2] = N$ from Definition~\ref{d:Lip}, this readily implies
	\[
		\P\bigg(
		\frac{\|\bx\|}
			{N^{1/2}}
		 \le 2\bigg) 
		 \ge 1-e^{-cN}\,,
	\]
which gives \eqref{e:confinement.subgaussian.basic.tail}.
	By Jensen's inequality,
	\[
		\frac{\E\|\bx\|}{N^{1/2}}
		\le 
		\frac{\E[\|\bx\|^2]^{1/2}}
			{N^{1/2}}
		 = 1
		 \,.
	\]
Since $\|\bx\|$ is $L$-subgaussian, for any $u\ge1$ we have
	\[\P\bigg(
			\frac{\|\bx\|}{N^{1/2}} \ge u
		\bigg)
		\le \P\bigg(
			\frac{\|\bx\| - \E\|\bx\|]}{N^{1/2}} \ge u - 1
		\bigg) 
		\le \exp\bigg(
			-\frac{(u-1)^2 N}{2L^2}
		\bigg)\,.\]
Integrating this bound gives
	\begin{align*}
		\E\bigg[\frac{\|\bx\|^k}{N^{k/2}}\bigg]
		&\le 2^k + \int_{2^k}^\infty \P\bigg(
			\frac{\|\bx\|^k}{N^{k/2}} \ge t
		\bigg) \,dt
		= 2^k + \int_2^\infty \P\bigg(
			\frac{\|\bx\|}{N^{1/2}} \ge u
		\bigg) ku^{k-1}\,du \\
		&\le 2^k + \int_2^\infty \exp\bigg(-\frac{(u-1)^2 N}{2L^2}\bigg) ku^{k-1}\,du 
		\le 2^k + 1\,,
	\end{align*}
	where the last inequality holds for all sufficiently large $N$.
	Since the mapping $\bG \mapsto \|\bG\|_{\op}$ is $1$-Lipschitz, the random variable $\|\bG\|_{\op}$ is $1$-subgaussian.
	Then \eqref{e:confinement.wishart.restated} implies that $\E[\|\bG\|_{\op}] \le C(\alpha) N^{1/2}$. Then, by a similar calculation as above, we obtain
	\begin{align*}
		\E\bigg[\frac{\|\bG\|_{\op}^k}{N^{k/2}}\bigg]
		&\le (2C(\alpha))^k + \int_{2C(\alpha)^k}^\infty \P\bigg(
			\frac{\|\bG\|_{\op}^k}{N^{k/2}} \ge t
		\bigg) \,dt \\
		&= (2C(\alpha))^k + \int_{2C(\alpha)}^\infty \P\bigg(
			\frac{\|\bG\|_{\op}}{N^{1/2}} \ge u
		\bigg) ku^{k-1} \,du \\
		&\le (2C(\alpha))^k + \int_{2C(\alpha)}^\infty
		\exp\bigg(
			-\frac{(u-C(\alpha))^2 N}{2}
		\bigg) ku^{k-1}\,du
		\le (2C(\alpha))^k + 1\,,
	\end{align*}
	where the last inequality holds for all sufficiently large $N$.
	This proves \eqref{e:confinement.subgaussian.basic.moment}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:13:18.495274+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dec1f14d27a1db30a6d8dabe2fe80c84dc4cfadfc7e265da9ef866b4244aced3","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 5 of arXiv:2608.30578, 'Compactly Supported Solutions near a Nehari Critical Value'] Let
\[
\mathcal R(u):=
\frac{\displaystyle\int_\Omega|\nabla u|^2\,dx}
{\displaystyle\int_\Omega|u|^2\,dx},
\qquad
\mathcal A:=
\{u\in H_0^1(\Omega)\setminus\{0\}:M(u)\geq0\}.
\]
Suppose that \(\bar u\in\mathcal A\) is a local minimizer of
\(\mathcal R\) on \(\mathcal A\). Then there exist
\(\mu_0,\mu_1\geq0\), with \(\mu_0+\mu_1>0\), such that
\begin{equation}
	\mu_0D\mathcal R(\bar u)=\mu_1DM(\bar u),
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
	\mu_1M(\bar u)=0.
\end{equation}
If \(DM(\bar u)\neq0\), then \(\mu_0>0\), and consequently there exists
\(\mu\geq0\) such that
\begin{equation}
	D\mathcal R(\bar u)=\mu\,DM(\bar u),
	\qquad
	\mu M(\bar u)=0.
	
\end{equation}
Thus, under the constraint qualification \(DM(\bar u)\neq0\), the
Fritz John conditions \cite{John} reduce to the usual Kuhn--Tucker
conditions. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:13:49.974155+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dec516930bba9db6dd4e2b2facaf1814e8cf8f8e593d06d54f06d2a35b357538","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:forests of arXiv:2411.07157, 'Rough differential equations in the flow approach'] Define $\mathcal{T}_{1,2}\eqdef\mathcal{T}\times\{0,1\}\times\{0,1,2\}$, and denote by $\tilde\tau=(\tau,r,u)$ an element of $\mathcal{T}_{1,2}$. 
We introduce a set of (ordered, unlabelled) forests
\begin{equs}
\text{$   \widehat\mathcal{T}$}\eqdef
\Big\{{\boldsymbol{\tau}}=(\tilde {\tau}_1,\dots,\tilde{\tau}_{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})})
=
\Big( (\tau_1,r_1,u_1), \dots, (\tau_{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})},r_{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})},u_{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})}) 
\Big)\in\text{$\mathcal{T}$}_1^{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})}:p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})\in[P]
\Big\}\,. 
\end{equs}

For two forests ${\boldsymbol{\tau}},{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}\in\widehat\mathcal{T}$ and a tuple $I=(i_1,\dots,i_{|I|})$ consisting of distinct elements of $[p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})]$, we define the forest ${\boldsymbol{\tau}}_{I}$ by
\begin{equs}    {\boldsymbol{\tau}}_I\eqdef\big(\tilde\tau_{i_1},\dots,\tilde\tau_{i_{|I|}}\big)\,,
\end{equs}
and we define the forest  ${\boldsymbol{\tau}}\sqcup{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}$, the concatenation of ${\boldsymbol{\tau}}$ and ${\boldsymbol{\sigma}}$, by
\begin{equs}    {\boldsymbol{\tau}}\sqcup{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}\eqdef(\tilde\tau_1,\dots,\tilde\tau_{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})},\tilde\sigma_1,\dots,\tilde\sigma_{p({\boldsymbol{\sigma}})})\,.
\end{equs}
Fix ${\boldsymbol{\tau}}=(\tilde\tau_1,\dots,\tilde\tau_{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})})\in\widehat\mathcal{T}$ and
suppose that for every $i\in[p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})]$, we are given tuples of times $(t_{i},s^{\tau_i})\in(-\infty,1]\times\R^{\mathfrak{s}(\tau_i)}$.
We then write
\begin{equs}
    t_{{\boldsymbol{\tau}}}\eqdef (t_{\tau_1},\dots,t_{\tau_{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})}})  \in (-\infty,1]^{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})} \,,\;\text{and}\;s^{{\boldsymbol{\tau}}}\eqdef(s^{\tau_1},\dots,s^{\tau_{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})}}) \in \R^{\mathfrak{s}({\boldsymbol{\tau}})} \,,
\end{equs}
where $\mathfrak{s}({\boldsymbol{\tau}})\eqdef\sum_{i\in[p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})]}\text{$\mathfrak{s}$}(\tau_i)$ is the \textit{size} of ${\boldsymbol{\tau}}$. We also write $\mathfrak{l}({\boldsymbol{\tau}})\eqdef p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})+\mathfrak{s}({\boldsymbol{\tau}})$. 

Finally, we define the \textit{scaling} of ${\boldsymbol{\tau}}$ by
\begin{equs}    |{\boldsymbol{\tau}}|\eqdef\big(p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})-1\big)+\sum_{i=1}^{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})}|\tau_i|\,,
\end{equs}
the \textit{order} of ${\boldsymbol{\tau}}$ by $\text{${\mathfrak{o}}$}({\boldsymbol{\tau}})\eqdef \sum_{i\in[p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})]}\text{${\mathfrak{o}}$}(\tau_i) $, and set $r({\boldsymbol{\tau}})\eqdef\sum_{i\in[p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})]}r_i$ and $u({\boldsymbol{\tau}})\eqdef\sum_{i\in[p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})]}u_i$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.198334+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_df26d27bad5c5d1eeef1c6602c0d167196e97df45a91ccf2597a76b1fb895a00","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Cor 125 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $J\equiv J(p,2\tep,\lambda/2)$ as  defined by \eqref{e:bad.times.J}. Then the coefficients from Definition~\ref{d:cts.coeffs} satisfy the estimates 
	\[
	\max\left\{
	\begin{array}{c}
	|\tbbb(t,y)^2
		-\Tbbb(t,y)^2|,\\
	|\tvvv(t,y)-\Tvvv(t,y)|,\\
	|\tuuu(t,y)^2-\Tuuu(t,y)^2|
	\end{array}
	\right\}
	\le \bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} \lambda
	\]
for all $(t,y)\in( [q_*,1]  \setminus J)\times\R$. 

\begin{proof}
Lemma~\ref{l:limit.coefs} gives
	\[\begin{aligned}
	\tB(t,y)&=\tB^N(t,y)+o_N(1)\,,\\
	\Tbbb(t,y)&=\Tbbb^N(t,y)+o_N(1)
	\end{aligned}\]
for all $(t,y)\in[q_*,1]\times\R$. Recall that $(p^N)'(t)$ converges to $p'(t)$ for almost every $t$. Therefore, for \emph{every} $t$, we can find $s\in[t-\tep,t+\tep]$ such that $(p^N)'(s)$ converges to $p'(s)$. If $t\notin J$, then $t\notin J^N$ for sufficiently large $N$ by Lemma~\ref{l:bad.times.JN.J}, so $p'(s)$ differs from $p'(t)$ by at most $\lambda/2$, while $(p^N)'(s)$ differs from $(p^N)'(t)$ by at most $\lambda$. Therefore, for $t\in[q_*,1]\setminus J$, we have
	\[
	\Big|\tbbb(t,y)-\tbbb^N(t,y)\Big|
	=\bigg|\frac{\tB(t,y)}{p'(t)^{1/2}}
	-\frac{\tB^N(t,y)}{(p^N)'(t)^{1/2}}\bigg|
	\le o_N(1)
	+ \bigg( \frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)}(\MAX_N)^2
	\lambda\,,
	\]
using the bounds on $\tB^N$ and $\tB$ implied by Lemma~\ref{l:sp.smooth.reg} and Corollary~\ref{c:reg.in.limit}.
Additionally, since $t\notin J^N$,
Lemma~\ref{l:t.smooth.domain} bounds the discrepancy between $\tbbb^N(t,y)$ and $\Tbbb^N(t,y)$.
Sending $N\to\infty$ gives the claimed bound on the discrepancy between $\tbbb(t,y)$ and $\Tbbb(t,y)$. The other bounds follow by similar arguments:
	\begin{align*}
	\Big|\tvvv(t,y)-\tvvv^N(t,y)\Big|
	&=\bigg|
	\frac{\tV(t,y)}{p(t)}
	-\frac{\tV^N(t,y)}{p^N(t)}\bigg|\,,\\
	\Big|\tuuu(t,y)-\tuuu^N(t,y)\Big|
	&=\bigg|\frac{\tU(t,y)}{[ p(t)
		\cdot t p'(t)]^{1/2}}
		-\frac{\tU^N(t,y)}{[ p^N(t)
		\cdot t (p^N)'(t)]^{1/2}}
		\bigg|\,.
	\end{align*}
Note in these cases that in the factor $L^{O(1)}$ appearing in the final bound, the $O(1)$ exponent can depend on the constant $\breve{c}$ from \eqref{e:breve.q.bounds}. We will remark on this point again in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:Lipschitz-SDE-approx}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.356532+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_df2ec02ab8113e2c74344a7c95930cb4ecc1735b76c9be1b5407fe24fca67876","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 234 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] There exist $C(\alpha) > 0$ and $C(\alpha,L,K) > 0$, such that the following holds for all sufficiently large $N$.
	If $\cA_N$ is an $L$-Lipschitz algorithm and $\cA_{N[K]}$ is as in Definition~\ref{d:truncated.lip.alg}, then 
	\begin{align}
		
		\max\{ 
		\|\mu(\cA_N)\|_{L^2}^2
		,\|\mu(\cA_{N[K]})\|_{L^2}^2
		\}
		 &\le C(\alpha)\,, \\
		
		\|\mu(\cA_{N[K]})\|_{L^4}^4 &\le C(\alpha,L,K)\,.
	\end{align}
	Furthermore, for $\mu_\bG(\bx)$ defined in \eqref{eq:proj-pursuit-def}, there exists $c = c(\alpha,L) > 0$ such that
	\beq
		\P\bigg(\|\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux))\|_{L^2}^2 \le C(\alpha)
			\bigg) \ge 1 - e^{-cN}\,.
	\eeq

\begin{proof}
	Throughout this proof $c > 0$ is a constant depending on $\alpha,L$ which may change line by line. Recall that we abbreviate $\bx\equiv\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)$. 
	We prove \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.tail} first. Recalling the definition of $\fm$ from Definition~\ref{d:truncated.lip.alg}, note that
\beq
		\|\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux))\|_{L^2}^2
		=\frac{\|\fm\|^2}{M} 
		= \frac{1}{M} \bigg\|\frac{\bG \bx}{N^{1/2}}\bigg\|^2
		\le \frac{(\|\bG\|_{\op} \|\bx\|)^2}{MN} \,.
	\eeq
	By \eqref{e:confinement.subgaussian.basic.tail} from Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.subgaussian.basic}, with probability $1-e^{-cN}$ the above is
	\[
	\le \frac{C(\alpha)^2 N \cdot 4N}{MN} 
		= \frac{4C(\alpha)^2}{\alpha}\,.
	\]
	This proves \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.tail} after adjusting $C(\alpha)$.
	Next, note that
	\[
		\|\mu(\cA_N)\|_{L^2}^2
		= \E \|\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux))\|_{L^2}^2
		= 
		\frac{\E[\|\fm\|^2]}{M} 
		\stackrel{\eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.step1}}{\le} 
		\frac{\E[(\|\bG\|_{\op} \|\bx\|)^2]}{MN} \,.
	\]
By H\"older's inequality and the bound \eqref{e:confinement.subgaussian.basic.moment} from Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.subgaussian.basic}, the above is
	\[\le
		\frac{\E [(\|\bG\|_{\op})^4]^{1/2} \E[\|\bx\|^4]^{1/2}}{MN} 
		\le \frac{C(\alpha,4)N^2}{MN} 
		= \frac{C(\alpha,4)}{\alpha}\,,
	\]
	for $C(\alpha,4)$ defined in Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.subgaussian.basic}.
This proves the first part of \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l2} after adjusting $C(\alpha)$. For the second part of \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l2}, we split into cases depending on whether $a\in S_K(\cA_N)$. Recall that the truncated algorithm $\cA_{N[K]}$ resamples the rows indexed by $S_K(\cA_N)$. If $a\notin S_K(\cA_N)$, then $\tilde{\fm}_a$ is equidistributed as $\fm_a$, so they have the same second moment. If $a\in S_K(\cA_N)$, then 
	\[\tilde{\fm}_a
		= \frac{(\bg^a, \tilde{\bx})}{N^{1/2}}\,.
	\]
where $\bg^a$ is independent of $\tilde{\bx}$, as $\cA_{N[K]}$ does not use the input $\bg^a$.
	Thus, the distribution of $\tilde{\fm}_a$ conditional on $\tilde{\bx}$ is a (one-dimensional) centered gaussian random variable with standard deviation $\|\tilde{\bx}\| / N^{1/2}$. It follows in this case that
	\[
	\E[(\tilde{\fm}_a)^2]
	= \frac{\E[\|\tilde{\bx}\|^2]}{N}=1\,.
	\]
Altogether this gives
	\[
	\|\mu(\cA_{N[K]})\|^2
	=\frac{ \E[\|\tilde{\fm}\|^2]}{M}
	\le
	\frac{ \E[\|\fm\|^2 + M]}{M}
	\le C(\alpha)+1\,.
	\]
This proves the second part of \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l2} after adjusting $C(\alpha)$.

Finally we turn to the proof of  \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l4}. Recalling the notations of Definition~\ref{d:truncated.lip.alg}, let
	\[
	\tilde{\fm}_a

		\Big)

where we recall that $\tilde{\bx}\equiv \cA_{N[K]}(\bG,\bg^{\aux+}))$. 
We then aim to bound

		= \E \Big[\|\mu_\bG(\cA_{N[K]}(\bG,\bg^{\aux+}))\|_{L^4}^4\Big]

	\]
To this end, we will show that there exists $C(\alpha,L,K)$ such that
	\beq
		\E[(\tilde{\fm}_a)^4] \le C(\alpha,L,K)
	\eeq
	for all $a\in [M]$, which implies \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l4}.

{"assumptions":["t>0.","The classical Ibragimov characterization for nondegenerate absolutely continuous laws."],"created_at":"2026-10-10T06:51:51.364956+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_df81d86c41a2e859c5a707fc5ae34d83a64ca8c89b34f2c04e48ecc49cc1f09a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked] This is a proved special case of Problem 3.11 of Takahiro Hasebe and Yuki Ueda's Large time unimodality for classical and free Brownian motions with initial distributions, ALEA 15 (2018), 353-374, DOI:10.30757/ALEA.v15-15 (arXiv:1710.08240). A probability measure is unimodal if, for some mode m, it is an atom at m plus an absolutely continuous measure whose density is nondecreasing to the left of m and nonincreasing to the right. Write boxplus for additive free convolution, the distribution of a sum of freely independent self-adjoint variables with the indicated laws, and * for classical convolution of independent real variables. Call lambda freely strongly unimodal if lambda boxplus nu is unimodal for every unimodal probability measure nu. For every t>0 the centered Cauchy distribution C_t with density t/[pi(t^2+x^2)] is not freely strongly unimodal: some unimodal nu makes nu boxplus C_t nonunimodal. The proof combines the Cauchy convolution identity with Ibragimov's characterization of classical strong unimodality by log-concavity of the density; the Cauchy density is not log-concave. This is an unrefereed campaign result.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["H is a complex Hilbert space","a one-parameter family of unitaries or an exponential e^{itT} is being used","the continuity and self-adjointness hypotheses are the ones at issue"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.772569+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, spectral theory, quantum dynamics","id":"claim_df9328ea820c9b58103e280388d82cc43f63148f9a76b0b2e1fdd63f459b8d1b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypotheses: (i) U(t) is unitary for every t ∈ ℝ and satisfies the group law on all of ℝ; (ii) t ↦ U(t)x is continuous (weak continuity or, on a separable space, weak measurability suffices, but some regularity is required); (iii) the generator is self-adjoint. What fails. Without any continuity: pick a discontinuous additive function φ: ℝ → ℝ (a Hamel basis construction) and set H = ℂ, U(t) = e^{iφ(t)}. This is a one-parameter group of unitaries with U(0) = 1, but φ is non-measurable and unbounded on every interval, so U(t) is not of the form e^{ita} for any real a; no generator exists. Hence 'one-parameter unitary group' without a continuity hypothesis carries no spectral information. Overshooting in the other direction: if one assumes t ↦ U(t) is continuous in operator norm, then the generator is necessarily bounded, so norm continuity is the wrong hypothesis for Schrodinger evolutions, where A is unbounded. With a symmetric but not self-adjoint generator: on L²(0, ∞) the right translation semigroup (T(t)f)(x) = f(x − t) for x > t, 0 for x ≤ t, is a C_0-semigroup of isometries that is not a group (T(t) is not surjective), and its generator is A = −d/dx on {f ∈ H¹(0, ∞) : f(0) = 0}, i.e. A = −iS with S = −i d/dx closed and symmetric with deficiency indices (1, 0). {"assumptions":["M is a compact Riemannian manifold and f a C^1 diffeomorphism of M","mu is an f-invariant Borel probability measure (compactness makes the Oseledets integrability condition automatic)","the exponents, multiplicities and subspaces are measurable and f-invariant; constant a.e. when mu is ergodic","the Oseledets splitting is measurable, generally not continuous, and the Pesin blocks are not invariant"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:09:43.732600+00:00","domain":"smooth ergodic theory, Lyapunov exponents","id":"claim_dfb0e656c58d4f14dd665a85b8ce62d25a662a2455b987541fa0436ab64565e1","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f be a C^1 diffeomorphism of a compact Riemannian manifold M and mu an f-invariant Borel probability measure. Since M is compact, log of the norm of Df and of Df^{-1} are bounded, hence integrable, so Oseledets' multiplicative ergodic theorem applies: for mu-a.e. x there are finitely many numbers lambda_1(x) > lambda_2(x) > ... > lambda_{k(x)}(x) (the LYAPUNOV EXPONENTS at x) and a Df-invariant splitting of the tangent space

  T_x M = E_1(x) + ... + E_{k(x)}(x),   Df_x E_i(x) = E_i(f x),

such that for every nonzero v in E_i(x) the limit of (1/n) log |Df^n_x v| as n -> +-infinity exists and equals lambda_i(x). The functions x -> lambda_i(x), the multiplicities dim E_i(x), and the subspaces are measurable and f-invariant; if mu is ergodic they are constant almost everywhere. The splitting is in general only MEASURABLE, not continuous, and the convergence is not uniform in x.

Two structural facts that every application uses. (1) TEMPEREDNESS: any measurable positive function that is subexponential along orbits -- such as the angle between the Oseledets subspaces, or the norm of the change to Lyapunov (adapted) coordinates -- can be chosen tempered, meaning (1/n) log of its value at f^n x tends to 0; this is what lets one build Lyapunov charts in which Df is uniformly contracting on the negative-exponent bundle at the cost of a chart size that shrinks subexponentially along the orbit. (2) PESIN BLOCKS: for each l one collects the points where the Oseledets estimates hold with uniform constants depending on l; the resulting sets Lambda_l are COMPACT (after discarding a null set and restricting the subbundles continuously), increase in l, exhaust a full-measure set, and carry uniform hyperbolic-like estimates. They are NOT f-invariant -- an orbit wanders between blocks -- which is exactly why non-uniformly hyperbolic statements are local-and-measurable rather than uniform.

A point x is called (non-uniformly) hyperbolic when no exponent at x is zero; the stable bundle E^s(x) is the sum of the E_i(x) with lambda_i(x) < 0 and the unstable bundle the sum of those with lambda_i(x) > 0. Zero exponents are the obstruction: nothing in this framework says anything about directions with zero exponent.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:03:59.375619+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dff9bffa0ab891c73511e0184790ef06096f22a114fc8353137b035d6e8368dc","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:stexist of arXiv:2507.08757, 'Strong existence and uniqueness of the tilt-indexed Busemann process in the planar corner '] There exists a stochastic process 
\begin{align}
    \bigl(B^{h{\scaleobj{0.8}{\boxempty}}}(x,y) : x,y\in\mathbb{Z}^2,\, h \in \mathcal{H},\, {\scaleobj{0.9}{\boxempty}} \in \{+,-\}\bigr)
\end{align}
on $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})$ with the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}  [label={\rm(\alph*)}, ref={\rm\alph*}]   \itemsep=3pt
\item \textup{(}No $\pm$ distinction at fixed $h$\textup{)} For each $h \in \mathcal{H}$, 
\[
\mathbb{P}\{B^{h-}= B^{h+}\}=1.
\]
When $B^{h-}(\omega) = B^{h+}(\omega)$, call the common cocycle $B^h(\omega)$.
\item \textup{(}Forward measurable Busemann function\textup{)} For each $h\in \mathcal{H}, B^h \in \mathcal K_c^+$.
\item \textup{(}Mean $-h$\textup{)} For each $h \in \mathcal{H}$ and $i\in\{1,2\}$, $\mathbb{E}[B^h(0,e_i)] = -h \cdot e_i.$
\item \textup{(}Monotonicity\textup{)} For $h,h'\in \mathcal{H}$ with $h \cdot e_1 \leq h' \cdot e_1$, all $x \in \mathbb{Z}^2$, and $\mathbb{P}$ almost every $\omega$
\[ 
    B^{h-}(x,x+e_1) \geq  B^{h+}(x,x+e_1) \geq  B^{h'-}(x,x+e_1) \geq  B^{h'-}(x,x+e_1)  
\]
and
\[ 
    B^{h-}(x,x+e_2) \leq  B^{h+}(x,x+e_2) \leq  B^{h'-}(x,x+e_2) \leq  B^{h'-}(x,x+e_2).
\]
\item \textup{(}Left-/right-continuity\textup{)} For $\mathbb{P}$-almost all $\omega$, all $h\in \mathcal{H}$, and all $x,y\in\mathbb{Z}^2$,
\begin{equation*}\begin{aligned}
B^{h-}(x,y) = \lim_{\substack{\mathcal{H}\hspace{0.5pt}\hspace{0.5pt}\ni\hspace{0.5pt} \hspace{0.5pt} h' \to h\\ h'\cdot e_1 \nearrow h \cdot e_1}} B^{h\pm}(x,y) \,\text{ and }\, B^{h-}(x,y) = \lim_{\substack{\mathcal{H}\hspace{0.5pt}\hspace{0.5pt}\ni\hspace{0.5pt} \hspace{0.5pt} h' \to h\\ h'\cdot e_1 \searrow h \cdot e_1}} B^{h\pm}(x,y).
\end{aligned}\end{equation*}
\end{enumerate}
Moreover, this process is unique in the sense that any two processes satisfying the above conditions are equal almost surely. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}
