{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:57:30.978276+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f69c0fe872d6b0c2de0d5b127f6bc48ad18dca028b41e0c3661273348c09782c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 2 (Structural representation and exact extraction) of arXiv:2608.12492, 'Weak Limits of Wiener Chaos: Primitive--Fock Classification and Hilbert--Stein Extraction'] For every represented subsequence of \eqref{overview:eq:packet}, the
following statements hold.

 \end{equation}

 \eqref{overview:eq:weak-closure}; collision-null replicas give the
 converse realization and the convergence of the finite contraction
 register.

 \item Put
 \begin{equation}
 a_Q=\sum_{r=1}^{Q-1}\binom{Q-1}{r}^2\binom{2r}{r},

 feedback energy and the coherently aggregated Gaussian self-plus-interface
 defect satisfy
 \begin{equation}

 \le\frac{\mu_Qa_QR^4}{J}.
 
 \end{equation}
 Consequently, along a further subsequence,
 \begin{equation}
 F_n\Longrightarrow A_*+G_C,
 \qquad G_C\indep A_*.
 
 \end{equation}
 This factorization is quantitative and unconditional, but the active
 factor $A_*$ need not be canonical.

 and the finite-level characteristic-function error is bounded by a

 \begin{equation}
 T=\mathsf A^{\can}+\mathsf G^{\can},

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.177619+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f6cf902830d44196232726e732f11132c890f43f7349e2277ad075f47de1989b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 78 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For $\hat{Y}$ the stopped martingale defined above, we can construct a deterministic time change $\tilde{Y}$ that can be expressed as the stochastic integral
    \[
    \tilde{Y}(t)
    =\tilde{Y}(q_0) + \int_0^t \tilde{w}_t\,d\tilde{W}(t)
    \]
for $t\in[q_0,\gamma(1)]$,
where
$\tilde{Y}(q_0)=\hat{Y}(q_0)=Y(q_0)$,
$\tilde{W}$ is a standard Brownian motion, and $\tilde{w}$ satisfies
the constraint $\E[(\tilde{w}_t)^2]=1$ for all $t\in[q_0,\gamma(1)]$.

\begin{proof} We will construct a  martingale $\tilde{Y}$ to essentially be the deterministic time-change of $\hat{Y}$ such that $\E[\tilde{Y}(t)^2]=t$ for all $t\in[q_0,\gamma(1)]$. Then, for $t\in[\gamma(1),1]$, we will take $\tilde{Y}$ to be any martingale ending at $\pm1$ almost surely, which exists by Lemma~\ref{lem:Yt-process-always-is-completable} below. To formalize the time reparametrization, since $\gamma:[q_0,1]\to[q_0,\gamma(1)]$ is nondecreasing, we can define its right-continuous generalized inverse 
\[\lambda:[q_0,\gamma(1)]\to[q_0,1]\,.\]
As a consequence of \eqref{e:gamma.prime} we must have $\gamma(t)-\gamma(s)\le t-s$ and $\lambda(t)-\lambda(s)\ge t-s$ for all $q_0 \le s\le t\le1$. It  follows by combining these inequalities with Proposition~\ref{p:gamma-1} that
    \beq
    \begin{aligned}
    s &\ge \gamma(s) \ge \gamma(1)+s-1 \ge s-4\epsilon^{1/2}\,,\\
    t &\le \lambda(t) \le \lambda(\gamma(1)) + t-\gamma(1)
    =1+t-\gamma(1) \le t+4\epsilon^{1/2}
    \end{aligned}
    \eeq
for all $s\in [q_0,1]$, and $t\in [q_0,\gamma(1)]$. It is clear from this that we must define $\tilde{Y}(t) = \hat{Y}(\lambda(t))$, so that
we will have $\E[\tilde{Y}(t)^2] = \E[\hat{Y}(\lambda(t))^2] = \gamma(\lambda(t))=t$. Since
    \[
    \hat{Y}(\lambda(t)) = Y(q_0) + \int_{q_0}^{\lambda(t)}
        w_u \ind\{u\le\tau\} \,dW(u)\,,
    \]
by considering the change of variables $u=\lambda(s)$ it is natural to define
    \beq
    \tilde{W}(t) = \int_{q_0}^{\lambda(t)} \gamma'(u)^{1/2} dW(u)\,.
    \eeq
Then $\tilde{W}$ is a local martingale with quadratic variation
    \[
    \langle \tilde{W}\rangle_t 
    = \int_{q_0}^{\lambda(t)} \gamma'(u)\,du
    = \gamma(\lambda(t))-\gamma(q_0) = t-q_0
    \]
for all $t\in[q_0,1]$, so by the L\'evy characterization it is a standard Brownian motion on $t\in[q_0,1]$, and is progressively measurable with respect to the time-changed filtration
$\tilde{\cF}_Y(t)\equiv\cF_Y(\lambda(t))$. We then define the modified control
    \[
    \tilde{w}_s
    \equiv
    \frac{w_{\lambda(s)}}{\gamma'(\lambda(s))^{1/2} }
      \ind\{\lambda(s)\le \tau\}\,,\]
where we define $\tilde{w}_s\equiv1$ in the case $\gamma'(\lambda(s))=0$ --- by Lemma~\ref{l:generalized.inverse.fn}, the set of such times $s$ is of measure zero. If $\gamma'(\lambda(s))=0$ then clearly we have $\E[(\tilde{w}_s)^2]=1$, and otherwise 
\eqref{e:gamma.prime} gives
	\[\E[(\tilde{w}_s)^2]
    =\frac{\E[(w_{\lambda(s)})^2 \ind\{
        \lambda(s)\le\tau\}]}
        {\gamma'(\lambda(s))}
    = 1\,.
    \]
We can then express the desired process as
    \[
    \tilde{Y}(t)
    = \hat{Y}(\lambda(t))
    =\tilde{Y}(q_0) + \int_{q_0}^t \tilde{w}_s\,d\tilde{W}(s)\,,
    \]
where $\tilde{Y}(q_0)=\hat{Y}(q_0)= Y(q_0)$. This concludes the proof.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

 T_h=sum_{t=h}^r M_t.

Over ALL generators, with source Mis_infinity<=c required in every
compatible world (including every compatible A support), the proposed
exact conditional worst-world false-mass frontier is

 V_D(c)=tau_ell*(T_ell-c)_+
        +sum_{h=ell+1}^r (tau_h-tau_{h-1})*(T_h-c)_+.       (1)

All formulas allow missing D_h and c in [0,1]. Exact score bins define
source Mis_infinity=TV(g,p_Pi), with p uniformly coarsened in each bin.

## Lower bound across arbitrary mixed bins

Average orientations fairly and A supports uniformly conditional on
containing their known identities. Let mu be the resulting mean law.
Every known true atom in a variable context has density

 a=(1/r+1/K)/(2N).

The uncertified atoms of a pair at count h have density b_h and false
probability tau_h under this artificial prior. Their total mu mass is
M_h across the D_h pairs. Known S atoms have density 1/(NK).

As h increases, tau_h increases and b_h decreases: directly,
b_h-b_{h+1}=(K-r)/(2Nr(K-h)(K-h-1)) when h<r. All safe densities
are >=1/(NK)>=b_h. Thus E_h, the union of uncertified atoms in pairs
with count at least h, consists of lower-density atoms than its entire
complement. For ANY partition Pi, uniform coarsening increases its mass:

 mu_Pi(E_h)>=mu(E_h)=T_h.

Indeed in each cell the mean density over E_h is at most the mean over
its complement, so replacing both means by the cell mean transfers
mass into E_h. This proves the assertion per bin, not merely globally.

Robust feasibility and linearity/TV convexity give TV(mu_Pi(g),g)<=c.
Hence g(E_h)>=(T_h-c)_+. Layer-cake decomposition of the artificial
average false risk gives

 max_world H(g)>=tau_ell*g(E_ell)
                   +sum_{h>ell}(tau_h-tau_{h-1})*g(E_h)
                >=V_D(c).

No joint-probability multiplication or actual-posterior identity is used.

## Matching construction

Start from mu. Remove mass min(c,T_ell) from uncertified groups in
decreasing h order, uniformly within each h group, and add it uniformly
to the fixed known S reservoir. All remaining g(E_h)=(T_h-c)_+.
Each pair's known-true group has h atoms from each sibling and invariant
source mass h*(1/r+1/K)/N. Its uncertified group has K-h atoms from
each sibling and invariant source mass (2-h/r-h/K)/N, regardless of
orientation or which residual truths occupy A. The constructed g is
constant on every such group. Exact score bins only merge invariant
groups, so p_Pi=mu_Pi in every compatible world. Since g_Pi=g,
Mis_infinity<=TV(mu,g)<=c. The uncertified false-atom fraction in each
h group equals tau_h in every world. Thus actual H equals V_D(c)
worldwise, proving conditional sharpness of (1).

## Same-data oracle and exact estimation penalty

If the true partition is additionally supplied, let

 A_h=D_h*(r-h)/(Nr), Q_h=sum_{t=h}^r A_t,
 alpha_h=(K-r)/(K-h)=2tau_h.

The same-data known-partition frontier, by the ordered known-A groups,
is

 O_D(c)=alpha_ell*(Q_ell-c)_+
        +sum_{h>ell}(alpha_h-alpha_{h-1})*(Q_h-c)_+.       (2)

Here A_h is the posterior mass of unknown true candidates of the actual
A contexts, and their densities decrease while their false risks rise.
The same mixed-bin tail proof and transfer-to-S construction apply.
Thus V_D(c)=O_D(c)+[V_D(c)-O_D(c)] is an exact matching decomposition,
with nonnegative difference because giving the partition enlarges
feasibility. At c=0 it simplifies to the explicit positive penalty

 V_D(0)-O_D(0)
   =sum_{h=ell}^r D_h*h*(K-r)^2/(2NrK(K-h)).             (3)

The penalty is zero at h=0, and at h=r contributes kappa/(2N) per pair,
recovering C013's unresolved full-verifier value. In general it depends
on the factual-support histogram, not merely VC dimension or a single
unweighted classification-error scalar. A fair completion among the
2^d support-consistent ERM orientations has conditional expected
classification error 1/N per pair; (3) weights that error by
h*(K-r)^2/[2rK(K-h)]. This is a specified ERM, not an optimal posterior
classification claim. The conditional minimax lower bound is not
silently averaged into a global expected lower bound; C014 forbids
that shortcut at positive budgets.

## Scope

This removes supplied tags and retains actual factual identities for
every balanced outcome, all n,K,r,ell and all calibration budgets. It
allows different h across pairs, but does not cover unequal sibling
counts, already identified pairs, or an unconditional exact expected
frontier. Equal h in every pair reduces the conditional formula to the
corresponding earlier C008 experiment with that many known truths;
the histogram, actual untagged-data applicability and explicit oracle
penalty are the proposed extension, not a claim that C008 was unknown.
Primary basis: Kalai--Vempala 2311.14648v3 Definitions 1--2 pp.8--9;
own earlier C008/C009 are unaudited drafts. No novelty or target score
is certified until independent mathematical and priority review.

## Extension: include identified pairs under a coverage ordering

The same theorem extends as follows. Partition the d pairs into resolved
and unresolved pairs. A resolved pair has a context with >r distinct
known truths, logically forcing S and identifying its sibling as A.
Let E_j count these known A contexts with j distinct known truths,
ell<=j<=r. Each unresolved pair still has balanced count h<=r; D_h
now counts just these unresolved pairs. Require

 j>=h_max for every resolved A, where
 h_max=max{h:D_h>0}.                                    (4)

If no unresolved pairs exist, condition (4) is vacuous. Known facts
in identified S and fixed S contexts are all safe and have density
1/(NK), irrespective of their observed identities or counts.

There are two positive-risk group types under the artificial compatible
prior (independent fair unresolved orientations and uniform compatible
A supports):

* Unresolved count h: mass M_h as before, risk tau_h, density b_h.
* Resolved A count j: mass L_j=E_j*(r-j)/(Nr), risk
  alpha_j=(K-r)/(K-j), density a_j=(r-j)/(Nr(K-j)).

Groups at j=r can have zero factual mass and risk one; retain them
without dividing by their mass. All safe groups have density >=1/(NK).
For resolved groups, j increasing makes risk increase and density
decrease. Across the two types condition (4) implies

 alpha_j>=alpha_hmax=2tau_hmax>=tau_h,
 a_j<=a_hmax<=b_hmax<=b_h.

Thus ALL groups are ordered in opposite directions by density and risk.
Let 0<xi_1<...<xi_s<=1 be their distinct risk values; aggregate masses
at equal risk into m_i, and let R_i=sum_{k=i}^s m_k, xi_0=0. The exact
combined conditional robust frontier is

 V(c)=sum_{i=1}^s (xi_i-xi_{i-1})*(R_i-c)_+.             (5)

The same arbitrary-bin tail argument proves the lower bound. Remove
mass in decreasing risk order, uniformly inside each group, and transfer
to fixed S for the upper bound. Resolved A certified and uncertified
groups have world-invariant p masses because all residual supports
have the same size and contain the known truths. Unresolved balanced
groups have the invariance proved earlier. Consequently exact score
mergers remain valid for every compatible support and orientation.
False fractions equal the specified risks in EACH actual world, so
the construction attains (5) worldwise, not just on artificial average.

The same-data partition oracle is formula (2) with A_h replaced by

 (D_h+E_h)*(r-h)/(Nr).

At c=0 its exact difference from (5) is still formula (3), now summed
over unresolved pairs only. The identified-pair terms cancel. At any
c, both explicit formulas match their respective conditional minima.
When ell=r, every resolved A has j=r and condition (4) always holds;
this reduces (5) to C013's conditional frontier for arbitrary mixtures
of resolved and unresolved pairs. For ell<r this is a larger untagged
partial-verifier data regime than the all-unresolved case.

Unequal sibling counts or failure of (4) are NOT covered. No exact
global expected minimax value follows by averaging (5). This extension
has a separate route check, logs/route_014_extension_check.txt, and its
finite exact verification is kept separate from the general derivation.

## Zero-budget pointwise scope and an explicit control

If all pairs are unresolved and share ONE count h, every atom of the
artificial mean law has density at least b_h. Robust zero calibration
implies g=mu_Pi, hence g(atom)>=b_h. Each actual world has exactly
d(K-r) false atoms. Consequently every such generator obeys the
POINTWISE bound H>=d(K-r)b_h=V_D(0), and the construction attains it.
This separate observation applies regardless of actual orientation
likelihoods. It does not extend to varying h by the same argument.

In fact varying h can destroy even a zero-budget pointwise version of
the conditional bound. Take N=5,d=2,K=3,r=2,ell=0 and counts h_0=0,
h_1=1; use C_2=C_3={0}. These are possible actual untagged data, e.g.
the two observations (2,0),(3,0). Form a bin B containing all three
atoms of context 0 and the four uncertified atoms of contexts 2 and 3.
Its source mass is 1/5+7/30=13/30, independent of orientations and
residual A supports; set g=13/210 on its seven atoms. Other bins are
all of context 1 (g=1/15), both certified atoms of contexts 2 and 3
(g=1/12), and all fixed-S context 4 (g=1/15). Merging the equal 1/15
scores preserves invariance. This g is robustly source-calibrated at
zero in every compatible world.

If context 0 is A its actual false mass is 13/105, strictly below
V_D(0)=1/8 by 1/840. If context 1 is A, its false mass is 9/70,
strictly above 1/8. This is a real compatible-world control, not a
violation of (1) or (5): the theorem is conditional WORST-WORLD, and
the latter world meets that lower bound. It forbids silently replacing
the conditional maximum by a per-world bound even at zero budget in
the varying-count family. No claim about the global sampling minimax
value follows from this single outcome.

For parameters $v, t \geq 0$, we have the probability inequalities

{"assumptions":["Rate-independent random recursive tree attachment.","The cited recursive-tree height estimate and standard root-subtree size limit."],"created_at":"2026-10-10T06:51:51.364062+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f8302037ad42a1dd803c8611710c6292f630e9af8a604deb9e7eedb3628d95f2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked; the combinatorial identities (layer = second-largest branch height, maximum layer = floor(diam/2) <= height) were verified by brute-force leaf stripping on 40 random recursive trees of sizes 6 to 120 (480 vertices), with the 5-vertex path as a control] This is the layer part of the campaign answer to Conjecture 2 of H. Stepanyants, P. L. Krapivsky, H. Hartle and D. Krioukov, The rank and layer distributions in random recursive trees, arXiv:2608.04303. For each integer n>=3, let T_n be a random recursive tree on vertices 1,...,n, in which each vertex j>=2 chooses its parent independently and uniformly from 1,...,j-1. Repeatedly remove all vertices of degree at most one, assigning layer zero to the first removed set and successively increasing the layer. Let L_n be the maximum layer. As n tends to infinity, L_n=e log n-(3/2)log log n+O_P(1), where logarithms are natural and O_P(1) means that the centered sequence is bounded in probability. Under this removal rule, L_n=floor(diameter(T_n)/2); other conventions for the last vertex left standing change the maximum by at most one. The proof uses the recursive-tree height estimate of Addario-Berry and Ford (Corollary 1.3) and the fact that the root's normalized subtree sizes have a stick-breaking limit whose second-largest term is positive almost surely. The maximum-rank part of Conjecture 2 is not addressed. This is an unrefereed campaign result.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:37:08.311265+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f89142b3ce3207a5f8a77e9d9fadf6b6d2e60a06c33b0f009a7d0dd0e6b49e25","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:quagmire of arXiv:2608.28505, 'Quagmires and large Suslin forests'] Given an uncountable cardinal $\kappa$ and a set $S \subseteq \mathrm{Lim}(\kappa)$, a\linebreak \emph{$(\kappa, S)$-quagmire} is a quadruple $(T, {<}, {\lhd}, Q)$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[label={(Q\arabic*)},  start=0]
\item 
\begin{enumerate}
\item $(T, <)$ is a $\kappa$-Kurepa tree,
\item $\lhd$ is a binary relation on $T$ whose restriction to each level of $T$ is a strict linear order; nodes of distinct heights are $\lhd$-incomparable,
\item the function $Q$ is a partial function from $T^2$ to $T$ whose domain consists of the pairs $(x, y) \in T^2$ such that $\mathrm{ht}(x) < \mathrm{ht}(y)$ and $x \lhd \pi_{\mathrm{ht}(x)}(y)$,
\end{enumerate}

\item if $(x, y) \in \mathrm{dom}(Q)$, then $x < Q(x, y) \lhd y$,
\item if $(x, y) \in \mathrm{dom}(Q)$ and $y < z$, then $Q(Q(x, y), z) = Q(x,z)$,
\item if $(y, z) \in \mathrm{dom}(Q)$ and $x \lhd y$, then $Q(x, Q(y, z)) = Q(x, z)$,
\item if $x \lhd y$ and $\mathrm{ht}(x) \in S \cup \{\kappa\}$, then there exists $\alpha < \mathrm{ht}(x)$ such that $\pi_\alpha(x) \lhd \pi_\alpha(y)$ and $x = Q(\pi_\alpha(x), y)$.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

Then, a \textbf{relaxation rate map} consists of a smooth fiberwise map $\mathscr B=\mathscr B(\beta,\zeta)\in\mathscr E^*$ defined for all future timelike $\beta$ and all $\zeta \in \mathscr F$, satisfying the following conditions.

\bei 

\item \emph{Stable equilibrium property:}
\bel{eq:pot-relax-map}
\mathscr B(\beta,0)=0,
\qquad
\zeta_{\alpha\beta}\mathscr B^{\alpha\beta}(\beta,\zeta)\geq0,
\qquad
\zeta_{\alpha\beta}\mathscr B^{\alpha\beta}(\beta,\zeta)=0
\Longleftrightarrow
\zeta=0.
\ee

\item \emph{Positivity property:}  Its linearization along the equilibrium manifold $\mathbb M$ given by 
\bel{eq:pot-relax-linearization}
\mathbb M^{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}(\beta)
\coloneqq
\frac{\del\mathscr B^{\alpha\beta}}{\del\zeta_{\gamma\delta}}(\beta,0)
\ee
must be symmetric under interchange of the two index pairs and positive definite on~$\mathscr E$, namely
\be
\eta_{\alpha\beta}\mathbb M^{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}(\beta)\eta_{\gamma\delta}>0
\qquad
\text{for every nonzero }\eta\in\mathscr E.
\ee
\eei
Furthermore, the associated \textbf{production term} is
\bel{production-term-value}
\mathfrak d_{\mathscr B}
\coloneqq
\zeta_{\alpha\beta}\mathscr B^{\alpha\beta}

component $\mathcal C$ with $r_{\mathcal C}\le L\log n$ nonconstant
slots, one physical anchor, and its complete packet/root channel.
A hard ordinary supernode is one fused physical time containing either a
nonsingleton packet resource or the time-indexed linear Jacobi child
$-2N^{-1}W_i$.  The coupled pure-Weyl root is a special hard symbol; the
total number of special root symbols is bounded by an absolute constant
$B_0$.  Aggregate Ricci is not present in this ported theorem and is
treated separately in the aggregate-Ricci synthesis below.

For every fixed $L$ there are $A_L<\infty$ and a numerical exponent
$B<\infty$ for which the estimate below holds.

Suppose $\mathcal C$ contains a hard resource and reserve its
chronologically earliest resource-bearing hard supernode as the endpoint,
breaking a same-node tie by the fixed ribbon-slot order.  Let
\[
\begin{aligned}
 b_{\mathcal C}&=\#\{\text{surplus ordinary hard supernodes}\},\\
 o_{\mathcal C}&=\#\{\text{all }\mathsf S^\pm
                         \text{ singleton supernodes}\},\\
 v_{\mathcal C}&=\#\{\text{all }\mathsf V
                         \text{ singleton supernodes}\},\\
 t_{\mathcal C}&=b_{\mathcal C}+o_{\mathcal C}+v_{\mathcal C}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{3.4.1x}
\]
If $\mathfrak e_{\mathcal C}$ is the selected endpoint resource and
$\mathfrak a_{\Gamma,\mathcal C}$ is the remaining normalized terminal
amplitude, then, for $\delta=1/16$,
\[
 \boxed{
 \sum_{\substack{\text{weak orders, equality blocks, finite gaps,}\\
                  \text{and typed states on }\mathcal C}}
 |\operatorname{Contr}_{\Gamma,\mathcal C}|
 \le A_L^{r_{\mathcal C}}(r_{\mathcal C}+1)^B
 \mathfrak e_{\mathcal C}\mathfrak a_{\Gamma,\mathcal C}
 n^{-\delta t_{\mathcal C}}.}
\tag{3.4.1x$_1$}
\]
The estimate holds at the application horizon $m=cN$ for each fixed

{"assumptions":["(a_n)_{n >= 0} is a real sequence","the second differences a_n - 2a_{n+1} + a_{n+2} are nonnegative for every n >= 0 (convexity)","a_n -> 0 as n -> infinity","consequences used and derived from these: a_n >= 0, a_n nonincreasing, n(a_n - a_{n+1}) -> 0, sum (n+1)(a_n - 2a_{n+1} + a_{n+2}) = a_0","integrability is with respect to Lebesgue measure on the circle"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:07:38.815245+00:00","domain":"Fourier analysis, trigonometric series","id":"claim_f95cf78453cad9016df951c8497b0e8bcbb54049fe66f88a10ab868d7db99aa2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (a_n)_{n >= 0} be real numbers which are CONVEX, meaning the second differences D2 a_n := a_n - 2 a_{n+1} + a_{n+2} are >= 0 for every n >= 0, and which tend to 0. (These two hypotheses already force a_n >= 0 and a_n nonincreasing: the first differences a_{n+1} - a_n are nondecreasing, so if one of them were positive the sequence would tend to +infinity. They also force n(a_n - a_{n+1}) -> 0, since the differences are monotone.) THEOREM (Young; Zygmund, Trigonometric Series, Ch. V). Put S(x) = a_0/2 + sum_{n >= 1} a_n cos(nx). Then: (1) the series converges for every x not in 2 pi Z, uniformly on every compact subset of (0, 2 pi); (2) S(x) >= 0 for all such x; (3) S is Lebesgue integrable on (-pi, pi), with (1/(2 pi)) times the integral of S over (-pi,pi) equal to a_0/2; (4) the series IS the Fourier series of S, that is a_n = (1/pi) times the integral over (-pi,pi) of S(x) cos(nx) dx for every n >= 0. The whole theorem rests on one identity: with K_n(x) = (1/(n+1)) (sin((n+1)x/2) / sin(x/2))^2 >= 0 the Fejer kernel, normalised so that (1/(2 pi)) times the integral of K_n over (-pi,pi) is 1, double summation by parts gives S(x) = sum_{n >= 0} (n+1) (D2 a_n) (1/2) K_n(x), with sum_{n >= 0} (n+1) D2 a_n = a_0 < infinity. Nonnegativity is then read off from D2 a_n >= 0 and K_n >= 0, and integrability from the normalisation. SHARP EDGES. (a) It is CONVEXITY, not monotone decrease, that does the work: monotone decrease to zero gives convergence off the origin by Dirichlet's test, but it does not produce the Fejer representation and therefore gives neither nonnegativity nor integrability of the sum. (b) The SINE analogue is false in this form. If (b_n) is convex and decreases to 0, then sum b_n sin(nx) still converges pointwise off 2 pi Z, but its sum is Lebesgue integrable if and only if sum b_n / n converges. The classical counterexample is b_n = 1/log n for n >= 2, which is convex and decreases to 0 while sum 1/(n log n) diverges: the resulting series converges everywhere but is not the Fourier series of any Lebesgue integrable function. Never transport the cosine statement to the sine case. (c) 'Integrable' cannot be improved to 'bounded': for a_n of order 1/n the sum behaves like log(1/|x|) near 0, which is integrable and unbounded. (d) The conclusion S >= 0 is on (0, 2 pi); nothing is claimed at x in 2 pi Z, where the series may diverge (it diverges precisely when sum a_n = infinity). (e) Convexity is only assumed for n >= 0 on the given sequence; a sequence that is eventually convex gives the same conclusions after subtracting a trigonometric polynomial, but then nonnegativity of the sum is lost.","status":"unverified"}

    \[

            \Big(\prod_{\substack{x\in\Lambda,\,y\in\Lambda^c\\x\sim y}}p_\beta(\sigma_x,\zeta_y)\Big);

    \end{multline}
    Notice that the Hamiltonian is defined somewhat atypically and incorporates

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:07:35.014292+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f9f11b2cef699280406131b0616cabc55e67dab81fb1661a6541cc44001fcfc3","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 6 of arXiv:2609.02878, '2609.02878'] A \emph{limiting point} at time \(T\) is an element
\(\xi\in M_T\) of Bamler's metric-flow slice at the limiting time
\cite[Definition~2.32 and the paragraph following
equation~(2.34)]{BamlerStructure}.  We represent it by a probability
conjugate heat flow
\[
 \xi=(\mu_t)_{t<T},\qquad d\mu_t=v_t\,dV_{g(t)},
\]
where
\[
 \partial_tv_t=-\Delta_{g(t)}v_t+R_{g(t)}v_t,
 \qquad v_t>0,
 \qquad \int_Xv_t\,dV_{g(t)}=1.
\]
The representation has the following two properties of the limiting slice:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(P\arabic*)},leftmargin=3em]
\item \(\xi\) is a subsequential limit of point conjugate heat flows
whose pole times increase to \(T\);
\item for \(D=2n\),
\begin{equation}
 \Var_{g(t)}(\mu_t)
 :=\iint_{X\times X}d_{g(t)}(x,y)^2\,d\mu_t(x)d\mu_t(y)
 \le H_{2n}(T-t).
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
The limiting point is called \emph{fixed} when it is chosen before any
sequence of blow-up scales.  Every tangent argument below keeps this
same limiting point while the scales vary.","status":"unverified"}

For random walk in a random environment on Z^d satisfying a directional transience condition, such as Sznitman's condition (T) or the stronger (T') in a direction l, or a simpler ballisticity/non-nestling condition, one constructs regeneration times tau_1 < tau_2 < ... at which the walk achieves a new running maximum in direction l and never backtracks below that level afterward. Under condition (T'), or the weaker (T), the increments (X_{tau_{k+1}} - X_{tau_k}, tau_{k+1} - tau_k), for k >= 1, form an i.i.d. sequence, reducing the walk, which is not itself Markovian once the environment is averaged out, to a genuine i.i.d.-increment structure from which a law of large numbers (a deterministic limiting velocity) follows directly, and, with additional finite-moment control on the regeneration increments, a central limit theorem follows via classical tools for sums of i.i.d. variables. This does not establish the directional transience condition itself, verifying (T) or (T') for a given environment law is typically the hard remaining step; it does not directly give a central limit theorem without separately checking finite second moments of the regeneration increments, which can genuinely fail in slow or near-critical regimes; and it is specific to the static, fixed-in-time environment model. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:34:33.543019+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_fa18f25af7b7b7bf663f7e66579a87c2a4d4c15e3c11603a7ee5fb076d7082d4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 19 (The models are EFIIDs) of arXiv:2603.28734, 'Free energy analyticity of the disordered XY model and Debye screening in the 2D Coulomb g'] All three models alluded to above are EFIIDs.
    More precisely, we obtain the following results.
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[\emph{\textbf{XY}}] Consider the XY model in dimension $d\in\Z_{\geq 2}$
        at inverse temperature $\beta\in[0,\beta_c(d))$.
        Then the infinite-volume Gibbs measure $\mu_{\XY,\beta}^{+1}$
        is an EFIID.
        \item[\emph{\textbf{SWM}}] Consider the SWM in dimension $d\in\Z_{\geq 2}$
        at inverse temperature $\beta\in\R_{\geq 0}$.

        is an EFIID.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.190930+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_fa474a8a4624814fe97709dafbef801fb0755ea4276210b20d5a5f868b3d8f3d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 109 (regularity for spatially smoothed coefficients) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] The coefficients from Definition~\ref{d:sp.smooth} are continuously differentiable in the space coordinate, and satisfy the bounds
	\[
	\Big(
	\|\sB^N\|_\infty
    +
    \|\partial_y\sB^N\|_\infty\Big)^2
	+ \max\bigg\{
    \|\tilde{A}\|_\infty
    +\|\partial_y\tilde{A}\|_\infty
    : \tilde{A}\in\{ \sV,\sU,\srrr,\swww\}^N
    \bigg\}
	\le 
	\bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2\,,
	\]
with $\MAX_N$ as in \eqref{e:MAX.N} and Proposition~\ref{p:Y.kolmogorov}.

\begin{proof}
We continue to use the abbreviations introduced above. To simplify notation, we mostly suppress the dependence on $N$ inside the proof. Consider
	\[
	\sB(t,y)
	=\frac{\overline{\varrho_{D,t}*\sphi}(y)}
		{\overline{\varrho_t*\sphi}(y)}
	\equiv \frac{\Num(t,y)}{\Den(t,y)}\,.
	\]
We first aim to lower bound the denominator $\Den$.
Recall from Definition~\ref{d:sp.smooth} that $\sphi$ has support $[-\sep,\sep]^3$, and is $\ge \Omega(1)/\sep^3$ on $[-\sep/2,\sep/2]^3$. 
From the construction of $\vX^\frozen$ and $\vY^\frozen$
(Definitions \ref{d:trunc}--\ref{d:rerand.Ising}), we see that $\varrho_t$ gives measure at least $\Omega( \sep^3 /\trK^{O(1)} )$ to any box of side length $\sep$ contained in $[-2\trK,2\trK]^3$. It follows that, for all $\vy\in[-2\trK+1,2\trK-1]^3$,
	\[
	\varrho_t*\sphi(\vy)
	\ge \int_{[-\sep/2,\sep/2]^3}
		\sphi(\vy-\vx)\,\varrho_t(d\vx)
	\ge \frac{1}{\trK^{O(1)}}\,.
	\]
Integrating over $\vy\in H(y)$ (as defined by \eqref{e:hspace.y}) gives
	\beq
	\Den(t,y)
	= \overline{\varrho_t*\sphi}(y)
	\ge \frac{1}{\trK^{O(1)}}
	\eeq
for all $y\in[-5\trK,5\trK]$. Next note that since particles outside $[-\trK,\trK]^3$ are frozen (see Definition~\ref{d:trunc}), the numerator $\Num(t,y)$ must be zero for $y\notin[-3\trK-1,3\trK+1]$. For $y\in[-3\trK-1,3\trK+1]$, we bound
	\begin{align*}
	|\Num(t,y)|
	&=\Big|\overline{\varrho_{D,t}*\sphi}(y)\Big|
	=\bigg| \int_{H(y)}
	\int_{\R^3} \sphi(\vy-\vx)B(t,\vx)\,\varrho_t(d\vx) \,d\vy\bigg|\\
	&=\bigg| \int_{\R^3}
	B(t,\vx) \overline{\sphi}(y-(\underline{1},\vx))\,\varrho_t(d\vx)\bigg|
	\le \|\overline{\sphi}\|_\infty \cdot \int_{\R^3}
	|B(t,\vx)|\,\varrho_t(d\vx)
	\le  \bigg(\frac{L}
		{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)}
		\MAX_N\,,
	\end{align*}
where the last step uses the quenched moment bound on $\bbb$ from Lemma~\ref{l:barD.I.second.quenched}, together with the bound $(p^N)' \le  L^2$ from \eqref{e:sdelimits.pprime}. Combining with \eqref{e:denominator.lbd} gives
	\[\|\sB\|_\infty 
	\le \bigg(\frac{\trK L}
		{\sep}
		\bigg)^{O(1)}
		\MAX_N\,.
	\]
We can also apply \eqref{e:denominator.lbd} to obtain
	\beq
	\Big|\partial_y \tilde{B}(t,y)\Big|
	\le \trK^{O(1)}
	\bigg|
	\frac{\partial}{\partial y} \Num(t,y)
	- \tilde{B}(t,y)
	\frac{\partial}{\partial y} \Den(t,y)
	\bigg|\,.\eeq
The first term on the right-hand side of \eqref{e:sB.quotient.rule} can be bounded by
	\begin{align*}
	\bigg|\frac{\partial}{\partial y} \Num(t,y)\bigg|
	&=\bigg|\frac{\partial}{\partial y}
	\overline{\varrho_{D,t}*\sphi}(y)\bigg|
	=\bigg| 
	\int_{\R^3} B(t,\vx)
	\overline{\sphi}' (y-(\vec{1},\vx))
	\,\varrho_t(d\vx)
	\bigg|\\
	&\le
	\|\overline{\sphi}' \|_\infty
	\int_{\R^3} | B(t,\vx) | \,\varrho_t(d\vx)
	\le \bigg(\frac{L}
		{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} \MAX_N\,.
	\end{align*}
The second term on the right-hand side of \eqref{e:sB.quotient.rule} can be controlled using the preceding bound on $\tilde{B}$, together with a similar  calculation as above:
	\[
	\bigg|\frac{\partial}{\partial y}
		\Den(t,y) \bigg|
	=\bigg|\frac{\partial}{\partial y}
	\overline{\varrho_t*\sphi}(y)\bigg|
	\le  \| \overline{\sphi}' \|_\infty \cdot
	\int_{\R^3} \varrho_t(d\vx)
	\le \frac{1}{\sep^{O(1)} }\,.
	\]
Combining the above gives the claimed bound on $\partial_y \sB$.
The bounds on $\sV$, $\sU$, $\srrr$, and $\swww$ follow by the same argument, using the quenched moment bounds from Lemma~\ref{l:tQ.first.quenched}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:54:34.576894+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_fa483578692ebb64fd65c90d7dd282dc4a175130c5fa82aad1ee8b96558013a2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop 10 of arXiv:2606.14812, 'Joint convergence in Wiener chaos via transport hierarchy and Malliavin covariances'] Consider two integers $p, q\geq 2$ and let
		\[
		X_N = I_p(f_N), \qquad Y_N = I_q(g_N),
		\]
		where $f_N\in H^{\odot p}$, $g_N\in H^{\odot q}$, and assume that $X_N$ 
		satisfies \eqref{c1} and $Y_N$ is bounded in $L^2(\Omega)$. Write 
		$q = ap + r'$ with $a\geq 1$ and $0\leq r' < p$. For $r\geq 1$, let 
		$Y_{r,N}$ be given by \eqref{yr}. Then the following hold.
		
		\begin{enumerate}
			\item For every integer $r\geq 1$ with $rp\leq q$,
			\begin{equation}
				Y_{r,N} = C_{r,p,q}\,
				I_{q-rp}\!\left(f_N\widetilde\otimes_p^{(r)} g_N\right)
				+ R_{r,N},
			\end{equation}
			where $f_N\widetilde\otimes_p^{(r)} g_N$ denotes the 
			$r$-fold iterated contraction of $f_N$ with $g_N$, 
			defined recursively by $f_N\widetilde\otimes_p^{(1)} g_N 
			= f_N\widetilde\otimes_p g_N\in H^{\odot(q-p)}$ and
			\begin{equation*}
				f_N\widetilde\otimes_p^{(r)} g_N 
				:= f_N\widetilde\otimes_p 
				\left(f_N\widetilde\otimes_p^{(r-1)} g_N\right)
				\in H^{\odot(q-rp)},
				\quad r=2,\ldots,a,
			\end{equation*}
			i.e.\ at each step the $p$ variables of $f_N$ are 
			fully contracted with $p$ of the remaining variables 
			of the kernel from the previous step. Also,  $C_{r,p,q} = (p!)^r\frac{q!}{(q-rp)!}$ and 
			$R_{r,N}\to 0$ in $L^2(\Omega)$ as $N\to\infty$.
			
			\item \textbf{Non-critical case} $ap < q < (a+1)p$: 
			\begin{equation}
				Y_{a+1,N} \to _{N \to \infty}0 \quad \text{in } L^2(\Omega).
			\end{equation}
			
			\item \textbf{Critical case} $q = ap$: taking $r=a$ in \eqref{14m-2b} gives
			\begin{equation*}
				Y_{a,N} - \mathbf{E}[Y_{a,N}] \to  _{N \to \infty}0 \quad \text{in } L^2(\Omega).

{"assumptions":["H_k the Sylvester Hadamard matrix of order 2^k, disc(A) = min over sign vectors x of ||A x||_inf"],"created_at":"2026-09-24T23:46:59.335012+00:00","domain":"combinatorics/Boolean functions","id":"claim_face5f144efa4b4e9a635b179d81577f","kind":"counterexample","schema_version":1,"statement":"Conjecture 13 of the Randomstrasse 2024 problem list asks whether the Sylvester Hadamard matrix H_k of order 2^k has discrepancy disc(H_k) = sqrt(2) sqrt(2^k) for odd k, where disc(A) = min over sign vectors x of the sup-norm of Ax. In plain terms: take the 2^k x 2^k matrix of plus and minus ones whose entry in row a and column u is (-1) to the mod-2 dot product of the k-bit strings a and u, and ask for the smallest possible largest absolute entry of the product Hx over sign vectors x. Indexing H_k by (-1)^{a.u} and reading x as the +-1 truth table of a Boolean function f on k variables, H_k x is the Walsh transform W_f, so disc(H_k) = min_f max_a |W_f(a)| = 2^k - 2 NL_max(k), where NL_max(k) is the largest nonlinearity of a Boolean function on k variables (the covering radius of the Reed-Muller code RM(1, k)). The conjectured value is exactly the bent-concatenation bound NL = 2^{k-1} - 2^{(k-1)/2}, which is beaten for odd k = 15 (Patterson and Wiedemann, 1983) and for every odd k > 7 (Kavut, Maitra and Yucel, 2006), and is optimal for k <= 7. So the conjecture holds exactly for k in {1, 3, 5, 7} and fails for every odd k >= 9. The numbers: for k <= 7 the maximum nonlinearity equals the bent-concatenation value (the covering radius of RM(1,5) is 12, Berlekamp and Welch 1972; of RM(1,7) is 56, Mykkeltveit 1980; k = 1, 3 by hand); for k = 9 functions of nonlinearity 242 exist (Kavut, Maitra and Yucel 2006), so disc(H_9) <= 512 - 484 = 28 < 32; for every odd k = 9 + 2j the direct sum of such a function with a bent function on 2j variables has largest Walsh coefficient 28 * 2^j, below 32 * 2^j, since the Walsh spectrum of a direct sum is the product; and Patterson and Wiedemann's nonlinearity 16276 on 15 variables gives disc(H_15) <= 216 < 256.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the point process is exactly determinantal, or Pfaffian with the analogous but distinct formula, with a well-defined correlation kernel K satisfying the standard positivity and boundedness conditions","the conditioning event is of the specific form covered by the Schur-complement formula, i.e. an exact configuration on a subset, or the corresponding L-ensemble conditioning","invertibility, or a well-defined limiting or pseudo-inverse procedure, for the relevant diagonal block appearing in the formula, e.g. K_AA - I","the block partition A, B is taken with respect to the same index set on which K is originally defined"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.998694+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_faf3e83a28894a41c1931704cf7a671a579f690c334933aa41076761cbab8d22","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For a determinantal point process with correlation kernel K, Hermitian and satisfying 0<=K<=I in the discrete finite-space setting, the conditional law of the process restricted to a subset given the exact configuration on the complementary subset is again determinantal, with a kernel given by a Schur-complement formula. Partitioning the index set into A, the observed subset, and B, the remaining subset, and writing K in block form with entries K_AA, K_AB, K_BA, K_BB, the conditional kernel on B given the exact points observed in A is expressed via a Schur-complement expression such as K_BB - K_BA (K_AA - I)^{-1} K_AB, with the precise form depending on the convention used (correlation kernel versus L-ensemble) and on whether one conditions on points being present or absent in A. This identity is the fundamental tool for analyzing conditioning, dynamics, and Gibbs-type properties of determinantal processes, including eigenvalues of random matrices, non-intersecting paths, discrete orthogonal polynomial ensembles, and, via the transfer-current theorem, uniform spanning trees, reducing conditional analysis to linear algebra on the kernel matrix. It does not apply outside the determinantal class of point processes, or its Pfaffian analogue for orthogonal and symplectic ensembles, which has a related but distinct formula, and the exact form of the Schur complement depends sensitively on the specific conditioning event and on invertibility of the relevant block, which can fail or require a pseudo-inverse or limiting argument at special parameter values. Typical failure: Applying a Schur-complement conditional-kernel formula derived under one convention, such as conditioning an L-ensemble on a fixed exact sample, to a different conditioning question, such as conditioning on a sub-event like at least one point in a region, or mixing up the correlation-kernel and L-ensemble conventions, without re-deriving the correct formula; determinantal-process conditioning identities are convention-sensitive, and mixing them up produces a kernel that still looks plausible, expressed via some Schur complement, but does not correctly describe the actual conditional process. Canonical reference: Shirai and Takahashi, 2003, Journal of Functional Analysis; Borodin and Rains, 2005, Journal of Statistical Physics; Lyons, 2003, Annals of Probability.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f is Lebesgue integrable on R^d","convention: kernel e^{-2 pi i x.xi} with no normalizing constant"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:39.261959+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis on Euclidean space","id":"claim_fb60e476216b9503fe6cf25758a518637c753a94a69a4d29f3d7163257a33360","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"For $f \\in L^1(\\mathbb{R}^d)$ define $\\hat f(\\xi) = \\int_{\\mathbb{R}^d} f(x) e^{-2\\pi i x\\cdot\\xi}\\,dx$ for every $\\xi \\in \\mathbb{R}^d$; the integral converges absolutely for every $\\xi$. The inverse transform of $g\\in L^1$ is $\\check g(x)=\\int g(\\xi)e^{2\\pi i x\\cdot\\xi}\\,d\\xi$. With this convention Plancherel reads $\\|\\hat f\\|_2=\\|f\\|_2$. Convention warning: texts using $\\int f(x)e^{-ix\\cdot\\xi}dx$ have inversion with a factor $(2\\pi)^{-d}$ and $\\|\\hat f\\|_2=(2\\pi)^{d/2}\\|f\\|_2$; the unitary convention puts $(2\\pi)^{-d/2}$ in front of both. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:11:11.696375+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_fb7ce0904ba6cc883fce5c582837e5c506adcefa9c9da36941d7a705dd34d6b5","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:centers of arXiv:2609.00645, 'Global persistence of nearly radial concentrated vortices in a bounded domain'] Let $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^2)$ be nonzero and nonnegative, and set
$\kappa:=\|f\|_1$.  Then $\mathsf C(f)$ is nonempty and compact, and
$\mathcal A(f)<2\kappa$.  Moreover, the following statements hold:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item if $\operatorname{supp}f^*\subset B_r(\mathbf0)$ for some $r>0$,
then every $\mathbf b\in\mathsf C(f)$ satisfies
\begin{equation}
  \int_{\mathbb R^2\setminus B_r(\mathbf b)}f
  \,\mathrm d\mathbf x
  \leq\frac12\mathcal A(f);
\end{equation}
\item if, for some $r,s>0$ and $\mathbf a\in\mathbb R^2$,
\[
  \operatorname{supp}f^*\subset B_r(\mathbf0),
  \qquad
  \operatorname{supp}f\subset B_s(\mathbf a),
\]
then
\begin{equation}
  |\mathbf b-\mathbf a|\leq r+s
  \qquad(\mathbf b\in\mathsf C(f));
\end{equation}
moreover, the mass center $\mathbf X_f$ defined by (equation eq:mass-center of the paper) satisfies
\begin{equation}
  |\mathbf b-\mathbf X_f|
  \leq\frac{r+2s}{\kappa}\mathcal A(f)
  \qquad(\mathbf b\in\mathsf C(f));
\end{equation}
\item if $\operatorname{supp}f^*\subset B_r(\mathbf0)$ for some $r>0$
and $\mathcal A(f)<\kappa$, then
\begin{equation}
  \operatorname{diam}\mathsf C(f)\leq2r;
\end{equation}
\item for any nonzero, nonnegative $f,g\in L^1(\mathbb R^2)$,
\[
  |\mathcal A(f)-\mathcal A(g)|\leq2\|f-g\|_1;
\]
\item the set-valued map $f\mapsto\mathsf C(f)$ has a closed graph with respect
to strong $L^1$ convergence: if $f_n,f\in L^1(\mathbb R^2)$ are nonzero and
nonnegative, then
\[
  f_n\to f\ \text{in }L^1(\mathbb R^2),\qquad
  \mathbf b_n\to\mathbf b\ \text{in }\mathbb R^2,\qquad
  \mathbf b_n\in\mathsf C(f_n)
  \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  \mathbf b\in\mathsf C(f);
\]
\item the set-valued map $f\mapsto\mathsf C(f)$ is upper semicontinuous\footnote{See
[AubinFrankowska2009] for this standard definition.} with
respect to strong $L^1$ convergence: for every nonzero, nonnegative
$f\in L^1(\mathbb R^2)$ and every open set $O\subset\mathbb R^2$ with
$\mathsf C(f)\subset O$, there exists $\delta>0$ such that
\[
  g\in L^1(\mathbb R^2),\quad g\geq0,\quad g\not\equiv0,\quad
  \|g-f\|_1<\delta
  \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  \mathsf C(g)\subset O.
\]
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["two-dimensional planar lattice model satisfying the FKG inequality","translation invariance and, in the classical gluing constructions, reflection symmetry of the lattice","an a priori lower bound on square-crossing probabilities, which is a hypothesis to be separately established, not a free consequence of RSW","independence, or at least positive association, of the underlying edge or site variables"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.974286+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_fb8fff362c8249e98704b89baabf231efeaf842e818303da3b033c4ea1e6cfba","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). In two-dimensional critical or near-critical percolation, RSW theory states that if crossing probabilities of n x n squares are uniformly bounded away from 0 as n grows, then crossing probabilities of rho n x n rectangles, for any fixed aspect ratio rho, are also uniformly bounded away from 0 (and from 1) by a constant depending on rho but not on n. The classical proof glues together several square-crossing events using the FKG inequality and translation and reflection symmetry of the lattice. RSW estimates are the essential multi-scale input for proving arm-exponent bounds, conformal-invariance-adjacent results, and, via the Duminil-Copin-Tassion approach, for establishing sharpness of the phase transition without relying on exact self-duality. RSW does not by itself prove existence of a scaling limit as n -> infinity, does not give the exact value of any crossing probability, only two-sided bounds; and the classical form required exact self-duality (p=1/2 on the square lattice), so extending the theory to general planar lattices or to p != 1/2 required a genuinely new, duality-free argument (Tassion, 2016). Typical failure: Assuming that RSW-type bounded-away-from-0/1 crossing estimates transfer automatically to a new planar model merely because it is monotone and planar; RSW requires either exact self-duality or the more robust but still nontrivial Tassion-style construction, and models without FKG, or with strong enough long-range dependence, can fail to admit the needed gluing arguments even though they look superficially similar to Bernoulli percolation. Canonical reference: Russo, 1978, Zeitschrift fur Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie und verwandte Gebiete; Seymour and Welsh, 1978, Annals of Discrete Mathematics; Tassion, 2016, Probability Theory and Related Fields.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Ω bounded open with Lipschitz boundary, n ≥ 2","1 ≤ p < ∞ for existence, boundedness and kernel; 1 < p < ∞ for the fractional-space range description","Green's identity form: u ∈ H^2(Ω), v ∈ H^1(Ω)"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:57.492614+00:00","domain":"Sobolev spaces, boundary traces, elliptic boundary value problems","id":"claim_fb9c6a675246add69d2d408b990ef27f4904b933fa93e1e739f05b2304fd2786","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Ω ⊂ R^n (n ≥ 2) be a bounded open set with Lipschitz boundary, dS the surface measure and ν the outward unit normal (defined dS-a.e.), and let 1 ≤ p < ∞.

(1) Existence and boundedness. There is a unique bounded linear operator T : W^{1,p}(Ω) → L^p(∂Ω, dS) such that Tu = u|_{∂Ω} for every u ∈ W^{1,p}(Ω) ∩ C(Ω̄). Tu is the trace of u, and ||Tu||_{L^p(∂Ω)} ≤ C(Ω, p) ||u||_{W^{1,p}(Ω)}.

(2) Kernel. ker T = W^{1,p}_0(Ω), the closure of C_c^∞(Ω) in W^{1,p}(Ω). A W^{1,p} function vanishes on ∂Ω in the trace sense exactly when it is a W^{1,p}-limit of compactly supported smooth functions.

(3) Range (Gagliardo). For 1 < p < ∞ the range of T is exactly the fractional Sobolev space W^{1−1/p, p}(∂Ω), and T has a bounded linear right inverse W^{1−1/p, p}(∂Ω) → W^{1,p}(Ω). In particular T : H^1(Ω) → H^{1/2}(∂Ω) is bounded and onto, and every g ∈ H^{1/2}(∂Ω) has an extension u ∈ H^1(Ω) with Tu = g and ||u||_{H^1(Ω)} ≤ C ||g||_{H^{1/2}(∂Ω)}. For p = 1 the range is all of L^1(∂Ω). Since H^{1/2}(∂Ω) ↪ L^2(∂Ω) is compact, T : H^1(Ω) → L^2(∂Ω) is a compact operator.

(4) Integration by parts with traces. For u ∈ W^{1,p}(Ω), v ∈ W^{1,p'}(Ω) with 1/p + 1/p' = 1 (p' = ∞ for p = 1) and each i,
   ∫_Ω u ∂_i v dx + ∫_Ω v ∂_i u dx = ∫_∂Ω (Tu)(Tv) ν_i dS.
Hence for u ∈ H^2(Ω), v ∈ H^1(Ω) Green's first identity ∫_Ω ∇u·∇v dx + ∫_Ω (Δu) v dx = ∫_∂Ω (∂_ν u)(Tv) dS holds with ∂_ν u := ν · T(∇u) ∈ L^2(∂Ω), and for u ∈ H^1_0(Ω) all boundary terms vanish.

Where it fails. There is no trace operator on L^p(Ω): ∂Ω has Lebesgue measure zero, an L^p class has no boundary values, and an estimate ||Tu||_{L^p(∂Ω)} ≤ C||u||_{L^p(Ω)} is false (the full W^{1,p} norm is needed). For p > 1 the range is NOT L^p(∂Ω): a general g ∈ L^2(∂Ω) has no H^1(Ω) extension. The kernel and range statements use the Lipschitz boundary (a segment / extension property); for domains with cracks, slits or cusps the boundary is not Lipschitz and these statements need modification (a crack has two sides with two different traces). The trace of ∇u exists for u ∈ H^2(Ω), not for a general u ∈ H^1(Ω), so ∂_ν u is not defined in L^2(∂Ω) for arbitrary H^1 functions.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Fresh IID noiseless samples, theta_star in the real Hilbert space, theta_0=0.","H=E[X tensor X] with E||X||^2<infinity; E[||X||^2*(X tensor X)]<=R*H for R>0.","4*gamma*||H||<=1."],"created_at":"2026-10-21T15:47:35.222188+00:00","domain":"Last-iterate stochastic optimization","id":"claim_fba342b2f98a71f9314f2d3f6f4afc268c939556965484423f9701824918011d","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a random vector in a real separable Hilbert space with E||X||^2<infinity and covariance H=E[X tensor X]. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:51:11.954305+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_fbda79203ede6d57ec8d3728064ded883d9621c89fa12574c9dcd8f137c061bc","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 17 (Vanishing diagonal regularization) of arXiv:2608.07820, 'Linear Spectral Statistics for Entrywise-Transformed Spiked Wigner Matrices under Shifted '] Let \(\widetilde H\) be a bounded centered array with zero diagonal and an
exactly stochastic, uniformly flat off-diagonal variance matrix
\(\widetilde S\).  Let \(\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_N\) be independent, centered,
variance-one, uniformly bounded random variables, independent of
\(\widetilde H\).  For fixed \(\eta\in(0,1)\), set
\begin{equation}
 \widetilde H^{(\eta)}_{ij}
 :=\sqrt{1-\eta/N}\,\widetilde H_{ij}\quad(i\ne j),
 \qquad
 \widetilde H^{(\eta)}_{ii}:=\sqrt{\eta/N}\,\chi_i.
\end{equation}
Then the variance matrix of \(\widetilde H^{(\eta)}\) is exactly stochastic
and satisfies the uniform lower and upper bounds required by the
generalized-Wigner theorem, with constants allowed to depend on \(\eta\).
For every finite family of functions analytic near \(\Gamma\),
\begin{align}
 \limsup_{N\to\infty}\left|
 \E\Tr\varphi(\widetilde H^{(\eta)})
 -\E\Tr\varphi(\widetilde H)
 \right|&\le C_{\varphi,\Gamma}\eta,
 \\
 \limsup_{N\to\infty}\Var\!\left(
 \Tr\varphi(\widetilde H^{(\eta)})
 -\Tr\varphi(\widetilde H)
 \right)&\le C_{\varphi,\Gamma}\eta.
 
\end{align}
Moreover, the Li--Xu expectation and covariance formulas converge to their flat
zero-diagonal versions in the order \(N\to\infty\), then
\(\eta\downarrow0\).  Consequently the joint CLT for
\(\widetilde H^{(\eta)}\) transfers to \(\widetilde H\).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-06T03:36:16.695247+00:00","domain":"harvested statement (arXiv 2512.18592, 2025): mathematics","id":"claim_fc21f9d2a26045039443f93d58f41d89","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 2.6 (Maximum–entropy characterisation) in the first version of arXiv:2512.18592, 'Wavelet Latent Position Exponential Random Graphs'] Fix $n\\in\\mathbb{N}$, latent positions $U=(U_{i})_{i=1}^{n}\\in(0,1)^{n}$, and a finite index set $\\mathcal{I}\\subset\\mathbb{N}_{0}\\times\\mathbb{N}_{0}$. Let $\\Omega:=\\{0,1\\}^{\\binom{n}{2}}$ and identify $A\\in\\Omega$ with an undirected adjacency matrix by setting $A_{ji}:=A_{ij}$ and $A_{ii}:=0$. Using the statistics $S_{00}(A)$ and $S_{rs}(A,U)$ defined in Section 2.4, fix target moments $m_{00}\\in\\mathbb{R}$ and $(m_{rs})_{(r,s)\\in\\mathcal{I}}$ and define $\\mathcal{Q}(m):=\\Bigl\\{Q\\text{ pmf on }\\Omega:\\;\\mathbb{E}_{Q}[S_{00}(A)]=m_{00},\\;\\mathbb{E}_{Q}[S_{rs}(A,U)]=m_{rs}\\ \\ \\forall(r,s)\\in\\mathcal{I}\\Bigr\\}.$ Assume $\\mathcal{Q}(m)\\neq\\varnothing$. (i) Existence and uniqueness. There exists a unique maximiser $Q^{\\star}\\in\\mathcal{Q}(m)$ of Shannon entropy $H(Q):=-\\sum_{A\\in\\Omega}Q(A)\\log Q(A),$ where $\\log$ is the natural logarithm and $0\\log 0:=0$. (ii) Exponential-family characterisation (attainable moments). For $\\theta=(c,(s_{rs})_{(r,s)\\in\\mathcal{I}})$ define $P_{\\theta}(A\\mid U):=\\exp\\Bigl\\{c\\,S_{00}(A)+\\sum_{(r,s)\\in\\mathcal{I}}s_{rs}S_{rs}(A,U)-\\Psi_{n}(\\theta;U)\\Bigr\\},$ with $\\Psi_{n}(\\theta;U):=\\log\\sum_{A\\in\\Omega}\\exp\\Bigl\\{c\\,S_{00}(A)+\\sum_{(r,s)\\in\\mathcal{I}}s_{rs}S_{rs}(A,U)\\Bigr\\}.$ If there exists $\\theta^{\\star}$ such that $P_{\\theta^{\\star}}(\\cdot\\mid U)\\in\\mathcal{Q}(m)$ (equivalently, $\\mathbb{E}_{\\theta^{\\star}}[S_{00}(A)]=m_{00}$ and $\\mathbb{E}_{\\theta^{\\star}}[S_{rs}(A,U)]=m_{rs}$ for all $(r,s)\\in\\mathcal{I}$), then $Q^{\\star}=P_{\\theta^{\\star}}(\\cdot\\mid U).$ In particular, if one restricts $\\theta$ to the WL–ERG subfamily (e.g. by imposing symmetry constraints inherited from a symmetric coefficient matrix), then any moment-matching WL–ERG member must coincide with $Q^{\\star}$ and hence is the unique maximum–entropy distribution under the constraints. The maximising distribution is always unique; the canonical parameter $\\theta^{\\star}$ is unique whenever the exponential family is minimal.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["driftless subordinator, Levy measure nu = sum_{m>=1} a_m delta_{x_m}","x_m = 4^{-m^2}, a_m = 2^{-m} 4^{m^2}"],"created_at":"2026-09-24T23:46:59.329215+00:00","domain":"probability/Levy processes","id":"claim_fc2810725f4f4b23a924b0d3f7cc75c4","kind":"counterexample","schema_version":1,"statement":"Question 5 of Hu and Sun's survey on Hunt's hypothesis (H) (arXiv:1908.06825) asks whether every pure-jump subordinator with infinite Levy measure satisfies (H). The classical sufficient conditions bound Im psi by a multiple of 1 + Re psi; the oldest, Kanda-Forst, asks |Im psi(z)| <= M (1 + Re psi(z)) for all z. The driftless subordinator with Levy measure nu = sum_{m>=1} a_m delta_{x_m}, x_m = 4^{-m^2}, a_m = 2^{-m} 4^{m^2}, has sum a_m x_m = 1 and sum a_m = infinity, and along z_m = 1/(m x_m) its exponent psi(z) = int (1 - e^{izx}) nu(dx) satisfies |Im psi(z_m)| / (1 + Re psi(z_m)) = 4m + O(1) (computed at high precision: 23.999 at m = 6, 32.000008 at m = 8), so the Kanda-Forst ratio is unbounded and the classical route to (H) is closed for it. It is not a counterexample to (H): an octave-by-octave estimate of the Kesten-Bretagnolle integral int Re(1/(1 + psi(z))) dz suggests the integral diverges, so points would be polar - a heuristic, not a proof. The example is atomic, outside the survey's type-(alpha, beta) density class, and the survey's Theorem 2.8 and Remark 2.21 anticipate processes of this kind, so it is an explicit witness with a computed rate rather than a new phenomenon.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:07:48.566545+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_fc38cad5596897daed2d2be8002e6feb9e18c80afa03e5ecaecf7e18b92fee3a","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 29 of arXiv:2609.01460, 'On cost-induced Santal\'o-type inequalities \\ in Polish measure spaces'] Let $L\subset M_{n,m}(\R)$ and $K\subset \R^n$ be compact sets of positive volume whose convex hulls contain the (appropriate) origin in their interiors.     \[
    \vol[nm](K^{\star,Q})\vol[n](K)^m \leq \vol[nm](K^{\star,Q})\vol[n]((K^{\star,Q})_{\circ,Q})^m 
    \] 
    and 
    \[ 
    \vol[nm](L)\vol[n](L_{\circ,Q})^m \leq \vol[nm]((L_{\circ,Q})^{\star,Q})\vol[n](L_{\circ,Q})^m,
    \]
    with equality only for invariant sets (up to sets of Lebesgue measure zero). 
    
    In particular, the following two statements are equivalent:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item if $K$ or $K^\circ$, has center of mass at the origin, then
    \[
    \vol[nm](K^{\star,Q})\vol[n](K)^m \leq \vol[nm]((\B)^{\star,Q})\vol[n](\B)^m 
    \]
    with equality if and only if $K=E$ for a centered ellipsoid $E\subset\R^n$ up to removal of null sets; 
    \item  if $L_{\circ,Q}$ or $(L_{\circ,Q})^\circ$ has center of mass at the origin, then
    \[
    \vol[nm](L)\vol[n](L_{\circ,Q})^m \leq \vol[nm]((\B)^{\star,Q})\vol[n](\B)^m
    \]
    with equality if and only if $L=E^{\star,Q}$ for a centered ellipsoid $E\subset \R^n$ up to removal of null sets.
    \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-02T00:34:53.670589+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_fc52ec0e15850831ffd97ae17424e764b5317a72e2ceda6bf212c67cb8e796cd","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In probability theory and mathematical physics, a random matrix is a matrix-valued random variable—that is, a matrix in which some or all of its entries are sampled randomly from a probability distribution. Random matrix theory (RMT) is the study of properties of random matrices, often as they become large. {"assumptions":["mu(Omega) < infinity for the global statement; a set of finite measure for the local statement","f_n measurable, f_n -> f mu-almost everywhere, all functions finite a.e."],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.752876+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_fc6b659554c68f681ea95004be9535b37b79d34316ba22807d81906efef118ad","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Egorov's theorem states that on a FINITE measure space, almost everywhere convergence of measurable functions implies almost uniform convergence: for every eps > 0 there is a measurable E with mu(E) < eps such that the convergence is uniform on the complement of E. Finiteness cannot be dropped. On R with Lebesgue measure let f_n = 1_{[n, n+1]}; then f_n -> 0 at every point, but for ANY set E of finite measure the complement meets [n, n+1] for infinitely many n, so sup over the complement of E of |f_n| equals 1 for infinitely many n and the convergence is not uniform off any set of small measure. What survives on a sigma-finite space is the LOCAL statement: for every measurable A with mu(A) < infinity and every eps > 0 there is E contained in A with mu(E) < eps and uniform convergence on A minus E; equivalently, almost everywhere convergence implies almost uniform convergence on each set of finite measure. The converse implication holds in general: almost uniform convergence always implies convergence almost everywhere and in measure, on any measure space. [standard; e.g. Folland, Real Analysis, 2nd ed., Theorem 2.33 and Exercise 2.39]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:54:12.567809+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_fc7bc3237410cbf6b684188ecc94f3fab7661bb876adf67616a89e224e9e86d5","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop P:half-space-KPZ-horizon-marginals of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] As $n\to\infty$, the process $R^{(n)}$ has a distributional limit $R^{\mathsf{KPZ}}=\{R^{\mathsf{KPZ}}_i\}_{i=1}^k$, under the uniform-on-compact topology. 
    We can describe the process $R^{\mathsf{KPZ}}$ explicitly as follows.
	
Let $\mathcal{B} = (\mathcal{B}_1, \mathcal{B}_2, \ldots, \mathcal{B}_{2k})$ be $2k$ independent Brownian motions on $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ of diffusivity $1$, with drift $-\gamma_i$ for $\mathcal{B}_i$ and $\gamma_i$ for $\mathcal{B}_{2k+1-i}$, for each $i\in\llbracket1, k \rrbracket$.
We consider the O'Connell-Yor polymer partition function (see [OYbb]) across $\{\mathcal{B}_i\}_{i=1}^{2k}$, defined as
\[
Z_{\mathcal{B}}(x,i;y,j) = \idotsint_{x=x_i\le \cdots \le x_j \le x_{j+1}=y} \exp\left( \sum_{i'=i}^j \mathcal{B}_{i'}(x_{i'+1})-\mathcal{B}_{i'}(x_{i'}) \right) dx_{i+1}\cdots dx_j,
\]
for any $1\le i \le j \le 2k$, and $0\le x \le y$.

Next, let $\{X(-i, j) : i\in\llbracket1, k \rrbracket, j\in\llbracketi, 2k +1 - i \rrbracket\}$ be an array of inverse gamma random variables, independent of each other and $\mathcal{B}$, satisfying 
\[X(-i, j) \sim \begin{cases}
1 & j =i,\\
\operatorname{Gamma}^{-1}(\gamma_j-\gamma_i), \qquad &j\in\llbracket i + 1, k \rrbracket, \\
\operatorname{Gamma}^{-1}(-\gamma_i- \gamma_{2k + 1 -j}), \qquad &j\in\llbracketk + 1, 2k - i \rrbracket, \\
\operatorname{Gamma}^{-1}(-\gamma_i+\alpha), \qquad &j =  2k + 1- i.
\end{cases}
\]
Then:
\[
R^{\mathsf{KPZ}}_i(x)=
\begin{cases}
\log\left(\frac{\sum_{i\le \ell \le 2k} \big(\sum_{\pi\in P[i,\ell]}\prod_{v\in \pi}X(v)\big)Z_{\mathcal{B}}(0,\ell; x, 2k)}{
\sum_{\pi\in P[i,2k]}\prod_{v\in \pi}X(v) }\right), \qquad & x\ge 0,\\
\log\left(\frac{\sum_{i\le \ell \le 2k} \big(\sum_{\pi\in \hat{P}[i,\ell]}\prod_{v\in \pi}X(v)\big)Z_{\mathcal{B}}(0,\ell; |x|, 2k)}{
\sum_{\pi\in \hat{P}[i,2k]}\prod_{v\in \pi}X(v) }\right), \qquad & x< 0,
\end{cases}
\]
where $P[i,\ell]$ is the collection of all up-right paths in $\mathbb{Z}^2$ from $(-i,i)$ to $(-1,\ell)$, and  
$\hat{P}[i,\ell]$ is the subset of such paths that intersect $\{(x,x+2k+1): x\in \mathbb{Z}\}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-06T03:36:16.740440+00:00","domain":"harvested statement (arXiv 2603.27659, 2026): owner_math","id":"claim_fc8a3d9866d34e7685dd03fa09662144","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 3.11 of arXiv:2603.27659, 'Operator Norm Bounds for Multi-leg Matrix Tensors and Applications to Random Matrix Theory'] Let $m,k,N\\in\\mathbb{N}$, let $\\sigma_{1},\\ldots,\\sigma_{k}\\in\\mathcal{P}^{\\prime}([m])$ be partial permutations, let $A_{1},\\ldots,A_{m}\\in M_{N}(\\mathbb{C})^{\\otimes k}$, let $Y$ be the matrix resulting from the partial trace evaluation $(\\mathrm{Tr}_{\\sigma_{1}}\\otimes\\cdots\\otimes\\mathrm{Tr}_{\\sigma_{k}})(A_{1},\\ldots,A_{m})$, and let $q=\\sum_{j=1}^{k}(m-|D(\\sigma_{j})|)$ with $D(\\sigma_{j})$ the domain of $\\sigma_{j}$, so that $Y$ acts on a space of dimension $N^{q}$. {"assumptions":["γ is a closed piecewise C^1 curve (or a cycle) in C","the point a does not lie on the trace of γ"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:42.483563+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_fcf7242c6dd1f3172a2cc112bfa1af26bdbbd80032c909e06e994d0138efa1ef","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let γ : [α,β] → C be a closed piecewise C^1 curve and let a be a point not on the trace of γ. The winding number (index) of γ about a is n(γ,a) = (1/2πi) ∫_γ dz/(z - a). It is always an integer; as a function of a it is constant on each connected component of the complement of the trace of γ, and it is 0 on the unbounded component. The definition extends additively to cycles (finite formal integer combinations of closed curves) and, via continuous branches of the argument, to merely continuous closed curves. A cycle γ lying in an open set U is called null-homologous in U (homologous to zero) if n(γ,w) = 0 for every w in C minus U. An open connected U ⊂ C is simply connected if and only if every cycle in U is null-homologous in U, if and only if the complement of U in the Riemann sphere is connected. The homology form of Cauchy's theorem reads: if f is holomorphic on U and γ is a cycle null-homologous in U, then ∫_γ f(z) dz = 0 and n(γ,z) f(z) = (1/2πi) ∫_γ f(ζ)/(ζ - z) dζ for every z in U off the trace of γ.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["k algebraically closed (over R, for example, x^2 + 1 has no zero and the weak form fails)"],"created_at":"2026-08-29T02:26:24.138161+00:00","domain":"commutative algebra / algebraic geometry","id":"claim_fd299ef0d812bc84f4e522b64f80b42912c4b2149be4e4eed7dcbbb09198fcc4","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let k be an algebraically closed field and R = k[x_1, ..., x_n]. Weak form: every proper ideal I of R has a common zero, that is, V(I) = {a in k^n : f(a) = 0 for all f in I} is nonempty; equivalently every maximal ideal of R has the form (x_1 - a_1, ..., x_n - a_n). Strong form: for every ideal I, the ideal of polynomials vanishing on V(I) is the radical of I: if g in R vanishes on V(I) then g^m in I for some m >= 1. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T00:48:45.312498+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_fd3771e65f917fea5d179b280898c754cbb7c13e975ed28cafdad6ec9c7e3c95","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:cone of arXiv:2411.14921, 'A boundary Harnack principle and its application to analyticity of 3D Brownian intersectio'] For any $u_1>1$, we choose a small constant $d_0>0$ and a large constant $n_1>64\, d_0^2$ such that the following construction is possible for all $n>n_1$ and $1\le m\le n$.

        \item On each surface $S_i\cap\partial \mathcal{B}_0$, we further pick $m$ points $v_{i,j}$ along an arc such that the following properties hold.
        Let $c_0$ and $c_1$ be two small positive constants. Consider two smaller cones
        \[
        T_{i,j}:=\mathsf{C}(v_{i,j},u_1^{-n}) \quad \text{and} \quad V_{i,j}:=\mathsf{C}(v_{i,j},c_0m^{-1}n^{-1/2}).
        \]
        For any $i,j$, we have $T_{i,j}\subseteq V_{i,j}\subseteq S_i$, $\mathrm{dist}(v_{i,j},\partial S_i)\ge c_1\, n^{-1/2}$, and $V_{i,j}\cap V_{i,l}=\varnothing$ if $j\neq l$. Moreover, if $1\le j<l\le m$, then $ |z/|z|-v_{i,l}|\geq c_1|j-l|/(m\sqrt n)$  for every $z\in V_{i,j}$.
    \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["uniform m-point toy probability space for the control","square lattice boundary for the endpoint count"],"created_at":"2026-10-10T08:26:09.577725+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_fd6b445eae37cb373a9bde3c564247ad5cd3fd1a4430b0ce0a03296d79f4809f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"An elementary probability control, not an FPP counterexample. If J is uniform on {1,...,m} and A_i={J=i}, each deterministic event has probability 1/m, while P(union_i A_i)=1. Equivalently, each threshold indicator has mean 1/m and their maximum is always one. Therefore an estimate for every deterministic pair of endpoints does not automatically control a pair chosen after observing the environment. For the square boundary S_n in Z^2 there are 8n sites and at most 64n^2 ordered endpoint pairs; a raw union bound needs a per-pair bound o(n^-2) to vanish. Qualitative midpoint decay supplies no such conclusion. Independence of the resampled edge from its outside environment is valid; multiplying success probabilities for correlated endpoint capacities or selected corridors needs an additional justified filtration or independence argument.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:39:12.419501+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_fdf17a2196d1cd144b6bea42b0864612ee5dc28726429d62afb8ae8373930a0d","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 3. dfn: functor of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] [{Functor}] 
  We call $\tau$ a \textit{functor} on $\mathfrak{M}_{c}$ if it satisfies the following.
  \begin{enumerate} [label = (\roman*)]
    \item 
      For every $ (S, d^{S}, \rho_{S}) \in \mathfrak{M}_{c}$,
      one has a metric space $(\tau(S, d^{S}, \rho_{S}), d_{\tau}^{S, \rho_{S}})$
      where $\tau(S, d^{S}, \rho_{S})$ is a set and $d_{\tau}^{S, \rho_{S}}$ is a metric on it.
      We simply write $\tau(S) \coloneqq \tau(S, d^{S}, \rho_{S})$.
    \item 
      For every $(S_{i}, d^{S_{i}}, \rho_{S_{i}}),\, i=1,2$ 
      and root-and-distance-preserving map $f: S_{1} \to S_{2}$, 
      one has a distance-preserving map $\tau_{f}: \tau(S_{1}) \to \tau(S_{2})$.
    \item 
      For any two root-and-distance-preserving maps $f :S_{1} \to S_{2},\, g : S_{2} \to S_{3}$,
      it holds that $\tau_{g \circ f} = \tau_{g} \circ \tau_{f}$.
    \item 
      For any $(S, d^{S}, \rho_{S}) \in \mathfrak{M}_{c}$, 
      it holds that $\tau_{\id_{S}} = \id_{\tau(S)}$.
  \end{enumerate}
  Similarly, we call $\tau$ a functor on $\mathfrak{M}$ if it satisfies the same conditions 
  not for $\mathfrak{M}_{c}$ but for $\mathfrak{M}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.167944+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_fe447b18dfa7282dbfab6cf2ff317c394d4162a056ee29db06a85660230bbec2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 60 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] The set $\sM^{\Lip}(\alpha,1)$, as defined by \eqref{e:sM.Lip.q0}, is a singleton set consisting of the standard gaussian measure:
$\sM^{\Lip}(\alpha,1)=\{\cN(0,1)\}$.
\begin{proof}
    Consider any $\mu \in \sM^{\Lip}(\alpha,1)$. By the definition \eqref{e:sM.Lip.q0}, this means that for any $\epsilon > 0$, there exists $L>0$ and a sequence of $L$-Lipschitz algorithms $(\cA_{N_j})_{j\ge 1}$ such that
    \begin{align*}
        &\WERR(\cA_{N_j}, \mu)
        =\max\bigg\{
            \bbW_2\Big( \mu(\cA_{N_j}), \mu \Big),
            \bbW_2\Big(\mu^{\Ising}(\cA_{N_j}), \cP(\{\pm 1\}) \Big)
        \bigg\} \le \epsilon\,, \\
        &q_0(j) \equiv \chi_{\cA_{N_j}}(0) 
        = \frac{\|\bbE \bsig_j\|_2^2}{N_j} 
        \stackrel{j\to\infty}{\longrightarrow} 1
        \,,
    \end{align*}
where we abbreviate $\bsig_j\equiv \cA_{N_j}(\bG,\bg^\aux)$. 
    Define the perturbed (deterministic) algorithm $\tilde\cA_{N_j}$ by setting 
    \[
        \tilde{\bsig}_j
        \equiv \tilde\cA_{N_j}(\bG,\bg^\aux) 
        = \frac{\bbE\bsig_j}{q_0(j)^{1/2}} \,.
    \]
This clearly satisfies $\bbE[\|\tilde{\bsig}_j\|_2^2]  = N_j$, so $\tilde\cA_{N_j}$ is a $0$-Lipschitz algorithm in the sense of Definition~\ref{d:Lip}.
Since $\tilde{\bsig}_j$ is a deterministic vector in $N_j$ dimensions of norm $(N_j)^{1/2}$, we have $\mu(\tilde \cA_{N_j}) = \cN(0,1)$.
    Note that
    \begin{align*}
        \frac{\bbE[
            \|\bsig_j - \tilde{\bsig}_j\|^2]}{N_j} 
        &= \frac{1}{N_j} \bbE\bigg[ \bigg\|
            \bigg(\frac{1}{q_0(j)^{1/2}} - 1 \bigg) 
            	(\bbE\bsig_j)
            - (\bsig_j - \bbE\bsig_j)
        \bigg\|^2 \bigg] \\
        &= \Big(1 - q_0(j)^{1/2}\Big)^2 + \Big(1 - q_0(j)\Big)
        \le 2\Big(1-q_0(j)\Big)\,,
    \end{align*}  
again using that inequality $|x^{1/2}-y^{1/2}| \le |x-y|^{1/2}$ for $x,y\ge0$.
    Then, by Lemma~\ref{l:control.problems.approx}, with constants $c_0$, $C_1(\alpha)$, $C_2(\alpha,L)$ as defined therein, we have
    \[
        \bbW_2\Big(\mu(\cA_{N_j}),
        	\mu(\tilde \cA_{N_j}) = \cN(0,1) 
	\Big)
        \le \bigg\{
        C_1(\alpha) 2(1-q_0(j)) + C_2(\alpha,L) e^{-c_0N_j} \bigg\}^{1/2}\,.
    \]
Combined with the assumption that $\bbW_2(\mu(\cA_{N_j}), \mu) \le \epsilon$ for all $j$, we find $\bbW_2(\mu,\cN(0,1)) \le \epsilon$.
    Since this holds for all $\epsilon > 0$, we conclude $\mu = \cN(0,1)$.
    We have thus shown $\sM^{\Lip}(\alpha,1) \subseteq \{\cN(0,1)\}$.
    The reverse inclusion $\cN(0,1) \in \sM^{\Lip}(\alpha,1)$ is witnessed by the (sequence of) deterministic algorithms
    \[
        \cA_N(\bG,\bg^{\aux}) = (1,\ldots,1) \in \bbR^N\,, 
    \]
    which are $0$-Lipschitz with $\mu(\cA_N) = \cN(0,1)$, $\mu^{\Ising}(\cA_N) = \delta_1 \in \cP(\{\pm 1\})$, and $\chi_{\cA_N}(0) = 1$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:09:43.712563+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_feaba3cd7651eeae98cfef872e7da6be688c330e8fd8c20a8243d425094ea1e9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition t.randomfieldCLT-new of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] Let $M=\{M(x)\}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^d}$ be a random field in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with values in a Polish space
$\mathbb {M} $ and $\zeta: \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb {M}  \to \mathbb{R}$ a  measurable function. 
Let $\mathcal{P}$ be a simple point process on $\mathbb{R}^d $,
independent of the random field $M$. 
Consider empirical random measures $(\hat{\sigma}_{n}^{\zeta(M)})_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ as in (equation linearstatBsigma of the paper).
\begin{enumerate}[wide,label=(\roman*),labelindent=0pt]
\item 
Assume that $\mathcal{P}$ has fast mixing correlations 
as in Definition~(d.omegamixing of the paper)(i.mixing-ground-fast of the paper). Assume that either (a) the random field $M$ satisfies the fast $\mathbb{B} $-mixing condition of Definition~(d.omegatmixing-field of the paper)(i.B-mixing-field of the paper)-(i.mixing-field-fast of the paper) or (b) 
$M$  satisfies the fast \textnormal{BL}-mixing condition of Definition~(d.omegatmixing-field of the paper)(i.BL-mixing-field of the paper)-(i.mixing-field-fast of the paper)
and $\zeta(x,\cdot)$ is Lipschitz. If $\zeta$ satisfies the $p$-moment condition~(equation e:M-p-moment of the paper) with respect to $M$ for all $p>1$ then the central limit theorem holds for
    $(\hat\sigma_{n}^{\zeta(M)}(f))_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$, i.e., as $n \to \infty$

\[   ({\rm Var} \, \hat\sigma_{n}^{\zeta(M)}(f) )^{-1/2}\Big( \hat\sigma_{n}^{\zeta(M)}(f) - \mathbb {E}  \hat\sigma_{n}^{\zeta(M)}(f) \Big) \stackrel{d}{\Rightarrow} Z,
  \]
for $f \in \mathbb{B} (W_1)$,  provided
${\rm Var} \, {\hat{\sigma}_{n}^{\zeta(M)}(f)} = \Omega(n^{\nu})$ for some $\nu > 0$.

\item  
Suppose the random field~$M$ and the point process~$\mathcal{P}$ are stationary 
(necessarily jointly so, due to their independence) with~$\mathcal{P}$ having intensity~$\rho$, 
and suppose that~$\zeta$ is translation invariant, 
i.e., $\zeta(x,\cdot) = \zeta(\cdot)$. Also assume $\zeta$ satisfies the $(1+\epsilon)$-moment condition~(equation e:M-p-moment of the paper) with respect to $M$ for some $\epsilon > 0$.
Then the mean empirical field satisfies for all $f \in \mathbb{B} (W_1)$
\begin{equation}
n^{-1} \, \mathbb{E}  \, \hat\sigma_n^{\zeta(M)}(f)
= \rho\, \mathbb {E}  \, \zeta(\0,M(\0)) \int_{W_1} f(x)\, \mathrm{d} x, \quad n\in\mathbb{N},
\end{equation}
which holds  without assuming mixing conditions on~$\mathcal{P}$ and~$M$ nor  Lipschitz conditions on $\zeta$. Moreover, under either of the mixing assumptions (a) or (b) of part~(i.CLT-infinite-zeta-field-mixing of the paper) we obtain for all $f \in \mathbb{B} (W_1)$
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty} n^{-1} {\rm Var} \, \hat\sigma_{n}^{\zeta(M)}(f)
= \sigma^2(\zeta) \int_{W_1} f(x)^2\,\mathrm{d} x,
\]
where
\begin{align}  
\sigma^2(\zeta) 
&:= \rho\, \mathbb {E}  \, \zeta^2(\0,M(\0)) \\
&\quad + \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} 
\Big( 
\mathbb {E} [\zeta(\0,M(\0))\, \zeta(x,M(x))]\, \rho^{(2)}(\0,x)
- \rho^2\, \mathbb {E} [\zeta(\0,M(\0))]\, \mathbb {E} [\zeta(x,M(x))]  
\Big)\, \mathrm{d} x \in [0, \infty) \nonumber
\end{align}
provided that~$\zeta$ satisfies the $(2+\epsilon)$-moment condition~(equation e:M-p-moment of the paper) for some $\epsilon > 0$.
\item  Let
$\boldsymbol{\zeta} := (\zeta_1, \ldots, \zeta_m)$ be a vector of translation-invariant, real-valued measurable functions 
on $\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb {M} $, with each $\zeta_i$ satisfying the $(2+\epsilon)$-moment condition~(equation e:M-p-moment of the paper) with respect to $M$ for some $\epsilon > 0$. 
Under either of the mixing assumptions (a) or (b) of part~(i.CLT-infinite-zeta-field-mixing of the paper), and under the stationarity assumption of part~(i.EVar-infinite-zeta-new of the paper)
 the multivariate central limit theorem holds as in Theorem~(t:multcltmarkedpp of the paper).
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.357430+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_feb7ff89f7ecb021ab1aa195f46a8f119ae55386714824dd65634a1101bfea88","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 241 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $\alpha,\iota > 0$ and $\fq\in [1,2)$ there exists $\epsilon = \epsilon(\alpha,\iota,\fq) > 0$ such that 
	\[
	\max\bigg\{
	\bbW_\fq(\mu,\ocM^{\Ising}(\alpha)) 
	: \mu\in \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)
	\bigg\}
	\le \iota\,.
	\]
The same statement holds with
$\ocM^{\Ising,\sym}(\alpha)$ and
$\cM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha;\epsilon)$ in place of $\ocM^{\Ising}(\alpha)$
and $\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)$. (The sets mentioned above specified by Definition~\ref{d:achievable-msrs}, \eqref{e:cM.Lip.union.L}, and \eqref{e:cM.Lip.union.L.SYM}.)

\begin{proof} Let
$\cA_N$ be an $L$-Lipschitz algorithm. 
If $\mu \in \cP_2(\R)$ satisfies $\bbW_2(\mu(\cA_N),\mu) \le \epsilon$, then Lemma~\ref{l:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound} gives, for $N$ large enough,
	\[
	\|\mu\|_{L^2} 
	\le 
	\|\mu(\cA_N)\|_{L^2} 
	+ \bbW_2(\mu(\cA_N),\mu)
	\stackrel{\eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l2}}{\le} 
	C(\alpha)^{1/2} + \epsilon
	\le (2C(\alpha))^{1/2}\,,
	\]
where the last bound holds for $\epsilon$ small enough. For such $\epsilon$, it follows by recalling \eqref{e:cM.Lip.union.L} and \eqref{e:cM.Lip} that 
	\[\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon) 
	\stackrel{\eqref{e:cM.Lip.union.L}}{=}
	\bigcup_{L>0}
		\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;L,\epsilon) \subseteq \cP_2(\R,2C(\alpha))\,.
	\]
For $\iota > 0$, define the set
	\[
		S_\iota = \Big\{\mu \in \cP_2(\R,2C(\alpha)) : \bbW_\fq(\mu,\ocM^{\Ising}(\alpha)) \ge \iota\Big\}\,.
	\]
	Now suppose for contradiction that $\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)$ intersects $S_\iota$ for all $\epsilon > 0$.
	Recall from Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.cPp.compact.Wq} that the $\cP_2(\R,2C(\alpha))$
	endowed with the $\bbW_\fq$ metric
	 is compact.
	The set $S_\iota$ is closed with respect to this metric. Thus, for any sufficiently small $\epsilon > 0$, the set
	\[
		S_\iota \cap \overline{\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)}
	\]
	(where the overline now denotes closure with respect to the $\bbW_\fq$ metric) is a nonempty closed subset of $\cP_2(\R,2C(\alpha))$ indexed by $\epsilon$, hence also compact.
	These sets form a nested family of nonempty compact sets, so their intersection is also nonempty.
	However, their intersection is
	\beq
		S_\iota \cap \bigcap_{\epsilon > 0} \overline{\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)}
		\subseteq  
		S_\iota \cap \bigcap_{\epsilon > 0} \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;2\epsilon)
		\stackrel{\eqref{e:sM.Lip}}{=} 
		S_\iota \cap \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha)
		\stackrel{\textup{Thm.~\ref{thm:control.problems.main}}}{=} S_\iota \cap \ocM^{\Ising}(\alpha)
		= \emptyset\,,
	\eeq
which yields a contradiction.
This proves that there exists $\epsilon$ such that $\bbW_\fq(\mu,\ocM^{\Ising}(\alpha)) \le \iota$ for all $\mu \in \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)$.
	The analogous claim for $\cM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha;\epsilon)$ and $\ocM^{\Ising,\sym}(\alpha)$ is proved similarly, using Theorem~\ref{thm:control.problems.sym} in place of Theorem~\ref{thm:control.problems.main} in \eqref{e:confinement.cM.lip.to.nbd.of.ideal}.
\end{proof}","status":"unverified"}
